Mexico arrests alleged cartel leader and fuel smuggler "The Tank"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Alleged Jalisco cartel leader and fuel smuggler dubbed "The Tank" is arrested in Mexico
Security forces in Mexico have arrested an alleged leader of a notorious cartel who is accused by the U.S. of drug trafficking and a large-scale fuel smuggling operation, authorities said Tuesday.
Ivan Cazarin Molina (a.k.a. "El Tanque"—meaning "The Tank"), was captured on Monday in the town of Zapopan in Jalisco state, security minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said in a social media post.
Mexican authorities say Molina, the alleged regional leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), runs a massive fuel theft network and is linked to homicides, kidnappings and drug trafficking. He is accused of being involved in the attack on a Mexican Army helicopter in Jalisco in 2015 that killed members of the Army and the Federal Police.
Harfuch posted several images of Molina being apprehended by National Guard members and being escorted in handcuffs.
Th U.S. Treasury sanctioned Molina in September 2024, saying he was part of the inner circle of "El Mencho," the infamous Jalisco cartel leader who was later killed in a military operation.
"Although primarily involved in fuel theft, El Tanque has also engaged in drug trafficking, extortion, and homicide," the Treasury said at the time. "El Tanque's fuel theft generates tens of millions of dollars per year for himself and CJNG."
U.S. authorities allege Molina manages a network of ostensibly legitimate retail gas stations where he sells stolen fuel. He is also accused of selling stolen fuel to third parties in Mexico, who in turn sell it to the U.S. market, often in Texas.
Fuel theft — more commonly known as huachicol in Mexico — has risen to the second most profitable revenue stream for Mexican cartels behind drug trafficking, according to the U.S. Treasury.
"Fuel theft and crude oil smuggling are cash cows for CJNG's narco-terrorist enterprise, providing a lucrative revenue stream for the group and enabling it to wreak havoc in Mexico and the United States," Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said in 2025.
One of Mexico's most powerful criminal organizations, CJNG is among eight cartels designated as foreign terrorist organizations by the U.S. government. In August, the State Department offered a $25 million reward for information leading to the capture of its new leader, Juan Carlos González, the California-born stepson of "El Mencho."

Russian Il-76s Flew 100+ Missions for UAE—and May Have Carried Weapons to Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:59:23 UTC
23:59:23 KST

- Category
- Investigations
Russian Il-76s Flew 100+ Missions for UAE—and May Have Carried Weapons to Sudan
A sanctioned Russian cargo airline with a history of transporting military equipment has flown more than 100 missions linked to the United Arab Emirates since mid-2025, including flights that may have supported weapons deliveries connected to the war in Sudan, according to reporting cited by Defense Express on October 6.
Defense Express, referring to an investigation by Defense News, identified the operator as Aviacon Zitotrans, a Russian airline that operates at least four Il-76 heavy transport aircraft and has previously been linked to military cargo missions for Moscow.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The carrier has also reportedly transported supplies for units of Russia’s Africa Corps and previously moved various types of weapons, including missiles, to customers in Asia.
Against that background, Defense Express noted that its growing work on behalf of UAE interests stands out as another example of the airline’s role in sensitive international logistics.
Flight tracking reviewed in the investigation reportedly showed Aviacon Zitotrans aircraft departing from locations directly associated with the UAE military, including Al Ain and Sweihan air bases.
Other flights originated from the Chandana airstrip in Pakistan, a location associated with hunting grounds used by members of the Emirati ruling families.
The Sudan connection is harder to verify directly. According to the reporting cited by Defense Express, the aircraft’s transponders were repeatedly switched off over the Gulf of Aden and only appeared again during the return leg.
That pattern has fueled suspicions that the Il-76s continued toward Sudan while deliberately avoiding public flight tracking.
The aircraft identified in the reporting carried the registrations RA-76842, RA-76502, RA-76846 and RA-76834.
Aviacon Zitotrans has already been subjected to international sanctions over its role in transporting military cargo.
Defense Express suggested that this could make the airline particularly useful for operations that governments or commercial carriers may be reluctant to perform, since the company already faces significant restrictions and therefore has less exposure to additional reputational or financial penalties.
The relationship also fits into the broader economic ties between Moscow and the UAE that have deepened since Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine. The Emirates have become an important hub for Russian trade and financial activity as Moscow looks for alternative routes around Western restrictions, Defense Express noted.
Earlier, Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) claimed responsibility for shooting down a Sudanese Air Force Il-76 Candid transport plane near the western town of Babanusa on November 4, reportedly killing everyone on board.
According to Russian military-linked Telegram channels, the aircraft was operated by a Russian civilian crew working under contract.

MOSCOW, October 6. /TASS/. An electronic intelligence (ELINT) plane of the Swedish Air Force spent almost seven hours over the neutral waters of the Black Sea, a source in the European Union’s air traffic control services has told TASS.
"The Swedish Air Force’s ELINT plane spent almost seven hours over the southern part of the Black Sea, flying from west to east and back at an altitude of about 13 kilometers," the source said.

The plane has already landed in Romania’s capital Bucharest.
Earlier, an air traffic source informed that flights by Sweden’s reconnaissance aircraft in the Black Sea are a rare occasion. However, its flight path coincides with the route of NATO’s Bombardier Artemis II reconnaissance aircraft, whose flights are often observed in the area.

The Hague court awards PrivatBank $180.9 mln against claims exceeding $1 bln
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:58:36 UTC
23:58:36 KST

THE HAGUE, October 6. /TASS/. An arbitration in The Hague has awarded Ukraine’s PrivatBank a payment of nearly $180.9 million for its allegedly "expropriated" assets in Crimea, which, excluding interest, is over five times less than the bank's original claims. The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA), which provides administrative support to the tribunal, announced the ruling.
The final award was issued on October 1. Interest accrues on the awarded $180.87 million from April 18, 2014, until the date of payment. The court also allocated the arbitration costs between the parties. The PCA did not disclose the interest rate or the cost-sharing ratio, and the text of the decision has not been made public.
PrivatBank previously stated that it was seeking more than $1 billion from Russia. The lawsuit was filed in April 2015, when oligarch Igor Kolomoisky (listed in Russia as a terrorist and extremist) was one of the bank's principal owners. PrivatBank was nationalized in December 2016 and is currently owned by the Kiev authorities.
Russia’s position
Russia did not recognize the jurisdiction of the Hague arbitration. In 2015, the Russian Justice Ministry stated that the 1998 intergovernmental agreement with Ukraine on the promotion and reciprocal protection of investments, cited by the bank, could not serve as a basis for resolving the dispute. Initially, the Russian side did not participate in the proceedings, and the arbitrator acting on its behalf was appointed by a competent authority rather than the defendant.
In 2019, Russia entered the proceedings and requested permission to present arguments regarding jurisdiction, the merits of the case, and the quantum of damages. The arbitration agreed to hear Russia only on the issue of the amount and on the objection that PrivatBank could not be considered a legitimate investor, as it had acquired its assets through corruption, fraud, and violence. In the final award, this objection was dismissed. Back in 2019, the arbitration had ruled that the claims of the second plaintiff, Finilon financial company, did not fall within its jurisdiction.
Russia’s interests in the proceedings are represented by the Prosecutor General’s Office of the Russian Federation and the International Centre for Legal Protection.
Russia challenged the 2017 and 2019 rulings — in which the tribunal affirmed its jurisdiction and found a breach of the agreement — in Dutch courts. The Hague Court of Appeal in 2022, and subsequently the Supreme Court of the Kingdom in December 2024, upheld those decisions. An application to set aside the final award may be filed with the same Court of Appeal within three months from the date the award is dispatched to the parties.
The bank’s exit from Crimea
PrivatBank ceased serving customers in Crimea in March 2014. On April 21, the Bank of Russia terminated the operations of the bank's branches on the peninsula, citing a failure to meet obligations to depositors. Compensation for residents of Crimea and Sevastopol — up to 700,000 rubles ($8,242) per person — was paid by Russia's Deposit Protection Fund. In September 2014, the State Council of Crimea nationalized assets located in the republic belonging to Kolomoisky and companies linked to him. Crimean authorities stated that proceeds from the sale of these assets were intended for PrivatBank depositors whose savings exceeded the compensation limit.
The bank itself also has outstanding claims against its former owners. In July 2025, the High Court of London found that they had misappropriated nearly $2 billion from PrivatBank, and in November, it ordered them to pay more than $3 billion, including interest and legal costs.
Crimea and Sevastopol became part of Russia following a referendum held on March 16, 2014 with a voter turnout exceeding 80%, 96.7% and 95.6% of participants voted for reunification with the Russian Federation, respectively. The treaty on the admission of the new constituent entities was signed on March 18 and ratified by the Federal Assembly on March 21. According to the arbitration’s findings, obligations under the agreement regarding Ukrainian investors in Crimea became binding on Russia as of that same date.

Pedro Sánchez is a master of the political comeback. But calling a snap election in Spain may be a gamble too far | Paolo Gerbaudo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:57:19 UTC
23:57:19 KST

To progressives across the west, Spain has been a rare glimmer of hope in a world where far-right parties are increasingly entering government. Under Pedro Sánchez, who became prime minister in 2018, the country has combined a post-Covid economic boom with a bold green energy transition programme, and a pro-immigration stance with a principled opposition to the war agenda of Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu. Yet, at the end of next month, this rare beacon of democratic progress could fall.
On Monday Sánchez called a snap general election, set for 29 November, after two decrees to address the country’s housing crisis were voted down in the lower chamber by politicians from rightwing parties. Speaking from the staircase of the Moncloa palace, Sánchez admitted that his government had not achieved all it had set out to do. “Many injustices remain to be corrected … particularly regarding inequality in public services and access to housing,” he said, adding: “To do more, we need to renew and expand public support.”
Sánchez attempted to pass the legislation after tens of thousands took to the streets to protest against the housing crisis, setting up camps reminiscent of the country’s 15-M anti-austerity movement and the global Occupy movement of 2011. But this explosion of popular anger has been long in the making. According to Spain’s national public opinion research institute Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS), housing has been the country’s top preoccupation since the end of 2024, as a growing number of people struggle to pay rent.
In the latest gamble of his long career as master of the political comeback, Sánchez hopes to ride the wave of popular mobilisation to turn public attention away from the Ceuta immigration crisis of July, which rightwing opponents exploited as a demonstration of the government’s failures, and focus attention on the housing crisis, an issue where the left holds stronger political ground.
But this time it will be hard to convince Spaniards that with a new lease of life, the progressive coalition government will solve an issue it had promised to address a long time ago.
Sánchez’s troubles provide useful lessons for progressives all over the world about the difficulties of translating policy achievements into a solid base of political support. They are also a reminder that – as championed by New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani – addressing the affordability crisis rather than promising abstract economic growth is of more significance to voters.
In the US midterm election campaign, Republicans are struggling because of rising prices at the gas pump, while in Brazil, rightwing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro just rode to an impressive result in the first round of the presidential elections partly due to discontent with living conditions and household pressures. In Spain, Sánchez’s government is facing similar concerns about affordability, which are obfuscating an otherwise impressive macro-economic performance.
Indeed, seen from the outside, Sánchez’s Spain may appear to be a dazzling political success. The country, which in the 2010s was derided as part of the European Piigs – a term coined to mock Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Greece and Spain as the eurozone’s weakest economies – has become an economic powerhouse. In the years after the Covid pandemic, Spain’s GDP grew at a rate of around 3%, while France, Germany, the UK and Italy grew at a miserly 1% or less.
Spain is also held up as a model of successful green transition, with renewables now generating close to 60% of the country’s power, which has also kept energy bills low and helped insulate the country from the energy shocks caused by international crises. Spain, enabled by significant Chinese investment, is also surprisingly becoming the leading European hub for electric car production, to the dismay of some of the country’s traditional allies.
To these economic and environmental achievements add the significant social improvements achieved under Sánchez, exemplified by the rise in the minimum wage from €736 to €1,184 per month since 2018.
Yet despite these measurable successes, Sánchez’s centre-left coalition is now trailing the right by about 7 percentage points in national polling. That’s partly because while minimum wages have increased, median wages have remained relatively stagnant. But it is real estate that Sánchez’s government has been judged as failing to deliver: during its eight years in power, house prices have risen by an estimated 50%, with rents rising by over 40%.
As climbing the housing ladder becomes prohibitive, a growing number of young people in Spain are forced to pay extortionate rents. This is acutely felt in large urban areas, where the presence of tourists and digital nomads further increases rents, forcing out local residents; this is enabled by private equity firms, who purchase entire blocks to expel local inhabitants in order to create Airbnbs. Sánchez’s government has repeatedly promised to take action on these issues, but its measures have been thwarted by political gridlock or otherwise proven indecisive, partly due to fear of alienating homeowners and antagonising international finance.
If Spain’s centre-left coalition falls, the country could be left with an alliance of the mainstream conservative Partido Popular and the far-right party Vox. It would be the most rightwing Spanish government since Francisco Franco’s dictatorship. The lesson for progressives everywhere is clear: economic growth and ambitious reform will count for little unless working people feel the benefits in their daily lives.
- Paolo Gerbaudo is a senior researcher at the faculty of political science and sociology of Complutense University in Madrid and a lead researcher at the Alameda Institute

Paris Police Prefect Patrice Faure, equivalent to the French capital's police chief, issued an order prohibiting a demonstration "against the genocide in Gaza and for respect of the ceasefire" slated to be held in Paris on Wednesday, the police confirmed on X/Twitter in a Tuesday post.
The order came at the request of French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, police said.
"In a context of heightened terrorist threat and while antisemitic acts remain at a historically high level in our country, such a demonstration on that day poses significant risks of disturbances to public order," Faure wrote.
"In the face of this, in particular, and in view of all the risks identified, my responsibility is to ensure the safety of all. I have therefore decided to prohibit this demonstration," he added.

French MP representing expats, including those in Israel, praises police's decision

Additionally, anti-Zionist groups, including Antifa's Lyon chapter, denounced the police chief's decision in posts on social media, questioning whether "it's forbidden to be against genocides and for ceasefires," and saying, "OK, fascists."
London's Metropolitan Police list conditions for student-led anti-Zionist march to go ahead
Meanwhile, London's Metropolitan Police (the Met), which initially requested that a student protest be delayed, listed conditions for the march after allowing it to go ahead in a Tuesday statement.
"The march and rally is expected to start at Kings College London Strand and end at University College London via London School of Economics and SOAS. We have imposed strict conditions: Those taking part in the event must form up by 12:30hrs and remain in the shaded area (Lincoln’s Inn Field) of the first map below until the procession begins," the Met wrote.
"The procession must start by 12:30hrs with participants moving along the prescribed route. Anyone taking part in the procession must not deviate from this route as shown on the second map below – Remnant Street, Kingsway, Southampton Row and Russell Square," the Met added.
"The rally assembly must conclude by 14:00hrs when participants are required to disperse. No one taking part in the form-up assembly, procession or rally may wear a face covering that conceals their identity," the Met stated.
"We have imposed robust conditions on a student march due to take place on Wednesday, 7 October in central London to prevent serious disruption to communities," Met Deputy Assistant Commissioner James Harman said.
"The event is being held on the third anniversary of the October 7 terrorist attack on Israel and the start of the ensuing conflict in Gaza. This will be a day of mourning and reflection for many in London. We know how concerned Jewish communities are at the timing of this event," Harman added.
"The stringent conditions will help us manage this event and minimize disruption. Anyone who breaches the conditions or commits offenses faces arrest," he added.
"We hear the calls for this event to be banned - Police cannot ban protests and can only ask the home secretary to do so if the risk of serious disorder is so high that it can't be managed by conditions. That high bar is not met here," Harman explained.

"We are also aware of a planned student protest at Marble Arch on 7 October between 13:00hrs and 16:00hrs. We will impose conditions on this protest requiring it to take place away from Marble Arch and local synagogues that congregants may wish to attend on this significant day," he added.

IDF expected to resume draft evader operations as High Court deadline approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:55:07 UTC
23:55:07 KST

The IDF expects to resume proactive enforcement operations against military draft evaders and deserters in October after such operations generally did not take place during the recent period, according to a Justice Ministry summary dated Tuesday.
Deputy Attorney-General Dr. Gil Limon said the absence of proactive enforcement for a significant period did not meet the country’s security needs, particularly after senior military commanders described expanding the regular army as a strategic necessity.
He said it was also inconsistent with the principle of equality, the state’s commitments to the High Court of Justice and a court ruling striking down a law that had prevented the arrest of yeshiva students.
The four-page document summarizes a September 23 meeting led by Limon and attended by senior representatives of the IDF, Military Police, Israel Police and the Population and Immigration Authority.
IDF plans renewed October enforcement against haredi draft evaders
Military officials said proactive enforcement operations, including arrests, generally had not taken place during the recent period because authorities were concentrating their efforts at border crossings and making adjustments for the holiday season.
They said proactive enforcement was expected to resume in October, with Military Police and the relevant Israel Police stations coordinating operations in advance. The coordination is intended to allow the two forces to prepare jointly and provide a police response if exceptional incidents occur.
Overnight Monday, hundreds of haredi protesters surrounded Military Police officers attempting to arrest a draft evader in Modi’in and prevented them from taking him into custody. Israel Police officers were called to restore order and escort the soldiers from the building.
The IDF condemned what it described as an organized attempt to obstruct the arrest and endanger soldiers, saying enforcement would continue equally and within its authority.
During a concentrated enforcement operation from September 1 to 22, authorities arrested 212 draft evaders and deserters at Ben-Gurion Airport, the Allenby Bridge and the Begin crossing near Taba, the summary said. Military officials estimated that 163 of those arrested were haredi (ultra-Orthodox).
Authorities initiated proceedings against all 212, mostly through military disciplinary proceedings.
Of the 188 people arrested at Ben-Gurion Airport, 64 were caught only when they returned to Israel, raising concerns about gaps in enforcing restrictions intended to prevent them from leaving the country.
The Population and Immigration Authority said it quickly closed the gaps identified in border enforcement. Cases involving suspected illegal crossings were transferred to either Israel Police or the IDF, according to the document.
The summary also said prosecutors filed 360 indictments against draft evaders between January 1 and September 23. Military prosecutors estimated that 49 involved haredi draft evaders.
Only 16 indictments involving that group had been filed as of June, indicating an increase in the months that followed.
Military prosecutors said they were advancing measures to shorten the period of evasion required before criminal charges may be filed from 18 months to one year. They also plan to prosecute people who desert during the induction process after 30 days.
Those changes have not taken effect yet. Military prosecutors said they had completed their review of arguments raised by the Military Public Defender’s Office and expected to respond during October, after which the measures would be implemented.
The dispute follows a series of Supreme Court rulings requiring the state to enforce the military draft equally.
In June 2024, the court ruled that the government had no legal authority to refrain from drafting yeshiva students after the legal framework allowing their exemptions expired, and that the state must enforce the existing draft law.
In November 2025, a five-justice panel ordered the government to formulate an effective enforcement policy within 45 days, including significant criminal-law enforcement measures and broad complementary economic and civil steps.
Last month, the High Court unanimously struck down a law shielding qualifying haredi yeshiva students from arrest, investigation and other enforcement proceedings over draft evasion.
The state must submit its next update to the court by October 15. Limon requested that the relevant agencies provide updated arrest, indictment, disciplinary and enlistment figures by October 12.
The document also said a separate meeting would examine the gaps discovered in border controls and enforcement at Ben-Gurion Airport and the measures taken in response.
Keshet Neev contributed to this report.

JPR study finds 50% of British Jews emotionally attached to Israel, up sharply since Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:55:07 UTC
23:55:07 KST

Half of British Jews now feel very emotionally attached to Israel, marking a sharp increase following the events of October 7, according to a major new empirical study by the Institute for Jewish Policy Research (JPR) released on Monday.
The report details how the post-October 7 landscape dramatically shifted emotional ties to the Jewish State and intensified concerns over antisemitism, even as core markers of domestic Jewish religious life and practice remained remarkably stable.
The study, called “October 8 Jews: The impact of October 7” on British Jewish identity, was conducted by Dr David Graham, a Senior Research Fellow at JPR.
Utilizing JPR’s longitudinal research panel, the study tracked the exact same group of 2,500 British Jews across multiple survey waves spanning a six-year period from July 2020 to June 2025. This allowed researchers to measure actual individual changes in attitudes and behaviors before and after October 7, 2023, rather than relying on retrospective accounts or single-snapshot polls.
The research aimed to examine whether widely discussed post-October 7 concepts applied to the UK, including the notion of the ‘October 8 Jew,’ describing individuals who experienced a renewed sense of Jewish consciousness and discovered that previously trusted progressive allies and spaces were no longer reliable, and the communal ‘Surge’, which refers to a broader rise in Jewish activity and engagement, particularly among previously unengaged Jews.
The report is organized into three core analytical sections that investigate how British Jews were impacted across different areas of life. The first section explores connections to Israel, the second shifts to experiences of antisemitism, and the third examines broader measures of Jewish identity, peoplehood, values, and religious observance.
UK Jews increasingly attached to Israel
The study first asked respondents about their connection to Israel through multiple indicators, revealing that overall emotional attachment rose from 72% in May 2023 to 76% in June 2024 and 78% by June 2025. Beyond that general rise, the report highlights a dramatic shift in intensity, with the proportion of those identifying as very attached surging from 38% prior to the attacks to 50% in June 2024 and holding steady at 51% in June 2025.
Analyzing these figures, the report explains that this represents an enduring change rather than a temporary spike, showing that Israel became far more central to personal identity.
Similarly, self-identification as a Zionist saw a statistically significant rise, climbing from 59% in November 2022 to 65% in June 2024, and holding at 66% in June 2025.
In contrast, the report notes that those identifying as anti-Zionist remained virtually unchanged at 9% to 10% across the same periods, while the proportion identifying as non-Zionist declined from 17% down to 14%, showing that people on the fence chose a side rather than shifting toward opposition.
The study also tracked the likelihood of making aliyah within five years, where the mean score on a scale from zero to ten increased from 1.38 in November 2022 to 1.95 in June 2024.
Analyzing these figures, the report notes that this post-October 7 rise in aliyah sentiment, while reflecting genuine increases in emotional attachment and Zionist sentiment, remained lower than the score of 2.29 recorded in July 2020 during the COVID-19 lockdown, explaining that such fluctuations likely reflect both a growing connection to Israel and changing perceptions of how comfortable and settled respondents felt living in the UK at different times.
Personal experiences with antisemitism rise in UK
The second section of the report evaluated personal experiences and perceptions of antisemitism, safety, and mental wellbeing. The survey found that personal experiences of antisemitism escalated drastically, with the proportion of respondents reporting that they had personally experienced at least one antisemitic incident jumping from between 17% and 20% in calendar years between 2020 and 2022 up to 29% in an 18-month tracking period spanning 2023 and the first half of 2024.
Public perception matched this reality; the proportion of respondents who viewed antisemitism as a very major problem in the UK nearly tripled from 17% in May 2023 to 47% in June 2024, reaching 50% by June 2025. This coincided with a sharp drop in average feelings of safety on a zero-to-10 scale, falling from 7.4 in May 2023 down to 6.2 in June 2024 and 5.8 by June 2025.
Consequently, the anxiety index mean score climbed from 2.99 in August 2021 to 3.76 in June 2024. Examining this sharp increase in anxiety, the analysis suggests that while rising antisemitism and declining safety certainly contributed, the elevated stress levels were likely driven primarily by concerns about antisemitism in the UK over and above concerns about Israel’s security, noting that anxiety increased uniformly across respondents regardless of their emotional attachment to Israel.
Furthermore, charitable giving priorities shifted notably, with the proportion of respondents prioritizing Israel charities nearly tripling from 6% before October 7 to 16% by June 2025. The report suggests that post-October 7 realities drove the Jewish population toward more particular Jewish causes at the expense of more universal general UK charities.
UK Jews report stronger ties to identity
The third section of the report investigated core dimensions of Jewish identity, peoplehood, and religious behavior. When respondents were asked to position themselves on a zero-to-10 scale regarding the strength of their Jewish identity, more than half chose nine or 10, with mean scores holding exceptionally steady at 8.29 in November 2022, 8.31 in June 2024, and 8.32 in June 2025.
When asked about the importance of feeling part of the Jewish People, 90% considered it important in May 2023, rising slightly to 92% in June 2024 before settling at 89% in June 2025, with those answering very important shifting marginally from 63% to 66% and 64% across those same waves. Similarly, when asked about participation in synagogue prayer services over the preceding 12 months, responses showed negligible movement, with 28% reporting no participation in November 2022 compared to 26% in June 2024 and 27% in June 2025, while regular attendees participating most or every Shabbat remained steady at 26%, 28%, and 27% respectively.
Self-described levels of religiosity also remained flat, with those placing themselves on the more strongly religious side resting at 49% in November 2022, 51% in June 2024, and 50% in June 2025. Taken together, these figures suggest that British Jews did not experience a broad-based transformation in religious observance or general identity strength following October 7.
The report concludes by emphasizing that October 7 acted as a profound watershed primarily regarding emotional connections to Israel and Jewish peoplehood rather than a total structural reinvention of British Jewish life. While solidarity, Zionist identification, and concerns over security heightened significantly, broader indicators of Jewish identity exhibited remarkable continuity with little to no measurable change.
In summary, the report noted that the “challenge facing Jewish leaders, educators and policymakers is how to translate these modest changes into deeper forms of participation, engagement and Jewish flourishing in the years ahead.”

Seventh arrest in RAF Fairford terrorism investigation
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:55:01 BST
23:55:01 KST

A seventh man has been arrested over the activity near RAF Fairford at the end of last month, and detectives have said they are still working to establish a motive, Counter Terrorism Policing has said.
The 22-year-old British national was detained in the borough of Westminster in London on Tuesday on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006, and a property in the same area has been searched.
Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, said: “This remains a live investigation and our specialist teams continue to pursue multiple lines of enquiry into the circumstances surrounding events near RAF Fairford.
“Once again, I’d like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this highly complex investigation.
“We’re acutely aware of the public interest in this investigation, and we are working around the clock, and at pace, to identify the motivation behind events in Gloucestershire. We remain committed to investigating all possible angles.”
More than a week after the first arrests, the motivation behind the activity in Gloucestershire has still not been established. Ms Evans said last week that officers were looking at all possible angles including possible foreign state involvement, and Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said earlier that they were considering whether the activity might have been committed by proxies or by individuals knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.
Six men in their twenties remain on police bail, five of them arrested in the early hours of Sunday 27 September and the sixth, a dual British and Iranian national aged 25, detained on Thursday 1 October and bailed at the weekend. Nobody has been charged.
The original arrests followed a report of suspicious vehicles near the airfield, which brought officers out initially on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and subsequently of preparation of a terrorist act. A major incident was declared and homes were evacuated in the village of Whelford beside the base. Three vehicles were examined and no improvised explosive devices were found in them, although a quantity of petrol was recovered.
Fairford is a United States Air Force forward operating location rather than a flying station of the Royal Air Force, and its long runway has made it the standing European base for American strategic bombers. B-1B Lancers have been operating from the airfield, and the base moved to its highest force protection condition before the first arrests were made.
Counter Terrorism Policing has asked anyone with information that might assist to report it through gov.uk/ACT or by calling the Anti-Terrorist Hotline on 0800 789 321.

European Commission proposes majority voting in EU on sanctions, opening of negotiation clusters
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:54:37 EEST
23:54:37 KST

The European Commission has proposed shifting from unanimous voting to qualified majority voting by European Union member states on issues such as sanctions, the opening of negotiation chapters, and interim decisions on enlargement.
These proposals are outlined in the so-called package of documents on the European Union's preparations for future enlargement, specifically in the sections dedicated to improving the governance system for an enlarged Union, the European Commission said on Tuesday.
In particular, the press release notes that, given the current geopolitical conditions, the EU must adapt its governance system to make the decision-making process "swifter and more effective."
"To this end, the Commission will continue to advocate the use of passerelle clauses to move from unanimity to qualified majority voting in key areas such as sanctions, tax fraud and fiscal measures in energy policy," the statement reads.
In addition, the Commission will review existing proposals to determine where enhanced cooperation could help overcome prolonged deadlocks.
In the area of enlargement, the Commission proposes using qualified majority voting to open negotiation chapters and adopt other interim decisions during accession negotiations, which will make the process more dynamic. The Commission also proposes to work with the European Parliament and the Council to explore ways to apply the procedures set out in Article 7 more effectively, particularly with regard to possible timeframes.
The European Commission noted that the annual reports on enlargement and the state of the rule of law will continue to serve as key monitoring tools, with their scope expanded to include other candidate countries as they become ready.
Commenting on the gradual integration of candidate countries into the EU, the Commission is convinced that closer integration should bring tangible benefits to citizens and businesses in both the EU and the candidate countries.

Spain's government on Tuesday approved two housing decrees whose rejection by parliament last week prompted Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap election.
The measures, which include rent caps, a temporary ban on evictions and limits on corporate purchases of residential property, were "based on plain common sense," Sanchez said in a press conference, arguing that opinion surveys showed the public was broadly in favor of intervention in the property market.

Measures to come into effect before being sent for approval
The measures will come into effect temporarily when the decree is published in the official state gazette but must then be sent for approval by the caretaker lawmakers who remain in place after parliament was dissolved, Sanchez said.
The standing body of 69 members, when including lower house speaker Francina Armengol from Sanchez's Socialist Party, has a slim majority in favor of the measures, according to state broadcaster TVE.
A second decree proposing the automatic renewal of rental contracts would only come into effect if approved by the reduced legislature since the government did not have a majority to validate it, Sanchez said.
The interventionist measures will only serve to drive away the investment needed to increase supply, said Carolina Roca, president of the Association of Property Developers of Madrid.
"The legal uncertainty inherent in both decrees will result in a sharp slowdown in the limited investment secured to date in the construction of affordable housing," she said.
The attempted eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid triggered nationwide protests including calls for a general strike before the election, which Sanchez said his government would respect.

“It's very difficult for me to go back there; it's very painful and even scary to stand in front of all the dear people who lost the most precious thing and sing, but this is the only and exact place where I want and need to be, and I'm grateful for the huge privilege of doing it," Raphael said in a statement ahead of the event, which will take place on the third anniversary of the massacres.
The event is being organized by the families of those killed at the Nova festival along with the Nova Tribe Community Association.

Kumu, Nova memorial events to be held on October 7 evening

While the Kumu event is set to take place in Tel Aviv and honors victims from across the October 7 attacks, the Nova memorial focuses on those killed from the rave communities.
There, at the Nova festival three years ago, Raphael was among the survivors as Hamas terrorists and others stormed the festival. Terrorists murdered 378 people, making it the deadliest single site of the massacres. Forty-four people were taken hostage.
Raphael herself hid in a roadside bomb shelter with at least 40 others crammed inside. Soon afterward, terrorists found the shelter and began firing inside.

The far-right Alternative for Germany convened for the first sitting of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament on Tuesday but, a month after its landmark election win, the party still lacks a clear path to forming what would be its first state government.
Despite winning the vote in the September 6 election in the eastern German state, the AfD fell three seats short of the absolute majority that candidate Ulrich Siegmund had aimed for.
Siegmund said before Tuesday's sitting that he aimed to win parliamentary backing to become state premier in a first round of voting that he said would only take place in December, giving him more time to build support. He did not elaborate.
The party has so far failed to secure enough support from potential partners or publicly win over defectors from rivals, leading to a stalemate in its efforts to form a government.
'Firewall' policy creates complications
The impasse underlines a challenge that has dogged the AfD for years: translating growing electoral support into executive power in a political system where mainstream parties have refused to cooperate with it under the "firewall" policy.
Founded in 2013 as a eurosceptic movement, the AfD won over voters with an increasingly hardline opposition to immigration after around a million people fled to Germany in 2015.
The party has since become a dominant political force in much of eastern Germany, especially among voters disillusioned with the mainstream parties, though many remain strongly opposed to cutting any deals with the AfD.
About 400 protesters gathered peacefully on Tuesday outside the state parliament in Magdeburg and read aloud Germany's constitution ahead of the session, with dozens holding up a long red banner that read: "No cooperation with the extreme right."
A symbolic victory
Tuesday's inaugural sitting, which the state constitution requires to take place within 30 days of the election, nevertheless offered the AfD a symbolic victory.
Tobias Rausch, a 35-year-old real estate entrepreneur and Siegmund confidant, was elected president of the state parliament with support from the left-wing populist BSW, becoming the first AfD member to hold one of the highest offices in a German state legislature.
Rausch used his inaugural speech to call on lawmakers to work together, adding that "the days of political firewalls should be a thing of the past."
The AfD's success in Saxony-Anhalt and two other state elections in September has put Chancellor Friedrich Merz's struggling government under pressure and raised questions within his conservatives about the effectiveness of the firewall.
The AfD has been working for weeks to win over lawmakers from Merz's party, whose support halved from the last state election, but no defections have been announced so far.
Reliable partners with the BSW?
Tuesday's vote was also closely watched for signs of whether the AfD can reliably count on the BSW, the only party that has not explicitly ruled out cooperation, though it has rejected the idea of joining the AfD in a coalition government.
The BSW, which, like the AfD, opposes mass immigration and wants to restore energy ties with Russia, has said it would abstain in any vote for Siegmund as state premier.
That could lead to the AfD forming a minority government with passive tolerance from the BSW, under a model seen in neighboring Thuringia, though Siegmund has previously rejected such a setup as making him too reliant on the smaller party.
Siegmund has also floated the possibility of new elections if he does not secure the required majority the first time around.
In Tuesday's secret ballot to become state parliament leader, Rausch secured 48 votes, suggesting he attracted support not only from his own party and the BSW - totaling 44 votes - but also from at least four other lawmakers.

How beavers are protecting a West London town from flooding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:53:05 UTC
23:53:05 KST

How beavers are protecting West London from flooding
To find a little wilderness in West London, take a left at the shopping mall and head under the highway. Near a McDonald's and within reach of the city's busy transport network, a family of beavers is reshaping a wetland and helping protect nearby streets and a Tube station from flooding.
Five Eurasian beavers were released into the town of Greenford in October 2023. They were the first to return to West London in about 400 years, part of an effort to bring back a species hunted to extinction centuries ago. The animals live within a fenced site that remains accessible to the public.
Veterinarian and conservationist Dr. Sean McCormack, one of the driving forces behind the Ealing Beaver Project, puts the chances of spotting one during a recent visit at 90%.
"Anytime from now you could see a beaver swimming across the lagoon here," he said.
But these animals were brought here to do more than draw an audience. They were offered a job.
The area around nearby Greenford Station had suffered repeated flooding during heavy rainfall. Local authorities were considering engineering works to hold back water before it reached the urban area downstream. McCormack and his fellow conservationists proposed a different approach: let beavers help manage it.
"They had planned a lot of expensive engineering works to create reservoirs to hold more water," he said. "And we said beavers could do that at a fraction of the cost and maybe more effectively."
The beavers got to work, felling trees, gathering branches and building dams. By July this year, they had constructed seven dams and created three ponds that help retain water.
Their engineering changes how rainfall moves through the landscape. Instead of rushing downstream, water is held in ponds, spread across the wetland and released more slowly.
The results came sooner than expected, McCormack said.
"By the second winter they were here — no flooding at all," he said of the downstream area the project was intended to help. "So we knew it would work in theory, we didn't realize they would do it so fast."
The project also reports that the dams have helped prevent flooding in Greenford Station's lobby and the surrounding residential area.
The transformation extends beyond flood protection. The beavers have built a lodge roughly 6 feet high, with an underwater entrance connecting it to the lagoon. Around it, their work is creating opportunities for other wildlife.
Beside a fallen tree, McCormack points out how a beaver chewed more deeply into one side of the trunk, bringing it down into the water.
"And then all that dead wood is going to provide habitat for beetles and woodpeckers and bats and all sorts of things," he says.
For visitors joining a guided evening beaver safari, the attraction is often simpler: catching sight of an animal going about its business in an unexpected corner of the capital.
Sometimes, baby beavers, called kits, make an appearance.
The breeding success has become another sign that the animals are settling in. The project reported that the parents, Willow and Woody, welcomed two more kits in 2026, their third consecutive year of breeding. McCormack has described their continued success as "nature's report card."
The lessons could reach beyond this patch of London: learning to live alongside beavers and harness their benefits could help communities facing the challenges of climate change, McCormack said.
And there is another benefit, harder to measure in flood levels or species counts.
"They make people smile," he said.

Authorities in Montenegro might not be able to catch the country's most notorious fugitive crime boss, but they are moving to dismantle his financial empire.
The Special State Prosecutor's Office asked Tuesday the High Court in Podgorica to permanently confiscate a sprawling portfolio of real estate and luxury vehicles it believes is in his or his wife’s possession. While the official statement only identified the targets by their initials, R.Z. and his wife, T.Z., the request appears to be detailing the hidden wealth of the reputed Kavač clan leader Radoje Zvicer and his wife Tamara Zvicer. Local media reports also name the two as the targets of this request.
The timing of this massive forfeiture request is no coincidence. It serves as one of the first major tests of Montenegro's sweeping new "Anti-Mafia Law," passed on September 4. The government hailed the legislation as a "historic step" that has already caused an "earthquake in criminal circles," specifically because it empowers the state to permanently confiscate assets in organized crime cases even before a final judicial verdict is reached.
Crucially, the law shifts the burden of proof, requiring accused cartel figures to prove their wealth was acquired legally. Following the law's passage, the government declared that crime will "never again be a business model" in the country.
The confiscation request was immediately welcomed by Deputy Prime Minister Aleksa Bečić. In an official statement reported by local media outlet Vijesti, Bečić noted that targeting illicit wealth and purging corrupt officials represent "the most deadly blows to the foundations of organized crime." Pledging that Montenegro will "never return to the dark ages of mafia occupation," he said the new legal framework allows the state to rapidly dismantle criminal infrastructure.
For Zvicer, the legal foundation for the seizure was triggered by his final 16-year prison sentence in Montenegro for drug trafficking and creating a criminal organization. However, his rap sheet stretches far beyond a single conviction.
In July 2026, he was handed a separate 40-year maximum first-instance sentence for orchestrating a drug smuggling and assassination syndicate alongside corrupt police officers. He also holds a final conviction in Serbia for identity forgery, while a raft of active indictments for murder and organized crime remain pending against him across Montenegro, Serbia, and Greece.
The 43-year-old, whose whereabouts have been unknown since 2021, remains the target of a sweeping Interpol red notice and is actively hunted across borders. Earlier this year, Austria's Criminal Intelligence Service offered a 20,000 euro ($22,540) reward for the armed and dangerous fugitive, seeking him for his role in organizing an 83-kilogram cocaine pipeline into Vienna.
According to Austrian authorities, the athletic, blue-eyed boss operates under at least 15 aliases and bears distinctive gunshot scars across the left side of his upper torso. The manhunt was so intense that in August, the Montenegrin Ministry of Internal Affairs escalated the stakes, offering a 500,000 euro ($562,834) bounty for information leading directly to his arrest.
Once a single Montenegrin syndicate smuggling South American cocaine into Europe, the Kavač and Škaljari clans violently fractured in 2014 over a botched drug deal in Spain. Their ensuing turf war for control of the billion-euro narcotics trade has claimed dozens of lives and deeply polarized the Balkan criminal underworld.
Prosecutors are now seeking to seize at least 54,567 square meters of property believed to have been purchased with criminal proceeds and carefully concealed behind a network of proxies, including front companies, legal counsel, and close family members.
The bulk of the targeted real estate is concentrated in the Kotor region on Montenegro's Adriatic coast, with heavy investments right in the clan's namesake stronghold of Kavač. Assets there include multi-story buildings, orchards, and more than 20,000 square meters of land and forest. Among the most prominent are a massive complex featuring a 355-square-meter duplex, as well as a separate residential space with an attic and garages—both formally registered to T.Z., according to prosecutors. Two other residential buildings and 10 garages are registered to multiple individuals, including her father, while a local company formally holds the rights to the majority of the forest, their documents say.
The seizures even reach into Škaljari, the ancestral territory of the Kavač clan’s deadly rivals, where the wife formally holds a half-share of a 188-square-meter courtyard.
Further along the Kotor coast, the dragnet caught a multi-story building in Dub containing five residential and ten non-residential spaces, alongside four commercial units. In Dobrota and Sutvara, prosecutors laid claim to a 140-square-meter apartment, a residential building with a private swimming pool, and tracts of meadows and forests formally registered to local businesses, associates, and a lawyer.
In the capital of Podgorica, authorities are targeting five apartments—including two duplexes—hidden behind a corporate entity. The remaining properties include 18,113 square meters of land in the Tivat village of Bogišići, and real estate registered to the fugitive’s mother in Herceg Novi.
Rounding out the seizure request are two heavily armored Mercedes G500 SUVs. While formally registered to an associate, prosecutors allege they belong to the crime boss’ illicitly acquired fleet. The prosecution noted its filing contains concrete evidence linking the entire portfolio directly to his criminal activities.

Yemen war puts Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact to first test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:51:56 UTC
23:51:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen war puts Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact to first test
Saudi Arabia's defence alliance with Turkey and Pakistan has moved from words to action for the first time, as escalating fighting in Yemen puts the two-month-old pact's collective defence commitments to the test.
The three members of the Mecca Alliance agreed at an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Sunday to begin the "practical implementation" of their collective defence commitments following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
They also agreed to make previously agreed military forces and capabilities available for rapid deployment to the kingdom.
But the move does not necessarily mean Turkish and Pakistani forces will join Saudi Arabia in directly fighting the Houthis.
Instead, experts told The New Arab that Pakistan could concentrate on territorial defence and military support inside Saudi Arabia, while Turkey provides capabilities including surveillance, air defence and drones.
For Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King's College London's School of Security Studies, the decision marks a significant evolution of the alliance.
"This is the first point at which I would describe the Mecca Pact as operational rather than primarily declaratory," Krieg told The New Arab.
"The critical development is not simply that the three governments have invoked collective defence. It is that Turkey and Pakistan are altering their military posture in response to attacks on Saudi Arabia and have committed to deploy previously agreed capabilities," Krieg said.
"That is the threshold the pact had to cross if it was going to have any deterrent credibility."
What will Pakistan and Turkey actually do?
The Mecca Alliance was established in August amid growing regional instability. Its collective defence principle means an attack against one member is treated as a threat to all three.
The arrangement has drawn comparisons with NATO's Article 5, but Krieg cautioned against taking the comparison too far.
"I would describe the pact as Article 5 language without Article 5 infrastructure," he said.
NATO has spent decades developing integrated military commands, common doctrine and joint planning. The Mecca Alliance has existed for only two months.
"This is meaningful activation, but it is the operationalisation of a flexible alliance rather than the creation of a unified war-fighting structure," Krieg said. "Yemen is now providing its first real operational laboratory."
The three countries have not publicly disclosed exactly which forces or military capabilities Turkey and Pakistan will deploy.
Krieg expects their roles to be substantially different.
Pakistan could provide territorial and air defence, training, advisers and manpower to protect strategic infrastructure, but is likely to be cautious about offensive operations against the Houthis partly because of its relationship with Iran.
Turkey could provide intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, radar and air defence, unmanned systems, electronic warfare and naval surveillance.
Saudi Arabia would remain the principal combatant.
"That allows all three states to say collective defence is functioning without requiring all three to fight the same war in the same way," Krieg said.
What does it change inside Yemen?
For Saudi Arabia, the most important effect may not be additional forces fighting inside Yemen but greater protection from attacks at home.
Maysaa Shuja al-Deen, a senior researcher at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, said the Houthis were likely among the threats Saudi Arabia had in mind when the agreement was designed.
Saudi Arabia is "the more vulnerable member state in this alliance, security-wise", she told The New Arab.
The Houthis have developed increasingly sophisticated missile and drone capabilities with Iranian support, allowing the group to strike targets well beyond territory it controls in Yemen.
Shuja al-Deen said Saudi Arabia's size and extensive economic infrastructure make defending against such attacks particularly demanding.
"No, it will not change the military situation inside Yemen," she said of the immediate effect of Turkish and Pakistani support.
Rather, "it will make the Saudis less vulnerable" to Houthi attacks.
That could nevertheless affect the war.
Saudi Arabia remains the principal external supporter of the Yemeni government and other anti-Houthi forces. If Riyadh reduced that support, Shuja al-Deen said, those forces would be placed in "huge trouble".
Stronger Saudi defences against missiles and drones - and the possibility of renewed Houthi ground operations towards the Saudi border - could therefore allow Riyadh to sustain its support for anti-Houthi forces for longer.
"When they become stronger in that sense, they can continue to support these anti-Houthi camp forces," she said.
Shuja al-Deen also warned that the threat to Saudi Arabia may not remain confined to missiles and drones.
She believes Houthi preparations and rhetoric indicate the group could eventually attempt another ground incursion across the Saudi border, although she stressed that it was unclear when such an operation might take place.
"I think the Houthis... are going to invade or to expand through the Saudi territories at some point in this war," she said. "I'm not sure when, but it seems from their preparation and from their discourse and media that they are going to do something like that."
The assessment comes amid heightened military activity in the Houthi stronghold of Saada along the Saudi border, where weapons and equipment have been moved towards frontier areas in recent weeks.
That possibility further increases the importance of the territorial defence Pakistan can provide, while Turkish and Pakistani support against missiles and drones could make Saudi Arabia better able to withstand Houthi pressure.
Turkish drones and Pakistani military expertise could provide additional support, Shuja al-Deen added, but she did not expect large numbers of Turkish or Pakistani troops to enter Yemen.
"Yemenis have plenty of fighters on both sides," she said.
Are Turkey and Pakistan now part of the Yemen war?
Direct Turkish or Pakistani intervention against the Houthis could risk widening a conflict already entangled with the regional confrontation involving Iran.
Shuja al-Deen said she did not currently expect the Houthis to retaliate directly against either country. Turkey is geographically removed from Yemen, while Pakistan occupies a sensitive position in Iran's regional calculations and maintains an important relationship with Tehran.
"I don't think they are going to widen the conflict at this moment to that extent," she said.
Krieg similarly expects Pakistan to remain wary of offensive action against the Houthis because Islamabad has strong incentives to avoid confrontation with Iran.
Turkey, meanwhile, is attempting to strengthen Saudi Arabia's position without closing the door to diplomacy.
Krieg said Ankara's preferred outcome was not the military destruction of the Houthis but a stronger Saudi negotiating position that could eventually produce a settlement.
Is the alliance aimed at Iran?
When Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan established the pact, they sought to reassure Iran that it was not intended as an anti-Iranian military bloc.
Its first activation has now come amid a war involving the Houthis, an armed movement closely aligned with Tehran.
Shuja al-Deen said the members had been explicit from the beginning that Iran was not the target.
But "it seems now, very obviously, that the Yemen war is the first test for this agreement", she said.
Krieg also cautioned against viewing the alliance simply as an emerging Sunni bloc designed to confront Iran.
"Iran and the Houthis are the immediate catalyst, but they are not the fundamental explanation," he said.
Instead, he sees the alliance as part of a broader Saudi effort to reduce the risks of relying overwhelmingly on the United States for its security.
Riyadh continues to depend on Washington for advanced aircraft, intelligence, missile defence, logistics and other high-end military capabilities, and is not attempting to replace its US security relationship.
"In that sense, I think Mecca is best understood as a supplement to the US architecture rather than an alternative to it," Krieg said.
Saudi Arabia brings financial resources and political weight to the arrangement, while Turkey contributes technology and its growing defence industry and Pakistan offers manpower, established military institutions and strategic depth.
"The Houthis triggered its first activation, but the alliance is really about how Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan intend to operate in a regional order where American power remains important but American reliability can no longer be taken for granted," Krieg said.

Book weighing over 200kg illustrated by Dalí and Cocteau stolen in Auvergne

On the night of 4 to 5 October, the "Book of the Apocalypse", a 210‑kilo volume with works by Salvador Dalí, Jean Cocteau and Bernard Buffet, was stolen from an art centre in Issoire, Puy‑de‑Dôme.
Another theft in the art world: the "Book of the Apocalypse", described as one of the most expensive (and heaviest) books in the world, was stolen from a private museum in Issoire, in Auvergne, overnight from Sunday to Monday, the Clermont-Ferrand public prosecutor’s office has said.
The original and unique copy of this book, conceived by the Auvergne publisher Joseph Forêt, was designed as a total work of art inspired by the Apocalypse of Saint John.
Weighing 210 kilos in total, this work made up of 150 parchments was produced between 1958 and 1961 by seven leading writers and seven leading painters of the time, among them Ossip Zadkine, Léonard Foujita, Jean Cocteau and Jean Giono. Salvador Dalí, for his part, sculpted the cover using the lost-wax casting technique.
A work that has travelled the world
After being shown in nearly 150 exhibitions around the globe between 1961 and 1972, the book disappeared from view for several years. Stored in Switzerland, it was eventually sold to Japanese collectors.
As they were preparing to auction it off, piece by piece, it was bought in 2003 by Christian Karoutzos, CEO of an art restoration company in Issoire. He decided to display the cover and several parchments in his contemporary art centre in the town until the autumn.
"It is a cathedral-like work, a masterpiece, unique in the world", the new owner lamented to ICI Pays d’Auvergne after the theft, adding that_"France was murdered last night, French heritage was murdered"_.
"This was a privately owned work kept in a small private contemporary art museum that also housed other, less valuable pieces", said Issoire’s mayor, Bertrand Barraud. He stressed that the loss was "incalculable" and that it was "the work of a lifetime".
An investigation has been opened by the Clermont-Ferrand gendarmerie’s research unit. The work is estimated to be worth several million euros.
This theft recalls the events at the Louvre on 19 October 2025, when thieves managed to steal jewels valued at 88 million euros_._

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev says drones have hit two commercial vessels, sinking one ship and wounding several people, in what he denounced as an “absolutely unacceptable” attack.
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Radev said the ships were attacked by sea drones and aerial drones at about 3am (00:00 GMT), about 70 nautical miles (130km) off Bulgaria’s coast, amid a rise in attacks on Black Sea shipping due to expanding drone attacks related to the Russia-Ukraine war.
“This is an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. It is a blatant violation of international law and maritime law,” Radev said.

The second vessel, the Palau-flagged Able, caught fire after the attack. A Bulgarian ferry and a naval fast boat evacuated all 18 crew members. Two sailors suffered serious injuries and were flown to a hospital in the port city of Varna, Radev said.
The Able was reportedly carrying wheat and sailing south, while the Alfa Watan was heading north. The Alfa Watan’s cargo was unknown, Radev said, adding that authorities were monitoring for possible oil spills and other signs of environmental pollution.
The origin of the drones was not immediately established, but the dual strike came a day after another ship caught fire and sank off the Romanian coast, killing one and leaving one missing, in what Ukraine said was a drone attack launched by Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described that attack as “a horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel” in neutral waters.
“What is happening is seriously disrupting shipping in the Black Sea, driving up insurance costs even further and making shipping extremely difficult,” Radev said after an emergency meeting on Tuesday.
Black Sea shipping has been heavily affected by the Russia-Ukraine war in recent months, and Radev warned that the war was expanding geographically and increasing the risk of global conflict.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said Budapest “stands in full solidarity with Bulgaria” after the attack on the two ships.

European Commission proposes suspending voting rights of prospective EU members failing to meet commitments
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:49:44 EEST
23:49:44 KST

The European Commission is proposing to introduce a series of precautionary measures for future European Union member states in the event they fail to fulfill their commitments, including the suspension of their voting rights in the EU Council.
These proposals are outlined in a package of documents regarding the European Union's preparations for future enlargement, specifically concerning sectoral and institutional safeguard measures.
In particular, the commission said future accession treaties should include "stronger safeguards against serious backsliding on commitments undertaken during the accession negotiations."
"Today, the Commission is proposing a common framework for these safeguards. Future accession treaties would strengthen the existing sectoral safeguards and introduce a new institutional safeguard. In particular, the period during which safeguards can be activated in areas such as the economy, the internal market, and justice and home affairs, would be significantly extended after accession," the press release reads.
Specifically, "the period during which safeguards can be activated in areas such as the economy, the internal market, and justice and home affairs, would be significantly extended after accession. A dedicated institutional safeguard would address serious breaches of Article 2 TEU values and the principle of sincere cooperation. In the most serious cases, measures could include the suspension of Council voting rights. Transitional arrangements could also be used where needed, including for the free movement of workers and services, agriculture, sensitive products, funding and participation in common systems. For a limited period, a new Member State could also commit not to block future enlargements because of bilateral disputes." the commission said.

Trump approves execution by firing squad for Fort Hood terrorist Nidal Hasan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:49:18 UTC
23:49:18 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump has formally approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan, the former U.S. Army psychiatrist who went on a shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, killing 13 people. Hasan’s execution would be the first carried out by the U.S. military itself, rather than the civilian justice system, since 1961.
The Pentagon said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recommended the death sentence be carried out by firing squad and Trump approved the recommendation. The date and location of the execution will be determined later. “Hasan’s day of reckoning has finally arrived,” the statement said.
Hasan, a U.S.-born Muslim of Palestinian descent, carried out the attack on Nov. 5, 2009. He entered a clinic at the sprawling military base, which at the time served as a staging point for troops preparing for deployment to combat zones in Iraq and Afghanistan, then pulled out two handguns and several magazines he had prepared in advance and opened fire on soldiers waiting for medical examinations and vaccinations while shouting “Allahu Akbar.”
The massacre was the deadliest shooting at a U.S. military installation in the country’s history. Hasan killed 13 people, including 12 soldiers, and wounded another 32, almost all of them service members. A civilian police officer responding to the attack eventually shot and incapacitated him, leaving Hasan paralyzed from the waist down.
Hasan, now 56, was born in the United States to Palestinian parents who had immigrated from the West Bank. His mother came from the town of al-Bireh. Years before the attack, Hasan himself visited the West Bank and remained in contact with relatives there. At the time, reports said his family owned several apartments in Ramallah and that one of his brothers had moved from the United States to the West Bank.
The investigation and trial that followed the attack found that Hasan had carried out the terrorist attack under the inspiration of the global jihadist group al-Qaida, after he said he had “switched sides” in what he called “America’s war against Islam.”
Hasan said he carried out the attack because he opposed the U.S. presence in Iraq and Afghanistan and wanted to prevent the military from sending troops there who would kill his Muslim brothers, including Taliban leaders.
Before the attack, he had been in contact with radical cleric and notorious terrorist Anwar al-Awlaki, a U.S. citizen affiliated with al-Qaida who was regarded as a “spiritual mentor” to prominent terrorists and was later killed in a U.S. drone strike in Yemen.
Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013, after a trial in which he chose to represent himself and refused to call witnesses or deny the charges against him. Court-appointed defense attorneys said at the time they feared he was deliberately seeking his own execution.
Hasan is now expected to become only the second person since 2010 to be executed by firing squad. Three other inmates are being held on death row in the U.S. military justice system and could also face a similar fate.
Since 1608, at least 144 civilian prisoners have been executed by shooting in what is now the United States, almost all of them in Utah. However, only four such executions have been carried out since 1977, the year capital punishment resumed after a decade-long suspension.
The most recent civilian execution by firing squad took place last year, when South Carolina carried out the death sentence of Brad Sigmon, who murdered the parents of his former girlfriend with a baseball bat.
This year, the U.S. Justice Department announced that it would allow executions by firing squad in an effort to increase the pace of executions for death row inmates.
In many U.S. death penalty cases, executions are delayed for years and sometimes decades through appeals or legal challenges over the planned method of execution and its effectiveness.
Just last week, controversy erupted after an attempt to execute convicted murderer Christa Pike in Tennessee failed when two lethal injections did not kill her and apparently caused her severe suffering. Pike’s lawyers had warned in advance that the injections might fail and even proposed that she be hanged instead.
At the state, nonfederal level, only five U.S. states currently allow execution by firing squad, all of them reliably Republican: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.

BRUSSELS - The European Commission proposed measures on Oct 6 to prepare the EU to take in countries such as Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine and Moldova in coming years while trying to reassure existing members about potential political and economic costs.
The proposals by the European Union’s executive body reflect a renewed interest among EU members in expanding the 27-nation bloc, driven largely by Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and Kyiv’s desire to join the bloc as part of a peace settlement.
The proposed reforms include a measure to allow other EU countries to suspend a new member’s voting rights during the first 15 years of membership if it stops adhering to the bloc’s values, and a plan to limit financial support to Ukraine’s large farming sector.
The Commission also proposed strengthening an existing policy of gradually integrating would-be members into EU programmes and economic sectors such as energy, transport, digital and defence. But countries would have to meet criteria for each scheme and align with the EU’s overall strategic direction.
The small Balkan state of Montenegro is likely to be the next country ready to join the bloc, possibly wrapping up negotiations by the end of this year, according to EU officials. Albania, Moldova and Ukraine are also seen as frontrunners but are probably at least still several years away from membership.
“As enlargement countries advance on their path of reform, the EU must be ready to welcome them,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a written statement.
“This means preparing our institutions, adapting our policies for new realities, and ensuring our budget reflects our shared ambitions.”
The Commission’s suggestions will require approval from the EU’s current 27 member states to become reality. Those countries are expected to begin discussions on the proposals in the coming days. REUTERS

Norway files FIFA ethics complaint over Infantino, governance concerns
Unknown

2026-10-06
14:48:53 UTC
