Meanwhile, the airline’s new business plan is approved in its entirety by the company’s board of directors, and the government has been informed of it and has given the green light for its implementation to stabilize the financial situation.
At the same time, it is essential for the ministry that the implementation of airBaltic business plan be carried out responsibly, in compliance with regulatory requirements, ensuring the company’s long-term financial stability and Latvia’s connectivity.
As reported, airBaltic could potentially lay off between 500 and 700 employees as part of the operational downsizing outlined in its business plan, according to a statement released by the airline to the media.
The airline currently employs approximately 3,000 people, meaning that about 20 percent of the workforce could be affected.
Based on current planning assumptions, airBaltic estimates that the planned changes could affect approximately 500 to 700 positions across its bases in Riga, Vilnius, and Tallinn. This is a current estimate, and the number may change in the course of the process.
The range reflects ongoing consultations with trade unions on potential reduced workload arrangements for pilots and cabin crew, as well as the development of new organizational structures for the rest of the company (expected to be defined by mid-October).
airBaltic has notified the State Employment Agency of the planned collective redundancy process. The company will continue to follow the applicable requirements and procedures as the process moves forward.
More detailed information will be provided to employees during October. As individual decisions have not yet been made, it would be premature to provide estimates for individual bases, functions, or employee groups.
Dace Kavasa, president of the Latvian Aviation Trade Union (LAA), told LETA that the union learned of the number of employees potentially facing layoffs just a few minutes before the presentation to employees took place, and that there had been no previous discussions regarding these figures.
The union has reportedly been requesting precise data on the number of people to be laid off since September 6, as required by both the Labor Law and a European Union (EU) directive, but has been refused.
Kavasa acknowledged that negotiations had taken place regarding an 85 percent work schedule (part-time), and that an agreement on this was planned to reduce the number of layoffs. According to her, the majority of LAA members have expressed a willingness to switch to such contracts.
She added that pilots and flight attendants could be offered this part-time job option, while negotiations regarding technicians and maintenance staff will begin in mid-October.
"It is currently unclear what is meant by these 500 to 700 employees," she said.
The airBaltic group’s revenue last year increased by 4.2 percent compared to 2024, totaling EUR 779.344 million. Meanwhile, airBaltic group’s losses last year totaled EUR 44.337 million, which is 2.7 times less than in 2024. The airline carried a total of 5.2 million passengers in 2025, which is 1 percent more than in 2024.
Last summer, Germany’s national airline, Lufthansa, became a shareholder in airBaltic. Currently, the Latvian government owns 88.37 percent of airBaltic’s shares, Lufthansa holds 10 percent, the company Aircraft Leasing 1, owned by Danish businessman Lars Thuesen, a financial investor, holds 1.62 percent, and 0.01 percent is held by other shareholders. Caring for Sick Parents and Military Service: The Supreme Court Clarifies an Important Principle
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:38:10 EEST
23:38:10 KST

Military service does not prevent a person from being appointed as the guardian of an incapacitated relative. At the same time, such an appointment is not automatic: the court evaluates the condition of the person in need of guardianship, the qualifications of the prospective guardian, family circumstances, and the availability of other individuals who can realistically provide care.
This point is highlighted by the Roman Satsyk Law Firm, which handles cases involving the declaration of legal incapacity, the establishment of guardianship, and the protection of the rights of families in which seriously ill relatives require constant assistance.
This problem is particularly acute for the families of military personnel. A person may be fulfilling their military duty, while at home, a father or mother, due to a serious health condition, is no longer able to independently meet their basic needs, address issues of medical treatment or social protection, or represent their own interests before government agencies.
One such case became the focus of the firm’s attorneys’ work. In this family, two sons were serving in the military. Their father, due to severe mental and physical health issues, required constant care from others, which his wife had provided for many years. After her own health deteriorated significantly and she underwent complex treatment, she, too, began to require constant assistance.
As a result, the family found itself in a situation where the seriously ill parents needed a close relative who could not only provide daily care but also legally represent the father’s interests.
Why Simply Caring for a Relative Is Not Enough
Ukrainian law distinguishes between the actual care of a person and the legal representation of their interests.
According to Article 39 of the Civil Code of Ukraine, an individual may be declared legally incapacitated by a court if, due to a chronic, persistent mental disorder, they are unable to understand the significance of their actions and/or control them. A diagnosis, disability, or advanced age alone does not automatically render a person legally incapacitated.
After a person is declared legally incapacitated, the court establishes guardianship over them and appoints a guardian upon the recommendation of the guardianship and custody authority. The law also provides that, when selecting a guardian, preference may be given to individuals who have a family or kinship relationship with the ward, but their actual ability to fulfill the duties of a guardian must be taken into account.
Can a Member of the Military Serve as a Guardian?
This issue has long posed practical difficulties, as the mere fact that a candidate is in military service was sometimes viewed as a circumstance that precludes them from performing the duties of a guardian.
On June 22, 2026, the Joint Chamber of the Civil Court of Cassation within the Supreme Court, in Case No. 305/1557/24, formulated an important legal conclusion: the mere fact of performing military service under mobilization is not an automatic and unconditional obstacle to appointing a person as the guardian of an incapacitated individual.
At the same time, the Supreme Court emphasized another fundamental point. In each specific case, it is necessary to determine whether there are other individuals who can effectively perform the duties of a guardian, as well as to assess the candidate’s ability and intent to safeguard the rights and interests of the ward.
Therefore, family ties or the status of a military servicemember do not, in and of themselves, determine the outcome of the case.
Guardianship does not mean automatic discharge from military service
This aspect is particularly important for families seeking a legal solution due to the need for constant care for their parents.
Under the Law of Ukraine “On Military Duty and Military Service,” during a state of martial law, one of the family circumstances justifying discharge from military service is the need to provide guardianship for a person whom a court has declared legally incapacitated, provided that no other persons are providing such guardianship.
Therefore, a court decision establishing guardianship may be relevant to the further exercise of a service member’s rights; however, each situation requires a separate review of documents, family circumstances, and legal grounds.
“In such cases, it is important not to start by asking how to obtain a certain status or discharge from service. The primary question is: who will actually protect the interests of a person who, due to their health condition, can no longer make legally significant decisions on their own? If there is effectively no other close relative capable of providing guardianship, the candidate’s military service alone should not be an automatic grounds for denial. However, the family must properly document all the circumstances and follow the procedure established by law,” explains Yaroslav Khlivnyi, an attorney at the Roman Satsyk Law Firm.
What Is Required to Establish Guardianship
The procedure may include gathering medical and other evidence, preparing a petition to the court to declare a person legally incapacitated, conducting a forensic psychiatric evaluation, interacting with the guardianship and custody authority, vetting a potential guardian, and the court’s review of the case.
A medical certificate or a determination of disability alone is not sufficient. The key factor is establishing whether the person, due to a chronic and persistent mental disorder, is capable of understanding the significance of their actions and controlling them.
It is also necessary to assess the family situation in advance: who else among the person’s close relatives is available, whether they can provide guardianship, who is actually providing care, and why the proposed candidate is capable of acting in the ward’s best interests.
For families of military personnel, it is particularly important to first conduct a comprehensive assessment of the legal situation, since establishing guardianship, deferring mobilization, and discharging someone from military service that has already begun are distinct legal procedures with different legal grounds.
About the Firm
The Roman Satsyk Law Firm provides legal assistance to individuals and legal entities in civil, administrative, commercial, and other types of cases. The firm’s practice areas include declaring a person legally incapacitated, establishing guardianship, and matters related to long-term care.
Attorney Yaroslav Khlivnyi is a member of the Roman Satsyk Law Firm and has been practicing law since 2017.

Saudi Arabia says East-West pipeline pumping 5.8 million bpd
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:38:09 UTC
23:38:09 KST

Saudi Arabia says East-West pipeline pumping 5.8 million bpd
Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman says capacity restored after major attack last month.
Saudi Arabia’s energy minister has said that oil pumped through the key East-West Pipeline reached a capacity of 5.8 million barrels a day (bpd).
Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman made the comments during a panel discussion at the GCC 2026 Forum in Bahrain’s capital, Manama, on Tuesday.
“Not everyone knows that within five or six days, we began using the pipeline again after the major attack that struck it,” he said according to Saudi media, referring to drone strikes blamed on Iraqi militia last month. “And, thank God, as of this morning we’re back up to 5.8 million barrels,” added Prince Abdulaziz.
The 1,200km (750-mile) pipeline links Saudi Arabia’s major oil-producing fields in the east with the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing the kingdom to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which has largely been closed since the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February.
The Saudi Ministry of Energy had said at the time of the attack in early September that pipeline had been temporarily shut as a “precaution”. Specialised teams had begun steps to “secure the pipeline and assess its safety”, according to the ministry.
The East-West pipeline, which is also known as the Petroline, was built in 1981.
It has a maximum capacity of 7 million bpd, although actual flows have been lower in recent months – about 2 million bpd in August, according to commodities data and analytics firm Kpler – the lowest monthly level since January, as attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group made the Red Sea route difficult to use.
Since the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted oil flows from Saudi Arabia and its Gulf neighbours through the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia has been using the pipeline to reroute some 4 million bpd, equivalent to about 4 percent of global supply, to Yanbu.

Kozlovskis hopes to secure adoption of port reform before change in government  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

RIGA - Transport Minister Rihards Kozlovskis (New Unity) hopes to secure adoption of the port reform before the new government is appointed; these reforms would provide for balanced representation of the state and local governments on port councils, selection of port council members and managers through open competitions, as well as changes to the regulations governing port territories, real estate, and the powers of port authorities, the minister told LETA.
He said that there may be enough time during this period to push forward the port reform and secure the law’s passage in the Saeima. He noted that amendments have been submitted to the Saeima national economics, rural, environment and regional policy committee.
"This bill has been on hold for two years. In my view, it could be adopted," the minister added.
He also said that the budget poses a major challenge, as there are no funds available, so, for example, regarding Rail Baltica, it is important to understand what Latvia can and cannot afford, and the issue of long-term contracts for passenger carriers and the necessary funding is also crucial.
Having failed to secure a seat in the next Saeima, Kozlovskis acknowledged that he currently plans to serve faithfully as minister for the remainder of his term and "we will see what happens then".
Information on the Saeima’s website indicates that the Ministry of Transport has requested that the bill be treated as a committee-initiated bill and designated as urgent, allowing for both readings to be considered during a single Saeima session.
The explanatory memorandum to the bill states that its purpose is to combine into a single bill the proposed amendments to the Ports Law that were included in a bill previously submitted to the Saeima, as well as proposals and feedback received from port authorities, the Ventspils municipality, and the Association of Small Ports. As a result of these consultations, the bill includes several proposals aimed at expanding opportunities for port development and addressing issues related to the application of the law that have been identified in practice.
The amendments included in the draft law aim to eliminate uncertainty in port management regulations and create a predictable legal framework for ports to facilitate long-term investments. The amendments address issues that have been recognized in the sector for several years, including bringing the legal status of port authorities into line with the actual situation, ensuring balanced representation of the state and local governments on the port council, and the division of the port territory into a core operational area and an industrial area.
The draft law includes significant changes to the regulatory framework for port management. The draft law clarifies the division of port territory into the port’s core operational area and the port’s industrial area, establishes a unified regulatory framework for port administration functions, the operation of port councils, and the management of real estate in ports.
To ensure professional, transparent, and competence-based port management, the draft law provides that members of port councils and port managers shall be selected through an open competitive process.
The draft law also includes transitional provisions that ensure the uninterrupted operation of port authorities after the law enters into force. During the transitional period, the functions of the existing administrative bodies will be maintained, establishing the procedures and deadlines for appointing members of the port councils, as well as ensuring that the terms of office of current port board members appointed by the Cabinet of Ministers continue until the new councils are fully established.
At the same time, the transitional provisions ensure the uninterrupted performance of the duties of port administrators, stipulating that the current administrators of the Freeport of Riga, Ventspils Freeport, and small port managers will continue to perform their duties until new managers are selected through an open competition, but for no longer than five years after the law enters into force.

Turkish justice minister details fund investigation and 'Terror-Free Türkiye' process
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:37:21 UTC
23:37:21 KST

Türkiye's justice minister said Tuesday that authorities have detained 85 suspects and taken action against 207 people as part of an ongoing investigation into alleged manipulation involving investment funds and stocks, stressing that the probe should not undermine confidence in the country's financial markets.
Speaking to Anadolu's Editors' Desk in the capital Ankara, Akin Gurlek said the investigation was launched following complaints and tips from the public, as well as an authorization granted by the Capital Markets Board (SPK) to launch the probe.
Gurlek said that during his tenure as Istanbul chief public prosecutor, in February 2025 authorities noticed unusual activity in some funds and stocks and sent an official notice. He said complaints from the public were received this August, after which the SPK gave its permission for a formal investigation.
He said authorities must distinguish between legitimate and illicit gains, pointing to profits allegedly made through the rapid buying and selling of so-called "bubble stocks."
"We noticed this ourselves, and our colleagues wrote to the SPK to request authorization for an investigation. We even held talks personally. Of course, our (Treasury and finance) minister was also following the process and had made statements on the funds. Authorization for an investigation was eventually granted following the memorandum we sent in August. The fund investigation began this way," Gurlek said.
He stressed that prosecutors can investigate the relevant offenses only after authorization is granted.
"Turkish markets and the Turkish economy are very strong. They are the apple of our eye. We should not generalize an incident that took place in a small part of this market," he said.
Gurlek said President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has been following the process from the beginning and that authorities give him regular updates. He added that he had held frequent meetings with Mehmet Simsek, the Treasury and finance minister, and that a Fund Coordination Board had been established under Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz.
"Daily routine transactions are entirely within the framework of the free market economy and are at the discretion of the relevant boards," Gurlek said, adding that prosecutors act on the basis of complaints, tips, and investigation authorizations.
Asked about the scope of the investigation, Gurlek said the SPK decided on Sept. 17 to liquidate the funds in question.
"As soon as the decision was made, the chief public prosecutor's office took all preventive measures under the scope of the investigation authorizations granted," he said.
“So far, 85 suspects have been detained, action has been taken against 207 people, and the assets of many people have been frozen. Our colleagues have also taken the necessary measures to prevent the transfer or concealment of assets."
Gurlek said authorities had prevented an attempted transfer of 40 million Turkish liras ($813,345) abroad by the spouse of a person who was detained two days after the investigation began.
He also said the State Supervisory Council had become involved to examine whether any public institutions had been negligent or whether there had been misconduct, intent, or bad faith.
According to Gurlek, prosecutors have been examining lists provided by the SPK, the Borsa Istanbul stock exchange, and the Central Securities Depository, and have imposed measures against individuals and companies suspected of making unusually large profits through manipulative transactions.
"We have already launched an investigation into these matters ... The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office has imposed precautionary measures against people who engaged in manipulative activity and obtained excessive or unusual profits in a short period of time,” he said.
"Their assets have been frozen. Some have been detained, while others are fugitives. There are also international travel bans. The process is ongoing. This is entirely under the supervision of the independent judiciary.”
Gurlek said the government is working to protect legitimate investors from being affected by the investigation.
"Turkish markets, the funds, and Borsa Istanbul are the apple of our eye. There’s an ongoing process here. We’re doing it meticulously. Our well-intentioned investors, our stocks, and our companies must not be affected by this process," he said.
On the return of funds, Gurlek said the SPK had decided to reimburse legitimate investors for losses of up to 1 million liras.
He said prosecutors had identified people who allegedly made substantial profits through manipulative transactions carried out over short periods and had frozen their assets, including the personal assets of portfolio and fund managers.
A mechanism has also been established at the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) to allow people to voluntarily return money, he said.
"I spoke with the TMSF head yesterday. Five people have returned money to these accounts," Gurlek said.
He added that the assets in question have been transferred to TMSF within the framework of the law and that it would notify prosecutors after the relevant repayments.
Gurlek also warned that those who repay losses should not assume that their criminal cases will automatically be dropped.
"Covering twice the amount of the damage is a reason for effective repentance, but this does not mean that the investigation or the case will be closed. It is simply a reason for a reduction provided for by law. The perception that no action will be taken against those who compensate for the damage is wrong. Action will definitely be taken against them," he said.
He said authorities have information on individuals and companies suspected of making excessive profits and had already taken steps to recover assets and funds allegedly transferred abroad.
"We have started judicial proceedings to bring back money sent to Switzerland. We have seized their personal assets and imposed precautionary measures. We have also placed measures on property records. We’re still investigating matters," Gurlek said.
He pledged that authorities would continue working to protect investors' rights.
"We will do everything within the framework of the law to recover our citizens’ money, to the fullest extent possible, from those who made excessive profits in a short period of time or entered the market after getting tips," he said.
Gurlek said all relevant state institutions are coordinating on this and urged the public to keep its confidence in Türkiye's economy and capital markets.
"Let them rest assured. Thanks to the ongoing investigations, our markets, Borsa Istanbul and our investors will definitely not be affected by this process," he said.
Gurlek also described the "Terror-Free Türkiye" process as a major priority, saying there would be no reversal.
"The Terror-Free Türkiye process is very important for us. We see it as a Türkiye Century project. For more than 40 years, our young people, our children and the security of the state have unfortunately suffered harm in every sense. There is no turning back from this process; the arrow has flown," he said.
Under the provisions of the law on strengthening national solidarity and social integration passed by parliament earlier this year with 467 votes, the law cannot take effect until the terrorist group PKK is dismantled in all its components, he explained.
He said a Monitoring and Evaluation Board had been established under Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz and that the Defense Ministry, National Intelligence Organization (MIT), and National Security Council are working to verify that the group has truly dismantled.
"There is an ongoing process. In particular, there is a mechanism for determining and confirming the dismantling of the group in all its components. Our Defense Ministry, our intelligence agency, and our National Security Council are working on this. The process is continuing. Thank God, it is going well so far," Gurlek said.
He warned against attempts to provoke the process, saying authorities are taking security measures at stadiums and coordinating with the Interior Ministry.
"We will not give them an opportunity to act," he said.
Gurlek said the completion of the process would allow people to direct their energy and resources toward investment and incentives while creating new employment opportunities for young people.
"We hope the process will be completed. It is very important for us. The Justice Ministry is following this process closely," he said.

Russians held at U.S. immigration detention center plan hunger strike over poor conditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:35:52 UTC
23:35:52 KST

Russians held at U.S. immigration detention center plan hunger strike over poor conditions
Fourteen Russians held in an immigration detention center in the state of Georgia have signed a collective complaint about the conditions of their detention and announced that they plan to begin a hunger strike. Copies of the complaint were obtained by Vot Tak, Agentstvo, and The Insider. Four sources familiar with the conditions in detention confirmed the document’s authenticity to Agentstvo. Here’s what we know so far.
Russians held in an immigration jail in Georgia say they are not treated for illness, are fed poorly, and have limited contact with the outside world
One of the most serious allegations in the collective complaint is the lack of medical care. The Russians say that while detained, they receive almost no treatment. Emergency care is only provided in cases of loss of consciousness or severe bleeding. For fever, high blood pressure, or acute pain, detainees may have to wait “a week or more” for treatment.
Alexei Kovalko, one of the authors of the complaint, said he once lost consciousness while having blood drawn. After he was revived, he asked staff to let him lie down, still feeling weak and dizzy. He was taken to a room that contained only a toilet and left lying on the bare concrete floor for several hours.
Kovalko said an even more acute problem is dental care. “My personal experience: numerous complaints about tooth pain and requests to see a dentist have been ignored for almost two years. They aren’t even registered in the system,” the Russian wrote in the complaint.
He and the other authors of the complaint also cite poor-quality water and bad food (they are mostly given canned and frozen food); cold cells (they have to sleep in their clothes); and noise in common areas (televisions there aren’t turned off until 2 a.m., which interferes with sleep, especially since earplugs are banned).
The complaint separately lists problems with communication: paper mail is delivered selectively, email is unavailable, and phone calls are expensive. Many of the people held at the jail are going through court proceedings over their immigration status, and these rules severely limit their ability to communicate with lawyers and defend themselves.
“The goal of this facility is to deport the maximum number of people and create conditions in which it’s impossible to defend your case in immigration court,” the complaint states. Its authors believe this is confirmed by the behavior of the detention center’s warden. He has repeatedly told the people held there that they will not be living in the U.S., and once told the Russians: “Don’t worry, we’ll send you back to your cozy Gulag.”
The immigration jail in Georgia was converted from a regular prison. Conditions there have largely remained the same
The immigration detention center named in the collective complaint is the D. Ray James Correctional Facility in Folkston, Georgia, named after a former mayor of the city. It is owned by GEO Group, one of the two largest private prison operators in the U.S.
The facility previously operated as a federal prison. In 2025, it was converted into an immigrant detention center. The people held there are not necessarily criminals and are not serving criminal sentences; for them, detention means being deprived of their liberty over a possible deportation while their case is being considered in immigration court. In practice, however, conditions in detention centers can resemble those in prisons.
Dmitry Valuev, president of the organization Russian America for Democracy in Russia (RADR), told Vot Tak that conditions in American immigration detention centers are difficult, but not everywhere are they as harsh as at the D. Ray James facility in Folkston.
“There are select detention centers where vegetables and fresh fruit are given out regularly, even daily, but there are many others where fruits and vegetables aren’t part of the regular diet. The same goes for medical services — people with chronic illnesses suffer a great deal, because treatment in detention centers is mostly very basic, without advanced diagnostics,” Valuev said.
He stressed that immigration detention centers are normally meant for short-term detention — up to several weeks — and that food and medical care standards there are designed with that in mind. In practice, however, people can remain in detention for years, and in those cases, the conditions effectively become torturous.
Russians (and detainees from other countries) plan to start a hunger strike. They want to be transferred to another facility
The collective complaint bears the signatures of 14 people. According to materials obtained by outlets that received a copy of the complaint, all of them are Russian. Among them are the complaint’s authors, Alexei Kovalko and Alexander Borovkov, and 12 other men who have been held in Folkston for five to 30 months. Kovalko, for example, has been in the jail for more than two years — 28 months.
The Russians relayed through relatives that they plan to declare a hunger strike on October 6 to protest the conditions of their detention. According to them, about 50 detainees in total plan to take part in the hunger strike — not only Russians but also Latin Americans, Iranians, Afghans, Chinese nationals, and people from other countries.
“Everyone wants to be released or transferred to other detention centers where they could get a fair hearing on their cases, bail requests, and petitions. At the same time, they’re demanding improved detention conditions,” Polina Gerdyukova, the wife of Andrei Gerdyukov — one of the signatories of the complaint who has been held in detention since February 2026 — told the independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo.
The flow of Russians seeking asylum in the U.S. increased after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. People who end up in immigration jails are usually those who crossed the border from Mexico and requested asylum in the U.S., or who were detained later while already in the country. As of spring 2026, RADR estimated the number of Russians in U.S. detention centers at 700–800 people.
After Donald Trump returned to power, U.S. authorities began detaining and deporting foreigners more aggressively. RADR believes that around 300–400 Russians may have been deported over the past year alone. They are being sent back to Russia even though they may face criminal charges or military conscription there.
At least two cases are known in which Russians who had sought asylum in the U.S. were detained on criminal charges after being deported back to Russia. The first involves serviceman Artem Vovchenko: after arriving in Russia, he was sent to a pretrial detention center on charges of abandoning his military unit, but he managed to get transferred to a civilian hospital and escaped from there. The second case is the prosecution of businessman and activist Leonid Melekhin, who was ultimately sentenced to six years on charges of justifying terrorism.

Russia denies plague death but quarantines hundreds without explanation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:34:22 UTC
23:34:22 KST

Rospotrebnadzor said Darya Shipilova, 28, died of "pneumonia of unknown aetiology" with no links to her work at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, but imposed quarantine on her contacts, confined 60 colleagues inside the facility and restricted access to hospitals including a maternity ward.
Russian authorities have insisted a lab researcher who died in Siberia last week did not have the plague while quarantining nearly 200 of her contacts, confining more than 60 colleagues inside their institute and restricting access to multiple hospitals, all without explanation.
Darya Shipilova, 28, a researcher at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, was admitted to Shelekhov District Hospital in late September and died last Friday night.
Russia's national health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said biological samples from her body found no microorganisms linked to her professional work and that she died from "pneumonia of unknown aetiology."
The agency said its special commissions had found no accidents involving pathogenic microorganisms at the institute. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters to rely solely on Rospotrebnadzor's statements.
Between 189 and 197 of Shipilova's contacts were placed under observation and quarantine, according to figures cited by independent and regional media.
Initial tests among those contacts returned negative. More than 60 staff members of the anti-plague institute were effectively confined inside the facility for several days.
Quarantine restrictions were also imposed on hospitals in Irkutsk, including a maternity ward, according to reporting by multiple regional and international outlets.
Patients at one facility said doctors cited plague as the reason. Relatives of a woman in labour were refused entry to the ward despite having paid for partner-assisted birth.
The head of neighbouring Buryatia, Alexei Tsydenov, initially said after Shipilova's death that she had died of plague, then amended this to "possibly plague".
Irkutsk regional authorities posted a message on Friday asking residents not to travel to the satellite town of Shelekhov because of plague, then deleted it.
Governor Igor Kobzev described the cause of death as "pneumonia of unknown aetiology" on Monday.
What are international authorities saying?
The World Health Organization said it assessed the public health risk from the incident as low to moderate for Irkutsk region, low for Russia as a whole and very low for the WHO European region.
It said Russian authorities had identified Shipilova's contacts and were monitoring them, and that they had detected no dangerous infectious disease agents among those contacts.
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control told Euronews it was "closely following the situation" and was in contact with the WHO.
"We are aware of a case of pneumonia of unknown origin in eastern Russia that is suspected to be plague. This suspicion has not yet been confirmed," an ECDC representative said.
US authorities are also monitoring developments, while Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan have strengthened sanitary controls at their borders with Russia.
Uzbekistan has also strengthened its public-health preparedness after reports of a suspected case of a particularly dangerous infectious disease in Russia’s Irkutsk region, while stressing that the diagnosis has not yet been confirmed.
Online theories swirl
Two unofficial theories have circulated in Russian media. The first, reported by Telegram channels SHOT and Baza, holds that Shipilova accidentally broke a test tube containing the plague pathogen in the laboratory.
Several specialists consider this unlikely, noting that work with high-risk pathogens is conducted inside sealed safety cabinets with protective suits and strict decontamination protocols.
The second theory is that the infection was acquired during field research in a region with natural plague reservoirs. The head of Buryatia publicly denied that Shipilova had visited the region.
The official diagnosis has not been confirmed or ruled out by published PCR test results.
Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Its most common form, bubonic plague, affects the lymphatic system. Pneumonic plague, which can spread between people via airborne droplets, is considered the most dangerous.
Russia's most recent confirmed human cases were recorded in the Altai region in 2014, 2015 and 2016, all involving people who handled marmots.
Human plague cases in Russia remain rare despite natural reservoirs existing in several regions.

Lithuania confirms natural tectonic earthquakes occurred within its territory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:31:00 UTC
23:31:00 KST

Lithuania’s Geological Survey has for the first time reliably confirmed that natural tectonic earthquakes occur within the country’s territory, the agency said Tuesday.
Two weak earthquakes were recorded in western Lithuania on December 14, 2025, with their natural origin also confirmed by experts from the University of Helsinki’s Institute of Seismology.
The first earthquake occurred at 08:35 and had a magnitude of 2.7. The second was recorded at 12:03 and had a magnitude of 2.4.
Magnitude measures the strength of an earthquake based on the amount of energy released.
“The earthquakes themselves were weak, but their scientific significance is great. For the first time, we collected reliable instrumental data confirming that natural tectonic earthquakes also occur within Lithuania’s territory,” Andrius Pačėsa, chief seismologist in the Geological Survey’s Division of Deep and Petroleum Geology, said in a statement.
The new data also allowed specialists to reassess an earlier seismic event and learn more about the activity of tectonic structures in western Lithuania.
The 2025 earthquakes were recorded in western Lithuania near the Gargždai fault zone. Earlier geological studies have shown that the area contains tectonic faults in both its crystalline basement and sedimentary rocks.
The Geological Survey said that, because of uncertainties in locating the earthquakes, they can be associated with the Gargždai fault zone but cannot be attributed with certainty to a particular fault or segment.
The 2.7-magnitude earthquake released about 2.8 times more energy than the 2.4-magnitude quake. The earthquake magnitude scale is logarithmic, meaning relatively small differences in magnitude can represent substantially different amounts of released energy.
For comparison, earthquakes of about magnitude 5 struck Russia’s Kaliningrad region in September 2004, with tremors felt in Lithuania, particularly in the western part of the country.
The new findings also prompted the Geological Survey to reassess a magnitude 2.1 seismic event recorded in western Lithuania on June 12, 2015.
At the time, available data were insufficient to determine conclusively whether the event was a natural earthquake or seismic activity caused by human activity.
Following the 2025 earthquakes, specialists conducted an additional analysis of seismograms held in the international GEOFON database and recalculated the location of the 2015 event.
The new analysis showed that the 2015 event was also a tectonic earthquake in western Lithuania, rather than an explosion, according to the Geological Survey.
The two earthquakes recorded December 14, 2025, and the June 12, 2015, event are therefore considered the first natural earthquakes reliably recorded and localised within Lithuania’s territory.

"We estimate that the bulk of the volume (1 million tonnes) was delivered via the SUMED pipeline and Egypt’s Sidi Kerir terminal. The remaining 0.3 million tonnes, by our calculations, were shipped directly from Yanbu, bypassing the SUMED infrastructure," the review said. Euler estimates that UAE shipments out of Gulf of Oman terminals have hovered around 3.7 million tonnes over the past two months.

====================================================================================================

Kharkiv mayor: No safe place left in the city as winter approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:27:00 UTC
23:27:00 KST

Kharkiv mayor: No safe place left in the city as winter approaches
The northern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv is now targeted by Russian drones as well as missiles, but the city lives on mayor Ihor Terehhov told ERR.
Being just 30 kilometers from the Russian border, Kharkiv has suffered a lot over the past four and a half years but is unbowed and is trying to rebuild what has been destroyed,
The mayor noted the coming winter will be very hard without any "energy truce", but the city survived the last winter and the previous ones too.
Mayor Terehhov was talkng to ERR at a time when Russia has been hitting Kharkiv in lethal strikes involving bombs, missiles and drones.
It is mid-autumn already and winter is approaching. How is Kharkiv preparing, and how did it survive the last winter?
If there is no so-called energy truce — Ukraine ending strikes on Russian oil refineries in exchange for Russia ending attacks on energy and other critical infrastructure in Ukraine, which is currently widely under discussion — then the coming winter will be very hard. We understand that perfectly.
I warned everyone last autumn that the winter would be tough, and so it has turned out to be. The enemy has been destroying energy infrastructure, targeting thermal power plants and water supply, leaving residents without basic utilities.
We all understand this all too well, yet we survived last winter, even though it, too, was hard. Due to the strikes on the power plants, we had not a single megawatt of electricity generation of our own. The heating system was damaged. There had been 50 attacks on electricity and heating networks. So it was a hard winter, but we held out. As for next winter, we are preparing for that too. We have been preparing since 2022.
Two years ago, in our previous interview, you spoke about the need to create energy "islands". What are these islands, and have they been created?
We wouldn't have survived last winter without those energy islands. I can't tell you everything, but if I were Estonia, I would be setting up energy islands too. It is effective. In essence an energy island is an autonomous energy source fed by small boiler houses. People get electricity, heat and water from it.
How many people currently live in Kharkiv? Initially people left, and then, as you said, they began to return. Two years ago you estimated the population at 900,000. Kharkiv has also become a destination for internally displaced people from the front line and occupied areas. What is the trend today?
During the war there have been times when the city's population fell to 350,000 and even to 320,000. But the trend has been positive, and currently around 1.4 million people live in Kharkiv, of whom 225,000 are internally displaced persons. This is a serious challenge for the city — these people have to be resettled and cared for.
Our hospitals cater to these people; their children attend our schools. They have lost everything, and it is our duty to care for them, but they also need help from the state. They have been left homeless, so the state should issue them housing certificates, but so far no state program has been implemented. So there are many challenges we face every day. But the fact that there are 1.4 million people living in Kharkiv today is actually good news.
How is responsibility for internally displaced people divided between the city, the oblast and the central government? Is the city obliged to provide them with housing?
In my view, providing housing for those who have lost everything — that is, internally displaced people — is the state's obligation. I mean a construction program for internally displaced people, so they have the opportunity to get living space where they want. The situation is not like this in Kharkiv alone. Yes, most of our people are displaced from Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts. So such a program is needed.
As for Kharkiv residents, we currently have 160,000 people who have been left without shelter. No other major Ukrainian city has suffered destruction like Kharkiv has. As of today, we have 10,000 damaged, severely damaged or completely destroyed residential buildings, but during the war we have managed to repair and restore nearly 4,000 buildings. Of course, the city's budget deficit is very large, and according to government forecasts it will be even larger next year.
Where is the money coming from?
Financial assistance from international partners is required. It is no secret that we depend on funds allocated by our international partners. This is public information; both the president and the government have said so. We have to use state and city budget funds very carefully.
On September 28, Russian attack drones destroyed practically the entire stairwell of a multi-story block. Do you have reserve apartments to relocate residents somewhere?
We offered people accommodation in a dorm. Two families initially agreed, but then said they would go to live with relatives. Most of the residents of that building are internally displaced people who were renting apartments there. And now they are looking for other apartments.
For our part, we closed the building shell (a temporary measure where holes in walls and broken windows are covered with plywood — ed.), restored the electricity supply and restarted the heating and water systems. All of this is financed out of the city budget. The victims have been documented and are receiving payments. But the stairwell is still destroyed, from the third floor to the fifth, and with this I think the state should already allocate money for restoration. At first we were restoring everything ourselves at our own expense, but the city budget is already exhausted.
So what is the city's current budget deficit? How much money do you need?
That is a complicated question. You could say there is a deficit, but also say there isn't, depending on how you calculate it. Without reconstruction costs, we are on the edge, but still not in deficit. If we want to carry out the programs we consider necessary, then a deficit comes up. For us, the most important thing is to ensure reconstruction support and that payments are not delayed, as sometimes happens.
I saw three buildings in [residential district of Kharkiv] Saltivka that had been heavily damaged at the start of the war, then repaired, and now they are in order and people are starting to return (apartment repairs are not the city's responsibility but the residents' — ed.). But the Saltivka area is not the safest place in Kharkiv, to put it mildly. Is it worth spending money on rebuilding something that could be destroyed again the very next day?
I am convinced that rebuilding is essential. If we don't do it, people will stay in other countries and not return. People do not come back to places where there is nowhere to live, work or educate their children. We consider it important that Ukrainians, Kharkiv residents, come back from abroad, which means we have to rebuild in any case. Moreover, the current situation is such that a strike can hit practically any Ukrainian city. There is no city in the country so safe that you could say it definitely won't be attacked.
Have you been taking part in international conferences on Ukraine's reconstruction? In June a conference like that took place in Gdansk, Poland; next January one is going to be held in Tallinn.
I was at the Gdansk one. We held a special event and we managed to attract money from international partners, specifically for preparing for the heating season. That meeting was a productive one for Kharkiv.
I was in the Pyatykhatky neighborhood, and anti-drone nets are being installed over the road there. At the same time, some nearby streets are not covered with nets; I saw at least one car destroyed by a drone strike. On what criteria do you decide what to cover with nets and what not to?
The nets are not installed by the city but by the regional military administration, and they are installed where the military says so. Only the military decides where the anti-drone nets get placed. For our part, we are also installing protection against fibre-optic FPV drones. We do this in conjunction with the military, but at the city's expense. This protection is our know-how, developed in cooperation with the military and engineers.
Which places in Kharkiv are currently the most dangerous, and which are the safest?
In Kharkiv, as in the rest of the country, there is no safe place. I can't tell you that Pyatykhatky is dangerous but the city center — say Shevchenkivskyi or Kyivskyi districts — is more or less safe, because at any moment it could be hit by anything, from a missile to an FPV drone. As long as the war continues, nowhere in Ukraine can be a hundred percent safe.
Do you have any advice for your Estonian colleagues — mayors, municipal leaders — on preparing for crises?
Estonia is a sovereign state and we respect that. If you need our advice, there is no problem there. We will talk and show everything as openly as possible, though that information is not intended for the wider public consumption.

“I hate to see them having it,” Trump said Monday. “It’s a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter, like an army.”
Asked whether he was concerned about the disease spreading internationally through travel, Trump appeared to downplay the immediate risk, saying little travel was headed toward the affected area.
During a joint press conference with Icelandic Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir in Reykjavík, Rubio was asked whether there was reason to suspect the incident involved the accidental release of an intentionally modified strain of plague developed by Russia, to which he cautioned against speculation.
“It would be irresponsible for me here to sit and speculate because we just don’t have all the information yet,” Rubio said.
He added Russia should “share more information with the world” so that other countries can better assess the situation and respond appropriately.
Fresh Intelligence Signals Massive Russian Strike Ahead, Zelensky Says
“Maybe there’s nothing there and maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know,” Rubio said, adding that the US and international agencies were monitoring developments “very closely, hour by hour.”
Rubio told reporters that Washington already has measures in place to respond if the situation proves more serious than currently acknowledged, adding that Washington would continue monitoring the situation and again urged Russia to be transparent.
“We encourage Russia to be transparent and share more information with the world,” he said, adding that any US decisions would depend on information still being gathered.
His statements come after a laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East died after developing severe pneumonia.
Russian health authorities have described the illness as pneumonia of “unknown origin” and said testing did not detect microorganisms associated with the woman’s work. They have also denied that any accident involving dangerous pathogens occurred at the facility.
Unconfirmed Russian media reports have suggested that the woman may have been exposed to pneumonic plague while working at the institute. Reports have also said that nearly 200 people who may have had contact with her were placed under medical observation or isolation, while several medical facilities introduced precautionary measures.
The reports have drawn particular scrutiny because the woman worked at a facility dedicated to studying plague and other dangerous pathogens.
US experts raise questions over Russian response
Former White House COVID-19 response coordinator Dr. Ashish Jha told CNN that the circumstances surrounding the death raised “a lot of red flags,” pointing to reports of widespread monitoring measures and the involvement of Russia’s security services.
Jha also pointed to the institute’s history and Russia’s alleged offensive biological-weapons program, saying the combination of factors warranted closer scrutiny.
He stressed, however, that there was no confirmed evidence that the researcher had been exposed to a weaponized pathogen.
CNN medical analyst Dr. Jonathan Reiner likewise urged caution, saying there was still no independent confirmation that the woman died from plague or clarity about how she became infected.
“It’s hard to know until we have more information,” Reiner said, warning against jumping to conclusions about either a major outbreak or an insignificant incident.
Russian opposition figure and former world chess champion Garry Kasparov also questioned Moscow’s account, arguing that the Kremlin’s history of withholding information made its statements difficult to trust.
He suggested the laboratory could have links to military biological research but provided no direct evidence connecting the woman’s death to a weapons program.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has said that, based on information available to it, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low.
Pneumonic plague is a severe form of plague that can spread through respiratory droplets. Unlike during historical outbreaks, the disease can be treated effectively with antibiotics when detected early.

Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir’s top elected official, Omar Abdullah, on Tuesday criticized an alleged eviction drive targeting Rohingya refugees in the region, saying they were being “singled out without cause” despite having lived there for years.
Abdullah, speaking to reporters in Srinagar, said people who entered India illegally from Bangladesh should face legal action, but Rohingyas who fled persecution in Myanmar were a “separate” case.
Indian authorities on Monday flew at least 150 Bangladeshi immigrants from Kashmir to the Indian state of West Bengal, which borders Bangladesh, saying they were staying illegally in the region.
Indian officials said a survey was conducted across the Kashmir region, during which around 600 Bangladeshi nationals were found to be allegedly staying there illegally.
“Those who entered from Bangladesh without permission - that is a separate issue. But the Rohingyas are being singled out without cause. They were driven out of their country (Myanmar), and we gave them shelter,” Abdullah said.
Government data shows some 7,656 Rohingyas were living in Jammu and Kashmir, including 6,737 in the Jammu division and 919 in the Kashmir Valley.
The eviction drive has intensified, with landlords reportedly ordered to remove Rohingya tenants or face criminal cases.
“At least 18 first information reports by local police have been registered against people accused of failing to report tenants to authorities,” Indian newspaper Deccan Chronicle reported Tuesday.
Human rights groups estimate that about 1,800 Rohingyas have been rendered homeless.
Many families say they have lived in Jammu for 15 to 20 years, working as laborers and holding UNHCR documents.
Abdullah said the federal government was directing the campaign, while Jammu and Kashmir police were conducting verification and eviction drives.
“They must not be treated like animals. They are human beings. You cannot let them starve or freeze,” he said.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party has alleged a “political conspiracy” behind their settlement in Jammu, while the opposition Congress party has called for adherence to international refugee norms.
The Rohingyas are a stateless Muslim minority from Myanmar who have faced decades of discrimination and displacement. More than 700,000 fled Myanmar’s Rakhine State following an outbreak of violence in August 2017, with most seeking refuge in Bangladesh.

ABUJA, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Nigeria has declared a three-day national mourning beginning Tuesday for the 32 Air Force personnel who were killed when a military aircraft crashed in the country's southwestern Ondo State on Monday.
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu, while declaring the mourning period late Monday, also directed that the national flag be flown at half-mast across the country to pay respect for the victims, including 25 passengers and seven crew members.
"This is a painful moment for our Armed Forces and for the entire nation," he said in a statement, ordering a comprehensive investigation into the incident.
The Nigerian Air Force confirmed earlier that the ATR-42 twin-engine turboprop aircraft, with the tail number NGR 931, was on a routine mission from Benin City in southern Nigeria to Lagos.
The aircraft plunged near the Naval Base in Igbokoda, a riverine community in Ondo State, according to Festus Keyamo, minister of aviation and aerospace development.

The Nigerian Air Force released the names of the personnel involved in the crash and opened a condolence register at its headquarters in Abuja on Tuesday morning.
Across the country, Nigerians mourned the victims of the crash, one of the deadliest involving a military aircraft in the history of the West African nation.
On Sept. 26, 1992, more than 150 military personnel were killed when a Nigerian Air Force aircraft crashed into a canal in a Lagos neighborhood shortly after takeoff. The victims were primarily middle-ranking officers attending a course in northwestern Kaduna State.
"This is a national disaster," Sharon Shiejir, daughter of one of the military officers who died in the 1992 crash, told Xinhua after Monday's incident.

Machine Gunner in the 12th &quot;Azov&quot; Brigade: Duties, Selection and Professional Training
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:25:00 EEST
23:25:00 KST

Machine Gunner in the 12th "Azov" Brigade: Duties, Selection and Professional Training
Kyiv • UNN
The 12th "Azov" Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine is looking for machine gunners and trains recruits from scratch. You can join through mobilization or under a contract.
Despite all the technological aspects of modern warfare, the position of machine gunner remains no less relevant. Wherever infantry operates, it is the machine gunner who provides the most substantial fire support, reports UNN.
The 12th Special Forces Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine, "Azov," has opened recruitment for candidates for the position of machine gunner. A lack of military training or experience handling weapons is not an obstacle. If there is motivation and a desire to learn, the unit's instructors will provide everything necessary from the very beginning.
Selection criteria: who can become a machine gunner
To take up the position of machine gunner in "Azov," prior combat experience is not required. Motivation and a willingness to work are valued most. It is also important to have certain basic qualities:
-  A desire to master heavy weapons and work toward the unit's common goal; 
-  Working with a machine gun and ammunition requires strength, but it is developed during training; 
-  The ability to remain calm and focused during intense combat; 
-  An understanding of one's role, since the safety of the entire group depends on one's work; 
-  No critical contraindications to military service. 
What a machine gunner's duties include
The machine gunner position in "Azov," in addition to working with large-caliber weapons, requires precise calculation and coordination:
-  Providing fire cover for infantry during defensive and assault operations; 
-  Suppressing enemy firing points and personnel, and restricting their maneuverability; 
-  Controlling and holding designated areas of responsibility; 
-  Maintaining weapons, monitoring ammunition expenditure, and quickly clearing malfunctions; 
-  The ability to promptly change firing positions and work as part of a team with other soldiers. 
From basic skills to full control of the weapon
The "Azov" brigade has a clear training system in place. First, every recruit completes an intensive basic combat training course. During the BCT course, the recruit develops physical endurance, tactical medicine skills, teamwork, and movement in combat conditions.
After BCT, the soldier undergoes a specialized stage. "Azov" combat instructors teach recruits to operate both conventional weapons and modern Western machine guns. The recruit practices firing from any position. Training concludes with tactical coordination as part of a squad, where teamwork and position coverage are honed to automaticity.
How can one join?
To become a machine gunner in the 12th Special Forces Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine, "Azov," you need to fill out an application on the azov.org.ua website or visit the nearest recruiting center. Recruiters will answer all questions, help with the Military Medical Commission, and guide applicants through every stage of the paperwork.
You can join the "Azov" brigade either through mobilization or under a contract. And if a candidate is already serving in the Defense Forces, recruiters will explain how to arrange a transfer from the Armed Forces of Ukraine to the National Guard of Ukraine, as well as from other structures.

Hungary plans to introduce wealth tax from 2027
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:24:52 CST
23:24:52 KST

BUDAPEST, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar announced Tuesday that the government plans to introduce a wealth tax from Jan. 1, 2027.
The tax will be 1 percent on wealth exceeding 1 billion Hungarian forints (3.1 million U.S. dollars) and 1.5 percent on wealth exceeding 100 billion forints (310 million dollars), Magyar said in a Facebook video.
It will cover property, investments and company stakes, including assets held abroad or through asset-management structures, he added. Debts will be deductible from the tax base, while property and vehicle taxes can be credited against the liability.
The first annual self-assessed payment will be due by Aug. 31, 2027, based on assets held at the end of 2026, Magyar said.
The proposed measure will undergo broad public consultation before being adopted. ■

Three of the vessels were under UK or EU sanctions. One received its cargo through a ship-to-ship transfer in South Korean waters, a method that can make a shipment’s origin harder to trace.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Finland-based think tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), told The Guardian that the shipments “undermine” Western sanctions and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.
The shipments do not appear to violate South Korean law, the report says, as Seoul’s sanctions on Russia primarily focus on export controls covering goods such as industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
However, the shipments also cast doubt on Seoul’s stance on the war in Ukraine, particularly as Seoul has publicly supported Kyiv while stopping short of providing lethal weapons.
South Korea has supplied Ukraine with humanitarian aid and non-lethal military equipment and pledged $2.3 billion in support in 2023, largely through loans.
At the same time, Seoul has sought to preserve its economic ties with Moscow and has ruled out directly providing weapons to Ukraine.
Fresh Intelligence Signals Massive Russian Strike Ahead, Zelensky Says
Fuel flows to Russia surge
The Guardian found that the sanctioned tanker Layla made two voyages from Ulsan to Vladivostok, carrying a combined 57,000 tons of diesel. On one voyage, it declared Vladivostok as its destination, while on another it listed Japan.
Another sanctioned tanker, the Russian-flagged Astoria, loaded nearly 11,000 tons of fuel at Ulsan before sailing to Vladivostok. The vessel is also under Australian sanctions.
The third sanctioned vessel, the Chongchon, did not enter a South Korean port. Instead, it received around 26,000 tons of fuel from the unsanctioned tanker Celeste I during a ship-to-ship transfer off Yeosu before heading toward Vladivostok.
The findings echoed a report from Reuters in early July, which said Russia sought jet fuel from Japan’s Chiba port to Russia via South Korea, though it’s unclear whether the operations relate to the latest findings presented by The Guardian.
In the rumored plans, the cargo was expected to arrive in Russia in the first half of July after a likely ship-to-ship transfer off Yeosu, South Korea. Its final destination remained unclear.
The reported route would mirror a similar shipment in 2022, when around 22,000 barrels of jet fuel were transported from Chiba to Russia’s Far Eastern port of Vladivostok via Yeosu.
South Korea declined to comment, while the Japanese and Russian ministries did not respond.
The owners and managers of the four tankers contacted by The Guardian did not respond to requests for comment.
Russia has faced growing fuel shortages after Ukrainian drone strikes disrupted its refinery network. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), Russian refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than two decades, while diesel production was down nearly 30% from a year earlier.
By July, Ukraine’s General Staff claimed to have knocked 43% of Russia’s refinery capacity offline.
According to The Guardian, Kpler data analyzed by CREA showed that Russia imported 368,000 tons of oil products by sea in August, more than seven times the previous month. However, the figure appears to be higher than the 172,000 tonnes listed by CREA in its August report.
The outlet also said South Korea accounted for 112,000 tons, or about 31% of Russia’s overall imports, second only to India, while CREA’s publication noted that Egypt, not South Korea, followed India in terms of volume.
Kyiv Post has reached out to CREA for clarification.
The increase began in July, around the time South Korean President Lee Jae Myung pledged $100 million for Ukraine’s reconstruction at a NATO summit in Turkey.
Diplomatic rift between Kyiv and Seoul
The fuel shipments come as relations between Seoul and Kyiv face a separate diplomatic dispute over two North Korean soldiers captured by Ukrainian forces.
The soldiers were captured in January 2025 while fighting alongside Moscow forces in Russia’s Kursk region and were reportedly transferred to South Korea in September 2026.
President Volodymyr Zelensky publicly disclosed the transfer during his address to the United Nations General Assembly in September, but South Korea says the transfer had been agreed to remain confidential to protect the soldiers and their families in North Korea.
Seoul subsequently demanded an explanation and apology from Kyiv.
South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said Tuesday that Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had apologized in messages exchanged over the incident, but that the apology did not meet Seoul’s expectations.
Cho added Seoul was considering several responses, including recalling its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Hee-chang.
Ukraine has described the dispute as a diplomatic misunderstanding. Zelensky’s office said Seoul had been informed of the president’s UN speech in advance and that the address did not disclose identifying information about the soldiers.
Cho said the soldiers’ safety, and that of their relatives in North Korea, had been the primary reason for the confidentiality agreement. He also suggested, while stressing that it was his personal interpretation, that Zelensky may have wanted to demonstrate at the UN that Ukraine had acted appropriately as a liberal democracy.

Lithuania takes further step towards lifting nuclear weapons ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:23:52 UTC
23:23:52 KST

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Lithuania’s move, alongside broader plans to expand US and NATO military infrastructure in the region, risked further escalating tensions.
Lithuania has taken a step towards removing a constitutional ban on nuclear weapons from its territory, bringing the Baltic state closer to the legal position of its neighbours as European allies debate how to strengthen NATO’s deterrence in the face of Russia.
The Lithuanian parliament, the Seimas, voted 106-18, with six abstentions, on Tuesday to advance a constitutional amendment removing a provision that bars weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases from Lithuanian territory.
The change still requires a second vote after a constitutionally mandated three-month waiting period. At least 94 of the Seimas’ 141 members must back it on both occasions. The final vote is expected on January 12.
“This constitutional amendment would enable Lithuania’s armed forces to participate fully in the planning and exercises of all of NATO’s deterrence measures,” said Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen, leader of the Liberal Movement parliamentary group.
Currently, Article 137 of the Lithuanian Constitution stipulates that weapons of mass destruction and military bases of foreign states may not be located in Lithuania, which borders Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave. This means that under current laws, allied aircraft or ships carrying nuclear weapons could not enter Lithuanian territory for deterrence purposes.
Added urgency in Lithuania's case
Supporters of the amendment argue that the constitutional provision has become a legal obstacle to Lithuania’s full participation in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements and leaves the country at a disadvantage compared with other NATO allies.
“Our neighbouring countries, such as Latvia, Estonia and Poland, have no such restrictions either,” Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the Seimas Foreign Affairs Committee, said during a parliamentary session in September. “We cannot be less protected than other NATO countries. We must send a signal that Lithuania is a full part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence.”
NATO describes nuclear deterrence as part of its collective defence, alongside conventional and missile-defence capabilities. The Alliance also says its nuclear policy remains consistent with its commitments to arms control, disarmament and non-proliferation.
For Lithuania, the issue has taken on added urgency. “NATO deterrence, including nuclear deterrence, is part of collective defence,” Motuzas said, adding that Russia has rapidly modernised its nuclear arsenal in recent years and deployed nuclear weapons close to Lithuania — in Kaliningrad and Belarus.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Lithuania’s move, alongside broader plans to expand US and NATO military infrastructure in the region, risked further escalating tensions, Reuters reported.
The warnings come as Russia has stepped up its nuclear rhetoric towards NATO. Moscow recently threatened nuclear retaliation in the event of what it described as attempts to isolate its Kaliningrad exclave, which borders Lithuania and Poland.
Finland has already made the move
Lithuania is not acting in isolation.
Finland, which joined NATO in 2023 after decades of military non-alignment, removed its own statutory prohibition on nuclear weapons earlier this year, citing the need to ensure that Finnish law did not restrict the country’s ability to fulfil its obligations as a NATO ally.
In June, the Finnish parliament approved amendments to the Nuclear Energy Act repealing the country’s ban on nuclear explosives. The legislation entered into force on July 1.
“This historic reform strengthens the security of Finland and of NATO as a whole,” Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said on X.
Helsinki has stressed, however, that the change does not mean Finland intends to acquire or host nuclear weapons, and that NATO has no plans to station them there.
Finland has since joined a French-led initiative aimed at strengthening European security through closer cooperation on nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron has proposed what Paris calls “forward deterrence” — closer cooperation with European allies around France’s independent nuclear capabilities.
The United Kingdom, Germany, Poland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, Denmark, and Norway have already signed up to France's initiative.

Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says some suppliers cannot build weapons ordered, and drops contracts to free $346 million for front
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:23:16 UTC
23:23:16 KST

Ukraine is canceling part of its planned military purchases and moving the money to other priorities. Ukraine's Defense Ministry has announced that it, together with the General Staff and the Logistics Forces Command, will free about $346 million by terminating some weapons contracts and dropping some planned purchases.
What the army planned to buy in 2024 and 2025 may no longer be suitable for the front, the ministry noted, because technology and tactics change quickly. The review comes four days after the Ukrainian government drew about $1.1 billion from the defense reserve to pay soldiers in October amid a looming economic crisis.
The ministry gives five reasons for the review: some weapons no longer match combat tasks, certain suppliers cannot build the planned volume, certain models have not been codified, partners already cover some needs, and cheaper means can perform specific jobs in larger numbers.
"For us, there is one criterion: does the item work for results in combat today. Every hryvnia released from irrelevant contracts must reach the troops as the weapons needed right now and in the right place," Col. Yurii Pohribnyi, commander of the Logistics Forces, says.
The procurement agency calls each producer
The General Staff set the final list of purchases for review, and the ministry forwarded the documents to the Defense Procurement Agency to implement the decision. For specific items, delivery volumes were adjusted rather than canceled, which the contracts allow when needs change.
Affected producers have been informed, and the agency is discussing each item with suppliers based on the status and payments of each contract. Artem Romaniuk, acting director of the agency, has explained that further steps on each contract will depend on the army's current needs and the contract terms. The list of weapons stays secret for security reasons.
Funds freed up by terminating contracts and canceling planned purchases will be redirected to the urgent needs of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
