Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.

Electric bicycle injuries in Denmark reached their highest level in six years as imports of the vehicles continued to rise.
In 2025, 200 electric bicycle riders were injured in traffic, including 133 who were seriously injured. Eleven riders died, according to Danish Road Directorate figures analyzed by insurance company Alm. Brand.
Electric bicycles can reach higher speeds and usually weigh more than standard bicycles, potentially making injuries more serious, said Mathias Kjær Sigvaldason, Alm. Brand’s accident insurance director.
Denmark imported 98,078 electric bicycles in 2025, up from 40,216 in 2017, Statistics Denmark reported.
Imports of standard bicycles fell from slightly more than 500,000 in 2017 to about 350,000 in 2025. Electric models now represent more than one in four imported bicycles.
The figures cover imports, not consumer sales, for which no combined national data are available.
The Danish Road Safety Council, an organization working to prevent traffic injuries, wants helmets to become mandatory for electric bicycle riders.
It also called for illegal electric bicycles to be removed from cycle paths.
Standard electric bicycles may assist riders up to 25 kilometers per hour and follow ordinary bicycle rules.
Approved speed pedelecs may assist riders up to 45 kilometers per hour. Helmets and lights are legally required when using them.
Most Danes support blocking social media for teenagers during overnight hours
A majority of Danes support requiring social media platforms to block teenagers ages 15 to 17 from viewing content between midnight and 6 a.m., a new survey found.
Voxmeter conducted the poll among 1,034 representative Danish adults for Digitalt Ansvar, an organization promoting responsible use of digital technology.
A total of 62.3 percent agreed or strongly agreed with an overnight block. Another 15.9 percent were neutral, while 17.4 percent disagreed or strongly disagreed.
The European Union’s proposed Kids Act includes an overnight block for users ages 13 and 14.
Digitalt Ansvar wants the measure expanded to include teenagers through age 17.
Director Ask Hesby Holm said nighttime social media use harms sleep and can leave students unprepared for school.
Aarhus University research found that more children arrive at school tired and that tiredness is linked to poorer academic results.
Previous studies reviewed by the researchers associated screen use, particularly before bedtime, with later, shorter and lower-quality sleep.
Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said action was needed but questioned whether a complete ban was the right solution.
“Social media should not be allowed to take our night’s sleep,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.

RITZAU
Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.
Source: Ritzau
G7 releases oil reserves – could it bring down Denmark’s record-high diesel prices?
Diesel prices in Denmark have climbed to record levels. Now the G7 countries are releasing up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves in an attempt to ease pressure on global energy markets.
Danish motorists could see some relief from record-high diesel prices after the G7 countries agreed to release emergency fuel reserves.
The move was announced Friday following a meeting of G7 leaders and will see up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil released over the next four months.
The release will be coordinated through the International Energy Agency and is intended to increase supply and help stabilise energy prices.
For Denmark, the move could take some of the pressure off diesel prices, according to Jens Nærvig Pedersen, senior commodities analyst at Danske Bank.
But motorists should not expect prices to return to normal immediately.
“It is not the grand solution that can cause prices to fall again,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“It does not solve the supply crisis in the oil market, which is primarily due to the conflict in the Middle East.”
Diesel has hit a Danish record
The price of diesel at Danish filling stations reached a record DKK 19.19 per litre in September.
The additional supplies from G7 reserves could help cushion the market, Pedersen said, but they cannot fully replace the supplies currently missing from the Middle East.
“For us to get lower and more normal prices again, a solution must be found to the current supply crisis,” he said.
The G7 announcement has already had an impact on international energy markets, with oil prices beginning to fall following the decision.
Why is the G7 releasing its reserves?
The decision follows mounting concern about global fuel supplies and sharply rising prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
It also comes after US President Donald Trump raised the possibility of stopping US diesel exports to Europe.
Europe is heavily dependent on imported diesel, making any restriction on US exports potentially significant for European supplies and prices.
Following the G7 agreement, Trump said Friday that he would not impose a diesel export ban.
The G7 countries have also agreed not to introduce restrictions on energy exports between member countries.
What happens to Danish fuel prices now?
The release of emergency reserves increases the amount of oil and diesel available on the market and could therefore put downward pressure on prices.
But the underlying problem remains the shortage of supply caused by the conflict in the Middle East.
That means Danish motorists could see some relief at the pump without necessarily seeing a return to the prices that prevailed before the current energy crisis.
The G7 consists of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Danish online banking fraud cases fall 51 percent from 2023 peak
Reported online banking fraud in Denmark has fallen sharply as banks improve detection and customers become more aware of scams.
Banks registered 2,571 cases during the first half of 2026, according to Finans Danmark, the main association representing Danish banks.
That was 51 percent fewer than during the first half of 2023, when reported online banking fraud reached its highest level.
Scammers attempted to steal 74.7 million DKK during the first six months of 2026. Actual losses totaled 38.1 million DKK, almost 16 percent less than during the previous six months.
More than half of the reported cases caused no financial loss.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, linked the decline to stronger fraud detection and greater public awareness.
He said banks had become better at identifying suspicious transactions and limiting the amount customers could transfer.
More than half of the cases involved contact fraud. In these scams, criminals call or otherwise contact victims while pretending to represent a bank, the police or another authority.
Consumers should remain alert when callers pressure them to act quickly, said Malene Gøttge Rasmussen.
“If you are just the slightest bit skeptical, hang up,” she said. “Better once too often.”

Legislation for departure centers outside the EU is now in place, says Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov
European Union countries will adopt legislation Thursday allowing the creation of departure centers outside Europe, Danish Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov said.
“Europe must strengthen the external borders,” Bødskov of the Social Democrats said before an EU ministerial meeting in Luxembourg.
The centers would hold rejected asylum seekers sent from Europe while authorities arrange their return. Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece are seeking agreements with non-EU countries to begin transfers next year.

EU ministers will also discuss a sudden arrival of migrants in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner recently proposed measures including closer cooperation with neighboring countries, improved monitoring and stronger action against human smugglers.
The plan would also strengthen deportations and allow visa restrictions or economic pressure against countries refusing to accept the return of their citizens. Bødskov said departure centers could support that effort.
More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.

Danish prosecutors are seeking a prison sentence and temporary nightlife ban for a 31-year-old Danish man accused of punching a 32-year-old Swedish man who died three days later.

The victim fell and suffered a ruptured artery. He died on July 3.
The defendant is charged under Section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers less serious violence. Prosecutors also cited Section 247 because he has previous convictions for crimes endangering others, including attempted murder.
That provision can increase a sentence by up to half.
A prosecutor previously said the Danish man could face eight to 10 months in prison. The indictment does not specify the requested sentence.
The nightlife ban would prevent him from entering bars and designated nightlife areas between midnight and 5 a.m. for a set period.
The trial begins October 7 at Copenhagen City Court. The defendant has been held since early July and denies guilt. His identity is protected by a court order.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.
Danish jewelry company Pandora is expanding production beyond Thailand for the first time in decades with a new facility in Ho Chi Minh City.
The factory opens Thursday following an investment of just under 1 billion DKK. Once fully operational, it is expected to employ 7,000 people and increase Pandora’s current production capacity by 50 percent.
The facility will eventually be able to produce 60 million pieces of jewelry annually, although production will be increased gradually as demand grows. Around 700 of the potential 7,000 positions have initially been filled.
Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier said the company chose Vietnam partly to reduce its dependence on a single production market.
“The reason why we are looking toward markets other than Thailand is that we want to create greater resilience and flexibility and avoid being dependent on a single market,” she said.
She added that Vietnam, like Thailand, has a strong tradition of jewelry manufacturing, giving Pandora access to workers with relevant skills.
Pandora makes its jewelry by hand, making access to employees who can be trained to meet the company’s craftsmanship standards important, de Pablos-Barbier said.
“We have not built the factory with a view to the next quarter, but instead with a view to the next decade,” she said.
The company expects to add employees and equipment as demand increases.
De Pablos-Barbier said she particularly expects future growth from consumers in the U.S. and Asia. The U.S. is currently Pandora’s largest individual market, while Asia is among its fastest-growing markets.
A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.

Danish consumer group files complaint over Red Bull advertising on influencer’s platforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:00:57 UTC
23:00:57 KST

Forbrugerrådet Tænk has asked Denmark’s Consumer Ombudsman to investigate whether Red Bull’s advertising through influencer Rasmus Søndergaard violates marketing law.
The Danish Consumer Council, an independent consumer organization, filed complaints against Red Bull Denmark, Søndergaard’s company and two marketing agencies.
Søndergaard publishes content on Twitch, YouTube and TikTok.
Danish law prohibits marketing energy drinks to consumers under 18 because the products are considered unsuitable for children and teenagers.
Forbrugerrådet Tænk described the Red Bull campaign on Søndergaard’s platforms as the most serious suspected violation of the Marketing Practices Act it had seen.
The organization said Red Bull products appeared frequently in his videos and argued that many viewers were younger than 18.
Miriam Michaelsen, chair of Denmark’s Media Council for Children and Young People, said Danish minors widely use the platforms carrying Søndergaard’s content.
Søndergaard rejected the complaint.
“I make content for adults, and children should not encounter advertisements that are not for them,” he said. “I completely disagree with the complaint, but we are listening, because we must protect the youngest.”
Søndergaard and Red Bull began a formal partnership in 2023.
The complaints also cover DayZeroAgency, which represents Søndergaard, and Ultra, which manages marketing and events for Red Bull.
Red Bull Denmark had not provided a comment.
Danish government proposes prison unit at Kærshovedgård departure center for convicted residents
Denmark’s government wants to build a prison unit at Kærshovedgård for departure center residents who receive prison sentences.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen announced the proposal Tuesday during her speech opening the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The unit could hold residents convicted of repeatedly violating requirements to report to authorities.
“Those residents who are sentenced to prison must be able to serve their sentence behind lock and key in a prison unit located in connection with Kærshovedgård,” Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said.
Kærshovedgård houses foreign nationals who have been ordered to leave Denmark or whose asylum applications were rejected but who cannot or will not return to their countries of origin.
Some say they would face persecution or torture. In other cases, their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities on returns.
Frederiksen said residents had caused problems for people living near the center, including theft, drug dealing and dangerous driving.
Authorities have previously introduced stricter reporting duties, removed some residents’ driving licenses and established electronic ankle monitoring.
The Danish People’s Party and others have called for all residents to be confined at the center.
The government rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving criminal sentences cannot legally be detained under international agreements.
The planned locked unit would apply only to residents convicted of crimes and sentenced to prison.

Large search bill alerted Danish authorities to breach of 8.8 million CPR records
An unusually large invoice led Danish authorities to discover that unauthorized people had accessed personal records on 8.8 million people, an official said Tuesday.
A small Danish company had legal access to search the national CPR register. Each search carries a fee, and extensive activity produced a large bill.
“There is a very large amount being invoiced, which makes one aware that there has been a lot of activity,” said Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization.
Unauthorized users abused the company’s access for about 10 days in September.
Authorities have not identified the company.
The accessed information consisted mainly of names and addresses, Leihardt said. The CPR system is Denmark’s national register of personal information.
Authorities do not yet know who was responsible or how the company’s access was compromised.
“It is too early to say at this point who is behind it and what method has been used,” said Henriette Erbs of NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit.
She said cases of this type often involve cross-border crime.
Laila Reenberg, director of Denmark’s Agency for Public Security, said digital fraud was an obvious possible motive.
However, she said authorities did not yet know who collected the data or how they intended to use it.

Residents with a specific suspicion that their CPR number is being used fraudulently can receive help creating a credit warning.
A credit warning alerts companies to conduct additional identity checks before approving loans or credit, making financial identity theft more difficult.
Authorities detected irregular activity in the CPR system on October 2.

The records cover living and deceased people, as well as those who have moved abroad.

More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.

This year’s Danish Christmas seal features 46 children holding hands in a design focused on friendship and community.

A low-pressure system approaching from the southwest will bring more typical autumn weather during the second half of the week.
Monday will begin with some sunshine in eastern Denmark, while most other areas will remain cloudy.
Light rain is possible in Jutland, and temperatures will reach between 15 and 19 degrees Celsius. The highest temperatures are expected locally on Funen or Zealand.
Winds will be moderate to strong from the southwest. Coastal areas near the Skagerrak could experience gales Monday afternoon.
Skies will clear overnight into Tuesday, bringing dry conditions. Temperatures could fall to eight degrees in some areas, though most places will remain between 12 and 15 degrees.
Tuesday will be dry with periods of sunshine.
A low-pressure system will approach from the North Sea during Tuesday evening and Wednesday, bringing rain and later showers.
Conditions remain uncertain through Friday. Temperatures are expected to fall gradually, reaching between 10 and 15 degrees Thursday and Friday.
Strong winds are also possible along some coastal areas.
Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.
Elk dies after collision with car on motorway north of Copenhagen
An elk died after being struck by a car on the Helsingør Motorway near Nivå on Monday morning, North Zealand Police said.
A 36-year-old woman was driving north in the inside lane when the animal suddenly appeared a few meters ahead of her, according to her statement to police.
The collision occurred at 6:10 a.m. between the Kokkedal and Humlebæk exits.
The woman was apparently uninjured. The car’s windshield and rear window were shattered, while its roof and hood were damaged.
The elk was found dead about 100 meters from the vehicle.
Denmark has no naturally occurring wild elk population. However, Swedish elk were introduced to Lille Vildmose in Himmerland beginning in 2015. That population had grown to about 20 animals by 2020.
Authorities also plan to release elk into Gribskov National Nature Park in North Zealand this year.
Wild elk are occasionally seen elsewhere in Denmark. The animals can swim across the Øresund between Sweden and Zealand.
In mid-September, a farm owner near Hundested reported that a roaming elk had damaged a fence before disappearing toward Ullerup Forest.
Morten Elmeros, a senior adviser at Aarhus University’s Department of Ecoscience, previously said that animal had probably swum from Sweden.
Such crossings occur about once every 10 years, he said.
Electric bicycle injuries reach six-year high as imports approach 100,000 in Denmark
Electric bicycle injuries in Denmark reached their highest level in six years as imports of the vehicles continued to rise.
In 2025, 200 electric bicycle riders were injured in traffic, including 133 who were seriously injured. Eleven riders died, according to Danish Road Directorate figures analyzed by insurance company Alm. Brand.
Electric bicycles can reach higher speeds and usually weigh more than standard bicycles, potentially making injuries more serious, said Mathias Kjær Sigvaldason, Alm. Brand’s accident insurance director.
Denmark imported 98,078 electric bicycles in 2025, up from 40,216 in 2017, Statistics Denmark reported.
Imports of standard bicycles fell from slightly more than 500,000 in 2017 to about 350,000 in 2025. Electric models now represent more than one in four imported bicycles.
The figures cover imports, not consumer sales, for which no combined national data are available.
The Danish Road Safety Council, an organization working to prevent traffic injuries, wants helmets to become mandatory for electric bicycle riders.
It also called for illegal electric bicycles to be removed from cycle paths.
Standard electric bicycles may assist riders up to 25 kilometers per hour and follow ordinary bicycle rules.
Approved speed pedelecs may assist riders up to 45 kilometers per hour. Helmets and lights are legally required when using them.
Most Danes support blocking social media for teenagers during overnight hours
A majority of Danes support requiring social media platforms to block teenagers ages 15 to 17 from viewing content between midnight and 6 a.m., a new survey found.
Voxmeter conducted the poll among 1,034 representative Danish adults for Digitalt Ansvar, an organization promoting responsible use of digital technology.
A total of 62.3 percent agreed or strongly agreed with an overnight block. Another 15.9 percent were neutral, while 17.4 percent disagreed or strongly disagreed.
The European Union’s proposed Kids Act includes an overnight block for users ages 13 and 14.
Digitalt Ansvar wants the measure expanded to include teenagers through age 17.
Director Ask Hesby Holm said nighttime social media use harms sleep and can leave students unprepared for school.
Aarhus University research found that more children arrive at school tired and that tiredness is linked to poorer academic results.
Previous studies reviewed by the researchers associated screen use, particularly before bedtime, with later, shorter and lower-quality sleep.
Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said action was needed but questioned whether a complete ban was the right solution.
“Social media should not be allowed to take our night’s sleep,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.
Danish government proposes 680 million DKK four-year plan for dementia care
Denmark’s government wants to allocate 680 million DKK over four years to improve support for people with dementia and their relatives.
The funding will be included in next year’s proposed Finance Act, Economic and Interior Minister Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party said.
The government has not completed the plan’s details. It will consider assigning permanent dementia coordinators to more people and providing additional training for care workers.
“What we are looking into is, of course, that we must provide something for the person with dementia, but also for the relative,” Dyhr said.
More than 100,000 Danes older than 65 have been diagnosed with dementia. That number is expected to increase as the elderly population grows.
About 400,000 people are relatives of someone with dementia.
Dyhr said the plan should create safer and more dementia-friendly environments, including at nursing homes, while providing greater support to families.
The previous dementia action plan expired in 2025. Its goals included assessing more people for dementia and halving the use of antipsychotic medication among those diagnosed.
The funding is part of a wider elderly care package.
The government will also allocate 30 million DKK in 2027 to expand a companion service helping older people with visual impairments leave their homes.
The Danish Association of the Blind estimates that about 1,000 people could qualify.

Denmark earned a 1-0 away victory over Wales in the Nations League on Sunday after Rasmus Højlund scored a second-half penalty.
The result gives Denmark six points from four group matches. Wales has three points and a worse head-to-head record against Denmark.

Greenland municipality imposes temporary alcohol ban
The Greenlandic government, Naalakkersuisut, has introduced a temporary ban on the sale and serving of alcohol in the southern Greenlandic municipality of Kujalleq.
Naalakkersuisut writes this on Friday, when the ban took effect, in a press release.
The ban comes following a request from the municipal council in Kujalleq.
– The purpose of the temporary closure of alcohol sales and serving is to eliminate the threat to children’s welfare and the safety of the population.
– Furthermore, Kommune Kujalleq has expressed concern and insecurity among the municipality’s population in recent times as a result of the fatal incidents that are a direct consequence of alcoholic beverages, the press release states.
It is not specified further which alcohol-related incidents have taken place in the municipality.
Malene Vahl Rasmussen, who is mayor of Kujalleq, confirms in a post on Facebook that she has asked Naalakkersuisut to temporarily halt the sale of alcohol in the municipality.
– Based on the negative consequences that alcohol consumption has on our surroundings, we can no longer defend the way we use alcohol, she writes.
In a press release, according to the Greenlandic media outlet Sermitsiaq, she elaborates further.
– We can no longer stand passively by and watch the negative consequences that alcohol consumption has on our surroundings, and merely wait for another serious incident to happen in our society, the mayor writes according to the media outlet.
The ban on the sale and serving of alcohol will last until the executive order is repealed, it is stated.
Thus, it is not clear how long the ban will remain in effect.
It is not the first time that an alcohol ban has been introduced in parts of Greenland.
At the beginning of the coronavirus pandemic, a ban was introduced for a period on the serving of alcohol with an alcohol percentage above 2.25 percent in Nuuk, Kapisillit, and Qeqertarsuatsiaat.
At that time, it happened with the justification that they wanted to protect children who were at home during the pandemic.

Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.
Source: Ritzau
G7 releases oil reserves – could it bring down Denmark’s record-high diesel prices?
Diesel prices in Denmark have climbed to record levels. Now the G7 countries are releasing up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves in an attempt to ease pressure on global energy markets.
Danish motorists could see some relief from record-high diesel prices after the G7 countries agreed to release emergency fuel reserves.
The move was announced Friday following a meeting of G7 leaders and will see up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil released over the next four months.
The release will be coordinated through the International Energy Agency and is intended to increase supply and help stabilise energy prices.
For Denmark, the move could take some of the pressure off diesel prices, according to Jens Nærvig Pedersen, senior commodities analyst at Danske Bank.
But motorists should not expect prices to return to normal immediately.
“It is not the grand solution that can cause prices to fall again,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“It does not solve the supply crisis in the oil market, which is primarily due to the conflict in the Middle East.”
Diesel has hit a Danish record
The price of diesel at Danish filling stations reached a record DKK 19.19 per litre in September.
The additional supplies from G7 reserves could help cushion the market, Pedersen said, but they cannot fully replace the supplies currently missing from the Middle East.
“For us to get lower and more normal prices again, a solution must be found to the current supply crisis,” he said.
The G7 announcement has already had an impact on international energy markets, with oil prices beginning to fall following the decision.
Why is the G7 releasing its reserves?
The decision follows mounting concern about global fuel supplies and sharply rising prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
It also comes after US President Donald Trump raised the possibility of stopping US diesel exports to Europe.
Europe is heavily dependent on imported diesel, making any restriction on US exports potentially significant for European supplies and prices.
Following the G7 agreement, Trump said Friday that he would not impose a diesel export ban.
The G7 countries have also agreed not to introduce restrictions on energy exports between member countries.
What happens to Danish fuel prices now?
The release of emergency reserves increases the amount of oil and diesel available on the market and could therefore put downward pressure on prices.
But the underlying problem remains the shortage of supply caused by the conflict in the Middle East.
That means Danish motorists could see some relief at the pump without necessarily seeing a return to the prices that prevailed before the current energy crisis.
The G7 consists of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

World Cup assault suspect convicted in separate case
Next week, a 31-year-old man is to appear in court in a case concerning violence against a Swedish man, who later died, at a big-screen event at Islands Brygge.
However, that is not the only case of violence the 31-year-old is involved in.
On Friday, at the Court in Svendborg, he was sentenced to three months of unconditional imprisonment for violence against another inmate in Nyborg State Prison in 2022.
B.T. and TV 2 report this.
In the case, two men of similar age have also been convicted. They have likewise received three months in prison, writes B.T.
The three men were charged with having assaulted an inmate in the prison with numerous punches and kicks to the face.
The victim suffered a concussion and broke both his nose and a rib, according to the indictment.
The three men were charged under the severe violence section, but were only found guilty under the mild violence provision – section 244.
It is also under this section that the 31-year-old man is charged when he appears in court next week in the case from Islands Brygge.
In that case, he is charged with having struck a 32-year-old Swedish man with a powerful punch.
The Swede died three days later.
The violence took place at a big-screen event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June at around 20:45. A screening of the football World Cup was held here.
According to the case’s indictment, the 31-year-old man at one point stood up on a bench, from where he, with a powerful overhand throw, threw two beer cans in the direction of a group of people – including the 32-year-old Swede.
Immediately after, the 31-year-old man dealt the Swede the powerful blow.
The blow hit the Swede on the left side of the head/neck, after which he fell to the ground.
Because of the blow, the Swede suffered, among other things, a rupture of the artery, which meant that the man later died.
In the case, charges have also been brought under section 247 of the penal code, which pertains to the 31-year-old man having previously been convicted of crimes against the person. Among other things, he has a conviction for attempted murder.
If one is convicted under section 247, the sentence can be increased by up to half.
A prosecutor in the case has previously stated that the man charged with violence faces between eight and ten months in prison.

Lidl to invest more than 100 million DKK renovating all Danish stores
Lidl plans to renovate all its supermarkets in Denmark under a new store concept, investing more than 100 million DKK over the coming business years.
The German-owned supermarket chain said the redesign would improve the use of space, create a consistent appearance and make shopping easier.
Changes will include allocating more space for products on shelves.
Lidl has tested the concept through renovations at several locations. The first store to open after the official introduction of the concept began operating in Holbæk on September 27.
More renovated stores are expected to open in the coming months.
“The goal is to have all stores in Lidl Denmark renovated within the next few years,” said Mads T. Nielsen, Lidl’s development, property and sales director.
He said customers had responded positively to the test stores and newly built locations using the same design.
Individual supermarkets will close completely while renovation work is underway.
Lidl has more than 170 stores across Denmark and expects the full renovation program to take between two and four years.
The chain also plans to continue opening locations as it works toward having more than 200 supermarkets in Denmark.
Lidl opened its first Danish store in 2005.
Suspected female wolf pup killed in traffic near Karup and sent for examination
A suspected female wolf pup has been killed in traffic on Hessellundvej near Karup, Danish authorities said Friday.
The Agency for Green Land Restructuring and Water Environment confirmed the incident to regional broadcaster TV Midtvest.
The Danish Nature Agency, which manages state-owned natural areas and wildlife matters, collected the animal Friday morning.
Officials believe it is a wolf and likely a female pup. The animal will be examined at the University of Copenhagen, though the specific purpose of the examination has not been disclosed.
Authorities could not provide further details about the collision Friday afternoon, including whether the driver involved contacted them.
Other wolves killed in traffic have previously been found and examined in Denmark.
Five dead wolves were examined in January, including three that had been struck by vehicles. The results were sent to the Natural History Museum Aarhus, which monitors Denmark’s wolf population and collects documentation.
“Through the autopsies, we gain an important understanding of the wolves’ health and way of life,” research director Kent Olsen said in January.
The examinations can include DNA testing and provide information used for research and wildlife management.
Wolves returned to Denmark in 2012 after being absent from the country for about 200 years.
The wolf is a protected species in Denmark and the country’s only apex predator.
Old systems and extensive personal data make universities vulnerable to hackers, expert says
Universities can be attractive and vulnerable targets for cyberattacks because they store large amounts of personal information and may rely on outdated computer systems, a Danish cybersecurity expert said.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, spoke after the Technical University of Denmark, known as DTU, reported a data breach Friday.
“Universities hold a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen said.
He added that several universities appeared to use older systems that might not meet the level of security expected in 2026.
More than 200,000 current and former DTU users could be affected by the attack, the university said.
Unauthorized people compromised several DTU user profiles to gain access to its database and retrieved “a larger amount” of information.
The exposed data could include CPR numbers, which are Denmark’s personal identification numbers, as well as home addresses and telephone numbers.
DTU has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many users were affected.

Copenhagen Airport records busiest September with 3.2 million passengers
Copenhagen Airport handled 3.2 million passengers in September, its highest total for that month.
The number was four percent higher than in September 2025, the airport said Friday.
“The peak season no longer ends with the summer vacation,” commercial director Peter Krogsgaard said. “In September, we had almost as many travelers as in the summer months.”
About 270,000 passengers traveled between Copenhagen and Norway, making it the largest country market.
Spain followed with 255,000 passengers, while routes to and from the United Kingdom carried 245,000.
London, Stockholm, Oslo, Amsterdam and Paris were the five most popular destinations.
Demand also increased for direct routes between Copenhagen and the United States.
Those flights carried 140,000 passengers, an increase of eight percent from September 2025.
Krogsgaard said both direct traffic and the number of American visitors to Denmark had increased.
Copenhagen Airport is Denmark’s only airport offering direct flights to and from the United States. Some American passengers visit Denmark, while others continue to destinations elsewhere in Europe.
The airport expects about 1.1 million passengers during Denmark’s October school holiday. More than 115,000 travelers are expected on the busiest days.
Spain, Italy and France are the most popular southern European destinations, with about 220,000 passengers expected around the holiday period.
Petrol-only cars fall below half of Denmark’s passenger vehicle fleet
Cars powered only by petrol now account for less than half of Denmark’s passenger vehicle fleet, according to figures from bilstatistik.dk.
Petrol-only cars make up 49.98 percent of registered passenger cars, down from 65 percent at the end of 2020.
The category does not include hybrid or plug-in hybrid vehicles because they use more than one source of power.
Over the same period, electric cars have increased their share of the Danish fleet. They now account for 24.3 percent of passenger cars.
Mobility Denmark, the main association representing Denmark’s automotive industry, said the figures showed how quickly the country’s vehicle fleet was changing.
“Pure petrol cars have for decades been completely dominant on Danish roads. Now they make up less than half of the passenger car fleet,” CEO Mads Rørvig said.
“That says something about how strongly electric cars have moved in a few years,” he added.

The Lego Foundation will invest 200 million DKK over five years in efforts to attract and retain more teachers and educators in Denmark.
The funding expands a partnership with Danske Professionshøjskoler, the association representing Denmark’s six university colleges.

The latest PISA study also showed historically weak results among Danish 15-year-old students.
The foundation’s total support for Danske Professionshøjskoler has now reached 565 million DKK since 2018.
The Lego Foundation is a Danish commercial foundation that owns 25 percent of the Lego Group.
Danish justice minister wants prosecutors barred from wearing religious and political symbols in court
Danish prosecutors should follow the same rules as judges and be barred from wearing visible religious or political symbols during court hearings, Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said.
“Neither Muslim nor other visible religious symbols must be allowed to weaken the public’s confidence that what takes place in Danish courtrooms is objective,” Wammen of the Social Democrats told Danish newspaper Ekstra Bladet.
Since 2009, Denmark’s Administration of Justice Act has prohibited judges and lay judges from wearing religious or political symbols during hearings. The rule does not currently apply to prosecutors.
The debate began after Zahra Sediqi, a prosecutor with the State Prosecutor in Viborg, wrote on LinkedIn that she was proud to be Denmark’s first prosecutor to wear a headscarf.
Dennis Flydtkjær, immigration spokesperson for the Denmark Democrats, said wearing a headscarf did not necessarily make a prosecutor biased. However, he said there should be no doubt about objectivity in court.
The Danish People’s Party has also criticized the different rules for judges and prosecutors.
The Association of Public Prosecutors said it did not understand the attention directed at Sediqi and supported her unconditionally.
The association said she had followed all current rules.
Denmark’s prosecution service confirmed that it has no internal rule preventing employees from wearing a hijab at work.
Sediqi has not commented.
Danish online banking fraud cases fall 51 percent from 2023 peak
Reported online banking fraud in Denmark has fallen sharply as banks improve detection and customers become more aware of scams.
Banks registered 2,571 cases during the first half of 2026, according to Finans Danmark, the main association representing Danish banks.
That was 51 percent fewer than during the first half of 2023, when reported online banking fraud reached its highest level.
Scammers attempted to steal 74.7 million DKK during the first six months of 2026. Actual losses totaled 38.1 million DKK, almost 16 percent less than during the previous six months.
More than half of the reported cases caused no financial loss.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, linked the decline to stronger fraud detection and greater public awareness.
He said banks had become better at identifying suspicious transactions and limiting the amount customers could transfer.
More than half of the cases involved contact fraud. In these scams, criminals call or otherwise contact victims while pretending to represent a bank, the police or another authority.
Consumers should remain alert when callers pressure them to act quickly, said Malene Gøttge Rasmussen.
“If you are just the slightest bit skeptical, hang up,” she said. “Better once too often.”

European Union countries will meet Friday to discuss a coordinated response to rising fuel prices, a European Commission spokesperson said, according to AFP.
The meeting follows pressure from the United States for Europe to help increase diesel supplies and lower prices.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told Fox News he was “very confident” that Europe would cooperate.
“Now is the time for a coordinated release of diesel stocks,” Wright said, citing the coming harvest and winter seasons.
The US government particularly wants France and Germany to release diesel from strategic reserves, AFP reported.
Washington has also threatened to ban diesel exports if European countries do not act, three unnamed sources told Reuters.

However, Trump said Wednesday that such a ban could instead push prices higher.
The average US diesel price has reached $6.39 per gallon, equal to about 42.52 DKK. A gallon is approximately 3.7 liters.
Diesel cost an average of $3.70 per gallon one year ago, according to AFP.

More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.

ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.

Too Russian for the NHL? The tensions behind Ovechkin’s farewell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:00:37 UTC
23:00:37 KST

There will be no doubt as to where the tomb of Alexander the Great II will be, or where he will see out the twilight of his career. But has one of the greatest modern Russian hockey stars been forced from the heady heights of the National Hockey League too soon?
When Alexander Ovechkin appeared in an election promo video for the United Russia party, I questioned his reasoning. I wasn’t alone. An NHL beat reporter posted in a WhatsApp group chat “Ovi’s about to quit Caps.” Of the other 30+ North American sports reporters in there with me, all speculated as to his next move, while also worrying about the backlash. There wasn’t long to wait.
The Ukraine troll farms ignited the fire that burned all the way into US media and Russophobic elements, and reached Washington Capitals owner Ted Leonsis. Leonsis, who also owns the Washington Wizards NBA franchise, refused to buckle to pressure from the US sports press corps, backing his star man to the hilt.
The Greek-origin billionaire has always been protective of Ovechkin and his other Russian players. In 2018, he told a popular English-language sports radio show in Moscow, called Capital Sports, that “we need to judge athletes on their performance and behavior, not color, country and so on.” However, the same cannot be said of the Capitals’ head coach, Spencer Carbery, who appears to have used the furor for his own ends.
“Spence wants a rebuild and he can’t do it with [Ovechkin] on board. He can’t blow up the team while [Ovechkin] is still on the roster,” a Capitals’ source told me on Tuesday morning. In the pre-season, Carbery said that he would play Ovechkin less and was, privately, against extending his contract.
When I questioned whether the political party video played any role in his ‘retirement’, the source said “definitely, but not from the club’s side. But there was a fallout with the coach.”
Igor Nazarenko, of St. Petersburg-based sports outlet Sport Day by Day warned of Ovechkin’s displacement in June after Washington signed American Alex Tuch from the Buffalo Sabres on an eight-year, $86 million contract. The sharpshooting winger’s arrival heralded, Nazarenko predicted, the replacement of the Russian as the on-ice leader.
Additionally, Carbery has focused on youth development, and has spoken about giving talents like Russia’s Ivan Miroshnichenko (22), Belarus’ Ilya Protas (20), and the US’ Ryan Leonard (21) more game time.
Scott MacPherson, former General Manager of Kunlun (now Shanghai) Red Star of the Kontinental Hockey League (KHL) and personal friend of Alexander Ovechkin predicted this would happen last year.
In early-2025, he told Capital Sports that Ovechkin wouldn’t “linger” in the NHL and instead return to his roots in Russia. “Ovi’s got nothing to prove [in the NHL], but he wants to be back in the KHL.”
I asked why. He made his debut at the top of Russian hockey aged 16; now at 41, why bother?
“He’s Russian. He loves his country and he wants to give back to fans. One, two years more in the KHL and it will be memorable.”
Russian sports media is already speculating about who will land him. Dynamo Moscow, his original Russian club, are favorites, while the other two big Moscow clubs, Spartak and CSKA, are already ruled out. SKA St. Petersburg has been mooted as his retirement vehicle, though that has been ruled out by the local media.
A couple of years in the KHL, followed by a career in politics, or sports administration, or even coaching, lies ahead of Ovi. His exit from the NHL was not as simple as stepping aside to let youth have its fling. Neither was it only because he made a video that riled up the anti-Russian trolls, as hockey fans see past politics and want to watch the best perform for them.
Yet it cannot be ruled out that the offer made by his current NHL team, according to MacPherson, of $1.5 million for one-year extension until 2027-28, was beyond insulting. If Russian sports media is to be believed, for two last-hurrah seasons with Dynamo Moscow, he will earn ten times that per year, and put the KHL front and center on the global stage.
In any case, Alexander the Great II is coming home to where his heart is.

People shift their political opinions to match the room in small group chats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:00:22 UTC
23:00:22 KST

When politics comes up in a small online group chat, people may adjust what they say to match the dominant viewpoint of the room, according to new research published in Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans. In two experiments in which participants chatted with AI agents playing coworkers, people randomly placed in conservative-leaning chats expressed more conservative positions than those in liberal-leaning chats, even after accounting for their own politics. The findings suggest that what people say in everyday political conversations does not always mirror what they privately believe.
Much of what we know about online political expression comes from studies of large, public platforms like X or Facebook. In those open spaces, people often tailor what they post because they know a massive, invisible audience might see it. If a topic is too controversial, users can simply stay silent and keep scrolling without anyone noticing. But a lot of daily communication happens in smaller, socially bounded digital spaces, such as neighborhood forums, family group texts, and workplace messaging apps.
In these closed spaces, individuals talk with people they know and expect to interact with again in the future. Because of these ongoing relationships, staying completely silent during a heated discussion can draw unwanted attention. People frequently encounter differing viewpoints in these daily environments. For example, a 2006 study noted that conversations at work are one of the primary ways individuals are exposed to political perspectives that challenge their own.
To manage their relationships, people may feel a need to closely monitor what they say. A 2016 study demonstrated that individuals often act like “political chameleons” in conversations, adjusting the opinions they voice to match whoever they are talking to. A study of Reddit users covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that right-leaning users used more moralized partisan language among political allies than in mixed spaces, while left-leaning users’ language stayed consistently moralized regardless of audience.
The current research was driven by a desire to understand these less-examined digital spaces, building on prior work exploring how the internet warps our sense of consensus. “One starting point was work by Claire Robertson, Kareena Del Rosario, and Jay Van Bavel on how social media can distort perceptions of social norms, including by making more moderate voices less visible,” Cleone Mitsui, a doctoral candidate in the Graduate School of Sustainable System Sciences at Osaka Metropolitan University and the study’s lead author, told PsyPost.
“This made us wonder what happens in small group chats, where people may have ongoing relationships and staying silent can itself be noticeable,” Mitsui continued. “These settings have received less attention than large, publicly visible platforms.”
Studying how this social calibration happens in private group chats is difficult, as it is ethically and practically tricky for researchers to manipulate conversations between actual acquaintances. To get around this, Mitsui and co-author Yuta Kawamura, an associate professor at the university, turned to artificial intelligence. As noted in a 2023 paper, AI agents can be programmed to simulate believable human behaviors, including forming opinions and interacting with others.
In the first study, the researchers recruited 180 American participants and randomly assigned them to either a liberal-leaning or a conservative-leaning group chat. Participants were told to imagine they had just joined a new company and were invited into a casual messaging group with three coworkers. The coworkers were AI agents, which participants were told about in advance, programmed to consistently express either liberal or conservative views. Each chat focused on one topic drawn at random from five: gun ownership, immigration, abortion, vaccine mandates for children, and gender education in elementary schools.
The chat interface was designed to look like a familiar mobile messaging app, complete with typing indicators, delayed thinking pauses, and randomly assigned names and profile pictures. One of the virtual coworkers would share an opinion on a political topic and prompt the participant to weigh in. Participants then engaged in five rounds of open text messages.
Afterward, an AI language model (GPT-5.2) reviewed the entire conversation and rated each participant’s overall expressed political stance on a scale from -2 (very liberal) to +2 (very conservative). The researchers verified this automated scoring, finding that it closely matched human ratings by the first author and produced nearly identical scores when re-tested with a different model, Gemini.
The researchers found that participants shifted their expressed political stance toward the prevailing attitude of the group chat. Those in the conservative-leaning chats expressed positions that were more conservative on average (0.21) compared to those in the liberal-leaning chats (-0.56). Over the five rounds of conversation, neutral positions decreased, and the participants’ text replies became increasingly aligned with the political tone set by their simulated coworkers. Additionally, participants who expressed views against the chat’s political lean reported more irritation and anger, and fewer positive emotions, after the interaction.
To see if this effect held up when accounting for a person’s actual underlying beliefs, the researchers conducted a second study with another 180 American participants. The setup was nearly identical, but this time participants were asked to report their own political ideology on a five-point scale before entering the chat room. They also rated their personal support for all five discussion topics. The AI model that generated the coworkers’ messages was upgraded to a newer version for this second experiment, while the same GPT-5.2 model scored participants’ stances in both studies.
As expected, the participants’ baseline political ideology was a strong predictor of what they said in the chat. However, even after adjusting for these preexisting beliefs, the ideological tilt of the chat environment still predicted how participants expressed themselves. Those assigned to the conservative chat group expressed more conservative stances (an adjusted average of 0.12) than those in the liberal chat group (-0.38). Still, baseline ideology accounted for considerably more of the differences between participants (22% of the variation) compared to just 4% for the chat setting.
“This suggests that what people say in a group chat can reflect the immediate conversational environment as well as their existing political orientation,” the researchers noted. “One implication is that apparent agreement in a conversation may give an incomplete picture of the views people privately hold.”
The effect of the chat environment was smaller than in the first study. The researchers note that this is expected once baseline ideology is accounted for, and that asking participants about their views beforehand may also have prompted them to commit to their positions. Still, the setting continued to shape the direction of what participants said.
“In the second study, participants’ baseline ideology remained a substantial predictor of what they said, alongside the effect of the conversational setting,” Mitsui added. “These are average differences between groups in a brief experiment; they do not tell us how much any particular person’s private beliefs changed.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study measured what participants typed into a chat window, which does not necessarily mean their deeply held political convictions actually changed. The authors suggest that when people soften opposing views in conversation, a group can appear more unified than its members really are, although the study did not measure such perceptions.
“We measured the political positions people expressed during the conversation, so the results do not establish changes in their private beliefs or lasting attitudes,” Mitsui explained. “We also cannot separate the influence of group norms from the persuasive content of the messages, because both varied together.”
This matters because AI chatbots can be persuasive in their own right. Research covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that brief conversations with politically biased chatbots shifted people’s opinions and budget choices toward the chatbot’s bias.
There are also a few things to keep in mind regarding the simulated environment. Participants were informed ahead of time that they were interacting with artificial intelligence. Because they knew the coworkers were not real people, they may have had less reason to worry about long-term social consequences, like making things awkward at a real office. This lack of genuine interpersonal stakes might have made some participants more willing to go along with the group, or on the other hand, it might have made them feel freer to disagree.
“A simulated coworker chat cannot reproduce the history or real-life consequences of conversations with actual colleagues, friends or family,” the researchers cautioned. “Finally, we did not directly compare these chats with public social media, so we cannot conclude that the effect is stronger in small groups.”
In addition, the AI agents in the study expressed their political views quite directly to establish an obvious group norm. The authors note that this explicitness might have tipped some participants off about the study’s aim. In natural everyday group chats, people tend to be more subtle about their partisan views to keep the peace. Future research could explore how people respond to more subtle political cues, and test how these dynamics play out in other types of closed networks, such as family text groups or hobby forums.
The study, “People shift political expression to fit the room in small online group chats: Evidence from AI-simulated chat experiments,” was authored by Cleone Mitsui and Yuta Kawamura.
