Rising electricity needs put Southeast Asia’s energy security at risk: report
The International Energy Agency report says Southeast Asian nations should share electricity and diversify where they get their power
Risks to Southeast Asia’s energy supplies are multiplying faster than nations are coming up with solutions to meet rapidly rising demand for electricity, according to an International Energy Agency report released on Tuesday.
Southeast Asia has a seemingly insatiable appetite for energy, but the region is now in a pinch as energy costs rise, partly due to the Iran war. Fast-growing Southeast Asian economies also need more electricity to power data centres and keep homes and businesses cool.
To boost regional energy security, the report says Southeast Asian nations should share electricity among each other and diversify where they get their power. But countries face multiple hurdles, from territorial conflicts between neighbours to differing types of national energy markets, according to analysts, who warn these barriers may keep the region vulnerable to energy shocks.
“Southeast Asia is one of the world’s most dynamic regions, but its rising needs for energy to power its economic growth face challenges in an increasingly uncertain global energy landscape,” Fatih Birol, the IEA executive director, said in a statement.

Who owns ‘brain rot’?: inside the international legal drama over a beloved meme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:00:16 UTC
23:00:16 KST

One of the most beloved characters in an absurdist genre of online video content has become the center of an international legal battle that could determine where human creativity ends and artificial intelligence begins.
Tung Tung Tung Sahur, also known as Triple T, was created in 2025 by an Indonesian teen who goes by the username Noxa, using OpenAI’s image-generation tool. Based on a kentongan – a type of drum used to wake south-east Asian Muslims for their pre-dawn meal during Ramadan – the character is an anthropomorphized version of the instrument with a broad smile and a vacant stare. He sits under the umbrella of “Italian brain rot” internet videos.
Since his creation, Triple T has become a global sensation: YouTube and TikTok host dozens of videos with hundreds of millions of views starring the character. People dress like Triple T at cosplay conventions and lovingly create fan art and animations of the stick-like creature, and his likeness appears on plushies, perfume and stickers.
The character has generated a great deal of money and stands to create much more – he will soon be joining Fortnite as a skin. But who should benefit from this virality?
That question is at the heart of a lawsuit filed in the US district court’snorthern district of California, where a games company is suing French creative agency Mementum, which represents Noxa, over the right to use Triple T as a character in a popular Roblox game.
Eben Jeda, co-founder of Mementum Lab, said he started the agency with the goal of modernizing economic infrastructure around internet-native works, the creators of which are often completely cut out of any resulting profit.
“Brain rot is one of the first highly visible manifestations of a much larger transformation: internet native creativity can now become global almost instantly, while the people who originate it can remain economically invisible,” he said.
Opponents argue no one person should own a meme whose ultimate value has been amplified by the online collective. Fabian Mosele, a self-described “Italian brain rot expert” who has made several Tung Tung Tung Sahur videos, said they see brain rot as collectively owned.
“There are a ton of creators who made these characters come to life,” Mosele said. “Before, they were really just images. Having been part of making the virality of these characters, to gatekeep it to the original prompter of this character doesn’t seem right.”
What constitutes ‘human authorship’ in the age of generative AI?
Tung Tung Tung Sahur is one of many characters that have emerged as part of the Italian brain rot genre of meme – a universe of strange, AI-generated characters beloved by generation Alpha and younger members of gen Z. These include the likes of Ballerina Cappuccina (a ballet dancer with a coffee cup for a head), Tralalero Tralala (a shark wearing sneakers), and a variety of other intentionally bizarre creations.
Capitalizing on the virality of these mascot-esque characters, video game company Do Big Studios released a game populated by recognizable personae in May 2025 called “Steal a Brainrot”, which quickly became one of the most-played games within Roblox, where users can create minigames.
But in September 2025, Spyder Games LLC and Speedy Simulator Gaming LLC – the owners of Do Big – received a cease and desist letter from Mementum regarding the use of Tung Tung Tung Sahur in the game. Do Big initially pulled the character and attempted to negotiate a resolution with Mementum, but ultimately Spyder and Speedy sued the company instead, stating in a complaint: “Mementum’s claimed rights do not exist. Under established law, copyright protection requires human authorship, and AI-generated material does not qualify.”
Copyright law in the United States applies only to human-made creations – but AI is challenging the interpretation of that rule. A 2025 report from the United States Copyright Office declared that copyright protects “original expression” in work created “by a human author” even if the work also includes AI-generated material, but that it “does not extend to purely AI-generated material, or material where there is insufficient human control over the expressive elements”.
The copyright office’s report does not offer a clear standard for ownership of creations that involve AI: “Whether human contributions to AI-generated outputs are sufficient to constitute authorship must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis.”
Do Big argues that, in the case of Tung Tung Tung Sahur, the level of human intervention in the character’s creation is not sufficient to claim ownership. Court documents filed by Mementum in a separate trademark-related dispute in France show that Tung Tung Tung Sahur was created over the course of 15 minutes using seven prompts before he achieved his final form. The prompts included basic instructions like, “draw a pentungan sahur with a face and legs”, then “human face”, and “no hands, legs like a human, and a human face”.
“We are not claiming in this case that AI-assisted work can never be owned by anybody,” said Aaron Moss, a copyright lawyer representing Do Big through the firm Mitchell Silberberg & Knupp LLP. “In a case where somebody makes real creative choices, there is human authorship that is subject to protection. But it’s our position that sparse prompts – typing in a few words and picking [the image] you like – does not constitute human authorship.”
Italian brain rot, global consequences
The blurry nature of authorship in the age of AI is not the only complicating factor in the case – the global reach of online content also makes enforcement difficult. An Italian brain rot character that was created by a TikTok user in Indonesia and largely popularized in Latin America is being claimed by a French company in a California courthouse. Jeda said that as a French company, Mementum does not “view this question exclusively through an American legal lens”.
Case in point: Mementum issued a takedown request under the EU’s Digital Services Act, requesting the removal of Tung Tung Tung Sahur from Do Big’s Steal a Brainrot game, which was successful. Mementum then countersued in the United States for trademark infringement. The company does not yet hold a trademark for Triple T in the United States, but in some cases trademark infringement can be argued before registration.
“Our client is pursuing a global strategy on all of this,” said Steven Stein, a partner at Greenberg Glusker, the US law firm representing Mementum Lab. “It is less about approaching it from a copyright law standpoint, and more about approaching it from the standpoint of – in this new wild west, where works are created with the involvement of AI, what can you do to make it so they are protectable under intellectual property law?”
How the lawsuit plays out will come down to a complicated, international web of legal dealings surrounding intellectual property laws – one that could have major implications moving forward, said James Grimmelmann, a professor at Cornell Tech and Cornell law school.
“This is the kind of case that could do one of two things: we could get a court decision that tells us, in a concrete setting, what is copyrightable and what isn’t when AI is involved,” he said. “It could also start establishing best practices and widespread norms on how people use AI.”
Such best practices could include better documenting creation processes, including what prompts are used to create characters. The prompt used to create Tung Tung Tung Sahur is at the center of this story – both in the legal case, where documentation of the process was revealed in pre-trial discovery – and online, where speculation over how Triple T was created has repeatedly gone viral.
Adam Aleksic, a content creator who has made multiple videos on the topic, said the frenzy over trying to back-solve the origin of the character reflects the mythological status and quasi-religiosity of brain rot characters.
“There’s this idea of origination when it comes to Tung Tung Tung Sahur – somehow out of the void, some memes are able to emerge into the cultural forefront, into our collective mainstream discourse,” he said.
The collective creation of such characters, which made brain rot popular in the first place, is exactly what makes it difficult to claim an origin for Tung Tung Tung Sahur, legally and culturally. When it comes to Tung Tung Tung Sahur, even speaking the name of the character has now come to inherently reference the absurdity central to brain rot, similar to how “skibidi toilet” became shorthand for “being really online”.
It is perhaps fitting, then, that of all of the Italian brain rot characters, the hero who has most come to represent virality itself has become a lightning rod for this kind of copyright battle.
“That’s the thing about archetypes – they are empty vehicles for you to project your expectations, desires, or narratives on to,” Aleksic said. “Triple T is a tool for you to tell your narrative, broadly, across the entire internet. That’s what memes do – they are a way for us to create our own stories in a time when it feels like our stories are meaningless.”

Chinese team creates ‘lifelike’ hydrogel that changes shape for smart devices
Light-activated hydrogel that can evolve with living tissue may ultimately help make more flexible brain-computer interfaces and robots
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Chinese researchers have developed a “lifelike” shape-changing hydrogel they say could provide a platform for next-generation developments, such as flexible tissue engineering scaffolds, brain-computer interfaces and humanlike robots.
Inspired by living organisms, the team created a light-triggered system called STERS, which uses liquid metal particles to generate slow, self-sustaining chemical reactions that allow a hydrogel to change its structure over time.
Capable of growing and changing alongside living tissues, this adaptive system could inspire next-generation biomedical materials and devices. It could also have broad implications in fields such as regenerative medicine and soft robotics, according to the researchers.
“This novel approach enables programmable, lifelike morphological evolution in hydrogels, spanning microscopic to macroscopic scales, minutes to weeks, and single to multiple transformation cycles,” the team said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Matter on September 4.

Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh held by ICE at Dulles, supporters say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:00:06 UTC
23:00:06 KST

US immigration authorities have detained Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh shortly after he landed at a Virgina airport, an advocacy campaign said.
"On September 24th, 2026, our friend and filmmaker, Arfat Sheikh was unlawfully detained by ICE coming off a plane at Dulles Airport (IAD)," the Support Arfat Sheikh's Release campaign said on Tuesday.
"Sheikh, along with award-winning, celebrated author and filmmaker Tara Dorabji, was en route to an Art as Resistance panel which was scheduled to take place at Busboys and Poets in Washington, DC. Sheikh was surrounded and arrested without a warrant by multiple ICE agents as he stepped off the plane at Dulles, even as he presented his immigration paperwork," the campaign added.
The 42-year-old artist, who resides in Alexandria, Virginia, arrived in the US on a student visa to pursue graduate studies in film at the Georgia State University.
He holds active work and residency authorisation under a pending immigration application.
Saffron Kingdom and Kashmir dispute
Sheikh is being held in the Caroline Detention Center in Bowling Green, Virginia, said his friend and author Azad Essa.
Sheikh is scheduled to appear before an immigration judge on Tuesday for a procedural hearing alongside a bond assessment.
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Department of Homeland Security have not issued an official comment regarding the detention.
Sheikh gained international recognition for his debut feature film, Saffron Kingdom, which screened in more than 100 theaters and was streamed in 175 countries.
The film explores the Kashmir conflict through a family's journey from Srinagar in India-administered Kashmir in the 1990s to US state of Georgia in 2019.
The production received honours including Best Feature Film at the Anatolian International Film Awards, Chicago Filmmakers Award, and Los Angeles Film and Documentary Awards, as well as an Emerging Filmmaker distinction at the Teaneck International Film Festival.
Supporters of Sheikh have launched a GoFundMe Campaign to help cover his legal representation and support his immediate community needs.
Sheikh, who grew up in India-administered Kashmir during the 1990s, told TRT World in a 2024 interview that "the film was born from his desire to reclaim his people's narrative, who have often been negatively depicted by Indian cinema."
"This film is my way of breaking Bollywood's hegemony over our narrative. It's about debunking the lies they have been peddling for years," he told TRT World.
In the interview he recalled traumatic memories of being locked in a room with his family while the Indian military tortured his uncle.
His father, a renowned Kashmiri musician, was murdered while travelling to northern Indian state of Punjab. "His death was reported in newspapers, but each paper had its own version of events. We were not even given his body," he said.
Kashmir is split between India and Pakistan, both of which claim it in full but control only parts. The two countries have fought three wars over the territory since the partition of British India in 1947. China also holds a silver of Kashmir, making Kashmir world's only nuclear tri-junction.
A significant proportion of Muslim Kashmiris favour the right to self-determination as promised by several UN Security Council resolutions, seeking either full independence or accession to Pakistan.
In May 2025, India and Pakistan fought a brief war using missiles, fighter jets, drones and other weapons, which ultimately led to US involvement.
US President Donald Trump helped broker a ceasefire during the military confrontation, an intervention later publicly praised by Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, while India maintained that the truce was reached through direct bilateral military communications and that Trump had played no role in it.

Norwegian princess Märtha Louise and husband sue ex-friends for ‘betrayal of trust’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:59:17 UTC
22:59:17 KST

The Norwegian princess Märtha Louise and her husband, the American businessman Durek Verrett, are suing several former members of their inner circle for defamation over what they described as a “calculated betrayal of trust”.
Court documents filed in Los Angeles on 14 September claim the former friends and colleagues took “private access once afforded to them and weaponised it”. The accused include “former intimate partners, trusted business associates, a family member”.
The documents allege that information including “confidential communications, disputed accusations and claimed insider knowledge” was used against Märtha Louise, Verrett and his company, Ohana, in what the couple describe as a “coordinated series of devastating public attacks”.
The compensation claims total in excess of $80m, the newspaper VG reported.
The legal action comes during a particularly challenging period for the Norwegian royal family. King Harald died in August aged 89, to be succeeded by his son, Haakon, who is Märtha Louise’s brother. Harald’s sister, Princess Astrid, died aged 94, two days after attending his funeral in September.
At the same time, the royal family has been embroiled in several scandals including revelations about Queen Mette-Marit’s friendship with Jeffrey Epstein. Her son Marius Borg Høiby was found guilty of two counts of rape in June. The queen, who has pulmonary fibrosis, underwent a lung transplant in the same month.
Märtha Louise and Verrett have been the subject of multiple headlines in recent years.
In 2023, before marrying Verrett, who describes himself as a sixth-generation shaman, the princess renounced her royal duties to focus on the couple’s alternative medicine business. Last year they starred in a Netflix documentary about their lives, Rebel Royals: An Unlikely Love Story.
The papers, filed to Los Angeles county superior court, state that the case was prompted by a “calculated betrayal of trust” and mention the “recent loss” of the late king. The alleged “incessant misconduct” was said to have started years ago, but “continued and escalated” in 2025 and 2026.
“During that period, plaintiffs experienced significant medical and personal circumstances, including Verrett’s serious kidney failure, dialysis treatment, health deterioration and recent kidney transplant, as well as Princess Märtha Louise’s recent loss of her father,” the papers state.
“Although plaintiffs would ordinarily have preferred to devote this period to their health, family, grief, and recovery, the timing of this filing is governed by applicable legal deadlines. Plaintiffs must proceed at this unfortunate time to preserve their claims and protect their rights arising from defendants’ publications and conduct in 2025 and 2026.”
The lawsuit says the accused people, “far from being distant critics reporting from the outside”, were “at one time in the inner circle of Verrett and Princess Märtha Louise”. It adds: “They had been welcomed into Verrett’s private life, family relationships, communications, client-related affairs and business operations through relationships of intimacy, trust, confidence, and professional responsibility.”
The couple’s US lawyer Richard Roth told VG: “Our clients’ reputations have been judged by the public for years. Now the facts will be tested in a court of law.”
Court documents list two future hearings for the case in December.
The palace and representatives of the couple have been contacted by the Guardian for comment.

Memorial initiative brings October 7 survivors’ stories to stage and screen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:59:09 UTC
22:59:09 KST

A staged reading of Love at the End of the Tunnel, a play about former hostages Aviva and Keith Siegel’s love story and captivity, will be performed at Habima Theatre on October 6 and 7.
It is the first production of the October 7 Global Memorial Project, an international initiative to preserve the memory of the Hamas massacre through theater, film, exhibitions, books, and other cultural projects.
Launched ahead of the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks, the initiative seeks to bring the stories of survivors and hostages to audiences in Israel and abroad, while documenting the events for future generations.
Eytan Schwartz, a public diplomacy and international relations specialist, founded the project after spending 15 years leading international affairs for the Tel Aviv-Jaffa Municipality. Since the outbreak of the war, he has focused on documenting October 7.
The Siegel play, a collaboration between Schwartz and playwright Michal Aharoni, stars Sandra Sade and Moni Moshonov. Performances are planned for the US.
A second production, a one-person play based on former hostage Omer Wenkert’s story, is scheduled to premiere in 2027. Schwartz and Meron Sasson are writing it.
The initiative is also developing an English-language feature film in partnership with Kastina Communications.
Funding for the October 7 Global Memorial Project’s productions will come from philanthropists, foundations, and organizations committed to documenting October 7 and preserving its memory.
Memorial initiative based on two October 7 documentaries
The new venture builds on two documentaries produced in partnership with Kastina Communications and philanthropists Carol and Joey Low: Screams Before Silence and The Children of October 7.
Screams Before Silence, featuring interviews conducted by Sheryl Sandberg, examines the sexual violence committed by Hamas terrorists during the attacks.
According to the organizers, it has screened at the White House, the US Congress, and 20 parliaments worldwide, aired on 20 television networks, and been translated into 18 languages.
The Children of October 7 features activist and social media influencer Montana Tucker in conversations with children who survived the massacre.
The organizers said Paramount+ acquired the documentary for streaming in 20 countries.
Other activities include bringing international journalists and influencers to the attack sites in southern Israel and advising on From Here We Rise, a video-mapping installation by photographer Ziv Koren and writer Noam Horev. The installation, documenting the past three years, is currently displayed on the rooftop of the Azrieli Mall in Tel Aviv.
The project’s advisory board brings together survivors, bereaved relatives of those killed on Oct. 7 or in the subsequent war, and specialists in documentation, diplomacy, and communications.
October 7 survivors amongst project's board members
Members of the board include Israel Prize laureate Dr. Cochav Elkayam-Levy, founder of the Civil Commission on October 7 Crimes by Hamas against Women and Children; Anat and Shimon Elkabetz, founders of Sivan’s House in Kibbutz Kfar Aza; and Ella Shani, a survivor of the massacre at Kibbutz Be’eri.
Also serving are Dr. Tsuriel Rashi of Ariel University; Uwe Becker, the German state of Hesse’s commissioner for combating antisemitism; Eran Masas, a recipient of Israel’s Medal of Civilian Heroism; and Joanna Landau, a nation-branding and strategic communications specialist.
“Documenting the stories of October 7 is the mission of our generation,” Schwartz said in a statement. “On that terrible morning, we awoke not only to a catastrophe of biblical proportions, but also to a machinery of denial on a scale humanity had never before witnessed.
“This new initiative is one piece of a much larger mosaic of people and organizations around the world working to ensure that the memory of these events continues to live on for generations to come.”

'Zionism is racism' vote sparks walkouts, condemnations from within Green Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:59:07 UTC
22:59:07 KST

The UK Green Party is facing a growing internal revolt over its adoption of a “Zionism is racism” policy, with senior members resigning or considering resignation and the European Greens distancing themselves from the party’s position.
As reported by The Jerusalem Post on Sunday, the UK Green Party voted in the controversial “Zionism is Racism” motion at its party conference in Brighton, UK, on Sunday, passing the motion 1,022 votes to 813.
In doing so, it became the first mainstream party in Europe to declare itself openly anti-Zionist.
Following the result, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar announced that Green Party leader Zack Polanski was barred from entering Israel.
Israel’s foreign ministry described the motion as a “clear antisemitic text” and beyond “the boundaries of legitimate political debate.”
UK politicians, Jewish groups condemn Green Party move
The passing of the motion has sparked condemnation from across the UK, including from politicians, Jewish groups and officials.
The Spectator revealed Monday that over a dozen Labour members of Parliament (MPs) – led by former Home Office minister Mike Tapp – reported the Green Party to Sussex Police and the Equality and Human Rights Commission over its “Zionism is racism” policy, and asked the commission to examine whether events at the Green conference may have crossed into criminally actionable racial or religious hatred against Jewish people.
However, some of the greatest losses have come from within the party itself.
Amnesty International UK chair Sandy Ruthven has left the Green Party following the party’s adoption of its “Zionism is racism” motion at its conference over the weekend.
Ruthven, who received 44% of the vote as Green candidate in the Bristol Mayor election in 2021, wrote on LinkedIn, “My heart has always been with the Green Party of England and Wales, and I have been a member for longer than I can remember. But this motion at conference marks the end of the line for me.”
“I have resigned my membership. In seeking to court the hard-left vote, we have failed to confront prejudice when it appears on our own side. In doing so, we have led ourselves into a political cul-de-sac. I sincerely hope the party finds a way back,” he said.
A man named Julian Mellor said he too was leaving the party, despite a long-standing membership.
“I first joined what was then the Ecology Party in 1981. Having spent a life supporting them, this motion seems to indicate that they’ve taken a direction different to my own. The fact that a motion that seems better suited to student politics made its way into the policies of what should be a serious national political party is a rather sad testament to the quality of leadership,” he said.
The chair of Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, told the BBC she will likely leave the party as a result of the motion.
Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today program, she said, “I haven’t decided yet… It is quite possible that I will leave the party… I’m giving it a little time and to talk with colleagues.”
Former party chief speaks out against vote
Former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas spoke against the motion during the debate.
Following the result, she posted a statement saying that even though she “views the Israeli government as racist, that its actions in Gaza amount to genocide and [supports] the BDS (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions) campaign,” she remains “firmly opposed to this motion.”
She went on to say that Zionism is “both racist AND a response to racism” and said there is “oversimplification at the heart of the motion [which leads] to many Jewish members feeling scared.”
Similar views were echoed by MPs such as Ellie Chowns and Carla Denyer.
The European Greens – the coalition of Green parties across Europe – announced it was distancing itself from the UK branch as a result of the motion.
In a statement, the EU Greens said it had contacted the UK Greens before the vote to express “deep concern” about the motion. The fact that the motion passed “goes against our agreed positions,” EU Greens said, adding that it therefore “unequivocally distances [itself] from it.”
“As EGP (European Green Party), we will immediately demand clarity from the leadership and parliamentary group of GPEW (Green Party of England and Wales) to understand the official party policy, how they position themselves toward the self-determination of Israelis and Jews as well as the protection of Jewish people.”
While the motion passed by 1,022 votes to 813, it is worth noting that this is only a tiny proportion of the Green Party’s overall membership. With 230,000 members, the vote represented less than 1% of the party.

First female Armored Corps combat company to begin IDF training in November

22:58:52 KST

The IDF Ground Forces have completed preparations to receive the Armored Corps’s first company of female tank soldiers designated for maneuvering combat, with the new track set to begin when recruits enlist in November, Walla learned on Tuesday.
Following a series of staff studies, pilot programs, and examinations of a dedicated training track adapted for women, and amid a heated public debate and opposition from rabbis, the High Court of Justice ruled in April that the IDF must establish an all-female maneuvering tank company as an organic combat unit without further delays.
The tank crews in the first company will consist entirely of female soldiers, who will serve for the first time as an operational maneuvering force in a role similar to that of male combat soldiers.
The IDF Ground Forces have not yet decided which armored brigade will receive the company.
Female tank soldiers have previously served in border defense missions under the 80th "Edom" Division along the Egyptian border. They fought during the October 7 massacre, at both Gaza border communities and at military posts in the sector overseen by the Gaza Division’s Southern Brigade.
The soldiers killed terrorists and prevented further attacks and attempted infiltrations into Israeli communities. Despite their actions, the IDF's General Staff did not authorize them to participate in maneuvering operations deep inside the Gaza Strip during the war.
Training for female Armored Corps soldiers slated to take place at different base to male compatriots
According to IDF Ground Forces plans, the training track for the female combat soldiers will be similar to that of male soldiers, but will take place at a separate base.
The ground forces also decided that the facility would serve as the recruits’ basic training base for the duration of training. The base currently serves as a facility for repairing IDF equipment in southern Israel.
The IDF’s training apparatus has made adaptations at the base ahead of the arrival of the female combat soldiers.
The recruits are scheduled to enlist in the dedicated track in November 2026.
The IDF also decided to establish additional medical and logistical support for the training program because of the base’s distance from the Shizafon base, home to the Armored Corps’ 460th Training Brigade.

In France, tens of thousands of people once again took to the streets in a protest by school students - schools were blocked and closed

In France, tens of thousands of people once again took to the streets in a protest by school students - schools were blocked and closed
Kyiv • UNN
In France, 86,000 people protested against the shortage of teachers, long school days, and the decline of schools. 1,800 lyceums were blocked.
Nearly 90,000 students, staff and parents took to the streets of towns and cities across France, as protesters blockaded hundreds of secondary schools during a nationwide day of action against extended school hours, teacher shortages and crumbling classrooms. UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
France’s Interior Ministry said 86,000 people took part in marches in cities including Marseille, Nantes and Lyon on Tuesday morning, 6 October, while as many as 40,000 people are expected to join the largest demonstration in Paris later that day.
The demonstrations follow two weeks of protests that began in the northern suburbs of the French capital and then spread across the country. They have been marred by frequent and often violent clashes with police, in which hundreds of people have been injured, some seriously.
Although many protests were peaceful, some demonstrators set fire to rubbish bins, vandalised bus stops and threw objects at police, who responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control projectiles. According to the Education Ministry, 24 schools have been burned or looted since the protests began.
According to the government, at least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been injured, while 6,100 people have been detained, nearly all of them minors. More than 1,800 people are facing criminal proceedings, 1,483 of them under the age of 18, the Justice Ministry said.
The National Union of Lyceum Students said that 1,800 of the country’s 3,700 secondary schools were blockaded or closed for the day on Tuesday, 6 October, although some local education authorities tried to move classes online.
Students on the marches held smoke flares and placards bearing slogans including "Beneath our textbooks lies anger" – a reference to the famous slogan from the student unrest of May 1968, "Beneath the paving stones, the beach" – and "Schools without money = a country without a future".
Many teachers also took part in the demonstration, the publication writes.
Trade union activists were also present at the marches, while CGT union leader Sophie Binet urged members to "stand up for upper-secondary students". Green Party leader Marine Tondelier called on local officials and parents to wear white and "go and protect our children during the demonstrations".
Trade unions and human rights organisations accused police of using excessive force against young protesters, while Amnesty International said the French authorities must "put an end to the disproportionate police repression witnessed in recent days".
On Monday, a 15-year-old had his arm torn off during a clash between protesters and police in northern France.
A 16-year-old lost his sight in his right eye after suffering a serious head injury on Wednesday during a blockade of a secondary school in Tours. Local prosecutor Catherine Sorita-Minard said the injury was "consistent with the impact of a defensive projectile known as a blast ball".
In another incident, a 14-year-old lost most of his teeth on Monday when a police officer appeared to fire a grenade at him from close range during a protest northwest of Paris. "His jaw is clamped shut, he can no longer speak and he eats through a straw," his mother told reporters.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu ordered his ministers to address the students’ main demands, including providing replacements for absent teachers, reviewing the length of the school day from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., and repairing ageing buildings.
However, the protests, seven months before a decisive presidential election that will determine Emmanuel Macron’s successor, have increased pressure on the government as it seeks to reduce the growing budget deficit amid rising investor concerns over France’s huge debt and weak economic growth.
The government accused the left-wing La France Insoumise (LFA) party of encouraging and even organizing the movement after numerous LFA lawmakers took part in blockading schools. Party veteran and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon strongly supported the protests, calling for nonviolence, the publication writes.

Three Iranian men spied on British-based dissident journalists on behalf of Iran's foreign intelligence service in order to attack them "as retribution for their criticism of the Iranian regime," prosecutors told a London jury on Tuesday.
The trio is accused of surveilling journalists working for Iran International, a Persian-language television station which is critical of Iran's government, between August 2024 and March 2025.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, have each denied two charges under Britain's National Security Act, brought in to give the authorities new powers to target threats from foreign states.
Their trial at Woolwich Crown Court began this week at a time of growing tension between Britain and Iran, which prosecutors say has repeatedly targeted critics and dissidents both inside the Islamic Republic and abroad.
"Eliminating hostile or critical voices... has effectively become a staple policy of the Islamic Republic of Iran," prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones told jurors.
Targeting of Iran International journalists, UK-based dissident Iranian news organization
He said the three defendants conducted research about at least two Iran International journalists, visiting addresses linked to them and taking photos and videos in preparation for an attack which Sepahvand was to carry out.
"Their ultimate objective was that one, perhaps more than one, of these targets would be subjected to serious violence, no doubt as retribution for their criticism of the Iranian regime and to try to silence and deter others," Emlyn Jones said.
He told the court the three defendants accepted going to places and taking photos and videos, but disputed why they had done so.
Emlyn Jones said Manesh and Noori's case was that they did not know they were doing so to assist Iranian intelligence, while Sepahvand accepted he knew but had been "bullied or threatened into doing what he did."

Smotrich: ‘Voluntary migration’ of Gazans to Muslim countries ‘is not racism’

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called on Tuesday for Muslim countries to absorb Gazans who voluntarily choose to leave the Strip, arguing that such a policy “is not racism,” while also calling for Israel to permanently apply sovereignty over territory it holds in Gaza and Lebanon.
Speaking at the National Conservatism Conference, or NatCon, in Jerusalem, Smotrich presented the proposals as part of a wider doctrine for ending Israel’s current wars and reshaping its regional deterrence.
“Encouraging the voluntary migration of Muslims who seek to leave conflict zones specifically to Muslim countries is not racism,” Smotrich said.
“The natural destination is the Muslim Arab countries, which share their language, religion and culture,” he added, stressing that he was calling for “a real, legal and dignified possibility” for those wishing to leave rather than forced removal.
The distinction is significant. International humanitarian law prohibits the forcible transfer or deportation of civilians from occupied territory. Arab governments have also repeatedly rejected proposals to resettle large numbers of Gazans outside the Strip.
Smotrich’s remarks build on a position he has advocated since shortly after the October 7 massacre. He previously called for Gaza’s population to be dramatically reduced through voluntary emigration, and last year proposed that Israel retain control of the Strip and “open the gates of Gaza for voluntary immigration.”
The idea has also moved beyond Smotrich: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in July that “voluntary migration” from Gaza remained under consideration, although he has been less supportive of reestablishing Israeli settlements there.
The debate comes as Israel continues to control more than 60% of Gaza nearly a year after the US-backed ceasefire took effect, while Hamas remains armed and reconstruction has largely stalled.

He has taken a hardline stance toward haredi conscription to the IDF, as his party’s platform seeks to cut all state funding for anyone evading military service and bar any exemptions from the IDF.
Bennett has also developed a plan to reform Israel’s education system, proposing that a government led by him would cut state funding to haredi educational institutions that do not teach core curriculum studies.

Reflecting on three years of arts coverage since October 7: Balancing culture, tragedy - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:58:13 UTC
22:58:13 KST

There were four cocktails I had never heard of at the bar that night - October 5, 2023 - and two of them were blue.
Trying to choose a drink at the awards ceremony of the Haifa International Film Festival was the defining “before-October 7” moment for me. I think all Israelis have a memory of that last “before” moment, when they still felt the world was normal.
I took one of the blue cocktails and sipped it while the winners were announced. Ironically, the award in the Israeli Feature Film Competition went to Dani Rosenberg’s The Vanishing Soldier, about a traumatized soldier fighting a war in Gaza who goes AWOL and hides in Tel Aviv as the rest of the country, thinking he has been taken hostage, searches for him.
In a further irony, about six weeks later, Rosenberg would start filming Of Dogs and Men, about a girl from Kibbutz Nir Oz searching for her lost dog just weeks after the Hamas massacre.
Over the past three years, as an arts and culture writer, I have tried my best to cope with the events of October 7 by striking a balance between writing about newly released movies and television series and covering art that chronicled and honored those who were killed or taken hostage in the massacre and the war.
Reconciling arts with ongoing tragedy
I did this while trying to make sense of what was happening.
At moments, I wondered if my work was futile: Did we even need arts coverage during this period? Why not another news page? But even in the panicked blur of October 7 itself, I started thinking about the most meaningful way I could help fill the arts pages.
First, I wanted to send David Brinn, who was then both the managing editor and the arts editor, as much material as possible as quickly as possible, so he could concentrate on the news.
I think the first article I wrote was about how people could get their money refunded for screenings on the last day of Haifa International Film Festival on October 7, which, of course, had been canceled.
After that, I thought about children. It looked as if they would be stuck at home till further notice, and as all parents know, uncertainty is hard for children to handle, as are frequent missile attacks, obviously.
During one of the trips to my building’s bomb shelter on October 7, I heard a child of about five ask her mother, “Can we still go to the playground today?”
At that moment, about five hours into the attack, we had heard nothing from any government or military official. It seemed that the attack was confined to the South of the country, but nobody knew anything for sure. “Not today,” her mother answered. “What about tomorrow?” the girl asked, and the mother said she didn’t know yet.
So, I spent part of October 7 disengaging from the news and going over all the children’s content available in Israel. I wrote articles recommending movies and series that I hoped children of different ages would love. Many TV providers made their children’s content free during this period.
The other option that occurred to me was museum websites. Many museums feature children’s content on their websites. Some added live, online activities. I wrote about as many of them as I could.
At a certain point, I knew I needed to start recommending some kind of escapist content for adults. This was a much trickier proposition. I knew that many people would not want to see anything featuring graphic violence.
If people wanted to see blood and death, they could watch the news. So, I recommended the movies and series I turn to regularly as comfort viewing, like comfort food, which were available in Israel. The main parameter was: Does this movie or series feature people I enjoy spending time with? Does it calm me?
But of course, it wasn’t all escapism. I wanted to keep the hostages present on every page of the paper. The arts community, like every community, had suffered losses on October 7. I follow a number of Israeli talent agencies on Instagram, which often promote their clients’ new projects. But the usual posts about this model’s acting debut or that musician’s new single were replaced by lists of funerals.
Quite a few of those who perished were trying to make it in the entertainment industry, like Tamar Goldenberg, an actress who had just gotten her big break, a role on the series Dismissed, but had not yet started filming. The producers dedicated an episode to her.
Yahav Winner, an independent filmmaker based in Kibbutz Kfar Aza, distracted Hamas terrorists so that his wife and baby daughter could escape, and he was killed. His last movie, The Boy, was released after his death and received an Ophir Award.
The cast and crew of Fauda, the series that depicts the exploits of the commandos in an Israeli counterterrorism unit, were directly affected by the war. Idan Amedi, an actor and singer who was one of its stars, was badly wounded fighting in Gaza.
Choosing to devote himself to his recovery and his music career, he opted out of appearing in the fifth season of the series, except for a wordless cameo.
Artists killed, kidnapped in Gaza
Matan Meir, a member of Fauda’s crew, was killed fighting in Gaza in November 2023, while Lior Waitzman, who worked in the sound department of Fauda, Tehran, and many other shows and movies, was murdered by terrorists in Sderot on October 7.
David Cunio, who had starred in Tom Shoval’s 2013 movie, Youth, was kidnapped from Nir Oz along with his wife, daughters, and brother Ariel. Shoval made a documentary about him, A Letter to David, which he edited again after Cunio was released in October 2025.
If anyone were to ask me what was the most difficult interview I ever did, I would not have to think for a second before answering, “Hen Avigdori.”
Avigdori is a television writer who is smart, funny, and warm - so why was he such a difficult interview? Because when we spoke, his wife and 12-year-old daughter were being held by Hamas, after they were kidnapped from Kibbutz Be’eri, where they were visiting relatives.
I found it hard to pick up the phone and call him, although I knew he wanted to do an interview because I couldn’t imagine how anyone in his position could speak calmly. But he was remarkably composed and articulate and said he welcomed the opportunity to keep his wife and daughter’s names in the news.
His wife, Sharon, is a drama therapist for people on the autism spectrum, and because my son is on the spectrum and greatly benefited from having this kind of therapy, we spoke a little about her work.
I felt a certain relief in his voice, a happiness at being able to speak about her gifts and the work that she loves, instead of just about her as a victim. Sharon and Noam were released in the first hostage deal.
Gradually, movie theaters began to reopen, and some version of cultural life resumed. One of the first movies to open was Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour, and I went to one of the first screenings in Jerusalem.
Many teen girls attended, some wearing sequined dresses and painting their nails every color of the rainbow in honor of seeing this movie featuring their idol.
I spoke to several of them, thinking it might make for a nice feature, but none felt comfortable giving me their names, and none were even old enough to consent to be quoted.
One said her brother was fighting in Gaza and that she had considered skipping the movie, which she had been looking forward to seeing for so long, but she was confident he would want her to enjoy herself. As we spoke, I felt that my questions were bringing them down, and I regretted approaching them.
Gradually, documentaries about the massacre were released, as well as feature films and series about the massacre and its aftermath, including Of Dogs and Men, Red Alert, and One Day in October.
Avi Nesher’s latest film, Our Loves, which just opened at the Haifa International Film Festival, tells a very human story about several people who think they are having the worst day of their lives on October 6, 2023, and then must fight for survival the next day. It will open in theaters throughout Israel on October 15.
Looking back, I wish I had found even more ways to keep the October 7 victims on the culture page, and I hope I was able to help people entertain their children and find TV content that took their minds off the news.
Thinking again about the blue cocktail array on the night of October 5, 2023, I remember that before I left, I thanked the festival public-relations manager for inviting me. “See you next year,” I said, and she replied with words that still echo in my mind: “I hope so, dear. But we never know what will happen.”

1 in 6 women in European Parliament targeted by deepfake pornography: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:58:05 UTC
22:58:05 KST

Aysu Bicer
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Fifty members of the European Parliament, including 46 women, have been targeted by deepfake pornography, according to new research released Monday by Germany-based civil society group Agora Digitale Transformation.
The findings mean roughly one in six female members of the European Parliament have been depicted in or associated with deepfake pornography, the report said.
Deepfake pornography, also known as AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII), involves the use of generative artificial intelligence to create sexually explicit depictions of people without their consent.
“AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII), colloquially known as deepfake pornography, is a systemic threat to women in European politics,” the report said.
Researchers examined hundreds of websites known to host or produce AI-generated sexual content, including sites associated with deepfake pornography, “celebrity leaks” and inappropriate candid images of women in public life.
They searched the names of all 720 MEPs across 200 of these websites using a Google Custom Search engine.
The analysis found that 50 MEPs — 46 women and four men — were depicted in or associated with deepfake pornography.
“Like in our recent audit of the exposure members of the EU’s national parliament face, we find that exposure to this harm falls overwhelmingly on women, is amplified by institutional visibility and affects all major groups across the political spectrum,” the report said.
The report said the findings show that the problem affects lawmakers across political groups and is linked to the visibility that comes with holding public office.
The EU is also taking steps to address AI-generated sexual content. It is banning AI-powered nudifier apps from Dec. 2 and investigating the use of similar technology involving Grok on the social media company X.
The report said the findings highlight the scale of non-consensual AI-generated sexual imagery targeting women in European politics.
“Our new analysis shows 50 MEPs — 46 women and four men — to be depicted in or associated with deepfake pornography. This translates to roughly one in six women MEPs,” the report said.

Russia was ordered to pay PrivatBank more than $327 million for the illegal expropriation of assets in Crimea
Kyiv • UNN
An arbitration court in The Hague awarded PrivatBank more than $327 million in compensation for the expropriation of assets in Crimea. The amount includes interest and costs.
The Arbitration Court ordered Russia to pay more than USD 327 million in compensation for damages caused by the unlawful expropriation of PrivatBank's assets in Crimea. As reported by the bank, this amount includes interest accrued from April 18, 2014 (which will continue to accrue until full payment), as well as other relevant costs and expenses incurred by PrivatBank, reports UNN.
Details
The Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague issued its Final Arbitral Award in Case No. 2015-21 in favor of PrivatBank (hereinafter, the Bank) against Russia (hereinafter, the Respondent) in the arbitration proceedings initiated by the bank in 2015 pursuant to the 1998 bilateral agreement on the promotion and reciprocal protection of investments.
The Final Arbitral Award is an obvious and important victory that culminated in PrivatBank's 11-year legal struggle to achieve justice and uphold the principle that unlawful expropriation must have consequences. The Arbitration Court confirmed the bank's right to substantial compensation, interest, and reimbursement of costs. We expect the arbitral award to be enforced and paid in full, and we will take all necessary measures to ensure payment and protect the interests of the bank and its stakeholders
PrivatBank has put Dnipro-Arena up for auction for the third time21.09.26, 20:18 • 5936 views
The decision is based on the Arbitration Court's preliminary findings that it has jurisdiction to consider PrivatBank's claims and that those claims are admissible, as well as that the Respondent breached Article 5 of the Agreement. In the final decision, the Arbitration Court rejected the Respondent's objections regarding the illegality of the investments and ruled that this did not deprive the court of jurisdiction or render the claims inadmissible, and awarded the Bank compensation and reimbursement of costs.
In addition
As previously reported, until April 2014, PrivatBank conducted substantial operations and held valuable assets on the Crimean Peninsula, including loans, real estate, and funds. Shortly after the unlawful occupation of Crimea, the Respondent took a number of measures that led to the unlawful expropriation of the bank's assets and the termination of its operations in Crimea.

Jim Bakker, televangelist who rose to fame and fell from grace, dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:55:29 UTC
22:55:29 KST

Jim Bakker, televangelist who rose to fame and fell from grace, dies
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
In the halcyon days of the televangelists, when Jim Bakker stood shoulder to shoulder with fire and brimstone preachers such as Jerry Farwell, Pat Robertson and Jimmy Swaggart, the collection plate always seemed bottomless.
For Bakker, it meant a Christian theme park in a leafy Charlotte, N.C., suburb, a fleet of black Cadillac limousines, vacation homes, regular orders of truffles flown in from Brussels, a gold-plated bathtub, mink coats for his wife Tammy Faye and an air-conditioned doghouse at the family compound.
In return for your unbending faith, he told viewers of his popular television show “The PTL Club,” God will bestow you great wealth and other blessings. And to get things rolling, he added, just call the 800 number on the bottom of your screen.
By the time it all fell apart amid a sex scandal and a fraud conviction, Bakker landed in prison and took stock of his life. He renounced the prosperity gospel he once had preached, wrote a raw and wrenching biography about his missteps and vowed to work with the needy and most vulnerable when he was released.
Once free, however, he set up camp at a Christian compound deep in the Ozarks, armed with a darker message. The End Times are upon us, he told viewers on his reborn television show, and the signs are everywhere — terrorist attacks, epic storms, thunderous earthquakes, frayed relations among world superpowers, a pandemic that refused to release its grip.
To get viewers to the Rapture he said was sure to come, Bakker sold buckets of freeze-dried food with a shelf life of 30 years, fuel-less generators, doomsday guides and a magical elixir — “Silver Solution” — that could cure the coronavirus and other unpleasantries. “Imagine — the world is dying and you’re having breakfast like a king,” he told viewers.
And, as before, the authorities were hot on his tail.
A man of confounding contradictions, Bakker died Monday, his wife announced in a statement on his Instagram account. He was 86.
“He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry,” read the statement from Bakker’s wife, Lori Bakker. “Jim loved people deeply. He loved this ministry, and he loved the friends and partners who stood with him throughout the years.”
Baby-faced with dark lacquered hair and oversized glasses, Bakker became the sunny alternative to the hell-fire bombast of Swaggart and Falwell when he and his wife introduced themselves to America when “The PTL Club” debuted in 1976.
The show, an acronym for Praise the Lord, was breezy and chatty, styled after a late-night talk show with a lineup of guests, performances by Christian musicians and the never-a-mean-word banter between Bakker and Tammy Faye, who would frequently burst into song, tears dribbling down her cheeks.
Together the Bakkers spoke of the souls saved and the hardships overcome by those who put their lives in the hands of the Lord. And as often, reminded viewers of the need for donations to keep their crusade barreling forward. Before long, according to evidence introduced at Bakker’s fraud trial, more than $1 million a week was pouring into “The PTL Club.”
Capitalizing on their fame and fortune, the Bakkers opened Heritage USA, a Christian theme park complete with a $12-million water park, a hotel, nightly Passion plays and a Disneyesque Main Street where guests could buy palm-size Jesus dolls, 24-carat gold crosses and boxes of Heavenly Fudge. As the guests rolled in, developers built condos and homes for those who wished to live in such a place.
Tammy Faye Messner, the mascara-laden former wife of televangelist Jim Bakker, the charismatic TV preacher with the choir-boy face with whom she appeared on their popular Christian talk-variety show until his downfall amid scandal in the late 1980s, has died.
It was all heady stuff for Bakker, who often said that as a youth he had few expectations. Born Jan. 2, 1940, James Orsen Bakker was raised in Muskegon, a commercial ship port in Michigan just across the lake from Milwaukee. He said his parents were deeply religious and so strict that even simple pleasures such as singing were forbidden.
At North Central University, a Minneapolis Bible college affiliated with the Assemblies of God, he met Tammy Faye LaValley. They married four months later, dropped out school and launched their television evangelism careers as hosts of a children’s puppet show on Robertson’s Christian Broadcasting Network. They eventually set off on their own to develop a show that paired church and pop culture, “The PTL Club.”
By the mid-1980s, “The PTL Club” had a daily viewership of roughly 5.7 million and more than 6 million visitors a year were rolling into Heritage USA. But it would all quickly vaporize.
It started with a rendezvous in a hotel room in Clearwater Beach, Fla., where Bakker met up with church secretary Jessica Hahn, a sexual encounter he successfully kept under wraps for years by reportedly paying her hush money. But when Swaggart caught wind of the tryst, he saw an opportunity to topple his rival and took the matter to the Assemblies of God, the church fellowship both preachers belonged to.
Accused of “moral failure” by the fellowship, Bakker resigned and Falwell replaced him as president of PTL. Once there, Falwell examined the company ledgers and realized he had a problem. Among other things, Bakker had offered nearly 160,000 people the opportunity to reserve a room at the 500-room Heritage Grand Hotel for three nights a year for life for $1,000 — a mathematical impossibility.
Bakker was eventually sentenced to 45 years in prison and fined $500,000 after jurors found him guilty on 24 fraud and conspiracy charges, which accused him of swindling his followers out of nearly $160 million and using much of it to fund his extravagance lifestyle. His sentence was later cut to eight years.
“Please don’t do this to me,” Bakker said before he was led away in handcuffs.
His attorney told The Times after his client was sentenced that Bakker had suffered a nervous breakdown during the trial and was overcome by vivid hallucinations, imaging that those packed in the courtroom were “frightening animals intent on destroying him.”
Behind bars, Bakker learned that Tammy Faye had filed for divorce, a final blow that left him questioning his faith, he later told Larry King. Ultimately, though, he said he “learned more in prison than in Bible college” and read the Bible in full for the first time, coming to realize that he had been leading “an ungodly arrogant lifestyle” as he chased wealth.
“You can worship money or you can worship God,” he told The Times when he moved into a small apartment in Burbank with his son after his release. “But you can’t worship both.”
The apartment served as a base camp after he released his memoir, “I Was Wrong,” and plotted a national book tour. He also did volunteer work at the Los Angeles International Dream Center, where he was welcomed warmly by the poor families and troubled youths who sought a fresh start there.
Tammy Faye Bakker says Jessica Hahn “knew exactly what she was doing” when she traveled to Florida in 1980 for the fateful meeting with Jim Bakker that eventually led to the PTL scandal.
It’s also where he met Lori Beth Graham, an evangelist and frequent speaker at the center who described herself as a survivor of an abusive marriage and a hard-partying lifestyle as a youth. Both were broke, and she told the Charlotte Observer she had to borrow a wedding gown when they married in 1988.
The newlyweds moved to rural Missouri, just north of the Arkansas boarder, and set up camp on 800 rolling acres that had been purchased by developer Jerry Crawford, a onetime PTL partner who credited Bakker with saving his failing marriage. Bakker put down roots quickly, establishing his Morningside Church and a studio for “The Jim Bakker Show.”
In many ways, Morningside was a miniature version of Heritage USA, with a street lamp-lined avenue called Grace Street, a faux town square with a 15-foot statue of Jesus and old-timey shops like Grace Street Creamery and Morningside Beauty Salon. Guests were free to wander in as Bakker and his wife taped their new show.
But if “The PTL Club” capitalized on the wealthier-the-better ethos of the 1980s, Bakker’s new show was filled with post-9/11 darkness and apocalyptic visions of what was to come. He claimed hurricanes, train derailments and mass school shootings were a judgment of God and predicted a second American civil war if President Trump wasn’t re-elected
Now white haired with a neatly trimmed beard and sunken cheeks, Bakker’s once upbeat delivery and playful repartee with guests had been replaced by a grim figure.
The soundstage where he and Lori Beth reached out to viewers was often filled with buckets of survival food — Tasty Pantry Deluxe Bucket (buttermilk pancakes, black bean burgers and more) and Fiesta Pail (refried beans, taco-flavored plant-based meat and more) and a sampler bundle he claimed was enough for 23,375 meals for a $2,500 donation. It could feed a family of four for years, he promised.
Not that it would matter much during the depth of Armageddon, reviews of Bakkers’ food buckets were less than glowing.
“We couldn’t agree on which was worse — the thick potato soup that felt like eating wet cement, the strong chemical overtones in the chocolate pudding or the disturbing radioactive orange of the macaroni and cheese,” a team of NPR tasters wrote in 2015.
But it was the Silver Solution and Bakker’s claims that it was a cure for COVID-19 that caught the attention of authorities. The Federal Trade Commission and the Food and Drug Administration sent him warning letters to cease making false medical claims and the attorney general in Missouri filed suit, alleging he was deceiving viewers by pushing a fake panacea for the virus.
In response, his program was dropped by World Harvest Television and GEB America Network — two of the few networks that carried his new show — and was cut off by credit card companies. Under mounting pressure, he agreed to pay restitution of $157,000 and stop pitching the product.
Telling viewers that he was, again, on the brink of bankruptcy, he urged viewers to save his ministry by sending him cash or checks.
“SOS, save our station, save our ship, help us stay on the air,” he said. “We need a miracle here.”
Bakker is survived by his wife and two children, Tammy Sue and Jamie, known as Jay. Tammy Faye Bakker died while battling cancer in 2007.

North Korea on Tuesday called South Korea’s claim that Pyongyang “deliberately planted” two mines inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), which exploded last month and wounded three South Korean soldiers, “blame shifting.”
“The ‘mine-explosion case’ is a sinister obstructive move intended to brand our fortification of the southern border, downright exercise of the sovereignty, as a ‘military invasion’ and delay and check it,” the North Korean Foreign Ministry said in a statement carried by the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
Pyongyang said the incident was “no more than a poor trick” by South Korea “to shift the blame for its own accident onto us.”
North Korea’s reaction came after Seoul said Monday that Pyongyang had “deliberately planted” the two mines and reiterated its demand for an apology.
“The military strongly calls on North Korea to offer a sincere apology to the South Korean soldiers injured in the mine blast and immediately remove the mines it planted in violation of the armistice agreement,” Lt. Seoul “seeks to hold” Pyongyang “accountable for the premeditated farce, fabricated and determined unilaterally by it, and tarnish the latter’s international image,” the North’s ministry said.
North Korea “categorically rejects the despicable attempt” and “solemnly clarifies that our state will exercise its just sovereign rights in a more resolute and bold manner to ensure the security of the southern border,” it added.
“We do not care about them trying to remove the mines irrelevant to us, and we have no reason to pay heed to such farce of the ROK,” the ministry said.
It warned that if “a jackboot or a spark of fire from the ROK goes even a millimeter beyond the border to violate our territory,” North Korean border guards would take “immediate and powerful counteraction.”
It added that if a similar incident occurs in the future, North Korea is “not responsible for it,” saying the side that sustains the incident would be “entirely accountable.”
The Korean Peninsula has remained divided since the 1950-53 Korean War ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty, leaving the two Koreas technically at war.

France test-fires new nuclear-capable missile from submarine for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:54:46 UTC
22:54:46 KST

"To be free, one must be feared," Emmanuel Macron has posted, weeks after vowing that hybrid attacks blamed on Russia would "not go unanswered".
France has test-fired its new M51.3 nuclear-capable ballistic missile from a submarine for the first time, in a launch President Emmanuel Macron said proved the credibility of the country's nuclear deterrent.
The missile, which carried no warhead, was launched on Tuesday from the nuclear-powered submarine Le Vigilant off Brittany. It came down in the North Atlantic, hundreds of kilometres from any coastline, the defence ministry said.
Macron watched from the warship Auvergne and posted a video of the launch on X.
"To be free, one must be feared. And to be feared, one must be powerful," he wrote. "This technical success further demonstrates the credibility of our nuclear deterrent, whose long-term viability is assured."
The ministry said the test was carried out "in strict compliance with France's international commitments", adding that the M51.3 missile "reflects the President of the Republic's commitment to maintaining the operational credibility of France's nuclear forces over the long term, at the level required by the international security environment."
The launch comes after Macron warned of a shift in "Russian aggression and threats" against European countries following a series of hybrid attacks blamed on Moscow. In mid-September he vowed they would "not go unanswered".
France is the European Union's only nuclear-armed state, and Macron proposed this year that European partners join its "advanced" deterrence framework.
Alexander Kazakevich contributed to this report.

The suspect was aware of the building’s civilian status and that it was protected under international humanitarian law and could not be a lawful target of attack

No, the AfD are not the Nazis – and neither are they Germany’s main problem right now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:54:24 UTC
22:54:24 KST

No, the AfD are not the Nazis – and neither are they Germany’s main problem right now
Unlike in countries such as Russia, the US, or France, the German presidency is not a powerful office. At least not in terms of what it can do directly or independently. Instead, Germany’s president is a largely representative figure, while real power to lead national policy belongs to the chancellor.
Yet the presidency is no mere decoration. According to a 2014 summary by Germany’s constitutional court, the authority of the office derives, above all, from the intellectual and moral influence it should exert, and whoever holds it “embodies the unity of the state.” In short, Germany’s president has two real jobs: to stand for national togetherness, especially when tensions increase and politics polarize, and to be a widely acknowledged moral authority.
Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the current president, has failed quite spectacularly on both counts, and his recent speech on the Day of German Unity has shown once again how and why. This is a scandal, but it is not a surprise. Even before his latest performance, Steinmeier had earned himself the nickname “Walter der Spalter,” which translates as Walter the Splitter.
And for good reasons: Although charged with integrating the nation, Steinmeier has a long record of explicitly calling for the marginalization and exclusion of large numbers of Germans, not only but in particularly those who dare represent or vote for the new-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
Usually implicitly but always clearly, the president has repeatedly smeared them as extremists beyond the pale of political participation. Last year, for instance, he used a major speech on November 9 – a date with several historical associations, including the massive pogrom of 1938 and thus the Holocaust – to, in effect, single out the AfD and its supporters as at least the successors of Nazism if not simply its new embodiment.
This year, in a revealingly snobbish sally, he has labelled them “vulgar democrats.” For Steinmeier, clearly, there is not merely a distinction between “democrats” and “non-democrats,” but also one between inferior (“vulgar”) and superior (presumably sophisticated) democrats. Steinmeier clearly sees himself as a distinguished example of the latter. On a personal level, the obvious smugness of his attitude is merely deeply embarrassing. What is worse is that taking popular sovereignty seriously – as prescribed by the German constitution – would look vastly different.
Now, in his German Unity Day speech, Steinmeier has taken aim at what he himself described as large numbers of Germany’s citizens. They, the president has correctly noticed, are displaying “distrust toward the political order.” That, for Steinmeier, is no reason to seriously examine what might be wrong with that order or to make a genuine effort to understand the reasons for that distrust. His scant and general remarks on Berlin’s own mistakes and the anxieties of ordinary Germans illustrated not humility but aloof and patronizing disinterest.
Generously conceding that maybe not all of those who have lost trust in the status quo are “against democracy as such,” Steinmeier explicitly kept all of them under precisely that suspicion. In essence, he conflated many Germans’ very plausible discontent with the devastating policies imposed by radical-Centrist establishment parties with rejecting the constitutional order or even democracy as such: If you are not for us, so the message, you’re not just against us but a virtually criminal misfit.
How convenient – if, that is, you are Frank-Walter Steinmeier and your whole political biography happens to represent precisely that establishment, its privileges, its obstinate refusal to learn, and its failure.
Steinmeier also had harsh words for a whole catalog of horrors, of typical Centrist paranoia, blame-shifting, and scapegoating: the “unbearable demagoguery of extremist forces” and their “joy of destruction”; “outside powers that seek to divide and weaken us” (meaning Russia, obviously); the “predominance of the internet” (read social media that didn’t exist when he was young and escape mainstream control now that he is old); “conspiracy fantasies”; caricatures of Germany produced by “Kremlin trolls,” “German right-wing extremists,” and “left-authoritarian cranks”; “unscrupulous internet oligarchs”; and, finally of course, simply “populists” and “Wutwahler” (literally, “rage-voters”) – a contemptuous term for those who dare articulate their frustration with Steinmeier’s establishment friends by actually voting against them.
Against this dark backdrop, the complacent, crusading president invoked the specter of Weimar – that is the collapse of interwar German democracy that was followed by the catastrophe of Nazism. Steinmeier insisted that today’s Germany is “not Weimar,” but he also made clear that he believes it could end in a similar crash.
That was ironic, as Steinmeier also warned that historical ignorance is unforgivable. Indeed. But then he should know that Weimar was destroyed by many things, yet it could have survived all of them, if its people had not been hit by the mass immiseration of the Great Depression. Yes, Nazis – and conservatives foolishly promoting them – killed that first German democracy. But they could only do so because the country was sinking into ruin, misery, and mass despair, while its establishment elites pursued a hopelessly misguided economic policy and – even if that is often forgotten now – massively curtailed democracy well before the Nazis finished off what was left of it.
Say what you will about the AfD; it is not the equivalent of the Nazi party. That is where Steinmeier’s implied analogy makes no sense. Indeed – deliberately or not – he is misusing history as a cheap rhetorical, not to say demagogic device.
The real parallel between today and the last years of Weimar is invisible to Steinmeier because he lacks the humility needed for self-reflection. Just as between spring 1930 and early 1933, Germany’s establishment is offering nothing but “stay-the-course” to voters desperate not simply for change but help.
It was precisely that spirit of irresponsible, privileged aloofness that the president, in his Unity Day speech, displayed when promising nothing but empty phrases and the same all over again: more so-called “reforms” at home which many Germans recognize as what they really are, namely deep cuts into their welfare and life chances.
And abroad, of course, more support for Ukraine, that is, the ultra-corrupt Zelensky regime that has committed the worst act of terrorism against Germany in its history. That as well, more and more Germans see for what it really is: a perverse national self-humiliation and an absurd waste of money to finance a highly corrupt regime as well as an avoidable, unwinnable, and disastrous – also for ordinary Ukrainians – proxy war against Russia; an indirect (if barely) German war against Russia that constantly escalates the risk of an even worse direct war between Berlin and Moscow, as German intelligence services acknowledge, if in a biased manner.
Steinmeier delivers his polarizing and divisive messages while performing a tired patina of wise statesmanship that betrays at least a clumsy effort to impress. One day after Steinmeier’s unfortunate speech, Chancellor Friedrich Merz chose the bluntest way possible to convey, in essence, the same message. Traveling to visit the Kiev establishment, where Merz – with his bottomless wallet fed by German taxpayers – may enjoy the popularity he absolutely lacks at home, the chancellor made it rudely, brutally clear once more: Germany’s current rulers care more for the Kiev regime, which they may or may not genuinely mistake for Ukraine as a whole, than for their own country and the citizens who have elected and pay them. And this is just one, if striking, outcome of the true core of Germany’s malaise: a widespread and very plausible sense that Germany’s establishment does not care about Germans. Even if you dislike the AfD or “populists” in general, they are a response to this sense of abandonment.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

Russian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into the use of forged quality certificates during the distribution of a popular canine vaccine blamed for the deaths of dozens of dogs over the summer, the Prosecutor General’s Office said Tuesday.
Inspectors discovered a falsified certificate uploaded to the state electronic database for a batch of the vaccine, the prosecutor’s office said in a statement, without identifying the maker or the medication by name.
Law enforcement sources told Interfax that the investigation targeted Moscow-based pharmaceutical company Vetbiochim, which produces the widely used Multican-8 vaccine.
At least 169 dogs have reportedly died since August across Russia, primarily in the Yaroslavl region, after receiving doses of Multican-8. Authorities revealed that samples from a batch of Multican-8 contained live Aujeszky’s disease virus, which is almost universally fatal to domestic dogs.
Vetbiochim recalled several batches of Multican-8 in late August following initial reports of illness and deaths from pet owners.
In comments to the RBC news outlet on Tuesday, Vetbiochim said it was fully cooperating with law enforcement and providing all requested documentation.
“We’re not avoiding responsibility, and we’re not hiding from the public or the investigation,” Vetbiochim said.
The company said it had launched an internal audit to determine how the contaminated batch and falsified documentation were released into circulation.
“We want an objective investigation to identify those responsible and to ensure they face proper consequences. We’ll do everything we can to make that happen,” Vetbiochim said.

On August 11, city authorities and Teremky residents agreed to check the possibility of laying the network along a different route and introduced a two-week moratorium on tree felling, and on September 1, the KCSA stated that the current project would be applied with maximum preservation of green spaces, in particular planning to preserve about 160 trees. Albares reaffirms Spain’s commitment to defence of Arctic and Baltic in Finland
Spain
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:52:15 CEST
