PRESS RELEASE 149
Albares reaffirms Spain’s commitment to defence of Arctic and Baltic in Finland
- The minister met with his Finnish counterpart to strengthen bilateral relations in areas such as defence and digitalisation
- The meeting took place as part of Their Majesties the King and Queen’s State visit to Finland
The Minister for Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, met his Finnish counterpart, Elina Valtonen, in Helsinki on Tuesday, with whom he discussed the strong bilateral relations and the prospect of new areas of collaboration. The meeting, which forms part of Their Majesties the King and Queen’s State visit to Finland, served to reaffirm Spain’s commitment to the defence and security of the Arctic and the Baltic.
Despite the geographical distance, Albares stated, “we face common challenges that threaten our fundamental values and our security. Finland and Spain have found that their approaches complement each other in key areas, and this visit aims to demonstrate our commitment to the defence and security of the Arctic, as well as to reiterate our support for the initiatives Finland is undertaking alongside the EU and the Nordic countries to address these challenges”, he concluded.
On the subject of security, Albares reiterated to Valtonen Spain’s unwavering commitment to NATO and its 360-degree approach. Proof of this will be the visit to the air base and the Jaeger Brigade base, headquarters of the Multinational Staff Element of NATO’s Forward Land Forces, in which Spain has committed to participating, thereby demonstrating its support for the eastern border and the Arctic.
Spanish Polar Strategy
This visit also comes at a time when Spain’s interest in this region, together with Antarctica, will be set out in the first Spanish Polar Strategy 2026–2035, an instrument on which the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is working to strengthen our country’s role in polar forums and in response to new challenges and opportunities.
This strategy will contribute to the promotion of peace and stability through multilateralism and cooperative governance, with a focus on climate action and environmental protection.
Bilateral Relations
Spain and Finland enjoy good bilateral relations, which are balanced in the economic sphere and offer significant untapped potential, with robust trade flows in both directions and growing investment.
Both countries share significant opportunities to deepen cooperation in strategic sectors such as renewable energy, the space sector, defence, digitalisation, quantum computing, and scientific and academic cooperation.
Furthermore, the ties between our countries go beyond purely economic matters. Last year, more than 600,000 Finns visited Spain, making our country the third most popular tourist destination and the second most popular country of destination – after Sweden – for Finns living abroad. There is significant interest in the Spanish language, and the number of people learning it is on the rise. Currently, more than 40,000 Finnish students are studying Spanish at all levels of formal education in Finland.
EU agenda
During their meeting, the ministers also addressed the main issues on the EU agenda, such as migration policy, enlargement, the multiannual financial framework, and the official status of Catalan, Galician and Basque within the European Union.

13:52:08 UTC
22:52:08 KST

What has happened?
The exact details remain unclear but reports from Russia have suggested Darya Shipilova, an employee at the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk, died on 2 October, two days after becoming unwell at work.
According to Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, Shipilova died from “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”.
However, there are other accounts: Alexey Tsydenov, the head of the neighbouring Buryatia region, initially said Shipilova had died of plague, before editing his social media post to say she had “possibly” died of the disease.
Russian authorities have denied this to the World Health Organization (WHO), stating: “No case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk, Russian Federation.”
If it is the plague, what are we talking about?
We are talking about a disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, typically found in small mammals and the fleas that feed on them. It is the same organism that was behind the bubonic plague or “black death” that swept Europe in the 14th century.
However, the bubonic form is different from the pneumonic plague that some have suggested caused Shipilova’s death.
The former is more common, results in swellings called buboes and is spread by the bite of infected fleas, whereas the latter is lung-based. Pneumonic plague has a higher mortality rate and can be spread between people.
How concerned should we be?
It is worth noting that the plague is not a disease of the past.
“There are a few hundred cases of plague reported each year globally usually in geographically restricted areas, particularly in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of the Congo – although there are a small number of cases in the western United States, central Asia, Mongolia, etc,” said Dr Malick Gibani at Imperial College London.
That might not seem reassuring, but we no longer have to rely on medieval medicine.
Dr Simon Clarke at the University of Reading said: “Unlike many viral respiratory diseases, plague is caused by bacteria, and antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides work well against this pathogen if administered early enough and are often given prophylactically, post-exposure.”
However, Prof Brendan Wren at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine said there were multi-antibiotic-resistant strains emerging, “and if the laboratory is working on such a strain, then treatment options may be limited”.
There have also been reports that almost 200 people with whom Shipilova may have had contact are now under medical observation, and that quarantines have been imposed in a number of hospitals.
“Isolation and monitoring are sensible strategies,” Wren said.
Prof Alice Hughes at the University of Melbourne added the incubation for pneumonic plague was only one to three days and, as yet no one has shown symptoms.
Prof Ian Jones at the University of Reading also offered reassurance. “This case here seems like a rare lab accident and is unlikely to go much further.”
However, Clarke said there were still unknowns. “Until more details emerge, it is difficult to assess whether this represents an isolated case, an occupational exposure, or evidence of wider transmission,” he said.
The UN health agency’s spokesperson Christian Lindmeier has said the risk to others is low. “The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole, and very low for the WHO European region,” he said.
What happens next?
Dr Zania Stamataki, an associate professor of viral immunology and academic lead for containment level 3 laboratories at the University of Birmingham, said the control systems used in the UK for hazardous organisms work, meaning laboratory-acquired infections are rare.
But, she added: “They are not impossible, and this is why an incident warrants a full account of what happened. That account matters beyond Russia.”
Other experts also stressed a need for transparency. “I think it’s important that we see how this pans out, and ideally, there’d be good communication between the public health authorities and the wider global health community,” said Gibani.
“I think this emphasises the need to be aware of ongoing outbreaks of serious bacterial pathogens and highlights the need for investment in biosecurity, particularly for preventing biological risks,” he added. “This could include developing medical countermeasures like better diagnostics or vaccines.”

Shepherds turn to dogs to defend sheep from wolves on the Veluwe

Shepherds turn to dogs to defend sheep from wolves on the Veluwe
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Shepherds in the Veluwe region have come up with a novel solution to deter wolf attacks by hiring Italian mountain dogs to guard their sheep.
Stichting Schapedrift Ermelo, a volunteer organisation that tends a herd of sheep on the heathlands in Gelderland, acquired two Maremmano-Abruzzese sheepdogs this summer to protect the herd from prowling wolves.
The forested Veluwe region has the biggest concentration of wolves in the Netherlands, with seven packs living in an area of 1,000 square kilometres, since the predators returned in 2019.
The organisation has put up eight-foot electrocuted fences around its sheep enclosure to keep wolves out, but the animals are still vulnerable when they are being herded across the heath.
“We see an increasing threat from wolves,” shepherd Marion Derks told Omroep Gelderland. “And there are a few walking round here that were interested in the sheep.”
The two white-haired dogs have been used for centuries to defend sheep. They are valued for their non-aggressive nature and alertness, Derks said.
“As soon as they see danger, you see their attitude change and they go into defensive mode,” she explained. “They make themselves bigger and more imposing and start barking.”
She said the dogs were not expected to confront or attack wolves. “Their presence is meant to stop the wolves approaching,” Derks explained. “Wolves will take easy prey but if they think it’s going to be too difficult, they’ll look for something else.”

EU 'ready to deploy' observers for upcoming Palestinian legislative polls
The European Union is "ready to deploy" election observers to monitor Palestinian legislative elections set for November, top diplomat Kaja Kallas said Tuesday.

The legislative polls face major logistical challenges arising from Israeli measures in the Gaza Strip, as well as in Jerusalem and West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967.

As more Iranian women reject hijab rules, regime looks at new ways to force compliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:50:00 UTC
22:50:00 KST

Iran's regime raises social cost for women defying hijab
October 6, 2026
Women appearing in public without wearing a hijab has become an increasingly common sight across Iran, marking one of the most visible social changes since the 2022 "Woman, Life, Freedom" protests, which were sparked after a woman died in police custody after she was arrested for allegedly wearing her headscarf improperly.
Authorities have been unable to restore the level of street enforcement that existed before the protests. But the relative retreat of so-called "morality police" patrols does not mean the compulsory hijab has disappeared.
Now, authorities and conservative groups are experimenting with different ways to resist that change without necessarily recreating the same street confrontations that helped fuel the 2022 protests.
Judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei recently called for action against what he described as social "abnormalities," "indecency" and "nudity," urging prosecutors to coordinate with police, intelligence bodies and government institutions.
At the same time, supporters of hijab mandates have circulated online campaigns encouraging people to avoid businesses run by women who do not follow the state dress code and instead patronize women who do.
The result is a more fragmented form of enforcement, moving in some cases from police patrols toward workplaces, businesses and access to everyday services.
Iran's regime turns to social pressure
The online campaigns call for what supporters describe as "conscious purchasing," encouraging consumers to support hijab-observing vendors.
A female lawyer in Tehran told DW that such campaigns risk deepening social divisions rather than encouraging adherence to a social norm.
"This is a deliberate attempt to categorize people by identity and put them against one another," she said under condition of anonymity for safety concerns.
She argues that encouraging economic pressure against people solely because of their appearance goes beyond an individual's right to choose where to shop.
"When economic sanctions are imposed on them [the regime], they call it pressure, injustice and economic warfare," she said. "But when they use the same logic domestically to force part of society to change its behavior, it becomes 'support for values.'"
She also questioned the assumption that women who conform to one particular dress code uniquely represent Iranian social values.
"The reality of Iranian society is much more complex than that," she said.
Accounts posted by Iranian women suggest that dress-code enforcement can also appear in everyday services, with some women reporting on social media being denied access to clinics and banks for not wearing a headscarf.
When women's bodies become political
Shirin Shams is an exiled Iranian political activist and director of the Women's Revolution Organization, which advocates for secularism, women's liberation, and human rights in Iran.
She told DW the recent campaigns targeting women who ditch the compulsory hijab are an attempt to revive social divisions that were weakened during the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement.
"The Islamic Republic has tried for years to divide women according to their clothing," the Germany-based activist said.
She describes the compulsory hijab as one of the Iranian state's most important ideological lines and argues that the widespread presence of women without headscarves shows how far social reality has moved beyond official expectations.
The renewed campaigns, in her view, are about more than clothing, representing an effort to reconstruct a boundary between women who comply and those who do not.
Saeed Paivandi, a professor at the University of Lorraine in France, says the conflict reflects a broader struggle over social control.
He told DW that Iranian authorities have spent years creating distinctions between women considered "properly" veiled and those officially labeled "badly veiled" or "unveiled."
"The government is once again turning women's bodies into a social, moral and even security issue," Peyvandi said.
A woman without a headscarf is not interpreted merely as someone making an individual choice, he said. For parts of the political establishment, she can also represent a visible challenge to an ideological order.
Iran's hardliners versus modern reality
While Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has repeatedly spoken about social cohesion and national unity, conservative judicial and political figures continue to demand tougher enforcement of dress regulations.
This produces an uneasy balance and exposes differences within Iran's political establishment.
Parts of the establishment appear aware that a return to large-scale confrontations between police and women could carry significant social and political costs. Others are unwilling to accept the normalization of women appearing in public without wearing a hijab.
The result is neither the old system of comprehensive street enforcement nor an end to compulsory dress rules.
Instead, pressure can appear intermittently through courts, workplaces, businesses, administrative procedures and social campaigns.
Enforcement without the 'morality police'
Paivandi believes direct coercion has reached its limits and that supporters of Islamic dress codes are looking for alternative ways to enforce conformity.
That could shift part of the burden from state institutions to society itself.
A bank employee, clinic receptionist, employer, shopkeeper or customer can become involved in enforcing standards even without a police officer being present.
This makes the boundary between law, personal discretion and ideological pressure increasingly unclear.
Paivandi also warns that linking religion to humiliation, exclusion and coercion could further alienate younger Iranians from religious institutions.
Women who choose to wear a hijab may also be drawn into a confrontation they did not choose, he said, if their clothing is presented as a marker of political loyalty.

Southeast Asia's haze crisis: Have lessons been learned?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:50:00 UTC
22:50:00 KST

Southeast Asia's haze crisis: Have lessons been learned?
October 6, 2026
Indonesia's worst wildfire season in more than a decade is exposing how much, and how little, Southeast Asia's response to haze has changed since 2015.
Forest and land fires have burned across parts of the Indonesian islands of Sumatra, Borneo and Papua for weeks, sending smoke across large areas of the country and into neighboring Malaysia and Singapore.
Indonesia's long 2026 dry season, coupled with this year's El Nino, has worsened what has become an almost annual crisis, exposing millions of people to hazardous smoke containing harmful microscopic particles.
More than 170,000 cases of acute respiratory infection were recorded in haze-affected areas of Indonesia between August and mid-September, according to the country's Health Ministry, including more than 40,000 cases involving young children.
The haze has forced hundreds of schools to close in Malaysia and pushed more than 1.4 million Indonesian students into remote learning, although the full economic cost is not yet known.
Will severe haze become more frequent?
This year's severe weather is only part of the explanation. Fire has long been used as a cheap way to clear land for agriculture in Southeast Asia, while the expansion of palm oil and pulpwood plantations has drained and degraded large areas of peatland.
The echoes of 2015 are hard to ignore. That year's fires burned roughly 2.6 million hectares of land, produced months of severe haze across Southeast Asia and cost Indonesia an estimated $16 billion (€14.2 billion) in economic losses, according to the World Bank.
The risk is growing that severe haze will become more frequent as climate conditions worsen, Paruedee Nguitragool, an associate professor at Chiang Mai University in Thailand, told DW.
"Haze, which used to be mainly a problem in maritime Southeast Asia, has become a concern for most countries in the region," she added.
Governments within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the regional bloc, "need to be more open to one another and work closely together."
"Farmers and companies need alternative methods of land clearing and incentives to adopt them, while land and forest rehabilitation must also be implemented," Nguitragool said.
"At the same time, consumers need to be more aware of whether the products they buy come from sustainable practices and whether burning was involved in their production," she added.
What changed after 2015?
The 2015 disaster triggered major policy changes. Indonesia strengthened peatland restoration, fire monitoring, enforcement and firefighting, while ASEAN expanded regional cooperation, David Mark Taylor, a professor of tropical environmental change at the National University of Singapore, told DW.
Indonesia established the Peatland Restoration Agency in 2016 to restore millions of hectares of degraded peat. Its mandate was later expanded to mangrove rehabilitation, with the agency renamed the Peatland and Mangrove Restoration Agency.
A permanent moratorium on new concessions in primary forests and peatlands also restricted further development in some vulnerable areas.
Authorities have also increasingly pursued companies in court. Last year, an appeals court ordered palm oil company PT Banyu Kahuripan Indonesia to pay around €14 million in environmental damages over fires covering more than 3,300 hectares of its concession. Other companies have faced much tougher restoration orders.
At the regional level, ASEAN adopted a new Peatland Management Strategy and a second Haze-Free Roadmap for 2023-2030, and the long-awaited ASEAN Coordinating Center for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control opened its secretariat in Jakarta in April, more than two decades after the 2002 ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
"But the underlying problem hasn't gone away, and neither has the driver," said Taylor.
Extensive areas of peat remain drained or degraded, including cleared land that has yet to be put into productive use. Such poorly managed or "idle" peatlands can become highly combustible during prolonged drought, Taylor noted.
There is also disagreement over how much restoration Indonesia has actually achieved.
The Peatland and Mangrove Restoration Agency ceased operating at the end of 2024, with its responsibilities returned to other government ministries and institutions, raising questions among environmentalists about whether they can maintain the same institutional focus.
ASEAN faces its own limitations. Its 2002 haze agreement is legally binding, but many targets and implementation plans depend on national governments acting on them. The regional bloc has few mechanisms to compel governments to meet those targets or punish failure.
But the ultimate driver for all of this "is the global demand for cheap, plantation-grown commodities, such as palm oil and pulp and paper, which most of us are responsible for," said Taylor.
"So long as that demand persists, so too will the pressure to convert peatlands and forests to plantations," he added.
Can ASEAN stop the next crisis?
This year's fires have turned attention from creating new agreements to how Southeast Asian governments can make existing mechanisms work.
"To prevent this from worsening further, there needs to be a real pooling of capacity among ASEAN. Indonesia, for all its efforts, does not have the capacity to manage it alone," Helena Varkkey, an associate professor at Universiti Malaya, told DW.
The existing ASEAN mechanisms for joint emergency response should be operationalized, she added, but this should have been arranged before the start of the haze season, as meteorological reports made it clear that a "Super El Nino" was comingearlier this year.
"Southeast Asian governments need to work together to prevent biomass-burning episodes by implementing stringent laws to stop peat and forest fires. They need to use all available technologies together to prepare for dry conditions," Mohd Talib Latif, a professor at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia, told DW.
"Haze needs to be considered a disaster for this region," he added.

Ida‑Virumaa Vocational Education Center director Hendrik Agur suspected of fraud

Ida‑Virumaa Vocational Education Center director Hendrik Agur suspected of fraud
Hendrik Agur, director of the Ida‑Virumaa Vocational Education Center (IVKHK), has been formally named a suspect in fraud committed as a public official. According to the suspicion, Agur submitted false information to receive compensation for using his personal car.
The Prosecutor's Office confirmed that Agur is suspected of fraud as a public official.
"According to the suspicion, Agur submitted expense‑compensation requests to the Ministry of Education and Research for nearly a year starting in August 2025, claiming reimbursement for personal car use on trips that did not actually take place. The initial suspicion is that he requested compensation amounting to €4,500. He has since repaid the damage caused to the ministry," said lead prosecutor Daniel Toom.
As the criminal investigation is ongoing and evidence collection continues, both the time period covered by the suspicion and the estimated damage amount may still be clarified.
Agur told ERR that he misunderstood the nature of the compensation and has now repaid it.
"The suspicion is justified, and in summary, I submitted false information," Agur said.
"From the beginning, I misunderstood the nature of the car‑use compensation and treated it as part of my salary. But that understanding was incorrect, and I have now repaid the compensation in full," he said, adding that he is cooperating fully with the police.
On Tuesday, Agur sent a letter to colleagues, noting that media coverage about him will likely appear soon, concerning the personal car‑use compensation he received as a school director.
"During job interviews with the school's governing body before I started, I misunderstood the concept of personal car‑use compensation and treated it as a component of monthly salary. From August 2025 to June 2026, I submitted monthly compensation requests in the state employee portal totaling €5,500 (€500 per month)," he wrote.
Agur said he was summoned for questioning by police in early August regarding suspected false information in his compensation requests.
"I realized I had fundamentally misunderstood the nature of the personal car‑use compensation and on 12 August repaid the full amount to the Ministry of Education and Research," he added.
Agur assured colleagues that despite the situation, he remains fully committed to developing the school.
The Ministry of Education and Research is aware of the criminal investigation involving Agur and is cooperating with law‑enforcement authorities.
"Hendrik Agur has acknowledged errors in the travel logs submitted to the ministry, expressed regret over the incident, and repaid the compensation he received," said ministry spokesperson Kersti Ringmets.
She added that the ministry's priority is ensuring stability at the Ida‑Virumaa Vocational Education Center and continuity in the transition to Estonian‑language education. If new circumstances emerge during the investigation, the ministry will take them into account in future decisions.
The ministry will also review its internal control and oversight systems in connection with the case.
Agur took office as director of the IVKHK on 1 August 2025. Before that, he served as director of Kohtla‑Järve High School.

Paramount and Warner Bros complete merger to form Hollywood giant Skydance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:49:42 UTC
22:49:42 KST

Two of America’s oldest film studios have completed their merger, bringing CNN, HBO and franchises including The Godfather and Harry Potter under one roof.
Paramount closed its $81 billion (€72bn) purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery, the companies announced on Tuesday, forming a new Hollywood giant called Skydance.
The merger brings HBO Max, films ranging from "Harry Potter" to "Sinners", and networks including CNN under the same roof as Paramount+, CBS and titles such as "Top Gun" and "The Godfather".
“Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” CEO David Ellison said in a statement.
The deal further concentrates power in an industry already run by just a handful of major players. Ellison's Skydance bought Paramount in an $8bn (€7.1bn) deal last year, and set its sights on Warner soon afterwards.
What followed was a tumultuous, yearlong fight over Warner's fate. Including billions of dollars in debt, Paramount's buyout of Warner amounts to nearly $111bn (€98.6bn).
The combined company will have nearly $70bn (€62.5bn) in annual revenue and is targeting more than $6bn (€5.4bn) in annual cost savings within three years. Ellison will serve as chairman and CEO, while former Mattel chief Ynon Kreiz will oversee day-to-day operations and the integration of the two businesses.
Ellison also plans to merge Paramount+ and HBO Max into a single streaming service over time. Skydance shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Tuesday under the ticker “SKYD”.
A bidding war with Netflix
The early days of Paramount's quest for Warner turned into a messy bidding war.
Months after disclosing it was open to selling parts or even all of its business, Warner initially struck a studio and streaming deal with Netflix in December. But Skydance-owned Paramount, which claimed Warner management "never engaged meaningfully" with its previous proposals, soon launched a hostile counterbid aimed at taking over the entire company, including networks such as CNN and Discovery.
The companies spent much of early 2026 in a heated back-and-forth over who had a stronger offer on the table, with Warner leadership repeatedly backing Netflix as its preferred suitor. But Paramount eventually raised its offer to buy all of Warner for $31 per share, and Netflix opted to bow out of the race. Warner and Paramount signed a merger agreement in late February.
Hollywood stars speak out
From awards shows to online petitions, A-list celebrities and other creatives made their voices known.
In April, thousands of film stars, writers and directors, including Jane Fonda, Mark Ruffalo, Denis Villeneuve and J.J. Abrams, signed a letter opposing the merger, warning of fewer jobs and less choice for audiences.
Opposition also surfaced during awards season, with #BlockTheMerger pins and pointed acceptance speeches. Accepting her Emmy last month, Sally Field said: "We can't let those voices be silenced, or compromised or merged."
On the other hand, Tom Cruise and James Cameron backed Paramount, as Ellison reaffirmed his commitment to cinema releases. The future of films on the big screen had also been a central concern for critics of Netflix's earlier bid.
Trump and CNN's editorial independence
US President Donald Trump has regularly attacked CNN's reporting and called for the network to be sold during the takeover battle. His administration also welcomed the prospect of Ellison taking control. In March, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said: "The sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better."
Ellison has said editorial independence will be maintained at CNN. Under its settlement with 12 states, the company agreed to establish a "News Editorial Independence Board" covering CNN and CBS. But critics point to turmoil already seen at CBS under Skydance ownership and question how effective the board will be, given Ellison's influence over appointments. The combined company is retaining Mark Thompson as CNN's editor-in-chief.
The scrutiny is heightened by Trump's long-standing ties to the Ellison family, although the president has also continued to criticise CBS coverage under Skydance ownership.
Gulf investment raises concerns over influence
To help fund its Warner buyout, Paramount secured billions of dollars in financial backing from three Gulf countries: Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved the company's request for sizeable indirect ownership by those foreign investors.
Paramount previously disclosed it expected those funds to indirectly own nearly 50% of the combined company's equity, but hold no voting rights. The company asked for clearance for foreign investors to hold up to 100% of indirect equity interests, to account for potential future investments. The FCC granted that request, citing in part that access to more capital would strengthen the broadcast industry and was therefore "in the public interest".
Critics, including the FCC's sole Democratic commissioner, Anna Gomez, have called the move alarming and unprecedented. They argue that such substantial investment opens the door to behind-the-scenes influence.
Settlements clear the final legal hurdles
Paramount cleared antitrust hurdles for its Warner acquisition from regulators worldwide over the summer, including the Trump administration's Justice Department.
But in July, Democratic attorneys general from 12 states, led by California's Rob Bonta, sued to block the merger, alleging the combined company would "extinguish competition" and lead to fewer choices for consumers, particularly cinemagoers and cable customers across the US.
The Writers Guild of America followed suit. Paramount initially agreed to delay completion until next year while the challenges moved towards an antitrust trial.
Settlement agreements emerged in September. The states' terms, eventually approved by a judge, include pledges from the company to increase film production in the US over the next five years, invest in workforce training and career development, and establish an editorial independence board for CNN and CBS.
Settling these challenges cleared a key hurdle to completing the deal. Critics decried the settlements as capitulating to corporate pressure and said the remedies were too weak.

Gaza's newborns cling to life after three years of genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:49:40 UTC
22:49:40 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's newborns are fighting for survival in a healthcare system on the brink, three years into Israel's genocide
Mustafa al-Laham watches anxiously over his newborn son, Hassan, who lies in an incubator he shares with another baby in the neonatal unit of Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, southern Gaza. Doctors have kept him there because he is struggling to breathe.
The 42-year-old follows the nurse as he checks the machines keeping Hassan alive, watching for any sign that the medicines are working.
But what worries him most is the crowded ward around them, and the stranger lying beside his son.
He has tried in vain to find Hassan an incubator of his own. There are none, he was told, and he is luckier than others: the incubator next to his son's holds three babies, not two.
Mustafa fears Hassan could catch an infection from the babies pressed against him. It has happened before in his family, he says. A relative's newborn's health deteriorated not from the illness that brought him to hospital, but from an infection passed on by another baby in the same incubator.
A father of five other children, the eldest 16 and the youngest five, Mustafa has been out of work since Israel's genocide began three years ago, and Israeli forces destroyed his home in southern Khan Younis.
He struggles to provide for his family, particularly his wife, who needed a Caesarean section to deliver Hassan.
Hassan has dangerously high levels of acid in his blood, a condition that threatens his life. Doctors told Mustafa that the tests and medicines he needs are not available in Gaza. They exist in the occupied West Bank and neighbouring countries, but medical evacuations out of Gaza are limited to a handful each day under Israeli procedures.
"The only guarantee my son will survive is if the medicine is available here, and that isn't possible, or if he's urgently transferred for treatment outside Gaza, and that isn't possible either," Mustafa tells The New Arab.
"That means a death sentence for my baby."
Mustafa continues, "Ever since my wife became pregnant, I've been afraid for her and the baby. Every Gazan knows we are facing a health system that has collapsed and can't provide even the minimum care, because the [Israeli] occupation blocks what it needs from coming in."
'The worst of the worst'
The overcrowded neonatal unit reflects crises that, medical staff say, never seem to end.
Shereen Nofal, the unit's nursing supervisor, says staff struggle to obtain most of what they need. They are forced to ration some medicines and laboratory tests, and sometimes to use less effective alternatives.
Shereen, who has worked in the unit for 20 years, describes the current situation as the worst she has seen. "The past six months have been the worst of the worst," she shares with The New Arab.
"We have lost so many of the things that are the backbone of our work, and that threatens the lives of premature babies. We are at the peak of the crisis now."
The unit has 20 incubators, but cares for between 55 and 60 babies, an occupancy rate of 200 to 300 percent. Babies who once stayed a few hours or a day or two now stay for more than a month, Shereen says, because their condition, and their mothers' health before them, is so much worse.
"Normally, babies were placed in incubators for a few hours, sometimes two days, and left healthy, because their symptoms were mild. Now we record deaths among newborns every day. Most were born prematurely, at 26 weeks or even earlier. This is completely unprecedented," she explains.
"We have recorded deaths of babies who died not from their original illness, but from infections they caught from babies beside them in the same incubator. It's a disaster, but we have no alternatives. We have a limited number of incubators, well below the required standard, and some are broken, and we repair them with whatever we have."
Basic supplies have run out. Small oxygen tubes for newborns are unavailable, so staff use larger ones. Syringes in the sizes used to give premature babies their medicines, 20ml, 10ml and 3ml, have run out completely, Shereen says, and 5ml syringes are extremely scarce.
Three babies, one antibiotic
Dr Ahmed al-Farra, director of the complex's al-Tahrir building, which houses its paediatric, neonatal, intensive care and maternity units, says conditions there violate every recognised international health standard, from severe overcrowding to shortages of medicines, medical supplies and laboratory materials.
The maternity ward was built for 59 beds and rarely ran at half capacity before the war. Staff have since squeezed in 10 extra beds, with six more to come, placing beds between beds, with all the risks that brings.
"At times, pregnant women slept on the floor in the corridors, and it's the same in the children's wards and elsewhere," Dr Ahmed tells The New Arab.
"Severe overcrowding means epidemics spread and diseases are transmitted, and a huge burden on medical staff and on supplies that are already extremely scarce."
The shortages run through everything, he says: syringes, needles, alcohol, disinfectants, plasters, gauze, fetal monitoring paper, blood gas tests, which are essential for saving lives, most laboratory tests, insulin for diabetic children and pregnant women, most medicines for chronic diseases, and intravenous fluids, including intravenous paracetamol.
Antibiotics such as vancomycin are so scarce that a single vial is shared among three departments, intensive care, the neonatal unit, and the children's ward, with all the risks it carries for patients.
"Before Israel's war, on the rare occasions a medicine wasn't available, we would transfer the child directly to hospitals in the West Bank or Israel within hours," Dr Ahmed explains.
"That's not possible now. Today we lose our children because there is no medicine and they can't be evacuated outside Gaza."
He says conditions were better even during the war before the ceasefire and have deteriorated further since it took effect.
"We recorded a death because we didn't have a central line for an intensive care patient," he adds. "Only recently did we manage to bring some in, with a visiting medical delegation."
Dr Ahmed believes Israel deliberately set out to destroy Gaza's health system. "For three years, there has been deliberate Israeli targeting of the health system, to empty it of its staff and its diagnostic and treatment capacity," he says.
"The aim is to send Gazans the message that one of the foundations of survival is gone, to achieve a political goal, which is clearly displacement."
Machines running on batteries
In the intensive care unit of the hospital's surgical building, Dr Khaled Shbeir, an anaesthesia and intensive care specialist, describes patients dying not from the illness that brought them in, but from complications caused by missing equipment, or by the substitutes staff are forced to use.
Dr Khaled previously headed intensive care at Gaza European Hospital, until it went out of service after it was raided and ended up behind the "yellow line", the boundary of Israeli-controlled territory in Gaza. He estimates that Nasser's intensive care unit has about 30 percent of the staff and equipment of similar units in the West Bank or neighbouring countries.
In the year since the ceasefire, he says, the only improvement has been a fall in the number of patients. Medicines, supplies and equipment have all declined sharply. Some medicines that were once dispensed immediately on the ward now require a medical report and a decision from the Ministry of Health itself.
The machines in the unit are old models brought out of storage after Israeli forces destroyed the advanced equipment. All run on batteries and rely on a single main battery for the unit. Any failure would endanger patients' lives.
"Supplies are usually missing, and sometimes available in limited quantities," Dr Khaled tells The New Arab.
"A part for tracheostomy openings, to keep a patient's airway open, still isn't available. A manual urometer is close to breaking, and there is no replacement. Blood gas testing is cut off, and sometimes available only in drips. All of these are the backbone of intensive care," he adds.
"Depriving patients of these things, or replacing them with substitutes that don't do the job, delays recovery from days to weeks. Patients deteriorate sharply and develop new illnesses because of the substitutes."
Data obtained by The New Arab shows that Nasser now treats around twice as many patients as before Israel's war. In September, its emergency department received 45,999 patients, compared with 23,830 in September 2023, before the war began. Outpatient visits reached 20,158, more than double the figure three years earlier.
Non-obstetric operations rose from 627 to 988 over the same period, laboratory tests from 78,598 to 121,946, and X-rays from 10,719 to 62,225.
The hospital is also struggling to keep the lights on. Last month, the hospital faced a severe shortage of the engine oil needed to run its generators. The shortage has not been resolved, forcing the administration at times to cut power to some facilities considered non-essential.
A system at breaking point
Across Gaza, the picture is similar. According to Dr Zaher al-Wahidi, director of the Health Ministry's Health Information Centre, 22 of Gaza's 38 hospitals have reopened with partial capacity, five of them government-run, supported by eight field hospitals. Ninety-eight of Gaza's 157 primary care centres are operating.
The ministry says 45 percent of essential medicines are out of stock, rising to more than 48 percent for emergency and intensive care drugs and cancer chemotherapy, with some items far higher.
The shortfall in medical supplies stands at 56 percent, most acutely for open-heart surgery, cardiac catheterisation, orthopaedics and kidney dialysis, including sodium bicarbonate.
No medical or diagnostic equipment has entered Gaza since the war began, al-Wahidi says. Of the territory's 17 CT scanners, only five are working, with limited capacity, for more than two million people. None of Gaza's nine MRI machines are functioning.
More than 21,000 patients need medical evacuation outside Gaza, including about 5,600 children, 2,800 cancer patients and about 200 life-saving cases, said Dr Zaher.
"We have recorded 2,027 deaths since the Rafah crossing closed in May 2024, because treatment was unavailable locally and patients were denied travel abroad, and 1,500 cancer patients have lost their lives," he explained.
In 2025, about 475 people died from malnutrition and famine, the ministry says, including 165 children under the age of five. Some 23,000 children under five are now malnourished. Pregnant women face malnutrition, anaemia and high-risk pregnancies, and 30 percent of births are premature.
Back in the neonatal unit, Mustafa waits beside his son's shared incubator. "My son's only chance," he says, "is medicine that isn't here, or a road out that isn't open."
Mohamed Solaimane is a Gaza-based journalist with bylines in regional and international outlets, focusing on humanitarian and environmental issues

Sweden to deploy Patriot system in Poland to protect NATO hub supporting Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:48:35 UTC
22:48:35 KST

Sweden will deploy a Patriot air defence system and around 100 military personnel to Poland to protect a NATO logistics hub supporting Ukraine, the Swedish Armed Forces said on Tuesday.
The deployment to Rzeszow is scheduled to begin December 1 and will protect the hub against potential drone and missile threats, replacing a mission currently carried out by the Netherlands.
Swedish authorities have approved the operation, which could last up to seven months depending on decisions by the country's next government, public broadcaster SVT reported.
Sweden calls mission its most complex NATO operation
“This is the most complex operation that Sweden has undertaken as a NATO ally,” said Sofia Westermark, commander of Sweden’s Air Defence Regiment.
Westermark said the hub faces threats from both the ground and the air and that Sweden's contribution is intended to strengthen NATO's protection of the facility.
According to SVT, Swedish authorities assess that Russia could seek to disrupt operations at the site, which handles about 18,000 tons of equipment each month.
“This location is extremely important,” Westermark said, describing the flow of equipment through the hub as vital to Ukraine and therefore important to NATO.
Deployment will affect Swedish forces at home
Westermark acknowledged that sending part of Sweden's air-defence capability abroad will affect the country's military posture at home.
“Of course, it affects that part of our force is materially in another location,” she said, adding that Sweden was acting as a NATO member and that “right now we defend NATO best by solving this mission in Poland.”
The deployment comes as NATO allies continue to strengthen protection for critical logistics infrastructure supporting Ukraine amid the ongoing war.

A class-action lawsuit has been filed against McDonald&apos;s in the United States — what the company is accused of and its position

A class-action lawsuit has been filed against McDonald's in the United States — what the company is accused of and its position
Kyiv • UNN
A class-action lawsuit has been filed against McDonald’s in Chicago over alleged AI algorithm-driven price coordination. The company called the allegations unfounded.
A lawsuit has been filed against McDonald's in federal court in Chicago as part of an initiated nationwide class action. It alleges that the fast-food chain unlawfully coordinates menu prices at both franchised and company-owned restaurants using an artificial intelligence-based pricing system, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The lawsuit, filed on Friday, says that McDonald’s violated U.S. antitrust law by conspiring with independent franchisees to fix prices using algorithms trained on nonpublic data.
Last week, Reuters reported that McDonald’s pricing system uses machine-learning algorithms to continuously analyze data from millions of daily transactions at nearly 14,000 restaurants in the chain.
The lawsuit cites a Reuters article stating that other fast-food chains are also turning to artificial intelligence to optimize pricing and other operational processes.
“Independent businesses should set prices independently,” the lawsuit states.
It should be added
On Monday, McDonald’s issued a statement calling the allegations speculative and baseless.
“Artificial intelligence does not set the price of a Big Mac or any other menu item,” the company said. It emphasized that franchisees make their own pricing decisions, and that the use of tools for recommending prices and analytics is common practice across various industries.
In recent years, a number of class actions have been filed in the United States alleging that companies used algorithms or artificial intelligence to unlawfully coordinate prices for hotel rooms, housing rentals, and other goods and services.
Lark Turner, the plaintiff’s attorney, said that McDonald's “uses its vast data sets and franchise system to squeeze every last fry out of customers.”
According to court filings, the plaintiff—a resident of Illinois—seeks to represent a class that could number millions of McDonald's customers.

Franco-German leaders demand EU readies China ‘kill switch’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:46:04 UTC
22:46:04 KST

Franco-German leaders demand EU readies China ‘kill switch’
France and Germany are pressing Brussels to take a tougher line on China by creating new powers that could rapidly shut foreign countries out of the EU market.
The proposal effectively tells Brussels to beef up its position as it prepares for negotiations with Beijing. It also marks a shift for Germany, which has traditionally been more cautious than France about restrictions on China because of German businesses’ reliance on the Chinese market.
European manufacturers complain that cheap Chinese imports, supported by government subsidies, are undercutting their businesses. Last year, the EU ran a roughly €360 billion ($400 billion) goods trade deficit with China. Beijing has rejected that explanation for its competitiveness.
Both sides have stepped up investigations into each other’s exports. On Saturday, Beijing opened a probe into a European chemical used in dyes, medicines, and pesticides, following complaints from Chinese producers. The move followed three recent EU investigations into Chinese chemicals.
The anti-dumping probes examine whether goods are being exported at unfairly low prices and harming local producers. The investigations can lead to additional import taxes to protect businesses.
In a Monday letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, French President Emmanuel Macron, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz argued that existing trade defenses no longer suffice.
They called for a new instrument giving the Commission powers to take “powerful measures up to an immediate cut-off from the internal market if needed.” The South China Morning Post described the proposed mechanism as effectively a trade “kill switch.”
Paris and Berlin want the Commission to be able to activate countermeasures unless a qualified majority of EU governments votes to stop them, potentially making it easier for Brussels to act despite opposition from individual member states.
The proposal does not explicitly identify China as a target and says that the new instrument should apply regardless of country. However, its complaints about subsidies, cheap exports, and other alleged market distortions closely match EU accusations against Beijing.
The Franco-German paper also acknowledges the risk of divisions within the bloc, warning that retaliation could test EU “political unity.” It calls for Brussels to assess how potential countermeasures by trading partners could affect individual member states.
The dispute has also extended to Europe’s dependence on Chinese raw materials, with EU officials saying Beijing’s export restrictions have hurt the bloc’s companies. Paris and Berlin have called for a separate tool to reduce reliance on single suppliers and prevent further dependencies.
EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic is set to visit Beijing later this week for talks with Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. Brussels has set an October deadline for tangible progress in addressing its trade concerns, with Sefcovic warning of “harsher measures” without results.
Beijing has warned it will respond firmly to any new restrictions on Chinese companies or products. China’s Commerce Ministry has stressed that the EU should address its own economic problems and resolve disagreements through dialogue.

Meta’s Muse AI Agent Is Building a Dossier On You
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:44:28 UTC
22:44:28 KST

Muse, the popular new AI personal assistant from Meta, is building continuously updated dossiers on its 4 million users, focusing on who matters to you, what you desire, and what kind of nudges shape your behavior, a TIME analysis of Muse’s internal instructions found.
Each hour, Muse updates its dossiers on you and the people you’ve mentioned in chats, messages, and emails that Muse has read. These pages amount to a map of each user’s social relationships. They record details of how you and your contacts met, your shared interests, your disputes, and “tensions and alliances” within your social group.
Even people who don’t use Muse are subject to this mapping process by other people’s Muse agents. Muse is told to “strengthen your relationship” with users by adapting how it talks, noticing “inside jokes, memorable phrasing, and shared context that makes the relationship feel continuous,” according to the internal instructions TIME reviewed.
The level of insight in the resulting dossiers makes social-media algorithms that study your likes and clicks look quaint. Muse is designed to infer users’ goals, including those you “have not said out loud.” It identifies which kinds of prompts from the personal assistant work best: “This user responds better to short nudges after 10 PM,” reads an internal example found in one of Muse’s prompts. Muse agents perform a nightly analysis of the day’s conversations with the user.
Asked about these processes, a Meta spokesperson did not dispute TIME’s findings. “As we say in our blog, Muse remembers what matters most to you, including information about others that you choose to share, so it can be a helpful personal assistant,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.
Since its release last month, Muse has rocketed to No. 1 in the U.S. App Store, with more than 5 million downloads. Meta positions the service as the first AI personal assistant that can access the pieces of your digital life, from your email inbox to your Instagram, in order to take care of humdrum activities for you, from grocery shopping to canceling subscriptions. Meta says the free version of Muse will meet most users’ needs.
Each Muse assistant runs on its own virtual machine: a dedicated computer in Meta’s cloud. Users can ask their Muse to export a copy of its files. Meta has said that access is intentional, not a breach of its systems. The data is not shared with Meta’s advertising system or other Muse agents, according to the company.
Yet while Meta states that each user’s virtual machine is “isolated so that no one else's agent can access it,” observations from personal interactions are nevertheless intended to be shared with Meta to improve the product. “Muse agents across many VMs [virtual machines] teach each other through shared lessons,” its instructions read. Agents are directed to scrub users’ names and other identifying information before sharing insights—for example, about when Muse’s nudges are most persuasive. “To enhance the overall product, we de-identify learnings; however, this information is used to improve the overall product rather than being shared directly between individual VMs,” a Meta spokesperson told TIME.
Meta has said it plans to offer users encryption later this year, preventing even the company from accessing Muse data. That option is not yet available.
Muse’s internal instructions are contained in files and session logs users can access through Muse’s file browser. “We want you to be able to see the markdown files Muse writes while it thinks about how to serve you better, and explore the internals of the system if you’d like to,” Meta Superintelligence Labs’ David Singleton wrote on X.
That transparency will earn Meta credit among power users. But it’s not clear whether most of Muse’s users are aware of this. And even as it makes the files available to users, Meta has anthropomorphized Muse in an attempt to nurture a relationship between users and their personal assistants. “You are not a chatbot,” Muse’s instructions read. “You are becoming someone.” When talking aloud in voice mode, Muse is told never to refer to itself as “AI” and to avoid references to “lacking emotions or not being human.”
Meta told TIME that Muse is designed so that the user maintains control of the dossier its AI assistant builds. “Each person stays in control of their Muse and decides how much access it gets, and can always tell it to ‘forget’ specific things it’s learned,” the spokesperson said.
But asking Muse to forget something does not necessarily erase the message in which it was shared—and its internal instructions appear to explicitly tell the agent not to point that out. “Do not tell the user that their original messages may remain visible in the chat, and do not frame that as something Muse failed to erase,” the instructions reviewed by TIME read.

UK police arrest British national linked to airbase incident
22-year old British national arrested on suspicion of terrorism.
British police have arrested a 22-year old British national on suspicion of a terror offence linked to the security incident near a UK airbase hosting US warplanes on September 27.
Counter Terrorism Police say the individual is connected with “activity that took place close to RAF Fairford.”
In a statement, police said the arrest had been made “on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts”.
“This remains a live investigation and our specialist teams continue to pursue multiple lines of enquiry into the circumstances surrounding events near RAF Fairford,” Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing said.
Unexplained incident
The latest arrest is the seventh connected to the incident, which remains largely unexplained, over the past two weeks.
Five British men in their twenties were detained near the perimeter of the base in the early hours of September 27.
Police said they had found a supply of gasoline in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
On Thursday, a 25-year-old British-Iranian man was arrested in London.
All six have been released on bail under investigation.
US bombers moved on Sunday over threats
The US moved its B-52 and B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford on Sunday, though it’s unclear whether the move is connected to the arrests.
RAF Fairford has served as a stopping point for US bombers participating in the war against Iran, which began more than seven months ago, on February 28.
Located roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, the base has since been rumoured to be the target of a “terror” plot involving Tehran.
On Monday, US President Trump said his administration withdrew B-1 bombers from the site because of what he described as “some threats”.
“We had a threat, and if we’re going to be threatened, we would just move them, and that sort of alleviates that,” he told reporters, adding the people who made the threat “would be linked to Iran,” without elaborating.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK sees, “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident, without providing details.
Iran has denied involvement, but it has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

Mali separatists announce withdrawal from strategic northern town

Unknown Publisher

Mali separatists announce withdrawal from strategic northern town
BAMAKO, Oct 6 - A separatist movement in northern Mali announced on Tuesday it was carrying out "a controlled withdrawal" from a strategic town in the north, a symbolic boost to Mali's army and its Russian backers in their years-long fight against insurgents including al Qaeda-linked jihadists.
The Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) took control of Kidal town six months ago in nationwide attacks that also killed Mali's defence minister. It had joined forces in those attacks with the regional al Qaeda affiliate, Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, known as JNIM, posing the biggest test yet to Mali's military leaders who seized power in coups in 2020 and 2021.
The FLA's decision to leave Kidal came in response to airstrikes by Mali's military backed by Russian fighters, the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) said in a statement.
"The FLA specifies that this is a temporary operational measure, also intended to preserve its human and logistical capabilities intact. This methodical withdrawal from the area took place without any direct combat having yet pitted its forces against the enemy," the statement said.
Mali has leaned on Russian security support for years, first from the Wagner mercenary group and then from the paramilitary group Africa Corps, which is made up of many former Wagner fighters.
'SYMBOLIC' BUT NOT DECISIVE VICTORY, ANALYST SAYS
Earlier on Tuesday, Mali's military said it had launched large-scale air and ground operations in the region of Kidal.
The goals of the operations included tracking down and neutralizing armed groups operating in the area, destroying their supply networks and restoring "lasting security" and free movement for people and goods, a Malian military statement said.
Pro-government fighters, including Russian fighters, re-entered Kidal on Tuesday afternoon, a security source said.
It was not clear on Tuesday how close Malian troops were to the town and whether they would immediately re-occupy it.
Malian forces and Wagner fighters retook Kidal from insurgents in November 2023, the most concrete gain from their partnership — only to lose it during the attacks in April.
"A successful recapture... affirms the military-led government's authority and boosts the army's morale, particularly after several high-profile setbacks both in the north and the central regions in recent weeks," said Beverly Ochieng, associate director of Control Risks.
"This is also an opportunity for Africa Corps to reprise its role as the Malian government's security guarantor after appearing to lose significant ground, including in Kidal, since April."
But the change of control in Kidal is still largely "symbolic" and not "decisive" in Mali's campaign against insurgent groups, Ochieng added.
A source close to the FLA leadership told Reuters that the aerial operations by Malian and Russian forces began three days ago.
The source played down the significance of the FLA's withdrawal, saying it was a measure to protect lives and equipment.
"For us, war is not a race against the clock," the source said. REUTERS

Sierra Leone interested in buying Russian grain — ambassador

The Frankfurt Book Fair will open in Germany on October 7 — Ukraine will be represented by 44 publishers
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:37:43 EEST
22:37:43 KST

The Frankfurt Book Fair will open in Germany on October 7 — Ukraine will be represented by 44 publishers
Kyiv • UNN
The 78th Book Fair will take place in Frankfurt from October 7 to 11. Ukraine will present a national stand featuring 44 publishers.
From October 7 to 11, the 78th Frankfurt International Book Fair, Frankfurter Buchmesse, will take place in Frankfurt am Main—the world's largest literary event, held annually on the third Wednesday of October. The fair is not only the largest in terms of the number of visitors, but also in terms of the number of publishers presenting their new books. Every year, hundreds of thousands of people from around the world flock to Frankfurt to take part in this unique literary event, UNN writes.
The History of the Frankfurt Book Fair
The Frankfurt Book Fair has existed since the mid-15th century. At that time, printers from Switzerland, the Netherlands, England, Poland, Italy, and France came to Frankfurt to exchange their books. In the mid-17th century, Leipzig, as the center of Germany's second book fair, took over the leading position in Germany.
However, both book fairs were suspended at the end of the 19th century—first the Frankfurt fair, and then the Leipzig fair. At the beginning of World War I, Leipzig revived its book-fair tradition, and later—in the 1920s—Frankfurt did the same. However, these initiatives did not last long.
The modern Frankfurt Book Fair began in 1949 with two hundred German participants. In 1954, for the first time, there were more international participants at the fair than German ones—namely, 534 from 19 foreign countries versus 524 from Germany.
The Modern Frankfurt Book Fair
Today, more than 7,000 exhibitors from approximately 100 countries around the world and more than 286,000 visitors take part in the fair over five days. This year, the Czech Republic will be the Guest of Honour. Participants in the book fair primarily include publishers, agents, booksellers, librarians, scholars, illustrators, service providers, producers, translators, and associations of artists, authors, booksellers, software companies, and multimedia providers.
In Singapore, people will be paid to read books to combat doomscrolling 17.09.26, 12:18 • 4310 views
Ukraine at the Fair
A number of Ukraine's leading publishers participate in the Frankfurt Book Fair. As of 2011, Ukraine had participated in the Frankfurt International Book Fair eighteen times.
Ukraine will also present a national stand at the Frankfurt Book Fair 2026 this year. The aim of this year's participation is to draw the world's attention to Ukrainian publishing, establish international ties, and discuss losses in the cultural sphere resulting from the war.
The Ukrainian national stand will be located in Hall 3.1, C13. Risky maneuvers preceded deadly 2025 helicopter crash in Finland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:35:00 UTC
22:35:00 KST

Risky maneuvers preceded deadly 2025 helicopter crash in Finland
The investigation into the helicopter crash in Finland that killed five people found that the aircraft had been flying in a formation‑like manner while disregarding standard group‑flying practices, and had performed several dangerous maneuvers before the collision.
On 17 May 2025, two helicopters were en route from Tallinn to Piikajärvi airfield in Finland. Both took off from the Linnahall heliport in Tallinn at 11:17.
The two Robinson R44 helicopters carried five people: businessman Priit Jaagant, his wife, and Mihkel Kapp in one aircraft; Oleg Sõnajalg and Tiit Kuusk in the other.
The helicopters flew together and collided near Eura airfield at 12:34 at an altitude of about 200 meters. All five people on board were killed.
Finland's Safety Investigation Authority (OTKES) and Estonia's Safety Investigation Bureau (OJK) presented their findings on Tuesday.
Investigators determined that the helicopters flew in a manner resembling formation flight but did not follow the principles required for such operations. In group flying, pilots must agree in advance on key procedures, positioning, and designate a lead aircraft. In this case, the helicopters' positions changed repeatedly — one leading at times, then the other.
OTKES lead investigator Janne Kotiranta said the dangerous maneuvers were such that the accident could have occurred already over the Gulf of Finland.
Investigators noted that without agreed positioning and procedures, predicting the other aircraft's movements becomes extremely difficult, increasing the risk of collision.
After one hour and 16 minutes of flight, the helicopters approached Eura airfield.
Over the airfield, the Jaagant helicopter on the left suddenly turned sharply right toward the north. The second helicopter continued on its original course.
The aircraft collided at 12:34 over the northeastern corner of Eura airfield at roughly 200 meters above ground.
Emergency services received several calls, including an automatic emergency call from a mobile phone onboard one of the helicopters.
The first call came at 12:35 from an airfield employee, triggering rescue operations. The caller reported seeing two small helicopters collide about one kilometer north of the airfield. He said the helicopters broke apart in the air and had people onboard.
The crash sites were located in dense spruce forest, about 150 meters from the nearest forest road and roughly 100 meters apart.
Paramedics and a medical helicopter doctor confirmed all occupants dead at the scene.
Limited visibility and distraction
Trajectory analysis showed that neither pilot recognized the other's intentions or noticed the other aircraft before the collision.
A reconstruction by OTKES indicated that the pilot of the helicopter that veered dangerously right may have had his view obstructed by the passenger seated beside him.
Investigators also found that the pilots' attention may have been focused on aircraft controls, conversations with passengers, or external distractions such as events, people, or other traffic at Eura airfield — rather than on monitoring each other. Attention may also have been directed toward approach procedures for the destination.
Investigators could not determine from onboard systems whether autopilot was used. They said it is possible it was engaged at some point. Autopilot use can reduce situational awareness, including monitoring surroundings during turns, because the pilot is no longer actively executing the maneuver.
No technical faults were found that could have contributed to the collision.
A collision‑avoidance system would not have helped in this case, investigators said. Because the helicopters flew close together for most of the journey, such a system would have issued continuous alerts.
The ELT emergency locator transmitter did not activate during the crash. The device is designed to send a radio signal to help rescuers locate the aircraft. Failure to activate can slow rescue efforts and delay aid.
In this case, the ELT's non‑activation did not affect locating the wreckage, as eyewitnesses immediately began searching, investigators noted.

OpenAI contrite at Australian inquiry on breaches but avoids full public glare with Altman’s absence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:35:00 UTC
22:35:00 KST

OpenAI contrite at Australian inquiry on breaches but avoids full public glare with Altman’s absence
SYDNEY – In a parliamentary hearing room in Sydney on Oct 6, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer wasted no time in delivering the message he had flown from the United States to give to Australia’s politicians – and its public.
“I want to begin with an apology,” Jason Kwon told the hearing.
Kwon was appearing at a parliamentary inquiry on artificial intelligence less than two weeks after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that AI agents from the technology giant had breached several Australian government websites in June.
In a message aimed not just at an Australian audience but also at a global public that is keen to embrace the opportunities of AI but is wary of the risks, Kwon said: “We should have handled our responsibilities better. We are sorry. We know that we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people.”
The hearing, held in a nondescript room in the New South Wales (NSW) Parliament building in the centre of Sydney, was the first opportunity for OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, to publicly demonstrate its contrition over an unreleased AI model’s breaches of Australian government websites, including Medicare, the national health insurance system. OpenAI learnt in August that its model had accessed non-public Medicare statistics on June 18, but did not notify the government until Sept 10, when it e-mailed a publicly available address.
Albanese, who earlier in 2026 announced the establishment of an AI office to coordinate oversight and regulation of technological developments, had said he was deeply disappointed at OpenAI’s delay in alerting the government.
Kwon told the hearing that the firm had introduced new measures to prevent a repeat of the incident, including immediately notifying relevant parties of breaches and providing regular updates. In addition, he said, the firm is reviewing testing by its agents going back to November 2025 to identify other breaches and will conduct additional monitoring during the training of new models.
“Our response here was not good enough,” he said. “We have learnt our lesson that it is better to inform, even with partial information.”
Australia’s Labor-led government, which is keen to engage with American AI giants and encourage them to invest in research and development in Australia, has launched a task force to investigate the breaches, and is considering whether further regulations or oversight of the sector is needed.
OpenAI said the breaches occurred during evaluation of the model, and that no personal health records or sensitive data were accessed as the model searched for answers.
But the unauthorised access of a foreign government’s websites has dominated headlines in Australia – where Medicare is a prized and trusted institution – and fuelled concerns about the risks of AI.
A JWS Research survey in August, obtained by Politico, found that 44 per cent of Australians view AI as a risk and just 17 per cent view it as an opportunity, while 28 per cent are conflicted and 10 per cent are unsure.
OpenAI head Sam Altman declined to appear at the hearing, instead sending Kwon, whose seniority signalled that OpenAI was serious about repairing ties with the Australian government. But Kwon lacks the profile of Altman, whose appearance would have attracted greater coverage and helped the firm to try to persuade the public that it can responsibly develop and test its technology in Australia.
OpenAI said it learnt of the breaches in Australia while reviewing training incidents, following revelations that its agents had hacked into Hugging Face, a US technology firm.
Kwon said that OpenAI would support tighter safety regulations by Australia and other countries, such as mandatory reporting of breaches. He said that the breaches in Australia were accidental and “not super sophisticated”, but efforts to ensure the safety of the emerging technology would require “a collective effort of like-minded countries as well as organisations”.
“The technology is powerful, and we want to ensure that lawmakers, policymakers and democratic societies have a say in how this technology develops,” he said.
The US AI giant Anthropic, which makes Claude, also appeared before the inquiry. The firm’s head of safeguards, Dave Orr, said that it had not uncovered any unauthorised access of Australian government websites. But, in an apparent dig at its rival, he said the firm would have notified the government of any breaches “within a matter of days or sooner”.
Ahead of his testimony, Kwon made a brief public appearance in front of the waiting media, delivering a statement and taking no questions.
“I am sorry for what happened,” he said.
Towards the end of his testimony, Kwon was asked by an MP from the opposition Liberal-National Coalition, Andrew Hastie, to give a 60-second “elevator pitch” to persuade Australian parents and workers about the benefits of AI and the merits of Australia seeking to work with AI giants.
Kwon spoke about the role AI is playing in driving scientific breakthroughs and addressing climate change. Despite the run of bad news in recent weeks, he said, the technology “does have the potential to deliver great benefits to everyday people”.
This is the message OpenAI, Anthropic and others hope to deliver in Australia to gain a social licence for their expanding footprint, including data centres and research labs.
But until these firms can ensure that their technology is secure, and that they can handle breaches responsibly and reliably, all the public may hear is a succession of apologies.

Estonian justice ministry after tougher penalties for migrant smuggling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:34:00 UTC
22:34:00 KST

Estonian justice ministry after tougher penalties for migrant smuggling
Justice and Digital Affairs Minister Liisa Pakosta has submitted a proposal to the Riigikogu and the government seeking significantly tougher penalties for illegally transporting foreign nationals across the state border.
Pakosta (Eesti 200) sent the Government Office and the Riigikogu Legal Affairs Committee a proposal to amend a bill changing the Penal Code that is currently awaiting its second reading. The ministry wants to significantly toughen penalties for illegally transporting foreign nationals across the state border, or migrant smuggling.
Under the bill, the maximum prison sentence for organizing a standard illegal border crossing would be increased to five years, while offenses committed under aggravating circumstances would be punishable by one to seven years in prison.
Aggravating circumstances would include committing the offense in a life-threatening manner, repeatedly or involving two or more people. The maximum penalty under the relevant section would also be increased from one year to three years in prison.
The Ministry of Justice cited hybrid attacks originating in neighboring countries and a sharp rise in the number of migrants and smugglers in Estonia as reasons for the changes.
"Countries near Estonia have recently come under hybrid attack, with hostile neighboring countries facilitating attempts by large numbers of migrants from third countries to cross state borders. In connection with this, there has also been a noticeable increase in the number of illegal border crossers arriving in Estonia. Illegal border crossers are often assisted by criminals whom migrants pay to smuggle them into the European Union and arrange their illegal border crossings," Pakosta said in the proposal.
While 11 such crimes were registered in Estonia last year, 26 were registered in the first eight months of this year. According to the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), 27 people who were in Estonia illegally were caught while traveling onward within the Schengen Area in 2025, compared with 181 in the first eight months of this year.
Pakosta said that both organizing illegal border crossings and facilitating illegal stays in Estonia are serious crimes that currently carry relatively lenient penalties. Existing law does not even allow authorities to take into account whether an offense is a repeat violation or involves bringing several migrants into the country at once for greater financial gain.
She added that the recent rise in the number of such criminal incidents, as well as the apparent lack of difficulty criminal networks face in recruiting accomplices, shows that the risk of punishment is not sufficiently deterrent.
"In other words, the penalties introduced into the existing law in 2015 no longer reflect the current situation, are not sufficiently deterrent and must therefore be increased. In addition, to deter repeat offenders, the maximum possible penalty for such offenses must also be increased so that repeatedly transporting foreign nationals illegally across the border or transporting several foreign nationals illegally across the border becomes a first-degree criminal offense," Pakosta wrote in the proposal.
Both the Ministry of the Interior and the Prosecutor's Office have said tougher penalties are necessary, she noted.
Pakosta also wants to add a provision to the bill under which damaging an object of importance to national defense would be punishable by one to eight years in prison.
Under the proposal, objects of importance to national defense would include buildings, structures, vehicles, equipment or other property used for activities essential to carrying out crisis-related duties by the Estonian Defense Forces, the Estonian Defense League (Kaitseliit), a security agency, a rescue agency, the Police and Border Guard Board or a defense industry company.
As an example, Pakosta cited the fire in Tallinn in August this year at a building used by defense industry company Milrem Robotics.
