Tigray war may spill over to Eritrea — helped by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's rhetoric
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:32:00 UTC
22:32:00 KST

Ethiopia: Abiy begins new term as regional tensions mount
October 6, 2026
Amid escalating conflict in Ethiopia's northernmost Tigray region, Abiy Ahmed has been sworn in for another term as Prime Minister of Ethiopia.
Shortly after the ceremony on Monday afternoon, Abiy reiterated his will to work toward giving the landlocked country direct access to the Red Sea.
"Based on the principle of give and take, we will work diligently to ensure that Ethiopia has an outlet to the sea," Abiy said, a remark that risks exacerbating tensions with neighboring Eritrea. The two countries have been at odds over Ethiopia's desire to control Eritrea's port of Assab.
DW correspondent Solomon Muchie, who followed the swearing-in ceremony in Addis Ababa, said despite the renewed mandate, Abiy faces challenging times ahead.
"The new term gives Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed stronger political authority," Solomon said. "But the country's complex internal and regional challenges could make it difficult to translate the authority into lasting stability."
Sunday's meeting in Cairo of countries that opposed Ethiopia was a case in point, Munchie said. "The leaders of Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan discussed regional issues, but Ethiopia was excluded from this meeting, so this is also what Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government will face in his tenure in the coming years."
Ethiopia still eyeing Eritrea's port of Assab
For analyst Abdurahman Sayed, who leads the London-based Horn of Africa Center for Regional Integration, Eritrea now faces an imminent threat of entering the war in Tigray. This comes after a three-year Ethiopian campaign to gain control of the port of Assab.
"Eritrea has legitimate concern of Ethiopia's intentions to occupy [the country] if it can, and then if not, then at least take the port of Assab, which is a very important port, not only for commercial purposes but also strategically," Sayed said.
"It oversees the Bab el Mandeb [Strait], which is the southern entrance to the Red Sea. Now, without that port, Eritrea's strategic significance would be reduced to almost nil, so there wouldn't be any importance of Eritrea."
Last week, Ethiopia severed its diplomatic ties with Eritrea and Egypt. According to Sayed, this might be a sign that the government is determined to pursue its push for the Red Sea port by force.
The renewed fighting in Tigray might point in that direction. Just days ago, the Ethiopian National Defence Forces took control of Tigray's capital, Mekelle.
On Monday, a pro-government media outlet reported that the Ethiopian army had begun mobilizing its troops towards the Eritrean border, following a movement of the opposed Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) retreating to the area near Adigrat, an important gateway to Eritrea and the Red Sea.
"The Tigrayan people have cultural, linguistic and religious links with those in southern Eritrea," Sayed said. "In fact, the ones in power in Eritrea have many more similarities with those in Tigray."
He added that there could be a spillover effect, especially now that the TPLF is out of Mekelle, and they might be out of major towns as well. "So they might go for a kind of ragtag fighting tactic."
According to Sayed, the Ethiopian government and army are only waiting for Eritrea to enter the war.
"They've already been making allegations without substantiating them, without any evidence, that the Eritrean army is already in Ethiopia fighting against the Ethiopian government. Although the truth is the Ethiopian rebel movements, they are quite well experienced in fighting, and they have plenty of armaments and so on," Sayed said.
"So there is not much need for the Eritrean army to be there physically to support them. But the Ethiopians would love to see that, so they can justify their attack on Eritrea by claiming that they were the first one to be attacked, and therefore they were now responding to that attack."
Calls for diplomacy
While allegiances in the Horn of Africa region and the Near East have been much debated in the context of the recent crisis, actors from the global North have remained relatively silent — though experts like Abdurahman Sayed have welcomed a statement by the United States for diplomatic efforts to be renewed.
One decisive factor, then, might revolve around access to Djibouti, the one Horn of Africa country with which Ethiopia has long been on good terms. At a recent webinar by the independent conflict monitor ACLED, the institution's senior East Africa analyst, Dr. Jalale Getachew Birru, elaborated on this.
"Ethiopia's main trade route is through Djibouti, and that is why we're seeing one of the fronts being within [Ethiopia's adjacent region] Afar. Just like in the previous war, the TPLF wants to control the main route from Djibouti to Addis Ababa," Jalale said.
She also said that, since Israel officially recognized Somalia's autonomous Somaliland region as an independent state, the past year has brought a new dynamic to diplomatic relations in the Horn.
"This also includes Djibouti sometimes aligning with Eritrea, Egypt and so on, but they're also trying to remain neutral," Jalale said.
At the moment, however, both Ethiopia and Djibouti seem to be determined to maintain the trade from which they both profit.
"There is also hyperinflation in Ethiopia," Abdurahman Sayed said. "And if there is a shortage of supplies and oil, that can cause major pressure on the Ethiopian government between yesterday and today."
Also, Djibouti, located strategically at the entrance to the Red Sea, hosts many international airbases, including those of the US, China, France, Italy, and Japan. Cutting off the country's trade route to mainland Africa could be the tipping point that finally prompts international players to speak up and pressure Ethiopia to end the conflict.

Ukrainian Ground Forces establish drone unit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Ukrainian Ground Forces establish drone unit
This was reported by a Ukrinform correspondent.
“Our Drone Forces are not a separate, newly formed branch of the military; rather, we have a deeply integrated system within the Ground Forces that includes not just a single UAV or unmanned aerial vehicle, but numerous units and a wide range of assets. And when videos of specific targets being struck appear in the media or on social media, everyone should understand that it wasn’t just the operator and the drone that carried out the strike—it’s an entire ecosystem. To strike a specific target, you need to train the pilot, plan the mission, and equip that pilot with the necessary resources. And behind every mission stands an entire team of people. That is why we believe that we created the Drone Forces precisely to ensure that it is an integrated system combining all components into a single whole,” emphasized Andrii Ostapenko, head of the Unmanned Systems Department of the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ Ground Forces Command.
He added that in many armies around the world, unmanned systems either constitute a separate branch of the military or are part of the Air Force.
“In our Army, however, unmanned systems units are present in all general-purpose units: in all artillery units, as well as in support units and reconnaissance units. In other words, unmanned systems are integrated throughout our forces,” Ostapenko explained, adding that unmanned systems units participate in both defensive and offensive operations and carry out various logistical and support missions, among others.
As event participants noted during the presentation, the Drone Forces—as a new philosophy of modern warfare—originated within the Army itself. It all began with the so-called “wedding drones,” which the infantry first adapted for tactical reconnaissance and improvised airdrops. In a matter of months, this amateur experience transformed into a systematic set of capabilities—from the first airdrops to high-precision, long-range “middle strike” strikes deep into enemy defenses.
“Today, drones on the front lines carry out the lion’s share of all combat operations. The numbers speak for themselves: up to 80% of strikes against enemy personnel and 70% of all reconnaissance are carried out by drones. Moreover, drones have taken over up to 90% of frontline logistics and account for half of all evacuations of the wounded from under fire. Drones are no longer an experiment. They have become the foundation of the Army’s combat power,” the event participants noted during the presentation.
The Army also noted that modern drones constitute a large-scale two-dimensional ecosystem. A full range of aircraft is in operation in the air—from precision strike FPV drones and heavy bombers to long-range reconnaissance drones and “middle strike” systems. On the ground, drone systems are being deployed across three critical areas: strike platforms for assaults and fire support, logistics platforms for delivering cargo and ammunition, and evacuation drones that extract the wounded from life-threatening zones.
To date, the Ground Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine have implemented a comprehensive vertical structure: every battalion has a drone company, every brigade has a drone battalion, and every corps has a drone regiment.
“The Army’s drone forces are not abstract technologies of the future, but a fully integrated, day-to-day combat component of combat units. They save the lives of our soldiers, enable instant decision-making, and provide absolute technological superiority along every meter of the front line. The Army is setting a new standard for modern warfare, one that the entire world is adopting right now,” the presentation participants emphasized.
During the event, spokespeople from various Army units spoke about their experiences in forming drone forces, as well as the recruitment and training of service members tasked with engaging the enemy using drones.
Responding to a question about the increased use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and drones on the front lines, Ostapenko noted that currently, most tasks previously performed by humans are now carried out by drones and robotic systems. These include the delivery of ammunition and food, medical evacuation, mine laying, and more.
Participants in the event also emphasized that drones and drone systems do not replace humans on the front lines, but they do change the way humans fight battles and wage war.
As reported by Ukrinform, over the past day, on October 5, 184 combat engagements between the Ukrainian Defense Forces and Russian invaders were recorded on the front lines, with the highest number occurring in the Pokrovsk direction.

The Gaza genocide permanently diminished the power of pro-Israel propaganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

For nearly 40 years, Gallup has been asking Americans a series of questions about the Middle East and U.S. policy in the region.
One of those frequent questions is, “In the Middle East situation, are your sympathies more with the Israelis or more with the Palestinians?“
In 2003, just 16% of Democrats said that they sympathized more with Palestinians than Israelis. When the annual survey was carried out this past February, that number had ballooned to 65%.
There are many reasons for this dramatic shift.
2003 was the year that the United States launched its war on Iraq, spurred by government lies and a post-9/11 bloodlust that permeated a sizable chunk of U.S. society. 2026 also saw the United States launch a war in the Middle East, but this one is broadly unpopular with the population, which has naturally grown skeptical of foreign conflict after 20-plus years of disastrous Forever Wars.
The tireless work of Palestine activists has also increased support for the cause, as Americans have developed a deeper understanding of Israeli apartheid and occupation. These efforts found particular resonance during the Black Lives Matter protests of 2020, as many activists stressed the connections between liberation at home and abroad.
However, the biggest reason for the jump is obviously the Gaza genocide and U.S. support for it. Since Israel’s war on Gaza began three years ago, conservative estimates say 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, and more than 175,000 have been injured. More than 1,400 have been killed and nearly 5,000 injured since the Trump administration declared a “ceasefire” on October 10, 2025.
Those Gallup results are just a small part of a vast trove of polling showing that Americans have completely flipped on the issue, and although Democratic voters have soured on Israel at a higher rate, the shift is certainly not limited to one political party.
Here’s some more:
- A Pew report from this past spring found that 60% of U.S. adults have an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 53% in 2025. The country is viewed unfavorably by 41% of Republicans, but that number is 57% among Republicans aged 18-49.
- In addition to Democrats, the aforementioned Gallup poll shows that Independents sympathize with Palestinians more than Israelis, 41% to 30%, for the first time since the analytics company began conducting the surveys.
- A recent Marquette Law School poll found that favorability toward Israel has been steadily declining for the last 20 months.
In a recent interview about AIPAC, investigative reporter Eli Clifton told Mondoweiss that, because of the country’s actions in the region, the propaganda of pro-Israel lobbying organizations just isn’t hitting like it used to.
“I think some of this is out of their control. Images of dead children and civilians continue to flow out of Gaza. The mainstream media hasn’t been the best at covering it, but with social media now, it’s very hard to suppress the scale of what is going on in Gaza, or the settler violence in the West Bank, or the violence against various communities, including Christians in Lebanon,” said Clifton.
“This stuff horrifies people, and it’s significantly responsible for shifting public opinion. People get facts on the ground in a manner that they had previously been denied and I think as long as the facts continue to be this way where Israel is occupying lands, people don’t have equal rights in Israel, they continue to engage in these wars on multiple fronts, they continue to engage in genocide in Gaza, there’s a limited amount that AIPAC can do.”
“They are deeply, deeply unpopular with Democrats and increasingly unpopular with Republicans and even with Christian evangelicals,” he added. “That poses a nearly insurmountable challenge for them.”
Similar sentiments have openly been expressed by Israeli leaders.
“What concerns me—and I believe it should concern every American leader—is a troubling trend in public opinion, particularly among younger Americans,” wrote former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett in a July Time op-ed. “Surveys show growing skepticism about Israel among the next generation of U.S. citizens. I do not believe this reflects their true values. American young people are, overwhelmingly, decent and justice-seeking. This is not merely Israel’s problem. It is America’s problem, too. In my opinion, the same forces working to delegitimize Israel are working to undermine the Western alliance, democratic institutions, and American leadership itself. Countering this shift is a shared responsibility—and an urgent one.”
Will Israel’s PR crisis actually result in a rethinking of U.S. foreign policy? There certainly doesn’t seem to be any big changes on the horizon, as Israel has continued to receive an effective blank check regardless of which party occupies the White House. In this sense, Israel has simply become yet another issue, like health care and the environment, where U.S. lawmakers are completely out of step with their constituents.
However, the ultimate fate of the “special relationship” remains unwritten, as the domestic struggle continues. Since the genocide, we have seen the issue permeate our political discourse and even watched some successful candidates highlight the issue on the campaign trail. Congress has even begun to slowly move. When Senator Bernie Sanders introduced an amendment aimed at blocking arms sales to Israel in November 2024, just 18 senators backed him. In April of this year, 40 of the 47 Democrats voted to block a sale of bulldozers to the country.
This is obviously wildly insufficient, but it’s clear that this is no longer a third-rail issue in Washington and, barring an absolute miracle, it seems unlikely that it will ever emerge as one again.

Feature: Chinese beekeeping expertise opens new opportunities for Kenyan women
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
21:29:35 CST
22:29:35 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Grace Cheserem, chairperson of the Lelkolo women's group in Kenya's Baringo County, still remembers her first honey harvest in 2022.
Wearing a protective veil, she carefully opened a beehive, hearing little more than her own breathing as she pulled out the first comb. The golden honey glistened in the sunlight, drawing cheers from the women gathered around her.
In local communities, beekeeping had long been regarded as men's work. Traditional hives were often placed high in trees, making honey harvesting physically demanding, while beekeeping was once considered taboo for women.
Today, the 21-member women's group has learned to manage beehives and harvest honey themselves, and has begun running their own honey business.
In 2025, the group harvested 612 kg of honey and earned about 500,000 Kenyan shillings (around 3,850 U.S. dollars) from sales.
Behind the change is agricultural extension officer Aholipama Chelagat Rutto, who brought beekeeping techniques she learned in China to the local community.
In 2017, Rutto traveled to China's Changsha, a central Chinese city, to attend a training program on bee production and oil-crop yield improvement, organized by China's Ministry of Commerce and undertaken by a local agricultural science and technology institution.
Before the trip, Rutto's knowledge of beekeeping was largely theoretical. "I learned some things at school, such as the history, life cycle and behavior of bees, but I had not learned beekeeping production in depth," she said.
In China, she received systematic training in apiary construction, colony breeding and hive management, and learned techniques for pest and disease control, honey maturity assessment and honey extraction.
One technique that particularly impressed her was artificial colony splitting. "Previously, beekeepers in Kenya would usually just put a hive there and wait for bees to move in," she said. "In China, I learned how to actively divide one colony into several colonies."
After returning to Kenya, Rutto began sharing what she had learned with local women. "I wanted them to gain more skills and become economically independent," she said.
In Baringo, where women often shoulder responsibilities including fetching water, doing household chores, and caring for children, Rutto saw beekeeping as a practical option for earning additional income. "It takes relatively little of their daily time and can provide income," she said.
Rutto began promoting modern hives, including Langstroth hives, together with protective clothing and specialized tools.
Compared with traditional hives, the equipment lowered the barriers to beekeeping and honey harvesting. Langstroth hives could be placed closer to the ground, while protective clothing and specialized tools enabled women to gradually handle the entire process themselves, from inspecting colonies to harvesting honey, according to Rutto.
As the women gradually mastered beekeeping techniques, changes also began to take place within their households.
"When the men saw that we were actually capable of doing the work, they also really accepted it," Cheserem said. "Now both my husband and I can share household responsibilities."
"We use the money from selling honey to buy livestock such as chickens and goats and to supplement our household expenses," Cheserem added.
For her, the more important change is that she no longer worries as much about paying her children's school fees. She now owns 10 beehives and has started managing her own household apiary.
For women in the area, beekeeping has also provided an alternative livelihood as crop farming becomes increasingly uncertain.
Faith Kittony, secretary of the women's group, said drought has severely affected some parts of the area this year, causing large reductions in crops such as maize and beans.
"Without the income from beekeeping, our lives would be very difficult," Kittony said, adding that beekeeping has become something they can rely on in the face of climate uncertainty.
As the women's beekeeping operation expanded, the group opened a shop selling its own honey and launched its own brand, attracting residents from neighboring villages who wanted to learn from their experience.
"People from nearby villages come and ask us how we did it and how they can start beekeeping," Kittony said.
Rutto is now introducing the idea of value-added honey processing to the group, encouraging the women to move beyond selling raw honey and explore other bee products.
"Next year, I plan to train them to make other bee products, such as body lotion, lip balm and beeswax products," she said.
Rutto has continued to apply and share the knowledge she acquired during her training in China. So far, she has passed the beekeeping techniques on to about 84 beekeeping groups in the county.
Looking back, Rutto said her biggest gain was being able to pass on the knowledge she acquired in China to more people.
"If I keep the knowledge only to myself, its value is very limited. Knowledge becomes truly valuable when it is shared with others," she added. ■

21:29:21 CST

LONDON, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Fewer than one in 10 adults in Britain smoked cigarettes in 2025, the lowest proportion on record, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said Tuesday.
Around 4.9 million people aged 18 years and over, or 9.8 percent of the population, smoked cigarettes in Britain last year, down from 10.6 percent in 2024, according to estimates from the ONS Annual Population Survey.
The proportion of current smokers has fallen by 10.4 percentage points since the data series began in 2011, when 20.2 percent of adults smoked.
People aged 45 to 54 had the highest proportion of current smokers in 2025, at 12.4 percent. Those aged 18 to 24 recorded the largest reduction in smoking prevalence among all age groups between 2011 and 2025, falling from 25.7 percent to 7.2 percent.
"This is the lowest proportion on record and continues the long-term decline in smoking. At the same time, e-cigarette use remains more common than smoking and has followed an overall upward trend since 2020," said ONS statistician David Mais.
Separate ONS figures showed that e-cigarette use remained widespread in Britain.
Around 5.4 million people aged 16 years and over, or 9.9 percent, used an e-cigarette daily or occasionally in 2025, according to the ONS Opinions and Lifestyle Survey. The proportion was broadly unchanged from 10.0 percent in 2024, but remained above the 6.4 percent recorded in 2020.
E-cigarette use was highest among people aged 25 to 34, with 16.4 percent reporting daily or occasional use in 2025. They overtook those aged 16 to 24 as the age group most likely to use e-cigarettes.
The latest figures come as the British government moves to phase out tobacco sales for future generations. Under the Tobacco and Vapes Act 2026, it will be illegal from Jan. 1, 2027 to sell tobacco products to anyone born on or after Jan. 1, 2009. ■

Targeted aid best shields poor from price shocks: IMF
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
21:29:19 CST
22:29:19 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Targeted financial support, rather than broad subsidies, is the most effective way to protect vulnerable households when inflation surges, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said Tuesday.
Targeted and temporary cash transfers can cushion poorer households against spikes in the prices of essentials while limiting the burden on public finances, the IMF said in its October 2026 World Economic Outlook, titled "Navigating a Shock-Prone World: Lessons from Cost-of-Living Crises."
Such assistance directs limited resources to those most in need while allowing higher market prices to signal scarcity and incentivize consumers to reduce consumption, the report said.
The IMF said support should be calibrated to the temporary portion of a price shock and include clear expiration dates, rather than compensate households for permanently higher prices. If governments broaden eligibility, assistance should remain tied to the average impact of the shock on lower-income households, it said.
The recommendations come after five years in which prices for everyday essentials, including food, electricity and fuel, have risen sharply in many countries, putting pressure on household budgets and, in some cases, threatening broader economic stability.
The IMF said the effects can persist long after the initial surge in food and energy prices fades. Inflation expectations can remain above pre-crisis levels for years, while falling real wages erode households' purchasing power.
With economies increasingly exposed to shocks, governments should strengthen social protection systems before crises hit, the IMF said. Doing so could make future interventions more effective while preserving fiscal space to respond to new shocks. ■

BANGKOK, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's headline inflation increased further in September, mainly due to rising fuel costs amid escalating Middle East tensions and higher food prices, official data showed on Tuesday.
The Southeast Asian country's consumer price index (CPI) rose 2.82 percent last month compared to a year earlier, accelerating from a 2.53-percent gain in August and registering the strongest reading since April, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
The September figure brings inflation closer to the upper bound of the central bank's 1 percent to 3 percent target range.
Core CPI, which excludes volatile fresh food and energy prices, climbed 1.50 percent year on year in September, quickening from a 1.44-percent rise in the previous month.
For the first nine months of 2026, the headline CPI grew 1.54 percent compared to the same period last year.
Looking ahead, the ministry expects headline inflation to remain in positive territory during the closing quarter of the year, supported by higher energy, food, and transportation expenses.
At a press briefing, it added that domestic flooding and El Nino weather conditions are not expected to have a broad-based impact on inflation.
The ministry narrowed its projection for headline CPI growth this year to between 1.8 percent and 2.2 percent, from 1.5 percent to 2.5 percent in an earlier forecast. ■

Demonstrators clash with riot police in France as education protests mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:28:54 UTC
22:28:54 KST

France suspends high school as protestors clash with police
School blockades and clashes intensify in France as frustration mounts over government inaction on educational needs.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has suspended high schools across France for the rest of the week as protests demanding education reforms rocked France and demonstrators clashed with police.
Authorities put the number of protestors nationwide on Tuesday at around a quarter of a million, but organizers estimated the number at closer to half a million.
Lecornu said the cancellation aimed to empower headteachers, teachers and pupils to pursue “internal democracy” to address concerns over school conditions.
“Burning down a high school does not improve the state of high school buildings” he said.
Clashes
Police fired tear gas at protesters blockading some French high schools as tens of thousands of students and activists rally across France in a mounting wave of protests demanding government improvements to the education system.
Students in Marseille, Nantes and Lyon began demonstrations on Tuesday morning, with demonstrators holding aloft signs which read “they don’t really care about us” and “survive or study”.
In Strasbourg, Lyon and Rennes, the protests turned violent at times, with police firing tear gas and protesters lighting fires in the streets and hurling projectiles.
The protests started two weeks ago in Paris’s disadvantaged suburbs, lighting a blaze that has spread across the country. The government said that the movement has turned into urban violence and has deployed riot police to some rallies.
Hand blown off
On Monday, a 15-year-old’s hand was blown off during clashes between high-schoolers and the police in northern France. The government said that around 200 to 250 protesters had thrown objects at the police.
A French newspaper, La Voix du Nord said that the teenager lost his hand and part of his arm after he picked a police grenade during the protest.
Nearly 2,000 high schools have been blockaded or closed for the day, according to the High School Students Union.
“When the answer is violence, it means democracy is no longer working,” said Hugo Vetzel, a recent high school graduate in Strasbourg preparing to attend France’s top universities. “There is such a gap between the elites and us.”
‘Troublemakers’
Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler who was at a march in Paris said more groups are joining the demonstrations.
“We’re seeing people from various unions, like the farmers union, energy workers, teachers unions who’ve also said they’re going to come out in support of the students.” Butler said.
“Parents and teachers said they want to be here not just to support their children but to protect them as they are worried about troublemakers who may infiltrate the protests and excessive police force” Butler added.
Al Jazeera’s Rosie Birchard was at a demonstration in Lille and said students from neighbouring Belgium came to show support.
Government pledges
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered ministers to address the students’ demands, including replacing underskilled teachers, making lunch breaks longer and changing the length of the school day.
Lecornu also said that the government will look into repairing old campuses, as he demanded ministers send in proposals by the end of October. But there are doubts about how quickly the government can respond.
“France is riddled with debt, France has a real budget crisis. Where would that money come from to put budget into public services” Al Jazeera’s Butler said.
France’s Ministry of Interior said that it has arrested 6,100 people since the beginning of the protests, the majority of them under the age of eighteen. The Ministry of Justice announced that over 1,800 will be prosecuted, including 1,483 minors.
During the protests, at least 215 teenagers have been wounded along with 715 police officers, according to Lecornu.

Swiss Ski vice-president Schmidhalter charged with fraud
The public prosecutor’s office in the Swiss canton of Valais has charged Swiss Ski vice-president Claude-Alain Schmidhalter with fraud and breach of trust.
Schmidhalter, who is also chair of the organising committee for the 2027 Alpine World Ski Championships, is due to appear in court on October 27.
Together with an accomplice, Schmidhalter is alleged to have defrauded his former business partner of a large severance payment. The two had run an engineering firm in the Upper Valais, as reported by the newspaper Blick and confirmed by the Valais judicial authorities to the Keystone-SDA news agency.
In the event that one of them retired, the two managing directors had agreed that the remaining owner would pay the other a severance payment. According to the Valais public prosecutor’s office, this payment was made, albeit at a lower amount than agreed.
To avoid paying the full sum, Schmidhalter and his accomplice are alleged to have reduced the company’s profits by transferring them to another company. According to the indictment, the retired business partner thus suffered a loss of over CHF300,000.
According to the indictment, the Valais Public Prosecutor’s Office is seeking a suspended prison sentence of 23 months, a fine of CHF10,000 and compensation of CHF55,000 to be paid to the victim.
The two defendants are therefore due to appear before the Brig-Glis District Court on October 27 to answer charges of fraud.

Burnout at work: MEPs call for stronger EU protections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:28:26 UTC
22:28:26 KST

MEPs called for EU-wide rules to tackle work-related stress, depression and anxiety, which affect almost one in three workers. Far-right groups opposed the text, arguing that it would place excessive obligations on businesses.
The European Parliament called on Tuesday for stronger EU action to tackle burnout, stress and other work-related conditions, addressing an increasingly common problem among European workers as digitalisation and AI reshape the workplace.
MEPs want new rules to recognise that psychosocial risks, including harassment, excessive workloads and unpredictable working hours, can give rise to occupational diseases, including mental health disorders.
“Illnesses linked to psychosocial risks, such as burnout, must be recognised as occupational diseases,” Belgian Socialist MEP Estelle Ceulemans, the report’s rapporteur, told Euronews.
According to the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA), 29% of EU workers experienced stress, depression or anxiety caused or made worse by their work in 2025. The figure rose to 32% among workers aged 25 to 39, as young people are disproportionately affected by those conditions, due to their intensive use of digital technologies and the often-precarious nature of their jobs.
MEPs urged the Commission to introduce EU-wide rules to protect workers, as existing provisions vary significantly across member states and do not always provide sufficient protection.
The resolution calls for binding obligations on employers, stronger labour inspections and a right to disconnect outside working hours.
It also features a reversal of the burden of proof in cases involving occupational disease. Where a worker establishes facts indicating exposure to work-related psychosocial risks and health damage consistent with that exposure, the employer would have to demonstrate otherwise.
The Parliament’s text also calls for telework to be voluntary. While remote working can improve flexibility and work-life balance, MEPs warn that it can also blur the boundaries between work and private life, particularly when imposed by employers.
The approach was considered too far-reaching by far-right groups, which voted against the resolution. “We must strike a balance between decent working conditions and the right of employers to manage and organise their business,” Spanish MEP Margarita de la Pisa Carrión of Patriots for Europe (PfE) wrote in a note on the resolution.
The next step now lies with the European Commission, which has been asked to come forward with legislation on psychosocial risks, stress and mental health at work. In the past, the Commission has regulated the minimum daily and weekly rest periods required to safeguard workers’ health and safety.

Your One Piece of Philosophy Grad School Advice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:27:53 UTC
22:27:53 KST

If you could give beginning philosophy graduate students just one piece of advice, what would it be?
I know that some readers will want to jump in to say “don’t”—either as a wisecrack or as sincere guidance.
But as humor it’s clichéd, and as advice it’s not helpful. All graduate students nowadays have heard some version of the warnings most of us know to give undergraduates who tell us they want to go to grad school in philosophy, and they’ve decided to go anyway. So let’s offer advice that will help them do well at what they’ve chosen to do.
I ask that commenters limit themselves to offering just one piece of advice, and to try not to repeat what other commenters have said.
(I know it’s probably too much to ask you all to refrain from raising problems regarding the individuation of advice, but try.)
I’ll start:
Communicate, don’t isolate. If you’re having trouble understanding something, if you’re struggling to keep up with all of your work, if you can’t quite figure out what to write or how to write it, if you feel inhibited from speaking up in class, if you don’t know what you are supposed to do, etc.—it is better to talk about it and seek guidance rather than to ignore or hide your issues, or absent yourself in significant ways from your department. If you have a faculty member designated as your advisor, talk to them; but feel free to approach other faculty as well. And of course your fellow grad students, especially those a few years into the program, may be of valuable assistance. Graduate school involves new tasks, but even familiar kinds of work takes place at a new level of difficulty or intensity, so it is not surprising that some students will be having a hard time. Know that many of today’s talented philosophers felt as you did once, sought advice, and succeeded.
Your turn, philosofriends.

India expands Navy’s BrahMos strike capability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:27:15 UTC
22:27:15 KST

India expands Navy’s BrahMos strike capability
India has contracted for more BrahMos missile launchers and fire-control systems for its Navy warships, expanding deployment of its primary maritime-strike weapon across the fleet.
The Defense Ministry signed the roughly $69 million contract with BrahMos Aerospace Private Limited in New Delhi on Tuesday. The order covers fire-control systems and launchers for Indian Navy ships and was made under a scheme to buy items that are indigenously designed and manufactured.
Several frontline Indian warships including destroyers and frigates already are armed with BrahMos missiles. New ships commissioned in recent years have received the system as standard equipment, while older vessels are being retrofitted in phases as part of a wider push to expand BrahMos deployment across the fleet by 2030, reports said.
BrahMos can be launched vertically or at an incline from naval platforms and is capable of striking both ships and land targets at extended ranges at supersonic speed.
The Indian Navy has operated BrahMos since 2005, when its anti-ship variant was integrated onto Rajput-class destroyers. The system has since become the service’s principal surface-to-surface weapon.
The latest purchase follows much larger contracts signed in 2024 when the missiles were ordered for the Navy’s combat and training requirements, along with additional shipborne BrahMos systems.
BrahMos Aerospace is a joint venture between India’s Defense Research and Development Organization and Russia’s NPO Mashinostroyenia. The program has produced ship-, land-, and air-launched versions of the supersonic cruise missile.
The new project will have at least 68% indigenous content and involve Indian companies, including micro, small, and medium enterprises. The ministry said the program is expected to generate employment over three years while increasing domestic participation in advanced military technology.

Germany's far-right AfD makes history again in Saxony-Anhalt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:27:00 UTC
22:27:00 KST

Germany's far-right AfD makes history again in Saxony-Anhalt
October 6, 2026
First thing in the morning, about 500 people gathered on Cathedral Square in the center of Magdeburg, the capital of the state of Saxony-Anhalt, to send a clear message that October 6 is not just another ordinary day. "Against Forgetting — Fascism Must Remain a Crime," read one of their banners. "No cooperation with the far right," read another.
Directly across from the imposing cathedral, in the state parliament building on the other side of the square, Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) was elected as speaker of the state parliament at 12:40 p.m. He received 48 votes — 9 more than the number of seats the AfD holds in the state parliament.
And this marks a turning point not only for Saxony-Anhalt but for all of Germany. For the first time since the end of World War II, a German state parliament has elected as its president a representative of a party that the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the domestic intelligence agency, has classified as right-wing extremist.
'The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt is a right-wing extremist party'
The parliament's inaugural session was opened by Eva von Angern, a member of the socialist Left Party and the senior-most member of the parliament, who had earlier been outside participating in the demonstration across the square. She noted that only a few women in German history had held such a high office. Among them, Von Angern said, was communist Clara Zetkin, who served as senior member of the Reichstag in 1932 — shortly before the Nazis seized power.
Nobody in the AfD caucus showed any support for these words. "Human dignity shall be inviolable," Von Angern then quoted from Germany's Basic Law. This includes, she added, people of different genders, worldviews, religions and skin colors. And she quoted former Federal President Richard von Weizsäcker. "He said: 'One expresses one's own dignity by respecting the dignity of others.'" Once again, no one in the AfD expressed any enthusiasm.
Allegations of nepotism against Rausch
Tobias Rausch, a 35-year-old real estate agent, is little known outside of Saxony-Anhalt. Many observers describe him as relatively approachable, and he describes himself as "not a hardliner." However, his name made headlines nationally at the beginning of the year when numerous AfD politicians were accused of nepotism.
Rausch himself admitted to employing several of his friends from his soccer club in his legislative office. That did not prevent his caucus from nominating him as president of the state legislature. Officially, the office is the highest-ranking position in the state.
After his election as parliamentary speaker, Rausch asserted: "I will not serve in this office as the speaker of a single parliamentary group, but as the speaker of all parliamentary groups." He added: "Rules must apply even when the majority changes."
A large AfD bloc — in the center of the chamber
Not everyone in the state parliament trusts this gesture of goodwill. During the first session following the election, a glance at the seating arrangement of the packed plenary chamber underscores the sheer force with which the AfD intends to shape policy here going forward: The AfD parliamentary caucus — composed of 37 men and two women — had taken its seats in the center, keeping a firm gaze on the lectern. The fact that this can be intimidating is clearly intentional.
Not everyone in the state parliament trusts this gesture of goodwill. During the first session following the election, a glance at the packed plenary chamber underscores the sheer force with which the AfD intends to shape policy here going forward: The parliamentary caucus — composed largely of men — seated itself prominently in the center where they could keep a firm eye on the lectern. Observers remarked that this can be intimidating.
Unlike in other parliaments, where the far-right party would normally sit far to the right, it has positioned the "old parties" that it despises — namely the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the socialist Left Party and the environmentalist Greens — around the edges. The AfD was able to push this seating arrangement through in preliminary talks before the state parliament convened to vote. The message is clear: We are the center. A new era has begun in Saxony-Anhalt.
A regional election that drew international attention
The election that took place on September 6 of this year in Saxony-Anhalt was certainly the most closely watched regional election in Germany in many years. Several hundred journalists, including several from international media, traveled to Magdeburg for the election.
Among the 1.7 million eligible voters in this German state, located between the Elbe River and the Harz Mountains, one thing was clear months before election day: the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — which has been partially classified as right-wing extremist — would emerge as the strongest party. Some polls even predicted that the party would secure an absolute majority of the votes.
In the end, the AfD garnered 39 of the 83 seats, just shy of the 42 seats it would have needed for an absolute majority.
Added together, the CDU, the Left Party, the SPD and the Greens also come to a combined total of 39 seats.
The Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), founded by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht, holds just five seats and yet could be the deciding factor in whether AfD's top candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, can actually become the state premier. The BSW had announced that it would vote for Rausch as parliamentary speaker, but not for Siegmund as head of the state government.
Nevertheless, Siegmund plans to stand for election in the state parliament in December. It will again take place by secret ballot. Siegmund has been displaying confidence, saying he intends to win in the first round of voting. And if he fails, he intends to call fresh elections.
On this point, the new parliamentary speaker, Tobias Rausch, commented on private TV channel RTL the morning before his election: "If we don't have a majority in the first round of voting, we won't have a majority for the rest of the legislative term either — in that case, it means the parliament doesn't want us to govern." Whatever happens, Saxony-Anhalt is facing turbulent times ahead.

Witnesses also reported two Israeli demolition operations in areas under Israeli occupation east of Gaza City, saying evacuated Palestinian homes and buildings were destroyed.
According to an Anadolu reporter, one explosion took place east of the Shujaiya neighbourhood and another east of Al-Tuffah.
Israeli warships also opened machine-gun fire towards fishing boats off the Gaza City coast. No injuries were reported.
Thousands killed since ceasefire began
Gaza's health ministry said Israeli forces have killed at least 1,460 Palestinians and injured 5,116 others since the October 10, 2025 ceasefire agreement.
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed by Israel and over 175,000 injured, according to Palestinian figures. The figures also put the destruction of Gaza's infrastructure at about 90 percent.
The latest casualties come as the ceasefire agreement remains under strain, with reports of continued Israeli military fire and other attacks across the enclave.

Paramount closes deal with Warner Bros., creating a media giant

Paramount closes deal with Warner Bros., creating a media giant
Kyiv • UNN
Paramount acquired Warner Bros. Discovery, giving David Ellison control over Skydance and a vast media empire. The company inherited $82 billion in debt and plans to cut costs.
Paramount closed its deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery on October 6. This gave the heir to a technology empire, David Ellison, control over a vast media empire that controls many of Hollywood’s most valuable projects. The New York Times reports, according to UNN.
Details
The deal immediately puts the combined company, now called Skydance, at the forefront of the streaming giants’ competitors, such as Netflix and YouTube, directly behind giants like Disney and Amazon.
"Today is a historic day not only for Skydance, but for our entire industry," Ellison said in a statement on Tuesday.
"We are incredibly excited to get to work," he added.
The new company is a hard-won prize, the publication notes. Ellison "snatched" Warner Bros. Discovery from rival bidder Netflix after a months-long tug-of-war that prompted him to make nine offers for the company. It was created despite objections from a coalition of state attorneys general, who sued to block the deal on antitrust grounds.
The lawsuit was ultimately settled after the attorneys general secured a series of concessions, including the creation of an editorial independence board to protect CNN’s integrity and Ellison’s pledge to spend an additional $1.5 billion on films over the next five years.
Hundreds of Hollywood insiders said the deal would sharply strengthen corporate power, leading to job losses and further stagnation in Hollywood. Skydance argued that the merger was a necessary counterweight to major technology companies.
David Ellison now controls:
-  film studios: Paramount Pictures, Warner Bros., Skydance; 
-  streaming services: Paramount+, HBO Max, Pluto TV; 
-  news organizations: CBS News, CNN, TVN24 (one of Poland’s most popular news channels); 
-  cable networks: Comedy Central, Nickelodeon, TNT, TBS, HBO, MTV, Food Network; 
-  major franchises: DC Universe (including characters such as Batman, Superman, and Wonder Woman), the Wizarding World of Harry Potter (The Wizarding World of Harry Potter), “Star Trek” (“Star Trek”), “Mission: Impossible” (“Mission: Impossible”). 
Now he just has to run it all, the publication notes.
The new company is making its debut in an industry undergoing profound changes. Cable television, one of media’s biggest "cash cows," is still profitable but is experiencing a terminal decline. Streaming has yet to replace those profits. Trust in the news business is low. And technology companies such as Amazon and Apple are entering the market for films, television shows, and sports rights, driving up content costs, the publication writes.
These challenges, it notes, will pose a serious test for 43-year-old Ellison, who until last year had never run a publicly traded media company. He and his team must convince Wall Street that the new company can handle these challenges while simultaneously paying down $82 billion in debt, an astonishing sum for a traditional media company. He must also unite tens of thousands of Warner Bros. and Paramount employees; both companies have experienced near-annual layoffs in recent years.
The situation, as noted, is further complicated by Ellison’s relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump, which has raised concerns among some CNN employees. This spring, Ellison hosted a dinner "honoring Trump’s White House" ahead of the annual White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, and later joined Trump at an Ultimate Fighting Championship bout at the White House (Paramount owns the media rights to the UFC).
Ellison allayed some of these concerns by keeping Mark Thompson, CNN’s chairman, in his position. In a memo to employees on Monday, Thompson said he had spoken with Ellison and was convinced that Skydance’s leadership would support "the independent news CNN has always stood for."
One of Ellison’s biggest challenges will be winning over Hollywood’s creative class in an era of declining box-office receipts, artificial intelligence, and algorithmic personalization. He has promised to invest in content, pledging to release at least 30 theatrical films annually. Within two years, that number will rise to 32 films. He has also promised to substantially overhaul the company’s technological capabilities.
But he must do all this while cutting $6 billion in costs this year over the next three years—a goal he will likely achieve, in part, by eliminating thousands of jobs, the publication writes.
Some of these cuts will likely result from combining parts of the company that have overlapping functions. CNN and CBS News are possible targets, as are some Paramount and Warner Bros. administrators. This process is already well underway: David Zaslav, the chief executive of Warner Bros. Discovery, has decided to step down from the deal, as has Cindy Holland, Paramount’s chief executive for streaming, the publication notes.

US court rejects Bashar Masri’s bid to pause discovery in alleged Hamas support,  Oct. 7 lawsuit

Unknown Publisher

13:25:07 UTC
22:25:07 KST

A US federal judge rejected a request by Palestinian-American businessman Bashar Masri and other defendants to halt evidence gathering in a lawsuit accusing them of providing material support to Hamas in connection with the October 7, 2023, attacks.
Judge Darrin P. Gayles of the US District Court for the Southern District of Florida denied the motion on October 1, following a hearing that day. He ordered the parties to submit a joint scheduling report and proposed scheduling order by October 16.
The decision allows discovery, the process through which parties seek documents, testimony, and other evidence, to proceed. The order addressed the timing of evidence gathering and made no finding on the underlying allegations.
The civil lawsuit was brought by American victims of the attacks and victims’ relatives and estate representatives under the US Anti-Terrorism Act. It alleges that Masri and companies he controls assisted Hamas and provided infrastructure used by the terrorist organization.
The plaintiffs allege that properties Masri owned, developed or controlled, including two Gaza hotels and the Gaza Industrial Estate, concealed Hamas tunnels and entrances. They also allege that solar installations at the properties supplied electricity to the tunnels.
Masri decries allegations of Hamas ties as 'baseless'
Masri has previously denied wrongdoing. His office called the lawsuit “baseless” when it was filed in April 2025 and said neither he nor the businesses involved had supported violence or militancy.
In a May 2026 motion seeking dismissal, his lawyers argued that the plaintiffs had failed to establish that he knew his conduct could help Hamas carry out attacks, Reuters reported. They said the defendants condemned Hamas’s violence and characterized the allegations as speculation based on participation in Gaza’s economic development.
Masri is known for developing Rawabi, a planned Palestinian city in the West Bank. He resigned from the dean’s council at Harvard Kennedy School in April 2025 after the lawsuit was filed.
The plaintiffs initially filed their case in Washington in April 2025 before voluntarily dismissing that action and refiling in Florida, according to a January court order. The October 1 ruling requires both sides to propose a timetable for the proceedings.

EXPLAINER - Why renewed Tigray fighting is raising fears of another Ethiopian war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:24:50 UTC
22:24:50 KST

Ethiopia is facing its most serious security crisis in years as fighting has returned to the northern Tigray region, raising fears of a new civil war and a wider regional conflict.
The fighting that intensified on Sept. 23 is the most severe since the 2020-2022 Tigray war, which killed hundreds of thousands of people before a peace agreement was signed in South Africa.
The latest conflict has already spread beyond Tigray, while relations between Ethiopia and neighboring Eritrea have deteriorated sharply.
The International Crisis Group warned in a statement that northern Ethiopia was facing a “dangerous descent back into war,” urging African leaders and key outside powers, including the US, to push both sides to de-escalate, show restraint and return to negotiations.
“The situation in Tigray is dangerously close to returning to full-blown war," Murithi Mutiga, Africa director at the International Crisis Group, said in a statement. "A new war would impose unbearable costs on northern Ethiopia’s long-suffering civilians.”
The EU in a statement Monday called for immediate de-escalation on all fronts, urging those involved to refrain from actions or rhetoric that could heighten tensions.
Here is what is happening in the country.
The 2022 Pretoria agreement ended the large-scale war between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), but left disputes over territory, security and political arrangements unresolved.
The latest major escalation began on Sept. 23, when Tigrayan forces seized the federally administered airports of Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, Axum and Shire, according to the African Union.
An offensive also opened fronts in and around neighboring Amhara and Afar.
The International Crisis Group said the attacks appeared to mark the first coordinated military operation by a newly formed opposition alliance against federal forces and their allies.
The TPLF-led regional administration said its forces were responding to federal air and artillery attacks. The African Union said the airport seizures were inconsistent with the Pretoria agreement and urged the parties to resume direct talks.
The battlefield has since shifted. Federal forces and allied fighters regained control of Mekelle over the weekend after Tigrayan forces withdrew. The TPLF said its regional administration would be “temporarily moved out of Mekelle and operate from somewhere else.”
The withdrawal did not end the fighting. Airstrikes and artillery fire were reported in northern Tigray on Oct. 5.
Federal troops and allied groups, including the government-backed Tigray Peace Forces, are fighting the TPLF and other armed opposition movements.
Government officials blamed the TPLF for the erupting conflict.
The TPLF dominated Ethiopia’s ruling coalition for nearly three decades before Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power in 2018. Its subsequent split with the federal government helped set the stage for the 2020-2022 war.
However, the TPLF is now part of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, a seven-group coalition announced in September that has pledged to remove Abiy and establish a transitional administration.
Alongside the TPLF, the coalition includes the Amhara Fano National Movement, Oromo Liberation Army, Ogaden National Liberation Front, Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front, Benishangul Peoples’ Liberation Movement and Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement, according to its founding statement read on Tigrai TV.
The statement accused the government of presiding over conflict, displacement, poverty and the erosion of rights.
The alliance brings together groups with different political goals and territorial claims. Its formation does not mean they operate as a unified army, but some have already coordinated attacks.
According to the International Crisis Group, Tigrayan forces and Amhara Fano fighters jointly attacked federal troops in Amhara near southern Tigray, while an Afar opposition group fought alongside the TPLF on the Tigray-Afar border.
The cooperation marks a shift from the 2020-2022 war, when Amhara forces fought alongside federal troops against the TPLF. Tigrayan fighters are now also on opposing sides, with the Tigray Peace Forces supporting the federal government.
The federal government is led by Abiy, whose political base is largely associated with the Oromo community, and allied forces from other parts of the country.
The Pretoria agreement, signed on Nov. 2, 2022, formally ended the two-year Tigray war and provided for a permanent cessation of hostilities, disarmament and a political process.
The African Union has described the Pretoria agreement as the "cornerstone" of peace, stability and reconciliation in Ethiopia and urged the parties to return to direct talks.
But key disputes remained, including questions over territory, the return of displaced people and the political and security arrangements in Tigray.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' office said in September that it was "particularly troubled" by reports of drone use and civilian casualties, urging all sides to "exercise maximum restraint" and resolve their differences through dialogue under the Pretoria framework.
The African Union has also called for "utmost restraint" and an immediate end to actions that could escalate tensions.
The crisis also has a regional dimension because Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting forces opposed to Abiy's government.
The three countries have denied the allegations.
Egypt and Sudan, both downstream from Ethiopia, are in a dispute with Addis Ababa over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile and have sought a binding agreement on its filling and operation.
Cairo fears the project could affect its annual water allocation of 55.5 billion cubic meters (1.96 trillion cubic feet).
Eritrea was an important military ally of Ethiopia during the 2020-2022 Tigray war. Eritrean forces fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops against the TPLF.
But the relationship has since deteriorated dramatically. One major source of tension is Ethiopia's demand for access to the Red Sea.
Abiy reiterated the importance of sea access after being sworn in for another five-year term this week, saying "Ethiopia's modernization cannot be realized without sea access."
The diplomatic crisis escalated last week.
Ethiopia ordered the closure of its embassy in Asmara and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats persona non grata.
Eritrea subsequently announced that it was severing diplomatic relations with Ethiopia.
The immediate concern is the impact on civilians.
The renewed fighting threatens civilians still recovering from the previous war, including those who remain displaced, the UN has warned.
Humanitarian operations have already been disrupted by road closures, communications outages and the seizure of aid vehicles.
The UN reported that a drone strike in northwestern Tigray hit a truck carrying food assistance for displaced people.
Internet and telephone services were reportedly disrupted in Mekelle and parts of Amhara, while roads were blocked in parts of Afar. Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to Mekelle, Axum and Shire after the TPLF seized the three airports.
“I am deeply alarmed by the recent escalation in hostilities between Ethiopian Government forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front and its allies, and the harmful impacts it is already having on civilians,” UN human rights chief Volker Turk said in late September.
He warned that communications outages could prevent civilians from finding safe routes out of affected areas and hamper aid workers’ efforts to reach those in need.
Turk also condemned what his office described as a campaign of forced mass recruitment by the TPLF, including of children and former fighters demobilized in late 2025.
People who resisted recruitment and their relatives had faced killings, torture, arbitrary detention, forced displacement and other reprisals, his office said.

Switzerland played role in Nobel Prize-winning research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:24:32 UTC
22:24:32 KST

Switzerland played role in Nobel Prize-winning research
Francis Halzen’s Nobel Prize in Physics has a Swiss connection. Researchers from the University of Geneva are involved in the IceCube experiment, for which Belgian-born physicist Halzen was honoured this year.
The research group led by Geneva-based physicist Teresa Montaruli is part of the international IceCube collaboration. They work with data from the giant detector, using it to investigate, amongst other things, the origin of high-energy neutrinos.
“I am so happy,” Montaruli told the Keystone-SDA news agency. She said the Nobel Prize was recognition for a field of research that offers a completely new perspective on the universe.
IceCube detects neutrinos by tracing the light trails created when these particles interact – albeit rarely – with the Antarctic ice. Because neutrinos interact very little with their surroundings, they can travel to Earth from great distances almost unimpeded.
“You can see neutrinos coming from very far away,” explained Montaruli.
The particles thus open “a completely new window” onto high-energy astrophysics. Unlike when observing light, neutrinos allow us, so to speak, to “peer into the depths of the sources”, said the physicist.

October 7 victims, bereaved families file NIS 5 billion lawsuit against PA, PLO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:24:10 UTC
22:24:10 KST

Days before the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre, 835 plaintiffs, including bereaved relatives, terror victims and soldiers wounded in combat, filed a NIS 5.151 billion civil lawsuit against the Palestinian Authority, the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), and former Palestinian prisoners’ affairs chief Qadura Fares, who formerly headed the PA’s Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs, which handles Palestinian prisoners’ affairs.
The Jerusalem District Court received the lawsuit on Sunday and assigned it to Judge Eran Shilo. Shilo is already overseeing a coordinated process concerning other October 7-related lawsuits brought by more than 8,000 plaintiffs, focusing first on the shared question of the PA’s potential civil liability.
The lawsuit alleges that the defendants helped finance Hamas, knew about the planned massacre, and participated in preparations for it. It also alleges that money and other support provided by the defendants helped finance and train terrorists who participated in the attack.
These are allegations made by the plaintiffs and have not been tested or established in court; the defendants have 60 days from the date they are served to submit a defense.
The complaint was filed by Prof. Gideon Fisher’s law firm and attorney Mordechai Heller.
Plaintiffs allege PA, PLO funds enabled Hamas's terror plot
It alleges that preparations for the attack began in 2018, when Hamas, PLO factions, and other terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip established a joint operations room that coordinated military exercises and training.
According to the plaintiffs, PA and PLO funding for civilian ministries and governing bodies in Gaza enabled Hamas to direct other resources toward its military operations. The lawsuit further alleges that organizations affiliated with the PLO participated in the joint operations room and in exercises that preceded October 7.
The plaintiffs are seeking compensation under the 2024 Terror Victims Compensation Law, alongside damages for the deaths, injuries, and psychological harm they allege the defendants caused.
The 2024 law allows the heirs of a person killed in a terrorist attack to seek NIS 10 million in exemplary damages, and a victim left with a permanent disability to seek NIS 5 million, from those who carried out the attack or paid rewards for it. These damages may be awarded in addition to other compensation.
The lawsuit includes relatives and estates of four people who were killed, and 824 people who the complaint says suffered physical or psychological harm in the massacre or the war that followed. It says 193 of the injured plaintiffs were left with permanent physical or psychological disabilities.
The remainder comprises claimed financial losses and compensation for emotional suffering.
The complaint lists two related cases already pending in the Jerusalem District Court. One is an NIS 4.491 billion lawsuit filed by Fisher’s office in March 2025 on behalf of more than 500 plaintiffs against the same three defendants.
Plaintiffs include bereaved families
Among the plaintiffs in the new lawsuit is Omer Ohana, whose fiancé, Maj. Sagi Golan, was killed in the battle of Be’eri in the early hours of October 8, 2023.
“Three years have passed, but it feels as though it happened yesterday,” Ohana told The Jerusalem Post. “People always say that time will take its course and heal, but in practice, time only makes it harder. The pain has turned into suffering.”
Golan, 30, was an officer at the IDF’s counterterrorism school. He held a bachelor’s degree in philosophy, economics, and political science from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and a master’s degree in public policy.
He also volunteered for nearly six years with Paamonim, a nonprofit that provides financial guidance to individuals and families, and helped families facing food insecurity manage their household finances.
“He was the perfect partner,” Ohana said. “He was handsome and smart and funny and silly. He was colorblind and did not know how to dress at all.”
The couple had been together for six years and were planning a weekend celebration in the desert on October 20. They called it a “celebration of love” rather than a wedding because Israel does not perform same-sex marriages, Ohana said.
On October 7, Golan put on his uniform, assembled his team and left their home in Herzliya to fight. Ohana said Golan helped rescue families trapped in safe rooms in Be’eri’s Kerem neighborhood before he was shot while responding to a commander’s call for assistance.
The family learned of his death several days later.
Ohana said he decided to join the lawsuit after discussing it with other bereaved families.
“At the end of the day, this is a lawsuit with many, many families seeking to hold the PLO and other actors responsible for October 7,” he said. “Hamas did not act alone, and they need to bear responsibility.”
He said monetary compensation could never provide what bereaved families truly wanted.
“They cannot bring these people back to life, and that is the only thing a bereaved family really wants,” Ohana said. “But they should be compensated. Those responsible should pay everything the law requires them to pay.”
Lawsuit follows previous suit filed in US
The lawsuit follows other cases filed by Fisher’s office in the United States, including separate $500 million lawsuits against Iran and Syria, as well as litigation alleging that Binance founder Changpeng Zhao and the cryptocurrency exchange provided services that enabled Hamas financing.
Fisher said his office was also examining which of the new plaintiffs hold US citizenship and whether they could pursue claims against the PA and PLO in a US federal court.
Fisher cited the US Supreme Court’s 2025 decision in Fuld v. PLO, which upheld a federal law allowing US courts to exercise personal jurisdiction over the PA and PLO in specified terrorism cases. The ruling concerned jurisdiction; it did not establish the PA and PLO’s liability in any particular case.
“The new lawsuit joins an international legal campaign that our firm has conducted since October 7, in Israel and the United States,” Fisher said.
“Our aim is to create a cross-border legal campaign that will hold those involved in supporting terrorism accountable and obtain the maximum compensation possible for the victims.”

"This trip confirmed for me that there is an active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort underway to hide the costs of this war and the implications of this war from Congress and the American people," Murphy told a small group of journalists in Riyadh, the second stop on his trip.
He also said that the Pentagon refused to set up a briefing for him on the war while he was in the region.
"I've never encountered anything like this in my time in the Senate and it's part of a deliberate campaign of obfuscation that my Republican colleagues in Congress should demand an end to," he said.
Murphy made clear, however, that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had facilitated his visit, including arranging meetings with diplomats, a stance he contrasted with that of the Pentagon.
During his trip, Murphy met with Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani and with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman as well as other senior Gulf officials. REUTERS

UK prog band Marillion to perform in Tallinn
In April, the neo‑prog band Marillion will give two full‑length concerts in Tallinn on two consecutive evenings, each with a different setlist.
Marillion will take the stage in Tallinn on Friday, 16 April, and Saturday, 17 April — together forming a single, cohesive Marillion Weekend.
Marillion Weekend is a format created by the band itself, built around specially curated setlists for each night and offering fans a chance to experience Marillion's work more broadly than during a typical concert.
Since 2002, Marillion Weekend repertoires have ranged from well‑known concert favorites to rarely performed tracks and long epics, and in some years have included full albums played in their entirety.
Marillion will perform a different concert programme on each of the two nights. Only two-day tickets will be available for the event, providing admission to both concert evenings.
Each evening will also feature a local guest act: Indrek Patte band on 16 April and Pantokraator on 17 April.
Formed in Aylesbury in 1979, Marillion became one of the best‑known representatives of emotionally charged, dramatic progressive rock in the 1980s. The band, whose name was inspired by JRR Tolkien's "Silmarillion", released its debut studio album in 1983. In total, they have released 20 albums, the most recent in 2022.

Hong Kong and mainland Chinese residents will have to register with immigration authorities on both sides of the border to use automated “joint clearance” channels at the revamped Huanggang Port crossing, with around 100,000 travellers a day expected to use the control point when operations begin.
Hong Kong’s Immigration Department would deploy sufficient manpower to help passengers register at the checkpoint, assistant director Jacky Wong Ki said on Tuesday.
“The whole registration process at the automated channel is very quick, it takes a few seconds to complete,” Wong said.
The “joint clearance” model will enable passengers to complete both departure and entry clearance procedures by presenting one identity document required by their destination and passing through a three-gated automated channel.

Yemen conflict escalating into regional war
Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have launched a major offensive against the Iranian-backed Houthis, with both sides claiming territorial gains as battles rage around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait connecting the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
The escalation comes after the Houthis took over the key territory around Bab el-Mandeb in September, one of the world’s most important shipping chokepoints, which has gained particular significance amid disruptions at the Strait of Hormuz caused by the US-Iran war.
On Monday, the Yemeni army claimed to have pushed north along the Red Sea coast toward Mocha, while announcing “a strategic offensive operation on Sanaa,” which serves as the de facto capital of the Houthi movement.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, agreed with Türkiye and Pakistan to rapidly deploy military forces under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, also known as the “Muslim NATO.” The coalition already announced that 100 warplanes are supporting the Yemeni offensive.
The Houthis have denied the government gains, claiming to have made headway around Taiz, some 80km from the Red Sea coast. The group has also retaliated with ballistic missiles and drones against Saudi targets, claiming strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, military bases, and Aramco oil facilities, including the Rabigh refinery. Saudi Arabia has confirmed damage from Houthi attacks on airports at Jizan and Najran.
The Houthis have consistently accused Riyadh of waging an “aggression” and blockade against Yemen, arguing that Saudi military operations serve US and Israeli interests. Their Yemeni opponents, meanwhile, view Houthis – who identify themselves as part of the “Axis of Resistance” – as “terrorists” and insurgents who overthrew the internationally recognized government in 2014.
The conflict in Yemen in its current form began when the Houthis seized the capital of Sanaa more than a decade ago, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention. However, fighting largely subsided after a 2022 truce.
Amid the fighting in Yemen and continued US-Iran standoff, US President Donald Trump argued that record gas prices are being driven not by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz but by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.

The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed in August, links Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan under a collective-defense pledge, which treats an armed attack on one member as an attack on all. It has been widely dubbed “Muslim NATO” for its similarity to the Western military bloc’s Article 5. On Monday, the three countries agreed to implement collective-defense measures and arrange the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia following Houthi attacks. In 2013, Hanning testified in a London court case as a security expert, backing businessman Oleg Deripaska in a dispute over the sale of a stake in Rusal.
Hanning also worked as a consultant in the Russian division of the London consulting firm G3 and served on the supervisory board of the Latvian PNB Banka. While working at PNB, he acted as a mediator in a dispute between two businessmen of Russian origin. Security firms linked to Hanning also include people with ties to Russia.

Former German spy chief arrested for espionage
Former German intelligence chief August Hanning has been arrested on charges of espionage and treason, the country’s federal prosecutor’s office announced on Tuesday.
The 80-year-old former spymaster headed the BND from December 1998 to November 2005 and remained in government until late 2009, when he moved into the private sector. He was previously embroiled in a high-profile kidnapping case in Germany.
Hanning is accused of abusing his relationship with his former chief of staff, an official identified by German authorities as “Manfred D.” The man remained a trusted aide during Hanning’s government career and later served several successive BND chiefs after Hanning left office.
Since 2010, Hanning allegedly bought state secrets from Manfred D. that were useful to him in his work as a security consultant. The alleged arrangement continued until at least June 2022, with nearly 2,000 internal documents intended exclusively for BND leadership, many of them classified, changing hands, prosecutors said.
In one case, Hanning allegedly used BND material to prepare an analytical report for an employee of a foreign intelligence service. The federal prosecutor’s office did not identify the country involved and said investigators could not determine whether the report was ultimately delivered.
Hanning is also accused of dealing with a member of another unnamed foreign intelligence service, partly on the basis of material he allegedly received from Manfred D.
The charges were announced after both suspects were arrested and their homes searched. The case was reportedly based on evidence found at Hanning’s residence in Hamburg, for which local law enforcement obtained a warrant in September 2025 as part of a separate investigation involving businesswoman Christina Block.
Block, an heiress to the Block House restaurant group founded by her father Eugen Block, is at the center of a high-profile custody scandal involving her children and is on trial on kidnapping charges. Security firm System 360, run by Hanning and his business partner, former state criminal police officer Thorsten Mehles, was reportedly hired by Block in connection with the dispute and allegedly took part in efforts to discredit the Danish father of her children.
The trial of Block and her alleged co-conspirators has yet to conclude. Hanning is not a defendant in that case, but remains under investigation over his alleged role in the affair.
