Gallery: Young Estonian artists' fall exhibition opens in Tallinn
The "Buy Young Art" fall exhibition has opened at Tallinn's Art & Tonic gallery where visitors can see works by 88 young Estonian artists free of charge. The exhibition will conclude with an art auction on October 23.
Nearly 400 works by 203 artists were submitted for this year's fall exhibition, with the jury selecting works by 88 artists. According to Reigo Kuivjõgi, organizer of "Buy Young Art" and gallerist at Art & Tonic, this year's selection is characterized by the high quality and diversity of the works.
"I am pleased that this time the selection includes more completely new artists than usual who will make their debut at the fall auction. This also makes the exhibition particularly interesting, as young artists with very different styles and approaches have come together under one roof," Kuivjõgi said.
Now in its 11th year, the "Buy Young Art" exhibition and auction gives young artists an opportunity to introduce their work to a wider audience while also bringing young Estonian art closer to enthusiasts and buyers.
"This year's selection is truly diverse and offers an opportunity to explore different artistic media, as in addition to painting, it also features graphic art, drawing, collage, photography and sculpture. The prices of the works also vary widely and start at just €1. When it comes to young art, there is always something for everyone, whether an experienced collector or someone buying art for the first time," Kuivjõgi explained.
Entrepreneur and art enthusiast Kristjan-Thor Vähi, head of Invego and a member of the selection jury, said the high quality of the works made choosing among the candidates quite a difficult task.
"There are many different approaches and truly fresh ideas in the work of young Estonian artists and I really like the fact that they dare to experiment. The exhibition offers a good opportunity to become better acquainted with their work and see what our young artists are doing right now," he said.
According to Vähi, initiatives such as "Buy Young Art" are important for young artists because they help their work reach a broader audience beyond the art world.
"When an artist is at the beginning of their career and is still relatively unknown, an opportunity like this to show their work is very important. It is important for young Estonian art to be visible and accessible and the more young art reaches the public, the more confident people will become about buying it and thereby supporting local artists," he said.
The "Buy Young Art" fall exhibition is open at the Art & Tonic gallery through October 22. All works displayed at the exhibition will be offered at a public auction on October 23.

From desalination to irrigation: How countries are adapting to water scarcity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:00:18 UTC
22:00:18 KST

From desalination in the UAE to modernising irrigation systems in Uzbekistan, countries facing water pressure are finding ways to secure supplies and reduce losses.
Roughly half the world's population experiences severe water scarcity for at least part of the year, according to the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, a figure climate change, population growth and rising demand are expected to push higher.
The pressures vary by location. In the UAE, where rainfall is scarce and no permanent rivers exist, most drinking water comes via desalination of seawater. In Uzbekistan, agriculture depends on irrigation networks moving water across dry landscapes. Both countries are turning to technology and infrastructure to stretch limited supplies further.
Securing water in an arid climate
In the UAE, limited rainfall and the absence of permanent rivers have long shaped how communities obtain and use water.
Efforts to manage scarce resources predate modern desalination by centuries. Traditional falaj irrigation systems channelled water through settlements and agricultural areas allowing communities to sustain local economies.
Abdulla Balalaa, the UAE's Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs for Energy and Sustainability, said such systems were engineered over 1,000 years ago.
Today, much of the country's drinking water comes from desalination. Balalaa said the UAE has achieved universal access to water and is also applying newer technologies, including artificial intelligence, to the sector.
As populations and cities grow, limiting water use and reusing existing supplies are becoming increasingly important.
Few places demonstrate that principle as clearly as the International Space Station.
Emirati astronaut Dr Sultan Al Neyadi spent six months aboard the station, where water is needed for drinking, hygiene, food preparation and oxygen production.
“Every drop on board the International Space Station is accounted for,” Al Neyadi said. “We recycle about 95% of our water.”
Water passes through several stages of filtration before being used again, providing an example of how a limited resource can be repeatedly recovered rather than discarded when there are no other options.
The UAE is also seeking to push water higher on the international agenda. It will co-host the 2026 UN Water Conference with Senegal in Abu Dhabi from 8 to 10 December. The event will bring together governments, international organisations, businesses and other stakeholders, with investment, technology and innovation among the areas under discussion.
Balalaa said solutions will vary by location. Technology and innovation can help bridge gaps, he said, alongside financing and cooperation needed to turn ideas into active projects.
In Uzbekistan, the pressures are different. Much of the country's agriculture relies on moving water over long distances, limiting losses along the way and ensuring it reaches farmland when it is needed.
Getting water to Uzbekistan's farms
Canals, reservoirs and pumping stations carry water across Uzbekistan's dry landscapes. In some areas, scarcity is therefore also a question of whether available water can reach agricultural land at the right time.
In the Fergana Valley, a World Bank-backed project launched in 2017 has modernised irrigation infrastructure.
At one site, water from local springs is collected and pumped around nine kilometres to areas where access has historically been difficult. The pumping station and pipeline are expected to improve irrigation for around 9,740 hectares of farmland.
More reliable irrigation has also allowed previously difficult-to-cultivate land to be farmed.
At one orchard in the valley, drip irrigation is used to deliver water to peach trees planted in 2024. The farm harvested around 200 tonnes of fruit the following year.
Moving water across the desert
Farther west, water from the Amu Darya is pumped across the desert through the Amu-Bukhara Machine Canal. The wider network irrigates more than 350,000 hectares across Bukhara and Navoi regions and supplies drinking water to Bukhara and Kogon.
The new Amu-Bukhara-1 pumping station replaced older infrastructure as part of a wider modernisation effort. Its digital control system tracks water and electricity use, and the new equipment has cut energy use by up to 15%.
Moving water over long distances is only one part of the process; preventing it from disappearing before reaching farms is another.
In parts of Bukhara, water losses through seepage previously reached around 37%, according to Sherzod Sharipov, a representative of the regional water delivery service. Canals are now being lined with concrete to reduce losses and provide steadier flows to farmers.
Farmer Hikmat Nazrullayev said large amounts of water once disappeared before reaching wheat and cotton fields. Since canals were lined, he said, irrigating crops has become easier.
Water beyond the fields
The irrigation network also connects agriculture with the wider environment.
Drainage and return flows from farmland feed Dengizkul, a wetland of international importance in Bukhara region and an important resting and wintering site for migratory birds.
Professor of Water Engineering Malika Ikramova said the lake receives water from precipitation and groundwater as well as drainage returning from irrigation systems. Its water is highly mineralised, but supports fisheries and provides habitat for migratory birds.
As populations grow and climate conditions change, Ikramova said reducing losses, improving water accounting and expanding water-saving irrigation will remain important.
“We are going to have to adapt,” she said.
From desalination in the Gulf to irrigation canals in Central Asia, the methods differ considerably. But the underlying task is similar: reducing losses and making limited water supplies go further.

Remaking scents: could fragrance tech help take pressure off endangered plants?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:00:15 UTC
22:00:15 KST

Many of the world’s most expensive perfumes begin with a wounded tree. When some Aquilaria trees are damaged, they produce a dark, fragrant resin that becomes agarwood, or oudh – an ingredient so valuable that wild trees have been illegally felled in its pursuit.
The result has devastated wild Aquilaria populations. But what if perfumers could create the smell without cutting down the tree?
With the help of AI, scientists are learning to predict how molecules that have never been made will smell, reconstructing scent-producing genes from flowers believed to be extinct. Others have collected microbes from clouds and used them as a starting point for new perfumes.
Now scientists and biotechnology companies say advances could soon allow the fragrance industry to reproduce scents and compounds from endangered plants without repeatedly harvesting them.
“Being able to recreate the scent of an endangered plant would be a huge win for both the environment but also the brands,” said Alex Wiltschko, the founder of Osmo, a Google Brain spin-off that has raised $130m to develop artificial intelligence capable of predicting and recreating smells.
Osmo has recreated the scent of a rare tree from a piece of bark “the size of a finger”, Wiltschko said. A spectrometer analysed the sample, its AI reconstructed the chemical formula and the scent was reproduced in its laboratory.
BioHarvest Sciences says it has created a stable cell culture from an endangered south-east Asian fragrance plant, allowing its valuable compounds to be produced without cultivating or harvesting the original plant.
The plant has not been named for commercial reasons but BioHarvest has announced an agreement anticipating production of 20 tonnes of the fragrance composition, with limited production potentially beginning next year.
“The challenge is that human demand can be effectively unlimited while biological supply is not,” said BioHarvest’s chief executive, Zaki Rakib. “We believe biotechnology can help close that gap, not by replacing nature but by allowing us to use what nature has given us without continually putting the source under pressure.”
But conservationists and perfumers say such claims risk giving advances in fragrance technology an environmental gloss they have not yet earned.
“Calling this conservation is greenwashing,” said Mandy Aftel, the pioneering natural perfumer, author and founder of the Aftel Archive of Curious Scents. “Making a synthetic version of an endangered plant’s smell doesn’t save the plant.” She said producing a substitute did not stop people buying the original – or address other causes of a species’ decline.
Rhian Smith, of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, agreed. She pointed to the Aquilaria tree. AI could help design an alternative to oudh, she said, but wild-sourced material remained highly prized. “It doesn’t completely take the pressure off wild plant species,” she said.
There is also the question of motivation. Wiltschko admitted that conservation was not “an explicit priority” for Osmo’s work.
Synthetic perfume itself is nothing new: the industry has relied heavily on synthetic ingredients for more than a century, and machines have long been able to identify molecules in a scent.
“What’s changed is what happens after the data comes off the machine,” Wiltschko said. “What’s new is prediction.” He claimed Osmo had trained its AI on more than 5m human responses to smells. “That means it can predict how combinations of molecules will be perceived,” he said.
Elsewhere, AI is claimed to be changing the whole world in which perfumers work. Christina Agapakis is not a perfumer, but her work reconstructing genes from preserved flowers has produced fragrance compounds that perfumers can use to create new scents.
Another perfumer, Future Society, has gone into the clouds, making two flights in a small plane to collect living microbes. Thirteen were identified, producing 57 scent molecules, which became the starting point for Cloud Reverie, a perfume launched this year.
Even AI has its limits: a flower’s scent can contain hundreds of molecules and change according to which part of the plant they come from and the conditions in which it grows.
It is still not enough for the purists. “The smell we got was this ghostly fragment of what had been lost,” Agapakis said of her project. She could not recreate the living organism, or the soil, climate, season and ecology that produced its scent, she said.
“What we have to remember is, ultimately, however powerful AI is, a smell is not simply a formula or dataset.”

What to know about Mistral's ML4 as it bets on EU sovereignty in the US-China open-weight AI race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:00:07 UTC
22:00:07 KST

Known as “Le Chonk,” the new frontier AI offering from French company Mistral says it will be the strongest open-weight AI outside China, as it bets that European "sovereignty" can win customers in a race increasingly framed as US versus China.
French artificial intelligence champion Mistral AI on Tuesday launched a public preview of a new frontier model that it says will be the most capable open-weight model developed outside China once its weights are released.
The launch comes as the race over open-weight AI, in which a model's parameters can be downloaded and run by anyone, has taken on a geopolitical edge.
Chinese developers have set the pace, while many American companies, such as OpenAI, keep their most capable systems closed. Meanwhile, the debate over safety has grown since AI agents have been found to go rogue and hack websites.
Mistral is betting that its new open-weight model, called ML4, which has strong defence capabilities, will attract customers who want a European alternative built around "sovereignty."
Here is everything to know about the model.
ML4, nicknamed "Le Chonk," meaning the large chunky one, is "a new generation of models," Guillaume Lample, chief scientist and co-founder of Mistral, said in a press conference that Euronews attended.
The model focuses on cybersecurity and defence capabilities, which the company claims are stronger than those of its Chinese competitors.
“The cyber defence capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyber attacks,” said Lample.
Mistral’s launch comes just a day after Reflection, a US startup, unveiled Beam as its first open-weight model and a Western counterweight to Chinese open models. Its weights are due later this month, and its performance claims have not been independently verified.
The rogue AI agents
Pierre Stock, Mistral's first employee and vice president of science, said that building a new AI model was "like building a spaceship".
He said every AI company is "moving at full speed". Though Mistral is only three years old, it is "definitely closing the gap" with its competitors, and in some aspects its new model is "basically stronger than China’s models from this summer," he said.
Last month, the company announced it raised €3 billion at a valuation of more than €21 billion, which it says is the largest equity round ever completed by a European technology company.
The model's release also comes as AI companies report AI agents acting on their own and hacking websites.
Stock argued that this has created a narrative for US companies to "market rogue events" as "only a few trusted players can take care of the technology."
He added that the "monopoly is controlled by the Americans but that open-weight models allow people to access models."
The company also said it leads open-weight models on manufacturing and finance tasks and on multimodal use, and that in coding it is closing the gap with other frontier models. Mistral also claimed the best results of any model — closed ones included — on grounding capabilities, and top-level performance on semiconductor benchmarks.
The French company said ML4 will get better, as training is not finished and reinforcement learning will conclude in the coming days.
Made in Europe
Mistral said ML4 was trained from scratch over two months on 4,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in its own European data centres.
ML4 covers more than 160 languages, including every official EU language, and works across Latin and non-Latin scripts.
When will it be available?
The model is now available through Mistral's API on Mistral Studio. Mistral plans to release the weights on October 27.
Until then, developers, cybersecurity leaders and state authorities will be able to test the model in real-world settings.

The world’s loudest bird could drown out a rock concert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

The bare-throated bellbird is loud. Very, very loud.
The explosive, metallic mating call of the snow-white male — a stout bird with a broad bill and distinctive blue-green throat patch — can top 130 decibels, louder than a jackhammer or a front-row seat at a Counting Crows concert.
That makes this South American forest dweller a contender for the title of world’s loudest bird. And now researchers think they know how it and other avian loudmouths produce such eardrum-rattling vocalizations.
Bigger bodies and, especially, wider beaks help these feathered screamers belt it out, behavioral ecologists João Menezes and Jeff Podos of the University of Massachusetts Amherst report September 29 in Evolution.
But what pushed some birds to evolve such volume in the first place remains a mystery. The researchers looked at mating behavior, habitat density and flight ability, but found no explanation that consistently held across species. “We weren’t able to find an overarching pattern that applies to birds in general,” Menezes says.
The quest to understand these sonic extremes dates back to 2019. That is when Podos and a colleague crowned the white bellbird (Procnias albus), an Amazonian cousin of the bare-throated bellbird (P. nudicollis), as a record-setting vocal powerhouse. Its 125-decibel calls were the loudest bird calls ever measured at the time.
Beyond the attention-grabbing number, the finding raised a broader question: What makes some birds so extraordinarily loud?
The honk of a Canada goose, for example, can reach chainsaw volume (100 decibels), while the chatter of a starling rarely rises above a dishwasher-level hum (70 decibels) — and ornithologists have surprisingly little understanding of why. Although scientists have spent decades cataloging the timing and frequency of birdsong, hoping to decode what birds are saying, the sheer loudness of bird voices has gone largely unexplored.
To get a read on the racket, Podos lugged a high-grade sound meter, the kind used to monitor noise levels in industrial workplaces, and a laser rangefinder into the woods, swamps and open fields around his home in western Massachusetts. He measured the calls of whatever birds he could find — warblers, sparrows, robins and more.
After logging a few dozen species, he enlisted Menezes, a then-grad student who at the time had recently joined his lab, to help turn the collection into a broader evolutionary analysis. Menezes measured bird vocalizations across his home country of Brazil, from the Atlantic Forest near São Paulo to the mountains surrounding Rio de Janeiro and beyond. He captured everything from the soft chirps of the dusky-throated hermit hummingbird to the piercing yelps of the red-legged seriema, a shaggy type of grassland bird.
All told, he and Podos compiled vocal volume data on 123 species, creating what they say is the largest such dataset to date.
The heftier the bird, the louder its call tended to be, and the same went for birds with broader beaks — a connection between anatomy and acoustic performance that biophysicist Gabriel Mindlin from the University of Buenos Aires in Argentina finds “sensible and plausible.”
“Larger birds have the potential to generate greater respiratory pressures and flows, while morphological features such as beak opening can affect how efficiently acoustic energy radiates,” says Mindlin, who studies birdsong but was not involved in the work.
Why evolution cranked up the volume on these avian megaphones, though, is a puzzle that remains, for now, unhatched.

A First Ride With Lightfoot, a Solar-Powered Scooter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

I stepped out of a building in New York City, put on my helmet, and was about to hop onto my scooter. That’s when I caught a passerby staring at the thing I was about to straddle: a funky-looking solar-powered two-wheeler called the Lightfoot. We locked eyes, and he asked, “Did you make that?”
That's essentially what the Lightfoot feels like—something tinkered into existence in a garage, rather than a factory overseas. It's like a rectangular pod on wheels, with two large solar panels on the side and a bench seat up top that fits a rider and a passenger. It's designed to be ridden in the bike lane—without pedals, it's designated as an electric scooter rather than an ebike—and has a top speed of 20 miles per hour.
Almost everyone who sees it says it looks ridiculous, but in a fun, whimsical sort of way. No doubt that's why its maker dubs it the “smile machine.” No other vehicle I've ever ridden has commanded this much attention. People have commented on the Lightfoot at traffic lights and even mid-ride, where several cyclists precariously pulled out their phones to take photos.
The Lightfoot hails from Otherlab, a research and design company founded by inventor Saul Griffith, who also cofounded Rewiring America, a nonprofit that helps US households switch from fossil fuels to clean energy. Griffith tells WIRED that the project started several years ago after publicly available data showed that 52 percent of all US passenger trips across all modes of transportation were less than three miles. Instead of relying on a car, why not try a simpler vehicle for short trips that can also recharge itself during the day?
“Solar can make a meaningful contribution. There's a nice pathway here for an easy vehicle that people really engage with that's simple and robust,” Griffith says.
Making it a scooter instead of a bike gives it a broader appeal too. “I think for every one person who wants something with pedals, there's nine people who don't give a fuck about pedals,” Griffith says.
I've been living with the Lightfoot for a little over two weeks. Unfortunately, for most of that time, New York City has been facing heavy rainfall—with a nor'easter sprinkled in. Not ideal conditions for a solar-powered scooter. That's why Otherlab is initially focusing on selling its $4,495 vehicle in California—it's now officially on sale (in sky blue or solar orange), and you can reserve one for $100.
Eventually, Griffith says, the company plans to expand into more southern states, beelining toward the Sunshine State, Florida, then gauging interest in northern states. Griffith says the company is talking to resorts, campuses, and fleet managers and plans to sell the Lightfoot in countries like Vietnam, where Hanoi will heavily restrict gas-powered scooters starting in 2027. But that's the larger vision—for now, the focus is to produce enough vehicles and get them to initial customers first.
“If you look at the bloodbath that is people who've done micromobility companies, they nearly all raised too much money and tried to be gigantic immediately,” Griffith says. “We just didn't want to do that.” He says that the first couple of production runs should prove that people like the Lightfoot and allow the company to study how people are using it.
Part of that involves servicing, and Griffith says the company wants to establish a service infrastructure as it expands. However, he points out that the Lightfoot uses common off-the-shelf components that should make repairs easy for most mom-and-pop bike shops (after removing the solar panels).
More evidence that the Lightfoot isn't built for New York City? If you're facing a slew of cloudy days, the only other way to charge it is by plugging it directly into an outlet. You cannot remove the battery. Also, the 137-pound vehicle is designed to be parked outside, meaning you'll need access to a power source that can reach the sidewalk or your patio. I'm lucky enough to have a secure backyard space with an outlet, so I was able to top it up despite the cloudy conditions.
Also, the Lightfoot is a very simple machine. There's no app, no speed modes, no turn signals, nothing. You can set a PIN to secure the thing when you leave it locked up, but that's about it. Unlike ebikes like Infinite Machine's Olto, which feature an alarm system and an always-on GPS to track the vehicle, you'll have to rely on a trusty bike lock and your preferred Bluetooth tracker to keep it safe.
The Power of the Sun
Riding the Lightfoot has been tremendous fun. (That might partly be because it's the first two-wheeled vehicle I've been able to ride since I broke my foot earlier this year.) It has a low center of gravity, and the suspension is excellent, even on rough Brooklyn roads.
It quickly vaults to its 20-mph top speed via the twist throttle, though the torque may be a little too much for some. There's also a small delay from when you twist to when the Lightfoot starts moving, which can feel a little awkward, but I got the hang of it after a few minutes. Power isn't a problem at all. Most e-bikes and scooters I've tested slow down on steeper inclines, like going up and over any of the bridges in New York City, but the Lightfoot maintained its 20-mph speed throughout. (Griffith says it's designed to handle San Francisco's hilly terrain.)
I rarely used the hydraulic disc brakes, instead relying entirely on the aggressive regenerative braking system that kicks in as soon as you stop throttling. Griffith says you can get back about 15 to 20 percent of battery life just from this regen system.
I have some qualms about the Lightfoot's fit and finish. There's a small gap between one of the panels and the scooter frame, and a similar seam between the bench seat and body, meaning some water can get into the inner storage area. The kickstand is also hard to access—it needs a lip that sticks out from under the frame—and when I make tight turns, the kickstand slightly scrapes the road. Griffith says his team is aware of these issues; my unit is a preproduction model, and many of these gripes have already been addressed or will be.
The most underrated feature is the internal storage compartment. It's so nice to toss a backpack or groceries in here instead of carrying them on your back or dangling them off the handlebars. You get two keys to lock the compartment, but I wouldn't leave anything precious in there. Someone could probably break into it with little effort.
Gauging the range is a little tough for something designed to suck up power when it brakes and by just sitting on the street. The company claims 37 miles, and I'm pleased to say I achieved 36 miles on a single charge. It's rare that I get this close to the quoted range, especially considering I'm 6'4" and 220 pounds; these range estimates are usually tested by people with more average heights and weights.
In one day, I scooted from my home in Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, to Bryant Park in Manhattan for a doctor's visit. Then I rode down to a meeting in Chelsea and another in lower Manhattan. I rode back home and didn't plug in. The next morning, I took the Lightfoot back over the bridge for a meeting in the Financial District, then rode home. A full 36 miles, and the vehicle didn't even slow down when the battery was almost gone, the way some electrics do.
Again, how much of that comes from the regen assistance and sun power is hard to say. I tried to park the Lightfoot in sunny areas as best I could (point one panel toward the sun to get the most power), but this isn't as easy as it sounds in a city dense with tall buildings. Coupled with the rainy days, I didn't see the battery bar gain any power while the scooter sat in my backyard for several days.
Then the sun broke the clouds. Finally, on a sunny Saturday, I parked the Lightfoot at the front of my house where it gets the most sunshine. After about six hours, the solar panel was finally doing its job—the battery meter went from around 50 percent to 60 percent. The next day, it sat in the same spot to bask in the sun, and it rose to 72 percent.
Those aren’t huge gains, but again, the Lightfoot isn't designed for a place like New York City. Otherlab claims its solar panels can add up to 18 miles of range in a day under good conditions—around 3 miles per hour of quality sunlight. That seems too good to be true, but I couldn't test it in those conditions.
Still, I nearly leaped for joy when I saw the battery meter ticking upward for the first time. The power of the sun in the panel of my scooter. It's ridiculous. And amazing.

After three years of genocide, Gaza’s olive harvest is going extinct
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Before 2023, Mahmoud Dweima, 75, would look forward to September and October more than any other time of year.
When the olive harvest arrived, he would gather his sprawling family, all 14 sons and daughters, and their children, and prepare for a day of agricultural work that resembled a family picnic.
They packed tall ladders, plastic sheets and tarps to spread beneath the olive trees, buckets for collecting the olives, and enough food to last the day. They brought a small portable gas stove, tomatoes, potatoes, olive oil, za’atar, and bread. Then, early in the morning, they would leave their home in Gaza City’s Shuja’iyya neighborhood and head east toward Juhr al-Dik, where Dweima owned a plot of land planted with over 200 olive trees.
The journey was barely seven kilometers, but Dweima remembers the anticipation around the harvest felt as if theywere traveling from one country to another. The family waited for it all year.
Like thousands of Palestinian families who own olive trees, the harvest was not simply about collecting a crop. It was a season unto itself, a time when families gathered outdoors from dawn to dusk, eating together, working, and returning home with buckets and sacks full of olives.
Today, when October rolls around, Dweima’s family has no olive trees to harvest.
For the third consecutive year, that season has all but disappeared from Gaza. Israel’s war has devastated Gaza’s olive sector, destroying groves, uprooting trees, damaging olive presses, and cutting farmers off from large areas of agricultural land. Much of Gaza’s most productive olive-growing land lies in the eastern parts of the enclave, including areas now behind what has become known as the ‘yellow line’, which demarcates over 64% of Gaza that is now under Israeli military control, and where Palestinian landowners are prohibited from reaching their property.
For farmers like Dweima, the destruction has meant far more than the loss of a crop. A vital source of income cultivated over decades and making up an entire seasonal way of life has been erased, severing families from land passed down and cared for across generations and interrupting one of the most deeply-rooted social rituals in Palestinian life.
According to Gaza’s Ministry of Agriculture, the Strip has lost roughly 90% of the land that was once planted with olive trees. The ministry says the number of olive trees has fallen from around 2 million to approximately 150,000, while annual olive production has plunged from about 40,000 tons to roughly 5,000 tons. Olive oil production, meanwhile, has fallen from approximately 5,000 tons annually to around 700 tons.
In July 2026, Palestinian Agriculture Minister Rizq Salimiya said that more than 1.6 million olive trees had been destroyed in Gaza during the genocide.
For Dweima, those numbers can be measured in the disappearance of every tree he once owned. “Not a single branch is left,” he said. His land was completely bulldozed.
Dweima had spent decades tending his trees, watching them mature and eventually bear fruit. He speaks of them in almost familial terms: he raised and cared for them as his own sons until they began producing fruit like children growing into adulthood.
Before the war, his grove yielded between 70 and 80 containers of olive oil per year, each holding about 16 liters. The family also harvested large quantities of olives for pickling, some of which they kept and others they distributed among neighbors. Giving away part of the harvest was itself part of the tradition.
“Every year, the oil we produced was enough for me to cover living expenses until the next season,” Dweima said. “I would give dozens of pounds of olives to the neighbors, the people who would see us leaving for the harvest and then returning with sacks full of olives.”
For Dweima, this was not simply generosity. It was part of the culture surrounding the harvest. Olive growers, he said, believed that sharing the crop with neighbors and loved ones brought blessings to the remaining groves.
The olive tree, for Dweima and his family, was never merely an agricultural crop. “It represented heritage and identity,” he said.
An uprooted economy
The destruction of the harvest has also affected Dweima’s economic security.
For much of his life, he depended on the olives he harvested, the olive oil he sold, and the olives he preserved. Selling olive oil alone could bring him between $13,000 and $15,000 a year, in addition to income from selling the fruit itself. That annual income is now gone.
Since the war began, Dweima said, his financial situation has deteriorated year after year. Today, even when olive oil is available in Gaza, he says he cannot afford to buy a single 16-liter container. And even if he could, he says, it would not be the same. He cannot find the pure oil he once pressed from his own trees.
Shaher al-Rifi, director general of rural development at Gaza’s Ministry of Agriculture, describes the transformation of the olive sector in similarly stark terms.
“All the lands that were rich with olive trees are gone,” al-Rifi told Mondoweiss. “Inside the yellow line, what remains are small plots here and there with some olive trees.”
According to al-Rifi, Gaza had approximately 44,000 dunams (4,400 hectares) of land planted with olive trees in 2022. The sector produced around 31,000 tons of olives destined for oil, which was pressed in 41 olive presses across the Strip.
Today, he said, only about 5,000 dunams of olive groves remain across Gaza, producing approximately 4,000 to 5,000 tons of olives. Some of the fruit goes to presses for oil production, while the rest is preserved for eating.
Only nine olive presses are currently operating, al-Rifi said, concentrated in Gaza City and the central Gaza Strip.
Keeping those presses running has become difficult. The Ministry of Agriculture is working with other organizations to reduce operating costs, al-Rifi said, as the presses contend with Gaza’s energy crisis and severe fuel shortages. A working olive press can require roughly 20 liters of diesel an hour, fuel that is both scarce and extraordinarily expensive in Gaza.
The ministry, therefore, treats the surviving presses as strategic facilities, al-Rifi said, because they form an essential link in what remains of Gaza’s agricultural production chain.
But the economic importance of the olive season extends far beyond farmers and press owners.
Before the war, the season generated more than 22,000 daily work opportunities across Gaza, according to al-Rifi. Workers were needed to pick olives, transport the harvest, operate presses, package the oil, and market and sell the final products. The residue left after olives were pressed was then used for heating, fertilizer, and soap production, creating additional use from the crop.
For a territory with few natural resources, al-Rifi said, agriculture had long been one of Gaza’s most important productive sectors. He described the olive tree as a witness to the Palestinian experience itself, a tree endowed with a cultural and symbolic memory that extends far beyond its economic value.
“Now, all of that is gone,” he said.
A community built around the harvest
The olive harvest in Gaza was never confined to the trees themselves.
For two weeks, sometimes a month, the groves became gathering places. Families carried everything they needed to remain on their land from sunrise until sunset. Children played between the trees. Women sorted the harvested olives. Relatives and neighbors joined in. Meals were prepared and eaten outdoors.
The work was exhausting, but it was also a celebration.
For many families, the season embodied a connection to land and heritage, reproduced every year through small rituals: separating green olives from black ones, picking out the leaves, cooking lunch over a fire, taking the first harvest to the press, and tasting the season’s first oil.
In Beit Lahia in northern Gaza, 59-year-old Mazouna Abu Riyash once owned land planted with more than 40 olive trees and dozens of lemon trees.
Beit Lahia was renowned for its fertile soil and the diversity of its crops. Abu Riyash’s family cultivated several kinds of fruit, but the olive harvest remained special in its own way. Everyone wanted to participate.
Today, Abu Riyash is displaced in Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza. “The most beautiful time of the entire year was when we began harvesting the olive trees,” she said.
By harvest season, Gaza’s intense summer heat would have begun to fade. As the family worked, the air sometimes became cool enough that they would light small fires to sit around. Then they would cook.
One of the meals Abu Riyash most closely associates with the harvest is “galayet bandora,” a traditional Palestinian stew of tomatoes cooked in olive oil from last year’s season.
But another meal had to wait for the first oil of the season. Once the family had taken their olives to the press and brought back the fresh oil, they would prepare “musakhan,” a Palestinian dish made with bread, onions, chicken, sumac, and generous amounts of olive oil.
The meal would then be served at lunch for everyone working in the grove.
“We would prepare it there in the field, in front of everyone, and they would all eat together,” Abu Riyash said.
These memories, Abu Riyash said, “reveal what has been lost beyond the agricultural devastation itself. The rituals of the harvest were fundamentally social. They connected relatives, neighbors to families, and families to the land they cultivated.”

Slovenia has struck digital gold, courtesy of the White House. Since US President Donald Trump signed an executive order rebranding artificial intelligence as "super intelligence"or "SI", buyers have been scrambling for the country's .si web domains.
Users around the world are rushing to buy .si domains in anticipation of businesses needing to switch their branding from artificial intelligence to super intelligence or “SI”, following an executive order by Donald Trump.
The US President officially renamed artificial intelligence to “super intelligence” after hosting a summit of America’s leading AI companies.
According to web hosting company Hostinger, 22,800 domains have been registered by 8,000 buyers since Trump first made his comments at the UN on 23 September.
Activity peaked during the first two days of October, with 5,300 registrations made each day.
Traffic slowed during the weekend to 2,246 registrations on Saturday and 2,804 on Sunday, albeit these figures are five times the pre-order daily average of roughly 520.
Growth is expected to pick up again this week.
Users from the US and India made up about half of all registrations, recording 5,640 and 5,560 respectively, with Morocco coming in third at roughly 1,320 domains and ahead of the UK, UAE and Canada.
Buyers in Morocco average 4.9 domains each versus 2.8 overall, which suggests people are buying domains to resell later.
Despite this glut of activity, the domains being registered have little to do with artificial intelligence, with just 3% of registrations including explicit AI terms.
Meanwhile shorter names are the most registered at 13%, followed by tech.
Trump first mentioned his preference for super intelligence over artificial intelligence during a speech at the UN general assembly just two weeks ago. He argued that “artificial” makes it sound fake when it is actually “amazing,” claiming that “super intelligence" is a more accurate description.
Top AI companies have not publicly opposed Trump's push to rebrand AI as SI. Elon Musk went further, later announcing that his AI company, SpaceXAI, would become SpaceXSI.
Since then, users around the world have been rushing to purchase digital real estate — in this case, domains — using artificial intelligence’s new SI moniker.

Von der Leyen turns to Europe’s refineries as shrinking capacity raises energy security concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:57:56 UTC
21:57:56 KST

Europe wants to reduce its dependence on fossil fuels, but while it still relies heavily on oil — particularly diesel — reducing the infrastructure that processes that oil has increased vulnerability during the green transition.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced on Tuesday a new "strategic dialogue" on European refineries, drawing attention to a growing vulnerability for the EU: its shrinking refining capacity, which has been declining since 2009.
European refineries — which convert crude oil into refined products such as diesel or jet fuel — have been closing or reducing capacity for years as ageing plants became less profitable and demand patterns shifted.
As a result, the European Union has become increasingly reliant on imports of finished fuels from places such as the disrupted Middle East, the less predictable United States and India.
Under the bloc's green ambitions, the shift away from fossil fuels has left the EU with fewer traditional fuels over the past years, while global conflicts make it harder to secure reliable energy.
"The aim is to bring down costs and to ensure we have the supplies needed also for defence," von der Leyen told European Union lawmakers ahead of the gathering of EU heads of State on 15 October.
The political talks will be chaired by Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen and Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius.
The latest emergency oil stocks release announced by the G7 was meant to provide short-term relief from rising energy prices.
Securing oil from global markets has become more costly, with Brent crude averaging $101 per barrel in September and tensions escalating in the Middle East.
Since the US and Israel bombed Iran on 28 February, the EU has paid more than €100 billion in additional costs for fossil fuel imports, without importing actual fuel, according to Commissioner Jørgensen.
Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, coupled with China’s suspension of fuel exports, are worsening an already precarious situation, raising the risk that the EU could draw down its emergency oil reserves faster than anticipated.
Saudi Aramco's chief Amin Nasser recently warned that the world’s oil stockpiles are "scarily thin".
Europe can import crude oil relatively easily, despite major disruptions in key chokepoints, but its declining refining capacity can't guarantee the refined diesel, jet fuel and petrol it needs.
20% oil refining capacity lost since 2009
At the end of 2025, the EU-27, UK, Norway and Switzerland had 72 mainstream refineries with 625.4 million tonnes a year of primary refining capacity — 167.6 million tonnes less than in 2009, according to industry data from Concawe, the scientific division of the industry body FuelsEurope, representing nearly 100% of the oil refining capacity in Europe.
The EU-27 alone accounted for 567.4 million tonnes in 2025.
By 2025, two more refineries were closed. At least five of the closed facilities have undergone a "transformation process," abandoning crude oil entirely to convert into biorefineries.
Germany remains the biggest refining centre in the figures, with 98.7 million tonnes of capacity, followed by Italy at 78.6 million, Spain at 70.6 million, the Netherlands at 59.7 million and France at 57.4 million. Belgium has 32 million tonnes.
The debate around refining is often framed as a question of the past, a FuelsEurope spokesperson told Euronews, noting that it is a matter of Europe's future resilience.
"The real question is whether Europe will continue to produce a significant share of them domestically while transforming its industry, or become increasingly dependent on imports from regions with different regulatory, environmental and geopolitical conditions," the FuelsEurope spokesperson added.
The trade-body association argued that the latest concerns raised by the G7 put the spotlight on the European refining sector. It noted that the 20% reduction in refining capacity, due to 35 refinery closures since 2009, is coming back to bite.
Ben McWilliams, affiliate fellow at the think tank Bruegel, said that emergency stocks are no replacement for domestic refining capacity and stressed that the EU's ability to refine oil is of "significant strategic relevance".
"Europe needs to ensure that it carefully maintains a domestic resource of oil refining capacity, particularly to meet the unique demands of each fuel (including diesel, gasoline, kerosene, and naphtha for the chemical industry)," McWilliams told Euronews.
Replace demand, not capacity, says Green MEP
EU lawmaker Michael Bloss (Germany/Greens) said that the EU is "dangerously" being pushed to deplete its emergency stocks just before winter.
"We are being blackmailed and don't control our own energy. Right now the US is pressuring us over our own diesel stocks, Russia is withholding diesel as leverage over sanctions, and China has paused exports," Bloss told Euronews.
Bloss argues that refineries have closed because of declining oil demand and shrinking profit margins.
"Those were business decisions, and oil demand will continue to collapse, so probably they were right," the German lawmaker added.
But he flagged the "real mistake" being the lack of refined products in the bloc's emergency stocks.
"We keep our emergency stocks mostly as crude, while our actual weak spot is diesel and jet fuel. Blaming climate policy for refinery closures gets the story backward," Bloss added.
The more ecological way to face this crisis, according to Bloss, is to replace the demand rather than the refining capacity, noting that starting a new refinery from scratch or repurposing it would take years and the bloc would still be dependent on crude oil.
"Europe should put its money into electrifying road transport, logistics and rail freight. That also means no further weakening of the CO2 standards for cars and trucks: every rollback there is a vote for more diesel dependence," Bloss said.

South Korea has become one of Russia’s biggest fuel suppliers. Some shipments are arriving on sanctioned tankers.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:57:24 UTC
21:57:24 KST

South Korea has become one of Russia’s biggest fuel suppliers. Some shipments are arriving on sanctioned tankers.
By the end of summer, South Korea had become Russia’s second-largest supplier of petroleum products, and sanctioned tankers were among those used to ship the fuel, The Guardian reported.
Tankers made 14 voyages from several South Korean ports to Russia’s Far East in July and August, carrying 176,000 tons of fuel, mostly diesel, according to The Guardian.
Seven tankers plied the routes, three of them under British and EU sanctions. One, the tanker Chongchon, did not even enter South Korean ports: its fuel was transferred from another vessel at sea, a method that conceals the cargo’s origin.
In at least two more cases, sanctioned tankers loading at South Korean ports officially listed Japan as their destination but instead headed for Vladivostok. Exactly who owned and sold the fuel remains unclear.
Russia imported 368,000 tons of petroleum products by sea in August, with 112,000 tons supplied by South Korea. Only India supplied more fuel to Russia that month.
South Korea’s Foreign Ministry declined to comment on the shipments or the use of sanctioned tankers. It said only that Seoul “supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”
South Korea has supplied Ukraine with humanitarian aid since the full-scale war with Russia began, along with non-lethal military equipment such as body armor and demining vehicles, The Guardian reported. But Seoul is trying to balance its support for Kyiv against its desire to maintain good relations with Moscow, and has only partially joined Western sanctions, mainly through export controls on industrial equipment and high-tech goods.
The fuel shipments, amid a crisis in Russia caused by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries, could expose Seoul as a “weak link” in Western efforts to pressure the Kremlin, The Guardian concluded.
The Guardian’s report on fuel shipments from South Korea to Russia came amid a diplomatic row between Seoul and Kyiv. At the U.N. General Assembly in late September, Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had transferred to South Korea two North Korean soldiers captured in early 2025.
Seoul accused Zelensky of violating an agreement to keep the transfer secret, noting that Ukraine itself had originally insisted on the secrecy. South Korea demanded that Kyiv issue an official apology.
Today, South Korea’s foreign minister, Cho Hyun, said he had received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, but that its level was different “from the level we expect.” He said Seoul now intends to “take firm measures.”

The India mood: Confidence in the country, anxiety about careers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:54:46 UTC
21:54:46 KST

A sense of collective pride, and yet a feeling of individual disquiet. This is probably the most accurate description of the mood among India's more connected, urban-skewed population. There is confidence in the larger macroeconomic story, even as there is lingering uncertainty about the jobs market and an apparent weakening of the old assumption that education is a sure-shot route to upward mobility. Ipsos's September surveys capture that dilemma between hope and anxiety. India ranks first among 30 markets on consumer confidence but 16th on jobs, and unemployment is the issue Indian respondents worry about most.India's consumers are upbeat about the economy. In Ipsos's September 2026 Global Consumer Confidence Index, India scores 66.9, the highest among the 30 markets, compared with a global average of 48.4. Ipsos says its India sample is more urban, educated and/or affluent than the general population and hence the results should be read as reflecting the views of a more "connected" segment.
High on confidence about India, not so much about jobs
India's Current Index, an indicator of how people rate present conditions, is 70.7, and its Investment Index is 73.2, both the highest among the 30 markets in the published survey.
Its Expectations Index, at 66.4, ranks fourth, so respondents are also buoyant about the future.The contrast is particularly sharp against the world's major advanced economies. Among the G7, the US has the highest overall consumer-confidence score at 50.5, followed by Great Britain at 48.2 and Canada at 47.3. Italy scores 43.0, Germany 41.4, France 40.6 and Japan 39.4. India, at 66.9, is therefore 16.4 points above the best-performing G7 economy.Across the countries surveyed, India is the most confident market, followed by Sweden at 60.0 and Malaysia at 54.8. At the other end, Türkiye is lowest at 35.3, followed by Argentina at 37.8 and Japan at 39.4. The gap between India and Türkiye is more than 31 points. Only one number breaks the pattern. India's Jobs Index is 59.3, putting it in 16th spot. On current conditions and investment, India sits more than 30 points above the 30-country average. On jobs, its lead is just 1.6 points.
Jobs top the worry list
In the September edition of Ipsos's What Worries the World survey, 47% of Indian respondents name unemployment among the three issues they find most worrying in the country, making it the most frequently cited concern in India. The global average is 29%. South Africa, Argentina, Singapore, Indonesia and Chile are the only countries with a higher share of respondents citing unemployment as a worry.Among the G7, unemployment is cited as a top concern by 28% in Canada and Italy, 20% in the US, 19% in Great Britain, 16% in France and 13% each in Germany and Japan, well below India's 47%. Across the 30 countries surveyed, concern is highest in South Africa, at 69%, and lowest in the Netherlands, at 6%.The same survey also finds strong optimism among Indian respondents. Seventy per cent say the country is heading in the right direction, against a global average of 38%. Only Singapore, at 80%, records a higher figure. Meanwhile, 79% describe the current economic situation in India as good, again compared with a global average of 38%.
People most worried about unemployment
Here too India stands apart from the G7. The share saying their country is heading in the right direction is 44% in Canada, 36% in Japan, 28% in Great Britain, 27% in the US, 23% in Italy, 14% in Germany and 11% in France. Singapore does best on this measure at 80%, while France is at the bottom at 11%.The jobs concern, in other words, does not stem from general economic pessimism. The more connected Indians Ipsos surveys can be positive about the economy and still name unemployment as one of the country's most worrying problems.
Education is second in the list of worries
Ipsos switched its India consumer-confidence sample from a mixed methodology to online-only in April 2026, a break that the September report flags. Long-term comparisons therefore need caution.
What the government data show
Do the official numbers help explain this contrasting mood?Real GDP grew 7.8% year-on-year in the April-June quarter of 2026-27, according to MoSPI estimates. Private final consumption expenditure, the broad measure of household consumption, increased 7.1%, while gross fixed capital formation rose 11.9% at constant prices. Those numbers are broadly consistent with Ipsos's strong readings for current conditions and investment sentiment.The labour market data are more mixed. The government's monthly Periodic Labour Force Survey put India's unemployment rate for people aged 15 and above at 5.0% in August on the Current Weekly Status measure, marginally lower than 5.1% in July. But the improvement came from rural India. Rural unemployment fell from 4.5% to 4.1%, while the urban rate was almost unchanged, moving from 6.7% to 6.8%. The urban Worker Population Ratio was also 47.0%, unchanged from July and below 47.5% a year earlier.These figures are not directly comparable with Ipsos's Jobs Index. PLFS measures actual labour-market status; Ipsos measures perceptions of job security and the employment environment. There is another limitation to headline unemployment numbers. NITI Aayog has also highlighted job quality, informality and underemployment as labour-market concerns, dimensions that an unemployment rate alone cannot fully capture.Taken together, the data help explain how the seemingly contradictory findings can coexist.
The classroom-to-career gap
Education is India's second-most cited concern, at 36%. That is the highest among the 30 countries, against a global country average of 13%. India's top two concerns, unemployment and education, are both closely tied to economic opportunity. The government's labour survey tracks one measure that spans both. In the latest PLFS annual report, covering 2025, 25.0% of people aged 15-29 were not in employment, education or training, or NEET. Among those aged 15-24, the share was 21.0%.The same report put the unemployment rate at 9.9% for 15-29-year-olds, 13.6% for urban youth and 6.5% for people with at least secondary education. NEET is not an unemployment measure: it also includes young people who are neither working nor studying but may not be looking for work. So for Indians, confidence in the economy, current conditions and investment is higher than in any other market. The Jobs Index is the exception, and the official data point to where some of the strain lies: among urban youth and the educated.
That is the lived reality the surveys capture. The pride is collective: it is about where the country is heading. The disquiet surfaces when the conversation turns to jobs and education. With technology rapidly changing the nature of work, continuous learning and reskilling are becoming an economic necessity. But many workers and young people still lack the support, guidance and pathways needed to navigate that transition.The surveys offer a snapshot of that churn.

The price of doing business in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:54:43 UTC
21:54:43 KST

The price of doing business in Russia
Seagull walks on a logo of Raiffeisen bank atop a building behind a monument of Soviet country founder Vladimir Ulyanov, also known as Lenin in Moscow on April 12, 2022. (Kirill Kudryavtev /AFP via Getty Images)
When Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, most global businesses rushed for the exit.
Swiss food and drink firm Nestlé was not among them. The company hunkered down, a decision it framed as ensuring local people's "right to food."
It made little difference to the Kremlin. On Sept. 17, the Russian government placed Nestlé Russia under temporary external administration, a move that could lead to the company's ultimate confiscation or nationalization.
Nestlé now says it is "assessing the situation and its options." It is not alone. In recent weeks, French supermarket chain Auchan and German food wholesaler Metro have been among those who have also seen their assets placed under external control.
Auchan told Russian news outlet RBC that it was continuing operations and had sought further clarification from the government. Metro said that the effects of the decision were "currently being analyzed."
But there seems to be little prospect of returning to business as usual, with the Kremlin tying its decision to geopolitics and its war on Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters that the companies were from "unfriendly countries" that were "actively involved in military actions against our nation, and involved in strikes carried out by Kyiv," he said.
read also
High risk, no reward
When foreign businesses moved into Russia after the collapse of the Soviet Union, they found a market with both high risks and high rewards.
Multinational companies made phenomenal returns in Russia throughout the 1990s and early 2000s, says Charles Hecker, the author of Zero Sum: The Arc of International Business in Russia.
But they also made assumptions about how Russia would develop economically and politically.
"Companies failed to keep pace with the political change in the country," Hecker says. "They were making life-changing sums of money in Russia. And I think that that distracted us from some of the political and geopolitical realities."
Today, the Russian market is as risky as that of the 1990s, but offers little in the way of returns. While leaving is still an option, companies that do so face steep penalties. Foreign firms from so-called "unfriendly countries" must sell assets at an eye-watering 60% discount, while also paying a "contribution" to Russia’s state budget equal to 35% of those assets' market value.
Some companies paid up. Others hoped they would benefit from playing the long game, says Christopher Hartwell, a professor of international business policy at the ZHAW School of Management and Law.
"You think, maybe if I just keep my head down, it'll blow over. You think, if I'm going to come back in 10 years, after (Russian President Vladimir) Putin dies and this war is over, it's going to be very difficult to get back into the market because you have competitors who are using all of your assets. So maybe we need to stay here in terms of, you know, just keeping our foot in the door," he says.
Moscow also signaled goodwill toward such firms. In March 2025, Putin told a congress of Russian industrialists that Western companies that left but kept their staff and technology, with Russians running them under a different brand, had "made an independent and responsible choice."
Yet there had already been grave warnings of what was to come. Even if companies in 2022 could not have imagined their assets being expropriated by the Russian state, their calculations would have quickly changed when the Russian subsidiaries of companies such as Danone and Carlsberg were similarly placed under external administration in 2023.
Russian state news agency TASS reported on Sept. 29 that 135 companies linked to foreign firms had been placed under such controls.
"Anybody could have seen this coming from a mile away," says Hartwell.
All for the war
A transnational corporation such as Nestlé is a greater prize for the Kremlin, and its assets are likely to be used to buy the loyalty of groups on which the Kremlin relies, says geopolitical analyst Alexander Kokcharov.
Danone and Carlsberg are good examples of what is yet to come.
In 2023, Yakub Zakriev, reportedly a relative of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov, was named head of Danone's Russian subsidiary, before it was sold on to another firm linked to a former Chechen official. Another Putin ally, Taimuraz Bolloev, was also named head of Baltika, the Russian brewer formerly owned by Carlsberg, before it too was sold on.
Many of these groups would usually receive money of some kind from Russia’s state budget, says Kokcharov. But as Russia’s economy continues to struggle and resources are instead pushed toward the war, gifting business assets can make up the shortfall.
As Moscow's war on Ukraine consumes Russian society, buying that loyalty and shoring up budgets have become more important than maintaining business relationships, says Kokcharov. Meanwhile, Nestlé's case suggests that the Kremlin is giving up on the idea of returning to "business as usual."
"My understanding was that the Kremlin saw war in Ukraine as temporary. The sanctions are temporary. The disruption of business relationships is temporary. And once Russia achieves what it wants in Ukraine, there would be some sort of a thaw, some sort of a reset," Kokcharov says. "My guess is that now they realize that this is not happening."
This shift in outlook means it's unlikely that Nestlé, Auchan, or Metro will be the last Western companies to face their assets being taken out of their control.
"If you're a Western company still trying to do business in Russia, you are playing with fire," says Kokcharov. "The entire political system is concentrated on the war, and it doesn't care about Western businesses or reputations, for that matter."
For those companies that have chosen to shelter in place in the Russian market, it is another stark warning to add to an increasingly long list.
"You can have a good run if you get in bed with authoritarians, but at some point you're going to wake up and realize that your wallet and your kidneys are gone," says Hartwell. "And was it really worth it?"

Key aircraft incidents that reshaped aviation safety rules since 9/11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

Key aircraft incidents that reshaped aviation safety rules since 9/11
Oct 6 - A flydubai co-pilot stabbed his captain with an emergency "crash axe" in what UAE prosecutors have called a terrorist attack, with the plane plunging 16,000 feet in 30 seconds before it was brought under control by passengers and a stand-by crew.
It landed safely thanks to some heroics from the injured captain, with all on board surviving. The co-pilot is being questioned, with Israeli officials saying that he had planned the attack even before joining the airline.
The incident on the flight bound for Tel Aviv from Dubai has once more put on-board security and pilot-screening procedures under scrutiny, after previous incidents from 9/11 to the 2015 Germanwings crash led to changes in safety protocols.
Here is a timeline of some of the major commercial aviation incidents since 2001 and how they changed aviation security or cockpit access rules.
9/11 ATTACKS
On September 11, 2001, al Qaeda hijackers took over four US passenger jets, crashing two into the World Trade Center in New York and one into the Pentagon outside Washington. Nearly 3,000 people were killed.
The attacks reshaped aviation security, with US airport screening beefed up in November that year and the federal air marshal programme greatly expanded.
US airlines had to install reinforced cockpit doors built to withstand forced entry and gunfire by April 2003. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) later made the doors a worldwide requirement.
A US rule requiring a second barrier to protect the cockpit whenever the door is opened in flight took effect for new aircraft in August 2026.
'SHOE BOMBER'
On December 22, 2001, British national Richard Reid tried to blow up an American Airlines jet flying from Paris to Miami with homemade explosives hidden in his shoes. Crew and passengers subdued him as he tried to detonate the bomb and the flight diverted safely to Boston.
The foiled attack led US airport security to require passengers to remove their shoes at security screenings starting in 2006, a mandate that was lifted in 2025.
MOZAMBIQUE AIRLINES
An Embraer regional jet operated by Mozambique Airlines crashed in Namibia on November 29, 2013, after it began a sudden descent, killing 27 passengers and 6 crew members.
Investigators found the aircraft started losing altitude after captain Herminio dos Santos manually changed the settings while his co-pilot had gone to the bathroom. Dos Santos locked the co-pilot out of the cockpit and brought the plane down after altering the plane's speed and altitude several times.
In its final report, the Namibian agency investigating the incident recommended Mozambique regulators ensure two people are always in the flight deck and called on ICAO to create standards to stop authorized crew members from being locked out of the cockpit.
GERMANWINGS CRASH
An Airbus A320 operated by Lufthansa's low-cost carrier Germanwings crashed in the French Alps on March 24, 2015, after co-pilot Andreas Lubitz locked the captain out of the cockpit and deliberately flew the aircraft into a mountainside, killing 150 people.
Investigators said Lubitz, whose death was ruled a suicide, had shown symptoms consistent with a "psychotic depressive episode" months before the crash.
Three days after the crash, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency issued a temporary recommendation that two people, one of them a pilot, remain in the cockpit at all times during flight. It later softened its position, leaving airlines to decide case by case, but tightened mental health rules, adding a mandatory psychological assessment for pilots. REUTERS

Affordable HIV prevention injection to be offered in the MENA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:53:15 UTC
21:53:15 KST

Breadcrumb
New $40 HIV drug could transform prevention across MENA
A new HIV prevention drug that requires just two injections a year will be made available for around $40 annually in eleven countries across the MENA region and Afghanistan, its manufacturer Gilead Sciences has told The New Arab.
Lenacapavir, sold under the brand name Yeztugo in the US, is a long-acting form of HIV prevention that could offer an alternative for people who find taking preventative medication every day difficult.
Its rollout comes as the Middle East and North Africa is moving against the global trend, with the number of new HIV transmissions rising sharply in the region.
While new HIV infections globally fell by around 40% between 2010 and 2024, they rose by 94% in MENA over the same period, from an estimated 12,000 to 23,000 a year, according to UNAIDS.
Lenacapavir is a form of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), medication taken by people who do not have HIV to prevent transmission. The most common form of PrEP is currently a daily pill containing tenofovir disoproxil and emtricitabine.
The twice-yearly injection could therefore offer an alternative requiring far fewer doses.
But there is a vast difference in how much the drug will cost depending on where a patient lives.
In the US, Gilead's Yeztugo costs $28,218 per year. Under voluntary licensing agreements reached by the company, six generic manufacturers will be able to produce cheaper versions of lenacapavir for use in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
The generic version is expected to cost around $40 per person per year, with widespread availability expected in 2027 following a limited rollout in late 2026.
In the region, Afghanistan, Djibouti, Egypt, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, Tunisia and Yemen are covered by the agreements.
Egyptian pharmaceutical company Eva Pharma is among the six manufacturers licensed to produce generic lenacapavir.
"The licensing territory reflects multiple considerations, including HIV burden, economic context, financing capacity and where generic access can have the greatest public health impact," Gilead Sciences told The New Arab.
The company said its access strategy was developed "with a focus on speed, volume, affordability and coordinated delivery to help ensure broad and sustainable access".
But several MENA countries are not covered by the agreement, including Lebanon and Iraq.
Their exclusion raises questions over access in lower- and middle-income countries that do not qualify for the cheaper generic version but where the price of Gilead's branded drug could put widespread use out of reach.
The issue has drawn wider criticism from Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), which has raised concerns over countries excluded from Gilead's voluntary licensing agreement and restrictions on where licensed generic manufacturers can sell the drug.
Gilead is also working with the US State Department through the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) and the Global Fund, a worldwide partnership tackling AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria, to expand access to lenacapavir while generic production is scaled up.
The company has committed to supplying lenacapavir at no profit for prevention in certain eligible countries until generic versions become available.
PEPFAR does not operate in any countries in the Middle East or North Africa, while the Global Fund told The New Arab that it was currently supporting the rollout of lenacapavir in 21 countries, including Morocco, and is preparing for a major global expansion.
Access to HIV testing and treatment remains particularly low across the region.
Only around 63% of people living with HIV in the Middle East and North Africa know their status, while fewer than half are receiving treatment, according to UNAIDS.
Around 48% of people living with HIV in the region are receiving antiretroviral treatment and 44% have achieved viral suppression, well below UNAIDS' global targets.
UNAIDS has pointed to stigma and discrimination as major barriers to accessing HIV testing, prevention and treatment in the region. HIV disproportionately affects some groups, including men who have sex with men, sex workers and people who use drugs, who can also face criminalisation across much of the Middle East and North Africa.
Effective treatment allows people living with HIV to live long and healthy lives. People who maintain an undetectable viral load through treatment also cannot sexually transmit HIV, a principle known as U=U, or "undetectable equals untransmittable".
Without treatment, however, HIV can progress to AIDS, severely weakening the immune system and leaving people vulnerable to tuberculosis, some cancers and other illnesses.

Former German spy chief arrested on suspicion of treason and espionage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:52:28 UTC
21:52:28 KST

Former German spy chief arrested on suspicion of treason and espionage
August Hanning’s former chief of staff was also arrested on suspicion of ‘aiding and abetting attempted treason’.
Germany’s former foreign spy chief has been arrested on suspicion of espionage and treason, prosecutors have said.
August Hanning, 80, is under investigation for attempted treason and acting as an agent for a foreign intelligence service, the Office of the Federal Public Prosecutor General confirmed on Tuesday.
Hanning was president of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service between 1998 and 2005.
He was arrested in Bad Toelz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany. His former chief of staff, partially identified as Manfred D, was arrested in Steinfurt in western Germany on suspicion of “aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage”.
The prosecutor’s office said, “On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service.”
Prosecutors said Manfred D also served as the chief of staff for Hanning’s successors between 2012 and 2026, and used his role to gain access to confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning “in exchange for remuneration”. Hanning then used the information in his private consulting work, prosecutors added.
“The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said.
The statement did not reveal who the two men were suspected of spying for or which country the foreign agent worked for, adding that “it has yet to be determined if the material reached the intended recipient”.
German MP Marc Henrichmann told the AFP news agency that Germany “will not tolerate the betrayal of secrets”.
Henrichmann, who chairs the German parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, said, “Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out.”
The premises of Manfred D and Hanning were being searched in several locations, including in the capital, Berlin.

Israel puts military on high alert for Oct 7 anniversary, warns Gazans
JERUSALEM – Israel’s defence minister said on Oct 6 he had put the military on high alert before the anniversary of Hamas’ Oct 7, 2023 attack, warning that Gazans would pay a “heavy price” if the forces were harmed.
The office of Defence Minister Israel Katz said the instruction came “in the light of intelligence regarding Hamas’ intentions to attempt to carry out attacks and terror operations against our forces in Gaza on that day”.
“If, heaven forbid, our forces are harmed, the ones who will pay the heavy price will be Hamas and the population of Gaza – beyond all proportion,” the statement added.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu suggested on Oct 6 during a government meeting that Hamas could try to attack Israel ahead of elections later in October.
“We are prepared for this; first and foremost, we will thwart such attempts, and, in any case, we will respond with overwhelming force if they make this mistake,” Netanyahu said.
Israelis will head to the polls on Oct 27, with Netanyahu locked in a tight race for re-election.
Hamas’ Oct 7, 2023 attack was the deadliest in Israel’s history, resulting in the deaths of 1,221 people.
Militants also dragged 251 hostages into Gaza, 44 of them already dead.
In response, Israel launched a military offensive that has left most of Gaza in ruins and killed more than 74,200 people, according to Gaza’s health ministry.
Since a ceasefire was declared last October, Israeli forces have killed more than 1,440 people in Gaza, according to the ministry.
On Oct 5, during a state ceremony to mark three years since the attack, Netanyahu said there would be “no Hamas rule in Gaza” and vowed to continue targeting anyone who was involved in the attack or who held hostages. AFP

Yemen rivals marshal forces for new ‘war of resources’ – RT reports (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:52:04 UTC

Yemen rivals marshal forces for new ‘war of resources’ – RT reports (VIDEO)
Yemen’s internationally recognized government has vowed to retake territory held by the Houthis, raising the prospect of a new phase in a conflict that has ravaged the country for more than a decade.
The Presidential Leadership Council (PLC) has ordered its armed forces and security formations to begin implementing plans “until the country is liberated from the grip of terrorist militias,” while also calling for a general mobilization.
But the balance of power is more complicated than the lines on the map suggest, RT’s Oumaima Ichchar reports.
“The government may control more of Yemen on the map, but it is the Houthis who control most of its people,” she said. The PLC is estimated to hold around 60.4% of Yemen’s territory, while the Houthis control about 22.8%, including the capital Sanaa and some of the country’s most densely populated areas.
The Houthis are estimated to have around 350,000 fighters, while estimates for the fragmented PLC forces range from 40,000 to 250,000. But, as Ichchar notes, “even hundreds of thousands of fighters mean little if you can’t properly arm or supply them.”
The Houthis have spent years developing long-range missiles and drones, as well as domestic weapons production, while PLC forces remain closely tied to Saudi military and financial support.
The Houthis have also built a “parallel economy” in the territory they control, collecting taxes, customs duties, religious levies and other revenues estimated at around $2.5 billion a year. The PLC, meanwhile, remains heavily dependent on outside financial support, particularly from Saudi Arabia.
With manpower, weapons, money and foreign backing all potentially determining what comes next, Ichchar examines the comparative strength of the warring sides and what she describes as the “ultimate war of resources.”

EU Parliament spat as MEP challenges Metsola’s claims over Israeli flag
