The 'death' of back-office jobs: office work in the AI storm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:41:50 UTC
21:41:50 KST

From insurance payouts to banking, AI is taking over tasks that once took hours or days of human work – which office jobs are first in line for automation?
Two years ago, processing a health insurance claim at one of Greece's largest insurance companies took on average 14 days. Medical opinions, test results, invoices and policy details all had to be checked and cross-referenced before payment was given the green light.
Today, the processing time has been cut to around one minute and the compensation is paid out the following day.
Driving this change is AI Flows, an artificial intelligence tool for document processing and workflow automation developed by the Greek company Archeiothiki. The system handles around 1,500 claims a day, "reads" the documents, extracts the necessary information and cross-checks it against the policy and the insurance company's rules.
Above all, though, it enables something that was previously practically impossible: checking 100% of cases rather than just a sample. This makes it possible to spot potential fraud that would otherwise have gone unnoticed.
The example of the Greek insurer offers a snapshot of a much broader transformation unfolding in offices across Europe.
From 16 hours to a few minutes
In banking, similar technology is used to assess the ESG (environmental, social governance) criteria of companies seeking finance.
The process involves around 300 questions. To verify the answers, staff must hunt for data in company reports running to hundreds of pages, ranging from the ratio of men to women to information on environmental performance and corporate policies.
This check used to require about 16 hours of human labour. Now, an AI system can search for the necessary information even in reports running to 400 or 500 pages, identify the relevant passages and process them in a fraction of the time.
The final assessment of ESG criteria influences the interest rate at which the company will be financed.
Jobs on the frontline
Archeiothiki currently applies AI Flows to around 100 different workflows for ten clients, mainly banks, insurance companies and businesses in the healthcare sector.
But what is happening in Greece is far from unique.
Office roles that have traditionally formed the back office of companies are among those most exposed to the new generation of artificial intelligence.
According to the report "Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure", published in May 2025 by the International Labour Organization (ILO) and the Polish research institute NASK, administrative and clerical occupations remain the category of jobs most exposed to generative AI.
Among the most exposed roles are data entry clerks, staff involved in accounting and bookkeeping, and administrative secretaries. In high-income economies, roughly one in three jobs shows some degree of exposure to generative AI.
Artificial intelligence has already entered European workplaces on a large scale. According to the study "Digital Monitoring, Algorithmic Management and the Platformisation of Work in Europe" by the Joint Research Centre of the European Commission, published in October 2025, 30% of workers in the EU already use AI tools in their jobs. Use is particularly high in office work.
The transition also has a clear gender dimension. More recent ILO research shows that occupations where women are in the majority are almost twice as likely to be exposed to generative AI as those where men predominate: 29% compared with 16%.
One key reason is the greater presence of women in administrative, clerical and support roles.
"I will not hide it. There are jobs that are lost too," was the response of Archeiothiki executives when asked about this by Euronews.
The picture they sketch, however, is more complex. In many cases, automation is not used simply to carry out the same volume of work with fewer people. It allows companies to take on tasks that were previously practically impossible to perform at this scale.
One client, for instance, had around 50 people working on a single process and still built up a year-long backlog. In other cases, where only a sample of cases could previously be checked, now the entire set can be examined.
This aligns broadly with the ILO's assessment. The organisation warns that the "exposure" of a job to artificial intelligence does not necessarily mean that role will disappear. Few occupations consist solely of tasks that can currently be fully automated. For this reason, the most likely outcome for now is the transformation of jobs rather than their complete replacement.
The next data reservoir: the public sector
In Greece, the next major field may lie in the millions of documents that have already been digitised in the public sector.
According to Archeiothiki's chief executive, Andreas Papadakis, the company has carried out around 15% of the relevant digitisation projects for the state.
The problem is that much of this new digital archive remains effectively "blind". Physical documents were turned into digital files and given basic metadata so they could be searched. Their content, however, was not necessarily converted into structured data that can be analysed and put to use.
The first stage of digitisation was to turn mountains of paper into digital files. The next stage is already under way.
AI systems are no longer confined to reading and recording documents, but can extract information, cross-check it and execute entire workflows.
This shifts automation away from repetitive data-entry tasks to a much larger portion of the traditional back office.

====================================================================================================

Archaeologists may have finally solved a 100-year-old Florida mystery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:41:48 UTC
21:41:48 KST

Archaeologists may have finally solved a 100-year-old Florida mystery
- Date:
- October 6, 2026
- Source:
- Florida Museum of Natural History
- Summary:
- Ancient pottery from Tampa Bay appears to have been made by migrant craftspeople who brought specialized Mississippian pottery-making knowledge hundreds of miles south. Remarkably, they even incorporated crushed fragments of older homeland pottery into new vessels, preserving a physical link to their past across generations.
- Share:
About a century ago, archaeologists excavating pottery fragments around Tampa Bay encountered something puzzling. Some of the pieces carried decorations that looked strikingly similar to pottery found hundreds of miles farther north. On appearance alone, the fragments seemed connected to the Mississippian culture, which emerged more than 1,000 years ago and reshaped social, economic and political life across much of southeastern North America.
For decades, however, maps of the Mississippian world generally left out peninsular Florida. The Tampa Bay pottery suggested that the region's relationship with that culture may have been more complicated.
"It's been this open debate for a century," said Neill Wallis, curator of Florida archaeology, bioarchaeology and the Ceramic Technology Laboratory at the Florida Museum of Natural History. "Tampa Bay sites had some Mississippian-like traits such as platform mound-village complexes and iconography, but lacked others, like maize agriculture and shell-tempered pottery. The Mississippian-looking pottery has always begged the question: How did this stuff wind up in Tampa Bay?"
Mississippian pottery could provide some of the strongest evidence linking Tampa Bay communities with the broader culture. But decorative similarities alone could not reveal where the vessels had actually been made. Lacking the necessary technology and expertise to answer that question, museum curators stored the mysterious fragments while competing explanations remained unresolved.
Researchers at the Florida Museum have now conducted a study aimed at determining where the pottery came from and who made it.
"We were curious to find out if these vessels were imported from the heartland by trade, if they were local imitations of Mississippian motifs, or, as we ultimately found, if they were made by migrants who had made their way into communities in Tampa Bay to take up shop and residency there," said Trevor Duke, who began conducting the research for his doctoral dissertation at the University of Florida. In the years since, Duke and his colleagues have expanded on the initial scope of his dissertation to compile more evidence from a larger collection of samples.
By examining details of pottery production that are almost invisible from the surface, the researchers traced the decorated vessels to a small community of skilled craftspeople who likely traveled hundreds of miles from the Mississippian heartland before settling in Tampa Bay. Compared with the plain molded pottery widely used in the area, the decorated vessels were made with different clay, tempering materials, and production methods. Those differences suggest the migrants possessed specialized expertise and access to resources unavailable to many local residents.
Mississippian Culture Spreads Across the Southeast
Around 1000 A.D., a new cultural system developed in the Mississippi River Valley and spread across large parts of what are now the Midwest and eastern United States. In its core regions, Indigenous communities became organized into political hierarchies, with powerful chiefdoms exerting influence over surrounding settlements. Large areas were planted with maize, while enormous quantities of earth were moved to construct mounds topped by temples and residences for leaders.
Tampa Bay lay far outside those major northern centers.
The regional culture that occupied Tampa Bay and nearby areas during this period is known as Safety Harbor. Like Mississippian societies, Safety Harbor communities formed smaller chiefdoms and constructed flat-topped mounds. The region's largest settlement was home to the Tocobaga, while smaller Mocoso, Pohoy, and Uzita chiefdoms were scattered nearby.
Yet important differences remained. None of these groups accumulated the same level of political power seen in the major Mississippian centers farther north. Tampa Bay communities also never adopted the extensive maize agriculture associated with Mississippian society, relying instead on fishing and other marine resources.
Because of this mixture of similarities and differences, archaeologists have long struggled to determine how closely Tampa Bay was connected to the Mississippian heartland. The discovery of pottery decorated in Mississippian styles only deepened the mystery.
To investigate, Duke and other Florida Museum archaeologists assembled 58 plain and decorated pottery fragments from Tampa Bay. Both kinds of vessels were likely used for preparing and serving food, although the decorated pieces may have been reserved for special events.
Mississippian potters of the period commonly mixed crushed freshwater shell or fragments of older pottery, known as grog, into their clay. They also built vessels by stacking coils of clay rather than molding them.
Those manufacturing details offered researchers a way to distinguish genuine Mississippian traditions from local copies. If the decorated Tampa Bay vessels had been imported or produced by potters trained in Mississippian methods, the fragments should preserve evidence of these techniques. If local potters had simply copied the decorative appearance, the underlying construction would instead reflect familiar Tampa Bay practices such as sand tempering.
Local Clay, Distant Pottery Traditions
The researchers first used neutron activation analysis to measure the chemical composition of the pottery. They compared those results with raw clay deposits from the Tampa Bay area.
The chemistry matched, showing that the vessels had been produced locally. That finding ruled out the possibility that finished pottery had been manufactured in the Mississippian heartland and transported south through trade. It did not, however, eliminate the possibility that Tampa Bay potters had copied northern designs.
The team then examined thin slices of the fragments under a microscope using a technique called petrography. Researchers polish a section of pottery until it is roughly half the width of a human hair, allowing light from a polarizing microscope to pass through it. Tiny grains, cracks and empty spaces can then reveal how the clay was prepared and what materials were mixed into it.
"Looking at the section under a microscope, you can identify the minerals in it based on their color and shape. From that, we can figure out what was added to it. It's a sort of fingerprint of the people who made it," Wallis said.
That microscopic examination produced some of the study's most revealing evidence.
Several decorated fragments contained grog, the crushed pottery temper associated with some Mississippian traditions. Adding grog improves the durability of a vessel and helps it tolerate the intense heat of firing and cooking.
"This grog tempering is not something that we saw previously or in the plain samples in Tampa Bay," Duke said. "But up in the Tallahassee Hills, where the nearest massive Mississippian mound center is located, it's common in all vessels. It's the plain-Jane tempering technique there."
The connection extended beyond manufacturing technique.
The Tallahassee Hills lie roughly 200 miles north of Tampa Bay. Inside the grog used in the decorated vessels, researchers found mica, a reflective silicate mineral that is common in the Florida Panhandle but unusual in peninsular Florida. Although the surrounding clay in the vessels came from Tampa Bay, some of the crushed material mixed into it appears to have originated farther north in the Mississippian heartland.
Grog appeared in 80% of the decorated pottery analyzed, but researchers did not find it in a single piece of plain pottery. Most of the plain vessels instead contained dry clay fragments or sand, materials that had been used in local pottery traditions for about 3,000 years.
Other differences reinforced the distinction. The decorated vessels were constructed using the Mississippian technique of coiling clay and followed more consistent clay recipes, suggesting a higher degree of specialized knowledge. Plain vessels, in contrast, were molded. That simpler technique became increasingly common as the region's population grew and could be learned quickly by people without advanced pottery experience.
Migrants May Have Carried Pieces of Home
Together, the evidence points toward potters who migrated from the Mississippian heartland and brought both their technical knowledge and materials with them.
As these craftspeople traveled south from northern Florida, they may have carried pieces of older pottery made from clay found in their homeland. Once they reached Tampa Bay, those vessels could have been crushed, ground into small fragments, and mixed into newly gathered local clay.
The practice may have carried cultural meaning as well as practical benefits.
The migrants appear to have specifically selected decorated pottery from their homeland for use as grog. Every grog tempered vessel examined by the researchers contained what is known as multigenerational grog, in which one fragment of grog contains an even older piece of grog inside it. In effect, pottery from one generation had been incorporated into the pottery of the next.
"It's sort of like Russian nesting dolls because you have grog within grog within grog. You can trace this back several generations of pots," Wallis said. "And they're not using vessels from just anywhere. They're crushing up the same decorated vessels that include pieces of decorated pottery from before."
These embedded fragments were tiny physical pieces of the migrants' homeland that continued to be incorporated into vessels made generations later in Tampa Bay.
Their pottery expertise and their connection to Mississippian traditions may also have helped the newcomers establish a valuable role in their adopted community. Skills that were ordinary in their homeland could have become highly specialized and desirable once they moved south.
"Migrant communities often had to figure out their own niche in a new place," said Andrea Torvinen, collections manager of the Ceramic Technology Lab and Florida Archaeology at the Florida Museum. "What would have made these migrants stand out? How would they have established a role in this new area? Bringing a specialized knowledge of pottery production seems to have been one way they could do so."
Evidence suggests those skills were highly valued. The advanced techniques appear almost entirely in decorated pottery, while everyday plain vessels continued to be made with simpler local methods. Decorated pots were also produced using higher quality clay, suggesting that the migrant potters were allowed access to scarce, superior materials for their work.
How Specialized Pottery Skills Stayed Exclusive
The divide between decorated and plain pottery continued for centuries, raising another question: Why did local residents not simply learn the migrants' more advanced techniques?
The researchers suggest that the knowledge remained concentrated within a small group of craftspeople who worked closely together. Whether intentionally guarded or simply transmitted within tight social networks, the techniques were not widely shared.
"The group of potters making the decorated vessels likely had some kind of special status that they maintained through this secretive practice, even if it wasn't a secret in the sense that no one knew about it," Wallis said. "In fact, for secrets like this, you do have to broadcast some of the details so that people know there is a secret."
High quality decorated vessels would likely have circulated widely and been prized throughout the community. But many of the features that made them distinctive, including grog tempering, coiled construction and carefully standardized clay preparation, were hidden inside the finished pottery and therefore difficult to copy.
Without direct access to the small circle of migrant potters who knew these methods, Tampa Bay residents would have had little opportunity to learn them.
"People with specialized skills have direct relationships with the people learning from them. That's how we see knowledge passed down. When it's the way your mentor has always done it, that's how you're going to do it," Torvinen said. "And in this case, there could have been a more meaningful reason behind it. By tying the homeland pottery into this enchainment, they're bringing those pots with them into the next generation."
The study was published in American Antiquity.

Evelin Kasenõmm: Asia puts drones to work — Estonia should follow suit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:40:00 UTC
21:40:00 KST

Evelin Kasenõmm: Asia puts drones to work — Estonia should follow suit
Europe may lead on drone rules, but Asia leads on putting them into practice — and Estonia's first move should be establishing two or three permanent drone corridors, writes Evelin Kasenõmm.
A new economic layer is emerging in Asia, often called the low‑altitude economy, meaning business activities and public services operating in low airspace, along with the infrastructure needed for them.
There is no point for Estonia to compete with Asian countries in drone manufacturing volume. Our opportunity may instead lie in developing digital services needed for safe and automated drone use. Estonia's long‑term experience in spatial data and 3D city models provides a strong technological foundation for this.
China is building an industry out of low‑altitude airspace
China has made the low‑altitude economy a national economic policy area, covering drones, air taxis, logistics, agriculture, urban monitoring, rescue operations, and the necessary infrastructure. According to China's civil aviation authority, by the end of 2025 the country had nearly 3.3 million registered drones — 51 percent more than the year before. Low‑altitude traffic service stations were already operating in 23 provinces1. In major Chinese cities, drones are used for delivering food and medical supplies, firefighting, urban monitoring, and maintaining public order.
Rapid growth has also brought stricter control: in 2026, mandatory drone registration and electronic identification requirements took effect, and conditions for airworthiness and operating permits for larger drones were clarified.
Japan uses drones to solve labor shortages
In Japan, drone adoption is accelerated by an aging population, labor shortages, mountainous terrain, and the difficulty of serving sparsely populated areas.
A framework created in 2022 allows compliant drones to fly beyond the pilot's line of sight even over populated areas. This enables inspection of power lines, railways, or coastlines without the pilot needing to follow the entire route.
Japan's next step is a national drone corridor system. A drone corridor is a digitally managed flight path with predefined routes, permitted altitudes, obstacles, network quality, possible landing sites, and safety requirements.
Technical specifications, guidelines, and a nationwide development map for the corridors were completed in 2025. Corridor management software was published as open source, and an official registration system is planned for 20262.
Drone logistics focus mainly on mountainous regions, small islands, and depopulating areas, where mail, medicines, and small parcels are delivered. Drones are also used in disaster zones. In agriculture, they are integrated with autonomous machinery, satellite data, and shared data platforms to reduce labor needs and improve precision.
Japan's experience shows that drone services are most likely to become permanent where they solve a clear and growing societal problem.
South Korea turns trials into standardized services
South Korea is expanding its drone industry through municipalities and standardized service models. Since 2019, drone delivery, rescue, monitoring, and other public services have been tested. In 2025, 26 municipalities participated.
In the national drone delivery program, services were launched in 2024 on 32 islands, 17 parks, and one port, with flight bases, delivery points, routes, ordering apps, and real‑time flight monitoring. In 2025, the service expanded to 166 areas. Korea is also testing medical logistics, safety monitoring, and transporting island‑produced goods to the mainland3.
Standardization is at the core of Korea's model. The state creates a unified safety and service model that different regions and companies can use. Drone delivery is becoming a practical service that people can order.
The country is also investing in the K‑UAM program. UAM (urban air mobility) refers to air taxis and other new aircraft used in and between cities. Although air taxi timelines have proven overly optimistic, the infrastructure created by the program enables smaller cargo and service drones.
Europe leads regulation, Asia leads implementation
Are Asian industrial countries far ahead of Europe in civilian drone use? Such a generalization would be misleading. The European Union has created one of the world's most comprehensive drone regulatory frameworks. The rules are based on flight risk rather than whether the drone is used for hobby or business.
Europe's strength also includes U‑space, whose legal framework has been in force since 2023. Essentially, it is a digital drone traffic management environment that allows filing flight plans, checking restrictions, issuing flight permissions, tracking drones, and avoiding conflicts with other aircraft.
SESAR — Single European Sky ATM Research — is Europe's joint air traffic modernization program. It has tested cooperation between drone service providers, integration of drones with conventional air traffic, medical logistics, and simultaneous beyond‑visual‑line‑of‑sight flights. Trials show that the technology can work in urban and cross‑border environments4.
Europe's bottleneck is slow and fragmented implementation, as decisions are made by member states. As a result, Europe has many successful pilot projects but fewer everyday services. Europe leads drone regulation; Asia leads drone deployment.
Estonia's opportunities
Estonia's strengths in the drone field include high‑quality spatial data, digital public services, a small and relatively manageable airspace, strong communications and cybersecurity competence, and the ability to integrate state and private‑sector information systems5.
We also have practical use cases. Islands are suitable for transporting medicines and small parcels. Power lines, railways, coastlines, and wind farms require regular inspection. Security agencies need rapidly collected spatial information. Estonia's variable and cold weather allows testing systems in conditions valuable for many foreign markets.
Currently, Estonia often treats drone flights as individual operations where the operator checks restrictions, requests permission, plans the route, and conducts the flight. In a service‑based world, much of this information exchange must happen automatically.
A flight‑planning system should be able to request up‑to‑date data on airspace restrictions, buildings and obstacles, terrain height, weather, and mobile network coverage. The system could evaluate the route, submit a permit request, and transmit drone identification data during the flight. Creating such a digital layer may be Estonia's opportunity.
I see Estonia's first step as creating two or three permanent drone corridors. One would serve logistics between islands and the mainland, another would support energy infrastructure inspection, and a third would handle coastal, forest, or rescue monitoring. A corridor must include reliable connectivity, spatial and weather data, agreed safety requirements, digital permitting, and shared infrastructure for multiple companies. Pilot projects for drone corridors are already underway in Estonia.
In parallel, public‑sector demand must be created. Multi‑year service contracts for detecting power line faults, assessing forest damage, or transporting lab samples and medicines would give the private sector reason to invest in automated solutions and create validated services in Estonia that could later be exported.
In the drone economy of the next decade, a significant part of the value will come from systems that allow drones to fly safely, with minimal human intervention, and legally. Estonia has succeeded before by turning a complex state process into a simple digital service. Opening our low‑altitude airspace to new services could be the next such field — but we must act much faster than we are now.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Air Force is 75% staffed with pilots, says deputy commander
According to Ukrinform, Colonel Yurii Cherevashchenko, deputy commander of the Ukrainian Air Force for air defense, made this statement during a meeting of the Temporary Investigative Commission.
“There is no widespread understaffing at the moment. We have made significant efforts to prevent pilots from being transferred to other branches of the Armed Forces. Currently, staffing levels are about 75%,” he said.
At the same time, Cherevashchenko noted that technological solutions are currently the main bottleneck for air defense. According to him, once the technological issue is resolved, the next constraints may be scaling up operations and the number of trained pilots.
“We will be able to retrain some of our current pilots to operate jet interceptor drones. In addition, we have a pool of former pilots who can also be enlisted,” added the deputy commander.
Thus, according to Cherevashchenko, there is a reserve for increasing the number of pilots. At the same time, the Air Force has other options for expanding its personnel, but does not currently plan to disclose them publicly.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Ukraine is preparing new contracts for air defense systems and missiles for air defense and is calling on partners to provide more anti-ballistic defense capabilities to protect infrastructure.

Jharkhand protest: Congress workers scuffle with police outside CEO office.
The youth wing and activists of Jharkhand Congress clashed with police on Tuesday while they were trying to cross the barricades during a protest happening outside the office of the chief electoral officer's (CEO) situated in Ranchi.These workers were protesting against the Election commission while demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the chief election commissioner (CEC). According to the PTI report, some demonstrators blackened the commission's official nameplate after being stopped from entering the premises.The hundreds of congress and youth wing workers marched from the area near the old assembly building to the CEO's office in Dhurwa.They were carrying placards raised slogans, "Where will you find the vote thief? In the BJP office", "Gyanesh Kumar Resign" and "Vote thief, vacate your seat of power".Former Union minister Subodh Kant Sahay, who participated in the demonstration, alleged that people across the country had prepared a "chargesheet" against the CEC."People of the country have prepared a chargesheet against the CEC. Two other members of the Election Commission had raised questions on Gyanesh Kumar's style of working, but now irregularities committed by him have come out," said Congress Ranchi Mahanagar president Kumar Raja.
Raja said the electoral process could not be made fully transparent unless Gyanesh Kumar stepped down as Chief Election Commissioner. He added that the Congress would continue its campaign on the issue.The protest followed a report by The Indian Express, which claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections on at least 14 occasions over the past 10 months to certain decisions and orders were issued without their knowledge, they said.The report further said the objections were raised even as the nationwide rollout of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) was being conducted under the supervision of the full Election Commission.

Announcement of the 2015 Defence Employer Recognition Scheme Gold winners.
Update to Defence Employer Recognition Scheme silver and bronze award holders.
The Defence Employer Recognition Scheme (ERS) encourages employers to support defence and inspire others to do the same. The scheme encompasses Bronze, Silver and Gold awards for employer organisations that pledge, demonstrate or advocate support to defence and the armed forces community, and align their values with the Armed Forces Covenant.
The ERS is designed primarily to recognise private sector support although public sector organisations such as the emergency services, local authorities, NHS trusts and executive agencies are also eligible to be recognised.
Pledge your organisation’s support via the Bronze award or express your interest in applying for Silver or Gold award, contact us to find out more.
Privacy policy
You can read our Privacy policy to find out more about how we process data.
Bronze award
Bronze award holders must have:
Signed the AFC and registered their interest for a Bronze award (via the ERS website).
Confirmed their understanding of the AFC and ERS and what it means to be a supporter of the Armed Forces community with the appointed DRM.
Informed their workforce of their positive support for the Armed Forces community.
Desirable Criteria. Factors which add value to an application. Note that the description of these allows for an assessment of evidence in the context of the scale, business model and market sector of the employer. The employer is willing to consider:
How to develop a suitable HR framework to enable Reserve mobilisation for members of their work force.
Provide additional leave for Reservists (i.e. Part Time Volunteer Reserves) to conduct training.
How they would promote volunteering and support to the Cadet movement through official Cadet Force channels.
How they ensure that Service personnel/Armed Forces community are not unfairly disadvantaged as part of their recruiting and selection processes.
Silver award holders in addition to Bronze Criteria must have:
ERS Bronze Award status and have held it with sufficient time to have put in place the necessary essential policies and evidence to support their application. It would be unusual for an organisation to achieve Silver status within 12 months of gaining Bronze.
Proactively demonstrate that Service personnel and Armed Forces community are not unfairly disadvantaged as part of their recruiting and selection processes.
Actively ensure that their workforce is aware of their positive policies towards the Armed Forces community. E.g. Internally publicised positive HR policy on Reserves in their workforce. In the case where no HR policy exists this should be demonstrated by specific references in job descriptions/organisation’s website.
Support Active Reservists (PTVRs) by:
Having Policy in place to support mobilisations or have made a commitment evidenced by their DRM that they understand the mobilisation process and would support a mobilisation if practicable. E.g. Employers of reservists must be aware of the role of Unit Employment Support Officers (UESO) and how they support the Reservists in their work forces.
Demonstrated support to their training by providing at least 5 days additional annual leave (ideally paid).
A proactive relationship with their DRM, which can be demonstrated through various interactions, including but not limited to personal contact, automated communications, and engagement with supporting products or resources.
The employer must allow flexibility for employees who are Cadet Force Adult Volunteers to fit their working hours in with their volunteering.
Desirable Criteria. Factors which add value to an application. Note that the description of these allows for an assessment of evidence in the context of the scale, business model and market sector of the employer. The employer is willing to consider:
Scoping opportunities to support the Cadet movement (via official Cadet Force channels) through the following example activities: sponsorship, supporting the development of cadets’ wider skills to enhance their future opportunities; or providing employment advice and guidance.
Employ at least one individual from the Armed Forces community .
Hosting a Reserve recruiting event on their premises in partnership with a local Reserve Unit or Military Command recruiting teams.
Have inclusive policy in place to support Strategic Reserves (those with an Ex-Regular and Callout liability).
Gold award holders in addition to Silver Criteria must have:Hold ERS Silver Award and have held it with sufficient time to have put in place the necessary essential policies and evidence to support their application. It would be very unusual for an organisation to achieve Gold status within 12 months of gaining Silver.
Be an exemplar within their sector, advocating for the AFC and or ERS to partner organisations, suppliers and customers with tangible positive results. E.g. demonstrate proactive steps/activity and clear success in encouraging partner organisations and their supply chain to engage with and sign the AFC, and or mentor others in progressing through the ERS.
Actively encourage a positive workplace environment for Active Reservists (Part Time Volunteer Reserves) by ensuring that positive policies in support of Reservists within the workforce are communicated to line managers and support their training by providing at least 10 days additional paid leave annually.
Demonstrate support to the Cadet movement by committing resources to improving the outcomes for cadets. This is to be achieved by verifying they deliver one or a combination of the following through official Cadet Force channels:
1) Sponsorship (e.g. for additional resources, competitions, events and specific activities such as overseas expeditions);
2) Supporting the development of cadets’ wider skills to enhance their future opportunities;
3) Providing employment advice and guidance.
Promote volunteering with the Cadet Forces by having policies in place that cater to offer additional paid or unpaid leave to employees who are Cadet Force Adult Volunteers.
Engaged with CTP to support recruitment of Service leavers and have registered with the Forces Families Jobs website.
Desirable Criteria. Factors which add value to an application. Note that the description of these allows for an assessment of evidence in the context of the scale, business model and market sector of the employer. The employer is willing to consider:
Support to Reserve Service and the wider Armed Forces community through internal and external communications, amplifying DRM social media messaging around Armed Forces Week, Reserves Day, ERS Gold /Silver announcements etc.
Actively finding out the numbers of Reservists employed and have a declared target for the number of Reservists within their workforce. Ideally, they will have relationships with the relevant Unit Employment Support Officers (UESO) for reserve units in their local area.
If there are Reservists within the workforce, the employer has positively engaged with them on how the company would support their mobilisation.
Host a Reserve recruiting event on their premises in partnership with a Reserve Unit or Military Command Recruiting Teams.
Where scale and business models permit, the employer should actively encourage and support an internal Armed Forces community network within their organisation.
Nominations will be validated to determine the level of defence personnel employment within the nominated organisation and to check that the organisation has signed the Armed Forces Covenant.
Once the nomination has been validated it will be considered by a selection board at national level for gold awards and regional level for silver awards. The selection boards will be a panel chaired by a senior military officer and they will consider each nomination against the award criteria. Organisations selected for gold and silver awards will be formally notified in writing and invited to the relevant award event.

Plague epidemic risk in Russia low after death of lab technician, WHO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:38:58 UTC
21:38:58 KST

The World Health Organization has said the risk of an epidemic in Russia is low after the sudden death of a lab technician who worked at a plague research institute in Siberia.
Darya Shipilova, who was 28, died last week, two days after falling ill. Russian media reports suggested she may have become infected after an accident at her workplace, where dangerous pathogens are kept and studied.
Russian authorities have downplayed the incident and say Shipilova died of “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. Strict quarantine measures have been imposed at the research centre in the city of Irkutsk and in several neighbouring hospitals.
Christian Lindmeier, a WHO spokesperson, said on Tuesday that there was no sign of a wider outbreak. “All of the patients’ contacts have reportedly been identified and are being monitored for illness, and none to date have shown symptoms of illness,” he said.
Russian officials were still investigating whether viral pneumonic plague caused Shipilova’s death but the WHO had assessed the health risk as “moderate to low” for Irkutsk, “low” for the rest of Russia and “very low” for Europe, he said.
According to Russian media, 60 of Shipilova’s colleagues have been locked in the institute where she worked since Friday, sleeping on the floors and chairs while tests are carried out. Similar measures have been imposed in five hospitals, with relatives forbidden to see patients.
The Kremlin’s spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, urged people on Tuesday not to listen to rumours but to rely on statements from Russia’s health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor. It said the situation in Irkutsk was stable, with no new infectious disease cases reported among institute employees.
Washington has been watching developments closely. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, called on Moscow on Tuesday to release more details about the case. “I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” he said. “We’re watching it very closely, hour by hour.“
Donald Trump had said earlier that his administration was willing to offer assistance. “I hate to see them having it. We’ll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we’ll always help,” he told reporters at the White House when asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague coming from Russia.
In an apparent mirror response, Rospotrebnadzor announced that Russia was prepared to assist the US in combating its own outbreaks of infectious diseases.
“The situation regarding dangerous infectious diseases remains unstable,” it said, highlighting a “significantly worsened” measles situation in three US states and a “fatal case of plague” recorded in New Mexico in June.

Schools blockaded as tens of thousands of protesters take to streets in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:38:33 UTC
21:38:33 KST

Nearly 90,000 students, staff and parents have taken to the streets in cities across France as protesters blockaded hundreds of high schools in a nationwide day of action against long hours, missing teachers and crumbling classrooms.
The French interior ministry said 86,000 people took part in marches in cities including Marseille, Nantes and Lyon on Tuesday morning, with up to 40,000 more expected to join the largest demonstration, in Paris, later in the day.
The demonstrations come after a fortnight of protests that began in the capital’s northern suburbs before snowballing across the country. They have been marred by frequent and often violent clashes with riot police that have left hundreds injured, some severely.
While many protests have been peaceful, some demonstrators have set dustbins on fire, destroyed bus shelters and thrown projectiles at police, who have responded with batons, teargas and riot-control rounds. Twenty-four schools have been burned or ransacked since the start of the protests, according to the education ministry.
At least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been wounded, according to government figures, while 6,100 people have been arrested, almost all minors. More than 1,800 are being prosecuted, 1,483 of them under 18, the justice ministry said.
The national union of lycée students said 1,800 of the country’s 3,700 high schools were blockaded or had been closed for the day on Tuesday, although some local education authorities attempted to move classes online.
Students on the marches held aloft smoke flares and placards with slogans including “Under our text books, anger” – a reference to a celebrated slogan from the May 1968 student riots, “Under the paving stones, the beach” – and “Schools with no money = country with no future”.
Océanne, 18, was among the marchers in Marseille. “We just want to save our education and be educated,” she said, adding that she had suffered from absent teachers who were replaced either by “pointless substitutes” or not all.
Many teachers were also demonstrating. In the western city of Rennes, Romain Dubourg said he and “about 30 colleagues” had “talked about the police brutality that we’ve witnessed, and decided to be there for our students if they need us”.
Trade unionists were also on the marches, with the head of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, urging members to “protect high school students”. The Green party leader, Marine Tondelier, urged local officials and parents to wear white and “go and protect our children during demonstrations”.
Trade unions and rights groups have accused the police of unnecessary force against the young protesters, with Amnesty International saying French authorities should “put an end to the disproportionate police repression seen in recent days”.
Anne Savinel-Barras, the president of Amnesty France, said: “The images and testimonies widely circulated over the past week raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of teargas, batons and policing techniques by the police.” The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said police had launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started.
On Monday, a 15-year-old’s hand was blown off as protesters battled riot police in northern France.
A 16-year-old lost the use of his right eye after he was seriously injured in the head on Wednesday during the blockade of a high school in Tours. The local prosecutor, Catherine Sorita-Minard, said the wounds were “compatible with the impact of a defensive bullet of the blast ball type”.
In another incident, a 14-year-old lost most of his teeth on Monday when a police officer appeared to fire a grenade at him at close range during a protest north-west of Paris. “His jaw is sealed shut, he can no longer speak and he eats through a straw,” his mother told reporters.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has ordered his ministers to tackle the students’ core demands which include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8am to 6pm school day, and repairing ageing buildings.
But the protests, seven months before crucial presidential elections to choose a successor to Emmanuel Macron, have piled pressure on a government trying to reduce a ballooning budget deficit amid mounting investor concern over France’s mountainous debt and weak economic growth.
The government has accused the radical-left La France Insoumise party of encouraging and even orchestrating the movement after numerous LFI MPs attended school blockades. The party’s veteran leader and presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has strongly supported the protests, while urging non-violence.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on Oct. 6 praised his government’s expansion of higher education across Türkiye, saying it had improved equal access to education for students regardless of their income or where they live.
“We brought quality higher education to every corner of Anatolia. We mobilized the resources of our state so that the children of this country, regardless of which income group they come from, could receive an education in the cities where they live,” Erdoğan said at an event in Ankara.
He said the government had abolished university tuition fees, increased scholarships for undergraduate, graduate and doctoral students and upgraded the infrastructure and digital facilities of universities and student dormitories.
“We did not want the child of the poor to be deprived of higher education while the child of the rich studies,” he said. “We did not want them to have to postpone their dreams or start life five goals behind.”
Erdoğan also defended his government’s policy of opening universities across all 81 provinces and increasing the number of international students in Türkiye, rejecting criticism that universities had been expanded too widely.
“Opposing the expansion of universities means opposing equal opportunity in education,” Erdoğan said.
He argued that education remained a key driver of social mobility in Türkiye and said opposing wider access to higher education effectively told the children of workers and farmers to remain in the same social position.
Erdoğan also defended the internationalization of Turkish universities, saying countries including the United States and Britain generate significant revenue from international students and use education as an instrument of cultural, commercial and scientific policy.
“If anyone is disturbed by Turkish universities opening up to the world, they do not want our country’s soft power to increase,” he said.
Erdoğan also highlighted the rising share of women among academics, saying women now account for around 47 percent of academic staff at Turkish universities.
He said a law passed by parliament on July 30 had reopened access to universities for young people whose education had been interrupted for various reasons.
Erdoğan said the number of universities in Türkiye had risen from 76 when his government first came to power to 208, while the number of student dormitories increased from 190 to 877. Dormitory bed capacity rose from 182,000 to 1 million, he said.
He also pointed to Türkiye’s performance in international university rankings, saying six Turkish universities entered the global top 500 in 2026, including two in the top 300. “These figures are important, but in our view they are not enough,” the president added.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:37:04 UTC
21:37:04 KST

War or not, foreign investment and government tech initiatives are soldiering on in Ukraine.
The Global Tech Kharkiv forum brought together participants willing to commit to Ukraine’s economy in August. Major announcements included large-scale mergers and acquisitions, the broadening of the Diia.City tax initiative, and a strategic shift in defense tech financing toward local component production.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
France’s Credit Agricole expands local presence
French financial group Credit Agricole is finalizing its acquisition of Bank Lviv, signaling continued European confidence in Ukraine’s wartime banking sector.
“Our shareholders, the French Credit Agricole group, are invested in our growth here,” said Ihor Kuropii, director of corporate business and financial markets at Credit Agricole.
“We are in the final stages of acquiring Ukraine’s Bank Lviv. In terms of investing in the Ukrainian economy, our words match our actions,” he added.
The Lviv-based bank had been a small lender in western Ukraine until Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion started. Since then, it has become a partner for international financial institutions (IFIs), and its location far from hostilities has made it an attractive vehicle for lower-risk transactions.
Bank Lviv was registered in 1990, according to data from business analytics platform YouControl. Its current major shareholders include Switzerland’s Responsibility Participations AG (41.15%), New Progress Holding (nearly 21%), and the Nordic Environment Finance Corporation (NEFCO) (over 10%). The western Ukraine-based lender focuses on small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and development financing, serving over 37,000 retail customers and 8,400 SME clients.
Why Russia Wants Western Embassies Out of Kyiv – and Why They’re Staying
Crédit Agricole Ukraine has been operating in the country for over 30 years. Headquartered in Kyiv, the universal bank serves 380,000 customers through a network of 137 branches and is owned by the French Crédit Agricole Group.
Brave1 bets on component localization
Brave1, Ukraine’s state defense cluster, is pushing for components to be produced locally to strengthen resilience.
“As domestic drone production scales rapidly, the Brave1 defense cluster is redirecting its Hr.7 billion [$170 million] budget toward localizing component production,” said Oleksandr Bornyakov, chairman of the Brave1 supervisory board, who added that many of Ukraine’s drone components and explosives were imported.
“Anyone who masters the manufacturing of these components today will build a resilient business for decades,” he added.
                                                                                                                                                                         From left to right: Ihor Kuropii, director of corporate business at Credit Agricole; Oleksandr Bornyakov, chairman of the Brave1 supervisory board; and Ihor Fedirko, executive director of the Ukrainian Armorers' Council, at the Global Tech Kharkiv forum in August 2026. (Photo by Kharkiv IT Cluster)                             
Ukraine’s defense tech sector has expanded from fulfilling a state order of just seven drones in 2022 to supporting over 500 active companies today.
The influx of venture capital into the sector is growing exponentially: After attracting just $1.1 million in 2023, investments have already surpassed $150 million in 2025, with market projections hitting half a billion dollars by 2027, said Ihor Fedirko, executive director of the Ukrainian Armorers’ Council.
Currently, foreign investment in Ukrainian defense tech is primarily driven by German and Danish funds, while other European venture capital remains constrained by bureaucratic hurdles.
Diia.City to include BioTech, MedTech
Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation is preparing to expand Diia.City, a legal and tax initiative for the tech sector in Ukraine.
A new technological sandbox for BioTech and MedTech companies will be launched shortly to attract foreign enterprises and capitalize on Ukraine’s growing expertise in wartime medical tech, according to the ministry.
“Unfortunately, many still perceive Ukraine merely as a testing ground, but this is just the beginning,” said Nataliya Denikeieva, deputy minister of digital transformation. “In the near future, we will launch our first tech sandbox for BioTech and MedTech, which will attract additional foreign companies.”
The ministry also announced the launch of “Diia.City Invest,” a specialized tool designed to simplify and secure venture capital investments into resident companies.
Diia.City Invest is a dedicated fast-track program that aims to attract capital into the Ukrainian tech sector. The initiative aims to create an environment that encourages investment in innovative companies, rather than relying on conservative instruments like bank deposits or real estate purchases.
                                                                                                                                                                         Nataliya Denikeieva, deputy minister of Ukraine’s digital transformation, at the Global Tech Kharkiv forum in August 2026. (Photo by Kharkiv IT Cluster)                             
UK Aid, Mercy Corps launch “Digital Booster” program for frontline SMEs
To support traditional businesses operating near the front lines, the Kharkiv IT Cluster, backed by the UK government through UK Aid under the BLOOM program, has launched the “Digital Booster” initiative.
The program will provide direct financial vouchers to 150 local SMEs to upgrade their operational software, specifically focusing on eradicating legacy Russian systems like 1C.
                                                                                                                                                                         Vicki Aken, Mercy Corps’ country director for Ukraine, at the Global Tech Kharkiv forum in August 2026. (Photo by Kharkiv IT Cluster)                             
The use of Russian software like 1C and its alternatives is considered a direct threat to Ukraine’s national security and cybersecurity. The primary danger lies in the potential leak of strategic data to Russian intelligence services, as these accounting programs hold comprehensive information on a company’s finances, logistics and personnel.
Ukraine’s National Security and Defense Council (RNBO) also officially banned this software, and the lack of legitimate updates leaves it highly vulnerable to destructive cyberattacks.
The program functions as a networking platform that directly connects frontline businesses with Ukrainian IT integrators to sustain capital circulation within the national economy.
“Sustainable economic recovery in Ukraine depends on stronger domestic markets, where Ukrainian companies buy from one another, implement innovations, and create jobs,” said Vicki Aken, Mercy Corps’ country director for Ukraine.

Russians in ICE Detention Plan Hunger Strike to Protest Poor Conditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:36:44 UTC
21:36:44 KST

More than 50 detainees, including Russian citizens, are planning to launch a hunger strike this week to protest what they have described as unbearably harsh conditions at one of the largest U.S. immigration detention centers, according to three people familiar with the matter.
The detainees are located at the Folkston D. Ray ICE Processing Center, a privately run Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center in Folkston, Georgia, that was expanded last year under a $47-million contract with the Department of Homeland Security.
A document written by detainees dated Sept. 14 and seen by The Moscow Times describes a range of issues. Among them: a lack of adequate medical and dental care, problems communicating with people on the outside, disparaging attitudes from staff and poor living conditions at the facility, part of which is a converted former prison.
Detainees complain of having limited time outdoors, being unable to sleep, mold on ceilings and mattresses and poor ventilation. One of the document’s authors said that he had not had a dental cleaning in his nearly two-year stay at the facility.
The document, originally written in Cyrillic, was authored by two Russian-speaking detainees and signed by 14 of them in total. The wife of one man who signed the document said it was submitted as a formal complaint to multiple federal oversight bodies.
“According to my husband, the most serious problems include food, the inability to sleep and rest properly, difficulties obtaining necessary medical care and the overall conditions of long-term detention,” said another Russian woman whose husband is detained in the facility.
The two women gave similar accounts of the center’s conditions and recent developments, as relayed by their husbands, in separate text exchanges with The Moscow Times. Both requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation.
The women said that detainees and their family members on the outside have previously tried to raise the issues with staff, including through formal complaints. The first woman said little had changed — until an inspection was announced for Oct. 6.
After that, “conditions inside the facility, according to my husband and other detainees, began to noticeably change,” she said. “In particular, the food and some living conditions improved.”
Detainees are skeptical that those changes will last, however.
The hunger strike, a drastic form of protest that puts a participant’s health at risk, was initially scheduled to begin Tuesday, the day of the inspection. The first woman said that some people had already begun refusing food on Monday.
She said the goal is to “disrupt this show, draw the inspectors’ attention to real, everyday problems, and demonstrate that people have serious grievances against the facility.”
Both women said their husbands told them that staff had gathered the would-be participants last week after learning of the planned hunger strike and tried to persuade them to call it off.
“[The women’s husbands] say they were warned of the consequences if they continued, including possible separation and isolation,” the second woman said.
Neither ICE nor GEO Group, the private contractor managing the Folkston D. Ray ICE Processing Center, responded to a request for comment.
On its website, GEO Group states that the facility provides basic services including “around-the-clock access to medical care,” “dietitian-approved meals” and in-person and virtual visitation. It also says that the center is accredited by the American Correctional Association.
Hundreds of Russians have fled to the U.S. to seek political asylum in recent years. A growing number of them have wound up in ICE facilities under the administrations of Presidents Joe Biden and Donald Trump, at times facing prolonged detention while their asylum applications are processed. Some have been forcibly deported back to Russia.
The planned hunger strike will involve detainees of several nationalities. The Moscow Times could not establish how many Russian citizens are planning to participate.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The New Taipei Fire Department and Chunghwa Telecom signed an agreement Tuesday to develop and test drone delivery of emergency blood supplies to remote areas, according to a press release.
The city’s fire department and the telecom company signed an MOU to transport blood products by drone. The project covers the northern coastline and mountainous communities.

The fire department will provide testing sites and emergency-response scenarios and assist with landing-zone planning and administrative coordination.

The validation process will cover mission intake, medical assessment, preparation of blood products, drone delivery, and on-site handover. Chunghwa Telecom will provide mobile network coverage, flight controls, location tracking, abnormality alerts, and temperature monitoring to support the operation.
Both parties will plan additional pilot programs and establish standard procedures connecting 119 emergency reports, medical assessments, blood preparation, drone transportation, and on-site delivery. They will also work with civil aviation, healthcare, and blood-supply agencies.
The parties aim to replicate the project in remote communities and outlying islands across the country. Chunghwa Telecom added that the project is part of a broader initiative integrating undersea cables, fiber optics, mobile and satellite communications, drones, and AI applications.

Israel's 2026 election: What will it mean for the Middle East?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:34:08 UTC
21:34:08 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's 2026 election: What will it mean for the Middle East?
Israel’s 27 October election could produce a major political turning point domestically. However, it is unlikely to lead to any dramatic shifts in Israeli foreign policy that many around the world might hope for.
A victory for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would likely strengthen the influence of Israel’s far-right parties, while a government led by figures such as Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, or other opposition leaders could bring a less confrontational tone and greater diplomatic flexibility.
Nonetheless, there is notable continuity across Israel’s political mainstream regarding Iran, Lebanon, and the Palestinians. This month’s election, therefore, is unlikely to fundamentally change how Tel Aviv approaches the region.
Three years after the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, Israel remains at war, its relations with certain Western countries have significantly deteriorated, and tensions with Jordan and Egypt are increasingly tied to developments in Gaza and the West Bank.
Yet, the election offers no obvious choice between fundamentally different visions of Israel’s regional role. The opposition has a shot at defeating Netanyahu, but the leading candidates largely agree on the centrality of military power, threat perceptions of Iran, Hezbollah, and Hamas, and the rejection of basic rights for Palestinians.
Nonetheless, this is not to say that the question of who will be Israel’s prime minister is not important. Netanyahu has become increasingly dependent on far-right partners such as Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose influence extends well beyond their electoral strength.
Their leverage has helped push settlement expansion, the weakening of the Palestinian Authority (PA), and a harder line on Gaza and the West Bank toward the centre of government policy. Netanyahu securing another victory could reinforce the political power of such extremist forces.
However, replacing Netanyahu would not necessarily mean replacing the strategy that has brought Israel into its current confrontation with various regional state and non-state actors.
A government led by Eisenkot, Bennett, or another opposition figure would probably be less dependent on the far right, more receptive to American pressure, and more cautious in its rhetoric.
Perhaps such a post-Netanyahu Israeli government could rein in settler violence to some degree, take a more cooperative approach to Gaza’s reconstruction, and give Jordan and Egypt greater diplomatic space, albeit with far narrower differences when it comes to the larger questions - chiefly Iran, Hezbollah, Israeli control of Palestinian territory and Palestinian statehood.
Israel’s political centre has moved so far to the right since the “Oslo years” (1993-2000) that a government led by one of Netanyahu’s challengers could change the tone and tactics of Israeli policy, albeit without making fundamental changes in direction.
“Chances are that a successor to Netanyahu would find himself handling the same regional issues using the same tools, in pursuit of mostly the same interests. There would be some variance, to be sure, and perhaps Israel would frame its involvement in places like Lebanon, Syria, and Iran differently. But the overall trajectory might be similar,” explained Aron Lund, an associate fellow at the Swedish Institute of International Affairs, in an interview with The New Arab.
“Israel would likely want to hold captured ground, weaken its enemies, and extract a steep price for any concession,” he added. Other experts agree. When discussing the possibility of a post-Netanyahu government resulting from this month’s election, Dr Rouzbeh Parsi, an affiliated researcher at Lund University, said we should not expect any change in Tel Aviv’s foreign policy strategy.
“Eisenkot, Bennett, and Lapid bicker with Netanyahu over the fine-tuning of the approach, the weight of diplomacy, etc. - not whether the wars are necessary or the way they are conducted as such. While they may be more willing to accommodate any US administration on tactics, they will follow the same strategy,” he told The New Arab.
“Capitals in the region are less concerned with who becomes prime minister since all the candidates will stay the course on the large issues.”
Gaza and the West Bank
Some observers see Gaza as a place to look at in terms of meaningful difference with a post-Netanyahu government that is less dependent on Smotrich and Ben-Gvir in charge.
There might be reason to expect such an Israeli government to be more willing to cooperate with the international efforts aimed at rebuilding the genocide-ravaged enclave and to accept some form of Palestinian administration rather than allowing the current stalemate to persist.
Perhaps this government could also be more responsive to pressure from Washington, Cairo, and other governments seeking to stabilise Gaza after the war.
Still, the room for change would have severe limits. Hamas’s disarmament, Israeli security demands, and the sensitive question of who will ultimately govern Gaza are unlikely to be resolved in the foreseeable future regardless of who Israel’s prime minister is.
At the same time, Israel’s political mainstream has little appetite for a return to the pre-7 October status quo. Therefore, while a post-Netanyahu government might make Gaza policy less confrontational and more diplomatically manageable, it is difficult to imagine it fundamentally ending Israel’s military control of the coastal territory or taking meaningful steps that could resolve the underlying conflict.
The West Bank could prove an even more consequential test of whether an Israeli government has genuinely changed course. Under Netanyahu, settlement expansion, settler violence and measures that strengthen Israeli control over Palestinian land have accelerated, while the Palestinian Authority has been weakened economically and politically.
A key concern is not necessarily an immediate, formal annexation, but a slower process of making Palestinian life increasingly difficult through a form of “soft transfer” that could gradually encourage Palestinians to leave.
A less right-wing government could put the brakes on some of these policies and restore greater restraint to the security forces and settler movement. However, that would still fall well short of reversing the occupation, and the leading opposition figures have shown no signs of being prepared to put Palestinian statehood back at the centre of Israeli policy.
“An Israeli government that doesn’t depend on the likes of Smotrich and Ben Gvir would probably be more flexible on the margins in relation to Gaza and the West Bank, and certainly in terms of rhetoric and public framing. Post-Netanyahu, Israel would have a cabinet less prone to saying unhinged, extremist things. With or without an actual policy change, it might help appease Western governments and enable some diplomatic advances,” Lund told The New Arab.
Jordan's growing concerns
The stakes are truly high for Jordan. The leadership in Amman has witnessed the deterioration of the West Bank with growing alarm. It is a given fact that any significant displacement of Palestinians across the Jordan River would have direct consequences for the Hashemite Kingdom’s own political and economic stability.
“Israel's government is pushing the territory to the brink like never before. This has happened since Bezalel Smotrich [became] Finance Minister [and] has funnelled benefits to the settlers whilst protecting violent extremists in their midst. He has also withheld revenue from the [Palestinian Authority (PA)],” explained Dr Rob Geist Pinfold, who teaches International Security at King’s College London, in an interview with The New Arab.
“This is a toxic combination: the PA is weaker, broker, and less legitimate than ever before. Israeli ministers openly talk of annexation and ethnic cleansing, both of which would mean that Jordan could see an influx of Palestinian refugees,” he added.
Jordan already faces serious fiscal pressures and unemployment, and the question of Palestinian identity is deeply embedded in its domestic politics.
Therefore, a new influx from the West Bank would potentially pose a grave threat to Jordan’s existing political order, leaving Amman with few attractive options.
Jordan can appeal to Washington and other Western governments to pressure Tel Aviv, pursue diplomatic and legal measures internationally, or, in an extreme scenario, reconsider aspects of its relationship with Israel, which normalised in 1994.
From Amman’s perspective, the most important question after the Israeli election is whether the next government, regardless of who leads it, is prepared to stop the West Bank from moving toward a point of no return.
Egypt's red lines
Egypt is primarily concerned with preventing the war in Gaza from becoming a new source of regional displacement and instability. Cairo’s overriding red line is any Israeli policy that effectively pushes Palestinians out of Gaza and across the Rafah border into the Sinai Peninsula.
Egyptian officials also want to preserve their role as a central mediator and to play a major part in rebuilding Gaza. This is both because of the security implications and because of Egypt’s longstanding interest in maintaining regional influence.
Perhaps a less confrontational Israeli government could give Cairo more room to pursue those objectives, particularly if it were willing to cooperate with an international reconstruction effort and accept a Palestinian governing structure in Gaza.
Yet, unless Israel and Hamas can agree on security, disarmament, and governance, Egypt will continue to face the risk that Gaza's unresolved conflict spills directly across its border.
Iran and Hezbollah
Iran and Hezbollah are two files where continuity in Tel Aviv’s foreign policy will most likely prove strong. Confronting Iran and weakening Hezbollah are consensus positions within Israel’s political mainstream.
A post-Netanyahu government might be more willing to listen more to Washington, place greater emphasis on diplomacy, or exercise more restraint in choosing when and how to use military force.
However, that is not to say it would abandon the key goal of thwarting the Islamic Republic and its regional allies and partners from rebuilding their military capabilities and reducing their perceived threats to Israel.
This brings us to a distinction which is necessary to draw between strategy and tactics. If Netanyahu loses, the next government could be less provocative and more predictable without being substantially less willing to use force. Ultimately, it is safe to say that a change of Israel’s government would not necessarily translate into a quieter Middle East.
“The Iranians will certainly be watching carefully; although while they will be happy to see Netanyahu lose, and potentially even serve jail time, they are under no illusion that Israeli policy toward Iran will change in any dramatic fashion,” explained Hooman Majd, an Iranian-American author, journalist, and NBC News contributor.
“And if Netanyahu’s party is able to form a government, the Iranians will be on a more serious alert for sabotage and/or assassinations. It does appear that so far Israel, having dragged the US into a war, is happy to see Trump finish it, and it is likely that the next government, even if headed by the opposition, will maintain that policy,” he told The New Arab.
The Washington factor
At the end of the day, in terms of Israel’s relationships with other countries, the election may have the greatest impact on Tel Aviv’s alliance with Washington.
A government without Netanyahu and his far-right partners could be easier for the Americans to work with and more receptive to pressure from Washington, particularly over Gaza, the West Bank, and regional diplomacy.
A post-Netanyahu government could also help repair some of the political damage caused by the current government’s increasingly strained relations with Western allies.
But there is a danger in attributing all of Israel’s declining popularity in the United States to Netanyahu. As Lund observed, the shift in American attitudes toward Israel may reflect a deeper structural change that an Israeli election cannot easily reverse.
A new government might therefore have an opportunity to improve the relationship in the short term without being able to halt the longer-term erosion of support for Israel among parts of the American public and political system.
What changes after 27 October?
Depending on the electoral outcome, Israel might have a new government that is less extreme in its rhetoric, more receptive to Washington, and more willing to accommodate its regional neighbours.
However, those changes can matter only if they translate into different policies on the ground. The crucial questions will be whether it can restrain settler violence and the expansion of settlements in the West Bank, find a workable path toward reconstruction and governance in Gaza, and manage its confrontation with Iran without drawing the Middle East into another cycle of war that brings more chaos, death, and destruction.
Just as important will be whether the United States and other international actors maintain pressure once the immediate drama of the election has passed.
A Netanyahu defeat could create an opening for change. But it will not by itself resolve the conflicts that produced Israel’s current isolation and its reputation as a rogue state that its genocidal war in Gaza and borderless aggression across the region have earned it over the past several years.
The world must not mistake a change in tone for a change in direction while allowing the underlying policies to continue.
For Israel’s neighbours and its international partners, what happens after 27 October will matter far more than who wins the election.
Giorgio Cafiero is the CEO of Gulf State Analytics
