October 7 exposed Israel’s vulnerabilities. The Gaza war deepened them.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:34:01 UTC
21:34:01 KST

The Hamas resistance group’s October 7 blitz exposed a profound failure at the heart of Israel’s security model, shattering the long-held belief that military superiority, intelligence and deterrence could guarantee the security of its citizens.
In response, Israel launched a genocidal war in Gaza, presenting it as necessary to restore security and prevent another such attack.
Three years of genocide have instead widened the crisis, deepening political divisions inside Israel and damaging its standing abroad.
It has raised broader questions about Israel’s political leadership, its decades-long mistreatment of Palestinians, and the future of a state built on the continued occupation of Palestinian land.
Over the same period, the Israeli public has moved further to the right, according to Alon Liel, former director general of the Israeli Foreign Ministry and an expert on Israeli politics.
“The October 7 attack was deeply traumatic, and the government's response to it was a huge failure. The scale of the damage and the embarrassment of the government were channelled into a more nationalistic sentiment and a desire for revenge,” Liel tells TRT World.
“The media, in the years since, has focused overwhelmingly, perhaps 95 percent of the time, on our suffering, the casualties, the hostages, the destruction inside Israel and so on. As a result, the public has become very angry and nationalistic, strengthening right-wing political parties.”
According to Liel, the result is not only an ideological shift towards more anti-Palestinian and anti-Arab positions, but also an erosion of democratic norms.
“We have 20 percent Arab citizens, and hostility towards them has grown, leaving them increasingly isolated,” she says.
“When you intensify pressure on Palestinians in Gaza, the West Bank and, in some ways, inside Israel itself, you also become less democratic.”
A crisis of political trust
The political fallout from October 7 has continued well beyond the initial failure of Benjamin Netanyahu's government to prevent the attack.
The attack exposed serious failures across Israel's political and security establishment, while the absence of a state commission of inquiry has prolonged the dispute over responsibility.
Netanyahu has resisted calls for such an inquiry, while victims' families and opposition figures have continued to demand accountability.
For Palestinian scientist and author Professor Mazin Qumsiyeh, who was nominated for the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize, the war has exposed deeper problems within Israel's political system.
“The period following October 7 has shown how fragile and unsustainable the pre-existing status quo since 1948 has been, and the systemic inequalities and limitations of relying on military might to maintain a colonial, racist occupation,” Qumsiyeh tells TRT World.
“It has made clear that lasting stability cannot be achieved without addressing the root causes, including self-determination, human rights, and equal justice for all people in the region.”
“Rather than enhancing security, the three years of genocide have brought the end of this racist regime closer,” Qumsiyeh adds.
Public dissatisfaction with the government's handling of the war has also remained high.
According to an INSS survey conducted for the third anniversary, only 34 percent of Israelis were satisfied with the government's management of the war on Gaza.
Meanwhile, 75 percent supported establishing a state commission of inquiry into the failures surrounding October 7.
“I think Israel is safer militarily because we have inflicted significant damage on Iran [during US-Israeli offensives] and the Syrian military [during and after the fall of Assad regime]. But the problem we are facing is political and societal,” Liel says.
“Israeli society is more divided than it was before; particularly over democracy, corruption and the way the country is governed.”
“The opposition is deeply worried about the erosion of democratic institutions, the media and the country's bureaucracy, as well as attacks on state institutions,” Liel adds.
The security doctrine exposed
Three years of war have exposed the limits of a security doctrine heavily reliant on military force and inflicted unprecedented destruction on Palestinians in Gaza.
The mass displacement of Palestinians and destruction of homes and civilian infrastructure have meant that Palestinians have borne the overwhelming human cost of Israel’s military offensive.
For many Israelis, meanwhile, the war has failed to restore a sense of security.
The same INSS survey found that 59 percent of Israelis believed an attack similar to October 7 could happen again in the coming years from the Gaza border.
Only 38 percent considered Israel's security situation better than before the attack, while 32 percent said it was worse.
The figures expose a contradiction within Israel's security narrative: overwhelming military force has not restored a sense of security among much of the population, while Palestinians bear the catastrophic consequences.
“The carpet bombing of Gaza and the lies perpetrated around it have shown the true nature of the Israeli regime: genocide and ethnic cleansing as central features of its artificial and fragile system of hegemony,” Qumsiyeh says.
“Sustainable security can only come from justice, the right of refugees to return, and adherence to international law,” he adds.
Liel also questions whether Israel's military response can provide lasting security, pointing instead to its longer-term political and moral consequences.
“The Israeli public has largely adopted the narrative that we are fighting barbaric Islamic extremists,” Liel says.
“I see what we have done in Gaza as an overreaction driven by Israeli Jewish fears and feelings of revenge. We have killed 74,000 Palestinians, destroyed Gaza and carried out numerous aggressive actions against civilians in the [occupied] West Bank,” he tells TRT World.
“I see this as a moral problem. We have overreacted and violated international law, and I consider this a long-term problem for Israel and perhaps for the Jewish people, who will have to carry these crimes on their shoulders.”
Reputation irreversibly tarnished
Before October 7, Israel maintained extensive diplomatic, economic and security relationships, particularly with Western governments.
Its international image was already contested because of its occupation of Palestinian territory, settlement expansion and treatment of Palestinians.
But the genocide in Gaza has brought those issues into sharper international focus.
The shift is reflected in polling.
A June 2026 Pew Research Center survey across 36 countries found that a median of 67 percent of respondents held an unfavourable view of Israel, compared with 25 percent who viewed it favourably.
In the United States, unfavourable views reached 60 percent, while in the United Kingdom they stood at 69 percent.
Israel's international standing has deteriorated dramatically over the past few years, according to Liel.
“Years ago, we were very close to establishing diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia. The main goal was to normalise relations with the Saudis without paying any price on the Palestinian issue.”
“Then came the attack, followed by what I see as our overreaction, the destruction in Gaza and the enormous number of casualties. Israel is now seen as a trigger-happy, colonialist and aggressive country,” Liel explains.
The deterioration in public perceptions has unfolded alongside significant international legal developments.
In July 2024, the International Court of Justice found Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful and said it must end as rapidly as possible.
The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The warrant for Netanyahu remains in force, potentially exposing him to arrest if he travels to a country that enforces it.
“The shift in global public opinion, diplomatic relations, and international legal scrutiny has put enormous pressure on Israel's standing in the world,” Qumsiyeh says.
“This growing isolation is unfortunately not affecting Israeli politics or its institutions. Most Israelis live in this self-created Zionist bubble.”
“It is an inferiority-superiority complex: ‘We are a chosen, superior people, but we are also always persecuted and hated, yet we do not care’,” he adds.
Three years on, the consequences of October 7 continue to reshape Israel both at home and abroad.

'Populist theatre' — Finns Party members tour East Helsinki, but stay on bus
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:33:41 EEST
21:33:41 KST

On Saturday, a group of Finns Party members were scheduled to visit the Puhos shopping centre in Eastern Helsinki as part of a party networking event.
The roughly 60-year-old Puhos shopping centre has become a hub for immigrant communities in recent years, and the site has also drawn gatherings organised by far-right groups.
Finns Party member and Raisio city councillor Sini Laine told Ilta-Sanomat that the purpose of the visit was to see Puhos for themselves.
"The idea was that we would see for ourselves what Puhos looks like. We have representatives from all over Finland, for example from Lapland, where there aren't very many immigrants," Laine told the newspaper.
However, the visitors stayed on the bus, after security personnel assessed that there could be a security risk.
Those on the bus included Finns Party Vice Chair Simo Grönroos and MP Pekka Aittakumpu.
"Apparently it was because there were identifiable Finns Party members who were present, and the security guards assessed that there could be a security risk," Laine told Yle.
Laine filmed a video in which she claimed that she could not see "a single ethnic Finn" in the area. She posted the video on her Facebook page, using the hashtag "send them back" in the caption.
Initially, Laine told Yle that parliamentary security staff had been on the bus. However, Aaro Toivonen, parliamentary security chief, told Yle that this was not the case.
The Finns Party later clarified on Monday that the security personnel were members of the party's own security team, not parliament's.
Locals question security threat
People who work and spend time at Puhos say they do not recognise the area as dangerous.
Shakur Nuur, who works at a shop at Puhos, and Joonas Kervinen, one of the authors of a recently published book about the area, told Yle they had never experienced threats there.
Kervinen described the Finns Party's visit as "populist theatre", arguing that negative perceptions of Puhos are often based on preconceived ideas rather than people's experiences of the area.
Nuur noted that Puhos is a multicultural area where anyone is welcome to visit.

Increased threat: Katz threatens war against PA as Netanyahu warns of Hamas election attacks
Israel raises its Gaza alert ahead of the October 7 anniversary, while Katz outlines a sweeping offensive if Palestinian security forces turn their weapons on Israelis in the West Bank
Defense Minister Israel Katz warned Tuesday that Israel would launch a comprehensive military offensive against the Palestinian Authority if its security forces or affiliated Tanzim groups attacked Israeli settlers and soldiers, while separately ordering heightened military readiness in Gaza ahead of the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre.
Addressing a government meeting, Katz said the military was preparing for the possibility that PA security personnel and affiliated groups would turn their weapons against Israelis in the West Bank and communities along its boundary.
“The IDF is preparing for a scenario in which there would be a reversal of allegiance by the Palestinian Authority’s security apparatus and the Tanzim organizations affiliated with it, against the settlers and IDF forces in Judea and Samaria and in the seamline communities,” Katz said.
He said such an attack would trigger war against the PA under a contingency plan approved by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and himself.
“In such a case, war will be declared against the Palestinian Authority and the IDF will launch a comprehensive attack in accordance with an organized plan that has been formulated and approved by Prime Minister Netanyahu and myself,” he said.

White House approves permanent US base in Poland, president's aide says
A political decision to establish a permanent US military base in Poland has already been made, with the White House giving the project a 'green light,' a senior aide to Poland's president said on Friday.
"President Donald Trump explicitly wrote about this on September 17," Marcin Przydacz told reporters after the meetings he had held at the White House and the State Department in Washington.
"Now the Pentagon, the Polish Ministry of National Defence, and the Polish military must implement this decision," Przydacz continued, adding that it would be certain whether the base has been established only when President Trump eventually travels to Poland to inaugurate it.
"Only then will we be 100 percent sure that the base has been launched. At this stage, there is a political decision that needs to be implemented," he added.
Przydacz made the statement when asked about President Trump's words, according to which the issue was under review by his administration but which also suggested that he might have already taken the decision.
Referring to his meetings in Washington, Przydacz said he had held talks with Deputy National Security Advisor Michael Needham and two deputies of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
According to Przydacz, information regarding a concrete US presence in Poland will be announced in a review of global American military deployments, which will likely be published by the Pentagon in November.
Przydacz took part in the third G20 sherpa meeting in Washington aimed at preparing the group's summit in Miami in December. He said that all of Poland's key priorities had been included in a draft declaration of G20 leaders and confirmed that President Karol Nawrocki, invited by President Trump as a special guest, would represent Poland at the summit.
Reacting to these developments on Saturday, Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said that Nawrocki's "main, and essentially only, state task" is to leverage his perceived closeness with Trump to enforce this decision and ensure the base is established.
According to Sikorski, the Polish government has already fulfilled its role by passing a resolution formally declaring Poland's readiness to host and financially cover the costs of the new base. While the existing US missile defence base in Redzikowo, northern Poland, was opened in 2024, Poland is now specifically seeking a second base, this time for US Land Forces.
Sikorski also commented on the recent Russian airspace violations in neighbouring Moldova, which he described as part of Vladimir Putin's ongoing strategy to escalate tensions and cut off foreign aid to Ukraine. "Even if the United States were to reduce its overall troop numbers in Europe, they should strengthen their presence here, where the real threat lies," Sikorski concluded.(PAP)

Russians use AI to plan attacks on cities – Air Force deputy commander

Russians are using artificial intelligence to plan attack routes and identify targets, and the Air Force is acting similarly, Deputy Commander of the Air Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Yuriy Cherevashenko has reported.
"It is difficult to accurately assess the scale [of Russia's use of artificial intelligence], but we see elements of AI in their work. In particular – in strike planning. There were attacks on Odesa that lasted a long time, in waves, with very short pauses. In my opinion, without AI, this would be extremely difficult," Cherevashenko said on Tuesday in the Verkhovna Rada at a meeting of the Temporary Commission of Inquiry (TCI) investigating potential violations of Ukrainian legislation in the sphere of defense, anti-corruption legislation, and compliance with human rights and freedoms under martial law.
He expressed confidence that Russians are already planning at least attack routes and target recognition with the help of AI.
To the question of what the Armed Forces of Ukraine can counter this with, Cherevashenko said: "The same thing. We are also introducing artificial intelligence. For example, in automated turrets."
Cherevashenko also noted that the most difficult situation for air defense forces is in the Black Sea. From there, it is significantly easier for Russians to attack Ukraine. "It is much harder to control the sky over the sea. Some of our capabilities simply cannot be used there as effectively as over land. We can often only operate on a head-on course," he said, noting that an additional negative factor is the weather. "Storms, fog, difficult weather conditions—all of this seriously complicates the work. And the Russians, conversely, find that the sea gives them more freedom for routes and launches."
According to Cherevashenko, to protect ports and the coastline, so-called "drone motherships"—platforms that carry other drones—are used, among other things. This makes it possible to increase their operating time in the air and effectively organize a constant patrol of drones in the required areas.
He also added that defense at sea and along the coast "has its own specifics, which is why we combine various available means."

Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in Physics for work on ‘ghost particles’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:31:16 UTC
21:31:16 KST

Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in Physics for work on ‘ghost particles’
Belgian physicist worked to build Antarctic observatory that tracks neutrinos from deep space.
Belgian physicist Francis Halzen has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for creating a giant detector in Antarctica that captures neutrinos, the so-called “ghost particles” from space that scientists believe offer clues to how the universe evolved.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the prestigious award in Stockholm on Tuesday, crediting Halzen with a central role in building the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.
The neutrino interactions collected by the observatory provide information about how high-energy neutrinos are created and may even reveal previously unknown phenomena, the Academy said.
“It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn’t expect it,” Halzen said, speaking to the committee by phone from Italy, in a call broadcast at the news conference to announce the winner.
The 82-year-old said it was predicted before that he would win the Nobel Prize, but the announcement still made him feel “strange”.
“I am working on a proposal, and I hope that this prize will help getting it approved,” he said to chuckles from the audience.
‘Information from the cosmos’
Neutrinos have nearly no mass and carry no electric charge, so they can cross between planets, stars and human bodies without being altered, making them rare and hard to catch. There are roughly 100 trillion solar and cosmic neutrinos that pass through our bodies every second.
Halzen first proposed the IceCube project in 1988, realising that the clear ice beneath the South Pole could act as a detector, so on the rare occurrence a neutrino strikes an atomic nucleus, it gives off a flash of light that buried sensors can record.
Richard Fitzgerald, editor-in-chief of Physics Today, said although hundreds of people built the observatory, it “all started with one person”, noting that the physics prize has rarely gone to one sole winner in recent years.
“People joined him in the quest for these neutrino messengers. The messenger is bringing information from cosmos,” committee member Eva Olsson said during the news conference. “They opened the door to distant galaxies and tell us about the processes of exploding stars.”
Eva Lindroth, a researcher in Stockholm and a member of the Nobel Committee, told Al Jazeera that Halzen’s observatory has helped scientists understand high-energy particles.
“The nice thing with neutrinos is that they come straight at us,” she said. “That way we can ultimately understand these sources of high-energy particles and understand more about how things in the universe, like how galaxies are formed and the roles of the black holes in that process.
“It gives a new way to study the universe,” Lindroth added. “They give us information which we cannot get in any other way.”
Last year’s award went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for experiments on quantum physics.
On Monday, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to two American scientists for discoveries that helped explain how the brain works.
The next award will be the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, which will be announced on Wednesday in Stockholm.
Nobel laureates will receive their awards in a ceremony on December 10, marking the anniversary of Swedish chemist Alfred Nobel, who established the award; members of the royal families of Sweden and Norway will be in attendance.

The crumbling firewall: Why German democracy faces its sternest test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:31:02 UTC
21:31:02 KST

In German building regulations, a Brandwand is a solid wall between two adjoining buildings.
It does not extinguish a fire. It only stops the flames from spreading next door long enough for the fire brigade to arrive.
German politics has long relied on a similar idea.
Known as the Brandmauer, or “firewall”, it is a strict political consensus among Germany’s mainstream parties that they will not form coalitions or governing agreements with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).
For years, the Brandmauer has kept the AfD isolated from government. But as the party attracts a growing share of the electorate, particularly in eastern Germany, that consensus is coming under unprecedented pressure.
On September 6, voters in the eastern federal state of Saxony-Anhalt cast their ballots in an election that has seriously questioned the establishment of German politics and the system.
The AfD had been polling at a staggering 43 percent ahead of the vote, a significant share in German politics.
Their lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund represents a regional faction that the domestic intelligence agency has explicitly classified as a proven right-wing extremist organisation.
The agency notes that these factions promote an ethnic understanding of national identity that fundamentally conflicts with the democratic constitutional order habituated within the country.
On paper, the firewall held again on September 20.
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern the AfD came first with 38.2 percent, yet the Social Democratic premier Manuela Schwesig announced talks with the Left Party and the Greens, leaving the AfD, in its lead candidate’s words, as the “sole opposition”.
In Berlin the AfD rose from 9.1 to 16.3 percent.
Two weeks earlier it had taken 43.8 percent in Saxony-Anhalt, a result that, according to Chatham House, no party labeled extreme right had achieved in a German state election since 1945.
Yet no AfD politician sits in a state cabinet. The concept carries more weight than its technical name suggests.
It draws on the lesson of 1933, when conservative elites believed they could tame Hitler by bringing him into government.
In 2018 the Christian Democrats (CDU) formalised it, rejecting “coalitions and similar forms of cooperation” with both the AfD and the Left Party.
When CDU legislators in Thuringia helped elect a premier with AfD votes in 2020, Angela Merkel called it “unforgivable,” and he resigned within days.
Such a firewall rests on three pillars.
The first is arithmetic, meaning enough seats outside the AfD to govern. The second is legitimacy, the public’s acceptance that exclusion defends democracy rather than a cartel of incumbents.
The third is performance: governments formed behind the wall must deliver. September strained all three at once.
Saxony-Anhalt shows the arithmetic failing. The AfD holds 39 of 83 seats, and the CDU, Social Democrats, Greens and Left Party together hold exactly 39.
The remaining five belong to the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which has agreed to exploratory talks with the AfD.
Because a third ballot for premier needs only a plurality, the CDU cannot stop Ulrich Siegmund, whose state party the regional intelligence service classifies as confirmed right-wing extremist, without Left Party votes that its own resolution forbids.
A porous wall
The firewall has left the CDU choosing between two of its own taboos.
Mecklenburg-Vorpommern shows the price of holding the line.
The CDU fell to 4.9 percent the first time it has failed to enter a German state parliament, and the AfD, with 32 of 71 seats, will be the only opposition.
A parliament in which the largest party is also the sole opposition hands that party every grievance against the next government.
Legitimacy is eroding too.
In February, a Cologne court ruled that the federal intelligence agency may not, for now, label the national AfD as confirmed extremist. Locally, the wall is porous.
In the town of Demmin, CDU and AfD representatives voted together against continuing a federally funded democracy program, and an independent district administrator argued that people “should at least be able to see what happens when the AfD governs”.
Abroad, US President Donald Trump celebrated the Saxony-Anhalt result, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz postponed a call with him. A boundary contested from the town hall, the courtroom and the White House is hard to sell as a national consensus.
Performance is the weakest pillar for the federal government.
The Brandmauer implicitly promises that the parties behind it will govern better.
Yet only 13 percent of Germans are satisfied with Merz and 15 percent with his government, according to ARD’s DeutschlandTrend, while the AfD leads national polls at around 28 percent, nine points ahead of the CDU.
Merz called the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern result a “disaster,” saying his party had been “ground down” between the AfD and the Social Democrats.
There is also an economic aspect of this shift.
In Saxony-Anhalt, 65 percent of voters who called their finances poor chose the AfD, against 37 percent of those doing well and popularity of the far-right is also spreading among unsatisfied middle classes all around Europe.
Explaining the situation as primarily a choice of “lower” or less educated echelons of the society.
The limits of firewall
The state lost Intel’s planned Magdeburg chip plant, once billed as the largest foreign investment in German history, when the company abandoned it in 2025.
Energy costs since the break with cheap Russian gas, and the fiscal weight of support for Ukraine, feed a sense that decisions made in Berlin and Brussels are paid for in the east.
That explains more than the familiar story of East German nostalgia for Moscow in contrast to many believe among the media. There is also fear of a possible AfD government would deter skilled workers and companies.
Berlin adds another layer. The Left Party came first with 25.7 percent, and its lead candidate Elif Eralp, whose parents came from Türkiye, could become the city’s first governing mayor with a migrant background.
The Left is not the AfD. But for a CDU whose 2018 resolution excludes both, being squeezed from two sides leaves less and less room behind a double firewall.
Europe offers no clean exit. Belgium’s cordon sanitaire against Vlaams Belang and its predecessor has broadly held since 1989. Sweden’s center-right has governed with the support of the Sweden Democrats since 2022.
The Dutch coalition that included Geert Wilders’ PVV collapsed within a year. Italy offers another model, where Giorgia Meloni’s government has at times aligned more closely with the political mainstream after taking office.
Neither exclusion nor inclusion offers a simple solution. What matters is whether mainstream parties use the time a firewall buys them.
That is the real lesson of September.
Relying solely on the Brandmauer to protect democratic institutions is no longer a viable long-term strategy. If established parties want to halt the AfD’s momentum in upcoming elections, they will need to look beyond the rhetoric of defending democracy.
That means addressing voters’ economic frustrations, streamlining a sluggish bureaucracy and showing that centrist coalitions can deliver on the domestic and foreign policy issues that affect everyday life.
Otherwise, the firewall may not just fail to hold back the tide. It will become the very structure that traps the political centre as the ground collapses beneath it.

Taiwan’s Maritime Law Enforcement Operation Has Sparked Anger in Chinese Society
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:31:00 UTC
21:31:00 KST

On October 1, a Chinese mainland fishing vessel came into a confrontation with a Taiwan Coast Guard vessel near the Pratas (Dongsha) Islands. After the fishing boat refused to leave the waters, the Taiwan Coast Guard vessel used a water cannon against it, eventually forcing it to leave the area.
Just one day earlier, the Taiwan Coast Guard had detained another Chinese fishing vessel near Penghu and taken control of its seven crew members.
The incident quickly attracted widespread attention on Chinese social media. Videos showing a Taiwan Coast Guard vessel spraying the Chinese fishing boat with a water cannon were widely circulated, prompting widespread criticism of what many described as the Taiwanese vessel’s heavy-handed conduct. Some commentators interpreted the incident as a deliberate provocation by Taipei on the National Day of the People’s Republic of China.
However, much of the criticism was directed not only at Taiwan, but also at the Chinese government itself. Some argued that Beijing’s repeated “concessions” toward Taiwan had encouraged Taipei to become increasingly assertive. Others even questioned whether Beijing is capable of effectively protecting Chinese fishermen. The reaction reflects the existence of a particularly hardline strand of opinion on Taiwan in mainland Chinese society, which frequently criticizes the government for being “too weak” toward Taiwan.
This challenges a narrative in which Beijing is portrayed as the main driver of coercive pressure against Taiwan, while mainland Chinese society simply passively absorbs Chinese Communist Party (CCP) propaganda about national (re)unification. In fact, in recent confrontations between Taiwan’s government vessels and civilian vessels from the mainland, Beijing has often exercised restraint and refrained from using its superior military capabilities in response.
Following the October incident, for example, the Taiwan Affairs Office of the PRC State Council merely called on Taiwan not to “use dangerous methods to treat mainland vessels and crew members in a heavy-handed manner.” Beijing has so far refrained from escalating the situation through its maritime forces.
This resembles Beijing’s handling of the February 2024 fishing boat incident near Kinmen, in which two mainland fishermen died after their vessel capsized during a confrontation with Taiwan’s Coast Guard. At the time, visible anger emerged on mainland Chinese social media. Related Weibo posts received more than 50 million views, accompanied by calls for retaliation against Taiwan. However, Beijing ultimately responded in a relatively restrained manner.
This raises an important question. Beijing has conducted repeated military drills around Taiwan in recent years, and confrontations between Chinese fishermen and the Taiwan Coast Guard might appear to provide convenient opportunities to demonstrate Chinese military power. So why has Beijing refrained from doing so?
Beijing must strike a balance between military deterrence and the image of itself as a guarantor of peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. A forceful response to Taiwan might satisfy public anger in the short term, but it could also reinforce Taiwanese society’s perception of the mainland as a security threat over the longer term.
Beijing frequently uses military exercises as a signal to Taipei and the international community of its determination to safeguard national unity. However, although Beijing continues to insist that such activities are directed only at the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and “Taiwan independence separatist forces,” polling suggests that a substantial share of the Taiwanese public regards these activities as a threat to Taiwan. Against this backdrop, any retaliatory action by the China Coast Guard or the People’s Liberation Army Navy against Taiwan could be presented by Taipei as further evidence of a military threat from the mainland.
Therefore, it is necessary for Beijing to calibrate the use of force carefully, lest coercive measures produce the opposite of their intended effect and undermine the credibility of deterrence. This may help explain why incidents such as fishing boat confrontations are not necessarily regarded in Beijing as occasions warranting a military response.
However, growing public dissatisfaction with Taiwan in mainland China could push cross-strait relations into a more dangerous direction. It could transform tensions between the CCP and the DPP into a broader conflict between two societies across the Taiwan Strait. Although direct interaction between people on the two sides has declined substantially since 2016, the remaining interpersonal, economic, and cultural ties between the two societies continue to play an important role in preserving peace across the strait.
A recent poll found that mainland respondents still held broadly positive attitudes toward Taiwan. Their average feeling toward Taiwan rose from 57 points in 2025 to 61 points in 2026, on a 100-point scale. At the same time, 38 percent agreed that force should never be used to achieve (re)unification under any circumstances, while 47 percent disagreed. When asked what measures could be taken if Taiwan formally declared independence, 81 percent supported “limited military operations on offshore islands,” but only 32 percent supported “a full-scale military attack.”
When asked why (re)unification between the mainland and Taiwan was important, 71 percent pointed to the two sides’ shared cultural heritage. These findings reveal an important ambivalence in mainland Chinese attitudes toward Taiwan: Opposition to the independence of Taiwan coexists with a sense of cultural affinity toward Taiwanese society.
Maritime confrontations, however, could cause this attitude to deteriorate, and the Chinese government itself could become an early target of public anger. For years, alongside military deterrence, Beijing has sought to improve Taiwanese attitudes toward the mainland through economic incentives and other forms of preferential treatment. However, these policies are often interpreted within mainland Chinese society as evidence of the failure of Beijing’s Taiwan strategy. These sweeteners have not persuaded Taiwanese society to move toward support for (re)unification. When PRC citizens see Taiwan’s Coast Guard forcibly enforcing its regulations against mainland fishing vessels, Beijing’s preferential policies toward Taiwan may instead be interpreted as a betrayal of the interests of the Chinese people. Beijing is therefore caught in a difficult position: Its restraint toward Taiwan can frustrate nationalist sentiment at home, while a more forceful response could undermine its longer-term efforts to influence Taiwanese society.
If such public sentiments continue to intensify, they could place pressure on Beijing to adopt a harder line toward Taiwan. A historical example can be found in the 2012 China-Japan dispute over the Senkaku (Diaoyu) Islands. Although Beijing initially sought to balance a demonstration of resolve toward Japan with the need to preserve Sino-Japanese relations, growing domestic demands for a tougher response contributed to pressure for escalation. After Japan proceeded with the nationalization of the islands, Beijing significantly intensified its response.
Managing the expansion of radical voices within society will therefore be important to keeping cross-strait tensions under control. However, this is not solely Beijing’s responsibility. Taiwan’s firm maritime enforcement may appear to reinforce the DPP’s longstanding hardline position toward Beijing, but its immediate effect may be felt not only by the Chinese government but also by Chinese society. Therefore, Taiwan will also need to calibrate its actions carefully to avoid turning maritime confrontations into triggers for a much broader conflict.

PROFILE - Who is Francis Halzen, the Nobel Physics laureate behind Antarctic ‘ghost particle’ hunt?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:29:49 UTC
21:29:49 KST

- His decades-long work helped create a new way of studying the most powerful objects in the universe
Francis Halzen’s idea was as audacious as the setting in which it would be tested: transform a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice into a telescope capable of observing almost invisible particles arriving from the farthest reaches of the universe.
Nearly four decades after he began pursuing that plan, the Belgian-American scientist was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his leadership of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos originating in space.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences honored Halzen “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.”
Mark Pearce, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics, said Halzen had led an international team that created an extraordinary scientific instrument.
“His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy,” Pearce said.
 
From Belgium to Wisconsin
Halzen was born on March 23, 1944, in Tienen, Belgium. He studied mathematics and physics at KU Leuven, where he received his master’s degree in 1966 and completed a doctorate focused on the broken symmetries of hadrons in 1969.
After working as a scientific associate at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) in Geneva, he was invited to the University of Wisconsin-Madison for what was initially expected to be a six-month research visit.
Halzen joined the university’s physics faculty in 1972 and remained there for more than five decades. He became a Vilas Research Professor and Gregory Breit Distinguished Professor, working at the intersection of particle physics, astrophysics and cosmology.
His early career coincided with the development of the Standard Model of particle physics, and he worked on its applications to particle colliders and cosmic rays. He also co-authored Quarks and Leptons, a textbook that became widely used in particle physics courses.
By the mid-1980s, however, his attention had turned toward neutrinos, electrically neutral particles with extremely small masses that rarely interact with matter.
Their elusive nature earned them the nickname “ghost particles,” but it also made them potentially valuable astronomical messengers. Unlike light, neutrinos can pass through gas, dust, planets and other matter without being absorbed or deflected.
Studying them, Halzen said, could allow scientists to “see things in the universe you couldn’t see any other way.”
 
Building a telescope beneath the ice
The difficulty was detecting them. A neutrino may cross enormous distances without striking a single atom, meaning researchers needed an exceptionally large and dark detector to observe the rare interactions that did occur.
In 1987, Halzen began working on the Antarctic Muon and Neutrino Detector Array, known as AMANDA. The project tested whether sensitive light detectors could be installed deep inside the Antarctic ice.
Researchers drilled holes thousands of meters into the ice using hot water and lowered cables fitted with optical sensors before the water froze again. AMANDA demonstrated that the deep ice was sufficiently clear and stable to act as a particle detector.
The experiment became the technological foundation for the much larger IceCube observatory.
Construction of IceCube began in 2004. Its final cable, or “string,” was lowered into the ice in December 2010, and its first fully equipped scientific run began in May 2011.
The completed observatory contains 5,160 optical sensors embedded in approximately one billion tons of Antarctic ice. When a neutrino occasionally collides with an atomic nucleus, it produces a charged particle that emits a faint blue glow known as Cherenkov radiation. The sensors record that light, allowing researchers to estimate the neutrino’s energy and direction.
“We started small and, to our own amazement, we overcame all these hurdles,” Halzen said.
 
Opening neutrino astronomy
IceCube’s breakthrough came in 2013, when the collaboration reported evidence of high-energy neutrinos arriving from beyond the solar system. The finding established that particles produced by some of the universe’s most powerful objects could be detected through Antarctic ice.
A further breakthrough followed in September 2017, when IceCube detected a neutrino with an estimated energy of 290 trillion electron volts and rapidly alerted other observatories.
Follow-up observations connected the particle to TXS 0506+056, a distant active galaxy powered by a supermassive black hole about 4 billion light-years from Earth. It provided the first compelling evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic neutrinos and demonstrated the potential of combining neutrino detections with conventional telescopes.
IceCube has since been used to study cosmic rays, dark matter, neutrino properties, the Milky Way and active galaxies including NGC 1068.
Halzen received numerous honors before the Nobel, including the Balzan Prize, Bruno Pontecorvo Prize, IUPAP Yodh Prize and the American Physical Society’s 2026 Medal for Exceptional Achievement in Research. He was elected to the US National Academy of Sciences in 2024.
Now 82, Halzen received the Nobel while in Italy and described the news as an unexpected surprise. As the sole laureate, he will receive the full prize of 12 million Swedish kronor, approximately $1.2 million.

Poland to allocate US$26bn for funding shelters and uninterrupted power supply
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:29:00 EEST
21:29:00 KST

Poland to allocate US$26bn for funding shelters and uninterrupted power supply
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has announced that on 6 October, the government will adopt a draft resolution approving the Population Protection and Civil Defence Programme for 2027-2031, providing funding of PLN 102.4 billion (US$26.4 billion), primarily through investments.
Source: European Pravda, citing Poland media outlet PAP
Details: Donald Tusk stated that he would like to draw attention to a key project due to be adopted on 6 October, namely the draft resolution of the Council of Ministers on the adoption of the Population Protection and Civil Defence Programme for 2027-2031. He explained that there would be five years of full funding for the programme, involving very significant funds guaranteed for population protection and civil defence, noting that those would primarily be investments.
"Local authorities had persistently demanded – and quite rightly so – that the programme be longer and more heavily funded so that investment programmes for civil protection and civil defence could be launched," the prime minister said, adding that this would amount to PLN 102.4 billion for 2027-2031.
Tusk noted that under similar programmes up to now, Poland funded primarily emergency purchases, such as generators when power outages posed a threat.
Priorities in the area of civil protection to be funded under the new project include protective structures – specifically all types of shelters – equipment, rescue bases and the capacity to ensure uninterrupted water and energy supplies, including sites and procedures for stockpiling reserves for critical situations, not only wartime scenarios but also other emergencies like natural disasters. Additionally, the government will fund warning systems and the security of IT and telecommunications systems.
Of the promised sum of over 102 billion złotys, more than a third – approximately 30 billion (about US$7.7 billion) – will be made available to the regions through their voivodeships. Local government bodies will be able to submit applications to gain a vote and decide which type of investment they need most.
Background: Poland is preparing a law on a so-called "pre-war state" designed to define rules of action in a situation where the country is formally not yet at war, but the threat level is significantly higher than in peacetime.

Russia’s Newest Submarine Just Went Hunting in the Baltic—and Scored a Torpedo “Kill”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:28:44 UTC
21:28:44 KST

- Category
- World
Russia’s Newest Submarine Just Went Hunting in the Baltic—and Scored a Torpedo “Kill”
Russia has put its new Project 677 submarine Velikiye Luki through a series of underwater combat trials in the Baltic Sea, including an exercise in which the vessel detected and engaged a simulated enemy submarine with a training torpedo, Zona Militar reported on October 6.
Russia’s United Shipbuilding Corporation, or USC, said the submarine first completed a series of preparatory maneuvers before diving to the required depth and moving into position for the torpedo exercise.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The scenario required the crew to locate a submerged target representing an enemy submarine, track it, and then carry out a simulated attack.
According to USC, Velikiye Luki completed the task successfully, reaching its assigned firing position and striking the target with a training torpedo. The exercise marked another step in the testing program for one of Russia’s newest conventional attack submarines.
The Project 677 design has a displacement of roughly 2,700 tons, a length of 66.8 meters, and a beam of 7.1 meters. The submarine is operated by a crew of about 35 and can reportedly reach submerged speeds of up to 21 knots. Its endurance is listed at as much as 45 days at sea.
Velikiye Luki is designed around six 533mm torpedo tubes and can carry torpedoes, naval mines, and missile weapons. The class also incorporates acoustic-reduction measures intended to make the submarine harder to detect, along with modern sonar equipment for tracking surface ships and submarines.
The new vessel is part of Russia’s long-running Project 677 program, intended to provide the navy with a quieter and more capable successor to older diesel-electric submarine designs. The Baltic trials are aimed at validating the submarine’s propulsion, sensors, weapons, and ability to carry out its primary combat missions before it enters regular operational service.
“These submarines are designed to combat enemy submarines and surface ships, protect naval bases, coastlines and sea communications, as well as launch missile strikes against enemy coastal targets,” USC said.
Earlier, a Russian Navy corvette stationed at Kronstadt has been painted to resemble a waterfront building and fitted with protective netting, as Moscow continues adapting its Baltic Fleet vessels against Ukrainian drone attacks.

Reuters: U.S. officials believe the likelihood of China “invading” Taiwan before 2028 is getting increasingly low. What’s the foreign ministry’s response?
Guo Jiakun: The Taiwan question is China’s internal affair. Resolving the Taiwan question is a matter for the Chinese ourselves that brooks no external interference. The U.S. side needs to implement the important common understandings reached at the meeting between the two presidents, abide by the one-China principle and the three China-U.S. joint communiqués, and act prudently on the Taiwan question.
Reuters: Taiwan recently received two F-16V fighter jets purchased from the United States and plans to receive another 64 within the year. What is the foreign ministry’s response? (Also raised by AFP)
Guo Jiakun: China’s position is clear. We remain firmly opposed to U.S. arms sales to China’s Taiwan region.
Reuters: U.S. authorities arrested a California woman on Sunday and accused her of spying on a son of Taiwan’s Lai Ching-te at the behest of Chinese officials, the FBI said. Does the foreign ministry have any comment? (Also raised by AFP, NBC and The Wall Street Journal)
Guo Jiakun: I am not familiar with what you mentioned. China opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called “Chinese spy” narrative.
AFP: Could the foreign ministry comment on accusations from the Philippines that China’s military and coast guard on Sunday harassed Filipino government aircraft and boats in two areas of the South China Sea?
Guo Jiakun: China has sovereignty over Huangyan Dao and Nansha Qundao, including Zhongye Dao and Tiexian Jiao, as well as their adjacent waters, and has sovereign rights and jurisdiction over relevant waters. The scope of Philippine territory is defined by several international treaties. China’s Huangyan Dao and Nansha Qundao lie beyond that scope. Over the past few days, Philippine aircraft and vessels have intruded into airspace and waters under China’s jurisdiction without China’s permission, disrupting China’s normal law enforcement operations. This is a serious violation of China’s sovereignty and jurisdiction, and a deliberate attempt to undermine peace and stability in the South China Sea. It’s fully legitimate and justified for the Chinese military and coast guard to respond by taking measures in accordance with law.
China firmly opposes any actions by the Philippines that undermine China’s sovereignty and rights and interests, and will continue to take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests in the South China Sea. The Philippine side should immediately stop its infringement and provocations.
Reuters: U.S. officials told Reuters that they believe Iran has obtained satellite-based positioning intelligence and possibly other positioning data from China. What’s China’s response?
Guo Jiakun: China strictly fulfills its due international obligations. We oppose using the conflict as a pretext to frame and smear China.
Financial Times: It is reported that the UK is looking to impose higher tariffs on Chinese NEV exports. What is your comment?
Guo Jiakun: I’d refer you to competent authorities for the specifics. Let me stress that economic and trade relations are about leveraging respective comparative advantages to achieve mutual benefit. China’s EV industry offers competitive options for global consumers, including those in the UK, contributes to green and low-carbon transition, and constitutes high-quality production capacity in high market demand.
NBC: An employee of a Russian anti-plague institute in the remote Siberian region of Irkutsk has reportedly died of a suspected pneumonic plague infection. The U.S. State Department said that they are monitoring the situation closely. Are Russian authorities reaching out to Chinese authorities and experts on possible cooperation to deal with this problem?
Guo Jiakun: China and Russia maintain close exchanges and cooperation on the prevention and control of infectious diseases, including plague.
Bloomberg: It’s reported that Germany and France sent a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urging the European Union to adopt new powers that would enable the bloc to cut off access to its single market if other nations destabilize trade relations. The letter also calls for an instrument that would force Europe to reduce various supply chain dependencies on foreign countries. While the letter does not specifically mention China, the EU is currently exploring ways to rebalance its trade relationship with the country. What’s the foreign ministry’s comments on this latest call? How would this affect EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic’s China visit later this week?
Guo Jiakun: Between China and the EU, the industrial and supply chains are highly integrated and mutually dependent, and our economic and trade relations are mutually beneficial in nature. It is hoped that the EU will work with China in the same direction and resolve each other’s concerns through dialogue and consultation, so that the two parties can jointly keep the global industrial and supply chains stable and unimpeded and promote the sound and steady development of China-EU economic and trade relations. As for your specific question, I’d refer you to China’s competent authorities.

A seventh man has been arrested in London on suspicion of terrorism offences related to the suspected RAF Fairford terrorism plot, police have said.
The 22-year-old British national was arrested in Westminster, central London, on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006, counter-terrorism policing said.
Five men in their 20s were arrested in the village of Whelford, Gloucestershire, outside the RAF base in the early hours of 27 September after police were alerted to suspicious vans in the area. They were later released on bail.
On Thursday, a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national was arrested in Westminster on suspicion of terrorism offences. He was released on bail on Saturday.
Speaking on Tuesday, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing, Vicki Evans, said: “This remains a live investigation and our specialist teams continue to pursue multiple lines of inquiry into the circumstances surrounding events near RAF Fairford.
“Once again, I’d like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this highly complex investigation.
“We’re acutely aware of the public interest in this investigation, and we are working around the clock, and at pace, to identify the motivation behind events in Gloucestershire. We remain committed to investigating all possible angles.”
Tensions have been high at RAF Fairford since Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that the base was a legitimate target. Iran’s embassy in London has denied any involvement in the events of the past few days.
Ministers have been briefed that Iran has various reasons for hiring proxies, who sometimes are unwitting, to carry out acts that aim to eat up resources and create chaos.
The Iranian embassy in London has said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” of Iranian involvement.
Senior US politicians, including the president, Donald Trump, have expressed surprise that the suspects were released on bail.
Counter-terrorism policing last week defended the move. “I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers,” Britain’s head of counter-terrorism police said.

Third President of Ukraine Viktor Yushchenko has criticized statements by certain Ukrainian political figures calling for "linguistic concessions," reflections on "parity," and the abandonment of the Euro-Atlantic course under the guise of achieving peace.
"Today, when the trials of our resilience demand the highest discipline of spirit and unwavering faith, we once again witness how poisonous seeds of despair are being thrown into our war-torn space. Certain political figures, striving for quick hype or yielding to weakness of heart, allow themselves faint-hearted passages about 'parity,' about 'linguistic concessions,' about abandoning our Euro-Atlantic choice, and about 'peace at any cost.' I deliberately will not name the surname of this politician. The wise Ukrainian people understand perfectly well who is in question without any announcements. But I persistently urge this figure—as well as everyone who ventures to speak on behalf of society—to immediately sit down with books and figure out the basic, fundamental categories and definitions," Yushchenko wrote on the Facebook social network.
In his appeal, Yushchenko compared such initiatives to the Munich Agreement of 1938, noting that attempts to satisfy the aggressor's appetites instead of achieving genuine peace lead only to illusions, disgrace, and an even greater catastrophe. He emphasized that whoever chooses disgrace between disgrace and war ultimately gets both.
"When the enemy came to deny your right to existence, any bargaining around language, faith, or national security is not a peace plan. It is a plan for national suicide. For our Ukrainian statehood, for every Ukrainian word, the best sons and daughters of our nation have given their lives for centuries. Mykhailo Hrushevsky and Symon Petliura, Yevhen Konovalet and Stepan Bandera, Yaroslav Stetsko and thousands of indomitable UPA warriors fought for it. How is this politician going to look into the eyes of their memory? How will he look into the eyes of our today's heroes who hold the front at the cost of their own lives?" the third president appealed.
He stressed that the Ukrainian position must be as unshakeable as granite.
"Identity is not a subject of bargaining. Language, church, and our history are the fundamental shield of our nation," Yushchenko emphasized.
According to him, the only true guarantee of peace for the state remains a strong army and full membership in NATO, rather than another piece of paper on neutrality.
"True peace is possible only when the aggressor is stopped, punished, and deprived of the opportunity to commit evil. Therefore, I call on our politicians to be responsible for every spoken word. The time for the decolonization of consciousness requires firmness. We have no right to bargain with what has been won by the blood of many generations," Yushchenko summarized.
As reported, the European Solidarity party on Monday evening distributed a statement regarding the exclusion of Oleksiy Honcharenko from the composition of the parliamentary faction of the same name following his recent statements. "Oleksiy Honcharenko's public positions regarding the end of the war and Ukraine's future security architecture diverged from the position of European Solidarity and its ideological foundations. That is why the European Solidarity faction – we made a decision that now we cannot continue our shared political path due to ideological differences. This decision does not cross out years of joint work. But party unity cannot be a formality behind which fundamentally different answers to questions about the state's future are concealed," the statement says.
The political force emphasized that their team is "not just a faction, but tens of thousands of party members, the most authoritative of whom are our colleagues who are currently in the ranks of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and whose opinion and position on defending the country is fundamental for us."
Honcharenko was also included in the Myrotvorets database. He is accused of "conscious, systemic, and deliberate actions aimed at the demoralization of society and the suppression of its will to resist Russian aggression."
Earlier, on October 2, Honcharenko published a series of posts on Telegram calling to initiate negotiations with Russia on agreements to stop strikes on ports, enterprises, schools, hospitals, residential buildings, and bridges. Following this, according to him, it would be possible to move on to discussing more complex issues, in particular Donbas and Ukraine's neutral status.
Honcharenko is not a member of the European Solidarity party, but belongs to the parliamentary faction of the same name. He is a member of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Budget, the permanent delegation to the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, numerous interparliamentary relations groups with other countries, heads the Verkhovna Rada Temporary Commission of Inquiry (TCI) on investigating potential violations of Ukrainian legislation in the sphere of defense, anti-corruption legislation, and compliance with human rights and freedoms under martial law, and is also a member of other TCIs.
In the previous 8th convocation of the Verkhovna Rada (2014-19), he was a member of the Petro Poroshenko Bloc party faction and a member of the party of the same name, but after its reformatting into the updated European Solidarity party (led by Petro Poroshenko) did not join it and ran in the last parliamentary elections as a non-partisan self-nominated candidate in election district No. 137 (Odesa region).

Türkiye’s orbital ambitions, constellations, equatorial spaceport take center stage at IAC summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:25:18 UTC
21:25:18 KST

Emirhan Yilmaz, Tugba Altun and Emir Yildirim
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Türkiye’s expanding orbital ambitions, highlighted by a mega-constellation and an independent spaceport in Somalia, take center stage at the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC).
A wide-ranging panel mapped out the future of space exploration at the event running from Monday until Friday, during which aerospace leaders detailed how national infrastructure projects and private space stations are reshaping the global orbital ecosystem.
Organized by the International Astronautical Federation (IAF), with Anadolu as its global communications partner, the congress is being held at the Antalya NEST Congress Center under the coordination of the Industry and Technology Ministry and co-hosted by the Turkish Space Agency and SAHA Istanbul.
Türkiye’s Aselsan revealed plans to launch the first satellite of its state-of-the-art Astralink (Gokbagi) low-Earth-orbit (LEO) constellation within two years as part of a broader 198-satellite communications network.
The project was initiated late last year to serve Türkiye and its allies, while the planned orbital network is expected to integrate over 1 million terrestrial user terminals deployed across operational fields, Aselsan CEO Ahmet Akyol said during the panel.
Building on 50 years of experience, Akyol stated that the constellation will run on domestic microchips, proprietary communications waveforms and subsystems developed by the Turkish defense ecosystem to ensure secure and uninterrupted connectivity amid a broader shift from solitary satellites to interconnected constellations, mirroring the global paradigm shift in modern defense, the economy and public infrastructure.
Arif Karabeyoglu, a board member of the Turkish Space Agency (TUA), stated that developing independent access to Earth’s orbit has become key for mid-sized spacefaring countries, as global launch capacity surged tenfold over the past decade from 300 tons to 3,000 tons, while costs went down.
Karabeyoglu said that launch capabilities have become all the more important for countries like Türkiye, which is building a spaceport in Somalia that will provide technical advantages such as immediate proximity to the equator, range safety controls and ideal atmospheric conditions for launches, both for domestic vehicles and global operators.
Astronaut Michael Lopez-Alegria, senior vice president of human spaceflight at Axiom Space, stated that Axiom aims to prepare its commercial platform before the International Space Station (ISS) is eventually decommissioned and deorbited, while praising Türkiye’s growing role in crewed spaceflight with the successful Ax-3 mission that carried the nation’s first space traveler, Alper Gezeravci, into orbit.
Hasan Huseyin Ertok, CEO of Fergani Space, stated that the space and telecommunications sectors have developed rapidly in the past five years and will become even more prominent in the coming decades, while a major race is underway in the geostationary sector, with every firm and country seeking new solutions and services in the field.
Mehmet Nefes, director of Türkiye’s Scientific and Technological Research Institution (Tubitak) Space Institute, said that the country’s lunar exploration program involves domestic research institutes, universities and defense firms, going beyond a simple surface landing.

He also placed responsibility for the instability in the Middle East on Western countries that meddle in the affairs of this region.
TASS has summarized the top diplomat’s key statements.
NATO’s statements
Moscow hears NATO’s statements about preparations for a war with Russia and stays alert: "We hear that and we are keeping an eye out, as people say. The most important thing is that we keep working to achieve the goals set by the president as part of the special military operation: to prevent any threats to Russia from our Western neighbors."
Lavrov says he is "taking a philosophical view" of reports about NATO's "defensive" plan for its eastern flank: "You know, I'm taking a philosophical view of this. Because today they say one thing, and tomorrow another."
Russia’s response to threats to Kaliningrad
Russian President Vladimir Putin has made it clear what Russia's response will be in the event of an attack on the Kaliningrad Region or any other region of the country: "At the Valdai forum, the president answered the question very clearly about the idea of the Kaliningrad Region ultimately facing an attack. He said: ‘There will be one answer to the Kaliningrad Region, to any other region."
West’s responsibility for Middle East destabilization
Western countries that interfere in the region’s affairs are to blame for the instability in the Middle East: "Problems arise because our friends within the Moscow Format on Afghanistan are experiencing the harmful, very serious, and severe consequences of the West’s blatant interference in this region."
Russia is concerned that the unfolding situation around Iran is having a negative impact on the global economy: "We are deeply concerned about this situation, as it is taking an extremely heavy toll on the entire global economy. We hope that the good offices currently being offered by many regional states--including Egypt, Pakistan, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia--will ultimately succeed in keeping this situation within diplomatic and political channels."
Situation in Asia Pacific
The United States and a number of European countries are seeking to create bloc structures in the Asia Pacific region: "Our Western colleagues - both the United States and a range of Europeans, let alone Australia and Japan - are trying to set up their own closed bloc-type structures, of three or four, in contrast to the ASEAN-centric concept that rests on inclusivity and consensus."
This tendency caused concern in Russia: "Naturally, this trend is a cause for concern not only for us. A number of association members wish to preserve its commitment to the core principles upon which it was founded and which have appealed to all the partners ASEAN has established broad relations with."
Afghanistan
The failure to adopt a final document on Afghanistan within the Moscow format is an unfortunate but not unexpected outcome: "This is not a very pleasant development, but I wouldn’t make a big deal out of it, because there were reasons to anticipate this outcome."
Russia is making efforts to promote the resolution of problems between Afghanistan and Pakistan: "I have not the slightest doubt that both Afghanistan and Pakistan are interested in normalizing their relations. Russia is doing its best to help them settle the existing and newly-emerging problems."
Cooperation with East Timor
Russian economic operators stand ready to expand energy supplies to East Timor: "Very little has been achieved so far regarding trade and economic ties, but quite promising prospects were confirmed today. There is a mutual commitment to developing joint investment projects in energy, mining, fisheries, and tourism. I conveyed to the Minister our readiness - and that of our economic operators - to expand energy supplies to East Timor."
Russia welcomes East Timor’s plans to open its embassy in Moscow and is ready to help it to do this once it asks: As soon as we receive concrete requests, we will offer all-round assistance without fail."

Scientists say this simple habit could strengthen your marriage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:23:37 UTC
21:23:37 KST

Scientists say this simple habit could strengthen your marriage
Working out together, even with a simple walk, may help couples communicate better, handle conflict more peacefully, and strengthen their marriage.
- Date:
- October 6, 2026
- Source:
- Brigham Young University
- Summary:
- Couples who exercise together report better communication, healthier conflict resolution, and lower marital stress than those who work out alone. Even something as simple as taking a walk together may create valuable opportunities to talk, listen, and feel more connected.
- Share:
Exercise is well known for supporting physical fitness and mental well being. New research from BYU suggests it may also offer benefits for marriage, particularly when spouses are active together.
The study, recently published in Family Relations, found that couples who exercised together reported better communication, more effective conflict resolution and less marital stress than couples who did not share physical activity.
The research was led by BYU School of Family Life professor Jeremy Yorgason with co-author Ashlyn Hiatt Mildenhall, who first became involved in the project as an undergraduate researcher at BYU.
"Our findings suggest that conjoint exercise facilitates, in a small but significant way, the ability to resolve conflict peacefully," Yorgason said. "People reported more positive outcomes in communication and conflict resolution when they exercised together."
Exercising Together Shows Stronger Relationship Benefits
To investigate the connection between exercise and marriage, researchers examined survey responses from nearly 1,700 young married couples enrolled in the nationally representative Couple Relationships and Transition Experiences (CREATE) study. The BYU project has tracked newly married couples throughout the United States for more than a decade.
The researchers looked at both individual exercise and physical activity done together as a couple. They then compared those habits with three measures of relationship health: communication, conflict resolution and marital stress.
Both individual exercise and shared exercise were associated with healthier marriages. However, physical activity done together consistently showed stronger links to positive relationship outcomes than working out separately.
"About 60% of husbands and wives in the sample said they exercised, but only about a third exercised together," Yorgason said. "That means about half the people who exercise are not exercising with their spouse. While the impact is not necessarily large, it is very consistent, which gives me confidence that it is influencing relationships in some meaningful way."
Why Shared Exercise May Help Couples Connect
Previous research has shown that spending leisure time together can benefit couples. This study narrowed the focus specifically to shared physical activity.
Researchers suggest that exercising together may naturally create more opportunities for conversation and positive interactions. Repeated moments of connection like these could help strengthen a relationship over time.
"Out of all three outcomes, exercise had the biggest impact on communication," Mildenhall said. "That's why it was interesting that walking was the number one reported exercise. It naturally provides opportunities to communicate."
Walking was the most common form of shared exercise reported by couples in the study. That finding suggests spouses may not need costly gym memberships or elaborate home workout equipment to experience the potential relationship benefits of being active together.
Couples who exercised together also reported better listening and stronger feelings that their spouse heard and supported them. According to Yorgason, those interactions may help explain why shared physical activity was associated with healthier communication and better conflict resolution.
A Simple Habit, Not a Relationship Cure
The researchers emphasize that exercising together is not a solution for every relationship difficulty. For young couples, particularly those raising children, finding time for shared physical activity may require deliberate planning.
Still, the researchers say conjoint exercise can be one of several healthy habits that give couples regular opportunities to connect. Amid the competing demands of school, daily life and parenting, even something as simple as walking together may create valuable time for conversation and connection.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Brigham Young University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Ashlyn Mildenhall, Matthew L. Núñez, Jeremy Yorgason. Conjoint Exercise among young married couples: Exploring associations with couple conflict, conflict resolution, and communication. Family Relations, 2026; DOI: 10.1111/fare.70260

Mapping where US bombers are based around the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:22:54 UTC
21:22:54 KST

Mapping where US bombers are based globally
The US has pulled its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford amid Iran fears. Here’s where else they can fly from.
Over the course of Sunday, a dozen B-1B bombers took off from Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford in western England and flew home to the United States. Their departure abruptly ended the base’s role as a launchpad for US strikes on Iran, which began on February 28.
The base, roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, is the US Air Force’s only European airfield for heavy bombers and a key forward operating location for deployed bombers.
Over the past two weeks, six people were arrested on suspicion of “terrorism”. They were all released on bail.
US President Donald Trump said on Monday the bombers were moved because “there were some threats”, which he believed were linked to Iran. “So we moved them around a little bit, not very far,” he told reporters at the White House.
Hours earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio played down any link to the alleged plot, saying it was “not unusual to see rotations happen” and that he had confidence in the security of US bases.
What happened at RAF Fairford?
On September 27, police arrested five men on suspicion of plotting to plant explosives near Fairford in the United Kingdom. They were released on bail a day later.
Investigators found petrol but no explosive devices in their vans, though UK officials say the men remain under investigation. On Thursday, police arrested a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national in London on suspicion of plotting an attack on the airbase. He was also released on bail on October 3.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested that “Iran played a part” in the alleged plot but declined to give details. Iran has denied any such scheme and summoned the UK ambassador in Tehran in protest at the arrests.
What bombers does the US have?
The US Air Force flies three types of bombers, with a fourth on the way.
The B-52 Stratofortress is the oldest. The B-52H model currently in service was built in the early 1960s. With a wingspan of 56 metres (185 feet), it is the largest US bomber and can carry about 31 tonnes of weapons, including nuclear bombs and cruise missiles.
The B-1B Lancer, which entered service in the mid-1980s, is the fastest of the three. It can reach 1.2 times the speed of sound and has a swing-wing that sweeps back for high-speed flight. It carries the largest conventional payload, about 34 tonnes, but no longer carries nuclear weapons. These were the aircraft that left Fairford.
The B-2 Spirit is a flying-wing stealth bomber designed to slip past air defences. Only 20 were built, of which 19 remain in service. It can carry both nuclear and conventional weapons, including the 13,600kg (30,000lb) “bunker buster” bomb used in US strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites in June 2025.
The B-21 Raider, a smaller stealth bomber, is still in flight testing, and it remains on track for delivery in 2027. Over the next decade and a half, the air force plans to replace the B-1B and B-2, leaving a future fleet of B-21s and upgraded B-52s.
Where do these bombers fly from?
All US bombers are permanently based in the US, at five main airbases:
- B-52H: Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana and Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota
- B-1B: Dyess Air Force Base in Texas and Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota
- B-2: Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri
- B-21: Due to arrive at Ellsworth in South Dakota in 2027
All of these bases have long, wide runways, typically exceeding 10,000 feet (3,048 metres).
That makes bomber runways about as long as those at a big international airport. What limits where bombers can operate is not tarmac but security, weapons storage and support.
For missions abroad, the US rotates bombers through a handful of forward bases. Other important overseas operating locations include Andersen Air Force Base in Guam and Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean.
Beyond these, the air force sends small groups of bombers to allied airbases for a few weeks at a time, in what it calls Bomber Task Force deployments. Recent rotations have included B-52s at Moron in Spain, B-1Bs at Orland in Norway and Misawa in Japan, and B-52s at Tindal in northern Australia, which arrived in September.
The bombers can also go on a strike mission from the US with the help of aerial refuelling. Bomber missions during the US-Israel war on Iran lasted more than 30 hours there and back. Each group of three bombers needed six to nine tanker aircraft to refuel them along the way.
