2026-10-06
14:57:58 EEST
20:57:58 KST

The Digital Transformation Office launched by the Energy Ministry is working on more than 20 projects related to the digitalization of the energy sector, Deputy Energy Minister Denys Shuhaliy said.
"We have more than 20 projects in the works. Some of them are already nearing completion, and some are just starting and are at the design stage," Shuhaliy said on Monday at the Code of Economy conference in Kyiv.
The aim of such projects is above all to bring information about energy facilities into shared systems that allow them to be seen in real time, so that necessary decisions on their operation can be taken quickly, he said.
This approach is very relevant given the construction of a large number of energy facilities of various capacities, and monitoring and managing them is a challenge for the power system, Shuhaliy said.
"Digital projects in energy are divided into two parts. The first is development projects aimed at improving the sector. The second is what helps restore and protect energy. Of course, no digital technology can restore a thermal power plant or grids, our power engineers do that through heroic efforts, but making their work safer and helping them find damage and ways to fix it faster is the task we face today," he said.
The Digital Transformation Office is now testing several models for analytics on attacks on energy and their consequences, as well as on outages, "so that there is a fairer distribution," he said.
Asked about the consequences of Russian strikes on data centers, Shuhaliy said a hybrid system of measures is used to protect against such strikes, including multi-layer data backup and stress tests.
"Five years ago everyone thought the main threat to IT systems was cyberattacks, and now we understand that the main threat is when two missiles arrive and destroy a data center. So changes in protection are needed," Shuhaliy said.
Cyberattacks on the power system happen all the time, two to three times a week, but so far none has been impossible to repel, he said.

Ukraine’s battlefield gains may be pushing Putin to shift focus to early winter strikes, ISW says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:57:49 UTC
20:57:49 KST

Ukraine's battlefield successes appear to be forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to reevaluate his theory of victory and shift focus toward long-range strikes to compel Ukraine to surrender, rather than advances on the battlefield, the Institute for the Study of War said on 4 October.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia used more than 800 jet-powered drones during the week of 27 September to 4 October. Ukraine currently intercepts only 50–60% of jet-powered drones, leaving it vulnerable to the large number of new drones Russia is deploying.
The late-September start and the campaign's aim
ISW said Russian forces began their winter 2026–27 strike campaign against Ukraine's energy infrastructure in late September and that the campaign is aimed at making civilian life unbearable enough to force Ukraine to capitulate.
Russian forces would step up attacks on military facilities, defense industry sites, and related infrastructure in Kyiv and elsewhere in Ukraine, the Russian Defense Ministry said on 4 October, according to Reuters. The announcement followed Zelenskyy's vow to increase attacks on Russian oil refineries.
The ministry also claimed its recent strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions were a response to alleged Ukrainian attacks on civilian targets inside Russia. Among the grievances it named were Ukraine's strikes on Leningrad Oblast during the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum in June and alleged strikes on electoral infrastructure in Moscow during the 18–20 September State Duma elections, according to ISW.
ISW called the Russian Defense Ministry's framing of the recent strikes as retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilian targets unfounded, saying many of its specific claims are "blatantly false." Russia has provided no evidence that Ukraine targeted electoral infrastructure, and Ukraine's 19–20 September strikes on Moscow targeted oil refineries and warehouses, the think tank said. The Russian strikes "are not an actual response to specific events," it concluded.
The 135 drones, the bridges struck seven times
Overnight on 3–4 October, Russia launched 135 Shahed-type and Gerbera-type drones, while also using decoy drones and Banderol or Dan-T loitering munitions. Ukrainian forces downed 123 drones and two loitering munitions, and strikes hit five locations, according to ISW, which cited the Ukrainian Air Force. Russian forces struck Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges seven times between 1 and 4 October in an effort to disrupt Ukraine's economy and daily civilian life, ISW said.
Ukraine builds new layers of defense against jet drones
More than 12 .50-caliber machine-gun turrets are already working in Kyiv against jet-powered drones, and eight more will be installed in Kyiv Oblast, Zelenskyy said, Suspilne reported. He added that F-16s help a lot against the drones, according to Ukrinform. Ukraine is set to receive 2,000 Bars interceptor drones through joint production with Germany, RBC-Ukraine reported.
Ballistic missiles may be Russia's next wave
Zelenskyy said Ukraine estimates Russia has up to 700 ballistic missiles in reserve and produces 130–140 a month. He made the remarks at a joint media briefing with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv, Ukrinform reported. Russia is likely stockpiling ballistic and quasi-ballistic missiles for intense strikes after its jet-powered drones lose their current advantage, ISW assessed. ISW also cited an ongoing shortage of Patriot interceptors.
OHCHR has verified some 15,280 civilian casualties in Ukraine in the first eight months of 2026, 55% more than in the same period of 2025, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said on 2 October.

Switzerland’s Partners Group set to wind up UK fund
Swiss asset manager Partners Group is set to wind up its private equity fund, Partners Group Private Equity (PGPE), which is listed on the London Stock Exchange.
A large majority of investors, representing 74.12% of the share capital, voted in favour of exiting this fund by converting their securities into so-called ‘realisation’ shares, according to a press release dated Monday. The threshold for approving this proposal was set at 40%.
In June, against a backdrop of fears of a private equity bubble, PGPE had given its shareholders the choice of continuing their involvement in the company’s long-term strategy following a restructuring, or opting for a tradable security that would guarantee liquidity.
This latter option will therefore be the only one put forward for shareholders’ approval at the extraordinary general meeting scheduled for Wednesday. Should it be adopted, the board of directors would proceed with a controlled liquidation of the entire investment portfolio.
Should it be rejected, the fund will continue to be managed “in accordance with its current investment objective and policy, and the directors will reassess the options available at that time”.
The reorganisation proposal has, meanwhile, been withdrawn.
This decision comes at a turbulent time for Partners Group, which has come under criticism for its exposure to private markets.
In June, the firm had restricted redemptions from its “evergreen” funds – those with no maturity date – which led to a fall in its share price.
Last week, the asset manager reorganised this perpetual fund. Global Value SICAV, with assets under management of €6.6 billion (CHF6.16 billion), has thus been incorporated into a fund with separate sub-funds, which will be divided into two sub-portfolios.
One of these aims to generate long-term capital gains, whilst the other is designed to facilitate easier exit.

Francis Halzen wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:56:55 CST
20:56:55 KST

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics is announced in Stockholm, Sweden, Oct. 6, 2026. Francis Halzen has been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics 2026 for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced Tuesday. (Xinhua/Lyu You)
STOCKHOLM, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Belgian scientist Francis Halzen has been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics 2026 for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced Tuesday.
"Francis Halzen realized that ice at the South Pole could be used to track particles known as neutrinos. His vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory -- a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors," the Academy said in a statement.
Using IceCube, researchers can capture neutrinos from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe, said the Academy.
"Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument. His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy," said Mark Pearce, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics.
"I didn't expect it. It's a great pleasure to hear about this prize." Halzen said in a phone interview with the Academy after the prize was announced, adding that he would like to point out this project began through collaboration with many people giving their assistance.
Halzen was born in Tienen, Belgium, on March 23, 1944. He is now a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the United States. ■

Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said the final vote is expected on Jan. 12.
Lithuania's Constitution prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on its territory.

Lithuanian lawmakers opposing the constitutional change said a decision of such significance should be put to voters in a referendum. ■

The U.S. Navy has awarded Lockheed Martin a $209 million contract modification to keep building the AN/SLQ-32(V)6, the electronic warfare system that warns U.S. Navy surface ships of incoming anti-ship missiles and the radars guiding them.
The U.S. Department of War announced the award, made Sept. 30. The modification includes options that, if exercised, would bring the cumulative value of the contract to about $1.7 billion. Work is scheduled to run through September 2029.
The AN/SLQ-32, known to sailors as the “Slick-32,” has been the U.S. Navy’s main shipboard electronic warfare system for decades. The (V)6 version is the product of the Surface Electronic Warfare Improvement Program, or SEWIP, Block 2. It adds new antennas, a more capable receiver and an open interface to the ship’s combat system, along with a high-gain, high-sensitivity sensor developed under an earlier SEWIP phase.
It picks up radar and radio signals from enemy ships, aircraft and missiles, identifies them and pinpoints their direction. According to the U.S. Navy, the (V)6 is meant to improve anti-ship missile defense, help ships avoid being targeted and tracked, and give crews a clearer picture of who is emitting around them. Crews can run it manually from a console, or the ship’s combat management system can control it automatically.
Lockheed Martin won the SEWIP Block 2 development contract in 2009. The first AN/SLQ-32(V)6 was installed on the destroyer USS Bainbridge (DDG 96) in 2014 for at-sea testing, and the system entered full-rate production in 2016. The U.S. Navy awarded a follow-on full-rate production contract in January 2020 covering the standard (V)6 and smaller variants, including a “Lite” version sized for ships with less room and power to spare.
The next step in the program, SEWIP Block 3, adds an electronic attack capability that can actively jam threats. That version is designated AN/SLQ-32(V)7 and is built by Northrop Grumman.
Most of the money obligated on this award comes from the U.S. Navy’s shipbuilding account. About $129.5 million, or 62 percent, is fiscal 2026 shipbuilding and conversion funding, which typically pays for equipment going onto ships under construction. Another $78.5 million comes from fiscal 2025 and 2026 other procurement funds, which are generally used to upgrade ships already in service, and about $1 million is research and development funding.
Lockheed Martin will do 78 percent of the work at its Rotary and Mission Systems site in Liverpool, New York, near Syracuse, where the company runs its electronic warfare business. The remaining 22 percent will be done in Lansdale, Pennsylvania. Naval Sea Systems Command in Washington, D.C., is the contracting activity.

KATHMANDU, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- The World Bank has projected Nepal's economic growth to slow to 3.7 percent in the current fiscal year 2026-27, which began in mid-July, from its earlier projection of 4.2 percent, reflecting disruptions to industry and services.
Releasing its flagship publication on Nepal, Nepal Development Update: Building Back Differently for the Future, on Tuesday, the global development institution said the Aug. 26 floods in Nepal are expected to have a material negative impact on the country's economic prospects in the short term.
A total of 1,455 people have been confirmed dead and 5,285 remain missing to date following the disaster, which devastated communities and infrastructure along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).
According to the Rapid Disaster Needs Assessment (RDNA) report prepared by a joint technical team of the National Planning Commission and the NDRRMA, the recent floods and landslides are estimated to have caused losses of 2.69 billion U.S. dollars.
The RDNA report said an estimated 4.77 billion dollars will be required for the reconstruction and recovery of affected infrastructure and assets.
The World Bank said industry is expected to be the main drag on growth, reflecting extensive damage to hydropower, solar energy, electricity transmission and transport infrastructure, which will constrain electricity generation and production and disrupt the movement of goods.
"Services are expected to be affected through disruptions to trade, transport, tourism, and financial activity, while agricultural losses are expected to have limited effects on aggregate output but significant impacts on livelihoods in affected areas," the bank said in its report.
Besides the impact of the floods, other key downside risks include a prolonged conflict in the Middle East, which could reduce tourist arrivals and remittance inflows, dampen consumption and services activity, and slow overall growth.
"Disruptions in fertilizer imports could raise production costs and reduce agricultural output, while fuel supply constraints could weigh on investment and economic activity more broadly," the global development lender said. "The risks to the outlook are tilted to the downside."
Domestically, the main risks include delays in relief, reconstruction and restoration of infrastructure damaged by the August floods, according to the World Bank.
"This could prolong disruptions to transport, trade, tourism, hydropower generation, and private sector activity," it said. ■

COLOMBO, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka's economy has returned to its 2018 level after 12 consecutive quarters of expansion, but household incomes, employment and poverty indicators continue to lag behind the recovery, the World Bank said Tuesday.
In its latest Sri Lanka Development Update, the World Bank projected economic growth of 4.4 percent in 2026, supported by strong industrial activity and steady services growth.
Growth is expected to ease to 4.2 percent in 2027 as the post-crisis rebound loses momentum and weak productivity constrains expansion. The bank also warned that global energy market volatility and a possible El Nino event could affect productivity and food security.
Fiscal conditions have improved, with the primary budget surplus increasing sharply, the update noted.
Despite signals of continued recovery, the country's poverty level remains at 16.9 percent, well above pre-crisis levels, while inflation has risen in recent months due to higher food and energy prices.
The report said Sri Lanka's next phase of growth would require greater reliance on private investment, exports and productivity rather than government spending.
The report identified agribusiness as a major source of the country's future growth, noting that the agrifood system, consisting of food processing, logistics, trade, and food services, contributes about one-sixth of GDP, more than 40 percent of employment and nearly 30 percent of goods exports.
It recommended reforms covering trade policy, infrastructure, agricultural research, climate-smart technologies, land tenure, financing, digital traceability and cold-chain logistics to attract private investment and raise productivity. ■

VIENTIANE, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- A warm and celebratory atmosphere is taking hold across Laos as schools, students and families prepare flowers, gifts and activities for Lao National Teacher's Day, a day dedicated to honoring those who devote their lives to shaping the next generation.
Across Laos, schools are preparing ceremonies, performances and activities to honor teachers, while students choose flowers and gifts for the people who have taught them, encouraged them and helped shape the paths they are taking.
For teachers, seeing those familiar faces return with a flower, a small gift or simply a word of thanks can bring a quiet but overwhelming warmth.
For primary school teacher Somvilay, the National Teacher's Day brings the same feelings every year -- warmth, happiness and pride.
"My students are still young, full of energy and sometimes a little too playful. Our days in the classroom are often filled with laughter, noise and unexpected moments," Somvilay told Xinhua on Tuesday.
But when Teacher's Day arrives, she said, something changes. Those same playful students find their own ways to put a smile on Somvilay's face and warm her heart. Some sing for her, others offer words of gratitude, while some bring small gifts, flowers or fruit, and wish her good health.
"All of these moments remind me why I work hard, why I chose this profession and why I keep coming back to school each day to help shape the future of our young generation," she said.
Watching her students grow gives Somvilay a deep sense of pride. For her, Teacher's Day is more than a celebration. It is a moment to look at the children in front of her and remember why she chose to teach and why she continues to do so.
Lindar, a high school student in Lao capital Vientiane, said Teacher's Day is a chance to show appreciation in a simple but meaningful way. This year, she is preparing small gifts for her teachers while also taking part in school activities organized to honor them.
She said she has come to understand how demanding it can be for a teacher to stand in front of a classroom and guide dozens of students every day, each with different personalities, abilities and needs.
"I really respect our teachers for being able to teach and take care of so many students every day. It is not an easy job, and I think their patience and dedication deserve to be appreciated," she said.
For some people, Teacher's Day is also a time to remember the teachers who helped shape who they have become. Noudchaly, a university student in Vientiane, makes time each year to return to her former high school and visit the teachers who once taught her.
She may not always have a gift to bring, but she said that simply showing up is enough to bring smiles to her former teachers.
"When I go back to my old school and see my teachers, I can see how happy they are. Sometimes I don't have anything special to give them, but I think visiting them and talking with them are already a way of showing that I still remember them and appreciate what they have done for me," she said.
As the National Teacher's Day arrives on Oct. 7, teachers and students alike share moments of warmth and joy, surrounded by laughter, smiles and celebrations that make the day a meaningful one for everyone. ■

The Stock Exchange of Thailand index drew early support in September from rising optimism in artificial intelligence and data center investments, which boosted electronics shares, said FETCO chairman Paiboon Nalinthrangkurn.

Looking forward, Paiboon said investors are tracking third-quarter earnings projections for listed companies, along with the government's economic stimulus measures and their implementation.
He added that eyes remain on capital deployment trends in tech sectors and data centers, as well as the impact and risks of domestic flooding on economic activity and supply chains. ■

SARAJEVO, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- From historic streets and religious landmarks to local neighborhoods and natural landscapes, Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH), is attracting a growing number of Chinese travelers seeking deeper cultural experiences rather than simply checking in at tourist sites.
During China's National Day and Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, Chinese photographer Chen Liwei traveled to BiH with a group of 10 photography enthusiasts on a 14-day tailored tour, capturing the country's diverse scenery and cultural heritage through their lenses.
"We had never visited the Balkans before, but we have long been fascinated by the region, partly due to classic Yugoslav films such as Walter Defends Sarajevo," Chen said.
The group, all photography lovers who had previously traveled to dozens of European countries, chose BiH for its rich history and unique cultural blend.
Rather than following a standard itinerary, they sought to experience local life and gain a deeper understanding of the Western Balkans, capturing through their lenses Sarajevo's old town streets, religious sites and everyday scenes of local residents.
"BiH has not only beautiful landscapes, but also warm and friendly people. Many locals greeted us with 'ni hao' when they saw us," Chen said.
The experience of Chen's group reflects a broader trend: customized and in-depth tours are becoming increasingly popular among Chinese visitors to BiH.
Zhao Yiming, a local tour guide, said demand for private and tailored Balkan tours has increased by more than 30 percent over the past two years.
"In the past, Chinese tourists mainly traveled in large groups with fixed schedules. Today, more travelers want trips designed around their interests, group size and preferred pace," Zhao said.
The shift has encouraged travel agencies to develop more diverse itineraries, including routes featuring historical sites, cultural experiences and less-visited destinations beyond traditional tourist attractions.
Tourism insiders said different generations of Chinese travelers have different interests. Many older visitors, influenced by films such as Walter Defends Sarajevo, are interested in locations connected with the movie and wartime history. Younger travelers tend to prefer city walks, cultural experiences and longer stays to experience local life.
Xiaoxin Xu, a representative of Hotel Grand Sarajevo, said the hotel's 20 rooms reserved for Chinese tourists were fully booked during the National Day holiday, while the restaurant received 200 to 400 Chinese visitors per day.
"September and October are traditionally the peak tourism season in BiH, and this year's National Day holiday saw strong demand from Chinese travelers," Xu said.
The growing popularity of tailored tours reflects closer people-to-people exchanges between China and BiH. With its historical heritage, diverse cultures and natural scenery, BiH is becoming an increasingly attractive destination for Chinese travelers.
Chen said he planned to share his travel experiences through social platforms to introduce BiH to more Chinese audiences.
"I hope more people will come to BiH and experience this beautiful country for themselves," he said. ■

A campaign group insists that the public must have their say on all major projects linked to the European Organization for Nuclear Research's CERN research facility in Switzerland.
The group launched a Geneva cantonal constitutional initiative and criticised the recent consultation on the Future Circular Collider (FCC) as “biased” and a “denial of democracy”.
“It is about regaining control at local and democratic levels,” said parliamentarian Christina Meissner. “The State Council has handed over all power to the Confederation and deprived us of it.”
The FCC has been placed under federal control, on a par with airport planning or military infrastructure. However, cantonal powers in the field of building law could very well have been applied, according to parliamentarian Raphaël Mahaim.
More
CERN’s next giant leap is a machine that could unlock the universe
Members of the Co-CERNés coalition include Noé21, Swiss Heritage Geneva, WWF Geneva, the Presinge Association for a Future without the FCC, Seymaz-Vie and Bien Vivre à Puplinge. These organisations believe that the FCC will undermine the sustainable policies adopted by the Grand Council and the local population.
Similar mechanisms
According to the initiative, any cantonal consultation on construction and infrastructure projects linked to CERN that require a permit should be put to a public vote. The advisory result would then form the canton’s position.
Mahaim cannot imagine that the Federal Council, or the other members of CERN, would simply “sit back” in the face of a democratic rejection. Similarly, he does not “believe for a second” that the initiative will be declared invalid. Similar mechanisms exist, notably in the canton of Vaud with regard to nuclear power.
The FCC is set to become the largest construction site in Europe, according to the coalition. It will onvolve thousands of heavy goods vehicles on the roads for ten years, millions of tonnes of rubble to be dumped, arable land being sacrificed and more than 100 km of underground construction sites.
No decision before 2028
They also raise concerns about the volumes of cooling water and greenhouse gas emissions. Electricity consumption would be equivalent to that of a city with several hundred thousand inhabitants, according to the petition organisers.
The FCC is a proposed 91-kilometre-long particle accelerator project, intended to succeed the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) from 2045. Costs are estimated at CHF15 billion, but opponents believe they will double.
CERN, for its part, is promoting the project as a world-leading facility. The decision will rest with the institution’s 25 member states in May 2028, barring any postponement.
The signatures for the initiative – 5,696 to meet the threshold – are expected to be submitted in mid-February 2027. Supporters admit that the timetable will be tight for a referendum to take place before CERN’s decision.

Suspected Russian Plague Death: How Much Should We Worry?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:51:43 UTC
20:51:43 KST

A suspected case of pneumonic plague killing a laboratory technician in Russia has sparked global alarm about the possibility of wider transmission. But how easily does pneumonic plague spread, how dangerous is it today, and why are laboratories working with the bacteria that causes it?
RFE/RL spoke to Brendan Wren, a professor of microbial pathogenesis at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, whose research includes studying Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague, about the situation and Russia's moves to deal with it.
RFE/RL: If this was pneumonic plague, how does it spread between people, and how easily can it spread?
Brendan Wren: Pneumonic plague is transmitted by the respiratory route but is not particularly transmissible and certainly not as transmissible as the respiratory SARS virus.
The unfortunate incident in Russia is clearly an isolated occupational infection and to date has not been transmitted to another person, so is not an outbreak. Other persons may have been in contact with the infected person, so isolation and observation of those potentially affected is a sensible measure.
RFE/RL: How rare and how dangerous is pneumonic plague? Can it be treated effectively?
Wren: It is such a rapid and fatal infection that can kill within 24 hours, so although antibiotics may be available, it may be too late if administered when the infection has taken hold. There are also increasing reports of antibiotic-resistant Yersinia pestis strains, the causative bacterial agent of plague. So some antibiotics may not work.
There are approximately 1,000 cases of plague worldwide each year. It is endemic in parts of Russia, China, and the United States.
RFE/RL: Why would a laboratory be working with plague bacteria in the first place? What are such laboratories studying or trying to achieve?
Wren: Generally, to make improved vaccines that could be used in regions of the world where plague is endemic. If Yersinia pestis was weaponized, a vaccine for military personnel may be desirable.
RFE/RL: Based on what is publicly known so far, how concerning is this case? Does it pose any meaningful risk to the wider public?
Wren: In my view this is an isolated case. We no longer live in medieval times, and plague is not particularly transmissible in modern times. It would seem that the authorities are taking sensible procedures to contain this single laboratory-acquired case.

Trump defers diesel tax for truckers as fuel costs bite weeks before US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:51:30 UTC
20:51:30 KST

US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order deferring tax payments on red-dyed diesel used on public roads, as near-record fuel prices linked to the Iran war weigh on the Republican Party weeks before the midterm elections.
Truckers, farmers and other diesel users in the US could benefit from deferred tax payments on fuel normally reserved for tractors and other off-road machinery, as the White House moves to ease a fuel squeeze that threatens to hurt the Republican Party in the midterm elections next month.
US President Donald Trump signed the order on Monday at a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, where he was campaigning to fire up Republican voters.
Trump told supporters the order would "officially waive the off-road requirement and allow anyone to purchase tax-free red-dyed diesel for any reason."
Trump also conceded he was no expert on the fuel. "I don't know what the hell it is, but whatever it is, it's supposed to be very good," he joked.
The dyed fuel is almost identical to ordinary diesel but is exempt from highway taxes, and using it on public roads normally carries penalties.
"The federal diesel tax is 24.4 cents per gallon, or about $60 on a 250-gallon fill," the White House stated in a press release, adding that savings would top $100 per fill where states follow suit. For a large truck taking on 250 gallons, a fill costs about $1,580 including tax at Monday’s average diesel price.
However, the order itself is narrower than Trump's pitch to the crowd suggested.
It does not abolish the levy but postpones payment on dyed diesel used on roads between 5 October and 31 December, free of interest and penalties, and asks US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to find ways, including legislation, to "eliminate the obligation to pay the amounts deferred," the executive order said.
It relies on a law that lets the US Treasury postpone tax deadlines for people affected by disasters or military action, and gives Bessent five days, in consultation with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, to determine whether those conditions are met and which taxpayers qualify.
Unless the Trump administration finds a way to cancel it, the deferred diesel tax will still be owed once the relief period ends on 31 December.
While the White House has pitched the measure at truckers and farmers, the order itself does not single them out, in line with Trump's promise that anyone could buy the fuel. In practice, the relief matters mainly to those running diesel trucks and farm vehicles, as most American cars run on petrol.
Federal authorities and state governors may also choose to suspend inspections and drop the tax, the White House added.
Diesel squeeze
The average price of diesel in the US stood at $6.32 a gallon on Monday, according to motoring group AAA, just below the record $6.53 set on 22 September and more than 70% higher than a year ago.
Prices have soared since the Iran war began in February, disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while Russia has curbed fuel exports after Ukrainian attacks on several of its refineries.
The White House announcement did not mention Iran, instead blaming "the Russia-Ukraine war and a lack of refining capacity around the world", as well as "Democrat-led states that chose to shut down their refineries in the name of 'Green Energy' policies".
Trump also pointed to the G7 deal struck last week to release 100 million barrels of refined diesel from strategic stocks over the next four months, after he had threatened to ban US diesel exports.
American farmers, who are in the middle of the harvest, welcomed the order.
"Every cent per gallon matters when you're running a fleet of grain trucks or hauling cattle hundreds of miles," said Zippy Duvall, president of the American Farm Bureau Federation, the country's biggest farm lobby.
Oil prices eased further on Tuesday as oil exports from the Gulf excluding Iran recovered towards pre-war levels.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped below $100 a barrel in early trading, down roughly 2.5%, while the US benchmark West Texas Intermediate also fell 2.5% to under $88.

Government weighs NIS 9m. assistance after flydubai suspends Israel flights - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:51:27 UTC
20:51:27 KST

The government is expected to approve on Tuesday an assistance mechanism of up to NIS 9 million for Israeli airlines operating flights from Dubai to Israel, after flydubai suspended flights and left thousands of Israelis without a way to return home.
Under the proposed resolution circulated to ministers by the Transportation Ministry, the state would, if necessary, help cover the cost of flying empty aircraft from Israel to Dubai and would also fund the transfer of passengers' baggage to Israel on separate cargo flights.
Flydubai is normally permitted to operate scheduled flights between Dubai and Israel, and according to the document, the possibility of returning through intermediate destinations is also limited because flights offering onward connections have insufficient capacity.
Thousands of Israelis who relied on the airline's flights were left in Dubai without a solution.
Israeli airlines began operating flights to bring citizens home on Friday, but security restrictions have made the operation complex and expensive. Under instructions from the relevant authorities, aircraft must fly from Israel to Dubai without passengers, while passengers' baggage currently cannot be loaded into the aircraft hold on the return flights.
The Transportation Ministry has expressed concern that the cost of the empty outbound leg will make the flights economically unviable and lead airlines to operate fewer flights than required.
The Transportation Ministry's proposed solution is a safety net for the airlines. Israelis seeking to return home will continue purchasing tickets from the airlines as usual, while the state will contribute toward the expenses only if passenger revenue does not cover the cost of the flight.
The assistance will not exceed the costs resulting from the requirement to operate the empty flights or from the need to transport baggage separately. The mechanism is intended to allow flights to continue at the necessary volume without subsidizing services that would already be economically viable.
The Civil Aviation Authority will publish procedures setting out the conditions for receiving the assistance, including limits on its duration and scope, as well as a cap on the cost of each flight segment. The document stresses that the decision does not automatically entitle airlines to receive assistance and does not grant any right to the traveling public.
UAE demanded Israel make arrangements for passengers' baggage
A separate solution is also required for passengers' luggage. Following a demand by the United Arab Emirates that arrangements be made for the baggage of passengers leaving Dubai, the Transportation Ministry will work through the Defense Ministry to bring the luggage to Israel on separate cargo aircraft.
The arrangement will remain in place until security procedures allow baggage to be loaded onto passenger flights or until an alternative solution is found, but in any case no longer than the duration of the government decision. The Transportation Ministry will fund the service through the Defense Ministry.
The total cost of the measure will be capped at NIS 9 million. NIS 5.5 million will come from funds allocated under a government decision to implement coalition agreements in 2026. As a result, the amount allocated under the relevant budget item will be reduced from NIS 6 million to NIS 500,000.
A further NIS 3.5 million will come from the Transportation Ministry's budget. The arrangement will remain in effect until Thursday or until flydubai resumes flights to Israel, whichever comes first. The Civil Aviation Authority will notify the airlines accordingly and ask them to inform passengers of the relevant date.
Finance, defense ministers agree to civil aviation authority's proposal
The finance and defense ministers have agreed to the proposal. Because it is being brought before the government during an election period, the government also examined its legal permissibility.
The legal opinion attached to the proposal states that, during such a period, an outgoing government must exercise "restraint and moderation" in using its powers on matters not subject to particular necessity or urgency.
In this case, however, the Transportation Ministry's legal adviser determined that the decision was necessary because of the exceptional circumstances created by the incident, the need for a rapid solution, the short duration of the assistance and its limited scope.
Accordingly, the opinion concluded that "there is no legal impediment to approving the proposal at this time."
The government used a similar mechanism earlier this year. In July, following Operation Roaring Lion, the government approved financial assistance for Israeli airlines on a larger scale.

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey defense pact faces first test in Houthi offensive - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:51:14 UTC
20:51:14 KST

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey have agreed to “activate collective defense commitments amid ongoing threats,” Saudi Arabia’s Arab News said on October 6. This is an important step.
The new alliance has emerged over the last several months. The Houthi offensive in September in Yemen presented the coalition with its first major test. This is because the Houthis launched missiles at Saudi Arabia and directly harmed Saudi citizens.
Arab News said that “Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey on Monday agreed to immediately implement collective-defense commitments under the previously agreed Mecca Defense Alliance, including the swift deployment of agreed forces and other military capabilities to the Kingdom amid ongoing threats.”
Saudi Arabia has been working over the last month to prepare a counter-offensive in Yemen. This initiative came after setbacks hit the forces of the internationally recognized government of Yemen, which lost ground around the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
Many observers wondered whether Pakistan and Turkey would come to Riyadh’s aid. All of these countries are either partners or close allies of the US, and they have access to advanced military equipment, partly as a result of their US affiliation.
However, it was not clear that Turkey would want to get involved in a conflict in Yemen. In part, this is because Ankara tries to balance relations with Iran, with which it shares a border. Pakistan also has ties with Iran and shares a border with Iran.
Now, Turkey and Pakistan appear to be increasing their support for Riyadh. “The decision was announced following an emergency meeting of the alliance’s Strategic Political and Defense Committee in Riyadh to discuss security developments and threats Saudi Arabia is facing during the regional conflict with Iran and its proxies. The alliance was formed by an agreement signed on August 7,” Arab News observed.
Saudi defense minister hails collective deterrence
Saudi Defense Minister, Prince Khalid bin Salman, wrote on X/Twitter that the meeting “affirms the solidarity and unified stance of our countries in confronting the sinful aggressions that targeted the Kingdom and the Holy Sanctuaries, activating collective deterrence against these aggressions, and against all those standing behind them within the framework of the [Mecca] Defense Alliance.”
The new committee of the alliance has “reviewed the outcomes of political and military consultations and approved recommendations affirming the commitment of the alliance to collective defense and a unified response to threats.” It appears that forces with various types of unnamed capabilities will now be deployed.
This could include Pakistani aircraft or air defenses. Similarly, Turkey could deploy defensive solutions. Intelligence and targeting are also important. Reports indicate the US has also been working closely with Saudi Arabia, although it does not want to directly intervene in Yemen for now.
This could enable important coordination between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan and help their militaries work together and streamline various processes to get the alliance off the ground. Some have argued that the Middle East could be moving toward a regional NATO. What has made NATO unique since its founding is how its members often train and work together.
This kind of cooperation cannot happen overnight. It means the Yemen conflict could help accelerate processes in real time. This will be good for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its partners.
Changing US commitments push regional powers toward deeper cooperation
In a changing world order where the US is shifting its commitments, many regional powers need to step up. All the countries in the new alliance are regional powers. Turkey, for instance, is not only in NATO but is a country with a strong industrial defense base. Pakistan has faced struggles in recent years due to instability at home and insurgent movements in places like its Baloch areas bordering Iran.
Saudi Arabia, a major purchaser of American defense products, has sometimes struggled to put the pieces together in the field to achieve its goals. This was especially true in Yemen, where Riyadh has backed the national government since 2015. However, its intervention in Yemen did not go as easily as planned. Iran armed the Houthis, and drones and missiles targeted Saudi Arabia.
According to Arab News, “Pakistan and Turkey commended the Saudi Armed Forces for their vigilance, state of readiness, and professional performance and efficiency in confronting threats and protecting the Kingdom.” The report added that “as part of efforts to establish the institutional structure of the alliance, the committee appointed retired Lt. Gen. Numan Mahmud of Pakistan as its first secretary-general, for a three-year term.
The alliance members welcomed his appointment and expressed confidence in the contribution he would make to developing the pact and advancing its objectives.”
Defense pact shifts from agreement to operational planning
The Mecca Agreement will now need to produce practical measures. Turkey’s TRT state media heralded the moves taking place in Saudi Arabia, noting that Turkey “was represented by Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, National Defense Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu. The meeting comes amid renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and wider concerns over regional security.”
TRT added that “Fidan said the three countries discussed steps to support Saudi Arabia’s defense while also examining ways to resolve regional issues peacefully through dialogue. The alliance was established in August by Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, with the three countries subsequently agreeing to build permanent institutions and strengthen collective deterrence and defense capabilities.”
Meanwhile, in Saudi Arabia, the General Authority of Civil Aviation announced on Tuesday that King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Jazan and Najran International Airport, in the south of the Kingdom, experienced “two attacks” targeting their facilities on Monday evening.
In addition, TRT noted that “the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has carried out a targeted military operation against the Houthi movement in the Red Sea province of Hudaida, destroying naval weapons depots and thwarting planned attacks on international shipping lanes. The national Yemeni army has said that government forces had seized the Dhubab district and strategic positions around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait following clashes with the Houthis.”

Russia starts production of upgraded tank recovery vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:49:11 UTC
20:49:11 KST

- Uralvagonzavod said it completed testing of an upgraded BREM-80 armored recovery vehicle with a mechanized coupling that lets crews tow tanks without leaving the vehicle.
- The company said serial production has started and vehicles are being delivered to Russian troops, without disclosing quantities.
Russian tank maker Uralvagonzavod says it has completed testing of an upgraded BREM-80 armored recovery vehicle that lets its crew hook up and tow damaged tanks without leaving the vehicle, a change the company says came directly from combat experience in Ukraine.
The company, part of Russia’s state-owned Rostec corporation, announced the end of the test cycle on Oct. 6. It said serial production is already underway and the vehicles are being delivered to Russian troops. Uralvagonzavod did not say how many have been built or delivered.
Armored recovery vehicles drag disabled or stuck tanks off the battlefield so they can be repaired. The job usually means getting close to where a tank was hit, and crews have traditionally had to climb out to attach heavy tow cables by hand. Uralvagonzavod said recovering damaged vehicles has proven to be one of the most dangerous tasks in the war in Ukraine.
The main change on the upgraded BREM-80 is a mechanized coupling device, which connects the tow to the damaged vehicle from inside. The company said this cuts the risk of crew injuries several times over. During testing, engineers ran the coupling under heavy loads while towing armored vehicles across rough terrain, the company said.
Uralvagonzavod said the vehicle also has reinforced armor against shaped-charge warheads, drones and artillery fragments. It carries what the company calls sixth-generation radio equipment, which it said was tested for resistance to jamming under active electronic warfare conditions.
The BREM-80 is built on the chassis of the T-80 tank and keeps the T-80’s gas turbine engine. According to the company, the vehicle can start at minus 40 degrees Celsius (minus 40 Fahrenheit) within minutes. Uralvagonzavod said its pulling power lets it tow several tanks at once, including heavier Western-made armored vehicles. At the Rembat-2018 competition, the company says, a BREM-80 towed six coupled T-80 tanks with a combined weight of more than 270 tonnes (about 298 tons).
The vehicle also carries hydraulic winches, a crane and a dozer blade that clears paths and anchors the vehicle in place while it pulls. Earlier manufacturer data for the BREM-80U put the crane’s lifting capacity at up to 18 tonnes.
The upgrade has been in the works for some time. A version shown at the Army-2024 exhibition near Moscow in August 2024 carried explosive reactive armor on the front of the hull and an electronic warfare counter-drone system built into a cage over the top. In February 2026, Rostec said Uralvagonzavod had delivered a batch of modernized BREM-80s to the Russian Ministry of Defense and had begun serial production.
Russian ground forces operate T-72, T-80 and T-90 tanks in Ukraine, and the T-80 chassis allows the BREM-80 to keep pace with T-80 units.

Spanish judge lifts arrest warrant for former Catalan leader Puigdemont, opening door to his return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:48:20 UTC
20:48:20 KST

The former regional president has lived abroad since Catalonia's unilateral declaration of independence in 2017, and left the country without being detained after a brief public appearance in Barcelona in 2024.
Spanish Supreme Court judge Pablo Llarena has revoked the national arrest warrant for Carles Puigdemont after Spain's Constitutional Court endorsed applying the amnesty law linked to Catalan's independence drive that culminated in a 2017 referendum. The decision removes one of the main legal hurdles to the former president of Catalonia's regional government returning to Spain.
Llarena's move follows a Constitutional Court ruling in favour of former Catalan regional minister Dolors Bassa.
Until now, the Supreme Court had refused to apply the amnesty, a 2024 law covering those prosecuted over the "procés", to embezzlement connected to the bid for independence. The Constitutional Court rejected that approach when it upheld Bassa's appeal.
Puigdemont had faced arrest if he returned to Spain. Lifting that measure substantially alters his legal situation and opens the door to his return.
The core issue was whether the use of public funds to finance the 1 October 2017 independence referendum could be covered by the amnesty law. The Supreme Court ruled that it could not, arguing that its organisers had obtained a personal financial benefit. The Constitutional Court has now rejected that interpretation and in turn the Supreme Court has lifted the arrest warrant.
What does this mean for Puigdemont?
Llarena's decision has an immediate consequence for Puigdemont. The former Catalan president has lived outside Spain since October 2017, when he left the country following the application of article 155 of the Spanish Constitution, which allowed the central government in Madrid to take direct control of the region.
The adoption of the amnesty law in 2024 opened up the prospect of his definitive return. However, Llarena initially kept the national arrest warrant active.
Puigdemont made a brief return to Barcelona in August 2024 to take part in an event coinciding with the investiture of Salvador Illa as Catalonia's regional president. He appeared in public and later left Spain without being arrested.
Puigdemont has called a press conference on Tuesday evening at Waterloo, Belgium, where he lives, for an "institutional declaration" at 6pm CET, alongside former regional ministers Antoni Comín and Lluís Puig, according to Infobae.

As Russia’s Foreign Ministry noted, removing the Taliban’s terrorist designation opens the way for establishing full-fledged partnership with Kabul in the interests of the Russian and Afghan peoples.
In the summer of 2025, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow had recognized the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan and that the country’s ambassador arrived in Moscow on July 1.

Drones strike merchant vessels in Black Sea off Bulgaria and Ukraine, killing at least one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:47:58 UTC
20:47:58 KST

Drones strike merchant vessels in Black Sea off Bulgaria and Ukraine, killing at least one
Drones reportedly struck several merchant vessels in the Black Sea on Oct. 6, including two ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. A Russian strike on a separate civilian vessel killed at least one crew member and injured several others.
One crew member, a steward, was killed, and seven others were injured when a Russian drone struck a merchant vessel flying the Marshall Islands flag in the Black Sea, according to Odesa Oblast Governor Oleh Kiper. The vessel was carrying rapeseed oil and was damaged in the strike, with a fire breaking out in the superstructure.
"By deliberately targeting civilian shipping and port infrastructure, Russia is grossly violating the norms of international law, thereby posing a threat to global food security," Kiper said.
Separately, two merchant ships, the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and the Palau-flagged Able, were hit by drones of unknown origin about 112 kilometers (70 miles) off Bulgaria's coast on Oct. 6, according to Bulgarian broadcaster Nova. The incident is believed to be the first reported drone attack on commercial shipping inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
The Togo-flagged vessel suffered severe structural damage and sank. The fate of its crew remains unknown, with the search for survivors continuing. NOVA reported that life jackets had been spotted near the vessel, but no people had been found.
The second vessel caught fire following the attack. All 18 crew members were rescued by a Bulgarian ferry. Two sailors were seriously injured, one with severe burns, the other with a head injury. The crew members are Indian and Turkish nationals, according to Nova.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev convened an emergency meeting with representatives of state institutions following the attacks. He described the attacks as a "gross violation of international law" and warned that such attacks pose growing risks to Black Sea shipping, increase insurance costs, and further complicate maritime transport.
The incidents come amid a growing number of attacks and incidents involving civilian shipping in the Black Sea, raising concerns over the security of one of the region's key trade routes.
A day earlier, on Oct. 5, a cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast after a Russian drone strike killed two people and injured at least 11 others, prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.

3 mayors in Mersin jailed pending trial on graft charges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

11:47:53 UTC
20:47:53 KST

(AA Photo)
A court early on Oct. 6 ordered Mersin Mayor Vahap Seçer and the mayors of two district municipalities jailed pending trial over corruption allegations, following an investigation into local government contracts.
The operation, launched on Oct. 1, targeted Mersin Municipality as well as the Yenişehir and Mezitli district municipalities in the southern province as part of a corruption investigation.
After nearly five days of judicial proceedings, the court ordered all three mayors, including Yenişehir Mayor Abdullah Özyiğit and Mezitli Mayor Ahmet Serkan Tuncer, jailed pending trial in the early hours of Oct. 6.
At least 10 of the 59 suspects detained in the operation were also jailed pending trials.
Seçer, who is also the head of the Union of Turkish Municipalities (TBB), was elected from the ranks of the opposition Republican People’s Party (CHP), as were Özyiğit and Tuncer.
The investigation alleged that public losses totaling around 331 million Turkish Liras ($6.75 million) were incurred in 13 tenders and 63 direct-procurement contracts at Mersin Municipality.
The alleged public loss was estimated at 1.01 billion liras at Mezitli Municipality and 105 million liras at Yenişehir Municipality.
The arrests come amid a broader series of investigations targeting mayors elected from opposition parties, which have intensified over the past year.
Several opposition mayors and senior municipal officials, including Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, have been jailed pending trial as part of the investigations.
In a separate operation on Oct. 6, authorities detained 46 suspects in a corruption investigation targeting the western province of İzmir’s Bayraklı Municipality. Among those detained was former Bayraklı Mayor Serdar Sandal.

Rubio urges Russia to be transparent over plague incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:47:15 UTC
20:47:15 KST

Muhammed Yasin Gungor
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russia on Tuesday to provide full transparency and share detailed information with the international community regarding a fatal biological laboratory incident in Siberia.
“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Rubio told reporters during a joint news conference with Icelandic Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir in Reykjavik. “That’s what they should do. That’s what we hope they will do.”
Rubio emphasized that whenever an infection occurs inside a specialized facility anywhere in the world, concerns naturally arise, pointing to lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic.
However, he cautioned against drawing unsubstantiated conclusions about whether the incident involved an intentionally altered pathogen. He said it would be “reckless” to speculate without comprehensive facts, adding that the US could not determine whether the situation represented a minor occurrence or something broader.
Rubio said multiple domestic and international agencies were tracking developments “hour by hour” to ensure partner governments could respond appropriately once verified information became available.
The diplomatic appeal followed reports that a 28-year-old female researcher at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died after contracting “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” Russian state news agency Tass reported.
While local outlets alleged that the death stemmed from accidental laboratory exposure that prompted hospital quarantines and factory mask rules in nearby Shelekhov, Russian consumer safety watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said the epidemiological situation remained stable.
US President Donald Trump said Monday that Washington was closely following the situation and remained prepared to assist Moscow. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov welcomed the gesture, saying mutual offers of aid were always positive.

How Palestinian reporters defied Israel’s genocide to redefine journalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:47:03 UTC
20:47:03 KST

How Palestinian reporters defied Israel’s genocide to redefine journalism
Western media have come under scrutiny for buying into the Israeli narrative rather than standing up for vulnerable journalists in Gaza and elsewhere.
Israel has killed about 250 journalists since launching its genocidal war on Gaza on October 7, 2023. That is more than the number of journalists killed in all wars in the past 150 years combined.
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) says Israel has engaged in “the deadliest and most deliberate effort to kill and silence journalists” that the media watchdog has ever documented.
Jonathan Dagher, the head of Reporters Without Borders’ Middle East desk, called the targeting of journalists “a tragedy for journalism”, while the United Nations human rights chief, Volker Turk, called Gaza “a ‘death trap’ for journalists”.
Yet, beyond the statements and condolences, Israel has never been held accountable for its killing of Palestinian journalists – a practice that long predates the genocidal war on Gaza, but that took on an industrial scale over the past three years.
Instead, the silence of the international community and lack of solidarity from Western media professionals emboldened Israel as it pursued the genocidal war and normalised journalists’ killings.
But despite trying to suppress the truth about its massacres and attempts at ethnic cleansing, Israel – historically an acknowledged master at propaganda – has largely failed in its efforts over the past three years, thanks to the bravery of the very voices it tried to silence.
That too is the story of how journalism has changed since October 7, 2023.
‘Neutral’ amid genocide
Western media outlets and their prominent faces often claimed to be “neutral” in their coverage of the genocidal war.
But the very concept of neutrality in journalism has come under question amid the genocide.
The Western media were rarely neutral when viewed according to the basic tenets of journalism and professional standards. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza so far. But Western outlets often framed headlines in the passive tense when reporting on these killings, conveniently shielding Israel from blame.
Palestinians were killed by Israel, mostly in circumstances that violated rules of war. These details were not highlighted, and the Israeli narrative that Hamas was using Palestinian civilians as a “human shield” was amplified.
When Al Jazeera journalist Anas al-Sharif was killed in a targeted attack in front of al-Shifa Hospital in August 2025, CNN carried the Israeli accusation that he worked for a Hamas cell in its second paragraph, an allegation Al Jazeera has rejected.
Weeks before the killing, Irene Khan, the UN’s special rapporteur on freedom of opinion and expression, had warned against “repeated threats and accusations” against al-Sharif by the Israeli army.
Israel killed 22 people, including five journalists – one of whom worked for Al Jazeera – in a “double-tap” strike in September 2025. It claimed that it had targeted a “Hamas camera.” Most media outlets ran the story. The Reuters news agency, whose journalist was also killed in the attack, confirmed that the camera belonged to it.
Similarly, when Israel targeted media personnel in Lebanon early in the war, a Sky News post on X called it a hit on a “Hezbollah-linked” broadcaster.
Israel has also been accused of jailing and torturing Palestinian journalists for doing their job. During the genocidal war, it has tried to control the narrative domestically too, cracking down on Haaretz for its critical coverage of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s failures on October 7, 2023, and the atrocities in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The Netanyahu government imposed a ban on Al Jazeera, calling the network a security threat. Al Jazeera described the shutdown as a “criminal act” and warned that Israel’s suppression of the free press “stands in contravention of international and humanitarian law”.
This was not the first time Al Jazeera has been targeted. In 2021, a Gaza building housing Al Jazeera’s office was destroyed in an Israeli missile strike. Israel has killed many Al Jazeera journalists even before October 2023.
Shireen Abu Akleh, considered a voice of Palestine, was killed by an Israeli soldier while she was reporting in the occupied West Bank in 2022. Her killer was never charged for the murder.
Assal Rad, an activist and Middle East historian, has accused the Western media of enabling attacks on journalists.
“When you’re repeating what Israel says, you’re creating space to legitimise the targeting of their own colleagues,” she said in an interview with Columbia Journalism Review on September 30.
Double standards
While reporting on Russian aggression against Ukraine, media around the world rightly humanised the victims.
But that same journalistic standard was missing, far too often, when Western outlets reported on Palestinians killed by Israel. Instead, they were at times portrayed as collateral damage, their deaths the result of fighting between two sides.
Israel has killed more than 21,000 children in Gaza in the last three years. But the faces of thousands of babies, children and mothers, and their suffering and despair, were frequently buried under statistics. They were nameless, faceless, their lives and stories deemed unworthy of human treatment.
Moreover, Western reporting often lacked historical contextualisation, erasing the history of Israel’s brutal occupation, territorial expansion and the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. More than 750,000 Palestinians were expelled or displaced from their homes, leading up to the formation of Israel in 1948. Israel has since forcibly displaced more Palestinians from the occupied territory.
Israeli leaders now publicly oppose the establishment of Palestinian statehood as part of the so-called two-state solution and successive governments have expanded illegal settlements on Palestinian lands.
Western media often present settler violence and government-backed illegal settlement expansion as separate, when in fact, the Israeli government has armed, funded and granted impunity to those involved.
Fundamentally, treating Israel – an occupying power in Gaza and the West Bank – and Palestinians as equal sides is itself problematic. It is not objective journalism; it is far from it. It misses the asymmetry inherent in this equation. On the one hand is a major military power in illegal occupation of another people’s land, waging a genocidal war on them and seeking to ethnically cleanse them; on the other is a Palestinian resistance movement consisting of multiple strands united only in their struggle to achieve self-determination, a right guaranteed under the UN Charter.
Objectivity requires that news reports highlight Israel’s use of disproportionate force and the firing of banned weapons at civilian areas – violations of the rules of war and war crimes. Instead, Palestinian experts and commentators were the ones grilled and pressed to condemn Hamas as a condition for even being heard.
The challenge
Still, the Western media’s lopsided coverage did not go unchallenged. It triggered rebellion in several newsrooms, including the BBC and The New York Times.
More than 1,500 Western journalists from various news organisations signed an open letter in protest against the coverage of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Eight BBC journalists wrote an open letter, accusing the broadcaster of failing to accurately report on the Israel-Palestine conflict.
They accused their organisation of running with pro-Israel editorial biases, downplaying Palestinian casualties and suppressing terms like “genocide”, “apartheid” or “occupation”. Many journalists of colour resigned in protest.
This has dented the credibility of Western media’s reporting on critical international issues at a time of global upheaval.
However, the unprecedented Israeli attacks on journalists did not deter Palestinians from reporting. They risked their lives to get the story out via social media, especially TikTok and Instagram.
“They take revenge on us through our children? It doesn’t matter. We will stay. We will continue. This is our path, and we chose it knowingly. We will not stop,” said Wael al-Dahdouh, Al Jazeera Arabic’s then-Gaza bureau chief, after Israel killed his wife, daughter, two sons, and a grandson in separate Israeli air strikes.
People across the world, including young Americans who primarily consume news on social media, were horrified by the graphic images coming out of Palestine despite the efforts of legacy media outlets to sanitise the Gaza genocide.
It triggered student protests at Columbia University that soon spread to other campuses.
Palestinian journalists became “the eyes of Gaza”, showing the world what rights organisations dubbed Israel’s “livestreamed genocide” against Palestinians.
One of them, Bisan Owda, who won an Emmy Award for her reporting on daily life and survival during the genocidal war on Gaza, is known for her resilience as a Palestinian journalist.
“Hello, my name is Bisan, and I am still alive…” became Owda’s signature greeting in her social media posts.
“I no longer have any dreams. My only dream is to survive this, to tell the story of the people who didn’t,” she said on the 27th day of the genocidal war.
She and hundreds of Palestinian journalists have done just that. In the process, they have upended a media landscape where giant organisations beholden to power have long controlled who gets to be heard and seen.
Ultimately, Israel’s genocide in Gaza has also been a war on truth. Thanks to Owda and her Palestinian colleagues, that is a war Israel has lost.

'The enemy is Gaza': Israel party leader says killing Palestinian babies 'moral'
Israeli politician Moshe Feiglin has described the killing of Palestinian infants in Gaza as a "moral" response to the 7 October attacks.
In an interview with The Jerusalem Post, the former Likud MK called for the rest of the Palestinian territory to be wiped out and for Jewish settlements to be rebuilt.
Feiglin leads the Zehut party, which has allied with Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism in the upcoming general election. He is running second on the two parties' common list behind the far-right finance minister.
"The enemy is Gaza, not Hamas", he told the English-language newspaper on Monday.
"The baby that will be born tomorrow in Gaza will do exactly the same," he said, in reference to the 7 October attacks.
Israeli forces have killed more than 20,000 children during their three-year genocidal assault on the Gaza Strip, according to the local health ministry. Tens of thousands of others have been injured.
This isn't the first time the extremist leader has called for the killing of infants. In 2025, he told Israel's Channel 14 that "every child, every baby in Gaza is an enemy" and that "not a single Gazan child will be left".
During the interview, he was asked about his previous comments.
"Because I'm Jewish and I guess I'm a little bit weak morally, I don't want to see babies killed. Morally, that's what should have been done," he said.
The interviewer asked: "Is it a Jewish point of view to wipe out all of Gaza and annex the West Bank?"
"100 percent," he replied.
Palestinians and Israeli soldiers have testified to the widespread intentional targeting of children by Israeli forces, including during the so-called ceasefire that was supposed to come into effect in October 2025.
A UN inquiry last year concluded that Israeli forces target Palestinian children using precision weapons such as quadcopters and snipers, and by bombing schools, displacement camps and residential areas.
Feiglin also expressed disappointment that the far-right Netanyahu government had not already re-established Jewish settlements in Gaza.
"We should have seen by now the Gush Katif villages built already. We should have seen now the new Israeli international airport almost finished," he said.
Feiglin has a long history of making genocidal, racist, and homophobic statements.
In 2024, he favourably quoted Adolf Hitler to justify Israel's genocidal assault on Gaza.
The British government barred him from entering the country in 2008, saying his views "would not be conducive to the public good".
Zehut is one of several far-right parties participating in the 27 October general election. Recent polls project its bloc with Religious Zionism to win between five and seven seats in the Knesset.

World Space Week highlighting ‘Revolution in Satellite Launch Vehicles’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:45:32 UTC
20:45:32 KST

World Space Week highlighting ‘Rocket Revolution’
TEHRAN – Iran is marking the 26th World Space Week, being held from October 4 to 10 under the theme “Rocket Revolution,” with a wide range of promotional, educational, and scientific programs organized across the country.
The programs, targeting students, children, and adolescents, aim to promote awareness of space science and technology and encourage younger generations to explore the field through educational and scientific activities.
Iran has been celebrating World Space Week since 2000. In 2025, the country ranked among the top 10 nations in terms of the diversity of programs held to mark the occasion, hosting a total of 234 events nationwide, IRIB reported.
This year, the week began with a ceremony on Sunday at the Ministry of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in Tehran. The ICT Minister Sattar Hashemi, the Government spokeswoman, Fatemeh Mohajerani, and other officials attended the event. During the ceremony, the event unveiled five books on space technology for children and young adults.
The week’s educational programs primarily target children and students from schools and universities to make them more interested in space science.
These programs are being implemented in cooperation with the Institute for Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults (IIDCYA), the Ministry of Education, research centers, specialized space organizations and centers, organizations utilizing space services, universities and scientific institutions, private associations and institutions, private sector companies, and knowledge-based enterprises nationwide.
The World Space Week programs include contests for students, online educational events for seventh- and eighth-grade students, and specialized meetings. Moreover, conducting 5 space observations and distributing educational materials and books in underprivileged areas in the country are among other parts of the programs.
The days of the week in Iran are named after homegrown rockets. Sunday, October 4: Safir; October 5: Simorgh; October 6: Zoljanah; October 7: Qased; October 8: Qaem; October 9: Qoqnous; and October 10: Sarir.
World Space Week is an international celebration of science and technology, and their contribution to the betterment of the human condition. The United Nations General Assembly declared in 1999 that World Space Week will be held each year from October 4-10.
The dates commemorate two events: October 4, 1957: the launch of the first human-made Earth satellite, Sputnik 1, thus opening the way for space exploration, and October 10, 1967: The signing of the Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies.
World Space Week consists of space education and outreach events held by space agencies, aerospace companies, schools, planetaria, museums, and astronomy clubs around the world in a common timeframe.
The week aims to provide unique leverage in space outreach and education, educate people around the world about the benefits that they receive from space, encourage greater use of space for sustainable economic development, demonstrate public support for space programs, excite young people about science, technology, engineering, and math, as well as foster international cooperation in space outreach and education.
The 2026 theme focuses on the rapid transformation of space launch. Once limited to a small number of government programs, access to space is now expanding through commercial launch providers, reusable rockets, university teams, startups, and new national space actors. This shift is changing who can reach space, how often launches happen, and what space is used for.

Iceland 'sits at center' of regional defense questions as threats grow: Rubio
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

20:45:06 KST

Yasin Gungor and Necva Tastan Sevinc
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Iceland occupies a pivotal strategic position across the High North that places the nation at the center of regional defense calculations as security challenges expand, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday.
"The location of this country between the United States and Europe and the High North means that it sits at the ... center of many of the questions surrounding the security and defense of our shared region," Rubio told reporters during a joint appearance with Icelandic Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir in Reykjavik, warning that “today, those threats are growing, which is why this focus on the Arctic in general and Iceland in particular is so critical.”
Rubio pointed to geopolitical friction in the polar expanse, cautioning that "potential adversaries and real competitors," along with associated commercial entities, are operating against allied interests. He argued that military deterrence offers “the best prevention of violence and the best preventer of war.”
Asked about a potential US military buildup in Iceland, Rubio said Washington "would never do anything without cooperating" with Iceland, noting "there's a willingness to do more together."
 
Undersea infrastructure and commercial ties
 
Rubio raised alarms over vulnerabilities spanning the High North, citing "irregular measures, covert measures that are happening, but also threats to undersea cables, threats to shipping lanes" as key factors driving the heightened focus on the Arctic.
On the economic front, Rubio ruled out comprehensive multilateral accords, arguing that "the era of free trade agreements for the foreseeable future is probably not going to be there" while advocating for a reciprocal bilateral trade understanding.
He highlighted Reykjavik's contributions beyond security, noting that Icelandic landscapes served as training grounds for the Apollo program and "continue to host training missions for the Artemis missions," alongside joint opportunities in geothermal energy, biotechnology, and marine sectors.
Addressing Ukraine's push for NATO integration, Rubio said that membership "is not on the table as we speak" due to required alliance consensus, adding that Washington remains focused on bringing the war to an end.
 
Defense ties with US remain ‘strong’
Iceland’s foreign minister, meanwhile, said the two countries enjoy a strong and enduring friendship.
“We are allies, we are friends, and we will continue working very closely to strengthen and deepen our good relationship,” Gunnarsdottir said.
Highlighting the countries’ 1951 bilateral defense agreement, Gunnarsdottir said they work together to safeguard the High North, North Atlantic, and Arctic.
Asked about US forces being needed elsewhere, she said Rubio had explained Washington’s reasoning during their meeting.
“I want to underline our really strong cooperation in terms of defense and security, and there is no change in that,” she added.
Talks also covered opportunities to expand investment in geothermal energy, data centers, pharmaceuticals, and infrastructure, alongside Russia’s war in Ukraine, the Middle East, and China, she further said.
 
Bilateral diplomacy and regional visits
During his trip, Rubio met Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir and toured Hofdi House, the historic site of the 1986 Reykjavik Summit between US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev.
Rubio and Frostadottir "explored new opportunities" for economic collaboration, including avenues for increasing Iceland’s electricity output, deepening technology cooperation, and increasing cooperation on pharmaceuticals, according to a statement by the US State Department.
The two also discussed Iceland’s "inaugural defense and security policy and reaffirmed the strength of the bilateral defense partnership," the statement said.
The visit follows recent bilateral friction after US President Donald Trump alarmed Icelanders by sharing an image displaying US flag colors across Greenland and Iceland. Gunnarsdottir summoned US Ambassador Billy Long to protest the post as unacceptable.
Rubio will travel to Greece and Portugal before returning to Washington on Thursday.
