U.S. Army’s newest Bradley arrives with active protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:45:00 UTC
20:45:00 KST

- The U.S. Army's 1st Cavalry Division is fielding the M2A4E1 Bradley, equipped with the Iron Fist active protection system, to its 6th Squadron, 9th Cavalry Regiment.
- The division's 2nd Battalion, 82nd Field Artillery Regiment, is also fielding the M7A4E1 Bradley Fire Support Team Vehicle with improved mobility, power and digital systems.
The U.S. Army’s 1st Cavalry Division has started fielding the M2A4E1 Bradley Fighting Vehicle, the first Bradley version fitted with an active protection system designed to destroy incoming anti-tank missiles, rockets and drones before they hit the vehicle.
The division said in a social media post that its 6th Squadron, 9th Cavalry Regiment, is receiving the new infantry fighting vehicles. The M2A4E1 carries Elbit Systems’ Iron Fist active protection system, along with more electrical power generation and an upgraded digital architecture. The division did not say how many vehicles the squadron is receiving or when fielding will be complete.
A second unit, the 2nd Battalion, 82nd Field Artillery Regiment, is fielding the M7A4E1 Bradley Fire Support Team Vehicle. That version carries the forward observers who find targets and call in artillery and air strikes. The division said the M7A4E1 brings improved mobility, power and digital systems to those teams. The post did not mention an active protection system on the M7A4E1.
The 1st Cavalry Division is based at Fort Hood, Texas, and is one of the U.S. Army’s main armored formations.
Iron Fist is a hard-kill system. Radar and infrared sensors mounted around the turret detect an incoming threat, and launchers fire an interceptor that detonates close to it, knocking it off course or destroying it before impact. Elbit says the system can counter anti-tank guided missiles, rocket-propelled grenades, loitering munitions and drones, and that its interceptor uses a combustible casing to reduce fragmentation risk to nearby infantry.
Drones and anti-tank missiles have destroyed large numbers of armored vehicles in Ukraine, including Bradleys supplied by the United States. The U.S. Army has looked at adding an active protection system to the Bradley for years and tested earlier Iron Fist configurations on the vehicle before settling on the current design.
The Army first showed the M2A4E1 publicly in April 2024 at a ceremony in Saco, Maine. At the time, the Program Executive Office for Ground Combat Systems said the Army had received funding to buy an M2A4E1 for every Bradley it had sent to Ukraine. Besides Iron Fist, that version includes an improved high-definition thermal gunner’s sight and a new environmental control unit for the crew and passengers.
Elbit has since received several contracts for Bradley protection systems. A $37 million order in 2024 was followed in January 2026 by a $228 million follow-on contract to supply Iron Fist systems for Bradley upgrades under a program led by General Dynamics, as the U.S. Army moved from testing and limited fielding toward wider use across its Bradley fleet.
The Bradley is built by BAE Systems and has been in U.S. Army service since the early 1980s. The M2A4E1 is the latest step in upgrades that have kept the vehicle in service while the Army develops its successor, the XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle.

Yemen’s Houthis claim attack on Riyadh airport, deny losing territory
SANAA – Yemen’s Houthis claimed an attack on the main airport in the Saudi capital while also denying on Oct 6 losing territory to government forces, as fighting intensified.
After declaring a counter-offensive, government forces claimed on Oct 5 to have pushed the Houthis out of the Bab al-Mandab area, a key shipping route in the Red Sea, as well as the port city of Mocha, which was captured in September.
Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify with the situation on the ground moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed on Telegram that the group still held all territory recently seized, including strategic areas along the Red Sea coast.
Their fighters “have full control over all their advances on the ground”, he said.
He said the Houthis had carried out dozens of strikes in the previous few hours targeting government forces in Yemen’s Al-Jawf and Marib regions, while also attacking Taiz governorate.
On the night of Oct 5, the Houthis said they had struck Riyadh airport and a refinery belonging to Saudi state oil giant Aramco.
Loud explosions rattled the Saudi capital on the evening of Oct 5.
On Oct 6, Saudi Arabia’s civilian aviation authority said at least three people were also wounded in attacks on the Jazan and Najran airports near the Yemeni border on Oct 5.
Saudi Arabia, the main backer of the Yemeni government, has been providing air support for a counter-offensive launched by government forces.
‘Victories on several fronts’
Yemen’s government forces claimed late on Oct 5 that they had achieved “victories on several fronts”, but military sources with the government nevertheless refrained from officially confirming taking Mocha, only saying they had cut the one supply route to the area.
They also said they expelled the Houthis from several areas in Taiz in the south-west, where fighting has surged in recent days.
Yemen’s government has announced a goal of retaking all Houthi territory – home to most of the country’s population, and much of it held for more than a decade.
Yemen’s civil war flared up again in July after years of relative calm, opening a new front in the wider Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
The Houthis in September seized control of the entire western coastline of Yemen along the Red Sea in the country’s deadliest fighting in years.
Since then, they have regularly targeted oil and military installations in Saudi Arabia and have declared a maritime blockade on its ships.
Pakistan and Turkey have pledged to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia under a mutual defence pact following weeks of Houthi attacks.
The Yemen conflict has caused a humanitarian crisis.
Since the renewed fighting broke out, more than 184,000 people have been displaced from their homes, according to the United Nations.
A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting”.
He condemned “the continued Houthi cross-border attacks” on Saudi Arabia. AFP

Kenya has confirmed its first imported case of Ebola after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo died in Nairobi, Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale said on Tuesday.
The man had lived in DRC for seven years and became ill about a month before returning to Kenya, according to the health ministry. He received treatment at several health facilities in DRC before travelling by road to neighbouring Uganda.
He later flew from Uganda to Kenya on a Jambojet flight carrying 23 passengers, landing at Nairobi’s Jomo Kenyatta International Airport at about 1:10 pm local time (1010 GMT) on Saturday, October 3.
The ministry said the patient underwent routine public health screening at the airport before clearing immigration. Relatives and friends then took him directly to Nairobi Hospital, where he was immediately isolated.
He subsequently tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola and died.
Over two dozen contacts identified
Health authorities have identified 28 people who had contact with the deceased, including family members and health workers, as officials work to prevent further transmission.
The man’s journey through DRC and Uganda, his commercial flight to Nairobi and subsequent contact with relatives and medical staff are now part of the government’s contact-tracing operation.
Kenya had already strengthened disease surveillance at airports and land border crossings in response to the Ebola outbreak in DRC, including measures to improve screening, laboratory capacity and preparedness at health facilities.
Ebola is transmitted through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or through contaminated materials.
Health authorities are monitoring the identified contacts for symptoms as surveillance continues following confirmation of the country’s first imported case.

‘Terrorists could enter in disguise’: Lebanon struggles to seal Syrian border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:42:01 UTC
20:42:01 KST

Human smuggling from Syria into Lebanon has returned to the headlines in Lebanese and Arab media in recent weeks, adding another major challenge for the Lebanese army as it struggles to control a long and porous border. Some of those crossing intend to remain in Lebanon, while others use the country as a transit point on their way to Europe.
The issue comes as the Lebanese military is already contending with continued tensions in southern Lebanon, efforts to expand state control there and attempts to restore a degree of stability while Hezbollah continues to reject demands that it disarm.
On September 24, Lebanon’s Al-Jadeed television aired footage showing people crossing mountainous terrain in the northern Akkar region. “Dozens of people cross the border almost every day, amid continued activity by smuggling networks and fears that the severe humanitarian and economic situation is being exploited,” the channel reported.
It was not clear exactly when the footage, which was also circulated by other Lebanese and Arab outlets, was filmed or who recorded it, but it renewed debate over the phenomenon.
A day later, the Saudi newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat reported, citing a Lebanese military source, that human smuggling from Syria had again moved high on the Beirut government’s agenda after information emerged that networks had recently resumed operations.
The source stressed, however, that the activity remained limited and was not exceptional. “What is happening falls within the framework of limited, ongoing operations through illegal crossings,” the source said. “The army is carrying out its duties in monitoring the border, but the intermingling of Lebanese and Syrian villages and the length of the border make full control extremely difficult. This is a problem many countries around the world suffer from.”
Lebanese lawmaker Jimmy Jabbour, who represents the northern Akkar region, told Asharq Al-Awsat that human smuggling between Syria and Lebanon had not stopped after the fall of the former Syrian regime and had at times even increased.
He said one reason was that legal entry into Lebanon requires special authorization from the country’s General Security agency. Jabbour said the smuggling creates a heavy economic and social burden for Lebanon and also carries security risks. Terrorist elements, he warned, could enter the country under cover, including by claiming they were simply looking for work.
On September 29, Lebanese media reported an accident involving Syrians who had been smuggled into Lebanon across the country’s northern border. A passenger bus carrying them veered off the road near the village of Ghalboun in Mount Lebanon and plunged into a ravine. According to the reports, 14 Syrian nationals were aboard. One was killed and the others were injured.
Lebanese newspaper An-Nahar reported that after Syrians cross the border, smugglers often move them along mountain roads using off-road vehicles, medium-sized buses or small trucks in an effort to bypass security checkpoints set up to stop the traffic.
An-Nahar reported on September 25 that, according to information it had obtained, smugglers charge between 150 and 200 dollars to bring one person from Syria into Lebanon. “With at least 20 people smuggled on each trip, the smuggler earns about 4,000 dollars from a single journey,” the newspaper reported.
A security source quoted by the newspaper did not deny that people were being smuggled from Syria, but pushed back against reports suggesting the crossings had become a daily mass phenomenon. “The situation is not as it has been portrayed in recent days, and it is not correct to say that this happens every day,” the source said.
The source said such smuggling had existed for many years and was a problem common to borders around the world, arguing that the scale of the issue should not be exaggerated. According to the source, Lebanese security agencies are working to stop the crossings, which often develop into maritime smuggling journeys toward Europe, though not always. In some cases, the source said, the person crossing may simply be a Lebanese citizen who left the country illegally and is seeking to return to family.
The source added that controlling the land border is an enormous challenge and can only be achieved through security cooperation between Lebanon and Syria, an effort that began several months ago but still requires further development because of the border’s length.
On September 8, the Lebanese army said the country’s navy rescued 23 people from a boat that broke down off the coast of Tripoli in northern Lebanon during an attempted smuggling voyage. The operation was carried out in cooperation with the Lebanese Air Force, Civil Defense, the Lebanese Red Cross and other civilian organizations, according to the army.
Qatar-based Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reported at the time that the incident came amid repeated attempts at irregular migration from Tripoli, one of the Lebanese areas hit hardest by the country’s economic and social crises.
Since Lebanon’s economic crisis deepened in 2020, the city has become a major departure point for migrant boats crossing the Mediterranean, the outlet reported, contributing to repeated deadly sinkings. Lebanese and Syrian migrants, it said, continue to risk their lives at sea in search of better opportunities abroad. Human smuggling is only one part of the broader challenge along the Lebanon-Syria border.
For years, authorities have also contended with attempts to move weapons, ammunition and drugs through both legal and illegal crossings, some of which have repeatedly been targeted over alleged weapons transfers to Hezbollah. The concern over people-smuggling is therefore not only economic or humanitarian. Lebanese officials also view uncontrolled movement between countries as a potential security threat.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun recently stressed the need to strengthen the army’s ability to enforce state authority. “It is essential to provide the Lebanese army with the necessary resources to expand the authority of the state, given the extensive missions it carries out outside the south, including combating terrorism and smuggling, securing the eastern and northern borders, preserving civil peace, protecting institutions and more,” he said.

Nvidia is approaching the world's first $6 trillion market capitalization
Kyiv • UNN
Nvidia shares rose 28%, bringing the company's market capitalization to nearly $5.8 trillion. The company approved a record $150 billion share buyback.
Nvidia Corp. is on the verge of becoming the first company with a market capitalization of $6 trillion. This comes as investors once again turn their attention to the AI chipmaker. UNN reports this, citing Bloomberg.
Details
The shares once again reached a record high after the company provided an optimistic revenue forecast and announced the largest share buyback in its history, taking advantage of a valuation close to multi-year lows. These two pillars — strong growth and a cheap multiple — stand out, especially given high interest rates and sluggish economic data, the publication writes.
"Nvidia is attractive from both a growth and a value perspective, and it appears to be a refuge from any harm that higher rates may inflict on the economy," said Jim Awad, senior managing director at Clearstead Advisors, which owns Nvidia shares. "All of that makes it such an attractive proposition here and a place people should continue to turn to if they have concerns," he noted.
The shares have risen 28% this year, driving a $1.2 trillion increase in Nvidia's market capitalization and bringing it close to $5.8 trillion. The company is also the largest contributor to the S&P 500 Index's 14% gain in 2026.
The move is particularly impressive given that on March 30 the shares were down 11% for the year, as investors questioned the hundreds of billions of dollars spent on artificial intelligence infrastructure. Since then, sentiment toward AI has changed, and more existential questions about the potential threats it poses to humanity are now at the center of attention. Meanwhile, inflation risks and the likelihood of the US Federal Reserve raising interest rates have made mega-cap technology companies such as Nvidia relatively safe for investors, the publication writes.
"As concerns about higher rates materialize, money starts moving into these large-cap technology stocks because they are somewhat more resilient to rising rates," said Larry Tentarelli of Blue Chip Daily, adding that the semiconductor sector has also experienced an AI-driven recovery fueled by Meta Platforms Inc.'s Muse AI agent. There is "a significant rotation into semiconductor companies, a significant rotation into mega-cap companies, and both of these factors are favorable for Nvidia."
The appeal to investors was underscored by Nvidia authorizing an additional $150 billion under its existing share-buyback program, which Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said "reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunities ahead." Before that, he called Nvidia "the world's first and only appreciating asset stock."
Wall Street generally likes buybacks because they represent payouts to shareholders and reduce the number of shares outstanding, boosting earnings per share. Nvidia's buyback is unique among major technology companies, which are largely using their funds for artificial intelligence spending, with the exception of Apple Inc., the publication writes.
The buyback "is what investors want to see" because it shows that the company is "sharing the wealth of its insanely high profits with investors," Mizuho Securities analyst Jordan Klein wrote in a September 28 note to clients.
Although there is an argument that share buybacks are merely a way for companies to inflate their earnings per share without organic growth, that is unlikely to apply to Nvidia. In its previous report, the chipmaker forecast that sales would grow by 70% in fiscal 2028, significantly above the expected 45% growth, the publication notes.
"The reason the company is able to make this enormous buyback is that it is growing so quickly that it has more money than it knows what to do with," said Awad of Clearstead. "It remains at the forefront of the artificial intelligence revolution, which shows no signs of slowing, and the demand it is seeing appears insensitive to rising rates, adding confidence in its resilience."
Nvidia's net income is expected to double in fiscal 2027, which ends in January, while revenue is projected to rise 90%. A year earlier, both figures increased by 65%.
But even taking all this into account, Nvidia is still trailing the broader semiconductor sector this year. The Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index has risen 86% in 2026, driven by companies such as Micron Technology Inc., Marvell Technology Inc. and Intel Corp., whose share prices have climbed more than 200%, even though they are trading below the record highs reached earlier this year.

Fourth meeting of the informal working group on European competitiveness
6 Ottobre 2026
In view of the European Council meeting to be held on 15 and 16 October, President of the Council of Ministers Giorgia Meloni, German Federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever today hosted another video conference meeting of the Heads of State and Government of the informal working group on European competitiveness.
In addition to Italy, Germany and Belgium, the video conference was attended by the European Commission, Austria, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia and Sweden.
The discussion focused on three issues: energy costs, simplification of EU rules and international trade relations.
President Meloni stressed that the next European Council meeting needs to provide clear and concrete policy guidelines, with particular regard to reducing energy costs and safeguarding the competitiveness of European industry. In this context, she highlighted the joint initiative with the Czech Prime Minister, Andrej Babiš, which sets out proposals to reduce costs linked to the ETS, support the most exposed industrial sectors, limit the impact of CO2 costs on electricity prices and further postpone the entry into force of ETS2. The importance of Europe’s refining capacity for energy security was also underscored.
With regard to simplification, it was highlighted that unnecessary, disproportionate or counterproductive European obligations need to be eliminated or revised, starting with the forthcoming entry into force of the EU Methane Regulation, which could make it more difficult and more expensive to turn to alternative energy suppliers.
As far as international trade relations are concerned, the discussion focused on the need to bolster Europe’s ability to compete on global markets, ensuring a more level playing field and better access to foreign markets for European companies.

Argentina will stop Falklands exploiting offshore oilfields, foreign minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:40:03 UTC
20:40:03 KST

Argentina’s foreign minister has told an audience that included the British ambassador that his government would stop the Falkland Islands from exploiting its offshore oilfields as part of a strategy to take sovereignty.
During a speech at a thinktank event in the Argentinian capital, Pablo Quirno condemned the British government for failing to open negotiations over the islands and facilitating a significant offshore oil project in its waters.
Among those in the audience was David Cairns, the UK’s ambassador to Argentina. Cairns, who was photographed listening to Quirno, left the event shortly after the foreign minister returned to his seat.
Quirno told the audience at the event organised by the Argentine Council for International Relations that his country’s president, Javier Milei, had a strategy for the “peaceful” assertion of Argentinian sovereignty.
He said: “The British government not only refuses to enter into negotiations to resolve the sovereignty dispute, but is also taking unilateral measures regarding the exploitation of natural resources in the maritime areas that are part of the controversy.
“Preventing the exploitation of our resources from consolidating the British occupation is part of a strategy to recover, through peaceful means, the full exercise of our sovereignty.”
Last month, Milei told the UN general assembly in New York that the international organisation had failed his country as he condemned the Sea Lion project, an oil development in the North Falkland Basin, as an “unlawful act”.
Argentina has accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands.
On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline stop the oil project or face arbitration and a binding decision under annex VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (UNCLOS) at the international tribunal for the law of the sea.
The UN does not officially recognise British or Argentinian sovereignty and maintains that the archipelago’s status remains a disputed matter that must be resolved through bilateral negotiations. It has repeatedly invited both governments to find a peaceful solution to the dispute that erupted into conflict in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces.
The 74-day war ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentinian military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders.
The UK government has said that the islands, known as Las Malvinas in Argentina and which are home to approximately 3,600 people, will remain a British overseas territory for as long as it is the wish of those who live there. In a referendum in 2013, on a turnout of 92%, 99.8% voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.
In a statement issued last week, the Argentinian government rejected “the manipulation of the principle of self-determination of peoples that the United Kingdom seeks to impose upon it”.
In his speech on Monday night, Quirno also warned third parties that they should not assist Falkland islanders in the exploitation of the natural resources.
A new shipping link is due to be opened between Chile and the Falkland Islands by the end of the year.
Quirno said: “Whoever contributes, directly or indirectly, to the illegitimate exploration or exploitation of resources that belong to all Argentinians will hardly be able to aspire to share in the benefits of our country’s growth.”

Russia plague quarantine following lab death: Should we be worried?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:40:00 UTC
20:40:00 KST

Russia plague quarantine following lab death: Should we be worried?
Plague is still endemic to Siberia, the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak.
Dozens of people have been quarantined in Russia’s Siberia after a laboratory worker at a plague research institute fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances.
Russian news outlet People of Baikal reported the woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube and died.
Plague is a severe, life-threatening infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Between 1346 and 1353, the bubonic plague – one of three forms of the disease – was known as the Black Death. It caused one of the most fatal pandemics in the world across Eurasia and North Africa. Some 30-60 percent of the population of Europe is believed to have died in that outbreak.
Pneumonic plague is less common than bubonic plague. It is a severe form of the infection that can spread from person to person.
What happened in the Russian lab and should we be worried?
Here’s what we know:
What happened in the Russian lab?
On Monday, Russian media reported that a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working at the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died from suspected pneumonic plague last week.
According to Russian media reports, Shipilova became ill while at work on September 30 and died two days later at a hospital in the nearby town of Shelekhov. Several media reports suggest there may have been an accident at the lab, but this has not been officially confirmed.
About 200 people who came into contact with the dead woman have since been quarantined, and parts of the hospital where she died have also been cordoned off. An aluminium plant nearby has instructed its workers to wear masks.
Anna Popova, head of Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk to meet with Governor Igor Kobzev and other officials four days ago.
In a statement quoted by the TASS news agency, Rospotrebnadzor said officials in the Irkutsk region had detected two cases of COVID and two cases of rhinoviruses among people who had been in contact with the researcher. No other cases of infectious diseases were noted.
Later on Monday, Russian authorities said they found no evidence that the woman’s illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with and said the situation was under control.
Kobzev said in a statement that the woman had died of “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, adding: “Importantly, over the past few days, no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention have been identified.”
He added that the situation was under control and that all known contacts with the dead woman had been identified, examined and placed under medical supervision.
What is plague and what are its symptoms?
The bacterium which causes plague, Yersinia pestis, is carried by small wild mammals and their fleas. In Siberia, where it is endemic, it is rare for Russians to fall ill with the plague, however. But cases occur every year in other parts of the world, notably in Africa.
According to the Centres for Disease Control (CDC) in the US, plague has been detected in people of all ages, from babies to those aged in their 90s. Half of the cases occur in people aged 12 to 45. Men and women are susceptible, although it has been slightly more common among men.
There are three main types of plague, affecting different parts of the body. These are bubonic, septicaemic and pneumonic. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), bubonic plague is the most common clinical form. Symptoms include painful swollen lymph nodes or “buboes”.
Septicaemic plague infects the blood while pneumonic plague affects the lungs.
The WHO describes septicaemic and pneumonic plague as “less common, but severe forms” of plague.
A fourth type, pharyngeal plague, is rare. It can be contracted by eating infected meat.
According to the US-based Cleveland Clinic, besides swollen lymph nodes in the case of bubonic plague, those infected with any of the forms of plague can display the following symptoms:
- Fever and chills.
- Headaches and body aches.
- Weakness and fatigue.
- Dizziness.
- Nausea.
- Vomiting and diarrhoea.
Specific symptoms for Septicaemic plague, which can occur as a complication of bubonic plague, include abdominal pain and blackness in tissues, particularly on figures, toes and the nose, according to the CDC.
Pneumonic plague, which occurs when bacteria from bubonic or septicaemic infections reach the lungs, is accompanied by shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing and sometimes bloody mucus.
Other complications can also arise from plague if it is untreated, according to the Cleveland Clinic. These include:
- Meningitis – a severe infection that causes inflammation of the lining of the brain and spinal cord.
- Tissue death and loss of limbs from gangrene.
- Respiratory failure.
- Organ failure.
Bubonic plague has a death rate of 30 to 60 percent. Pneumonic and septicaemic plague are fatal if left untreated within one to six days, the WHO says.
If identified quickly, however, all forms can be treated with antibiotics.
How does plague spread?
Plague most commonly spreads through the bites of fleas carried by rodents, but can also be transmitted from person to person.
According to the CDC in the US, people can also become infected through exposure to sick pets, especially cats.
These are the main ways the disease can be transmitted:
Flea bites
According to the CDC, people and animals can contract plague from dead rats carrying the disease, as well as being bitten by fleas that have bitten infected rats. “Dogs and cats may also bring plague-infected fleas into the home. Flea bite exposure may result in primary bubonic plague or septicemic plague,” the CDC states.
Direct contact
Humans can contract plague through contact with the tissue or body fluids of an infected animal. This form of exposure most commonly results in bubonic plague or septicaemic plague, according to the CDC.
Infectious droplets
Droplets coughed out by humans and animals infected with pneumonic plague can hang in the air and be inhaled by another person. The CDC states that this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague, and it is the only way the disease can be transmitted from person to person.
According to the CDC, the last documented case of person-to-person pneumonic plague transmission was in 1924. However, there have been more recent cases of pneumonic plague transmitted to humans by sick cats.
“Cats are particularly susceptible to plague and can be infected by eating infected rodents. Cats with plague pose a risk of transmitting infectious plague droplets to their owners or to veterinarians,” the CDC states.
Where does plague exist?
Ian Jones, professor of virology at the University of Reading, told The Associated Press news agency that “plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia.”
Worldwide, there are between 1,000 and 2,000 cases of plague every year, according to Cleveland Clinic in the US.
Plague is endemic to Siberia, which is the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak. Besides Russia, plague is also endemic in several countries, according to the WHO. Between 2019 and 2025, most new cases recorded by the WHO occurred in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar.
There have been rare cases elsewhere. In July 2025, an Arizona man who worked with cats died of pneumonic plague – the first such death since 2007.
There was a major outbreak of bubonic plague in Los Angeles in 1924-1925, after it was first recorded in the US in 1900, brought by infected rats on steamships. Bubonic plague has made up 80 percent of an average of seven cases per year in the US since then. Most of these have occurred in northern New Mexico, northern Arizona, southern Colorado, California, southern Oregon and western Nevada, according to the CDC.
Why has this incident triggered global alarm?
While authorities in Russia have stressed that postmortem tests carried out on the woman did not detect that she had plague, the incident has raised global alarm.
Several authorities have called on Russia to give more clarity about what exactly happened to the woman at the lab.
In Washington, United States President Donald Trump said he was watching the situation with concern and that the US would be willing to help, though he said he had not spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the situation.
“It’s a rough disease. You know, that’s a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They’re like an army,” Trump told reporters outside the White House.
“Even with great advancement, the germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don’t work as well any more,” he added.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that he does not believe there is cause for alarm, but that the US is watching the case closely, aware that “it could spread quickly” despite the quarantine and other public health protocols.
Should the world be worried?
On Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the public and media should follow official statements from Rospotrebnadzor, rather than “rumours or speculation”.
“It is difficult to comment with confidence given the relatively limited information currently available,” Malick Gibani, clinical associate professor in bacterial vaccinology at Imperial College London, said in a statement to the media.
“Based on reports, there appears to be a suspected index case, and contacts have been quarantined. If there is an exposure in a laboratory to a potentially dangerous pathogen, the usual procedure would be to undertake a risk assessment of who may have been exposed and the nature of their contact.”
He added: “People considered at risk can then be monitored and, where appropriate, screening, quarantine, or post-exposure prophylaxis with antibiotics may be offered. I think it’s important that we see how this pans out, and ideally, there’d be good communication between the public health authorities and the wider global health community.
“I think this emphasises the need to be aware of ongoing outbreaks of serious bacterial pathogens and highlights the need for investment in biosecurity, particularly for preventing biological risks. This could include developing medical countermeasures like better diagnostics or vaccines,” Gibani said.

Ukraine preparing to possibility of Russia's increase jet drones speed

Source: Yurii Cherevashenko, Deputy Commander of the Air Force, at a meeting of the parliamentary Temporary Commission of Inquiry (TCI); MP Oleksii Honcharenko, head of TCI, on Telegram

Test flights are already being conducted by 14 companies. Among them, six companies have achieved certain results in destroying jet drones and three companies have results that the Air Force considers promising.
Answering the question of when to expect the supply of jet drone interceptors on the required scale, Cherevashenko replied: "Not earlier than the end of November."
Background: Colonel Oleksandr Dmukhovskyi was appointed as commander of Ukraine's Close Air Defence, the branch responsible for protecting troops and critical facilities against aerial threats at short range. Yurii Cherevashenko oversees Ukraine's Close Air Defence and coordinates this area within the Air Force.

EXPLAINER - Why are French students protesting?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:38:45 UTC
20:38:45 KST

- French government promises action with initial decisions to be presented before end of October
A student-led movement in France led to the full or partial closure of up to 500 schools on Monday.
The students, aged between 15 and 18, say their schools are understaffed and classrooms are overcrowded. In some cases, the buildings are inadequately equipped.
Blockades and demonstrations have spread from the Paris suburbs to cities including Marseille, Lyon, Lille, Nantes, Montpellier, Bordeaux, Toulouse and Rennes.
Student organizations have called for another nationwide mobilization Tuesday, with university students and several education and labor unions joining the action.
 
How did the protests begin?
The movement is traced to Lycee Saint-Exupery in Creteil, southeast of Paris, where students, teachers and parents gathered outside the school on Sept. 21 to protest unfilled teaching positions and insufficient resources.
Similar complaints were already present in other schools, particularly in lower-income suburbs where teacher absences, staff turnover and aging buildings are longstanding problems.
Protests were reported at about 60 high schools in the Paris region later that week.
The Union Syndicale Lyceenne (USL), a high school student union, subsequently called for blockades nationwide on Sept. 29, coinciding with a wider public-sector protest.
Within eight days of the Creteil action, demonstrations or blockades were reported at about 410 high schools.
The number of affected institutions continued to rise, reaching more than 1,000 on Oct. 1 before falling to 735 on Oct. 2, according to government figures.
 
What are students demanding?
The movement does not have a single list of demands shared by every school, but several complaints are common.
Students want vacant teaching positions filled and absent teachers replaced more quickly.
They are also demanding smaller class sizes, additional education and support staff, safer and better-maintained buildings and less demanding daily schedules.
Some schools have reported long gaps between lessons because of timetable and staffing problems, while students say teacher absences can leave them preparing for national examinations without completing parts of the curriculum.
The movement has also taken aim at Parcoursup, France’s university admissions platform. Critics argue that the system lacks transparency, increases anxiety and disadvantages students from less affluent schools.
The USL and Union Etudiante, another student union, have broadened the campaign to include university funding, student poverty and social and racial inequalities within education.
 
Who is being affected?
France has approximately 3,700 high schools.
But the disruption has extended beyond high schools.
Around 100 middle schools were affected last Friday, largely because they were situated within the same educational complexes or near protesting high schools.
Some universities have also experienced blockades.
Closures have forced students to miss lessons or move temporarily to remote learning, a measure teachers’ unions say can deepen inequality because pupils do not have equal access to equipment or suitable study environments at home.
Education staff have also been caught in the unrest.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said 78 employees had been injured and 24 institutions had been burned or ransacked since the protests began.
 
Why has the movement grown so quickly?
Student unions transformed scattered local actions into coordinated blockade days, while videos and messages circulated rapidly through social media.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has identified online mobilization as one reason for the movement’s unexpected scale.
Support from parents and organized labor has given the campaign additional momentum.
France’s largest parents’ federation, the FCPE, said the protests reflected concerns families had raised for years.
Several labor and education unions have called on members to join Tuesday’s demonstrations or strike in solidarity.
The movement also expanded after a Friday meeting between student representatives and the education minister.
Organizers said they left without sufficiently concrete commitments and announced what they called a third stage of mobilization for Tuesday.
 
Are the protests becoming more violent?
The movement is mostly peaceful, but some violent incidents have been reported.
Authorities recorded urban violence near 158 schools last Friday.
Incidents have included fires, attempts to force entry into schools, property damage and attacks on staff and police.
Over the past week, police arrested more than 5,000 protesters.
Nunez said about 85% of those detained were minors.
The government says far-left activists and other outside groups have infiltrated and hijacked the student movement.
Student and teachers’ unions acknowledge that outsiders have been involved in violence at some locations but reject attempts to portray the entire campaign as rioting.
Police tactics have also become part of the dispute.
Amnesty International has documented allegations of excessive force against minors and called for the suspension of rubber-ball launchers during the protests.
 
How is the government responding?
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered work on five areas: replacing absent teachers, renovating buildings with regional authorities, improving timetables, making Parcoursup more transparent and ensuring student proposals receive formal responses.
The government says initial decisions, including funding and implementation schedules, will be presented before the end of October.
It is also accelerating proposed legislation intended to make those responsible for vandalism pay for the damage they cause.

Festival of Kindness: supporting children and protecting their right to education
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

Festival of Kindness: supporting children and protecting their right to education
TEHRAN – As the new academic year begins across Iran, the annual Jashn-e Atefeha, literally meaning the Festival of Kindness, is once again bringing together people, charities and public organizations in a nationwide effort to support students from underprivileged families and help ensure that financial hardship does not keep children from education.
The festival, traditionally held at the beginning of the Iranian school year, calls on citizens to contribute school supplies, clothing, educational materials, and financial assistance to children and families in need.
The initiative is mainly organized by the Imam Khomeini Relief Foundation, in cooperation with other charitable and public institutions.
Hamed Sabouri, the deputy education minister, said that the 35th edition of the festival will be held in schools for a full week this year for the first time, giving students, families and the education community more time to take part in the charitable initiative.
Sabouri added that the event is being held under the central slogan, “A Breeze of Kindness with Students’ Charitable Spirit.” Under this year’s plan, the festival will continue in schools for one week starting October 6, he noted.Bottom of Form
The primary aim of the festival is to promote equal access to education and ease the financial burden faced by low-income families. Donations collected during the event are used to provide essential school necessities for disadvantaged students, allowing them to start the academic year with the basic resources needed for their education.
The initiative dates back to the early years following the establishment of the Islamic Republic of Iran and has gradually developed into one of the country's best-known public charity events. Over the years, the festival has attracted participation from government bodies, charities, businesses, schools, volunteers and ordinary citizens.
The festival's name conveys the idea of affection, compassion and caring for others, reflecting the spirit behind the initiative. It seeks not only to provide material assistance but also to strengthen a culture of solidarity and social responsibility.
Donation drives are held in cities and towns across the country, with collection points set up at public venues and through participating organizations. In recent years, online and electronic payment channels have also made it easier for people to contribute.
The festival has thus become more than an annual charity drive. It serves as a reminder of the importance of collective responsibility in supporting children and protecting their right to education, particularly at a time when economic challenges can place additional pressure on vulnerable families.

Indonesian Special Forces Field Ukrainian-Made Vulkan Assault Rifles
Ukrainian-made Vulkan bullpup assault rifles have been spotted with personnel from Indonesia’s Air Force rapid reaction corps, providing a rare documented example of the weapon being used outside Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on October 5, photographs published by Indonesian defense outlet KERIS Reborn show members of Kopasgat, the Indonesian Air Force’s special operations and rapid reaction corps, carrying Vulkan rifles chambered in 7.62×39 mm.
The personnel were identified by their Kopasgat unit patches, while the rifles can be distinguished by their characteristic bullpup configuration, receiver design, and controls.
It remains unclear how many Vulkan rifles the Indonesian unit has received or whether they have been formally adopted. There is also no publicly available information about a serial procurement contract between Indonesia and the Ukrainian manufacturer.
Kopasgat, formally known as Korps Pasukan Gerak Cepat, is a specialized corps within the Indonesian Air Force responsible for protecting air bases and other facilities, conducting special operations, and supporting aviation missions.
The Vulkan is a Ukrainian assault rifle based on a bullpup layout, with the magazine and firing mechanism positioned behind the pistol grip. The configuration allows the weapon to retain a 415 mm barrel while keeping its overall length to approximately 712 mm.
Its operating system is derived from the Kalashnikov rifle family but was substantially redesigned for the bullpup configuration. The Vulkan is produced in 5.45×39 mm, 7.62×39 mm, and 5.56×45 mm versions and can use compatible Kalashnikov-pattern magazines.
Development began with the Malyuk project in 2005, with prototypes provided to the Security Service of Ukraine’s Alpha special operations unit for testing in 2006. The weapon underwent further development after 2014 based on requirements and combat experience provided by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence.
Ukraine’s Armed Forces formally adopted Vulkan rifles chambered in 5.45×39 mm and 7.62×39 mm in 2017. The weapon has since been documented with Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, Special Operations Forces, Air Assault Forces, and Marine Corps.

Two Commercial Vessels Struck by Drones Off Bulgaria in First Reported Attack of Its Kind
Two commercial vessels were hit by drones in Bulgaria’s Exclusive Economic Zone in the Black Sea, killing at least two people and triggering a major search and rescue operation, Novinite reported on October 6, citing Bulgarian and Romanian authorities.
The strikes occurred around 80 miles off the Bulgarian coast, east of Cape St. Atanas and the town of Byala. Reports cited by Novinite described the incident as the first known drone attack against ships within Bulgaria’s Exclusive Economic Zone.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The vessels were identified as the Togo-flagged general cargo ship ALFA WATAN and the Palau-flagged ABLE.
The ALFA WATAN sustained severe structural damage and later sank off Bulgaria’s eastern coast. Initial reports did not provide details on the condition of its crew, but Romania’s Ministry of Internal Affairs subsequently reported two deaths and the rescue of 11 people in connection with the incident, according to Novinite.
The second vessel, ABLE, caught fire after being struck, prompting all 18 crew members to evacuate the ship. They were taken aboard the Bulgarian-flagged ro-ro passenger ferry DIOSCURIA, which had been redirected to the area to assist with the rescue effort.
Some of the rescued crew members were injured and received first aid aboard the DIOSCURIA. Bulgarian rescue services are coordinating efforts to transfer those requiring further treatment to medical facilities on shore.
Romanian authorities are also involved in the operation, deploying Coast Guard vessels and a helicopter from the General Inspectorate of Aviation. The Romanian Interior Ministry said injured survivors had been transported for emergency medical care, the outlet reported.
The circumstances surrounding the strikes remain under investigation, including the origin and ownership of the drones involved.
The incident follows another deadly drone strike on civilian shipping in the Black Sea a day earlier. Two people were killed after two Russian drones struck a civilian cargo vessel near Romania’s coast.
Romania’s Interior Ministry later reported that 11 crew members were rescued after the vessel caught fire approximately 30 nautical miles south of Sfântu Gheorghe.

France Prepares First Submarine-Launched Nuclear-Capable Missile Test in Three Years
France is preparing its first submarine-launched ballistic missile test in three years, with the nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine Le Vigilant expected to fire the new M51.3 during a long-range trial over the Atlantic, according to French outlet Ouest-France on October 5.
Strategic weapons analyst Étienne Marcuz said the missile is expected to travel roughly 4,700 kilometers, or about 2,920 miles, although that distance is well below the weapon’s estimated maximum range.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The M51.3 will be launched without a nuclear warhead from waters off France’s Finistère coast, where maritime restrictions have already been imposed through October 21.
The test comes after Le Vigilant completed an extensive maintenance period that began in fall 2023 at France’s Île Longue strategic submarine base.
The overhaul included work on the vessel’s nuclear reactor, weapons systems, and other critical equipment. French ballistic missile submarines typically undergo sea trials after such major maintenance, with an M51 launch serving as one of the most important checks that the submarine’s strategic weapons complex is fully operational.
A similar test was carried out by Le Terrible in April 2023 following its own major refit. This time, however, France will be testing the newest operational version of its sea-based deterrent missile.
The M51.3 officially entered operational service in October 2025. Compared with earlier versions, the new variant is reported to offer improved range, greater accuracy, and better ability to penetrate missile defenses. It is also designed to carry France’s new TNO-2 nuclear warhead.
France conducted the first qualification launch of the M51.3 in November 2023 from a land-based test facility at Biscarrosse. That missile was also unarmed and flew toward the Atlantic Ocean.
The M51.3 is a three-stage, solid-fueled submarine-launched ballistic missile developed as the latest evolution of France’s M51 family. Paris does not disclose its exact performance, but earlier M51 versions have been estimated to reach approximately 8,000 to 10,000 kilometers, or roughly 5,000 to 6,200 miles, at speeds of up to Mach 25.
Previous M51.1 and M51.2 missiles could carry multiple thermonuclear warheads with individual yields estimated at roughly 110 to 300 kilotons. The M51.3 is believed to retain broadly similar dimensions to its predecessors, measuring around 12 meters long, 2.3 meters in diameter, and weighing roughly 52 metric tons.
The missile is also expected to become the primary strategic weapon of France’s future SNLE 3G ballistic missile submarines, which are scheduled to begin replacing the current Le Triomphant-class fleet after 2035. ArianeGroup develops and manufactures the M51 family.
Earlier, France’s Air and Space Force has rehearsed one of the country’s most consequential military missions: breaking through hostile defenses and delivering a nuclear-armed missile to a precise launch point using Rafale fighters.

Ukraine Quietly Fields Turkish Korkut Air Defense Guns Against Russian Drones
Ukraine is already operating Turkish-made Korkut gun-based air defense systems against Russian drones following a previously undisclosed delivery from Türkiye.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 5, citing Middle East Eye, a small number of the systems have entered Ukrainian service and are already successfully intercepting Russian drones. The delivery had not previously been publicly announced by either Ukraine or Türkiye.
An unnamed Ukrainian official told Middle East Eye that operators initially encountered some difficulties with the systems, but the issues were resolved through relatively minor adjustments. The official also said the Korkut’s price was considered appropriate for its capabilities and that Ukraine was interested in acquiring additional systems.
The exact Korkut variant delivered to Ukraine has not been officially disclosed. However, Middle East Eye’s reporting cited the use of 25 mm programmable ammunition against FPV drones, including fiber-optic-controlled UAVs—a detail that Defense Express said could point to the Korkut 100/25 SB.
Developed by Turkish defense company Aselsan, the Korkut 100/25 SB is a short-range air defense system built around a 25 mm automatic cannon. It can fire ATOM programmable airburst ammunition, which detonates near an aerial target rather than requiring a direct hit.
According to Defense Express, the Korkut 100/25 SB has an effective range exceeding one kilometer and a rate of fire of up to 600 rounds per minute. Its targeting suite includes an active electronically scanned array radar, thermal imaging cameras, a laser rangefinder, and AI-based algorithms for target detection and engagement.
The combat module can be integrated onto different vehicle platforms, including 4×4 armored vehicles such as the Ejder Yalçın.
Defense Express, citing Middle East Eye, reported that a Korkut system supplied to Ukraine consists of three gun vehicles and a command-and-control vehicle. It remains unclear, however, whether that configuration corresponds specifically to the Korkut 100/25 SB or another member of the Korkut family.
Aselsan also produces Korkut variants armed with 35 mm cannons, which offer an engagement range of up to approximately four kilometers and are designed to counter drones and other low-flying aerial threats, including cruise missiles.
Ukraine has previously selected 35 mm Korkut systems for its Ada-class corvettes, including the Hetman Ivan Mazepa and Hetman Ivan Vyhovskyi.
Neither Ukraine nor Türkiye has publicly confirmed the number of land-based Korkut systems delivered or identified the exact variant currently operating in Ukraine.
Earlier, Ukraine publicly revealed its Rheinmetall Skyranger 35 air defense system for the first time, with footage suggesting the German-built 35 mm gun system may have been operating in the country for months before its presence was officially acknowledged.

Ukrainian Drone Attack Hits Oil Facility Supplying Moscow’s Major Airports
A major oil storage facility in Russia’s Moscow region caught fire following a large-scale Ukrainian drone attack overnight on October 6, Russian outlet Astra reported, citing its OSINT analysis of footage from the area.
According to Astra, the Moscow region came under drone attacks for several hours overnight. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed that 650 drones were flying toward the region between 8:30 p.m. on October 5 and 5 a.m. on October 6, with most allegedly intercepted by Russian air defenses at longer ranges.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Sobyanin said 105 drones were destroyed while approaching Moscow but did not report any damage or casualties.
Analyzing footage published by the Supernova+ channel, an Astra OSINT analyst geolocated one of the fires to the village of Konstantinovo in the Ramensky district of the Moscow region. The footage itself was recorded from the nearby settlement of Volodarskogo.
According to the analysis, the source of the fire was located on the grounds of the Volodarskaya Linear Production and Dispatch Station (LPDS Volodarskaya). Astra noted that no previous attacks on the facility had been reported.
LPDS Volodarskaya is described as the largest oil storage facility in the Moscow region and is part of Transnefteprodukt. The facility can separately store and transport gasoline, aviation fuel, and diesel through pipelines, with an annual turnover of approximately 3 million tons of petroleum products.
The station receives supplies from the Moscow and Ryazan oil refineries. Its pipeline network also directly connects the facility with Moscow’s major airports, including Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Sheremetyevo.
The Volodarskaya fire follows a series of Ukrainian long-range strikes on Russia’s oil infrastructure. Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said on October 4 that such operations had put 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity out of operation.
According to Khmara, recent operations have targeted a number of Russian oil refineries and related facilities, including KINEF, Ust-Luga, Moscow, Yaroslavl, Perm, Ilsky, Saratov, and Syzran.

Russia Finally Unveils Its New Pantsir-S1M—Ukraine Had Already Blown One Up Before the Premiere
Russia has officially unveiled a new version of its Pantsir-S1M air defense system mounted on a Belarusian-made MZKT chassis—but Ukraine had already encountered and struck one near temporarily occupied Mariupol months before its public premiere.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 6, Russia displayed the Pantsir-S1M configuration during the Center-2026 military exercises, marking the first official public demonstration of the system in this form.
The unveiling comes more than seven months after Ukrainian drone operators targeted what appeared to be the same rare Pantsir configuration near the Azovstal steel plant in temporarily occupied Mariupol.
In late February 2026, operators from the 413th Raid Regiment of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces struck the air defense system, which stood out because it was mounted on an MZKT chassis rather than the KamAZ platform commonly used for Russian Pantsir systems.
Defense Express now identifies the vehicle targeted near Mariupol as one of the MZKT-based Pantsir systems and reports that Russia has already lost one of the systems before officially presenting the configuration.
The new version uses the Belarusian MZKT-7930 wheeled chassis produced by the Minsk Wheel Tractor Plant. Russia has experimented with Pantsir systems on MZKT platforms before, including a prototype demonstrated at the MAKS-2009 aerospace exhibition.
The number of the new systems may remain limited. Defense Express cited a Belarusian opposition investigation published in April 2026 that claimed Russia ordered 18 MZKT-7930-312 chassis from Belarus in 2024 specifically for use with Pantsir air defense systems.
If the reported chassis order corresponds to the current production batch, the fleet could consist of around 18 vehicles. Defense Express noted that the MZKT-based configuration has been publicly observed only twice in 2026—the system targeted near Mariupol and the vehicle subsequently displayed during Center-2026.
The switch to the Belarusian chassis may also address shortcomings associated with the KamAZ platform traditionally used for Pantsir systems, particularly its stability and cross-country mobility.
The Pantsir family combines surface-to-air missiles and automatic cannons for short-range air defense against aircraft, missiles, and drones. The Center-2026 appearance provides the first official look at the MZKT-based Pantsir-S1M—after the configuration had already appeared within range of Ukrainian forces.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces destroyed Russia’s new Sarma 300 mm multiple launch rocket system for the first time during a mechanized assault in the Donetsk region. The HIMARS-like system, first displayed by Russia in 2025, was struck by a Ukrainian attack drone.

Ukraine Offers Interceptor Drones and Air Defense Technology to JEF
Ukraine is ready to deepen its defense partnership with the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) by sharing combat-tested drone, counter-drone, and battlefield data-integration technologies, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported on October 3.
Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara outlined the proposal in an address to participants at a JEF meeting, emphasizing that Ukraine’s wartime experience directly overlaps with the force’s security priorities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine had previously become the first non-member state to receive Enhanced Partnership status with the JEF, opening the way for joint exercises, defense-industry cooperation, and deeper coordination on drones, air defense, and hybrid threats.
“Ukraine is ready to build a mutually beneficial partnership with you. We need it. So does the security of our region. And of the entire continent. Our shared future lies in this partnership,” Khmara stated.
The JEF’s mandate includes countering UAVs and hybrid threats in the Baltic and North Atlantic regions, protecting undersea infrastructure, and responding to Russia’s shadow fleet of sanctioned oil tankers.
“We see how Russia uses drones for reconnaissance, sabotage and strikes on infrastructure. And we have already built solutions that work in real combat,” Khmara noted.
Ukraine highlighted several capabilities it is prepared to bring into deeper cooperation with JEF members, including mass-produced low-cost interceptor drones, detection systems, and platforms that combine data from multiple sources into a single real-time air picture.
The Defense Ministry stated that these technologies could be used to protect the Baltic Sea and critical undersea infrastructure from threats already faced by JEF countries.
Kyiv also proposed expanding cooperation through existing programs, including Drone Deal agreements for exporting Ukrainian drone technology, Train with Ukraine, and Build with Ukraine, which supports joint production of drones and counter-drone systems.
The JEF was established in 2015 at the initiative of the United Kingdom and includes Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, and Sweden.
EU-Ukraine defense cooperation is also expanding through new joint projects. The European Commission recently outlined plans to direct about $22.2 billion in unallocated SAFE program funding toward ventures involving EU member states and Ukraine, including projects built around Ukrainian defense innovation.

Russia is out to break Ukraine’s economy this winter, Jetten says—and the Netherlands will help keep Ukraine’s drone-hunting F-16s in the air
Unknown

20:37:25 KST

The Netherlands will help Ukraine with maintenance, spare parts, and ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten promised in a statement on 5 October. He made this and other statements following a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Russia attacks Ukrainian cities with drones every day, increasingly with jet-powered ones. F-16 fighter jets are one of the effective options for shooting down these UAVs, but Ukraine has far too few of them. The F-16s are used very frequently and therefore require maintenance. About half of the aircraft spend extended periods abroad undergoing repairs and maintenance, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times this month. The process of returning the aircraft has taken too long, and Ukraine has lost time when the jets were most needed to protect Ukrainian airspace, he said.
“A further strengthening of Ukraine’s air defense is literally vital,” the prime minister said.
Russia’s aggression continues to escalate, and F-16 fighter jets can help stop it
Russia is deliberately attacking civilian facilities and energy infrastructure and wants to make Ukrainian cities uninhabitable, Jetten said, adding that “we must not allow this to happen.”
One effective solution is the use of F-16 fighter jets, while Ukraine faces shortages of both these aircraft and the missiles for them.
Ukrainian F-16 pilots lack air-to-air missiles and take off with only the aircraft’s cannon during some daytime missions, the War Zone reported on 2 September. The M61A1 Vulcan 20mm rotary cannon can pose a danger to civilians on the ground, the outlet noted.
Poland promised to provide Ukraine with F-16 missiles back in September, and several partners, including Poland, have already begun the process of transferring ammunition this month. Other partners include Spain and Belgium, which Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha mentioned during a meeting with journalists, Hromadske reported on 1 October.
Ukraine critically needs this ammunition, especially as Russia prepares new strikes, Sybiha said.
“Against the backdrop of the fact that we have not yet built up the capability to repel jet-powered drones, against the backdrop of preparations for new strikes, it was critically important to help our military shoot down these drones. The most effective right now—apart from air defense systems, which are very expensive to use constantly against drones—are F-16 fighter jets,” the minister said.
Zelenskyy held talks with the president of France and the prime ministers of Poland and the Netherlands about means of protecting against Russian strikes, he said in his address on 5 October. In particular, he thanked the Dutch prime minister for his prompt response.
Whether Belgian maintenance delays are the reason for the low number of operational F-16s in Ukraine remains disputed
Fewer than 50% of the F-16s delivered to Ukraine may be operational, Defense Express reports, citing a Wall Street Journal (WSJ) editorial published on 29 September.
The Belgian company that services F-16s for Ukraine takes as long as 40 weeks to complete the work, retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery told the WSJ.
That day, Zelenskyy had already announced that Belgium would send three of its fighter jets to Ukraine this year. Ukraine will receive them under an accelerated procedure, he said.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs refutes claims that Ukrainian fighter jets have a catastrophically low operational availability rate and excessively long maintenance times.
“Contrary to these claims, our industrial sustainment partners are not only continuing to deliver overhauled aircraft, but are doing so at an increasing pace. Turnaround times are decreasing, not increasing,” Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said on 2 October.
Reports about the condition of Ukraine’s F-16s should not undermine confidence in international funding supporting F-16 maintenance or cast doubt on the need for additional F-16s from the stockpiles of partner countries, Tykhyi warned.

Belgian physicist wins Nobel for turning Antarctic ice into a telescope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:35:13 UTC
20:35:13 KST

Belgian Francis Halzen, 82, turned a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice into the world's largest neutrino detector. On Tuesday, his hunt for "ghostly messengers" from the distant universe won him the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Buried deep in the ice at the South Pole sits a detector the size of a cubic kilometre, built to catch some of the most elusive particles in the universe. On Tuesday, the man who dreamt it up won the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Belgian physicist Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics on Tuesday for pioneering work that uses Antarctic ice to capture neutrinos from the far reaches of the cosmos.
"This year's prize is about ghostly messengers from space," Ellen Moons, secretary general of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, told a news conference in Stockholm.
The jury honoured Halzen "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin".
The academy said his work had been fundamental to the observatory, which it described as "a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors," and that it had "paved the way for a new kind of astronomy".
The detector lets researchers capture neutrinos, rare subatomic particles, "from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe".
Halzen, 82, was born in Tienen, Belgium, and is a US citizen. He is a professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, where he directs the Institute for Elementary Particle Physics.
Speaking to the news conference by phone from Italy shortly after the announcement, he said, "it was a great surprise, and I obviously didn't expect it."
"But it's a great pleasure to hear about this prize," he added.
A giant eye in the ice
High-energy neutrinos form in the same violent cosmic environments as other particles. Unlike the others, though, they travel through space in a straight line and arrive intact.
"Neutrinos reach us without changing direction or losing energy. This means they can provide information that is not available in any other way," the academy said in a statement.
The catch is that they are fiendishly hard to spot. "Cosmic neutrinos with extremely high energies are very rare, so an enormous volume of ice is needed to observe an adequate number of collisions," the jury said.
Halzen first floated the idea of the observatory in 1988, and it quickly won over other researchers. Preliminary tests followed a few years later, but the detector was not completed until 2011.
He has served as principal investigator of IceCube, located at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station in Antarctica and the world's largest neutrino detector.
"For me, the main pleasure of it, besides winning the Nobel Prize, is that I hope this reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in the beginning of this project," Halzen said.
From Leuven to Antarctica
Halzen earned a master's degree in physics from KU Leuven in 1966 and a doctorate in 1969.
Since the 1970s, he has been a leading figure in cosmic ray and astroparticle physics, publishing research on cosmic ray anomalies and quark matter.
He has also sat on advisory committees including those of the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory in Canada and Germany's Max Planck Institutes.
Halzen's award is the second Nobel of the season. On Monday, the medicine prize went to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work in optogenetics, which uses light to control nerve signals.
The chemistry prize follows on Wednesday, with the literature laureate due on Thursday. The most closely watched award, the peace prize, will be announced on Friday.
US President Donald Trump lobbied hard for it last year, and Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, who won it, later gave him her Nobel medal. The committee is aware he will be watching closely again.
The economics prize closes the Nobel season on Monday 12 October.
Each Nobel comes with a diploma, a gold medal and 12 million Swedish kronor (€1.1mn), shared if a prize has more than one winner.
The laureates will receive their awards at a formal ceremony on 10 December, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev condemned drone attacks on two ships in Bulgaria’s Black Sea exclusive economic zone early on Tuesday, calling them “absolutely unacceptable” and a flagrant violation of international law.
One of the vessels, sailing under the flag of Togo, sank, while the other was hit and caught fire in the attacks, which took place at around 3 a.m., Radev said. The crew of the second ship was rescued by the Bulgarian roll-on/roll-off vessel Dioscuria, which was in the area.
“The crew of the Dioscuria saw the explosion on the first ship and headed towards the scene. They found an overturned boat and life jackets, but no members of the sunken ship’s crew,” Radev said.
The 18 rescued sailors, 11 Turkish and seven Indian nationals, were brought ashore by Border Police boats. Two, including the captain, were seriously injured and admitted to a military hospital in Varna.
One of the ships was carrying wheat and heading south, while the other was sailing north with an unknown cargo, Radev said, without specifying which vessel had sunk.
“I said long ago that unless this war is brought to an end, things will get very bad. All kinds of international laws are being violated, and civilian vessels are being attacked,” the prime minister said.
Radev also said authorities were monitoring a ship damaged near Odesa in August that remained adrift.
“We are monitoring whether it might enter our territorial waters, and if it heads towards our coast, we will act immediately. We will not allow drifting ships to pose a threat to the Bulgarian coast,” he said.
Meanwhile, the search for the crew of the sunken vessel continues. Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said a Su-25 aircraft would carry out an aerial search for survivors.

President Donald Trump said that the United States would consider the possibility of establishing a permanent military base in Lithuania, after which the Baltic state's government offered to cover the costs. Bloomberg reports, UNN writes.
Details
"We will certainly consider it," Trump told reporters in Washington on Monday, responding to a question about the possibility. "They are wonderful people. I know so many people in that country."
Several hours later, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius wrote on social media that Lithuania would "cover the costs associated with it."
U.S. troops have been stationed in Lithuania on a rotational basis since 2014, with the contingent usually numbering around 1,000 service members. This summer, its size was reduced as Washington conducted a broader review of its military presence in Europe.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said last month that two battalions were heading to Lithuania, which would restore the U.S. military presence to the level of recent years.
"If the military infrastructure of a leading NATO country is approaching our borders, then, of course, this cannot be perceived as anything other than a step toward escalating tensions," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, as quoted by Interfax. "Russia will be forced to take all necessary measures to reliably ensure its own security."
As the publication notes, a permanent military base in Lithuania would represent a significant change from the rotational-presence model that has defined the U.S. military presence in the Baltic states since NATO began strengthening its eastern flank following Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.
Trump's statement about the possibility of establishing a permanent base came against the backdrop of his remarks about "significant progress" in plans for a new U.S. Army base in neighboring Poland.

Ukraine’s Ukrposhta postal service and drone maker Athlon Avia have issued a new set of postage stamps documenting the history of the Furia, Ukraine’s first fixed-wing reconnaissance drone.

The stamps, along with an illustrated envelope and postcard, were presented at Kyiv’s War Museum ahead of Ukraine’s Defenders and Defenders’ Day and Veterans’ Day.
“Over more than 10 years, much has changed, but one thing has remained unchanged – the people who continue this work,” said Artem Vyunnyk, co-founder of Athlon Avia. He said the company wanted the Furia’s history to become part of Ukraine’s national history rather than remain only in its archives.
The Furia underwent state testing and was subsequently adopted by Ukraine’s National Guard and Armed Forces. The drone is used for aerial reconnaissance, identifying enemy positions and adjusting artillery fire.
One of the earliest combat chapters in the Furia’s history dates back to 2014, when the first reconnaissance drone was delivered to the Donbas battalion. It was used during Ukraine’s operation to liberate Popasna in the Luhansk Oblast, serving as the “eyes” of Ukrainian artillery.

The stamp designs include archival photographs from Athlon Avia showing the Furia and its operators during some of its first combat deployments.
Another stamp features Taras “Sheriff” Vynarchyk, a veteran and Athlon Avia engineer who previously commanded a unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) battery with the 15th Separate Artillery Reconnaissance Brigade “Black Forest” in 2022-23.
After being wounded and leaving military service, Vynarchyk joined Athlon Avia, where he continued working with the Furia and used his battlefield experience in the drone’s further development.
“For the museum, it is important to preserve not only individual objects, but also the context in which they appeared,” said Yurii Savchuk, director general of the National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War.
In 2026, a Furia aircraft was transferred to the War Museum for a future exhibition dedicated to modern military technologies.
The postal issue was designed by Ukrainian artist Yurii Denysenkov, who works across painting, video and installation. His work focuses on themes including memory, fear, ruins, and human experience.
Athlon Avia has been developing and manufacturing unmanned aerial systems since 2014. Its flagship A1-SM Furia system is used by Ukraine’s Defense Forces for aerial reconnaissance, artillery adjustment, and other battlefield missions.
