Former UN food agency official claims he was fired for highlighting hunger in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:31:00 UTC
20:31:00 KST

A former senior UN food agency official has alleged he was fired last week for his work highlighting hunger in Gaza, and has launched an appeal against his dismissal.
Benjamin Davis said the leadership of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) had refused to renew his contract as director of its rural transformation and gender equality division because his team had published a brief on hunger in Gaza and held a seminar on the subject last year, and because he had taken part in weekly “moment of silence” vigils on FAO grounds for those killed.
The seminar on hunger in Gaza last September triggered a complaint from the Israeli mission to the FAO, which also sent a diplomat to take pictures of staff taking part a moment of silence gathering last October, according to a FAO staff report filed at the time.
Davis, 62 and a Spanish-American dual citizen, left the FAO last week after 26 years of service. Video of the event shows FAO staff standing and applauding him as he left the Rome headquarters for the last time.
“It’s a nice feeling that I’m not alone, that other people are behind me in this,” Davis said. “I was stopped constantly in the hallways by people, even those that I didn’t know, just to shake my hand or just to thank me or just to say that they supported me or that they were upset.”
The FAO did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment on Monday, but the organisation’s director general, Qu Dongyu, appeared to refer to Davis’s dismissal in public remarks last Tuesday, in which he threatened to fire more people for what he deemed to be political activism.
“We are not going to allow you to play the game here of human rights,” said Qu, a veteran Chinese agronomist. “Of course human rights are very important, but they have a human rights agency in Geneva. If you want to take care [of human rights], go there.”
“Thats why [when] some senior members play political games here, I fire him,” he said, suggesting that Davis had violated staff regulations. “I’m a very soft person. I didn’t fire that many. I’m going to use my last year … to fire more if they’re against the law.”
Davis said he and fellow FAO staff members had been stunned by Qu’s remarks.
“Even more than the threat about firing people was just what he said about human rights. I think that really shocked people because it undermined the foundations of why we’re here basically, or why FAO is part of the United Nations and why the United Nations exists,” he said.
“We’re surely an organisation which is based on human rights, right?” Davis added, pointing to the FAO slogan: “Leave no one behind.”
The official letter informing Davis that his contract would not be renewed said that Qu was “no longer confident in your ability to discharge your obligations in the manner required of a senior international civil servant”.
The letter cited paragraphs in the official code of conduct for international civil servants regarding “honesty, truthfulness, impartiality and incorruptibility” and limits on public expression of personal views on “controversial matters”.
In his written response, Davis said that approach taken by FAO leadership was “simply wrong”.
“Silence in the face of suffering and injustice is not neutrality, it is complicity,” he wrote. “Shutting down discussion on the starvation of the Palestinian people weakens the reputation of the organisation and the legitimacy of our mandate. Being true to our mandate calls for a frank and open discussion around starvation, famine, and genocide in Palestine and elsewhere.”
Davis said that FAO leadership had previously criticised him for a briefing paper published by his team in May last year describing the level of hunger in Gaza and setting it in the context of international humanitarian law.
“The current conditions in the Gaza Strip … reflect a gross violation of the right to food and the unlawful obstruction of humanitarian assistance,” the report said. It was removed from the FAO website a few weeks later on the orders of its leadership.
Davis led a seminar on the same subject in September 2025, which led to a complaint from the Israeli mission to the FAO and other Rome-based international agencies.
Davis said he had also been criticised for taking part in moment of silence gatherings held by concerned staff in the FAO car park every Thursday, in remembrance of those in Gaza who had died of hunger. There was an altercation there on 23 October when a woman identifying herself as an Israeli diplomat appeared and took photographs of those attending.
“The person explained she was the permanent representative of Israel, and asked if we were allowed to do these events, and asked specifically who says we could not take photographs,” a report by a FAO witness on the day of the incident said.
On being told she could not take photographs, the woman complained to FAO security that she was being harassed, the report said. The Israeli embassy in Rome said it had no comment on the report.
Davis said that the Gaza briefing paper, the associated seminar, and the weekly moments of silence had all been approved by FAO management, and he had not been told at the time that they represented violations of the code of conduct. He said he had lodged a formal appeal against his dismissal.
“I filed the appeal mostly as a matter of principle, not because I’m looking for or expecting any monetary compensation or anything like that,” Davis said. “I have requested to be reinstated, and also for them to take back the accusations that they made against me.”

Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for work on ‘ghostly messengers’ from outer space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for work on ‘ghostly messengers’ from outer space
STOCKHOLM – Belgian physicist Francis Halzen on Oct 6 won the Nobel physics prize for groundbreaking work using South Pole ice to capture neutrinos originating in the distant cosmos, providing insight into the far reaches of space.
“This year’s prize is about ghostly messengers from space,” Ellen Moons, secretary-general of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, told a news conference. Halzen was honoured “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”, the jury said.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said Halzen’s work had been fundamental for the observatory – “a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors” – and has “paved the way for a new kind of astronomy”. Using the observatory, researchers can capture neutrinos – rare subatomic particles – “from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe”.
Halzen, 82, was born in Tienen, Belgium and is a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the United States, where he is a citizen. “It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn’t expect it,” he told the news conference by telephone shortly after the prize was announced. “But it’s a great pleasure to hear about this prize.”
Courageous people
The academy explained that high-energy neutrinos are created in the same environments as other particles. “However, unlike other particles, neutrinos reach us without changing direction or losing energy. This means they can provide information that is not available in any other way,” it said in a statement.
Halzen first presented his idea for the observatory in 1988 and his idea quickly gained support from other researchers. Preliminary testing was conducted just a few years later but the observatory was not completed until 2011. “Cosmic neutrinos with extremely high energies are very rare, so an enormous volume of ice is needed to observe an adequate number of collisions,” the jury explained.
“For me, the main pleasure of it, besides winning the Nobel Prize, is that I hope this reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in the beginning of this project,” Halzen said.
The award is the second Nobel of the season, after the medicine prize was awarded on Oct 5 to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel. The researchers were honoured for their pioneering work in the field of optogenetics, which involves controlling nerve signals with light.
Peace prize lobbying
In 2025, the Nobel Prize in Physics went to Briton John Clarke, Frenchman Michel Devoret and American John Martinis for putting quantum mechanics into action and enabling the development of all kinds of digital technology from cellphones to a new generation of computers.
The physics prize will be followed by the chemistry one on Oct 7. The literature laureate will be revealed on Oct 8, with some pundits suggesting the Swedish Academy could follow up 2025’s award to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a woman writer, possibly from Latin America.
The most keenly anticipated award – the peace prize – is due on Oct 9. US President Donald Trump lobbied intensively in 2025 to get it, and Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado ended up giving him her Nobel medal. The committee is aware he will be watching closely again.
The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on Oct 12.
The Nobel consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a 12 million kronor (S$1.5 million) prize sum, which is shared if there is more than one winner in a discipline. The laureates will receive their prizes at a formal ceremony on Dec 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of scientist Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will. AFP

On the barricades with wheelie bins and shopping trolleys: Paris students rage at politicians and police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:28:44 UTC
20:28:44 KST

Before dawn on Tuesday outside the Lycée Sophie-Germain in central Paris, hundreds of teenagers dragged wheelie bins, metal barriers and shopping trolleys to build a barricade outside the front door of their secondary school.
Climbing to the top of the piles of bins, pupils held banners calling for more funding and greater equality in French schools. But they were also protesting against French riot police, who have been accused by human rights groups of using disproportionate force against children in what is fast becoming the biggest youth protest movement in decades.
“Everyone hates the police,” chanted a group of 15- and 16-year-olds. At least 215 teenagers, 715 police officers and 85 teaching staff have been injured in clashes in recent days, according to the government.
“We’re teenagers with wheelie bins, and the police have heavy weapons, it’s totally mismatched,” said Livia, 17, who was studying theatre at a lycée in northern Paris and did not want her real name published. “The police are extremely violent in France. This is state violence and it’s horrible seeing police allowed to target children. It’s important to remember this is institutionalised violence, it’s planned and deliberate.”
Ten investigations into possible police brutality are under way after injuries allegedly involving the use of police weapons, including one 15-year-old who lost his hand, another who lost his eye and a boy whose jaw and teeth were shattered, leaving him, as his mother said, barely able to eat with a straw in hospital.
“The policing is catastrophic, people have been mutilated by weapons – one boy has lost an eye – it’s horrible,” said Lily, 17 (not her real name), who was studying social sciences in her final year of school and demonstrating for more funding in what she called a discriminatory education system that left poorer children behind. “My parents support me being on the barricades and at the protests. They’re worried about the policing, but they said they’d come and get me from the police station if I was arrested.”
Teenagers nearby held up cardboard signs protesting against the use of teargas and riot police. “A state that gases high school students is a weak state,” read one banner. “Gas rapists, not children,” said another sign in reference to calls for tougher laws against sexual violence. Another banner read: “Not here to riot.”
The unprecedented protest movement that began outside one school in a low-income Paris suburb has spread across the country, taking the government by surprise.
Hundreds of high schools have been barricaded and forced to close as pupils protest against teacher shortages, crumbling buildings and overcrowded classes. The justice ministry said 5,060 people had been arrested since the protests began, 87% of them being minors. More than 1,800 people had been prosecuted, including 1,483 minors, the ministry said, without specifying the crimes. It said 790 cases had been dismissed. The government said 24 schools had been burned or ransacked.
“In more than 20 years of teaching, I’ve never seen protests this big,” said one teacher at Sophie-Germain high school who planned to join the Paris demonstration on Tuesday afternoon. “The students in central Paris have shown a great sense of solidarity with those in the Paris suburbs who face much worse conditions in their schools. There’s a feeling of solidarity and generosity between teenagers that flies in the face of the notion that we live in an era of selfishness. No one knows how long this will go on for.”
Tens of thousands of students, trade unionists and parents are expected to march in support of the protests across France on Tuesday afternoon, including in Paris, Toulouse, Nice and Bordeaux, with riot police on alert.
Isabella, 16, said she had the backing of her parents, who work in film and music. “Young people have been teargassed for doing nothing but trying to express their opinion. Everybody told us that school was the great leveller, but today that is not the case at all. A teenager in the banlieue [suburbs] of Paris is never going to have the same opportunities as a student from the city centre. That’s why we’re here today.”
Lionel, 17, who was in his final year at school and hoped to study English, said: “The aim isn’t to riot or smash things up, we just want to protest peacefully.”
Teenagers also chanted songs against Marine Le Pen, the far-right, anti-immigration candidate in the 2027 presidential election, who is high in the polls as Emmanuel Macron steps down after a decade in office. Many teenagers were worried about the election. “We’re also protesting against the growth of the far right,” said Aislinn.
Justine, 17, who had been at the barricade since before dawn, said she hoped the protest would continue and grow into a “massive” movement. “For years, there has been a mental health crisis among young people in France and anger at rundown schools and the stresses of the education system. We need the government to listen to us and make radical change.”
Maya, an 18-year-old sports science student, had spent two days on a barricade at her university building in Bobigny in solidarity with school students, and joined the Paris protest march on Tuesday. She had attended high school in Drancy in Seine-Saint-Denis outside Paris, in a school she said had mould on the walls, not enough chairs for class and absent teachers who often were not replaced.
“It’s only when we spoke to other students at university who came from different types of schools in the countryside or city centres that we realised our experience was so different and that there was a real injustice to the conditions we had to learn in,” she said.
Julie, 46, a self-employed parent of two high school children from Levallois, in the west of Paris, had joined her husband to accompany her sons to the Paris march. She said: “We’re here to support our children but also to protect them from what is going on with the police and the violence we’ve seen with the police these last few days. We’ve seen our own child teargassed many times in front of his school ... It’s unbelievable.”
Students’ names have been changed.

Trump blames Ukraine for US fuel price surge (VIDEO)

Trump blames Ukraine for US fuel price surge (VIDEO)
US President Donald Trump has blamed Kiev for record-high fuel prices in the US, saying they are no longer driven by the Iran war but by Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries. He also pointed to policies pursued by Democrat-led states as a contributing factor.
In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump said: “What’s driving up gasoline is no longer the Strait of Hormuz, because record numbers of barrels are coming out now on an almost daily basis, but the word, ‘refineries,’” adding that Russian refineries “are being blown up by Ukraine.”
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian refineries and other petroleum-linked facilities in recent months, disrupting production and contributing to fuel shortages and price hikes.
Moscow responded by restricting exports of gasoline, diesel, and other petroleum products. The diesel ban is currently in effect until the end of October. Russian President Vladimir Putin acknowledged that the strikes cost around 1% of GDP, but said damaged facilities are being quickly restored and the country’s energy system has significant reserve capacity.
https://t.co/FuWlIHEEeZ
— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) October 5, 2026
This is not the first time Trump has lashed out at Kiev over the strikes. During a visit to Ireland last month, he blamed Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky directly, saying: “Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia… Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.”
Earlier, Trump said Ukrainian attacks caused Russia to lose “control of its diesel oil industry,” calling for and end to “this ridiculous and never-ending war,” as “the whole world suffers.” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also said Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy assets and refined products are contributing to a wider “energy shock.”
Despite repeated warnings about the global fallout, Zelensky vowed over the weekend to intensify strikes on Russian oil facilities. The Ukrainian Defense Ministry also claimed that its long-range attacks have disabled 51% of Russia’s refining capacity, though Moscow has not corroborated the figure.
Russia, which has retaliated by expanding strikes on Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities and severely disrupting Ukrainian logistics and Black Sea shipping, pledged on Sunday to step up its campaign.
Can Trump blame his way out of the fuel crisis?
With the midterm election just weeks away, Trump also blamed high fuel prices on the Democrats, lashing out at the “Dumocrats” for jeopardizing supplies “in Blue States, like California” through refinery closures.
California has lost around 17% of its refining capacity following the closure of two major facilities. The US Energy Information Administration warned that this could tighten supplies and increase price volatility. State officials reject claims that policy alone drove the closures, citing broader industry changes, although refiners have pointed to pressures linked to California’s regulatory environment.
Trump has also sought to play down the impact of the Iran war. The months-long disruption of the Strait of Hormuz – which once handled around 20% of global oil supplies – earlier pushed crude oil above $100 per barrel. Crude oil flows have since largely recovered through pipelines and ship-to-ship transfers, but refined oil supplies, particularly diesel, remain constrained. US diesel prices hit a record $6.52-$6.53 a gallon on September 22 and remain near historic highs, with prices in states such as California exceeding $8.21 a gallon, while regular gasoline stood at around $4.36 as of October 5.
The price surge has prompted emergency measures. In Texas, Governor Greg Abbott declared a disaster over record diesel costs, temporarily allowing truckers to use cheaper red-dyed diesel, normally reserved for agricultural and off-road equipment, and raising truck weight limits to 95,000 pounds to reduce trips and fuel use. Nine other states have since temporarily allowed dyed diesel for some on-road use.
Trump signed an executive order on Monday expanding the measure nationwide and deferring the federal fuel tax through the end of the year. However, an AP-NORC poll found that 65% of Americans blame Trump’s policies for the high prices, and 69% said the economy is worse off now than when he returned to office.
With fuel costs squeezing truckers, farmers, and consumers, the issue has become a political liability for Republicans heading into the midterms. RT’s Caleb Maupin reports on the mounting pressure – and whether voters will make Trump pay at the ballot box.

He also confirmed there are now two types: classic rotor-driven interceptor drones and fast jet-powered ones.
"And we consider both as real tools of air defense," he said.

Gallery: Estonian artist Urmas Viik brings dynamic graphic show to Viljandi
Urmas Viik's latest exhibition, "Personal Mythology," brings tribal foxes, fantastical flowers and novel visual connections in a changing format to Viljandi's Rüki Gallery.
The exhibition centers on two graphic series, "Tribalfoxes" and "Megaflowers," which merge in the gallery into a constellation of new connections and associations.
"Tribalfoxes" combines the words "tribal" and "werefoxes," blending visually pared down imagery associated with clans, tribes and gangs as the mythical werefox blurs the boundaries between the exotic and the everyday, the archaic and the urban, and the sensual and the comic.
"Megaflowers" drew its initial inspiration from 19th-century botanical engravings and fantastical medieval travel accounts, but has since transformed, fragmenting and branching out in different directions to become increasingly difficult to precisely define.
Urmas Viik is an Estonian artist, graphic artist and lecturer whose work spans printmaking, drawing, illustration, installation and digital art.
"Personal Mythology" will remain on view at Rüki Gallery through November 14.

Türkiye, Pakistan activate Mecca pact to support Saudi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:24:32 UTC
20:24:32 KST

Pakistani Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Foreign Affairs Ishaq Dar (L), Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud (C), and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan pose during a Strategic Political and Defence Committee meeting in Riyadh, on 5 October 2026 (AFP Photo)
Türkiye and Pakistan agreed on Oct. 5 to activate collective deterrence measures under a mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia and rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities to the kingdom following attacks claimed by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis.
The decision was announced after the three countries’ defense and foreign ministers held an emergency meeting in Riyadh. It marked the first time the alliance, known as the Mecca pact, has been invoked since it was signed Aug. 7.
The accord stipulates that an attack on any of the three countries will be treated as an attack on all three, echoing a central provision of NATO’s founding treaty.
Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the talks focused on ways to support Saudi Arabia’s defense as well as efforts to resolve the crisis through dialogue and peaceful means.
Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman said the committee had agreed to “activate collective deterrence measures” under the alliance in response to the attacks and those responsible for them.
He said the three countries had also reaffirmed their “solidarity and unity” in confronting attacks against Saudi Arabia and its holy sites.
A joint statement issued by Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said the three countries would “provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment” to Saudi Arabia.
The commitments will be carried out under “approved arrangements” and in accordance with each country’s laws, the statement said.
The announcements came hours after forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government launched a counteroffensive to retake territory seized by the Houthis last month.
Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, said they had retaken the Red Sea port city of Mocha and taken control of the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The Saudi-led coalition has confirmed its participation in the offensive, saying about 100 of its fighter jets were providing air support.
The Houthis, meanwhile, claimed attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an Aramco refinery in the coastal city of Rabigh. The group also claimed to have struck several other sites, including an airport, an air base and other critical facilities.
The Mecca pact emerged amid escalating regional tensions following the outbreak of war between the United States, Israel and Iran.
The defense agreement was signed in August, shortly before the Houthis launched their offensive in Yemen, which has included attacks targeting Saudi Arabia.

Expert says moving Estonia's units near border has limited strategic impact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:24:00 UTC
20:24:00 KST

Expert says moving Estonia's units near border has limited strategic impact
As Estonia strengthens its defenses, the country is shifting military units closer to the Russian border and expanding long‑range strike capability. Security expert Rainer Saks says moving units by less than 100 kilometers offers little strategic benefit, arguing that Estonia's real vulnerabilities lie in air defense and attack‑drone capacity.
Recently, the EDF's 1st Infantry Brigade moved its Jõhvi staff company and brigade headquarters from Tapa, and next year a company will relocate from Jõhvi to Narva. The shift toward the eastern border is part of preparations for active defense.
"I wouldn't call this a strategic advantage. It's more routine work. A decision was made years ago that we begin defending the country at the state border. It makes sense to move certain functions and units closer to the border," said Tarmo Kundla, commander of the 1st Infantry Brigade.
"So that in a crisis we don't have to start moving there — we're already there. If someone thinks this makes us a target, they're right. If we're sitting in our bases as targets when war breaks out, then we've done something very wrong," said Defense Minister Martin Herem.
According to Saks, relocating units may be justified in terms of military planning, but strategically the change is minor.
"No matter where we place our forces, they are vulnerable if we lack air defense. If the air‑defense issue is solved, that becomes a major achievement in defense planning. Until air defense is sufficient, placing units at specific points is less important," Saks said.
Herem says air defense is improving month by month. Additional ammunition for existing systems will arrive this year, and long‑range strike capability is being developed.
"We have HIMARS. We previously received loitering munitions — essentially winged drones similar to Russia's Lancet. We already have them in Estonia, and the unit is trained," Herem said.
Some HIMARS munitions have already arrived, though not the 300‑kilometer‑range missiles.
"Russia could previously plan operations against Estonia knowing it could mass forces right near the border, use aircraft from close range, and fire missiles from close range. If Estonia could bring that 300‑kilometer zone under fire control, it would be a major change," Saks said.
The Financial Times reported on Monday about changes in Estonia's defense planning. Saks says it is important to show foreign media that Estonia is preparing countermeasures — sending a message to both Russia and allies that Estonia's defense forces are capable.

“Test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens in any of the contacts,” the update said, according to the WHO.

Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Rubio said in the Icelandic capital of Reykjavik.

Petition to repair Kyiv's Paton Bridge falls short of votes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:21:47 EEST
20:21:47 KST

Another petition on the Kyiv City Council website calling for major repairs and restoration of the Paton Bridge has failed to gather the number of votes needed for consideration.
According to the council's petition platform, the initiative was submitted on Aug 7, and as of Oct 6 it had gathered only 1,000 of the 6,000 votes required.
"The Paton Bridge is a critically important transport artery connecting the left and right banks of Kyiv, as well as a monument of architecture and urban planning. In recent years the bridge has been in disrepair. Partial traffic restrictions and temporary measures do not stop the degradation of the metal and concrete load-bearing structures. Further delay creates a real threat to the safety of thousands of daily passengers and a risk of collapse of the city's transport system," the petition said.
The author proposed allocating the necessary funds for full restoration and major repairs, starting anti-emergency and restoration work immediately, and publishing a clear schedule of work naming those responsible and the final deadline for each stage.
First Vice President of the National Academy of Sciences Vyacheslav Bohdanov has said on Feb 25 that the technical condition of the Paton Bridge gives specialists serious concern. Scientists assess the structure's residual life as zero, and corrosion processes are becoming less and less predictable, he has said.
In early 2026, the National Committee of Ukraine on Theoretical and Applied Mechanics appealed to the government with proposals on organizing and financing major repairs of the bridge.
In March, the director general of the Ukrainian Institute of Steel Structures said repairs and reconstruction of the Paton Bridge should begin without delay.
On March 5, 2026, the Kyiv City State Administration said a meeting held at the municipal enterprise Kyivavtoshlyakhmist with representatives of the Shymanovsky Ukrainian Institute of Steel Structures concluded that the Paton Bridge can still be used, but traffic must comply with the restrictions set earlier.
The bridge was commissioned in 1953 and until 1965 was the only road crossing of the Dnipro within Kyiv. The international route E95 and several trolleybus and bus routes run across it. A main pipeline built under the bridge in 1962 supplies heat to about 200 high-rise residential buildings in the Rusanivka and Berezniaky neighborhoods, but it suffered a major breach in early March 2020.
Tram tracks were removed from the bridge in 2004, and since then current repairs have been carried out only on small sections. Specialists have repeatedly pointed to the bridge's emergency condition, and in 2017 traffic was restricted, with the first lanes closed in both directions.
In 2018 the bridge was declared unfit for operation, meaning in an emergency condition. In 2023 a commission set up to inspect bridge structures under a National Security and Defense Council decision found that anti-emergency measures were carried out only on individual piers in 2018 and 2019, and the city authorities spent UAH 15 million on them. Experts then confirmed that the bridge is in the fifth operational condition category, meaning unfit for operation. No repairs were carried out after that up to the date of the commission's inspection.

“Neither of these moves will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent. On the contrary – and to our regret – they will mark yet another significant escalation of tensions,” Peskov said.

The remarks come as the Lithuanian parliament, the Seimas, voted earlier Tuesday to advance a constitutional amendment that would remove a ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons on the country’s territory.
According to public broadcaster LRT, the amendment passed its first reading with 106 lawmakers voting in favor, while the final vote for the amendment is scheduled for Jan. 12.
The parliament conducted a vote late last month on amendment, receiving 99-13, with five abstentions, in favor of the proposal.
Peskov also commented on remarks by US President Donald Trump concerning reports of cases of pneumonic plague in Russia, saying it is always good when mutual assistance is offered.
He said Russia's public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor is providing "comprehensive information" on the situation in the country's Siberian region of Irkutsk.
Last week, Russian media outlets said Rospotrebnadzor defined the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region as stable amid reports of a person being diagnosed of a “pneumonia of unknown etiology.”
The reports said measures had been taken in connection with the case, which involved an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East. The employee has died.

Bulgarian authorities take an injured crew member to a hospital after two commercial vessels were attacked in the NATO member's Black Sea economic zone on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, Varna, in what was the first such attack on shipping in the area. (Bulgarian News Agency via AP)
Bulgarian authorities launched a major search operation on Oct. 6 for the missing crew of a ship that sank in the Black Sea after drones struck two merchant vessels, in an attack Prime Minister Rumen Radev called “absolutely unacceptable.”
The search was launched about 70 nautical miles east of the coastal town of Byala after the Togolese-flagged vessel sank, authorities said.
A Bulgarian ferry, the Dioskuria, which was in the area, witnessed the explosion and rushed to the scene, where it found overturned life rafts and life jackets but no members of the missing crew, Radev told reporters.
A Bulgarian Navy fast boat later joined the operation and rescued two crew members, one suffering from burns and the other from a head injury.
The remaining 16 crew members were rescued by border guard patrol boats.
The rescued crew comprised 11 Turkish and seven Indian nationals, according to Radev.
The second vessel, registered in Palau, was also hit by a drone and caught fire, but all of its Turkish and Indian crew members were rescued.
Some media reports said the two cargo ships were Turkish-owned, although authorities have yet to confirm the reports.
“Two merchant vessels were attacked by sea and air drones. This has been formally confirmed by the crews, and both ships were hit,” Radev said.
He described the incident as “a flagrant violation of maritime law and, more broadly, of the rules of navigation,” saying an attack within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone was “absolutely unacceptable.”
The Bulgarian government said it would convene an emergency meeting on Oct. 6 to discuss the strikes.
The incident came a day after a Turkish-owned grain ship caught fire and sank off the Romanian coast, killing one crew member and leaving another missing. Ukraine said the vessel was targeted in a Russian drone attack.
Shipping in the Black Sea has faced growing risks linked to the Russia-Ukraine war in recent months.
Türkiye’s Chamber of Maritime Commerce (IMEAK) said last month that 226 civilian and commercial vessels had been attacked in the Black Sea since the war began in February 2022, with the vast majority of the incidents occurring this year.

A History of U.S. Philosophy Via APA Presidencies (guest post)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:19:49 UTC
20:19:49 KST

With which universities have APA Presidents been affiliated?
Joshua Paschal, a recent philosophy PhD out of Indiana University Bloomington, took up that question, gathered the data, and discusses it in the guest post, below.
It’s a look at one kind of the institutional history of philosophy in the United States, one that may inform or complement our understanding of the sociology of the profession.
A History of U.S. Philosophy Via APA Presidencies
by Joshua Paschal
The presidency of the American Philosophical Association (APA) is a glimpse into the history of academic philosophy in North America. While only a partial picture, we can get some valuable insight into the history and tendencies of our discipline, as well as find some interesting outliers along the way. The dataset still has a few gaps, but any observable trends should hold regardless of those missing tokens.
Before the longer write-up with commentary below, here are some standout stats:
- Only 53 Ph.D.-granting institution’s graduates have ever served as a divisional President of the APA, with 22 only represented once.
- Harvard is dominant in terms of Ph.D.-granting institutions, accounting for 72 Presidential terms (with 1 two-termer, Blanshard), with the “2nd tier” appearing much later: Cornell (25), Columbia (24), and Princeton (23).
  - Harvard is also first for all divisions individually: 29 (Eastern), 13 (Western/Central), and 16 (Pacific).
  - This also holds post-1980, with Harvard at 26 and Princeton at a sole 2nd tier at 19.
- Yale is 7th in terms of Ph.D.-granting institutions but, barring any unfortunate data gaps, has not been represented since Benhabib in 2006-7.
- International institutions are present fairly consistently for Ph.D.-granting institutions, most notably Oxford (8) and Freiburg (5)
  - The German-speaking institutions were mostly represented before 1980, perhaps most notably with Marcuse (1968-69), the most recent Freiburg-associated President.
  - Since 1980 for Ph.D.-granting institutions: Oxford (6), Toronto (4), KU Leuven (1), and Paris (1).
- The University of Michigan is where the plurality of Presidents started their careers post-Ph.D. (13), followed closely behind by Columbia (11), Harvard (10), and a tie between Cornell (9) and UC Berkeley (9).
- APA Presidents have started their careers at 111 distinct institutions, and 65 since 1980.
- In terms of institutions while serving as President, 89 distinct institutions appear in the data
  - UC Berkeley is first (20), followed closely by Harvard (19), Chicago (17), Michigan (15), Princeton (14), and a few others.
  - The on-offs are interesting here and include CCNY, Scripps, Manitoba, Grinnell, just as some examples of APA Presidents serving from outside the typical elite.
- Only Columbia has had active faculty members who have served as Presidents of every division (something I am attempting to verify and find an explanation for).
- APA Presidents tend to end their careers at more prestigious, legacy institutions: Berkeley (20), Harvard (19), Chicago (15), Michigan (14), and a three-way tie between Columbia, UCLA, and Yale (13).
- APA Presidents have ended their careers (or are currently at) 95 distinct institutions, minimally, which is actually a greater diversity than their affiliations during their terms. (I suspect this is due to endowed chairships used to recruit “big names”).
- There is significant deviation from the patterns outlined here and the PGR’s ranking of the Ph.D. granting institutions, discussed in a comparison toward the end of this post.
Here is a table listing the presidents of the different divisions of the APA and their precursors.
The Early Period to the Post-War Period
Before 1920, there were the Western Philosophical Association and the American Philosophical Association, with inaugural Presidents Frank Thilly (Western, 1900-2) and James Edwin Creighton (American, 1901-2). Interestingly, both were Cornell faculty members, though Thilly was at the University of Missouri during his term. Interestingly, Thilly even wrote a Philosophical Review article about Creighton, evidence of ties between the two organizations.
That early period before the post-1920 divisional structure featured an interesting blend of institutional affiliations. Of their Ph.D.-granting institutions for the Western Presidents of that period: Cornell, Yale, Berkeley, Chicago, Harvard, and Columbia feature among the American institutions, as well as Berlin twice (Woodbridge and Sharp) and Freiburg (Tufts). A number of gaps persist in the data in the very early 20th century, sadly, so it is hard to extrapolate much more about trends beyond one.
Many of these early Presidents were connected through the University of Chicago, in part due to the influence of John Dewey’s move there in 1884. Of the American Presidents, so titled, a similar blend can be seen regarding Ph.D.-granting institutions: Johns Hopkins features twice through Josiah Royce and John Dewey, as well as Harvard, Berkeley, and Columbia, and once again some German institutions: this time Freiburg and Leipzig (Münsterberg).
Mary Whiton Calkins (American President, 1918-1919) is an interesting exception to the norms of that time: she was the first woman to be President of both the American Philosophical Association and American Psychological Association as a professor as Wellesley College, even after Harvard administration had blocked her from her formal Ph.D. (Harvard webpage on this, for those curious).
The modern structure of the APA divisions came about in the 1920s, with the Eastern being named from the American at-large in 1920 and the Pacific being founded in 1924. In this period, Harvard and company’s dominance is striking. 6 of the 10 Eastern Presidents in the 1920s were Harvard graduates! The other divisions’ data is currently lacking for this period, but from 1931-1950 at least 7 Pacific Presidents were also Harvard graduates.
Putting aside alma maters, there was some interesting institutional diversity in this early period.
In the Eastern Division, the Ivies are well-represented up to the 1950s: Harvard, Yale, Brown, Dartmouth, Columbia, Penn, and Princeton. Amherst, the City College of New York, Boston, Ohio State, and Swarthmore also make early appearances.
In the Western Division (Central, pre-1984), the data is spotty, but regional flagships dominate: Chicago, Michigan, Wisconsin-Madison, Iowa, Kansas, UIUC, Nebraska-Lincoln, and Minnesota all make early appearances as affiliations during the presidents’ terms.
In the Pacific, a few schools jump out from the early 20th century (since 1924) in terms of faculty affiliations. UC Berkeley dominated early on, with 10 different presidents alone before 1952. Stanford, Oregon, Nebraska, USC, Washington, and UCLA also all make early appearances. Pacific schools, however, are notably absent from the Ph.D.-granting column: most of the early Pacific Presidents were Harvard Ph.D.s, perhaps surprisingly.
Post-War to the Late 20th Century
The most interesting trends in this period grew from the impact of the Second World War and the wave of immigrants who came to the United States in this period. A handful of Presidents held Ph.D.s from German-speaking institutions in this time: Reichenbach (Pacific 1947, Erlangen), Hempel (Eastern 1961, Berlin), Feigl (Central 1962, Vienna), Bergmann (Central 1967, Vienna), and Marcuse (Pacific 1968, Freiburg). This clearly parallels the influence of both logical positivism and critical theory in this period.
Unless there’s a missing data point, this group would be the last Central European degree-holding Presidents outside of McMullin (Central 1983, KU Leuven).
Outside of this, Harvard’s dominance is striking, especially in the Eastern Division, accounting for the Ph.D. institutions of around 1 in 4 Presidents, including a four-year run from 1965 to 1969, a trend that would reemerge in the late 1990s and early 2000s. And many of those who held other Ph.D.s were faculty at Harvard during their terms, such as Rawls, Cavell, and Nozick.
In the Western/Central, the degree institutions are more mixed, but there is a clear trend of University of Michigan faculty members in this time: Stevenson (1961), Frankena (1965), Brandt (1969), Burks (1972), Curley (1990), Sklar (2000), Gibbard (2001), and Darwall (2003). The University of Wisconsin at Madison also features prominently as faculty institutions: Dretske (1984), Singer (1985, Marcus, not Peter), and Sober (1998), and has reemerged in recent years with Atherton (2012), Nadler (2013), Shafer-Landau (2020), and Brighouse (2025).
In the Pacific, there is similar preference to the prestige institutions of the East Coast regarding degree-granting institutions, with some exceptions. UCLA features thrice in 5 years alone: Fingarette (1976), Salmon (1977), and Kaplan (1980). But the Pacific Division overwhelmingly supports UC-system faculty members, accounting for around half of all Pacific Presidents since the mid-20th century.
Since 1980 and Comparison to the Philosophical Gourmet Report
What’s most surprising is how diverse the institutions of affiliation have become in recent years, both in terms of degree-granting institutions and work affiliation. It has become incredibly rare for any form of affiliation to repeat in nearby years across divisions, which readers are welcome to go view for themselves in lieu of overly long lists here. But since 1980 alone, APA Presidents have started their careers at 65 different institutions, served from 61 distinct institutions, and ended their careers or currently work at 60 unique institutions, all of which are greater diversity than their degree-granting institutions.
The most striking difference (which, while not marked directly in the data, I have estimated separately) is the gender gap. Before 1980, less than 5% of APA divisional Presidents were women—since 1980, around 1 in3, assuming my cursory assessment of the data is correct, have identified as women. Perhaps more recent comparisons would yield different results.
Outside of that, it is also interesting how different the picture this data sketches compares to another common touchstone of our discipline: the Philosophical Gourmet Report (PGR). While the PGR is controversial, it is, like the APA presidency data, a similar screenshot into the sociology of philosophical academia.
Some observations:
- Harvard (PGR #10) dominates overall appearances at 84 unique appearances in the data.
- The “Second Tier” for overall appearances in the data also capture a wide range of PGR ranks
  - Top 10 and high-appearing: Princeton (#3, 38 counted), Berkeley (#6, 35 counted), Michigan (#4, 33 counted), Yale (#4, 27 counted), UCLA (#10, 24), and Pitt (#8, 16 counted).
  - Under the top ten appearing equally high: Columbia (#21, 38 counted), Cornell (#16, 35 counted), Chicago (#16, 33 counted), Stanford (#14, 23 counted), Wisconsin-Madison (#24, 15 counted), Brown (#23, 12 counted), Minnesota (#43, 12 counted), Johns Hopkins ($16, 11 counted), Ohio State (#25, 10 counted), and UIUC (#49, 10 counted)
  - These lists together exhaust the number of schools that appear 10 or more times in the overall data with redundancies corrected for.
- Some of the top schools appear striking low in the data
  - NYU appears only 7 times and has never had a doctoral alumni serve as a divisional president: all have been faculty members (Likely a testament to their relatively recent rise to their position in the last couple of decades of the 20th Century, as Justin noted to me in preparing this post).
  - Likewise with Rutgers (PGR #2), except they appear only 5 times (But they were only founded as a unified department in 1982!)
  - USC (PGR #6) also appears only 5 times, though one alumni is counted for them in the data.
  - UT-Austin is also down here, appearing 8 times in the data (Above NYU and Rutgers)
- Only two schools fail to appear in this data that are listed in the PGR: UConn (PGR #35) and Miami (PGR #39)
  - This suggests, contrary to the internal variance, significant overlap of the underlying social environment this data tracks.
  - Major public flagships tend to appear equally low in both sets of data, such as Indiana, Colorado (Boulder), Maryland, Virginia, and Utah.
Overall, this data reflect what I take to be a common consensus: both that traditionally dominant institutions within the discipline generally remain in that elite position, yet there has been noticeable diversification over time. I will cut off my discussion of this data there. It has been an interesting project for me and I welcome comments.

Travolta’s daughter made her runway debut at Paris Fashion Week
Kyiv • UNN
John Travolta’s 26-year-old daughter walked in the Miu Miu show alongside Gigi Hadid and stars of “The Crown.” She previously made her debut in film and music.
John Travolta’s daughter, Ella Bleu, made her runway debut at Paris Fashion Week. UNN reports this, citing Page Six.
Details
The 26-year-old daughter of John Travolta and the late Kelly Preston appeared on the runway on Sunday, October 4, at Miu Miu’s spring 2027 show.
She shared the runway with "The Crown" stars Olivia Colman and Emma Corrin, "Half Man" drama star Jamie Bell, and supermodel Gigi Hadid.
Ella Bleu Travolta wore a muted green pantsuit with contrasting brown lapels and carried a dark leather bag while attending the after-party for the Miu Miu show at the Palais d’Iéna in Paris.
Sunday’s show was not Ella’s first appearance with Miu Miu this year. She chose a 1950s-style floral dress by the brand for the May New York premiere of "Propeller One-Way Night Coach," her father’s directorial debut and her first major on-screen role.
"This whole week has been a dream, as has this dress," she wrote on Instagram at the time.
The film, which 72-year-old John directed based on his 1997 children’s book of the same name, was screened in Cannes earlier that month, and the father-daughter duo toured the festival hand in hand.
During a joint appearance on the show "Today," the star of "Saturday Night Fever" discussed casting Ella as a flight attendant in the film: "I had a plan to introduce Ella to the world as an adult, in the style of Audrey Hepburn and Grace Kelly… it made a big impression, so, you know, I’m so proud of her."
The rising star made her runway debut in 2022 at Karl Lagerfeld’s "Cara Loves Karl" show during New York Fashion Week, and in April she appeared on the red carpet at the Fashion Trust US Awards ceremony.
Ella is also involved in music, releasing her debut EP "Colors of Love" in 2024. One track, "Little Bird," is an ode to her mother, Kelly Preston, who died of breast cancer in 2020 at the age of 57.
"When you lose someone, at least for me, even if there is so much love and support from other people, sometimes other people’s emotions or feelings can get in the way of your own," she told Hunger magazine while writing the song.
"You don’t always know what you’re feeling or what message you want to convey to that person, but it was really nice to express it in the form of music. I think music is one of the best forms of communication," she noted.
Preston and John also have a son, Benjamin, 15; their older son, Jett, tragically died in 2009 at the age of 16.

Russia says no plague cases detected among contacts of deceased lab worker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:19:10 UTC
20:19:10 KST

No plague cases detected in Siberia, Russia says, and locals play down scare
SHELEKHOV, Russia, Oct 6 - Russia's health watchdog said on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with a Siberian plague institute laboratory worker who died last week, and locals said their lives had barely been disrupted.
Authorities say the 28-year-old woman died on Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in a case that has prompted international concern, including from US President Donald Trump.
Rospotrebnadzor, the watchdog, said in a statement that no infectious diseases had been reported among the staff of the same plague research institute in Irkutsk over the past 10 days and that extensive testing had found no microorganisms in the deceased woman's body linked to her work.
"A comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures was immediately organised and implemented in full in accordance with public health legislation," the watchdog said.
"This included identifying the widest possible circle of individuals who had been in contact with the patient and arranging for them to be placed under medical observation in hospital with daily laboratory tests."
It said the results had revealed two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection, but that no pathogens causing other infectious diseases had been detected.
"None of the contacts showed any changes in their state of health associated with infectious disease," it added.
Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, said what she called a "dangerous diagnosis" had not been confirmed.
She added that 60% of those placed under quarantine as a precaution had already been released. Local media said around 200 people had previously been quarantined.
TRUMP'S OFFER OF HELP
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov expressed appreciation for an offer of help on Monday from Trump, although without making clear if Moscow planned to accept it.
"It's always good when mutual assistance is offered," Peskov told reporters.
Trump on Monday described the situation as a "big problem for Russia". US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday it was incumbent on Moscow to share more information.
The World Health Organization in Geneva said on Tuesday that Russia had told it there were no cases of plague in the city of Irkutsk. Reuters could not immediately establish if this meant they could rule out plague in the lab worker's case.
In the town of Shelekhov, where the lab worker is reported to have died in hospital, locals said their lives had barely been disrupted although they said some people in shops had initially worn surgical face masks as a precaution.
A resident who gave her name only as Anna said the situation was calm and that people had been prepared for restrictions to be introduced, but that life had gone on pretty much as usual.
"Everyone had face masks at home and wore them for no more than 24 hours," she told Reuters.
Denis, another resident, said news of the lab worker's death had been widely discussed in the town and that the local hospital had temporarily stopped doing diagnostic tests but had since resumed normal business. REUTERS

Transport Ministry rejected Shin Bet help in securing flights before flydubai hijacking - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:17:59 UTC
20:17:59 KST

Despite agreeing last year to take responsibility for securing foreign flights, the Transportation Ministry failed to allocate or use additional resources for the task, Army Radio reported Tuesday morning, less than a week after the flydubai attempted hijacking.
The report also claims the ministry rejected or stalled several attempts by the National Security Council (NSC), Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), and the Finance Ministry to help it carry out the task.
The ministry, headed by Transportation Minister Miri Regev, agreed to accept responsibility for the task as part of discussions held with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Security Cabinet, and defense officials in mid-2025.
Shin Bet attempts to assist waved off by Transport Ministry
As part of the discussions, it was suggested that an official from the Shin Bet would serve as the ministry's "head intelligence officer" and assist in the security analysis and assessment of both foreign and charter flights entering Israel, Army Radio reported, citing three sources familiar with the discussions.
Ministry officials opposed the suggestion, Army Radio said, citing one source who said Avri Cohen, the head of the Transportation Ministry's Security, Emergency and Cyber Division, led the opposition to the plan because he feared Shin Bet personnel would "intervene" in his department's work.
Another proposal made to the ministry involved the training of its officials on aviation security, the classification of airports around the world, aviation security assessments, airport security plans, and threat modeling by the Shin Bet. It was further proposed that the Shin Bet share operational methods, tools, and ideas with the ministry to help it fulfill its responsibility for securing foreign and charter flights.
The ministry failed to implement any of the actions suggested by the security agency.
Ministry did not use funds, positions given to secure foreign flights
The Army Radio report also noted that the Transportation Ministry received some NIS 10 million, and 10 new positions to fill within the ministry, to carry out said tasks. According to sources cited by Army Radio, the ministry has not filled a single position.
The report comes less than a week after flydubai Flight FZ1073, en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv, was the target of an attempted terror attack after its Omani co-pilot stabbed the captain and attempted to take control of the aircraft, which was carrying 166 Israeli passengers, as well as others.
The passengers and crew members subdued the co-pilot, while the wounded captain managed to open the cockpit door and allow others to intervene. The plane subsequently made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
The incident has since triggered scrutiny in Israel over who was responsible for vetting foreign pilots and securing foreign flights entering Israel. The Transportation Ministry has denied responsibility for conducting intelligence background checks on foreign crews, while information that has come to light since the incident has shown the ministry is responsible for overseeing foreign airlines' security procedures.
In a statement given to Army Radio, the Transport Ministry explained that "as part of the budget discussions, and in light of the ministry's additional responsibility for charter flights, the ministry demanded additional funding and positions in the aforementioned amount as a condition for accepting the additional responsibility.
"Unfortunately," the ministry continued, "and despite a written commitment from the Finance Ministry in the budget agreement and repeated requests from us to honor the agreements, the funding and positions have not yet been received. Therefore, the claim that the ministry received the resources about a year ago and failed to act to utilize them is incorrect."
On Sunday, Netanyahu instructed NSC Head Shmuel Ben-Ezra to appoint an overseer to conduct a thorough review of all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel.

Israel's Consul-General in New York, Ofir Akunis, invited New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday evening to view the 47-minute film documenting the October 7 massacre, which will be screened in New York to mark three years since the attack.
Akunis extended the invitation to Mamdani during a memorial ceremony held by the Israeli Consulate in the city, attended by some 1,000 people, and simultaneously sent him a formal letter.
"In less than 48 hours, on October 7, we will screen in New York City the 47-minute atrocity film produced by the IDF," Akunis said in his speech. "I invite Mr. Zohran Mamdani, the mayor, to come and watch the film. For the first time, he will be able to see what the people he supports actually did, and perhaps he will stop his relentless incitement, hatred, and blood libels against the State of Israel."
In the letter sent to Mamdani, Akunis wrote that the film documents the events of October 7, including footage recorded by Hamas terrorists themselves.
"Your words against the State of Israel are a significant factor in the rise of antisemitism in New York," he wrote. "Perhaps after watching the film, you will understand why the existence of the State of Israel as the state of the Jewish people is so important and why we will continue to defend ourselves at any cost."
Akunis hits back at international criticism of Israel
In his speech, Akunis also addressed leaders and elected officials around the world who criticized Israel during the war.
"Three years after the massacre, this is an opportunity to ask world leaders, presidents, prime ministers, elected officials and mayors who continue to criticize us: What would you do if those savage people invaded your country or your city and brutally murdered innocent civilians?"
"What would you do if a member of your family, your son, your daughter, were burned before your eyes?" he continued. "We are done listening to your empty criticism. We are not impressed by your cowardly actions, your hypocrisy and your weakness."
Akunis concluded his invitation to Mamdani with the message: "Anyone who watches the film and has a human heart will understand who the real enemy is."
Akunis, Mamdani feud over Israel
Akunis and Mamdani have clashed several times in recent months over the mayor's approach toward Israel.
After Mamdani rescinded orders issued by his predecessor, including the adoption of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism, Akunis warned that the move "places the city's Jewish communities in immediate danger."
In February, Akunis announced that he would not meet with Mamdani until the mayor recognized Israel as a Jewish state.
In May, after Mamdani decided not to participate in the city's Israel parade, Akunis called him "a true hater of the State of Israel" and said he was not welcome at the parade.
In June, after Mamdani said he could not support a state that gives preference to one religion, Akunis responded: "No one needs your recognition of Israel."

Students, teachers and parents marched in cities across France on Tuesday, and protesters blockaded hundreds of schools, in the biggest day of action in a wave of demonstrations demanding the government tackle understaffed and dilapidated classrooms.

A teenager's hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France on Monday. François-Xavier Lauch, prefect of Pas-de-Calais, declined to comment on the exact circumstances, saying some 200 to 250 protesters had been hurling objects at police.
The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord said the 15-year-old lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police dispersal grenade.
The High School Students Union said 1,800 high schools were blockaded or would close for the day. Some local education authorities have tried to move classes online. The education ministry did not immediately release numbers.
“When the answer is violence, it means democracy is no longer working," said Hugo Vetzel, a high school leaver in Strasbourg now taking classes for the entrance exams to France's top-tier universities. "There is such a gap between the elites and us.”
Prime Minister Lecornu orders ministers to tackle protesting students' demands
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students' leading demands. Those include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day and the need for longer lunch breaks.
The government would also look at repairs needed to aging school buildings, said Lecornu, who demanded ministers send in their first proposals by the end of October.
But finding spare cash will be difficult.
The protests have piled pressure on a government trying to narrow a ballooning budget deficit as investor concerns about France's growing debt, weak growth, and reluctance to rein in spending push bond yields higher. The yield on France's 10-year bonds briefly hit a 24-year high of over 5% last week.
The surge in French borrowing costs has started to spill into the broader euro area, with the sliding euro currency the latest alarm bell for policymakers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Tuesday that the European Central Bank has no need to step in.
Marine Le Pen, the far-right euro-skeptic populist leading the presidential race ahead of next spring's election, set out plans to slash public spending if elected, seeking to establish her fiscal credibility as the bond market crisis deepens.
Interior Ministry says over 6,000 people arrested since protests began, majority are minors
France's interior ministry said 6,100 people have been arrested since the protests began, the overwhelming majority of them minors. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted, including 1,483 minors, the justice ministry said, without specifying the crimes.
At least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been injured in clashes, according to Lecornu's office.
Six months before an election to replace Macron, his government and Le Pen's National Rally party have accused hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) lawmakers and mayors of stoking the protests. The LFI denies the accusation.
Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of Saint-Denis, a poor Paris suburb, said he opposed violence but stood beside the protesting students.
"I stand by being on the side of my residents, and high school students are my residents," he said.

Why we could not stop cholera in Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:16:44 UTC
20:16:44 KST

Cholera has existed for centuries. We know how to prevent and treat it. Yet in 2024 and 2025, Sudan endured the deadliest cholera outbreak recorded in its modern history.
The disease reached all 18 states for the first time, with more than 124,000 cases and 3,500 deaths, as stated by the World Health Organization.
I have spent much of my medical career working in emergencies. What haunts me about this outbreak is not simply that it happened, but that so many cases and deaths could have been prevented.
Sudan has faced at least 16 cholera outbreaks since the 1960s, including major waves in 2006, from 2016 to 2018, and in 2019. Seasonal rains and weak infrastructure exacerbated those outbreaks.
Over the past two years, war altered the pattern. Since fighting erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces in April 2023, our teams have seen cholera follow the routes of conflict and the poor living conditions in displacement sites. Cases surged in Port Sudan, Al-Gedaref, Khartoum and Kosti during the dry season, months before the rains that usually accelerate transmission.
In February 2025, a strike hit the power station supplying Kosti, in White Nile state. The city’s water treatment plant stopped working, and families had little choice but to collect water from the river and buy water carried by donkey carts. Within days of the attack, hundreds of severely ill people arrived at Kosti Teaching hospital with watery diarrhoea symptoms. By 5 March 2025, less than one month later, more than 3,000 cholera patients had been admitted and over 100 had died.
The same chain of events appeared elsewhere. In Khartoum, attacks on power stations in May cut electricity to pumps supplying safe water. Blackouts also disrupted water treatment and health facilities. Chlorine and other essential supplies were delayed or ran short. Funding gaps forced water-trucking services to stop, leaving families to choose between unsafe water and water they could not afford.
Two years on, we can now speak of what we have learned. These surges followed the rhythms of war rather than the seasons or the weather. The greatest burden fell on people with the least protection: families displaced within Sudan, often living in overcrowded camps or informal settlements without clean water, sanitation services, or healthcare close to home. In some places, outbreaks had begun within days of new arrivals.
These surges followed the rhythms of war rather than the seasons or the weather.
Dr Micaela Serafini, President of Médecins Sans Frontières in Switzerland
Cholera did not spread in a vacuum. Conflict created and deepened the conditions that allowed it to develop: damaged water and power systems, mass displacement, blocked humanitarian access, and a response lacking resources. The disease is preventable. The repeated failure to prevent it in the past reflects political choices to not protect civilians, to target and accept damage to civilian infrastructure, to block fast-track aid, and to cut funds allowing proper preparedness.
Médecins Sans Frontières was far from alone in this past response. Humanitarian organisations worked under extraordinary constraints. Where international teams could not go, Sudan's volunteer-run Emergency Response Rooms often acted first. They organised water points, alerted health authorities to new cases and kept people alive before larger responses arrived. Much of the response was carried out by the Sudanese health workers and the communities themselves.
This large outbreak was contained by March 2026, but the danger has not ended. A new outbreak was declared in West Kordofan state in June, after acute watery diarrhoea cases had appeared in May, before the rainy season was fully underway. Cases also emerged in North Kordofan state, though numbers have been decreasing. Once again, conflict, lack of clear surveillance data, and inadequate access to safe water created conditions for the disease to appear.
What did we learn? Sudanese responders, health authorities and humanitarian organisations have all worked to prepare, to some extent, for future outbreaks. What is still missing is speed: delay is paid for in lives. Two things must happen now, together.
The first is the sense of urgency, we must move at the speed this outbreak demands. My message to the donor community, to Sudan's Federal Ministry of Health, and to other humanitarian organisations is simple: timeliness matters as much as the investment itself. Surveillance must be strengthened to identify cases early.
The response cannot stay centralised; we need decentralised ways of working that strengthen surveillance on the ground and get ahead of transmission. That means investing urgently in preparedness. That includes vaccination plans and water and sanitation services. Where a life can be saved from a disease as preventable as cholera, we must do everything we can. 
The second is accountability. Parties to the conflict, and those with influence on them, must respect their obligations under international humanitarian law and the Geneva Conventions to protect civilian infrastructure, such as water and power systems, essential to people's survival. These are not optional safeguards. When a power station or water treatment plant is attacked, the consequences go far beyond the destruction of infrastructure: it is seen in the next cholera ward, filled with patients, some of whom will die.
The lesson we learned from the past cholera outbreak could not be clearer. The only real question left is whether those involved are finally willing to learn from it, through humanitarian action that funds and fast-tracks preparedness, and political will that protects civilians and infrastructure, before history repeats once more.

Drones sank two merchant ships and set a third on fire in the Black Sea economic zones of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria on 5 and 6 October, killing at least two seafarers, Romanian and Bulgarian authorities reported. Ukraine blamed Russia for the first attack. Neither Bucharest nor Sofia has said who launched the drones.
Russia has spent months striking ships bound to and from Ukrainian ports while denying responsibility or staying silent. Now merchant vessels are sinking inside NATO members' economic zones without either government naming the attacker, so Moscow pays no political price for hitting allied waters.

The Royad Mammadov, a Turkish-owned ship carrying grain from Ukraine's port of Izmail to Italy, sank on 5 October near Romania's Pescăruș offshore platform, 20 nautical miles from the Romanian coast, Digi24 reported. The Romanian Naval Authority described the incident as a fire on board. Romania's Interior Ministry said 11 crew members were rescued and two people died.
Three injured sailors aged 22 to 50 were taken to the Constanța county hospital, conscious and stable, with multiple injuries. Adrian Mihălcioiu, the leader of Romania's Free Seafarers' Union, said the ship was attacked by Russian sea and aerial drones in waters Romanians consider safe.
"It is a commercial ship, a ship that is not part of the war… people who have nothing to do with the war, it is not their war," he said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed the attack on "two Russian drones" and said the ship was in neutral waters carrying corn. Citizens of Azerbaijan and India were on board, and the captain was killed, he said. Romanian authorities have not attributed the sinking to Russia.
Two more ships hit in Bulgaria's zone
A day later, drones struck two merchant ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone east of the town of Byala, the first known attack on ships there, Maritime.bg reported. The Togo-flagged Alfa Watan, sailing from Al-Arish, Egypt, to Sulina, Romania, suffered critical hull damage and sank, Militarnyi said. The Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria found only an overturned lifeboat and life jackets at the scene, and the search for the crew continues, Euronews reported.

Two sailors with severe injuries were flown to a hospital in Varna, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said, according to AP. Sea and aerial drones hit the ships at about 3 a.m., he said, calling the attack "a blatant violation of international law and maritime law."
Radev called an emergency meeting of four ministries, the presidency, and the security services. No one from the Alfa Watan has been found, he said, warning that if the war is not ended in time, it "will continue to expand its spatial scope." The origin of the drones is still being clarified, Maritime.bg said. Several Bulgarian media outlets cited sources as saying the drones were Russian, Sofia Globe reported.
Russia's war on Black Sea shipping
Russia had already killed the captain of a Tanzanian-flagged ship in September, and days later it struck another civilian vessel, killing its captain too. Ukraine says that route carries 90% of its farm exports.
Romania has destroyed a sea drone near its Neptun Deep gas project and found Russian drones floating in its economic zone. In September, ISW linked drone crashes in Romania and Moldova to a wider Russian pattern of pressure on NATO.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas called for a moratorium on Black Sea attacks. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said Ankara was stepping up diplomacy to restore grain exports. Türkiye and the UN are organizing new Black Sea truce talks between Russia and Ukraine, Bloomberg reported, citing a diplomat. Russia earlier dismissed Kyiv's offer of a Black Sea ceasefire.

Kenya reports first-ever Ebola death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:14:00 UTC
20:14:00 KST

Kenya reports first-ever Ebola death
October 6, 2026
Kenyan health authorities announced the country's first death from Ebola on Tuesday.
Health Minister Aden Duale said a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo died after returning to Kenya via Uganda over the weekend.
It makes Kenya the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in the DRC in mid-May. Neighboring Uganda has reported 20 cases and France has lodged one.
What did the Health Ministry say about the case?
Duale told reporters the deceased patient fell ill about a month ago and had been receiving treatment in the DRC. He then traveled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before taking a flight to Nairobi on October 3.
The patient was suffering "fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites," Duale said.
The man subsequently tested positive for Ebola and died Monday night. He was expected to be buried later on Tuesday in line with public health recommendations.
The health minister said 28 people who came into contact with the patient — including relatives and health workers — had been identified and would be quarantined. Another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the flight from Uganda were also being traced, he added.
"I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease," he said.
What is the status of the outbreak?
Congolese authorities officially declared an Ebola outbreak on May 15, but experts believe the virus may have already been circulating for some time before that point.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has recorded more than 4,000 Ebola deaths out of 8,400 cases since then.
The current Ebola outbreak is the fastest-growing in history, and the WHO has warned it could also become the deadliest because poor health resources and ongoing violence in the DRC have hampered efforts to contain it.
The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare type of Ebola that has no approved vaccine or treatment.
Ebola is spread between people by direct contact with bodily fluids. It can cause fever, fatigue, and muscle pain, followed by vomiting and diarrhea. Some patients also develop internal or external bleeding.
The disease has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.

François Picard is pleased to welcome Philip Ingram, journalist and former British military intelligence officer. The events surrounding RAF Fairford are not an isolated incident, explains Ingram. It's part of a much wider security issue in which conventional military operations, intelligence activity and gray-zone tactics increasingly overlap.
The withdrawal of the U.S. B-1 bombers can plausibly be understood as a routine operational rotation: Fairford is a forward operating base, the aircraft have been deployed for several months, and both crews and equipment require respite and deeper maintenance. At the same time, however, the timing of that withdrawal, the ongoing counterterrorism investigation and the broader debate over British defence spending make it impossible to consider the episode purely in operational terms.
From his perspective, the most important point is that much of the relevant information necessarily remains outside the public domain. The arrests and subsequent releases on bail may reflect tactical decisions within a much larger intelligence and counterintelligence operation. He also sees the possibility that the activity around RAF Fairford forms part of a broader threat shared by British and American intelligence services.
More broadly, he would place this episode within the growing pattern of gray-zone activity across Britain and Europe. Russia, China, Iran and their proxies are increasingly operating below the threshold of conventional conflict, using activities that can test security arrangements, probe intelligence networks or create uncertainty without necessarily producing an immediately visible attack.

Influencer Abeeeer caught cheating after claiming Berlin Marathon personal best, dropped by sponsor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
