Russia Continues to Develop Cheap Cruise Missile Substitutes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:58:30 UTC
19:58:30 KST

An Oct. 5 report by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) says Russia is increasingly turning to cheaper, maneuverable “quasi-cruise” missiles to supplement its conventional strike capabilities, a tactic that is pressuring Ukraine’s already overstretched air defenses.
Building on the relative success of the jet-powered variants of the Iranian-designed Shahed/Geran kamikaze drones, Russia has been introducing the so-called Banderol and Dan-T weapons and is believed to be developing other variants, increasing production and testing new launch platforms.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Mass attacks combining these new weapons with ballistic and conventional cruise missiles and jet-powered drones are exacerbating Ukrainian interceptor missile shortages.
While Ukraine is developing countermeasures including faster interceptors, electronic warfare and artificial intelligence-enhanced automatic gun towers, these will, as President Volodymyr Zelensky has admitted, take time to develop and bring into service. Meanwhile, Kyiv will struggle to protect itself from the onslaught these weapons will unleash.
The Banderol
Russia’s S8000 “Banderol” (meaning a small parcel in Russian) is a jet-powered medium-size cruise missile analog manufactured by the Kronshtadt Group.
It uses the Chinese Swiwin SW800Pro-A95 turbojet engine, giving it a range of up to 500 kilometers (312 miles) at speeds up to 650 kph (400 mph) and a 150-kilogram (330-pound) warhead.
Power Cuts Return After Russian Strikes Damage Grid
The Ukrainian Air Force describes it as a “hybrid of a drone, an aerial bomb, and a missile.”
It first appeared during a strike on the Odesa region in early 2025 before taking part in 40 separate strikes between May and September this year, while Ukraine’s Main Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR) reported in July that Russia had completed testing and the weapon had entered mass production.
They have been used in attacks targeting ports, logistics hubs, terminals, food warehouses and infrastructure in Kharkiv, Odesa, Zhytomyr and Kyiv.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Kyiv’s presidential commissioner for sanctions policy, said in July that Banderols had been used in 80% of Russian strikes on the Odesa City port.
The Dan-T
Russia unveiled its Dan-T at the El-Alamein airshow in Egypt in September. It is based on the 1990s Dan-M target aircraft, which was designed to simulate US Tomahawk cruise missiles for air-defense training.
According to the ISW report, Russia’s state-owned arms conglomerate Rostec, which makes the missiles, converted Dan-M stockpiles into air-launched loitering munitions by adding 135-kilogram (300-pound) warheads. It has an all-up weight of 270 kilograms (600 pounds) and a 500-kilometer (312-mile) range.
ISW assesses that construction of Dan-Ts has not yet reached scale but is another indication of Moscow’s efforts to repurpose existing technology into strike weapons. As an example, Soviet-era RM-48U missiles – originally designed for S-400 air defense training – have been converted into ballistic missiles for ground attacks on Ukraine.
The extent of Dan-T use is unclear. While Rostec and some Russian milbloggers claim hundreds have been successfully used in strikes on Ukraine, it was not until Sept. 13 that Ukraine began to differentiate between Banderols and Dan-Ts.
Launch platforms
Banderols and Dan-T were initially designed to be air-launched from Orion drones, helicopters and tactical aircraft – which some estimates say would potentially double their range.
HUR has reported ground launches from occupied Crimea, with Ukrainian analysts suggesting Dan-T could eventually launch from ground and naval systems.
Cost versus performance
These “quasi-cruise” missiles have inferior performance to conventional missiles, but their cost allows more to be manufactured and used, while their capabilities are more than sufficient for Russia’s purposes.
Compared to the Kh-101 cruise missile’s 2,500-kilometer (1,560-mile) range, 1,000 kph (625 mph) speed, and 480-kilogram (1,050-pound) warhead, the Banderol has a 500-kilometer (312-mile) range, speed of up to 650 kph (400 mph), and a 150-kilogram (330-pound) warhead.
The cost differential is even more stark. A Ukrainian aviation expert estimates that each Banderol costs less than 10% of the approximately $2million cost of a domestically produced Kh-101 cruise missile.
Banderols present especially difficult targets when used in attacks that combine them with Geran/Shahed drones and conventional missiles. They are maneuverable and have a smaller turning radius, which complicates tracking and interception.
Russian mass production
The report claims that Russia has prioritized production of jet-powered drones and quasi-cruise missiles in order to increase its strike capability at an affordable cost.
In September, Zelensky claimed that Russia would spend $12 billion on the weapons, with Ukrainian defense analyst Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov saying that Russia not only aims to increase the numbers of Banderol, Dan-T, Dan-M and jet-powered drones, but also aims to boost speeds to 750 kph (470 mph) while improving low-altitude flight and maneuverability.
HUR estimated in August that Russia was producing about 80 Banderols a month, with Beskrestnov setting the target at 120 and Ukrainian sources estimating Dan-T production at 14,000 in 2027.
Ukrainian countermeasures
Ukrainian developers recently unveiled upgraded interceptors, such as the LITAVR+ and Sting 2.0, capable of taking on jet-powered Geran/Shaheds flying at speeds over 400 kph (250 mph).
Beskrestnov said up to five such interceptors are in development and still require testing. Ukrainian developers have also reportedly deployed unspecified Banderol countermeasures and are scaling production.
Electronic warfare could reportedly play a role, as both Banderol and Dan-T reportedly rely on satellite and inertial navigation for guidance.

Ukraine launched a record-breaking number of drones and missiles at targets across Russia over the past 24 hours on Tuesday, according to Russia’s defense ministry.
Russian air defenses claimed to have intercepted and destroyed 1,750 fixed-wing drones and 17 Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missiles, as well as two guided aerial bombs and a US-made HIMARS rocket.

The reported drone total exceeds the previous record of 1,671 Ukrainian drones claimed by Russia on Aug. 18, when attacks were reported across 15 Russian regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.
The number of Flamingo missiles reported over the 24-hour period is also unprecedented. Russia had previously claimed to intercept no more than three to six Flamingos in a single day.
The figures have not been independently verified.
Moscow among the main targets
The record-breaking barrage included repeated attacks on Moscow and the surrounding region.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 650 drones were heading toward the capital early on Oct. 6, with 105 destroyed as they approached the city. He later reported another 68 drones intercepted by air defenses.
Moscow Region Governor Andrei Vorobyov said 185 drones were destroyed across 16 municipalities.
According to Vorobyov, two people were killed and nine injured. Forty-seven private homes were damaged in several towns, while an apartment building in Lobanovo, near Domodedovo, was also hit.
Major oil facility targeted
Among the reported targets was the Volodarskaya Linear Production and Dispatch Station, a major Transneft facility and one of the Moscow region’s key fuel-storage and distribution hubs.
Power Cuts Return After Russian Strikes Damage Grid
The facility handles up to 3 million metric tons of petroleum products annually, including gasoline, jet fuel and diesel supplied from the Moscow and Ryazan refineries. Some of the fuel is delivered to airports serving the Moscow aviation hub.
The extent of any damage to the facility was not immediately clear.
The scale of the attack also disrupted air travel across Moscow. More than 200 flights were reportedly delayed or canceled at the capital’s airports from midnight.
The Sheremetyevo airport saw the largest disruption, with around 47 departures and 106 arrivals affected. The Vnukovo airport reported disruptions to 28 departing and 23 arriving flights, while four flights were affected at the Domodedovo airport.

Singapore refers eight civil servants to police over property purchases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:55:46 UTC
19:55:46 KST

Singapore refers eight civil servants to police over property purchases
Minister announces referrals after think tank paper finds link between purchases and unannounced MRT stations.
Singapore has referred eight civil servants to the police following an inquiry into the suspected use of nonpublic information to buy properties near planned railway stations.
Coordinating Minister for Public Services Chan Chun Sing announced the referrals on Tuesday after a working paper by a United States-based think tank found that civil servants were disproportionately likely to buy homes near future Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) stations.
In remarks to Parliament, Chan said the government had identified eight individuals who warranted further examination following a review of property transactions by 191 civil servants.
“Let me emphasise that a referral does not mean that wrongdoing has been established,” Chan said.
“The police will look into the facts independently and due process will be followed.”
Chan said the government took the misuse of government information seriously and would act “firmly” in any cases where wrongdoing was established.
“The fundamental principle is clear,” he said.
“Public officers must never use information obtained through their official duties to advance their own private interests or those of others.”
The announcement comes after the National Bureau of Economic Research last month published research suggesting that Singaporean civil servants were 60 percent more likely to buy homes in areas where planned MRT stations had yet to be announced.
The paper, written by economists at Stanford University, Columbia University and the University of Hong Kong, found that purchases were concentrated among mid-level officials linked to public transport planning and generated “meaningful” financial gains for those involved.
Singapore has long prided itself on being a leader in clean governance, proclaiming zero tolerance for corruption.
The city-state’s public sector was ranked third-cleanest in Transparency International’s annual Corruption Perceptions Index last year, trailing Denmark and Finland.
In 2024, a Singaporean court sentenced S Iswaran, a former transport minister, to 12 months in prison for obstructing justice and accepting gifts worth more than $300,000 while in office.
Iswaran’s conviction marked the first prosecution of a cabinet official in Singapore since 1975, when then-Environmental Minister Wee Toon Boon was found guilty of receiving kickbacks from a local businessman.
In 1986, Teh Cheang Wan, a minister for national development, was under investigation by the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau. He died before charges were brought against him.

Dali artwork worth millions stolen in French museum heist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:54:38 UTC
19:54:38 KST

Dali artwork worth millions stolen in French museum heist
A multimillion-euro artwork featuring a massive bronze cover designed by Salvador Dali has been stolen from a museum in central France. It is the latest in a string of high-profile thefts targeting the country’s cultural institutions.
Thieves took the artwork from the Centre of Contemporary Art in Issoire overnight to Monday. Prosecutors described it as an “exceptional and unique” work of “great value” and opened a criminal investigation.
The stolen work is Joseph Foret’s ‘Livre de l’Apocalypse’ (The Book of the Apocalypse), a monumental 210kg volume produced between 1958 and 1961 with contributions from prominent figures in 20th-century art and literature, including Dali, Jean Cocteau, Bernard Buffet, and Jean Giono.
Its roughly 150kg bronze casing, designed by Dali, is decorated with gold, precious stones, and seashells. The one-of-a-kind book has been described as among the world’s heaviest and most expensive, with its value estimated at several million euros.
The Issoire theft is the latest in a string of high-profile robberies to hit French museums. In September, thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer in southeastern France and grabbed four paintings from the walls. Two were abandoned in the museum garden as the thieves fled, while two remain missing. The four were initially valued at €9 million ($10.1 million), with the missing pair later valued at €4.2 million.
In July, three masked thieves raided the Lalique Museum in northeastern France, escaping with 27 valuable pieces worth €4.5 million in just 11 minutes. Despite the museum receiving “special attention” after the Louvre robbery, its security company reportedly failed to alert gendarmes when the alarms went off, leaving a cleaner to call police.
The wave of robberies follows a spectacular Louvre heist in October 2025, when thieves stole eight pieces of the French Crown Jewels worth around €88 million in broad daylight. Hours later, nearly 2,000 prized coins were reportedly stolen from the Denis Diderot House of Enlightenment in northeastern France. A month earlier, thieves had broken into the National Museum of Natural History in Paris and made off with 6 kg of rare gold nuggets, with the loss later estimated at around €1.5 million.
The string of thefts triggered a national scandal over museum security. A parliamentary inquiry released in May found widespread shortcomings, pointing to aging infrastructure, staff shortages and inadequate surveillance. Only 23% of French museums had an emergency and risk-prevention plan in 2024, while just 54% had video surveillance, according to the report.
Following the Louvre robbery, the Lalique Museum was designated a “sensitive site” and placed under “special attention.” Yet a source close to the investigation said the additional protection was “not sufficient.” The government unveiled a new 33-point museum-security plan in July, but did not specify how the measures would be funded.
France has also cut heritage spending while ramping up military expenditures. The country’s 2026 heritage budget was reduced by €106 million, or 8%, while the Louvre lost €5 million in funding. By contrast, the defense budget rose by €6.7 billion to €68.4 billion as the government accelerates what it calls France’s “rearmament.”

Chentsov: Adopting bill No. 15412 at this time could jeopardize opening of EU integration clusters
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:54:28 EEST
19:54:28 KST

Vsevolod Chentsov, Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration of Ukraine, urged lawmakers to pass Bill No. 15412 "On amendments to certain laws of Ukraine regarding ensuring the status of Ukrainian as the state language" at the first reading only after consultations with the European Commission and other stakeholders.
Specifically, during a committee meeting on Tuesday morning, discussing the bill on the educational rights of national minorities (No. 16119), which aims to unblock the opening of two negotiation clusters on Ukraine's EU accession by lifting Hungary's veto, Natalia Pipa (Holos faction), a member of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Education, Science, and Innovation, proposed that before the parliamentary vote on that bill, the Rada should pass Bill No. 15412 ("On amendments to сertain laws of Ukraine regarding ensuring the status of Ukrainian as the state language") at the first reading.
In turn, Roman Hryschuk (Servant of the People faction) also supported this idea: "This is the right moment—not just for the opposition, but for society as a whole—to explain why the Rada passed the bill on national minority languages and significantly expanded the use of language in the educational process. Bill No. 15412 would balance the situation. My position is that we should ultimately pass both."
"We must approach the adoption of this bill (No. 15412) in a highly responsible and measured manner. You are absolutely right that strengthening and protecting the Ukrainian language is our sovereign right. However, we are currently engaged in a negotiation process. And this is not just about the Hungarian community. We have an action plan regarding national minorities, approved by the European Commission, the Council of Europe, and the High Commissioner on National Minorities, and we need to present a comprehensive picture to our partners. This law will become part of a broader body of legislation regulating the use of both the state language and the languages of national minorities. This bill has already raised questions from the European Commission," Chentsov said at a meeting of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Education, Science, and Innovation on Tuesday.
The Deputy Prime Minister added that he understood the logic behind the MPs' proposals to pass Bill No. 15412 at the first reading, with consultations and further refinement to follow.
"If we hadn't found ourselves in the current situation regarding the adoption of the education bill (No. 16119) and the opening of accession clusters, we might have been able to do this. But the risk is very high. There could be a negative reaction from the European Commission and national minority groups, which is quite possible, and we have many opponents, primarily the Russian Federation, who are watching our every move very closely," he emphasized.
In light of this, he urged the MPs to first work through Bill No. 15412 "calmly" with the European Commission and other stakeholders, and only submit it to Parliament for a first reading after this review process.
"We could manage these risks. That is my proposal. I have already discussed this with Mr. Poturaev [Mykyta Poturaev, Head of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Humanitarian and Information Policy] and with other MPs. If we want to achieve our goal, we need to be extremely cautious right now. Because we risk both failing to pass the education bill and falling short on the state language protection law," the Deputy Prime Minister stated.
Earlier, a number of civic initiatives and organizations called upon the Rada, as well as parliamentary factions and groups, to vote for Bill No. 16119 only on the condition that Bill No. 15412 is first adopted at the first reading.
"We urge you to submit both of these bills to the upcoming plenary session and demonstrate a balanced, responsible approach to protecting and supporting both the Ukrainian state language and the languages of national minorities," the open appeal states.
As previously reported, in August, the Committee on Humanitarian and Information Policy recommended that the Verkhovna Rada adopt Bill No. 15412 "On amendments to certain laws of Ukraine regarding ensuring the status of Ukrainian as the state language" at the first reading.
In September, the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Education, Science, and Innovation also recommended that parliament adopt Bill No. 15412 at the first reading.
Specifically, the bill proposes expanding the list of individuals required to be proficient in the state language and to use it while performing their official duties. This requirement applies, among others, to Members of Parliament, heads of state scientific and cultural institutions, private enforcement officers, insolvency administrators, auditors, and other individuals.
Furthermore, the bill proposes strengthening the protection of the right to use the Ukrainian language in the workplace by guaranteeing this right at the hiring stage, rather than only after an employment relationship has been established. The document also outlines requirements for ensuring official documents comply with state language standards and aims to improve state oversight mechanisms and specific complaint-handling procedures.

Nearly 3 in 4 Estonian educators have experienced bullying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:53:00 UTC
19:53:00 KST

Nearly 3 in 4 Estonian educators have experienced bullying
A University of Tartu study found nearly 3 in 4 educators have experienced bullying at some point in life, affecting how they perceive their workplace.
Researchers at the university's Institute of Education examined whether bullying experiences affect how educators perceive psychosocial factors at their current workplaces.
"We wanted to see how experiences with bullying affect how educators perceive psychosocial factors at their current workplace," said Minni Aia-Utsal, one of the study's authors.
The study revealed that nearly three-quarters of respondents had experienced bullying at some point, either as a target or perpetrator.
The researchers used the short version of the Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire (COPSOQ-II) to assess four aspects of the work environment: predictability, role clarity, leadership quality and social support.
'Bullying doesn't happen in a vacuum'
Aia-Utsal said they focused on workplace relationships and leadership because bullying is also a social phenomenon involving relationships.
"Bullying requires social relationships; it doesn't happen in a vacuum," she explained. The study thus examined how educators who have experienced bullying perceive workplace relationships.
She added that all four dimensions relate to workplace relationships and leadership, noting that social support, for example, can be emotional or practical, or involve sharing information to help employees feel they're part of the team.
Because the study relied on a questionnaire, its findings reflect respondents' subjective perceptions of their work environment.
Educators with no bullying experience gave the highest ratings across all four areas measured. The lowest ratings, meanwhile, came from those who had been bullied both at school and at work, suggesting that such experiences can have a lasting negative effect on how educators perceive workplace relationships and leadership.
Those whose bullying experiences were limited to school, however, gave more positive ratings. Aia-Utsal said this suggests a supportive workplace can help people overcome earlier negative experiences.
Bullying prevention for students and educators
School employees can be bullied by parents, colleagues or students, Aia-Utsal said, making it important for school leaders to prevent bullying and support not just students, but also teachers and other staff. Schools should also have systems in place to help educators who have experienced bullying.
"The most important thing is that a teacher or support specialist doesn't have to face the problem on their own," the co-author said. "There needs to be support from the organization and clear systems in place."
Co-authored by Aia-Utsal and Kristi Kõiv, the study was published in the Open Journal of Social Sciences (JSS) last month.

Over 20,000 migrants entered Djibouti from Ethiopia since Sept. 10: UN migration agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:51:53 UTC
19:51:53 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
More than 20,000 migrant movements from Ethiopia into Djibouti have been recorded since Sept. 10, while thousands of migrants have been stranded along dangerous routes in the country, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Tuesday.
Alexandre Coissac, the IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, told reporters in Geneva that migrants continue to travel along the Eastern Route, which connects the Horn of Africa with Yemen and the Gulf, and is one of the "busiest and most dangerous" migration corridors.
Migrants are also returning from Yemen toward their home countries through Djibouti, with the IOM recording 539 Ethiopian returnees since Sept. 10.
Between Sept. 20 and 30, more than 3,000 stranded migrants were observed along migration routes in Djibouti, facing dehydration, exhaustion and shortages of food and water.
The IOM warned that migrants are increasingly using secondary routes, making it more difficult to reach those requiring assistance.
The agency said it is providing stranded migrants with immediate assistance, including food and water, and helping those who request voluntary return.
Djibouti is simultaneously receiving people fleeing Yemen, as well as migrants traveling toward and returning from the country, the IOM said, warning that the scale and complexity of the movements are stretching existing resources and services.
The agency called for increased international support, and said that migrants need safety, protection and assistance.
According to the latest IOM data, more than 184,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since Aug. 1 as fighting between the Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthi rebels intensifies.

Russia Strikes Kryvyi Rih Hospital, 3 Wounded
The government in Vilnius describes Russian hybrid operations as a systematic campaign against NATO rather than a series of unrelated incidents.
Recent cases include the attempted explosive-drone attack at Germany’s Leipzig-Halle Airport, which Berlin formally attributed to Russia, as well as drone incursions and suspected sabotage across Europe.

Russia has repeatedly denied conducting sabotage or preparing attacks against NATO members.
Article 5 threshold
Hybrid operations create a particular problem for NATO because they are designed to cause damage while maintaining uncertainty over who was responsible and whether the incident qualifies as an armed attack.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has said the alliance deliberately avoids announcing the precise threshold for activating Article 5, its collective-defense clause, so adversaries cannot calculate how far they can escalate without triggering a joint response.
Since 2016, the alliance has maintained that a sufficiently serious hybrid operation could lead NATO members to invoke Article 5, although any decision would be made collectively and depend on the circumstances.
Rutte recently described the term “hybrid attack” as too mild for operations involving drones, sabotage, and cyberattacks. He said NATO possesses both public and undisclosed response options and does not necessarily have to retaliate in kind.
NATO is also developing broader plans to confront a possible Russian attack by combining conventional forces with drones, artificial intelligence, and integrated battlefield systems.
Lithuania’s warning
Sinkevičius warned that a Russian victory in Ukraine could encourage Moscow to search for “other directions” for expansion or pressure.
He urged European governments not to become fatigued by the war, stressing that Ukrainians were fighting not only for their country but also for peace across Europe.
The Lithuanian prime minister also said Russian President Vladimir Putin had successfully subordinated much of Russia’s economy to the war, making the Kremlin more difficult to predict despite its internal economic problems.

christopher glass made plaid explode and skyscrapers tilt for boots riley’s latest film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:50:38 UTC
19:50:38 KST

christopher glass made plaid explode and skyscrapers tilt for boots riley’s latest film
from his work on spike jonze's apple ad to the jungle book's live action sets, the production designer reveals how to create movie magic.
designing for the movies with christopher glass
Production designer Christopher Glass has recently come off the wild and colorful sets of American director Boots Riley’s latest film, I Love Boosters, starring Keke Palmer, Demi Moore, and Eiza González. In the film, Moore plays the salacious fashion designer Christie Smith, whose office is in a fictional version of San Francisco’s Millennium Tower, which has been sinking into the ground, causing the luxury skyscraper to tilt. In Riley’s film, Smith’s offices, complete with sketches, racks of clothing, and colorful accoutrements, lampoon the structural deficit, creating an egregiously slanted office that causes those who enter to slip, slide, and struggle to close the door.
This set was actually created at a 15-degree angle (although the script said it was 45 degrees). Many of the effects in the film, like a giant threatening ball of junk that follows Palmer and plaid that explodes off a dress, were practical effects created by Glass and his team. In conversation with designboom, Glass chats about creating all types of film sets, from the physical-digital world of The Jungle Book to the ribbon-filled halls of Spike Jonze’s HomePod commercial for Apple.
On creating inside the Boots Riley universe
‘It’s a very strange, interesting universe and he comes up with things that that you would truly never think of,’ says Glass on Riley’s imaginative movies, which often include miniatures, puppets, stop motion, and fantastic costumes. ‘[Riley’s] actual stories are not entirely surreal! I know that sounds weird after working on a movie where there’s a giant trash ball stalking somebody and skinless people and whatnot. But I think there’s a kernel in his stories that are that are grounded and something that we can all relate to.’ The trash ball Glass refers to was a product of miniature magic. They built tiny versions of the Bay Area’s sloping streets so this ominous ball of scrapped clothing and eviction notices could roll up behind the film’s protagonist.
All these effects and concepts, collaged into one movie, were a creative challenge for the production designer. He recalls creating a scene where Keke Palmer’s character, Corvette, has on this dress where the plaid print explodes off the textile. ‘We didn’t want to do any computer-generated visual effects or anything like that,’ says Glass of how he started to conceptualize the dress. ‘I’ve done a lot of stuff with ribbons before, so I said, why don’t we just get a bunch of ribbons. It’s already made it’s already pre-cut and comes in very long lengths that you can use.’
From blockbusters to commercials
Glass is specifically referencing the expanding apartment set of Spike Jonze’s HomePod commercial, Welcome Home, which he created for Apple in 2018. In the commercial, FKA Twigs, playing a character dejected from her humdrum nine-to-five, comes home from work. Upon asking Siri to play her some music, her apartment begins to expand in a colorful flurry of rainbow stripes. To create this set involved a complex series of moving set pieces that would spin open, hallways of tightly bound ribbons, and FKA Twigs dancing with a body double.
‘What’s funny is that, when I was making it, I thought it was the end of my career. I was like, this is it! This is all gonna collapse and it’s not going to work,’ mentions Glass on the technical challenges that arose around that project. Nevertheless, the visually striking advertisement went on to win a Grand Prix at the Cannes Lions festival. ‘Commercials can be very experimental or they used to be because there was more of a desire for what’s called “branding creative” where a commercial expresses an aspiration instead of focusing on solely the product feature’. He goes on to say, ‘it does give you a playground to do weird, experimental, or more risky visual ideas.’ Glass has also created a growing house for Leroy Merlin, a world for a giant financial adviser for Experian, and a noir world for Jim Beam’s Willem Dafoe ad.
When to go real and when to go digital
Glass’s work has taken him beyond the real and into high-action universes like Marvel’s Ms. Marvel or DC’s Batgirl. Back in 2015, he worked on The Jungle Book, a live-action movie that followed in the success of James Cameron’s Avatar, a pioneering film in merging computer graphics with real performances. ‘It used a lot of the same techniques as [Avatar], but we had to have a real kid [play Mowgli] and he’s really the only human actor in the entire film,’ Glass says on when and where the production decided to create physical sets or CGI surroundings. ‘So almost everything that he’s he interacts with physically we created, like the leaves, the snake skin he pulls up. If he’s climbing up a log and has to like duck under a branch or push it aside. [These elements are] all different sizes depending on what the action was like. Sometimes it’s very narrow if it’s a pathway and sometimes it was wider because we needed his shadow.’
Ultimately, through his wide range of production, Glass has seen, and taken part in, the creation of movie magic. Although his role is designer, he admits that sometimes he can’t help but get involved in the paint and the props. He talks about his time on 12 Strong, the war-action movie starring Chris Hemsworth, saying, ‘I was very hands-on in the battlefield dressing, like dark ash all over the place and setting up body parts for blown up people. It’s just because I’m a nerd for filmmaking and and if I if I’m not doing something I start to feel too separated from the process.’

The mysterious Voynich Manuscript may have been read in the wrong order for centuries
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:49:38 EEST
19:49:38 KST

The mysterious Voynich Manuscript may have been read in the wrong order for centuries
Kyiv • UNN
Researchers believe that the pages of the Voynich Manuscript were bound in the wrong order in the 15th century. The restored sequence may help decipher it.
The famous Voynich Manuscript — a medieval manuscript written in an unknown alphabet — has remained undeciphered for more than a century, partly because its pages were bound in the wrong order as early as the 15th century. This is the conclusion reached by researcher Colin Layfield and paleographer Lisa Fagin Davis. The work was published in the journal Digital Medievalist, reports the Guardian, writes UNN.
Details
The manuscript’s parchment, preserved in the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library at Yale University, was dated by radiocarbon analysis to 1404–1438. The authors established that the sheets originally existed as separate folded bifolios — “singletons.”
Later, in the mid-to-late 15th century, they were sewn together again into nested quires, disrupting the original sequence. As a result, the text and illustrations were read in the wrong order for five centuries, which partly explains why all attempts to decipher the manuscript repeatedly failed.
To restore the original sequence, the researchers applied latent semantic analysis — a method that identifies similarities between textual fragments on different pages and makes it possible to infer which sheets were originally located next to one another. In addition, the scholars relied on instrumental analysis of the ink and marginal marks, as well as the placement of water stains, which can reveal how the bifolios were nested inside one another.
Davis notes that the common perception of the manuscript as the work of a single “mad genius” is not supported by the material evidence.
Many people wanted the Voynich Manuscript to have been created by a single mad genius. In fact, the evidence points to a more collective object
The conclusion that the manuscript was bound incorrectly is important because most decipherment attempts are based on the current order of the pages: if that order was disrupted, then both the statistics of recurring combinations of symbols and the connection between the text and drawings of plants, astronomical diagrams, and human figures could have misled researchers for years.
The authors hope that the restored sequence of the sheets will provide more meaningful material for those continuing attempts to read the text, and they plan to release the code and data openly.

The EUDI wallet: Building trust, unlocking growth in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:48:12 UTC
19:48:12 KST

Europe is about to place a digital identity wallet in the hands of every citizen. Writes Jacques Van Zijp in an OpEd for Euronews. It could become the trust layer of the European economy and a growth driver in a single market that works at digital speed. A model that has value well beyond Europe.
Anyone who has recently opened a bank account, rented a flat or signed up to a new service knows the routine. Photograph your identity document. Upload proof of address. Enter the same information again. Then wait for it to be verified. Try the same in another Member State and the process can become even more cumbersome.
This is not merely an irritation or a privacy issue. It weighs on European economies through abandoned transactions, duplicated verification costs, slow onboarding, fraud losses and cross-border friction that a single market is supposed to have removed.
By the end of 2026, under the European Digital Identity Regulation, every Member State must make a digital identity wallet available to its citizens. The deadline is often discussed as a compliance obligation. That framing undersells what is at stake. The European Digital Identity (EUDI) Wallet is a transformational opportunity for Europe.
From identification to verification
The significance of the EUDI Wallet does not lie in producing a digital duplicate of an identity document on a smartphone. It changes what we are asked to prove.
Today, identity systems largely work by identification: you reveal who you are, and the other party determines whether you qualify. The Wallet enables verification: proving the specific fact that matters. A citizen could, for example, demonstrate that they are over eighteen without disclosing their name, address or date of birth.
This gives the citizens greater control over the information they share, while reducing the volume of personal data circulating through the economy.
Dissolving a false trade-off
For two decades, digital services have largely been designed around an assumption that security, privacy and performance pull against one another. More security meant more friction. More privacy meant less convenience.
The Wallet can change that equation. A credential certified by a trusted authority can be verified instantly, in person or remotely, without manual review. Data disclosure can be limited to what the transaction actually requires, while simpler processes reduce reduces the friction at which customers give up.
Less data disclosed. Stronger assurance. Faster transactions. Three objectives that used to compete can now move in the same direction.
Where the growth comes from
The potential applications are broad: verified bank account and employment information, driving licences and diplomas, electronic signatures, or confirmation that someone is authorised to act on behalf of another person or a company.
For businesses, this can lower costs, accelerate onboarding, strengthen authentication and reduce abandoned journeys. In complex and sensitive sectors such as energy, transport, health and defense supply chains, trusted professional credentials can also simplify secure access.
For the single market, the prize is larger still. Portable credentials can make it easier for citizens and businesses to operate across Member States, removing administrative barriers that continue to inhibit cross-border activity.
This is also where digital sovereignty becomes tangible. Anchoring these exchanges in European law, standards and identity infrastructure gives Europe the opportunity to develop its own model of digital trust, combining interoperability with privacy, and innovation with democratic control.
That model could have relevance beyond Europe, as governments across Africa, Asia and Latin America develop their own digital identity systems. But its value lies not in the technology alone. Proportionality, user control and data protection are fundamental to its success.
Availability is not yet adoption
None of this happens automatically. Launching a Wallet is a milestone, not the objective. Success depends on whether citizens use it and whether public authorities and businesses integrate it into the services people rely on.
At IN Groupe, our work supporting Wallet and credential pilots for public and private issuers across several Member States points to four conditions that are likely to shape adoption.
The first is enrolment. Activating the Wallet and obtaining credentials must be simple, reliable and accessible from the outset.
The second is inclusion. Citizens have different levels of digital confidence and access to technology. Support, alternative channels and delegation mechanisms will be essential to ensure digitalisation does not create new barriers.
The third is recourse. Information can be incorrect, credentials can fail and devices can be lost. Clear mechanisms for correction and recovery will be essential to maintaining trust.
The fourth is the ecosystem. Businesses may hesitate to invest without sufficient users, while citizens may see little reason to adopt a Wallet until it works with services they value. Governments can help break this deadlock by enabling high-value public and working with private sector providers to create compelling every day use cases for citizens.
The regulatory framework has created the opportunity. The technology is ready. What remains is the harder, more valuable work: building services that citizens choose to use. Europe has legislated trust.
Now we must earn it. The growth will follow.
Jacques Van Zijp is Executive Vice President Europe at IN Groupe, a French state-owned company that specializes in secure identity and document systems and a global leader in secure identity and trust services.

Saudi Arabia says three wounded in attacks on airports near Yemen border

Saudi Arabia says three wounded in attacks on airports near Yemen border
Saudi aviation authority reports severe injuries and damage following Houthi strikes on Jazan and Najran airports.
Saudi Arabia says three people have been wounded in attacks on two airports near the Yemen border.
King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz airport in Jazan and Najran airport were hit in the attacks on Monday evening, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Aviation Authority said in a statement on Tuesday.
“The attacks resulted in three minor injuries and material damage,” it said.
Yemen’s Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), said late on Monday that their forces targeted sites across southern Saudi Arabia, including airports and military sites.
The attacks caused injuries of “varying severity” and material damage, and the injured have been taken to hospital, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
“Specialised teams dealt with the attacks immediately upon their occurrence,” the authority said, adding that it will continue to assess the damage and is taking measures to protect passengers and staff.
Gulf Cooperation Council Secretary-General Jassim al-Budaiwi called attacks on airports and civilian facilities “a dangerous escalation”, and urged the international community to take a “firm stance against these attacks”.
Kuwait’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also condemned the Iran-aligned group’s “continued brazen and disgraceful attacks” on Saudi Arabia, accusing it of targeting civilians and economic facilities.
Fighting escalates
The attacks on Saudi airports come amid an escalation in fighting in Yemen, where forces loyal to the internationally recognised government, backed by Saudi Arabia, are battling the Houthis.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said early on Tuesday that it destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in Yemen’s capital Sanaa, which the Houthis have controlled since 2014.
It also said it destroyed a storage facility in Saada that had 20 ballistic missiles, according to the official Saudi Press Agency.
The announcements came after forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched a counteroffensive to retake territory the Iran-aligned Houthis captured last month. The Yemeni government-aligned forces said they have retaken the port city of Mocha on the Red Sea and are now in control of the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The Saudi-led coalition has confirmed its participation in the Yemeni government offensive, saying 100 of its fighter jets are providing air support. Saudi naval forces have also launched an operation against the Houthis in Hodeidah governorate, the coalition said.
Fernando Carvajal, a former United Nations Security Council adviser on Yemen, told Al Jazeera that Mocha would be key to the next phase of clashes.
He said government forces will have to prove that they can hold on to the city, which is “surrounded by Houthis from all three sides”, before using it as a staging point.
Meanwhile, Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under a mutual defence pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter Houthi attacks.
“The committee agreed to activate collective deterrence measures, within the framework of the Alliance, in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them,” Khalid bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, said in a social media post.
He said the alliance had “reaffirmed the solidarity and unity of our countries, in confronting the heinous attacks against the Kingdom, and holy sites”.
Carvajal said it remains unclear what practical support they will provide. He said Pakistan might try to mediate between the warring sides, but that the Houthis would likely only want to talk to the Saudis, which would leave the Yemeni government excluded.

A nationwide moment of silence, convoys, protest installations, survivor testimony and a central memorial ceremony will mark three years since the October 7 massacre on Wednesday, with events planned at around 400 locations across Israel.

Events will be held at the site of the Nova music festival near Re’im and at the Sha’ar HaNegev arches junction, where the flag will be lowered to half-staff. Protests are also planned at additional locations, while families affiliated with the October Council will participate in installations and protest activities in Caesarea and Jerusalem.
At 7:00 a.m., several protest groups will hold memorial ceremonies outside the homes of ministers who served in the government on the day of the massacre. Ten minutes later, a vehicle convoy will leave Caesarea for Tel Aviv along what organizers are calling the “Route of Abandonment.”
At 8:30 a.m., the women’s protest group “From Abandonment to Responsibility” will hold an event at Trumpeldor Beach in Tel Aviv, centered on an installation symbolizing the events of October 7.
At 10:00 a.m., convoys are expected to leave northern, southern and central Israel for Ben Shemen Forest, where a memorial ceremony for those killed in the attack will be held later in the afternoon.
From 11:00 a.m., bereaved families from the October Council will take part in memorial services and events for their loved ones across the country.
At 11:47 a.m., a special ceremony will be held beside the yellow container at the Nova site, led by bereaved father Yoram Yehudai, whose son Ron Yehudai was murdered at the festival.
At 12:00 p.m., the October Council plans to hold a nationwide minute of remembrance at hundreds of locations.
The council said municipalities, businesses and organizations have already announced that employees will be allowed to participate.
Among those joining are Soroka, Ichilov, Sheba, Rambam, Hadassah, Schneider, Wolfson and Hillel Yaffe hospitals; the Weizmann Institute of Science, Technion, Ben-Gurion University, Tel Aviv University, Hebrew University and Reichman University; as well as the municipalities of Haifa, Herzliya and Givatayim and dozens of regional councils, kibbutzim and moshavim.
Companies and organizations including Taboola, Ness, Keter, TLV Partners, the Israel Bar Association, CET and the Amal school network have also joined the initiative, along with dozens of schools.
The October Council called on additional organizations to participate and urged the public to stop at noon, step out of workplaces, schools and homes and stand for one minute in memory of those murdered.
At the same time, the “Space Left Behind” exhibition will open to the public at the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation in Jaffa, displaying personal belongings of dozens of people murdered on October 7. A short ceremony will also be held there with representatives of families from the October Council.
From the afternoon into the evening, protests will be held across Israel. Demonstrations involving protest groups and members of the October Council are planned in Haifa, Afula, Tzemach Junction, Rosh Pina Junction and Sde Boker.
At 6:29 p.m., a ceremony will be held at the Nova site in Re’im Forest with bereaved families and members of the Tribe of Nova association.
At 7:30 p.m., a stage for survivor and witness testimony will open at the Sha’ar HaNegev arches junction.
The day’s events will culminate at 9:15 p.m., when the national memorial ceremony organized by the families of October 7 begins at Yarkon Park in Tel Aviv. The ceremony will also be screened at locations across the country and will be hosted by former hostage Eli Sharabi and actress Shani Cohen.
This will be the third year the ceremony has been held. Organizers say the aim is once again to create a “national, all-Israeli, unifying and hopeful” event giving voice to different groups across Israeli society. Performers will include Shlomo Artzi, Ivri Lider, Miri Mesika, Valerie Hamaty and Harel Skaat.

Cancer rates rising faster among younger people, global study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:45:47 UTC
19:45:47 KST

Dilara Hamit
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Cases of seven cancers have risen significantly among people under 50 in England, according to an analysis published Tuesday by the World Cancer Research Fund International.
The organization examined official cancer registry data for 12 cancer types in England between 2001 and 2023. Significant increases in case numbers were recorded for breast, colorectal, kidney, liver, pancreatic, prostate and uterine cancers.
The sharpest proportional increase was seen in prostate cancer. The number of diagnoses among men under 50 rose from 158 in 2001 to 640 in 2023, more than fourfold. The incidence rate increased from 1 to 3.6 cases per 100,000 men.
Despite the increase, prostate cancer remains rare in this age group, with fewer than four cases recorded per 100,000 men in 2023.
Early-onset colorectal cancer also rose markedly. Among women, the rate increased from 3.8 to 8.3 cases per 100,000, while among men it climbed from 4 to 8.4 per 100,000.
Uterine cancer rates more than doubled, from 1.8 to 3.9 cases per 100,000 women. Kidney cancer increased from 1.2 to 2.3 cases per 100,000 women and from 1.9 to 3.6 among men.
Breast cancer remained the most commonly diagnosed cancer among women under 50, with its incidence rate rising from 42 to 47.5 cases per 100,000. Smaller increases were also recorded for liver and pancreatic cancers.
The analysis also examined registry data from the US and the Netherlands. Significant increases were identified in five cancer types in the US — breast, colorectal, kidney, pancreatic and uterine — and four in the Netherlands: cervical, colorectal, kidney and liver cancer.
 
Causes not fully understood
The World Cancer Research Fund cautioned that the analysis identified trends but did not establish what caused them.
“The short answer is we don’t completely know yet,” it said, adding that several interacting factors were probably influencing the figures.
Population-level changes in obesity, physical activity and diet may explain part of the increase. Diets high in red and processed meat, fast food and sugary drinks, as well as diets low in fiber, are associated with a higher risk of certain cancers.
Smoking, alcohol consumption and excessive sun exposure are among other modifiable cancer risks. However, the organization stressed that such factors probably explain only part of the changing pattern and should not be interpreted as proof that personal choices caused individual cases.
Researchers are also investigating whether pollution, chemicals, plastics, antibiotic use and changes to the gut microbiome could be affecting cancer risk across generations.
Improved awareness and diagnosis may account for some of the rise because younger adults are now more likely to recognize symptoms and seek medical attention. Better testing can also detect cancers that might previously have gone unnoticed.
The fund said improved detection could not explain the entire increase, particularly for cancers for which mortality is also rising.
Cancer nevertheless remains predominantly a disease of older adults. The average or median age at diagnosis in developed countries is above 60, and early-onset cancer remains uncommon compared with cancer among people over 50.
The English figures were calculated using age-specific incidence rates, which account for the size of the under-50 population but not changes in its internal age distribution. The fund said further research into genetics, environmental exposure, tumor biology and the microbiome would be needed to explain why some cancers are becoming more common among younger generations.

Flemish particle physicist wins Nobel Prize in Physics (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:44:00 UTC
19:44:00 KST

The Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded to the Flemish particle physicist Francis Halzen (82) from Tienen (Flemish Brabant). This is only the second time a Belgian has won the Nobel Prize in Physics, following François Englert in 2013.
Francis Halzen has been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering research into neutrinos, also known as ‘ghost particles from the universe’. Neutrinos are high-energy, elementary particles that have almost no mass and pass right through everything, including our bodies.
Neutrinos are of great interest in helping us understand the universe, including galaxies and black holes.
Watch how the prize announcement was made in Stockholm
Who is Francis Halzen?
Francis Halzen was born on 23 March 1944 in Tienen, Flemish Brabant. He studied physics at KU Leuven/UC Louvain and between 1969 and 1971 worked as a scientist at CERN, the European research centre known for its large particle accelerator.
Since 1972, Halzen has been a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the United States.
Francis Halzen came up with the idea of building a large detector at the South Pole to detect neutrinos, ‘ghost particles from the universe’. He led the project during its construction and scientific development. The observatory was built between 2005 and 2010.
What did Francis Halzen discover?
Francis Halzen discovered that ice at the South Pole can be used to detect neutrinos. Neutrinos float everywhere throughout the universe, but because they interact with almost nothing, they are almost impossible to detect.
However, when a neutrino collides with an ice particle, it does produce a faint flash of blue light. Halzen therefore decided that a giant detector needed to be built in Antarctica to detect these flashes of light.
“Francis Halzen’s discovery and scientific leadership have been of fundamental importance to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a cubic kilometre of ice equipped with light sensors,” says the Nobel Committee of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
“Using IceCube, researchers can detect neutrinos originating from extremely high-energy processes in the distant universe.”

Three Iranians on trial in UK for spying on dissident journalists
LONDON, Oct 6 - Three Iranian men spied on British-based dissident journalists on behalf of Iran's foreign intelligence service in order to attack them "as retribution for their criticism of the Iranian regime", prosecutors told a London jury on Tuesday.
The trio are accused of surveilling journalists working for Iran International, a Persian-language television station which is critical of Iran's government, between August 2024 and March 2025.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, have each denied two charges under Britain's National Security Act, brought in to give the authorities new powers to target threats from foreign states.
Their trial at Woolwich Crown Court began this week at time of growing tension between Britain and Iran, which prosecutors say has repeatedly targeted critics and dissidents both inside the Islamic Republic and abroad.
"Eliminating hostile or critical voices ... has effectively become a staple policy of the Islamic Republic of Iran," prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones told jurors.
He said the three defendants conducted research about at least two Iran International journalists, visiting addresses linked to them and taking photos and videos in preparation for an attack which Sepahvand was to carry out.
"Their ultimate objective was that one, perhaps more than one, of these targets would be subjected to serious violence, no doubt as retribution for their criticism of the Iranian regime and to try to silence and deter others," Emlyn Jones said.
He told the court the three defendants accepted going to places and taking photos and videos, but disputed why they had done so.
Emlyn Jones said Manesh and Noori's case was that they did not know they were doing so to assist Iranian intelligence, while Sepahvand accepted he knew but had been "bullied or threatened into doing what he did". REUTERS

Russia Holds Major Nuclear Accident Drill at Beloyarsk Plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:43:23 UTC
19:43:23 KST

More than 1,000 people began a two-day emergency exercise at Russia’s Beloyarsk nuclear power plant on Tuesday, testing how staff and emergency services would respond to simultaneous accidents at two reactors.
The exercise in the Sverdlovsk region, which organizers said is the largest in Russia’s nuclear industry this year, will simulate a natural disaster compounded by failures in reactor safety systems.
The plant’s reactors will continue operating normally throughout the exercise, its communications department said.
Emergency crews will extend the drill to the nearby town of Zarechny on Wednesday to rehearse the response to a simulated nuclear accident.
Crews in protective equipment will use fire engines and military vehicles to clear debris, extinguish simulated fires and set up decontamination facilities. They will also practice sheltering and evacuating residents.
Plant management has asked residents to remain calm during the exercise, which may include sirens and loudspeaker announcements.
The drill is part of an annual program in which different Russian nuclear plants take turns hosting large exercises. Plant officials said the scenario combines highly unlikely events to test emergency preparedness.
Russian federal regulations require nuclear plant operators to hold exercises involving specialist support teams and emergency services at least once a year.
International Atomic Energy Agency safety standards also call for regular drills to test coordination between plant staff and outside agencies. The agency’s guidance includes exercises involving emergencies at multiple reactors on the same site.
Participants at the Beloyarsk drill include plant employees, specialists from nuclear plant operator Rosenergoatom and state nuclear corporation Rosatom, rescuers, police, medical workers and local officials.
Military radiation, chemical and biological defense units are also taking part, along with observers from Belarus and Kazakhstan.
Beloyarsk supplies about 16% of the Sverdlovsk region’s electricity. Its two operating units use BN-600 and BN-800 fast-neutron reactors, which began operating in 1980 and 2015, respectively.
The exercise comes amid reported drone strikes on Russian nuclear infrastructure, though its announced scenario centers on a natural disaster and equipment failures.
Rosatom said drones struck cooling towers at the Kursk II nuclear power plant twice this year, hitting unit 2, which is under construction, on July 6 and unit 1 on Sept. 17. The company said neither incident affected plant operations or radiation levels.

New spatial plan pushes development toward compact regional centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:43:00 UTC
19:43:00 KST

New spatial plan pushes development toward compact regional centers
Estonia has prepared a new national spatial plan that outlines development priorities through 2050, calling for stronger regional centers linked by a rail network. Municipalities hope the strategy will translate into real investment, especially for rural areas, rather than remain a paper exercise.
As of Tuesday, the national spatial plan is on public display, outlining the directions for Estonia's spatial development for the next couple of decades.
Minister of Economic Affairs and Industry Liina Vahtras noted that at a time when development is increasingly concentrated around the capital, thoughtful spatial decisions are needed to support a more balanced distribution of settlement across regions.
The keywords of the national plan are balance and compactness, said Ivan Sergejev, deputy secretary general for planning at the Ministry of Economic Affairs.
"We want people to have the opportunity to thrive anywhere in Estonia without necessarily having to move to Tallinn. Regional centers should be strong enough to offer both living and working opportunities. That would be balanced development," Sergejev said.
"The second keyword is compactness, because compact development is more sustainable — both from a budget perspective, since you don't need to build new infrastructure but can use what already exists, and from the perspective of service accessibility and the environment," he added.
Simply put, the goal is to encourage people to live closer to services. This does not mean everyone must live in cities, Sergejev emphasized.
"When municipalities consider how to develop, they should aim for density rather than sprawl. Sprawl automatically means building new infrastructure — new schools, kindergartens, and so on — and we wouldn't be able to reuse what already exists," Sergejev explained.
"But the idea is not to push people into cities. Services are already available at multiple levels. Some services are accessible in almost every small settlement, while others only in regional centers. The system works, but it could be more thoughtfully structured."
The Association of Cities and Municipalities generally agrees that development should move toward compactness, said deputy director Heiki Hepner.
"We agree that high‑quality natural land should be used last. All other options should be exhausted first," Hepner said.
Municipalities also stress the importance of autonomy in spatial planning. Initially, the plan envisioned ten regional centers, but after pressure from municipalities, the number has been increased to 15, Hepner noted.
"In that sense, the plan has moved in the right direction — we now have 15 regional towns across all counties that deserve development, plus a separate cluster of four towns in Northeast Estonia," Hepner said.
Hepner added that while the plan sets priorities and directions, the state must follow up with concrete actions.
"The state must take steps in funding and public services — whether at county centers or smaller hubs — and public transport is crucial. Rail transport is highlighted, but we know Rail Baltic is currently on hold, the Haapsalu line is incomplete, and we cannot yet move quickly toward Tartu. These are bottlenecks. A practical action plan is needed to show how all this will actually be implemented," Hepner said.
The national spatial plan can be viewed at riigiplaneering.ee, and feedback is invited until 4 November.

Indonesia’s Prabowo taps Widodo’s allies as advisers amid falling approval rating

The council, which advises the president on the direction of government policy but has no power to set or control it, comprises allies of former presidents, political commentators and Muslim leaders.
“These are figures who have influence, connections and mass followings. By keeping them in Prabowo’s orbit, Prabowo can feel a bit more at ease that no opposition is being built outside through these figures,” said Yoes Kenawas, a political analyst with the Indonesian Survey Institute.
On Friday, Prabowo designated 26 political figures, civil society representatives, Muslim leaders, businessmen and activists to the council, which had been vacant since he became president in October 2024.

When the UN agreed with the UK Green Party on Zionism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:41:01 UTC
19:41:01 KST

Breadcrumb
When the UN agreed with the UK Green Party on Zionism
The Green Party’s decision to adopt a motion classifying Zionism as a form of racism has caused uproar in the UK. The motion calls Zionism an ideology which supports an “ethnonationalist Jewish state” and calls for a “single democratic state in all of historic Palestine”.
The Green Party’s leader, Zack Polanski, did not vote on the motion, but found himself banned from Israel as a result.
Rabbi Charley Baginsky of the Movement for Progressive Judaism described the motion as “incredibly sinister” and told LBC she was “really distressed” at the vote, saying that Zionism was a key part of many Jewish people’s identity.
The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that the move would stoke “anti-Jewish hatred”, citing attacks on Jews in the UK in the past year.
The resolution was even opposed by leading members of the Green Party itself.
Caroline Lucas, the party’s former leader and its first-ever MP, said, “I view the Israeli government as racist, I believe its actions in Gaza amount to genocide, and I support the BDS campaign. And yet I remain firmly opposed to this resolution.”
She justified this by claiming that Zionism was historically a response to the racist persecution of Jews in Europe.
Media coverage in the UK has been extremely critical, with The Economist calling the motion “shameful” and the Daily Mail suggesting that the Greens were now the UK’s “first openly anti-Semitic party”.
It is often forgotten, however, that the UN itself once classified Zionism as racism.
UN condemnation of Zionism
While the UN was instrumental in the creation of Israel, with the majority of its members voting in favour of the 1947 Partition of Palestine, by 1975, African and Asian states had gained independence from European colonial rule and formed a large proportion of the world body’s membership. Most of these voted for UN General Assembly Resolution 3379, which determined that Zionism was “a form of racism and racial discrimination”, alongside the Arab League countries which sponsored and proposed it.
The Soviet Union, which was one of the first countries in the world to recognise Israel, had by that time become an ally of Arab countries and, along with its East European allies, also voted in favour. The resolution passed with 72 votes for and 35 against, with the US and its Western European allies voting against.
The vote took place at a time when Israel’s 1967 occupation of the West Bank and Gaza was relatively new. Israel subjected the Palestinian population of those territories to military rule while denying them citizenship. It also began establishing settlements in the territories in violation of international law.
Memories of the 1948 Nakba, in which Zionist forces expelled the vast majority of the Palestinian population, were also much fresher than they are today.
South Africa and Israel
Israel at the time was also a close ally of apartheid South Africa, with the two countries cooperating in defence, intelligence, and the development of nuclear weapons, with both viewing themselves as outposts of “civilisation” in a hostile environment.
As a South African government publication put it at the time, “Israel and South Africa have one thing above all else in common: they are both situated in a predominantly hostile world inhabited by dark peoples."
It was very easy to draw parallels between the two countries and the statements of Israeli leaders themselves appeared to confirm them. As Yitzhak Navon, Israel’s president between 1978 and 1983, said, “The very point of [the Israeli] Labor [party’s] Zionist programme is to have as much land as possible and as few Arabs as possible!”
These parallels helped explain the overwhelming African and Asian support for the UNGA resolution.
Israel, however, bitterly rejected the resolution, with its ambassador, Chaim Herzog (father of Israel’s current president), claiming that some of Israel’s Palestinian citizens – within the 1948 boundaries – had gained high-ranking positions within its government and military.
US ambassador to the UN Daniel Patrick Moynihan told the UN that it was “about to make anti-Semitism international law."
Repealing the resolution for ‘peace’
By 1991, the global environment had changed. The collapse of the Soviet Union had deprived Arab countries of a key strategic ally and supplier of weapons and changed the balance of power across the world. The Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and the subsequent Gulf War had left the US in a much stronger position in the Middle East.
Israel demanded that the UN repeal Resolution 3379 as a precondition for its participation in the 1991 Madrid peace conference, which eventually led to the 1993 Oslo Accords between the PLO and Israel.
The UN General Assembly duly repealed the resolution under US pressure, with even some Arab countries – such as Egypt, Morocco, and Oman – staying away rather than voting against.
However, all of the original factors behind the 1975 resolution remained. The Oslo Peace Process ended up entrenching Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, its settlement policies, and its encirclement and siege of Palestinian communities – notably Gaza.
The number of Israeli settlers in the West Bank has gone up from just a few thousand in 1975 to around 700,000 today.
Human rights groups such as Amnesty International have concluded that Israel is committing “the crime of apartheid” both within its 1948 boundaries and in the West Bank and Gaza, long after apartheid as a ruling system ended in South Africa.
Israeli leaders are engaging in much more bloodthirsty rhetoric than Navon’s “as few Arabs as possible” remarks, with far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir recently calling for “30-40” Palestinians to be killed every day.
What may have changed, however, is the increasing censorship regarding discourse on Israel and the growing and deliberate conflation of criticism of Israel with anti-Semitism.
Singers who chant “Free Palestine” at music concerts are attacked on the grounds that they make Jews feel unsafe, while artwork by Palestinian children displayed at a UK hospital is removed for the same reason.
By passing a motion equating Zionism with racism, the Green Party only stated a position once held by a significant section of global opinion. However, it did so at a time when Israel is far more aggressive in pushing its narrative than it was 50 years ago.

Drone sinks ship off Bulgaria, as fears grow about hybrid attacks by Russia

It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack by air and sea drones about 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, but there are growing concerns about hybrid attacks by Russia as it wages war in Ukraine.
Shipping sources said it appeared to be the first such attack in the waters of Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.

A search has been launched for the missing crew and for any signs of an environmental threat.
A maritime security source said initial assessments of the strike suggested it had probably been a Russian attack.

DISTRESS SIGNALS REPORTED

google japan puts gboard on conveyor belts so the keys come to you
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:25:51 UTC
00:25:51 KST

google japan puts gboard on conveyor belts so the keys come to you
the latest experiment from the gboard team reverses the usual logic of typing: this time, the keyboard does the moving.
GOOGLE JAPAN GBOARD KURUKURU PUTS THE KEYBOARD IN MOTION
Google Japan has looked at the conventional keyboard and decided that perhaps our fingers have been doing too much of the work. Developed by the Gboard team, the new Gboard Kurukuru Version places its keys on moving conveyor belts, allowing characters to travel toward the user rather than asking the user to reach across a fixed layout. The experimental device turns one of the most familiar tools on a desk into something closer to a miniature production line, with typing becoming a matter of catching the right character as it rolls into place.
Four continuous belts make up the keyboard, with 29 keys arranged along each one for a total of 116. As they rotate, users can keep their hand relatively still and press the desired character when it arrives beneath their fingers. Uppercase and lowercase letters can be entered directly, while the moving layout is designed to make the full character set accessible with one hand or even a single finger. In other words, the keys have finally been asked to meet us halfway.
FOUR CONVEYOR BELTS BRING 116 KEYS TO YOUR FINGERTIPS
The mechanism quietly reverses the basic relationship between hand and interface. On a standard keyboard, muscle memory tells the fingers where to go; with Kurukuru, the fingers wait while the interface comes to them. Google Japan imagines the one-handed setup leaving the other hand available for a mouse — or, in the team’s own more leisurely scenario, a cup of tea. For those unwilling to abandon two-handed typing altogether, using two Kurukuru keyboards at once is also floated as a possible route to greater productivity.
Kurukuru arrives as the 15th entry in Google Japan’s long-running series of unconventional Gboard experiments. Previous editions have stretched the keyboard into a single elongated row, twisted it into a double-sided loop and, in 2025, replaced traditional typing with rotary telephone-style dials. The latest version continues that habit of taking an everyday interface far too literally, then engineering it seriously enough to work. Google is also considering color variations, a high-speed mode and longer or more portable short versions, although none have been announced as commercial products.
OPEN-SOURCE GBOARD KURUKURU TURNS THE JOKE INTO A DIY BUILD
As with earlier Gboard experiments, the moving keyboard is more than a visual gag. Google Japan has released open-source build files so makers can construct a similar device themselves, bringing together 3D-printed components, switches and the mechanical system required to keep the belts circulating. The result sits somewhere between computer peripheral, kinetic object and desktop machinery, exposing all the movement that a conventional keyboard usually hides beneath a very stationary rectangle.
There are no plans to put Gboard Kurukuru on sale, which may be just as well for anyone who prefers their vowels not to escape before being pressed. Instead, the project works as a deliberately exaggerated rethink of an interface that has remained remarkably stable for decades. Google Japan unveiled it on October 1 — a recurring nod to the familiar 101-key keyboard — but behind the wordplay is a simple design question: why should the human body always adapt to the machine? With Kurukuru, for once, the keys do the commuting.

designer: Gboard team, Google Japan | @googlejapan

Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. That ship, the Able, was flying the flag of Palau and transporting grain.
Its last reported position was five nautical miles (9km) from the Alfa Watan.
Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law".
He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable."
He did not accuse Russia of carrying out the strikes, but referred to the war in Ukraine, saying: "As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning.
"Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea," she said. "While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning."
"Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable."
Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea.
A separate attack on Tuesday, near Odesa, saw a crew member killed and seven more injured. The ship was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, according to Ukrainian media.
On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
