COP31 eyes modest steps as climate disasters multiply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:36:51 UTC
19:36:51 KST

Mining vehicles extract coal from a lignite coal mine as the Elbistan thermal power plant is seen in the background in Elbistan, Kahramanmaraş, Türkiye. (AFP Photo)
Nations reeling from a year of climate devastation gather for COP31 next month, but negotiations are not expected to deliver major progress in cutting the fossil fuels driving the crisis.
The conference follows deadly heat waves and fires in Europe, catastrophic floods in Nepal and record temperatures around the world, testing whether the United Nations-backed talks can keep pace with reality.
As leaders meet in Antalya in Türkiye’s Mediterranean shore, an exceptionally powerful El Nino pattern will be approaching peak strength, threatening to amplify weather chaos worldwide and drive global heat to unprecedented highs.
Concerns over energy security will also loom large, with no end in sight to the Middle East war that has sent oil and gas prices soaring and hit fossil fuel-importing nations hard.
With a new agreement on fossil fuels unlikely, Türkiye is rallying support for a voluntary “electrification” pledge it says could cut heat-trapping emissions and reduce reliance on energy imports.
“In many ways, the defining contexts for this year’s climate summit will be heat and Hormuz,” said David Waskow from the World Resources Institute, referencing the vital strait that carried one-fifth of the world’s hydrocarbons before the Iran war.
Unusually, Türkiye must navigate these complexities with Australia, a major fossil fuel exporter, after both countries agreed to share COP31 duties following a bruising hosting battle.
Australia’s Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations in Antalya starting Nov. 9, said this year’s extreme events “show climate change is not a future challenge.”
“It is a present reality and the costs of inaction are rising,” he said.
A “pre-COP” meeting began on Oct. 5 in the climate-vulnerable Pacific with a leaders’ retreat in Tuvalu and government meetings in Fiji.
Unlike recent COPs, where nearly 200 nations forged landmark pacts on phasing down coal or moving away from fossil fuels, the negotiation agenda at COP31 is light on big-ticket items.
There are more than 100 items on the table but many deal with technical matters, like approving indicators to track progress on climate adaptation.
“Much of the Antalya summit will be a ‘roll up the sleeves’ effort. Governments need to make concrete headway in negotiations, though there may not be dramatic outcomes this year,” Waskow told AFP.
Nations are not expected to adopt new binding commitments to reduce the burning of fossil fuels, the leading cause of climate change.
Türkiye says it is not realistic to expect all countries to move at the same pace.
“Any proposal that fails to reconcile our climate objectives with social and economic realities will be doomed to fail,” said Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.
Türkiye is curating an “action agenda” alongside the negotiations that encourages countries to support non-binding pledges on issues from artificial intelligence to waste management.
There is broad support for its centerpiece goal: Raising the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20 percent today to 35 percent by 2035.
The electrification target does not state how that extra power should be produced. One-third of electricity is generated by coal, and there are concerns the target could provide cover for expanded fossil fuel use.

Three years of genocide: Evictions, demolitions deepen pressure on Palestinians in East Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:34:47 UTC
19:34:47 KST

- Israeli elections fuel competition over who will violate Palestinian rights more, says rights group official Rami Saleh
- Palestinian women have been forced to give birth at checkpoints amid movement restrictions, says women rights activist Randa Siniora
For Rae'd Basbous, the loss of his family home in occupied East Jerusalem was the culmination of an 11-year legal battle that began when his children were still young.
It ended with a phone call and less than 24 hours to vacate the house.
Basbous, 49, said their house was built in 1963 on land his grandfather bought in the Batn al-Hawa neighborhood in the Palestinian village of Silwan.
For more than six decades, the house was the center of their family life.
His father and uncles lived there with his grandfather. Later, Basbous and his brother raised their own families in the same building.
Then, in 2015, they received an eviction order sought by Israeli occupiers.
"We appointed lawyers, submitted documents, and opposed this eviction order in different courts," Basbous told Anadolu.
Israel's Supreme Court, however, rejected the family's appeals in 2026.
Basbous said his family's experience was not an isolated case.
He estimates that about 86 Palestinian families live in Batn al-Hawa, with more than half either already evicted or facing final eviction orders.
"What happened to the families in Batn al-Hawa neighborhood is a part of Israeli policy,” he said.
They want to alter Jerusalem’s demographic makeup by pushing Palestinians out of the city and bringing in Jewish families instead, Basbous said.
For Basbous, the international response has been deeply disappointing.
“No one supports us,” he said, as Israel's genocide in Gaza nears three years.
While the war in Gaza has been marked by relentless bombardment, Palestinians in East Jerusalem have faced mounting pressure through evictions, home demolitions, settlement expansion and other measures.
 
Broader pattern of displacement
Palestinian rights organizations say the pressure on residents does not come through evictions alone.
Home demolitions, construction restrictions, illegal settlement expansion, land confiscation and residency policies all affect Palestinians living in East Jerusalem.
Rami Saleh, Jerusalem branch director of the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center, said Palestinians were being used as bait for the upcoming Israeli election.
"Right now we are heading to the Israel elections... and this is from our experience: Israelis are using Palestinians as fuel to the Israel elections," he said.
Each election, he said, is a competition over “who will violate Palestinian rights more.”
Saleh cited figures collected by his organization that showed 5,100 new illegal settlement housing units had been approved in East Jerusalem during the first eight months of this year.
What they want in East Jerusalem is “ethnic cleansing of Palestinians," he said.
Pointing to Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement, which commits both parties to respect human rights and democratic principles, he said: "Everybody knows that Israel is not respecting human rights.”
“They can stop this agreement … and this will be helpful for Palestinians because putting pressure on Israel will make them think again and again about … (what) they are doing in the occupied Palestinian territories," Saleh said.
 
'You become a stranger'
East Jerusalem has been occupied by Israel since 1967, and is physically and administratively separated from much of the occupied West Bank due to a complex system of Israeli residency rules, checkpoints and a separation barrier.
The result is a city in which Palestinian communities can find themselves simultaneously inside Jerusalem's municipal boundaries and physically disconnected from much of the city.
Samer Daoudi, director of the Jerusalem Human Rights Consortium, described a pattern in which restrictions that Palestinians once experienced as temporary have become normalized.
It's gotten worse in the last three years, he said.
"Dehumanizing and demonizing” Palestinians has become the norm, he added.
"So you become a stranger in the country that you've grown up in," Daoudi said.
He recalled cases involving Palestinians seeking permits to travel, women trying to reach medical facilities and families attempting to register children. "Everyone in East Jerusalem, and across the occupied Palestinian territory has a story," he said.
"Some people died because they didn't get a permit because they have travel bans."
He said such stories had become increasingly normalized.
"You hear the stories, but then it becomes normalized... People become numb to them, and that has to be broken," Daoudi said.
For Daoudi, the issue is ultimately about whether international rules are applied consistently.
"I think there is a moral stance, a collective moral stance.
"If you see one of the countries not abiding by them … then there should be some sort of accountability," he added.
He warned that allowing violations to go without consequences could have repercussions beyond the Palestinian territories.
 
Women and children pay another price
Randa Siniora, director of the Women's Center for Legal Aid and Counseling, said women and children are disproportionately impacted.
Siniora highlighted the effects of movement restrictions, checkpoints and the separation of East Jerusalem from other parts of the occupied Palestinian territory.
She said Palestinian women had experienced problems accessing health care and traveling between communities, while some had gone into labor and given birth at checkpoints.
Siniora also described sexual harassment and sexual violence during arrests and said women living near agricultural land can be particularly exposed to occupier attacks.
"Women are always around their homes, around their agricultural land, and therefore they are at the forefront with the settler violence, which is in complicity with the soldiers and the police," she said.
She called on the international community to fulfill its legal and moral obligations under international law and to challenge the “culture of impunity.”
Siniora urged the European Union and other international actors to take an active role in addressing the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, arguing that decades of occupation had produced realities on the ground that could not be reversed through statements alone.
"The whole call for a two-state solution is becoming irrelevant under the facts on ground," Siniora said.

After 53 years behind the wheel, Nir Oz ambulance driver returns to rebuild his shattered kibbutz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:34:32 UTC
19:34:32 KST

For more than half a century, when someone in Kibbutz Nir Oz needed an ambulance, Giora Zehavi was one of the people they could count on. Zehavi completed his Magen David Adom ambulance driver course in 1973 and spent the following decades serving the community, part of a small group of drivers and medics who took turns keeping the ambulance stationed at the kibbutz and ready for an emergency. 
Nearly three years after Oct. 7, 2023, Zehavi is again putting on his MDA uniform, returning to ambulance work and helping rebuild the emergency infrastructure of a kibbutz where roughly one in four residents was killed or abducted during the Hamas-led attack. “We’re pioneers here, rebuilding the kibbutz,” he said.
Zehavi’s connection to Nir Oz stretches back even further than his years with MDA. He arrived in 1965 with a Nahal group from the Hashomer Hatzair youth movement and became a member of the kibbutz. When MDA began looking for volunteers to train as ambulance drivers, particularly in communities close to the border, Zehavi volunteered.
“At the time they were looking for people who would volunteer to take an ambulance drivers’ course and staff ambulances in the communities, especially the communities near the border,” he recalled. “In the beginning, most kibbutzim had ambulances stationed there, and we had a very small team of drivers and medics who took turns being on call.”
By the eve of Simchat Torah in October 2023, Zehavi had already spent decades answering those calls.
That evening, the MDA Negev dispatch center contacted him and asked whether he could take responsibility for an ambulance stationed in Nir Oz. Zehavi, who at the time was staying with his partner in nearby Kibbutz Magen, immediately agreed.
He even asked whether he should take the ambulance with him to Magen or leave it at Nir Oz, just a few minutes away. He was told there was no need to move it. Hours later, on the morning of Oct. 7, that decision took on an entirely different meaning.
According to Zehavi, one of the first things the invading terrorists did in Nir Oz was destroy the ambulance and other emergency infrastructure. “The first thing the Nukhba terrorists did was blow up the ambulance,” he said, adding that they appeared to know where essential facilities and equipment were located inside the kibbutz.
Zehavi was meanwhile trapped inside a safe room in Magen with his partner. Through Nir Oz’s internal communication network, they could hear what was happening only a few kilometers away.
They could not reach anyone. “We heard everything that was happening in Nir Oz over the internal communications,” he said. “Of course, we couldn’t help.”
Some of the words he heard remain with him. “‘He died in my arms.’ ‘We’re choking from the smoke, the safe room is burning.’ ‘Come rescue us, come rescue us.’ ‘He died in my arms,’” Zehavi recalled. “But we couldn’t help.”
For a man whose instinct for more than 50 years had been to respond when someone called for medical assistance, that helplessness was among the most painful parts of the day. “That was the hardest thing,” he said. “That we couldn’t do anything. We weren’t allowed to do anything either.”
Residents in the surrounding communities had been instructed not to leave their safe rooms amid the attack. Zehavi believes that being in Magen that morning may have saved his life.
“I have a feeling that if I had been in my own home in Nir Oz that day, I wouldn’t be talking to you right now,” he said. “My house in Nir Oz was completely destroyed and burned.”
The scale of the catastrophe soon became clear. Dozens of Zehavi’s friends and neighbors in Nir Oz had been murdered or abducted. Magen David Adom itself lost seven of its personnel on Oct. 7, while additional members of the organization were killed over the course of the war. For Zehavi, however, there was never much doubt about where he ultimately belonged.
After Oct. 7, the surviving Nir Oz community was evacuated. Zehavi spent an extended period in Kiryat Gat, living far from the home and community that had defined most of his life.
He found the displacement deeply difficult. “From my perspective, it was always about going back,” he said. “There was no other way.”
He described the period in Kiryat Gat, where members of the community lived in a 12-story building, as one of profound disconnection. “Not living at home, being completely disconnected,” he said. “And now we’re here, pioneers, rebuilding the kibbutz.”
On June 6, Zehavi and his partner moved into a new home in Nir Oz.
The community is still far from what it was before the massacre. Zehavi said that about 23 kibbutz members are currently sleeping there regularly, while the population can rise to between 100 and 130 when members of a pre-military academy and a Hashomer Hatzair group staying at the kibbutz are included.
For Zehavi, rebuilding Nir Oz means more than reconstructing houses. It also means restoring the systems that allow a community to function and protect its residents. One of his goals is to establish a functioning local emergency medical team so that Nir Oz can once again have an ambulance stationed inside the kibbutz. “I don’t want to be the only one,” he said. “I want at least another two or three people with me.”
A young woman from the Hashomer Hatzair group living in Nir Oz has recently completed paramedic training at Ben-Gurion University, he said, giving him hope that a new team can gradually be assembled. “I hope that slowly we’ll be able to establish a team here,” Zehavi said.
The same process is underway with other lifesaving equipment. After the evacuation, defibrillators that survived the Oct. 7 attack were taken from Nir Oz to Kiryat Gat. Zehavi is now helping return them to the kibbutz as residents come back.
Three defibrillators have already been installed. “We’re slowly beginning to build a team with young people,” he said, including former military medics and people with medical training from youth movements. “Slowly, we’re stabilizing the situation.”
Young volunteers have become an important part of that process. Zehavi continues to work with participants spending a year of national service in Nir Oz before entering the military. He sees their energy and initiative as part of the kibbutz’s future.
“We pass on to them whatever we can, and we rely a great deal on their initiatives,” he said. “They’re young, energetic people.” Then he added, with characteristic determination: “Together we will rebuild Nir Oz. Nobody is going to stop us.”
His own return to MDA has also been gradual. Before Oct. 7, Zehavi had continued volunteering at MDA stations in Be’er Sheva and later in Tzohar, often stepping in when additional help was needed.
“Because I’m already veteran enough, I didn’t stand in line to get shifts,” he joked. “When they needed me, they called me.”
After the massacre, he took a break. Recently, he has begun volunteering again at the MDA station in Tzohar. He is not yet working regular ambulance shifts, but remains in constant contact with the regional station and keeps first-aid equipment for emergency responders in his car. “If they need something, I have equipment,” he said. “I do the best I can.”
His earliest journeys in an MDA ambulance after Oct. 7 were not ordinary emergency calls. They were funerals. “In the first times, we accompanied funerals from the funeral home in Rishon Lezion to the cemetery in Nir Oz,” Zehavi recalled. “That was a very difficult experience.”
Along the route, however, he also remembers seeing something else. “We saw the beautiful, good people of Israel along the roads,” he said.
Today the ambulance once destroyed in Nir Oz has become part of a larger mission for Zehavi: restoring the ability of the community to care for itself.
After 53 years with MDA, the veteran driver is again working toward the same basic goal that brought him to the organization in 1973: making sure that when someone in Nir Oz calls for help, someone is there to answer.

The Immigration Department said travellers can register for the “collaborative inspection” automated channels at the new Huanggang port on site or through its mobile application.

“The whole registration process over the automated e-channels is very quick. I think it takes a few seconds to complete the whole process.”
Wong said travellers who are not eligible for the automated channels can also use traditional manual counters.

What to know after U.S. Marine arrested for murder in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:34:08 UTC
19:34:08 KST

A U.S. Marine is accused of killing a woman in Japan. Here's what to know.
A woman's murder allegedly committed by a U.S. Marine in Okinawa has triggered public outrage, prompted Japan's premier to slam a "heinous crime" and rekindled controversy over the heavy military presence on the southern island.
 Here are five things to know about the latest case and Okinawa's thorny relations with the U.S. military bases.
What happened?
Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media.
Security camera footage showed a man entering the hotel with the woman and later leaving alone.
Ballard was arrested when a patrolling officer saw him walking later Saturday in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 15 miles northeast of Naha. His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo News agency reported.
Why are so many bases concentrated in Okinawa?
Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today Okinawa hosts 70% of America's military facilities and most of the 50,000 U.S. troops based in Japan today, despite comprising just 0.6% of Japan's landmass.
In the wake of World War II, Japan regained its sovereignty under the San Francisco Peace Treaty of 1952, but Okinawa remained under American control, making it a hub of U.S. military build-up.
 The 1972 return of Okinawa's sovereignty to Japan did little to diminish the number of US bases on the island, leading to the disproportionate burden it is saddled with today.
Why is it so controversial?
There has been anger over increasing crime linked to the U.S. military on the island. The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to prefectural police.
The heavy U.S. presence has led to a host of issues, from helicopter crashes and noise pollution to crimes involving servicemen, including the 1995 gang-rape of a local 12-year-old schoolgirl.
That rape by three U.S. soldiers in Okinawa fueled widespread calls for a rethink of a 1960 pact that outlined the legal status of Japan-based U.S. military personnel.
The latest incident has sparked widespread anger.
"I'm outraged and flabbergasted to hear that a suspect came to the (entertainment area) after committing a murder," Kenji Higa, who lives in Okinawa City, told the Okinawa Times.
People in Okinawa have long opposed the heavy U.S. military presence on the island, but some have come to see its strategic value due to what is widely viewed as a growing threat from China.
 Some also argue the military bases create jobs and help boost Okinawa's local economy, accounting for around 5% of the region's annual income.
How does jurisdiction work?
The 1960 Japan Status of Forces Agreement is often accused of rendering U.S. military bases virtually extraterritorial and immune to Japan's domestic laws.
Japanese authorities are, for example, hard-pressed to conduct an on-site probe into alleged environmental pollution inside the bases and regulate low-altitude flights of their aircraft.
Among the most contentious is Japan's lack of primary jurisdiction over crimes committed by US military personnel while on duty.
Even if crimes are committed while off-duty, as long as the individual responsible remains on base, their custody won't be handed over to Japan until they are indicted, according to the Japan Federation of Bar Associations.
In this case, Kyodo reported that a police officer questioned and detained the suspect as he walked alone on a street in Naha's entertainment district late Saturday.
Japanese prosecutors started examining the suspect's case on Monday to determine whether to press formal charges in coming weeks.
 If convicted, he could face life in prison or the death penalty.
How sensitive is the issue for Japan?
Despite the controversy, Japan -- which has a pacifist constitution -- relies on U.S. military might as a deterrent against any potential attack, stressing the importance of American soldiers being trained and on standby 24/7.
But Japan's safety is not necessarily America's only concern.
Experts say Washington essentially sees Okinawa as its strategic foothold to deploy militarily in the region and beyond, and the island is seen by both countries as important for monitoring China, the Taiwan Strait and the Korean peninsula.
In the past, American troops were mobilized from Okinawa to participate in conflicts such as the 1990 Gulf War and the 2003 Iraq War.

FAO boosts Iran’s capacity to protect date palms from pests and diseases

FAO boosts Iran’s capacity to protect date palms from pests and diseases
TEHRAN – The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) is strengthening national and provincial capacities to prevent, detect and manage key pests and diseases affecting date palm production in the Islamic Republic of Iran, supporting healthier orchards, reduced production losses and more sustainable livelihoods for date-producing communities.
This support will be advanced through a newly signed Letter of Agreement between FAO and the Agricultural Education and Extension Institute (AEEI) under FAO’s project “Technical Assistance to Improve Integrated Pest Management of Key Date Palm Insect Pests and Diseases”. The agreement was signed on October 5 in Tehran and will enable a multi-provincial capacity-development programme targeting approximately 1,720 farmers, agricultural extension officers and technical staff across nine provinces.
The ceremony was attended by Mr Golmohammadi, Deputy Minister of Agriculture.
“Strengthening the capacity of farmers and agricultural extension services is essential to ensuring that pest and disease management measures are effective, timely and sustainable,” said FAO Representative in the Islamic Republic of Iran, Farrukh Toirov. “Through this cooperation, FAO is supporting the application of science-based and environmentally responsible approaches that can help protect date palm production, reduce losses and strengthen the livelihoods that depend on this important sector.”
The Islamic Republic of Iran is one of the world’s leading date-producing countries, producing approximately 1.3 million tonnes of dates annually. Date palms are cultivated across around 260,000 hectares, with an estimated 40 million trees nationwide. Date production provides an important source of income and employment for farming families and rural communities, particularly in southern and central provinces, while also supporting a wider value chain encompassing harvesting, processing, packaging, transportation, trade and export.
The health and productivity of date palm orchards are therefore closely linked to the resilience of rural livelihoods and the competitiveness of the date sector. Pest and disease outbreaks can reduce yields and fruit quality, increase production costs and contribute to economic losses for farmers and other actors across the value chain.
“Through this initiative, FAO is supporting efforts to improve the management of major threats to date palm production, including the Red Palm Weevil, date palm borers, Dubas bug and important date palm diseases and disorders. The project focuses on strengthening surveillance, monitoring and early detection, while promoting effective, innovative and environmentally responsible Integrated Pest Management and Integrated Disease Management approaches,” Mr Toirov stated.
The newly signed Letter of Agreement will translate these objectives into practical capacity development in the field. Under the agreement, training activities will be carried out in Sistan and Baluchestan, Kerman, Hormozgan, Fars, Bushehr, Khuzestan, Yazd, South Khorasan and Isfahan provinces.
The programme will strengthen participants’ knowledge and practical skills in identifying pests and diseases, conducting surveillance and monitoring, recognizing threats at an early stage and applying appropriate integrated management measures. For farmers, improved knowledge of early signs of pest and disease incidence can support timely action and help prevent damage from becoming more severe. For extension officers and technical staff, strengthened capacities can support more effective field-level advice, monitoring and response.
By bringing technical knowledge and practical training closer to farmers and field-level agricultural professionals, the programme aims to support the wider application of integrated pest and disease management practices across major date-producing areas.
“The cooperation is expected to contribute to healthier date palm orchards, reduced production and economic losses, stronger farmer livelihoods and improved quality and competitiveness of Iranian dates in domestic and international markets.
Through the Letter of Agreement, FAO and its national partners are investing in the capacities, knowledge and institutions needed to support a more resilient and sustainable date palm sector in the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Mr Toirov concluded.

Escape from Oleshky — 12 people reached Ukraine-controlled territory in September, official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:32:50 UTC
19:32:50 KST

Escape from Oleshky — 12 people reached Ukraine-controlled territory in September, official says
Twelve people reached Ukraine-controlled territory from the Russian-occupied front-line city of Oleshky in September, the local military administration head told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 6.
Oleshky in the occupied part of Kherson Oblast has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make it almost impossible to evacuate safely.
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help people from Oleshky leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips through Russia and Belarus. Now, they said, the risk of Russian attacks and mines has made organized evacuation impossible.
In recent weeks, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky to the neighboring village of Radensk alone or in pairs, on roads mined by Russian forces.
Tetiana Hasanenko, exiled head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, said that while over 60 people left the city of Oleshky in September this year, only twelve managed to reach Ukraine-controlled territory.
The others either left for the neighboring settlement of Radensk, approximately 15 kilometers (10 miles) away to find food and return, or stayed in other occupied towns in Kherson Oblast.
"Most (of those who left the city in September) are still in the occupied territory. Some people have no documents, and most of them were forced to return to Oleshky because they have relatives there who cannot get about on their own, or they have children whom they simply cannot lead through a minefield," Hasanenko said.
While Russian troops occupy Oleshky and the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Kherson Oblast, the Ukrainian military controls the western bank. Russian troops use towns and villages on the eastern bank to launch attacks across the river, including on the liberated city of Kherson.
Russian forces have placed guns, mortars, and mines in and around residential neighborhoods due to the city's proximity to Ukrainian-controlled territory, Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration, told the Kyiv Independent.
Hasanenko previously told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 30 that four people were attempting to leave the town when they stepped on a mine and were injured, while a man collecting nuts was killed by another mine. The incidents occurred along routes used by civilians to leave the occupied town.
"These people left Oleshky at 6 a.m. and must have failed to spot something before stepping on a landmine. One woman suffered a back injury and injuries to her limbs. She was taken to the hospital on a bicycle. The others were transported in garden trolleys," Hasanenko said.
The local hospital, which is operating without basic medical supplies, electricity, or running water, is also struggling to function, Hasanenko said. Four doctors, all elderly former hospital staff, continue to work there, she said.
"But there are absolutely no medical supplies. The only thing they can do is stop the bleeding. There are no medicines," Hasanenko said.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said that around 2,000 people, including nearly 50 children, remained in the occupied town with severely limited access to food, drinking water, electricity, and other basic services.
Russian forces are preventing Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing the occupied territories to provide aid.
Oleshky lies on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, less than 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from the regional center of Kherson.

Fieldwork turns dilapidated building into mansard-roof-topped home and studio
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:30:54 UTC
19:30:54 KST

Fieldwork turns dilapidated building into mansard-roof-topped home and studio
Local studio Fieldwork has transformed a run-down building in west London into a home and casting studio with "a sense of drama and atmosphere".
Fieldwork stripped back and expanded the two-storey building, adding a mansard roof and a double-height side infill extension to increase the internal floor area by over 60 per cent.
This created a 245-square-metre three-storey building that houses a casting studio on its ground floor, with a two-storey apartment and roof terrace above.
"The new mansard roof creates additional floor space, which allowed us to meet the clients' accommodation requirements," Fieldwork director James Owen told Dezeen.
"The space accommodates a bedroom and ensuite; a bespoke timber and glass partition separates it from the stair landing while maintaining a visual connection to a new roof terrace."
Both the mansard roof and the extension, which sits where there used to be a covered garage, were clad in zinc shingles.
The studio chose to work with zinc because of the juxtaposition it creates with the existing exterior.
"The textured finish and shape of the shingles contrast with the render on the existing main facade, creating a distinction between the old and the new," Fieldwork director Tim Gibbons told Dezeen.
Inside, the studio designed the space around a central staircase.
"The concept focused on a new central staircase that reorganises an existing dilapidated building," Gibbons said. "The stair becomes the organising element of the design, allowing movement to flow around it, drawing natural light from above and pulling airflow up through the building."
The staircase also separates the working and living spaces, with the ground-floor casting studio weaving around it.
Above, the first floor houses a bedroom, living room and kitchen area as well as a bathroom, while the second floor has a bedroom and ensuite.
Fieldwork used different materials for the workspaces and residential areas to create a functional studio space.
"Internally, microcement is used in the bathrooms, while light oak joinery is combined with Douglas fir linings to introduce warmth and texture," Owen said.
"Additional acoustic insulation was incorporated into the walls and ceiling of the casting room, alongside a cork floor, to help control reverberation and improve acoustic performance."
Fieldwork also added multiple skylights to the mansard roof extension, including one right above the central staircase that helps draw light into the building.
The shape of the circular skylights was drawn from the round softbox lights used in the ground-floor casting studio.
"Positioned above the casting studio and within the main roof, the rooflights draw natural light into the deeper areas of the floor plan while accentuating the curved forms of the walls and joinery below," Gibbons said.
"As well as reducing the need for artificial lighting, the rooflights create a changing interplay of light and shadow throughout the day," he continued.
"Shadows are cast through the timber slats of the staircase and across the curved walls, creating a sense of drama and atmosphere within the interiors."
Other recent London extensions include a home renovation designed to capture changing light and a De Beauvoir home with a textured material palette.
The photography is by French + Tye.

South Korea says it received 'insufficient' apology from Ukraine over North Korean POWs, mulls envoy recall

Cho said the apology was among the messages he received from Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
"But there is a difference from the level we expect, so we intend to take firm measures," the South Korean chief diplomat said, according to Yonhap.
The minister noted that the South Korean government is considering several options, including a potential recall of South Korea's Ambassador to Ukraine, an idea proposed by a lawmaker.
President Volodymyr Zelensky angered Seoul by disclosing information on two North Korean POWs transferred to South Korea during his speech on Sept. 23 at the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
South Korea claimed this breached a non-disclosure agreement and demanded an apology. In response, the Ukrainian Presidential Office said no such agreement existed, calling it "strange" to keep the transfer a secret.
The disagreement escalated on Oct. 2 when South Korean President Lee Jae Myung wrote on social media that Kyiv's denial of the agreement's existence was "branding the head of state of the other country a liar," warning of "additional measures" if Kyiv does not apologize.
"This is a matter concerning the dignity of the Republic of Korea's citizens and the nation, we cannot overlook it," he wrote on X.
During a parliamentary audit on Oct. 6, Cho emphasized that the arrangement was meant to keep North Korean soldiers and their families safe, noting that the Ukrainian side was the first to introduce the non-disclosure idea.
Sybiha has previously dubbed the incident a "diplomatic misunderstanding," adding that he hopes the situation is resolved promptly as South Korea is an important ally.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry has not commented on whether Kyiv issued an apology to Seoul.
Ukraine announced the capture of two North Korean soldiers in early 2025 as an estimated 11,000 North Korean troops were deployed to Russia's Kursk Oblast.

Should we be worried about a plague outbreak in Russia?

PRESS REVIEW – Tuesday, October 6: The death of a researcher in Siberia, reportedly from the plague, sparks concern despite Russian authorities' denial. But first: French high school protesters are promising "Act 3" of their protest movement against learning conditions. Also, Le Monde speaks to the editor of Russian independent outlet Novaya Gazeta ahead of the 20th anniversary of the murder of investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya. Finally, it appears that butter is back in fashion.
French high schoolers are promising "Act 3" of their protest movement and there is great concern in the press about how it is going to unfold. French left-wing daily Libération worries about the police crackdown on the high schoolers. It calls on police to "act with discretion". The Communist paper L'Humanité evokes the "rage of student protesters". In its editorial, the paper pays tribute to a generation who have grown up with social anxiety: they learned to read with soldiers patrolling their schools in 2015 (due to terror attacks), they hit puberty during the social distancing years of Covid-19 and they are finishing school amid two wars and rising inflation. The right-wing paper L'Opinion, however, is less sympathetic. It expresses concern about how violent the protests will become and says the student movement has "no instruction manual", calling it "a movement that has been, up to now, volatile, violent and unable to be controlled by the government."
The movement is garnering a lot of interest in Europe too. The British daily The Times says the French government is "bewildered" by the anger and fury of the high school students. The conservative daily quotes a Paris school principal as saying that in 20 years she has seen strikes, blockades and protests, but never as violent as what is happening now. Germany's Frankfurter Allgemeine explains the movement by France's economic woes, which were exacerbated by the 2024 dissolution of parliament and by the emergence of artificial intelligence while Le Soir, the Belgian daily, reports that the movement is starting to spread to Belgium as well. Students in Liège told the paper that they too want to fight against a "sick" educational system.
Meanwhile, authorities in Russia are playing down fears after a researcher in Siberia died of the plague. Time magazine reports that dozens of people have been quarantined and outbreak control measures are underway at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. A 28-year-old lab worker known as Darya Shipilova died in unknown circumstances. A local report says she died after being exposed to the plague via a broken test tube, but those reports are no longer available online. Local authorities say there is no evidence to support this. But experts have been quick to play down fears of an outbreak. The Times of London explains that the pneumonic plague can be spread through close contact and is dangerous if untreated. However, it can be managed with antibiotics and outbreaks can be controlled if cases are caught early and isolated and treatments are respected.
We stay in Russia for our next story. Wednesday marks the 20th anniversary of the death of Russian journalist Anna Politkovskaya, who was assassinated in Moscow on October 7, 2006. As Le Monde notes, Politkovskaya was killed for "understanding Putin before anyone else did". Her reporting from Chechnya foreshadowed the war in Ukraine. The paper interviews Dmitry Muratov, the founder of the independent Russian media outlet Novaya Gazeta, where Politkovskaya worked. He notes that her belongings are still in the office, including a yellowed copy of the Russian penal code opened to the last page she had consulted before her death. For Muratov, her death was clearly orchestrated by the Russian government.
Finally, it appears that butter is back in fashion, at least according to the Guardian. Here in France, butter was never out of fashion but elsewhere, butter is enjoying a renaissance right now: from butter sculptures, to a quest for a butter sommelier, to after-dinner "butter and crackers". This summer, a young entrepreneur opened Le Butter in Paris, a shop dedicated to 50 different varieties of butter. An Egyptian American artist has carved fragments of Michelangelo's David out of butter. Butter is back – butter late than never!

Kevin Roose Didn’t Use AI to Write His Book About AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

For most people, the AI Era we’re now living in started sometime around the end of 2022, when OpenAI released the first consumer version of ChatGPT to much fanfare—and, ultimately, over 100 million downloads within a few short months.
In reality, as WIRED readers know, the story of artificial intelligence stretches back decades. And the work informing today’s generative AI products, from chatbots to agents and beyond, has been more than a decade—of blood, sweat, tears, and furious rivalries—in the making.
It’s that recent history, told through the interweaving stories of three generative AI leaders—OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google—that’s chronicled in Kevin Roose’s compelling new book, The AGI Chronicles. Roose, a longtime tech journalist who most recently served as a columnist and podcast host for The New York Times, conducted more than 150 interviews with AI insiders to compile what he hopes becomes something of a historical document, an accurate, in-depth retelling of the people and the institutions, the bloodbath and the drama, that brought Silicon Valley to where it is to today.
I spoke to Roose in late September, a few days after he and Casey Newton—with whom Roose previously cohosted the New York Times’ Hard Fork podcast—announced the creation of their new media company Machine Gods Media, alongside a podcast distribution deal with NPR. We talked about what Roose and Newton hope to accomplish with the new show, why traditional media companies have a talent problem, and, of course, all things artificial intelligence.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
KATIE DRUMMOND: You and Casey Newton recently announced that you were launching a new media company, called Machine Gods Media. And your podcast is also called Machine Gods, correct?
KEVIN ROOSE: Yeah, a name so nice we used it twice.
When you first announced that you’d be leaving The New York Times, you described your vision for what you wanted to do as one that, quote, “takes AI progress seriously, is clear-eyed about the capabilities and risks of powerful AI systems, and tries to empower and entertain people in the face of radical uncertainty.”
As you look at the landscape of tech coverage and AI coverage, what’s missing from the reporting and commentary that you and Casey want to address with the new show?
We just feel like it was high time that two men had a place to talk about AI.
I've been saying this for years. I want more men talking about tech.
Look, there is obviously no shortage of podcasts and YouTube shows and mainstream media coverage of AI. It’s the biggest story in the world right now. But when Casey and I looked out at the media landscape, we saw some issues. One was there are people who just are getting very famous and having a lot of success saying that all this AI stuff that’s going on is fake, it’s hype, it’s a giant financial bubble, no one is using these tools, they’re not going to have any impact on the economy. You know, OpenAI is going to go bankrupt. Anthropic’s going to go bankrupt.
This is sort of a genre of popular criticism, and it’s not just a few people. I hear this from friends of mine who don’t pay close attention to tech news and just assume that what’s going on is just fleeting and trivial and that it will all go back to normal soon.
There’s another genre of AI coverage that is purely hype. It’s look at the 17 amazing ways that Claude can supercharge your enterprise SaaS business. You can go on LinkedIn and see example after example of people who are purely excited about this technology and don’t really care to talk about the risks.
We both thought there’s a large gap in the middle for what Casey calls AI realism, which is basically this idea that you can take AI seriously, acknowledge that the tools are powerful and impressive and in many cases dangerous, and that you can help people understand that and demystify this area without slipping into boosterism, and that you can also have a good time while you do it.
The show you announced recently is being published in partnership with NPR. Why was that the right partner?
A bunch of reasons. Both Casey and I are big fans of NPR. We like the fact that they have a broad independent reach and mandate. We like the fact that they’re going to let us own the show and make the creative decisions, and it will be a distribution partnership rather than a full acquisition, so we will still have some operating distance.
We think this is a really critical time and a really important story, and we like the idea that people might be in their cars just listening to their local NPR member station and happen on our podcast.
Maybe that’s going to be someone who works in policy, or maybe that’s going to be someone who is involved in local government. Maybe that’s going to be someone who has a very different point of view on AI. We don’t just want to have the opt-in, self-selected tech audience listen to us.
I am going to ask you a crass question. A Bloomberg report recently said you both were fielding offers of up to $5 million for the show. It’s a startling sum of money. Kevin, how much are you making?
It's not $5 million.
Is it more than $5 million?
So much more, Katie. No, look, they have made us a good offer. We could have gotten more money elsewhere.
When I heard NPR, I thought to myself, “There’s no way NPR’s giving those guys $5 million,” with all due respect to NPR.
Public radio is not traditionally where people go to get rich in media. We loved their new chief content officer, Nadine Zylstra. She’s just a total force of nature, and we’re very excited to work with her.
We thought they had a lot of things to offer us beyond money, like their distribution on radio. People don’t realize how big radio still is. The reach of radio, and especially public radio, is still quite large. We’ve had this show, Hard Fork, for the last four years. We built up a pretty good-size audience, but the Times owns that show and owns the feed.
We are looking to grow our show as quickly as possible, and we just thought that the combination of commitment to journalistic excellence, their wide distribution, and their investment in helping us grow the show was the right combination of factors.
This brings me to another thing I’m curious about: The idea that a great reporter, a great commentator, can spend time somewhere “traditional” like The New York Times. They can build a brand, and then they realize that they can just go do it themselves, and they don’t actually need that institution anymore to exist in the world as talent, and often to make a lot more money than they would in traditional media. What’s your take on that?
Look, I don't have anything bad to say about The New York Times. I had nine wonderful years there. It was my second stint at the Times. I’ve spent the vast majority of my career at The New York Times and inside these big media institutions.
I do think we are entering this moment where at least for some portion of the audience, they want to connect with individuals more than institutions. We’ve just seen this in wave after wave. I don't know. I am not doing this for ideological reasons. I’m doing this because I thought it was a really exciting opportunity. But I do think that organizations that want to retain and attract very talented people will just need to be more flexible about these kinds of arrangements.
Some people aren’t going to wanna give up their Substacks and go inside a media institution. Some people aren’t going to want to have all of their work published by one publication. I think there are some media organizations that are starting to experiment with different, more flexible ways of bringing people in part way or having them maintain their independent operation but also contribute on an ongoing basis.
I think there are a lot of ways this can work, but I think it all has to start from a recognition that the journalistic career path where you go in the mail room and you work your way up and you spend 25 years at the same employer and you eventually become an editor and then a manager of editors, that has broken down. That is regrettable. I don’t think that’s a good thing that it’s broken down, but it has broken down.
I think institutions should grapple with the fact that there’s now a generation of media entrepreneurs who just don’t find what they have to offer all that appealing.
When you think about the talent piece of that, when you think about AI, are you optimistic about journalism and the industry of journalism?
I am very optimistic about the application of AI to journalism. That is one place where I have wanted to do more experiments, not with having AI write for me or do all my reporting, but like ways of extending journalism using AI.
What's an example of an experiment you would love to do?
I have former colleagues at the Times who have done incredible document analysis on a scale that wouldn’t have been possible before, using satellite imagery to determine whether a munitions factory has moved or something like that.
That’s the kind of thing that I don’t do much in my own life but that I would like to see other organizations trying, because I think that’s really cool. I have used AI to research and edit and improve my own work for months now. I have found that very helpful. I think the caliber of my work is better, and I would love to see more institutions in the media experimenting with these tools to improve the output of their journalists. Not just like, you know, filling their websites with slop but actually helping these be tools to make journalists better.
I want to talk about your book, The AGI Chronicles. When did you decide “I’m going to commit years of my life and my career because there's a book here.” What was that moment for you when you realized that this was a big deal?
I know exactly when it was. It was early last year, 2025, and I was in the car on the Bay Bridge stuck in traffic, and it just kind of hit me, like an epiphany. It was like I have been following this story in all the incremental detail for years now.
I’ve interviewed all the major AI researchers and CEOs. I’ve spent time with the papers. I’ve gone to all of the companies and reported on what they’re doing. But there was this larger story that I was missing. I hadn’t really zoomed out and tried to take a more panoramic view of something that was just weird.
I felt living in the Bay Area, being immersed in San Francisco tech culture, I had kind of gotten acclimated to that, and it no longer seemed as strange to me that there were these companies racing to build the machine superintelligence that could either save or destroy humanity.
Right.
I sometimes feel like I am in Los Alamos, New Mexico, in 1943 when the Manhattan Project rolls into town, and I’ve just kinda got my lawn chair and I’m looking at trucks rolling in and trying to make sense of what’s happening.
I believe that this technology is important and that the people and the companies who built it will be important historically. So when I thought about who is actually doing the work of writing all of this down, it was nobody. Nobody was doing it.
I just felt like it would be a tragedy if all this just disappeared in a bunch of Signal messages and Slacks that auto-delete, and if we just end up with no durable historical record of this really strange decade in AI when things went from not working at all to threatening the future of humanity.
I spent about a year reporting and writing. I talked to more than 150 people. I should have probably taken more time, because it was very hard and intense. But I think what came out of it was an artifact that people and future AI systems can look back at to say, “Here is how this happened. Here’s who made it happen. Here were the key decisions and moments along the way.”
The book follows three key companies, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, in their pursuit of this technology. What were your big-picture learnings about those companies and the key differences between them that you think is important for people to know?
The companies are very different from one another, both in the makeup of their personnel and also in their ambitions.
Let’s start with Google, because they’re the oldest. They have had for decades now an advanced AI research effort. They were pioneers in AI. They developed the transformer, which is the T in ChatGPT, the sort of foundational technology that all of this other stuff rests on, and then there were these two guys, Elon Musk and Sam Altman, who got very worried about how well they were doing, about Google racing ahead, and they decided to start OpenAI …
To imagine that now …
Yeah, it’s wild, and we have the emails. It's all there in the record where they're basically like, “We have to start a lab that’s going to beat them or at least challenge them so that they don’t run away with the whole game.” So they start OpenAI, and they do a couple years of that, and then this guy at OpenAI, Dario Amodei, he takes six of his colleagues, and they leave and start Anthropic basically to make sure that OpenAI doesn’t get to this critical threshold of AGI first. So the whole industry spawned out of itself. These people all used to work together, and now they run these companies that are mortal enemies. Like, I was shocked. This was actually my biggest surprise. I thought this was more like Coke and Pepsi, but this is not a buddy-buddy industry. This is like a blood feud.
From all of the reporting that you did, who do you trust? Who do you trust with our future in the context of artificial intelligence?
I don’t trust any single person.
None of them.
What I learned through reporting this book is these are people, they are flawed, they are fallible, they have moments of weakness. Their motives are never 100 percent pure. Some of these people are quite nice. Some of them are very thoughtful. I think we have in some ways gotten very lucky with the people who are running these AI companies, who I think are, on the whole, much better suited to build powerful technology and release it into the world than the social media barons were.
So there is a marked difference between the Facebook era and this AI era?
Oh, yeah. For one, they are just way less naive. You know, the social media guys came in and they said, “We’re going to change the world. We’re going to free communication from the bottlenecks that hold it back. We’re going to distribute the benefits of technology to everyone.”
And they really didn't start thinking about the problems until they were being questioned in front of Congress.
I will say some of these AI guys talk a lot about saving the world. They talk a lot about how great this will be for humanity.
If you go back and look at the founding emails of OpenAI, they have been very consistent that they think this is a potentially very dangerous technology.
Now, they’re racing toward it, so maybe their words don’t mean that much. But I think you can’t accuse them of being naive, because they just have such a long track record, all of them, of saying that, “Yeah, this could be great for humanity, but it’s not a given that it will be, and we need to build it really carefully and thoughtfully to make sure that it's actually going to turn out well for us.”
What kind of responsibility do you think falls on their shoulders in the context of AI safety?
This was something that I’ve asked all of them about at various points. Like, why don’t you just stop?
Yeah.
Why do you get up every day and try to make these systems more powerful if you’re worried it could end the world in some cases?
Some of them, including Dario and Sam, genuinely believe that this technology is inevitable. The recipe for AI is not that hard. You get a lot of compute, you get a lot of data, you build the right scaffolding and grow the model in this organic process of stochastic gradient descent and reinforcement learning, and out comes a superintelligent model.
It is their sincere belief that it’s not that hard to build this stuff if you understand the basics and that, because it's not that hard, someone will do it. And whether that someone is a US AI company or a Chinese AI company or a terrorist group or an academic research lab, someone will do this.
So it is in the best interests of humanity for someone who thinks a lot about safety to be the first to get there, because they can set standards for the rest of the industry. Now, I don’t know if I fully buy that, but that is their logic, and that is the reason that they feel validated getting up and doing this every day.
The book ends in an interesting way, and I have a couple questions about that. It ends, essentially, with you saying, “I really hope these guys get it right. I really hope that they slow down so that I can keep living my life the way I live it now.” It’s funny timing that the book is coming out right as these very acute conversations around AI safety are happening, and it feels like every other day a company is disclosing some new breach, something that went wrong with one of their models. How scared are you right now, Kevin Roose?
I am actually feeling quite hopeful right now relative to where I was a few months ago, and it’s largely because we are now having this conversation.
There have been people, including many of the people I spoke to for the book, who have been worried about runaway AI, rogue AI, a possible AI takeover for 10, 15 years, who have been trying to sound the alarm about this, and no one believed them. Outside their little bubble of AI safety people, everyone was sort of like, “Yeah, yeah, yeah.” Now I feel like we have finally reached this point where this stuff is inside the Overton window.
I think that some of what I see on social media and some of what I see in the news media is really hyperbolic and is really dramatic. I’m not saying that the stakes aren’t dramatic, but my assessment of the situation is that if something does go horribly wrong with artificial intelligence, it will be much more boring than we might think, and it will have more to do with human error than we are sometimes attributing.
Yeah, I totally understand that, and to be clear, I’m not saying I know exactly the risks that we should be most afraid of. I just think there’s this whole category of risk that has kind of been written off or downplayed or just, you know, those are just those weirdos in Berkeley talking about it. Now we can have conversations about it.
People are worried, they’re taking this seriously, and I think we really have a window here where we can actually make some changes or take some steps to make sure that this goes better for humanity. I don’t think that was possible a couple of months ago.
So I think that’s why I’m feeling more hopeful, because even though I think objectively the models are getting worse and scarier and more dangerous, we are also much better positioned to recognize and talk about and perhaps prevent those risks.
In that last page of the book, and I don’t want to ascribe an emotion to you, but I felt fear there from you and a reluctance to see your life change too quickly. I think that is something that is very much universal.
Absolutely. I think this is where the people inside the AI bubble do not understand the world. I think the people at the AI companies building this technology are generally people who enjoy the prospect of large, unannounced social change.
Unannounced social change. Hard to imagine a bigger nightmare for me personally.
Like, they love when things get weird. That’s part of why they moved to San Francisco. They wanna live in the future. The prospect of radical upheaval does not scare them.
Doesn’t that seem like a huge problem to you?
Yes, because normal people don’t think like that. Normal people want to live a life that is recognizable to them. They want their kids to grow up in a society that resembles the one that they grew up in. We don’t manage change very well as a society, and we never have. But I think this is why I wish that there had been more types of people involved in the critical conversations around this technology.
Because, as I said, 50 people in San Francisco, give or take, made all of the relevant decisions, and they are not a representative sample. They are very weird. They see the world differently. They have a higher tolerance for change than most people, and I think it led to them making some decisions that we can’t really take back now.
I mean, do you think that if two years ago we had had more philosophers, more artists, more creatives, more journalists, lawyers, whoever it may be, involved in those conversations, that it really would’ve moved the needle when there is so much money on the other side of that conversation?
I guess what I’m saying is that, sure, it’s all well and good for a broader coalition to be having those conversations, but Greg Brockman’s donations to the Trump administration get him that phone call, right? They have the president’s phone number. The access to the decisionmakers is bestowed upon those 50 people in San Francisco by virtue of their wealth and their power.
I think it can help at the margins, and I’ll give you an example. One of the people I write about at some length in the book is Amanda Askell. She is a longtime employee at Anthropic and was at OpenAI before that. You just had a story in WIRED about searching for the most powerful woman in Silicon Valley. I think she’s gotta be up there in the top two or three.
She has been in charge of Claude’s character. They call her the Claude mother at Anthropic. She’s a virtue ethicist. She has a PhD in philosophy. She went into AI specifically to think about this question of what should a good AI system do? How should it act? What values should it represent? How should it decline to do certain things or volunteer to do certain things? How can you instill something like virtue ethics in a chatbot? This was a very fringe area of research. She was, to my knowledge, the first person ever to do this kind of work inside one of these AI companies.
It has resulted in them having a really sophisticated way of thinking about the morality and the ethics of Claude. She now has a whole team. They have many people that are devoted to this, and I think it has probably made Claude not just safer and better behaved, but has also inspired other labs to hire their own philosophers and come up with their own ways of training their AIs for something like moral goodness.
I think there’s a really strong argument for having lots of people from lots of different disciplines engaging with this technology, because it should not just be engineers doing this.
As someone with a bachelor of arts degree in philosophy, I have to say it is a boom time for my people.
There was a lot in the book to me that was troubling. What stands out to you that is hopeful when you think about the book, when you think about the technology? Aside from the fact that we may actually make some meaningful progress toward regulation, was there something you discovered in your reporting that made you feel optimistic?
A lot of the optimism that I feel around this stuff has to do with science and medicine. I lost my father to cancer. I know lots of other people who have lost loved ones to rare diseases that have not been cured, not because we lack ingenuity, but because it’s just a question of resources and manpower. I think that AI can do incredible things for people who suffer from disease. I don’t think that’s all marketing BS.
There’s a story in the book about the DeepMind protein-folding AI system that won the Nobel Prize, and there’s this incredibly touching moment where a mother of a kid who has a life-threatening genetic condition writes to the DeepMind researchers after this breakthrough and asks them, “Could this help my kid?” They have to give her the honest answer, which is probably not, because this stuff takes time. You have to get it through clinical trials. Even if you have these amazing breakthroughs in science, you have to design the drugs, you have to test the drugs, you have to get the drugs approved.
It can be a decade before these things actually make it to saving people’s lives. But I want that to happen faster. I want there to be more AI-designed drugs. I want us to get them to market quickly. I don’t want people to suffer from the same diseases that have killed previous generations.
So that’s where I feel a lot of optimism right now. Ask me in two weeks, maybe it’ll be something else, but right now that’s where I’m feeling good.
I’m curious about your own process with AI. You have published three books prior to this one. Your first was published in 2009, well before any of this technology was available. How did it change the book-writing process for you? I know you're very open with how you use AI, sometimes to much controversy among your journalistic peers.
There’s a whole section in the beginning of the book about how I did and did not use AI, ’cause I thought it was important first and foremost to be transparent.
Kevin, I’m going to be transparent with you. I ran your book through Pangram.
How did it do?
The book is written by a human being. Presumably by you.
Yeah, it was written by a very tired, overworked, underslept human being. I also had a researcher help me with this, Jasmine Sun, and had a bunch of great human editors at FSG.
The book is fully human-written, but how did you use the tech?
I had a giant notebook on NotebookLM filled with all of my research materials, interview transcripts, magazine articles, and academic papers. And the most basic way I would use that is just to query it about things that I needed to know. So like, “Give me all of the stories that I’ve heard about the pre-training of GPT-4,” and then it would pop back a list, sort of like a supercharged search function.
I also did it to help with some reporting tasks, like who would the three people have been in the room when this decision was made, and what are their contact details? It helped with organizing my notes, with fact-checking. Actually, at the end, I had a human fact-checker, but I also had an AI swarm doing fact-checks and catching some things that honestly neither I nor the human fact-checker had caught.
Then I used it for editorial feedback. I have what I call a Council of Claudes, which is my team of Claudes that are assigned to different personalities and vantage points. So I have one who’s a hardcore LLM skeptic who goes through the draft and tells me, “Oh, this is what I object to. You’re anthropomorphizing here. It’s not really thinking here.” I have one that’s a Kurzweil-type futurist that wants to expand the vision of the future in the book. Like some of this was just slop and probably wasted more time than it saved, but there were a couple things that the Council of Claudes said to me where I was like, “Oh yeah, that’s a good point. I should go back and revise that.”
How do you think about the premium on human-generated writing? Do you think in five years, the average person will care that Kevin wrote this book as opposed to an AI writing that book? Do you think it matters to people?
I do. I think it matters a lot to people. I know this because they’ve done studies where when people read a sample of writing that is generated by AI, but they don’t know it’s generated by AI, they give it very high marks. They prefer it to human-written text in a blind test. But then the minute you tell them this was generated by AI, they hate it.
Their approval of it plummets. I think this has a lot to do with human psychology. We like to think that people work really hard to make something for us, that it represents their authentic view. So people will still continue to be offended when they find out that their favorite writer has used AI to generate their latest book or essay or whatever. But I think that’s basically only if they detect it, only if they can tell, and I don’t think they can tell or will be able to for much longer. I think as long as Pangram exists, it will probably be a useful tool. But I also think that, in the abstract, people just don’t know the difference. When you tell them the difference, they care, but before that, they don’t.
That’s really interesting. It is the psychological value of wanting to know that someone’s fingerprints were on something and wanting to know that you were getting their voice and not the voice of Claude.
Totally.
I think it’s important for writers to show their process for this reason. To talk about and literally film themselves working so that people can connect with the labor involved in making something. I think that’s going to be important for humans of all creative stripes.
Is that going to be a social video series that you and Casey come up with?
Yeah, I’m streaming myself writing 16 hours a day on Twitch. Go check it out.
Sounds like hell. Kevin, congratulations on the book. Thank you so much for being here. This was fascinating.
Thank you, Katie. You’re the best.

Russia testing Europe's defenses below threshold of open war, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:29:35 UTC
19:29:35 KST

Russia is testing how far it can push Europe without triggering open war — from drones crossing NATO airspace to sabotage and cyberattacks across the continent. Experts warn that Europe has strengthened its defenses since 2022, but key gaps remain, including in air defense, communications, intelligence, and joint command.
Russia is testing the limits of Europe's security without formally crossing into open war. Its attacks on Ukrainian cities have intensified in recent months, including strikes on civilian infrastructure. Russian drones entering NATO airspace have also become a recurring occurrence, while Western officials have raised the alarm over a rise in Moscow's hybrid operations across Europe.
In September, Germany accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport in early August. The incidents are raising a broader question: how far Moscow can escalate its pressure on European countries without prompting a direct military response.
The Kyiv Independent spoke with participants of the Ukraine Recovery Lab, sponsored by Erste Foundation and organized as part of the European Forum Alpbach in Austria, held Aug. 24-Sept 4.
What may look like a string of hybrid incidents increasingly resembles a sub-threshold war against Europe, says Olena Davlikanova, a security policy expert.
The Everywhere War Tracker records a sustained campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks, military provocations, and airspace violations, which has grown more intensive and audacious since 2024 as Moscow has tested how far it can push Europe without triggering open conflict.
"Russia is waging a war against the European model of freedom, equality, and solidarity, and against the institutions that sustain it, especially the EU. This is a war fought in small steps," says Leopold Schmertzing, а strategic foresight and security and defense policy expert.
"I struggle to see it ending without a fundamental change in either the current Russian model or the European one."
Schmertzing argues that, despite Europe contributing far more to Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine than it did to earlier conflicts, most Europeans still experience it as a war happening somewhere else.
"My fear is that we will only fully wake up when our own capitals are attacked and our citizens are killed. By then, it will be too late to prepare," he added.
Experts believe Europe is better prepared for a potential confrontation with Russia than it was in 2022, but important gaps remain. Air defense, drones, communications, intelligence and joint command remain weak points, they say, while European militaries have yet to fully adapt to the realities of modern warfare.
Ukraine's experience shows that unmanned systems can have an outsized impact, but European defense spending has yet to reflect that lesson.
More than 80% of Russian targets destroyed on the battlefield are hit by drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in January.
"That is how the modern war looks like," says Kateryna Mykhalko, managing director of the German-Ukrainian defense industry consortium New Age Defense.
"At the same time, the technology delivering 80% of battlefield results receives only roughly 2% of European defense budgets," she adds.
The EU and Ukraine have sought to deepen cooperation in the sector. The EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance aims to accelerate the development and production of drones and counter-drone systems, combining Ukraine’s battlefield experience with Europe’s industrial capacity.
For Europe, the challenge is therefore twofold: closing military capability gaps while developing a response to forms of Russian aggression that experts believe are already unfolding across the continent.
"Russia is a hard nut to crack because it is deeply vulnerable in some respects and remarkably insulated in others," Schmertzing says. "We have a great deal to learn from Ukraine about where pressure works and where it doesn't."

WHO says ‘low’ risk in Russia following plague reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:29:25 UTC
19:29:25 KST

This undated photo released in 2019 by the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East, shows the institute workers in a lab. (The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East via AP)
The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Oct. 6 that it deemed the public health risk in Russia to be low, following reports that a laboratory technician had died of plague.
A worker at the anti-plague institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk region reportedly died of pneumonic plague, and news of their death sparked alarm last week.
“The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole, and very low for the WHO European region,” the U.N. health agency’s spokesman Christian Lindmeier said.
“A woman who worked at a laboratory in Irkutsk oblast has died, and the authorities are looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death,” he told a press briefing in Geneva.
The lab technician, named as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, worked at an institute that studies dangerous pathogens in a part of Siberia where plague occurs naturally in wild animals, the spokesman said.
“The illness initially presented as a typical acute respiratory viral infection,” he said.
Lindmeier said Russian authorities had identified the people she was in contact with and had been monitoring them.
“According to the test results, no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts,” he said.
“WHO is following the situation closely, working with headquarters to keep other countries informed,” and stands ready to support the Russian authorities if they ask.
Russia’s consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor insisted yesterday that a document circulating online indicating heightened sanitary-epidemiological measures and restrictions in the Irkutsk region was fake.

Portugal's PM seeks to keep Costa, Metsola in EU top jobs until 2029
LISBON, Oct 6 - Portugal is pushing to reappoint Antonio Costa and Roberta Metsola as heads of the European Council and European Parliament, respectively, Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said on Tuesday, saying that continuity would strengthen the European Union's stability.

Hong Kong’s Generation Y unhappiest amid housing and economic pressures, poll finds

Hong Kong’s Generation Y unhappiest amid housing and economic pressures, poll finds
Hong Kong’s happiness index falls to 5.87, staying below passing level of six out of 10 for fourth year, but remains above 2024 low
Hong Kong’s Generation Y residents – those aged 30 to 45 – are the city’s unhappiest age group, largely because of dissatisfaction with economic and housing conditions, a poll has found.
The Hong Kong Happiness Index stood at 5.87 out of 10, according to a survey of 1,039 adults conducted by HK.WeCare, an initiative under non-profit organisation Wofoo Social Enterprises.
The score remained below the passing level for a fourth consecutive year, despite an overall upward trend since 2024.
More than 40 per cent of residents reported moderate to severe depressive symptoms. Respondents also reported only moderate levels of community belonging and trust, scoring 3.13 and 2.81, respectively, out of five. Both factors were found to be directly linked to happiness.

‘Situation Is Changing Dynamically’: Ukraine Says It Holds Tactical Initiative Near Vovchansk
