A Ukrainian military spokesperson on Tuesday refused to directly comment on the battlefield situation east of Vovchansk, where much of the fighting is taking place in the gray zone.
Viktor Trehubov, spokesperson for the Joint Forces, said the situation is “changing quite dynamically.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are currently refraining from actively commenting on this area because most of the operations there involve a struggle for control of the gray zone, and the situation is changing quite dynamically,” Trehubov told Ukrinform.
Trehubov was responding to an assessment by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) that Ukrainian forces had retaken around 10 square kilometers (4 square miles) of wooded terrain east of Vovchansk.
He warned that battlefield information can become outdated even before it is publicly reported.
“I would wait for a clearer stabilization of the situation,” Trehubov said, adding that he believes Kyiv has gained a tactical upper hand.
“After the summer, the Russians have somewhat run out of steam and reduced the intensity of their offensive operations. They have moved on to creative psychotherapy – drawing fantastic maps where they control Bilyi Kolodiaz, Vovchanski Khutory, Polohy and even Kupiansk,” he said.
Vovchansk, located in the northern Kharkiv region just south of the Russian border, is a strategically important stronghold.
Russia’s Jet Drones Kill 1, Injure 8 in Kharkiv Amid 205-Drone Overnight Barrage
Control of the area gives Russia positions from which to pressure Ukrainian defenses and threaten deeper advances toward the region, while forcing Ukraine to maintain significant forces along its northeastern frontier.
Russian forces have repeatedly sought to push Ukrainian troops farther from the border and toward positions from which Kharkiv could come under greater military pressure.
The Vovchansk and Kupiansk sectors are also part of interconnected Russian efforts in the Kharkiv region. Russian military planners have sought to establish positions in the region that could facilitate further advances toward Velykyi Burluk and the Oskil River, potentially putting additional pressure on Ukrainian positions farther south.
Ukraine’s preferred outcome, Trehubov said, is to push Russian forces back to the international border, which would reduce the threat of infiltration and shelling against territory between the border and Kharkiv.
Ukrainian forces repelled four Russian attacks in the Southern Slobozhansky direction on Oct. 5, according to Ukrinform.

Keith Haring retrospective opens at Rome’s Palazzo Braschi with more than 140 works

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:28:22 UTC

Pop artist Keith Haring began his career covering New York City's subways with his instantly recognisables designs. Now 140 of his artworks are on display at an exhibition in Rome.
The exhibition includes early works when he first began creating art in New York, to sculptures, paintings and art that reflects his activism. Among the work on show are the famous ‘Subway Drawings’ that kicked off Haring's career when he drew with chalk on New York subway panels.
There are also the iconic panels he painted with spray paint in 1984 along Manhattan’s FDR Drive, as well as his monumental 'Altarpiece: Life of Christ', a triptych altarpiece made during the final year of his life.
‘Keith Haring: Retrospect’ runs until 11 April 2027 at the Museo di Roma at Palazzo Braschi.

Pneumatic, pneumonic, whatever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:28:19 UTC
19:28:19 KST

Pneumatic, pneumonic, whatever
« previous post | next post »
"Trump calls reported pneumatic plague outbreak ‘big problem for Russia’: ‘The microbes and the germs have gotten stronger’", NY Post 10/5/2026.
President Trump gave an ominous assessment of the suspected outbreak of pneumonic plague in Siberia Monday, calling it a “big problem for Russia” and adding cryptically that “the microbes and the germs have gotten stronger.”
The article's author, Steven Nelson, used the conventional term pneumonic plague, but the editor (?) who wrote the headline changed the word-internal '…on…' into '…at…' to get pneumatic plague.
In the press encounter cited by the article, Donald Trump simply refers to the outbreak as "pneumonia".
The Wikipedia article on "Pneumonic plague" surveys the various forms of the disease and the terminology involved. And Wiktionary tells us that pneumonic refers to the lungs, whereas pneumatic refers to "air or other gasses".
We'd make it easier for our editors if we used more native compounds in place of Greek, as German has lungenpest for our "pneumonic plague".
For an informed discussion of the actual dangers associated with this case, see here.

Belgian physicist Francis Halzen wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:27:13 UTC
19:27:13 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to the Belgian physicist Francis Halzen on Tuesday for his contributions to IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of astrophysical high-energy neutrinos.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said Halzen was awarded the prize "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin."
Halzen recognized that the ice at the South Pole could be used to detect particles known as neutrinos, a vision considered "fundamental" to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors.
Using IceCube, researchers can detect neutrinos produced by extremely energetic processes in the distant universe.
Extremely high-energy neutrinos can travel without changing direction or losing significant energy, allowing researchers to gather information about the universe that cannot be obtained through other means.
Halzen was born in Belgium in 1944 and is a professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the US.

Drax datacentre could create nearly twice the yearly emissions of all Gatwick flights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:27:03 UTC
19:27:03 KST

Drax’s planned datacentre could produce nearly double the emissions of all flights out of Gatwick airport each year by burning 4.9m tonnes of wood annually, an analysis has shown.
Campaigners say this would make it “one of the dirtiest datacentres out there”.
Last year, the energy company Drax unveiled plans to convert part of its biomass power plant in North Yorkshire into a datacentre in response to the increase in demand for AI capability.
AI datacentres use a massive amount of electricity to power servers and cooling equipment, and to run facility systems. There are 315 datacentres in the queue to connect to the UK’s electricity grid, representing 73GW of demand. This is almost double the peak winter energy demand for the entire UK.
In public documents, Drax says it is developing options for a 1.2GW datacentre, with 100MW of this energy coming from the electricity grid and the rest from its own power station.
The Drax power station currently burns millions of tonnes of imported wood to create energy. This has been touted as a clean way of producing energy that could even result in “negative emissions”, as replacement forests take up CO2 from the air when they are grown.
However, scientists and environmental experts strongly contest this accounting approach, with researchers finding such systems could take 150 years to be “carbon negative”.
Based on information in Drax’s 2025 annual report, the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) estimated that if built, Drax’s datacentre will require 4.9m tonnes of wood each year.
The campaign group calculated the total emissions from this to be 8.6m tonnes of CO2 a year. This is based on an assumption that the datacentre would run at a constant rate for all hours of the year.
This is nearly double the total CO2 emissions of all flights from Gatwick airport, which measured 4.79m tonnes in 2024.
Matt Williams, a senior advocate for NRDC, said this would make it “one of the dirtiest datacentres out there”.
Oliver Hayes, head of policy at the campaign group Global Action Plan, said, “Burning millions of trees to power server farms is indefensible.”
The datacentre has not yet entered the formal planning process but Drax said it could be fully operational from 2031 if secured the necessary consents.
“The government must urgently set minimum standards for datacentres and rule out dirty energy generation like burning trees,” Williams said.
There is growing pressure for more transparency over how these energy intensive datacentres will align with the government’s legally binding net zero targets.
In response to previous reports that just two planned datacentres in Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, Toby Perkins, a Labour MP and chair of the Commons environmental audit committee, said: “Without the right measures in place, datacentres could represent a serious threat to the environment and to our legally binding climate goals.”
Hayes said the absence of coordinated government policy was a “dereliction of duty”.
“The only sensible solution at this point is a moratorium on datacentres until very basic questions about how many we need, what for, where, and how pollution will be avoided are answered satisfactorily by the government,” he added.
The government has previously ruled out issuing a moratorium on datacentres, stating that doing so would send investment and good jobs abroad. In Scotland, MPs voted in September to pause all new datacentre planning applications for up to a year until a national strategy can be developed.
A Drax spokesperson said: “The potential plans for datacentres at Drax Power Station can support UK economic growth as well as helping meet the government’s ambitions for industrial renewal, in places like North Yorkshire, as well as AI sovereignty.
“NRDC are a longstanding anti-biomass campaign group and have no positive vision for our Selby site. Their inaccurate assertions are not independently verified and are rooted in basic errors regarding the international standards for GHG accounting of biomass and bioenergy and on the potential datacentres’ power mix.”

The talks focused on bilateral relations, security, the development of infrastructure links, economic cooperation, and historical dialogue.
The meeting was held on 2 October. Separately, a broader discussion took place with representatives from the ministries of the Interior and Administration, Culture and National Heritage, Infrastructure, Energy, Climate and Environment, as well as Education. The interlocutors agreed that the arrangements adopted during the Polish–German intergovernmental consultations in Berlin on 1 December 2025 should be consistently implemented. They stressed the importance of joint measures to strengthen the security of NATO’s eastern flank and emphasised the urgency to improve Poland-bound transport links.
“We need road and rail connectivity that is fit for the 21st century. It is crucial for not only people-to-people contacts or economic cooperation, but also enhanced military mobility,” said Henryka Mościcka-Dendys, the Chair of the Council for Cooperation with the Federal Republic of Germany.
Historical issues, including the commemoration of the Poles who perished during World War II and the restitution of the looted cultural goods, were also high on the agenda. The matter of teaching the Polish language in Germany was discussed as well.
***
The Council for Cooperation with the Federal Republic of Germany is an auxiliary consultative body established by the Order no. 6 of the President of the Council of Ministers of 23 January 2026 (“Monitor Polski” Official Gazette of 2026, item 136). On 30 January 2026, Henryka Mościcka-Dendys was designated as the Chair of the Council.
The Council is composed of representatives of selected ministries: the Ministry of Development and Technology, the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of the Interior and Administration, the Ministry of Climate and Environment, the Ministry of National Education, the Ministry of Infrastructure, and the Ministry of Science and Higher Education. The chair of the Polish limb of the Polish–German Intergovernmental Commission for Regional and Cross-Border Cooperation and, optionally, the chair of the Polish–German Parliamentary Group also take part in the Council’s work.

Bulgaria searches for missing crew as drones hit two Black Sea ships
Bulgarian authorities on Tuesday launched a search for missing crew members of a boat that sank in its economic zone in the Black Sea after drones hit two merchant vessels. Black Sea shipping has been hit by growing fallout from the war in Ukraine in recent months.
Bulgarian authorities launched a major search on Tuesday for the missing crew of a ship that sank in the Black Sea after drones hit two vessels in what the prime minister slammed as an "absolutely unacceptable" attack.
The dual strike came a day after another ship caught fire and sank off the Romanian coast, killing one and leaving one missing, in what Ukraine said was a drone attack launched by Russia. Black Sea shipping has been hit by growing fallout from the Ukraine-Russia war in recent months.
A search operation was launched 70 nautical miles east of the coastal town of Byala, authorities said. The ship that sank was Togolese-flagged, according to the Maritime.bg specialised website.
The second ship, registered in Palau, was set alight by the drone but its Turkish and Indian crew members have been rescued.
A boat that rushed to the scene discovered overturned life rafts and life jackets near the ship that sank, but no members of the crew have been found, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told reporters, without specifying how many people were missing.
The attack "constitutes a flagrant violation of maritime law and, more broadly, of the rules of navigation", Radev said.
"Such an attack within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable," he told reporters.
"Two merchant vessels were attacked by sea and air drones. This has been formally confirmed by the crews, and both ships were hit," Radev added.
European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen said Tuesday that attacks on civilian shipping in the Black Sea were "unacceptable".
"While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning," von der Leyen wrote online.
A Bulgarian ferry, the Dioskuria, which was in the area, witnessed the explosion of the first ship and proceeded to the scene, joined by a Bulgarian Navy fast boat, which rescued two crew, one suffering from burns and the other from a head injury.
The other 16 crew members were rescued by border guard patrol boats.
Eleven of the rescued crew are Turkish and seven are Indian, according to Radev.

"As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict," Radev added.

Asos customers receive ‘hack’ message threatening to leak personal data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:24:31 UTC
19:24:31 KST

Asos is investigating unauthorised access to its app system after shoppers received a notification claiming hackers had “fully compromised” its data.
The online fashion retailer said basic personal information including name and contact details might have been accessed by an unidentified third party but it did not believe that payment card records or passwords had been compromised.
It said in a statement: “We are investigating unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms that we use to communicate with customers. We took immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms and are working with our internal and external specialist advisers, as well as all relevant authorities.
“Our website and app are operating as normal, with no current disruption to any aspects of our operations. Customer trust is incredibly important to us, and if the situation changes an update will be provided as appropriate.”
The value of Asos’s shares on the London Stock Exchange dived more than 14% after thousands of customers received a notification titled “Asos hacked” with a link that sent them to the Telegram messaging service.
Shares later recovered to about 11% down after Asos said it had cybersecurity insurance with a large global provider, including business continuity insurance. However, the company added: “It is too early to quantify any potential impact on trading.”
The message sent out to customers said: “Dear Asos DPO [data protection officer] and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance.”
Snowflake is a cloud platform used to store, process and analyse data including transactions and demographic information such as clothing sizes and body measurements. It also enables push notifications to phones.
The Telegram channel operated by the purported hackers, who have named themselves the Xuanye Group, carried a message assuring Asos customers that “payment information is not affected” and a further post stating “the app is safe to use”.
Indicating that Asos had been set some form of deadline, the post added: “The incident involves customer information, it is safe on our server, and it will not be touched for a designated period.”
The National Cyber Security Centre, part of the government’s GCHQ intelligence agency, is offering its assistance to Asos.
Dray Agha, the senior manager of security operations at Huntress, an online security firm, said: ““Sending a ransom demand directly to consumer devices is an aggressive extortion tactic designed to force the business into a quick negotiation. I strongly advise shoppers to watch out for targeted phishing attempts while we wait for official confirmation of a data breach.”
The link directed Asos customers to a Telegram channel apparently operated by the Xuanye Group. Cyber experts said they had not heard of the group before and the push notification might be an attempt to grab wider attention.
“It’s not unusual to see new groups emerge, and often they wait until they have what they see as a significant opportunity before they announce themselves so as to enter the ecosystem with ‘credibility’,” said Aiden Sinnott, the principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity firm Sophos.
Xuanye had not been mentioned before on hacker forums or other Telegram channels. Sophos added.
Marijus Briedis, the chief technology officer at the online service provider NordVPN, said: “High-profile cyber incidents create ideal conditions for phishing attacks. Criminals may exploit the publicity by sending emails and texts claiming to be from Asos, perhaps asking customers to reset a password, confirm payment details, check an order or claim a refund.”
The potential hack comes after a string of British retailers, including Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods, suffered cyber incidents last year. M&S and the Co-op experienced stock shortages and the former was forced to close its website for several weeks as it battled to ensure its systems were clean.

Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad: All to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:21:53 UTC
19:21:53 KST

Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad: All to know
The US Army is averse to capital punishment and has not carried out an execution in decades.
United States President Donald Trump has approved the death by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan, a former army officer convicted of carrying out a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, an army base in Texas.
The move, if it proceeds, will revive executions in the army, which has not carried one out since 1961.
Death sentences, as well as executions in the US military, are rare and require presidential approval.
Under the army’s code of military justice, premeditated murder does carry the death penalty, but the process is often strict and prolonged.
However, the Trump administration has shown more willingness to seek death penalties for serious crimes, including against civilians.
Here’s what we know about the case:
What is the presidential order?
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had initially recommended an execution order for Hasan, and Trump has now approved it, according to an X statement posted by Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell.
Parnell said the time and date of the execution will be set by Army Secretary Adam Telle, who is serving in an acting capacity.
“Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” he wrote.
What happened at Fort Hood?
On November 5, 2009, the US-born army major, Hasan, a psychiatrist in the force, walked into an army processing centre in Fort Hood, shouted “Allahu Akbar” (God is great) and opened fire on fellow staff members waiting to get medical attention.
Thirteen people were killed, including a pregnant soldier, and 32 others were wounded during 10 minutes of shooting. Analysts have called it the worst shooting at a US military base targeting members of armed forces.
Hasan was shot several times after two officers engaged him and remains paralysed from the waist down.
What happened during the trial?
Hasan was immediately court-martialled, and military prosecutors, from the start, sought the death penalty against him.
However, the process would play out over the course of several years even after his conviction – largely because the US military is averse to capital punishment.
During the trial, Hasan represented himself and admitted to the attacks, saying he was trying to stop deployments to Afghanistan and the killing of his fellow Muslims. He was due to be deployed weeks later.
Investigations revealed Hasan had exchanged emails with Yemeni-American scholar Anwar al-Awlaki, accused of ties to al-Qaeda, before the shooting. He had also repeatedly voiced opposition to the US wars in Iraq and Afghanistan to colleagues and the treatment of Muslims in the army.
Hasan made little effort to defend himself, and his assigned lawyers claimed his testimony aided the opposing side.
He was charged and convicted on 13 counts of premeditated murder in 2013, and jurors recommended the maximum sentence of death. Controversially, Hasan was charged with “workplace violence” because the military justice code does not address the crime of “terrorism”.
The judgement was further delayed by appeals mandated by the military, not because Hasan sought them.
In 2020, the US Army Court of Criminal Appeals upheld the death penalty for Hasan, and in 2023, the US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces did the same. In March 2025, the US Supreme Court denied a mandatory petition for a judicial review.
In September 2025, Hegseth announced he was seeking presidential approval for Hasan’s execution.
At the time, there was no report of Hegseth specifically seeking death by firing squad.
The president holds the ultimate authority to specify the designated method of execution.
Other forms of execution could have been lethal injection or hanging, which the US military has used in the past.
What next?
While Trump’s approval will begin a series of steps towards preparing for the execution, Hasan can still put the process on hold for years with an appeal in the civilian federal court system.
However, that might be unlikely as Hasan made no effort to defend himself during the trial.
He has been remanded to the US Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas, where three other men have also been on the military death row for years.
Among them is Hasan Akbar, convicted of two counts of murder after attacking fellow army members on a Kuwait base in 2003, during the invasion of Iraq.
Another is the convicted serial killer and rapist Ronald Gray, who was found guilty of four counts of murder and eight counts of rape in 2008. He was approved for execution in the same year under President George W Bush, but the process was put on hold by a judge.
Timothy Hennis, a former sergeant, was convicted in 2010 of a triple murder and is also on death row.
The last military execution took place in 1961, when former soldier John Bennett was hanged for the rape of an 11-year-old girl.

Ohio early voting begins with US Congress control on the line
MEDINA, OHIO, Oct 6 - Early voting begins on Tuesday in Ohio, where the winners of November's midterm elections will help determine whether Republicans or Democrats control the US Congress for the next two years, given the state has one Senate seat and two House seats seen as "Toss Ups" by Cook Political Report.
When polls open across the Midwestern state early on Tuesday, voters will be casting ballots at a time when discontent throughout the United States runs deep, especially over rising prices.
The political party out of power usually benefits in midterm elections and with Republicans holding the White House and both chambers of Congress at a time when President Donald Trump's approval rating is at a record-low 32%, Democrats are feeling increasingly competitive less than a month before the November 3 elections.
INFLATION, WAR ON BALLOT
Political analysts will be watching closely what unfolds in Ohio, as Trump has been a dominant force, especially among blue-collar workers who used to align with the Democratic Party.
But with inflation running at around 3.4%, every visit to a grocery store stirs that discontent because of rising food prices, but also due to rapidly escalating energy and housing costs.
The US war with Iran, launched by Trump on February 28 for reasons that he has not clearly presented to the nation, also has voters worried that it will become yet another "forever war."
The president won Ohio and the state's 17 electoral votes handily in 2016, 2020 and 2024, despite losing the 2020 presidential race to Democrat Joe Biden.
In this election, all eyes will be on whether some of those disaffected Democrats return to their party and if a significant number of independents turn their backs on Trump's Republicans.
SENATE SEAT
Former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, is trying to return to the Senate, where he served for 18 years before being defeated two years ago by Republican Senator Bernie Moreno.
This time around, Brown, a populist Democrat who long railed against US trade deals with foreign competitors, is attempting to unseat Republican Jon Husted in a special election with the winner holding the seat through 2028.
Political analysts see the race between Husted and Brown as a toss-up.
With Republicans currently holding a 53-47 majority in the Senate, Democrats are hoping for a net gain of at least four seats, including in Ohio, in order to control the chamber.
CLOSE HOUSE RACES
Meanwhile, two US House races could help determine next year's majority in that chamber, which Republicans currently hold with a 218-214 margin. One independent is aligned with Republicans and there are two vacancies that will be filled in the midterm elections.
In the seventh congressional district, which includes Medina, just south of Cleveland, incumbent Representative Max Miller, a Republican, is in a tough race in seeking a third term.
While he has raised far more funds than his Democratic opponent and has Trump's endorsement in a Republican-leaning district, Miller's campaign has been hit by allegations of domestic violence, which he denies.
Democrat Brian Poindexter, a labor union iron worker and member of a suburban city council, is mounting an aggressive campaign to unseat Miller.
Meanwhile, in Ohio's 9th congressional district that covers most of northwest Ohio and hugs the shores of Lake Erie, Democratic Representative Marcy Kaptur, a moderate who was first elected in 1982, is battling in another toss-up race against Republican challenger Derek Merrin, who nearly defeated her in 2024. 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics awarded to Francis Halzen, pioneer of high-energy neutrinos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:18:41 UTC
19:18:41 KST

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded to Francis Halzen for “decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.” Halzen is a Belgium-born physicist, a professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and principal investigator at the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica.
“It’s a great pleasure to hear about this prize,” said Halzen during the press conference that followed the announcement. “I hope this reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in the beginning of this project.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“It’s very exciting,” says Michael H. Moloney, CEO of the American Institute of Physics. “It’s a timely and an important recognition of the extraordinary work that Dr. Halzen did to open up a whole new window on the universe.”
Indeed, IceCube—Halzen’s brainchild—gave humankind a fresh glimpse of the cosmos when it came online in 2010. Unlike the majority of the globe’s telescopes. which gather starlight, this unique observatory sees the universe via ghostly messengers called neutrinos. Combining the two has improved our understanding of some of the most distant and violent physical processes in the cosmos.
Neutrinos are the least understood of the 17 fundamental particles known to exist. They nearly always move through matter as if it isn’t there. So massive detectors are required to capture and study their exceedingly rare collisions with atoms.
IceCube does this with arrays of specialized sensors dispersed in the crystal-clear ice a mile beneath the surface of Antarctica. A high-energy neutrino, accelerated at the center of a faraway galaxy, will usually zip right through this subsurface deep freeze. But occasionally, it will hit an atom in a molecule of water ice, producing a shower of light that the sensors collect and use to reconstruct the neutrinos’ energies and directions of origin.
After just a couple of years, IceCube confirmed it had measured the first high-energy neutrinos from beyond the solar system. Thanks in large part to IceCube, astronomers are heralding a new era of “multimessenger astronomy,” where neutrino measurements, traditional telescopes and gravitational-wave detectors together triangulate to pinpoint and scrutinize distant, obscure phenomena.
“People didn’t know that the extragalactic sources would be bright enough to be detected, so it was a risk,” says Jonathan Bagger, a theoretical physicist and CEO of the American Physical Society. “Halzen analyzed this subject and wrote proposals and got them through peer review—this was ultimately a testament to the system working.”
The observatory is an ambitious and unprecedented feat of engineering. It was constructed by boring deep holes across a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice using jets of hot water and then carefully lowering long strings of sensors into them. It remains the largest neutrino telescope in the world. This year’s Nobel therefore awards exactly the kind of modern, large-scale experimental science that is under financial threat in places like the U.S., where IceCube originated. (The Trump administration’s budget proposal for 2027 calls for halving IceCube’s funding.)
“It’s big, publicly funded science,” Moloney says. “It shows that when we design audacious experiments, we can discover extraordinary things.”
The Nobel Prize in Physics, first given in 1901, was previously awarded 119 times to a total of 229 individuals. Those recipients included Marie Curie, who was awarded in 1903 for making sense of radioactivity; Albert Einstein, who was awarded in 1921 for discovering how light and matter interact; I. I. Rabi, who was awarded in 1944 for discovering what would become the science behind magnetic resonance imaging (MRI); and Frederick Reines, who was awarded in 1995 for discovering low-energy neutrinos. Before Halzen’s win today, the last time the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to a single person was in 1992, when it went to French physicist Georges Charpak.
More recently, the physics Nobel Prize recognized a tool for studying the motion of electrons in 2023, the development of core techniques for building many of today’s artificial intelligence models in 2024, and the creation and study of weird quantum phenomena in macroscopic, handheld devices in 2025.
The prize will be presented in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death.

Estonia allocates €2.2M to set up nuclear safety regulator
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:18:00 UTC
19:18:00 KST

Estonia allocates €2.2M to set up nuclear safety regulator
The government has set aside €2.2 million towards building its nuclear regulatory body.
The money has been given to the Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority (TTJA) to set up the regulator in 2027.
The TTJA will issue permits and conduct nuclear oversight, hiring 13 specialists initially and aiming for around 40 over four years.
Though no nuclear plant is currently under construction, building one, including Small Modular Reactor (SMR) types, has long been discussed.
The explanatory memorandum to the Nuclear Energy Act, passed this summer, notes the state's aim is to create the legal framework needed to enable the development of nuclear energy in Estonia in a safe and responsible manner. Estonia has had no competent authority when it comes to nuclear safety supervision, the document notes.
The TTJA is now being designated as that authority, and will begin issuing permits and conducting nuclear oversight.
Maanus Urb, an adviser at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications, said the planned nuclear regulator will assess nuclear safety. He added that although no nuclear plant is currently being built in Estonia, the regulator is still required, given the potential locations for a plant are being scoped out.
"These are being mapped. Once they are mapped, it will be possible to move to the next stages. So this is being done in phases. For that, an adequate authority is needed that knows how to assess it," Urb said.
TTJA deputy director general Lauri Kütt said new personnel will be hired to get the nuclear regulator off the ground.
"According to the current plan, the aim is to hire 13 specialists, but across the whole project over four years the goal is to reach around 40 people," Kütt explained.
Kütt added that the €2.2 million the authority is receiving has a set purpose, that is, to allow the state to carry out independent oversight. The funds will be used for training and personnel costs. Expert opinions will also be commissioned, Kütt noted.
Although under current plans the nuclear regulator project is valid for four years, Kütt believes this may change over time.
Several potential locations have been earmarked for a proposed nuclear power station, all of them close to the Baltic Sea coast to meet the requirements for the cooling water needed in the process.
Estonia has never had a nuclear power station, though two reactors operated at the nuclear submarine base in Paldiski during the Soviet occupation. These were decommissioned after independence.

Foster + Partners extends Bilbao Fine Arts Museum with bridge-like gallery

Foster + Partners extends Bilbao Fine Arts Museum with bridge-like gallery
British studio Foster + Partners and local architect Luis María Uriarte have expanded the Bilbao Fine Arts Museum in Spain with a 55-metre-long elevated gallery.
Named Agravitas, the bridge-like extension sits on large V-shaped columns that straddle the existing museum, not touching the original building fabric.
Foster + Partners and Luis María Uriarte designed the extension to improve the connection between the museum's multiple buildings and extensions, which have a U-shaped layout with an extended wing.
"In the great tradition of Bilbao, a city with a rich industrial history and an outstanding ability to reinvent itself, this project is about bridging the past, present, and the future," said Foster + Partners founder Norman Foster.
"The flexible new building looks ahead to the future and responds to the ever-changing form of contemporary art, while remaining respectful of the site's storied history," he continued.
"Working in collaboration with local architect Luis María Uriarte and the museum teams, the design reinforces the museum's role as one of the city's major civic attractions, with enhanced permeability, expanded gallery spaces, and a new social heart for the museum."
Locally produced steel was used to build Agravitas, aiming to celebrate the industrial heritage of Bilbao.
The extension spans the existing museum and a former outdoor space at the centre of the complex, creating a ground-floor hall enclosed by a glazed facade and filled with sculptures.
The upper level contains column-free gallery spaces topped with skylights that can let daylight in or be blacked out depending on exhibition requirements.
Foster + Partners also introduced office space and roof terraces to give views across the city.
Overhanging roofs were designed for solar shading, while photovoltaic panels have been added to the rooftop.
The transformation also involved restoring Bilbao Fine Arts Museum's existing buildings and reopening the original 1940s entrance for the first time in decades.
Foster + Partners worked on the design for Agravitas with Spanish engineer Julio Martinez Calzón, founder of MC2 Estudio de Ingeniería, who passed away in 2023.
Other projects recently completed by Foster + Partners include an art gallery in Shanghai lined with tubular glass and the Zayed National Museum on Saadiyat Island, which is characterised by soaring ventilation towers.
The photography is by Nigel Young.

Ofcom investigates Meta over Instagram Instants safety checks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:15:31 UTC
19:15:31 KST

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta is under investigation for a potential breach of the UK’s digital safety laws after launching a Snapchat-style feature on Instagram.
The communications watchdog, Ofcom, is investigating whether the $1.9tn (£1.4tn) company infringed the Online Safety Act (OSA) by failing to carry out adequate checks on whether its Instagram Instants product could show illegal content or be accessed by children.
Social media companies are required to carry out risk assessments before making significant changes to their service’s design or operation. Breaching the OSA carries a range of potential actions, from a formal warning to a fine of up to 10% of global revenue.
George Lusty, the director of enforcement at Ofcom, said risk assessments were a vital step in keeping tech platforms safe for users. “You wouldn’t launch a new car without testing it properly, and it’s the same for online services,” he said. “Safety by design must be built in, not bolted on, and today’s investigation shows we’ll take action where we have concerns that providers are failing to comply.”
Instagram’s Instants feature allows users to send images that disappear after viewing. The company said it had conducted a risk analysis of Instants and talked to Ofcom on a number of occasions before launching it. It said the feature carried protections such as blocking forwarding and included all the safeguards under its teen account settings, the default mode for under-18s on Instagram, Facebook and Messenger.
“We will of course cooperate with Ofcom during this investigation,” a Meta spokesperson said.
The Molly Rose Foundation, a charity established by the family of Molly Russell, a teenager who took her own life after viewing harmful content on Instagram, said it was crucial that Meta was “held to account for their failures under the Online Safety Act”.
Ofcom is already investigating whether Meta breached the law by failing to comply with a request for information related to its WhatsApp platform.
Zuckerberg’s company is challenging Ofcom in court over the OSA. It is suing the regulator in the high court over how it charges tech firms fees to cover its operating costs and, in a further case, it is challenging Ofcom for placing WhatsApp and Instagram in a new category under the act that subjects it to additional duties.
Meta has also joined TikTok and Elon Musk’s X in a court challenge over the amount of information Ofcom is demanding they provide under the online safety regime.

Nobel prize in physics goes to Francis Halzen for south pole work on neutrinos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:11:01 UTC
19:11:01 KST

The Nobel prize in physics 2026 has been awarded to a researcher who turned an enormous block of ice at the south pole into a detector for ghostly particles called neutrinos that reach Earth from outer space.
Prof Francis Halzen, a Belgian particle physicist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, led work on the IceCube neutrino observatory, which made the first detection of high-energy extraterrestrial neutrinos in 2013, soon after it was switched on.
To build the observatory, scientists, technicians and engineers embedded thousands of basketball-sized light detectors into a cubic kilometre of ice to detect faint flashes of light that can result when neutrinos from space crash into atomic nuclei.
Announcing the prize on Tuesday, the Nobel committee said Halzen won “for decisive contributions to the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”. He receives a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000).
“It feels strange,” Halzen told a press briefing on winning the prize. “I hope it reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in the beginning of this project when no really respectable, conservative physicist would have joined me, but many talented people did.”
Neutrinos are mysterious particles that are as elusive as they are ubiquitous. They pass through almost everything they encounter, from people to planets. Every second, billions of neutrinos from the sun pass unnoticed through the body. But every now and then, a neutrino will interact with the nucleus of an atom in a collision that can be picked up by a sensitive detector.
Halzen realised that brief flickers of light from neutrino collisions could be detected in clear, glacial ice and in 1988 put forward a plan to convert a chunk of the south pole into a neutrino observatory. The detector uses Earth to shield against the background noise of cosmic rays, and has downwards-facing light sensors to detect neutrinos passing through the planet from the northern hemisphere. Apart from a hostile environment for the team, the site benefited from being far from sources of interference and the risk of vibrations from earthquakes.
After the first detection of high-energy extraterrestrial neutrinos in 2013, scientists working on IceCube identified the first cosmic source of neutrinos 3.7bn years away.
The observatory has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy. Until now, researchers have learned about the cosmos from light, other electromagnetic radiation, and gravitational waves. Neutrinos are considered messengers from the cosmos and provide fresh clues as to how the universe evolved.
Halzen, who received the news while travelling in Italy, said he was working on a new proposal and hoped that winning the prize would help in getting it approved.
Dr Patrick Dunne at Imperial College London welcomed the prize. “For all of human history the only way we’ve been able to understand things outside our solar system is with light. Detecting neutrinos from astrophysical sources opens up a new lens, so it isn’t overstating things to liken this to when Galileo first pointed a telescope at the stars,” he said.
“Neutrinos are the most abundant massive particles and their ability to pass through matter much more easily than light makes them ideal for observing distant phenomena or the inside of extreme phenomena like those seen by IceCube,” he added.
Other experiments to understand neutrinos include the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (Dune) in the US and the Hyper-Kamiokande detector in Japan.
The observations of cosmic neutrinos have led some scientists to speculate that the ghostly particles could be used by alien civilisations to send messages across the universe. Asked what he made of the idea, Halzen said: “I don’t think I’ll go there. We have enough realistic problems to deal with right now [to] make neutrino astronomy a reality rather than worry about this.”
But he added that when astronomers have opened new windows on the universe, they often make unexpected discoveries. “I’m sure this will be true for neutrinos 50 years from now,” he said.
On Monday, three scientists won the Nobel prize in medicine for optogenetics, a powerful technique that has allowed researchers to shed unprecedented light on the workings of the brain. The Nobel prize in chemistry is announced on Wednesday.

Kremlin warns Lithuania that its move to lift a nuclear arms ban risks further escalation
MOSCOW, Oct 6 - The Kremlin on Tuesday warned that a preliminary decision by NATO member Lithuania to lift a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear arms on its territory could lead to a new round of escalation in the region.
Lithuania's parliament voted in favour of removing the ban on Tuesday, in a first of two ballots required for the change.
Asked by reporters how Russia viewed that development, as well as a proposal floated this month by US President Donald Trump to build an American military base in the Baltic country, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said:
"If the military infrastructure of what is, in effect, NATO's leading country (the US) is moving closer to our borders, then, of course, this cannot be perceived as anything other than a step towards escalating tensions."
He added: "The same applies to the deployment of nuclear weapons on the territory of a neighbouring state. Neither of these developments will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent; on the contrary, they will, much to our regret, mark yet another significant escalation of tensions."
Lithuania, a member of the EU and NATO, borders Russia and Moscow's close ally Belarus. The US has kept an armoured battalion of almost 1,000 troops there since 2019, in overlapping rotations, meaning the troops arrive and leave every few months.
The legal overhaul of the nuclear arms ban, which requires a two-thirds majority in two parliamentary votes to go into effect, is set to remove prohibitions put in place more than three decades ago after Lithuania broke away from the Soviet Union. REUTERS

NEW DELHI: The INDIA bloc on Tuesday stepped up its protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, with opposition parties demanding his resignation, scrapping of the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise and restoration of deleted names from electoral rolls.The demands were raised as INDIA bloc MPs marched from Parliament towards the Election Commission of India headquarters in New Delhi, alleging irregularities in the electoral roll revision process.
CEC's resignation: The opposition demanded the immediate removal and resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged unilateral changes to voter registration forms and centralisation of power.
Scrap SIR, restore old rolls: The bloc called for suspension and repeal of the ongoing Special Intensive Revision process and sought the use of pre-SIR electoral rolls.
Notice before deletion: The opposition demanded that voters receive prior notice and have access to a formal and transparent appeal mechanism before their names are removed from electoral rolls.
Simpler first-time registration: The bloc called for a simpler and more accessible voter registration process for first-time and young voters.
Return to ballot papers: The opposition also demanded the scrapping of Electronic Voting Machines and a return to traditional ballot paper voting.
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge accused the government of trying to undermine citizens' voting rights and alleged that the Election Commission was functioning at the government's direction."Look, we are fighting against the injustice of the fact that the government is stripping away everything—all the rights of the people. And today, the universal adult franchise that we received after Independence—this government is working to finish it off," Kharge said.He alleged that the CEC was "merely a puppet of the government" and claimed the poll panel acted according to directions from Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah."And the Election Commission, the CEC is merely a puppet of the government. Whatever Modi and Shah tell them to do, that is exactly what they do," he said.
Kharge further alleged that such functioning of institutions would harm democracy and the Constitution."Because of this, democracy will be destroyed in this country, the Constitution will be finished, and Hitler-like rule will take over," he said.
Opposition targets SIR, voter forms

Anybody over the age of 18 and a citizen of India has a fundamental right to vote. But the exercise of the SIR, undertaken by the Election Commission of India, is disenfranchising our citizens from their fundamental right," Chidambaram said.He said Form 6, which is used for enrolling first-time voters, contains questions about whether an applicant's parents and grandparents were voters and where they voted."Your right to vote is not dependent on the fact whether your parents were voters or not. This is not a question which can be asked in Form 6. Who inserted these questions into Form 6? If you can't go past that question, you can't enroll yourself as a voter," he said.Chidambaram also questioned whether the Election Commission had taken the decisions unanimously or through a majority."The Chief Election Commissioner cannot take decisions unilaterally. If these decisions were taken unilaterally by the Chief Election Commissioner, then it's an illegal decision, and the entire exercise is completely illegal and ultra vires," he said.On Form 7, Chidambaram alleged that the process meant for reporting voters who had died or moved away was being used for mass deletion of names."It has been brought to light in Karnataka that one party worker of the BJP has filed 7,000 Form 7 applications to delete voters," he alleged."This is a complete abuse of the process. There is an illegality, abuse of process, and disenfranchisement happening in the SIR, which is depriving the right to vote, which is fundamental to us," he said.Chidambaram demanded that the Election Commission reform itself and Kumar resign."So, the Election Commission must immediately reform itself, and the Chief Election Commissioner must resign forthwith," he said.
Kharge warns of continued protest

First, leave the seat. Otherwise, there will be a commotion in the country. The people of the country will not sit quietly. This is my warning to them," he said.

The government should be destroyed," Kharge added.Congress MP Rajeev Shukla also demanded Kumar's resignation."It is certain that Gyanesh Kumar will have to resign; people have lost faith in the Election Commission," Shukla said.Congress MP Syed Nasir Hussain said, "Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar should go. The company, which was behind the blockbuster Barbie film featuring Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling in 2023, has struggled to turn around its business as sales of the Barbie doll and other toys have declined.
Discussions of a sale come after Mattel named its new CEO and chairman, Roger Lynch in September, taking over from predecessor Ynon Kreiz. Kreiz led the company for eight years.
Last week, brand licensing firm Authentic Brands expressed takeover interest in Mattel with a potential offer valued at about $6 billion, according to reports. Mattel's shares rose 20% on the news.

UniCredit gets Putin’s approval to sell part of its Russian business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:06:06 UTC
19:06:06 KST

The Italian bank plans to keep its international payments business while selling its other Russian operations. The approval contrasts with Moscow’s recent moves to place several Western companies’ local assets under temporary management.
On Monday, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree allowing Italian bank UniCredit to sell part of its Russian business, paving the way for the Milan-based group to scale back its presence in the country.
UniCredit Bank has been operating in Russia since 1989. It continued its activities in the Russian Federation after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
In May, the bank announced plans to sell part of its Russian subsidiary to "a well-established private investor in the United Arab Emirates" with "long-standing ties to the local institutional and business community", while retaining part of the business linked to payment services.
The newspaper Kommersant previously reported that the investor eyeing the assets represents Alfa Group, an international conglomerate in good standing with the Kremlin. One of its founders is Mikhail Fridman, who was recently removed from the EU's sanctions list.
The decree "permits the reorganisation" of the company in Russia, envisaging the separation of part of the Russian legal entity UniCredit Bank into a new company that will remain under the ownership of the Italian UniCredit group.
Under the decree, the Italian group is permitted to sell 100% of its shares in the Russian UniCredit Bank.
The carved-out "new bank" will stay in Italian hands and will focus on international euro and dollar payments for corporate clients who are not under sanctions.
The rest of the business will pass to the buyer, whose name UniCredit has not disclosed.
The Italian group has estimated the negative impact of the deal on its financial results at €3–3.3 billion.
UniCredit said in May that it expected to complete the transaction in the first half of 2027, subject to binding agreements, the separation of the businesses and regulatory approvals.
Conditions for leaving Russia
Without the personal approval of the Russian president, the deal would not have been possible, writes RFE/RL. Since 2022, under a decree on special measures regarding so-called "unfriendly" countries, UniCredit Bank has been on a list of banks for which any share transaction requires special permission.
In 2025, the Russian central bank's press service published a list of systemically important credit institutions, with 12 lenders on it, including UniCredit and Raiffeisenbank.
This came amid pressure from the European Central Bank on both banks to reduce their Russian operations and the banks' own declarations that they were winding down their activities in the country.
In addition to these two Western "systemic" banks, Italy's Intesa Sanpaolo continues to operate in Russia on a more limited scale through its corporate banking business. It received presidential approval to leave in September 2023 but has yet to complete its exit. Hungary's OTP Bank also continues operating through its Russian subsidiary.
Alongside the need for a "Kremlin blessing" to leave Russia, the conditions for doing so were made much tougher in October 2024: for affected foreign asset sales, the discount must be at least 60% off market value, and there is an additional exit tax of no less than 35%, according to UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD).
In response to repeated calls from European authorities and regulators to pull out of Russia, UniCredit argued that it was simply impossible to do so without the Kremlin's green light. Chief executive Andrea Orcel had repeatedly said the bank was unwilling to sell its Russian assets too cheaply, according to Kommersant.
Since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, hundreds of foreign companies have fully withdrawn from Russia or at least curtailed their operations there.
The fate of those who stayed has not always been smooth.
One example came on 17 September, when Putin signed a decree transferring the management of assets linked to 16 companies, including Nestlé, Auchan and several other Western groups, to a little-known firm, L.E.V. Management, which later turned out to have ties to Russia's security apparatus.
Another example followed on 28 September, when German wholesaler Metro AG lost operational control of its Russian subsidiary under a presidential decree. Control passed to UK Torg RUS, while ownership remained with the German group.
Asked whether the Russian subsidiaries of UniCredit or Austria's Raiffeisen could be next, an unnamed senior Russian government source told Reuters: "Let them be scared."

Former German spy chief arrested for espionage and treason
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:05:42 BST
19:05:42 KST

Former German spy chief arrested for espionage and treason
- Published
Former German spy chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says.
Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant.
Prosecutors allege that he used classified intelligence to "draft an analysis" for one foreign intelligence service and maintained contact with another foreign spying service. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved.
Police also arrested former BND employee Manfred D, accusing him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents for money.
Manfred D, who was Hanning's bureau chief and remained in the BND until this year, is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
Local media reported Hanning was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near Münster while Manfred D was arrested in Bavaria. Hanning is due in court on Wednesday and Manfred D will appear on Tuesday.
Prosecutors say Manfred D, who also served as the chief of staff for Hanning's successors between 2012 and 2026, used his role to gain access to highly confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning "in exchange for remuneration".
"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement says.
"On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence ... to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service," prosecutors said, noting it was not clear if "the material reached the intended recipient".
Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D, for several years".
Local media say Hanning's alleged possession of intelligence documents came to light during a separate case relating to German steakhouse heiress Christina Block.
Hamburg public prosecutor's office accused Block of orchestrating the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Investigators allege Hanning was involved in an earlier attempted kidnapping of the children, which he denies.
State criminal police officers reportedly discovered an electronic data storage device containing sensitive information including recent BND documents.
It is not the first time the BND has faced similar controversy. A high-ranking German intelligence officer was charged with treason in 2023 for allegedly passing state secrets to Russia.
Prosecutors alleged Carsten L shared intelligence about the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and received roughly €400,000 ($450,000; £340,000). His trial is ongoing.

Drones aimed at ambulances
Between 22:00 and 22:25, the Russian army deliberately directed two FPV drones at ambulances parked on a Kramatorsk street, prosecutors said. Three workers of the ambulance service were injured while trying to save the vehicles after the first hit. They suffered blast injuries, shrapnel wounds to the body and limbs, burns, and concussions, and received medical care. Three ambulances were damaged.
FPV drones are flown by an operator watching a live camera feed until the moment of impact. Prosecutors called the strike targeted.
A woman killed at home
At 22:10, a Russian drone hit a residential high-rise in the city. A 49-year-old woman was killed. Another resident, a 68-year-old woman, suffered a broken foot, shrapnel wounds to the body and limbs, and a concussion, according to prosecutors. The Kramatorsk district prosecutor's office has opened criminal proceedings over war crimes.
Across Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed three people on 5 October, in Sloviansk, Druzhkivka, and Sukhanivka, and injured 11, Donetsk Oblast head Vadym Filashkin said. His morning tally, posted before the prosecutors' report, did not include the Kramatorsk death.
Kramatorsk under the drone hunt
Russian drone operators have hunted people in Kramatorsk for months. In June, a Russian pilot chose to kill a man he saw on a city street. Russia strikes the city daily, and in August it dropped eight FAB-250 bombs on Kramatorsk, killing one person and injuring 18.
The same drone hunting of civilians has run for years in Kherson, where Ukraine's Security Service has named 10 Russian servicemen it ties to the "human safari." A UN inquiry has traced the Kherson campaign up the chain of command. In April, ISW found Russians using such tactics across southern Ukraine, including in Nikopol.
Medics have been repeated targets. In March, a Russian FPV drone killed two medics in an ambulance in Kharkiv Oblast, and in February, Russian drones hit an ambulance and a shop there, killing three. In Kyiv, a Russian missile attack damaged a maternity hospital in September.

====================================================================================================

AI models keep hacking real systems during tests. What does this mean?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:05:00 UTC
19:05:00 KST

Can AI kill humans? What rogue AI agents can actually do
October 6, 2026
Let's start with people's real world fears about AI. Here's a sample of people we asked:
Sebastian, 22, says it'll be an AI-powered robot uprising that finally wipes out humanity: "I think that'll take some time," he says, admitting his dystopia owes a lot to the 2004 film "I, Robot."
Luisa, 19, has heard the rumors too. Her fear is what happens when these tools get into the wrong hands. "I'm more afraid of people," she says. "Powerful people."
Pilar, 25, is pessimistic about humanity's prospects. "The world is going down," she says. "Hopefully after my lifetime."
In 2026, AI systems have repeatedly slipped out of human control — and at some of the world's largest AI companies.
What happens when AI agents go rogue?
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta have all disclosed in 2026 that their AI agents escaped the controlled test environments.
Agents are AI systems that don't just answer questions but act — running code, browsing the web, clicking through systems — on their own.
Thorsten Holz, scientific director at the Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy in Germany, is among the researchers who test AI systems.
"It feels a bit crazy how powerful these models have become." Holz told DW. "I didn't anticipate they'd be so obsessed with solving tasks and that they'd start to do things we never [foresaw]."
Holz is one of 16 authors of ExploitGym. ExploitGym is an AI benchmark published in May 2026 by a team led by the University of California, Berkeley, with researchers from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. It is a standardized test of cybersecurity capabilities and vulnerabilities.
Its 898 challenges test whether AI agents can turn known software bugs into working attacks. Each one runs inside a sandbox — a sealed-off digital space, cut off from the internet, so nothing the agent does can reach anything real. That's the theory, anyway.
In July, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI models had escaped from their sandbox.
They were running an internal ExploitGym test with the models' safety refusals switched off, a setting that lets evaluators measure what a model is capable of rather than what it will decline to do.
Failing the task, the models went looking for a shortcut instead, and found a flaw in the software meant to keep them sealed in. It let them onto the open internet.
From there they worked out that Hugging Face, a site where AI developers store and share models and data, probably held the answer to the test.
So, they broke in and went looking for it, organizing the effort on message boards they set up themselves. The behavior was not instructed, according to OpenAI's account of the incident.
Hugging Face detected the intrusion and shut it down before OpenAI connected it to its own test. No customer data was reportedly taken.
"What happened is really a bit of science fiction," Holz said.
Then, Google confirmed that its Gemini model had guessed or found login credentials and accessed three real companies' websites during a May test run by the independent evaluator Irregular — an intrusion Google learned of in July 2026 and disclosed weeks later.
Anthropic's and Meta's escapes happened in sandboxes run by the same firm, which has said it notified the labs in late July 2026 and that it has since fixed the flaws.
In late September 2026, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent had broken into a statistics portal belonging to Medicare, Australia's public health system, reaching non-public files and writing data into a government server. No patient records were reportedly touched.
Could AI decide to wipe out humanity?
The incidents have revived older fears. If agents can program each other, where does that end? Could it lead to what philosopher Nick Bostrom has called a "paperclip maximizer"?
Bostrom's thought experiment imagines a machine given one simple goal: Make as many paperclips as possible.
The machine pursues the task so single-mindedly that it eventually treats humans as raw material standing in the way.
"For the intermediate future, I do not see any kind of scientific evidence that there could be this super intelligence that autonomously decides, 'Okay, let's kill,'" said Holz.
Rogue software needs vast datacenters to run, he said, which makes it visible. And the internet is built from parts that can keep working independently of one another.
But the AI escapes and hacks in 2026 were noticed late. Google learned of Gemini's intrusions two months after they happened, and OpenAI told Australia about the Medicare breach nearly three months after the event.
Holz said he expects a different kind of threat: Bad actors turning capable AI on critical infrastructure, mass compromise of ordinary machines, or chatbots used to manipulate information at scale and destabilize politics.
Can Europe compete with US and Chinese AI?
No, Europe cannot easily compete with China, according to experts.
France's Mistral and Germany's open-source Soofi project lag behind the frontier labs — a handful of US and Chinese firms building the most advanced models. Europe lacks the datacenter capacity to train systems at that scale, which leaves it dependent on non-European models, and largely subject to US or Chinese export controls.
For Holz, the more pressing gap is expertise. "What we definitely need to see is how we can build up more competence in the area of security, AI, and especially the intersection of both," he said.
How worried should you be about AI?
Be skeptical of what the companies themselves claim, Holz said. They have a financial interest in the conversation, he said, particularly ahead of a stock market listing. "There's also fear mongering, or a bit of hype, about how advanced these models get."
Holz uses AI daily, as do his children. His nine-year-old generates coloring book pages. His 12-year-old uses it for homework, but has already learned the hard way that it lies and that "it's sometimes wrong."

Electrification, AI and fossil fuels: What to expect as Türkiye hosts major climate summit next month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:04:55 UTC
19:04:55 KST

The UN talks in Antalya next month will be backdropped by the energy crisis, extreme heat and Nepal's flood disaster.
All eyes will be on Türkiye next month as the country hosts the world's biggest climate summit.
COP31 opens in the seaside city of Antalya on 9 November, bringing 197 countries together to grapple with record global temperatures, mounting climate damage, and growing pressure to shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.
While Türkiye won out as host country, the marathon negotiations will be steered by Australia in an unprecedented arrangement reached after both nations bid to stage the world's premier climate gathering.
This year's formal UN talks are set to be light on big-ticket items, with voluntary climate pledges taking centre stage.
Alongside these, the host intends to push electrification as one path to reducing emissions and dependency on fossil fuels. Critics have warned that electrification must be pursued in tandem with clean power if it is to deliver on decarbonisation.
How will a devastating year of climate disasters and turmoil in global energy markets shape discussions inside and outside the negotiating rooms?
Will a fossil fuel phaseout be on the table at COP31?
Efforts to reach a global consensus on setting concrete targets or pathways for phasing out fossil fuels have stalled and the perennially thorny issue is not a formal item in the COP31 negotiations.
In the absence of consensus, Brazil is expected to release a voluntary 'roadmap' to guide the transition away from coal, oil and gas after nations failed to agree on the process at last year's COP.
But frustration over the fossil fuel impasse could reignite in Antalya. This year, about 60 nations demanding faster action on fossil fuels staged their own breakaway conference outside the United Nations process.
It is unclear how they may be accommodated at COP31 but Türkiye and Australia have promised predictability at COP31 and no last-minute surprises.
Why a focus on electrification could be problematic
Türkiye and Australia want the focus instead on electrification – essentially, replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels directly, like diesel cars and gas heating, with electric alternatives.
Their flagship initiative in Antalya urges countries to commit to a voluntary target to raise the share of final energy demand met by electricity from about 20 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035.
The hosts say boosting electrification could cut heat-trapping emissions and reduce reliance on costly fossil fuel imports – a major concern for nations after the Middle East war triggered a global energy shock.
But around one-third of the world's electricity is still produced using coal, and the electrification target does not explicitly state how that extra power should be produced, raising questions of credibility.
What voluntary climate pledges are expected on the sidelines of COP31?
Apart from the centrepiece electrification goal, Türkiye is spearheading a range of voluntary initiatives on themes including artificial intelligence, methane and waste reduction, and climate-resilient cities.
These non-blinding pledges are slated for a separate 'action agenda' which runs parallel to the formal COP talks, where decisions are taken by consensus and nations must agree on every line of the text.
This year the hard-fought negotiations contain few headline-grabbing items and deal mostly with technical issues carried over from previous conferences.
Climate finance in the wake of the Nepal floods
Another recurring sore spot at COPs, the amount of financial assistance provided by wealthy countries will be scrutinised again in Antalya, especially after devastating floods in Nepal linked to climate change.
Kathmandu's appeal for assistance has revived longstanding calls for historic polluters to cough up more to help poorer nations shift to renewable energy, adapt to climate impacts, and recover from disaster.
Türkiye has pitched itself as a bridge between developed and developing countries and incoming COP31 President Murat Kurum said closing the climate finance "chasm" would be a key priority in Antalya.
Who will host COP's 'global stocktake' in 2028?
At COP33 in 2028, countries will undertake a 'global stocktake' of progress on climate action. These take place every five years and assess where the world has fallen short in meeting the goals of the Paris Agreement.
But this crucial COP doesn't have a host yet after India withdrew its candidacy.
China is mulling a bid, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Beijing seeks to burnish its reputation as a global leader on climate change, particularly in the absence of the United States.
A decision does not have to be taken this year but the prospect of a politically-charged Beijing COP is expected to be a hot topic in Antalya.

Experts say drug policy Chiang opposes does not exist in Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:01:19 UTC
19:01:19 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) said Saturday he would not allow drugs or needles to be provided within communities for injection, a policy that experts say does not currently exist in Taiwan.
“Do we allow drugs and needles to be provided in our communities for people to take drugs?” Chiang, who is running for re-election, wrote in a Facebook post, questioning whether Taipei residents would agree to the idea.
Chiang’s post was a response to a 2014 article by Puma Shen (沈伯洋), the DPP’s mayoral candidate for Taipei. In the think piece, Shen discusses three approaches to drug use and suggests that Taiwan could “follow the footsteps of other countries by setting up community centers to provide drugs and clean needles and introduce social workers to help them.”
Experts said they were unsure what Shen meant by “community centers” in his post, but said no institution in Taiwan offers drugs or needles for injection.
At Taiwan’s drug prevention centers, which are based in hospitals or affiliated with local health departments, health workers teach people how to properly disinfect and use needles and locate veins to reduce the risk of conditions including phlebitis and myocarditis, said Ko Nai-ying (柯乃熒), a distinguished professor of nursing at National Cheng Kung University with decades of experience treating people who use drugs.
These facilities also provide needle-exchange services to reduce the risk of disease transmission.
“We do not provide drugs to people who use drugs,” she said. “We also do not inject them. We simply tell them what they need to be aware of.”
Two decades of harm reduction
Taiwan introduced its harm-reduction program following a sharp rise in HIV infections among people who inject drugs.
The Centers for Disease Control began implementing needle-exchange and methadone treatment programs in late 2005, after which new HIV infections among people who inject drugs quickly declined. In that year, more than 2,400 injecting drug users were infected with HIV, accounting for 72% of confirmed cases, but the CDC has recorded fewer than 100 such cases in recent years.
“When we talk about sharing needles, we used to think it meant simply someone using another person’s needle, but it goes beyond that,” said Ko, who also sits on the Cabinet’s advisory committee on AIDS prevention and control. “We’ve seen people who use drugs dilute heroin in a plastic bottle cap and then take turns using the same needle for injection.”
A study by Taiwanese scholars found that Taiwan’s 2006 harm-reduction program produced a decline in the first-time offense rate for heroin use equivalent to 6.88 years of the previous downward trend.
Methadone, a synthetic medication taken orally to treat dependence on heroin and other opioids, is regulated as a Schedule II controlled drug under Taiwanese law. Patients enrolled in the methadone treatment program are required to visit a facility daily and take the medication under supervision.
“You might not be able to stop using drugs completely because of substitute treatment, but at least you can make sure you won’t get HIV, hepatitis C, or myocarditis,” Ko said. “Harm reduction efforts allow marginalized individuals to start anew.”
In 2011, the Ministry of Health and Welfare began offering buprenorphine sublingual tablets as a longer-lasting alternative that does not require daily visits to medical facilities.
"Zero tolerance"
Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) told reporters Monday, in response to the disagreement between the Taipei mayoral candidates, that the government has maintained a “zero-tolerance” stance on drug use. He also highlighted the importance of science in policymaking.
Lee Szu-Hsien (李思賢), a professor of health promotion and education at National Taiwan Normal University and chair of the Taiwan Harm Reduction Association, said methadone was originally introduced as a substitute drug to prevent the spread of infectious diseases but believed it should play a greater role in treating people with drug dependence.
“The biggest benefit of methadone is that it keeps people clear-headed throughout the day,” he said. “Once they are clear-headed, we can help them find jobs and provide vocational training, so they can eventually contribute to society again.”
According to government statistics, he said, the daily subsidy for methadone treatment is NT$3 (US$0.09) per person.
“In Taiwan, people often lump everything together,” he said. “As long as it involves drugs, whether using or trafficking, it is considered a crime and something bad that should be dealt with through harsh penalties.”
He proposed drafting a special law that would clearly distinguish people who use drugs from those who manufacture, transport, or sell them. Such a law would improve treatment for drug users at facilities and give doctors opportunities to develop treatments for different substances.
