The Ghosts That Haunt Egypt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

I grew up in Cairo under Hosni Mubarak, who had ruled for longer than I had been alive. I was 15 when the revolution erupted in January 2011, a high school student just coming into political consciousness as the streets around me cracked open with possibilities for otherwise futures.
Two years later, politics had permeated our homes, our friendships, our classrooms, our morgues. In July 2013, the military, led by Gen. Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi, overthrew Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood, who was Egypt’s first democratically elected president. Over the following weeks, Morsi’s supporters camped and protested in eastern Cairo near the Rabaa al-Adawiya mosque. In August 2013, the military and police opened fire on the protesters in what came to be known as the Rabaa massacre. The father of a dear friend was among those killed.
Enraged, I joined the street movement against the coup. On Oct. 6, 2013, I was arrested at a mass protest near Tahrir Square and spent the next six years and three months as a political prisoner. Released by a chance miracle in 2020, I fled Egypt for the United States.
Gen. el-Sisi crowned himself field marshal and president and continues to rule Egypt. The revolution has been crushed, tens of thousands remain imprisoned, and economic hardship has broken the backs of Egyptians. When I look back at my country, I see an Egypt structured by ghosts: four relentless hauntings that explain what has become of the country in the wake of those fleeting blue mornings in January 2011, when we were last touched by a dream.
That bridge in Cairo
Something always draws me back to Qasr El-Nil bridge. Even in my prison cell, I often closed my eyes and returned to the faded bronze of the two lions at its threshold. To Jan. 28, 2011, the "Friday of Rage," three days after the spark of the Egyptian revolution. Specifically: the famous video of clashes atop the bridge between protesters and police.
Throughout the clip, security forces push the protesters back; armored vehicles accelerate to drive bodies back. Tear gas canisters sizzle through the air, leaving cloudy trails as they sail toward the advancing sea of bodies. Water cannons slam into protesters, catapulting them backward. Rubber bullets crack bones.
Yet something wondrous keeps happening: each time the police push the protesters off the bridge, the protesters surge forward again. And each time they return, they push and trespass farther. Push. Return. Trespass. Push. Return. Trespass. Until something ruptures: the masses start running not away from but toward the forces.
And you can tell that everyone on that bridge feels the rupture rip through the air, because for a split second, even the police freeze, confounded. And once the rupture takes hold, the soldiers—those who have never been run toward—turn and flee. The crowd erupts—cheering, screaming, cursing—as if shocked by the very movement of their bodies, the bodies they have always moved but have never moved this way before. This is the second haunting. I begin with the second because I write from and toward the rupture.
The eagle family
To grasp Egypt's ghosts today, we must understand its first haunting: the Eagle Family. Since the Free Officers overthrew the monarchy in 1952, Egypt’s political order has remained, in practice, under military rule. Officers emerged from that coup as the architects of the new state and cast themselves as the custodians of its national interest.
The military’s authority has been sanctified over seven decades, and that exalted status extends to the broader security apparatus: police, prosecutors, judges, and intelligence officers. Together they form the Eagle Family, named after the emblem on the Egyptian flag that also adorns officials’ uniforms. The eagle became shorthand for an implicit social contract: those who bear it personify the nation; those outside its ranks are expendable.
Then, the expendable subjects rose up in revolt on Jan. 25, 2011. After decades of repression, Egyptians were shaken by the brutal 2010 torture and killing of Khaled Saeed, a 28-year-old from Alexandria, who the police claimed had died after swallowing a packet of drugs. The photographs of his bashed-in face surfaced online, and the images became one of Egypt’s earliest cases of social media virality, igniting public outrage that helped coalesce into the uprising that ousted President Hosni Mubarak. The revolution was an unthinkable event: one that fundamentally contradicted the ruling order’s conception of the relationship between civilians and eagles.
As protests intensified, state media unleashed a frenzied smear campaign, casting Egyptian protesters as foreign agents and outside agitators. State media claimed that revolutionaries had been trained by Israel and tied them, simultaneously, to the United States, Iran, Hamas, al-Qaeda, the Muslim Brotherhood, and international NGOs. State media outlets even circulated the absurd accusation, later immortalized as a running joke, that protesters were being fed and financed by Kentucky Fried Chicken.
Protesters went on to torch police stations across the country, overrun national security headquarters in multiple governorates, storm torture chambers, and unearth archives of horror and abuse. The headquarters of the National Democratic Party was set ablaze. Founded by Anwar Sadat in 1978 and led by Hosni Mubarak from 1981 until 2011, the party had long dominated Egypt’s political system as its de facto ruling party. Its headquarters were left smoldering on the banks of the Nile.
To the Eagle Family, these scenes were sacrilege. Their untouchable status was profaned before millions. And by whom? Lowly civilians. The “Friday of Rage”, and especially the clash on the bridge, remains an open wound in the Eagle Family’s psyche, feeding its fury, fears, and insatiable hunger for revenge. Since then, the one-way street has become a two-way street: the Eagle haunts the civilian; the civilian haunts the Eagle.
The founding massacre
Between Mubarak’s fall and the 2013 coup, military violence resurged. The Supreme Council of the Armed Forces, while posturing as the guardian of a democratic transition, governed through massacres and military tribunals. When the Muslim Brotherhood’s Mohamed Morsi won the 2012 elections, the Brotherhood proved incompetent to govern a fractured nation under the shadow of a military establishment that had never surrendered real authority.
By mid-2013, mass disillusionment with the Brotherhood provided fertile ground for a military comeback. Demonstrators filled the public squares, demanding early elections. The military and police, who saw the Brotherhood as their archenemy, openly backed the anti-Morsi demonstrations and even recruited participants. Their backing attracted hordes of counterrevolutionaries and Mubarak loyalists. On television, I watched officers carried and celebrated by the crowds as saviors. And in July 2013, Gen. el-Sisi, the minister of defense, staged a coup and took over the country.
From the first moment, the 2013 coup regime hurled itself toward a singular goal: the eradication of every possible reminder of the January 2011 rupture. One of its earliest preemptive spectacles of violence became our third haunting: the Rabaa massacre.
On Aug. 14, 2013, security forces stormed the Rabaa al-Adawiya Square in eastern Cairo where supporters of Morsi had entrenched themselves in a sprawling sit-in demanding his reinstatement. Police bullets seared flesh, shattered skulls; the air filled with thuds, shrieks, and the hiss of flames. The Egyptian police and military, killing at least 1000 protesters, committed what would be recorded as one of the deadliest massacres in modern Egyptian history.
Rabaa ended the Arab uprisings. The regime transmuted its coercive force into political legitimacy through the spectacular destruction of dissident bodies, restoring reverence for the Eagle. For the Brotherhood, Rabaa became the defining catastrophe of its post-2013 political memory, upending its organization, self-conception, and belief in its own permanence.
Some secular activists say they are still haunted by how the military exploited them, even as they now find themselves sharing prison cells with the very Brotherhood members they once opposed. The deep state had appropriated their opposition to the Muslim Brotherhood, redeploying it as justification for the massacre.
Most disturbing were those who celebrated the killings: artists, media figures, and segments of the public who blessed the dispersal in the name of stability or anti-Brotherhood conviction. Once one blesses mass killing, there is no going back: they must continue to sanction the violence they had endorsed again and again.
Today, Egypt’s prisons hold no fewer than 60,000 political prisoners. Thousands have spent more than a decade behind bars for a passing protest, a stray chant, or a post on a screen. Hundreds have died under torture, in overcrowded cells, or from medical neglect. Thousands have been swallowed by enforced disappearance. Most of those with release orders are denied their freedom and held in prison on new, fabricated charges.
Egyptian media operates under a single, unchallenged state voice; independent outlets are suppressed or banned; journalists face unending detention. Television and cinema have been converted into instruments of state-managed production geared toward “patriotism,” the eradication of any mention of the revolution except as a catastrophe, and the re-sanctification of the Eagle Family through propaganda shows.
When even an unregulated utterance can end a life, and when such utterances are made to go unwitnessed, what remains? What meaning can sacrifice ever hold again? The force that keeps this machinery running with such ruthless efficiency is, in my view, the fourth and most defining haunting of contemporary Egypt: political prisoners as state-manufactured ghosts.ghosts.
Manufacturing ghosthood
These ghosts haunt me. Recently, I wanted to write again about my incarcerated best friend, Ayman Moussa. Ayman was 19 when we were arrested at the same protest in 2013, tried in the same case, and handed the same 15-year sentence. He is 32 now; the bars have swallowed his entire twenties.
I had run out of new pictures of him to post. I have posted every iteration: laughing at a joke he might no longer recall, staring to the right as if something has just escaped the frame, doing a backflip, doing a handstand, doing a silly dance at his prom with his feet in the air, moving in that way he moves, as if gravity never learned his name. But his face, his frozen face, has reached a point where it has saturated the minds of onlookers, no longer catching anyone by surprise.
I am lucky. I carry contraband memories of him that the world has no access to. I remember the soft migrations of his features, the new edges and lines, the ones etched into our faces when prison time pressed too hard against our skin. I caught myself thinking of the nearest anniversary and realized I was writing eulogies. I was mourning Ayman, and I was tired of mourning him when he is here. He is here, right across the wall. He is not a ghost; he has been ghostified.
Ayman is but one of over 60,000 lives behind bars. There’s a famous Egyptian prison prayer that goes: “Lift this suffering off us, us, us, us, us, us, O God!” A prisoner would yell it from the opening in his cell door, and the whole cell block would shake in unison: O God! This call-and-response always fascinated me in prison. The lifting was assumed, God was the obvious entity being addressed, but what mattered most was the us, us, us. A prayer seeking—more than divine deliverance—to be witnessed. A prayer of ghosts.
I spent over six years standing at the same cell doors myself, shuffled from jail cell to pretrial detention center to maximum-security prison. I know something about the seething despair that settles in when your years dissolve before your eyes and the outside world moves on without you. Locally, almost no one dares utter your name. You see friends sent for release only to be recycled into the same machinery on new, fabricated charges; you watch your prison mates die one after another.
Abroad, you open the state newspapers and watch the military regime imprisoning you receive extensive financial and political support from the United States government, primarily to serve the objective of maintaining Israel’s security and enforcing the siege on Gaza. You watch the European Union announce a $8.3 billion package for Egypt meant to incentivize its regime to curb migration and guarantee E.U. security. You understand, inside your cell, that your body carries no value against the interests that make the regime holding you useful to others; that those others are, in fact, invested in your crushing.
In the official lexicon of the state, political prisoners do not exist. Egyptian officials have repeatedly insisted that they have no prisoners of conscience. Within Egypt, then, to speak of political prisoners is to enter a linguistic vacuum, mark oneself as suspect.
Over time, the knowledge of the thousands held in cells, disappeared into detention sites, or trapped in unending pretrial detention begins to discipline public conduct by way of anticipation: people train themselves not to know. Paradoxically, this kind of cognitive dissonance is possible precisely because of the saturation of public awareness with this knowledge and the hefty costs of acknowledging it. Because to acknowledge the ghosts is to risk becoming one.
To the bridge in Cairo, I return
I have had a ritual since 2013: on the eve of each anniversary of the revolution, I take out my copy of Egyptian poet Mostafa Ibrahim’s poetry collection, Manifesto, and recite it from cover to cover. Published in the wake of the 2011 revolution, Manifesto has become a kind of literary scripture for many of the politically engaged members of my generation. Ibrahim moves through the splintered dreams, among comrades who once shared a square, a sidewalk blanket, and a barricade. In the quiet of the night, I let its lyricism hold me, and I mourn. I always return to one iconic poem about Tahrir Square, “So-and-So.”
So-and-so: I never learned
his name, so I called him
cousin, and that was
enough.
The anonymous “so-and-so’s” continue until the end of the poem, and I cannot stop thinking about how, at the time of writing that poem, each was flesh and blood: a face we could summon from memory, a stranger turned friend whose number sat in our phones. Now, it has become a poem of ghosts that calls forth immense pain.
Yet, every year, I sit by my copy on the night of January 25 and choose the haunting. We are haunted not by romantic nostalgia, but by the ephemeral moment when the unthinkable became thinkable. When we were shocked, then giddy, at the chants tumbling from our lips, daring and transgressive as if each were testing the limits of the possible. In her 1996 memoir, The Stillborn, Arwa Salih, one leader of Egypt’s 1970 student movement, speaks wistfully about the naïveté her generation felt whenever they recalled the revolutionary rapture of their crushed movement. “But I find far harsher,” she writes, “the hand dealt to the generations who never got to know such abundance.”
We were intoxicated by revolution. We understood that we were, forever, of the rupture, so we embraced it, and when we embraced it, the rupture held us back. And for a fleeting moment, we could imagine otherwise. I am blessed to have known such abundance. I accept the haunting. I embrace the ghosts of defeat.
And so, I argue for a counter-haunting, one that pierces openings beyond the Eagle-controlled pores, letting the unsanctioned ghosts seep through. The state’s machinery is built to erase the memory that another world was—and therefore is—possible. Our task is to summon the tender ghosts of revolution, to do justice to the ghosts of state massacres, and to unghost, unpast the us, us, us banished behind bars.
I know how difficult it is to remain held open in taut receptivity. It is often draining, even for someone like me, who shared the handcuffs and the prison cell. But it begins here, haunting our way back to the bridge.

From Parliament to Akashvani Bhawan - Rahul climbs barricades, MPs detained
NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi climbed atop barricades during the INDIA bloc MPs’ march from Parliament towards the Election Commission headquarters in New Delhi on Tuesday, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, NCP-SP MP Supriya Sule and several other opposition leaders also joined the march, which was held amid heavy security and barricading around Parliament and the EC office. Security personnel stopped the march near the NITI Aayog office as the MPs raised slogans of “Vote Chor, Gaddi Chhod”.
Rahul Gandhi led several INDIA bloc MPs in a march from Parliament towards the Election Commission headquarters in New Delhi, with protesters carrying placards and cutouts of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The opposition MPs were demanding Kumar’s removal over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process.The INDIA bloc had announced the march from Parliament to Nirvachan Sadan as part of its campaign against the Election Commission’s handling of the electoral roll revision. The protest route saw heavy security deployment, with barricades placed across central Delhi and Rapid Action Force personnel deployed around Transport Bhawan ahead of the march.
Security personnel stopped the MPs near NITI Aayog, preventing them from proceeding towards the ECI headquarters. Several opposition MPs then sat in protest near Parliament Street.The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) skipped the march, saying it would pursue the issue through its own means.
Opposition leaders detained
Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc MPs tried to enter the Election Commission office during their protest march against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, but were stopped by security personnel. After being prevented from entering the EC office complex, Congress leaders staged a sit-in outside the premises. The INDIA bloc MPs had marched from Parliament towards Nirvachan Sadan, demanding Kumar’s resignation.Earlier, Rahul Gandhi climbed atop heavy iron barriers near the NITI Aayog office and waved the tricolour while advancing towards the EC headquarters. Tensions escalated as Delhi Police detained Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, party General Secretary KC Venugopal and several other INDIA bloc leaders near the NITI Aayog office, where police had barricaded the route to prevent the opposition MPs from reaching Nirvachan Sadan.
Rahul, Priyanka Gandhi enter Akashvani Bhawan premises during EC protest

After being prevented from proceeding further, they sat on the road in protest. Rahul Gandhi and TMC MP Abhishek Banerjee later climbed atop a police barricade, while Priyanka Gandhi was taken to a waiting bus for detention.Priyanka Gandhi soon alighted from the bus and joined Rahul Gandhi at the Akashvani gate. Despite being stopped by police, Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi and Congress MP Deepender Hooda entered the Akashvani Bhawan premises through the reception gate and were later seen sitting under a tree.
Security tightened around protest route
The march began amid heavy security deployment and barricading in and around Parliament and the Election Commission headquarters. Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut questioned the security arrangements, saying the MPs intended to proceed peacefully. He also alleged that the CEC had “no moral right” to continue in office, while CPI leader P Sandosh Kumar called him a “Cheating Election Commissioner”.Kharge, Akhilesh target EC over SIR as INDIA bloc MPs press for poll reformsCongress president Mallikarjun Kharge alleged that the Modi government was trying to take away the public’s right to vote and accused Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of acting at the government’s direction. “After independence, the public was given the right to vote, which the Modi government is trying to end. Opposition steps up attack over SIR
The protest is part of the opposition’s sustained campaign against the SIR exercise and its demand for greater transparency from the poll panel. Congress MP Dharamveer Gandhi alleged that 13 crore votes had been deleted and called it the “biggest fraud in Indian political history”. Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar must go; he should resign. The SIR (Special Intensive Revision) should be scrapped. All the voters who have been removed or deleted under SIR must be restored back onto the voter list,” Congress Rajya Sabha MP Syed Naseer Hussain told ANI. He also demanded a high-level inquiry into alleged political interference in the election machinery.
Form 6 row fuels political clash
The march comes a day after the Supreme Court said it had not approved any modified version of Form 6 and said it would examine the Election Commission’s records to determine whether changes had been made and who had authorised them. The EC had earlier said the declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR had been upheld by the Supreme Court and that the forms prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, would be used outside the SIR period.Senior Congress leader P Chidambaram said, “How can the BJP blatantly deny that the Chief Justice of India did not say that... he said it clearly, 'we have not approved any modifications to Form 6.' I have seen the declaration...
the declaration is indeed a modification of Form 6.”Rahul Gandhi had accused the CEC of changing the application used by citizens to register as new electors “illegally and unilaterally”. BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra, however, accused Gandhi of misleading the public, saying the Supreme Court had not declared Form 6 illegal and had only agreed to examine allegations concerning changes to the form. The Election Commission has rejected allegations of differences within the three-member poll panel and maintained that decisions relating to SIR were taken unanimously.

Nobel body eyes those building peace in shifting world order, secretary says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:59:39 UTC
18:59:39 KST

Nobel body eyes those building peace in shifting world order, secretary says
OSLO, Oct 6 - The Nobel Peace Prize committee is closely watching the reshaping of a world order in turmoil, and those fostering new ways of cooperating that match the award's goals, its secretary says.
Kristian Berg Harpviken, secretary of the five-member Norwegian Nobel Committee, prepares its dossiers and joins the deliberations but does not vote. This year's announcement is on Friday.
Speaking in general terms about the committee's work in an interview on Monday, Harpviken said it was closely following the changes in the international order.
"We know what we're leaving behind, we don't know how much of it will survive, and in what form, and we certainly don't know what will come," he said.
"That is something that the committee, of course, takes very seriously in its discussions, also because some of the trends we are seeing internationally are trends that are threatening to many of the values that the Nobel Peace Prize has upheld throughout its history."
Created by Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel in 1895 in his will, the Peace Prize goes to the person "who has done the most or best to advance fellowship among nations, the abolition or reduction of standing armies, and the establishment and promotion of peace congresses".
Asked whether the committee could at some stage name a laureate concerned with how this new world order should look, Harpviken said:
"Of course, it's clear that people who are able to, within the transition period we are now seeing, start to stake out new institutions, new initiatives, new ways of working, that would be in harmony with the very objectives that Alfred Nobel defined in his will.
"Because, ultimately, that is of course the yardstick for what the committee does. That would obviously be something that the committee would be looking for."
The fact that the world is in upheaval does not mean that there is a want of candidates, or that the Peace Prize is losing its relevance, Harpviken said, adding:
"I'm not worried about the prize, but I am worried about where the world is heading." REUTERS

2026 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for research on neutrinos and contributions to IceCube
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

2026 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for research on neutrinos and contributions to IceCube
Kyiv • UNN
Francis Halzen became a laureate of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his contribution to IceCube and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos.
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Francis Halzen "for decisive contributions to the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of astrophysical high-energy neutrinos." The Nobel Committee announced this on October 6, UNN reports.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences decided to award the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics to Francis Halzen "for decisive contributions to the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of astrophysical high-energy neutrinos"
The 2026 Physics laureate Francis Halzen realized that the ice at the South Pole could be used to track particles known as neutrinos. His vision and scientific leadership were fundamental to the IceCube neutrino observatory—a cubic kilometer of ice equipped with light sensors. Using IceCube, researchers can detect neutrinos produced by extremely high-energy processes in the distant Universe, the Nobel Committee noted.
The interactions of neutrinos continuously recorded by IceCube will provide researchers with new knowledge about the turbulent processes in which high-energy neutrinos may be produced, and may even reveal previously unknown cosmic phenomena.

Pneumonic plague suspected in Russia: What we know and what is the risk to Europe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:59:28 UTC
18:59:28 KST

The death of a staff member at an anti-plague institute in Russia following a laboratory accident has put the spotlight on plague and how it spreads.
A staff member at the anti-plague institute in Irkutsk, Russia, died after a test tube broke in the laboratory, regional media reported, citing unnamed sources close to the region’s security services.
Russian authorities said they found no evidence that her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with. But the case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
Russian media reported that around 200 people, who had been in contact with the deceased worker, were under strict medical observation and that several hospitals in the region were closed and placed under quarantine.
“As ... the contagion was in a lab (and has presumably well disinfected) and people were rapidly quarantined, it is highly unlikely that it will spread further- and thus, whilst it is contagious, it is unlikely to have the opportunity to spread,” Alice Hughes, professor of conservation science at the University of Melbourne, said in comments to the Science Media Centre.
Yet, public health authorities are following closely any developments.
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) told Euronews that it is “closely monitoring the situation” and is in contact with the World Health Organization.
“We are aware of the case of pneumonia of unknown origin in eastern Russia that is suspected to be the plague. That suspicion is not yet confirmed,” a spokesperson said in a written statement.
The spokesperson added that based on the limited information currently available, there are no reports of secondary cases or sustained human-to-human transmission, and noted that there is “little travel” between Irkutsk and the European Union and European Economic Area countries, “particularly at present due to Russia’s war against Ukraine”.
Plague has been absent from Europe for more than 50 years; however, human cases are reported in Africa, particularly in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Madagascar.
What do experts say about the risk?
While the information surrounding the suspected case in Russia is very limited, experts noted that sporadic pneumonic cases are not rare.
“Plague is not a historical disease,” said Zania Stamataki, associate professor of viral immunology at the University of Birmingham in comments to the Science Media Centre. “It remains endemic in rodent populations across Africa, Asia and the Americas, and human cases occur every year, including outbreaks of the pneumonic form.”
According to Brendan Wren, professor of microbial pathogenesis at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, “there shouldn’t be too much concern as the transmission of Yersinia pestis between humans is generally poor”.
What is pneumonic plague?
Pneumonic plague occurs when plague, an infectious disease caused by bacteria, infects the lungs.
Pneumonic plague is the most serious form of the disease and is the only form of plague that can be spread from person to person. If left untreated, it has a case-fatality ratio of 30% to 100%.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), it is especially contagious and can trigger severe epidemics through human-to-human transmission via respiratory particles. However, recovery rates are high if the disease is detected and treated in time.
The incubation period can be as short as 24 hours and any infected person may pass it via respiratory particles to other humans.
What are the symptoms?
Pneumonic plague develops when bacteria spread to the lungs of a patient with untreated bubonic or septicemic plague, or when a person inhales infectious droplets coughed out by another person or animal infected.
Symptoms typically appear one to three days after infection. They include severe respiratory problems such as shortness of breath and coughing, often with bloody or watery mucus.
What is the treatment?
If untreated, pneumonic plague can be rapidly fatal. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential for survival and to reduce complications. Common antibiotics used against enterobacteria can effectively cure the disease if given early.
“Plague is a serious infectious disease. However, it can be diagnosed and treated with antibiotics readily available in Europe,” the ECDC spokesperson noted.
In cases of pneumonic plague, patients should be isolated and their contacts traced and treated, the agency says on its website.
Are there vaccines?
The WHO does not recommend vaccination except for high-risk groups, such as laboratory personnel who are constantly exposed to infection and health-care workers.
Because human plague is rare in most parts of the world, public health agencies see no need to vaccinate people other than those at particularly high risk of exposure.

Francis Halzen wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Francis Halzen wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics
STOCKHOLM, Oct 6 - Belgian-American Particle physicist Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for "decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin", the award-giving body said on Tuesday.
The winners of the Nobel physics prize are selected by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences and receive a prize sum totalling 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million), which is shared among the winners if there are several.
The Nobel Prizes were established under the will of Swedish inventor and entrepreneur Alfred Nobel, whose fortune was built in part on the invention of dynamite. First awarded in 1901, the prizes honour achievements in science, literature and peace, with the economics award added later by Sweden's central bank.
Physics occupied a prominent place in Nobel's will and the prize remains one of the discipline's highest distinctions. Over the decades it has recognised discoveries that have fundamentally reshaped humanity's understanding of the universe.
Among past laureates are some of the most celebrated figures in science, including Albert Einstein, Marie and Pierre Curie, Max Planck and Niels Bohr, whose work helped establish the foundations of modern physics.
Last year's physics prize was awarded to US-based scientists John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for experiments that demonstrated the principles of quantum physics in action, research seen as helping to advance the next generation of computing and other digital technologies.
The award was the second of this year's Nobels to be unveiled, following Monday's medicine prize announcement, with chemistry next on Wednesday.
Nobel medals are presented to the winners by Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf at a ceremony in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death. The awards are followed by an elaborate banquet at Stockholm City Hall.
The peace prize, the only Nobel not presented in Sweden, is awarded separately in Oslo. REUTERS

House China committee chair urges Fed to review Hong Kong’s access to dollar lifeline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:58:14 UTC
18:58:14 KST

The chairman of an influential congressional committee is urging the Federal Reserve to consider cutting off a potential financial lifeline extended to Hong Kong during Covid-era market turbulence.
The Fed should review the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's access to the Foreign and International Monetary Authorities Repo Facility, Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., said in a letter sent to the U.S. central bank last week and exclusively obtained by CNBC. Moolenaar chairs the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.
The FIMA facility allows central banks to effectively borrow dollars from the Fed with those countries' Treasury holdings as collateral. It was conceived as a means to ensure governments could get access to dollars in a crisis without having to sell Treasurys, which could create a downward spiral for prices.
The push to potentially limit Hong Kong's access to a source of dollar liquidity comes as China is making efforts to promote its currency, the yuan, as an alternative to the dollar as the bedrock of the global financial system. The U.S.-China relationship remains fraught despite the cheerful tone of President Donald Trump's recent meeting in Washington with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
The Fed is in receipt of Moolenaar's letter and plans to respond, a spokesperson said.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority declined to comment.
A 'very tenuous truce' between the U.S. and China
Still, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is unlikely to take a step that could be seen as interfering with China policy at a sensitive moment, said Shehzad Qazi, managing director of China Beige Book, a research firm.
"That said, this is an example of the novel ways Congress could begin asserting its role in China policy," Qazi said. The "very tenuous truce" between the two countries remains highly vulnerable, he said.
FIMA has been used only sparingly since its creation in 2020, though in August Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Japan to utilize it to support the yen.
The dollar remains secure in its status as the premier global reserve currency. It makes up 56.7% of global central banks' official foreign reserves, according to the International Monetary Fund, and is widely used to settle global trade. Investors treat short-term U.S. Treasurys as equivalent to cash.
Those attributes give Americans major advantages by lowering the cost of financing the outsized U.S. debt and allowing them to conduct business abroad in their own currency.
China has ambitions to edge out the U.S. dollar, though it is starting from a major disadvantage. The yuan makes up 2.1% of reserve holdings, according to the IMF.
Still, Beijing is taking steps to change that, and is making Hong Kong its laboratory for the creation of an alternative global financial architecture.
As a longtime British territory, Hong Kong developed its own financial and legal systems in parallel to China. But China now has firm control over Hong Kong, a factor Moolenaar cited in his letter.
The Fed needs to take into account "the complete dismantling of the legal and institutional autonomy that has historically distinguished Hong Kong from mainland China and justified its preferential treatment under U.S. law," he said.
The Fed should consider that shift in combination with China's recent efforts to boost its currency as an alternative to the dollar, Moolenaar said.
The dollar's prominence
The People's Bank of China in June launched its own version of the Fed's FIMA facility, to allow central banks to make short-term loans of Chinese government bonds. Hong Kong was its first user, PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng said in July. The PBOC is China's central bank.
"The Federal Reserve's own facilities should not be a passive participant in that process, nor should the Chinese Communist Party be allowed to copy and paste the U.S. system for its use," Moolenaar said.
But removing Hong Kong's access to a source of dollar liquidity could create its own risks, said Eswar Prasad, an economics professor at Cornell University. "FIMA's repo facility, if anything, increases the prominence of the dollar in global finance and also bolsters U.S. Treasury securities' role as a global safe asset," Prasad said.
"So it is hard to imagine that restricting access to this facility would in any way bolster the dollar's dominance or remove any threats to it," he said.
The Fed's protective umbrella helps the dollar's appeal among global investors, who can't be fully confident that funds invested into authoritarian China can be safely taken out of the country.
The FIMA facility was created to ensure authorities could get access to dollars in a crisis, on top of a network of swap lines that allow countries to trade their currencies for dollars. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority was one of the earliest central banks given access in 2020. Fed officials said then that Hong Kong "could be a template for others."
The Fed reports overall levels of usage of the FIMA facility but doesn't reveal the breakdown of which central banks borrowed how much. The Fed's most recent data show no one was using the facility as of Wednesday.
Hong Kong drew up to $1.4 billion from the facility in May 2020, but has not materially used it since, Moolenaar said in his letter.
"Precisely because the current financial stakes are modest, now is the appropriate moment for deliberate review rather than reactive action under crisis conditions," he said.

Poland and Lithuania prepare to evacuate one million Baltic residents to Poland in event of war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:58:11 UTC
18:58:11 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland and Lithuania are jointly preparing plans for the evacuation of one million or more residents of the Baltic states into Poland in the event of a war or other major crisis, amid growing concern in the region over potential Russian aggression.
On Monday, the two countries’ interior ministers met to discuss the issue following a recent large-scale Lithuanian mobilisation exercise that also involved Polish officials. The pair also addressed their joint response to the migration crisis on the borders orchestrated by Russia’s ally Belarus.
“In crisis situations, it is best to cooperate. It is best to prepare such plans through mutual understanding, thus attempting to address potential situations,” said Lithuanian interior minister Martynas Katelynas, speaking alongside his Polish counterpart, Marcin Kierwiński, at the Budzisko-Kalvarija border crossing.
“As for this crossing here, this place that connects us with Poland, this plan foresees approximately one million, and perhaps even more, refugees who will be able to be evacuated from our countries in the event of war,” he added.
The three Baltic states – Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – are seen as a primary potential target for Russian aggression. NATO states, including Poland, have in recent months warned of the growing possibility of Moscow conducting some form of “provocation” against the alliance’s eastern members.
Lithuania last week finished a major exercise testing its national mobilisation system in the event of war or other crises. For the first time, it included elements relating to cross-border evacuation of civilians from the Baltic states to Poland.
Alongside thousands of Lithuanian officials, a 20-person Polish team, led by representatives of the interior ministry, took part in the exercise.
This has allowed Poland to develop “an agenda and action plan for what must be adjusted very quickly: cross-border evacuation plans, infrastructure and alternative border crossings in an emergency, as well as reception points”, said Kierwiński, adding that “we will begin intensive work” on implementation.
Poland already has extensive recent experience in receiving civilians fleeing conflict. In 2022, it became the primary destination for the millions of refugees fleeing Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Poland’s government and civil society quickly implemented measures to support the refugees, almost one million of whom remain in the country.

The two ministers also used their meeting to discuss their joint response to illegal migration. Both countries have been the target of a crisis engineered by Russia’s ally Belarus, which has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross into Poland, Lithuania and Latvia.
In response, Poland last year introduced checks on its borders with Lithuania and Germany. Those measures have been repeatedly extended, including last week, when Poland announced that they would remain in force until at least March 2027.
“Border controls with Germany and Lithuania allow us to catch people illegally crossing the border from the Baltic states,” said Kierwiński on Monday. “As soon as there are grounds to end these controls, we will discontinue them. But for now, we have decided that they will remain in place for at least another six months.”

He also noted that an agreement between the two countries on cooperation between police, border guard and customs services is currently being finalised.
“Poland and Lithuania are like brothers and sisters who support each other and will continue to do so,” said Katelynas.

Last month, Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental.
Poland has already recently suffered airspace violations by Russian drones, a missile and a helicopter. It has also been the primary target for Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
In response, the Polish government has moved to expand the network of warning sirens along the Ukrainian border, launched a campaign informing the public how to respond to aerial threats, and started more clearly marking bomb shelters.
The Polish-Lithuanian border area, which sits between Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and is known as the Suwałki Gap, is seen as a potential target for Russia in the event of war. Poland and Lithuania held joint military exercises there in 2024 to test their defensive capabilities.

Ukraine unleashes drone barrage on Moscow, ships hit off Bulgaria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:57:00 UTC
18:57:00 KST

A Ukrainian drone barrage, involving approximately 650 aircraft, targeted the Moscow region overnight, killing two people and damaging dozens of residential buildings, Russian authorities said Tuesday.
Most of the drones were destroyed by air defenses at long range, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin wrote on Telegram. He said 105 drones were destroyed as they approached the Russian capital.
In addition to the two deaths, nine people were injured in the attack, according to Andrei Vorobyov, the governor of the Moscow region. It was not initially possible to verify these figures.
Vorobyov said 47 residential buildings had been damaged. Local reports said a fire had broken out in a warehouse in the village of Litvinovo.
The drone attacks continued into the morning, Sobyanin said, forcing Sheremetyevo Airport, the largest in the country, to suspend operations temporarily.
If the Russian figures on the number of drones shot down are accurate, they would point to a major Ukrainian attack.
Citing eyewitnesses, the Kyiv Independent reported that an oil production facility around 40 kilometers from Moscow was targeted.
Russian sources said the facility in the village of Konstantinovo is the region's largest reservoir and a key hub for Moscow's fuel supply. No official statement has been made regarding the target.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russia's oil industry to hit energy exports that provide important revenue for Moscow's war effort.
Ukraine has been defending itself with Western support against Russia's full-scale invasion for more than four and a half years and regularly targets sites deep inside Russian territory as part of its defense.
Russia, meanwhile, systematically attacks targets across Ukraine with drones and missiles, killing civilians and damaging homes and critical infrastructure.
At least six people were killed by Russian aerial bombs in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv Monday, according to authorities.
Investigators said 59 people were injured, while rescue workers continued searching the rubble of a residential building for possible further victims.
Also Tuesday, unidentified drones hit two commercial ships in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria, sinking one of the vessels, the government said.
While the sailors from the sunken ship were missing, those from the second ship were rescued, Rumen Nikolov, head of the local rescue operations in Varna, was quoted as saying by the BNR public radio.
Rescuers were scouring the area for the missing sailors, about 150 kilometers (90 miles) east of the coastal city of Byala, the radio said.
The government said it would convene an emergency meeting later Tuesday to discuss the strikes.
According to the Maritime.bg specialist site, the ship that sank was flying under a Togo flag.
The other ship was flying under a Palau flag, with 18 crew members evacuated by a Bulgarian ferry after the strikes.
Tuesday's strikes came a day after Romania reported that a grain ship had caught fire and sand near its coast, with two crew members killed, in an attack Ukraine blamed on Russia.
Türkiye's Chamber of Maritime Commerce (IMEAK) said last month that since the start of the war, 226 civilian and commercial vessels have been attacked in the Black Sea, the vast majority this year.

How does Switzerland use fossil fuels?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:55:45 UTC
18:55:45 KST

Switzerland’s trains may run on mostly on renewable electricity, but the country still depends heavily on fossil fuels. Transport accounts for the biggest share, driven by cars, trucks and frequent air travel. At the same time, roughly half of residential buildings are heated with oil or natural gas. Reducing Switzerland's dependence on imported fossil fuels will be critical if it is to meet its net-zero goal for 2050.

Nobel Physics Prize goes to Francis Halzen for neutrino work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:54:00 UTC
18:54:00 KST

Nobel Physics Prize goes to Francis Halzen for neutrino work
October 6, 2026
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences on Tuesday awarded the Nobel Prize in physics to Francis Halzen.
He received the award for this "decisive contributions to the IceCube neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin," the academy said.
The committee described the neutrinos as "ghostly messengers from space."
What Francis Halzen said about his Nobel prize
Born in Belgium, the 82-year-old is a physics professor University of Wisconsin–Madison in the United States. Halzen acknowleged the prize as he was called on the phone by the panelists who presented the award.
He told the Nobel academy that he was "surprised" to get the prize and thanked the many contributors to the project, adding that the discoveries required a lot of "luck."
"This was kind of an adventure, where success was not guaranteed. It was a long journey, but it finally worked," Halzen said.
The Belgian scientist said that he hoped his Nobel Prize reflects on the "really courageous people" who believed in the project. "No really respectable conservative physicists would have joined me, but many talented people did, and that's why I'm here," Halzen added.
Belgium's Prime Minister Bart De Wever extended his "heartfelt congratulations" to Halzen. He noted that Halzen is the 11th Belgian to win a Nobel, and the second in physics.
What is the IceCube neutrino Observatory?
Neutrinos are tiny cosmic particles of ultra small mass that are present everywhere. They come from stars like the sun and trillions of them pass through our bodies every second.
Scientists are not able to observe the so-called ghost particles zooming around on their own, so they measure what happens when they collide with other bits of matter.
Halzen's idea of capturing neutrinos at the Earth's South Pole dates back to the 1980s. The IceCube Neutrino Observatory was subsequently built at the South Pole in Antarctica as a dedicated facility to capture and study the neutrinos.
"The neutrinos we detect are like fingerprints that help us understand the objects and phenomena where the neutrinos are produced," the group said.
"IceCube collaborators address several big questions in physics, like the nature of dark matter and the properties of the neutrino itself," the organization says.
Some 450 physicists from 58 institutions in 14 countries make up the IceCube collaboration.
The Nobel prizes awarded this week
The physics prize has been awarded 119 times to 230 laureates between 1901 and 2025.
Last year, it went to three scientists for their research on the strange behavior of subatomic particles called quantum tunneling that enabled the ultra-sensitive measurements achieved by MRI machines and laid the groundwork for better cellphones and faster computers.
It is the second Nobel announced this week, after the medicine prize was awarded to three scientists whose work on optogenetics has helped unravel how the brain works.
Further laureates are set to be named in chemistry, literature and peace in the days up to Friday.
The prizes will be presented at ceremonies on 10 December.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million; €1 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.

Putin Warns Russia Must Not Create an “Intellectual Elite” Taught to Think
Russian leader Vladimir Putin stated that against the backdrop of artificial intelligence development, society must not be divided into an "intellectual elite" taught to think and people whose intellectual development falls into the background.
Speaking at the plenary session of the Valdai Forum on October 1, Putin also spoke about the risks associated with the development of artificial intelligence, according to The Moscow Times on October 5.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
He cited warnings from experts who believe that AI could become another attempt to "bring everyone to a common denominator."
Putin also touched upon the issue of national digital sovereignty. He stated that as state structures become increasingly digitized, governments must balance technological openness with national security and cultural identity, avoiding isolation from global technological advancement.
The State Duma previously passed a new law on artificial intelligence development in its second and third readings. The legislation introduced definitions for sovereign and national AI models into Russian law, requiring them to comply with traditional Russian spiritual and moral values.
Under the new regulations, sovereign models had to be created entirely by Russian companies, with development, training, and data storage restricted exclusively to domestic data centers. National models could use open-source foreign components, but both categories required government confirmation of alignment with traditional values before gaining official status.
The law placed national AI strategy under Vladimir Putin, while the government managed framework implementation, state support, and mandatory usage cases ahead of its September 1, 2026 effective date.

Le Pen vows to save €140 billion by 2032 if elected to prevent French 'default'
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen said she would make drastic savings to bring France's public deficit back in line if she wins next year's presidential election. The government forecasts the national debt will hit 5.4 percent this year despite the EU setting a 3 percent limit for member states.
French far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen said Tuesday that she would implement €140 billion ($157 billion) in cost savings by 2032 if elected next year, warning that without change France was "heading towards default" on its debt.
The current frontrunner in the presidential race made the announcement in a bid to stake out her credibility on the economy and regain momentum after her top ally Jordan Bardella was accused of making antisemitic comments, which he has denied.
Le Pen also vowed to bring France's public deficit back to below the EU limit of three percent of GDP by 2030, while urging the European Central Bank to "ease the burden" of interest rates.
France's deficit – the annual shortfall of revenue to spending – came in at 5.1 percent of GDP last year, and instead of reducing that level as originally planned the government now forecasts it will hit 5.4 percent this year.
It plans to borrow €340 billion ($385 billion) in 2027, around €28 billion more than this year, to help finance government spending and repay debt coming due.
Read moreFrench PM presents belt-tightening 2027 budget, including frozen wages and new taxes
But those forecasts could be jeopardised by rising interest rates, which have seen France's government bond yields soar in recent weeks.
"If the French do not choose a political break, France is heading towards default," Le Pen said.
She slammed the successive governments of President Emmanuel Macron for failing "to anticipate the slightest economic, financial or budgetary policy capable of preventing the noose of interest payments from strangling France".
Le Pen also lamented that "productivity has completely fallen behind that of the United States, and our research spending is incapable of giving us the slightest comparative advantage in the technological battle that is raging".
She also reaffirmed her proposal to introduce via referendum a budget "golden rule" to oblige an annual reduction in debt.
But Le Pen will have to find areas to make significant cost savings, given she also wants to lower the retirement age to 62, or even 60.
She promised cost savings of 15-20 billion euros within pensions alone by correcting "inefficient and unfair" measures in the current system.
A poll last week showed Le Pen was on course to easily win not just the first round of the presidential elections next April, but also the second round against any challenger.
But the accusations last week that Bardella made antisemitic comments on Facebook Messenger in 2013 dealt a blow to her campaign. She has made clear she still has full confidence in Bardella.

Scientist Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on subatomic particles at the South Pole, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm announced on Tuesday.
Halzen was honoured "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin", the Nobel jury said.

The announcements of this year's prizes began Monday with the Nobel Prize in Medicine being awarded to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.
This week's awards continue Wednesday with the chemistry prize and literature on Thursday. After Friday’s peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Monday.

‘He brought honor to 1.4 billion’: India rallies around flydubai hero pilot

It is rare to see a country rally so strongly around a national hero, let alone a country of nearly 1.5 billion people. Across India, people are embracing the flydubai pilot who became a national hero overnight and holding their heads high with pride. Smit Machchhar, who was wounded while helping thwart an attempt to crash Flight 1073, is drawing praise from all quarters.
On Indian social media, people have traced the story of Machchhar, who fought the terrorist and enabled Israeli passengers and relief pilots to take control of the plane. He grew up in Mumbai’s Ghatkopar neighborhood in a family originally from Gujarat, a state in western India. His family was in the textile business and although he initially studied textile engineering, he later trained as a pilot in New Zealand.
In Ahmedabad, one of Gujarat’s major cities, the sense of pride is evident in conversations with residents. “Machchhar really fought heroically and saved many lives,” declared Meet, a city resident. Vedant also used a word that has repeatedly appeared in local coverage: hero. “Everyone is emphasizing his courage. He is a hero.”
Everyone wants to take part in honoring him. Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel announced that Machchhar would receive an award and called him “Gujarat’s brave son.” At the Somnath Temple, an important Hindu pilgrimage site in the state dedicated to the god Shiva, prayers were held for his recovery. The chief minister of neighboring Maharashtra, where Mumbai is located, also expressed pride in “Mumbai’s son.”
On Friday, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi also spoke with Machchhar, praising him and saying he had brought honor to his 1.4 billion fellow citizens. The pilot burst into tears, apologized to Modi and said he had never imagined that he would speak with him.
“I saw that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also praised him highly,” said Gaurav, whom we met in Ahmedabad. He said the incident presented an opportunity to bring the two countries closer. “We already have good relations with Israel, and I hope that after this incident the relationship will grow even stronger.”
Another interviewee, Siyas, linked the episode to the familiar Indian concept of “Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam,” meaning “the world is one family.” He said the closeness between India and Israel is also reflected in official ties: During Modi’s visit to Israel in February, relations between the two countries were upgraded.
At the same time, within India itself, national pride exists alongside tensions that simmer beneath the surface and occasionally emerge. Hindus make up about 80% of the population, while Muslims account for about 14%. Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, is associated with Hindu nationalism, while Muslim support for the opposition has strengthened in recent years. At the same time, 95% of Muslims said they were very proud to be Indian.
Unsurprisingly, support for relations with Israel is stronger among the Hindu majority than among the Muslim minority, though for now there is no disagreement when it comes to the heroic pilot, who is Hindu. A poll published in June, before the incident, found that 32% of Indians had a favorable view of Israel, 28% had an unfavorable view and 40% did not respond.
We did not see those poll results reflected on the streets of Ahmedabad. Quite the opposite. Pride in the pilot and appreciation for the lives he saved went hand in hand with affection for Israel.
Meanwhile, Rinkel and Salma want Israelis to know that this friendship stands by them even in difficult times. “We just want to say one thing: India will always support Israel under any circumstances.”
Meanwhile, it was reported Monday that Shin Bet personnel had arrived in the United Arab Emirates and are participating in the interrogation of Omani terrorist pilot Hammam al-Hammami. During questioning, he has so far said that he acted out of a desire to take revenge on Israel for its actions in Gaza. He also confirmed that his plan was to crash the plane at Ben Gurion Airport.

Who is Nauman Mahmood, the Mecca Defence Alliance chief?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:51:55 UTC
18:51:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Who is Nauman Mahmood, the Mecca Defence Alliance chief?
Retired Pakistani Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood has been appointed the first secretary-general of the Mecca Alliance for Defence, putting the former intelligence official and field commander at the centre of the new Saudi-Pakistani-Turkish military alliance.
The 57-year-old will serve a three-year term as secretary-general as Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey move to turn their mutual defence agreement into practical mechanisms for military coordination.
His appointment comes at a formative moment for the alliance, which was signed in August and activated for the first time on Monday in response to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Mahmood brings more than three decades of military experience to the role, with a career spanning field operations, military training, intelligence analysis and strategic planning.
From military instructor to field commander
Born in 1969, Mahmood joined the Pakistan Army in September 1987 and was commissioned into the Baloch Regiment.
Early in his career, he served at the Command and Staff College in Quetta, the capital of Pakistan's southwestern Balochistan province, where he held a number of teaching and training positions and eventually became a senior instructor.
He also underwent advanced military training and studies in Pakistan and Egypt and studied at the National Defence University in Islamabad, where he earned a master's degree in war studies.
As a major general, Mahmood went on to command an infantry division in North Waziristan, one of Pakistan's most sensitive security regions, where the military has conducted years of operations against armed groups.
The posting marked a significant period of field command in his career before he moved into intelligence and strategic analysis.
Intelligence and Afghanistan
Mahmood later served as director-general of the Analysis Directorate at Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence agency, better known as the ISI.
His work there involved analysing domestic, regional and international political and security developments, giving him experience in national security and Pakistan's external security relationships.
In April 2019, Mahmood was promoted to lieutenant general and appointed inspector-general of communications and information technology at the Pakistan Army's General Headquarters.
Eight months later, in December 2019, he was appointed commander of XI Corps, also known as Peshawar Corps, one of the Pakistan Army's major formations.
The command is particularly significant because of its responsibility for areas close to the Afghan border.
Mahmood headed the corps during a period of major change in neighbouring Afghanistan, as the United States moved towards ending its two-decade military presence and security concerns mounted along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border.
He remained in the position until November 2021, when he returned to military academia as president of the National Defence University in Islamabad, one of Pakistan's leading institutions for strategic and national security studies.
Mahmood headed the university until retiring from the Pakistan Army in April 2023.
First chief of the Mecca Defence Alliance
Three years after his retirement, Mahmood has returned to a prominent regional defence role.
Pakistan announced his selection as the first secretary-general of the Mecca Defence Alliance, with the alliance's political, strategic and defence committee confirming his appointment on Monday for a three-year term.
The alliance's secretariat will be based in Riyadh, with Pakistan holding the secretary-general position for the first term. The post is expected to rotate among the three member states in subsequent terms.
Mahmood takes up the position as the alliance moves rapidly from a mutual defence agreement towards an operational military framework.
The Mecca Alliance for Defence was established under an agreement signed on 7 August by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
The pact states that an attack on one of the three countries will be treated as an attack on all.

Finnish Refugee Council faces up to 15 job cuts
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:51:08 EEST
18:51:08 KST

The Finnish Refugee Council will start change negotiations covering 21 employees as the organisation prepares for cuts to state funding. Up to 15 employees face dismissal, while the duties of another six workers could change as part of a restructuring.
The negotiations will begin on 8 October and affect employees whose positions depend on grants from the Funding Centre for Social Welfare and Health Organisations, known as STEA.
The talks will also cover employees whose work could be affected by organisational changes. The council said possible measures include redundancies, changes to job descriptions, transfers to other positions and a reorganisation of work.
The government plans to cut state grants for social welfare and health organisations by €84 million next year. The reduction represents about one-third of the grants awarded this year.
The Finnish Refugee Council said the funding cuts had forced the organisation to prepare changes to its operations.
“When funding falls this quickly and significantly, we also face difficult choices and have to adjust our operations,” executive director Annu Lehtinen said in the council’s statement.
She said the decisions would affect both employees and the support provided to people served by the organisation.
The Finnish Refugee Council specialises in forced migration and has worked with refugees and other displaced people for more than 60 years. The organisation said the restructuring aims to protect its work with people affected by forced migration as funding declines.
The council will receive about €1.3 million in STEA grants in 2026. Helsingin Sanomat reported that around 80 per cent of the funding for its work in Finland comes from those grants.
The newspaper also reported that Lehtinen warned in June that the organisation’s domestic operations faced closure from the start of next year. Her assessment followed proposed funding criteria from Social Affairs and Health Minister Wille Rydman.
The criteria were later changed. Finland’s Chancellor of Justice had raised legal concerns about the original criteria. The government subsequently decided to set the grant criteria through a government decree.

France's Macron observes test of new nuclear-capable missile without warhead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:50:08 UTC
18:50:08 KST

Macron observes test of new nuclear-capable missile without warhead
French President Emmanuel Macron on Tuesday observed the test firing of a new nuclear-capable missile without a warhead, according to the Elysée Palace and the Ministry of Defence.
France on Tuesday test-fired for the first time its new M51.3 nuclear-capable ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine, the defence ministry said. It was not carrying a warhead.
The missile, a variant of France's M51 missile, was fired from the Le Vigilant submarine off Brittany and impacted "in the North Atlantic, hundreds of kilometres from any coastline", it said. President Emmanuel Macron witnessed the firing from a French warship, an official told AFP.
It said the launch was conducted without a payload and in strict compliance with international obligations.
While the announcement made no mention of Russia, the test comes after President Vladimir Putin warned the West last week not to escalate a standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which is wedged between EU members Poland and Lithuania and which Moscow has made clear it would defend with nuclear weapons if necessary.
Macron hails clear message
NATO has said none of its "exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation". Putin also said Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully.
"Today we are stronger. The message has been sent loud and clear for wherever it must be received,” Macron said in a video on X showing him watching the launch.
Macron said in March France would expand its nuclear arsenal and launched an initiative offering European partners joint exercises, the possible short-term deployment of nuclear-capable assets on allied territory and deeper consultation.
Since then, the message of being prepared to bear the costs of defending France's values and security has been a constant theme.
France spends roughly €5.6 billion ($6.04 billion) a year to maintain its stockpile of 290 submarine- and air-launched weapons — the world's fourth-largest arsenal. Britain has 225 nuclear warheads. Russia and the United States have more than 5,000 each.
The M51.3 is the latest version of the missile that entered service in October 2025 as part of the modernisation of France's nuclear deterrent.
Paris does not disclose the range of the M51.3. Publicly available estimates for the M51 family generally place its range at around 9,000 km (5,600 miles) or more, while French officials have said the new version can travel further.
France maintains a nuclear arsenal based on air- and sea-launched weapons, with four ballistic missile submarines forming the backbone of its ocean deterrent.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Expert Insights: Belonging starts after five o’clock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:50:00 UTC
18:50:00 KST

In my very first column, I wrote about my early months back in Denmark: a new job in Vojens, a small room I lived in alone, and colleagues who knew I was alone and still never invited me for dinner. I took it almost as rejection. Later I explained it to myself, and to you, with a neat cultural rule: in Denmark, social life happens at the workplace, not in private homes.
I still think that is true. But I now think it is only half the story.
Every one of my previous columns has, in some way, been about the workplace: how trust is built there, how hiring works, how misunderstandings get resolved on a cleaning shift. But something kept nagging at me while writing about TRASBO’s weekly shared breakfast and summer party. The strongest Danish relationships I’ve seen, the ones that actually last, rarely start at work at all. They start in a forening.
The infrastructure nobody mentions in the onboarding email
Denmark has one of the highest rates of associational life in the OECD. At some point in their life, roughly a third of Danish adults will sit on the board of a voluntary association, a sports club, a choir, a parent-teacher group, a local sauna society. Interpersonal trust in Denmark runs north of seventy percent, compared to the thirties or forties in most large countries.
The political scientist Robert Putnam, in his famous study of American civic life, Bowling Alone, made an observation that applies almost perfectly here: trust is not built by people trying to build trust. It is a side effect of people showing up, week after week, for something else entirely, a training session, a rehearsal, a board meeting about the clubhouse roof. Denmark industrialised that side effect. The forening is not a nice cultural tradition. It functions as public infrastructure, quietly producing the very trust that later shows up at work as “flat hierarchy” and “we don’t need it in writing.”
No one puts this in an onboarding email, because no Dane thinks of it as a system. It’s just Tuesday handball practice.
Hygge: The glue, and sometimes the wall
If the forening is the infrastructure, hygge is usually described as the glue, cosiness, candles, trust among people who already know each other well. What gets left out of the export version of hygge is that “among people who already know each other well” is doing a lot of quiet work in that sentence.
Susan Ahmed, a singer with Iraqi-Danish roots who was born and raised in Denmark, has described experiencing two different versions of hygge, one among Danes, another reserved for people like her, despite having lived her entire life in the country. Hugette, who has lived in Denmark for 24 years after moving from Burundi, says she still cannot experience hygge the same way Danes do with each other, because she always feels like the difference in the room. Siana Ivanova, who moved from Bulgaria to Aarhus seven years ago, has made exactly two Danish friends outside work in that time, and describes Danes as people who would rather stay in their comfort zone than actively pull someone new into it.
The linguist Carsten Levisen has put it more bluntly still: “The Danes are not a nation… they are a tribe.” The anthropologist Jeppe Trolle Linnet, who has studied hygge academically, notes that it “establishes its own hierarchy of attitudes, and implies negative stereotyping” of whoever sits outside it. None of this means hygge is fake. It means hygge was never designed to be an onboarding tool. It was designed for people already on the inside.
Gentle withdrawal, not hostility
This is where it gets genuinely hard to name, let alone fix. Researcher Julia Jones, who has studied foreign workers’ experience of Danish work-life balance, describes a specific pattern: Denmark has low conformity pressure in private life and high conformity pressure in public life, almost the reverse of what many internationals expect. Danes are famously relaxed about how you live at home. But stepping into the shared, public spaces where belonging actually gets negotiated, the clubhouse, the staff kitchen, the summer party, comes with unspoken expectations that are rarely explained, because no one had to learn them.
The result, in Jones’s phrase, is “gentle withdrawal and disconnection” rather than overt exclusion. Nobody is rude. Nobody says you don’t belong. People simply, quietly, don’t pull you in, and over time, the absence of an invitation starts to feel like its own kind of answer.
It is worth connecting this to something from column #5: the Deloitte finding that sixty percent of employees report “covering”, downplaying part of their identity to fit in, within just the past year. Gentle withdrawal is what makes covering feel necessary in the first place. If belonging depends on blending into a hygge you weren’t raised inside, smoothing yourself out can feel like the only lever available.
So what actually works?
None of this means joining a forening is pointless, quite the opposite. It is, by most accounts, still the single most effective way into Danish social life, precisely because it runs on Putnam’s logic: showing up repeatedly, for a shared reason, produces trust almost as a by-product. A badminton club doesn’t require you to already have Danish small talk mastered. It requires you to show up on Tuesdays.
But it is worth being honest about the limits, rather than selling it as a guaranteed fix. Hugette has been in Denmark for 24 years and still describes feeling the difference in the room. Belonging here is not a problem that competence or patience alone solves, which is the same conclusion my last column reached about the workplace. If the forening and the hygge inside it stay only legible to people raised inside the code, no amount of individual effort from newcomers will close that gap on its own. Clubs, like companies, can choose to actively invite people in rather than simply leaving the door unlocked and assuming that is enough.
For internationals, the practical version of this column’s advice is probably: join something boring and recurring, show up even when no one makes it easy, and don’t mistake a slow build for a rejection. For Denmark, the harder question is one this column keeps circling back to, whether a culture that prizes trust so highly is willing to extend the same patience to the people trying to earn it from outside.

Booking.com goes to court to force staff to go to the office

Booking goes to court to force staff to go to the office
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Website Booking.com has asked a court to order its employees to work at least two days a week in the office to settle a long-running internal dispute.
The company’s works council has refused to sign off on a change to its working conditions that would require its 7,000 staff at its head office in Amsterdam to travel in to the capital twice a week.
Booking.com issued guidance at the end of the coronavirus lockdowns in 2022 advising its staff to spend 40% of their working time in the office, but some workers still work almost entirely from home, a spokesman told the Financieele Dagblad.
Any change to working locations needs to be approved by the company’s works council (Ondernemingsraad) under Dutch law, but the council refused to endorse the plan, forcing Booking.com to take the case to court.
The company argues that homeworking is bad for teambuilding and productivity, while staff surveys indicate that most workers find it easier to collaborate with their colleagues when they are in the office.
The new rules would allow staff to choose which days they come in to work: one day to be agreed within members of a team and the other on an individual basis.
The works council has said there is no business case for compelling employees to be present in the office two days a week.

Its initial assessment put the risk at "moderate to low" for Irkutsk, "low" for Russia overall and "very low" for the WHO European region.
