Fear and disruption for Ukraine's rail passengers as Russia escalates drone attacks
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:48:37 BST
18:48:37 KST

Fear and disruption for Ukraine's rail passengers as Russia escalates drone attacks
- Published
Ukraine's railways have kept the country running since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. But attacks are intensifying, with more than half of all strikes on locomotives since then occurring this year alone, according to the state-owned operator.
Yuliia Ponomarenko, 27, a marketing specialist from Kharkiv, found her journey to Warsaw last month suddenly interrupted just short of the Ukraine-Poland frontier.
"The border guards started running around and shouting "Run! Get out of the carriages! There's shelling!"
A Russian drone had just hit a locomotive near the same border, and a special train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European dignitaries, had passed through minutes before.
Passengers on Yuliia's train were kept waiting for six hours while the fire up ahead was put out and the line cleared, she says: "We were really lucky that we were delayed a little and it wasn't our train."
She is among an increasing number of Ukrainian passengers facing disruption and long delays, as air raid alerts trigger emergency evacuations far from the battlegrounds of the east.
In September alone, 5,831 trains had to be evacuated due to Russian drone attacks, state owned railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia told AFP news agency on Monday. This meant on average each day, 205 trains were stopped.
It appears to be part of a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure, with two bridges attacked in Kyiv in the past few days and passengers of a metro train caught up in one of the strikes.
Seventeen-year-old Anastasiia Ryvbalchenko has also experienced a narrow escape.
She and her fellow passengers were forced to leave their train at 4am, towards the end of a long of a journey from Odesa to Kirovohrad on 16 September.
"On my way to Odesa, there had been a lot of evacuations and now on my way back it was happening again," she says. "I was already thinking that if there was another evacuation, I just couldn't take it any more."
An hour and a half later, as passengers waited in the dark, a drone struck nearby.
"There was an extremely loud explosion and everyone started running into the woods," she said.
It is not clear what the target was, and in this case the train was not damaged, but with further explosions lighting up the night sky, Anastasiia decided not to linger, continuing her journey on foot before being picked up by her parents.
"I'm not going to travel by train anymore," she says.
Anastassia's journey was more dramatic than most, but delays – some brief, others that last for hours – are now commonplace.
Since Russian drones first started attacking moving passenger trains towards the end of 2025, the routine for passengers has become increasingly familiar: leave the train, scroll Telegram channels for updates on drone and missile launches, send messages to warn friends and family that the train is delayed.
For a railway company proud of its record for punctuality, this year's disrupted schedule is posing a major challenge.
"We used to say that that during times of war we performed better than some railways in Europe in regular times,"the head of rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia, Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, told us.
"But now the life of our passengers and crew members is the utmost priority."
Russia's defence ministry denies targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.
The dangers are very real. Attacks on Ukrzaliznytsia's rolling stock and stations have risen sharply.
Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, almost 60% have been this year, according to statistics released by the company. Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.
"The latest wave of escalation and real war with railways is becoming extremely intense," said Pertsovskyi.
"It's a combination of the deadly force of their shahed drones and precision that they achieve with cameras and mesh networks so they can hit moving targets."
According to Pertsovskyi, some of Russia's most recent drones are equipped with AI tools and image recognition. Ukraine is understandably cagey about how it goes about confronting this increasingly sophisticated threat, but electronic methods to disrupt the drones' connectivity are high on the list.
"Unfortunately, this is always a cat-and-mouse game," he said.
- Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign 
  - Published6 days ago
We were given rare access to an underground bunker in Kyiv, dubbed – appropriately enough – the "Iron Command Centre", where railway staff monitor threats in real time.
On one huge video screen, colour-coded passenger and freight trains could be seen making their way along the arteries of Ukraine's vast railway network.
We watched as a red icon representing a drone appeared to loiter over Kyiv, practically above our heads at one point.
Each drone had a 100km (62-mile) circle around it. Any passenger trains inside the circle would already have been evacuated, with customers not allowed to reboard until the train was outside the circle and the drone was still moving away.
"Our mission is not to let our train or our crew members be in that immediate attack area," Pertsovskyi said.
The company's precautions appear to have kept casualties low. Its figures for 2026 show that eight company employees have been killed, six of them when a ballistic missile struck a locomotive depot in Kyiv.
During our visit to Iron Command, another air raid siren sounded in Kyiv. The city's main railway station, we were told, was being evacuated.
On a later visit to the busy station, we found passengers waiting outside the main entrance or sheltering in underground passageways. Over the tannoy came news of steady stream of delays.
Everyone knows the coming months could be among the most difficult yet.
With winter not far off, Ukrzaliznytsia is already figuring out how to deal with evacuations when the outside temperature can reach -20C or below and snow is lying heavy on the ground.
Along with international donors, the company is preparing winter evacuation packs, mobile shelters and bus services in areas where evacuations become too frequent.
"We might be a slightly different railway, a reinvented railway," Pertsovskyi said. "But we'll keep connecting the country, no matter what, be it winter, be it summer, no matter how hard the enemy hits us."
Extra reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko

SBU arrests collaborator suspected of setting up repeater stations for Russian drones in Kyiv
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), together with the National Police, detained a Russian collaborator, allegedly hired by the Federal Security Service (FSB) to help direct long-range mass attacks on the Ukrainian capital.
The man was suspected of "collecting data on defense facilities and critical infrastructure to adjust massive attacks on Kyiv from September 21 to 24 this year," the SBU said on Telegram on Oct. 5.
According to the case materials, the attacker tracked potential "targets" for four days in order to direct Geran-5 type jet drones and ballistic missiles at the capital.
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Russian collaborators helping Moscow's war effort inside Ukraine have been a consistent focus of the work of Ukrainian counterintelligence.
In recent weeks, Russia’s daytime jet-powered drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital have become notorious not only for their difficulty to intercept, but also for their precision, highlighted by the targeting of bridges across the Dnipro River.
This has been enabled by the use of mesh radio networks, built around a decentralized network of radio repeaters that allows both airborne drones and ground-based repeaters to constantly share radio and control signals between them in real time.
On October 3, presidential advisor Serhii "Flash" Beskretnov asserted that the increased precision of Russian strikes on central Kyiv must have been enabled by the existence of mesh radio repeaters located inside the Ukrainian capital, something that suggested the presence of well-resourced collaborators assisting the Russian strikes.
The news comes after Russian jet-powered drones hit two of the most important bridges across the Dnipro River in Kyiv, the southern and northern bridges, several days in a row.

New European ski lodges and hotels opening in winter 2026-2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:45:25 UTC
18:45:25 KST

The winter sports season will see the arrival of many new properties in Europe. Highlights include The First Cortina in Cortina d’Ampezzo and the aptly named Ski Lodge in Verbier, while several properties are also returning after renovations.
Winter is coming and that means only one thing – it’s time to dust off the skis and get ready to hit the slopes.
In Europe, we’re lucky to have the world’s most developed ski market, with the Alps a traditional favourite alongside resorts in the Dolomites, Pyrenees, Scandinavia, the Balkans, and Central and Eastern Europe.
In fact, according to the Skiresort.com database, Europe is home to more than 3,900 resorts, with 37,800 kilometres of marked slopes and more than 16,800 ski lifts.
With so many ski destinations to choose from, there’s no shortage of places to stay. Here are some of the hotels and lodges opening or reopening this winter.
New ski hotels and lodges in Europe
Fahrenheit Seven Les Menuires, France
Fahrenheit Seven will open its Les Menuires hotel on 11 December 2026, adding a third Alpine address to its collection after Val Thorens and Courchevel. Set on the ski front in the Preyerand district, it promises direct access to Les 3 Vallées, along with an in-house ski boutique, bar, restaurants, terrace and indoor pool.
The First Cortina, by The Pavilions, Italy
The First Cortina, by The Pavilions is scheduled to open in early December 2026 on Corso Italia, in the centre of Cortina d’Ampezzo. Its 76 rooms and suites put guests within reach of the Dolomites while offering a base in town. Some suites even have private wellness facilities and terraces with mountain views. Dining options include Zuma (contemporary Japanese) and Velo (Italian) and there will also be a dedicated ski room and REVĪVŌ Spa.
The Green Resort, Zillertal, Austria
The Green Resort is due to welcome guests in Uderns from December 2026, combining a Zillertal ski base with a substantial wellness offering. Its 3,300-square-metre indoor and outdoor spa area includes pools, saunas and steam baths. For snowsports fans, the hotel offers a seven-night winter ski package which includes accommodation, meals, a six-day Zillertal Super Ski Pass per person, plus wellness treatments.
The Ski Lodge, Verbier, Switzerland
Opening in December 2026, The Ski Lodge is a 36-room boutique hotel close to Verbier’s Place Centrale. As well as its location, other highlights include a spa and a bar. The state-of-the-art spa will have an indoor swimming pool, cold plunge, sauna, hammam and a relaxation area. While the hotel’s bar, The Listening Room, will be open for guests and visitors.
Schiefergut Family Resort, Flachau, Austria
Families heading to Flachau in Austria will have a new option when Schiefergut opens in December 2026. The four-star resort has 28 suites and chalets and is located close to the ski lifts, Snow Space Salzburg, the Achter Jet lift, and cross-country trails.
Hôtel Le Tremplin, Morzine, France
Following an extensive three-year renovation, Hôtel Le Tremplin in the heart of Morzine is opening 13 self-contained holiday suites for the 2026-2027 ski season. This marks the full reopening of the property after the bar, restaurant and après-ski terrace returned last winter.
Garance Hotel & Spa, Morzine, France
The former Les Airelles hotel in Morzine is set to return as Garance Hotel & Spa in December 2026. Close to the ski lifts, and the legendary slopes of the Portes du Soleil ski area, the four-star Mont-Blanc Collection property will have 65 rooms, a brasserie, cocktail bar and spaces for children and teenagers. Its wellness facilities are planned to include a pool, Nordic spa, treatment rooms and areas for yoga and fitness.
Also on the horizon
Les Gets celebrates 90th year with new snowpark
While not a new property, Les Gets resort in Haute-Savoie, France, is celebrating a milestone year – the 90th anniversary of its first ski lift – and will welcome a new snowpark in 2026.
Designed for beginners, the snowpark beneath the La Croix chairlift will replace the mini boardercross course.
Les Gets plans a partial opening on 12 December 2026, subject to snow conditions, followed by full opening on 19 December 2026. The season is scheduled to run until 11 April 2027.
Raffles and One&Only in Courchevel 1850
Ok, so these next two luxury properties will not be ready for a few years just yet, but they are certainly worth adding to your winter travel bucket list.
Slated to open in 2028, Raffles Hotels & Resorts will debut its first ever-alpine resort in Courchevel 1850, one of skiing’s most iconic addresses which sits at the heart of Les 3 Vallées in the French Alps, the world's largest interconnected ski area.
Then a couple of years later in 2030, One&Only Resort and Private Homes will also open in Courchevel 1850, the brand's first resort in the French Alps.

FlyDubai flight incident: Did aviation miss the insider-threat warning?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:44:53 UTC
18:44:53 KST

The incident took place on a FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. (Photo: Reuters)
The FlyDubai incident has raised a difficult question for the aviation industry: what happens when the threat is already inside the cockpit?Aviation safety expert Captain Amit Singh believes the incident should be a wake-up call for everyone - especially the global aviation industry. In an interview with me on Times Axis channel, he pointed to gaps in information sharing, pilot background checks and the growing danger of insider threats.The incident took place on a FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The co-pilot, an Omani national, attacked the captain while the aircraft was in flight.
Reports have suggested that the co-pilot may have intended to take control of the aircraft and crash it in Israel.
Reports suggested that co-pilot may have intended to take control of aircraft and crash it in Israel.
Singh said the sequence of events was consistent with such a possibility. His assessment was that the attack on the captain could have been an attempt to take control of the aircraft. When that failed, the co-pilot may have tried to bring the aircraft down.These are questions for investigators to establish. The cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder will be crucial in reconstructing what happened.But there is another question that Singh believes needs urgent attention.
How did the warning against this pilot get lost when he moved from one country and airline to another?
The flight data recorder should provide a much clearer picture.
Reports have said the pilot had previously been barred from flying in Oman over concerns about extremist views. He later worked in other countries before joining FlyDubai. Singh said this raises questions about how far back airlines and aviation authorities look when checking a pilot's history. A pilot may move from one country to another and obtain a new licence. Does a new employer get the complete picture?“If somebody, say, his licence was suspended in Oman, then he goes to Morocco, he gets a new licence, he gets a Moroccan licence. And then he shifts somewhere else, he gets a third-country licence, then he comes to Dubai. So Dubai will only check the past licence, not the past three or four licences. So this is a matter of debate.”The larger problem, he argued, is the lack of seamless information sharing across jurisdictions. That is where the concept of the insider threat becomes important.
The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) issued an Insider Threat Toolkit in 2022. Singh pointed out that an insider does not necessarily mean someone who has entered an airport illegally. It could be a baggage handler, a member of the catering staff, cabin crew, an engineer or even a pilot.All of them have legitimate access to sensitive areas and systems. The industry, he said, has known about such risks for years. There have been cases involving insiders taking control of aircraft or helping explosives get on board.But he feels that a separate regulation cannot exist for every possible threat. The industry also needs a culture in which small warning signs are reported and information is shared.A disturbing social media post may appear insignificant. So may a warning issued to an employee. But repeated incidents can form a pattern.The challenge is making sure that pattern reaches the people responsible for security. Singh described these early signals as “murmurs”. The question is whether aviation is listening to them.
The aircraft had only seconds before it would have hit the ground.
The 30-second window
There was another extraordinary element to the FlyDubai incident. The captain managed to open the cockpit door after being attacked. Passengers then entered the cockpit and restrained the co-pilot. One passenger, identified as an Israeli plumber, took the controls while the aircraft was in a steep descent. Singh estimates that the aircraft was descending at around 25,000 feet per minute - about ten times the normal rate of descent, according to his assessment. The aircraft was under enormous stress. The passengers needed to act quickly. According to him, the aircraft had only seconds before it would have hit the ground. Therefore, the captain's decision to open the door was critical. That decision may have saved the aircraft. But Singh believes there was something else unusual about the combination of people on that flight.“The pilot was an Indian and the passengers were Israeli. Had there been different nationalities, the outcome would have been different,” he said.Singh said the captain's resilience and his faith helped him push through his injuries and reach the cockpit door. He also believes the Israeli citizens’ military training and their instinct to respond quickly helped prevent the aircraft from crashing. He called it their “survival mode”. The point, Singh said, was not that the passengers knew how to fly. It was that they did not freeze. The distinction is important. They were not flying the aircraft in the conventional sense. They were responding to an extreme emergency with almost no time to think. And that is what makes those 30 seconds so important.
Did aviation miss the warning?
What happens next?
Videos recorded by passengers have already fuelled speculation about what happened inside the aircraft.Singh identified one detail that could be significant: emergency lights appear to come on during the incident. Those lights can be activated during a loss of electrical power. In Amit Singh's view, this raises the possibility that both the aircraft's engines may have temporarily lost power or may have been deliberately shut down.That cannot be established from the videos alone. The flight data recorder should provide a much clearer picture. But the larger lesson may extend well beyond FlyDubai.Aviation security relies on layers of checks. Licences are checked. Backgrounds are checked. Security clearances are issued.
PM Modi and President Murmu praised Capt. Smit Machchhar.
But an individual's history can cross several countries and employers. A single database may not capture all of it. Singh believes aviation needs better information sharing, continuous background checks and technology – especially AI and biometrics.People working in aviation must also feel they can report unusual behaviour without being punished for raising a concern.The aviation industry cannot afford to ignore this question: Are we still looking for terrorists outside the system when the next threat may already have legitimate access from inside it?

ROUNDUP - Yemen fighting intensifies as government forces report gains against Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:44:40 UTC
18:44:40 KST

Sahin Demir
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Yemeni government forces reported new territorial gains against the Houthis in southwestern Taiz province on Tuesday, expanding a major military offensive launched a day earlier that has seen them retake strategic areas along the country’s western coast and around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Taiz Military Axis said government forces retook Jabal al-Manzara, al-Asharif and Dhiban in the Hayfan district of southern Taiz.
Control of the mountains overlooking several key areas in Hayfan gives the government forces an advantage in monitoring surrounding territory and securing supply routes.
Earlier Tuesday, the army said around 100 Houthi fighters were killed and 150 others wounded during separate operations across Taiz on Monday, while five drones were downed and six military vehicles and a tank were destroyed or damaged.
The operations targeted fronts north, south and west of Taiz city, and formed part of the first day of the government’s newly launched “Dawn of Yemen” offensive.
 
Offensive expands to western coast
The latest advances followed significant territorial changes reported Monday along Yemen’s western coast.
Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said Monday the “Dawn of Yemen” operation aims to restore state institutions, retake the capital Sanaa and end Houthi control.
Pro-government Southern Giants Brigades and Nation’s Shield forces took part in the operation, supported by air cover from the Saudi-led coalition.
Government forces subsequently said they had regained control of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb area, including positions around Dhubab, following clashes with the Houthis.
Government forces also announced the recapture of Mokha, the strategic Red Sea port city in Taiz province that had fallen to the Houthis during their advances in September.
The developments effectively opened several fronts stretching from inland Taiz toward the Red Sea coast and Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints.
The Saudi-led coalition, which supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government, said Monday that 100 fighter jets participated in the opening phase of the “Dawn of Yemen” operation.
The coalition said its aircraft struck 324 “high-value targets” and were providing round-the-clock air support to Yemeni government forces, including air protection around Bab el-Mandeb.
 
Houthi denial
The Houthis have disputed government accounts of some of the battlefield advances and accused their opponents of announcing “imaginary victories.”
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Tuesday that the group carried out dozens of strikes against what he described as Saudi-backed forces east of the northern Al-Jawf province.
He also claimed attacks against forces east of Raghwan in central Marib province, saying the strikes caused casualties and destroyed military vehicles.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia or the Saudi-led coalition of the Houthi claims.
The Houthis have also stepped up missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia amid the fighting.
The group said Monday it targeted several sites across the kingdom, including airports and military and economic facilities.
Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said Tuesday that King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Jazan and Najran International Airport were attacked Monday evening, leaving three people with minor injuries and causing material damage.
The latest offensive comes after the Houthis made significant gains along Yemen’s western coast in September, seizing key areas in Al-Hudaydah and Taiz provinces, including Mokha and Mayun Island overlooking Bab el-Mandeb.
The current government offensive seeks to reverse those gains while increasing pressure on Houthi-held territory on several fronts.
The latest escalation is among the most significant rounds of fighting in Yemen since a UN-brokered truce in April 2022 ushered in a period of relative calm.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Golmohammadi: Iran U23 option or Team Melli coach?
TEHRAN - Yahya Golmohammadi has emerged as a name increasingly linked with Iranian football’s national teams following his recent departure from Iraqi side Duhok. While reports have connected the experienced coach with the vacant Iran U23 head coach position, there is growing speculation that Golmohammadi could be a more suitable candidate for the senior national team.
The Iran U23 job became available after Hossein Abdi resigned as head coach, leaving the position open at a crucial stage for the country’s young players. Golmohammadi’s name has subsequently appeared in media reports as one of the possible candidates to take charge of the Olympic side.
However, it remains unclear whether there is any concrete agreement or serious negotiation between Golmohammadi and the Iranian Football Federation. Much of the current discussion appears to be based on media speculation rather than an officially confirmed proposal. His recent resignation from Duhok has naturally fueled those reports, but leaving an Iraqi club does not necessarily mean that the former Persepolis coach is preparing to take charge of the U23 team.
At the same time, another possibility deserves serious consideration.
The pressure surrounding Amir Ghalenoei has increased following a series of disappointing performances by the Iranian senior national team. Although Ghalenoei remains in charge, criticism of his tactical approach and the team’s overall performances has led to speculation about a possible change in the future.
This is where Golmohammadi could become a particularly interesting candidate.
The 54-year-old coach has considerable experience managing Iranian clubs and has already worked under intense pressure at one of the country’s biggest football institutions, Persepolis. His teams have generally been associated with organization, defensive discipline and an ability to compete under pressure. Those qualities could make him a logical candidate if the federation eventually decides to make a change at senior level.
Of course, appointing Golmohammadi to the U23 team could also make sense. Working with younger players would give him an opportunity to build a new generation and potentially prepare footballers for the senior national team. Yet, considering his experience and current profile, the senior team may represent a more natural challenge for him.
For now, the link between Golmohammadi and the Iran U23 team should be treated cautiously. There is no official confirmation that he will replace Abdi.
What is certain, however, is that Golmohammadi is available again. If the situation surrounding Ghalenoei becomes more complicated, the former Persepolis boss could move from being a media-created U23 candidate to a serious contender for the biggest coaching job in Iranian football.

Govt allows cut in diesel duties to elapse
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:44:04 CEST
18:44:04 KST

The last in a long series of measures to cut duties on diesel, which Premier Giorgia Meloni's government had brought in to help people and businesses cope with soaring fuel prices, elapsed on Tuesday. 
The first such cut was approved in March in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war and in recent months there has been a 17-cent-per-litre reduction in diesel duties, which was gradually brought down to 12.2 cents and then to 6.1 cents. 
Eni said its cap on fuel prices in its gas stations in Italy would rise as a consequence of the end of the cut in duties,going from 2.19 to 2.25 euros for a litre of diesel, with the cap for unleaded petrol remaining at 1.99 euros per litre.
Encouraged by the government, the State-owned energy giant brought in the 30-day cap last week and several other companies running petrol stations in Italy followed suit. 
Consumers association Codacons said the government had failed to respect a promise to bring in a new Flexible excise-duty offset mechanism to replace the cut in diesel duties.

Germany faces a triple threat from Russia, China and domestic far-right extremists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:41:00 UTC
18:41:00 KST

Germany's triple threat: Russia, China, far-right extremists
October 6, 2026
The heads of Germany's intelligence agencies rarely provide information openly. What members of the Bundestag's Parliamentary Control Committee discuss in their bug-proof meeting room with the presidents of the Federal Intelligence Service, or Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), and the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), as well as the president of the Military Counterintelligence Service, is strictly confidential.
Since 2016, however, a public meeting has been held once a year, open to journalists, as well as citizens who register in advance. At this year's meeting, held Monday, intelligence officials seemed extremely alarmed. They painted a picture of a country in the midst of a confrontation with Russia.
"The military scenarios envisioned for the year 2029 have already become a reality today in the shadowy world of intelligence," BfV President Sinan Selen said, referring to a recent assessment by NATO experts that, under certain conditions, Russia could be capable of launching an attack on the alliance in a few years.
BND President Martin Jäger said there were no indications of an imminent military attack. Instead, Moscow is waging a "shadow war" through sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation, and espionage. "No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany," Jäger explained, adding: "Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia."
In Russia's crosshairs
Germany plays an essential role in supporting Ukrainethrough military, financial and humanitarian efforts. Jäger said that this makes Russia see Germany as a "major obstacle to Russia's hegemonic power projection in Europe." "If Germany were to falter, all of Europe — and Europe's support for Ukraine — would begin to unravel," Jäger concluded.
The intelligence agency heads expressed concern over the course of the war in Ukraine. Russia is expected to step up the pressure on the country this coming winter. At the same time, Moscow is attempting to hinder Western arms deliveries.
The intelligence services find that Russia is deliberately attempting to create uncertainty and weaken societal resilience in the European Union and elsewhere. Selen spoke of "coldly calculated destabilization operations."
When asked whether Germany would be safer if it did less to support Ukraine, Jäger said unequivocally that aid to Kyiv is in the national interest.
In addition to espionage, there are an increasing number of acts of sabotage and even assassination operations. Transportation routes, military infrastructure, and the defense industry are particularly at risk.
As an example, authorities cited this summer's attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, in which Russia is the prime suspect. In August, a drone rigged with explosives was discovered there near a Ukrainian cargo plane. Selen, head of the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany's domestic intelligence agency, again pointed to clear evidence of Russian involvement.
'Disposable agents' and organized crime
Germany's domestic intelligence agency is particularly concerned about the increasing use of so-called low-level agents, or people who are recruited locally via digital channels, for example, for espionage, transport services or acts of sabotage. "Social media plays a central role here," Selen stressed.
The intelligence chiefs also said Russian services were collaborating with organized crime groups. An increase in this area is a development that security agency heads say they will need to prepare for more thoroughly in the future.
According to the BND, Russia is gradually pushing boundaries through targeted actions. Examples cited included drone overflights of NATO territory and airspace violations in Moldova. "Russia is very deliberately shifting the bar here toward a kind of new normal," said Jäger.
Jäger said covert operations against individual NATO countries, particularly in the Baltic states, were conceivable, recalling events in Crimea in 2014, when Russian troops appeared as covert units without any insignia. Now the agency heads suggest similar operations could be conducted to test the alliance's ability to respond.
China's long-term challenge
In addition to Russia, China continues to be a concern for security agencies. The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution once again warned against attempts to gain access to German know-how through research collaborations and universities. Particular focus is on artificial intelligence, quantum technology, hypersonic technology and biotechnology.
The authorities are also watching the spread of Chinese technology products with concern. Data leaks from connected vehicles or household appliances could be misused. In extreme cases, it is even conceivable that systems could be shut down remotely.
Right-wing extremism on the rise
The topic of extremism also took up a significant portion of the discussion with the parliamentary committee. Regarding right-wing extremism, Selen spoke of an "extremely alarming trend" toward groups of young actors who are prone to violence and are increasingly forming international networks.
MAD President Martina Rosenberg reported an increase in suspected cases of extremism within the Bundeswehr. The increasing radicalization of society is not sparing the armed forces either.
Against the backdrop of growing threats, the heads of the BND and BfV defended a planned expansion of intelligence powers. The plan is to significantly expand agencies' powers regarding the collection, storage, and automated analysis of data. In addition, the agencies are to be given the ability for the first time, to actively combat threats such as acts of sabotage or hacker attacks through counterattacks.
"Amid geopolitical instability, conflict-prone systemic rivalry and hybrid aggression, there is a greater need than ever for tailored capabilities and robust security systems," Selen said.
Jäger said: "If we have these powers, then we will use them. And our adversaries will feel the consequences."
Critics in Germany, however, warn against blurring the line between intelligence gathering and police intervention. In light of these expanding powers, Konstantin von Notz, a member of the Parliamentary Control Panel with the opposition environmentalist Greens, is also calling for greater oversight of the intelligence services. He expects the Federal Constitutional Court to address the plan to expand the powers of the intelligence services.
This article was originally written in German.

Former German spy chief arrested for treason and espionage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:40:33 UTC
18:40:33 KST

Former German spy chief arrested for treason and espionage
One of the greatest potential intelligence breaches in post-Cold War German history comes at a particularly sensitive time for the country’s scandal-plagued foreign intelligence agency.
BERLIN — A former chief of Germany’s foreign intelligence service was arrested early Tuesday on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason amounting to potentially one of the greatest intelligence breaches in the country’s post-Cold War history.
An allegedly paid informant who held high positions inside the foreign intelligence agency, or BND, is accused of providing August Hanning — the former head of the agency from 1998 to 2005 — with nearly 2,000 documents, many of them classified, over a period of a dozen years up to 2022, according to the German Federal Prosecutor’s Office.
Hanning is alleged to have used the information to profit as a private consultant, according to prosecutors. In at least one case, prosecutors say Hanning allegedly used classified information to create an assessment for an employee of a foreign intelligence service.
Advertisement
“The accused Hanning is under strong suspicion of espionage constituting treason,” the prosecutors’ statement read.
The allegations amount to a huge embarrassment for Germany’s scandal-plagued foreign intelligence agency. The BND has a history of being infiltrated by other foreign intelligence services — at times making Western spy agencies reluctant to share sensitive information with the agency.
In 2022, authorities arrested former BND department head Carsten L. on suspicion of spying for Russia, charges he denies in a court case that is still ongoing.
The new allegations come at a particularly sensitive moment for the BND as the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz moves to grant it major new powers to hit back at Moscow, giving the agency much broader authority to perpetrate acts of sabotage, conduct offensive cyber operations and carry out espionage more aggressively.
Many questions will now be raised in Germany about how such a massive intelligence breach could have gone on undetected for more than a decade.
The alleged informant accused of having worked with Hanning was identified as Manfred D., Hanning’s former chief of staff. Following Hanning’s departure, Manfred D. went on to serve as chief of staff to several subsequent BND presidents from March 2012 to March 2026, according to prosecutors.
Advertisement
The material Manfred D. provided Hanning was used to brief the agency’s leadership for regular meetings at the chancellery attended by senior officials from ministries and security agencies, according to prosecutors.
Manfred D. is charged with “aiding and abetting attempted treason and espionage in the interest of a foreign power,” according to the prosecutors’ statement.
It was not immediately clear which foreign intelligence service employee Hanning is alleged to have prepared an assessment for using classified information provided by Manfred D.
In addition to that case, Hanning was also allegedly engaged “in an intensive exchange” with a member of another foreign intelligence service over several years, providing “political information” some of which was based on material received from Manfred D., according to prosecutors.
In neither case were Russian or Chinese intelligence agencies involved, according to a German intelligence official granted anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.
At the same time, Jäger welcomed current draft legislation giving his agency new powers to counter the threat posed by the Kremlin. “We will be a different, a new BND,” he said. “We are aware that additional powers entail greater responsibility.”
On Tuesday, however, Jäger was forced to defend his agency amid mounting concerns that the massive intelligence breach had undermined its ability to counter ongoing threats.
“For the BND and for me, there can be no compromises when it comes to internal security,” Jäger said in a statement. “None of my goals, none of my priorities are called into question by this incident.”
That is unlikely to ease concerns among German lawmakers that the BND has suffered serious reputational damage at one of the most sensitive moments in its history, as it prepares to hit back against rising Russian espionage and sabotage.
“The allegations against August Hanning are grave and appalling,” Greens lawmaker Konstantin von Notz, the deputy chairman of the parliamentary committee that oversees intelligence agencies, told WELT. “Any damage caused to the intelligence services must also be identified and investigated both promptly and comprehensively.”

In Kyiv, a Telegram channel admin was detained in a joint operation with the FBI — what he is suspected of

The SBU and FBI detained a Kyiv resident suspected of calling for terrorist attacks and distributing instructions on how to make explosives. The channel was blocked.
In Kyiv, the founder and administrator of a Telegram channel suspected of calling on subscribers to carry out terrorist attacks were detained. The operation was conducted by the SBU and the U.S. FBI. The Office of the Prosecutor General reported this on October 6, UNN reports.
Under the procedural guidance of the Office of the Prosecutor General, the SBU, in cooperation with the U.S. FBI, exposed and detained in Kyiv the founder and administrator of an extremist Telegram channel. He called on subscribers to carry out terrorist attacks and disseminated instructions for making explosive devices
Details
According to the investigation, in 2025–2026, the man created a channel through which he publicly called for terrorist attacks against civilians and law enforcement officers in Ukraine and partner countries. He also published materials and video instructions on making improvised explosive devices and hazardous substances.
"In his apartment, the suspect set up a ‘research laboratory,’ where he synthesized chemical explosives for loading into homemade bombs. He also provided subscribers with instructions on using electric detonators, assembling explosive systems and other components of improvised devices. During the search of the detainee’s residence, approximately 10 kg of explosives, 6 explosive devices, 200 cartridges, factory-made and homemade electric detonators, chemical explosives and poisonous substances, as well as equipment for synthesizing them, were seized. In addition, computer equipment containing evidence of the creation and administration of the Telegram channel was seized," the post reads.
The man has now been notified of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 258-2 and Part 1 of Article 263 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — public calls to commit a terrorist act and illegal handling of weapons, ammunition or explosives.
"At the prosecutor’s request, the suspect is being held in custody without the right to bail. The Telegram channel has been blocked," the post reads.

Ukraine is fielding Turkey’s Korkut air defense guns, a Turkish cousin of the Gepard. One kind of Russian drone may be too fast for them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:39:27 UTC
18:39:27 KST

- Ukraine has acquired new Korkut air defense guns from Türkiye
- The Korkut is a pair of fast-firing guns on a tracked or wheeled chassis
- Ground-based guns are effective defenses against drones
- But the Russians are launching faster drones, and more of them are getting through
Ukraine has reportedly purchased Korkut self-propelled anti-aircraft guns (SPAAGs) from Türkiye. Effectively a Turkish take on the classic German-made Gepard SPAAG, a mainstay of Ukraine's defense against Russian one-way attack (OWA) drones, the Korkuts could help stiffen Ukrainian air defenses as winter looms and Russia intensifies its terror attacks on Ukrainian cities and power plants.
The problem for Ukrainian air defenders is that the latest jet-propelled Russian drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, are getting through. They fly at around 500 km/h, nearly three times as fast as an older, propeller-driven Geran-2, and in September Ukraine shot down just 55% of them, by Zelenskyy's count, against at least 90% of the slow ones, one analyst calculated. The Korkuts arrive in that gap. Ground-based guns are arguably Ukraine's most cost-effective anti-drone weapons, but they may not work so well against the fastest drones.
That means more Russian munitions are getting through. More Ukrainian homes are burning. More power plants are going dark. It's a crisis now. It'll be an even greater crisis when winter arrives and the temperature drops.
All that is to say, the handful of Korkut systems Ukraine has received from Turkish firm Aselsan are welcome, but they're not silver bullets against Russian drones.
A Korkut battery includes a command vehicle plus three tracked or wheeled vehicles armed with pairs of fast-firing, radar-cued 35-mm autocannons. The exact variant Ukraine received hasn't been disclosed; Middle East Eye's mention of 25-mm ammunition suggests it may be the smaller Korkut 100/25, built mainly to stop frontline drones. The Ukrainian Korkuts join a sizeable fleet of SPAAGs in Ukrainian service, most notably including potentially 90 or more 1960s-vintage Gepards with twin radar-cued 35-mm guns.
Ukraine is running short of its best missiles for hunting Russia’s jet drones. Now MiG-29s are firing 1970s weapons
The tracked Gepards are old but effective. They, like all SPAAGs, can only engage incoming drones and other targets at fairly short range: just a few kilometers. But they're cheap. A SPAAG might fire a few hundred dollars' worth of shells to bring down a $50,000 Geran. A surface-to-air missile can hit a Geran from much farther away, but even the cheapest missiles cost tens of thousands of dollars apiece—and the supply is limited.
Gepards and other gun-based air defenses, along with wide-area strategic radio jamming, were the twin keys to Ukraine's temporary victory over Russian Gerans as recently as late last year. That's when the Russians were still mostly launching propeller-driven Gerans, and the Ukrainians were shooting down most of them.
Slipping interception rates
Vanquishing the slow Gerans didn't solve a separate air defense problem—how to shoot down supersonic ballistic missiles—but it did minimize Ukrainian casualties and mitigate the overall damage to Ukrainian infrastructure. Only the best, priciest, and rarest Ukrainian air defenses such as the Patriot and SAMP/T can hit incoming ballistic missiles. As missiles have run out for those batteries, more Russian ballistic missiles have gotten through.
But now more Gerans are getting through, too. On 26 September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 2,730 jet-powered Gerans at Ukraine that month and that Ukrainian air defenses were shooting down 55% of them. Analyst and mapper Clément Molin set that against Air Force totals: of 5,437 drones launched between 1 and 26 September, the remaining 2,707 were slow Geran-2s and Gerbera decoys, and at least 90% of those were downed. The overall interception rate, he calculated, has fallen to close to 70%, from 86% to 90% earlier this year.
Ukrainian forces are scrambling to acquire more inexpensive surface-to-air missiles as well as faster interceptor drones. But they're racing against time and the growing preponderance of jet-propelled OWA drones. The Ukrainians' air defense problem may get worse before it gets better.
"Ballistic missile defense is a serious problem, but the increasing production of Geran-4, Geran-5, Banderol, and Filin jet-powered OWA drones/cheap cruise missiles will also be a growing challenge this fall and winter," Rob Lee, an analyst with the Foreign Policy Research Institute in Philadelphia, warned in August.
Winter weather reduces the effectiveness of interceptor drones and helicopters, Lee noted, and Ukraine will need more high-speed interceptors to counter the jet drones. "The interception rate for OWA drones will likely decrease."
But that doesn't mean the Korkut isn't helping forestall an even worse dip in the overall interception rate for incoming Russian drones. Ukrainian officials are reportedly pleased with the Turkish gun. "Korkut has been pretty much successful in countering the Russian attacks," a Ukrainian official told Middle East Eye. "There were of course some problems but nothing that couldn't be overcome through some small adjustments."
According to Middle East Eye, the Ukrainians are considering acquiring more Korkuts.

India’s ‘million mutinies’ are puncturing Modi’s aura of invincibility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:39:03 UTC
18:39:03 KST

India’s ‘million mutinies’ are puncturing Modi’s aura of invincibility
Across India, students and opposition parties are turning disparate grievances into a broader reckoning with unaccountable power.
This October, India is a country where a million mutinies are gathering force.
India’s “cockroaches” — supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) — are back on the streets, marking Mahatma Gandhi’s 157th birth anniversary with non-violent disobedience. Once again, the atmosphere was carnival-like: plenty of students; a phalanx of marching, fist-waving women, arm-in-arm with young men, punching the air and shouting: “Gyanu, it’s done, bro”.
Surreally enough, they already talk of “Gyanu” — India’s Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar — in the past tense. What will follow — what system or person — is a question that has been put on hold. That’s for later. For now, the protestors are unified with a single, concentrated message: they want Kumar, accused of manipulating voter rolls in favour of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party, to resign.
Young women and queer students have taken to the streets over women’s safety in Delhi after a 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang-raped in Aastha Kunj Park in southeast Delhi by three men who posed as police officers. Concurrently in Mumbai, the parents of Sahil Wakode, a second-year BTech student at IIT Bombay, have launched an indefinite hunger strike after he died by suicide earlier this month. They are demanding the arrest of his teachers and alleging severe caste-based harassment. In Pune, Maharashtra Public Service Commission aspirants are on the streets demanding the chairman’s resignation over a range of concerns about alleged examination irregularities, transparency issues and uncertainty surrounding examination results.
The rest of India — those not out on the streets — is umbilically tethered to a computer or phone screen, riding alternating currents of buoyancy, pessimism, doubt and rage.
The sudden convergence of these volatile protests has effectively caught the Modi government in a pincer movement of domestic unrest. The overlapping waves of unrest represent a dangerous shift in the national mood, effectively uniting a fragmented Gen Z demographic against the Centre, re-energising and bringing together the opposition as a national force, and transforming disparate grievances into a cohesive, highly visible movement that the government can no longer contain.
Besides, central Delhi and parts of Mumbai are locked down under heavy security — on Gandhi Jayanti, no less — compounding the crisis of optics. Modi no longer provides stable governance. At this point, he rules not by legitimacy but by brute force and fear — of losing power and the legal reckoning that might follow once power is lost. For much of Modi’s political history, hierarchy has carried its own justification. His foundational axiom is that voters work for him and not the other way around. When he was popular, it worked. He could get us to queue in front of ATMs; lock us down without food, money, or scientific justification; abrogate Kashmir’s special constitutional status and beat up farmers and students.
When he was no longer popular, with the Election Commissioner — protected by lifelong immunity — tilting the system in his favour, he could dispense with popularity as well as a popular mandate altogether. But he no longer has the luxury of power without consequence. For three terms he wielded the combined power of popular legitimacy and institutional control. That era has ended. He no longer has a mandate like the one he had in 2014, and no institution — media, parliament, election commission or judiciary — is left to absorb the shock on his behalf.
The protests are disparate, but their underlying demand is strikingly similar: power comes with responsibility. The Chief Election Commissioner, the upper-caste teachers at IIT Bombay and the gang rapists who posed as cops are all being pulled into the same reckoning.
After the CJP’s first victory in July — which culminated in the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan — Modi retreated into his office, with some of his old swagger missing. Pierced by the relentless ridicule of Instagram reels and memes, the giant balloon that is Modi’s self-esteem is leaking from a thousand cuts. History will note that the first cracks in his powerful regime appeared not with an electoral defeat but when ordinary students stopped believing that nothing can be done.
This new wave of protests, the second in three months, challenges the inevitability of Modi.
The nationwide protests will continue all through October. Besides the “cockroaches”, India’s opposition parties will organise five big rallies around the nation. Besides the demand for Kumar’s resignation, the parties want a return to ballot papers, rather than Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs), arguing that electronic voting has made the recording and counting of votes vulnerable to manipulation. Leader of the opposition, Rahul Gandhi, has accused Kumar of high treason and warned of consequences once he is removed from the post.
Modi, meanwhile, has no plans to yield any of his authority.
He began the day at Gandhi’s samadhi, laying flowers before the apostle of non-violence while deploying paramilitary cordons and anti-riot vehicles across Delhi and Mumbai to stop protestors from gathering. Roads leading to Jantar Mantar in New Delhi — the designated protest site — are barricaded. The few who get past the blockades are being detained by police. The irony is almost too neat to be accidental. There were mass detentions on Friday. Fresh detentions on Saturday. Despite repeated detentions, protestors keep returning to the sites, pressing their demands.
Modi has, in fact, revived some of the very instruments of repression that Gandhi spent his political life resisting: restrictions on public assembly, curfews, preventive detention and the policing of dissent. The more precarious his hold on power, the more nakedly he reaches for brute force.
If there’s anything Gandhi taught, it was the limits of power and force.
Over the coming days, Modi may well succeed in emptying the streets, imprisoning protesters, confiscating placards and silencing dissent. What he will not be able to do, at least not indefinitely, is compel Indian voters to believe that power is legitimate simply because it is powerful.
In an exhausted democracy like India’s — with its institutions crumbling under the weight of unchecked power — the sight of Indians rising in a million mutinies is one of the more beautiful things I have seen in my life. The month of agitations is going to be messy, irreverent and noisy. The spectacle will also invite romanticism. There will be a temptation, when looking at this young movement with such extraordinary visual energy, to dwell on its purity, youthful exuberance, or incandescent rage.
It would be a mistake.
India’s new protest culture should neither be romanticised nor categorised in some tight box. It is something more, something rare: it is unfinished.

Gaza's children born since 2023 only know Israel's genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:38:37 UTC
18:38:37 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's genocide since 2023 shape a generation of Gaza's children
Three years of Israel's genocidal war have taken more than time from Gaza's children, the war also took away virtually every ordinary experiences that should shape a normal, healthy childhood: school, play, family life, and the feeling of being security and safety.
An entire generation's childhood in Gaza has been shaped by how to survive Israel's genocide.
On 9 October 2023, two days after Israel's genocidal war began, Suha Abdul-Wahid was born in Jabalia, northern Gaza. She has never known what Gaza was like before the war. Her earliest memories are of displacement, bombardment, shortages, and fear, according to her mother, Hibatullah.
"She grew up amidst the war and all its details," the mother told The New Arab. "Suha has never experienced a stable home or the kind of carefree play that children once took for granted," she said. "Even her first words reflected the world around her."
"Her first words were 'shooting' and 'missile'," her mother recalled. "I had hoped she would grow up like any other child, safe and living a normal childhood, but the war robbed her of that from the moment she was born."
Like all Gazan children, Suha grew up hearing explosions and moving with her family from one place to another in search of safety. By the time she was young enough to understand what was happening around her, war had already become the lens through which she understood the world.
Arkan Mahdi from al-Mughazi refugee camp in central Gaza was three years old when the war began. This year, he is around six; he finally started school.
But there was no school building, classroom, or playground waiting for him. Instead, Arkan entered a school set up inside a tent.
"When I saw him walk into that tent, I felt as though we had been set back decades in time," Mahdi, his father, told TNA.
Before Israel's war, Mahdi had bought uniforms for his three older children and shared their excitement as they prepared for each new school year. Unfortunately, Arkan never had that experience.
"The war deprived him even of the little things that bring a child joy," Mahdi said.
The damage has extended beyond his education. Mahdi explained that Arkan has become more withdrawn, developed a stutter and sometimes responds with irritability or aggression.
For him, the tent is not simply a substitute for a classroom. It is a symbol of a childhood that has been reshaped before it could properly begin.
Teens, lost to war
Jalal Abu Rajeh was 13 when the genocidal war began. Now 16, he told TNA that the past three years have made him feel far older than his age.
"I lost more than 120 members of my extended family, including my three brothers," he described, saying that "I also witnessed scenes of death and destruction that I never imagined encountering as a child."
Before 2023, Jalal focused on school and what he wanted to become. Now, much of his time is consumed by the basic struggle to survive.
Queuing for water, searching for food and helping his family secure necessities have replaced activities that should have filled his teenage years.
He said the war has also changed the way he sees the future. Before, he knew what he wanted to become. Now, even tomorrow feels uncertain.
"All I want is for the war to end so I can return to school, live a normal life and build a future for myself," he said.
For Janna, three-years-old, Israel's war left her with a different kind of loss: an unanswered question about her family.
Three years ago, the baby arrived at a hospital amid the chaos of mass casualties. No one knew who had brought her or where her family was.
With medical teams overwhelmed by the number of dead and wounded, identifying some children and tracing their relatives became extremely difficult.
After the necessary procedures were completed, Gaza-based Rami Arouqi became her guardian.
"Over time, Janna became part of my life," Arouqi, who has no children, told TNA. "She came to recognise me and look for me."
As Janna grew, she learned to speak, express her needs and emotions, and form a strong bond with the man who cared for her. He became a source of safety in a life marked by uncertainty.
But one question remains: where is her family?
"If her family appears, Janna has the right to know them," Arouqi said.
Arouqi knows that such a moment could be painful for him, having become so attached to the child, whom he has come to regard almost as a daughter.
But he said he would not stand between her and her family if they were found.
"Until that day," he added, "I will remain by her side and her only father."
A generation under trauma
The experiences of Suha, Arkan, Jalal and Janna reflect a wider crisis among Gaza's children.
According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, more than 22,000 children have been killed and over 44,000 injured since the war began, including more than 1,000 amputations. Tens of thousands have lost one or both parents, while around 700,000 students have been deprived of education.
Behind the figures is a generation deprived of the conditions needed to grow. Schools have become shelters, homes have become memories, and play has been replaced by queues for water and food.
Abdullah Al-Jamal, an official at the Gaza Community Mental Health Programme, told TNA that children have endured an accumulation of trauma, from bombardment and displacement to the loss of family members, hunger and the destruction of homes and schools.
"When a child endures all of this for an extended period, war ceases to be merely an experience they have lived through; instead, it becomes part of their psychological makeup," he said.
Some children develop withdrawal, aggression, persistent fear, sleep disturbances and difficulty expressing emotions, while others may appear calm without having overcome their trauma.
Al-Jamal noted that the impact can be even deeper for children born during the war.
"A child born during the war has had no opportunity to form a normal memory of safety," he said. "For them, the sounds of bombing, displacement, life in tents, and the disruption of services may become part of how they define the world."
He also warned that losing school and play deprives children of essential development.
"For a child, play is not a luxury," he said. "When a child is deprived of school and play, spending their day in water queues, foraging for food, or moving from place to place, we are depriving an entire generation of a fundamental part of its development."
The psychological impact will not end when the fighting stops, Al-Jamal said. Children who have lost parents, siblings, homes, or schools may need years of psychosocial support to regain a sense of safety.
"What we see today is not a normal childhood in Gaza, but a generation trying to survive in abnormal circumstances," he said.

Lithuania’s parliament votes to remove ban on nuclear weapons deployment

09:37:29 UTC
18:37:29 KST

VILNIUS, October 6. /TASS/. Lithuania’s Seimas (parliament) has voted to lift a ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons in the country.
A second vote in three months is required for the decision to come into force.
A total of 106 lawmakers voted to abolish the constitutional provision banning the deployment of nuclear weapons in the country, while six abstained and 18 voted against.
"Lifting the ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons removes legal restrictions in the field of security that were different from those in other EU and NATO countries," Seimas Speaker Juozas Olekas said.
The Seimas decision means that Article 137, which bans the deployment of weapons of mass destruction, including nuclear weapons, in Lithuania, will be removed from the constitution. The same article also bans the presence of foreign military bases in the country. Vilnius is currently pushing for the establishment of a US base.
The Seimas is supposed to hold two votes on any constitutional amendments with a three-month interval between them. An amendment requires the support of a qualified majority of 94 of the 141 lawmakers. The second vote is set for January 12.

Human cost of war: 30,000 wounded since Oct. 7, 63% face psychological trauma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:36:58 UTC
18:36:58 KST

Nearly 30,000 wounded IDF soldiers and members of Israel’s security forces have entered the Defense Ministry’s Rehabilitation Department since the October 7, 2023 massacre, with about 63% suffering psychological effects, according to figures released Tuesday ahead of the war’s third anniversary.
The figures underscore the growing human cost of three years of fighting. The department now treats 91,200 people wounded across Israel’s wars and military operations, including 42,500 dealing with mental health conditions and post-traumatic stress. Its budget has risen 88% over the past three years to 10 billion shekels, and officials estimate the total number of patients could reach 100,000 by 2028, half of them requiring mental health care.
Nearly half of those wounded since October 7 are under 30, while 62% are reservists and about 8% are women. Sixty-three have been classified at the 100%+ disability level, 249 have complex head injuries, 29 are blind or have permanent visual impairments and 106 are amputees. The ministry said 95% of the amputees have received advanced prostheses, including models adapted for sports and recreational activities.
The numbers have risen sharply over the past year. In October 2025, the ministry reported that about 20,000 wounded service members had entered rehabilitation since the massacre and 56% were experiencing psychological effects. At the time, 56 were classified at the 100%+ disability level and 168 had complex head injuries. Those figures have since risen to 63 and 249 respectively.
The increase came as Israeli forces continued routine security operations along the borders, fought another round against Iran and conducted a campaign in southern Lebanon marked by repeated drone attacks on troops.
Following last year’s figures, Defense Minister Israel Katz and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, together with the IDF Disabled Veterans Organization, established a public committee headed by Prof. Shlomo Mor-Yosef to examine ways to expand national support and treatment for wounded service members.
- The Defense Ministry’s One Soul support line for wounded service members and their families is available 24 hours a day at *8944.

Britain probes Meta over risk assessment of Instagram Instants
LONDON – Britain’s communications regulator said on Oct 6 it has opened an investigation into whether Meta Platforms breached British online safety laws by failing to properly assess risks posed by its Instagram Instants feature before launching it in May.
Instants allows content shared by users in social media platform Instagram to disappear after being viewed.
Ofcom said its formal investigation would establish if Meta carried out a “suitable and sufficient” assessments into the risk of illegal content in the feature or any possible risks posed to children before launch.
George Lusty, director of enforcement at Ofcom, said: “Our online safety laws are clear – significant changes to platforms must be risk assessed before they’re launched.”
He said safety by design had to be built in and not bolted on.
“Today’s investigation shows we’ll take action where we have concerns that providers are failing to comply,” he added.
Meta said it took its regulatory obligations under the Online Safety Act seriously.
“We conducted a risk analysis and briefed Ofcom about this feature on a number of occasions before launching it,” a spokesperson said.
“Instants has in-built protections, including blocking screenshots, reshares and forwarding, no public feed, and Teen Account protections on automatically.”
“We will of course co-operate with Ofcom during this investigation,” it added.
Meta has launched legal challenges against Ofcom over its implementation of the Online Safety Act, including the scale and the scope of the information it has to provide to the regulator, and the level of fees it charges. REUTERS

Ukrainian forces strike Russian telecommunications hub and UAV and ammunition warehouses

“What we are standing for is a right to say no”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:33:18 UTC
18:33:18 KST

Meet Antonia Burke who is standing up for Indigenous rights in Australia
For more than a decade, Antonia Burke travelled across Australia listening to First Nations people describe the impacts of government decisions on their lives. Over the years, she heard stories of oppression, injustice and intergenerational trauma. As a First Nations woman from the Yanyuwa and Garrwa people from the Northern Territory, Antonia understands first-hand how government policies can shape lives. That understanding took on new urgency when she saw the extent of offshore oil and gas development across the Arafura and Timor Seas, waters that sustain communities, cultures and marine life across Australia, Timor-Leste, Papua New Guinea and Indonesia. First Nations people in Australia call these waters “Sea Country” – a source of identity that holds stories and songlines that have guided people for generations.
As Founder and Director of Sea of Nations, Antonia works with First Nations people and coastal communities to hold decision makers accountable for ensuring meaningful consultation and consent before decisions affecting their territories are made. Here, she shares her experience:
My name is Antonia Burke. I am an Aboriginal woman from the Northern Territory. I was born to a mother whose entire existence was impacted in a negative way by government decisions. Oppression, dominance, control, which led to intergenerational trauma, and caused a lot of pain and disempowerment for my immediate family.
Growing up knowing the story of what happened, and how it happened, instilled something inside of me that always made me want to stand up, and just do something. It created this deep sense of responsibility. And it’s this responsibility that required finding the truth and speaking out.
Working with and listening to First Nations communities across Australia, it was clear that the sicker the land or the country, the water, the air, the environment, the sicker the people are. The healthier the environment is, the healthier the people are.
“It felt like a new wave of colonization”
Whilst sitting in the Australian Government Federal Resource Minister’s office in 2022, I saw a map on the wall that showed the entire ocean in the Arafura and Timor Seas and all the way down the west coast of Australia that had been sold off to mainly international stakeholders, to be exploited for oil and gas drilling. I was the person who had to stand in front of my community and show them what the government had been planning. It set my community into a spiral, a familiar feeling of government control, dominance and oppression. People were feeling a sense of disempowerment again and it felt like a new wave of colonization.
For over 60 years, the Australian Federal Government has been drilling into the ocean in the Arafura and Timor Seas for oil and gas exploration, without telling people who live on the coastline. They only consulted with businesses like fisheries, shipping and tourism operators. Every single coastal community where First Nations people live and rely on the sea for their economy, their food source, their cultural heritage, all of them were ignored for over 60 years.
Under the law and the regulations applicable in Australia, they were supposed to consult with anyone on the coastline who would be impacted by drilling into the sea. This requirement was already in the law. They just weren’t doing it.
So, my community and, elders – had to take our own government regulator to court to say, you need to comply with your own laws.
“Let’s do this together”
They have failed to consult with people from Timor-Leste, Indonesia and Papua New Guinea, West Papua and Australia. Coastal peoples from all four countries were being ignored by everyone who lived on the coastline, so Sea of Nations stood up and said: “Let’s do this together. We should all have a right to say no, and at the very least have a right to be consulted about what the governments are planning in the sea.”
In the Arafura and Timor Seas alone, in Australian waters, there are 758 wells that have been drilled into the ocean – without consulting coastal communities. There are 51 fossil fuel leases that have been sold off.
Because of this, our home, on the Tiwi Islands is the most vulnerable place in the Timor Sea.
Everything that happens out there in the sea, we feel it first. We’re the first people that are impacted. We are the frontline.
Everything that happens out there in the sea, we feel it first.
We’re the first people that are impacted. 
We are the frontline.
Antonia Burke
“What’s at stake is our very existence”
Not only this, the Federal Government and the Northern Territory Government gave approval for an oil and gas company to lay a pipeline just five kilometres off the Tiwi Islands coastline without telling Tiwi people.
What’s at stake is Tiwi peoples’ very existence.
Climate change is already creating erosion on Tiwi Islands coastlines. What Sea of Nations are resisting is further industrialisation of the Arafura and Timor Seas from the fossil fuel industry. That’s what we’re resisting. We don’t want them there.
What we are standing up for is a right for all Australians to say no. And for Island Nations to be placed into the centre of decision making when it comes to the sea that we live in.
Today, Sea of Nations has brought together coastal community leaders to stand up together, to make sure that these four governments comply with international laws.
We are doing the job of our governments. That sense of responsibility feels like trying to live life and just be a normal human being, with the added pressure of doing the government’s job.
My hope for the future (is): that whales feel safe to swim through these waters with their babies and have enough to eat; that turtles can lay their eggs and crawl back into the water and swim across the sea to the next beach without worrying about industrialization; that people who live on the coastline of the sea can maintain the wilderness of it.
My hope for the future is that transboundary laws are introduced between all four countries that share the Arafura and Timor Seas, that governments stop what they’re doing for a moment and really look at the impacts, and come up with another solution instead of developing fossil fuel projects in the seas and transition to renewables.
I truly believe that we’re going to achieve our vision of maintaining healthy seas, thriving coastal communities and strong cultures, and working together has made us so much stronger.
I truly believe that we’re going to achieve our vision of maintaining healthy seas, thriving coastal communities and strong cultures, and working together has made us so much stronger.
Antonia Burke
Antonia believes that protecting the Sea Country means ensuring that future generations inherit a clean, healthy and sustainable environment, thriving culture, and the right to decide what happens in the places they call home.

Victoria will hold its state election on Nov. 28, with One Nation fielding candidates across all 88 lower-house electorates.

Irkutsk Maternity Hospital Screens Patients for Plague After Lab Worker’s Death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:31:12 UTC
18:31:12 KST

A maternity hospital in Siberia’s Irkutsk region has started screening pregnant patients for possible plague exposure and restricting visitors following the death of a local anti-plague institute employee, the independent outlet Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal) reported Monday.
Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, died last week after being hospitalized with pneumonia symptoms in the nearby town of Shelekhov. Her death has fueled fears of a possible plague outbreak, though authorities have not publicly confirmed that she had the disease.
Blogger Ulyana Gavryunina told the outlet that staff at the Irkutsk City Perinatal Center gave her a “Checklist for Suspected Plague” when she arrived for an examination on Oct. 5. The questionnaire asked about symptoms and contact with sick people or recent arrivals from abroad.
Gavryunina said the center has barred entry to everyone except pregnant patients since Friday and that staff checked her temperature and asked her to show her tongue when she arrived.
Staff reportedly cited unconfirmed information about an unidentified infection as the reason for the restrictions. The center also introduced a mask requirement and temporarily barred partners from attending births, she added.
Unconfirmed reports have suggested Shipilova contracted plague during a work trip to the neighboring republic of Buryatia or after accidentally breaking a test tube containing the plague bacterium in a laboratory. Neither account has been officially confirmed.
The Shelekhov hospital was subsequently placed under quarantine and 189 people who had been in contact with Shipilova were placed under medical observation, according to earlier reports.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday urged Russians to disregard rumors of a possible plague outbreak and rely on statements from the consumer protection and public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor.
The agency said the Irkutsk region’s public health situation remained “stable” following an investigation.
Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan have stepped up precautions amid the reports. U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration is also monitoring information about the suspected case.
The World Health Organization said Tuesday that Russian authorities had identified Shipilova’s contacts and that none were showing symptoms. It said it had requested more information from Russia about her death.
Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which circulates among small mammals and their fleas. According to the World Health Organization, people can become infected through flea bites or contact with infected animals or tissues.
The most common form, bubonic plague, causes painful, swollen lymph nodes and rarely spreads between people. Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and can spread through respiratory droplets during close contact.
Both forms can be treated with antibiotics, though early treatment is critical.
