South Korea considers steps to force North Korea apology for DMZ mine blast
Seoul has urged the North to remove any other mines planted on the southern side of the military demarcation line.
South Korea is weighing measures to force an apology from North Korea over a recent landmine blast that wounded three soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) between the two countries, a Defence Ministry spokesperson has said.
A joint South Korean-United Nations investigation concluded on Monday that two landmines that exploded last month in the DMZ were planted by North Korean forces about a year ago, prompting Seoul to demand an official apology.
“We are not ruling out any options or prejudging anything when it comes to additional measures,” Defence Ministry spokeswoman Chung Bin-na told reporters on Tuesday when asked if steps were being planned to force an apology from Pyongyang.
Chung did not offer specifics about what actions might be employed.
Seoul has also called on nuclear-armed North Korea to remove any other mines planted on the southern side of the military demarcation line (MDL) that runs through the DMZ, the heavily fortified frontier that has divided the Korean Peninsula since the 1953 Armistice Agreement.
Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the September 21 blast, with Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea’s leader, slamming the call for an apology as “despicable”.
Chung said Seoul is calling on Pyongyang to come to the table to discuss a misalignment of the MDL. Differing views of the border line are one factor contributing to tension in the area, she said.
The comments come a day after South Korea’s military carried out a mine-clearing operation south of the MDL. It pledged to continue with clearing operations in the area if Pyongyang fails to remove the remaining explosives. The United States-led UN Command (UNC) confirmed the mine placement violated the 1953 agreement.
Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul told the Yonhap news agency on Tuesday that the military’s “decisive” response was “unprecedented in history”.
“All responsibility lies with North Korea,” Kang told reporters, adding that armed forces would “respond decisively” to any actions threatening national security.
The escalation comes as Pyongyang rejected diplomatic overtures from Seoul. Unification Minister Chung Dong-young proposed on October 2 that both sides jointly resurvey the MDL, noting that only about 200 of 1,292 original boundary markers remain intact and that Seoul and the UNC differ on roughly 60 percent of border coordinates.
Kim Yo Jong rejected the proposal as a “wild dream”, declaring Pyongyang would define its sovereign boundary “by the use of force, not by means of negotiation”.

on le corbusier’s 139th birthday, why ronchamp chapel still challenges modern architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:58:28 UTC
17:58:28 KST

on le corbusier’s 139th birthday, revisit his iconic ronchamp chapel through paul clemence’s lens
light, texture and sculptural form come together in a building that still feels remarkably contemporary more than seven decades after its completion.
LE CORBUSIER’S RONCHAMP CHAPEL THROUGH PAUL CLEMENCE’S LENS
Born Charles-Édouard Jeanneret on October 6, 1887, Le Corbusier would have turned 139 today. To mark the anniversary, designboom revisits one of the architect’s most singular works through a photographic portfolio by Paul Clemence, whose images turn their attention to the light, textures and sculptural surfaces of Notre-Dame du Haut in Ronchamp, France. Le Corbusier himself reduced the thinking behind the project to an unusually concise formula: ‘the place: the four horizons; the means: the crab shell.’ Both ideas — the surrounding landscape and the object-like form of its roof — became fundamental to a chapel that seems to shift with every viewpoint.
Rising from Bourlémont hill in eastern France, Notre-Dame du Haut occupies the site of an earlier pilgrimage chapel destroyed during bombing in 1944. In the years following World War II, the site’s owners and the diocese of Besançon set out to rebuild it, eventually entrusting Le Corbusier with the commission. The choice formed part of a broader postwar movement to bring contemporary art and architecture into the Catholic Church, championed by figures including Dominican priest and art critic Father Marie-Alain Couturier, an influential advocate of Le Corbusier’s religious work. Work began in 1950 and the chapel was completed several years later, before being officially inaugurated and blessed on June 25, 1955. Rather than reconstructing what had been lost, the architect used the project to reconsider what a place of worship could be.
FOUR HORIZONS SHAPE THE ARCHITECTURE
Ronchamp marked a striking departure from the rational grids and orthogonal geometries commonly associated with Le Corbusier’s earlier modernist work. Here, walls swell, taper and bend; towers emerge as rounded volumes; and the roof sweeps over the composition like an independent sculptural object. For Clemence, photographing the chapel 70 years after its inauguration also became an exercise in looking at a canonical work from the present. ‘With this photo essay I wanted to show this modern landmark through a sensibility of today, let a contemporary eye tell the story,’ he tells designboom. Before beginning the design, Le Corbusier spent hours on the hill studying and drawing the landscape around him. The plains, valleys and distant Vosges mountains became what he called the site’s four horizons, with the architecture conceived not simply as an object placed within them, but as a response to their presence.
He later described Ronchamp as a ‘contact with a site’, suggesting an architecture that speaks to its surroundings rather than merely occupying them. This dialogue becomes clearest when circling the building. No single facade explains the chapel: each elevation changes its proportions and expression according to the landscape it faces. Curved walls extend outward or retreat, openings appear and disappear, and the silhouette continuously rearranges itself against the sky. Clemence was particularly struck by the way the building asserts itself on the hill without becoming imposing — monumental in presence, yet inviting in scale.
A CRAB SHELL BECOMES A CONCRETE ROOF
Inside, light becomes a construction material of its own. The thick south wall is perforated by an irregular constellation of openings, varying in size, depth and orientation. Some contain colored or painted glass, allowing fragments of red, blue, yellow and green to spread across the otherwise restrained interior. Rather than the continuous stained-glass windows of a traditional church, Le Corbusier created individual points of illumination whose appearance changes according to the hour, season and position of the sun. That tension between material solidity and colored light also shaped Clemence’s final edit: he chose black and white for the exterior photographs, emphasizing form, texture and shadow, while keeping the interiors in color with a subtle watercolor quality.
The chapel was conceived for both private contemplation and collective pilgrimage, with three smaller chapels incorporated alongside the main nave and an outdoor choir allowing ceremonies to extend into the landscape. Nearby, the Pyramid of Peace adds another layer to the site, built by Le Corbusier from rubble of the previous chapel destroyed during World War II. More than seven decades after its inauguration, Notre-Dame du Haut remains one of Le Corbusier’s most radical explorations of architecture as an emotional and sensory experience. Since 2016, it has formed part of the 17 works by Le Corbusier inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, while a major restoration carried out between 2022 and 2025 has renewed its concrete surfaces, glasswork and interiors. Seen through Clemence’s contemporary eye, Ronchamp emerges not as a frozen modernist icon, but as a building whose relationship with mass, light and landscape continues to feel immediate.
LIGHT PIERCES THE THICK WALLS
Inside, light becomes a construction material of its own. The thick south wall is perforated by an irregular constellation of openings, varying in size, depth and orientation. Some contain colored or painted glass, allowing fragments of red, blue, yellow and green to spread across the otherwise restrained interior. Rather than the continuous stained-glass windows of a traditional church, Le Corbusier created individual points of illumination whose appearance changes according to the hour, season and position of the sun.
The chapel was conceived for both private contemplation and collective pilgrimage, with three smaller chapels incorporated alongside the main nave and an outdoor choir allowing ceremonies to extend into the landscape. More than seven decades after its inauguration, Notre-Dame du Haut remains one of Le Corbusier’s most radical explorations of architecture as an emotional and sensory experience. Since 2016, it has formed part of the 17 works by Le Corbusier inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, while a major restoration carried out between 2022 and 2025 has renewed its concrete surfaces, glasswork and interiors. Seen through Paul Clemence’s photographs on what would have been the architect’s 139th birthday, Ronchamp continues to make Le Corbusier’s four horizons visible through architecture.

Lithuania takes 1st step to lift nuclear weapons ban amid Russian threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:57:46 UTC
17:57:46 KST

Lithuania's parliament voted on Oct. 6 to advance a constitutional change that would remove the country's ban on deploying nuclear weapons on its territory.
The move comes as Vilnius seeks to strengthen its deterrence amid growing security concerns in the region because of Russia's aggressive posture.
The parliament approved the proposal in its first reading by 106 votes to 18, with six lawmakers abstaining. The measure would repeal Article 137 of Lithuania's constitution, which currently prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory.
The proposal comes as Lithuania expands its defense cooperation with NATO allies, including the permanent deployment of a German military brigade, and as France considers expanding its nuclear deterrence role in Europe.
The amendment now faces a second and final vote, which cannot take place for at least three months. It would require the support of at least 94 of the 141 lawmakers to pass.
Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said before the vote that removing the constitutional ban would strengthen Lithuania's resilience and deterrence.
"This would mean that we secure the strongest possible support," he said.
Olekas said the final vote could take place on Jan. 12.
Lithuania has significantly increased its defense spending in recent years. The country also hosts a NATO multinational force, with Germany permanently expanding its military presence there.
Lithuania's security concerns are also shaped by its location between Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast and Belarus. Both countries host Russian military capabilities, while Kaliningrad borders NATO members Poland and Lithuania.
The proposed repeal would remove the constitutional provision itself rather than directly authorize a specific nuclear deployment.

Two of China's most closely watched AI developers are edging towards public markets, with Moonshot AI, the company behind the Kimi chatbot, lining up a flotation as rival DeepSeek attracts far more investor cash than it originally sought.
Beijing-based Moonshot AI has completed its last private funding round, valuing it at about $50 billion (€44.6bn), up from $31.5 billion (€28.1bn) in a round this summer, according to Bloomberg, which cited people familiar with the matter.
It is now preparing an initial public offering in Hong Kong, targeting the first quarter of 2027, that could raise up to $5 billion (€4.46bn), though the timing could still change, they added.
The company has also started organising early-look meetings to test investor demand, possibly from this month. Bank of America is coordinating the deal, with China International Capital Corp, Deutsche Bank and Goldman Sachs acting as sponsors, according to Bloomberg.
Moonshot's annual recurring revenue has climbed from $300 million (€268mn) in June to about $1 billion (€892mn) and is expected to reach $2 billion (€1.78bn) by December.
The company was founded in early 2023 by Yang Zhilin, a graduate of Tsinghua University, often dubbed “China’s MIT”, who previously worked at Meta AI and Google Brain.
Backed by Chinese tech giants Alibaba and WeChat operator Tencent, the company drew global attention in July with its Kimi K3 open model.
If the IPO goes ahead next year, it would become the latest Chinese AI developer to tap Hong Kong investors, after rivals Zhipu and MiniMax listed in January, with MiniMax's shares more than doubling on their first day of trading.
DeepSeek's bumper round
Hangzhou-based DeepSeek is also close to securing at least 80 billion yuan (€10.6bn) in a round with Tencent and battery maker CATL among the largest investors, according to Bloomberg.
Strong investor demand could push the total towards 100 billion yuan (€13.3bn), double the roughly 50 billion yuan (€6.66bn) the start-up initially sought.
DeepSeek, which relied mainly on money from founder Liang Wenfeng's hedge fund High-Flyer until this year, had reportedly targeted a valuation of about 500 billion yuan (€66.5bn) for the round.
Its low-cost R1 model rattled global markets in January 2025, wiping almost $600 billion (€535bn) off chipmaker Nvidia's market value in a single day. DeepSeek has since released its V4 models, adding a faster V4.1-Flash version in September.
It also recently teamed up with Huawei to develop programming tools for the Chinese tech group's Ascend AI chips, as Beijing pushes to cut its reliance on Nvidia.
Both companies are being investigated by the Cyberspace Administration of China, the country's internet regulator, according to reports last month, over whether they routed sensitive user data to Claude, the chatbot of US firm Anthropic. The US-based AI company has accused them of using its model to train their own.
It is currently unclear how the probe could affect their IPO plans.
DeepSeek has hired Chinese brokerage CITIC Securities to prepare for a potential listing on Shanghai's STAR Market, a board for technology companies, though the timing, valuation and size of any offering have yet to be decided and confirmed publicly.

George Fenton, British composer behind David Attenborough’s Earth Trilogy, dies aged 76
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:56:34 UTC
17:56:34 KST

Best known for his award-winning film scores and long-lasting partnership with director Ken Loach, George Fenton also created the music for what became known as David Attenborough's Earth Trilogy: The Blue Planet, Planet Earth and Frozen Planet.
Celebrated British composer George Fenton has died aged 76.
The five-time Oscar-nominated composer wrote numerous scores for film, television, and theater over a career spanning more than five decades – including scores for Ghandi, Cry Freedom, Dangerous Liaisons, The Fischer King and Groundhog Day.
In a statement, Fenton's family said: "We are very sad to announce that George Fenton passed away unexpectedly today (Monday 5 October). He is survived by his loving wife Amanda, ex-wife Jane, children Gemma, Grace and Bridget, and grandchildren Lola, Audrey, Alfred, George, Frank and Beatrice, and a life of music."
Some of Fenton’s most notable film work as a composer also includes The Jewel in the Crown, Mary Reilly, The Object of My Affection, You’ve Got Mail, Anna and the King and Bewitched. He also maintained a long-lasting partnership with director Ken Loach, scoring most of the director’s films, with music for My Name Is Joe, Sweet Sixteen, The Wind That Shakes the Barley, The Angels’ Share, I, Daniel Blake, Sorry We Missed You, and The Old Oak.
Fenton’s work for television includes several of beloved wildlife broadcaster David Attenborough’s documentary series, including The Blue Planet, Planet Earth, Frozen Planet, as well as the 2023 series Wild Isles.
Over his career, Fenton won two Emmys (for The Blue Planet and Planet Earth), three BAFTAs (Bergerac, The Monocled Mutineer, The Blue Planet), five Ivor Novellos (Ghandi, The Jewel in the Crown, The Monocled Mutineer, Cry Freedom, Shadowlands), and earned two Grammy and three Golden Globe nominations.
He also wrote many well-known theme tunes British audiences will be familiar with, including the BBC's One O'Clock News, Six O'Clock News, Nine O'Clock News, Newsnight, The Money Programme, and Radio 4's PM Programme.
In 2023, Fenton was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire for services to music.
His final film score was for Trudie Styler’s Up Against It, which premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival last month, on 12 September.
RIP George Fenton 1949 - 2026

US televangelist Jim Bakker, ensnared in fraud and sex scandal, dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:55:03 UTC
17:55:03 KST

The US televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar empire and lived in opulence before being disgraced by a sex scandal, a conviction for defrauding followers and divorce from his television co-host Tammy Faye, has died aged 86.
The death of Bakker, whose journey from the TV pulpit to a prison cell in the 1980s inspired comparisons to the corrupt character of the fictional preacher-huckster Elmer Gantry, was revealed on social media by his second wife, Lori Bakker.
“It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening,” she wrote on the Facebook and Instagram pages of her husband’s latest television ministry.
She paid tribute to Bakker as a “pioneer of Christian television”. The cause and circumstances of his death were not revealed.
Bakker revived his career as a television preacher after prison with a new wife and new television show in 2003, later becoming a staunch supporter of Donald Trump.
Bakker had been among the most popular of the Christian preachers who thrived on US television in the 1980s, achieving fame on the show The PTL Club. PTL stood for “Praise the Lord” and “People That Love”. Detractors, pointing to his unabashed daily exhortations to viewers for donations to his ministry, said PTL should have stood for “pass the loot”.
Bakker spent four and a half years in prison after being convicted in Charlotte, North Carolina, in 1989 of defrauding followers in a scheme involving holidays at his Heritage USA Christian theme park and resort.
Prosecutors painted him as a selfish and petty conman driven by greed and lust for power. “Those of us who do have a religion are sick of being saps for money-grubbing preachers and priests,” Judge Robert Potter told Bakker before sentencing him.
Bakker had quit the PTL ministry in 1987 after revelations of a 1980 sexual encounter with Jessica Hahn, a former church secretary who later posed nude in Playboy magazine, and a subsequent $265,000 payoff with ministry funds to gain her silence. Bakker was later defrocked.
Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker, his first wife, had started with a small TV ministry and eventually created a multimillion-dollar operation with 2,000 employees and the 2,300-acre (930-hectare) Heritage USA complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina. At its peak, the PTL ministry drew 13 million viewers on 200 TV stations and raked in $129m a year.
With his working-class upbringing, the affable Bakker related well to common folk. He did not deliver fire-and-brimstone sermons like other televangelists, instead offering a friendly Christian message – although it was larded with requests for money donations.
Tammy Faye was more much more flamboyant, with her enthusiastic singing and penchant for tears that left her heavy makeup smeared on her face.
Bakker was convicted after a six-week trial in federal court on all 24 fraud and conspiracy charges brought against him. Prosecutors said he defrauded followers of $158m by selling promises of lifetime annual vacations that he could not provide. They said he siphoned $3.7m to bankroll a lavish lifestyle that included several homes, luxury cars, mink coats, diamonds, servants – and an air-conditioned dog house.
The judge ordered Bakker to serve 45 years in prison but the sentence was later reduced. “I have sinned,” Bakker told the court. “I have made mistakes. But never in my life did I intend to defraud anyone.”
Bakker’s chief aide Richard Dortch served 18 months of an eight-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to reduced charges in exchange for testifying against Bakker.
Tammy Faye was never charged. She stood by Bakker at the trial, even singing to reporters after his conviction, but divorced him in 1992 while he was in prison. She died of cancer in 2007.
Bakker started his life over after leaving prison in 1994, renouncing the “prosperity gospel” he once preached and writing a book titled I Was Wrong.
“I’ve had a second chance at life. And I have a beautiful wife who loves me,” Bakker told CNN in 2000, referring to his second wife, Lori, whom he married in 1998.
They started a TV ministry together in 2003. In 2008, they began taping The Jim Bakker Show at a 600-acre development called Morningside near the tourism city of Branson, Missouri. It bore similarities to Heritage USA. Bakker once again pleaded with his followers for donations.
In 2020, he drew the ire of state and federal officials for selling a false treatment for Covid-19 during the pandemic.
Bakker said in 2017 that Christians would launch a civil war if Trump were to be impeached. Trump later became the first US president to be impeached twice.

The US Embassy in Riyadh warned US citizens on social media to be vigilant about possible drone or missile attacks.
The group formally known as Ansar Allah said they had captured more territory in the southwestern part of Yemen, taking a key town in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward a strategic provincial capital in the region.
The Saudi-led coalition spokesman, Major General Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets supported government forces. He said the coalition secured "air protection" of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets.
Yemen Dawn advances
The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen's war after a four-year ceasefire.
On Sunday, the Houthis captured the town of Turbah, which sits on a main road linking the provincial capital of Taiz with the port city of Aden, which serves as an interim seat of Yemen's government. Over the years, the town was a major post for government forces defending Taiz.
Earlier, the Houthis seized several villages and areas on Taiz's outskirts, paving the way for the group to encircle Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.
The Houthis made a swift push on the country's western coast on the Red Sea in early September, capturing the strategic city of Mokha and several Red Sea islands, gains that enabled them to control the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb, through which 12% of global trade transits.
The Saudi-backed government said Sunday it was mobilising troops across government-held areas.
Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, said in a televised speech that the operations were aiming at "recovering the remaining territories" controlled by the Houthis. He called on the international community to provide support to his government.
Hours after al-Alimi's declaration, the Saudi military spokesperson al-Malki vowed "full operational support" to Yemeni government forces until the Houthis are "eliminated."
Al-Alimi said in a post on X on Monday that the operation — dubbed Yemen Dawn — had started with the aim of "restoring state institutions, liberating" the Houthi-controlled capital Sana'a, and ending "the Houthi terrorist militia coup".
Al-Nazili said government forces were carrying out a "strategic offensive" on the capital. The Houthi media office reported multiple airstrikes on their territories, including Sana'a.
The group's taking of Turbah will likely constrain government forces' ability to reinforce and resupply front-line positions across Taiz province and the provincial capital of Taiz, according to the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank.
Also on Monday, the foreign and defence ministers of Pakistan and Turkey agreed with Saudi Arabia to deploy military forces to the kingdom under their defence pact.
A joint statement released by Pakistan's Foreign Ministry after an emergency meeting in Riyadh did not specify troop numbers, identify which countries would contribute forces or give a deployment timetable.
The three countries condemned what they described as attempted attacks on Mecca and Medina, as well as continuing attacks on Saudi cities and civilian and economic facilities. The statement did not identify who was responsible.
Concerns over humanitarian crisis spike
Yemen's war began in 2014 when the Houthis launched an offensive from their northern stronghold, capturing Sana'a and forcing the government to flee into exile in Saudi Arabia. It created one of the world's worst humanitarian disasters, resulting in the deaths of more than 150,000 people.
The latest bout of violence has killed at least 959 people and wounded over 4,200 others, according to the WHO. The flare-up forced about 174,097 people to flee their homes inside Yemen, according to the UN migration agency. More than 3,000 others fled across the waters into Djibouti, the agency reported.
Last week, Yemen's health ministry — part of the internationally recognised government — warned about the war's impact on health facilities and medical staff across Taiz province.
The ministry said in a statement on Friday that health facilities in coastal, western and southern areas of the province have closed or are barely functioning.
A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting" and condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis are tied to Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

France: Trade unions join students in major demonstration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

France: Trade unions join students in major demonstration
October 6, 2026
About 256,000 people took to the streets of France for nationwide blockades and protests led by high-school and trade union groups. Police were out in full force and fired tear gas at protesters.
The demonstrations are part of a movement that sprung in recent weeks demanding that French President Emmanuel Macron's government tackle understaffed and underfunded schools.
Protests that began in Paris' struggling suburbs have now spread across the country, including pupils from affluent areas who have joined in solidarity.
Hundreds of high school entrances have been blocked by student protesters since late September. The students have decried poor learning conditions, such as missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that are not suitable for high temperatures.
While many of the demonstrations have been peaceful, some protesters have lit trash can fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police, who have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds, with authorities accusing the movement of having devolved into urban violence.
Police accused of brutality towards children
The country's Justice Ministry said 5,060 people have been arrested since the protests began. Some 87% of those taken into custody were minors.
Over 1,800 people face charges, including 1,483 minors, the ministry said, without providing details of what they had been accused of, although some 790 cases have already been dismissed.
Trade unions and human rights groups have accused the police of using disproportionate force on children. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Monday that police have launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started.
The reports include the cases of:
- a 15-year-old lost his hand at a protest in the northern town of Lens
- a 16-year-old lost the use of his right eye after being seriously injured in the head in the central town of Tours
- a 14-year-old lost most of his teeth when a police officer in Saint-Ouen-L'Aumone, northwest of Paris, appeared to fire a projectile at him at very close range
Government promises response to students' demands
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Tuesday there can be "no room for tolerance of violence."
"Burning down a high school does not improve the state of high school buildings. Lynching a teacher does not help replace teachers," he told parliament, adding it was a "lie" to suggest the government had ordered "police repression" against demonstrators.
Lecornu also said earlier that he had ordered government ministers to study the students' demands.
Among the demands the government will be tackling are ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day and the need for longer lunch breaks.
The government has promised to also look at repairs needed to ageing school buildings.
Lecornu said ministers are expected to submit their first proposals by the end of October. The protests have put pressure on a government that has sought to narrow a ballooning budget deficit.

Global fuel reserve release unlikely to lower Estonian diesel prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:49:00 UTC
17:49:00 KST

Global fuel reserve release unlikely to lower Estonian diesel prices
The G7 plans to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel fuel from strategic reserves, but the move is unlikely to bring down diesel prices in Estonia.
G7 countries — Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the U.K. and the U.S. — are releasing the fuel under U.S. pressure to ease global energy supply problems. Although Estonia has previously contributed to international reserve releases, it is not part of the latest release.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) said its member countries, including Estonia, have so far released 325 million barrels of oil and petroleum products from strategic reserves. In March, they committed to releasing 400 million barrels in total, meaning 75 million barrels have yet to be released.
"That's not an additional 100 million," clarified Alan Vaht, a board member of Estonian fuel retailer Terminal. "It's not 400 million plus 100 million."
He said it remains unclear whether G7 countries or the IEA will release an additional 25 million to bring the total to 100 million barrels.
Estonia released a proportional 10 percent of its reserves in March but has not been asked to contribute to the latest release.
According to Estonian Stockpiling Agency (EVK) figures, the country currently has about 83 days' worth of fuel reserves, said Jaanus Uiga, deputy secretary general at the Ministry of Climate.
"That varies by fuel type," Uiga said. "The standard is 90 days, and that's where we are with diesel."
He said Estonia had released less diesel in the spring after determining it had a small surplus, and released more gasoline instead.
No price drop in sight
Vaht, meanwhile, said global fuel inventories have worn "extremely thin," with stocks about 20 percent below the five-year European average. Damage to more refineries has also made crude oil processing more expensive.
"The market for finished products is still in a critical state," he noted, pointing to a widening gap between current and future delivery prices.
Releasing reserves can ease the supply shortfall, but diesel is nonetheless likely to remain expensive at Estonian gas stations. Alexela board member Tarmo Kärsna said recent price spikes have eased but prices remain as high as they were in early September.
"Unfortunately, we shouldn't expect a major drop in prices," Kärsna acknowledged, noting that winter demand and the approaching heating season will put further pressure on the market.
"Prices are likely to remain at these levels until the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz is resolved," he added.

Cornell rape allegations fuel calls for safer US campuses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:48:44 UTC
17:48:44 KST

Cornell rape allegations fuel calls for safer US campuses
- A lawsuit accuses seven men of gang-raping a Cornell student in 2024 and criticises the university for failing to protect victims and enforce safety policies in fraternities.
- Many students distrust Cornell’s handling of sexual assault, with low confidence in fair investigations and meaningful action, sparking protests and national attention.
- Experts call for urgent reforms, including education on consent and bystander intervention, and urge faster, serious university responses to prevent sexual violence.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – As 19-year-old Jane Wang read a lawsuit accusing seven men of gang-raping a former Cornell University student in 2024, she felt a chilling sense of recognition.
The lawsuit’s account of how the university handled the case mirrored her own experience in reporting sexual assault at the Ivy League institution.
“It literally felt like a carbon copy, like a copy-and-paste version of something I had gone through with the administration,” said Wang.
In the lawsuit, the student, identified anonymously as Jane Doe, said she was coerced into consuming drugs before being gang-raped at a fraternity house on campus in 2024.
After campus police made no arrests and the district attorney declined to pursue criminal charges, Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the men and the university. All the men deny wrongdoing. Four said their sexual contact with Doe was consensual; the others denied participating, according to The New York Times.
Doe said Cornell failed to protect her and did not enforce policies to keep students safe, even though it knew sexual violence was prevalent in its fraternity houses.
The case has ignited outrage at the Ivy League institution and fuelled calls across the United States for safer campuses.
In Jane Doe’s frustration with the university’s administration, Wang saw her own experience.
Wang, whose family immigrated to the US from China, initially feared that reporting the assault would jeopardise her scholarship or alert her professors to what had happened. She reported it anyway. Six months later, she said, her case had gone nowhere.
During repeated follow-ups, Wang said Cornell’s Title IX office, which handles sexual misconduct complaints, told her it was backed up and would contact her when it could.
“Every single time I was more and more discouraged to continue following up to continue trying to see through this case and pursue it to the end.”
The cases reflect a national pattern: One in five female students in the US says they were assaulted during college, yet most cases go unreported. Those who come forward can face lengthy university procedures and difficulties proving what happened, particularly when drugs or alcohol are involved.
But the outcry over Doe’s case has intensified demands for universities to investigate complaints promptly and hold those responsible accountable.
The frustration reflects broader distrust among the Cornell student body. Just 5% of students said they trusted the university to handle sexual assault reports fairly, while the same proportion believed a report would lead to meaningful action, according to a survey by the campus newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun.
National attention
Jane Doe’s case has drawn national political attention, with New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez condemning what she called a “culture of rape” at elite institutions during a Sept 27 town hall event attended by more than 1,200 people in Ithaca, close to Cornell University’s campus.
Ocasio-Cortez recalled her own experience with sexual harassment during her time at university in the US. “Within maybe 10 seconds of me walking into a party, at a gym, at a school facility, someone had touched me inappropriately,” she said.
“Jane Doe, that survivor, lost her education because you can’t stay in school when something like that happens to you.
“She had to lose her education, and those men were protected by an institution and granted an Ivy League degree as a reward. Never again.”
Cornell did not respond to requests for comment. In a video sent to the campus community on Oct 3, president Michael Kotlikoff said the university “must do better”, pledging to improve support for survivors and investigate allegations “rigorously and fairly”. He also said that Cornell would examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus.
“We must do everything we can to prevent what happened to Jane Doe – and everyone before her and anyone after her – from ever happening again.”
By Oct 5, anger had reached the university’s administrative building, where activists smashed a door and painted messages in red on the walls, including “at Cornell rapists are protected”.
Protesters called for Kotlikoff to resign, urged the university to restore an independent judicial system and demanded mandatory sexual assault prevention training for students.
“We are known as the rape school,” Saya Taylor, a member of Students for a Democratic Cornell, told protesters. “We can be known as leading a nationwide reform movement.”
The uproar reflects frustration with a persistent problem at US universities. Women attending university face a 74 per cent higher risk of sexual violence than women who do not, according to an analysis of national crime data by Washington State University researchers. Women living on campus were especially vulnerable.
‘Heartened by the outcry’
Many blame a culture of coercion, barriers to reporting and uneven accountability. But some experts hope universities will heed the students’ demands.
“I’m heartened by the outcry,” said Jane Stapleton, a sexual violence prevention specialist who has worked in the field for four decades.
“Yes, there are people who are continuing to support this culture. But there are a lot more people who are saying ‘This is not okay’. And there are a lot of men who are saying ‘I don’t want to be part of this club’.”
Stapleton is president of Soteria Solutions, which trains bystanders to intervene to prevent sexual violence. She urges universities to teach students how to recognise coercion and challenge their peers. First-year students can be especially reluctant to speak up as they build friendships far from home, she said.
“You’re not living in your family’s home or a caregiver’s home. You’re in a peer group, particularly as a first-year student where you don’t have a lot of social capital,” she said.
In Doe’s case, she said, any of the men present could have intervened. “At any point in time, any of those seven men who were close to the nucleus could have said, ‘OK, stop… this is not what she consented to, and we need to stop.’ But they don’t have the training and the courage to say, ‘Hey, this is not OK.’”
Katie Koestner helped bring national attention to campus rape when she spoke publicly about being raped by a fellow student at the College of William and Mary four decades ago. Now head of the Take Back The Night Foundation, which works to prevent sexual violence and support survivors, she said universities must examine where assaults happen and who controls those spaces.
Fraternities and sororities
Fraternities and sororities are student social organisations with houses on and off campus that often serve as hubs of campus life. Koestner argues that parties, alcohol and pressure to fit in can enable sexual violence and discourage intervention, while financial ties to wealthy alumni and donors can complicate oversight.
“The locations of rape and sexual assault are some of the most important parts of the problem. For the most part, the fraternity houses are owned, operated and controlled by some of the wealthiest and most privileged men and alumni,” she said.
“There’s a major conflict of interest that no one’s willing to address.”
For students like Wang, delays in investigating an assault can compound a sense of powerlessness. Discouraged by months of waiting for the university to take action, she eventually withdrew her complaint.
“Cases of sexual assault and sexual violence cannot be treated with urgency and seriousness only when Cornell’s reputation is on the line,” Wang said.
“The investigations need to happen as quickly as we can possibly make them happen... That’s the only way we can change the rhetoric on campus to one where sexual assault is not tolerated.”

Former German spy chief detained on suspicion of espionage and treason
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:48:03 UTC
17:48:03 KST

Germany’s former foreign intelligence chief August Hanning was arrested Tuesday on suspicion of treasonous espionage and other offenses in an investigation involving the alleged transfer of roughly 2,000 intelligence documents, federal prosecutors said.
Hanning, 80, headed Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service, or BND, the country’s counterpart to Israel’s Mossad, from December 1998 until November 2005. Prosecutors said he is strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason and espionage.
A former aide, identified only as Manfred D. under German privacy rules, was also arrested Tuesday. Hanning was detained in the Bad Tölz-Wolfratshausen district in southern Germany, while Manfred D. was arrested in Steinfurt in western Germany.
Prosecutors said Manfred D. had served as Hanning’s chief of staff and later worked as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from March 2012 until March 2026, giving him access to confidential information.
According to the investigation, the two men agreed in spring 2010 that Manfred D. would continuously provide Hanning with valuable BND intelligence in exchange for payment. Prosecutors said he eventually supplied Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many containing classified information intended exclusively for internal BND use, including executive intelligence briefings.
Hanning allegedly used the material in his private consulting activities after leaving the intelligence service. Prosecutors said that on one occasion he used classified information supplied by Manfred D. to prepare an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service. They did not identify the country involved and said it remains unclear whether the material reached its intended recipient.
Bild reported additional details surrounding the investigation, saying the case initially grew out of suspicions that Hanning was involved in an attempted kidnapping of the children of German heiress Christina Block, an affair in which former Mossad operatives were also reportedly involved.
According to Bild, investigators subsequently uncovered indications that information had been leaking from the BND. A search of Hanning’s home last year reportedly turned up a storage device containing classified material.
Authorities are also examining whether Hanning passed intelligence to China or Russia, countries with which Bild said he maintained direct contacts. The newspaper reported that highly sensitive documents concerning Iran’s nuclear program and the Russian military were among the materials found in his possession.
Manfred D. is suspected of aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
Authorities searched premises linked to both men on Tuesday as the investigation continued.

Kenya confirms first Ebola case and says patient has died
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:47:51 UTC
17:47:51 KST

Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May.
This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment.
A Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for seven years died after returning to Kenya, the Kenyan health minister Aden Duale told reporters.
The man, who has not been named, had been treated in the DRC after falling ill about a month ago. He then travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before flying to Nairobi on 3 October.
Kenya has previously never reported a case of Ebola, but neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 – almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August.
Duale said the man was taken by a relative and a friend from Nairobi’s international airport to Nairobi hospital, where he was immediately isolated, suffering from “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”.
He said the man was subsequently screened and confirmed positive for the virus, but “regrettably passed on last night at around 1130” in the evening (2030 GMT).
Duale said officials had listed 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and healthcare workers, but that so far “only one test has turned positive and is the one that we have just discussed”.
He added that authorities were looking for another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight with the man and that “arrangements” for quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” he said.
Duale said a “safe and dignified burial” of the man had been planned for later in the day, in line with public health standards, but did not give further details.
Kenyans reacted furiously to government plans earlier this year to allow the US to set up an Ebola facility at Laikipia airbase, about 125 miles from Nairobi.
After starting in the DRC’s north-eastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the country’s north and east.
The response to the virus in the vast central African country has been hindered by instability, including clashes between armed groups, mistrust of authorities – which has led to violence against health workers and other officials – and a lack of resources amid huge cuts in international aid.
The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda. The province now accounts for 40% of all new Ebola cases, compared with 24% at the end of August, the NGO said.
“It is like fighting a megafire,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in the city of Butembo. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations.”
The wider Butembo health zone is home to around 2 million people and only has four Ebola treatment centres, two of which only opened recently, MSF said.
Hoffman said: “Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment.”
North Kivu is particularly affected by conflict, with 134 violent incidents there in the past month, according to tracking group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, more than any other province.
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

Malaysia’s Anwar to host Myanmar leader as repatriations near 10,000
Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing to visit Kuala Lumpur ‘in the next few days’, Anwar Ibrahim says.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says about 10,000 people have been sent back to Myanmar since January, despite safety warnings by human rights groups and the United Nations refugee agency.
Anwar told parliament on Tuesday that a number of those deported were sent back by planes arranged by the Myanmar government, while nearly 1,500 were returned by sea last week as part of a bilateral arrangement.
Anwar acknowledged concerns by rights groups and lawmakers over the potential safety risks faced by those being repatriated, especially those from the Rohingya Muslim minority, but said Myanmar authorities had given assurances that they would not be harmed upon their return.
“The conditions that we placed on Myanmar is that they must bring home their citizens,” Anwar said. “Secondly, it is that they treat their people fairly so that there are no abuses, coercion or rights violations.”
Anwar said he would continue to discuss the matter with Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing, who is due to visit Kuala Lumpur “in the next few days”.
The visit is part of a diplomatic push for legitimacy by the Myanmar leader, whose 2021 coup plunged Myanmar into civil war and who led a 2017 military crackdown that forced hundreds of thousands of Rohingya people to flee the country.
Malaysia insists all returnees agreed to repatriation, but rights monitors have raised concerns that Myanmar refugees had little choice.
The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said last week that its staff was not allowed to meet the Myanmar nationals to confirm whether their decisions to return “were genuinely free and informed”.
The deportations come amid escalating raids on refugee communities in Malaysia by immigration officials, which led to the detention of more than 50,000 refugees in 2026.
Rohingya make up the majority of Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, but it remains unclear how many members of the persecuted group were among those deported.
Malaysia took in about 193,000 refugees from Myanmar, according to UN data.
While Malaysia is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants, it is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the UNHCR.
Myanmar has been accused of committing genocide against the Rohingya. Earlier this year, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) opened its first genocide case it has heard in full in more than a decade.
The UNHCR and rights groups said returnees could face persecution and forced military conscription in an active war zone. Myanmar has been embroiled in a civil war since the military seized power from the elected government in 2021.
The war has killed more than 100,000 people since the coup, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) project.

What are Banderol weapons?
Ukraine’s Air Force classifies the Russian Banderol, also known as the Dan-T, as a loitering munition. Military experts have also described it as a hybrid between an attack drone and a cruise missile.
The weapon is powered by a jet engine, making it faster and more difficult for mobile air-defense teams to intercept than conventional propeller-driven drones such as the Shahed.
The Banderol can reportedly reach speeds of approximately 500-560 kilometers per hour (310-350 miles per hour) and carry a warhead weighing up to 135 kilograms (300 pounds).
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 5, 2026
Russia has increasingly used Banderol systems alongside Shahed-type drones, decoys, and conventional missiles during combined attacks intended to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses.
Photographs circulated by Russian sources earlier this year also indicated that Moscow had developed mobile ground launchers for the weapon, which was previously believed to be launched primarily from Orion drones and Mi-28 attack helicopters.
Kryvyi Rih repeatedly targeted
Kryvyi Rih, a major industrial center in Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk region and President Volodymyr Zelensky’s hometown, has faced repeated Russian missile and drone attacks.
An overnight Russian barrage on Sept. 11-12 killed two people in Kryvyi Rih, left another person missing, and wounded three. The strikes damaged an industrial facility, apartment buildings, schools, and a healthcare center.
In August, a Russian strike on a shopping center in the city killed at least 16 people and wounded more than 130. Nine people, including two children, were initially listed as missing following the attack on the crowded mall.
Russian strikes have also repeatedly damaged the city’s industrial and energy infrastructure, forcing businesses to suspend operations and placing additional pressure on municipal services and hospitals.

Mumbai airports restrict cargo shipments on Russian airlines – reports

Mumbai airports restrict cargo shipments on Russian airlines – reports
Airports in India’s financial capital, Mumbai, have stopped allowing cargoes booked on Russian airlines, reports have said.
Cargoes booked with Russian carriers Aeroflot and Volga-Dnepr have been held up at Mumbai’s main airport for nearly two weeks, while a Volga-Dnepr charter was rerouted to Delhi after being denied permission at the Navi Mumbai airport, amid concerns over compliance with US sanctions. 
Navi Mumbai is a satellite city of Mumbai, and both airports are owned and operated by the Adani Airport Holding Ltd, owned by Indian billionaire Gautam Adani. Adani Airports raised $1 billion through the sale of shares to investors, including US funds managed by BlackRock, last month.  
Delmos Aviation, which represents the two Russian carriers, has sought intervention from India’s Civil Aviation Ministry as about 2.5 metric tons of cargo is currently held up at Mumbai airport, while another 12.5 metric tons await clearance. 
Airport officials linked the restrictions to US sanctions on Russia, the Economic Times quoted Delmos Managing Director Naveen Rao as saying. 
India does not implement or enforce unilateral sanctions imposed by the US or the European Union, according to a 2026 India sanctions guide published by Chambers and Partners. Indian businesses, nevertheless, face growing exposure to US and EU secondary sanctions over continued commercial ties with Russia, leading private companies to adopt their own compliance measures.  
In July, US tech major Microsoft restored IT services – suspended under EU sanctions – to the Russian-backed Indian oil refinery Nayara Energy after a court challenge. 
Aeroflot operates daily flights between Delhi and Moscow. Bonded cargo, which is imported goods held under customs control before duties and fees have been paid, from Mumbai is normally processed through customs before being moved by truck to Delhi for onward shipment to Russia. That process has stalled for the two airlines, with trucks carrying some shipments forced to return to their point of origin.
Delmos has questioned whether the restrictions should apply to shipments where an Indian logistics company handles the physical movement and neither the shipper nor consignee is itself a sanctioned entity. It has also asked why the same restrictions don’t apply to Russia-related cargo carried from Mumbai by other international airlines, including Emirates, Turkish Airlines, and Ethiopian Airlines.
Delmos is seeking a “clear, written and uniformly applicable policy,” Rao said in a September 30 letter to the ministry, reports said. The company is not seeking exemptions from Indian law, customs requirements, or airport security procedures.
India and Russia are seeking to expand bilateral trade, which now stands at around $60 billion annually. The two countries also signed multiple trade agreements around the BRICS summit in New Delhi last month, as they seek to deepen economic and industrial cooperation.

designboom listens to andreas angelidakis’ imaginary worlds
What does an artist listen to while building imaginary worlds? For Andreas Angelidakis, music sits alongside a practice that moves between sculpture, installation, architecture, digital culture and mythology. Based in Athens, Angelidakis draws on the ruins, stories and contradictions of the city around him while looking equally toward virtual worlds, pop culture and speculative futures. For the next edition of designboom listens, the Greek artist shares the songs that accompany his creative life, from the tracks that get him started in the studio to the ones that bring back a particular place or memory. His selections offer another way into a practice concerned with how we construct realities, remember the past and imagine what might come next.
Trained in architecture at the Southern California Institute of Architecture and Columbia University, Andreas Angelidakis has exhibited and curated internationally, including at documenta 14, the Chicago Architecture Biennial and, most recently, the Venice Art Biennale. But architecture is only one of the languages through which his work operates. His installations, sculptures and digital projects treat buildings as characters, ruins as archives, and technology as another space in which collective fantasies can take shape. His recent Escape Room for the Greek Pavilion at the 61st Venice Art Biennale, curated by George Bekirakis, turned the pavilion into a contemporary Plato’s Cave, questioning how images, history and constructed realities shape what we understand as truth. Here, the Athens-based artist tells us what he listens to while making, thinking, remembering and getting unstuck. Pneumonic plague in Russia: What do experts say about the risk?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:45:50 UTC
17:45:50 KST

Russian authorities are investigating the death of a laboratory worker from an unexplained respiratory infection after unconfirmed reports suggested pneumonic plague. Experts say the disease is treatable with antibiotics and is unlikely to spread widely.
Russian authorities are investigating the death of a laboratory worker in Siberia after she contracted pneumonia of an unknown cause. Unconfirmed reports suggested she may have died from pneumonic plague, a rare and severe form of the disease.
Experts say there is little risk of the disease spreading widely beyond close contacts.
Dr Glenn Wortmann of MedStar Washington Hospital Center said pneumonic plague is not easily transmitted and can be treated with antibiotics. He said there was little chance of the disease spreading widely in Russia or reaching the United States.
The infection can be transmitted through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs, but Wortmann said transmission generally requires close, face-to-face contact because the droplets do not travel far.
People who may have been exposed should take precautions, according to Simon Clarke, an infectious disease expert at the University of Reading. He advised those at risk to self-isolate and take antibiotics.
Clarke also stressed that plague is not a disease confined to history books. Although often associated with the Middle Ages, the bacteria remains present in wild animals in parts of the world. “People think the plague is gone,” he said. “It’s not. It’s here amongst us.”

Trump Expands Access to Tax-Exempt Dyed Diesel to Try to Lower Fuel Costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:45:00 UTC
17:45:00 KST

President Donald Trump will allow road vehicles to use untaxed diesel typically used in farm operations as part of an effort to ease rising fuel costs.
Trump signed an executive order on Monday to temporarily allow anyone to pump so-called red-dyed diesel, which is normally not allowed in road vehicles.
“For many years, farm vehicles, construction equipment and other off-road vehicles have used what’s known as red-dyed diesel. You know what that is? I don’t know what the hell it is, but whatever it is, it is supposed to be very good,” Trump said at a campaign rally in Grand Island, Neb., in support of Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts. The order would “officially waive the off-road requirement and allow anyone to purchase tax-free, red-dyed diesel for any reason,” he said.
“This order will also drive down the costs of all goods, including groceries,” he added.
Fuel prices have soared across the country since Iran disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and attacked Middle Eastern refineries in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28. Average diesel prices in the U.S. hit $6.32 a gallon on Monday, according to AAA. That’s up from $3.76 a gallon before the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran began, although below the Sept. 22 peak of $6.53 a gallon.
The spike in diesel has been magnified by Ukrainian attacks on refineries in Russia, one of the world’s top diesel exporters, and export restrictions in China. Diesel has risen 77% this year, putting it on track for the largest year-on-year percentage increase since AAA started tracking the data in 2000.
In recent days, several Midwestern and Southern states have already sought to tamp down the rising diesel costs by increasing access to dyed diesel for use in highway vehicles.
Here’s what to know about the order.
What is dyed diesel?
Dyed diesel is essentially the same as regular diesel, but it is exempt from the federal highway tax of 24.3 cents per gallon, as well as certain state highway taxes. State taxes and fees on diesel, which are typically used to fund road construction and maintenance, averaged 35.5 cents per gallon as of January 2026, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Dyed diesel is not available at most ordinary gas stations or truck stops, and it is normally prohibited for highway use. Instead, it is used off-road by farm vehicles like tractors. The fuel is marked with a small amount of red dye, so that inspectors can distinguish it from regular diesel.
What does the order say?
The order directs the secretaries of Transportation, Agriculture, Defense, and the Treasury to “temporarily allow off-road ‘dyed’ diesel for highway use and defer the applicable Federal excise tax, lowering costs for Americans.”
That means that vehicles can use dyed diesel fuel on highways without immediately paying federal taxes, while the Administration seeks to eliminate those deferred tax obligations entirely. The order also encourages states to halt inspections and suspend state taxes for on-road use of dyed diesel.
The waiver will last through the end of the year.
“We’re not going to need it long, I hope, we’re not going to need it long because your prices are plummeting and they’re going to really be plummeting,” Trump said.
What does this mean for consumers?
The direct benefit for prices at the pump may be limited because most gas stations don’t sell dyed diesel to standard consumers.
But consumers may see some indirect savings on groceries and consumer goods through lower supply-chain costs, as the exemption seeks to lower costs for farmers and truckers.
Currently, to fill an 18-wheeler with 250 gallons of diesel would cost around $1,580, which is around $700—or 80%—higher than the beginning of the year when diesel averaged about $3.52 a gallon. Waiving federal taxes would save truckers about $60 per fill-up. If states follow suit by waiving state taxes, the White House suggests truckers could save more than $100 per fill-up.
The order also aims to help farmers, historically a key voting bloc for Republicans. Farmers have been squeezed by soaring fuel and fertilizer costs, as well as the fallout from Trump’s trade war with China and lingering tariff-related uncertainty.
Farm Bureau economists argued, before the federal order, that removing highway taxes for dyed diesel could produce meaningful savings across large fuel volumes.
The Michigan Farm Bureau, which called on Gov. Gretchen Whitmer to provide statewide relief on dyed diesel, also said waiving the penalties on highway use of dyed diesel would produce “an immediate, meaningful, and targeted relief from record fuel prices.” The bureau said farmers already have significant stores of dyed diesel for off-road use, making it an easily accessible option for use on highways.
Ten states—Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Louisiana, Missouri, Nebraska, North Carolina, North Dakota, Oklahoma, and Texas—already temporarily permitted the use of dyed diesel fuel for some on-road use.
These state measures largely target agricultural and timber haulers by temporarily waiving fines and penalties when dyed diesel is found in the tanks of vehicles on public highways.
“Record-high diesel prices are squeezing our ag producers, and this is a meaningful and timely step we can take to provide temporary relief and help our farmers and ranchers through the harvest season,” Gov. Kelly Armstrong of North Dakota said last week. The state executive order allows farmers to use dyed diesel in highway vehicles engaged in agricultural operations. North Dakota charges 23 cents a gallon in state taxes on regular diesel, as compared to 4 cents a gallon on dyed diesel.
Arkansas, Indiana, Missouri, Nebraska, and North Dakota also offered state tax relief for certain highway use of dyed diesel.
In an Oct. 1 letter to Trump, American Farm Bureau President Zippy Duvall said a waiver of the federal tax on regular diesel would “provide immediate cost relief for farmers, ranchers, and agricultural haulers that continue to rely on taxable clear diesel.” Earlier this year, the Farm Bureau called for suspending fertilizer tariffs and facilitating safe passage through Hormuz.
Some analysts, however, questioned how much relief the waiver can deliver without addressing underlying diesel supply constraints.
Others have said that a large influx of on-road commercial vehicles purchasing dyed diesel could strain dyed diesel inventories, potentially driving up costs for farmers during harvest.
What other measures are on the table?
The Trump Administration has pursued other measures to lower fuel prices. Last week, the Group of 7 countries, which includes the U.S., agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil reserves over four months.
In August, the Administration also extended the Jones Act Waiver, allowing foreign-flagged vessels to transport gasoline, diesel, and other energy products between U.S. ports in an effort to ease shipping bottlenecks and lower fuel costs.
Last month, Trump weighed a ban on U.S. diesel exports, backed by some farm-state Republicans. But the President has not yet followed through on such an action, which would cut off global supplies from the world’s largest diesel exporter and likely worsen shortages around the world.
Analysts warned that any initial relief for Americans from a diesel export ban could eventually come at the expense of higher gasoline and jet fuel prices because U.S. refineries would process less crude in order to store unsold diesel. The global price of diesel would also likely rise, which could “boomerang” back onto American consumers. Some farm economists warned that such a ban could also expose U.S. agricultural exports to retaliation.
Some states have also pursued broader fuel tax relief. Georgia and Ohio temporarily suspended state taxes on gasoline and regular diesel, while Indiana extended its suspension on gasoline sales taxes. Earlier this year, Illinois postponed a scheduled gasoline tax increase, and Kentucky temporarily cut gasoline and diesel taxes by 10 cents a gallon. Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey also proposed a two-month gasoline and diesel tax holiday, which remains pending before the state legislature.

Storm leaves thousands without power as first snow approaches Finland
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:44:55 EEST
17:44:55 KST

Strong autumn winds swept across Finland on Tuesday, cutting electricity to thousands of households and bringing gusts above 20 metres per second to western parts of the country. Forecasters expect colder air to follow the storm, while another low-pressure system is due later this week.
More than 5,000 households were without electricity at around 11am, according to an electricity outage map maintained by Finnish Energy. The Ostrobothnia rescue service had received 12 damage-prevention assignments by that point.
The Finnish Meteorological Institute issued wind warnings across Finland apart from Lapland. Western winds were forecast to reach dangerous levels in places during Tuesday afternoon, with the main risk concentrated in western and central regions.
Meteorologist Heikki Sinisalo said in the institute's forecast that damage was possible across most of Finland outside Lapland.
“The situation looks worst in the Ostrobothnia regions, Pirkanmaa and Central Finland,” Sinisalo said.
The strongest inland gusts were forecast to exceed 20 metres per second.
Forecasters expect falling trees and power cuts in areas affected by the strongest winds. Ostrobothnia, Pirkanmaa, Satakunta and Central Finland face some of the highest wind speeds.
Winds are forecast to ease during Tuesday evening. Gusty conditions will continue across parts of Finland on Wednesday, with the strongest winds shifting north.
A change in temperature will follow. Colder air from the north-west will move across Finland behind the low-pressure system.
Foreca meteorologist Sara Salonen wrote that precipitation around Kilpisjärvi on Wednesday could fall mainly as snow. Fell tops in the area could receive their first continuous snow cover of the season.
Another low-pressure system is expected from Thursday. Rain will spread into western Finland before becoming widespread south of Lapland on Friday. Some areas could receive substantial rainfall.
Temperatures will also fall. Southern Finland started the week with daytime readings around 15 °C, but temperatures are expected to remain below 10 °C in many areas later in the week. Northern Lapland will approach 0 °C during daytime by the end of the week.
Despite the colder spell, the ECMWF monthly forecast issued on 4 October points to a milder and wetter October than the seasonal norm across much of Finland. The forecast places temperatures above the long-term average nationwide during 12–18 October, alongside above-average rainfall.
For 19 October through 1 November, the monthly outlook continues to favour temperatures above seasonal averages, though confidence falls for the later forecast periods.

How hunger is devastating Yemen’s children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:42:10 UTC
17:42:10 KST

How hunger is devastating Yemen’s children
Al Jazeera travels to Yemen’s displacement camps to measure the toll of malnutrition on the country’s children.
“My daughter is dying. Save her,” Tahani’s father pleaded, after years of knocking on the doors of officials and aid organisations in the hope they would be able to save his eight-year-old daughter.
More than 2.2 million children under five in Yemen are acutely malnourished, over half a million of them severely, the United Nations says.
The war, which began about 12 years ago, has left more than 22 million people in need of humanitarian assistance and 18.3 million facing acute food shortages. Yet the country has received only a fifth of the $2.2bn it needs to help them this year.
Tahani’s case led Al Jazeera Arabic to investigate the stories of other children enduring the same suffering, and to ask: where do the billions in aid sent to Yemen go, and why does it not prevent children from reaching dire levels of hunger and malnutrition?
Al Jazeera visualises where malnutrition is severe in Yemen, how aid funding is distributed, and why experts say aid is treating the symptoms rather than the causes.
Severe malnutrition rising among children
The search for answers took Al Jazeera to displacement camps, nutrition centres and hospitals.
The family of Jiyad Mohammed Jalal, who has not turned two yet, resides in the al-Khadeesh camp in Abs district of Hajjah governorate. The war forced them out of Haradh district. Jiyad is severely malnourished. His weight has fallen to dangerous levels and he needs continuous treatment, so the hospital has become part of the family’s routine.
Children like Jiyad reach nutrition centres only after displacement and poverty have taken their toll. He is not an isolated case. According to ground reports obtained by Al Jazeera, more than 200 malnutrition cases have been documented in Abs over the past three years. In Dhale governorate, Al-Nasr Hospital received 269 acutely malnourished children between January and August 2026.
Almost a quarter of Yemen’s acutely malnourished children, 516,157, have the severe form of the condition.
Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health and Population stated that between January and July 2026 there was an increase in cases of “severe” malnutrition among children under five compared with the same period in 2025.
According to the Health Ministry and data analysed by Al Jazeera Arabic, Taiz had 11,982 cases of severe malnutrition in children, followed by Aden (7,339) and Dhale (6,710).
These local figures do not, on their own, provide a national measure of the prevalence of malnutrition, but they reveal something else that is more important in fieldwork: that cases do not appear in a single centre, and that pressure on nutrition services is distributed across different parts of the country.
Taiz had 24,529 cases of moderate malnutrition, followed by Abyan (15,366) and Lahj (11,893).
Treating the symptoms, but returning to the same conditions
At clinics, treatment depends on severity. Children with severe malnutrition need a full medical assessment and those with complications may need to be admitted to hospital.
Stable cases can be treated and followed up as outpatients under the approved medical protocol.
Moderate cases are monitored at the clinic, where they receive therapeutic foods or nutritional supplements and have their weight and growth checked regularly.
In al-Sumayya camp in Marib, Dr Muajiba al-Mansouri runs a government nutrition clinic. Over the past year, she told Al Jazeera, it treated 33 children with severe acute malnutrition, 85 with moderate acute malnutrition and 84 mothers.
Lack of food or poor diet, illness, social conditions and feeding problems are all made worse by war, poverty and displacement, she said. The World Food Programme (WFP) supports treatment of moderate cases, while supplies for severe cases come through UNICEF and the governorate health office.
When al-Mansouri spoke to Al Jazeera, her clinic had recorded no deaths from malnutrition, thanks to timely treatment. In her clinic, four severely malnourished children regained their appetite and weight after their mothers learned therapeutic feeding. But a child saved in the clinic often returns to the same conditions that caused the problem.
Mothers are also facing the same risks. Some 1.3 million pregnant and breastfeeding women are estimated to suffer from malnutrition.
A mother feeding a child also needs food and care herself, but she lives in the same economic and health conditions as her family.
Expanding need and shrinking response
According to UN agencies, some 14.4 million people need water, sanitation and hygiene services, and only about 59.3 percent of health facilities are fully operational.
Funding has never matched declared need. According to Humanitarian Response Plan data, in 2022, $2.27bn of the required $4.27bn was funded. In 2024, the figure was about $1.51bn of the $2.71bn required. The 2026 plan seeks about $2.16bn but is only 20.6 percent funded. These figures cover all sectors, not just malnutrition.
The lack of full funding comes as Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, recorded a sharp rise in cases at the facilities it supports during the first half of 2026.
UNICEF said the shortfall in funding has forced programmes to prioritise life-saving treatment over prevention and has limited access to children in the areas most in need.
The Health Ministry said severe cases among children below five rose during January-July 2026 compared with the same period in 2025. The ministry said falling WFP funding roughly halved the programme’s reach, from 122 districts to 62, so a drop in some registered cases does not mean the situation is improving. It added that government support through the budget, therapeutic food and health workers is lacking.
Billions for the response yet malnutrition persists
As the investigation expanded, Al Jazeera contacted organisations about Tahani’s case. When they called her father back, they learned she had died. According to him, she died of hunger.
While Tahani was struggling, millions were being allocated to humanitarian projects. According to documents obtained by the investigation, a Norwegian Refugee Council project in Hajjah had a budget of about $1.1m and allocated roughly $353,000 to activities tied to its objectives. One beneficiary said he received cash assistance only once. A WFP project with Relief International, worth about $4.86m, included more than $2m for salaries and allowances and about $1.84m for storage.
Mousa Alaya, a specialist in humanitarian aid and war economies, argues that the question is not only how much money entered Yemen but what it changed. Aid, he says, operates within a network of interests and actors. It can save lives, but it cannot restore salaries, jobs or public services, or end the war economy.

"Microbes are getting stronger, like an army": Trump says US will help Russia with plague problem
US President Donald Trump has offered to help Russia after a laboratory worker at a plague research institute in Siberia fell ill and died.
Source: European Pravda with reference to CNBC
Quote from Trump: "We'll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we'll always help. [...] That's a disease we used to be able to control. Somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and stronger, they're like an army."
Details: The US president said he had not spoken to Russian officials about the incident but described plague as a "rough disease".
"We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners. Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly," a state department spokesperson who did not wish to be identified told CNBC.
The World Health Organisation said in an emailed response that the cause of death had not been confirmed and investigations were ongoing. It said it was in contact with Russian officials and had offered support if needed, while assessing the risk to the wider public as low based on the information currently available.
It remains unclear whether Moscow has requested assistance.
Background:
- According to Russian media reports, on 25 September, Daria Shipilova, who worked at a plague research institute in Russia's Irkutsk Oblast, broke a test tube containing the pathogen that causes pneumonic plague.
- She was admitted to hospital on 29 September and died on the night of 1–2 October, prompting local authorities to quarantine nearly 200 people.
- The White House subsequently said it was monitoring reports of a suspected case of plague and related quarantine measures in Russia.
- The European Commission also said it was very closely monitoring the suspected outbreak of pneumonic plague in Siberia and was prepared to coordinate response measures among EU member states if necessary.
