Ukrainian Pilots Will Soon Begin Rafale Training in France, Zelenskyy Says
Ukrainian pilots will soon begin training on French Rafale fighter jets in France, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared on October 5 following talks with French President Emmanuel Macron.
Zelenskyy announced the plans on his official Telegram channel after discussing Ukraine’s air defense needs and new French military assistance with Macron.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Ukrainian pilots will begin training on French Rafale aircraft in France in the near future,” Zelenskyy wrote. “This is a strong step for Ukrainian combat aviation.”
France is also preparing a new defense package for Ukraine, which Kyiv expects to receive soon. Zelenskyy noted that the two leaders discussed the package’s contents but provided no details about the weapons or equipment involved.
Ukrainian and French teams are additionally working to localize the production of French missiles and aerial bombs in Ukraine. Zelenskyy added that preparations for the FREYJA system are advancing and that the sides discussed ways to accelerate the work.
The Dassault Rafale is a French twin-engine multirole fighter designed for air superiority, air defense, precision ground strikes, reconnaissance, and long-range missions, with a maximum speed of Mach 1.8 and a capacity for up to 9.5 tons of external weapons and fuel.
In Ukrainian service, the aircraft could strengthen both air defense and strike aviation, using weapons including MICA and long-range METEOR air-to-air missiles, AASM precision bombs, and SCALP cruise missiles.
The agreement also provides for accompanying air-to-air and air-to-ground weapons, while Zelenskyy confirmed on October 5 that Ukrainian pilots would begin training on the Rafale in France in the near future.
Preparations for the Rafale program have been underway for months, and instruction for Ukrainian pilots and technicians was expected to begin in France as early as July, before the end of the year.
The early stages of the pipeline rely on GROB G 120TP trainers and Dornier Alpha Jet aircraft, which allow pilots to master navigation, flight controls, and combat maneuvers before moving on to frontline fighters. Kyiv and Paris have agreed on an initial batch of 16 Rafales, with the first four slated for transfer once training is complete.
The first aircraft are expected in Ukraine in 2028–2029, while plans reported in November 2025 envisioned as many as 100 Rafales over the longer term.
France's push to equip Ukraine with the Rafale builds on earlier fighter support for the Ukrainian Air Force. In February 2026, Ukraine was reportedly set to receive two Mirage 2000 jets from France by the end of the first quarter, along with additional training for pilots and maintenance crews. Over the long term, Ukraine was expected to field at least six French Mirage 2000 fighters.

Government forces also announced Monday that they had retaken the Red Sea coastal city of Mokha and the strategic Bab el-Mandeb area from the Houthis.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree, meanwhile, disputed government accounts of battlefield advances and said the group maintained control of its positions.

Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Mazda electric crossover gets an external speaker without a profanity filter
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:15:41 EEST
16:15:41 KST

Mazda electric crossover gets an external speaker without a profanity filter
Kyiv • UNN
The electric Mazda CX-6e allows users to broadcast their own messages and live speech through an external speaker without effective filtering. In Australia, improper use may result in a fine of up to 6,000 Australian dollars.
The new Mazda CX-6e electric SUV is equipped with an external speaker that allows the driver to broadcast their own messages or voice in real time. Testing showed that the system has virtually no filtering and even allows profanity to be played. Motor1 reports, as UNN writes.
Details
The CX-6e is a Chinese-made electric vehicle that, as of October 2026, is sold in Europe and Australia, among other markets, but not in the United States. Its external alert system was originally developed as a safety feature. The driver can activate prerecorded messages in a digitized voice intended to warn people crossing the road in front of an almost silent electric vehicle.
In addition to ready-made warnings, the system allows the driver to enter a phrase on the vehicle’s 26.45-inch touchscreen and save it as a shortcut for subsequent playback. The same speaker can also function as a microphone in real time, turning the vehicle into a mobile public-address system directed at people standing in front of the bumper.
This dual function distinguishes the system from backup warning sounds, which are already mandatory for hybrid and electric vehicles sold in the United States. Such signals play a fixed sound approved by regulators, rather than any sound created by the driver. Mazda has previously used unconventional solutions in its cabins, including replacing a physical control knob with a touchscreen in other models.
Custom messages, profanity and legal consequences
Reviewers who tested the feature found that the system plays almost anything entered into the shortcut-creation field, including profanity. No effective filter intercepts swear words before they reach the external speaker, and the ability to broadcast live speech through the same system has the same limitations.
The lack of a real filter may already have consequences in Australia. Road rules in states such as Queensland and New South Wales restrict drivers’ use of horns and other warning devices. Authorities may issue fines for offensive language used in public places, but official guidance does not provide for a separate offense specifically related to the improper use of an external speaker.
Western Australia also provides for penalties under road traffic and public order laws. Current legislation sets a maximum fine of 6,000 Australian dollars (US$4,170), which may be imposed for the offensive or improper use of a vehicle’s external loudspeaker.

For more than six decades, Plácido Domingo has remained one of the central figures in international musical culture.

RENK wins $35M gearbox order for Patria TRACKX vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:14:22 UTC
16:14:22 KST

- RENK Group won a €30 million (about $34.8 million) Patria order for HSWL 076 transmissions for the TRACKX tracked vehicle, with deliveries starting in 2027.
- Finland and Sweden began buying TRACKX in late September, with Sweden ordering five pre-series vehicles for testing and evaluation.
German transmission maker RENK Group has won a €30 million (about $34.8 million) order from Finland’s Patria to supply HSWL 076 transmissions for the TRACKX, a new tracked armored vehicle that Finland and Sweden began buying at the end of September. RENK said on Oct. 6 that deliveries under the order will start in 2027.
RENK did not say how many transmissions the order covers. It follows a smaller pre-production batch Patria ordered from RENK at the start of 2026, and RENK described the new contract as significantly larger.
The TRACKX is designed as an armored personnel carrier with an empty weight of 12 tonnes (about 26,500 pounds) and a payload of 3.5 tonnes, with room for ten soldiers in a compartment fitted with blast-attenuating seats. Patria says it is meant to replace the aging M113 and MT-LB tracked vehicles still used in Finland and Sweden. The vehicle runs on wide rubber tracks with adjustable hydropneumatic suspension and was developed under the multinational FAMOUS program, co-funded by the European Defence Fund.
The two countries’ first purchases are small. Sweden will buy five pre-series vehicles for testing and evaluation, while Finland has not disclosed how many it is acquiring. Finland has also signed a letter of intent with Patria covering possible future serial deliveries. Patria plans to begin serial production of TRACKX in 2027 or 2028.
“The announced vehicle procurements by Finland and Sweden are a key step towards series production for TRACKX. We have been involved with this vehicle family through the development, testing and pre-production stages, and will now be continuing this cooperation with Patria,” said Michael Masur, CEO of Vehicle Mobility Solutions at RENK Group.
The HSWL 076 was built for light tracked vehicles in the 10- to 20-tonne class. It weighs about 700 kg (1,540 pounds) and combines steering, braking and propulsion in a single, digitally controlled drivetrain. Because the vehicle’s movement is handled electronically, RENK says the same transmission can support remote control, platooning, where several vehicles follow a lead vehicle automatically, and future autonomous driving.
That is the basis for a separate project between the two companies. At Eurosatory 2026 in Paris in June, RENK and Patria showed a concept for a heavy unmanned ground vehicle that pairs the TRACKX platform with the HSWL 076 and RENK’s drive-by-wire system. RENK says the setup can be used in crewed vehicles, optionally crewed vehicles and tracked vehicles designed from the start to operate without a crew. Neither company has announced a customer for the unmanned version.
Patria is owned by the State of Finland, which holds 50.1%, and Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace, which holds 49.9%. RENK, based in Augsburg, Germany, makes transmissions for a wide range of military vehicles and reported revenue of about €1.4 billion (about $1.6 billion) for 2025.

Bestselling British author and scandal-plagued Conservative politician Jeffrey Archer has died aged 86.
Archer died “suddenly and peacefully” at his home yesterday, a day before the global release of his final novel, “Adam and Eve,” publisher HarperCollins said.
The new book out today, like his bestselling novel “Kane and Abel,” follows a pair of biblically named characters born on the same day to different social classes. "Kane and Abel", released in 1979, remains one of the best-selling novels in the world, with an estimated 34 million copies sold globally.
Kate Elton, HarperCollins UK CEO and Archer's editor, said: "It has been one of the great privileges of my publishing life to have been Jeffrey Archer's editor. He was the master storyteller and an editor's dream - phenomenally hard-working, utterly committed to completing draft after draft to get every word as perfect as possible, and a true champion of the 'team' nature of great publishing."
Archer sold more than 300 million books in his five-decade writing career, including "Not A Penny More, Not A Penny Less", the William Warwick series, and the Clifton Chronicles, which started with 2011’s "Only Time Will Tell" and spanned seven novels up until 2016’s "This Was A Man".
The former Conservative MP and Conservative Party deputy chairman was imprisoned in 2001 after being found guilty of lying and cheating in his 1987 libel case against The Star newspaper. He had sued the newspaper that accused him of paying a sex worker and won £500,000 in damages.
A jury found that Archer had fabricated an alibi during the case and he was sentenced to four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice. Archer was released early in 2003 and he returned to the House of Lords, politically non-affiliated, until he retired in 2024.

Estonians still returning bottles despite unchanged 10-cent deposit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:12:00 KST

Estonians still returning bottles despite unchanged 10-cent deposit
People in Estonia continue to return bottles at high rates despite the 10-cent deposit losing value to inflation, giving the state little incentive to raise the fee.
Eesti Pandipakend collected more than 355 million single-use containers last year, about 1 percent more than in 2024. Return rates reached 86 percent for glass, 91 percent for metal and 88 percent for plastic.
The deposit was last changed in 2015, when rates for different types of beverage containers were standardized at 10 cents. Since then, prices have risen significantly, but bottle return rates have remained high despite the deposit staying at 10 cents.
Dagny Repp, head of packaging waste at the Climate Ministry's Circular Economy Department, said there is no need to raise the deposit amount while return rates remain stable.
"We should consider changing the deposit if return rates start to noticeably dip," she said.
Some deposit containers never make it back to bottle-return machines because they are thrown in regular trash or recycling, damaged or, as Repp noted, taken out of Estonia, such as when visitors from abroad take purchased beverages with them.
Others may not be reflected in the statistics until later, as bottles can be purchased one year and returned the next.
Bottle return service provider Eesti Pandipakend posted €55.5 million in revenue and a net profit of €2.15 million last year.
Most of its sales revenue comes from deposits on containers placed on the market, followed by revenue from selling packaging waste and handling fees paid by packaging companies.

====================================================================================================

From snake oil to biohacking: The quackery and science of longevity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:08:39 UTC
16:08:39 KST

Scientists still have no convincing answer as to whether medicine can substantially extend human life, but enormous sums are being invested in research on the subject: in March 2026 alone, the U.S. government agency ARPA-H allocated $144 million to developing biomarkers of aging and testing drugs to slow it. According to the WHO, by 2050 the number of people over 60 worldwide will double to 2.1 billion, while the number over 80 will triple to 426 million. Alongside extending lifespan, this makes extending youth – that is, increasing the healthy and productive years of life – an increasingly urgent goal. So far, however, the most advanced anti-aging treatments are available only to the very wealthy – and they almost always prove to be quackery.
For millennia, people have long tried to restore their youth and extend their lives. Gilgamesh sought plants of rejuvenation. China’s first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, took mercury. Six other Chinese rulers died from an “elixir of immortality.” And one of them unsuccessfully drank menstrual blood. But attempts to extend youth through scientific means began relatively recently – in the late 19th century.
From Brown-Séquard to Altos Labs
1889. Seventy-two-year-old French physiologist Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard injected himself with an extract from the testicles of dogs and guinea pigs and said he had experienced a “return of strength and increased capacity for work.” A century later, calculations showed that the dose of testosterone in the extract was roughly four orders of magnitude below what was required, meaning any result was merely a function of the placebo effect.
1903–1907. Russian biologist Ilya Mechnikov founded scientific gerontology and the doctrine of orthobiosis (a complete and happy life cycle ending in a peaceful natural death). In 1904, he delivered a lecture in Paris titled “Old Age,” linking aging to putrefactive bacteria in the large intestine while attributing Bulgarian longevity to the consumption of sour milk.
A year later, Bulgarian microbiologist Stamen Grigorov isolated from Bulgarian yogurt the bacterium that would be named Lactobacillus bulgaricus. Mechnikov embraced the discovery, consumed a pure culture of the bacterium himself for the rest of his life, and set out his sour-milk hypothesis in his 1907 Studies of Optimism. The hypothesis quickly became a commercial proposition as sellers of fermented dairy products promised customers longevity long before there was any evidence to support the claim.
1912–1937. German physiologist Eugen Steinach began performing vasectomies on elderly men, believing the procedure would increase the production of sex hormones. More than a hundred Viennese doctors and professors underwent it. Sigmund Freud opted for the procedure at 67, while William Butler Yeats did so at 69 and claimed to have experienced a “second puberty,” prompting the press to dub him an “old man with glands.” But this, too, proved to be a placebo effect.
1920. French surgeon Serge Voronoff performed the first transplantation of chimpanzee testicular tissue into a human, and by the early 1930s, more than 500 men in France and thousands worldwide had undergone this form of “rejuvenation.” But by 1935 it had become clear that the transplanted tissue was rejected and that the reported improvements were due to autosuggestion.
1926–1928. Russian physician Alexander Bogdanov founded the world’s first blood transfusion institute in Moscow and experimented on himself with blood exchanges involving other people, seeing them as a means of “physiological collectivism.” In 1928, the experiments ended with his death – the result of one of the exchange transfusions.
1930–1946. Ukrainian pathophysiologist Alexander Bogomolets linked longevity to the condition of connective tissue and won government backing to produce antireticular cytotoxic serum (a preparation intended to stimulate wound healing and slow aging). He was awarded the Stalin Prize in 1941 and the title of Hero of Labor in 1944. In 1946, Bogomolets died at 65, and four years later his doctrine was declared unscientific.
2013–2026. Google founded Calico to study the biology of aging, while Yuri Milner’s Altos Labs raised $3 billion for life-extension research. In the U.S., the PROSPR program support efforts to extend people’s lifespan and healthspan.
A lifelong experiment
In 2020, the WHO counted one billion people over 60 worldwide. By 2030, it projects, that number will reach 1.4 billion, and by 2050, 2.1 billion. Over the same period, the number of people over 80 will triple to 426 million.
Life-extension research, however, still faces several natural obstacles. To prove that a technology has actually added years to someone’s life, it is necessary to wait for those years to pass, meaning trials can take decades, with control groups numbering in the tens of thousands aging alongside the study groups. An experiment capable of demonstrating an effect can outlive both its investor and its principal investigator.
To prove that a technology has actually added years to someone’s life, you have to wait for those years to pass
It is hardly surprising, then, that of the three measures of longevity – how long someone lives, how long they remain in good health, and how much their lab markers change – the market is most interested in the third. This creates demand for markers that change within months and can provide a rough estimate of future effects.
Along with that demand comes the temptation to pass off a surrogate marker as a real result.
A serious attempt: epigenetic clocks
Researchers are constantly working on surrogate measures that reliably reflect biological aging. So far, the most successful example is the epigenetic clock. The model was trained to estimate a person’s age from chemical markers on their DNA that change predictably over time.
The first such clocks were published in 2013: a universal clock, developed by U.S. researcher Steve Horvath and designed to work with data from any tissue in the body, and one developed by fellow American Gregory Hannum using data from blood cells. In the second generation, PhenoAge (2018) and GrimAge (2019), the model learned to predict mortality and disease rather than simply chronological age. The third generation, the DunedinPACE epigenetic clock (2022), measures the rate of biological aging: the number of biological years a person ages in a single calendar year.
There are three main criticisms of epigenetic clocks. Early versions showed considerable variability when the same sample was analyzed again: results depended on the reagent batch and the laboratory, so the same test tube could produce age estimates differing by several years. In 2022, the clocks were recalibrated, reducing that variability.
The second criticism is that it is impossible to predict how long any particular person will live. Mortality is higher among people with faster-running clocks than among those with slower ones. But this does not work as a practical prediction for any one person, because lifespan is shaped by genetics, past illnesses, lifestyle, and chance, while the model is trained on an average population pattern.
Lifespan is shaped by genetics, past illnesses, lifestyle and chance, while the model is trained on an average population pattern
The third criticism focuses on the divergence between different clock models. Horvath’s clock may show the same person as younger than their chronological age, while GrimAge may show them as older. Which is closer to the truth, and what accounts for the discrepancy, remain subjects of debate.
All of these are examples of a broader problem that can be illustrated by one story. Patients who have suffered a heart attack often develop irregular heart rhythms – extra beats visible on an ECG. In the 1980s, drugs emerged that eliminated these irregularities, making the ECG look more normal. But when a trial was completed, the drug group turned out to have twice as many deaths as the placebo group.
A measure used in an experiment becomes evidence only after it has been validated against actual outcomes – and epigenetic clocks have yet to reach that point.
Why the U.S. does not approve anti-aging drugs
The U.S. is the world’s largest market in the field of anti-aging biotech. In 2024, it was home to 57% of the world’s longevity companies and accounted for 84% of all venture investment in the sector.
But the U.S. drug-approval system requires a treatment to be indicated for a specific disease on the FDA’s list – diabetes, hypertension, dementia, and so on. Aging is not on the list and is mentioned only as a risk factor for actual illnesses, meaning a company developing a molecule that targets the mechanisms of aging has to choose a disease on the FDA’s list and prove the drug works against it. As a result, the anti-aging industry talks about defeating aging, while the regulatory filings for drugs developed for that purpose list conditions such as “heart failure” or “liver fibrosis.”
To resolve this contradiction, scientists proposed the TAME trial, which the FDA approved 15 years ago. Three thousand people aged 65–79 will be divided into two groups and followed for six years at 14 research centers. One group will take metformin, the other a placebo.
It might seem like a routine study, but instead of measuring a single disease, the researchers propose tracking several outcomes at once: heart attacks and strokes, cancer, dementia, and death. They hope that slowing aging will show up across several diseases at once, and if successful, the study would give regulators a framework for evaluating such drugs. Unfortunately, its launch is still delayed, as the organizers are still raising funds.
Meanwhile, life-extension drugs for dogs are already being approved in the U.S. Loyal is developing LOY-002, a drug for dogs over 10, with its indication stated explicitly: life extension. In February 2025, the FDA’s veterinary division agreed that the data submitted were sufficient to support such a claim, and a second drug targeting the same goal has also received FDA support.
The difference lies in the more flexible requirements: unlike human drugs, veterinary drugs can receive conditional approval while developers continue to collect data. And a dog’s lifespan fits within a timeframe that is foreseeable for both the company and its investors.
Candidate No. 1
The first approved geroprotector for humans may turn out to be a drug already sitting on pharmacy shelves. At a conference on aging in Copenhagen in the summer of 2025, executives from Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly suggested an idea later echoed in an editorial in Nature Biotechnology: GLP-1 receptor agonists – semaglutide and related drugs – could well become the first longevity drugs.
In patients with obesity and diabetes, these drugs reduce overall mortality and cardiovascular events, with only about one-third of the cardiovascular benefit being explained by weight loss. The rest is attributed to anti-inflammatory and other mechanisms – effects that act throughout the body.
In a study of 108 participants, semaglutide slowed the rate of aging measured by DunedinPACE by about 9%. The author, however, makes an important qualification: slowing individual biological processes and rejuvenating a person are two entirely different things. “We’re not saying that semaglutide reverses aging or makes people younger. We’re seeing a signal that it may slow some biological processes of aging,” cautions Michael Corley, the study’s lead author.
Things are finally moving
In the spring of 2026, the U.S. agency ARPA-H awarded up to $144 million under its PROSPR program to seven recipients: four university teams and three biotech companies.
The interventions being tested are unremarkable: metformin, rapamycin, semaglutide, and calorie restriction. Nothing exotic – all the drugs have long been approved for other indications, and half are available at regular pharmacies. Yet the agency has agreed to use functional changes as outcomes: how fast a person walks, how they perform on cognitive tests, how well they maintain their independence, and how often they are hospitalized.
One team is developing a composite measure designed to predict mortality, disease onset, and hospitalization over a 20-year horizon, and a Phase 3 trial will test whether three approved drugs slow age-related declines in physical and mental function in healthy people over 60. Biomarkers are also part of the program – including chemical markers on DNA – but their role is secondary; they will be measured against functional outcomes.
PROSPR is built around the goal of evaluating trial results within three years using measurements that can be taken at home with wearable devices. It is a direct attempt to solve the problem at the heart of this story: the endpoint lies decades in the future, while money and human resources are spent for years.
The program’s goal is stated openly: to pave the way for the approval of drugs that target aging itself. In parallel, in 2024 the agency launched the PATH project for the Buck Institute (with a contract worth up to $52 million).
In other words, a precedent has been set. For the first time, the government has funded an effort to answer a question that had been sidestepped for more than a century: can a person at 70 retain the abilities they had at 60? And how can that be measured in a way that regulators will accept?
The bigger the budget, the fewer the promises
Companies investing serious money in the fight against aging tend to be cautious and avoid grand promises. Life Biosciences raised $80 million and took its cellular rejuvenation program into clinical trials for a narrow indication – optic neuropathy, with the effect assessed by an ophthalmologist based on the patient’s vision.
Altos Labs launched in January 2022 with $3 billion from Yuri Milner, Jeff Bezos, and ARCH Venture Partners. Its president, Hans Bishop, made clear at the time that the company was focused on extending healthy life, while extending overall lifespan would be an “incidental consequence.” It was a disarming formulation: a company with a budget the size of a small country’s was distancing itself from the promise of a longer life that anti-aging clinics routinely sell.
Calico, founded by Google in September 2013 to defeat aging, remained silent about its results for 12 years. In November 2025, its partner AbbVie ended the collaboration after investing about $1.75 billion in the research, but its drug, Fosigotifator, failed trials as a treatment for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. In other words, the most highly funded anti-aging effort of the decade ended in a very public failure.
Clinics, meanwhile, have no qualms about aggressively marketing rejuvenation services: hormone therapy, cellular treatments, infusions, and biomarker panels. MIT Technology Review describes the market as being built around interventions that lack evidence. The market’s poster boy is billionaire Bryan Johnson, who has turned the daily publication of his own test results into a genre of its own.
The offshore biohacking bonanza
Over the past 12 years, aging research has received funding on a scale that gerontologists of the last century could only have dreamed of, but the money has come from a relatively small circle. Calico was founded with funding from Larry Page and Sergey Brin. Altos Labs received $3 billion from Jeff Bezos and Yuri Milner. Sam Altman, the head of OpenAI, invested $180 million in Retro Biosciences. All these people have one thing in common: they can buy almost anything except extra years of life.
They and their somewhat less wealthy peers are buying anti-aging treatments for themselves. Ambrosia once offered clients plasma from young donors for $8,000 a liter or $12,000 for two liters, but in February 2019 the FDA warned that the procedure had not been tested in clinical trials and that it carried risks of infection, allergic reaction, and adverse cardiovascular effects. The company shut down that same day.
On the Caribbean island of Roatán in Honduras, startup Minicircle offers gene therapy to boost production of the protein follistatin for $25,000 per injection. The treatment has no FDA approval, the company has published very few clinical-trial results, and it chose the site in a special economic zone with looser regulations. Bryan Johnson underwent the therapy himself for free, but neuroscientist Christine Glorioso put her conclusion bluntly in Fortune: interventions like these will sooner or later kill someone through cancer or liver failure.
Fountain Life, a clinic founded by Peter Diamandis and Tony Robbins, sells an annual program for $19,500–$21,500 that includes whole-body MRI, a CT scan of the heart’s blood vessels, more than 100 blood markers, genome sequencing, and epigenetic tests. Across the industry, annual costs range from $10,000 to $150,000. Johnson himself spends about $2 million a year on his protocol.
In short, the people whose companies spend years guiding drugs through the approval process and carefully framing their claims about extending life are themselves buying treatments that sidestep that process: transfusions of other people’s plasma, injections on an island governed by looser regulations, and annual memberships built around dozens of tests. Billionaires’ money is funding both halves of the industry at once – genuine science in the laboratory and the sale of hope in the clinic.
Putin’s modest anti-aging program
Russia is trying to address these challenges through the national project “New Technologies for Health Preservation.” It comprises five federal projects: management of medical science, development of drugs and medical devices, biomedical and cognitive technologies, and production of medicines in demand. The fifth, particularly interesting project is titled “Regenerative Biomedicine, Preventive Medicine Technologies Ensuring Active and Healthy Longevity.”
The program was designed by Mikhail Kovalchuk, head of the Kurchatov Institute and brother of an oligarch believed to be Vladimir Putin's money manager. The genomics program is overseen by Putin's daughter Maria Vorontsova, an endocrinologist by training.
According to The Wall Street Journal, the program brings together tissue bioprinting, cryotechnologies, xenotransplantation (using organs grown in mini-pigs), and gene therapy targeting cellular aging. Its stated goal is to save 175,000 lives by the end of the decade.
Estimates of the project’s cost vary widely. The WSJ put the program at $26 billion, though when the national project was launched, industry media reported that a mere 210 billion rubles ($2.5 billion) would be allocated. As elsewhere in the world, the hype is backed by little substance. Only about 1.85 billion rubles ($22 million) is earmarked through 2030 for work directly related to aging and longevity.
Alexander Ostrovsky, who founded Invitro and 3D Bioprinting Solutions before leaving Russia in 2022, summed it up succinctly: “If there are no publications, there are no real results, and their claims should probably be viewed as aspirations, if not dreams.”
The identity of the main client, meanwhile, is well known: Putin. After all, he is the one who told Xi Jinping about the possibility of extending human life to 150 years.
130 years later
Ostrovsky’s remark goes to the heart of every life-extension project. Since Brown-Séquard, technologies and budgets have changed dramatically, but the pattern remains the same: promises outpace evidence, and instead of demonstrating longer lives, scientists point to changes in individual parameters that can be measured quickly.
The 72-year-old physiologist’s sense of well-being, the number of patients treated with Bogomolets’ serum, the number of technologies introduced under the national project, the figure on a biohacking clinic report – all are measures of activity, while the real question is how many additional years people actually live. In Russia, where men live about 68 years on average, longevity is a pressing issue. And how success is measured matters: by the number of technologies introduced or by the number of people who reach 70 in good health.
The Russian program lists technologies and funding and expects results by 2030. But there is no sign of publications, controlled trials, or clearly defined endpoints. Nor is it clear what will happen to its funding amid sanctions and the protracted war.
The U.S. PROSPR program differs in one crucial respect: experts agreed in advance on how trial success would be measured and chose criteria that people themselves can assess. Walking speed, memory, independence, and hospitalization rates are measurable outcomes that directly reflect health.
In a few years, we will know whether the program works, and the answer may well be disappointing. Metformin and rapamycin may well prove to have no beneficial effect on healthy people in their 60s, but even such an outcome would still provide the first real answer in 130 years to the question of whether life can be extended – instead of yet another empty promise of immortality.

Massive Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow and surrounding region kills two, sets region’s largest oil depot ablaze
Update. A Ukrainian drone attack killed two people and injured nine in the Moscow region, Governor Andrei Vorobyov said. Forty-seven private homes were damaged in seven municipalities.
A massive Ukrainian drone strike killed one person and injured six others in the Moscow region, Governor Andrei Vorobyov said.
The victim was a 20-year-old resident of the village of Radumlya in the Solnechnogorsk district. Residents of Istra and the Volokolamsk and Domodedovo districts were also injured, and three of them are hospitalized.
In Istra, 10 private homes were damaged in Safontyevo, Torlopovo, Gorki, and Yadromino, along with outbuildings and two cars. In Domodedovo, a private home caught fire in the village of Lobanovo, and another was destroyed in Barybino.
Citing photos and videos from witnesses, Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channels (1,2), as well as the independent Telegram channel Astra, claimed that a fire broke out at the linear production and dispatching station (LPDS) “Volodarskaya” in the Moscow region. Open sources describe it as the largest oil depot in the Moscow region, as well as a key node for supplying petroleum products to Moscow and the surrounding region. The LPDS is part of JSC “AK Transnefteprodukt.” Local authorities have not reported the fire.
In all, air defense forces and electronic warfare systems destroyed 185 Ukrainian drones over the Moscow region, Vorobyov said. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 650 drones began flying toward the city and the region on the evening of October 5, and air defenses shot down a large share of them “at distant approaches.” Air defenses destroyed 105 of the drones on approach to Moscow. Sobyanin later said air defenses had shot down another 29 Ukrainian drones flying toward Moscow.

Southeast Asia’s energy chiefs meet against backdrop of Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:07:47 UTC
16:07:47 KST

Southeast Asia’s energy chiefs meet against backdrop of Iran war
ASEAN ministers to discuss energy security amid energy crunch caused by the war on Iran.
Southeast Asia’s energy ministers are meeting this week to discuss regional energy security against the backdrop of supply disruptions caused by the US-Israel war on Iran.
The gathering of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Wednesday and Thursday comes as the region is seeking to lessen its dependence on energy supply chains upended by conflict in the Middle East.
The meetings in Manila, the Philippines, are expected to discuss various initiatives on energy cooperation and clean energy, including a framework on fuel-sharing and the integration of the region’s power grids.
ASEAN, one of the world’s fastest-growing economic blocs with a combined gross domestic product (GDP) of more than $4.2 trillion, is heavily dependent on imported oil and natural gas.
ASEAN’s 11 member states imported about half of their oil needs from the Middle East before the start of the Iran war in late February, leaving them highly exposed to supply constraints stemming from the effective shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz.
The Philippines, the current chair of ASEAN, declared a national energy emergency within weeks of the start of the war amid warnings that fuel supplies could run dry in 45 days.
Other ASEAN economies, including Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia, rolled out energy-conservation measures ranging from work-from-home arrangements to fuel rationing.
Rising demand
“What happens in global energy markets can quickly reach our shores, affecting the cost and availability of fuel, disrupting industries, and putting pressure on households,” Philippine Energy Secretary Sharon S Garin said in a statement issued on Sunday ahead of the meetings.
“Our ASEAN Chairship is an opportunity to translate regional cooperation into practical arrangements that strengthen our collective ability to prepare for and respond to disruptions.”
While Southeast Asia’s per capita energy demand has risen by nearly 30 percent over the past decade, oil production in the region has fallen by 40 percent from its 1990s peak, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
Electricity demand in the region, home to more than 700 million people, is projected to rise by an average of 5.4 percent annually from 2026 to 2030, according to the IEA.
IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol warned on Monday that Southeast Asia would face challenges meeting its growing energy needs amid an “uncertain global energy landscape”.
“Energy security must be built into decisions across the whole system from oil stocks and gas infrastructure to electricity grids and more efficient use of energy,” Birol said in a statement.
“By working more closely together, ASEAN countries can make better use of their collective resources and respond more effectively when disruptions occur.”
Dinita Setyawati, head of Southeast Asia research at the energy think tank Ember, said that ASEAN ministers will bring different priorities to the table during their discussions.
“For the Philippines, this would be to take part of the ASEAN Power Grid via secured funding and governance that would oversee undersea cable connections,” Setyawati told Al Jazeera.
“For Singapore, it is probably to further solidify commitments from neighbouring countries to export clean electricity to the country, for example, Singapore-Indonesia connections,” Setyawati added.
“There will be countries who are interested in developing a regional carbon market to expand clean energy financing.”
Integration struggles
Despite efforts going back decades, ASEAN has struggled to follow through on its plans for deeper energy integration across the bloc.
Only nine of 18 projects identified as priorities under the ASEAN Power Grid initiative have been completed since the plan was first mooted in the late 1990s.
Unlike the European Union, ASEAN lacks a central, supranational authority and cannot pass or enforce laws, a structure critics say hampers the bloc’s effectiveness.
Laurence Delina, an associate professor at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology who specialises in energy policy in Southeast Asia, said ASEAN’s rhetoric has long exceeded its achievements, with cooperation largely limited to bilateral energy-sharing agreements.
“It has no enforcement power like in the EU,” Delina told Al Jazeera.
Delina said integrating the region’s energy grid would be as much a political as a technical challenge.
“I don’t know if I can see it eventuating in my lifetime,” Delina said.
“Although it’s a region, the context is really different across countries,” he added.
“It’s not actually a regional market. It’s very different from country to country.”
Setyawati at Ember expressed optimism that ASEAN ministers will commit more funding to renewables and electrification to reduce the region’s dependence on fuels.
“Current data for Southeast Asia shows electrification is around 25 percent from total final energy consumption,” Setyawati said.

Latvia’s national airline airBaltic is continuing to implement its new business plan, gradually adapting the company to its future operating model. One of the steps under the plan is a review of staffing levels to ensure that the company’s structure and cost base are aligned with its future scale, the airline said in a statement.
According to current forecasts, the changes could affect approximately 500 to 700 positions at airBaltic’s bases in Riga, Vilnius and Tallinn. The exact number of positions has not yet been determined and may change as the process progresses.
The range reflects both ongoing consultations with trade unions on possible reduced-workload arrangements for pilots and cabin crew and the development of new organisational structures across the company. These are expected to be defined by mid-October.
The airline currently employs around 3,000 people.
The staffing review is one of the measures included in the new business plan.
 As previously reported, its priorities include strengthening the airline’s financial stability, creating a more focused route network and improving overall operational efficiency.
The plan also envisages a smaller Airbus A220-300 fleet and closer year-round cooperation with ACMI partners – aircraft leased together with crew – while maintaining reliable connectivity for Latvia and the wider Baltic region, the airline said.
Erno Hildén, President and CEO of airBaltic, commented: “We recognise that the upcoming changes are highly significant for our employees. Therefore, our priority is to act responsibly, transparently and with respect for every colleague, providing timely information about the company’s next steps.”
“At this stage, no decisions concerning specific individuals have been made,
 and the necessary discussions and consultations are taking place beforehand. The entire process will be carried out in full compliance with the applicable legal framework and established procedures.”
More detailed information will be provided to employees during October. As no individual decisions have yet been made, the airline said it is currently too early to specify the potential impact on individual bases, company functions or employee groups.
airBaltic has informed Latvia’s State Employment Agency about the planned collective reduction in staff numbers. Further steps will be taken in accordance with the procedures established by law.
The airline will gradually provide further information on significant developments concerning both staffing changes and the implementation of its new business plan as a whole.
The changes will not affect airBaltic’s flight schedule. The airline continues to operate as usual, and all scheduled flights are being operated according to plan.

Wearable counter‑drone tech enters frontline service across US, Ukraine and IDF units
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:06:08 UTC
16:06:08 KST

Autonomous Guard’s Wearable Kit counter-drone system has been used by Ukrainian troops and undergone operational testing with the US Army in Europe and maneuvering forces in Gaza by the IDF, Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post.
The system is a compact RF detection and jamming device that can detect hostile drones up to two kilometers away, providing early warning for units on the move. Its jamming capability extends to three kilometers, enabling forces to disrupt drone operations before the aircraft reaches visual range. It provides directional alerts, allowing troops to take cover or reposition before a drone identifies their location.
When interception is required, SkyLock’s RF guns, which are handheld jamming devices that do not require precise aiming, can be used to neutralize incoming drones. The company says this combination of early warning and rapid response is designed to reduce exposure during reconnaissance and targeting cycles.
SkyLock’s Sky Spotter Pro, a wearable system used at higher command levels such as battalion forward command posts, allows operators to preload friendly drone data during mission planning, reducing false alarms and improving identification accuracy. This helps troops distinguish between hostile and friendly platforms.
Sky Spotter Pro can detect drones at ranges of up to five kilometers, or three kilometers in complex terrain. It can also identify the drone operator's location, enabling units to direct fire and close the operational loop more quickly. Additionally, SkyLock provides a wearable module that identifies friendly drones to prevent accidental interception.
Wearable counter‑UAS systems have seen widespread use in the Russia‑Ukraine conflict, where both sides rely heavily on small drones for reconnaissance and targeting. According to Autonomous Guard, interest in wearable systems is increasing among militaries, police forces, border units, and prison services.
The system has been sold to hundreds of US Army operations in the US European Command (EUCOM) and other combatant commands worldwide, including Ukraine’s Armed Forces. In July, EUCOM tested the system during a large-scale exercise in Germany. The Defense Post reported that participants included the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, a 4,800-person agile unit stationed at the Rose Barracks in Vilseck that specializes in a full spectrum of operations in support of EUCOM and the NATO alliance.
As AI‑enabled drones are becoming more resilient to jamming, defense officials say wearable counter‑UAS systems are likely to play a growing role in infantry protection by providing mobile coverage in environments where aerial threats are persistent, adaptive, and increasingly autonomous.
‘Hunted by autonomous systems’
In a keynote address at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference in Maryland in September, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine said US forces should assume they will be “hunted by autonomous systems, jammed across the spectrum, and tracked in real time,” citing lessons from the Russia‑Ukraine war.
According to a report in DefenseScoop, Caine said FPV drones equipped with AI‑enabled computer vision can now continue toward targets even when GPS signals or control links are disrupted.
“We have to transition the joint force to be prepared to fight and win our future wars by generating and delivering lethality at scale with an agile, optimized, high-low mix of combat capabilities to give the young members of the 2.8 million-member all-volunteer joint force the tools that they need before they need them,” Caine said.
Referring to the Russia-Ukraine war, Caine said that the life expectancy of a new Russian recruit on the frontline in certain areas was as little as 20-30 minutes.
“Think about that. This is what happens when low-cost precision [weaponry] is fielded fast, adapted quickly, and scaled across the battlefield. The price of lethal exchange is decreasing day over day,” he said.
“In the future fight, advantage will go to the side that can see first, who can understand first, decide first, and act first, and along the way be a learning organization,” Caine said, adding that “AI is here now and it’s already changing the way militaries see, sense, decide and act.”

Leonardo DRS completes Australian sniper thermal sight deliveries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:05:51 UTC
16:05:51 KST

- Leonardo DRS completed delivery and training for INOD Block III clip-on thermal weapon sights for Australian Army snipers under LAND 159 Tranche 1.
- The company did not disclose the number of sights delivered or the contract value; NIOA is the prime contractor for the program.
Australian Army snipers have finished receiving clip-on thermal weapon sights from Leonardo DRS, the U.S. company said on Oct. 5, completing deliveries and operator training under the first tranche of Australia’s LAND 159 small arms program.
The sight, the Improved Night/Day Observation Device (INOD) Block III, lets snipers and special operations troops find and engage targets in darkness, smoke, haze and bad weather. Leonardo DRS did not say how many sights it delivered or what the contract was worth.
The INOD Block III mounts on the rifle in front of the sniper’s existing daytime scope. Because the day optic stays in place, the shooter keeps the scope’s zero and does not need to re-sight the rifle when switching between day and thermal use. The company says the sight works with scopes from 5x to more than 25x magnification.
At its core is a 640-by-480 mid-wave infrared sensor with a miniature cooler. Cooled thermal sensors are generally more sensitive than the uncooled sensors found in many cheaper thermal sights, which helps at the longer ranges snipers work at. The micro-cooler keeps the size and power demand down enough for a rifle-mounted sight.
The sight runs on lithium batteries that can be swapped without shutting it down, and it can draw external power for long periods of static surveillance. Controls include a rear-facing focus knob, a wired remote and one-handed operation designed for use with gloves.
According to Leonardo DRS, Australian snipers will now carry the same generation of thermal sight that U.S. Army special operations forces use. The company also supplies individual weapon sights and thermal targeting systems to the U.S. Army, including under the Family of Weapon Sights program.
“Completing delivery and training for the Australian Army is an important milestone for our team,” said Jerry Hathaway, senior vice president and general manager of the Leonardo DRS Electro-Optical and Infrared Systems business unit. “The INOD Block III provides a thermal sighting capability intended to support sniper operations in demanding conditions, and the training helps ensure personnel are prepared to operate and maintain the system.”
Leonardo DRS staff trained Australian Army personnel to operate and maintain the sights as part of the deal.
LAND 159 is the Australian Army’s program to replace and upgrade soldiers’ small arms and related equipment, including sniper systems. Australian defense company NIOA is the prime contractor for Tranche 1 and handled local program management and delivery logistics for the Australian Army, with Leonardo DRS supplying the thermal sights.

Trump allows cheaper, dyed diesel on highways to blunt historic fuel-cost spike ahead of midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:05:36 UTC
16:05:36 KST

President Donald Trump has allowed the use of cheaper red-dyed diesel, typically reserved for farm operations, to be used more broadly in an attempt to bring down record-high fuel costs.
Trump signed an executive order Monday evening stateside to temporarily allow truckers and farmers to use red-dyed diesel — which is exempt from highway fuel taxes — and deferred related taxes on the fuel through the end of this year.
The tax-free diesel is typically used by farm equipment, construction machinery, trucks and other off-road vehicles. It is therefore exempt from a 24.4-cent-per-gallon tax applied to diesel fuel sold for highway transportation.
Using dyed diesel in vehicles operated on public roads is considered illegal, and could result in fines for tax evasion. But several states this year have relaxed restrictions on the tax-exempt diesel to help Americans cope with surging fuel prices.
The U.S. national average price of diesel topped $6 a gallon in September for the first time ever, as fuel supply disruptions triggered by the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran pushed up transportation costs across the country. Americans are spending about $700 million more per day on gas and diesel than they did a year ago, according to Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy.
The White House said truckers could save more than $100 per fill-up.
The order also directed the Treasury secretary, in consultation with the Department of Defense, to defer collection of the federal excise tax on highway diesel through the end of 2026, without interest or penalties, according to a fact sheet released by the White House. The Treasury is also directed to "explore pathways to eliminate the obligation to pay the deferred taxes" altogether.
The Trump administration cited tight global supply tied to the war in Ukraine and a lack of refining capacity as pushing up diesel prices and household costs. The Group of Seven nations also agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude reserves, after pressure from Trump who had floated a ban on U.S. exports of the fuel.

Brazil ex-President Bolsonaro wins big without his name on the ballot
BRASILIA Oct 6 - The biggest winner in Brazil's blockbuster weekend election did not even appear on the ballot.
Banned from public office, former President Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest, serving a 27-year sentence for a coup plot after his 2022 election loss. The 71-year-old watched from confinement on Sunday as his eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, scored an upset victory over leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the first round of the presidential election.
The result, which pundits linked to a right-wing wave sweeping the region and Lula's own campaign missteps, made Flavio the favorite to win second-round voting on October 25. The shock victory represented a stunning reversal of his father's fortunes as the rehabilitated Bolsonaro family and ideological movement emerged stronger than ever.
Candidates from Bolsonaro's right-wing Liberal Party won up and down the ballot, demonstrating growing traction for the brand despite his legal woes, which the new right-wing Congress could resolve when it takes office in January.
Along with Flavio's surprising success, four more members of the family won public office on Sunday including Senate seats for Michelle Bolsonaro, the ex-president's wife, and second son Carlos while brother Renato and youngest son Jair Renan took seats in the lower house.
"In Brazilian political history, I do not remember any political clan that ever managed to elect so many members all at once," said political analyst Antonio Flavio Testa, who served on the former president's transition team in 2018.
When the imprisoned ex-president tapped his son to run for Brazil's highest office in December, markets tumbled and center-right allies turned up their noses. Flavio enlisted a little-known lawmaker from his own party, Alfredo Gaspar, as running mate because no other major party would join the ticket.
Flavio's most important ally could not appear in public even virtually to campaign for him but still loomed large over the race. An AI-generated avatar of the elder Bolsonaro gave a controversial endorsement of Flavio at his campaign launch.
The real Jair Bolsonaro has moved from serving his sentence in prison to house arrest since March due to ill health including complications from a 2018 stabbing. The Supreme Court prohibited visits from his eldest son for the past three months.
Their Liberal Party nearly doubled its bloc in the 81-seat Senate on Sunday to 28 seats, the strongest result for a party since Brazil's constitution was enacted in the 1980s after the country's return to democracy.
That will put amnesty for the elder Bolsonaro at the top of Congress' agenda next year, according to a close aide of Flavio who requested anonymity to speak openly. A vote on the matter could come even sooner if Flavio wins and the current Congress decides to curry favor with the incoming government.
Flavio said in early September that he hoped he would be inaugurated with his father present. "I ask God for the opportunity to walk up the ramp of Planalto Palace next year alongside President Jair Messias Bolsonaro," he said.
Bolsonaro and Lula, who got 47% and 45% of Sunday's vote respectively, go head-to-head in a second-round vote that political consulting firm Think Policy said would be "very difficult, but not impossible" for Lula to win.
To do that, Lula needs to get 62% of voters who backed conservative candidates other than Flavio in the first round, Think Policy estimated.
With prospects for Flavio's victory promising, Liberal Party President Valdemar da Costa Neto told Reuters that the elder Bolsonaro could once again play a role in government under his son. REUTERS

Three years after Oct. 7, Israel’s children face a crisis of trust that may last for years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:03:43 UTC
16:03:43 KST

Three years after the war began, the psychological damage suffered by many Israeli children has not faded. A child should not have to wonder whether home is safe, whether their parents can protect them or whether the state will keep them secure. Yet after October 7, mental health professionals say many children and teenagers were forced to confront exactly those questions.
Experts are now identifying another dimension of the trauma: a breakdown of trust in the people and institutions that were supposed to protect them. The frustration and confusion created by that crisis can emerge in many forms, professionals say, including verbal and physical violence, vandalism, anxiety and challenges to the authority of parents and teachers.
Prof. Asher Ben-Arieh, a researcher specializing in child welfare and rights and chairman of Ofek, the Hebrew University’s National Center for Innovation in Resilience, Trauma and Children’s and Families’ Mental Health, said the events created a form of trauma whose full characteristics are still not understood.
"A different kind of trauma was created, some of whose characteristics we still do not understand," he said. "One of the most prominent is the dimension of betrayal. Children were harmed precisely in the place that was supposed to be safest for them, while their parents, through no fault of their own, were unable to protect them."
Ben-Arieh said that may be only the beginning of what researchers will eventually discover.
"If we compare what happened to other forms of prolonged trauma, whether sexual, physical or emotional, in which children are repeatedly harmed over years by someone who was supposed to guard and protect them, or in which those protectors fail in their role, there is a certain similarity to what happened on October 7," he said.
"We are seeing similar consequences among teenagers, including violence, difficulties at school, depression, anxiety and more."
Still, Ben-Arieh stressed that much remains unknown about the psychological impact of October 7. "The element of betrayal is only one aspect that characterizes it, and from that we can begin pulling at a thread in our attempts at treatment and rehabilitation," he said. "But it will take many more years to understand what we went through and how it should be treated."
Ofek was established following the October 7 massacre and is now seeking to translate those insights into new rehabilitation models through programs it operates in schools.
Noa Petrushka-Afek, a doctoral student in social work at the Hebrew University and director of Ofek, said the center was founded on the understanding that the trauma created by October 7 and the war was different from previous crises.
"The feeling of betrayal is only one element," she said. "Children and teenagers are suffering from the consequences and the symptoms that accompany it."
She said the crisis of trust can be seen in relationships with state institutions, families and other authority figures.
"We are seeing vandalism and violence on an unusual scale among teenagers, and even protection rackets," Petrushka-Afek said. "All of these are expressions of distrust and resistance to the system. They don’t want treatment, they don’t trust adults and they don’t talk to adults about what happened to them."
She said new responses must be built by listening directly to those who were affected, constantly testing approaches against reality and being willing to change course when existing tools fail.
According to Ofek, 69 children have been killed since the beginning of the war and more than 1,500 have been hospitalized because of war-related injuries.
The center said that during the second year of the war, the number of teenagers diagnosed with anxiety rose by about one-third compared with the previous year, while diagnoses of eating disorders increased by roughly one-quarter.
About 275,000 children also grew up during this period with a mother or father serving for extended periods in the military reserves, according to the center.
Educational psychologist Yona Burstein, chairwoman of the Israel Psychological Association and a representative of a forum of organizations supporting public psychological services, said the war had created new forms of trauma, including one rooted in the loss of trust and the collapse of a basic sense of safety.
"In different crises, we guided parents to create a sense of protection and calm," she said. "When a child receives a calm message, what is happening outside does not affect them in the same way."
Young people themselves describe the consequences in similar terms. Rotem Getreide, a 12th-grade student and chairman of a student council, said the situation had emotionally destabilized many teenagers.
"There is a feeling of confusion, that at any moment something is about to happen," he said. "Vandalism and violence come from distress and helplessness, and there really are young people who find it difficult to trust others."
Lian Hajaj, 16, chairwoman of the student and youth council in Ofakim, said teenagers had been forced to deal with experiences far beyond what should be expected at their age.
"We found ourselves dealing with things that teenagers our age should not have to deal with," she said. "So many friends are dealing with anxiety and fear. What they define for us as a ‘return to routine’ does not really feel like routine."
Talia Ben Baruch, 17, of Beit She’an, who chairs the student and youth council in Israel’s Northern District, said the end of the war had not ended its psychological impact.
"The war may have ended, but we, the youth of the north, are still dealing with what it left behind: anxiety, sleepless nights, disconnection and prolonged loneliness," she said. "I watched friends from communities along the confrontation line lose their homes and move from one temporary framework to another."
The Education Ministry said it did not have the center’s findings but stressed that since October 7, professionals from its psychological and counseling services had been providing ongoing support to students and educational staff.
The ministry said focused support had been provided to students and families directly affected by the war, while counseling hours and educational psychology services had been expanded.
It added that new tools had been developed to identify distress and provide appropriate responses, alongside dedicated training for professionals.
"The education system continues to monitor the changing needs of children and teenagers and adapt the support provided to them, with the goal of strengthening resilience, belonging and continuity," the ministry said.

Writer Jeffrey Archer, author of a NYT bestseller, dies at 86
Kyiv • UNN
Jeffrey Archer died in London at the age of 86. The author of "Kane and Abel" sold hundreds of millions of books and left behind more than 40 works.
British writer, politician and former convict Jeffrey Archer died at his home in London at the age of 86. His death was announced by publisher HarperCollins. The New York Times reports, UNN reports.
Details
According to the publication, Archer became famous for thrillers and novels about wealthy and influential people. His books have sold hundreds of millions of copies worldwide. One of his best-known works was the 1979 novel "Kane and Abel," which has sold more than 50 million copies since its publication and topped The New York Times bestseller list. Archer's first novel, "Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less," was published in 1976. Before becoming a writer, he worked in public relations and was a politician.
"Where I come from, in Western Australia, we say: 'Tell them a story, (...) and make them turn the pages, and you can't go wrong,'" Archer explained about his approach to writing books.
Jeffrey Archer was a Member of the House of Commons and deputy chairman of Margaret Thatcher's Conservative Party. He later took a seat in the House of Lords with the title of Baron Archer of Weston-super-Mare.
In 2001, he was convicted of perjury.
"A political Houdini, he survived many twists and turns, including a 2001 conviction for perjury, when he was found guilty of fabricating diaries and inventing a story to win a court case over whether he had slept with a prostitute whom he had paid to keep silent," the publication writes.
Despite the political scandal, Archer continued his writing career and published more than 40 books.
"Storytellers are very rare, but they arouse a great deal of envy. The people who survive are storytellers," he told writer Anthony Horowitz in an interview in 2011.
Jeffrey Archer died on Monday in London. His final novel, "Adam and Eve," was due to be released the following day.

Voyager to build satellite dispensers for U.S. Space Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:00:58 UTC
16:00:58 KST

- Voyager Technologies won a $22.4 million U.S. Department of War agreement to prototype flight-ready small satellite dispensers for launches with unused payload capacity.
- The Strategic Capabilities Office funded the effort, which aims to transition the technology to the U.S. Space Force; quantities and timelines were not disclosed.
Voyager Technologies has won a $22.4 million agreement from the U.S. Department of War’s Strategic Capabilities Office to build prototype satellite dispensers that would let the U.S. Space Force fit extra small satellites onto launches that would otherwise fly with unused room.
The Denver-based company announced the award on Oct. 5. It is an Other Transaction Agreement, a contracting tool the Pentagon uses to fund prototypes faster than through standard procurement rules. Voyager said the goal is to move the resulting technology to the U.S. Space Force.
Voyager did not say how many dispensers it will build, when they are due, which rockets they are meant for, or when the first one could fly. The company described the hardware as prototypes that will nonetheless be flight-ready.
Many launches lift off with spare mass and volume left over after the main payload is mounted. Dispensers and adapters mounted alongside or beneath the primary spacecraft can use that space to carry smaller satellites, which are released once the main mission is safely deployed. The U.S. military has flown secondary payloads this way for years, often on adapter rings fitted between the rocket’s upper stage and the primary satellite.
Voyager said its dispensers are being designed to get more out of launches that leave payload capacity unused, without interfering with the primary mission.
“This award reflects Voyager’s confidence in our ability to move rapidly from concept to on-orbit capability,” said Matt Magaña, president of Space, Defense and National Security at Voyager. “We’re excited to work with the DoW on this R&D effort that has the goal of providing the Space Force new tools to put more capability on orbit faster, and without displacing primary mission objectives.”
The Strategic Capabilities Office was set up in 2012 to find new military uses for existing technology and get them to combatant commanders quickly. It works on a project basis and typically hands successful prototypes to a military service to field. In this case, that service would be the U.S. Space Force.
Voyager has a long track record with small satellites. Its Nanoracks business has deployed large numbers of CubeSats from the International Space Station, and the company handles payload integration, launch coordination and on-orbit operations for civil, commercial and national security customers. Voyager is also leading development of Starlab, a planned commercial space station, and went public on the New York Stock Exchange in 2025 under the ticker VOYG.

Bar Shrimp uses laser-etched acoustic panels to balance music and conversation

Bar Shrimp uses laser-etched acoustic panels to balance music and conversation
Cocktail bar and restaurant Bar Shrimp combines red velvet interiors with bespoke acoustic panels from Autex Acoustics to balance music and conversation, shown in this video produced by Dezeen.
Located in Manchester, Bar Shrimp has a custom sound system and a dark interior with floor-to-ceiling red velvet curtains and plush banquettes, reminiscent of vintage New York bars and music lounges.
The design was informed by the founders' experience of bars around the world, where co-founder Richard Cossins said they were struck by ones with particularly good sound.
"When we first saw the space, we wanted to create a relaxed and comfortable environment, where guests could spend numerous hours within the space," Cossins told Dezeen.
The existing space had a concrete floor and glass walls, prompting the team to introduce softer materials to improve the acoustics.
Autex Acoustics worked with the team from an early stage, supplying a bespoke Frontier Axis ceiling system and Mirage wall panels to reduce reverberation and echo.
The acoustic treatment was designed to complement the interior rather than disappear into it, with laser-etched patterns giving the Mirage panels a textured finish inspired by natural materials.
"We're looking at it from a technical perspective, but also from an aesthetic perspective," said Autex Acoustics UK, EU and the Middle East director Daniel Senior.
"We laser etch a pattern into a panel," he continued. "That allows us to create some really intricate designs, to create real depth and texture to a panel, all taking inspiration from natural materials."
Bar Shrimp also features a custom MasterSounds Clarity M-1215 Audio system – a large-format modular speaker system designed to provide high-quality sound throughout the space.
Cossins said the acoustic treatment was intended to make the bar comfortable even when music is playing at a high volume.
"It's an aspect of the guest experience that doesn't necessarily get noticed, but when you walk into a space and you don't have to shout and you can hear your guests and your dining companions with real clarity, I think it goes a long way," he said.
The project continues a six-year-long collaboration between Cossins and Autex Acoustics, who also worked together to design the interiors of Higher Ground, Bar Shrimp's sister restaurant located next door.
Founded in 1967, Autex Acoustics produces sound-dampening products for offices and mixed-use interiors.
In 2025, the brand created a forest-like installation using its signature acoustic material at LA Design Festival in downtown Los Angeles.

The UK has a food waste problem and a food poverty problem – and we have a plan to fix them both | Charlotte Hill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:00:06 UTC
16:00:06 KST

How often does this happen? You open the fridge and find some ingredient you meant to use but didn’t get round to, and even though it’s still edible you think perhaps it’s just easier to throw it away. In the UK it’s estimated that an average household wastes about three meals a week, or 156 meals a year.
Household fridges are one thing. But across the food sector more than 1bn meals’ worth of easily accessible surplus food is wasted each year in the UK for the same reason: because it is easier to throw it away. That equates to 470,000 tonnes – enough to feed every child in the UK three meals a day for a month. When so many people are struggling to afford food, that is a staggering amount, and what’s even more shocking is that it is good quality and nutritious.
We hear a lot about grocery stores and restaurants throwing out perfectly edible food, but truthfully, they are a minor part of the problem. The vast majority of the food waste, about 850m meals, comes from farms, followed by food manufacturing facilities with 178m meals, another 71m come from the hospitality and food service sector, and finally the retail sector accounts for 12m meals.
And when I say easily accessible, I mean this is food we have the capacity to rescue and get to people. The organisation I head, Felix, is a food rescue charity. We recover edible surplus food that would otherwise go to waste and get it to more than 8,000 organisations doing amazing work feeding people in need. This food sustains lunch clubs for older people where friendships are forged and isolation is addressed. It supports food pantries, where families can access a weekly bag of shopping for just a few pounds. And it can provide meals in homelessness shelters and refuges. But with the levels of food insecurity growing, the need for our food is also rising. So we must rescue more of that billion-meal surplus.
In our food system, unavoidable surplus food is generated at every stage of the supply chain. On farms, unpredictable weather, grading standards and mismatches between harvest volumes and buyer orders contribute to the enormous quantities of edible produce without a home. But we are working with farmers to ensure this food is getting to people’s plates; almost half the food we gave out last year was fresh fruit and vegetables.
In manufacturing, production overruns, packaging changes and quality control measures create surplus that cannot be sold through normal channels. But there are bright spots, and an incredible example is food manufacturer Premier Foods. When their noodle nests don’t pass quality control, we take them and use a partner organisation to repack and label them. We are doing a similar project with 2 Sisters Food Group, a huge manufacturing company that uses late-night surplus factory capacity to repack breaded chicken with minor visual defects.
We are also working with the supermarkets such as Asda, Co-op, Ocado, Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Waitrose. They give us a huge amount of stock that we get straight back out to every part of the UK.
So many companies are doing their bit, but the reason many are not is economics. It is cheaper for a business to waste food than to give it to people: the corporation tax system does not reward food donation in the same way it does a financial one. In addition, public subsidies for alternative disposal routes – such as turning food waste into animal food or biogas – provide profit. This creates a market that actively pulls surplus away from human consumption. We must change this.
That is why Felix has started the Redistribution Revolution. Felix, City Harvest, Community Shop, The Bread and Butter Thing, His Church, Feeding Britain, Neighbourly and the wider Felix and Xcess Networks have formed the Food Redistribution Partnership UK, working together to rescue more food. Backed by the government we have launched a national programme to redistribute surplus food, which aims to triple the amount of food we redistribute over the next decade. According to our research, about 1% of all excess food in the UK food system is redistributed by charities. France redistributes about twice that, while the USA does three times more.
Our revolution needs food businesses to make redistribution the default route for all surplus food, and view it as an opportunity for social good. We need philanthropists to invest in the infrastructure required to store and move the food. And we need the government to change the tax system and make it more financially viable for companies to get food to people.
Finally, we need donations and volunteers to help us rescue and deliver more food.
We know surplus food is out there, and while it is very important to recognise that redistribution is not a systemic solution to poverty, we are certain that good food is going to waste, and rescuing it can be a powerful way to alleviate the symptoms of food insecurity, and to support organisations that are helping people tackle the challenges in their lives.
- Charlotte Hill is chief executive of the food redistribution organisation Felix
