Here is a look at the latest news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, October 6, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
WATCH: What does an AfD state speaker mean for Germany?
Germany’s far-right AfD party took a significant step toward exercising political power in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
One month after winning 44% of the regional vote, the party secured the presidency of the state parliament, with Tobias Rausch elected as speaker of the house.
What does this moment mean for Germany? DW reports from Magdeburg.
AfD will also field a deputy speaker in Saxony-Anhalt parliament
Parliamentarians in Saxony-Anhalt have also voted for AfD politician Hans-Thomas Tillschneider to be one of the deputy speakers in the chamber.
This follows Tobias Rausch of the right-wing populist AfD being voted into the speaker's role earlier on Tuesday.
Tillschneider received 44 votes in favor in Tuesday's session, while 38 parliamentarians opposed his appointment. Nobody abstained from the vote, which was by secret ballot. The AfD has 39 seats in the chamber.
Lawmakers decided to elect three deputy speakers in total, with elections for the others expected to follow later.
Tillschneider, aged 48, is the deputy chair of the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt parliamentary group. He's an AfD veteran, having joined the party in 2013 soon after it was founded.
Tillschneider is a member of the identitarian movement, and was a member of the two AfD fringe groups — the so-called Flügel (wing) and its "Patriotic Platform" — that have since been formally disbanded. He also had close ties to the Pegida and Legida groups that organized anti-migrant protests in eastern Germany.
As well as his strong views on Islam and migration, Tillschneider is also known for his ties to Vladimir Putin's Russia. He was one of three AfD parliamentarians to visit Russia in September 2022, barely six months after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in a visit that AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel rapidly disowned as a "private trip" and "not productive."
Since 2023, Tillschneider has written a monthly column for the Vedomosti newspaper in Russia. He attended the 73rd birthday celebrations for Putin at the Russian Embassy in Berlin last October.
CDU state premier: Where did the votes for Rausch come from?
The outgoing premier of Saxony-Anhalt says he can't explain where an additional four votes backing the AfD's Tobias Rausch as the state's new parliamentary speaker came from.
In a first for the far-right party, 35-year-old Rausch was elected to the post on Tuesday with the help of the populist BSW party (see entry below).
The Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group leadership had recommended that its 15 lawmakers in the state parliament abstain from voting.
But CDU regional leader and current state Premier Sven Schulze said it had become clear by this morning that not all the party's lawmakers planned to do so.
Some indicated that they planned to vote "no," Schulze said in comments to the German press agency DPA. "But none of us said we would vote 'yes,'" he added. "Not a single one."
Rausch was elected with 48 votes in favor and 29 against from 82 eligible votes in the secret ballot. There were five abstentions.
The AfD holds 39 seats in the parliament and the BSW five, meaning Rausch also got backing from members of other parties besides the AfD and BSW.
The center-left Social Democrats demanded answers, with the party's general secretary, Tim Klüssendorf, calling for the CDU to "immediately clarify who from within its ranks may have considered this disastrous decision to be right."
Klüssendorf also criticized the BSW for supporting Rausch's election.
"The BSW has made a conscious decision to elect, for the first time since 1945, a politician from a far-right party to the leadership of a German parliament," Klüssendorf told the Rheinische Post newspaper.
In addition to the CDU, the Social Democrats and the BSW, the Left party and the Greens are also represented in the state's parliament. Except for the BSW, the other parties have refused to work with the AfD, but some combination of them cast a secret vote for Rausch.
Bank board member agrees to quit, but cleared of wrongdoing in brothel loan inquest
The Volksbank Köln Bonn in western Germany has agreed to part ways with a board member, Jürgen Neutgens, after a scandal over a loan he authorized to Cologne's large brothel, Pascha.
It made the announcement on Tuesday, several months after placing Neutgens on leave and commissioning an independent law firm to investigate the transaction for potential wrongdoing.
"The investigation ... found no indications of financial irregularities or actions contravening obligations in the loan processes or the business relationship," the bank said in a press release. "Nevertheless the past weeks have weighed considerably on everyone involved."
Against this backdrop, the bank said the parties involved had mutually concluded that "a trusting and candid cooperation for the future can no longer be continued on the appropriate foundation."
It said both sides had agreed to confidentiality on the further details and terms, and thanked Neutgens for his service and wished him well for the future.
The loan was issued amid the restrictions of the COVID pandemic, which took a severe toll on the sex industry in Germany and led to the Pascha brothel in Cologne filing for insolvency and then changing ownership.
A family from China, or more specifically the autonomous casino-rich region of Macao, bought the business. But they needed a bridging loan of around €5 million (roughly $5.6 million at today's exchange rates) to cover part of the purchase price when their funds were held up in Hong Kong.
Pope receives German Christmas cake gift by car from Saxony
A typical German Christmas speciality intended as a gift for Pope Leo XIV was driven to Rome in an official vehicle from the state of Saxony after it was deemed unsuitable for air transport, officials revealed on Tuesday.
The 4-kilogram (8.8-pound) cake, a so-called stollen, which was made in the Ore Mountains in eastern Germany, was taken by Saxon Premier Michael Kretschmer to the Vatican for a private audience at the end of September.
The cake was reportedly too large to be taken into the cabin and too fragile to be placed in the aircraft hold, the officials said.
No information was provided on the cost by the officials at the Saxon State Chancellery.
The vehicle also transported other presents and documents.
Greens leader in Saxony-Anhalt says border has been crossed
The leader of the Green parliamentary party in Saxony-Anhalt, Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz, has vowed to defend democracy following the election of a member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), Tobias Rausch, as parliamentary speaker.
The election of the member of a confirmed right-wing extremist, anti-constitutional party as house speaker meant that a "border" had been crossed, she said.
"We will not allow ourselves to be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights here or those of the people in this state are to be curtailed," she added.
Earlier in her address, she said that if the AfD were to take power in the state, her party would "speak out if people were denigrated because of their origins, beliefs or lifestyle."
Sziborra-Seidlitz said Saxony-Anhalt could not afford for "exclusion to become the political brand of this parliament and our state."
The AfD emerged from September elections as the strongest single force in parliament but has so far failed to find parties willing to enter into a coalition with it.
The Saxony-Anhalt chapter of the party has been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the domestic intelligence agency in the state.
Among other things, the party advocates a hard-line anti-immigration agenda and an intolerant stance toward LGBTQ+ rights.
Far-right AfD candidate elected state parliamentary speaker
Tobias Rausch, the far-right Alternative for Germany's (AFD's) nomination for speaker in Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament, has been elected with the help of the populist BSW party.
Rausch gained 48 votes in favor to 29 against from 82 eligible votes. There were five abstentions.
The AfD holds 39 seats in the parliament and the BSW five, giving Rausch the majority he needed to win the post, as the other parties combined — all of which reject working with the AfD — also hold 39 seats.
The result, however, means that members of parties besides the AfD and BSW voted for him.
Rausch, 35, thus becomes the first member of the AfD — a party classified by domestic intelligence in Saxony-Anhalt as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization — to become speaker in a state parliament in Germany.
The new speaker is a real-estate entrepreneur by profession and has been a member of parliament for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt since 2016.
The parliamentary session was accompanied by several anti-AfD protests in front of the parliament building.
The vote for speaker is separate from that for state premier.
The AfD's lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, who won the September election with 44% of the vote — thus falling short of an absolute majority — intends to stand for the position in December.
As no other party so far wants to form a coalition with his party, it is still in question whether he can win a vote or form a government.
The AfD says it is in dialogue with the BSW and individual parliamentarians to seek the necessary support.
EU chief warns against German-led push to cut budget
Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, warned on Tuesday against major cuts to the European Union's next long-term budget.
"I am aware that balancing all of these constraints is not easy. I am also aware of the difficult budgetary situation in the member states," von der Leyen told the European Parliament in the French city of Strasbourg.
"But I would like to caution against large cuts. They would risk undermining critical priorities that we have all agreed upon," she added.
Negotiations on the long-term budget for the 2028-2034 period are currently underway. The EU's long-term budget, also known as the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), is the European Union's seven-year spending plan that sets how much the bloc can spend and on which priorities, such as agriculture, regional development, research, defense, migration, and climate policy.
The European Commission has proposed a budget of around €1.76 trillion (about $1.98 trillion). The budget is financed mainly through contributions based on the size of member states' economies.
The current MFF for 2021-2027 amounts to around €1.2 trillion.
Traditionally, Germany has opposed increases to the proposed budget, while other countries favor maintaining subsidies for economically disadvantaged regions. This time has been no different, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz calling for major cuts.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating EU presidency, is expected to present a new compromise proposal in the coming days.
European Council President Antonio Costa aims to secure an agreement on the new budget by the end of the year.
Applications to refuse military service on the rise
The number of applications from people wishing to refuse military service on grounds of conscience has risen sharply.
Altogether 12,102 such applications were made in the first eighth months of the year, according to figures from the Federal Office for Family Affairs and Civil Society Functions (BAFzA) — more than triple the number in the whole of 2025 (3,879).
The sharp increase comes after Germany's new military service law came into effect on January 1.
That law foresees mandatory medical screening for young men born in 2008 or later, with an eye to recruiting volunteers to expand the armed forces.
Although compulsory military service has been suspended in Germany since 2011, it remains enshrined in Germany's Basic Law.
The right to refuse armed military service as a conscientious objector also remains in place.
Parliament can decide to introduce needs-based conscription if recruitment targets are not reached under the current voluntary system.
German Economy: Recovery faces setback as factory orders plunge
In August, orders from German factories fell faster than expected, marking the first decline in four months. Orders were down 10.6% compared to July.
According to the statistics agency Destatis, the decline in orders from large German manufacturers highlights the fragility of the recovery in Europe's largest economy.
Germany's economy has been stagnant for an extended period and has only been recovering slowly, supported by massive public spending. However, recent data have shown signs of strengthening.
The German Economy Ministry said that August's orders data represented a "significant setback." It also noted that, excluding the drop in large orders, the overall situation was virtually unchanged from July.
The August decline was driven by weaker domestic demand. Orders fell by more than 60% in the category that includes military vehicles, aircraft, ships, and trains.
Germany raises military spending
Orders in this sector have increased as Germany spends vast sums on its military to confront an increasingly hostile Russia and amid concerns about US security guarantees for Europe.
The ministry stressed that the growing importance of public procurement has made orders "highly volatile."
By comparison, new orders from June to August were 1.3% higher than in the previous three-month period.
The energy crisis stemming from the conflict in the Middle East has created additional challenges for Germany's economic recovery, but the economy has weathered the impact better than initially feared.
Experts recently doubled their growth forecast for this year to 1.3%.

Police in Lower Saxony have been deployed to a high school in the town of Langwedel after being alerted to a possible rampage attack by an alarm, according various German media.
Later, officers confirmed that the situation was resolved. It remained unclear if a false alarm was triggered or if a serious security threat had been brought under control.
German-Russian man jailed over helping Russian military
A German-Russian man has been sentenced in Latvia to seven years in prison and one year on probation after being found guilty of collecting and supplying money and goods to Russian military personnel.
The man was detained by Latvian authorities while on one of his car trips allegedly transporting the goods across the Latvian-Russian border.
The man denied supplying sanctioned goods, saying he was transporting humanitarian aid such as wheelchairs, crutches and nappies.
The Latvian news agency LETA cited the responsible court in Riga as having said he was in fact carrying goods including night-vision devices and telescopes.
Prosecutors used correspondence, photographs and videos found on the man's mobile phone to back their case against him.
The verdict against the man, who holds both German and Russian citizenship, is not yet final and can be appealed.
Wadephul warns of climate change as security risk
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has highlighted the consequences of climate change for global security as the Berlin Climate and Security Conference kicks off in the capital.
"Particularly in fragile states, climate change exacerbates poverty and hunger — and can thus also become a fertile ground for extremism and terrorism or lead to waves of migration," he said.
Wadephul also emphasized the importance of climate protection in enhancing national security.
"When Russia once more deliberately attacks the energy infrastructure in Ukraine, decentralized, renewable energy sources could become a form of life insurance," he said.
"Investment in climate protection is also investment in our security," he added.
The Berlin Climate and Security Conference, which has been held annually since 2019, brings together some 250 international actors in the fields of climate, peace and security.
Participants include representatives from countries particularly affected by climate change and from the UN, EU and scientific and civil society organizations.
New Saxony-Anhalt parliament sits to choose speaker
The newly elected state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt is poised to hold its first session on Tuesday, over four weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won elections there with almost 44% of the vote.
The AfD holds 39 seats in the legislature, the same number of seats as the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the Left Party, Greens and Social Democrats (SPD) together.
During the session, parliamentarians are to vote for a speaker, with the AfD, as the strongest force, empowered to nominate the first candidate.
The AfD has put forward long-serving parliamentarian Tobias Rausch, 35, for the post, a choice that the populist BSW, which holds 5 seats, has pledged to back.
All the other parties refuse to work with the AfD under a policy known as the "firewall," and the CDU chairman in the state has advised members of his party to abstain from the vote.
If Rausch is elected, he will become the first AfD speaker of a state parliament in Germany.
However, if he fails to be elected in a first round of voting, all the other parties can put forward their own candidates.
There will be no vote on who will lead the state.
The session will be accompanied by protests by civil society groups who see the AfD, which has been classified as a "confirmed extremist" organization by domestic intelligence in the state, as a danger to Germany's democracy.

I have said that the triple lock is our policy and it remains our policy. I don’t think going after pensioners is the right thing when there are loads of people who can work, who won’t work.
When we are going to reverse Labour’s policies, I say we are going to reverse their policies.
I have said that we are keeping this policy, but if they take that money and they spend it on something that we can’t get it back from, then it would be difficult for me.

Welsh government announces plans to tackle two notorious road bottlenecks
Steven Morris
Steven Morris is a Guardian reporter covering Wales.
Welsh ministers have announced ambitious – and expensive - plans to tackle two notorious traffic bottlenecks by building a new bridge and widening a road tunnel.
The government, led by Plaid Cymru, wants to create a third crossing of the Menai Strait in north Wales, which separates the island of Ynys Môn (Anglesey) from the mainland. The price for the new crossing is put at about £750 million.
It is also planning to get to grips with the M4 around Newport in south Wales, which is often snarled up with traffic.
Proposals there include expanding the Brynglas Tunnels from two to three lanes each way, which might cost £1.7bn.
In addition, junctions into and out of the city could be closed to cut down traffic using the M4 for short journeys.
The government has not said where the money is coming from but will look at all options, including, for example, asking for help from the UK government for funds as both schemes are important for Britain as a whole.
The deputy minister for transport, Mark Hooper, said:
We will carry out an 18-month study to consider a range of road-based solutions for the M4 around Newport. People on Ynys Môn and across the north of Wales have waited a long time for greater certainty about the future of the crossings.
The afternoon session ended with a Ukrainian school choir singing the Ukrainian national anthem, and the British national anthem. The choir also sang earlier, at the start of the afternoon session.

Shadow DWP secretary Helen Whately says UK 'in deep trouble' because of number of working-age adults on benefits

We’re spending £170bn a year on working age welfare, two and a half times more than we spend on defence. And that’s paying for the benefits of six million people who are not working. Conference, six million!
We must, of course, look after people too sick to disabled to work. We’re a civilised society. We’re compassionate. We want a safety net to be there for people in desperate need.
But that’s not six million people. It’s simply not true that one in seven people of working age in this country is unable to work. Adam Smith wrote that the nation’s prosperity depends on the share of its people in useful work. By that measure, we are in deep trouble.
Whately also said that at the last conference she had her team had already identified cuts that would save £23bn.

Historian Niall Ferguson tells Tories it's not 'alarmist' to say another world war may happen, and UK must prepare
At the Tory conference Tom Tugendhat’s speech was followed by a Q&A with the leading global historian, SirNiall Ferguson. Many of Ferguson’s books have been about war and he told the audience that he was attending a Tory conference for the first time because he wanted to spread the message that “there is only one responsible party when it comes to national security, and it is the Conservative party”.
Ferguson also told the conference that a third world war was possible. He said:
I don’t think it’s alarmist to say that we may be on a path to another world war, because remember how the world wars began? There were regional wars before they broke out in the Balkans before 1914. And then there were wars before the war of 1939, wars in Asia, civil war in Spain. Germany’s rise didn’t begin in 1939. It began with the reoccupation of the Rhineland.
We must remember the lessons that our grandparents – and in the case of younger people here, our great-grandparents – had to learn through bitter experience. We never again want to have to see British kids in air raid shelters.

Australia opposition pledges ‘biggest cut to immigration’ in history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:18:14 UTC
15:18:14 KST

Australia’s opposition coalition has pledged what it calls the “biggest cut to immigration” in the country’s history, proposing to reduce net overseas migration to 100,000 a year during its first two years in government.
Opposition leader Angus Taylor unveiled the plan on Tuesday as the Liberal-National Coalition seeks to link immigration levels to housing availability and pressure on public services.
The proposal would reduce the number of temporary visa holders by about 650,000 over four years, while permanent skilled migration would remain capped at 185,000 places a year.
Students might face restrictions
International students would face tighter restrictions, including a cap of 240,000 new student commencements. The coalition also plans to abolish most Temporary Graduate Visas, with exemptions for PhD students and those studying health and education or attending regional universities.
The coalition would also halve Australia's humanitarian intake to 10,000 places a year and require most applicants for second or subsequent temporary visas to apply from outside the country.
‘Australia is not a hotel’
“A temporary visa should mean temporary. Australia is a home, not a hotel,” the coalition said.
Under the plan, net migration would gradually increase after the initial cuts, reaching 160,000 in the fourth year.
Migration has become a major political issue in Australia amid housing and cost-of-living pressures.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's Labor government has also tightened migration rules, including for international students, while arguing that migration remains important for addressing critical skills shortages.

US televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar empire and lived in opulence before being disgraced by a sex scandal, a fraud conviction for bilking followers, and a divorce from television co-host Tammy Faye, died on Monday at age 86.
The death of Bakker, whose journey from the TV pulpit to a prison cell in the 1980s inspired comparisons to the corrupt character of the fictional preacher-huckster Elmer Gantry, was revealed on social media by his second wife, Lori Bakker.
"It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening," she wrote on the Facebook and Instagram pages of her husband's latest television ministry.
She paid tribute to Bakker as a "pioneer of Christian television," but the cause and circumstances of his death were not revealed.
Bakker revived his career as a television preacher after prison with a new wife and a new television show in 2003, later becoming a staunch supporter of President Donald Trump, known for his own brand of right-wing populism.
Bakker rose to fame through ‘The PTL Club’
Bakker had been among the most popular of the Christian preachers who thrived on US television in the 1980s, achieving fame on the show "The PTL Club." PTL stood for "Praise The Lord" and "People That Love."
Detractors, pointing to his unabashed daily exhortations to viewers for donations to his ministry, said PTL should have stood for "pass the loot."
Bakker spent 4-1/2 years in prison after being convicted in Charlotte, North Carolina, in 1989 of defrauding followers in a scheme involving vacations at his Heritage USA Christian theme park and resort.
Prosecutors painted him as a selfish and petty con man driven by greed and lust for power.
"Those of us who do have a religion are sick of being saps for money-grubbing preachers and priests," Judge Robert Potter told Bakker before sentencing him.
Bakker had quit the PTL ministry in 1987 after revelations of a 1980 sexual encounter with Jessica Hahn, a former church secretary who later posed nude in Playboy magazine, and a subsequent $265,000 payoff with ministry funds to gain her silence. Bakker was later defrocked.
Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker, his first wife, had started with a small TV ministry and eventually created a multimillion-dollar operation with 2,000 employees and the 2,300-acre (930-hectare) Heritage USA complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina.
At its peak, the PTL ministry drew 13 million viewers on 200 TV stations and raked in $129 million a year.
With his working-class upbringing, the affable Bakker related well to common folk.
He did not deliver fire-and-brimstone sermons like other televangelists, instead offering a friendly Christian message - although it was larded with requests for money donations.
Tammy Faye was much more flamboyant, with her enthusiastic singing and penchant for tears that left her heavy makeup smeared on her face.
Fraud conviction brings Bakker’s empire crashing down
Bakker was convicted after a six-week trial in federal court on all 24 fraud and conspiracy charges brought against him.
Prosecutors said he defrauded followers of $158 million by selling promises of lifetime annual vacations that he could not provide.
They said he siphoned $3.7 million to bankroll a lavish lifestyle that included several homes, luxury cars, mink coats, diamonds, servants - and an air-conditioned dog house.
The judge ordered Bakker to 45 years in prison but the sentence was later reduced. "I have sinned," Bakker told the court. "I have made mistakes. But never in my life did I intend to defraud anyone."
Bakker's chief aide, Richard Dortch, served 18 months of an eight-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to reduced charges in exchange for testifying against Bakker.
Tammy Faye was never charged. She stood by Bakker at the trial - even singing to reporters after his conviction - but divorced him in 1992 while he was in prison. She died of cancer in 2007.
Bakker started his life over after leaving prison in 1994, renouncing the "prosperity gospel" he once preached and writing a book titled "I Was Wrong."
"I've had a second chance at life. And I have a beautiful wife who loves me," Bakker told CNN in 2000, referring to his second wife, Lori, who he married in 1998.
They started a TV ministry together in 2003. In 2008, they began taping "The Jim Bakker Show" at a 600-acre (240-hectare) development called Morningside near the tourist city of Branson, Missouri, that bore similarities to Heritage USA.
Bakker faced scrutiny for promoting false COVID remedy
Bakker once again pleaded with his followers for donations.
In 2020, he drew the ire of state and federal officials for selling a false treatment for COVID-19 during the deadly coronavirus pandemic.
Bakker also said in 2017 that Christians would launch a civil war if Trump were to be impeached. Trump later became the first US president to be impeached twice.
James Orson Bakker was born on January 2, 1940, the son of an auto parts factory worker in Muskegon, Michigan, who maintained a strict fundamentalist Christian household.
He met Tammy Faye LaValley at North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, and they married in 1961. Both dropped out of school to become traveling evangelists as he pursued the career of a minister of the Pentecostal Assemblies of God denomination.
Their big break came in 1964, when televangelist Pat Robertson aired a children's religious puppet show with them on his fledgling TV network.
Setting out on his own in the 1970s, Bakker used the emerging world of cable and satellite TV to build an empire.

Somaliland seeks deeper security ties with Israel, sees Turkey as growing threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:12:35 UTC
15:12:35 KST

Somaliland is seeking to deepen security cooperation with Israel, including by obtaining air-defense systems, amid Turkey's growing military presence in Somalia, senior Somaliland presidential foreign affairs adviser Mohamed Osman Fadal said in an interview with Middle East Eye published this week.
"We need air-defense systems," Fadal said. "We want Israel to support us against Turkey."
According to Fadal, the deployment of Turkish F-16 fighter jets in Somalia and Ankara's expanding drone capabilities are among the reasons officials in Hargeisa want to strengthen Somaliland's defenses. Turkey deployed military aircraft to Somalia this year, and three Turkish F-16s participated in an April flyover over Mogadishu as part of celebrations marking Somali Armed Forces Day.
The remarks offered a rare glimpse into how Somaliland views its developing relationship with Israel. In recent months, reports have also increased regarding the possibility of an Israeli military presence at the port of Berbera.
Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud claimed on Friday that Israel was planning to establish a naval base in the city and also use its airport.
Somaliland denied that such an agreement exists. Its defense minister said in June that there was no Israeli military presence and no negotiations over establishing a base. He did, however, confirm that Israel provides training to Somaliland's military and police.
Somaliland sees Israel as counterweight to Turkey, Somalia ties
Officials in Hargeisa have described Israel as a potential counterweight to the increasingly close cooperation between Somalia and Turkey.
Mohamed Abdirahman Hassan, director-general of Somaliland's Foreign Ministry, told Middle East Eye that officials in Hargeisa fear the Somali government is considering military action against Somaliland and that Turkey could assist it.
The claim has not been independently verified, however, and Somalia's federal government has not announced any plan to invade Somaliland.
Turkey is considered one of Somalia's main strategic allies. In 2017, Ankara opened its largest overseas military training facility in Mogadishu and has since trained thousands of Somali security personnel.
In 2024, Turkey and Somalia signed a 10-year defense and economic cooperation agreement that includes assistance in building, training, and equipping Somalia's navy and strengthening maritime security. Turkey has also expanded its involvement in the energy sector, including oil and gas exploration off Somalia's coast.
Analysts question Somaliland's warnings over Turkey
Not everyone is convinced by Somaliland's warnings.
Mogadishu-based analyst Ahmed Abdi told Somalia Today that, in his view, Turkey does not pose a significant threat to Somaliland and that the statements are largely aimed at audiences outside the region.
According to Abdi, Somaliland is seeking to position itself alongside Western actors that criticize Turkey or support Israel, hoping the secure greater international support and further recognition.
Abdi assessed that the strategy was unlikely to succeed, in part because Turkey is a NATO member and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan maintains ties with US President Donald Trump.
He said Somaliland would have a stronger case if it based its demand for recognition on its own achievements and status rather than on opposition to other countries.
The reports also challenge the assumption that closer security ties between Israel and Somaliland are driven primarily by the Houthi threat across the Gulf of Aden.
Hassan told Middle East Eye that Somaliland does not support confrontation with the Houthis and instead prefers direct political dialogue.
Somaliland, Israel differ over approach to Houthi threat
That position differs significantly from Israel's approach, after the Houthis have attacked Israel and shipping routes in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden over the years.
The gap may indicate that, from Somaliland's perspective, Turkey and its relationship with the Somali government currently represent a more central security concern than the Houthis.
Somaliland declared independence from Somalia in 1991 and has since maintained its own governing and security institutions. According to the report, Israel is currently the only country to have formally recognized it as a sovereign state.

EU discusses tighter restrictions on Russian diplomats amid hybrid attacks – Euronews
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:12:00 EEST
15:12:00 KST

EU discusses tighter restrictions on Russian diplomats amid hybrid attacks – Euronews
EU countries are discussing tighter restrictions and additional checks for Russian diplomats amid a wave of hybrid attacks in Europe.
Source: European Pravda, citing Euronews
Details: The movements and activities of Russian diplomats have come under closer scrutiny as the European Union tackles a series of hybrid attacks, some of which have been directly linked to Moscow and which have shaken its collective security. Euronews reported that this issue could be the next step in the EU's sanctions regime.
Hungary expelled 10 Russian diplomats last month, accusing them of "unacceptable" conduct under the 1961 Vienna Convention. Moscow responded in kind.
Other worrying incidents, including a suspected arson attack on a defence company facility in Estonia and the discovery of an unexploded drone at Leipzig Airport in Germany, both linked to Russia, have further increased concerns.
The discussions, which are still at an early stage, are a continuation of the mechanism introduced by the EU last year as part of its 19th sanctions package. This requires Russian diplomats working in the EU to notify the authorities of their intention to travel to another member state or transit through one outside their host country at least 24 hours before their planned entry.
This applies to diplomatic and consular representatives of all ranks, including ambassadors, as well as administrative, technical and service staff and their family members.
Although the system has given European authorities greater powers to monitor the movements of Russian diplomats, it does not in itself restrict their movements.
Member states can introduce a stricter procedure requiring Russian diplomats to apply for permission to transit. If permission is refused, the diplomat may not cross the border. However, this procedure is optional. So far, only two countries have introduced it.
"As the system has only been in place since January 2026, experience is limited," a European Commission spokesperson said.
According to Euronews, discussions in Brussels will have to strike a balance with the Vienna Convention, which grants diplomatic representatives broad rights and protections in their day-to-day work. This document is considered one of the most significant achievements of international law.
Background:
- The Estonian Internal Security Service established that an arson attack on the building of the defence company Milrem Robotics in Tallinn on the night of 14-15 August was an act of sabotage ordered by Russian intelligence services.
- Germany directly accused Russia of carrying out a hybrid attack at Leipzig Airport in early August and announced retaliatory measures, including the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House Russian Houses are cultural centres established in other countries to promote Russia's language and culture and Russian education. They also serve as platforms for Russian state propaganda and soft power in Berlin.

Ukraine hits Moscow with one of its largest drone attacks in two years
Ukraine launched overnight one of its largest drone attacks on Moscow in the past two years, killing two men and injuring several people in the Russian capital, local officials said on Tuesday.
Hundreds of drones hit Moscow overnight, killing two men on the outskirts of the capital and injuring nine others, Russian authorities said Tuesday.
Overnight, "650 drones were launched toward the Moscow region", Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram, stressing that "most (were) destroyed by air defences at long range".
Moscow Region governor Andrei Vorobyov said 185 drones were "destroyed or neutralised" overnight over 16 municipalities in the region.
But he said on Telegram that the attack killed two men, aged 71 and 20, in two different locations on the outskirts of Moscow, while nine others were injured.
And 47 houses across seven municipalities had been damaged, as had four apartments in a residential building in the village of Lobanovo, he said.
According to the Russian state news agency TASS, the pummelling was the second largest drone attack in the past two years on the Russian capital and its surrounding region – hundreds of kilometres from the Ukrainian border.
Operations at Moscow's four airports were meanwhile disrupted by the attack, with air traffic restrictions imposed multiple times during the night and morning, according to the Russian civil aviation agency Rosaviatsia.
Both Ukraine and Russia have stepped up long-range strikes in recent months on civilian and industrial targets, including energy, transport and port infrastructure, as well as ships in the Black Sea.

Russia, which launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, has said it plans to increase strikes on infrastructure targets, including in Kyiv, as winter approaches.

As geopolitical tensions and technical dependencies escalate while simultaneously becoming increasingly interdependent, Europe’s policymakers and industry will meet on stage and off to discuss the greatest threats to European security, sovereignty, and resilience at Techritory 2026.
The 9th annual Techritory forum will take place on October 21-22, 2026, in Riga, Latvia, gathering over 600 speakers and guests – industry leaders, policymakers, researchers, and innovators. This year’s main focus will be Europe’s digital security, sovereignty, and competitiveness.
Rather than serving as a passive showcase, Techritory 2026 will serve as a strategic engine for European and transatlantic cooperation, with a particular focus on Persian Gulf states. Across two main stages, interactive workshops, and high-level roundtables, participants will confront critical priorities from building true technological sovereignty and scaling defense tech to balancing AI-driven data center expansion with grid capacity. The forum will also tackle independent satellite networks, telecoms integration under the Digital Networks Act, the roadmap to 6G, and expanding digital partnerships across Eastern Europe, Asia, and the Middle East.
“Nearly ten years ago, Techritory started as a showcase for future tech. Today, that future is here. We’ve grown from forecasting innovation to mobilizing real-world action, bringing decision-makers together to ensure emerging technology serves European security, strength, and progress,” says Neils Kalnins, Director of Techritory Ecosystem.
This year’s speaker lineup includes some of the most influential voices in global innovation, research, and politics, including Tomas Lamanauskas (Deputy Secretary-General of the ITU), Erzsébet Fitori (Executive Director of SNS JU), Yasushi Masaki (Deputy Secretary-General of the OECD), Peteris Ustubs (Director of Central Asia, Asia and Pacific, DG International Partnerships at the European Commission), and 80+ other industry leaders.
Reflecting Techritory’s expanding geopolitical footprint, the 2026 forum will host key international delegations, including official representatives from Moldova, the United Arab Emirates as well as representatives from Central Asia.
In an acknowledgment of technology’s increasingly critical impact on geopolitics, Techritory will formally sign a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the World Governments Summit Organization, highlighting its growing global reach. The agreement will establish a strategic framework for both organizations to combine their global platforms to advance technology development and deployment. The partnership aims to align global governance with rapid digital transformation, reinforcing both events as critical meeting grounds for governments, telecom leaders, researchers, and decision makers.
Registration is free of charge, and the complete forum agenda is available at www.techritory.com.
Techritory 2026 is organized by the Electronic Communications Office of Latvia, with LMT, DELSKA, Nordic Council of Ministers, and the Ministry of Smart Administration and Regional Development of Latvia as strategic partners.

New mass protest by thousands of school students is expected in Paris after clashes with police
Kyiv • UNN
Up to 40,000 demonstrators are expected in Paris on October 6 over problems in education. Since the protests began, 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured.
In France, tens of thousands of demonstrators are expected to take to the streets of Paris on October 6 for protests at schools demanding improved learning conditions. This comes as influential French trade unions join high school students amid a wave of protests that have already seen clashes with police. UNN reports this with reference to AFP.
Details
The authorities expect between 20,000 and 40,000 demonstrators in Paris.
New protests are expected on Tuesday after classes were disrupted at 589 of the country’s 3,700 lycées and 32 universities, according to the education ministry and the student union.
The protests have been ongoing since late September. Students then began blocking the entrances to hundreds of secondary schools for 15- to 17-year-olds, complaining about a lack of teachers, overloaded schedules, run-down classrooms, and buildings unable to cope with rising temperatures.
Many of the protests were peaceful. But some students set fire to garbage bins and bus stops or clashed with police, who responded with batons, tear gas, and riot-control projectiles, the publication writes.
Since the movement began, 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured, according to the authorities, while a 15-year-old teenager lost an arm on Monday, October 5, when he picked up a grenade fired by officers.
Several trade unions accused police of using disproportionate force against protesters. Police have launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests began, France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said late Monday.
The government has tried to address these complaints while accusing left-wing activists of hijacking the protest movement.
According to the education minister, 24 schools have been burned or looted since the movement began. More than 5,000 people, 87 percent of them minors, have been detained. Lecornu’s office reported that 85 teachers were also injured.
The unrest erupted just months before the 2027 elections, in which the successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron will be elected after his maximum two terms in office.

Kosovo police use tear gas on protesters demanding curbs on war crimes court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:08:18 UTC
15:08:18 KST

Anger has been building since former president Hashim Thaci, viewed by many as a hero of the independence struggle, was sentenced last month over crimes committed during the 1990s war against Serbia.
Riot police used tear gas and a water cannon on protesters outside Kosovo's parliament on Monday night, after lawmakers ended their session without passing a bill to limit the powers of the country's war crimes court.
Several hundred demonstrators had spent most of the day outside the building, vowing to blockade it until the law was approved. When the session closed in the evening, they moved towards police lines to try to stop lawmakers from leaving.
Tear gas was aimed at the crowd, while some protesters threw firecrackers at officers. Bins were set alight near the parliament and projectiles were hurled at police, who responded with a water cannon and armoured vehicles.
During the hours-long stand-off, demonstrators denounced the sentencing last month of former president Hashim Thaci for war crimes committed during the 1990s war of independence against Serbia.
Thaci and three other senior guerrilla figures received heavy sentences after being found criminally responsible for murders, illegal arrests, torture and cruel treatment carried out by Kosovo Liberation Army fighters.
The verdict prompted outrage and rallies in the Balkan country, where the four men are widely seen as heroes of the independence struggle.
The bill cleared its first reading on Monday but was not passed into law. It would strip the Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC) of the power to try war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the war between ethnic Albanian guerrillas and Serb armed forces. Its jurisdiction would instead be limited to crimes committed inside Kosovo in the immediate aftermath of the war.
The KSC is established under Kosovo law but based in The Hague. Opposition parties and war veterans' organisations have long criticised it.

Imre Kaas: Save the rescuers!
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:08:00 UTC
15:08:00 KST

Imre Kaas: Save the rescuers!
Estonia relies heavily on volunteers to bolster its internal security, but low pay for professional rescue workers risks making that reliance increasingly necessary.
Estonia has done very well so far because there are so many kindhearted people around us. One is a neighbor with a knack for fixing things who goes around clearing clogged sewer pipes in the neighborhood or comes over to help stack firewood, another serves as an assistant police officer, a third spends every weekend training with the Estonian Defense League and a fourth volunteers at the local rescue station.
Of course, it is entirely possible that all these activities are undertaken by the same person, simply because they cannot sit around doing nothing.
For a volunteer, what matters is the act itself — giving society something it would otherwise lack. Even if that something is security. And internal security matters, even if greater emphasis has been placed on ensuring external security in recent years and in light of Russia's military activity.
The defense budget, artillery shells, hybrid attacks, the threat posed by drones. All of these might seem like matters of external security, but in reality they are domestic issues, too. When you insure your home, you are bound to wonder whether your policy covers damage caused by a stray drone.
Everyone in Estonia expects that if something happens to them or their home, help will already be on its way. The swift arrival of rescue workers, paramedics or police officers is taken for granted and whenever the pay of those responsible for internal security comes up again in public debate, many people are surprised to learn just how meager their incomes still are.
Of course, people can and should complain about such pay, even if doing so incurs Finance Minister Jürgen Ligi's displeasure. After all, the minister said on ETV's "Esimene stuudio" that rescue workers' salaries would rise faster than inflation, or by roughly the same amount, and that those receiving such favorable treatment should not complain. The remark quite rightly provoked a storm of indignation because complaining is just about the only thing that is still free.
Even the host had to remind the minister that rescue workers' pay is among the furthest behind and that it is difficult to make ends meet on it. Ligi nevertheless described it as a matter of choices, adding that, to put it mildly, he disliked the tone rescue workers used when asking for money.
Having listened to and read the comments made by those asking for higher pay, I see nothing behind them but concern about making ends meet. There is nothing inappropriate about their tone. I am also reminded of a telling sign from a past demonstration demanding higher pay: "Save the rescuers!" And we are still in the same situation.
Of course, there is little point in comparing Jürgen Ligi's own €7,800 salary with that of rescue workers, but the figures are worth setting out nonetheless. Among Estonia's 1,668 professional rescue workers, 112 earn the minimum salary of €1,606 a month. A rescue worker's average base salary is €1,758. In the new year, they will receive a pay increase of just under €50 a month. That will at least allow a rescue worker to afford one more basket of groceries, although the finance minister himself acknowledged that, in the worst-case scenario, wages will rise only in line with inflation and such an increase will bring no measurable improvement in quality of life.
The Rescue Board and trade unions have said that a fair level of pay for rescue workers would be 1.2 times Estonia's average salary or about €2,700 a month. Reaching that level would require an additional €25 million or so a year for the payroll budget and that calculation concerns average pay. That is, of course, a large sum and not one that can simply be taken from somebody else's budget line. As an election promise, however, it would sound impressive.
Despite their poor pay, professional rescue workers do a good job and there is no indication that water flows through their hoses any more slowly because of it. On the other hand, motivation is a complicated thing and pay an important part of it. Salary is among the first things mentioned in employee satisfaction surveys and there is probably no one whose pay clearly exceeds their expectations. In the case of rescue workers, the situation is even more prosaic: Even outsiders can see that this level of income buys only enough food to stave off starvation a little longer.
So I fear that the role of volunteers will grow even further simply because there will not be enough professionals. Estonia already has 119 volunteer rescue stations alongside 71 professional ones. This gives the country an enormous amount of additional capacity for ensuring internal security, but that capacity depends on people's free time and motivation. Nor can those 3,241 volunteer rescue workers and assistant explosive ordnance disposal specialists be expected to sit on a tree stump armed with nothing but a bucket and an ax.
For example, volunteer rescue worker Hendrik Tali wrote in Delfi that they scrape together every cent needed to keep operating. They, too, are affected by the cost of electricity and fuel because without them the lights at rescue stations do not stay on and the vehicles do not move. And when you hear that some volunteers respond to emergencies in vehicles built 50 years ago, your arms almost drop helplessly to your sides.
Volunteers — assistant police officers — also provide the police with a significant amount of additional manpower. Estonia currently has 1,300 assistant police officers who have performed a total of 111,616 hours of police work this year. Eighty-eight percent of assistant police officers are active, meaning they serve regularly. Fortunately, assistant police officers do not have to buy their own handcuffs or batons and their vehicles are somewhat more modern than those used by volunteer rescue workers.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Strong winds sweep Finland on Tuesday
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:07:26 EEST
15:07:26 KST

Winds on Tuesday morning picked up to dangerous levels in parts of Finland.
A low-pressure system will lie to the northeast of Finland in the afternoon, bringing strong winds across the country.
The fiercest winds and gusts will be concentrated in western Finland and over sea areas, where gusts could exceed 20 metres per second. Winds in the west will gradually ease towards evening, though the weather will remain gusty.
A broad band of rain is also sweeping across Finland, leaving more than 20mm in some areas overnight. Conditions should ease in the south by afternoon, though scattered showers will persist across the central and northern parts.
Daytime temperatures will range from 5 to 15 degrees Celsius on Tuesday. Cooler air will reach the north in the evening, bringing the possibility of sleet showers in northwestern Lapland.
Power cuts and rescued hikers
Strong winds have knocked out power to roughly 2,000 households, mainly in western Finland.
The Lapland rescue service meanwhile brought two hikers out of the wilderness on Monday evening in Pallas-Yllästunturi National Park.
Wednesday should be mostly dry, with sunshine breaking through across much of the country. Strong, gusty winds will persist in the north and parts of the east, while temperatures will be a couple of degrees lower than on Tuesday.

====================================================================================================

France's sovereign debt crisis explained: How dangerous could it be?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:02:38 UTC
15:02:38 KST

French borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2002, and the gap with Germany is the widest since 2011. What is driving France's debt crisis and how far could it go?
For most of the past decade, lending money to France was considered almost as safe as lending money to Germany.
That belief is now breaking down, and it is happening fast.
Last week, investors demanded up to 5% a year to lend to the French government for 10 years. France had not faced borrowing costs that high on its 10-year bonds since July 2002.
The extra return investors want to hold French debt instead of German debt rose to its highest level since the eurozone debt crisis of 2011-2012.
France now pays more to borrow than Italy and Greece, two countries that sat at the centre of that crisis.
This matters well beyond the bond market. Government borrowing costs influence the rates on mortgages and business loans and the interest bill that every French taxpayer ends up covering.
So how did the eurozone's second-largest economy get here, and how far could it go?
France's government debt has skyrocketed to 119% of GDP
The root of the problem is simple.
Every year, the French state spends far more than it collects in taxes, and it borrows to cover the difference.
This year, the gap, the deficit, is expected to reach 5.4% of the country's annual economic output, its gross domestic product (GDP).
EU rules set a deficit limit of 3% of GDP.
Year after year, those deficits pile up as debt.
French public debt reached €3.6 trillion in the second quarter of 2026. That equals 119% of GDP, up from 115.6% a year earlier, according to INSEE, the national statistics office.
The trouble starts when investors begin to doubt the repayment plan.
Why markets are losing patience with Paris
France has a plan. The problem is its track record.
Last Thursday, the minority government of Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu presented its 2027 draft budget, which proposes about €54 billion in spending savings and additional revenue.
It targets a deficit of 5% of GDP next year, down from 5.4% in 2026.
Around two-thirds of the adjustment in the budget would come from spending restraint and one-third from higher taxes and contributions.
Proposed measures include €6 billion of savings each in pensions and healthcare.
Government spending excluding interest and defence would be frozen in cash terms, squeezing budgets after inflation.
Yet, instead of calming investors, it worried them.
Lecornu has no majority in parliament, the National Assembly starts debating the text on 13 October, and a presidential election is due in spring 2027.
Stéphane Colliac, an economist at BNP Paribas, noted that France had already missed its budget targets in three of the four years between 2023 and 2026.
Interest payments and defence spending are both rising, so the government must find savings worth about 1% of GDP just to cut the deficit by 0.4 percentage points, Colliac calculates.
Supply adds to the pressure.
The French Treasury plans to issue €340 billion of debt in 2027, €20 billion more than this year, as pandemic-era borrowing comes due.
Even if everything goes to plan, Colliac expects debt to rise to 121% of GDP in 2027 and to stabilise only at 124% in 2032.
Enrique Díaz-Alvarez, chief economist at Ebury, said: “The political deadlock in Paris remains very much unresolved,” adding that the proposals had met with scepticism from the fiscal watchdog.
Student protests over underfunded schools have added to the pressure on the government.
Why France's sovereign risk is blowing up now
Beyond the rise in France’s 10-year bond yield to 5%, its widening gap with Germany shows investors are increasingly concerned about French debt.
Its premium over Germany’s equivalent Bund reached 152 basis points, or 1.52 percentage points, returning to levels associated with the 2011 eurozone crisis.
Intesa Sanpaolo strategists, led by Gian Marco Salcioli, argue that the speed of the move matters more than its level.
When yields jump this fast, they say, the fear shifts from the price of borrowing to the risk of not being repaid in full, and France is the clearest example.
"The move tends to transform rate risk into something broader, first and foremost credit risk," Salcioli said in a note to clients.
Díaz-Alvarez said this was "the largest weekly widening in said spread in seventeen years."
Could the crisis spread across Europe?
There are already warning signs.
ING strategists Michiel Tukker and Benjamin Schroeder reported that Italian and Greek spreads over German Bunds had widened by almost 15 basis points during the French turmoil.
“Debt dynamics are no longer deemed only a French problem,” they wrote.
Currency markets are also reacting.
Intesa’s currency analysts Luca Cigognini and Fabio Vacchelli noted that the euro touched $1.1161 in Monday’s Asian trading despite weaker US employment figures.
They warned that French fiscal concerns could push it towards $1.10.
For the ECB, that creates a difficult balancing act.
September eurozone inflation rose to 3.8%, strengthening the case for continued tightening. Meanwhile, stress in government bond markets bolsters the case for pausing and considering support.
“An ECB pause would weigh on the EUR from a rates-spread perspective, although the stabilisation of debt markets would return flows into the currency,” Ana Munera, BBVA’s director of global markets strategy, said.
The ECB does have a targeted bond-purchase tool, the Transmission Protection Instrument, to counter unwarranted market disruption.
But support depends on factors including debt sustainability and fiscal-policy compliance.
It is not an unconditional guarantee of French borrowing costs.
Such purchases can address disruptive differences in borrowing costs between countries without requiring the ECB to cut its main interest rates.
So how dangerous is it?
The immediate risk is that political deadlock prevents France from passing a budget.
BBVA's Munera warns that Lecornu could fail to secure sufficient parliamentary support and be forced from office.
Without an approved budget, France would again rely on an emergency law to maintain essential government financing, as it did in 2025 and 2026.
Each new delay has a price.
BNP Paribas' Colliac estimates that if serious deficit cuts slip to 2028, debt would reach 126% of GDP by 2032.
With borrowing needs of €340 billion next year, every extra tenth of a percentage point on France’s borrowing costs adds up quickly.
There are also reasons not to panic.
France is not a country that has lost access to markets. It is a country whose lenders want to be paid more and want to see a plan they can believe.
The first parliamentary test of that credibility begins on 13 October, when the Assembly starts debating the budget.

Knesset candidate met professor accused of plotting mass attacks on Arabs, didn’t alert police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

A right-wing attorney who recently said it would be "good" even if IDF soldiers were killed in a violent confrontation with Jewish settlers has acknowledged meeting the mathematics professor accused of planning terror attacks targeting hundreds of Arabs, but said he did not report the encounter to police. "It was a mistake in judgment. At the time, I had the impression that this was a man around 60 years old presenting a delusional plan," attorney Tamir Dortal said.
At the same time, a densely written letter the professor sent to Zehut chairman Moshe Feiglin has been revealed. Its title was "The people will carry out transfer," the phrase from which the professor derived the Hebrew acronym he allegedly used as the name for his plan.
The professor’s neighbors said they were stunned by the indictment against him. One woman said she witnessed the forces arriving to arrest him.
"I came back from work and saw them taking the guy who lived here, pretty much by force," she said. "They put him into a car. They weren’t wearing uniforms or anything. I asked one of them what was going on, and he told me they were the police and not to worry, everything was fine."
Another neighbor said the allegations appeared completely out of character. "It doesn’t fit him," he said. "Do you know how intelligent he is? He is very nice and mild-mannered. His clothes and appearance were a little strange, but he didn’t seem extreme at all. We even talked a little about politics. I understood that he was right-wing, but he didn’t strike me as an extremist."
Ron, who has lived on the street for 12 years, said he rarely saw the professor. "It’s a huge shock. This is a very quiet street," he said. "We would always say hello to each other. I knew he lived here alone and that he was pleasant."
Dortal told ynet that the professor had come to see him and "introduced himself as a retired professor who wanted to promote a bizarre and absurd theoretical idea."
"From the moment I understood the nature of the plan he was presenting to me, I completely opposed it and made clear to him that it was a grave, unacceptable and dangerous idea," Dortal said. "I told him the meeting was over and demanded that he leave my office. I made clear to him that his idea was terrible, both morally and in terms of the goals he himself claimed to believe in. I explicitly asked him whether he had a weapon, and he said no."
"I regret that I did not go to the police at that moment," Dortal added. "It was a mistake in judgment. I assessed that he was only speaking theoretically and did not pose a real danger."
Dortal said he nevertheless told the professor that he would contact the head of the Shin Bet and report what he had heard. "I had the impression that the warning deterred him and that he would stop spreading the idea," he said. "After I ordered him to leave, he initially refused to leave my office. Eventually, he agreed and left."
Dortal said that after the mathematics professor was arrested, he gave police everything he knew and cooperated fully. The professor’s name remains under a court-imposed gag order.
"I was never a partner in the plan, I did not support it and I did not help advance it," Dortal said. "On the contrary, from the moment I understood what it was about, I rejected it clearly and unequivocally and tried to make him understand that such a plan would actually harm the very goals he claimed to believe in."
Dortal hosts the right-wing political podcast "Al HaMashmaut." Last month, he sparked controversy after saying during an episode that even if soldiers were killed in a violent confrontation with Jewish settlers in the West Bank, that would still be "good" if it prevented a mass evacuation of Jews from the territory.
In a clip circulated on social media, Rabbi Benny Lau told Dortal that "anarchy is bad." Dortal then asked him: "If the sovereign Jewish people decided to carry out the ethnic cleansing of Jews from Judea and Samaria, is it good or bad if that is prevented by force and bloodshed?" Lau replied firmly: "It is bad." 
Dortal disagreed. "I think it is good," he said. "Even if IDF soldiers die in that event, and 20 or 100 times as many settlers die, but ultimately the event is prevented and the Land of Israel remains in our hands, that is good."
Dortal has previously hosted senior political figures on his podcast, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, Knesset Constitution Committee chairman Simcha Rothman and former ambassador and minister Gilad Erdan.
After the comments were publicized, Dortal issued a response seeking to explain the discussion but did not retract the statement itself.
"The clip being circulated is a short section from a long discussion in which we raised an extreme and hypothetical thought experiment: What should be done if the Israeli government decides to forcibly evacuate all Jews from Judea and Samaria?" he said. "It was a moral question within a debate, not a call to action, and certainly not a call to kill, shoot or harm IDF soldiers."
72 attackers in 12 cells
The mathematics professor from Bar-Ilan University, a Petah Tikva resident in his 60s, has been charged with planning attacks against hundreds of Israeli Arabs as part of a scheme he called by a Hebrew acronym derived from the phrase "The people will carry out transfer."
A court has barred publication of the defendant’s name for at least the next two days. The Central District Prosecutor’s Office has charged him with security offenses including preparation to commit an act of terrorism under Israel’s Counter-Terrorism Law, extortion by threats and obstruction of justice. Prosecutors are seeking to keep him in custody until the end of legal proceedings.
According to the indictment, the professor’s plan envisioned 72 Jewish attackers, at least half of them licensed gun owners, including himself. They would be divided into 12 cells of six people each.
The cells would allegedly arm themselves with weapons including handguns, rifles, axes and hammers and launch surprise mass attacks in mixed Jewish-Arab cities and Arab communities across Israel.
The plan also called for advance coordination with what the professor described as subversive elements recruited from within the IDF, who would provide assistance and support to the attackers. According to the indictment, the proposal included strikes on Arab population centers by the Israeli Air Force, Artillery Corps and Armored Corps.
Prosecutors said the professor also laid out a practical section describing how the plan could be carried out "here and now." According to the indictment, it called on participants to carry out mass killing, rapidly seize friction points, roads and entrances to and exits from Arab communities, mixed cities and hospitals, and continue despite pleas to stop.
Attempts to recruit supporters
Prosecutors say the defendant spent about a year and a half trying unsuccessfully to recruit supporters and partners for the plan. He also allegedly conducted a reconnaissance trip around the Arab town of Tuba-Zangariyye in northern Israel to study access routes and determine what he believed would be the best ways to attack the community, which he wanted to make a central target.
According to the indictment, his covert recruitment plan centered on approaching Moshe Feiglin, who heads the Zehut party and is running in the coming election for Israel’s 26th Knesset. The professor allegedly hoped to recruit Feiglin and, with his assistance, enlist additional activists.
Under the plan described by prosecutors, selected activists would be identified in advance and invited to a Zehut election gathering. During the event, they would allegedly be told that they had been recruited for a terror attack scheduled for the following day and would receive detailed operational instructions.
The professor attended two public events held by Feiglin and tried to arrange a meeting with him and give him a summary of the plan, according to the indictment. Feiglin did not agree to any of his requests. About a month ago, as the election approached, prosecutors say the professor wrote a threatening letter to Feiglin criticizing and insulting him over his refusal to cooperate.
The indictment alleges that the professor threatened to make the letter public unless Feiglin quickly agreed to cooperate and help promote the plan, believing its publication would cause Feiglin political damage ahead of the election.
About two days later, the professor allegedly went to Feiglin’s home and handed the letter to a neighbor who happened to be passing by, asking her to deliver it. She did so.
He later arrived at a Zehut party event at Jerusalem’s Mahane Yehuda market and, through another woman, gave the party’s director-general several copies of the letter along with another message containing a similar threat, according to prosecutors.
Zehut and Feiglin said after the indictment was filed that they contacted police immediately after receiving the letters. "Immediately upon receiving the extortion and threatening letters from the defendant, Moshe Feiglin and the party leadership contacted the Israel Police without delay and filed a formal complaint," they said.
"We thank law enforcement authorities for their swift and determined action and trust the security and judicial authorities to deal with those responsible to the full extent of the law. Zehut will continue to act with public responsibility and without fear."

“Over a three-year period, our players have achieved incredible things,” Montella said.

‘Bully in every way’: domestic abuse survivors say ex-partners behind far-right UK street patrols

During their relationship, Lisa’s ex-partner was controlling. He kept her at home where he was emotionally and physically abusive towards her, including once attacking her with a machete.
These days, he runs protests outside houses of multiple occupancy that he claims are housing asylum seekers. He coordinates groups of men to patrol the streets of his town, claiming to protect women but often using these patrols to profile and target men of colour.
“There’s nothing good about that man. He’s a bully in every way,” she says.
Lisa is one of seven women who have told the Guardian they are survivors of domestic abuse carried out by key figures in the anti-immigration street patrol movement. All have chosen to come forward to make the public aware of the patterns of violence behind this new form of activism.
At least 14 street patrol groups have been set up in towns and cities across the UK, receiving tens of thousands of pounds in public donations, as well as political support. The deputy leader of Reform UK, Richard Tice, has previously called for more patrols to take place.
Wearing hi-vis jackets and, in some cases, stab-proof vests and carrying handcuffs, these groups of men aim to be a visible presence conducting patrols through their towns and cities. Some have used their patrols to target men of colour, stopping and questioning individuals and demanding to see identity documents.
Despite using rhetoric of protecting women, the Guardian has been shown evidence that indicates the severity of the abuse carried out by men in these groups. Some of the women we have spoken to have been granted restraining or non-molestation orders. One was forced to move towns with the support of the police for her own safety.
“He likes power, and I feel like this is giving him some sort of power. It’s all about power and control in everything he does,” says Lisa, who met and began a relationship with a far-right activist when she was 16.
He is one of the main figures behind the branch of the Raising the Colours movement in his town. The far-right, anti-migrant campaign has hung flags from lamp-posts across the UK under the guise of “patriotism”.
Early in their relationship, Lisa’s partner became abusive and controlling, sometimes preventing her from leaving the house. This behaviour escalated after she became pregnant and had her first child. He would threaten her and her family if she attempted to end the relationship. “I still have nightmares to this day,” Lisa says.
The night that Lisa left him, he tried to attack her with a machete and gave her a black eye and several broken toes. Police attended the scene and arrested him but this was not the end of his abuse, Lisa says. “When I did get away, he was threatening me constantly. I had met somebody else eventually, and I was getting phone calls saying he’s going to kick the baby out of me when he sees me in the street.”
Despite the severity of this abuse, it never resulted in a conviction.
Claire was in a relationship with an anti-immigration activist for several years, during which she made various calls to the police due to his abusive and violent behaviour, which would often be carried out while her children were present.
He was verbally abusive to Claire while she was pregnant, as well as behaving aggressively towards hospital staff after the birth of their first child. This abuse continued after Claire’s pregnancy, including one occasion when he pulled Claire’s hair and gripped her by the throat.
He uses his elevated platform in the town to run street patrols, standing with men outside schools in the mornings and afternoons as children come and go, and erecting St George’s Cross flags on lamp-posts.
The Guardian previously revealed police data indicating patterns of intimate partner violence among 2024 rioters, and similar links can be observed for those involved in these forms of vigilantism.
Last August, Reece McCarron founded the Corby Guard, claiming he had been inspired to set up a group for the Northamptonshire town after seeing someone “making advances to a young girl on the way from school”. On early street patrols he was joined by James Kenna, who had a domestic violence protection order imposed on him in 2020.
A month later, McCarron broke into his former partner’s house, swinging a machete around the kitchen and threatening to kill her. He was later charged with a string of offences including rape, actual bodily harm and intentional strangulation, which have been dropped after support for prosecution was withdrawn by the victim. In May, he was convicted of coercive control, as the prosecutor told the courts “the victim said that she was very scared he would kill her. She couldn’t sleep for weeks.”
In Greater Manchester, Adam Farrell and Jamie Thomason formed the Heywood community guard. Several schools in Heywood were forced to go into lockdown when the guard ran patrols outside their gates.
Farrell was jailed in 2022 after a racist attack on a man that left him with life-changing brain injuries. Thomason has claimed he is “doing God’s work” protecting women and children. In 2018, he was convicted under section 4A of the Public Order Act after arriving at a former partner’s address, banging on her door, threatening to slit her throat and punching her car.
Names have been changed to protect the identity of the survivors of abuse.
