‘Pull the plug’: protesters resort to direct action against AI firms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:00:04 UTC
15:00:04 KST

In a bar below Waterloo Bridge, a cell of a fast-growing anti-AI protest movement met last week to plot their latest move: disrupting a tech industry dinner being addressed by a senior executive from the chip maker Nvidia.
Emma, a 28-year-old bartender, had never before taken direct action and was the most nervous of the four plotters from Pull The Plug, one of a growing number of AI-focused campaign groups around the world.
Around the table were a former climate protester and a campaigner versed in the anti-nuclear movement. Emma signed up after a summer of feeling rising alarm at the catastrophic risks of AI, first when a swarm of OpenAI agents escaped their training “sandbox”, cheated, deceived and conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website and then as Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, quit with an apocalyptic warning that superintelligent AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.
As darkness fell they crossed the Thames to the Claremont hotel where Emma filmed while two others unfurled a banner in a function room, shouting “Pull the plug on Nvidia” and “Pull the plug on Palantir”. Hundreds of protesters also staged a rally in front of Palantir’s London HQ last Thursday.
“We did not consent to the kind of build-out that you are planning here,” the activists yelled as they were wrestled out of the door. They edited a video clip – “activist disrupts elite AI network dinner – Nvidia edition” – and uploaded it to Instagram. It was a small gesture, but they had made their stand.
“I want to show other people that they don’t have to feel powerless among all of these articles coming out [about AI doom],” said Emma. “It’s easy to fall into a spiral that it’s too late. This shows people they can address the tech executives, disrupt their meetings, make them feel uncomfortable and get some answers.”
Pull The Plug was launched in January and has about 300 members – mostly aged from 20 to 40. It is backed by an anonymous funder who works in the technology industry, organisers said. Several campaigns resisting AI acceleration are funded by tech insiders.
Pull The Plug advocates direct action – a tactic other AI campaigns have rejected. Last month, one of its members climbed on to a chair in a packed AI conference in London addressed by speakers from OpenAI and Amazon and delivered an impassioned speech.
“Best case scenario: the men handling this technology are completely incompetent,” the female activist said in an outburst that garnered 153,000 Instagram likes and was picked up by the Washington Post. “Worst case scenario: we are all being led into a disaster.”
Other AI protest movements are gaining momentum after a torrent of news about AI dangers. Anthropic told investors this week that advanced AI could pose “existential risks to humanity”. Pause AI, a confederation of campaign groups in 17 countries, saw a fourfold jump in sign-ups when worrying news about rogue AI agents was breaking in August and last month.
“We have had a lot of volunteers who have suddenly decided to dedicate way more of their time to the cause,” said Maxime Fournes, a Cambridge-educated mathematician and deep learning engineer who is chief executive of PauseAI Global. Volunteer sign-ups doubled to about 100 a week after the Hugging Face incident and soared to 681 in the week of Coxon’s “kill us all” warning, when PauseAI organised protests in Paris, London and Berlin.
Donald Trump may be one of the movement’s most important recruiting sergeants. He announced last week that he wanted AI companies to “self-police” despite widespread demands, including from the companies, for federal and international rules to limit AI-enabled cyber-attacks and bioweapons.
The surge in worrying news has given campaigners like Fournes hope that “we could actually survive this situation”. He added: “Suddenly we have a large fraction of the world population that is waking up.”
Joseph Miller, an AI safety researcher who has suspended his doctoral studies at Oxford University to run Pause AI’s UK branch, noticed the shift while campaigning outside Brixton tube station in London. He said: “It was the easiest flyering we’ve ever done, because people would just come and talk to me … one every few minutes.”
People he spoke to were worried about cognitive decline in schools and AI resulting in sloppy work in the office. “I heard ‘killing everyone’ more from young people,” Miller added.
Pausing or halting AI is a cause that cuts across political and generational boundaries, according to campaigners. University students sign up because they fear AI will wreck career paths, while older conservationists rally against datacentre construction.
In Scotland, where at least 21 datacentres are planned, Action to Protect Rural Scotland, a 100-year old charity better known for campaigning for green belt land, said its supporter list had swollen from 400 to 4,000.
“I’ve never seen grassroots energy like this,” said Kat Jones, the charity’s director. She affectionately calls it “a campaign of nerds” with supporters probing the workings of AI datacentre cooling systems and the power grid and lodging freedom of information requests.
AI’s need for vast physical infrastructure has provided a “very physical, concrete object of protest”, said Fournes, and, in some cases, a target for direct action. In the last year, far-left or anarchist groups protesting over the climate crisis and AI have claimed responsibility for criminal attacks on infrastructure in France and Germany.
In August, Wynd Kaufmyn, became the first anti-AI protester believed to have been jailed for taking direct action – in her case blocking the entrance to OpenAI’s HQ in San Francisco. In April, another protester hurled a petrol bomb at the house of the company’s chief executive, Sam Altman. The same month, an attacker fired gunshots into the home of an Indianapolis politician in protest at datacentre plans.
Mauro Lubrano, assistant professor of terrorism and political violence at the University of Leiden, said that if rising demands for accountability, transparency, and democracy in AI governance were not met, more people could get drawn to violence.
“It’s quite likely that we will see anti-AI violence becoming more prominent as a driver to political violence,” he said, citing last month’s vandalism of a Canadian AI institute, Mila, and a nearby software company in Montreal. Windows were smashed and graffiti scrawled reading “burn the data centers”.
Some Pull The Plug activists have diverted their energy from Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion. One member of Emma’s cell glued herself to roads to protest against the climate crisis – tactics that have alienated the public.
Such direct action is “extremely counterproductive”, said Fournes who predicted it would trigger “an immune response” from wider society and would provide “a golden opportunity for the AI labs … to say, they are criminals and it is easier to turn the broader public against the movement against the development of AI”.
Whatever the tactics, a movement is stirring.

Fine scenery, historic towns and great pubs: a weekend walk on the Shropshire Way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:00:04 UTC
15:00:04 KST

Few pubs boast a more idyllic setting. As I emerge from the woods after a 15-mile hike, The Bridges, on the banks of the Onny River, in the rolling south Shropshire hills, glistens in the late afternoon sun. Inside it’s all wooden beams, with light streaming through stained glass and huge bunches of homegrown flowers adding splashes of colour. There’s time for a pint before general manager Sam Thompson shows me to my room in the recently converted stables.
I’m here exploring part of the 185-mile (297km) Shropshire Way, on a two-day Heart of the Hills hike – one of the county tourist board’s new Rail-Ready Short Breaks. Designed for people who don’t have time to tackle the whole route, the itineraries focus on loops that are easy to access by train, with illustrated PDF downloads, GPX files, accommodation suggestions and highlights of what to do along the way. My route will take me from Shrewsbury to Bishop’s Castle via Ratlinghope – about 27 miles, perfect for a weekend.
Shrewsbury itself is worth lingering in – the historic market town is crammed with independent shops and restaurants (I loved Csons for its creative small plates) and impressive Tudor architecture. But I’m most intrigued to learn that beavers have been reintroduced here by the council and the Shropshire Wildlife Trust. The first kit in the county in 400 years was born late last year and the Trust’s Tom Freeland shows me around the site, the Old River Bed nature reserve, just two miles north of the town centre. A boardwalk crossing wetlands allows an up-close view of the rewilding project. Although we don’t spy the elusive creatures (we see heron and plenty of moorhen), there’s still lots to learn. “It’s been a great success in inspiring the community to find out more about our local wildlife,” says Tom. Nature talks and guided tours of the beaver enclosure are in the pipeline, too.
Back at my base, the 16th-century Lion + Pheasant townhouse hotel, I dine on pan-roasted trout in the beamed restaurant (there’s a popular wine and tapas bar on site too) and the next morning set off to walk the first leg to Ratlinghope. Crossing the River Severn, the city soon peters out and quiet country lanes lead to Lyth Hill Country Park where expansive views open up across Shropshire.
It’s a steady climb to Wilderley Hill, past fields of rape, bright patches of yellow in a sea of green, and I stop under an oak tree to picnic. There’s no one around, just the songs of wren and chaffinch filling the air. The landscape changes on the approach to Ratlinghope as the route traces a brook, crosses wooden bridges and winds through pretty woodland. Just off the path lies the 12th-century St Margaret’s Church, the burial place of 19th-century farmer Richard Munslow, the last known “sin-eater”, whose job it was to eat bread and drink ale over corpses to absorb their sins.
I enjoy a drink instead in the pretty beer garden at The Bridges. The seven immaculate, minimalist rooms are round an adjacent courtyard – and guests have access to a lounge above the pub, too. The food in the bar includes Guinness rarebit and duck terrine, while the light-filled restaurant focuses on organic fare from the owners’ regenerative farm on the Linley Estate and the Welsh Marches. I feast on huge radishes with anchoïade, and hake with fennel, capers and crispy polenta. Breakfast the next morning – homemade granola and poached rhubarb – is equally delicious. It’s such a lively, friendly place I’m tempted to move nearby for the pub alone. They’ll even drive locals home if they’ve had one too many, Sam tells me.
Blue skies and gentle sunshine greet me for day two of the hike, a 12-mile yomp across rugged moorland and pastures to Bishop’s Castle. The pub lies on the edge of the Long Mynd, a heath and moorland plateau, but I’m heading north to the Stiperstones, a national nature reserve with a wild, dramatic ridge of quartzite rock formations that pierce the ground. I climb higher, passing Devil’s Chair tor, watching skylarks and buzzards soar overhead.
It’s a beautiful walk. After several hours, a magnificent avenue of Linley Beeches line the descent into Bishop’s Castle, a charming town of half-timbered houses. Bank House B&B, a Georgian renovation with an oak-panelled drawing room and five antique-filled rooms, is my home for the night. I pop into the Poetry Pharmacy where prescriptions are poems chosen to spark specific emotions, to be “taken” when required (I leave with a bottle of Joy). Although little remains of the medieval castle that once stood here and gives the town its name, the grand Castle Hotel, with its pretty gardens and welcoming restaurant, is worth a visit.
With more time, I could, of course, carry on and add another loop of the trail. But the train back home beckons – Craven Arms station is a short bus or taxi ride away – and I leave feeling pleased to have dipped my toe into a small segment of the Shropshire Way. As far as rambling weekends go, it’s ticked all the right boxes, and whetted my appetite to discover more.
The trip was provided by Visit Shropshire and train travel from London to Shropshire was by Visit England. The Bridges has rooms from £120 a night. The Lion + Pheasant has rooms from £140 a night. Bank House B&B has rooms from £110 a night. Luggage transfer was provided by Silver Sherpa and costs from £30 a day for 1-3 bags

Yemen: Huthis Prosecute UN, Civil Society Staff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Accused Face Death Penalty in Misuse of Espionage Charges
The Huthi de facto authorities in Yemen have sent at least eight people involved in human rights and humanitarian work for criminal prosecution, for espionage related charges punishable by death, since 18 August 2026, Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch said today. They include two United Nations employees, a UN consultant, and five people who worked with international and local civil society organizations on a range of issues, including health, human rights and humanitarian aid.
The Huthis should immediately halt these prosecutions and immediately and unconditionally release all eight people whose caes were sent for prosecution along with scores of other UN staff and civil society workers the Huthis have arbitrarily detained over the past two years.
The prosecution is the latest escalation in a crackdown by Huthi authorities on civil society in the part of Yemen they control, with successive waves of arrests of Yemenis targeting UN staff and civil society members since 31 May 2024. The Huthis have arbitrarily detained over 100 such staff and workers, holding them without charge and denying them access to lawyers and their families.
Many of the detentions started as forcible disappearances. An enforced disappearance happens when a person is deprived of liberty and their detention is denied or their situation or whereabouts concealed, placing them outside the protection of the law.
“As fighting once again escalates in Yemen, the Huthis have maliciously moved to prosecute at least eight UN and civil society workers on charges that could, if convicted, result in the death penalty,” said Diala Haidar, Yemen researcher at Amnesty International.
“Demanding the immediate release of Yemen’s UN and civil society workers should be a top priority for governments, and not an afterthought.”
Demanding the immediate release of Yemen’s UN and civil society workers should be a top priority for governments, and not an afterthought.
Diala Haidar, Yemen researcher at Amnesty International
Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International spoke to seven people with direct knowledge of the cases, including family members of those detained.
All eight transferred for prosecution remain in detention and have deteriorating health conditions, including at least two who have diabetes and have not been able to get adequate medical care, and one who is at risk of glaucoma. One has stomach cancer and has been undergoing chemotherapy while in detention.
Some family members said the detainees told them they had been forced to confess to espionage charges under torture or threats of torture.
Since 2015, Amnesty International has documented scores of cases in which Huthi authorities used spying charges to target political opponents and silence peaceful dissent. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have documented the Huthis’ use of torture to obtain confessions.
“It is outrageous that detainees are facing the risk of the death penalty simply for providing medical and food assistance or promoting human rights, peace, and dialogue,” said Niku Jafarnia, Yemen and Bahrain researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“It is critical for other governments to step up diplomatic efforts to secure the release of the dozens of arbitrarily detained members of Yemen’s civil society and UN staff, especially considering the attacks prisons have faced in the conflict.”
Imposing the death penalty after unfair proceedings makes its use as a punishment arbitrary and in violation of international legal standards, the organizations said. Further, under international human rights law, only the “most serious crimes” can legitimately attract the death penalty, which has been interpreted as limited to intentional killing. None of those facing prosecution have been accused of such actions. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch oppose the death penalty unconditionally, in any cases and under any circumstance.
The eight people transferred to the Specialized Criminal Prosecution in Sana’a, Yemen’s capital, are facing charges of “espionage” and “aiding the enemy” (articles 127 and 128 of Yemen’s Penal Code), both punishable by death. The Specialized Criminal Prosecution has also made vague and overly broad accusations about the detainees’ humanitarian and human rights work, alleging that they had “hidden and malicious goals” as part of a premeditated plan to “destroy the values of society.”
The Sana’a-based Specialized Criminal Court, established in 1999, has jurisdiction over a variety of security-related crimes and offences deemed detrimental to state security and public interests. As the Huthis consolidated their control over territories, they also consolidated their control over the judiciary, and the Court has been used as a tool for political repression.
All eight detainees have been denied adequate access to their lawyers.
Sami Kallabi, 41, who worked for the UN at the time of his arrest on June 6, 2024, has cancer and is undergoing chemotherapy at a military hospital. Despite his critical health situation, he has been denied family visits and the Huthi authorities are refusing to disclose where he is being held.
Labib Shayef, 57, is a consultant detained from his office in Sana’a, also on June 6, 2024. Since then he has only been allowed a single visit from his family, in August 2025. His health has severely deteriorated in detention. He has diabetes and contracted Hepatitis B in custody but has not been provided with adequate access to health care.
Prosecutors have questioned him about his work with local and international organizations, including on gender- and peace- related programmes.
At the time of his arrest, Dr. Ali Al-Mudhwahi, was a United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) consultant and an advisor to the Huthi’s Ministry of Public Health and Population, his wife, Safiah Mohammed, told Human Rights Watch. The authorities have subjected him to “solitary confinement, torture, and severe psychological pressure” throughout his detention, his wife said he told her over the phone.
The Huthis—who oppose vaccinations—have tried to force him to say that vaccines are “nothing but espionage tools” and that he is “a spy recruited by the World Health Organization,” his wife said.
Background
Starting on 31 May 2024, the Huthis carried out a series of raids in areas under their control, arbitrarilydetaining 13 UN staff and at least 50 staff from Yemeni and international civil society organizations. Since that time, the Huthis have arbitrarily detained dozens more UN staff and civil society workers. As of February2026, at least 73 UN staff and dozens of humanitarian and civil society workers remained in Huthi detention, all of them Yemeni nationals.
On 11 February 2025, an aid worker from the World Food Programme died in Huthi custody. His death heightens fears for the safety and wellbeing of others arbitrarily detained in Huthi-run detention centres, given the Huthis’ track record of torture and other ill-treatment of detainees.
Many of those detained were arrested without being shown arrest warrants, and were forcibly disappeared for months before their detention was acknowledged and whereabouts known. While some have received medical care, many have not, including some people with serious medical conditions.

Chao Yen-ching (趙彥清), director of Taiwan's representative office in Munich, said Tanja Graf, managing director of Literaturhaus Munchen, told him Chinese consulate officials had contacted the venue and asked it to cancel the event.

He said there is no direct evidence that China was behind the subsequent dispute over interpretation, but the approach raised concerns that Beijing could also have sought to influence participants.
Yang said the controversy reinforced her view that literature and politics cannot be separated, Mirror Media reported. The event later sparked a separate controversy over a local interpreter, who reportedly told Yang and others before the discussion that certain political topics could not be translated.
The interpreter, Cao Changzhen, arrived without notes and allegedly avoided translating references to the Republic of China, Taiwan, and China during the event. When Yang discussed China’s cognitive warfare against Taiwan, Cao reportedly rendered the term as “disinformation,” while translating a reference to the threat from China as “a very big neighbor.”
German journalist Kai Strittmatter, a Mandarin-speaking moderator and reporter for Suddeutsche Zeitung, intervened to clarify the remarks for the German audience, saying the “big neighbor” referred to China, according to Mirror Media. Taiwanese audience members subsequently protested the interpretation online, prompting Chao to express dissatisfaction to the organizers formally.
Springhill Publishing said it had recommended Taiwanese writer Lin Yu-li (林育立), who is based in Germany, for the event, but organizers instead recruited Cao through a local Taiwanese association to reduce accommodation costs during Munich’s Oktoberfest, per CNA. Literaturhaus later apologized to Springhill Publishing and said it would not use the interpreter again.
A reader from China asked Yang why she had written the novel from a colonizer's perspective. Yang responded that exploitation produced by colonial structures remains a fact and reiterated Taiwan’s refusal to be colonized.
Springhill Publishing said Lin would provide German interpretation for Yang's upcoming events in Germany, including the Frankfurt Book Fair and appearances in Hamburg and Berlin, CNA reported.

The European Commission will lay out long-awaited proposals Tuesday on how to keep the EU workable if new members are admitted as Ukraine and others push to join.
Russia’s 2022 invasion of its neighbour breathed fresh impetus into efforts to expand the European Union as Ukraine and Moldova joined the queue of countries seeking membership.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The ex-Soviet duo are now among four frontrunners, with Montenegro pressing to become the EU’s 28th member next year, and Albania not too far behind.
But while Brussels insists enlargement is crucial for the EU’s future, there are major fears that adding new members – especially war-torn giant Ukraine – could shred the EU’s budget and render the bloc unmanageable.
In a bid to alleviate the worries, diplomats expect Brussels to propose a series of “safeguards” to stop potential new members disrupting decisions or sapping too many resources.
Those could include getting them not to use their veto power in key areas and limiting access to subsidies from the EU’s mammoth Common Agricultural Policy.
Learning from the bitter experience of Hungary’s repeated blockages under former leader Viktor Orban, there are demands for more checks to stop new members rolling back on democracy or rule-of-law.
“We must make sure we do not let in Trojan horses,” EU enlargement commissioner Marta Kos said in August.
“Such measures are a must-have, not a nice-to-have. This is crucial to build confidence and unity inside our Union to accept new members.”

- ‘Roadmaps’ to membership -
Tuesday’s proposal has been delayed for months as various EU countries have pushed a variety of ideas.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz earlier this year floated giving countries an “associate membership” status before fully joining that could allow them to attend – but not vote – at EU meetings.
That plan received short shrift from a raft of EU countries and Ukraine, who saw it as a way of trapping wannabe members in a permanent halfway house.
There has also been pushback against any idea of speeding up the process.
“It is a positive sign that the commission finally may have listened to member states and dropped totally unrealistic or dangerous options, like enlargement light or a fast track,” said one EU diplomat speaking on condition of anonymity.
EU leaders will debate the proposals at a summit next week and officials are hoping they at least give a clear signal they are still open for enlargement.
In a bid to offset any complaints by the candidates, Brussels has said it will soon lay out “roadmaps” for the four frontrunners to try to pin down their path towards membership.
Moldova’s Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said in Brussels on Monday that his country remained set on gaining “full membership” as soon as possible.
“At the same time, we recognise the right of the member states to design an architecture that they consider most suitable for advancing the European idea,” he said.

Eastern palace eyes 250,000 visitors by year-end
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:56:42 UTC
14:56:42 KST

(DHA Photo)
Drawing history enthusiasts to Türkiye’s eastern province of Ağrı, the 18th-century Ishak Pasha Palace expects 250,000 visitors by year-end as officials launch digital projects.
Located in Doğubayazıt district at Mount Ağrı’s foothills, the complex has hosted 200,000 tourists this year. Included in the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List since 2000, the site features the world’s first central heating. Construction started under Çolak Abdi Pasha and concluded during grandson Ishak Pasha’s era.
Blending Selçuk, Ottoman, Gothic and Baroque styles, the structure has four crown gates, eight-pointed stars, rumi patterns, ivy designs and a life tree motif with an elevated lion. “It is the Ishak Pasha Palace in the east, like the Topkapı Palace in the west,” Ağrı Culture and Tourism Director Erhan Ağrı said.
Authorities plan to introduce an audio guide by year-end while the ministry conducts restorations. The site attracts tourists from neighboring Iran, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Nakhchivan and Armenia, drawing over 30,000 visitors in August and 25,000 in September. The monthly average recently reached 40,000.
Tour guide Ahmet Gülmez said the palace mesmerizes tourists from Australia, the U.S. and Canada. “They are fascinated when they see a grand Ottoman palace in the country’s east,” he said. The nearby Ahmed-i Hani Tomb and Old Beyazıt Mosque also serve as key historic stops.

Crystallized salt draws photographers to Türkiye’s Tuz Lake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:56:32 UTC
14:56:32 KST

(AA Photo)
Decreasing water levels driven by seasonal temperatures have formed unique crystallized salt structures across Tuz Lake in the central province of Aksaray, drawing photographers eager to capture the snow-like geological formations.
After surface water fully evaporated in the Eskil region of the lake, distinct solid formation, including mushroom-like structures, were exposed. Depending on the sun’s angle throughout the day, visitors walking across the dry bed experience shifting visual effects.
Photographer Nazmi Meral told state-run Anadolu Agency he monitored the area for about a month to capture the continuously changing landscape created by the interaction of nature, water and salt.
“We encounter completely different views every time we visit and plan to come again. Walking on the salt layer provides a different experience, it feels exactly like walking on snow,” he said.
Local resident Mustafa Güdendede said residents are accustomed to seeing a flat, watery surface rather than these textured features. The newly formed mushroom-shaped salt masses present unmissable, postcard-like scenery for photography enthusiasts visiting the region, he said.
Another resident, Mehmet Meral, compared the pristine white salt formations to the famous travertines of Pamukkale, inviting all visitors to see the natural area he described as a hidden paradise.
Tuz Lake is the second largest lake in Türkiye and one of the largest hypersaline lakes in the world. The shallow basin provides a significant portion of the country’s salt needs. It also serves as a crucial natural breeding ground for flamingos and migratory birds during the spring months before the waters naturally pull back to expose the crust.

Türkiye weighs new rules for foreign booking platforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:56:14 UTC
14:56:14 KST

A parliamentary committee is set to debate rules for foreign booking platforms on Oct. 6 under a bill that could allow Booking.com to resume domestic hotel reservations in Türkiye.
The proposal, before the Public Works, Zoning, Transport and Tourism Committee, would require foreign platforms to obtain a Culture and Tourism Ministry permit and appoint a representative in Türkiye.
Platforms would have to verify accommodation providers’ license details and display them in listings.
Total fees and commissions would be capped at 17 percent of the sale price, excluding value-added tax.
Booking.com stopped accepting domestic hotel reservations from users inside Türkiye following a 2017 court ruling in a case brought by the Association of Turkish Travel Agencies (TÜRSAB).
Bookings for Turkish properties made from abroad remain available.
Some industry representatives say the commission cap could initially lower hotel prices but warn that foreign platforms could gain excessive market power over time.
The bill would also allow platforms to sell flight tickets directly
Combined sales of transport and accommodation under its provisions would not be classified as package tours.
Disputes arising from licensed activities would be governed by Turkish law, with Turkish courts having exclusive jurisdiction.
Mehmet Gem, head of the Consumers Confederation’s (TÜKONFED) tourism commission, said appointing a local representative alone might not ensure effective redress for cancellations, room disputes or unfair deductions.
He warned that platforms could seek to avoid responsibility by describing themselves solely as intermediaries.
TÜRSAB President Firuz Bağlıkaya also opposed the proposal, saying it would allow foreign platforms to operate without establishing a company in Türkiye or meeting the same obligations as domestic travel agencies.
Speaking at a press meeting on Oct. 5, Bağlıkaya said the resulting competition would put local agencies at a disadvantage.
He rejected suggestions that the bill would attract more tourists, saying foreign platforms already accept bookings for Turkish hotels from abroad and the principal change would concern access to the domestic market.
Bağlıkaya warned that greater dependence on foreign platforms could increase commission payments flowing abroad and force domestic agencies to close.

'Targeted killing': Gaza intel chief at center of Oct. 7 failures says IDF singles him out for blame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:55:48 UTC
14:55:48 KST

Newly released court documents reveal how Lt. Col. Aryeh Amidror, the Gaza Division intelligence officer on October 7, fought to remain in the IDF after military leaders moved to end his service, arguing that he had been discriminated against and unfairly singled out over the failures surrounding the Hamas massacre.
The documents were made public after Israel’s Supreme Court permitted publication of Amidror’s identity at ynet’s request. They include the administrative petition he filed, relevant appendices, requests for interim relief and a publication ban, the state’s response and the transcript of a June 22 hearing. The opinion written by Deputy Chief of Staff Maj. Gen. Tamir Yadai was not released.
Amidror argued that senior military officials had failed to treat him fairly and described the decision to terminate his permanent service as “arbitrary, discriminatory and selective.” His petition said he was “the only commander in the IDF who is paying a real price, in the form of lost rights, for the failures of the military and the state.”
A central part of his complaint concerned the loss of pension and other employment benefits. His representatives argued that other commanders held responsible for October 7 had retained their full social and pension benefits, while officers in positions comparable to his had either been promoted or continued serving.
‘I was the one who ordered the exercise to be analyzed’
Amidror also challenged the way the military portrayed his exchanges with a female noncommissioned intelligence officer identified only as V., who this week received a certificate of appreciation from the IDF chief of staff for what he described as “intellectual courage and professionalism.”
According to Amidror, when he became Gaza Division intelligence chief he discovered that the division had for some time neglected intelligence collection aimed at examining Hamas’ ability to carry out its operational plans. He said he therefore instructed a unit within the IDF’s Unit 8200 signals intelligence branch to analyze Hamas training exercises in order to assess the group’s tactical capabilities.
“Following the instruction given by the petitioner, and on the orders of her commanders, NCO V. carried out the analysis of the exercise and put the findings in writing,” his petition said.
Amidror argued that an email exchange later cited against him took place before the full analysis had been distributed and represented only an initial discussion. At first glance, he said, the exercise appeared to contain elements that were widely considered unrealistic at the time by Military Intelligence and the IDF more broadly.
He said that after V.’s findings were circulated, he sought to distinguish between capabilities Hamas could realistically execute and training designed primarily to create an impression or motivate its fighters.
Amidror also claimed that additional exchanges omitted from the deputy chief of staff’s assessment showed he was encouraging deeper examination rather than dismissing the warning. In one message, he said he wrote that “there seems to be quite a lot of gold here to mine.”
In another, he wrote: “For the avoidance of doubt, the purpose of my email was not to lower but to elevate,” adding that as more material was circulated, the area of agreement would grow. He also said he ordered additional Hamas exercises to be analyzed and sought to challenge assumptions held by the Gaza Division and Military Intelligence about possible Hamas courses of action.
‘A sense of a targeted killing’
The petition also disputed investigations into Amidror's conduct on the night of October 6-7. His lawyers challenged the significance of material gathered against him and complained that they had not been given access to all the investigations and documents underlying the decision to remove him.
The IDF announced on November 23, 2025 that Amidror would be removed from his post, and the process to terminate his permanent service formally began on February 14, 2026.
At the June 22 hearing, one of Amidror's lawyers sought a postponement, arguing that the defense still lacked access to material used by the deputy chief of staff.
“We are racing after materials that form the basis of the deputy chief of staff’s opinion,” the lawyer said. “We know for certain that there are additional materials on which he relied, and they have not been presented to us.”
The lawyer said some of those materials concerned the period before October 7, including emails involving V., who had warned Amidror about Hamas preparations and readiness for a scenario that ultimately unfolded during the massacre.
“Our feeling is that there is some kind of targeted killing here, and it seems no one is interested in transferring the material to us,” the lawyer said, adding that none of four investigations reached a specific conclusion personally against Amidror.
The state rejected those arguments, saying the process had begun months earlier and that Amidror’s representatives had been shown the investigations forming the evidentiary basis for the administrative proceeding. Prosecutors stressed that it was an administrative, not criminal, process and said the petitioners could not expect access to every IDF investigation into October 7.
The state said the deputy chief of staff’s assessment contained “very concrete claims concerning a series of professional errors and failures in the officer’s conduct,” rather than a general allegation that his performance had been flawed.
Amidror also challenged the authority of the deputy chief of staff to prepare the professional assessment, arguing that the head of Military Intelligence, as his professional commander, should have done so instead.
“The deputy chief of staff is not his commander,” his representatives argued. “He does not know the petitioner and is not familiar with intelligence matters.”
Amidror further alleged that he had been personally targeted, saying that other officers described as bearing command responsibility for October 7 had not faced termination of their service contracts. The state responded that the allegations against him were reviewed at several levels, including by the head of the IDF Personnel Directorate and ultimately the chief of staff, and noted that Military Intelligence chief Maj. Gen. Shlomi Binder had himself received a command reprimand following another review.
State cites ‘significant professional and ethical error’
In its response, the state summarized the deputy chief of staff’s assessment as finding “a series of professional errors and failures in the officer’s conduct,” both during the night of October 6-7 and in the months preceding the attack.
According to the state, the recommendation to continue the process of dismissing Amidror was based in part on a “significant professional and ethical error” in his assessment of a document concerning Hamas’ elite Nukhba force training routine and an email exchange titled “Death in the kibbutz at any cost.”
The state said Amidror’s conduct fell “significantly short of what is expected of those engaged in intelligence work,” particularly the obligation to question assumptions, actively seek opposing views and give them a central place in intelligence analysis.
It also cited a series of professional errors on the night of the attack and Amidror’s command responsibility for the Gaza Division intelligence branch’s failure to issue a warning ahead of the Hamas assault.
The state rejected Amidror’s demand that the process be transferred to an independent senior reserve officer, saying such a demand had no basis in military regulations and would undermine the established chain of authority.
The court ultimately rejected Amidror’s petition and allowed the IDF process aimed at ending his permanent service to continue.

Evidence gathered at the scene raised suspicions that the explosion was caused by an explosive device, police said.

He had been a central police target and was under regular surveillance by the Jerusalem District Police, Central District Police, and Lahav 433, according to Walla.
Several years ago, Bar-Mucha was released from prison after serving a sentence for involvement in attempts to assassinate rivals, the report said. He later moved to central Israel, where he was suspected of becoming involved in a conflict with local criminal organizations.

Magen David Adom emergency medic Haki Har Kesef said medical teams arrived to find a vehicle on fire and debris scattered around it.

Aselsan has signed contracts worth 2.46 billion euros with Türkiye’s Defense Industries Secretariat (SSB) to supply hybrid air defense systems, the company announced on Oct. 5.
The agreements, disclosed to the Public Disclosure Platform (KAP), mark the company’s largest contract announcement to date. No delivery schedule was released.
The latest package brings the combined value of four SSB air defense contract announcements this year to about 5.72 billion euros.
A separate 1.23 billion euro agreement with Roketsan for air defense components takes the total to nearly 7 billion euros.
Aselsan chief executive Ahmet Akyol said continued mass production was strengthening Türkiye’s Steel Dome air defense network.
Steel Dome is designed to integrate systems including Korkut, Hisar and Siper with radars and command-and-control units to counter threats at different altitudes and ranges.
Aselsan supplies the Hakim command-and-control system, designed to coordinate these elements.
The company also unveiled its Gökbağı communications satellite project at the 77th International Astronautical Congress in Antalya on Oct. 5.
Known internationally as Astralink, the planned low Earth orbit network is intended to provide communications services for military, government and civilian users.
Akyol told Anadolu Agency that Aselsan had designed the project “from the chip level up” and planned to begin launching the first satellites within the next few years.
He said the company had also developed ground receivers that track satellites electronically without mechanically moving their antennas, drawing on its experience with active electronically scanned array technology.
Aselsan is also exhibiting the synthetic aperture radar payload for the Göktürk-3 satellite, designed to capture high-resolution images of Earth’s surface through cloud cover.
Akyol said the company was investing in facilities for its space activities at its Oğulbey campus.

Largest oil depot in the Moscow region caught fire following drone attack - OSINT analysis
Kyiv • UNN
Following a massive UAV attack, a fire was reported at the territory of the Volodarskaya Linear Production Dispatch Station. The station stores and transports 3 million tonnes of fuel annually.
The largest oil depot in Russia's Moscow Region is burning after a drone attack in the early hours of October 6. This is evidenced by an OSINT analysis by ASTRA, reports UNN.
Details
In the early hours of October 6, the Moscow Region was reportedly under a massive UAV attack for several hours.
"Between 8:30 p.m. on October 5 and 5 a.m. on October 6, 650 UAVs flew toward the Moscow region. Most of them were destroyed by air defense forces at long-range positions. 105 drones were destroyed on approach to Moscow," Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on his Telegram channel, without reporting any damage.
Based on a video posted by the Supernova+ channel, ASTRA OSINT analyst determined that the fire occurred in the village of Konstantinovo in the Ramenskoye urban district of the Moscow Region. The source of the fire was reportedly located on the territory of the Volodarskaya linear production and dispatch station (LPDS). No previous attacks on the Volodarskaya LPDS had reportedly been reported.
The Volodarskaya linear production and dispatch station (LPDS) is the largest oil depot in the Moscow region and is part of JSC "AK Transnefteprodukt." It can separately store and transport motor gasoline, aviation fuel, and diesel fuel through pipelines. Its annual turnover amounts to 3 million tonnes of petroleum products. The raw materials come from the Moscow and Ryazan oil refineries, while an extensive network of product pipelines directly connects the station with the key airports of the Moscow hub (Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Sheremetyevo).

Meanwhile, rain, thunderstorms, and gusty winds are forecast to cover up to 50 percent of the plain region and 60 percent of the plateau region.
"Based on this weather forecast, citizens are urged to remain highly vigilant against sudden downpours, lightning, and strong winds, especially those traveling by land or water," the ministry warned.
The ministry added that it will continue to monitor the weather patterns closely and provide timely updates if conditions change. ■

Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan agreed on Oct. 5 to arrange the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities to the kingdom under their joint defense pact, following attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.
The decision came at an emergency meeting of the Mecca Defense Alliance’s Strategic Political and Defense Committee in Riyadh.
The committee decided to “move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments,” a joint statement said.
The measures would be carried out in accordance with the countries’ national laws and agreed arrangements. The statement gave no troop numbers or deployment timetable.
The three countries condemned attempts to target Mecca and Medina, as well as continuing attacks on Saudi cities and civilian and economic facilities.
They reaffirmed that each member’s security was inseparable from that of the other two.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan attended alongside Defense Minister Yaşar Güler and Chief of General Staff Gen. Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu. Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan also took part.
Speaking after the meeting, Fidan said the participants discussed support for Saudi Arabia’s defense and ways to resolve the dispute through peaceful means and dialogue.
He said a meeting on the alliance’s institutional arrangements had already been planned, but developments involving Yemen and Saudi Arabia had prompted the emergency talks.
He described Riyadh’s approach to resolving the dispute as constructive.
The committee also appointed retired Pakistani Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood as the alliance’s first secretary-general for a three-year term.
Fidan said discussions covered the secretariat’s structure and the appointment.
The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed on Aug. 7, treats an armed attack on any member as an attack on all three.
Separately, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari welcomed the agreement as a promising development for regional security during a panel at Georgetown University in Doha on Oct. 5.
He said Qatar continued its mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran and that communication channels remained open.
Al-Ansari also warned that a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz would affect the entire world, stressing that vital waterways should not be used as instruments of pressure.

CANBERRA, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Petrol vehicle sales in Australia were down 36.2 percent year-on-year in September as electric vehicle sales continued to surge, the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries (FCAI) reported on Tuesday.
The report also said that diesel vehicle sales declined by 18.4 percent in September.
In the same period, the FCAI said that sales of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug-in hybrids more than doubled.
It said that BEVs accounted for 24.2 percent of all new vehicles sold in Australia in September, the second-highest market share on record behind the 24.9 percent reported in August.
It marked the fifth consecutive month of BEVs accounting for at least 20 percent of new vehicle sales after the milestone was first achieved in May.
The FCAI said that China was the largest source of vehicles sold in Australia in September, supplying 35.5 percent of the market compared to 22.5 percent supplied by Japan.
China became the leading source of new vehicles in Australia for the first time in February after Japan had been the country's leading supplier of new vehicles every month for almost 30 years.
As of the end of September, China's BYD had sold 76,614 new vehicles in Australia in 2026, up 102 percent from 37,923 at the same point in 2025. ■

Feature: Ancient characters, guqin music bring Chinese culture to life in New York
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:44:52 CST
14:44:52 KST

Chinese artist and guqin performer Nie Hui introduces artworks inspired by oracle-bone inscriptions during a cultural activity in New York, the United States, Sept. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo)
by Vivien Liu
NEW YORK, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- An ancient pictograph evolving into a Chinese character; a child's mouth forming the sounds of a word; a brush sweeping across paper; and the centuries-old notes of a guqin filling the air...
For students and visitors in New York, these became different entry points into Chinese culture -- ways to encounter it not just through books, but through sight, sound and direct experience.
A series of cultural activities, recently held at the State University of New York at Old Westbury and the Long Island School of Chinese, featured exhibitions of Chinese poetry, calligraphy, painting and seal carving, guqin performances and a lecture on the origins and evolution of Chinese characters.
At the center of the programs were Chinese artist and guqin performer Nie Hui and her husband, cultural researcher Xie Feidong, who have worked together for years to study and share traditional Chinese culture and arts.
In one session, children were invited to say the Chinese word for "laugh" and observe what happened to their faces. As they pronounced it, the corners of their mouths lifted into a smile.
The exercise connected language with something the children could immediately see and feel. The lesson then moved to the visual origins of Chinese writing.
Nie drew early pictographic forms of the sun and moon, showing how ancient characters resembled the objects they represented.
"Chinese characters were originally pictographic characters. They were a picture," Xie said.
A discussion of oracle-bone inscriptions offered another glimpse into the early development of Chinese writing and the ways ancient people drew upon images of the natural world to express meaning.
For Christian D'Ambrosi, an American student pursuing a master's degree in education at SUNY Old Westbury, the presentation further sparked an interest in China that had taken root years earlier.
"I was here to learn more about Chinese culture, because I've always loved Chinese history," he said. "I hope to teach about Chinese history in the future."
The activities also explored connections across cultures, including a discussion linking the ancient Chinese story of Dayu controlling the floods to the biblical story of Noah's Ark.
"Art and culture have no borders," Xie said.
Catherine Fan, a high school junior and volunteer at the Long Island School of Chinese who plays the guzheng, particularly enjoyed hearing Nie perform Liu Shui (Flowing Water) on the guqin.
The ancient melody has traveled far beyond the classroom. A recording of Liu Shui was included on the Golden Record carried aboard NASA's Voyager spacecraft, launched in 1977 with sounds and music selected to represent life and culture on Earth.
For Edmund Yan, a Chinese American attendee, the Chinese paintings were particularly striking.
"I think it's very impressive how detailed it is and how much personality you can put into it," Yan said. "Being able to show off the personality of the artwork with just black and white is very beautiful and very impressive."
Olivia Chen, a sixth-grade student who has attended the Long Island School of Chinese since second grade, said the program helped explain what lies behind the characters she learns in class.
"We actually learn the history of words and stuff like that here," she said. "In Chinese class, we learn how to read, write and memorize words."
"I hope that the children today can remember a particular character that touched them," Xie said.
Nie captured their approach in a single line: "Let art have the depth of culture, and let culture have the beauty of art." ■

TOKYO, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Several Japanese companies and a university have reported data breaches or cyberattacks since Monday, potentially affecting millions of customers, members, students and teachers in a series of separate incidents.
Osaka Metropolitan University said Monday that data on at least 130,000 students and teachers may have been leaked following a cyberattack that caused a system failure at the institution.
About 500 servers supporting the university's information system stopped operating after a suspected ransomware attack Friday last week, according to the university.
The campus network for students and the portal site for teaching staff remained unusable as of Monday, while lectures were canceled.
Japanese discount store chain operator Mr. Max Holdings Ltd. said Tuesday that personal data of up to 1.7 million customers may have been compromised following unauthorized access to a server handling its online shopping services.
The retailer has halted services, blocked the attack route and is working with external security specialists, regulators and police to investigate and strengthen monitoring.
Japan's internet service firm GMO Research & AI Inc. said Monday that up to 948,500 records of its members were stolen following unauthorized access to its server.
The company said some members' rewards, worth about 2.9 million yen (about 18,000 U.S. dollars), were illicitly exchanged for Amazon gift card codes.
Monogatari Corp., which operates the Yakiniku King barbecue restaurant chain, said Monday that more than 10 million pieces of customer information, covering almost its entire registered user base, were leaked following unauthorized access to a system supporting its smartphone app for restaurant reservations and rewards.
The leaked information included email addresses and phone numbers, the company said, adding that no misuse of the data had been confirmed.
Meanwhile, Daiwa Securities Group Inc. said Monday that data on around 110,000 customers of its securities brokerage unit, along with other nonpersonal information, may have been compromised following unauthorized access to a server operated by one of its contractors.
The company said that even if the information had been leaked, it could not be used to conduct transactions, including online transactions.
The incidents were separately reported by the organizations involved, and there is no indication from the information disclosed so far that they are linked to a common cyberattack. ■

Widowed twice: A Gaza mother’s story of loss and survival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:44:39 UTC
14:44:39 KST

Widowed twice: A Gaza mother’s story of loss and survival
A young mother has lost two husbands and two children during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Gaza City, Gaza — For three years, Nisreen Touman has gone to bed every night in tears, remembering all she has lost since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza in October 2023.
By the time Nisreen was 34, she had been widowed twice. First, she lost her husband and her two children in June 2024. Then in July 2025, eight months after she remarried, Nisreen lost her second husband while she was pregnant.
Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Nisreen lived a happy and stable life in her home in Nuseirat, central Gaza, with her husband, Sami, 35, and their two children, Mahmoud and Laith, who were aged five and two at the time of their deaths.
“I had a home and a complete family. I got along with my husband, and we were friends,” she says, fighting back her tears.
Everything changes
On June 8, 2024, Nisreen was returning home with her husband and children after visiting extended family, who had been displaced to al-Mawasi in Khan Younis.
“We arrived and the children were playing in the street. Everything was normal. I was upstairs with my husband when suddenly we started hearing heavy, very close, bombing and gunfire.”
Her husband rushed outside to bring their children and his brother’s and sister’s children inside, where 25 members of her family were staying.
He then went outside again to see what was happening, as aircraft flew overhead.
“That was the last time I saw him. I later learned that he had been killed by a gunshot to the head from a quadcopter that was flying over the area that day,” she said.
Minutes later, while trying to calm the children as the bombing and gunfire continued, the house was targeted by an Israeli aircraft.
“I lost consciousness for a few moments, then woke up to thick dust that completely blocked my view,” she said.
“As the dust began to clear, I started to understand our place was bombed. I heard the family screaming and saw blood and body parts. I started shouting, ‘My children, my children.’”
Nisreen breaks down as she recalls seeing her two children lying on the ground. One had suffered severe head injuries, while the other appeared to be sleeping.
“I knew from that moment that I had lost them. It was clear that they were dead,” she says, recalling how she was unable to move from the shock.
Her husband’s brother came and placed the children in her arms.
“I could not speak. I was completely unable to speak, just tears running silently,” she said. “Everyone around me was screaming and crying.”
For two hours, Nisreen held her children in her arms as the family, including those who were injured, remained trapped in the damaged home as gunfire and bombing continued.
After repeated requests to the International Committee of the Red Cross for help, the family were eventually evacuated to a hospital.
The killing of Nisreen’s family came on one of the bloodiest days of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. On June 8, 2024, Israeli forces launched a military operation in the Nuseirat refugee camp, central Gaza, to rescue four Israeli captives who had been held following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
The United Nations said 89 inhabited houses and residential buildings were targeted in nearly four hours of bombing. Gaza’s Health Ministry said that 274 Palestinians were killed and 698 wounded on that day alone.
Eighteen members of Nisreen’s husband’s family were killed, including her husband and children, her sister Sabreen, 36, her mother-in-law, two of her husband’s brothers and their children, as well as members of the extended family.
A difficult decision
Nisreen returned alone to her family’s tent in al-Mawasi south of Gaza, where she struggled with the trauma and grief of losing her family. Four and a half months later, Nisreen found herself facing a difficult decision when her late sister’s husband, who was also her first husband’s brother, proposed to her.
He wanted to marry Nisreen and have her help take care of their four children, who had lost their mother.
“I strongly opposed it at first. I did not want to start a family or get married,” Nisreen said. She eventually agreed because she wanted to care for her departed sister’s children, especially the youngest, who was only one year old.
Nisreen does not hide the fact that there were no romantic feelings behind her second marriage. “I had lost my husband, and he had lost his wife. I had lost my children, and the four children had lost their mother,” she said.
The marriage allowed two people to fill the roles of the ones they lost. Nisreen found in her sister’s children a small comfort for the absence of her own.
But her new life came with significant challenges, especially during the first months. She was still grieving her first husband and her children, as she and her new husband attempted to adjust to each other.
Their different personalities and the new situation presented challenges, but gradually their lives became more stable. Nisreen even considered having another child.
“I used to see my children who had died, in my dreams every day. I would drift into thoughts about them, and they never left my mind,” she said. “So, with encouragement from my mother, I decided to become pregnant and experience motherhood again.”
The second loss
But eight months later, on July 8, 2025, Nisreen faced something she had never imagined: the loss of her second husband.
“Mohammed woke up, had breakfast with the children and said he was going to see a friend. A few moments later, we heard a huge explosion,” she said.
Shortly after, Nisreen was told by a neighbour that Mohammed had been killed in a strike on a group of people near al-Awda Hospital in Nuseirat.
For Nisreen, this second loss was even harder to bear than the first. After believing she had finally settled into a new sense of stability, her life was once again turned upside down.
“I felt like I was back at zero again,” she said. “I thought about the baby who had not yet been born, the children of my sister who had now lost both their mother and father, and the new loss I was living through.”
The remaining months of her pregnancy were heavy for Nisreen. Four months after Mohammed’s death, she gave birth to their daughter, Sidra.
Born into grief
Sidra’s birth brought back to Nisreen the pain of everything she had lost – her two children, her first husband and Mohammed.
While her daughter, who turns one in October, has brought Nisreen a “little compensation” for three years of sadness, it pains her that she will grow up without a father.
“Becoming a mother again brought me joy, but that feeling was deeply incomplete. She was a little compensation,” she said
Caring for Sidra has become Nisreen’s main priority.
“I have become more isolated. I prefer to stay quiet for hours and focus on my daughter,” Nisreen says. “I am afraid of making any new choices or trying to start another life after everything that happened to me.”
Nisreen now lives with Sidra at her family’s home in Gaza, while her late sister’s four children are being cared for by their grandfather. She visits them from time to time.
No matter how much time passes, she says she is unable to overcome the series of tragedies that have shaped her life.
“I never imagined I would go through all of this in my life. Sometimes it feels like I’m in an Indian film because of everything that has happened,” she said. “But under the war, unfortunately, anything is possible.”

Child left behind on Tallinn tram raises questions over driver care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:44:00 UTC
14:44:00 KST

Child left behind on Tallinn tram raises questions over driver care
An incident at the weekend involving a family on a Tallinn tram prompted similar stories online accusing drivers of a lack of due care and attention.
Tallinn Transport (TLT) says it reviews mistakes and trains drivers on safety accordingly, including by replaying video footage.
Over last weekend, a child got left alone at a tram stop in Tallinn after their father was unable to get off the tram with a stroller before the doors closed. Pressing the door button and speaking to the tram driver did not help things, and the father had to dash to the next stop on foot to retrieve the child safely.
The story has spread on social media and has brought to light other similar incidents in which small children have ended up on one side of tram or bus doors, their adult carer on the other. In some cases, families got reunited at the same stop, while in others, as in the one outlined above, the vehicle continued on its way.
Kaido Padar, TLT board member, rejected the idea that the issue is a systemic one. He said the company gets about 270 complaints a month, but most of these concern schedule time-keeping rather than safety issues.
"Something like this has happened between one and four times during my four years here," Padar said, though noted the weekend's incident was the second this year.
According to the TLT executive, 750 of the company's 1,500 drivers undergo practical, video-based customer service training each year.
"This morning we already agreed that we would also look at the driver's perspective and videos, showing how to act in one situation or another," Padar added.
Regina Peegel, a board member of the transport section of the rail workers' union (Eesti Raudteelaste Ametiühing), said tram drivers can see what is happening around the tram doors either through cameras or mirrors. Drivers close the doors only once there is no longer any movement around them, she noted.
"One thing is certain: the driver did not do it deliberately. In fact, that is what the job is about — letting everyone off and then letting everyone on properly," Peegel said.
"You see, quite often passengers are on their phones and only at the last moment realize it is time for them to get off, then they run to the door and start pressing the buttons. But the driver can't see who is running where. From a driver's perspective, if no one is getting off anymore, they close the doors and start driving. That means you really need to be ready when it is time to get off," Peegel continued.
However, Padar conceded the recent incident also clearly illustrated a trend of tram drivers being unnecessarily distracted while driving, or in this case, not grasping fully what had happened.
"The tram driver said this morning that they didn't really understand what the person wanted, because people ask all sorts of things and some people do stupid things to drivers through the glass, something which has happened to us many times. It is even more common for people to try to provoke the driver. So these kinds of incidents do happen and, unfortunately, yes, people also get caught in the doors," Padar added.
Other recent reported incidents involving TLT trams include one from March this year, when a dog got left outside a tram with its leash stuck in the closed doors. A quick-thinking passenger pulled the emergency brake lever, thereby avoiding the worst. However, the driver then assaulted the passenger who had pulled the lever, both verbally and physically. TLT said the driver has been fired and that the passenger had acted "100% correctly".
In March 2025, reported this summer, a man on the tram lines on Peterburi tee was killed when a tram struck him. Surveillance footage from inside the tram showed the driver had been viewing a video on a dashboard-mounted smartphone at the time of the incident. The driver received a two-year suspended sentence.
The tram incidents come amid a wider pattern of serious public transport accidents in the capital. In August 2025, a 26-year-old Ukrainian woman died after being hit by a bus at Narva mnt; police found she had crossed against a red light while wearing headphones. Last month, a 65-year-old woman died after a bus struck her at a pedestrian crossing in Haabersti — she had crossed on a green light, but the driver did not spot her. The circumstances of that case are still under investigation.

In doing so, it takes into account, among other things, the requirements arising from NIS2, the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), the Net-Zero Industry Act (NZIA), the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), and the Cybersecurity Act 2 (CSA2), as well as the requirements of transmission and distribution system operators.

“Mere subjectivity, [Hegel] argued, insisting on the purity of its own principle, becomes entangled…”

“Mere subjectivity, [Hegel] argued, insisting on the purity of its own principle, becomes entangled in antinomies. It is brought down by its own mischief, by hypocrisy and evil, in so far as it is not objectified in society and state. Morality, autonomy founded on pure self-certainty, together with conscience, is mere illusion. […] This dialectical motif, operating on all levels of the system, is at once true and untrue. True because it unmasks the particular as a necessary illusion, the false consciousness of isolated things as being themselves alone and not moments of the whole; and this false consciousness it breaks down with the power of the whole. Untrue because the motif of objectification, ‘alienation’, becoming a pretext for bourgeois self-assertion of the subject, is degraded to a mere rationalization, as long as objectivity, contrasted by thought to bad subjectivity, is unfree and does not measure up to the subject’s criticism.”
– Theodor W. Adorno, Minima Moralia, 152
