COP31 eyes modest steps as climate disasters multiply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:12:00 UTC
13:12:00 KST

COP31 eyes modest steps as climate disasters multiply
PARIS – Nations reeling from a year of climate devastation gather for COP31 in November but negotiations are not expected to deliver major progress in cutting the fossil fuels driving the crisis.
The conference follows deadly heatwaves and fires in Europe, catastrophic floods in Nepal and record temperatures around the world, testing whether the United Nations-backed talks can keep pace with reality.
As leaders meet in Turkey, an exceptionally powerful El Nino pattern will be approaching peak strength, threatening to amplify weather chaos worldwide and drive global heat to new highs.
Concerns over energy security will also loom large, with no end in sight to the Middle East war that has sent oil and gas prices soaring and hit fossil fuel-importing nations hard.
With a new agreement on fossil fuels unlikely, Turkey is rallying support for a voluntary “electrification” pledge it says could cut heat-trapping emissions and reduce reliance on energy imports.
“In many ways, the defining contexts for this year’s climate summit will be heat and Hormuz,” said David Waskow from the World Resources Institute, referencing the vital strait that carried one-fifth of the world’s hydrocarbons before the Iran war.
Unusually, Turkey must navigate these complexities with Australia, a major fossil fuel exporter, after both countries agreed to share COP31 duties following a bruising hosting battle.
Australia’s Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations in Antalya starting Nov 9, said the extreme events in 2026 “show climate change is not a future challenge”. He said: “It is a present reality... and the costs of inaction are rising.”
A “pre-COP” meeting began on Monday in the climate-vulnerable Pacific with a leaders’ retreat in Tuvalu and government meetings in Fiji.
Stalemate
Unlike recent COPs – where nearly 200 nations forged landmark pacts on phasing down coal or moving away from fossil fuels – the negotiation agenda at COP31 is light on big-ticket items. There are more than 100 items on the table but many deal with technical matters, like approving indicators to track progress on climate adaptation.
“Much of the Antalya summit will be a ‘roll up the sleeves’ effort. Governments need to make concrete headway in negotiations, though there may not be dramatic outcomes this year,” Waskow told AFP.
Nations are not expected to adopt new binding commitments to reduce the burning of fossil fuels – the leading cause of climate change. Countries agreed in 2023 to move away from coal, oil and gas but since then efforts to negotiate concrete targets or timelines for that transition have gone nowhere.
At the summit in 2025, fossil fuels were not mentioned by name in the final agreement after oil and gas-producing nations prevented consensus on the issue.
“Everyone agrees there will be no real gain at the multilateral level at the moment,” Marta Torres-Gunfaus from the IDDRI think tank told AFP.
Fossil fuel emissions, meanwhile, hit record highs in 2025.
In September, the UN conceded that the milestone 1.5 deg C climate target will be missed in a matter of years.
Nations frustrated at the COP gridlock have sought progress elsewhere. Nearly 60 countries attended a fossil fuel phase-out conference without UN involvement in 2026. France, the Netherlands and Germany have published “road maps” with explicit deadlines for quitting coal, oil and gas.
UN Climate chief Simon Stiell has defended the negotiations while acknowledging their limitations. “No single COP can fix this global crisis, but each takes meaningful steps forward,” he said.
Pressure
Turkey says it is not realistic to expect all countries to move at the same pace. “Any proposal that fails to reconcile our climate objectives with social and economic realities will be doomed to fail,” said President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Turkey is curating an “action agenda” alongside the negotiations that encourages countries to support non-binding pledges on issues from artificial intelligence to waste management.
There is broad support for its centrepiece goal: raising the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20% today to 35% by 2035.
The electrification target does not state how that extra power should be produced. One-third of electricity is generated by coal, and there are concerns the target could provide cover for expanded fossil fuel use.
The Nepal floods would also put “a huge amount of pressure” on Western countries to increase financial support for climate disaster recovery, said Ajay Mathur, a former Indian government negotiator.
“We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying for it,” Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said. AFP

Why Russia Wants Western Embassies Out of Kyiv – and Why They’re Staying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:10:35 UTC
13:10:35 KST

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed months of Russian warnings for foreign diplomats to leave Kyiv, making clear that Moscow will not decide whether Washington maintains its presence in the Ukrainian capital.
“Look, we have an embassy presence there, and we’ll make the determination about whether it’s safe for them to be there or not,” Rubio told reporters Sunday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“They’ve been warning diplomats to leave for months, and I don’t think it’s a surprise to anyone that Kyiv is under attack. I think that’s well understood.”
Rubio said the State Department assesses the security of every US diplomatic mission daily and would change its posture if Washington believed conditions required it.
“We haven’t done that up to this point there,” he said.
The remarks were the latest Western rejection of a sustained Russian effort to warn – and increasingly pressure – foreign governments to pull their diplomatic missions out of Kyiv.
For Moscow, however, the issue goes well beyond embassy security.
An exodus of Western diplomats from the Ukrainian capital would hand the Kremlin a powerful symbolic victory: the image of Ukraine’s allies abandoning Kyiv under Russian military pressure, four years after Moscow failed to capture the city.
Europe says it is staying
Rubio’s comments followed a coordinated response from European governments rejecting Russia’s latest warnings.
Russian Drones Sink Turkish-Owned Grain Ship as Ankara Pushes Black Sea Security Deal
Germany, Italy, Spain and Sweden publicly declared that their embassies would remain in Kyiv, joining France, Poland, Estonia and the European Union in reaffirming their diplomatic presence.
“We are staying in Kyiv,” the embassies said in coordinated messages.
Kyiv Post previously reported that the statements came after Russia’s Foreign Ministry warned foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel that remaining in the Ukrainian capital represented a “mortal danger” as Moscow threatened further large-scale strikes.
The embassies called on Russia to respect the Vienna Convention and international humanitarian law rather than attempt to intimidate diplomatic missions.
EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová went further, saying none of the 25 EU member states maintaining embassies in Kyiv was preparing to leave.
“I am not aware of any embassy that is leaving – and certainly not embassies of EU countries,” Mathernová said.
The EU Delegation and the EU Advisory Mission also remain operational in Kyiv.
The European Commission separately said Russia’s threats would neither reduce EU support for Ukraine nor alter the bloc’s diplomatic presence.
Poland likewise rejected any suggestion it was preparing to withdraw its mission, describing Moscow’s warnings as an effort to intimidate European governments and weaken their backing for Ukraine.
Moscow has been sending the message for months
The current confrontation did not begin with Russia’s October warning.
Kyiv Post reported in May that Rubio had already addressed Russian warnings about the security of diplomatic facilities in Kyiv after Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov conveyed a message from Vladimir Putin to the Trump administration.
At the time, Rubio said Russia had not directly ordered the United States to evacuate its embassy, but had issued broader warnings about the danger facing diplomatic facilities in the capital.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accused Moscow of responding to US peace efforts with threats against Kyiv, calling the warning a “brazen provocation.”
Days later, another controversy erupted when reports suggested the US Embassy had left Kyiv.
Kyiv Post reported that the embassy publicly denied the claim.
“The US Embassy is open. There are no changes to our operations and reports otherwise are false,” the mission said at the time.
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry also rejected reports of an American evacuation.
Why an embassy withdrawal would matter to Moscow
Embassies are not merely administrative offices. Their presence in a wartime capital is an unmistakable political signal.
Foreign diplomats meet Ukrainian officials, coordinate military and economic assistance, host visiting delegations and maintain direct communications between Kyiv and allied governments.
Their continued presence also says something more basic: foreign governments continue to recognize Kyiv as a functioning capital whose government remains firmly in control.
That symbolism has carried particular weight since the opening weeks of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Before Russian troops crossed the border in February 2022, the US and a number of other countries temporarily moved diplomats away from Kyiv as Western intelligence warned that Russian forces could rapidly reach the capital.
Russia then attempted to seize Kyiv.
It failed.
As Ukrainian forces pushed Russian troops out of the Kyiv region, Western officials began returning.
On May 18, 2022, the US formally reopened its embassy in Kyiv and raised the American flag over the mission again. Then-US Secretary of State Antony Blinken explicitly connected the reopening to Ukraine’s successful defense of its capital.
“The Ukrainian people, with our security assistance, have defended their homeland,” he said as the embassy resumed operations.
The return of diplomats became one of the clearest visual markers of Russia’s defeat around Kyiv. A mass departure now would carry the opposite symbolism.
Making Kyiv appear unlivable
Russia’s latest diplomatic warnings coincide with an intensified campaign against the Ukrainian capital. Moscow has struck transport infrastructure, residential areas and other targets while openly promising additional large-scale attacks.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has described Russia’s evolving strategy as an effort to make Ukrainian cities increasingly difficult to live in by systematically attacking the infrastructure required to sustain them.
Four years after failing to seize Kyiv, Moscow is again trying to isolate the capital through missiles, drones and threats.
It has failed again.

Jim Bakker, televangelist whose Christian TV empire collapsed in scandal, dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:09:12 UTC
13:09:12 KST

American televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar evangelical television empire before sex and financial scandals brought down his ministry and sent him to prison for fraud, died Monday at 86, his family said.
Bakker became one of the most recognizable faces in American religious broadcasting alongside his then-wife, Tammy Faye Bakker. The couple rose to national fame through “The PTL Club,” a Christian television program launched in the 1970s that grew into a sprawling religious and business enterprise.
Their ministry eventually included a satellite television network and Heritage USA, a vast Christian theme park and resort in South Carolina that became one of the most prominent symbols of the Bakkers’ success. Their increasingly lavish lifestyle, financed as the ministry solicited donations from viewers, also drew mounting scrutiny.
The empire began to unravel in 1987 after revelations emerged about a payment connected to church secretary Jessica Hahn, who accused Bakker of sexual assault. Bakker denied raping her. The scandal forced him to step down from PTL, while investigations into the ministry’s finances exposed much broader allegations of financial misconduct.
In 1989, a federal jury convicted Bakker on 24 counts of fraud and conspiracy stemming from his fundraising operation. Prosecutors accused PTL of selling more than 150,000 “lifetime partnerships” promising lodging at Heritage USA while failing to build enough accommodation to fulfill those commitments.
Bakker was initially sentenced to 45 years in prison and fined $500,000. An appeals court later ordered a new sentencing hearing, and his prison term was reduced to eight years. He ultimately served nearly five years before being paroled in 1994.
Tammy Faye divorced Bakker in 1992 while he was in prison. She later remarried and remained a prominent cultural figure until her death from cancer in 2007. Bakker married Lori Beth Graham in 1998.
Despite the spectacular collapse of his first ministry, Bakker eventually returned to television, launching “The Jim Bakker Show” in 2003 and once again building an audience around evangelical Christianity, prophecy and apocalyptic themes. His later career ensured that he remained a controversial presence in American religious broadcasting decades after the scandal that had appeared to end it.
Announcing his death, Lori Bakker said her husband had “finished his race with faith” after dedicating decades of his life to Christian ministry. His son, Jay Bakker, also confirmed his death.

SEOUL, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's September foreign exchange reserves fell for the first time in four months, driven by reducing foreign currency deposits by financial institutions and asset entrustment for the U.S. strategic investments, central bank data showed Tuesday.
The total reserves sank 1.72 billion U.S. dollars from a month earlier to 440.56 billion dollars at the end of September, marking the first decrease since May, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The downturn was attributed to a decline in foreign currency deposits by financial institutions and asset entrustment to the Korea-U.S. Strategic Investment Corporation, a temporary state-run agency to manage South Korea's strategic investments in the United States worth 350 billion dollars.
A reduction in the U.S.-dollar-converted value of non-dollar assets also contributed to the sliding reserves. The dollar index, which gauges the U.S. dollar value versus six major peers, went up 1.7 percent last month.
By asset type, securities made up the largest share at 386.03 billion dollars, accounting for 87.6 percent of the total reserves.
Deposits amounted to 29.95 billion dollars, followed by special drawing rights with 15.48 billion dollars, gold holdings with 4.79 billion dollars and the country's IMF reserve position with 4.30 billion dollars. ■

Feature: A growing passion for Chinese language takes root in Central Asia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:01:44 CST
13:01:44 KST

ASTANA, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- At a light-rail station, passengers can buy tickets with a tap of the screen, with instructions available in Chinese, Kazakh, Russian and English. Outside, a ride-hailing driver greets passengers in halting Chinese. At restaurants, Chinese-language menus are becoming increasingly common.
Across Central Asia, Chinese is becoming an increasingly familiar part of everyday life, reflecting a growing interest in the language across the region.
In a classroom at the Confucius Institute at Al-Farabi Kazakh National University in Almaty, Kazakhstan's largest city, students spend the evening repeating Chinese phrases and answering questions.
After a day's work, 26-year-old Aiym Naurzbayeva joins more than 100 local learners for evening Chinese classes.
Naurzbayeva works for a local logistics company, where she regularly deals with Chinese business partners. The experience has shown her the opportunities that speaking Chinese can open up. She started learning the language in September.
"I hope to study in China next year and, after completing my studies, return and continue working in Kazakhstan-China cooperation," she said.
The Confucius Institute was jointly established by Lanzhou University and Al-Farabi Kazakh National University. Deng Hong, the institute's Chinese director, said interest in learning Chinese has continued to grow in recent years, with students ranging in age from 7 to 70.
The institute is also a center for Hanyu Shuiping Kaoshi (HSK), or Chinese Proficiency Test, serving more than 2,000 test takers each year. The number of applicants has continued to rise.
A similar trend can be seen in Tajikistan. Sun Jing, Chinese director of the Confucius Institute at Tajik National University, said the institute enrolls students twice a year, admitting more than 1,000 students each time. But the number of applicants exceeds 1,500 each time.
"Some parents travel long distances to bring their children to learn Chinese," she said.
Beyond Confucius Institutes, Chinese language learning is becoming increasingly diverse in Central Asia, with private language schools and individual tutoring growing in popularity.
In Astana, a search for "Chinese language courses" on a local lifestyle services platform yielded listings for 136 Chinese-language training institutions. Other major cities in the region also have dozens or even hundreds of similar institutions.
At the "Laoshi" Educational Center in Almaty, classrooms were filled with children, students and working adults studying together.
Tatyana Kaukenova, director of the center, said more local people are choosing to learn Chinese as economic, trade, logistics and technological ties between Kazakhstan and China deepen.
The center now offers classes at different levels. Kaukenova and her colleagues have also developed customized teaching materials incorporating Kazakhstan's local culture and traditions to help students learn and use Chinese more effectively.
Private tutoring has also emerged as a new trend. Roza, who completed her studies at the Confucius Institute at Al-Farabi Kazakh National University, now works as a private Chinese tutor and teaches 15 teenagers.
"Chinese culture is fascinating, and the Chinese language has opened a window for us to observe China," she said.
The growing interest in Chinese across Central Asia is no coincidence. Growing economic and trade ties, cultural exchanges and more favorable policies have helped make Chinese more than just a classroom language, opening doors to new opportunities for young people across the region.
Baikazak Sultanbekov, a Kyrgyz student at Jalal-Abad State University, has been learning Chinese for more than two years. Since Aug. 20, Kyrgyz citizens have been eligible for a 240-hour visa-free transit program and a 30-day visa-free entry policy for Hainan, China's southernmost province.
"I was very happy when I heard the news. It means my dream of seeing the sea in Hainan may soon become a reality," he said.
"All my family fully supports me in learning Chinese," said 17-year-old Muslima, who studies at the Confucius Institute at Tashkent State University of Oriental Studies in Uzbekistan.
During a study trip to Xi'an in 2025, she was deeply impressed by the city's historical sites and culture, sparking a strong interest in Chinese culture.
"I really want to see more of China," she said.
Gulnar Shaimergenova, director of the China Studies Center in Astana, Kazakhstan, said China's leading position in high-tech industries such as scientific and technological innovation and the digital economy has increased demand for bilingual talent in fields including artificial intelligence and financial technology, continuously driving demand for Chinese-language learning in the region.
Across Central Asia, Chinese is increasingly becoming a bridge between people, cultures and opportunities. With every new phrase learned and every conversation held in Chinese, ties between the people of the region and China are becoming more tangible. ■

Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:01:01 UTC
13:01:01 KST

Cases of seven types of cancer have risen sharply among younger people in England, major new research has found, prompting warnings that lifestyle choices are costing thousands of lives each year.
The number of people under 50 diagnosed with prostate cancer in England has quadrupled since 2001, while early onset bowel, kidney and uterine cancer diagnoses more than doubled.
Analysis of English, US and Dutch cancer data by World Cancer Research Fund identified “significant increases” in early onset cancers for seven cancer types in England, five types in the US and four in the Netherlands.
Although cancer has been increasing across all age groups globally, the rate rise in early onset cases is greater than other ages.
Experts said the figures reflected the growing global obesity epidemic, poor diets and insufficient exercise, as well as growing awareness of cancer and earlier diagnosis.
Cancer among the under 50s is still uncommon, with the median age at diagnosis above 60, but the trend is worrying, the authors noted.
Commenting on the findings, Mark Lawler, professor of digital health and the chair in translational cancer genomics at Queen’s University Belfast, called the problem “a ticking timebomb that we need to [defuse] as quickly as possible, otherwise the numbers will undoubtedly continue to grow”.
He went on: “The overall trend is also particularly worrying as it comes on the backdrop of lifestyle factors contributing to thousands of deaths.”
In England, of the 12 tumour types studied, incidence rates of prostate cancer among men under 50 jumped from one in every 100,000 people in 2001 to 3.6 in every 100,000 in 2023. Over the same period, rates of bowel cancer among the under 50s leapt from 3.9 in 100,000 people in 2001 to 8.4 in 100,000 in 2023, while early onset uterine and kidney cancers also doubled to 3.9 and 3 per 100,000 people respectively.
The rate of breast cancer among the under 50s increased, albeit less sharply, from 42 to 47.5 per 100,000 in 2023, while there were also increases in the incidence of early onset pancreatic and liver cancers.
In the US, analysis of official data since 2000 found that among patients under 50, incidence rates of kidney cancer more than doubled from 2.5 in 100,000 people in 2000 to 5.3 in 2023, while bowel, uterine and pancreatic cancers all increased by more than 50% and breast cancer by about 20%.
For the Netherlands, the researchers found significant increases in early onset bowel, kidney, liver and cervical cancers.
In contrast, rates of lung cancer among the under 50s declined in all three countries, reflecting continuing declines in smoking in those countries.
Dr Giota Mitrou, the executive director of research and policy at the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), called the trajectory “concerning”, and added: “Behind every figure is a person facing cancer earlier than they, their family and often their doctor would expect. While cancer is still much more common in older adults, these changing patterns among younger generations need to be treated as a serious research and cancer prevention priority.”
WCRF said risk factors such as growing obesity levels, poor diet, insufficient exercise, alcohol consumption, smoking and environmental exposures (such as pollutants, chemicals, plastics, water and air pollution) could be contributing to the trend. About 40% of cancers are linked to these kinds of modifiable risks. However, greater awareness of cancer symptoms also means that people are more likely to be diagnosed earlier.
“While we don’t completely understand why more cancers are occurring in people under 50 years of age, it is likely that risk factors related to cancer – for example, overweight and obesity, diet, alcohol, consumption and smoking – play a role,” said Dr Vanessa Gordon-Dseagu, research translation manager at WCRF.
“At the same time, the public are increasingly aware of the risk factors relating to cancer and the signs and symptoms of the disease to look out for, so are more likely to seek out healthcare when they experience them.”
While more cancers are being diagnosed at an earlier stage, “increased diagnosis does not explain the whole story and more research is needed to understand early-onset cancers” she added.
King’s College London has announced a new trial of 250,000 people, funded by Cancer Research UK, to investigate the increase in bowel cancer cases among younger adults.
The study will seek a clearer understanding of the balance between worsening risk factors and better detection in the rise.
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “These findings underline why early diagnosis is at the heart of our national cancer plan. To help catch cancer sooner, we’re investing in new technologies to speed up diagnosis, expanding genetic testing, and supporting research to better understand the causes of cancer and who may be most at risk.
We’re also prioritising research into less-survivable and rarer cancers, and our ambition is for three-quarters of people diagnosed by 2035 to be cancer-free or living well with cancer, saving 320,000 lives.
“Our newly announced national cancer board has a specific representative for children and young people, as we’re aware of the devastating impact of getting cancer at an earlier stage of life.”

Japan PM leads outcry after US Marine arrested over alleged killing of woman on Okinawa

04:00:41 UTC
13:00:41 KST

Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, has led public outcry over crimes committed by US servicemen after a marine suspected of killing a woman on Okinawa was arrested on Saturday.
In a speech in parliament, Takaichi described the alleged crime as “heinous” and urged US military authorities to enforce discipline among American servicemen stationed on Okinawa, an island 1,000 miles south of Tokyo.
Crimes and accidents involving US troops on Okinawa have been a constant source of tension between Tokyo and Washington and the target of protests among local people. The island hosts most of the 50,000 US troops in Japan and 70% of the country’s military facilities there.
Police said Devin Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal, had been arrested on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Okinawan capital Naha early on Saturday. He is also suspected of stealing her wallet and backpack. Ballard denied the allegations, police said.
If convicted, Ballard could face life in prison or the death penalty.
His arrest triggered anger in Okinawa days after voters elected Genta Koja, a pro-US base governor backed by Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic party, ending the eight-year-tenure of Denny Tamaki, a critic of the US military presence on the island.
Koja’s election had raised hopes that the US and Japan might finally make progress on the planned transfer of a marine corps base from a densely populated city to a remote off-shore location.
The relocation of Futenma air station, where Ballard is stationed, has been held up for decades amid opposition from people living near the alternative site and local politicians who want US military facilities moved off the island altogether.
Koja said the arrest had dealt a “major shock” to the island and “raises fears among Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to US bases”. He added: “It is absolutely unforgivable, and we are outraged.”
He said the case proved that US attempts to improve discipline among its troops had failed. “I’m enraged by the loss of a precious life of an Okinawan resident,” he told Lt Gen Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, and the US consul general in Naha, Andrew Ou, after Ballard’s arrest.
Watson said he recognised that the incident had caused “significant concern and anxiety among the residents of Okinawa, our neighbours”. He added: “We are committed to being good neighbours … and earning the trust of the Okinawan people.”
Anti-US sentiment on Okinawa intensified after the 1995 rape of a 12-year-old girl by three American servicemen. A year later, Tokyo and Washington agreed to reduce the US military footprint by closing Futenma and relocating its functions to the quiet fishing village of Henoko on the north-east coast.
Anger erupted again over the rape of a teenage girl by a US service member in 2024 and the delayed disclosure of the crime.
Crimes involving US troops on Okinawa have risen in recent years, from about 40 in 2020 to 101 last year, according to the prefectural police.
Okinawa plays a central role in regional tensions. Japan’s government insists US bases on the island act as a deterrent amid Chinese claims over disputed parts of the East and South China Seas and the emergence of a nuclear-armed North Korea.
Under the Japan-US status of forces agreement, Ballard, who was arrested in a civilian district while he was off duty, will remain in the custody of the Japanese authorities.
Security footage showed him entering the hotel with Yagi and later leaving alone.
Yagi’s family said they were “devastated” by her death. Her brother said in a statement: “Our parents are especially exhausted with grief after losing their daughter.”

====================================================================================================

‘It could knock a whole street down’: the art of defusing a second world war bomb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:00:02 UTC
13:00:02 KST

Everyone at Exmouth Marina knew there was an unexploded German bomb in the water. Old hands at the dock had been saying so since the end of the second world war. But the marina had been dredged and re-dredged and nothing had ever come up. It had started to sound like an old wives’ tale. The marina is a busy stretch of water: a commercial port until the late 1990s that had since been converted into a home to private yachts. A bomb, you’d think, would have a hard time staying hidden. But in the middle of the afternoon on Wednesday 14 January 2026, 81 years after the end of the second world war, Steve Hockings-Thompson, the manager of Exmouth Marina, got a call from the crew of a dredging vessel telling him he’d better come out to the boat. “I thought: ‘Oh crikey. We’ve got a bit of an issue here,’” Hockings-Thompson told me recently.
He went out to the dredger, a squat barge that hauls silt and other debris from the marina floor on to a flat deck that resembles a steel sieve. Sitting on the deck was a huge hunk of metal, caked in mud and stones. As Hockings-Thompson got closer and saw its distinctive conical shape, he knew it was a bomb – a big one. The dredger was loaded with 20,000 litres of diesel fuel, so if the bomb detonated, it would be disastrous. He called the police, who quickly came to the scene. “And then,” he said, “all hell broke loose.”
To deal with the explosives, they called in the army. The call was picked up at the control centre at Vauxhall Barracks in Didcot, a small town in Oxfordshire. This is the headquarters of the 11 Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Search Regiment (11EOD), a specialist army division responsible for all kinds of bomb disposal – from improvised devices planted by terrorist groups to second world war-era munitions.
When the Exmouth bomb was called in, Maj Andrew Boyce, who was managing operations for the regiment, was confused. “We were talking about ‘the bomb’, which I’d been told was a 50kg,” he recalled. “And then somebody on the phone tells me it’s a 250kg. I’m like, how have you confused a 50kg bomb, which is the size of a fire extinguisher, with a 250kg bomb, which is the size of a hot water tank?”
The reason for the confusion soon became clear: the Exmouth Marina bomb was not the first to be discovered that day. Another second world war bomb had been unearthed a few hours earlier at a building site in Plymouth, 50 miles away.
In Plymouth that morning, Luke Templeton, director of S.I UXO, a private contractor that goes in ahead of construction companies to look for unexploded bombs, had known what he was looking for. His company’s historians had already spent a fortnight doing a detailed risk assessment of the site, drawing on historical documents showing the Luftwaffe’s flight paths and local records of airstrikes. From this, they’d worked out that it was highly likely there were two bombs buried somewhere on the building site. Using specialist equipment, they had found a 50kg bomb buried more than four metres down. After inspecting the bomb up close, Templeton called the police.
As far as Boyce knew, this was the first time since the immediate postwar period that two unexploded bombs had been discovered on the same day. The two bombs were in the same part of the country, and had been reported to the same police force, Devon and Cornwall. “We’re used to having confusion with location or devices. We’re not used to having two devices,” said Brig Darren Fisher, who at the time was a colonel overseeing the operations. Once the confusion had been straightened out – it was a 50kg bomb at the building site in Plymouth, and a 250kg bomb floating on the dredger in Exmouth – the response began.
When most people think of bomb disposal, they imagine a lone figure in a bomb suit carefully approaching an improvised device as bullets fly overhead, holding steady as they unpick wires, knowing that one wrong move will kill them. This image was forged in Belfast during the Troubles and Helmand province during the invasion of Afghanistan, and it is not unwarranted; bomb disposal is commonly described as the most dangerous job in the military. But, in Britain in 2026, the daily reality of the job is quite different.
Although the same team deals with terrorist incidents, such as the 2017 Manchester attack on an Ariana Grande concert, it is unexploded second world war munitions that make up the core work of the UK’s bomb-disposal teams. The Luftwaffe dropped more than 60,000 tonnes of bombs on Britain over the course of the war, and the Ministry of Defence estimates that roughly one in 10 of these failed to explode on impact. The reasons range from the grim – poor manufacturing quality due to a reliance on forced labour in concentration camps – to the prosaic: a bomb might have landed at an odd angle, or on soft ground that absorbed the impact before the fuze could fire. (“Fuse” is the general spelling for electrical safety devices and burning cords, while “fuze” refers to engineered explosive detonators.) Britain also dropped munitions on its own land during training exercises and deliberately buried surplus after the war in an effort at disposal. Eight decades on, the physical remnants of the war still account for about 2,000 of the 2,500 incidents that military bomb-disposal teams respond to in an average year.
The calls often come in from metal detectorists and magnet fishers, hobbyists who throw strong magnets into waterways to see what comes up. They surge on bank holidays, when people are out walking and notice things underfoot, or catching up on tasks such as clearing out a grandparent’s home. Not long ago, the bomb-disposal unit was called to deal with a 2in mortar that had been used for 20 years as a paperweight. Increasingly, calls come from construction sites, as buildings get taller and companies dig deeper, which has led to a growing industry of private contractors actively searching for unexploded bombs. “We’re expanding cities, building new homes, and an accident could happen,” said Templeton. “If a 250kg bomb went off in a city, it could knock a whole street down.”
The passage of time has not rendered these explosives less dangerous. In June 2010, three bomb-disposal experts in Göttingen, Germany, were killed by a 500kg American bomb found beneath the site of a new sports arena. In 2020, a 250kg bomb exploded beneath a crab boat off the Norfolk coast, seriously injuring five of its seven crew. In 2021, another bomb exploded beneath a drilling rig near Munich’s main railway station, injuring four. Because it was a global war, this is a global problem. This year, a second world war bomb beneath a stilt house in Indonesia detonated, killing five people and injuring 20.
These decades-old devices are difficult to read or predict. “You don’t really know why [a particular bomb] didn’t function, which is part of the problem,” said Lt Col Andy Hambley, the commanding officer of 11EOD. Years of corrosion, shifting ground and rust make the fuzes less predictable, the machinery harder to read.
That was exactly the issue facing two teams in two different corners of Devon on the afternoon of 14 January.
At about 1pm, PO Scott Dooley, a diver and bomb-disposal operator with the Royal Navy’s Diving and Threat Exploitation Group, arrived at the building site in Plymouth. Dooley, a tall man with a neatly trimmed beard and a soft Devon accent, grew up in the military; his father was in the Royal Engineers, doing bomb disposal. In recent years, he had acquired the nickname “the Doom Watch”, because every time he was on duty, the phone didn’t stop ringing (his record was 11 call-outs in a single week). In Plymouth, Dooley scanned the area for risk: there was a school nearby, as well as a glass-fronted hotel that could shatter if the worst happened. Police were already at work establishing a cordon and evacuating the area around the bomb.
When an operator approaches a bomb for the first time, they do not know what they are walking towards. The most important thing is to assess the fuze, a metal cylinder screwed into the side of the bomb. It is the first link in a chain. The fuze contains explosives, which fire a tiny, highly sensitive detonator, which sets off a booster charge, which sets off the main filling of the bomb, a comparatively stable “secondary” explosive. Most German fuzes were electrical, charged from the aircraft as the bomb was released. After 80 years, there is no charge left in them. But some German bombs were fitted with a mechanical delayed-action fuze, constructed from gears and springs, like a watch. Once triggered, this fuze ticks down before detonating between two and 72 hours later. The Luftwaffe deliberately fitted these fuzes to maximise disruption; hospitals, roads and factories were cleared for days at a time because the bombs could detonate long after impact.
Everything, therefore, turns on the fuze. If the fuze is judged to be sensitive, that usually means it is too dangerous to move the device. The safest option is to surround it with sandbags and detonate it where it is. If the fuze is stable, then it can be moved somewhere safer, such as out to sea.
Dooley had two things working in his favour: a 50kg bomb was less likely to have a ticker, and it was still half-buried, which suggested it hadn’t been badly jolted. On the other hand, the fuze was submerged in mud and he couldn’t see it. Bomb-disposal operators try to avoid moving a device until they’ve assessed the fuze, lest they trigger a ticker, but Dooley had no choice. Down in the pit, he and a colleague built a stable platform on a ledge of mud, surrounding it with sandbags, and set to work painstakingly unearthing it. Once it was out, he placed a listening device on it called a microphone stethoscope, or mic steth. He listened for ticking.
Silence. A moment of relief, quickly followed by further investigation. Silence only means that at that moment, no mechanical fuze has been triggered. Was there one in the bomb at all? Dooley needed to physically examine it. The bomb had been lodged more than four metres underground for decades and was caked in thick clay. Still listening for ticking on the mic steth in case his movements triggered anything, he poured water on the fuze to wash away the mud. “The fuze was absolutely more than gone,” he said. It was so degraded that none of the markings were visible. No markings, no information. They would have to X-ray it.
While this was unfolding in Plymouth, Capt Liam Kidman was anticipating a quiet couple of days at home. Kidman had just come off a gruelling week that ended in rural west Wales, cutting open a safe packed with explosives at the bottom of a dead man’s garden. (The man had apparently used the explosives for felling trees, and nobody knew where he kept the key.) Then, shortly after he had completed that job, the control centre rang to say two bombs had been discovered in Devon. The local team in Plymouth was already occupied with one of them. Could he go to Exmouth? Kidman was back on the road within the hour.
An energetic man from south Wales, Kidman ended up in bomb disposal almost by accident – when he joined the army more than 20 years ago, there was a shortage of ammunition technicians. As he climbed the ranks, dealing with improvised explosive devices (IEDs) in Afghanistan and second world war jobs in the UK, he came to love the problem-solving aspect of the work.
It was past 7pm when Kidman reached Exmouth Marina from his base in Gloucestershire. The closer he got to the marina, the emptier the roads got. The bomb was sitting out in the middle of the harbour, bobbing on the open deck of the dredger. It was so big that if detonated it could flatten the marina’s waterfront. The bomb was only accessible by sea, and the nearest naval team was tied up with the other bomb in Plymouth that night. Usually, the army handles incidents on land and the navy anything at sea, but the unexpected nature of two bombs being found on the same day had turned everything on its head.
The bomb had been handled roughly – hauled off the seabed and dumped unceremoniously on to a metal deck. “If there’s a mechanical fuze on there, that’s enough for it to be ticking down,” said Kidman. They had to get ears on it. Harry Griffin, the marina compliance manager, stepped up. Griffin knew there was a chance the bomb could go off, but reassured himself that it had been in the water for 80 years without incident. He ferried a sergeant from Kidman’s team over to the bomb to get a mic steth on to the device. “That’s the bit that gets the operator’s heart going,” said Kidman.
It was not ticking. But nobody relaxed. Just as in Plymouth, they did not know what kind of fuze they were dealing with.
On a bright day in June, I visited RAF Northolt, a base on the outskirts of London, to observe a training exercise on airdropped weapons. Learning how to correctly assess an old, rusting bomb takes time and practice. Bomb disposal is a dangerous job but, Hambley told me: “Knowledge dispels fear.”
Bomb disposal as a specialism was created in the second world war. Britain wasn’t ready for the blitz, and the early assumption was that police or air raid wardens could simply deal with any bomb that failed to go off. But as delayed-action mechanical fuzes – those ticking timebombs – became more common, it was clear that targeted intervention was needed. As the historian James Owen details in his 2010 book Danger UXB, in May 1940, the War Office handed the problem to the Royal Engineers, who formed 25 bomb-disposal sections armed with little more than picks, shovels and stethoscopes. By September 1940, they were dealing with more than 3,000 bombs a month. By some estimates, the average life expectancy of a bomb-disposal operator in this period was 10 weeks.
Those early teams mapped every bomb they dealt with, and the maps are still in use. Matt Fuller, a researcher at S.I UXO, the contractor that found the bomb in Plymouth, works through wartime bomb censuses and Home Office daily intelligence reports. Studying the bomb maps, he found that the Plymouth bomb most likely fell on the night of 21–22 March 1941. (The Exmouth bomb he puts at 24-25 February 1941.) Conducting risk assessments, Fuller is struck by the sheer number of places that were targeted, some of them small towns with tiny populations. “The last person to die from an unexploded bomb dropped in world war two probably hasn’t been born yet,” he told me. Fuller also marvels at the detailed records local wardens kept. They saw the danger that unexploded bombs would pose for future generations. In keeping those records, they reached out a helping hand from past to present.
In contrast to their second world war counterparts, modern bomb-disposal teams come armed with robot-mounted cameras, mic steths that can be operated from a distance, and X-ray machines that can penetrate thick layers of steel to examine the explosive content inside. “Risk to life comes above everything – for the public, but also for us – and risk to property comes second,” Hambley told me. But when a bomb is 80 years old, even this equipment can be unreliable.
At RAF Northolt, a 500kg German bomb was perched on a grassy verge. The bomb, which was inert, had been placed there, at an awkward angle, for bomb-disposal technicians to assess in pairs: what type of bomb is it? Which fuze? What action can be taken? I approached the bomb with Maj Matt Walker, the squadron duty officer. It was roughly the length of a two-seat sofa: a long, thin hunk of dull metal, its surface rough and textured with rust. Walker told me that a device this size would have a blast radius of “a few hundred to a thousand metres”.
Without clear markings, trainees would have to use their knowledge to work out whether the fuze had a mechanical timer, or an additional anti-handling fuze: a booby-trap built into the bomb that detonates it if anyone tries to move it or remove the main fuze. The trainees had to work out what to do next. “It’s extreme problem solving,” said Walker. “Someone described it to me the other day as – you start by juggling five books, then someone throws a glass ball and you have to keep that juggling as well. They then throw a ball of fire.” If you drop one of the balls, you and those nearby will probably die.
We left the 500kg bomb where it was and walked into the “museum”, a grand name for a few long, dusty shelves inside a garage that acts as a visual reference library. “Anything and everything will turn up here,” said Walker. He picked up a tapered, hollow metal tube. “This one is actually a kid’s baseball bat. But it got called in.” They’d hung on to this and other red herrings so that trainees could see, in practice, how easy it is to mistake something for a bomb. The other miscellanea included an internal part from the Citroën 2CV car that looks so much like a bomb that people regularly call 999 after finding it in a scrapyard. Until I looked at the items in the museum, I hadn’t fully grasped how little there is to go on: the munitions are not just rusted but distorted, sometimes missing pieces, completely blank. Translating these rusted lumps of metal into something legible requires an expert eye: a cylindrical shape with a curved end means it could be a German SC50, particular fuze pocket positioning can identify a British SAP250.
There is a generational difference between bomb-disposal technicians in the UK. People who qualified before 2012 cut their teeth in Afghanistan, where the Taliban laid an extraordinary number of IEDs. In 2011 alone, US-led forces recorded 16,800 IED incidents, roughly 46 a day. Those who qualified after 2012 tend to have mainly worked on second world war munitions. Hambley’s own career has mapped this change. His first job as a bomb-disposal officer was in Helmand in 2012, walking toward a buried device while live rounds tore past his ear. These days, the problems are different: orchestrating large-scale evacuations of civilians, trying to avoid property damage. “You’ve got a lot more latitude than when you’re deployed in Afghanistan,” Hambley told me. “In the UK, we own the ground, no one is going to shoot at us, we’ve got time, so we can afford to be as safe as we possibly can be.” Caution, though, is slow – and the moment a bomb is discovered, the clock is ticking to get people back into their homes.
Sitting at her desk overlooking Exmouth Marina, Fiona Bolt, a chartered financial planner in her 60s, could see the bomb on the dredger. At about 3pm on Wednesday 14 January, police knocked on the office door and told Bolt and her four colleagues to pack up and leave. “It was really quite scary,” she told me. By 8pm, the safety cordon had expanded from 100 to 400 metres and police started knocking on doors on streets near the marina. Some people went to stay with family members nearby, others in hotels. One of the Bolts’ neighbours ended up sleeping in their car.
As the night set in, Kidman’s team was out on the water, trying to see inside the bomb. The first X-ray images of the fuze were unusable: the steel casing, thickened and blistered by rust, defeated the beam. They spent seven hours cycling through different X-ray equipment, trying to get a clear image. As Kidman worked through the night, he could see lights going on and off at the far end of Exmouth harbour, in flats that would ideally be empty. Police can’t force anyone to leave. When someone refuses, police hand them a letter saying they’re staying at their own risk, and the regiment has to work around them. In Great Yarmouth three years ago, Hambley worked to render a 250kg bomb safe with a resident “teeth-chatteringly close” – less than 50 metres away.
When Bolt got up the next morning, she noticed her street, close to the marina, was eerily empty. When Bolt left the house she saw how far the exclusion zone had expanded along the seafront: it now encompassed 400 metres, and 2,000 properties. She didn’t have an office to go to. “I felt really lost, like a rabbit in headlights,” she said. “It was all just so out of my control.” The council had hastily assembled makeshift shelters out of a leisure centre and retirement home. When Bolt stopped by the leisure centre that day, she saw that camp beds and bedding had been brought in during the night, and Tesco had donated food. “If we’d been in wartime,” she said, “I imagine that’s what the community spirit was like.”
By about 5pm, it was clear Bolt would not be going home that night. Her house was deep within the cordon. She stuffed essentials into a rucksack and walked across town to her son’s house. By 9pm the cordon had crept up to 600 metres, encompassing a further 500 homes, cleared block by block by police officers. This was a big operation, but in Germany, where far more unexploded ordnance lies buried, even larger scale evacuations are common. In September 2017, 60,000 people were cleared from central Frankfurt, including two hospitals, so that a 1.8-tonne British “blockbuster” bomb could be defused. In 2025, the city of Cologne alone carried out 19 evacuations for wartime bombs, affecting almost 70,000 residents.
At their respective sites, Dooley and Kidman were both acutely aware of the disruption around them, which adds an intense time pressure to their work. In Plymouth, all the buildings within a 100-metre radius of the building site had been evacuated on Wednesday, including the school. Dooley’s first X-rays, taken with the standard equipment, had come out completely black. At around 4pm on Thursday, high-sensitivity X-ray plates arrived from elsewhere in the country. Finally, a readable answer. The bomb had no mechanical fuze, and no anti-handling device. Dooley breathed a sigh of relief. “People could just calm down a little bit,” he said. “It wasn’t going to tick if you knocked it.”
Soon afterwards, in the late afternoon, the high-sensitivity X-ray machine arrived in Exmouth. It went out on to the dredger. The team started scanning, and kept going for hours. Still nothing. Kidman reported back to the operations team: they couldn’t identify the fuze.
The forward base in Exmouth was the lifeboat station, and over the course of Thursday it filled up with marina staff, police, coastguard and emergency planning officers from the council. Briefings and strategy meetings took place every few hours. The position of the bomb severely limited the normal mitigation procedures. The regiment’s standard protection for a 250kg bomb is a sand-filled fortification weighing about 350 tonnes. This could not be built on a barge. Abrasive cutting, an advanced technique for cutting out the fuze, was not deemed appropriate. The next option was towing the dredger out to sea and blowing the whole thing up. Griffin, the marina’s compliance manager, phoned its insurers to ask whether this would be covered. Most marine policies carry an act-of-war exclusion, which raises a difficult question: after 80 years, is a Luftwaffe bomb still an act of war? “We went round in circles, really,” said Griffin.
This is a sensitive subject for 11EOD. In February 2021, a 1,000kg German bomb – one of the heaviest in the Luftwaffe’s arsenal – was discovered on a construction site next to Exeter University’s halls of residence. The team could not establish if the bomb was booby-trapped so it decided to do a controlled detonation where it was, with 400 tonnes of sand around it to absorb the blast. It was not enough. The explosion, which was heard for miles, left a crater the size of a double-decker bus in the ground and threw debris at least 250 metres, shattering windows of nearby buildings. The university claimed on its all-risks policy; the insurer, Allianz, declined, citing a clause excluding damage “occasioned by war”. The high court found in favour of the insurer. The military was not financially liable for this, but the experience of having every step of its process picked over in court made the unit even more cautious. “We are very aware that everything could end up in court and everything could be questioned,” said Hambley.
Caution pulled one way and time pressure – the need to get people back into their homes in Exmouth and kids back to school in Plymouth – pulled another. The idea of exploding the entire dredger was ruled out due to the risk of environmental pollution from the 20,000 litres of fuel on board and fragmentation of the vessel itself. That left only one option: get the bomb into the water and tow it away to detonate safely at sea. But this left a question: how to remove it?
By 11pm on Thursday 15 January, there was a plan for the smaller bomb in Plymouth: lift it out, place it in a 4x4 packed with sandbags, drive it 1km to the water’s edge, take it out to sea and blow it up there. By 12.30am, police and fire crews were going door-to-door to evacuate everyone who lived within 150 metres of the route. At about 2.30am, Dooley and another bomb operator lifted the 50kg bomb out of the pit with their hands, climbing up on a makeshift staircase they had built out of sandbags. The bomb, slick with mud, was cold and heavy. It was dark, and the steps, wedged deep in a muddy pit, were slippery. They placed the bomb carefully into the back of the waiting vehicle. The convoy slowly moved off, at walking pace. As the vehicles passed by, the police released the cordon, letting people back into their houses while the bomb was still crawling towards the sea.
Once it was at the water’s edge, the bomb was carried down on to a boat and lowered over the side, where a buoyancy device was waiting so that it could be dragged along underwater at a safe distance from the boat. Dooley was aboard the navy boat, which lowered the bomb into the water as it got further away from the harbour. He’d had two hours sleep in the preceding 36 hours.
The King’s Harbour Master, which controls shipping in Plymouth Sound, had given permission for the bomb to be detonated in a specific patch of sea, and they sailed out four nautical miles towards this spot. At the drop point, Dooley fixed an explosive charge to the bomb and had it lowered down to the seabed. A navy diver followed the rope down in the dark. It was pitch black and the water was thick with silt, rendering a torch useless. Working by touch, the diver undid the bolts, let the air out of the float and brought it to the surface.
When the diver came back up, Dooley took the boat back a hundred metres. From there, the only thing showing the location of the bomb was a small lit float attached with a line, bobbing on the surface of the water. The swell of the waves kept hiding it. Police drones confirmed nobody on shore was in danger. The navy confirmed there was nothing on radar at sea. The charge was initiated. Dooley counted down.
At 5.13am on Friday 16 January, the sea briefly lit in the dark. A plume of white water rose above the surface, then nothing. Eight decades after it was dropped, the bomb had been detonated.
As this unfolded in Plymouth on Thursday night and into Friday morning, Exmouth Marina was empty except for the military bomb-disposal team and the two marina staffers. “It was quite eerie,” said Hockings-Thompson, the marina manager. “It was like going back to Covid times.” They were all focused on how to get the bomb off the dredger. Someone suggested bringing the dredger in closer, but moving the boat meant moving the bomb, and nobody wanted to risk it.
Griffin went back into the office and called a local crane hire company, who agreed to bring a 55-tonne crane. The next problem was who would drive it. Senior officers including Fisher scrambled to find a military crane operator qualified to drive a 55-tonne crane, available at short notice. They could not. The civilian crane driver who had brought it over offered to do it himself. “I can’t own the risk of him driving that crane,” said Fisher, who held the military liability. That passed the question to the police, who had to decide whether to authorise a civilian to handle an unexploded bomb – and whose financial responsibility it would be if the crane was destroyed. “If the worst happens,” Fisher said, “we’ve got much bigger problems than losing the crane.” Eventually, they let him go ahead. (The crane driver declined to speak to me for this article.)
After midnight, in the early hours of Friday 16 January, bomb-disposal operator Lt Matt Bowden attached straps around the bomb casing and added a buoyancy device. He left the dredger and the crane lifted the bomb. As the 250kg lifted from the deck, the barge rose in the water. They had discussed this in advance: whether the dredger, suddenly lighter, would bob up hard enough to bump into the bomb and trigger something. The dredger heaved. The bomb swung out to the side and missed the steel vessel entirely. It was lowered into the water and attached to a navy boat.
Everything now depended on the tides. There was a fixed window in which it could be towed out and detonated. At about 4.30am, the boat picked its way through moored yachts with the bomb submerged and trailing 100 metres behind. By 6.30am, the bomb was so far out and deep underwater that residents were allowed back to their homes.
Hockings-Thompson and Griffin, who had been mostly awake for the preceding 48 hours, went aboard the dredger to bring it back into the marina. Then they walked up to a coffee shop on the seafront. They were in the queue at 8.13am when the bomb went off, a mile and a half out. “The whole seafront was full of people expecting to see a massive bang and a splash,” said Griffin. “All we got was a bit of a plop.” The sea had done its job and neutralised the blast.
By 11am, businesses around the marina were open again. Kidman was exhilarated. “No one died, there was no injury, no damage to infrastructure,” he said. After working for 36 hours straight, everyone went home to sleep. For Dooley, after his own successful operation in Plymouth, it was only a few hours later, when he was sitting with his family, that the magnitude of what had happened hit him. “You’re just doing your job,” he said. “Then you sit there and think, what have I done here? A 50kg could kill you as much as a 1,000kg.”
In late summer, about six months after the double bomb discovery, I sat in the bar at Vauxhall Barracks with Dooley, Kidman, Fisher, Boyce and others who had worked on the two operations. It was a wood-panelled room with a blue patterned carpet, the wall adorned with regiment photos and a framed Private Eye cover of the Queen meeting Martin McGuinness in a bomb-disposal suit. As I pressed for details, they found their recollections blurring. Was a particular memory from 14 January? Or was it the 250kg Plymouth bomb that was found in April outside an Aldi? The one found in June at a business park in Coventry? “So much has happened since then,” said Boyce. In fact, WO Sarah Rowland, who had worked with Dooley on the bomb in Plymouth, was unable to join the meeting as that morning she’d been called out to Staffordshire, where a 500kg bomb had been found in a quarry. (She texted Dooley to say she was collecting them all, “like Pokémon cards”.)
They are getting busier. Ten years ago, one or two large airdropped weapons were found each year. This year there have already been six. The latest was on 21 September, when a 115kg American bomb was found in the water off Pendennis headland, at the mouth of Falmouth’s harbour. The call went to Dooley, but he was already on another job. Kidman was assigned to it and drove down to Cornwall, where he spent almost all of the next three days awake, problem solving. The job was complicated. Blowing it up where it lay risked rupturing waste tanks 40 metres away and pouring sewage into the Channel. Instead, more than 300 households were evacuated while the navy lifted the bomb and towed it out to deep water. It was too dangerous to send a navy diver down, so the bomb was left on the seabed, far from anyone, while the regiment counted down the hours.
On 27 September, with the clock on the Falmouth bomb still running, another call came in: three white vans near RAF Fairford, a Gloucestershire base used by American bombers. A major counter-terror operation began. Kidman and Rowland drove to the scene. A robot searched the vans. X-rays followed. They helped each other out, catching some sleep in the car when possible. Kidman was still overseeing the bomb in Falmouth. On 28 September, they found that there were no explosives in the white vans. Kidman went home to sleep. At 2.25pm on 29 September, the timer was up on the bomb in Falmouth, so the team went back to detonate it at sea. “And then,” Kidman said, “we’re ready for the next bomb, I guess.”

“I don’t think I’m happy in the happiest country in the world”: The question that took an international from being a student to opening a restaurant chains in Copenhagen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Bruce Kim’s first months in Denmark left him with a question. He had moved from South Korea to a country repeatedly described as one of the happiest in the world, but after living there for six months, he was not convinced. “I don’t think I’m happy,” he remembers thinking.
Kim, now 40, had arrived in Denmark in 2010 as an exchange student at DTU, the Technical University of Denmark. He was studying transportation, and Denmark had not been some long-held ambition. In fact, it had been the only exchange option available through his university in South Korea. “If there had been more choices, I don’t think I would have chosen Denmark,” he said. To him, Denmark was an “unknown country,” associated with agriculture, cheese, milk, high prices and cold weather. He had also heard it was difficult to make friends. “Denmark wouldn’t have been my first choice.”
Today, Kim runs the restaurant chain Kopan, with four restaurants and a food truck and employs around 40 people. He never trained as a chef and did not come to Denmark to become an entrepreneur. Food was not even the original point. What eventually became a business started as an attempt to understand the country he had unexpectedly landed in, and Kim still does not see what he is doing today as entirely separate from that first experiment. “I think I’m still doing the same thing,” he said. “I’m still curious about Denmark as a society and about the happiness index.”
A reason to stay
Kim’s exchange semester at DTU was also the final semester of his bachelor’s degree in South Korea. “When I finished my exchange program at DTU, I automatically graduated from my university,” he said. Suddenly, he had several possible directions: return to South Korea to look for work, continue studying there or apply for a master’s degree elsewhere in Europe.
A professor at DTU encouraged him to stay after seeing how seriously he had approached his studies. Kim also applied to universities in Sweden and the United Kingdom, but Denmark had started to present him with a puzzle he wanted to solve.
Around the time he finished his exchange, Denmark was again receiving international attention for its place in global happiness rankings. Kim struggled to reconcile that reputation with his own experience. “Even though I had stayed in Denmark for six months, I didn’t think I was happy,” he said. Friends in South Korea were also asking him about it. They were seeing Denmark presented as an exceptionally happy country while South Korea was performing poorly in the same comparisons.
“My curiosity about the happiness index made me stay in Denmark for my master’s,” Kim said.
That curiosity deepened when a Korean broadcaster asked him to help with a documentary about happiness in Denmark. The subject was already on his mind, so he agreed. After the program aired in South Korea, he began receiving more questions from Korean viewers. “They asked me a lot of questions about what makes Denmark happy and how I felt about living in Denmark,” he said.
Kim did not feel he could simply answer them.
“I needed to find answers to those questions from the Korean audience,” he said.
By then he had completed his master’s degree. The obvious options were familiar ones: find a job, pursue a Ph.D. or return to South Korea. Instead, Kim decided to use part of the time he was allowed to remain in Denmark for something else. He gave himself a year and called the project “Delivering Happiness.”
“I wanted to know more about happiness from local people,” he said. But before he could ask Danes what made them happy, he needed a way to meet them.
Eight minutes with a stranger
Kim needed what he called a “tool” to make strangers stop and talk to him. At the time, he said, Korea was still unfamiliar to many of the people he met in Denmark. “A lot of people asked me, ‘Are you from North Korea or South Korea?’”
That gave him an idea. He could introduce a small part of Korean culture and, at the same time, ask Danes about their own society.
“I thought food might be a good way to meet people,” he said.
With permission from Copenhagen Municipality, Kim went onto the streets with a bicycle and began making Korean pancakes. The food itself was simple, but one detail made it particularly useful for his experiment: a pancake took around eight minutes to prepare.
“I thought eight minutes might be a good amount of time to have a small interview,” he said.
So while people waited for their food, Kim asked them about happiness. He spoke with students and other people he met on the street about education, satisfaction and what they believed made life in Denmark work. He then shared their stories online for the Korean audience that had been asking him those same questions.
The project gradually became known beyond the people who happened to encounter his bicycle. Kim said some Danes started approaching him specifically because they had heard about what he was doing and wanted to contribute. “They came to my bicycle and talked about their stories,” he said. “Not because they were interested in my pancakes, but because they were interested in my project.”
The idea, as Kim understood it, was that their experiences might offer something useful to people in South Korea. “They thought their interviews and their stories could also contribute to Korean society and maybe help increase happiness in Korea,” he said.
As a social experiment, Kim felt it was working.
As a food business, less so.
“I didn’t make much money,” he said. The pancake itself, he admitted, was not necessarily the main attraction. But that did not bother him. The calculation was different. More pancakes meant more conversations.
“If I sold 10 pancakes, that meant I had interviewed 10 people,” he said.
For a year, that was enough.
‘I kept it secret’
There was one group of people Kim was not interviewing about the project: his parents.
They knew their son had completed his studies in Denmark and was trying to establish his career abroad. They did not know that instead of working in transportation, he was cycling through Copenhagen and selling pancakes to strangers.
“I kept it secret,” Kim said. “I didn’t tell my parents about the project for a year.”
When he spoke with them, he presented a different version of his life. “I told them, ‘I’m looking for a job. I haven’t found one yet, but don’t worry about me. I still have two more years.’”
Eventually, the secret did not hold. His parents discovered what he had been doing through an interview Kim had given to a Korean broadcaster. They were disappointed that he had not told them the truth, and his father was also disappointed by the choice itself.
“My father was disappointed that I was selling pancakes on the street,” Kim said.
He understood the reaction. His parents had expectations for what would follow after their son went abroad and completed a master’s degree. Selling pancakes on the streets of Copenhagen was not the obvious next step.
Kim himself was still far from certain that it was.
After the first year of the project, he returned to South Korea. He told his family that he had enjoyed the experiment, but he would take a more conventional route when he went back to Denmark. “Maybe I’ll just find a job when I go back to Denmark,” he told them.
But when he returned, he still did not know what that job would be. “I only had two years left, and I hadn’t found a job,” he said. “I didn’t know what to do.”
Then something happened that changed the way he thought about the project.
A conversation after tragedy
During Kim’s journey back to Denmark in 2014, a passenger ferry sank in South Korea with many students on board. Kim first heard information suggesting the students had been rescued. “I felt relieved. I thought there was nothing to worry about,” he said.
When he reached Copenhagen Airport, he learned that many had died.
“The news caused me a lot of stress and worry,” he said.
In Copenhagen, Kim gathered with other Koreans at a church. “I shared how I was feeling,” he said. The people there had different lives and professions, and they began talking about their experiences in Denmark. Their conversations included the way Denmark approached safety, work and education.
“Those stories touched me,” Kim said.
He had spent a year collecting stories from Danes and sending them toward South Korea. Now he was listening to Koreans in Denmark describe what they themselves had experienced in the country.
The conversation gave Kim another idea. “I believed that if I wanted to bring more good stories from Denmark to Korea, I needed to bring more Koreans to Denmark so they could have their own experiences.”
That created a practical problem.
“In order to do that, I needed to create jobs.”
The pancake project went back onto the street.
When people started coming for the food
Starting again was not much easier. “It was a hard time for me,” Kim said. “The winter was long, very cold and rainy.”
There was another problem: the original pancake still was not particularly suited to Danish customers.
Kim’s Danish friends began telling him why they thought it was not working. The pancake was sweet, used sugar and was fried in oil. They suggested adapting it, including by adding kimchi.
Kim rejected the idea.
“In Korea, we don’t eat kimchi with bread,” he said. “We eat kimchi with rice.”
His friends kept insisting.
“Bruce, in Denmark people eat bread, not rice,” Kim remembers them telling him. “Maybe you can try.”
Eventually he did. Kim began making versions with fillings such as kimchi and bulgogi.
“Suddenly, we got a lot of attention from local people,” he said.
For perhaps the first time, people were not only interested in the social experiment. They also wanted the food.
The project eventually received a fixed spot at a Copenhagen food market. Kim said the opportunity was connected not only to what he was selling but also to the social purpose behind it. His project shared stories from Denmark with people in South Korea, and Kim also provided pancakes to homeless people in Denmark based on his sales.
“We were helping both Denmark and Korea,” he said.
The experiment had started to become a business, even if Kim had not set out to build one.
Four restaurants, almost by accident
A fixed location solved one problem but created another. During the summer, outdoor sales were strong enough for Kim to employ people. In winter, customers moved indoors and sales dropped.
That left him with a choice he did not like.
“In winter, people went inside, so we couldn’t sell many pancakes,” he said. “That meant I would have to fire my employees.”
Instead, he opened a restaurant nearby.
“To keep my employees and my staff, I needed to open a restaurant next door,” he said.
The first restaurant, then, was not simply an attempt to expand. It was a way to keep the people already working for him employed through the winter. The outdoor operation and restaurant could support each other across different parts of the year.
From there, the operation continued growing.
By the time of the interview, Kim said he had four restaurants as well as the food truck, with around 40 employees.
It is a long way from studying transportation at DTU, and an even longer way from the eight-minute conversations beside a bicycle. But when asked how it feels to have ended up in an entirely different career, Kim pushes back slightly against the premise.
“Denmark gave me the chance to choose something different,” he said. He had not been trained in food and had not entered Denmark planning to work in restaurants. “But my curiosity about Denmark and happiness brought me to this project and eventually to this business.”
To Kim, the method has changed much more than the purpose.
“I’m still curious about Denmark as a society and about the happiness index,” he said. “I still want to share what we have experienced in Denmark with Korea, and I want to bring more Korean people to Denmark.”
“If someone asks me why I run these restaurants, I still tell them I’m curious about Denmark,” he added. “I still want to bring more Danes to Korea too.”
‘I need to knock on many doors’
Turning the experiment into a company also exposed Kim to another side of being a foreigner in Denmark.
“The first thing was that there wasn’t much information,” he said.
Starting a business meant figuring out how to create a company, handle taxes and employ people. Kim said more information is available in English today, but when he started, finding those answers was difficult.
“I had to knock on many people’s doors,” he said. “‘Could you tell me how to open a company? How do I pay taxes?’”
His Danish friends became part of the process. “A lot of my Danish friends helped me with the project,” he said. “Otherwise, it would have been impossible to start a business or a project as a foreigner.”
That reliance on other people also shaped the way Kim sees the broader challenge of making a life in Denmark. He believes foreigners often arrive without knowing much about the country, while Danes may also have limited knowledge of the places newcomers come from. “There is an imbalance of information because people don’t know each other,” he said.
For people moving to Denmark, his advice is not to expect closeness to happen immediately. He believes newcomers need to make an effort to learn about Danish culture, study the language and build relationships.
“They’re not open in the beginning,” he said. “But if you make an effort to get closer to Danes and learn about Denmark, they open up slowly.”
“It takes some time.” Kim found his own shortcut, or at least his own starting point. “I feed them a lot of Korean food,” he said.
He would invite Danish friends home and offer them Korean barbecue. For someone who had once needed an excuse to spend eight minutes talking to strangers, sharing food became a way of getting past the distance he initially felt in Denmark.
“That’s why they really trust me through food,” Kim said.
Four restaurants and around 40 employees later, that part of the experiment has not changed very much. “That’s why I chose food for my project.”
