War-weary northern Israelis rethink loyalty to Netanyahu before election
- Northern Israelis, once strong supporters of Netanyahu, are reconsidering their votes due to dissatisfaction with his government's handling of ongoing conflicts with Hezbollah.
- The 2023-2024 war caused severe disruption, trauma, and displacement, shaking community trust and increasing calls for change amid prolonged violence and high living costs.
- Despite anger, some residents still back Netanyahu’s hawkish coalition, believing it offers the best protection against attacks and regional threats.
AI generated
Nahariya, Israel – On Israel’s border with Lebanon where Hezbollah fired thousands of rockets and drones, previous backers of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu say they are rethinking how they will vote in the first election since the war.
“Many I know were right-wing and were Bibi supporters, and today they’re not,” said plant nursery owner Sigal Malachi, using a nickname for Israel’s longest-serving premier.
In traditional strongholds of Netanyahu support, many told AFP they could no longer back his right-wing government in the Oct 27 vote, accusing it of failing to secure a lasting quiet with the militants.
Hezbollah, an Iran-backed Lebanese militant group, began firing into Israel in October 2023 in support of Hamas following the deadliest-ever attack on the country.
The barrages altered life in northern communities, displacing tens of thousands of Israelis and forcing people like Malachi to close shop for several years.
Northern Israelis are accustomed to incoming fire from the Lebanese side of the border, but they say that round of conflict was more intense.
“We grew up with Katyushas (rockets) and bombs,” said Malachi, whose plant nursery reopened in March. “This war was different.”
She described that “if you went outside, within a second you’d be running” for shelter.
The war was halted with a fragile ceasefire in November 2024, but evacuees were not allowed home until early 2025.
Life began slowly returning to normal, until the northern front reopened after the outbreak of the Iran war.
Maxim Zarbaylov, who was born in the former Soviet Union but has long lived in Nahariya, the northern-most Israeli town on the Mediterranean, is among those wavering. “All my life I voted for (Likud), for Bibi Netanyahu... But this year I want to vote for (Gadi) Eisenkot,” he said, referring to the former military chief who is Netanyahu’s main election rival.
Hezbollah has repeatedly dragged Lebanon into conflicts with Israel, most recently in March with rocket fire at Israel in support of Iran. Israel has in turn seized what it calls a “security zone” in Lebanon, where the authorities say Israeli attacks have killed more than 4,300 people.
At least 48 Israeli civilians and 30 soldiers have died on the Lebanese front since 2023.
‘Psychological catastrophe’
The prolonged violence has left border residents in limbo.
“After Oct 7, we don’t sleep well any more,” Malachi said. “I’ve thought about leaving. But the roots are so deep that I’m staying.”
In Shlomi, an Israeli border town, the enemy is a tangible presence behind a hill. Shadi Tuma, who owns a supermarket there, prides himself on running the only one that remained open.
“This area is under a trauma we haven’t seen before. There’s anger. The government is unable to provide a comprehensive response,” he said. “It’s a huge psychological catastrophe. Not everyone is able to cope with a war that lasts three years.”
The war has cracked the local support base for Netanyahu, Tuma said. In the last elections in 2022, the premier’s Likud party won 43% of the vote in Shlomi, compared with 23% nationwide.
Residents who backed Netanyahu “now want change because they no longer trust this government”, Tuma said.
He said the high cost of living was a major complaint.
“Many people I see are struggling to make it to the end of the month.”
For Tuma, the conflict is also personal. He was born in Lebanon, the son of a fighter with the South Lebanon Army, a militia that fought alongside Israel in the 1980s and that had many fighters granted Israeli citizenship.
‘Feel protected’
The war could have shifted longstanding political loyalties in towns like Nahariya, a sleepy resort of about 70,000 people.
In 2022, 38% of voters there chose Likud. But Zarbaylov says there is anger over the failure to stop Hamas’ unprecedented assault on the country.
“What happened on Oct 7, Bibi could have prevented it, but he didn’t,” he said. “The army, the top commanders, the chief of staff, could have prevented it.”
Others believe only the current hawkish coalition can protect them.
Patrice Haddad retired to Nahariya from Paris a year ago, drawn by the town’s “charm”.
Israel’s “Law of Return” allows any Jew anywhere in the world to immigrate and automatically receive citizenship.
Adjusting to life under the rockets was not simple at first.
“We were told we had 30 seconds to find shelter” after sirens blared, he said. “In reality, sometimes we only had 15, sometimes less.”
For his first election as an Israeli, he has made his choice.
“The left in Israel has done a lot of harm, it wanted to give up territories,” he said. “It’s important to vote for the right, because for me, with a government like Netanyahu’s, we will feel protected.” AFP

How Christian Networks in Asia Are Shaping Support for Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
02:59:00 UTC
11:59:00 KST

With much of the international discourse, specifically in North America and Europe, focused on criticizing Israel, a large group of international Christian leaders congregated in Jerusalem to show support. One of the key participants was senior Filipino pastor Bishop Dr. David A. Sobrepeña who leads a large evangelical community across the Philippine islands. Bishop Sobrepeña is the founder of Word of Hope Christian Ministries which includes 43 satellite churches and hosts 70 services on any given Sunday across Manila. Partaking in this year’s event, Bishop Sobrepeña stated, “For Christians in the Philippines, the opportunity to come here and pray in Jerusalem is deeply meaningful. We also come to listen to the people of Israel and to carry their stories back to the churches and communities we serve.”
The Bishop was one of more than 550 prominent Christian leaders with vast followings who recently participated in a 10-day Eagles’ Wings delegation organized in conjunction with Bishop Sterns and Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Attendees hailed from 51 different nations and congregated around the Jewish holiday of Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles) in Jerusalem, commemorating the third anniversary of the October 7th attack. The gathering offers a window into a less frequently discussed dimension of the Israel debate: the continued mobilization of Christian communities in parts of Asia and the wider Global South around Israel.
Taking a closer look at Israel sentiment in Western countries, antisemitism interwoven with anti-Israel sentiment is on the rise. In 2025 the Anti Defamation League (ADL) recorded 6,274 antisemitic events in North America alone. The Hillel organization reported 2,334 incidents across U.S. campuses in the 2024-2025 academic year, stating that, “Antisemitic incidents on campus are at a record high in the past school year.”
In Western Europe the Community Security Trust (CST) recorded a staggering 3,700 antisemitic incidents across Britain over the course of 2025, the second highest annual total of such events ever recorded. French authorities cited 1,320 antisemitic acts in 2025, with France’s Interior Ministry calling it a “historically high” figure.
As sentiment over Israel grows increasingly polarized in the West, there are a number of well-educated Asian evangelical Christian communities who unequivocally support Israel, comprising the backbone of its support in the region. South Korea is home to nearly 9 million evangelical and Pentecostal Protestants who display the Israeli flag during rallies and prayers. Roughly 8 percent of Singapore’s population run a network of influential evangelical megachurches while boasting an active Christian Zionist movement that mobilizes fundraising initiatives, educational tours and pro-Israel forums.
The Philippines is a particularly heavy hitter on the East Asian evangelical pro-Zionist front with an estimated 13 million evangelical adherents within a predominantly Catholic milieu. A Pew study surveying Pentecostals across 10 nations highlighted that 67 percent of Filipino Pentecostals surveyed said they sympathized with Israel.
In this context, Eagles’ Wings has been working for the last three decades to bring tens of thousands of evangelical Christians from around the globe to Israel. The organization was founded by Bishop Robert Stearns who is a staunch supporter of Israel and an outspoken supporter of moving the United States Embassy to Jerusalem. In Stephen Spector’s 2008 book Evangelicals and Israel: The Story of American Christian Zionism, Bishop Stearns discusses Israel’s regional threat profile while declaring himself willing to “die defending Israel.” He has spoken on Israel’s behalf both at the House of Lords in London and the Israeli Knesset.
Stearns founded Eagles’ Wings with a clear mission in mind: Firsthand encounters with Israel can be utilized to strongly shape how large Christian networks around the world understand Israel and antisemitism. They have been working to achieve this goal by having brought 25,000+ Christians to the Holy Land, organizing Nexus Leadership Missions which offer intensive educational tours to global pastoral leaders, as well as spearheading the Christian answer to Birthright, dubbed the ‘Israel Experience’, bringing college-age Christian students to Israel.
One of the key events as part of this year’s Eagles’ Wings 10-day delegation was “Awake Jerusalem at the Tower of David.” The event took place on October 3 at Jerusalem’s iconic Tower of David with hundreds of Christian leaders from 51 different countries in attendance. The event showcased international Christian artists while also including communal worship being covered and broadcasted by Daystar Television Network, a media partner of Eagles’ Wings.
For Israel, the challenges that lie ahead are not merely diplomatic. As the international stage becomes increasingly harder to navigate the relationships that Israel fosters with Asia and the Global South may become of increasing strategic importance. This gathering of 550 Christian leaders from 51 nation-states demonstrates merely one aspect of this shifting climate. Prominent religious communities from the Philippines to Korea and Brazil to Kenya will be able to shape the conversation about Israel within their respective societies. The mobilization of these groups shows the potential benefits that Israel stands to reap from fostering non-traditional alliances and that vis-à-vis culture, religion and interpersonal connections a new path to diplomacy may emerge.

AI borrowing binge rattles US markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
02:55:00 UTC
11:55:00 KST

AI borrowing binge rattles US markets
- Tech giants like Google, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft have borrowed around US$500 billion since 2024 to fund AI infrastructure, marking a historic surge in corporate debt.
- Investors demand higher returns for lending to these firms, causing increased borrowing costs and reducing demand for US government bonds, pushing up US interest rates.
- Experts warn of financial risks if the AI boom slows, with potential market shocks and contagion fears linked to companies like Oracle facing debt and project delays.
AI generated
NEW YORK – The world’s richest companies can no longer rely on their massive cash piles alone to stay in the artificial intelligence race and have suddenly started borrowing massively in a shift that is sending repercussions across the world.
Rising US interest rates, including on the Treasury bonds that anchor the global economy, are sending tremors through the financial world, and some analysts point to the AI borrowing bonanza as one of the culprits.
From next to nothing in 2024, tech sector borrowing has reached around US$500 billion (S$640 billion) in the nine months since January, as Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and others raise debt hand over fist to finance the chips, servers and data centres that power AI.
Goldman Sachs expects a further ramp-up in 2027, to US$1.2 trillion.
“This is not something that we’ve seen before,” said Chris Della Fave, senior vice-president at fund-raising advisory firm Post Oak Group, who estimates that AI now accounts for 25% of all corporate bond issuance, up from 4% two years ago.
In inflation-adjusted terms, the AI sector is expected to borrow more in 2026 than US cable operators did to build out the entire internet, or than railroad companies did during the 19th-century US rail boom.
So far, investors have eagerly snapped up the chance to lend to the tech giants, but they have demanded returns that would have been unthinkable for such blue-chip companies not long ago.
Even Meta has had to offer more than 7% a year, while riskier cloud data centre specialists have gone above 9%.
The impact reaches well beyond the companies building AI – their debt is even starting to crowd out demand for the US government bonds that anchor the financial system.
An investor who might otherwise buy a US Treasury bond “might decide to buy Microsoft” instead, said Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial, referring to the tech giant’s bonds.
That shift pushes up the rates Washington pays to borrow, he explained.
This adds to the other force driving up US borrowing costs: inflation, fuelled by the war against Iran and high energy prices.
The interest rate on 10-year US government bonds – Wall Street’s benchmark and widely seen as the most important number in global finance, setting the tone for everything from mortgages to car loans – is now above 5.3%, its highest level since 2002.
‘Sharper correction’
Adding to the volatility, hedge funds had piled into US government bonds like never before, holding 7% of all those in circulation at the end of 2025, though that share has since fallen.
Hedge funds, which place big bets on markets, move their money far faster than more cautious investors such as insurers and pension funds.
Even if the war and the oil situation stabilised, Della Fave said, “I wouldn’t expect the yields to dramatically reduce, to be honest, because of this influence of the AI debt situation”.
Beyond the rising cost of borrowing, some are questioning the risks of betting on an AI boom that could hit a wall, as the dot.com bubble did in 2000.
Even a moderate slowdown in the frenzied pace of construction, delays on certain projects or weaker-than-expected revenue growth could trigger a shock in financial markets, Malek warned.
In late September, the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee warned that “the risk of a sharper correction persists”, particularly if concerns about the pace of AI development or adoption hit earnings expectations.
In July, amid some second-guessing about the AI boom, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index fell nearly 7%.
Against this backdrop, cloud specialist Oracle is sometimes seen as a bellwether.
With massive debt (US$125 billion), cash reserves that shrink every quarter and a possible delay on a huge data centre project in New Mexico, several warning lights are flashing for Larry Ellison’s group.
“Let’s say Oracle has a problem... They can’t pay for something,” Malek said. Trouble with its debt “could trigger contagion” across AI finance as a whole, he added. AFP

UN rights council condemns attacks on civilians in Sudan, calls for truce

UN rights council condemns attacks on civilians in Sudan, calls for truce
Resolution demands an immediate ceasefire and extends the mandate of the mission investigating abuses in Sudan.
The United Nations Human Rights Council has condemned drone strikes and other attacks on civilians in Sudan, warning warring parties that there is “no military solution to the crisis” in the country.
The statement on Monday came as the World Food Programme said an air attack had hit a truck carrying food supplies in North Kordofan, killing one person.
In Geneva, the 47-member council adopted a resolution extending the mandate of its independent international fact-finding mission for Sudan by a vote of 28 to 10, with nine abstentions.
Sudan urged member states to reject the measure, stating the council had failed to take its reservations into account.
The war between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which began in April 2023, has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced more than 13 million, according to estimates cited by human rights groups.
The resolution demanded “an immediate and complete ceasefire by all parties, without preconditions”, along with an independent monitoring mechanism and the restoration of basic infrastructure.
It condemned widespread violations of international humanitarian law by both the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF, citing “indiscriminate attacks against civilians” and “indiscriminate aerial bombardments and drone strikes resulting in civilian deaths and the destruction of critical infrastructure”, including schools and hospitals.
Both sides have sharply increased their use of drones in recent months. UN figures show that drone strikes killed more than 1,100 people in the first five months of the year alone.
The council also condemned outside interference in the war, warning that illicit financial networks, illegal arms transfers and foreign mercenaries continue to fuel the fighting.
The fact-finding mission, which gathers evidence of abuses by both sides, concluded in February that the RSF’s siege and capture of the North Darfur capital, el-Fasher, bore “the hallmarks of genocide”.
As the last military stronghold in Darfur to fall after a months-long siege, el-Fasher saw civilians systematically deprived of food and medicine before facing mass summary executions, investigators found.
They documented ethnic killings aimed mainly at non-Arab groups, widespread sexual violence and the destruction of medical facilities.
Separately, the WFP said in a statement that the airstrike that hit its convoy travelling between Dilling and Kadugli in South Kordofan killed one driver and damaging life-saving food.
The agency stressed that the vehicles were clearly marked with official humanitarian logos. The attack took place on Saturday and came just 24 hours after another WFP vehicle detonated an explosive device in Dilling following a food distribution run, it said.
“Humanitarian workers and aid assets are not targets,” the WFP said, demanding a transparent probe to hold perpetrators accountable under international law.

‘We’re still short on combat troops’: IDF reserve chief warns of mounting strain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
02:53:24 UTC
11:53:24 KST

“We are at a historic moment, reshaping the entire Middle East for years to come. From the very first moment, the reserve force has fought shoulder to shoulder with the standing army, carrying out the same missions, and it continues to do so,” said Brig. Gen. Benny Ben Ari, the IDF’s chief reserve officer, nearly three years after Oct. 7, which dramatically expanded the reserve force and transformed it from a supporting element into a central fighting force.
The numerical growth of the reserve force has been significant. Exact figures are barred from publication due to military censorship restrictions, but since Oct. 7 the force has grown by more than 130,000 reservists — combat troops and combat support personnel.
“We understand that we are not going back to Oct. 6, so we are building the reserve force differently,” Ben Ari said. “Reservists used to serve 20 days once every three years.”
The IDF has taken a number of steps over the past three years to increase the number of reservists as much as possible and contend with the enormous strain involved in serving hundreds of reserve duty days a year. Among other measures, it expanded the number of personnel entering the reserves after completing mandatory service, brought inactive reservists back into service, raised the exemption age for certain positions to maintain operational continuity and issued a special call-up order allowing tens of thousands of people who had previously been removed from the reserve force to return to service even though they were still of reserve-service age.
In addition, the IDF General Staff held recruitment drives aimed at bringing reservists who had been inactive for various reasons back into service and assigning them to units and positions. In 2025, eight such drives were held, drawing 16,111 participants, 87% of whom were placed back into service. In 2026, four drives were held, with 94% of the 8,059 participants placed back into service.
Among the results has been the establishment of a number of new reserve formations, including the Hashomer Brigade and the 96th and 38th divisions.
‘We can’t provide certainty’
As impressive as those figures may be, they mask a troubling reality of almost unimaginable strain. While a significant portion of Israel’s population remains outside the circle of military service amid the absence of an equitable conscription law and widespread draft avoidance, the hundreds of thousands who do report for duty are buckling under the burden.
Ben Ari openly warns of the mounting strain and says the system is being stretched to its limits.
“Every time there was some kind of peak, everyone we called showed up. The problem is that we no longer have the ability to provide certainty. A reservist who knows when their service begins and ends can plan their life around it. But that’s not the situation. We have not been able to give them that certainty because different fronts have heated up, and they have been called up from time to time.
“The challenges a reservist faces during their first stint of reserve duty are very different from those they face during their third or fifth. It changes from one stint to another in many respects. We are at a point where the reservists are fully committed to us, and even the next time we call them, they will come. But they will probably pay a heavy price in the support systems around them. Those systems are already nearing their limit.”
According to Ben Ari, employment is particularly problematic.
“Reservists are protected from dismissal by their employers for 60 days. But a private employer who has someone in a managerial position and that employee is gone for three months is put in a very difficult position. Ultimately, managers will prefer someone who is there.
“There is a sense in the country that the period of intensive fighting is over, that there is no deep ground maneuver, but we still need large numbers of reservists. I also think workplaces that hold on to their reservists will benefit because, ultimately, these are the best people. Employers who know how to accommodate reservists will benefit in the long run.”
The defense establishment and the government have also sought to address the burden through an extensive support system developed through a series of government decisions over the years. These have ranged from assistance funds and special grants in 2023 to family grants, emotional support and subsidies for tuition and vacations in 2024, followed by expanded assistance for students, mental health support and digital wallets in 2025 and 2026.
In addition, the IDF Personnel Directorate launched the “Ma’agal HaSherut” (“Service Cycle”) program, a General Staff initiative intended to reduce burnout through dedicated unit budgets, mental health support and training for personnel assigned specifically to assist reservists. Targeted assistance has also been developed for groups at greater risk of burnout, including students, through tutoring and academic accommodations, as well as reservists who own small businesses.
‘We are still short on combat troops’
But despite all the assistance, repeatedly reporting for duty under immense strain ultimately depends on the reservists themselves.
“These are people who have spent more time with one another than they have at home, so they don’t leave us. Those who volunteered at the beginning of the war are still with us,” Ben Ari said.
“Being a reservist is not easy. It is challenging. We know that having a reservist serve 100 days a year wears them down. But today it is clear to everyone — the IDF, the State of Israel and its citizens — that without a strong reserve force, we will face serious challenges.
“Fortunately, despite the unimaginable price the reservists are paying — particularly combat troops — in terms of those killed and wounded, those suffering psychological injuries and the personal toll on the support systems around them, reservists continue to report for duty and fight.
“For the first time, there is an understanding both by the state and the IDF that we are responsible for reservists even when they are not in uniform. We are building mechanisms and tools to address the needs of reservists, and that is something they see.”
According to the chief reserve officer, there is no alternative.
“I think the war demonstrated in the clearest possible way the enormous importance of the reserve force to the State of Israel’s national security doctrine and the importance of keeping it fit, trained and equipped.
“For this system to withstand the challenges facing the State of Israel over time, reserve service must be elevated to a national status. The state must recognize and honor the reservist as its finest citizen for risking their life for the country.
“At the same time, the entire support system around reservists needs assistance: more help at home, with the children, at workplaces and at universities. To preserve that support system while maintaining such an intense level of reserve service, we in the IDF must do everything possible to reduce the burden on those serving.
“We are short on combat troops. That is no secret, and the burden falls on the reserves. The IDF needs to be larger. I can use the entire reserve force to its absolute limit, and we will still be short on combat troops.”
Nearly three years after October 7, Ben Ari said: “These are very significant days. We have lost many friends and subordinates. I think the reserve force is the element that unites and connects the people of Israel as we contend with this war.
“It represents everyone and shows that when everyone comes together, we are unbeatable. The reserve force has fought on every front, fulfilled every mission against the enemy and continues to defeat it again and again.”

Throngs of Cornell University students rallied on Monday voicing solidarity with a classmate whose gang-rape allegations have ignited a national uproar and demanding that the Ivy League school take firmer action against sexual violence on campus.
The protesters called for an external inquiry into how the matter has been handled by Cornell's administration. The alleged gang-rape victim, identified by the pseudonym Jane Doe, has said the university failed to adequately investigate and punish the campus fraternity members who were involved.
Demonstrators also called for the resignation of Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other members of his administration, saying their policies have perpetuated what protesters called a "culture of rape" on campus.
In a lawsuit filed last month, Jane Doe said she was plied with drugs and alcohol and then sexually assaulted by several members of the campus chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024 after she had become incapacitated.
Doe, who was 20 at the time, named seven Chi Phi members as defendants in the suit, along with the fraternity chapter, a local bar, her own sorority, and the university.
She had reported the alleged assault to police several weeks after the fact, leading to an internal university investigation and a law enforcement probe, but the local prosecutor declined to bring criminal charges in the case.
Cornell shuts down fraternity, disciplines members after rape accusation
Cornell, which has defended its response to the original report, shut down the Chi Phi chapter and imposed a range of discipline on the fraternity members involved, including expulsions and other sanctions.
The men all denied any wrongdoing, some saying the sexual activity was consensual and others disputing their participation, the New York Times has reported, citing Cornell documents.
The lawsuit criticized the university for having offered some of the alleged perpetrators a chance to mitigate their penalties by writing essays.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul last Friday appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor to take over a newly reopened criminal investigation, saying she was "deeply disturbed" by how local authorities originally dealt with the case.
Monday's boisterous but orderly demonstration included a march by several hundred students, faculty supporters and community activists - perhaps 1,000 or more - through the campus in the upstate New York town of Ithaca.
The protesters, chanting "One struggle, one fight" and "No justice, no peace," filled Cornell's Ho Plaza, the central pedestrian square and gathering space on campus, and spilled over into adjacent areas. Many carried signs with slogans such as "Justice for Jane Doe," "We Stand for Survivors," and "Prison Sentences, not Topic Sentences."
Cornell rape victim threatened after filing lawsuit
The rally came a day after Doe and her lawyer said they had received multiple threats since filing the lawsuit, which has prompted a public outcry, particularly on social media under the banner "#IamJaneDoe," over why law enforcement declined to pursue charges in 2024.
The uproar also stirred a backlash by others who have questioned whether keeping Doe anonymous was fair because it denied those implicated in the matter the chance to publicly face their accuser.
Addressing the controversy on Saturday, Kotlikoff promised in a video message to examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus, saying, "being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility."

Cuba says US contacts fall short of formal talks as Trump pressure mounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
02:50:55 UTC
11:50:55 KST

Cuba and the United States have maintained “channels of communication” but are not engaged in any formal negotiations, Havana’s top diplomat in Washington told Reuters, as the Trump administration pursues a pressure campaign against the Communist-ruled island.
In an interview on Monday, Lianys Torres Rivera, chargé d’affaires at the embassy in Washington, said Cuba remains open to a “respectful” dialog but is “not naive” about President Donald Trump’s threats and has increased preparations to defend itself against any US military action.
The latest US-Cuba diplomatic contacts have included meetings, phone calls and WhatsApp messages, but the two sides have made no progress toward a negotiating agenda or restarting official talks, she said.
“What we have with the US is channels of communication,” Torres Rivera said. She declined to provide details on the timing, topics and participants.
Her description of the communications appears to fall short of Trump’s assertion at the United Nations last month that Secretary of State Marco Rubio was “deep into negotiations” with Havana.
Trump also called Cuba a "failed state” and predicted its government would fall. The Cuban delegation walked out in protest.
US says talks are ongoing as oil blockade strains Cuba
A US State Department spokesperson said: "It does not come to our surprise that the Cuban regime is circulating this propaganda. In all reality, talks are ongoing, and the regime has been unwilling thus far to agree to anything that would help the Cuban people, ultimately, threatening its total control.”
Trump has openly stated that his goal is to fundamentally change Cuba's government. A US-imposed oil blockade has put the country under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.
UN human rights experts have condemned the oil blockade as a violation of international law.
Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said at the end of June that talks initiated earlier this year with the US had stalled, and in early September that no talks were under way or planned.
Cuba rules out negotiating changes to its political system
Torres Rivera said Cuba’s “red line” remains that Havana is unwilling to negotiate any changes in its political system, seeing Trump’s demands for the removal of the Cuban leadership as a violation of sovereignty.
She rejected the Trump administration’s claims that Cuba was a threat to US national security or is interfering in US domestic affairs, and said Washington was using such accusations as a pretext to continue squeezing the island economically in what she called “collective punishment.”
A US official, responding to Reuters questions, reiterated Trump's assertion that “we will not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep.”
US tightens restrictions as Havana prepares for possible military action
The Trump administration tightened the embargo against Cuba last week, further restricting travel there by Americans and access to US banking for its private sector.
Those measures, said Torres Rivera, contradict US insistence that it wants Cuba to expand private enterprise.
Facing US pressure, Cuba unveiled free-market reforms in June that, if fully implemented, would represent the biggest change to the island's socialist economy since former leader Fidel Castro took control in 1959.
But Washington says the reforms do not go far enough and has also called for "free and fair" elections.
Despite the gaps, Trump predicted late last month that the US and Cuba “will make a deal,” adding, ”I don't think we'll need the military.”
But the Cuban government remains wary.
“Cuba has always been preparing for an aggression from the US,” Torres Rivera said. “And we are increasing our capabilities now more than ever before … It is to defend ourselves.”

India's Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said trade talks with the U.S. had reached a plateau, adding to growing skepticism around a deal between New Delhi and Washington.
"Negotiations are still ongoing, although we'd like to believe that both sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very very difficult," Sitharaman said, speaking to the press at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi on Monday.
The finance minister's comments come just after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer last week said a trade agreement was not 'imminent' even as the negotiations were ongoing.
Sitharaman's comments mark the first time India has acknowledged the challenges it faces in closing the trade deal with the U.S.
She said the U.S. wants to "reduce" its trade imbalance with India, and they want to make up "for all that they've lost over these years."
"When you're talking of trade and trade imbalance being the sole criteria to reduce the imbalance, to what extent beyond negotiation can you go," Sitharaman said.
The U.S. goods trade deficit with India was $58.42 billion in 2025, a 27.8% increase ($12.7 billion) over 2024. In the first seven months of 2026, this figure was $28.4 billion, as per U.S. data.
Last week, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had reviewed bilateral trade, defense, energy and critical technologies during a call with U.S. President Donald Trump. While Greer said the call was "constructive," and Modi called it "productive," Trump did not comment on it.
Trump in February announced an interim trade deal with India, outlining that New Delhi had agreed to "BUY AMERICAN" at "a much higher level." India, meanwhile, has been seeking preferential tariffs from the U.S. that make its exports to Washington more competitive.
"Both countries stand to lose if no deal is finalized," Mark Linscott, former assistant U.S. trade representative and senior advisor at the U.S.-India Strategic Partnership Forum, told CNBC.
"US exports currently face higher tariffs in the Indian market," he said, adding that if India did not strike a deal soon, "it could face much higher tariffs than other countries, and that could be a real problem given that the U.S. market is critical for India."
Currently, Indian exports to the U.S. face a 10% tariff, following the conclusion of USTR's investigation into the acts, policies and practices of forced labor in 60 countries.
As per the Indian government, a substantial share of the country's exports to the U.S., such as generic pharmaceuticals and smartphones, remain outside the scope of the 10% duty.

The MAC said in a press release that China has repeatedly jeopardized the safety of Taiwanese and their families, adding that the council had recorded at least 140 cases of Chinese transnational repression.
China’s tactics target not only Taiwan officials but the entire Taiwanese population, seeking to create a chilling effect, the council said.
The FBI arrested a woman Monday in California for allegedly spying on President Lai’s son and his family for China in a case the Presidential Office called “a typical example of transnational repression.”
“Such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world,” said Karen Kuo (郭雅慧), spokesperson for the office.
The MAC said the government planned to amend the Anti-infiltration Act to criminalize transnational repression. Working as an agent for a foreign agent is a federal felony under US law, but there is no law against such an action in Taiwan, the council added.
Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗), deputy executive director at Tunghai University’s Cross-Strait Research Center, told Liberty Times that the US decision to arrest the suspect in Los Angeles and file criminal charges shows that China’s surveillance has “crossed a red line” for law enforcement and national security.
In another example of transnational repression, Chinese officials planned to stage a car collision targeting Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) during her visit to Prague in 2024, Czech intelligence confirmed.

Trump says taxpayers will no longer fund controversial TV ads after backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
02:32:00 UTC
11:32:00 KST

Trump: Taxpayers will no longer fund ads touting government
October 6, 2026
US President Donald Trump said Monday that taxpayer funds will no longer be used for television ads featuring him, which he claimed were a "standard thing to do," and said the cost will instead be borne by his super PAC.
The campaign-style ads, which cost at least $1.5 million (€1.34 million) in federal funds, drew criticism from lawmakers and ethics experts across the political divide.
What did Trump say about the ads?
Labeling the ads a "positive promotion for our Great USA," the US president said he decided to bear the costs himself and through his MAGA Inc. political action committee.
"This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
A White House official confirmed that MAGA Inc. would fund the ads going forward.
The MAGA Inc. super PAC had a war chest of more than $400 million by the end of July.
Trump ads warn of 'final battle'
The ads, which began airing in late September, feature Trump promoting his policies and warning against communism and of a "final battle" against "globalists."
They end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government.
Critics, including lawmakers from both parties, have questioned whether the ads violate restrictions on government propaganda and partisan political activity.
Democrats have said the administration transferred $20 million from the Department of Homeland Security to fund the ads and have called for independent investigations.
Trump has not said whether taxpayers will be reimbursed for the ads already aired.

Antisemitic conspiracy theories spread after attempted flydubai hijacking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
02:31:42 UTC
11:31:42 KST

A young girl steps out of the bathroom on a flight and glimpses a bloody scene unfolding in the cockpit: the co-pilot is attacking the pilot with an axe. She screams for help.
A handful of unarmed passengers, still tanned from their vacations in Thailand, rush by her, successfully grabbing the control wheel as the plane plunges 17,000 feet. They also manage to save the life of the bloodied pilot.
It sounds like the climactic scene from a high-stakes action movie, yet by now most people know that this is what happened last week on a Tel Aviv-bound flydubai jet.
Or did it happen? It is so fantastical that maybe it is just a fabricated story or an event staged by Israel’s Mossad? That is what millions of people on social media seem to be suggesting in online posts.
Even after nonstop media interviews with the hero pilot or with the ordinary passengers who took control of the plane, conspiracy theories about the attempted hijacking are swirling. Some mockingly insist the event never happened.
Others say it was a false flag operation. And many of the comments invoke deep-rooted antisemitic tropes.
Some accuse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of staging the incident for political survival or to divert attention from the war in Gaza. Others say it was an attempt by Israel to play the victim or garner global sympathy.
“Brought to you by Bibiwood Productions,” wrote one person commenting on a CNN report posted on Facebook.
“Just stop already,” wrote another person beneath CBS’s clip of interviews with the men who fought the rogue co-pilot posted to Instagram. “It’s seriously embarrassing at this point. We didn’t believe it when the news broke; we didn’t believe it the first time you aired this interview. Reposting clips will not convince anyone with half a brain.”
“Bulls–t,” wrote another person.
Researchers document thousands of hostile posts within hours
Monitoring online responses as the attempted hijacking was unfolding last Wednesday, the Combat Antisemitism Movement’s Antisemitism Research Center found that the first conspiracy theories were posted just 67 minutes after the plane sent its first distress signal.
Within five hours, the ARC documented 1,000 hostile posts, and after 12 hours, 2,963 posts. The posts generated at least 30,000 likes and more than 3 million views.
“The fact is that internet companies have promoted a much more open free-speech policy these days, especially on Instagram and X/Twitter,” said Sacha Roytman, CAM’s Chief Executive Officer, adding that it’s not just the posts that are problematic but also the comments they generate.
“They [the social media platforms] don’t control information anymore; they don’t want to control it,” he said.
Roytman added that another factor is that agitators – likely from Russia or Qatar – have learned how to build an effective bot network to spread misinformation. When the first post appeared after only 67 minutes, he said, “we knew it was not a human posting because no one cares to go online and start posting [that fast].”
“They were activated extremely fast and set up the stage to create an environment that’s toxic enough for other users to be inspired to find the stories they need to build their own claims,” Roytman said.
Information gaps help conspiracy theories spread
Amit Cohen, a research fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies and an expert in cyberattacks and digital fraud, said that during such events, “there is often a gap between what the public wants to know and the amount of verified information available at that moment.
“That is exactly the kind of environment in which rumors and conspiracy theories can develop very quickly,” she said. “In this case, claims appeared online within a short period of time suggesting that the event did not happen as reported, that the videos were fake, or that the incident was staged or a false flag.
“Posts like these are not necessarily the original source of the conspiracy theory,” she said, “but they can function as ignition points.”
Cohen said it was important to distinguish between those who “deliberately create disinformation and those who spread it.”
“Someone may share misleading content simply because it fits what they already believe, because it provokes a strong emotional reaction, or even because it seems interesting or ‘worth looking into,’” she said. “They do not need to know where the message originated, and they certainly do not need to be part of any coordinated campaign.”
Gal Yavetz, a senior lecturer of Artificial Intelligence at Bar-Ilan University, said the flydubai story was so incredible, it left many people “looking for answers.”
“Inevitably, some people will accept more natural explanations, and others, who are more extreme, will go and blame the Jews for it,” Yavetz said, pointing out that similar conspiracy theories arose over the summer when thousands of Moroccan nationals flooded Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta in July.
“Every time there is something that we can’t really understand, that we can’t really explain, we blame the usual suspects — the Jews, the Jews who control the world, the Jews who are the natural scapegoat,” he said, adding that since the October 7, 2023, deadly Hamas raids in Israel, conspiracy theories have become commonplace and all it takes is for a handful of people to start questioning the veracity of the events.
Social media posts invoke antisemitic conspiracy tropes
Posts by Egyptian-born, LA-based political satirist Bassem Youssef, known for his controversial comments about Israel and Jews, are a good example. In a series of videos, he mocks the flydubai event and raises suspicions about what really happened.
In one clip posted on X/Twitter and viewed 64,000 times, Youssef, whose career was supercharged in 2012 when he was boosted by Jewish comedian Jon Stewart, even terms it a “Hollywood movie,” drawing on what critics say are familiar antisemitic conspiracy tropes about Jewish control of Hollywood and, by extension, the world.
“I wish it was chatbots, but the truth of the matter is that social media is a breeding ground for this kind of discourse,” said Yavetz, who specializes in social media, political communication and the spread of misinformation and disinformation online.
“They are definitely helping to spread and to reshare most of this misinformation and disinformation, but we know from previous studies that it is really just a negligible number compared to just regular people who are going to the more extreme sides and just taking their own outrageous opinions to social media just because it is now so easy to do so,” he said.
“You don’t really need to do much; you just need to make sure that you can stand behind your claims, and all of a sudden an outrageous post will have 1,000 likes, then 10,000 likes, and these comments are just circulating again and again, going from Facebook to WhatsApp to Messenger and back to Twitter with screenshots and back to Instagram… It’s a flood that you can’t really stop by taking out an umbrella,” Yavetz said.
AI makes real evidence easier to dismiss
INSS’s Cohen, who is also a national security expert with the Dvorah Forum, a group that promotes women’s voices in foreign policy, said that “conspiracy theories are not new, but the digital environment has changed their speed, scale, and the ability to obscure where a message originally came from.”
She explained that “in the past, there were more intermediaries between the person producing information and a large audience. Today, a single account can post a claim and reach very large audiences within a very short time.”
And, Cohen added, AI has made the problem worse.
“Mainly because it has dramatically reduced the time, cost, and skill required to create convincing content,” she said.
It has also made it harder for people to believe what appears on their screens.
“The problem is no longer only that AI can create fake content that looks real. It also makes it easier to dismiss real content by claiming that it is fake,” said Cohen. “Once the public knows that convincing images, audio, and video can be artificially generated, the existence of visual evidence no longer necessarily ends the debate.”

Chinese, Caribbean women among contenders for Nobel literature prize

Chinese, Caribbean women among contenders for Nobel literature prize
- The 2026 Nobel Literature Prize may go to a Chinese or Caribbean woman, such as Jamaica Kincaid or Can Xue, to diversify the award traditionally dominated by Western male authors.
- The Swedish Academy faces pressure to recognise women and non-Western writers after past over-representation of Western males and recent reforms following a 2018 scandal.
- Other contenders include Latin America's Samanta Schweblin, while the winner will receive a US$1.2 million prize, gold medal, and diploma when announced on October 8.
AI generated
STOCKHOLM – The 2026 Nobel literature prize could go to a Chinese or a Caribbean woman when it is awarded later this week, literary critics say, in a bid to diversify an award that has most often gone to Western male authors.
There is no public shortlist for the Nobel, and with the deliberations of the Swedish Academy that awards the prize and the list of nominees remaining sealed for 50 years, Stockholm’s literary circles engage in frantic guessing ahead of the announcement.
The suspense will end on Oct 8 at 1pm (1100 GMT or 7pm SGT) when the 18-member Swedish Academy reveals its pick.
Antiguan-American author Jamaica Kincaid, 77, whose work explores Caribbean culture, family and identity as well as colonialism and race, has often been mentioned in Nobel speculation, as has China’s Can Xue, whose avant-garde experimental writing has been compared to that of Kafka.
“It’s about time for Jamaica Kincaid to get it,” Victor Malm, culture critic at Swedish daily Expressen, told AFP.
“She has been mentioned for a long time,” said Bjorn Wiman, culture editor at Sweden’s largest daily Dagens Nyheter.
Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai took home the honour in 2025.
Women under-represented
Kincaid’s 1990 novel Lucy is an autobiographical tale of an embittered young girl who travels from the West Indies to the United States to work as an au pair.
“It’s exactly the kind of book where it’s enough to read three lines to say: ‘OK, we’re talking about a Nobel laureate here’,” Wiman said.
Giving her the nod could also be interpreted as a political choice, given her fierce criticism of US President Donald Trump.
The Academy trod familiar ground in 2025 when it honoured Krasznahorkai – a male writer from Central Europe, of which there are many in the Nobel annals – and Wiman said the committee should “distance itself a bit” from that.
The institution has long been criticised for the over-representation of Western male authors since the prize was first awarded in 1901.
There are only 18 women among the 122 laureates, and only very few have bodies of work written in Asian or Middle Eastern languages.
No African languages are represented.
A 2018 sex assault scandal left the Academy in tatters, and more than half of its members ended up being replaced.
Since then, every other literature laureate has been a woman – making it likely that the nod in 2026 could go to a woman.
The Swedish Academy insists, however, that its only consideration is the quality of a writer’s work.
Argentina?
Lina Kalmteg, literary critic for Swedish public broadcaster SR, meanwhile said it was time for a Spanish-language author from Latin America.
“In recent years, there has been a lot of talk about the ‘Latin American literary miracle’, this new generation that came after the male authors devoted to magical realism, like Gabriel Garcia Marquez,” she told AFP.
“In this new wave, it’s women who are taking the lead, with writing often tinged with feminism, but also often quite dark and violent, punctuated by surreal touches,” she noted.
Argentinian author Samanta Schweblin, 48, would be an interesting and surprising choice in this category, she said.
“But she is surely still too young,” she added.
Literature laureates are honoured for their body of work, not a single publication.
The last writer from South America to be honoured was Peru’s Mario Vargas Llosa in 2010.
Other “usual suspects” mentioned regularly in Nobel speculation include Australia’s Gerald Murnane, his Aboriginal compatriot Alexis Wright, American author Thomas Pynchon and Mexican writer Cristina Rivera Garza.
Several new names getting Nobel buzz the past few years are Germany’s Jenny Erpenbeck, who won the 2024 International Booker Prize for the novel Kairos, and Duong Thu Huong, one of Vietnam’s most popular writers whose first books in the late 1980s were bestsellers before they were banned, and whose books are mainly published outside Vietnam.
The winner will take home a US$1.2 million (S$1.5 million) cheque, gold medal and diploma. AFP

Pentagon says Trump approves Army firing squad execution of Fort Hood killer Nidal Hasan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
02:23:18 UTC
11:23:18 KST

The Pentagon on Monday evening said that President Donald Trump has approved a recommendation by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to have convicted Fort Hood mass killer Nidal Hasan executed by a U.S. Army firing squad.
Hasan, 56, would be the first person executed after a U.S. armed forces court-martial since 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, for the rape and attempted murder of a girl in Austria.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC.
Hasan, a psychiatrist, was convicted and sentenced to death after a 2013 court-martial for the Nov. 5, 2009, shooting spree that killed 13 and injured 32 others at the Army base in Killeen, Texas, while he was an Army major.
During his court-martial, Hasan told a judge that he was motivated in the shooting to defend the "leadership of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, the Taliban."
Hegseth in September 2025 said that he had asked Trump to approve Hasan's execution.
Federal law says that a person convicted through court-martial and sentenced to death cannot be executed until approved by the president.
"Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009," Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a post on X on Monday.
"He killed 13 people and wounded 32 others while shouting 'Allahu Akbar' during the attack," Parnell said.
The spokesman also said the secretary of the Army "will set the time and place of the execution."
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell wrote.
Hegseth retweeted Parnell's post, writing "Justice."
The Supreme Court on March 31, 2025, denied a petition by Hasan to hear an appeal of his conviction, clearing the way for him to be executed.
In September 2025, Hegseth told The Hill in a statement, "I am 100 percent committed to ensuring the death penalty is carried out for Nidal Hasan."
"This savage terrorist deserves the harshest lawful punishment for his 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood," Hegseth said at that time. "The victims and survivors deserve justice without delays."
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Hasan is one of just four people currently on death row as the result of a U.S. military court-martial.

Britain's new car market records strongest September since 2017

11:19:50 KST

LONDON, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Britain's new car market accelerated in September, with registrations marking the 10th consecutive month of growth and the strongest September since 2017, data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed Monday.
A total of 350,536 new cars were registered last month, up 12 percent year on year, the SMMT said, noting that the overall growth was largely driven by intense competition as increased choices and attractive deals encouraged purchases.
Electrified vehicles helped power growth, taking a record 58.4 percent of registrations. Specifically, registrations for plug-in hybrid vehicles surged 55.5 percent to take a record share at 17 percent.
Battery electric vehicle (BEV) demand also climbed 36.3 percent to a record high volume of 99,201 units, with market share reaching 28.3 percent, the SMMT noted.
Since 2023, the number of BEV models on the market has more than doubled, with 178 now on sale. The country's electrified offering now represents more than three quarters of new cars available, according to the SMMT.
"September's record electrified vehicle performance is a major achievement. Drivers are increasingly embracing the growing choice of models made available and high fuel prices are also undoubtedly giving more consumers reason to consider going electric," said Mike Hawes, SMMT chief executive.
However, the organization pointed out that the number of new BEVs registered in the first three quarters of 2026 accounted for 26.2 percent of overall car registrations, which is significantly below the 33 percent mandated for 2026 and behind even last year's target of 28 percent. ■

Cornell students stage anti-rape rally in support of 'Jane Doe'

Cornell students stage anti-rape rally in support of 'Jane Doe'
ITHACA, New York, Oct 5 - Cornell University students staged a mass rally on Monday voicing solidarity with a classmate whose gang-rape allegations have ignited a national uproar and demanding that the Ivy League school take firmer action against sexual violence on campus.
The protesters called for an external inquiry into how Cornell's administration has handled the matter, independent hearings and uniform minimum sanctions for all sexual assaults on campus, and better training for campus police in responding to complaints of sexual violence and harassment.
The alleged gang-rape victim, identified by the pseudonym Jane Doe, has said the university failed to adequately investigate and punish campus fraternity members who were involved.
Some demonstrators also called for the resignation of Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other members of his administration, saying their policies have perpetuated what protesters called a "culture of rape" on campus.
In a lawsuit filed last month, Jane Doe said she was plied with drugs and alcohol and then sexually assaulted by several members of the campus chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024 after she had become incapacitated.
Doe, who was 20 at the time, named seven Chi Phi members as defendants in the suit, along with the fraternity chapter, a local bar, her own sorority, and the university.
She had reported the alleged assault to police several weeks after the fact, leading to an internal university investigation and a law enforcement probe, but the local prosecutor declined to bring criminal charges in the case.
Cornell, which has defended its response to the original report, shut down the Chi Phi chapter and imposed a range of discipline on the fraternity members involved, including expulsions and other sanctions.
The men all denied any wrongdoing, some saying the sexual activity was consensual and others disputing their participation, the New York Times has reported, citing Cornell documents.
The lawsuit criticized the university for having offered some of the alleged perpetrators a chance to mitigate their penalties by writing essays. The demonstrators on Monday demanded that Cornell expel or revoke the degrees of any student found complicit in the alleged gang rape.
'PRISON SENTENCES, NOT TOPIC SENTENCES'
New York Governor Kathy Hochul last Friday appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor to take over a newly reopened criminal investigation, saying she was "deeply disturbed" by how local authorities originally dealt with the case.
Monday's boisterous but orderly demonstration included a march by several hundred students, faculty supporters and community activists — perhaps 1,000 or more — through the campus in the upstate New York town of Ithaca.
The protesters, chanting "One struggle, one fight" and "No justice, no peace," filled the central pedestrian plaza on campus, and spilled over into adjacent spaces. Many carried signs with slogans such as "Justice for Jane Doe," "We Stand for Survivors" and "Prison Sentences, not Topic Sentences."
The march ended at Cornell's main administration building, which was defaced in Monday's predawn hours by unknown activists who smashed two glass panes of the front door and spray-painted graffiti on the entryway, including one message that read: "AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED."
Independent student newspaper the Cornell Daily Sun reported receiving a statement from the activists saying their vandalism was an act of protest of the alleged assault and "global systems of power that allowed this to happen in the first place."
The rally came a day after Doe and her lawyer said they had received multiple threats since filing the lawsuit, which has prompted a public outcry, particularly on social media under the banner "#IamJaneDoe," over why law enforcement declined to pursue charges in 2024.
The uproar also stirred a backlash by others who have questioned whether keeping Doe anonymous was fair because it denied those implicated in the matter the chance to publicly face their accuser.
Addressing the controversy on Saturday, Kotlikoff promised in a video message to examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus, saying, "being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility." REUTERS

Spanish election threatens to blow up Brussels’ political balance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
02:18:45 UTC
11:18:45 KST

Pedro Sánchez applauds during an extraordinary parliamentary session to vote on a government housing decree at the in Madrid on Oct. 2, 2026. | Javier Soriano/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — A defeat for Pedro Sánchez in Spain’s snap election risks destabilizing the EU by putting the Socialists and Democrats on the back foot in Brussels and pushing them into a more confrontational stance.
Sánchez, the only Socialist-aligned leader currently running a large EU country, has provided a center-left counterweight to decisions in a Council largely dominated by the center right. Spain’s lawmakers form the S&D’s largest national delegation in the European Parliament, and when Sánchez strikes a Council deal, Spanish MEPs can usually carry his position through the group, even over internal opposition.
A change of government in Madrid would disrupt that arrangement, senior S&D lawmakers told POLITICO. Polls suggest that the country will vote in an administration led by the center-right People’s Party, which would likely partner with the far-right Vox party.
Advertisement
“There might be a temptation to look more critically at Council positions if there is no [longer] a Socialist prime minister of a large country,” said René Repasi, head of Germany’s SPD delegation in Parliament.
A second senior S&D lawmaker said Sánchez helped “balance” decisions at the leaders’ table and that his absence would unsettle the informal alliance of the S&D, liberals and the center-right European People’s Party that Commission President Ursula von der Leyen relies on to pass legislation.
“If what comes out of the leaders’ table, and the guidelines it gives the Commission, becomes more conservative, it will be less appealing for progressives to feel part of that governing majority,” said the lawmaker, who was granted anonymity to speak about sensitive group matters.
The S&D has lost ground elsewhere in Brussels. Since the 2024 European election shifted Parliament to the right, the EPP has passed some legislation with far-right groups. The Socialists have less representation in national governments and fewer commissioners of their own, fueling repeated tensions and attempts to repair the alliance. With Sánchez gone, the last center-left leaders would be Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen and Malta’s Robert Abela — with Magdalena Andersson working to form a government in Sweden.
Spain’s election will sound the starting gun a year of consequential votes across major EU countries, including Italy, Poland and France, where the far-right National Rally is leading the polls ahead of the 2027 presidential election. Far-right forces in Brussels are pressing the EPP to drop its ban on cooperating with them and break with its traditional ties to the S&D.
Fewer incentives for compromise
The S&D, Parliament’s second-largest group, has repeatedly threatened over the past two years to withdraw support for von der Leyen, with some lawmakers urging a more forceful stance on EU policy.
Advertisement
Spain’s Iratxe García, who leads the group, has so far kept Spanish lawmakers in line. She faces a leadership vote on Oct. 21, though she is broadly expected to keep her post.
Should Sánchez lose his election, all the S&D’s largest national delegations — from Italy, Romania and France — would be in opposition at home. The only S&D parties still in government would be junior partners in Germany and Austria, alongside Denmark’s Social Democrats, whose hardline stance on migration limits their influence in the group.
Without a heavyweight prime minister from a large EU country to keep the S&D in line, von der Leyen would face greater pressure to make more concessions to lawmakers already frustrated by the center-right’s votes with the far right.
Iratxe García, who leads the S&D group in the European Parliament and has so far kept Spanish lawmakers in line, holds a press conference in Strasbourg, France on Feb. 10, 2026. | Magali Cohen/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
“If von der Leyen still delivers on S&D priorities, she will have the support of the group, and if that is not the case, then she will lose the support of the group,” Repasi said. A formal alliance between Spain’s EPP and far-right Vox, he added, “will drive us even more apart.”
The S&D would also have fewer “incentives” to compromise without Sánchez’s presence, the second senior lawmaker said, because the group would have less responsibility for maintaining stability in EU institutions.
“The institutional responsibility to guarantee support for the Commission and stability in the EU institutions will no longer be there,” the lawmaker said. A tougher line would be easier for the center-left “if the EPP continues striking deals with the far right, and the European Commission fails to offer a politically attractive agenda that progressives can sell to their voters.”
Advertisement
One diplomat called the Socialists’ threat to withdraw support for von der Leyen “not credible,” saying it would isolate the group further: “They just feel a need to send a signal to the EPP.” Weakening or firing von der Leyen also runs against the S&D’s interests, the diplomat added, because the EU has moved further to the right since she first took office and “the next person coming in would be much less inclined to work with them.”
Turbulence ahead
Brussels is set to become a battleground between Spain’s two main parties, with the Spanish lawmakers leading the Socialists in Parliament, while their rivals in the EPP form that group’s second-largest national delegation.
The election is also weighing on talks over the EU’s next seven-year budget, known as the Multiannual Financial Framework, which Brussels aims to conclude by the end of the year.
“It’s not going to do any good for the MFF,” a Commission official said, warning that Spain risks dragging its feet during already strained negotiations. The EPP and its allies will try to put debates on Parliament’s agenda to cause discomfort for Sánchez, the official said, likely making the talks more “turbulent.”
Spain’s underlying budget position will not change under a new government, a second diplomat said, but “the election will be distracting” and “won’t incentivize finding compromise.”
The EPP’s Siegfried Mureșan, Parliament’s lead budget negotiator, warned EU countries not to use the election to delay talks ahead of a leaders’ summit in mid-October. “The European Council shall not use the political situation in Spain as an excuse for further delays.”
Advertisement
EPP leader Manfred Weber declined to comment on what a Sánchez defeat could mean for the Socialists’ influence in Brussels, but voiced support for Spain’s opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo.
“Spain’s future is now in the hands of the Spanish people,” he said. “At a time when vision and reform are needed more than ever, the EPP is proud to stand firmly behind Alberto Núñez Feijóo. He has our full support.”
Zoya Sheftalovich and Tim Ross contributed reporting.

The Royad Mammadov, carrying corn from Ukraine’s Izmail port toward Ravenna, Italy, was hit by two Russian drones in neutral waters, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn,” Zelensky wrote on X.
Azerbaijani and Indian nationals were aboard the vessel. Zelensky said the captain was killed, while the fate of another crew member was initially unknown. Eleven sailors were rescued, one of them injured.
Romanian authorities later confirmed that two people had died and 11 crew members were rescued after the vessel caught fire and sank in Romania’s exclusive economic zone, roughly 30 nautical miles south of Sfântu Gheorghe.
Three crew members were injured and eight were unharmed, according to Romanian maritime officials, with the injured evacuated by helicopter.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha also condemned the Russian attack on the Turkish civilian vessel and offered condolences over the deaths. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry published his statement Monday as Kyiv called for greater international pressure over attacks on civilian navigation.
The Royad Mammadov was named after an Azerbaijani serviceman killed during the 2020 war over Karabakh.
European Solidarity Expels MP Honcharenko Over War-Ending Proposals
The ship is linked to Turkey’s Palmali shipping group, founded by Azerbaijani-born businessman Mübariz Mansimov.
Turkey has repeatedly voiced alarm over attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
Turkey, UN push for safer Black Sea corridor
The attack also comes as Turkey and the United Nations are seeking to revive talks on maritime security in the Black Sea, including proposals for a protected commercial shipping corridor.
Ankara has pushed Moscow and Kyiv toward arrangements aimed at halting attacks on civilian vessels and ports, drawing on the model of the 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative brokered by Turkey and the UN.
That agreement allowed millions of tons of Ukrainian agricultural products to reach global markets before Russia withdrew from the deal in 2023.
Turkey has since urged both sides to restore safer navigation and has presented proposals aimed at reducing attacks on commercial traffic and rebuilding confidence in Black Sea shipping.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan traveled to Baku on Sept. 15, where he held talks with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov. The Russo-Ukrainian War and the deteriorating security situation in the Black Sea were among the issues discussed.
Speaking alongside Bayramov in Baku, Fidan warned that mounting attacks on civilian vessels were threatening lives, property and freedom of navigation, noting that both Turkish and Azerbaijani sailors had already been killed. He said Ankara was continuing talks with the parties and working on proposals that specifically prioritize the Black Sea.
The timing of the visit underscored Ankara’s effort to build regional backing for renewed Black Sea diplomacy, although neither Turkey nor Azerbaijan publicly said that Fidan had asked Baku to formally join the initiative. It also remained unclear whether Azerbaijan had endorsed the proposed arrangement.
Turkey’s current effort, pursued alongside the United Nations, is aimed at reducing attacks on civilian shipping and establishing safer commercial navigation – an initiative that echoes the Black Sea Grain Initiative Ankara and the UN brokered in 2022.
Zelensky said Ukraine has repeatedly offered “concrete steps to de-escalate the situation and ensure security in the Black Sea,” while third countries have also put forward proposals.
“But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian vessels instead of normal maritime navigation,” he said. “Pressure is needed to restore global food security.”
The sinking of the Royad Mammadov adds new urgency to those efforts, particularly for Turkey as Turkish-owned vessels and seafarers are increasingly exposed to attacks in the expanding Black Sea drone war.

Tarek Chouiref
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
A classified CIA assessment has warned that deepening political, economic and social fractures could put Israel at risk of civil war or state collapse, according to a report published Monday.
The assessment, titled “Fracture From Within,” was prepared in August by the CIA’s Red Cell, a unit tasked with challenging prevailing intelligence assumptions, Drop Site News reported, citing two US sources familiar with its contents.
The CIA did not respond to the outlet’s request for comment.
The assessment points to a volatile mix of pressures ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 election, including economic strain, rising military spending, anger over exemptions from compulsory military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews and escalating violence by Israeli occupiers in the occupied West Bank.
It also identifies Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s fight to remain in power as a source of further political and constitutional tension.
Years of war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran have deepened existing divisions, according to the report, as soldiers return from prolonged combat, many suffering serious psychological trauma.
The military draft dispute has emerged as one of Israel’s sharpest internal fault lines, with resentment growing over exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men following repeated reserve mobilizations.
The assessment also points to Israel’s growing international isolation, including eroding support in the US, as another factor that could deepen internal instability.

studio 5.5 recombines sockets and switches into modular lighting and furniture building blocks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
02:10:16 UTC
11:10:16 KST

studio 5.5 recombines sockets and switches into modular lighting and furniture building blocks
volt face treats the switch as a starting point rather than a finishing detail.
Sockets and switches become VOLT FACE building blocks
Volt Face by Studio 5.5 reinterprets Schneider Electric’s Odace range of sockets and switches as a collection of lighting and furniture. Developed by Vincent Baranger and Anthony Lebossé, the project follows the studio’s approach of repurposing familiar everyday objects while retaining their original functions.
The collection includes a wall light, table, bedside table, pendant light, and other lamps that place switches and sockets at the center of each design. Components from the Odace range are recombined and repositioned to explore their materials, colors, finishes, and tactile qualities.
Volt Face Lamp, Vincent Baranger and Anthony Lebossé from Studio 5.5 for Schneider Electric
Studio 5.5 turns familiar switch into a point of interaction
Switches and sockets are usually installed at the end of an interior project, but Volt Face by Studio 5.5 treats them as starting points. The familiar act of pressing a switch becomes part of the physical interaction with each object, with the characteristic click contributing to the sensory experience.
The project also presents the Odace range as a modular design vocabulary. Instead of selecting individual products from a catalog, designers and interior architects can combine, repeat, and arrange the components as building blocks, using an industrial range as a starting point for new objects and configurations.
Volt Face Lamp, Vincent Baranger and Anthony Lebossé from Studio 5.5 for Schneider Electric
‘click’ becomes part of Volt Face’s tactile design language
‘We wanted to encourage people to try them, to make them want to touch them, to make them wonder whether everything is actually functional, whether it works when you press this one,’ shares the design team. The gesture becomes an integral part of the project. And so does the famous ‘click.’
Volt Face also invites us to look at an industrial range in a different way. The Odace range becomes a toolbox. Each socket, each switch becomes a building block that designers and interior architects can play with, repeat, combine, and build upon. An industrial range is not an end in itself. It is a vocabulary.
Volt Face Lamp, Vincent Baranger and Anthony Lebossé from Studio 5.5 for Schneider Electric
Volt table, Vincent Baranger and Anthony Lebossé from Studio 5.5 for Schneider Electric
