New York declares first US measles disaster emergency since 2025 surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
22:19:04 UTC
07:19:04 KST

New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on Monday over a measles outbreak, the first such declaration by a US state since cases began surging in 2025.
The state also expanded the pool of health professionals allowed to administer measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccines as cases rise in rural communities.
"No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease," Hochul said in a statement.
New York has reported 108 measles cases this year through October 3, including 92 since July 15 in under-immunized rural communities across 18 counties, well above typical annual levels, according to the executive order.
Seven of the cases are in New York City, and 101 are elsewhere in the state, the governor's office said. Local health departments have administered more than 1,000 MMR doses in rural areas since July 15.
Outbreak spreading in Pennsylvania
Neighboring Pennsylvania is battling a fast-spreading outbreak, with 977 cases and five deaths as of October 2, mostly in rural counties that border New York, the order said.
Pennsylvania health officials said on Monday the state's total had passed 1,000 cases, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades.
The US is having its worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 cases reported, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The order allows registered nurses to order tests for suspected measles and pharmacists to vaccinate children as young as two. It also requires all MMR vaccinations to be reported to state or New York City immunization registries within 72 hours, while waiving adults' consent for such reporting.
Vaccination itself still requires the consent of the patient or a legal guardian. The emergency took effect on Monday and runs through November 4.

Employee of Russian plague institute dies of suspected pneumonic infection, Trump offers help

2026-10-05
22:18:52 UTC
07:18:52 KST

Almost 200 people have been placed under medical observation in Russia after a worker at an anti-plague research institute in eastern Siberia died of what many have been reporting as a form of plague on Thursday.
The employee was hospitalized with severe pneumonia last Tuesday before dying in the hospital on Thursday, according to local news, which wrote on Friday that the 28-year-old Darya Shipilova was suspected to have fallen ill with the plague after returning from a work trip to Buryatia.
Early Russian reports wrote that Shipilova had contracted the pneumonia after breaking a vial of plague bacteria.
Alexei Tsydenov, head of the nearby Republic of Buryatia, where the woman had reportedly visited, stated that she had died from an unspecified form of plague.
Tsydenov later modified his statement to say she had possibly died from the plague.
Employee diagnosed with 'pneumonia of unspecified etiology', Russian watchdog says
Russia's public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor said on Sunday that the employee had been diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology," in a statement on Sunday, adding that no microorganisms linked to her work had been found.
According to Rospotrebnadzor, extensive anti-epidemic measures were put in place, including "identifying the widest possible circle of people who had been in contact with the patient, inpatient medical observation, and daily laboratory testing."
Aside from two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection (the most frequent cause of the common cold), no other infectious agents were found, according to the official watchdog agency.
However, many still suspect, as initial reports indicated, that Shipilova contracted pneumonic plague, one of the three kinds of plague caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium, the same one behind the infamous Black Death that affected Europe in the mid 1300s.
Pneumonic plague occurs when the bacteria attacks the lungs, resulting in severe respiratory symptoms, including shortness of breath and coughing, which can turn bloody.
Pneumonic plague is also the only form that can be transmitted between humans through inhaling respiratory particles from someone who is sick.
While pneumonic plague can be fatal if left untreated, if detected and treated within 24 hours of symptom onset, recovery rates are high, according to the World Health Organization.
Trump 'concerned' about plague while Kremlin warns against rumors
US President Donald Trump said that he was concerned about the suspected plague outbreak when asked by reporters on Monday, saying that it was "a big problem for Russia."
"Well, I hate to see them having it," Trump said. "It's a rough disease."
Trump also said that the US would be willing to provide help if needed.
"We'll help," Trump said. "Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we're always willing to help."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also told reporters that US authorities were monitoring the situation on Monday, warning that "if something like that gets out it could quickly spread."
"We're watching and monitoring it closely," he said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged Russians to listen to Rospotrebnadzor's report rather than "various rumors and speculation."

Trump’s approval hits new low among Hispanic voters ahead of midterms
Hispanic voters are twice as likely to favour Democratic Party over Trump’s Republican Party in the November elections.
A new poll from the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos has found that United States President Donald Trump’s approval rating remains at a record low as the midterm elections approach in November.
The six-day survey, completed on Monday, found that just 32 percent of US voters approve of the job Trump is doing as president.
While that low rate has held steady since September, the latest Reuters-Ipsos poll suggests his support among Latino voters is continuing to slide.
Trump’s approval rating shrunk this month to 24 percent among Hispanic voters, its lowest point in either of his two terms in office.
The Republican leader had previously made substantial inroads with that constituency.
The Pew Research Center estimated that Trump and his Democratic rival, Kamala Harris, were within three percentage points of each other in the 2024 presidential race, earning 48 percent and 51 percent of the Hispanic vote, respectively.
That rate marked a significant jump for Trump over the 2020 election, when he only earned 36 percent of the Hispanic vote.
Experts have credited the boost in Hispanic support with helping Trump win the 2024 race. His 2020 bid, by contrast, ended in defeat to Democrat Joe Biden.
The Monday poll found that Trump’s gains among Hispanics have largely evaporated.
About 52 percent plan to vote for the Democrats in the November midterms, compared to 26 percent for Republicans.
The upcoming midterm is largely viewed as a referendum on Trump’s second term and will decide whether the Republicans maintain their majorities in the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
Democrats have seized on Trump’s low approval ratings, hoping to translate frustration with the president into voter momentum for their party.
A Democratic majority in one or both houses of Congress would place substantial constraints on Trump’s agenda for the remainder of his time in office.
But Trump has also faced rumblings from within his Republican Party as the November 3 midterms approach.
One Republican incumbent, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, released a campaign advertisement last month that addressed Trump directly, saying, “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”
She cited Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown as a source of tension. “Some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she said, pointing to the detention and deportation of immigrants with no criminal record.
Experts have also warned that the president’s shrinking popularity, driven in part by concerns about the cost of living and his decision to launch a war on Iran, could weigh down Republican candidates in key races across the country.
Still, Trump has continued to express confidence about the prospects of his Republican Party in the upcoming midterms.
He has also defended his decision to place himself at the centre of the Republican election campaign strategy. Trump recently launched a 32-day blitz of cross-country rallies ahead of the November 3 midterms.
“Just so you understand, they all want me to go,” Trump said, denying that some Republicans would prefer he keep his distance. “They all want me to go campaign.”

Israelis and Palestinians need a new choice: Federalism - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
22:05:28 UTC
07:05:28 KST

In September 2025, as the war in our homeland continued to take an unimaginable toll in blood and destruction, a group of young Israelis and Palestinians traveled to the Italian island of Ventotene. We chose this location for a reason.
During the darkest days of World War II, political prisoners on this very island wrote a manifesto envisioning a united, federal Europe. They proved that even from the ashes of a devastating conflict, a new reality based on partnership, not endless war, could be born.
We arrived broken. As Israelis, we carried the painful scars of the October 7 trauma – a day that completely destroyed our basic sense of security. As Palestinians, we brought the heavy weight of an ongoing reality defined by endless destruction, widespread grief, and a completely blocked political and personal future, shaped by decades of military occupation and dispossession.
In this impossible reality, when the gap between our societies had never felt deeper, it felt almost impossible to imagine a shared future.
Yet, inspired by the history of the island around us, something deep changed. The experience of meeting the other side, face to face during the deepest pain of our peoples – and still managing to connect and listen – proved that our shared humanity can win. We argued and disagreed, but by resolving most of them, we became more inspired and determined than ever.
Meeting other side gave rise to Young Federalists movement
From that breaking point, we realized one simple, clear truth: Both of our nations share a deep historical and national connection to this land, and neither of us is going anywhere. This realization gave rise to the Young Federalists movement and the Federal Charter we wrote together.
Now, as the public prepares to head to the polls, the political arena is painfully empty of real vision. Candidates running for office offer us nothing but endless wars and zero political solutions. They promise only a never-ending cycle of bloodshed and conflict management that has led us straight into a disaster.
At the same time, the election debate traps us in a false choice: absolute separation that requires huge walls, endless military control, and deepens hatred, or a forced unity in a single state that threatens to erase our unique national identities. We refuse to cast our ballots for these failed ideas.
The upcoming elections in both Israel and Palestine must not just be about replacing politicians; they must be about replacing the entire paradigm.
The only practical path forward is an Israeli-Palestinian federal framework based on absolute equality, mutual recognition, and the principle of non-domination.
Most importantly, this model breaks away from past failed agreements. It does not push questions of rights and equal sovereignty into an unknown future, but builds strict non-domination and equality from day one.
Our vision proposes a political and civic union of two independent states, Israel and Palestine, based on the internationally recognized 1967 borders, with a united Jerusalem serving as the shared capital.
At the heart of our Federal Charter is the promise that neither state will ever control the other demographically, politically, or economically. Instead of walls and checkpoints that strip away daily human dignity, we imagine a shared space that guarantees freedom of movement for all.
Shared federal institutions with equal representation will manage our macro-economy, establishing economic unity (as promised in the 1947 UN Resolution 181), along with the joint management of natural resources and the defense of our outside borders.
At the same time, both Israel and Palestine will keep full sovereignty over their internal affairs, including education, culture, and civil law.
Security will shift from a system of separate, hostile defense to one of regional partnership. A joint federal command will focus strictly on regional defense, ensuring military forces are never again used against civilians.
This framework does not try to erase historical memory or ignore ongoing trauma. Instead, it provides a structural guarantee against future control, oppression, and dispossession.
Charter to be presented at joint Israeli-Palestinian event
This October, we will publicly present our charter at a joint event bringing together 100 Israeli and Palestinian peace activists. Federalism is not an unrealistic dream; it is a detailed political and civic roadmap that offers true security through mutual partnership.
As voters and citizens, it is time to stop managing the conflict and start building a home together.
Will we choose to keep bleeding in a cycle of endless revenge led by leaders with no vision, or will we finally dare to choose a federal alternative that guarantees security, dignity, and a prosperous future for both peoples? The choice is in our hands.
The writers are the co-leaders of The Young Federalists, a joint Israeli-Palestinian grassroots movement advocating for a federal political framework.

US approves $1 billion arms sale to UAE
The United States on Monday announced the approval of a $1 billion sale to the United Arab Emirates of up to 10,000 Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System guidance sections for rockets.
"The proposed sale will improve the United Arab Emirates' capability to meet current and future threats by developing and maintaining a strong and ready self-defence capability and improving interoperability with US forces," the US State Department said in a statement.
It "will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a major defence partner", the statement added.
The Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System converts unguided rockets into precision munitions that can be employed for purposes including shooting down drones, thereby avoiding the use of costly missiles to shoot down comparatively cheap aircraft.
The UAE and other US-allied Gulf countries have been hard hit by the war on Iran, during which Tehran's forces have repeatedly targeted them with both drones and missiles.
The State Department also announced on Monday the approval of a $400 million sale to Kuwait, another Gulf state, of "repair and return services" for Patriot missiles, which have played a key role in countering Iranian attacks in the region.
"Kuwait will use the enhanced capability to strengthen its homeland defence" and "will have no difficulty absorbing these articles and services into its armed forces," the department said in a statement.

CAIRO, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi said Monday that Egypt will defend its Nile water rights by all means sanctioned under international law.
In a speech marking the 53rd anniversary of Egypt's October 1973 war against Israel, Sisi described the Nile as "the very lifeline of Egypt and the cornerstone of its existence across millennia," saying that Egypt's water share is "an established historical and non-negotiable legal right that admits of no compromise or infringement."

====================================================================================================

World Insights: Three risks weigh on Europe's growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:02:31 CST
07:02:31 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Costly energy, rising inflation and higher borrowing costs together threaten to weaken Europe's economic recovery by squeezing household spending and business investment.
The euro area economy has proved more resilient than expected, prompting the European Central Bank (ECB) to raise its 2026 and 2027 growth forecasts in September.
Emergency fuel releases may ease the immediate supply strain, but reliance on imports leaves Europe exposed to further disruptions. The ECB must balance inflation risks against weakening demand, while governments face pressure from rising costs as they seek to cushion the energy shock.
FUEL RELIEF HAS LIMITS
A coordinated release of emergency reserves may ease Europe's diesel shortage, but declining domestic refining capacity leaves the region dependent on imports.
On Oct. 2, leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel over four months through the International Energy Agency, including substantial diesel supplies within the first 20 days. They also pledged to avoid export restrictions among member countries and called for coordinated refinery maintenance and higher utilization rates where feasible.
The agreement followed U.S. pressure on European governments to release emergency diesel stocks. Later that day, U.S. President Donald Trump said the United States would not impose a diesel export ban, easing concerns about a potential disruption to European supplies.
Releasing stocks may buy time, but can not solve insufficient production capacity. FuelsEurope, an association representing European fuel manufacturers, said that 35 European refineries had closed since 2009, reducing capacity by 20 percent. It said Europe's dependence on imported diesel and jet fuel could deepen and extend to other products without corrective action.
Additional crude supplies cannot fully relieve a diesel shortage if refineries lack the capacity to process them. The G7's focus on refinery operations alongside reserve releases reflects that problem.
Gas supplies pose another risk ahead of winter. Joachim Nagel, president of Germany's central bank, the Deutsche Bundesbank, said on Monday that low storage levels may force Europe to purchase substantially larger volumes during the heating season, leaving gas prices vulnerable.
High energy costs squeeze business profits and may prompt companies to raise prices. Higher fuel and heating bills also reduce households' spending power, weakening demand for other goods and services.
Philip R. Lane, a member of the ECB's executive board, said companies may have to pay higher energy and input bills before they can adjust production or selling prices, increasing their need for short-term financing.
INFLATION CREATES A POLICY DILEMMA
Annual inflation in the euro area rose to an estimated 3.8 percent in September from 3.2 percent in August, according to Eurostat's flash estimate. Energy prices rose 18.8 percent from a year earlier, up from 14.3 percent in August.
Underlying price pressures remained more contained. Inflation excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco edged up to 2.5 percent from 2.4 percent. Services inflation rose to 3.2 percent, while inflation in non-energy industrial goods eased to 1.1 percent.
The figures highlight the ECB's challenge: determining whether the energy shock will spread to other prices and wages or weaken demand enough to curb inflation.
"There are so far no clear signs that inflation has fed through to price and wage setting," Nagel said. Longer-term inflation expectations remained consistent with the ECB's 2 percent target, he added.
A prolonged shock, however, could encourage companies to pass on costs and workers to seek compensation for lost purchasing power.
The ECB raised its key interest rates by 25 basis points in both June and September, bringing its deposit facility rate to 2.5 percent. It said further rate decisions will depend on incoming data and assessments at each meeting.
On Monday, Lane said higher energy costs could weaken activity and reduce household incomes and business profits. Those effects, together with tighter financial conditions, could limit the monetary policy adjustment needed to bring inflation back to target.
DEBT MARKETS ADD PRESSURE
Concerns about government finances are adding to borrowing costs.
France remains a focus of investor concern. The spread between French and German 10-year government bond yields widened by about 5 basis points to 145.5 basis points in Monday early trading. Investors questioned France's ability to rein in its budget deficit amid political uncertainty ahead of the 2027 presidential election.
Borrowing costs can rise even without another ECB rate increase. Investors may demand greater compensation for fiscal risk, while higher government bond yields can feed into financing costs across the economy.
Global developments also matter. Lane said the worldwide artificial intelligence investment boom was plausibly contributing to higher long-term interest rates. "Especially since the scale of the European AI boom is not of the same order as the global AI boom, the increase in long-term interest rates constitutes a material tightening of financial conditions for the euro area," he said.
Governments face a difficult trade-off. Subsidies can cushion households and companies against energy costs, but financing them through additional borrowing can intensify investors' concerns about public finances.
Europe's resilience will depend partly on whether fuel supplies improve before expensive energy and credit force businesses to cut investment and households to curb spending. Emergency reserves can ease the immediate squeeze, but they cannot resolve the import dependence and capacity constraints that leave the region exposed to further shocks. ■

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is deeply concerned by increased fighting in Yemen and condemns Houthi attacks, a UN spokesperson said Monday.
"The secretary-general has wanted the sides to de-escalate tensions, and he continues to want that," said Farhan Haq, the deputy spokesperson for Guterres.
The spokesperson added that Guterres does not believe that further militarization of the conflict, including involvement by outside powers, will be helpful.
The International Organization for Migration said more than 180,000 people have been displaced since Aug. 1.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said the United Nations and its partners continue to support the humanitarian response wherever conditions allow, as escalating hostilities are causing more civilian casualties.
Since the start of August, at least 46 civilians have been killed, 24 of them children, and more than 130 others have been injured, including 84 women and children, OCHA said, citing the UN Human Rights Office.
According to OCHA, humanitarian partners have reported damage to civilian infrastructure, including homes and farms, as well as health, water and education facilities.
"OCHA continues to assess people's needs and the impact of the hostilities," it said. ■

South Africa's petrol, diesel prices for October set to rise sharply
China
Unknown Publisher

07:02:23 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- South African motorists and consumers face another economic blow this week as the Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources announced major monthly fuel price increases on Monday, set to take effect this Wednesday.
Driven by ongoing conflict in the Middle East and rising global crude costs, with Brent crude climbing above 100 U.S. dollars a barrel during September, the department confirmed that petrol prices will increase by between 3.12 rand (about 0.19 U.S. dollars) and 3.33 rand per liter, while diesel will rise by 2.84 to 3.24 rand per liter.
In its statement, the department highlighted that average Brent crude oil prices rose from 87.89 to 101.00 dollars per barrel over September as U.S.-Iran tensions escalated and threatened oil transit through the Strait of Hormuz.
The exchange rate provided minimal relief, as the rand appreciated slightly against the dollar, averaging 16.21 in September.
The steep price hikes come roughly a week after the South African Reserve Bank raised its benchmark repurchase rate by 25 basis points, coupled with annual inflation reaching 4.4 percent in September.
Commenting on the wider economic fallout, Azar Jammine, chief economist at Econometrix, an independent economic consultancy, warned that South Africa remains highly vulnerable to geopolitical shocks due to its import dependency.
"We are an oil importer. Worse than that, we have seen a deterioration in our fuel refining capacity over the last decade, making us even more dependent on imported refined fuels than in the past," Jammine told Xinhua in an interview.
"The entire economy will suffer as a consequence, and job creation will be negatively affected. At present, there seems to be very little scope for a major growth upswing," he noted. ■

PANAMA CITY, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- The Panama Canal Authority said Monday it will expand its Long-term Slot Allocation program to include a pilot program for the Panamax locks for the first time, covering transits from Jan. 3 to April 3, 2027.
The program, known as LoTSA, will continue at the Neopanamax locks, with bidding scheduled for Nov. 17. It will offer 36 packages totaling 270 transit slots, the authority said in a statement.
Bidding for the Panamax pilot program will take place on Nov. 24, with 51 packages totaling 288 slots available.
Slots will be allocated through sealed-bid competitions. The program is designed to allow customers to secure transit slots ahead of the dry season, giving shipping companies greater certainty when planning their operations.
The authority said the program is particularly relevant as the canal takes steps to sustain operations amid climatic conditions affecting water availability.
Remaining transit capacity is expected to continue being offered through the regular booking system and auctions, the authority added. ■

Britain's services PMI at 52.1 in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:02:00 CST
07:02:00 KST

LONDON, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- The purchasing managers' index (PMI) of Britain's services sector fell to 52.1 in September, but posted a sustained rebound in business conditions during the third quarter of 2026, data from S&P Global showed Monday.
The seasonally adjusted S&P Global UK Services PMI Business Activity Index went down from the four-month high of 52.5 in August, and stayed flat from July's 52.1, according to the company.
Moderate output growth was maintained across the UK services economy in September, albeit with a loss of momentum in comparison to August, said Tim Moore, economics director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, noting "subdued demand conditions and rising inflationary pressures contributed to weaker business activity expectations for the year ahead."
New orders increased at the slowest pace since the current period of growth began in July. And new business from abroad fell for the 7th successive month due to strong competition and lackluster global economic conditions, S&P Global said.
"Geopolitical tensions, squeezed consumer budgets and higher borrowing costs were cited as sales headwinds," Moore commented, taking resilient demand for technology services as the remaining main bright spot.
The data also marked two years of continuous job cuts across the sector, however, it showed that the rate of decline in workforce numbers was the slowest since October 2025.
Efforts to protect operating margins from rising fuel bills and elevated pay inflation contributed the fastest increase in prices charged by services firms since May, the company added. ■

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Tensions between South Africa and the United States have deepened following a fresh public exchange between South African International Relations and Cooperation Minister Ronald Lamola and U.S. Ambassador to South Africa Brent Bozell III.
On Monday, Bozell responded on social media platform X to remarks by Lamola, who said the U.S. envoy should "get out of the kitchen" if he was tired of dialogue and no longer believed in diplomatic engagement with Pretoria.
"So here we go again. Another Minister Lamola personal insult aimed at an American leader (this time me)," Bozell wrote, adding that the South African government then "wonders why relations are collapsing."
Lamola's remarks were published by the Sunday Times, a South African newspaper, on Sunday, days after South Africa issued a formal diplomatic protest, or demarche, to Bozell over what the government described as "undiplomatic conduct."
Lamola said he was "taken aback" by Bozell's remarks suggesting that Washington had grown tired of repeated discussions with Pretoria.
"You can't have a diplomat who says time for talking is over. It's our job to talk," Lamola was quoted as saying.
He also accused Bozell of interfering in South Africa's domestic affairs through his public statements and engagements.
On Sept. 29, South Africa's Department of International Relations and Cooperation summoned Bozell over what it described as "undiplomatic conduct." It was the third demarche made to the U.S. envoy since he arrived in Pretoria in February.
The latest exchange came as Bozell continued to publicly criticize the South African government. In an interview with Fox News Digital published Sunday, he accused South African President Cyril Ramaphosa of refusing to condemn what he described as incitement to violence associated with the controversial anti-apartheid struggle chant "Kill the Boer."
The South African government has repeatedly rejected allegations of systematic persecution or "genocide" against white South Africans. Pretoria has said violent crime affects South Africans across racial groups and that its economic transformation policies are intended to address inequalities rooted in the country's apartheid past.
Disagreements between Washington and Pretoria have also centered on South Africa's land policies, race-based economic transformation measures and foreign policy positions.
In an opinion article published on the U.S. Embassy's website on Sept. 29, Bozell cited rural farm attacks, race-based measures affecting U.S. companies and what he called South Africa's "steady drift toward our adversaries" among Washington's concerns. He also criticized South Africa's land expropriation policy.
Bozell argued that South Africa's economic policies were discouraging some U.S. companies from investing in the country and said Washington had grown frustrated with what he described as Pretoria's failure to adequately respond to U.S. concerns.
South Africa has maintained that differences with Washington should be resolved through constructive diplomatic engagement, while insisting on respect for its sovereignty and its right to determine its domestic policies. ■

06:01:49 CST

ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Yemeni government forces said Monday they had retaken the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha in southwestern Taiz province from the Houthi group in what would reverse a major recent Houthi gain near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
A military source was quoted by the state-run Saba news agency as saying that the Nation's Shield Forces, the pro-government Giants Brigades and the Tihama Resistance, backed by airstrikes, entered Mocha after fierce fighting on the city's outskirts.
The source said an unspecified number of Houthi fighters were killed, wounded or captured in the fighting, while others fled.
Government forces were carrying out clearing operations in the city and surrounding areas to secure their positions, the source added.
A Houthi military official on the ground told Xinhua on condition of anonymity that Saudi warplanes carried out scores of strikes on Houthi positions near Bab al-Mandab before government forces launched the offensive.
He estimated that more than 56 Houthi fighters were killed and dozens of others wounded.
However, a source on the ground disputed the government account, telling Xinhua that government forces had not taken control of Mocha or its port. The source described the announcement as a "premature" claim of victory and part of an escalating propaganda battle.
The Houthis seized Mocha in early September during a rapid advance that expanded their presence around the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
If confirmed, the government's recapture of the port city would mark a significant shift in the battle on Yemen's southwestern coast.
Mocha lies on the Red Sea coast north of Bab al-Mandab, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden -- a critical artery for international shipping between Asia and Europe.
The fighting came amid a wider escalation across southwestern Yemen. The government said the advance was part of its "Operation Dawn of Yemen," a broader offensive aimed at retaking Houthi-held territory, including the capital Sanaa, with Saudi Arabia providing extensive air support.
Yemen's conflict broke out in late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of the country's north, forcing the internationally recognized government out of the capital. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the government. The recent clashes marked the sharpest escalation since a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities in the war-torn country. ■

OSLO, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Norway's government on Monday proposed raising the minimum age for riding electric scooters from 12 to 16, citing a sharp increase in injuries among children and teenagers.
The Ministry of Transport said it had asked the Norwegian Public Roads Administration to submit the proposal for public consultation.
Transport Minister Kamzy Gunaratnam said stronger measures were needed to reduce serious accidents, noting that many people involved in e-scooter crashes were aged between 12 and 16.
An assessment by the roads administration found that the youngest riders had limited traffic knowledge, making it difficult for them to navigate complex situations and interact safely with other road users. Riders aged 14 and 15 were more frequently involved in accidents characterized by high speeds and risky riding.
Gunaratnam said several European countries had already introduced higher minimum ages, while many Norwegian rental companies required users to be at least 15 or 16.
Norway's existing rules include mandatory helmets for riders under 15 and liability insurance requirements. The government is also examining broader helmet requirements and measures targeting illegal e-scooters. ■

African telecom regulators call for strong AI governance to mitigate risks
China
Unknown Publisher

06:01:47 CST
07:01:47 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- The development and adoption of emerging technologies like artificial intelligence (AI) in Africa must be anchored in sound policy and legal guardrails to mitigate potential societal risks, telecom regulators said Monday.
Speaking at a meeting of Africa's information and communications technology (ICT) regulatory bodies running through Friday in Nairobi, the Kenyan capital, David Mugonyi, director-general of the Communications Authority of Kenya, noted that while AI has immense potential to transform economies, it also carries serious risks that require ethical deployment and oversight.
"As regulators, we are exploring ways to promote ethical deployment of AI within education or health sectors without compromising the safety of our citizens," Mugonyi said.
He added that regulators across the continent are actively sharing knowledge and best practices to draft forward-looking policies and laws, aiming to govern AI effectively without stifling innovation.
The five-day meeting, convened by the Communications Authority of Kenya in conjunction with bilateral partners, brought together senior policymakers, regulators, and industry experts from regional ICT regulatory bodies to bolster collaboration and institutional capacity as the continent prepares for an inclusive and resilient digital future.
Lafayetta Boye-Massaquoi, a junior licensing officer at the Liberia Telecommunications Authority, emphasized that sound, evidence-based, and people-centered regulations are vital to ensuring the safe adoption of AI and accelerating Africa's digital transformation.
She added that regulatory guardrails must be carefully balanced to avoid stifling innovation, particularly in key sectors like public services, banking, healthcare, education, and agriculture that stand to be revolutionized by AI.
"We are looking forward to collaboration with sister countries to see how AI can promote digital inclusion and protect consumer rights," Boye-Massaquoi said.
Brian Kalinga, a senior ICT officer at the Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority, stressed that for AI adoption to unleash positive impacts in Africa, governments should invest in digital infrastructure, training and the provision of seed capital to AI startups and innovators.
Telecom regulators on the continent should also ensure that access to AI tools among the marginalized, including persons with disabilities, is prioritized, Kalinga said.
"AI is going to transform this continent, increase efficiency, enable people to create, but we should learn from those who are ahead of us to make sure there are guardrails," Kalinga added. ■

Roundup: Ethiopia forms new gov't as Abiy Ahmed reappointed PM amid security challenges

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- The Ethiopian House of Peoples' Representatives (HoPR) formally established the country's new federal government on Monday, as the ruling Prosperity Party (PP) appointed incumbent Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed for another term in office.
RULING PP FORMS NEW GOV'T
The formation of the new government and the appointment of Abiy occurred during the inaugural session of the seventh HoPR tenure, completing the constitutional process that followed the general elections held on June 1.
During the election, the PP won a landslide victory by garnering 438 of the 486 contested seats in the HoPR, securing the parliamentary majority required to form the federal executive branch for a second term.
In line with Ethiopia's parliamentary political system, Abiy and the newly elected members of the HoPR, the lower chamber of parliament, took their oaths of office in the session.
Ethiopia's constitution places the HoPR at the center of federal legislative authority. It stipulates that the political party or coalition holding a majority of seats in the HoPR forms and leads the federal executive, with election results establishing the parliamentary basis for the formation of a new government.
The federal government's post-election transition follows regional council formations across the East African country, as regional states recently constituted their respective governments and elected their chief administrators.
OUTLINING STRATEGIC GOALS
During his acceptance speech at the inaugural session, Abiy presented key social, economic, and political directions his administration will pursue over the next five years for his government -- dubbed the "Medemer Government," an Amharic word for "coming together" or "synergy."
Abiy highlighted sustaining the country's socioeconomic development, ensuring national security and stability, as well as fostering national reconciliation and understanding as his government's major targets.
He stressed that the government will implement various initiatives to further strengthen the ongoing comprehensive national reforms, while also improving the effectiveness of public institutions.
Abiy further outlined ensuring macroeconomic stability, promoting green development, fostering digital transformation, and integrated urban development efforts as some of Ethiopia's primary socioeconomic development targets for the coming five years.
Highlighting past and existing regional and geo-political realities, he underscored that in an era of fast and unpredictable global shifts, "choosing and pursuing what is best for the nation remains the solemn duty of this generation."
Meanwhile, the prime minister called on citizens to join hands to help realize the East African country's aspiration for "national rejuvenation."
DOMESTIC, REGIONAL UNCERTAINTIES
Ethiopia's post-election transition is unfolding amid mounting uncertainties, as the East African country grapples with active conflicts, primarily in its northern region.
Upon formally forming its second federal government, the ruling party's new government has inherited pressing peace and security challenges as well as regional diplomatic tensions.
The formation of the new government came as military confrontations have escalated in recent weeks in the country's northernmost Tigray region, pitting the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) and its allied forces against troops loyal to the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allied armed groups.
The Ethiopian army and its allies are currently expanding territorial control across the conflict-hit Tigray region. Local residents who spoke to Xinhua on Sunday confirmed that the Ethiopian army and its allied forces, mainly the Tigray Peace Force, took control of the regional capital, Mekelle, late Saturday afternoon.
Experts and political analysts noted that the ENDF's control of Mekelle marks a new phase in the ongoing military escalation in northern Ethiopia, following the Sept. 20 announcement of a new alliance formed by seven Ethiopian opposition and armed groups.
These recent security tensions are set against the backdrop of the devastating two-year war between federal forces and TPLF-loyal troops from November 2020 to November 2022. The war left millions in urgent need of humanitarian assistance before the two parties signed the landmark Pretoria peace accord in South Africa to end hostilities.
As military tensions continue in northern Ethiopia, the situation has also raised concerns over the conflict's potential regional spillover. Recent developments have also ignited heightened diplomatic tensions, primarily among Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Egypt. ■

Explainer: Why 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awards optogenetics
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:01:44 CST
07:01:44 KST

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine is announced in Stockholm, Sweden, Oct. 5, 2026. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel were awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, the Nobel Assembly at Sweden's Karolinska Institute announced. (Xinhua/Lyu You)
STOCKHOLM, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.
The Nobel Assembly at Sweden's Karolinska Institutet awarded the prize for optogenetics and described it as a method that makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behaviours in the living brain.
WHO ARE THE LAUREATES?
Karl Deisseroth is a U.S.-born professor at Stanford University and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, both born in Germany, are professors at Humboldt University of Berlin and the University of Wuerzburg, respectively.
"Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel discovered a remarkable protein, channelrhodopsin, in a single-celled alga. Karl Deisseroth transformed the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells. The laureates have laid the foundation of a new era in neuroscience," the institute said in a press release.
The laureates will share a prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (about 1.19 million U.S. dollars).
WHAT IS OPTOGENETICS?
Optogenetics refers to a method for controlling nerve signals with light. The story began with a simple question: how can a single-celled green alga swim toward light even though it has no brain?
Peter Hegemann studied Chlamydomonas, an alga that can detect light and rapidly change its movement. He suspected that its light sensor might also act as an ion channel.
Working with Georg Nagel, Hegemann identified proteins known as channelrhodopsins. When exposed to blue light, these proteins open a channel through the cell membrane. Charged ions then flow into the cell, producing an electrical response.
Crucially, when researchers introduced the genes encoding these proteins into other cells, those cells also became sensitive to light.
Karl Deisseroth introduced the gene for channelrhodopsin into nerve cells from rats. In 2005, his team showed that flashes of blue light could trigger nerve signals with millisecond precision. Two years later, the approach was successfully used in the brains of living mice.
The method became known as optogenetics and gained global impact.
WHY DID THIS CHANGE NEUROSCIENCE?
The adult human brain contains around 90 billion nerve cells, or neurons, each forming thousands of connections with other cells. Neural pathways can stretch across distant parts of the brain, while neurons controlling very different functions may be packed closely together.
For decades, scientists could observe which parts of the brain became active when an animal moved, formed a memory or experienced an emotion. Such observations could show that brain activity and behavior were linked without revealing whether one directly caused the other.
Optogenetics changed that by allowing scientists to activate selected neurons and observe what happened next, making it possible to test cause and effect with far greater precision. Researchers have identified neural circuits involved in pain, social behavior, thirst, feeding, reward and attention. They have also pinpointed neurons that help regulate functions ranging from the body clock to fever responses triggered by the immune system.
"Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of," said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine.
COULD IT HELP TREAT DISEASE?
For now, optogenetics remains primarily a research tool, helping scientists investigate how brain circuits malfunction in conditions including depression, anxiety, Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease.
Anna Wedell, a member of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, said that researchers can first identify cells involved in conditions such as dementia and addiction in animal models, and then use imaging and other methods to explore how those findings may apply to humans.
Clinical research has also begun. Qiang Pan Hammarstrom, a member of the Nobel Committee and professor of Clinical Immunology at Karolinska Institutet, told Xinhua that optogenetics has already shown clinical potential in retinitis pigmentosa, a rare genetic eye disease, where light-sensitive proteins can be used to stimulate surviving retinal cells and partially restore vision.
The larger impact of optogenetics may lie in what it allows scientists to ask. By turning carefully selected nerve cells on or off, researchers can continue to unravel one of humanity's greatest mysteries: how the brain works. ■

Talking to yourself on psilocybin may be a good sign in alcohol treatment, small study hints
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
22:00:49 UTC
07:00:49 KST

People with alcohol use disorder who were still abstinent three months after psilocybin-assisted therapy tended to describe their first psychedelic session differently than those who had returned to drinking, according to a study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders. In interviews the day after their first dose, much of the talk about an inner dialogue, rethinking habitual patterns, and committing to change came from people who stayed abstinent, while talk focused on sensations, visions, and emotions came mostly from those who later drank. The exploratory findings suggest that how people engage with a psychedelic experience may be related to treatment response.
Psilocybin is a psychedelic substance that can temporarily alter perception, emotions, and patterns of thinking. In psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy, the drug experience is combined with preparation and follow-up sessions. The follow-up, or integration, sessions are intended to help participants make sense of what they experienced and connect it with their goals for recovery.
Previous studies have suggested that psychedelic therapy may help some people with alcohol use disorder, but it remains unclear why some participants improve more than others. Researchers have proposed that personal insights, emotional processing, changes in self-perception, and new approaches to coping may all contribute, but earlier interview-based studies of psilocybin for alcohol use disorder included only a handful of participants.
Led by Maria Garcia Garcia of Nîmes University Hospital and the University of Montpellier in France, the team analyzed recordings from the first integration session in the Psilocybin Alcohol Depression trial. In that randomized trial, recently detoxified patients received two psilocybin sessions three weeks apart, at either a high dose or a very low dose, alongside an intensive relapse prevention program.
The analysis included the 20 participants who received the high, 25-milligram dose. All had alcohol use disorder and continuing depressive symptoms, and they had a median age of 49 years; 11 were male and nine were female. Before dosing, participants took part in preparation sessions that included mindfulness exercises and setting personal intentions related to alcohol, which were read aloud at the start of the psilocybin session.
The integration sessions took place the day after the first dose. Eleven participants were abstinent from alcohol three months later, meaning they had not had a drink in the previous four weeks, while nine were not.
The sessions were transcribed and analyzed with software that uses an automated method to sort passages into groups based on the words they share, without the researchers specifying the groups in advance. The transcripts contained 127,760 words and were divided into 3,700 short segments. The software sorted 88.27% of these segments into two main language patterns.
The first pattern, which represented 44% of the classified segments, focused on sensory and emotional features of the psychedelic experience. Participants discussed physical sensations, visual experiences, emotions, and the setting of the session. This pattern came mostly from people who were not abstinent three months later.
The second pattern represented nearly 56% of the classified segments. It focused on inner dialogue, rethinking familiar ways of behaving, making commitments, working with the intentions set during preparation, and revisiting the role of alcohol in participants’ lives. This pattern came mostly from participants who remained abstinent, as well as from those with more trauma symptoms or greater sensitivity to social rejection.
The authors described the second pattern as involving “active cognitive processes, characterized by an inner dialogue.” They emphasize that this dialogue was something participants described having during the psilocybin session itself, often while freely recounting the experience, rather than something generated during the interview. One participant who remained abstinent recalled: “I told myself I don’t need alcohol to feel okay. I have people I love, and I have people who love me.”
A follow-up analysis comparing the words used by abstinent and non-abstinent participants painted a similar picture. People who stayed abstinent more often mentioned family members, pleasant emotions, and new ways of handling situations that used to trigger drinking. Those who returned to drinking more often mentioned negative emotions, physical pain, disappointment, and attempts to push unpleasant feelings away.
Difficult experiences were not necessarily a bad sign. Fear was the one negative emotion linked to abstinence, and it tended to appear when participants described facing old fears using coping strategies taught during preparation, such as holding a meaningful object. The authors suggest that what mattered was how people handled difficult content, not whether it appeared.
Notably, none of the participants directly described a mystical experience, and talk about the intensity of the experience was not more common among those who stayed abstinent. The authors suggest that preparation, including work on personal intentions, may help encourage the kind of inner dialogue that was linked to abstinence.
The study has some limitations. With only 20 participants, the findings are preliminary, and each language pattern was driven heavily by a handful of people. The analysis was exploratory and examined text segments rather than treating each participant as a separate statistical observation. Therapist questions were also included in the transcripts, so the conversations reflected an interaction rather than participants’ words alone.
The study also cannot show that inner dialogue caused abstinence. Participants received a second psilocybin session and continued an intensive relapse prevention program after these interviews, so the early differences might not have held up without the full course of treatment. The authors describe inner dialogue as a possible therapeutic mechanism to be tested in future studies rather than a proven one.
The study, “Insights from the psychedelic experience integration session: Verbatims differentiate 3-month abstinence in alcohol use disorder with depressive symptoms,” was authored by Maria Garcia Garcia, Dahbia Belahda, Carine Graux, Chris Serrand, Noé Igounenc, Felix Sergent, Thibault Mura, and Amandine Luquiens.

The predawn incident came ahead of a rally demanding “justice for survivors” by student groups on Monday.

“We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community,” Kimball said. “Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer.”

“We wanted to ensure that Day Hall, the centre of Cornell’s administrative function, was not able to continue business as usual,” the students told the campus paper.

IMF warns debt-financed tax cuts increase global interest rates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
21:45:51 UTC
06:45:51 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned that corporate income tax policies generate cross-border spillovers through profit shifting, investment reallocation and knowledge transfers.
The IMF released a chapter titled "Intangible Yet Real: Spillovers from Corporate Income Taxation" for its October 2026 World Economic Outlook, stating that tax competition remained a defining feature of the global economy while its nature changed over time.
Authors noted that the globalization of production, the rise of multinational corporations and the growing importance of intangible assets transformed the landscape of corporate income taxation.
The institution highlighted that multinational corporations accounted for more than 20% of global gross domestic product and approximately 15% of global corporate profits.
The study showed that differences in corporate income taxation generated cross-border spillovers as multinational corporations relocated profits and investments across countries to minimize tax liabilities.
The report warned that debt-financed tax cuts increased global interest rates and crowded out investment abroad.
Researchers emphasized that stronger anti-avoidance frameworks supported economic output while protecting tax revenues.
The organization added that a one percentage point increase in a country's corporate income tax rate relative to rates elsewhere caused a cumulative decline in foreign direct investment inflows of about 0.5% of gross domestic product over three years.

Lebanon to hold joint drills with Britain
Lebanon's army will hold exercises with the British military this month, both sides said Monday, and the drills will also involve personnel and representatives from countries including the United States and France.
Britain has been a key supporter of the cash-strapped Lebanese army and has provided millions of dollars in assistance over the years, including helping train Lebanese soldiers to secure the country's land borders.
The Lebanese army said that the joint "Pegasus Cedar 2026" exercise would begin on Tuesday and aimed to "bolster the capabilities of military units and raise the level of coordination between the Lebanese army and friendly armies".
It said the exercise would include "training on reconnaissance, raids and combat in built-up areas", among other activities.
A British embassy statement said British soldiers based in Cyprus would "join their Lebanese counterparts in the Air Assault Regiment in a landmark military exercise aimed at strengthening bilateral defence ties and enhancing operational readiness".
"Personnel from the armies of the United States and Italy will also take part, with representatives from the armies of France, Cyprus, Qatar, and Jordan joining as observers," it added.
The exercise, to be held over three weeks, builds on a previous UK-Lebanon military training exercise held in September 2023, the embassy statement added.
Lebanese authorities have called for increased support for the country's under-resourced army, which counts some 80,000 personnel and depends heavily on foreign aid.
The military faces enormous challenges in completing its deployment to south Lebanon under a framework agreement reached in June between Israel and Lebanon that involves the disarmament of militant group Hezbollah and the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces.
Israel has launched a series of massive airstrikes and a ground invasion in Lebanon in March.
While violence has dropped since June, Israel still carries out attacks and demolitions, and its troops are occupying a self-declared "security zone" running around 10 kilometres (six miles) inside Lebanon along the border.
The fighting followed another war that erupted in 2023 and led to an all-out war the following year.
Last month in Paris, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun met his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron and Jordan's King Abdullah II, and discussed international support for the country's military.

US 'watching closely' after plague researcher dies in Russia
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
22:33:49 BST
06:33:49 KST

US 'watching closely' after plague researcher dies in Russia
- Published
President Donald Trump says the US is looking "very strongly" at the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was watching closely amid concerns the incident could lead to the spread of pneumonic plague, but there was no cause for alarm.
Announcing the cause of death as "pneumonia of undetermined etiology", Irkutsk's governor said "no micro-organisms" linked to the woman's work had been found "in her biological samples".
Unconfirmed reports suggested the woman fell ill either after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
Asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague spreading from Russia, Trump said he had not spoken to the Kremlin about it.
"I hate to see them having it," he said, but added: "We'll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we'll always help."
No other cases of staff from the plague institute seeking medical attention since the lab technician's death had been reported, Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said, quoting Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor.
The watchdog said a biological safety team had inspected the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk and found no emergency situation there.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people not to "listen to various rumours" but "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements" instead.
Russian media reported last week that nearly 200 people known to have had contact with the dead woman were under medical observation as a precaution.
Asked by a reporter for an "update on the suspected plague case in Russia", Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread, at least internally - you've seen them do quarantine of this and that nature.
"If something like that gets out, it can quickly spread. So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and the cause to just keep an eye on it and we're doing that."
The woman who died, whose first name was given by Russian media as Daria and who was in her late twenties, had recently visited the Buryatia region on the border with Mongolia.
The plague bacterium or Yersinia pestis, external, which killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death, is found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, external was founded just over 100 years ago.
Dr Simon Clarke, an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the pneumonic version of Yersinia pestis was nearly always fatal if left untreated, but could be overcome with antibiotics.
"Pneumonic plague can transmit from person to person and that is why there is the concern around this," he said.
He added: "But of course people's thought with any outbreak of infectious disease at all runs to... lockdowns and Covid and that is just not what's going to happen here."
"People think, 'Oh the plague, that's gone, that went hundreds of years ago,' but it hasn't," Clarke said.
"It's still around and in certain parts of the world, it's a threat to human health and that's why they need to study it."
Asked if the pathogen might have been studied for potential use as a bio-weapon, the scientist agreed it was possible.
"Because this is Russia people's thoughts are running to that, but I think my earlier explanation is probably more likely," Clarke said.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.
People can be infected through:
- infected flea bites
- contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials
- the inhalation of respiratory particles.
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.

Romanian president signs law regulating bear population cull
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
21:32:46 UTC
06:32:46 KST

In recent years Romania has increasingly seen bears wandering into towns and villages, and the number of bear attacks has risen sharply.
Romania's head of state, Nicusor Dan, on Monday signed a law aimed at reducing the country's bear population, a bill he had previously challenged on constitutional grounds and sent back to parliament for reconsideration.
The legislation, which was re-adopted by the Chamber of Deputies on 16 September, allows the preventive shooting of 859 brown bears this year. A further 110 protected large wild animals may be hunted as an intervention measure if they pose a threat to human life.
In recent years it has become common in Romania for bears to appear in inhabited areas, and the number of bear attacks has risen sharply, with more and more fatal incidents.
According to the results of an earlier survey mapping the brown bear population, Romania is home to Europe's largest bear population and the greatest genetic diversity among bear species.
The study put the number of individuals at between 10,600 and 12,700.
Last week, Covasna County prefect Ráduly István warned that, because of the limited time available, it would be impossible to meet this year's quota. He pointed out that in the Szeklerland county 86 bears should be culled this year, of which 30 have already been removed, but there is not enough time left to reach the full quota.
The government's local representative said the law was much needed because both the number of bears and the damage they cause had increased significantly in the county. In the first eight months of this year, around 300 emergency calls were registered over bears straying into built-up areas and there were also two bear attacks.
Time running out to tackle overpopulation?
The law, initiated by the Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania (RMDSZ) and now revised, will enter into force once it is published in the official gazette. Some officials, however, warn that it is now impossible to fulfil this year's quota, as the months-long legal wrangle has left too little time to shoot several hundred large wild animals.
Nicusor Dan sent the draft law back to parliament in August after first lodging a constitutional challenge, which was rejected by the Constitutional Court. He asked parliament to review and supplement the legislation, arguing that the previously adopted law needed clarification on several points.
The Chamber of Deputies approved the bill without amendments, in the form already adopted by the Senate. During the debate some MPs urged that the law be put into practice as soon as possible.
Senator Tánczos Barna, acting deputy prime minister and one of the initiators, recalled that the alliance had requested nearly a year ago that preventive quotas be doubled for this year and for 2027.
He said this step followed a scientific survey which confirmed that the overpopulation of bears in Romania can only be curbed through more effective intervention, and that immediate action against dangerous bears does not replace broader population control measures.

Ukraine and Germany to deepen partnership to support war-affected businesses
The information comes from the Ministry of Economy and Environment, Ukrinform reported.
The ministers focused on two priority areas — a new mechanism for war‑risk insurance and the development of the joint Industrial Ramstein initiative.
Ukraine is currently designing an updated war‑risk insurance model that would raise compensation for affected businesses to USD 10 million.
“This is the first tier of losses the state will cover. We want the mechanism to be genuinely useful for large companies and create conditions for private insurers and reinsurers to join. Ukraine expects G7 support for this model, including Germany’s participation in establishing a dedicated fund for targeted financing,” Kravchenko said.
The discussion also centered on the needs of Ukrainian businesses amid ongoing attacks on production and logistics infrastructure, the restoration of industrial capacity, the attraction of German investment and technology, and further implementation of the Industrial Ramstein initiative.
The ministers devoted separate attention to shifting from emergency support for Ukrainian companies to systematic industrial modernization and deeper integration of Ukrainian manufacturing into European supply chains.
They discussed next steps to launch the pilot phase of the program and scale it up. Ukraine expects the mechanism to help not only replace equipment lost to the war but also upgrade production technologically and build long‑term industrial links between Ukrainian and German companies.
Ukraine also proposed expanding direct cooperation with German federal states and their industrial clusters, matching specific needs of Ukrainian enterprises with the technological specialization of individual German regions.
Other topics included expanding the presence of German companies in Ukraine, establishing joint ventures, localizing production, developing joint R&D projects, and advancing war‑risk insurance instruments.

New York declares first US measles disaster emergency since 2025 surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
21:24:02 UTC
06:24:02 KST

New York declares first US measles disaster emergency since 2025 surge
Oct 5 - New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on Monday over a measles outbreak, the first such declaration by a U.S. state since cases began surging in 2025.
The state also expanded the pool of health professionals allowed to administer measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccines as cases rise in rural communities.
"No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease," Hochul said in a statement.
New York has reported 108 measles cases this year through October 3, including 92 since July 15 in under-immunized rural communities across 18 counties, well above typical annual levels, according to the executive order.
Seven of the cases are in New York City and 101 are elsewhere in the state, the governor's office said. Local health departments have administered more than 1,000 MMR doses in rural areas since July 15.
Neighboring Pennsylvania is battling a fast-spreading outbreak, with 977 cases and five deaths as of October 2, mostly in rural counties that border New York, the order said.
Pennsylvania health officials said on Monday the state's total had passed 1,000 cases, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades.
The US is having its worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 cases reported, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The order allows registered nurses to order tests for suspected measles and pharmacists to vaccinate children as young as two. It also requires all MMR vaccinations to be reported to state or New York City immunization registries within 72 hours, while waiving adults' consent for such reporting.
Vaccination itself still requires the consent of the patient or a legal guardian. The emergency took effect on Monday and runs through November 4. REUTERS

The attack has intensified scrutiny of Israel’s system for securing foreign airlines and screening crews flying into the country. New questions have also emerged over potential conflicts of interest involving senior figures responsible for aviation security at the Transportation Ministry.
After Haaretz reported that Avraham “Avri” Cohen, head of the ministry’s Security, Emergency and Cyber Division, had held a second job in private security for eight years without final authorization, another senior figure in the ministry’s aviation security apparatus has come under scrutiny.
Dvir Rubinstein, one of the founders and the current director of the ministry’s Aviation Security Operations Center, known by its Hebrew acronym MAMLAT, is not a civil servant. He provides services to the Transportation Ministry as an outside contractor while also operating a private company that provides consulting and training services to airlines, including flydubai and Emirates.
That arrangement means Rubinstein has received private payment from flydubai while holding a central role in the Israeli system responsible for dealing with security matters involving foreign airlines, including flydubai.
MAMLAT serves as the Transportation Ministry’s operational center for aviation security and occupies a key position in the mechanism through which Israel approves and oversees security arrangements for foreign airlines operating flights to the country. It works regularly with airlines and government agencies in Israel and abroad.
As part of his role, Rubinstein is responsible for security approvals and permits required by airlines and flights seeking to enter Israel, both in advance and in real time. That makes him one of the principal officials maintaining direct contact with foreign airlines and handling security issues connected to their operations in Israel.
The arrangement has created a situation in which an official responsible through MAMLAT for security matters involving foreign airlines also maintains private business relationships with airlines falling within his professional sphere of responsibility.
The Transportation Ministry said Rubinstein’s outside activities were properly authorized and conducted outside the hours in which he provides services to the ministry. The ministry has not yet responded specifically to questions about his private work for airlines that fall within his professional responsibilities or the implications of those relationships for his MAMLAT role.
A long-running battle over responsibility
The attempted takeover of the flydubai flight has exposed what officials and previous government reviews have described as a broader structural problem in Israel’s security system for foreign aviation rather than an isolated failure.
At the center of the dispute is a position that has become increasingly entrenched among Transportation Ministry professionals: The ministry’s Security, Emergency and Cyber Division does not have the intelligence capabilities, resources or tools needed to assume responsibility for the security of foreign flights entering Israel.
Those concerns predate the current government.
During the tenure of former transportation minister Merav Michaeli and former ministry director-general Michal Frank, ministry professionals formally raised the issue. Frank held at least three dedicated meetings with the National Security Council in which she warned that the Transportation Ministry was not equipped to bear the responsibility.
The National Security Council continued to oppose changing the arrangement, however, and the interagency dispute persisted. Government decisions intended to clarify the division of responsibilities and establish a central coordinating body were not implemented for two years.
As government agencies argued over jurisdiction, aviation and cybersecurity were identified as among the most exposed areas in the security system, according to officials familiar with the discussions.
The organizational problems also extended inside the Transportation Ministry’s security division.
Questions arose over Cohen’s outside employment in private security while he headed the division responsible for protecting national transportation infrastructure. An arrangement allowing him to undertake the outside work had encountered resistance under Michaeli and raised questions about potential conflicts of interest and priorities. It emerged Monday that the approval process had never been finalized.
The concerns over foreign aviation security were raised again after Transportation Minister Miri Regev and ministry Director-General Moshe Ben Zaken took office.
Professional officials told Ben Zaken that the security division could not adequately carry out the mission and warned that the situation represented a genuine security risk. The issue was nevertheless put on hold, according to people familiar with the matter.
One official familiar with the discussions said Ben Zaken had been warned repeatedly but took no action, describing the ministry’s handling of the issue as part of a deep management failure.
Warnings but no dedicated meeting
A review of Regev’s publicly available calendars from 2023 through 2025 also raises questions about the priority given to the issue.
The calendars were analyzed as part of the “Minister Meter” project by Shakuf, an Israeli nonprofit investigative news organization focused on government transparency.
They show extensive attention to aviation matters, including efforts to persuade foreign airlines to resume service to Israel, responses to flight cancellations, aviation agreements and meetings with the Civil Aviation Authority.
But the calendars contain no dedicated meeting specifically addressing the screening of foreign flight crews or the broader security gap surrounding foreign airlines.
That absence stands out because the state comptroller had already warned about weaknesses in the system.
In May 2024, State Comptroller Matanyahu Englman’s office published the public portions of a classified audit examining international civil aviation security. The review covered foreign and private aircraft entering Israeli airspace as well as Israeli aviation abroad and flights departing Israel.
The comptroller recommended that the National Security Council work with the Transportation and Finance ministries, the Civil Aviation Authority, Shin Bet and police to conduct a comprehensive review of the entire civil aviation security system. It also called for a reassessment of government and security Cabinet decisions governing aviation security, some dating to the 1970s, and for clearer responsibility and allocation of resources.
Regev’s calendars show that she continued to meet directly with Civil Aviation Authority officials in 2025. Meetings were recorded Jan. 30, on consecutive days June 11 and 12 with Ben Zaken participating and in a June 27 conference call involving the heads of the Shin Bet and Civil Aviation Authority.
Despite those meetings, no dedicated discussion on the foreign-flight security gap was recorded, even though Cohen submitted several explicit requests for urgent meetings with Regev and Ben Zaken to discuss the deficiencies.
The public calendars provide only a partial picture. The data examined covers 2023 through 2025 and does not include Regev’s schedule in 2026. As is common with ministers’ public calendars, sensitive security consultations, routine briefings and informal conversations may also not appear explicitly or may be listed under broader headings.
Ministry priorities under scrutiny
The calendars also provide a broader picture of how Regev allocated her time during the three-year period.
From 2023 through 2025, she held 160 meetings with municipal leaders from 40 cities and local councils. According to the Shakuf analysis, most were associated with or supportive of Regev’s Likud party.
By contrast, the calendars show no meeting during that period with Tel Aviv-Jaffa Mayor Ron Huldai, a prominent critic of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government.
Those findings do not by themselves establish why particular meetings were or were not held, and the publicly released calendars may not capture every interaction.
The renewed scrutiny comes as investigators across several countries try to determine how al-Hammami was allowed into the cockpit of a Tel Aviv-bound aircraft despite reported warning signs in his background. The Associated Press reported that he had previously been flagged in Oman over extremist views and barred from flying there. No terrorist organization has claimed responsibility for the attack, and publicly available evidence has not established Iranian involvement.
The case has therefore opened two parallel investigations for Israel: one into whether al-Hammami acted entirely on his own or had outside support and another into how the security system designed to protect foreign flights bound for Israel allowed him to reach the cockpit in the first place.
