Jeffrey Archer, former Conservative politician and novelist, dies aged 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:42:02 UTC
05:42:02 KST

Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling author and former MP whose political career ended in disgrace when he was imprisoned for perjury, has died at the age of 86.
Archer, who was a Conservative MP for five years before serving as the party’s deputy chair, died “suddenly and peacefully” at his home “between writing sessions” on Monday, his publisher HarperCollins said.
He had a successful career as an author and was made a life peer in 1992.
During a run to become mayor of London for the Conservatives in 1999, his political career was in effect ended when it emerged he had lied in court over a decade earlier when a newspaper accused him of paying money to a sex worker. He was convicted of perjury and perverting the course of justice and imprisoned for four years.
An Old Bailey jury found that he had lied in a libel action he had brought against the Star newspaper in 1987 in which he had been awarded £500,000 in damages.
He was released early in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024.
Kate Elton, HarperCollins UK’s chief executive and Archer’s editor, said: “It has been one of the great privileges of my publishing life to have been Jeffrey Archer’s editor.
“He was the master storyteller and an editor’s dream – phenomenally hard-working, utterly committed to completing draft after draft to get every word as perfect as possible, and a true champion of the team nature of great publishing.”
Archer’s death came just one day before the publication of his new novel, Adam and Eve, on Tuesday 6 October.
His first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, was published in 1976, two years after he was threatened with bankruptcy, marked the end of his time as a sitting MP. This marked the beginning of an enviable writing career. Archer spent a total of 14 years and five months on the Sunday Times bestseller lists and over five years on the New York Times bestseller lists, selling 300 million books in 119 countries in 49 languages. His 1979 novel Kane and Abel remains among the best-selling books in the world, having sold more than 30 million copies to date.
His death came less than 24 hours after Archer had met and signed books for hundreds of fans at a sold-out event with broadcaster Gyles Brandreth at the Leicester Square Theatre in central London on Sunday, HarperCollins said.
Writing on X, Brandreth said: “Just yesterday I did a show with Jeffrey Archer to celebrate his new novel – he said it was to be his last.
“He was in the most wonderful, ebullient form and had such a great reception from a packed house. He was funny, engaging and self-deprecating – a great storyteller to the last.”
Archer was first elected an MP in a 1969 byelection for the constituency of Louth in Lincolnshire when he was 29 years old, having already worked as a Conservative councillor for Havering in north-east London, a period during which he also ran a Mayfair art gallery.
Archer cast himself as a centrist in parliament, frequently rebelling against the right wing of the Conservative party, but his political career stalled when he became the victim of a fraudulent investment scheme, which left him almost half a million pounds in debt. He said he would therefore not stand in the 1974 election “due to financial difficulties”.
His first novel was a direct effort to regain financial control – a move that paid off, and Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less was adapted for radio, and later, for TV. By the mid-1980s Archer had written several successful novels as well as short stories, plays and children’s books.
As his literary career bore fruit, Archer returned to politics, becoming a popular speaker at grassroots events, leading Margaret Thatcher to appoint him deputy chairman of the Conservative party in 1985.
But in October 1986 he became embroiled in scandal when the News of the World claimed he’d spent £2,000 to pay off a “vice girl”, a story immediately followed by a more detailed story in the Star alleging Archer had paid a woman named Monica Coghlan for sex. Archer sued the Star, and the case came to court the following year, winning £500,000 in damages but sowing the seeds for his downfall over a decade later.
In 1999, when allegations broke that he had lied in the libel trial, the leader of the Conservative party at the time, William Hague, said: “This is the end of politics for Jeffrey Archer. I will not tolerate such behaviour in my party.” Archer was expelled from the party in February 2000.
At the time he was charged with perjury in 2000, he was also making headlines by starring in his own West End play The Accused, which ran at the Theatre Royal Haymarket in London, and in which Archer’s character played an alleged murderer on trial and in which the audience voted on whether they believed Archer’s character was guilty or innocent at the end of each performance.
Archer’s perjury trial began on 30 May 2001, a month after Monica Coghlan was killed in a road traffic accident.
Following sentencing he was imprisoned at Belmarsh, a category A prison in London but later moved to four other prisons before his release in 2003, having served half of his sentence.
Despite retaining his seat in the House of Lords, Archer did not take an active role in the upper chamber of parliament and gave up his seat in 2024.
The former Tory minister, Nadhim Zahawi, paid tribute to Archer, writing on X: “Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey’s company.”
Archer had been due to be at the Cheltenham festival later in the month to discuss his forthcoming novel.
Archer is survived by his wife, Mary, and their sons, William and James.

Surging US interest rates 'a bigger problem for others'
The usual optimism from Rabobank global strategist Michael Every in his daily note.
"Monday saw Treasuries slump again, 10s up to 5.31% and 30s to 5.67%, the highest since early 2002," he observes.
"If we keep going like we have since February, we'll soon have 20th century yields again, a shock for the generation who weren't born in it and for elders who kept telling themselves "lower for longer" would hold after the geopolitical consensus couldn't.
"That's obviously a huge problem for the US but, as usual, it's proving a bigger problem for others."
Every cites civil unrest over the potential for austerity in France, but we can see the local dissatisfaction brewing over the RBA's string of rate rises, the latest of which had a strong flavour of response to rising US rates.
"Meanwhile, the US Nasdaq just hit a new record high, again taking us back to the turn of the century and its dotcom bubble," Every continues.
"That's another reason we can't expect yields to fall back easily — at least not until the miraculous deflationary impact of AI and SI (also referred to as AGI).
"Either way, SI is now the national security equivalent of the 20th century Manhattan Project and the 19th century investment surge into railways and steel. It won't stop easily.
"Neither will national security spending in general as wars rage on."
So, inflation is back and, in his view, not going away for a fair while, therefore meaning we'll have higher interest rates for longer and all the fallout that comes with that.
Key Event
Euro sinks, largely due to France's record debt and political uncertainty
The euro has dropped to a 17-month low against the US dollar.
It's also near a 22-month low against the Australian dollar.
Essentially, concerns about France's ability to rein in its budget deficit and a sharp bond market sell-off last week stirred fears of a return of sovereign debt crisis dynamics in the euro zone.
French government bonds have been sold off as expectations of higher policy rates and rising political uncertainty cast doubt on the ability of the euro area's second-largest economy to put its public finances on a more sustainable footing.
“Latest bond market dynamics are increasingly concerning and somewhat reminiscent of a sovereign debt crisis," Hauke Siemssen, strategist at Commerzbank, said.
The French government is seeking to enact an unpopular 2027 budget to lower its deficit and contain its record-high debt load, a tall order in a deeply divided parliament as political factions position ahead of next year's presidential election.
"We're pretty pessimistic about the euro. We think it's going to go down to under $US1.10," said Joseph Capurso, a currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank.
"We're not surprised that we've seen this weakness... For the euro to rise, you'd need a big decrease in oil prices... a big increase in expectations for European monetary policy tightening.
"Another one would be them starting to get their act together on reining in the budget deficit, though I think there's no chance of that happening anytime soon."
Analysts argued that France's fiscal problems were daunting enough on their own, but an upcoming presidential election and a hung parliament where compromise has often proved impossible make them even harder to address.
Planned budget cuts, which have deepened an already acute funding crunch in the education sector, have fuelled discontent and sparked protests across France.

Key Event
Directors cleared of wrongdoing in audit tender process: Macquarie statement
A key element of the intrigue around the Macquarie audit process was the involvement of non-executive director Michelle Hinchliffe.
She is a 35+ year veteran of KPMG, and also sits on the board of BHP.
The review "considered matters concerning two of Macquarie’s non-executive directors, Michelle Hinchliffe and Susan Lloyd-Hurwitz. The Boards sought independent advice on these matters from Tom Bathurst AC KC."
Here's what they deduced:
"Ms Hinchliffe met with KPMG staff before and during the audit tender process, in both a professional and personal capacity, in a manner consistent with Macquarie’s policies and audit tender protocols.
"Ms Hinchliffe interacted with the three firms participating in the tender process, in Macquarie’s interests, but recused herself from scoring and decision-making.
"Ms Lloyd-Hurwitz sent an email to a KPMG partner during the audit tender process, seeking a meeting in relation to general careers advice for one of her children which did not eventuate. Similar requests were made to other companies from a range of industries around the same time.
"In relation to these matters, Mr Bathurst concluded that neither Ms Hinchliffe nor Ms Lloyd-Hurwitz breached their fiduciary or statutory duties or Macquarie's policies or rules. In relation to Ms Hinchliffe’s interactions with KPMG staff before and during the audit tender process, Mr Bathurst concluded that any conflicts were managed appropriately and that Ms Hinchliffe did not give KPMG any unfair advantage over other firms in the process through her interactions or through any information provided."
So no harm, no foul. But the statement suggests that Macquarie might be getting that a lot of investors don't like the stench.
"Having considered the review findings, the Boards remain fully supportive of Ms Hinchliffe and Ms Lloyd-Hurwitz. They each make key contributions and their respective skills are highly valuable to the Boards’ effectiveness.
"While the review found no breach of duties, policies or audit tender rules, the Boards recognise that auditor independence, conflicts management and governance standards are of significant interest to shareholders and other stakeholders. The Boards acknowledge the importance of considering both actual and perceived conflicts and are committed to strengthening Macquarie's approach wherever improvements can be made.
So things will be different in future.
"For any future audit tender process, Macquarie's tender rules will be reviewed including with respect to restrictions on personal contact with participating audit firms during the tender period. As part of its usual annual refresh, the Board Conflicts of Interest Policy will also be externally reviewed for any potential improvements having regard to evolving best practice."

Key Event
Coalition sells migration policy as 'biggest' cut in Australian history
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has vowed to cut net overseas migration to 100,000 per year for the first two years of a Coalition government, before increasing to 160,000 by year four.
Net overseas migration was just over 300,000 in the year to December 2025 and peaked at 556,000 in 2023.
Mr Taylor described the proposal as the biggest cut to immigration in Australian history.
The Coalition's migration policy would also reduce the number of temporary visa holders by around 650,000 over four years.
It would abolish temporary graduate visas, cut the student visa intake to 240,000 and halve the humanitarian intake to 10,000 per year.
Mr Taylor said he was confident the plan was "budget neutral".

Key Event
Global oil and refined fuel inventory will deplete in 10-15 weeks, CBA analyst says
The Commonwealth Bank's commodities analyst Vivek Dhar is a voice worth listening to on the important concept of, "Do we have the stuff we need to keep our economy functioning?"
Specifically, oil.
Earlier in the year the Middle East conflict led our prime minister to tour South-East Asian nations on a smiling barter-fest, where we essentially cemented the future supply of crude oil and refined liquid fuels in return for something we have and they need: liquefied natural gas (LNG).
Do we have those supply issues again?
Dhar says, "Ship tracking data (shows) a significant uptick in Middle Eastern crude oil exports to levels close to pre-war levels (and by some measures eclipsing pre-war levels)."
That's a positive sign. But there's no concern about "oversupply" because the perception is that "the current upswing in Middle Eastern exports is unsustainable".
Even if the US navy can allow oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, a retaliation from Iran is likely imminent.
"The lack of belief that current oil flows through the Middle East are sustainable contrasts heavily with the recovery of flows following the US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on 17 June.
"The market’s reaction then was swift with Brent futures falling sharply –reaching a low of $US70/bbl on 2 July. But other market factors are also keeping markets participants reluctant to believe lower prices can be sustained."
The main issue is that very few believe the amount of oil being stored is high enough.
"Energy Aspects estimates that oil inventories have fallen to 5-year lows, giving the market less resilience to another supply disruption," Dhar added.
"It’s worth noting that the upswing in Middle Eastern oil flows likely means markets now have at least 10-15 weeks of oil and refined product left before depletion risks are realised in certain regions, with risks to the upside if current oil flows persist, up from our previous estimate of 5-10 weeks when Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline was temporarily offline. 
"But the calculation is sensitive to several factors. For example, higher global oil demand and rising Chinese imports can offset the impact of rising Middle Eastern oil exports. Shipping rates from the Arabian Gulf to Asia have lifted to new record highs, underscoring the tightness in the shipping market. Tight shipping markets highlight another aspect of the oil supply chain that has little tolerance for disruption."
Key Event
Number of job advertisements surge 13pc since last year, but ANZ expects unemployment will get worse
The jobs market is still holding up, despite the ABS recently confirming the unemployment rate has risen to 4.6%.
But that's very low by historical standards.
The number of job advertisements rose 2.2% in September, compared to the previous month, according to a new report from ANZ and Indeed.
It's a 12.9% increase over the past year and 24.4% higher than the average during the 2010s.
Although this suggests more jobs are available, the competition is intense. Seek (Indeed's main competitor) recently published data showing the number of applicants for each role has hit a record high.
Looking ahead, the situation will probably get worse for job applicants.
ANZ senior economist Jasmine Zheng said "labour market conditions typically respond to softer economic activity with a lag".
"As the impact of higher interest rates continues to flow through to the economy, we expect economic momentum and labour demand to slow.
"As a result, we anticipate Job Ads will gradually trend lower over the coming months …
"We expect the unemployment rate to gradually drift higher over the months ahead, although the rise is likely to be modest given the resilience in the Job Ads series."
Key Event
Falling prices don't necessarily mean affordable housing
Sarah Megginson, personal finance expert at Finder, says a further house price correction would be welcomed by most Australians, but won't be a silver bullet for housing affordability.
"Even when you include the recent correction, property prices have surged far faster than most people’s pay packets, leaving would-be buyers needing bigger deposits and bigger mortgages just to get through the front door," she says.
The federal government’s recent budget reforms to negative gearing and capital gains tax discounts for property investors have been credited with taking some heat out of demand.
"Investors have had a huge influence on the property market, so anything that takes some heat out of investor demand could give first-home buyers a better shot at getting their foot in the door," Megginson says.
But Megginson says a cheaper house doesn’t automatically mean an affordable one.
"Buyers still need to get through the deposit hurdle, service the loan and survive the other costs of home ownership," she says.
"With four cash rate hikes so far in 2026 and potentially another on the way, buyers should factor higher repayments into their budget and compare home loans carefully before committing to a property."

Key Event
Majority of Australians want house prices to drop further, according to one survey
A new survey from Finder shows the majority of Aussies want to see property prices continue to drop.
A Finder survey of 1,006 respondents revealed two in three Australians (66%) support the objective of bringing house prices down.
The research shows one in three (34%) strongly support the objective of bringing house prices down, while a further 32% say they support it.
That’s a total of 14.4 million people who want values to fall.
Of that number, younger Australians are the most likely to welcome a drop in prices, with 45% of gen Z strongly supporting the objective, and 33% saying they support it.
Baby boomers, on the other hand, only saw 28% strongly support the objective, and 29% saying they support it.
Key Event
Consumer sentiment hit again by fuel and interest rate rises, according to one economist
The head of Australian macro-forecasting at Westpac, Matthew Hassan, says Aussies remain "stuck in a cost-of-living nightmare" with no end in sight.
"At just over 80, the latest sentiment Index is amongst the forty worst reads since our monthly survey began in the early 1970s," he says.
"We have had two others in this unfortunate group already this year – in April and June – with another eight recorded in 2022–23.
"Altogether, this marks the worst period of recurring extremely weak sentiment since the disastrous recession in the early 1990s."
The survey details show consumer concerns focus on cost-of-living pressures and high interest rates.
The concerns are less about the more acute job and insolvency problems that arise during a recession.
"However, these pressures are still both broad and intense. Pessimists outnumber optimists in 102 of the 106 sub-groups we track, and by over 20% in nearly two thirds of these," Mr Hassan says.
"This speaks to the pervasive influence of higher fuel costs in particular. Average weekly pump prices have pushed back over $2.30/litre nationally, to be near the peaks seen back in April and up nearly 25% since the start of the year.
"Meanwhile the latest RBA interest rate move takes the cash rate to 4.6%, the highest since 2011, with the standard variable mortgage interest rate set to push above 9% for the first time since 2008."
Key Event
Westpac consumer confidence index drops
Westpac's Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment Index fell 4.7% to 80.4 points in October, from 84.4 in September.
Westpac says the responses over the survey week show a "very sharp pull-back" after last week's RBA rate hike.

foster + partners completes floating addition above bilbao fine arts museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:35:21 UTC
05:35:21 KST

foster + partners completes floating addition above bilbao fine arts museum
rising over the museum’s existing buildings, 'agravitas' adds galleries and opens a new public atrium below.
AGRAVITAS HOVERS ABOVE BILBAO FINE ARTS MUSEUM
A new volume now hangs above the Bilbao Fine Arts Museum, spanning architecture built several decades apart. Foster + Partners and Bilbao architect Luis María Uriarte have completed Agravitas, an expansion that adds around 6,000 square meters to the museum while leaving its 1945 building and 1970 addition clearly visible below. The new structure stretches 55 meters between groups of tubular V-shaped columns, forming a broad elevated bridge whose deep cantilevers project toward the surrounding city. The museum reopens to the public on October 6th, 2026.
From the street, this upper layer changes the museum’s silhouette immediately. Its long horizontal edges extend well beyond the older masonry facade, while glazed sections reveal the depth of the volume behind them. The earlier buildings remain distinct within a complex that has grown in stages for almost a century. Foster + Partners and Uriarte won the international competition for the project in 2019, proposing to expand upward into the open space above the site.
A NEW ROOM APPEARS UNDER THE BUILDING
Foster + Partners‘ strategy to lift the extension creates another major space underneath it. The former Plaza Arriaga has become a covered atrium of more than 1,000 square meters, sheltered beneath the underside of the gallery above. Francisco Durrio’s restored monument to Bilbao-born composer Juan Crisóstomo de Arriaga returns to the center of the space, beneath a six-meter circular opening cut through the overhead structure. Works by Eduardo Chillida and Richard Serra also occupy the atrium.
The atrium now sits at the center of a museum assembled through decades of additions. Visitors can enter again through the original doorway of the 1945 building, then cross the complex along a new north-south route that passes old facades, existing galleries, and the structure overhead. Changes in level have been smoothed out across the main public spaces, making the different parts of the museum easier to move between. The architecture stays visible along the way, with the older elevations becoming interior walls around the new shared space.
2,300 SQUARE METERS OF NEW EXHIBITION SPACE
Inside Agravitas, approximately 2,300 square meters are devoted to new exhibition areas. The upper level contains BBK Museoa, a large column-free gallery designed for temporary exhibitions. Technical functions are pushed toward the perimeter so the central room stays open and flexible. North-facing glazing brings daylight into the gallery while looking toward the neighboring park, and an adjoining terrace provides further space for sculpture.
The expansion also increases the area available for the permanent collection by 1,635 square meters. Below the main gallery, further spaces accommodate the museum’s architecture and design collection alongside educational uses. Across the wider complex, roughly 8,000 square meters of existing architecture have been renovated as part of Agravitas, including the 1970 wing by Álvaro Líbano and Ricardo Beascoa.
BILBAO’S INDUSTRIAL LANGUAGE RETURNS OVERHEAD
Steel does much of the visual and structural work. The elevated addition rests on large V-shaped columns, with its bridge-like frame extending outward above the older museum. Much of the structure was produced locally, drawing on manufacturing expertise in the Basque Country. The material feels closely tied to Bilbao, where steel production and engineering shaped both the city’s industry and its architecture.
The roof incorporates more than 500 square meters of photovoltaic panels, while the projecting facade shades the glazing below. Natural ventilation and daylight form part of the environmental strategy as well. The strongest move remains easy to read from outside: the museum has gained substantial floor area by occupying the air above itself. Agravitas sits high enough for the buildings below to remain visually independent, turning the space between different generations of architecture into one of the most active parts of the project.
project info:
name: Bilbao Fine Arts Museum | @bilbaomuseoa
architect: Foster + Partners | @fosterandpartners, LM Uriarte Arkitektura / Luis María Uriarte
location: Bilbao, Spain
completion: October 6th, 2026
previous coverage: July 2019

London to Chicago BA flight declares emergency after dropping 28,000 feet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:33:30 UTC
05:33:30 KST

A flight from London to Chicago declared an emergency after a sudden and steep descent of 28,000 feet over Ireland and was forced to turn back to Britain.
British Airways flight BA295 was bound for Chicago’s O’Hare airport but after a “technical issue” during which oxygen masks were deployed from the ceiling, the plane landed safely back at London Heathrow.
The aircraft, a Boeing 777-200ER, had departed Heathrow at 12.14pm on Monday for its scheduled transatlantic flight, and an hour into the journey had ascended to its cruising altitude of 37,000 feet.
According to passengers, the plane then encountered turbulence moments before the masks dropped, prompting “uncertainty” among those on board.
Pilots descended to below 10,000 feet and issued a 7700 emergency squawk to air traffic control – the international general emergency code – and made a U-turn to head back towards England.
Flight-tracking services showed the aircraft flying in a looping holding pattern over the Bristol Channel between Pembrokeshire and North Devon as the plane burnt off fuel in order to lower its weight, allowing the pilots to make a normal landing just after 5pm.
Passenger Tom Nicholls said there was a “sudden bit of turbulence” before the emergency was declared and that the quick descent to 9,000ft hadn’t been too uncomfortable.
He said: “The plane adjusted but it didn’t feel like it was descending rapidly. I’d say the pilots did a very good job.
“The oxygen masks popped out soon after and there was a bit of uncertainty onboard. The couple in front couldn’t get to theirs but by the time they’d found a spare seat with a mask, the captain announced we were below 10,000ft so they were not needed.”
A spokesperson for BA said: “The safety of our customers and crew is always our top priority, and the aircraft landed safely after our highly trained pilots returned to Heathrow following a technical issue.
“Customers disembarked the aircraft normally and our teams are working to get their travel plans back on track as quickly as possible.”
Photographs taken by passengers and shared on social media showed oxygen masks dangling from the ceiling as the plane made the return journey.
A rapid descent to below 10,000 feet and a 7700 emergency squawk are routinely associated with aircraft experiencing cabin depressurisation but the official cause of the emergency has yet to be confirmed by BA.
The Boeing 777-200ER is one of BA’s oldest planes in service, having been delivered to the carrier almost 30 years ago – in July 1997. Live streams showed the aircraft making its descent and safe landing back at Heathrow.
Many passengers have been booked on to new flights departing on Tuesday.

Barack Obama will head to Detroit this month to rally with Abdul El-Sayed, a show of establishment support for a progressive insurgent in Michigan, one of the most consequential Senate races in the country.
The former US president will appear with El-Sayed and the gubernatorial nominee, Jocelyn Benson, on 24 October, the state’s Democratic party announced on Monday. The rally falls on the first day of the state’s in-person early voting period and 10 days before election day.
“Get. Ready,” El-Sayed wrote on social media as he confirmed the appearance.
The event is a significant endorsement for a candidate who survived tens of millions in an out-of-state ad blitz to beat the congresswoman Haley Stevens by less than a percentage point in August, making the contest a national proxy battle over the party’s direction.
El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne county health director, ran on Medicare for All and a refusal to take corporate Pac money, and was backed by Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. He made opposition to US military aid to Israel and criticism of its conduct in Gaza central to his campaign, and has described Israel’s actions there as genocide.
Aipac and its allies as a result spent a record-breaking $30m trying to stop him, and in total Stevens and her allies outspent El-Sayed’s side nearly nine to one on advertising, according to AdImpact.
Stevens, a moderate, was backed by the Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, incumbent senator Gary Peters, and the party establishment.
Obama’s presence matters most in Detroit, where Black residents make up more than three-quarters of the population and where he is still highly popular. Stevens won Wayne county, which includes the city, with about 51% of the Democratic primary vote to El-Sayed’s 45%. Some ads backing her used old footage of Obama praising her, which critics called misleading because he had not endorsed in the race.
Kamala Harris, the first Black and south Asian vice-president, campaigned with El-Sayed last month, and Obama phoned him after the primary.
El-Sayed is running for the seat being vacated by the retiring Democrat Peters, against the Republican former congressman Mike Rogers, and the contest is one of a handful that will determine Senate control next year. Rogers was the Republican nominee in 2024, and lost that race against Elissa Slotkin, despite Donald Trump winning the state. A Marist poll of registered voters from late September had El-Sayed ahead 51% to 44%.
Still, El-Sayed, who has sworn off corporate donations and made his opposition to big money in politics a theme of his campaign, traveled to New York for a fundraiser where top “all-star” donors were asked to give $57,800, split among his campaign, the Michigan Democratic party and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, with Ocasio-Cortez and the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, expected to attend, the New York Times reported.
Obama has kept a relatively low profile this cycle, but is preparing a broader push. He has recorded about two dozen advertisements for Democratic candidates for governor and Senate, to be released in the coming weeks, and further stops are to be announced.
Earlier this year he campaigned in Texas with the Senate nominee James Talarico and the gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa, and featured in an ad for Josh Turek, the Iowa Senate candidate. This week he will headline a Washington fundraiser for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, his first with the group this cycle.

Finnish wildlife photographer Tapani Linnanmäki has reached the final of the 2026 Nikon Comedy Wildlife Photography Awards with a photograph of a white-tailed eagle walking across ice in southwest Finland.
Linnanmäki’s photograph is one of 40 finalists selected from more than 10,000 entries submitted from 112 countries. The photograph, taken in Kustavi, shows the eagle walking with its legs crossed as it moves across the ice.
The image is titled “Fashion fades. Feather coats are forever.”
Linnanmäki is no stranger to the competition. Another of his white-tailed eagle photographs reached the final two years ago and went on to win the public vote.
The photographer told Helsingin Sanomat that white-tailed eagles rank among his favourite birds to photograph. He said he has taken thousands of pictures of the species and has observed different ways in which the birds move and handle fish.
“Even if it is not always comical in them, it is at least full of personality,” Linnanmäki told the newspaper.
Linnanmäki lives in Kustavi, an island municipality on Finland’s southwest coast.
White-tailed eagles have also become a more common sight in Finland following the recovery of a population that once faced a threat of extinction in the country.
The annual Comedy Wildlife Photography Awards select photographs showing humorous moments in the animal world. The competition also seeks to draw attention to wildlife conservation and biodiversity.
This year’s finalists include photographs of animals from several species and countries. The competition will announce the winners in London on 8 December.
For Linnanmäki, the nomination marks his second final appearance in three years, with a white-tailed eagle once again providing his entry.

National Commission for Women issues safety guidelines to step-up monitoring of app-based and digital transport services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:27:46 UTC
05:27:46 KST

The NCW issued guidelines for the safety of women using app-based cabs (representative image)
NEW DELHI: Taking note of safety concerns emerging from across states the National Commission for Women has issued guidelines to states and UTs for safety of women passengers using app-based and digital transport services calling for appropriate verification of criminal antecedents, police verification and background of drivers before onboarding, monitoring of drivers operating during late-night hours and providing SOS buttons in every cab to send out alerts to the command-and-control centre.The NCW notes that as cabs, auto-rickshaws, bike taxis and other app-enabled transport services have become an integral part of everyday mobility, particularly for women travelling independently, ensuring safety throughout the journey has assumed greater importance.Instances relating to mismatch in driver or vehicle identity, route deviation, inappropriate conduct, harassment, stalking, unsafe drop-offs, delays in emergency response and inadequate grievance redressal underline the need for a coordinated and accountable safety framework.
The guidelines issued in this backdrop also take into consideration the recommendations of the Justice J S Verma Committee Report, 2013, and the regulatory framework under the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025, issued by the ministry of road transport and highways.NCW chairperosn Vijaya Rahatkar, has written to the chief secretaries of all states and UTs, requesting appropriate measures for implementation of the guidelines.
Bringing focus on verification of driver and vehicle, the guidelines lay down that the aggregators shall ensure that the driver and vehicle assigned to a passenger match the details displayed on the application. “Any unauthorised change in the driver or vehicle shall be appropriately flagged in the application and treated as a safety concern,” it asserts. The guidelines also call for mechanisms for real-time alerts for route deviations or suspicious stoppages.The guidelines also call for penalty-free cancellation in case of identity mismatch. The guidelines also lay down that the aggregators must strive to maintain a verified pool of women drivers, enabling women travelling alone with the option to request a woman driver through the application.
Calling for enhanced verification and monitoring of drivers operating during late-night hours, the guidelines set out measures ranging from mandatory driver photo verification at trip commencement, addressing driver intoxication, enhanced command and control centre monitoring and a safe-drop option at the end of the ride.
“Aggregators may establish a dedicated and time-bound grievance redressal mechanism for complaints relating to driver misconduct, harassment, assault, route deviation, unauthorised driver or vehicle substitution and failure of emergency-response mechanisms,” the guidelines state.

Justice Oswal concurred with the petitioner that the charges against him were vague and “bereft of necessary particulars”. The court said the state failed to identify the persons and associations with extremist leanings with which it alleged Shah maintained contact, nor did it specify who the youths were with whom the petitioner attempted to establish contact and when.

The Scam Industry Is Becoming a Big Problem in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:18:00 UTC
05:18:00 KST

On September 15, investigators raided three call centers in Pune and Patiala, finding around 220 people at work. According to India’s Enforcement Directorate, the premises were being used to defraud Americans. Investigators said that they were establishing the workers’ identities and roles.
Officers also searched a Chandigarh property linked to a suspected organizer. They seized 66 mobile phones, 13 laptops, and unspecified records. Investigators said that they were examining calling scripts, internet telephony systems, and payment routes.
The published account did not provide an overall figure for victims’ losses.
Months earlier, another investigation exposed the damage one India-based network could inflict. An American woman’s $1.7 million loss helped investigators connect other victims to the operation. The FBI subsequently attributed more than $48.7 million in reported losses among over 600 American victims to the network. Indian authorities arrested six alleged leaders in December 2025.
These cases reveal an enduring threat to American households, while also hurting India’s image abroad. Organized networks operating from India can reach victims thousands of miles away. As has happened with Cambodia’s scam centers, a raid may shut down one office while the people who hire workers, move the money, and coordinate from outside remain untouched.
The Business of Scamming
The criminal organizations behind these calls can resemble a conventional business. A 2024 study published by Itad and commissioned by Britain’s Home Office described larger Indian scam centers with management structures, staff shifts, human resources departments, and quality control functions. It also documented recruitment agencies, prepared scripts, English and accent training, and performance incentives.
Roles can be divided between “openers,” who establish contact, and “closers,” who persuade victims to surrender money. Beyond the telephone operators sit facilitators who supply websites, deceptive pop-ups, recruitment services, and various forms of money laundering. The study also identified markets for phone numbers, calling scripts, and victim profiles. These arrangements allow different participants to specialize in separate parts of the fraud.
Reuters reported in 2016 that former workers at scam centers near Mumbai described memorizing scripts, learning from floor managers, and receiving commissions or incentives. The accounts describe a workplace where securing a payment from a victim could increase an employee’s earnings.
Technology helps conceal the operation. In a Noida case announced in July 2025, Britain’s National Crime Agency described spoofed telephone numbers and internet calls routed through servers in several countries. The scam center in Noida targeted both British and American victims. A familiar-looking number on a screen offered no reliable indication of where the caller actually worked.
An office can make a scam look like a real business. Reporting from Maharashtra has described scam centers posing as IT or outsourcing firms, while poor verification of businesses made such operations harder to detect.
How Scammers Extract Money
The details differ between networks, but documented cases show a recurring progression from an alarming first contact to demands for money.
Stage one is intended to trigger initial fear and gain attention from the intended victim. In technical support fraud, a person browsing the internet sees a warning claiming that their computer has been infected or compromised. The message supplies a telephone number. Calling it connects the victim to someone offering to resolve the supposed emergency. In the Noida case, investigators said callers falsely presented themselves as Microsoft employees and charged for unnecessary repairs.
Other schemes begin with unsolicited calls claiming unpaid taxes, compromised identities or criminal investigations. The goal is to create a false sense of urgency and then urge action before the victim has time to check it.
Scammers reinforce their claims through multiple impersonations. A supposed technical support worker may introduce a bank representative, followed by someone claiming government authority. Each apparent handover makes the preceding story seem independently confirmed.
The FBI’s warning about “Phantom Hacker” scams describes forged correspondence on government letterheads and instructions to keep transfers secret. The victim is encouraged to distrust the very people who could interrupt the fraud. The caller says the conversation must stay private to protect the victim. That stops the victim from asking someone else for advice.
Some operators persuade victims to install remote-access software. This can allow the scammer to inspect the computer and watch as the victim opens financial accounts. The supposed repair becomes an opportunity to identify available savings. A second impersonator then claims those funds face immediate danger and must be moved to a supposedly secure account.
In other schemes, threats of arrest or deportation supply the pressure. American prosecutions have documented India-based callers impersonating tax and immigration authorities to extract payments. The victim is made to believe that following instructions will protect a home, retirement account, or legal status. That belief is central to the deception.
Payment methods vary. Gift cards and prepaid cards allow scammers to demand value without asking victims to send money directly to an identifiable caller. Once card details are surrendered, criminals can use or transfer the value.
Cryptocurrency offers another route. Victims may be instructed to withdraw savings, buy digital assets and send them to wallets controlled by the fraud network. Wire transfers can similarly move money into accounts controlled by intermediaries. These methods feature in documented call-center investigations.
Cash and gold introduce a physical collection stage. The FBI has warned that scammers direct victims to buy precious metals or withdraw cash for supposed safekeeping, then dispatch couriers to collect them. The person arriving at an American doorstep can therefore be part of a fraud directed from abroad.
Money laundering adds further distance between the victim and the organizers. In one India-based operation that was prosecuted in the U.S. state of Virginia, American authorities documented couriers, bank accounts, and hawala transfers used to move proceeds. Such arrangements complicate efforts to trace the money and identify who ultimately received it.
After the transfer, the scammers may cease contact, leaving victims with unanswered calls and missing savings. But some schemes continue demanding transfers over days or months, so the first payment does not necessarily end the manipulation.
Either way, by the time a victim recognizes the fraud, the lost money may already have moved through several hands.
The same methods are used against victims in other countries. Canada’s Project OCTAVIA targeted callers impersonating tax officials; reported losses to that particular scam fell from C$6.4 million in 2018 to C$1.4 million in 2019.
In Australia, police alleged that Hyderabad-based Ridge IT Solutions had taken 80-100 million rupees from Australians over roughly two years. The allegations included payments passing through Australian accounts before moving toward India.
Why Scam Centers Survive
India is not unique in hosting these scam centers. The online scam industry is global, and the financial scale is substantial. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) received 1,008,597 complaints in 2025, with reported losses of $20.9 billion. People aged 60 and older reported approximately $7.7 billion in losses. Complaints involving technical or customer support fraud and government impersonation together exceeded 80,000, with losses above $2.9 billion.
Those totals cover perpetrators worldwide, and IC3 also receives complaints from outside the United States. These figures cannot be presented as American losses caused entirely by India-based centers; IC3 has not established the share of the 2025 losses originating from operations in India.
Nevertheless, India’s role is well documented: in a 2022 podcast, the FBI said most technical-support and telephone scams targeting Americans originated from India. And while scam operations based in Southeast Asia, especially Cambodia, have received more attention of late, scam centers operating out of India remain less discussed.
Recovering money presents a daunting challenge. Investigators must identify recipients, trace subsequent transfers, and seek the necessary legal cooperation. American agents cannot simply conduct arrests in India. Even successful prosecutions do not guarantee that every victim will receive full repayment. Often, the scammers are able to keep their ill-gotten gains, and use them to fund further crimes.
Scam centers can reopen after raids because the system around them often remains in place. In December 2025, The Indian Express reported concerns from Maharashtra police about weak business verification, scrutiny of network connections and coordination. Its reporting also described operations shifting toward smaller towns offering cheaper premises and access to English-speaking workers.
Those conditions lower the practical barriers to reopening. A group with access to staff, scripts, communications services, and payment intermediaries can establish another office even after one address is exposed.
Jurisdiction adds delay. Victims report crimes in the United States, relevant records may belong to banks or technology companies elsewhere, callers operate in India, and accomplices handling payments may be in another country. Investigators have to connect those dots before evidence can support arrests and prosecutions.
Within India, policing is primarily a state responsibility, while networks may operate across state boundaries. The Itad study identified limited collaboration between jurisdictions as an obstacle to connecting linked operations.
The Noida investigation revealed the work involved. It took 18 months of cooperation involving the Indian CBI, Britain’s National Crime Agency, the U.S. FBI, and Microsoft before the July 2025 raid.
In July 2025, the CBI arrested two people at a Noida call center that British investigators said had contacted more than 100 people in the UK. British victims were believed to have lost more than 390,000 pounds. Canada’s Royal Canadian Mounted Police Hyderabad(RCMP) said its Project OCTAVIA investigation had helped shut down 39 illegal call centers in the Noida and New Delhi areas.
In November 2025, Hyderabad police arrested nine people at an alleged fake call center targeting Australians.
These cases form part of a wider enforcement effort. According to the FBI, cooperation with Indian agencies since 2022 has involved more than 1,200 information exchanges and more than 475 arrests across 27 joint operations. That includes about 175 arrests in 13 joint operations in 2025 alone.
The harder task is finding the people who run these scams, move the money, and help new centers open. Raids can close an office, but another may take its place. Victims also need a chance to get their money back.
Until that changes, these networks can keep making money by frightening people in the United States and beyond. They also hurt India’s global image at a time when the country wants to be seen as a reliable technology and services hub.

Indian alleged mastermind of online child abuse ring goes on trial in Paris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:15:18 UTC
05:15:18 KST

Indian alleged mastermind of online child abuse ring goes on trial in Paris
Rohan Rane, an Indian national who came to France to study before becoming a fitness coach, went on trial on Monday behind closed doors in Paris, on charges of torture and acts of barbarity against minors. Investigators say he is the leader of a neo-Nazi child exploitation ring that ran its operations via messaging platform Discord.
An Indian man went on trial behind closed doors in Paris on Monday, accused of running a neo-Nazi child exploitation ring in which young girls were allegedly coerced into performing sexual acts online and engaging in self-harm.
The group is believed to have abused mostly underage girls in countries including the United States, the Netherlands, Britain and Estonia.
Investigators say the perpetrators were men from Germany, New Zealand and the United States who communicated on the popular messaging platform Discord. They espoused racist and anti-Semitic views and expressed hostility toward feminists and the LGBTQ+ community.
Rohan Rane, a 29-year-old Indian national who came to France to study at a business school in the southeastern city of Antibes before becoming a fitness coach, is described by investigators as the group's leader.
The defendant, who was arrested in 2021, appeared in the dock wearing a white T-shirt.
He is being tried on charges including torture or acts of barbarity against minors, organised extortion and dissemination of child sexual abuse material. If convicted, he faces up to life in prison.
'Warlords' and 'slaves'
The case was triggered in November 2020 by a report from the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.
The child protection organisation discovered online images of a 12-year-old girl with her chest exposed while another user encouraged her to carve the name "Rohan" into her body.
Five American women, between the ages of 18 and 21, have joined the case as civil parties and were expected to testify by video link this week.
According to a court document released by the US Department of Justice, the internet-based group dubbed CVLT espoused "neo-Nazism, nihilism, and paedophilia as its core principles."
The investigation showed its members attracted vulnerable minors via Instagram or other social media platforms.
They persuaded them to send naked pictures then threatened to publish them – or blackmailed them by saying they would make a fake emergency call so security forces would turn up at their door.
The ring members – who called themselves "warlords" – then forced their victims, who were often Jewish or black girls they called "slaves", to perform sexual acts against their will – including with knives – or to carve the names of their tormentors or Nazi swastikas into their skin.
They also incited their victims – whom they also called "housewives" – to commit suicide by drinking bleach or by strangling themselves with a belt or leash.
One of these "warlords", a 26-year-old US citizen, has already been sentenced in his home country for having abducted and raped a 12-year-old girl in 2021.
Threatened US prosecutors
The Paris criminal court on Monday ordered the trial be held behind closed doors, following a request from US authorities.
The court defended its decision by explaining the group – which was allegedly led by Rane and had been particularly active in the United States – had already sought to intimidate victims and witnesses and had threatened US prosecutors.
It also noted that videos showing the torture and humiliation of victims – often under the age of 15 – were expected to be screened during proceedings scheduled to run through Friday.
Backed by child protection groups, Hippolyte Marquetty, a lawyer for the five US victims, had unsuccessfully opposed the closed-door proceedings.
He said his clients believed it was important to raise awareness of the dangers that teenage girls face on social media.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Cuba and US maintain ‘channels of communication’ but no negotiations, diplomat says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:13:51 UTC
05:13:51 KST

Cuba and US maintain ‘channels of communication’ but no negotiations, diplomat says
WASHINGTON – Cuba and the United States have maintained “channels of communication” but are not engaged in any formal negotiations, Havana’s top diplomat in Washington told Reuters, as the Trump administration pursues a pressure campaign against the Communist-ruled island.
In an interview on Oct 5, Lianys Torres Rivera, charge d’affaires at the embassy in Washington, said Cuba remains open to a “respectful” dialogue but is “not naive” about US President Donald Trump’s threats and has increased preparations to defend itself against any US military action.
The latest US-Cuba diplomatic contacts have included meetings, phone calls and WhatsApp messages, but the two sides have made no progress towards a negotiating agenda or restarting official talks, she said.
“What we have with the US is channels of communication,” Torres Rivera said. She declined to provide details on the timing, topics and participants.
Her description of the communications appears to fall short of Trump’s assertion at the United Nations in September that Secretary of State Marco Rubio was “deep into negotiations” with Havana.
Trump also called Cuba a “failed state” and predicted that its government would fall. The Cuban delegation walked out in protest.
A US State Department spokesperson said: “It does not come to our surprise that the Cuban regime is circulating this propaganda.
“In all reality, talks are ongoing and the regime has been unwilling thus far to agree to anything that would help the Cuban people, ultimately, threatening its total control.”
Trump has openly stated that his goal is to fundamentally change Cuba’s government. A US-imposed oil blockade has put the country under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure. UN human rights experts have condemned the oil blockade as a violation of international law.
Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said at the end of June that talks initiated earlier in 2026 with the US had stalled, and in early September that no talks were under way or planned.
Cuba’s ‘red line’
Torres Rivera said Cuba’s “red line” remains that Havana is unwilling to negotiate any changes in its political system, seeing Trump’s demands for the removal of the Cuban leadership as a violation of sovereignty.
She rejected the Trump administration’s claims that Cuba was a threat to US national security or is interfering in US domestic affairs, and said Washington was using such accusations as a pretext to continue squeezing the island economically in what she called “collective punishment”.
A US official, responding to Reuters’ questions, reiterated Trump’s assertion that “we will not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep”.
The Trump administration tightened the embargo against Cuba last week, further restricting travel there by Americans and access to US banking for its private sector.
Those measures, said Torres Rivera, contradict US insistence that it wants Cuba to expand private enterprise.
Facing US pressure, Cuba unveiled free-market reforms in June that, if fully implemented, would represent the biggest change to the island’s socialist economy since former leader Fidel Castro took control in 1959.
But Washington says the reforms do not go far enough and has also called for “free and fair” elections.
Despite the gaps, Trump predicted late last month that the US and Cuba “will make a deal”, adding, “I don’t think we’ll need the military”.
But the Cuban government remains wary.
“Cuba has always been preparing for an aggression from the US,” Torres Rivera said. “And we are increasing our capabilities now more than ever before… It is to defend ourselves.” REUTERS

Diplomat is Romania’s fourth prime ministerial candidate in five months

A senior diplomat will try to form a new government as Romania’s prime minister, in an attempt to end a five-month stalemate that threatens the country’s economic and political stability.
President Nicușor Dan named Luca Niculescu, secretary of state in the foreign ministry, as prime minister-designate on Monday. He is the fourth candidate tasked with leading a government since the coalition collapsed in May.
To be confirmed in the role, Niculescu will need to win a vote in Romania’s parliament within 10 days to show he has majority support for his new ministerial team and their program for government.
Advertisement
His task is formidable: Amid bitter divisions between the parties, lawmakers rejected two of Dan’s previous nominees, and a third didn’t even make that far. Dan made his announcement after holding talks with the parties at Cotroceni Palace on Monday afternoon.
After three previous candidates failed, the president is already facing calls to dissolve parliament for an unprecedented snap election. But he is reluctant to do so, fearing it would bring a far-right euroskeptic opposition party closer to power.
“My proposal for the position of prime minister is Luca Niculescu, a man who, as a diplomat, knows how to harmonize different positions,” Dan said on Monday evening. “It is necessary for Romania to have a government as soon as possible, because there are institutions that need rectification, and there is a need for a budget for next year. Prolonging the uncertainty will have effects on the lives of Romanians.”
One politician who refused to take part in talks with Dan on Monday was George Simion, leader of the hard-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians party, which currently leads opinion polls. Simion — who challenged Dan for the presidency last year — reiterated his demand for an election to end the chaos.
The president confirmed that the new government would have no place for parties that are anti-Western — which is his code for far-right groups, especially AUR. “I have the guarantee that a government with Luca Niculescu will maintain Romania’s pro-Western direction and will respect the financial targets and all the commitments that Romania has undertaken,” he said.
Dan said the uncertainty was affecting exchange rates, interest rates and investments in Romania. Over the past four years, Niculescu has led Romania’s accession process to the OECD, a major milestone in the country’s development. Dan said his candidate would have the freedom to decide whether the government was “political or technocratic.”
Accepting the nomination, Niculescu said Romania was grappling with a “long” period of uncertainty at a difficult time. “The first mission will be to build a parliamentary majority that will vote for a government that will be deeply anchored in Romania’s European and Euro-Atlantic direction,” he said. “I will have discussions with the parliamentary parties to build this majority and to agree on a realistic governing program.”

Six foreign volunteers bring Colours of Solidarity to Sofia

Six foreign volunteers bring Colours of Solidarity to Sofia
“Young Bulgarians are still not used to volunteering,” says Strashimir Dimitrov of the Values, Virtues, Integrity Foundation
Monday 5 October 2026 22:27
Monday, 5 October 2026, 22:27
PHOTO Sofia Municipality’s Oborishte District Administration
Font size
Six young people from different countries and continents came to Sofia with a shared purpose – to contribute their time, energy and creativity to making the city cleaner, more attractive and a better place to live.
For 40 days, they took part in the third edition of Colours of Solidarity, a project organised by the Values, Virtues, Integrity Foundation.
“We select people from countries with different backgrounds and histories, which is why we gave the project this name,” said foundation representative Strashimir Dimitrov.
“At the zoo, we worked to make the grounds more inviting,” he told Bulgarian National Radio’s Hristo Botev programme. “In South Park, we helped paint benches and painted designs on rocks along the main paths. We dismantled a stage at the Summer Theatre in Borisova Gradina Park and painted the benches in front of the National Palace of Culture. At the Rivers of Sofia festival – a real gem in the city’s summer programme – we helped with the preparations and the clearing up afterwards. We also had a stand where we presented EU youth exchange programmes.”
Strashimir Dimitrov, Alicia Sommer, Lorenzo Loconsole, Sandra Worwornyo and Barbora Mikanova (standing, from left to right), with Daria Tranzhina and Joaldo N’kom.
PHOTO Natalia Maeva
Since a good example can inspire others, are more young Bulgarians becoming interested in volunteering?
“Young Bulgarians are still not used to volunteering, although some are beginning to show an interest,” Dimitrov replied. “Our foundation’s main mission is to reach schoolchildren and young people, those who see the world through different eyes, and encourage them to get involved. Volunteering is not very widespread in Bulgaria, yet there is a real need for it.”
The six participants explain why they chose to give their time and effort, without payment, to help communities in another country:
PHOTO Sofia Municipality’s Oborishte District Administration
Daria from Estonia: “I came here because I’m an art student. This isn’t my first volunteering project, but it’s the first one that has something to do with my field of study. So it was an opportunity to develop my skills and do some painting.”
Alisha from Germany: “I came here because I wanted to learn something different – to volunteer and help out, even though I’m not a professional. I’m doing it for myself, but I really enjoy it. I’ll continue working with art, although I still don’t know exactly where things will lead.”
Joaldo from Angola: “My parents are from Angola and we speak Portuguese, but I’ve lived in Rome since I was 19, studying publishing. This project is an opportunity to embark on a new adventure, step outside my comfort zone and do something interesting in another country. You’re helping the community without being paid, and you feel proud of what you’ve achieved because people appreciate it.”
Sandra from Ghana: “I’m currently doing a master’s degree in circular economy in Italy. I wanted to try something new – to travel and see more of Europe – and this is my first time volunteering. It was a chance to meet new people and get to know Bulgarian culture. I’d read about Sofia as a European capital, and St Alexander Nevsky Cathedral was what impressed me most. The city has lived up to my expectations. There’s a lot to see here, the surroundings are interesting, and the mountain makes a beautiful backdrop.”
Barbora: “I’m from the Czech Republic, but I now live in Rome, where I’m finishing a master’s degree in art history. Since moving to Italy, I’ve been actively involved in volunteering – I cook meals for homeless people. I enjoy painting in my spare time, so I’m glad this project has a creative element. I’m very happy to be part of it.”
PHOTO BTA
Lorenzo from Italy: “It’s a pleasure to be here. I’ve visited Sofia many times before. When I was looking for volunteering opportunities for the summer, hoping to gain some experience during my holidays, I came across this project and thought it could be a great experience. The city faces the same problems as other capitals – pollution, litter and graffiti. I wanted to help make Sofia cleaner, remove some graffiti and take part in artistic projects.”
Having left their mark on Sofia and gained new experiences and dreams along the way, the young volunteers will carry with them lasting memories of an unforgettable summer – one that, in some ways, has changed them too.

'France has fallen': Far-right figures fuel Islamophobic claims with false student protest videos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:10:15 UTC
05:10:15 KST

'France has fallen': Far-right figures fuel Islamophobic claims with false student protest videos
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
France's student protests have become the target of a wave of false and misleading videos shared by far-right figures, including Alex Jones and Tommy Robinson. Old footage and unrelated videos have been shared to portray the demonstrations as evidence of an "anti-white" or Islamist uprising linked to uncontrolled immigration. But the protests are over school conditions, including large class sizes, teacher shortages and poor facilities, not immigration. Vedika Bahl fact-checks in Truth or Fake.
Student protests and school blockades in France are entering their third week, with demonstrations over high school conditions also seeing violence between demonstrators and riot police.
But alongside the unrest, a wave of false and misleading videos has been circulating online, shared by far-right figures in the US and UK to promote claims about immigration and social unrest in France.
Videos showing fires, clashes and large crowds have been presented as evidence of an immigration-fuelled "civil war", even when the footage is old or unrelated to the current demonstrations.
Alex Jones pushes 'anti-white civil war' claim
In the US, far-right conspiracy theorist Alex Jones has shared lengthy video compilations about the protests, using them to promote an Islamophobic narrative.
Jones has claimed that France is experiencing an "anti-white civil war", with "dead bodies everywhere". There is no evidence to support these claims. No deaths have been reported to date in the current protests, and the demonstrations are centred on concerns over the state of France's education system, including large class sizes, teacher shortages and poor school conditions, not immigration.
Jones uses a series of videos to illustrate his claims about supposed immigrant violence. But some of the footage predates the current protests by years. For example, one of his video compilations begins with footage of a burning bus, but it's a video of a school bus that caught fire in the southern French city of Nîmes in 2022, with no casualties reported. It's thus being used out of context to push Jones's narrative.
Jones has also claimed that Catholic institutions and clergy are being targeted during the protests. In one video, he says he has seen "at least a dozen videos of Catholic priests being set on fire".
We found no evidence supporting these claims in connection with the current student protests. The videos used by Jones to support his wider narrative of an "anti-white" uprising are also not evidence of an organised campaign against Catholic institutions or clergy.
Tommy Robinson shares old protest footage
Similar claims have been circulating in the UK. Far-right activist Tommy Robinson has shared footage of unrest in France while promoting an anti-immigration message.
In one post, Robinson described a video as evidence of a "green/Islamic holy alliance" spreading through Western Europe and the United States, claiming that what is happening in France would spread to other countries.
But the footage is not new. The video shows the aftermath of a protest in Paris and has been circulating online since 2022. It therefore cannot be used as evidence of the current student demonstrations.
Robinson has also posted about what he calls "occupied France," sharing footage showing violence and looting during recent demonstrations. Some of this footage is genuine and does show incidents linked to the current protests. But the fact that the footage is authentic does not substantiate the broader claims about immigration being made, and these videos are being misused to create a racist and xenophobic narrative.
'France has fallen' video is from a football celebration
Other anti-immigration accounts have also used genuine images from France but stripped them of their original context. One widely shared video is captioned simply: "France has fallen".
The footage, which has been viewed millions of times, shows smoke around the Eiffel Tower and large crowds gathering in the streets, but was filmed in May, when Paris Saint-Germain fans gathered to celebrate the club's Champions League victory.

SpaceX stock climbs to highest since June, returning Musk to trillionaire status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:10:13 UTC
05:10:13 KST

SpaceX shares rose almost 8% on Monday, reaching their highest since mid-June, shortly after Elon Musk's company held its record initial public offering. With the rally, Musk is once again a trillionaire.
The jump followed a Sunday note from Morgan Stanley analysts, who called SpaceX "cheap" at today's prices, and highlighted "future AI product releases, Starship progress, and additional neocloud contracts." They recommend buying the stock and have a $300 price target, representing an increase of about 75% from Monday's $171.09 close.
Late last week SpaceX conducted multiple historic flights in a single day, including sending a crewed mission for NASA to the International Space Station, and a separate launch of Google AI chips into orbit.
The Morgan Stanley analysts suggested investors buy SpaceX shares before the company's next planned test flight for its massive Starship rocket, and ahead of its third-quarter earnings report expected in late October.
Starship is SpaceX's next-generation spacecraft, the largest rocket ever built, and is designed to be fully reusable with both its upper stage and booster able to land safely back on Earth. The system is expected to supercharge SpaceX's business, bringing the company's Starlink satellites into orbit, as well as cargo and crews from other companies and agencies.
Should SpaceX attempt a Starship upper stage ship catch in its next test flight, that could be "the biggest positive catalyst since the IPO," the analysts wrote. In prior test flights, the Starship upper stage has made splash downs in the ocean, but hasn't been proven reusable.
SpaceX is also getting a boost from its artificial intelligence business, which it gained through the acquisition of Musk's xAI last year and expanded through the recent acquisition of Cursor. While the company's homegrown Grok model hasn't taken off compared to leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, SpaceX is generating hefty revenue by renting out capacity to the likes of Google and Anthropic.
Musk has the benefit of close ties to the Trump administration.
On Wednesday, the Pentagon appointed Musk as co-lead of Project Meridian, an initiative that involves identifying weapons, technologies and military capabilities the U.S. may need in future wars. SpaceX makes a large chunk of its revenue from the U.S. government and increasingly from defense contracts, earning over $12.7 billion to date from its work with the Defense Department, according to FedScout.
Musk said over the weekend he will be renaming SpaceX's AI division, known as SpaceXAI, as SpaceXSI, embracing President Donald Trump's new branding.
As his company's stock soared on Monday, Musk was notably absent from a New York City Council hearing, where city officials grilled AI leaders and researchers about how the technology should be regulated. Representatives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta were in attendance to testify.
Councilmember Shekar Krishnan noted, "AI has taken over our economy, inflated valuations, stealing our public land for data centers, and increasing the net worth of AI CEOs like Elon Musk, who became our first ever trillionaire."
According to Forbes' real-time billionaires list, Musk is currently worth $1.03 trillion, factoring in his holdings in Tesla and SpaceX.
SpaceX went public on June 12, and jumped to a record close of $201.80 on June 16. The shares started trending lower soon thereafter, bottoming in early August. They've since climbed about 58%.
SpaceX didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Russian Drones Sink Royad Mammadov Dry Cargo Ship Carrying Ukrainian Grain

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:09:46 UTC
05:09:46 KST

The Turkish dry cargo ship Royad Mammadov sank in the Black Sea following an attack by Russian drones. The ship was en route from Ukraine to Italy with a cargo of grain.
This was reported by the Romanian Ministry of the Interior.
The ship was attacked by two drones, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
“A horrific attack by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters that was carrying corn and belonged to Turkey,” Zelensky wrote.
There were citizens of Azerbaijan and India on board.
As of now, it is known that the ship’s captain was killed. The fate of one other person is still unknown. Eleven crew members were rescued, one of whom was injured.
At the time of the attack, the dry cargo ship was 20 nautical miles from the coast — approximately 37 km. The ship was carrying grain. Its final destination was the Italian port of Ravenna, where the Royad Mammadov was scheduled to arrive on October 12.
In mid-September, the ship departed from the Ukrainian port of Izmail, which is one of the key ports for Ukrainian grain exports.
The ship entered the Black Sea on the afternoon of October 3. The tracking service detected interruptions in AIS data transmission, the Automatic Identification System, on the morning of October 5, around 9:20 a.m. local time. It is likely that the ship was attacked at that very moment.
The Royad Mammadov flies the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis, but companies based in Turkey are responsible for its commercial and technical operations.
Earlier, last week, a civilian vessel flying the Liberian flag was attacked in a port in the Odesa region. One person was killed as a result of the attack.

Sybiha Condemns Russian Drone Strike on Turkish-Owned Vessel Carrying Corn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:09:18 UTC
05:09:18 KST

Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha condemned Russia’s drone strike on a Turkish-owned cargo vessel carrying corn in the Black Sea, warning that civilian shipping routes urgently need stronger protection.
The Royad Mammadov sank in Romania’s exclusive economic zone earlier on Monday, Oct. 5, after a fire broke out on board. President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a statement that two Russian drones had struck the ship, killing its captain, while the fate of another crew member remained unknown.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Freedom of navigation cannot depend on whether Moscow decides to observe it on one day or another,” Sybiha said in a statement published on the Foreign Ministry’s website.
Calls for pressure on Moscow
Sybiha warned that attacks on vessels carrying Ukrainian agricultural exports could have devastating consequences for vulnerable communities in Africa, Asia and the Middle East that depend on imported food, potentially leading to acute food insecurity, malnutrition or even famine.
He said Ukraine had repeatedly offered concrete steps to make Black Sea navigation safer, but that Russia had responded by widening the reach of its attacks.
“This trend will continue until the price of escalation becomes higher than the benefits that Moscow expects to get from it,” Sybiha said, calling for greater pressure on Russia, stronger protection for civilian shipping and accountability for attacks on vessels and their crews.
Russia Strikes Kharkiv With Guided Bombs Killing 6, Wounding 59, Including Children
His remarks echoed Zelensky’s earlier statement that Russia “consistently chooses terror and the sinking of civilian vessels instead of normal navigation.”
Sybiha described the attack as ‘cynical’
The attack, Sybiha said, proves particularly cynical given Turkey’s ongoing efforts to de-escalate tensions, advance peace initiatives and ensure security in the region.
The country has maintained diplomatic ties with both Moscow and Kyiv, despite being among the countries hit hardest by the escalating war at sea.
Since late June, at least 25 Turkish-owned or Turkish-operated merchant vessels have been damaged or caught in the crossfire in the Black Sea.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan repeatedly urged both sides to agree on a mutual moratorium on attacks against commercial ships.
In August, Ankara had begun restricting commercial transits through the Dardanelles toward the Black Sea, including routes to Russia’s port of Novorossiysk.
Just a month later, Turkey sent a draft memorandum of understanding to Kyiv and Moscow aimed at formally halting strikes on commercial shipping and civilian port infrastructure.
“We are trying to reach a conclusion. Frankly, both sides have demands and positions that are difficult to reconcile,” Fidan said on Sept. 20.
So far, Moscow has rejected all ceasefire proposals.
On Oct. 1, Bloomberg reported that Turkey and the UN had arranged new talks in Russia and Ukraine on a possible Black Sea ceasefire, aiming to bring together separate efforts to protect grain shipments as global food prices climb.
According to a senior diplomat cited by the outlet, the meetings are set for early October, with the Swiss-based Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue acting as mediator.
Ship sinking in Romania
The Royad Mammadov had left Ukraine’s Danube port of Izmail with grain and was heading for Ravenna, Italy, according to Romanian media on Monday morning.
The Romanian Interior Ministry said 11 crew members were rescued and two deceased people were identified.
Three injured sailors were airlifted for emergency medical treatment, while the remaining eight were taken aboard rescue vessels, Romanian broadcaster Digi24 reported.
The ship sank while the rescue operation was still underway.
The incident took place about 30 nautical miles south of the coastal village of Sfântu Gheorghe, outside Romania’s territorial waters.
The 140-meter vessel sailed under the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis, while shipping records list Turkey-based MG Shipping 5 Co Ltd as its registered owner.
Romanian authorities have officially confirmed only a fire on board and have not determined its cause, attributed the incident to Russia or established the origin of any drone involved.
Hours before the incident, Romania’s Defense Ministry said its radar had detected an airborne target near the border, east of the Ukrainian town of Vylkove.
Two Spanish F-18 fighter jets deployed to Romania for NATO air policing were scrambled, though the ministry said the target did not enter Romanian airspace. Authorities have not linked that incident to the fire on the ship.
Russia has not directly commented on the attack, though its Defense Ministry said it had struck two cargo vessels, the BBC reported.
