Mecca Pact allies pledge rapid military deployment to Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey confirmed their commitment to collective defense and a unified stance in confronting threats
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday to appoint the Mecca Pact's first secretary-general.
Pakistan’s Lt. Gen. Nauman Mehmood was appointed as the first secretary-general for a three-year term.
The forum condemned Houthi attacks on Mecca and Medina, as well as continued attacks on civilian targets in Saudi Arabia.
The three countries also confirmed their commitment to collective defense and a unified stance in confronting threats.
They agreed to provide "the agreed-upon military forces and capabilities" and rapidly deploy those forces to Saudi Arabia in accordance with the member states’ national legislation.
"This move aims to enhance readiness, military integration, and the collective capacity to confront and counter threats," Saudi Arabia said.
They emphasized the need to translate the Mecca Pact into practical measures that demonstrate the credibility of the joint defense commitment.

Earlier today, Russia’s Central District Military Court in Yekaterinburg sentenced activist Leonid Melekhin to six years in a penal colony on charges of “justifying terrorism,” according to a report by the independent outlet Mediazona. Melekhin was deported from the United States to Russia last summer after being denied political asylum.
The criminal case against Melekhin stemmed from a post in the Telegram channel “Bobr. There and back (an immigration diary),” run by fellow Perm activist Leonid Bobrov. The post showed Melekhin shortly after he crossed into the United States alongside an image of a poster depicting a mannequin hanging by a rope and a photograph of Russian President Vladimir Putin. The poster read:
“V.V. Putin is a murderer, fascist and usurper. All that is needed for evil to triumph is for good people to do nothing. Hang the fascist.”
The post appeared in August 2024, the same month Melekhin tried to enter the United States through the Mexican border in the hopes of receiving political asylum. He was placed in immigration detention before being denied asylum in the summer of 2025 and then arrested after being deported back to Russia.
Melekhin’s trial had been held behind closed doors since early May. Prosecutors later added a second count over an online comment whose contents have not been disclosed. Both episodes were classified as justification of terrorism under Russian law.
Before leaving Russia, Melekhin had repeatedly been detained by police for taking part in protests. The detentions continued through late 2023, prompting him to emigrate.

One of most expensive books in world, weighing more than 200 kg, stolen in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:03:59 UTC
05:03:59 KST

PARIS, October 5. /TASS/. One of the world’s most expensive and heaviest books, Joseph Foret’s "Apocalypse" featuring a hefty bronze-plated cover designed by Salvador Dali, has been stolen from a private museum in the commune of Issoire in central France, the Ici radio reported.
"This is a grandiose, masterful work with no equivalent anywhere in the world. Tonight, France suffered a death, the death of cultural heritage," the book’s owner, Christian Karoutzos, told the radio station.
The book was displayed at the town’s contemporary art center, which was also founded by Karoutzos. It was stolen from there overnight on October 4-5. The circumstances of the theft have not been disclosed. The Clermont-Ferrand gendarmerie was tasked with investigating the incident.
The work was created between 1958 and 1961 by gallery owner Joseph Foret, with the blessing of Pope John XXIII, based on the Book of Revelation, the final book of the New Testament, also known as "Apocalypse." Around 15 of the best-known artists and writers of the time, including Salvador Dali, Jean Cocteau, Bernard Buffet and Ossip Zadkine, contributed to the work. The book weighs 210 kg in total, with the Dali-created bronze cover weighing 150 kg.
When the book was published, it was valued at 100 million old francs. In 2003, Karoutzos bought it at an auction in Japan for "several million euros," regional newspaper Ouest-France reported.

Coalition's migration policy all about chasing One Nation votes: Labor
Assistant Minister Andrew Leigh has accused the opposition of chasing One Nation votes with its migration proposal.
The Coalition has vowed to slash the stock of temporary visas to 650,000 over four years with deep cuts to graduate, humanitarian and bridging visas.
It's insisted the policy would be budget neutral and is structured to not hurt the economy.
But Leigh insists that's not the case.
"What you're seeing from the Coalition are measures which would have a huge negative impact on the economy, where you're essentially chasing One Nation votes in delivering a policy which is going to be deeply damaging for Australians, for the living standards that we expect," he tells Afternoon Briefing.
Leigh says the policy, if adopted, would have a deep impact on the healthcare and construction workforce.
"Migrants aren't just mouths to feed. They're muscles to build and minds to inspire," he says.
Uncertainty over copyright laws could shut down investment
Microsoft executives say a lack of clarity over fair use and copyright obligations in Australia could drive big tech away from investing here.
The government is locked in negotiations with AI companies from the US who want to use work made and owned by Australian artists and creatives to train their AI models.
"We see your copyright laws as, providing a high level of uncertainty about the ability to engage in the training processes that are necessary to train a model," Microsoft executive Jordan Gimbel says.
OpenAI exec 'can't explain' mistrust of AI among Australians
Reporter Cam Wilson is in Sydney today listening to the parliamentary inquiry into AI and chased down OpenAI's Jason Kwon on his way out of the hearing room.
Asked about the potential benefits of artificial intelligence, Kwon says around half of all adult Australians are already using the technology.
But he was stumped when it came to explaining why Australians are among the most distrustful of the technology in the world.
"I can't explain the current sentiment, all we can do is get better," Kwon says.
'If it ain't broke, don't fix it': Canavan doesn't think backpacker visas are an issue
Nationals leader Matt Canavan doesn't think there needs to be a reduction in backpacker visas, declaring "if it ain't broke, don't fix it".
The Coalition has vowed to slash the stock of temporary visas to 650,000 over four years with deep cuts to graduate, humanitarian and bridging visas.
But the opposition vowed to overturn the government's caps on second and third-year visas extensions, opting instead to increase fees with exemptions for those who completed required regional work.
Canavan tells Afternoon Briefing that backpackers aren't the problem.
"The facts are that those on working holiday visas are often moving around a lot. Most of them do move around a lot because they're here on holiday and then they go to different parts of Australia," he says.
"So they're not taking up permanent accommodation and adding to those stresses.
"We should perhaps take some pressure off the cities but we always have that labor force need on our farms, in tourism businesses, in remote areas. And that will be a win-win for our country if more backpackers want to go there."
No recession risk under Coalition migration plan: Canavan
Nationals leader Matt Canavan is our first guest on ABC's Afternoon Briefing this afternoon, following the release of the opposition's migration policy.
The Coalition has pledged to reduce the stock of temporary visa holders by 650,000 in four years in what it has described as the "biggest cut to migration in Australian history".
It claims the policy will be budget neutral. Canavan is asked how that can be the case.
"The average skilled worker here in Australia contributes three times more in tax than those on some other visa classes. So we will be reducing those visa classes, like say temporary graduate visas, like bridging visas," he says.
Asked to guarantee there is no risk of recession from the policy, Canavan is sure.
"Yes I can because we've worked very hard to make sure our changes continue to allow the important industries, businesses in this nation to have access to skills," he says.
Coalition's migration cut would undermine economic growth: ACCI
The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) warns the Coalition’s proposed immigration cuts would hurt Australia's economic growth.
Under the proposal, net overseas migration would be slashed to 100,000 per year for the first two years of a Coalition government, before increasing to 160,000 by the fourth year.
The plan includes cutting 650,000 temporary visas over four years through a number of different measures like abolishing temporary graduate visas and cutting the student visa intake.
ACCI chief executive Andrew McKellar says the policy goes against what the economy needs.
"The Coalition say that their policy is the largest cut to migration in Australia's history. That is not a good thing and that's not what we need at this point in time," he said.
"The reality is if we are going to cut levels of migration to the extent that the Coalition says that it will, that will undermine the growth rate of the Australian economy and our future growth potential and that is not a good thing."
OpenAI says it doesn't know if its tech could break into a gas plant and operate it
OpenAI's Jason Kwon is answering questions about what his company's agents are capable of.
Could an agent, for example, break into an Australian gas or oil facility and remotely operate it?
Kwon says he doesn't know.
"It's going to depend on the safeguards and the infrastructure and the security controls that that particular company or provider has in place," he says.
"There are facilities that are probably better secured than others."
He says tech companies need to work with people operating critical infrastructure to stress test whether AI would be able to get in.
"The way we get to a better answer is for there to be some sort of arrangement that lets that experimentation happen," he says.
When did Sam Altman know about the Medicare breach?
Senator David Pocock is questioning OpenAI's Jason Kwon over who knew what and when regarding the Medicare hack.
He asks if OpenAI boss Sam Altman knew about the hack when he met with Deputy PM Richard Marles at the start of September.
Kwon says Altman did not know about the hack but agrees the "process" through which people inside the company became aware of the hack "could have been much better".
"I want to make sure something like that does not happen again," he says.
OpenAI 'learned lessons' from Medicare hack
OpenAI executive Jason Kwon says additional monitoring has been put in place since one of the company's artificial intelligence agents infiltrated a Medicare website earlier this year.
Kwon is appearing before the AI parliamentary inquiry and says training models are now monitored in real time during tests and an alarm is triggered if they interact with the internet in a way they're not meant to.
"It has led us recently to act ually detect an instance of this occurring, and immediate intervention of our staff," he says.
He admits the company should have told the Australian government sooner about the Medicare hack but says they didn't because they "wanted to understand more of the facts before informing parties".
"But we have learned our lesson, and it is better to inform impacted parties even if we have limited information," he says.

Anthropic gave off-camera evidence in AI hearing
If you're wondering why Anthropic's stint at the AI inquiry today seemed short, it's because we, the public, didn't get to the see the second half.
Chair Labor MP Jo Briskey confirmed that the AI company had provided "both public and in-camera evidence to us" just before the hearing paused for lunch.
It's unusual — but not unheard of — for committees to grant those appearing before committees the opportunity to speak to the committee to inform their findings but without the public listening in.
We were in the room when we got hushed out suddenly, and what we can confirm is that the Anthropic hearing continued in camera for another twenty minutes.

Technical difficulties are plaguing the tech giants' evidence as company reps, appearing via video link, struggle to hear people in the room.
If only we had an autonomous artificial tool to help us get back on track.
Key Event
Albanese passes on wearing 'fou' in Tuvalu for pre-COP event
There's been a revealing little moment in Tuvalu, where the Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and several Pacific leaders have touched down for a brief visit as part of pre-COP talks.
Albanese and the other leaders are now visiting a major coastal reclamation project designed to help the low-lying Pacific nation from rising seas, as they try to build momentum ahead of global climate negotiations.
But there was a slightly awkward exchange not long after arrival when Albanese declined to put on the hand-made floral head garland — known in Tuvalu as a "fou" — which was handed out to leaders as part of their traditional welcome.
When one attendant approached to offer Albanese the fou, she was (politely) waved away by Australia's Special Envoy for the Pacific and Ambassador to PNG Ewen McDonald, who seemed to signal that the prime minister would prefer not to wear it.
That was in sharp contrast with the Pacific leaders seated next to the prime minister, who were more than happy to be garlanded.
But a second attendant seemed to think that Albanese had been left out and went to put another crown on his head, before being stopped by Albanese, who put it in on his lap and then quickly handed it back to McDonald.
The incident is unlikely to generate any real offence — at least a few other dignitaries at the event also declined to wear the fou, and the ABC has been told it was "optional" for leaders.
But it suggests the prime minister might be very sensitive about the optics surrounding this event, which the Coalition has savaged as a "farce" and a personal vanity project for the prime minister and the Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen.
'No safe or easy days' for those who serve in ADF: PM
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says the nation's thoughts are with the family and loved ones of the soldier who died during a training exercise in the NT.
The 28-year-old male soldier was killed and five other personnel on board were injured after their military vehicle rolled over at the Mount Bundey Training Area.
In a statement, the prime minister said it was a reminder there were "no safe or easy days" for those who served in the ADF.
"This sad incident is a terrible reminder of what families take on when their loved one bravely puts on our nation's uniform," he said.
"Every loss and every incident is felt deeply by the broader Defence family, but by none more so than their mates who served alongside them. We think of them today and every day.
"We ask that all Australians respect the privacy of Defence members and families at this saddest of times.
"The ADF will provide further updates when possible."
Death of soldier during training exercise 'tragic': Marles
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles has described the death of a soldier during a training exercise as "a tragic loss of life".
The 28-year-old male soldier was killed and five other personnel on board were injured after their military vehicle rolled over at the Mount Bundey Training Area in the Northern Territory.
"Australia’s servicemen and women do an exceptional job training and fighting for our country," Marles wrote on social media.
"This work in the defence of our nation carries risk. Our thoughts in this difficult time are with their family and friends.
"Defence is currently working with and supporting all the families in this difficult time. While further information will be provided in due course, right now our focus is on providing this support."
Key Event
Anthropic would alert of accidental hack in 'matter of days'
Anthropic head of safeguards Dave Orr says the Australian government would be notified "within days" if the company had an accidental hacking event like OpenAI's hack of Medicare earlier this year.
"Our policy is that we do notifications to victims of this sort of thing," he says.
"And certainly, it would to the Australian government as soon as we detect anything of that nature ... within a matter of days, or sooner".
Company representatives say they'd welcome new laws to clarify reporting requirements, which already exist in places like California. 
Orr is also asked how confident he is that Anthropic has not already hacked an Australian government website.
"We have not found any cases where it interacted with Australian government systems in any sort of unauthorised way," he says.
But he warns that while the company has reviewed its own activity, it has less oversight over what users of its AI are doing and whether they are inappropriately accessing websites.
Key Event
Hanson claims credit for 'dragging' Labor and Coalition to migration debate
Pauline Hanson has responded to the Coalition's migration policy, claiming credit for kickstarting the debate.
"Liberal and Labor have both been dragged kicking and screaming into the immigration debate by One Nation," she wrote on social media.
"They’ve ignored Australians for decades on this issue and they’d prefer it if they didn’t have to talk about it at all."
One Nation has proposed cutting net overseas migration by 750,000 over three years, pushing the NOM into negative territory.
Anthropic questioned over copyright laws for creators
Anthropic is being asked to explain its position on Australian copyright laws, which continue to be a sticking point between the government and big tech companies.
The PM has previously given strong assurances to Australian musicians, writers and artists that they would maintain control over their work and get to name the price in any copyright deals with AI companies.
"Anything less is theft," Albanese said in July.
AI companies like Anthropic want to train their models using the content but have insisted there is a path forward that is fair for everyone.
Special envoy Jeffrey Bleich tells the AI parliamentary inquiry he understands the Australian government is "interested in exploring" what would be necessary to "incentivise training here" but said it would be done on "Australian terms."
"But you can't license the entire internet," says Bleich.
He pushes back on the idea that training models on Australian content would result in reproductions of that work.
"The training is about looking at documents and identifying styles and ways of processing information," he says.
Anthropic paints picture of an Australia which 'shapes' AI era
Anthropic is delivering its opening spiel at the parliamentary joint inquiry into AI.
It's delivered by Jeffrey Bleich, the company's special envoy, who is giving evidence via video link.
He starts his opening pitch with a question - will Australia help set the terms for the development of AI, or will it allow the terms to be set for them?
"If Australia takes this opportunity and gets a balance right, it will not simply participate in the era, it will shape it," he says.
Artists, creators return serve on AI copyright
We expected strong performances from rights holders and creative groups at today's AI inquiry, and they didn't hold back.
At the hearing in Sydney, representatives for music labels, writers and voice actors were questioned about whether Australia needed to strike some kind of deal with tech companies to pave the way for deals or build national AI sovereign capacity.
Uniformly, they rejected the premise that the status quo was not working and instead pointed the finger at the big AI companies for "mass theft" — echoing a line from the prime minister earlier this year — used to train their AI models.
Here's a taste of just some of their zingers:
ARIO/PPCA CEO Annabelle Herd said: "Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal."
Simon Kennedy compared the unauthorised use of Australian copyright material by the companies to sexual consent: "The men who run AI companies have been acting as if consent is assumed."
AWG CEO Claire Pullen said that the "companies are treating us like mugs".

Ukraine says Russian drone attack sinks ship in Romanian waters

Ukraine says Russian drone attack sinks ship in Romanian waters
The incident is the latest suspected Russian drone incursion, as fears grow that the war in Ukraine could spill over.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has blamed a Russian drone attack for the sinking of a ship in Romania’s section of the Black Sea.
Romania reported that two people were killed and 11 rescued when a grain ship caught fire and sank in its waters on Monday. The Ukrainian president’s claim suggests the incident is the latest in a series of suspected incursions along NATO’s eastern flank, and will fuel concerns that Moscow’s war in Ukraine could spill over.
“A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Turkiye,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media.
According to the Romanian Ministry of Internal Affairs, the coastguard was alerted at about 11am local time (08:00 GMT) that a fire had broken out on the ship, adding that it was in the country’s “exclusive economic zone”.
The ministry did not identify the cause of the fire.
Azerbaijani and Indian citizens were on board the ship at the time of the attack, it is reported.
Romania is among several NATO members to have reported incursions this year, as Russia and Ukraine have increasingly turned to launches of hundreds of drones and missiles.
In May, a Russian drone hit an apartment building. In June, a stray Ukrainian maritime drone exploded in the Black Sea port of Constanta. In July, Bucharest summoned Russia’s ambassador after air defences intercepted three drones within the span of one week.
Incursions by Russian drones into eastern European airspace are seen by some as a test of NATO and the European Union’s defences and response capabilities.
The Baltic states have also seen drones enter their airspace throughout the war, with airspace violations contributing to the collapse of Latvia’s government in late May after a dispute over how to respond to the incursions.
The incursions have also prompted Poland to bolster its air defence posture after accusing Moscow of violating its airspace in September. Suspected drones were shot down twice in Moldova.
Romania’s Ministry of National Defence said the Romanian Naval Forces had destroyed nine drifting sea mines in the Black Sea since the start of the war.

Five days after an Omani co-pilot attempted to crash a flydubai flight bound for Israel, heightened Israeli vigilance was evident again Monday when a TUS Airways flight from Bologna, Italy, to Ben Gurion Airport was delayed for three hours after three Georgian passengers were removed from the aircraft.
A ynet check found that the decision to remove the three passengers was made at the request of Israel’s Population and Immigration Authority.
The authority said two of the Georgian nationals had attempted to travel to Israel using forged Israeli passports, while the third was barred from entering Israel.
It remained unclear, however, how all three managed to pass through the full check-in, border control and security process before boarding the aircraft.
Following the decision to remove the three passengers, the rest of the passengers were also taken off the aircraft, along with their baggage, for additional checks.
Idit, one of the passengers, said: “After those three passengers were removed from the plane, all of us were taken off as well so our belongings could be checked again. They didn’t explain to us why the flight was delayed or why we were taken off.”
TUS Airways said in a statement: “The safety of passengers and crew is our highest priority. The company is cooperating fully with aviation authorities in Israel and around the world.”
The airline thanked passengers for their patience and understanding and stressed: “At no stage was there any danger to the crew or passengers.”
Kavei Hofsha, the tourism group that owns the airline, said: “Three passengers were removed from the flight for an additional check. In accordance with instructions from Israeli immigration authorities, the airline’s team at Bologna Airport was asked to remove three passengers from the flight for renewed screening.”
Earlier Monday, another unusual incident occurred on a TUS Airways flight when a passenger who had not completed the required border-control procedures managed to board an aircraft.
Minutes before takeoff, the crew detected a discrepancy in the passenger count. A quick check located the passenger and determined that she had not completed the required border-control procedures.
Local police were called to the aircraft, and the passenger was removed and transferred to the relevant authorities.

Elon Musk’s Exes Are the Most Damning Part of a Massive New Documentary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:58:38 UTC
04:58:38 KST

On Friday morning, Shivon Zilis, a top executive and lieutenant of Elon Musk at his brain chip implant company Neuralink—as well as mother of four of the 14 children he is known to have fathered—took to his social media platform, X, to announce an abrupt shift in their relationship.
“It’s hard to go from in love to let go in a week with no warning, but that’s just how it is sometimes,” Zilis wrote, sharing a screenshot of the X account @BigTechAlert that showed Musk had unfollowed her there. Zilis’ post continued: “I feel happy that I got to show Elon how it feels to be deeply understood, nurtured, and peacefully loved with stability and gentleness,” followed by warm praise and best wishes for Musk. “I do hope and pray he and I can be great friends and coparents,” Zilis concluded, leaving some ambiguity as to what exactly changed between them and whether she remains a director of operations and special projects at Neuralink, though it does not appear as if she has left the position.
While this was a strange revelation of a private matter, it seemed hardly out of the ordinary for Musk’s dizzyingly complicated family life. At this point, all four of the women confirmed to have had children with him—Zilis, ex-wife Justine Wilson, Claire Boucher (better known as Grimes), and Ashley St. Clair—have used X to share details of their time with him or push back against his own claims.
Both Wilson and St. Clair participated in filmmaker Alex Gibney’s sprawling new documentary Musk, in theaters nationwide on October 16 and screening at the WIRED World Fair in Miami next month. St. Clair, a former conservative influencer, alleges that she rejected a nondisclosure agreement worth $40 million that would have prevented her from talking about her tumultuous association with Musk. Among an ensemble of tech entrepreneurs, journalists, and former Musk employees, the pair stand out as arguably the most important critical voices in the film, shedding light on Musk’s rise in Silicon Valley as well as his turn toward MAGA extremism during the 2024 election.
At a run time of nearly four hours, Musk sounds like daunting viewing, though once it’s over, you’ll find yourself wondering if it could’ve been a 10-part miniseries. That’s how much ground there is to cover, from the unrealistic ambitions of landing on Mars and the corporate colonization of Texas to the fatal collisions involving “self-driving” Teslas and the annihilation of the US Agency for International Development by the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) at the beginning of Trump’s second term. (WIRED’s reporting is cited in the documentary, which features interviews with global editorial director Katie Drummond and contributing editor Zoë Schiffer.)
Alongside a fast-moving, comprehensive account of Musk’s career as an all-powerful and untouchable oligarch, his former romantic partners provide crucial context about exactly who he is, piecing together a devastating portrait of the type of man to “let go” of a significant other by unfollowing her on social media.
Wilson reflects movingly on the loss of their firstborn to a SIDS-related condition, which is juxtaposed with a Musk post on X in which he wrote that he held their infant son as he died—a comment to which his ex-wife replied, “not that it matters to anyone except me, because it is one of the most sacred and defining moments of my life, but I was the one who was holding him.”
In the film, she also addresses the pain of Musk repeatedly insisting that their transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, was “killed by the woke mind virus,” calling this an unconscionable comment given the actual loss of a child they experienced together. Musk goes on to tell Gibney that right after passing along the message that he would “always love” Wilson, he cut off their daughter’s health insurance and that he has “never tried to repair things” with her.
“He was constantly remarking on the ways he found me lacking,” Wilson says in recounting their marriage. She claims that when she reminded her husband that she was his spouse and not an employee, he told her, “If you were my employee, I would fire you.” Summing up their overall dynamic, she says: “I learned the term gaslighting through my relationship with Elon.”
St. Clair, defiantly outspoken against Musk since revealing in early 2025 that he had fathered a child with her, alleges that her whirlwind affair with the billionaire was a temporary illusion of compatibility that led to a messy and ongoing custody battle. (Musk also covers a custody dispute with Grimes that was eventually settled for undisclosed terms.) St. Clair says in the film that Musk lost interest in her once she was pregnant and claims that he sought to father children with other women. According to The Wall Street Journal, this included cryptocurrency influencer Tiffany Fong, whom he messaged with an offer to give her a child. (Musk did not immediately return a request for comment on this matter. Fong declined to comment publicly on the Journal’s story except to say that she had requested not to be included in the outlet’s reporting.)
“It’s like a Gatling gun of sperm in his DMs,” St. Clair quips. In the film’s interviews, both she and Wilson voice discomfort over their ex’s views on birth rates and ambition to father a “legion” of offspring, with Wilson claiming he regards the mothers of his children as replaceable “breeders.”
Elsewhere in the film, St. Clair covers her allegation that Musk retaliated against her by reducing his financial support for their son, Romulus. And her reluctance to touch on certain issues the filmmakers ask her about seems to serve as something of an answer in its own right. “I’m not at liberty to say,” she responds carefully when asked if she ever witnessed Musk using illegal drugs.
Gibney’s broad account of how Musk wove together a tech empire and his celebrity image through relentless self-mythologizing, then insulated it from government oversight by backing Trump and seizing power within his administration, is an utterly convincing one. But most of the story will be familiar to those who have kept up with Musk headlines for the past decade. What’s truly eye-opening in Musk is the way the women he was once close to talk about what they see as his boundless capacity for cruelty and narcissism.
Is there a world in which Zilis, too, comes forward to share her intimate conversations and correspondence with Musk? That surely depends on whether she has signed any legal documents like those presented to St. Clair. What’s more than evident, however, is that for all his resources, Musk can’t buy the silence of everyone he’s ever known, and if anyone can finally shred his aura of genius inventor-king, it’s the women he’s allowed—however briefly—to share his orbit.

The 14th edition of NAPEC, the trade fair and conference dedicated to energy and hydrogen in Africa and the Mediterranean, kicked off today in Oran, in western Algeria, with over 450 exhibitors and 230 speakers. Italy is officially participating for the first time with an Italian pavilion, organized by the ICE Agency in collaboration with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation.
                                    
The opening ceremony was attended by the Italian Ambassador to Algeria, Alessandra Schiavo, along with the Minister of Hydrocarbons, Mohamed Arkab; the Minister of Energy, Mourad Adjal; and representatives from Algeria’s oil and gas sector, as well as executives and representatives from international energy companies.
                                    
The head of the diplomatic mission in the North African capital visited the Italian Pavilion, where she met with representatives of Italian companies attending the event dedicated to the energy sector.
                                    
In a statement to ANSA, Ambassador Schiavo emphasized the importance of Italy’s first “collective” participation in NAPEC. “This is a market where Italy has always been present, but where the challenge today lies not only in continuing to be active, but also in expanding our operations,” the diplomat emphasized.
                                    
“That is precisely why we have brought 13 Italian companies—13 small and medium-sized enterprises—that are characterized by extraordinary know-how, cutting-edge technology, and strong managerial skills, as well as a willingness to share these capabilities with Algerian companies,” she added.
                                    
“The 13 companies in the Italian pavilion are here because they want to introduce themselves directly to the Algerian market, even though some of them have already been collaborating with Italian companies operating in the country for decades,” explained Schiavo.
                                    
Regarding Algeria’s importance to Italy in the energy sector, the ambassador said: “It remains extremely significant: Algeria is by far our largest supplier of gas, and therefore, obviously, it remains a crucial country for Italy’s energy supply.”
   The ambassador also highlighted Algeria’s great potential to further develop as a regional hub and as a link between Europe, Africa, and the Mediterranean. She emphasized that the geographical location of Algeria and Italy allows the two countries to serve as “the two ends of a bridge between Africa and Europe.”
   The event, scheduled for October 5–7, brings together Algerian and international exhibitors, including leading operators in the hydrocarbons, oil services, energy, and energy transition technology sectors.

Student protests erupt at Cornell over mishandling of gang-rape allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:52:32 UTC
04:52:32 KST

Mass protests erupted at Cornell University on Monday, with students criticizing officials’ handling of gang-rape allegations, demanding the president’s resignation and painting “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” on an administration building.
Thousands of students and faculty gathered for a demonstration, sparked by the high-profile case of a former student known as Jane Doe, who said in a recent lawsuit that she was plied with drugs and raped at a fraternity house in 2024. The case has prompted international outrage and intense scrutiny of college fraternities and sexual violence on US campuses.
Protesters shouted, “Ban the frats” and held signs saying, “At Cornell, rapists are safer than women” and “Stop rape culture.” Some demonstrators directed their anger at Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, arguing he had failed to keep students safe and chanting, “Kotlikoff, resign!”
The demonstration took place after some students had smashed a glass door at the entrance of Day Hall, a building that houses the president’s office, and painted messages on the facade at approximately 3am on Monday, the Cornell Daily Sun reported.
The messages in red paint read “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” and “AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED PROTESTORS ARE EXPELLED”. The security camera above one of the messages was also painted over.
The students who graffitied the building said in a statement to the student newspaper that they were protesting “the global systems of power that allowed this to happen in the first place”.
“We wanted to ensure that Day Hall, the center of Cornell’s administrative function, was not able to continue business as usual,” the statement added. The students’ painted message was a reference to arguments that campus officials had treated pro-Palestine protesters more harshly than students accused of sexual misconduct, with four student demonstrators suspended in 2024, according to the Cornell Daily Sun.
Kyle Kimball, a Cornell spokesperson, condemned vandalism in a statement on Monday.
“We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community. Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer,” Kimball said. “We are investigating the vandalism at Day Hall and will address it in accordance with University policy and applicable law.”
The student activists defended their actions in a manifesto obtained by the student publication. “We reject the dogma that would condemn our actions this morning as violent while excusing rape,” they wrote. “Property damage is not violent; condoning rape is.”
The demonstrations escalated as Cornell faces widespread backlash for its handling of Jane Doe’s case, with critics saying the university had been too lenient with the accused men and had failed the victim.
According to lawyers for Jane Doe, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours. Jane Doe dropped out of Cornell after the incident.
A third fraternity member, who had already graduated, was barred from the Cornell campus, the New York Times reported on Saturday. Two more were reportedly given suspensions and disciplinary probation.
Two other men, the outlet said, were ordered not to contact the sophomore and required to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and to write “reflection papers”.
The lawsuit claimed that the seven fraternity members allegedly involved in the incident were “afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell”.
The university has said that claim does not accurately reflect what occurred. The accused men have denied all wrongdoing.
One student protester who addressed the crowd on Monday said: “Too often, we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support. How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?”
And a professor, according to the AP, said to applause: “Rape should not be inevitable.”
Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, who is also under fire for his office’s handling of the original allegations, announced last week he was reopening the case. Van Houten said Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were “dramatically different” from the statement she gave to police two years ago. Jane Doe’s attorney has pushed back on those claims and accused the DA of failing to do a thorough investigation after the incident.
Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang rape at Cornell University.
Kotlikoff, the university president under fire, addressed the case in a video message on Saturday, saying the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the future. That included “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, Kotlikoff said.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

Unknown Publisher

National-Religious Jews serving in the IDF are being killed in wars because their rabbis “teach them twisted Torah,” Rabbi Dov Lando, leading haredi (ultra-Orthodox) Litvak rabbi and spiritual head of the United Torah Judaism party, said in a leaked recording published by N12 on Monday night.
Lando, head of the Slabodka Yeshiva, was recorded addressing a small group of rabbis at his home, where he was heard saying young haredi men who avoid conscription to the military should not feel remorse over the sacrifices made by the religious Zionist community.
"Those who are getting killed - they are being killed because we don't learn enough,” Lando was recorded as saying. “They are being killed because their rabbis teach them twisted Torah....They kill people for honor."
Instead, Lando argued that those studying Torah in yeshivas are the ones protecting the country's residents. "There is no explanation why Arabs don't unite to wash away the entire land, and mercifully spare them from exterminating everyone. There is no explanation [other than the Torah]," Lando added.
Haredi spiritual leader: Zionism at fault for Arab hostility
Lando was also recorded during a scathing attack on Zionism, blaming the movement for hostility from the Arab world. While acknowledging that Arabs had not historically been friendly toward Jews, he argued that Zionism had caused them to hate the Jewish people.
"Never in history have Arabs been so hated," he claimed.
Addressing the haredi community’s relationship with the State of Israel and the IDF, Lando compared the state to a group of robbers whose protection the community nevertheless relies on.
“What does it matter now? What to do now? If we live among the robbers and the robbers save us, what to do? It’s a problem, a big problem,” he said.
Lando also condemned secular Israeli society, accusing secular Israelis of having no connection to Judaism and describing the establishment of the State of Israel as an act of heresy.
“These are people who have no connection with Judaism, nothing. It’s terrible and horrible, in my opinion, it’s a very great blasphemy. That the people of Israel, who are with God, and have made a state of annihilation and heresy – this is a great lesson to be learned,” he said.
Looking back to the founding of the Israeli state, Lando also questioned the need for Jewish sovereignty.
"I don't know what would have happened if at first there was no state and they had established a UN government here - it would have been an excellent situation," Lando said. “It would have been quite good if Arabs ruled here, it would have been the best situation.”
Eisenkot: Lando's statements 'embody anti-Zionist in its purest form'
Shortly following the publication of the leaked recording by N12, opposition party leaders in the bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the October 27 election hit out at Lando's remarks, vowing that UTJ will not take part in the next coalition formed after the election.

New York declares state of emergency over measles outbreak
NEW YORK – New York Governor Kathy Hochul issued an executive order declaring a state of emergency in response to rising measles cases on Oct 5, as infections skyrocket nationwide.
The order allows the state to respond more quickly to the outbreak and speed testing and vaccination, Hochul said in a statement. As at Oct 3, New York has recorded 108 total cases, including seven in New York City. A majority of the infections were recorded since mid-July.
“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease,” she said.
The announcement comes as the US is grappling with one of the worst measles outbreaks in decades.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recorded 3,887 cases as at Oct 2 – the most reported in three decades.
The majority of cases currently are centred in Pennsylvania, which reported more than 1,000 confirmed infections, including five deaths, on Oct 5. It has become the largest singular outbreak in the US.
The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is 97% effective in preventing a measles infection after two doses, according to the CDC.
Vaccination rates nationwide have been declining and are now below the threshold needed to protect immunocompromised or vulnerable people in many areas, leading to the growing number of outbreaks. BLOOMBERG

Despite the defeat of Islamic State’s self-declared caliphate nearly a decade ago, the group retains sleeper cells in Iraq, Iraqi security officials told Reuters ahead of the US withdrawal.
The withdrawal had raised concerns that a security vacuum could provide an opening for Islamic State to regain strength, with some officials warning that Iraqi forces would now have to contain the group without the coalition’s military presence. REUTERS

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Iceland late on Monday to begin a three-nation European tour to advance US influence in the Arctic after Washington sealed a pact on Greenland.
Rubio will meet with officials in Reykjavik "to discuss economic and security collaboration," the US State Department said in a statement announcing the trip.
The lightning visit, as symbolic as it is political, comes after the US signed a security pact with Denmark and Greenland in late September on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
The agreement has apparently put an end to President Donald Trump's threats to buy or even annex Greenland, which soured relations with the European Union.
Before taking off, Rubio described Iceland as "a good friend of the United States."
"So it's an opportunity to stop there and meet with them... it really is a result of a conversation I had with their leaders at the NATO summit with the leaders earlier this year, and with their foreign minister, so I'm looking forward to it," he said.
Under the pact, Washington plans to establish two new military bases on Greenland, drawing the autonomous Danish territory further into US orbit.
Trump’s Arctic ambitions
With competition on the rise in the Arctic, Iceland has regained status as a strategic player, even as the island continues to rely heavily on the United States for security.
At the start of September, Trump sparked new controversy by sharing an AI-generated map that appeared to show all of North America, the Caribbean, Greenland and Iceland as "the United States of America."
In response, Reykjavik summoned the US ambassador "to convey a clear message that the image was wholly inappropriate," Iceland's foreign ministry said in a statement to AFP.
Icelanders had voted in late August 52.8 percent to 47.2 percent against resuming negotiations on joining the EU, which have been frozen since 2013.
The last US secretary of state to visit Iceland was Antony Blinken in 2021.
Since gaining independence in 1944, Iceland has never had a military. It relies on the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) for its security and on a bilateral defence pact signed with the United States in 1951.
Washington does not have a permanent base in Iceland, but is looking to consolidate its control over Arctic access routes coveted by Russia and China.
Trump again signaled his obsession with Greenland on Sunday, posting on his Truth Social platform an AI-generated image of his face looming over what appears to be its landscape, accompanied by the words "Hello, Greenland!"
Greece, Portugal
After Iceland, Rubio continues to Athens to participate in a "strategic dialogue" with NATO member Greece on regional and energy security, the State Department said.
The visit follows media reports about possible conflicts of interest involving the US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, a former fiancee of Donald Trump Jr. and ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom.
In a letter addressed to Rubio, Congressman Gregory Meeks sought clarification of a Wall Street Journal report alleging she had stated the United States could create "political change" in European countries.
Rubio will later wrap up his European tour with a brief stop in Lisbon.

Pro-Israel Samoa prime minister apologizes after Nazi salute video resurfaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:46:54 UTC
04:46:54 KST

The prime minister of Samoa, a remote island nation in the heart of the Pacific Ocean, was forced to apologize Monday over a 19-year-old video showing him shouting “Heil Hitler” and giving a Nazi salute during a family gathering. The embarrassing footage of Prime Minister La’auli Leuatea Schmidt is particularly striking given that he and his country are regarded as staunch supporters of Israel.
The Samoa Observer revealed Sunday the existence and contents of the seven-second video, which reports said was filmed at a Schmidt family gathering in Samoa in July 2007. A screenshot from the video shows Schmidt holding a microphone in one hand while raising the other, surrounded by others making the same gesture. The newspaper reported that Schmidt can be heard saying into the microphone: “Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler!”
Schmidt, who served as deputy speaker of Samoa’s parliament in 2007 and has led the island nation since his election victory in August 2025, did not deny the report. In a statement posted on social media Monday, he said: “I acknowledge that these words and the gesture were inappropriate and could have caused hurt and offense, and I apologize for using them.”
He added that the video was filmed “at a private family gathering — not intended for public viewing.” In the statement, he stressed that his conduct in the video did not reflect his personal beliefs or the views of the Samoan government or people, and said he rejected “Nazism, antisemitism, racism and every form of political extremism.”
According to the newspaper, it is not known what happened immediately before or after the clip, and Schmidt’s statement offered no further explanation.
The controversy erupted as news organizations across the Pacific region have condemned Schmidt’s continuing treatment of the Observer. The newspaper has been barred since November from covering news conferences and government events involving Schmidt and other officials after the prime minister accused it of misleading coverage.
On Friday, Schmidt confirmed allegations that photographs of him taken by an Observer reporter outside government buildings during an official event had been deleted from the reporter’s camera by an aide. He defended the move, arguing that the Observer, Samoa’s largest media group, had violated the ban imposed on it.
The Observer called Schmidt’s boycott “an authoritarian act,” while news organizations across the region have urged the prime minister to reverse course. The Journalists Association of Samoa said it was “deeply concerned” by the incident involving the deletion of the photographs.
Like several other leaders of small South Pacific island nations, Schmidt has previously voiced strong support for Israel. Since September 2023, three Pacific island nations, including Samoa, have been among the handful of countries to follow the United States in opening embassies in Jerusalem rather than Tel Aviv. Analysts attribute the support Israel enjoys in the region to deeply rooted Christian traditions woven into public life.
When Schmidt was sworn into office in September 2025, he even wore a Jewish prayer shawl during a ceremony that also included the blowing of a shofar. “Samoa will not retreat from its support for Israel as the nation of God’s people,” he told reporters after the event, according to local media reports.
Samoa is a tiny nation of about 220,000 people, located near Fiji and west of American Samoa, a U.S. territory in the eastern part of the Samoan island chain.
In the early 20th century, Samoa was under German rule and was a German colony, which is why many residents have German ancestry and German surnames. In 1914, New Zealand seized what was then known as Western Samoa from Germany and retained control until 1962, when the country gained independence.

AstraZeneca CEO says Summit drug could drive next generation of cancer combinations after $2 billion investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:44:30 UTC
04:44:30 KST

AstraZeneca CEO Pascal Soriot told CNBC on Monday that Summit Therapeutics' lead drug could help power next-generation cancer treatment combinations that could be the "future of cancer care."
Soriot's comments in an exclusive interview with CNBC come a week after the pharmaceutical giant announced a $2 billion equity investment and clinical collaboration with the biotech company to test potential cancer drug combinations.
At the heart of that investment is Summit's ivonescimab, which is a first-in-class bispecific antibody that works by attacking cancer through two pathways simultaneously: PD-1, which acts like a brake on immune cells, and VEGF, a signal that helps tumors grow new blood vessels.
Blocking both unleashes the body's immune system to attack cancer cells and cuts off the blood supply that tumors need to grow.
Soriot called that medication the "next generation" after an initial wave of drugs that only target PD-1, such as Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda. Ivonescimab made waves globally after head-to-head clinical trials showed it outperformed Keytruda – the reigning standard of care and one of the highest-grossing drugs in history – in patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer.
Soriot particularly sees an opportunity to combine Summit's drug with AstraZeneca's portfolio of targeted cancer treatments called antibody-drug conjugates.
Summit's drug "in particular is very exciting because it can help address a certain number of tumor types that can be better treated in combination with antibody-drug conjugates, better treated than with existing first-generation PD-1 agents," he said.
AstraZeneca's investment equates to a roughly 12% stake in Summit, and it's not an outright acquisition or licensing agreement. That means Summit retains full permission and commercial rights to ivonescimab, which has sparked massive interest and a multi-billion dollar gold rush into drugs that work the same way.
AstraZeneca's new R&D site
Soriot spoke with CNBC from the site of AstraZeneca's new more than $1 billion research and development facility in Kendall Square in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
The company on Monday announced the opening of the 570,000 square-foot site, where scientists will develop next-generation treatments across obesity, breast cancer, COPD and rare diseases, among other areas. AstraZeneca said those new products will help the company grow beyond 2030.
The center will use robotics, continuous automation and agentic AI to aid the drug discovery and development process, the drugmaker added.
"It's faster, lower cost of research and development, more products that are delivered to better products that are delivered to patients," Soriot said. "We are on the race against disease, and there's a lot of unmet needs out there."
He said about 20% of the investment in the site is going toward robotics and AI.
"The idea is to really leverage AI to invent new medicines faster, but also invest in robotics to simplify and accelerate the process of discovering and developing molecules throughout the preclinical phase in particular," Soriot said.

Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.

Mexico seeks evidence of border shooting that prompted US troop deployment

Unknown Publisher

Mexico seeks evidence of border shooting that prompted US troop deployment
Mexico’s Sheinbaum has expressed concern about US officials overstepping norms on security cooperation.
Mexico has asked the United States for evidence of a cross-border shooting that allegedly targeted US security personnel.
In her daily news conference on Monday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum explained that the US had reported “shots from the Mexican border”.
“We asked for all the evidence because we have no evidence,” Sheinbaum said. She added that Mexico’s National Guard, Army and Navy had not detected any shots being fired from Mexican territory towards the US.
Sheinbaum made her remarks a day after the US Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson wrote on the social media platform X about the shooting, which allegedly took place in Texas across from the Mexican state of Tamaulipas in late September.
Johnson said the targets were members of the US Coast Guard, and that the threat would be “swiftly addressed”.
“The U.S. Embassy in Mexico is helping coordinate with Mexican forces deploying to the border area where U.S. Coast Guardsmen were fired upon,” Johnson wrote.
“Together, we intend to patrol both sides of our shared border, protect our communities, and make it more difficult for criminal and terrorist organizations to operate.”
Some 500 US troops, along with helicopters, drones and anti-drone equipment, have been sent to the border since the alleged shooting.
Mexico has sent its own deployment in the border area, as part of a joint operation called Operation Mirror between the two countries to secure the frontier.
In Monday’s news conference, Sheinbaum confirmed that the Mexican deployment was designed “to forestall any issues” that may arise.
During their time working together, Johnson and Sheinbaum have repeatedly been at odds over questions of border security and national sovereignty.
A former US Army Green Beret who later served in the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), Johnson has served as ambassador to Mexico since May 2025, under US President Donald Trump.
Since returning to office for a second term, Trump has sought to increase US influence over Latin America, as part of a policy informally dubbed the Donroe Doctrine — a twist on the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine.
His administration has also taken a more active role in the region’s security, on the premise of combatting narcotics trafficking and criminal organisations.
Trump has repeatedly said he may carry out military strikes inside Mexico to attack the cartels he said are “running Mexico”, framing their presence as a threat to US security. Sheinbaum, however, has warned that such an operation would violate her country’s sovereignty.
Mexico’s tensions with the Trump administration have strained relations with Johnson. Sheinbaum has accused the ambassador of overstepping diplomatic norms, while Johnson has sought to push the Mexican government to cooperate with Trump’s demands.
In June, Johnson criticised Sheinbaum’s government on social media for turning the “fight against cartels” into a “political dispute”.
Sheinbaum responded the next day with a warning for Johnson, saying, “Ambassadors must respect the internal political affairs of their countries.”
Law enforcement agencies in the US and Mexico have long cooperated in counter-narcotics operations, but Trump’s militaristic approach has created friction with left-wing governments including Mexico.
On Monday, Sheinbaum took issue with Johnson for announcing the opening of an international police academy in the central state of Queretaro without her government’s knowledge.
“How can a groundbreaking ceremony take place with a US ambassador and a Mexican governor, but not with the federal security cabinet?” she said.
Under the Mexican constitution, the federal government must approve the activities of foreign forces on Mexican soil.
But that law was tested earlier this year, when two CIA agents were reportedly killed in an April car accident in the northern Mexican state of Chihuahua, alongside members of the state’s law enforcement.
What the CIA agents were doing in Chihuahua remains unclear. Reports emerged that the CIA agents may have been participating in a state-led raid on a local drug lab without federal authorisation.
One state official publicly denied that report, saying the agents were conducting an unrelated training on drone usage.
Sheinbaum said neither she nor her cabinet were informed of any CIA activities, and her government pledged to investigate the incident.

David Berson, president and chief executive officer of CBS Sports, will lead a newly formed global sports group that will oversee all networks, platforms and territories. The CBS Sports, TNT Sports and WBD Sports brands will roll up into the new group.
Sources familiar with the matter say Skydance is expected to make a formal announcement about Berson's move soon. A CBS spokesperson declined to comment.
The combined company, which last week announced it will be named Skydance, will own a large swath of sports rights, including NFL Sunday afternoon games, all of March Madness, college football, NHL, MLB, The Masters, and many others.
The Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery merger is expected to close tomorrow, Oct. 6.
Silberwasser joined TNT Sports in 2022 from Univision. Warner Bros. Discovery lost NBA live rights in 2025, concluding a 40-year relationship with the league.
Still, Silberwasser struck new multiyear deals to sublicense College Football Playoff games and air events such as All Elite Wrestling (AEW), the French Open and NASCAR races. That helped Warner Bros. Discovery reach distribution deals with pay TV providers and maintain distribution fees even without the NBA.
Berson must now look at his entire portfolio and decide which sports are worth keeping and which can be shed as Skydance looks to pay down nearly $80 billion in debt in the coming years.

Turkey, Pakistan agree on rapid troops deployment in Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
RIYADH – Turkey and Pakistan will undertake a “rapid deployment” of troops to Saudi Arabia as part of a new mutual defence alliance, the three countries said on Oct 5, as the Gulf kingdom faces escalating attacks from Yemen’s Houthis.
The trio in August signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, committing them to come to each other’s aid if attacked.
The pact unites NATO’s second-largest army, that of Turkey, with the Islamic world’s only nuclear-armed state, Pakistan, as well as the leading Gulf power, Saudi Arabia.
Their representatives held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Oct 5 where they noted recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, in particular those targeting the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, without mentioning the Iran-backed Houthis by name.
The three countries “reaffirmed their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the kingdom’s security and territorial integrity”, they said in a joint statement.
They also agreed “to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom”.
The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.
The kingdom has faced repeated Houthi attacks targeting its cities, oil infrastructure and ships ever since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July.
In September, the group launched a new offensive that seized swathes of territory from Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, which on Oct 5 launched a counteroffensive with Riyadh’s support seeking to retake all Houthi territory, some of it held for more than a decade. AFP

Russian Attack Destroys KUSUM Pharmaceutical Plant in Sumy, Killing Employee and Halting Production
A Russian attack destroyed the KUSUM pharmaceutical plant in Sumy on October 4, killing one employee and halting production at the facility.
KUSUM reported the destruction in a statement published on Instagram on October 4. The company identified the killed employee as Yevhen Volodymyrovych Miroshnychenko, who had worked in the plant’s engineering department since 2009.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The plant in Sumy has been destroyed. But KUSUM continues to work for the people who need our medicines every day,” the company stated.
The Sumy facility produced medicines that the company described as essential for Ukrainian patients. KUSUM is assessing the extent of the destruction and working to maintain uninterrupted supplies of its products in Ukraine.
The plant produced cardiovascular, gastroenterological, anti-inflammatory, antipyretic, antihypertensive, mucolytic, and pediatric medicines, including tablets, capsules, granules, suspensions, and syrups.
The company also operates manufacturing facilities in Indore and Bhiwadi, India, which it plans to use to reorganize production and sustain deliveries. KUSUM noted that the transition would depend partly on avoiding regulatory obstacles.
The attack follows an earlier major loss for the pharmaceutical producer, when one of its warehouses was destroyed. KUSUM emphasized that it continued operations after that incident and now intends to maintain medicine supplies despite the destruction of its Sumy plant.
The destruction of the KUSUM plant fits a broader pattern of Russian strikes on foreign-owned industrial facilities in Ukraine.
On September 3, a Russian drone strike caused a major fire at a Coca-Cola production plant in Velyka Dymerka, Kyiv region, one of Europe's largest beverage manufacturing sites.
Earlier, a drone attack on Dnipro damaged an oil processing facility owned by US agribusiness Bunge, spilling about 300 tons of oil onto roads and leaving the city's embankment routes impassable for two to three days.

Russia Hosts Regional Talks on Afghanistan With Taliban Delegation, Humanitarian Aid and Regional Security in Focus
Russia will regularly send humanitarian supplies to the Taliban-led administration in Afghanistan—a group designated as a terrorist organization by many countries —Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov announced at the opening of the Moscow Format consultations on Afghanistan.
Lavrov stated that the next delivery of Russian aid is scheduled to reach Kabul within the next month or two, noting that the humanitarian situation in the country remains difficult, as reported by The Washington Post on October 5.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A delegation from Afghanistan’s ruling Taliban government joined representatives from China, India, Iran, Pakistan and other nations for talks in Moscow on Monday.
Citing United Nations data, Lavrov said nearly half of the population—more than 17 million Afghans—could face food shortages this winter, while the total number of people needing assistance stands at around 22 million.
In addition, about 4 million Afghans have returned to the country from Pakistan and Iran since early last year, placing an extra strain on the economy, which Lavrov said requires management through specialized international bodies and bilateral efforts.
At the same time, despite these statements, the news outlet Afghanistan International reported that the Taliban is purchasing batches of weapons and drones in Belarus with Moscow's consent and through India's mediation, The Washington Post reported.
According to former senior Afghan officials, contacts between Minsk and Kabul intensified following a visit to Moscow by Afghan Defense Minister Mohammad Yaqoob in late May and early June.
Russia and Afghanistan signed a military-technical cooperation agreement. Such agreements typically involve the exchange of weapons, licenses, military technologies, and joint developments.
“Five years is a short time to overcome the consequences of many decades of occupation, yet your government’s achievements are evident, and we welcome them,” Lavrov said. He hailed the Taliban’s successes in combating the Islamic State group and other extremists, and its efforts to eradicate drug trafficking, according to The Washington Post.
In July 2025, Russia became the first country to formally recognize the Taliban-led government of Afghanistan after accepting the credentials of the new Afghan ambassador in Moscow.
The Russian Foreign Ministry stated that it saw strong prospects for developing bilateral ties and planned to expand cooperation in security, counter-terrorism, energy, transport, agriculture, and infrastructure.
The move marked a major step in ending the Taliban’s international isolation and reflected Moscow’s growing partnership with Kabul following the lifting of Russia’s ban on the Taliban movement earlier that year.

Businessman Oleg Varyukhin, who traveled to Russia after living in Ukraine for 27 years, has been charged with treason for paying Ukraine’s mandatory military levy into its state budget, Mediazona reported.
Varyukhin was detained in May 2026. In early August, his lawyer, Yuri Shel, said the treason charge stemmed from tax payments in Ukraine. At the time, it was unclear which tax the Russian authorities had taken issue with.
Officers from Russia’s Federal Security Service found records of the tax payments on Varyukhin’s phone during a search at the airport, his lawyer said.
Money transfers to support the Ukrainian army have previously led to treason prosecutions in Russia. But Varyukhin is the first person known to be prosecuted for treason for paying taxes into Ukraine’s state budget, Mediazona noted.
Varyukhin was born in Norilsk and moved to Ukraine in 1999, where he ran a perfume shop. He was unable to obtain Ukrainian citizenship and did not have a Russian passport either: he had left Russia with Soviet documents. In 2026, he flew to Russia via Moldova to update his documents. He was detained directly at the airport.
Shel called the treason charge absurd. “Anyone who works in any country is required to pay taxes. They have no say in that. As in any country, [Varyukhin] had no say in how the government allocated those taxes,” he said while challenging his client’s detention. But his arguments did not persuade the court.

Spain PM pins hopes on housing crisis to help win snap election
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:30:50 BST
04:30:50 KST

Spain PM pins hopes on housing crisis to help win snap election
- Published
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's decision to call a snap election for 29 November came on the back of a parliamentary defeat.
On Friday, the raft of measures he had presented to congress aimed at improving conditions for tenants and trying to address the problem of soaring rentals was narrowly rejected, as parties on the right voted against them.
That parliamentary result confirmed that Sánchez's left-wing coalition no longer commanded a majority.
But as has so often been the case throughout Sánchez's career, the calling of the election was not a knee-jerk reaction but a carefully thought-out manouevre.
His government has been struggling in recent months.
His Socialist Party has been mired in corruption, with cases implicating former senior figures in the party, Santos Cerdán and José Luis Ábalos, while the former Socialist Prime Minister, José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, is facing accusations of having benefited financially from the government's bailout of an airline. Zapatero has denied wrongdoing.
In addition, Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, is due to go on trial over allegations of misuse of funds and influence peddling - accusations that Gómez and Sánchez vehemently deny.
Meanwhile, Sánchez's administration has struggled to manage the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in North Africa, where more than 70,000 migrants suddenly arrived in July. Most have returned over the border to Morocco, but the city has become a political and logistical headache for the prime minister.
Although Sánchez had insisted until recently that he would see out the legislature and not call elections until next summer, his government had looked increasingly unlikely to make it that far.
The wave of outrage which has exploded in recent days over housing has provided him with the ideal reason to call elections early - and a welcome issue away from Ceuta and the allegations of corruption.
Appealing to his own party's voters and those further to the left on Monday, he called for voters to "mobilise and ensure that parliament gives us a much bigger, progressive majority with which to defeat the elites, conquer social rights and keep transforming Spain".
On the upcoming campaign trail, Sánchez can point to the fact that his adversaries on the right - such as the conservative People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox - voted against his government's housing measures, which sought to prevent the eviction of tenants, improving the conditions of their contracts and preventing investors from buying residential property.
The PP and Vox tend to oppose any initiative presented by the Sánchez government, which they have long cast as illegitimate due to its scandals and reliance on Catalan and Basque nationalists.
However, as a matter of policy, parties on the right tend to oppose the kind of direct intervention in the housing market that Sánchez has been advocating, warning that it can be counterproductive.
Earlier this year, when Sánchez's international profile rose due to his outspoken criticism of Israel's actions in Gaza and his clashes with US President Donald Trump, there was speculation that he might have used the political capital that gave him on the left and called an early election back then.
However, the housing issue, which is the biggest concern for Spaniards according to polls, appears more likely to mobilise support on the left.
Yet polls also show that the Socialists are trailing the PP. While the housing issue provides Sánchez with a potential fillip on the campaign trail, staying in power after these elections will be probably the biggest challenge of his career.

From making interceptors to guarding sky: Ukrainian drone maker gets its own private air defense unit and will pay for it from weapon sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:28:53 UTC
04:28:53 KST

A Ukrainian drone maker just got its own air defense unit, and says it has already downed Russian jet-powered drones. Ukraine's Defense Ministry has issued an order granting the Night Hornets, the anti-Shahed unit of interceptor maker Wild Hornets, the status of a private air defense, and the company announced it is starting to build its own network of remotely launched interceptor drones.
Russia has sharply increased its use of jet-powered Shahed drones, which cuts the reaction time of Ukraine's mobile fire groups from about a minute to as little as six seconds. Now, a private company joins the air defense line, while Ukrainian military intelligence says Russia is producing up to 500 Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet drones a month.
The planned network will combine remote-control centers, a grid of remote interceptor launches built on the company's Hornet Vision Ctrl technology, and field positions. Wild Hornets will not sell protection for individual sites and will pay for the unit from drone sales profit.
"The unit has more than 50 downed Shaheds to its name, including jet-powered ones. We create technologies that work. We use them ourselves to protect our country," the company says.
Air Force commanders will direct the crews
The crews already go on daily combat duty alongside the military and will take orders from the Air Force command. The unit draws on Wild Hornets instructors and test pilots, including veterans of the war and pilots who rose from beginners to instructors. The company wants to fold private air defense into the country's overall system, including over Kyiv.
Air alerts now swallow nearly a third of mall hours
Due to Russia's jet-powered drones, air-raid alerts covered 30.8 percent of shopping-center operating hours across Ukraine in September, a record, up from 22 percent in August and 14.1 percent a year earlier, the Ukrainian Council of Shopping Centers reports. The average mall has now lost 176.5 working days since the full-scale invasion, including 9.6 in September alone.
Kyiv shows the sharpest jump. The share of alert time during mall hours in the capital rose from 11.6 percent in August to 32.7 percent in September, the council said.
The damage reaches well beyond the malls. Ukraine's Economy Ministry expects losses from Russian strikes to reach up to $10 billion this year, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said on 12 September.

With the two presidents watching, Ariane TORO SOLER was aiming for the -52kg World title. Ranked 5th, she had been in excellent form, battling with determination. With the biggest prize within reach she had one final challenge between her and gold : ABE Uta, Olympic and five-time World Champion.
She worked her way into the final with the experience and composure expected of a champion. She came through the preliminaries with confidence and responded under pressure. ABE kept finding the answers to keep her bid for another World title firmly on course.
In the final, the contest was tactical and hard won, but it was the Japanese legend who would retain her title for another year. The six time World champion has never been defeated at a World Championships.
OTP Group CEO Mr Peter CSANYI awarded the medals.
In the -66kg category, Uta’s brother ABE Hifumi was the one to beat. The double Olympic and four time World Champion was chasing yet another World title. The Japanese star made it to the final, but could he regain the red backpatch?
David GARCIA TORNE would be his opponent. Marching towards his first ever World Championships final, the Spanish judoka was on great form in the preliminaries.
When it came to the final, ABE proved decisively why he would take home his fifth World title with an enormous ippon that electrified the crowd. A fitting finish from one of judo's biggest stars and another golden moment for the ABE siblings.
Olympic Council of Asia Vice President Mr Otabek UMAROV awarded the medals.
Another unforgettable day in Baku.
