Gerald Posner analyzes whether Hamas actions on October 7 meets the legal standard for genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:58:51 UTC
02:58:51 KST

Investigative journalist and author Gerald Posner released a new paper on Monday examining whether the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel meets the legal standard for genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention. Posner previously authored a legal primer titled Genocide for Dummies, examining whether Israel’s military campaign in Gaza met the genocide threshold under international law.
Now, he has turned his focus toward the actions of Hamas on October 7.
In his new analysis, titled "The Genocide Case Against Hamas," Posner addressed initial threshold questions regarding duration and non-state entities. He noted that the Genocide Convention does not require a prolonged campaign, explaining that a single act committed with the requisite intent can legally qualify, and that international tribunals and courts have previously established that genocide can be committed by non-state groups and individuals rather than governments alone.
To support this, Posner cited several historical examples, including the individual convictions of private individuals like Georges Rutaganda during the Rwandan genocide, the actions of the army of the Republika Srpska, a non-state entity, during the Srebrenica massacre, and the landmark genocide conviction of an ISIS member in Frankfurt for atrocities committed against the Yazidis.
The paper outlined the two core components required under international law: the actus reus, or guilty act, and dolus specialis, which is the special intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group as such. Posner explained that while mass killing, torture, and sexual violence clearly satisfy the prohibited acts under the convention, the more complex determination centers on proving special intent.
To evaluate intent, Posner examined both written records and public statements from Hamas leadership alongside the empirical evidence of what occurred on the ground. He highlighted explicit evidence from the 1988 Hamas Covenant, pointing to Article 7 and its quotation of a hadith calling for Muslims to fight and kill Jews, as well as statements from leaders such as Yahya Sinwar promising in 2022 to come in a “roaring flood” and Fathi Hammad calling in 2019 to “attack every Jew on the planet.”
Posner also cited recordings of participants during the attack, including a terrorist who boasted to his parents on the phone that he had killed 10 Jews with his bare hands. Posner contrasted these records with arguments raised by defenders of Hamas who point to a “Document of General Principles and Policies” published in May 2017, an updated text released to improve the group’s public image and present a fresher, less militant face.
Posner argued this 2017 text was merely a public relations rebrand driven by external pressures, such as Egypt designating the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist organization and Qatari hosts pushing for a softened public posture, noting that the document never formally repealed the 1988 covenant and that Hamas’s physical conduct on October 7 matched the earlier eliminationist rhetoric rather than a limited political dispute.
Proceeding to evaluate the empirical evidence of what actually happened, Posner examined the prohibited acts under Article II of the convention, focusing primarily on killing and causing serious bodily or mental harm.
Posner analyses Hamas violence against civilians
Posner analyzed the attack on more than 20 civilian communities, noting that at places like Kibbutz Be’eri, Kfar Aza, and Nir Oz, terrorists went house to house, set homes on fire, and executed families, with recovered-body data showing 80% of bodies at Be’eri had been tortured.
He argued that recovery data, recovered operational documents instructing fighters to “kill as many people as possible,” and targeted selections of Jewish communities demonstrate that civilian deaths were a central aim rather than an afterthought.
Addressing the Nova music festival, where 364 people were killed, Posner argued that, even if the site was found rather than pre-targeted, the subsequent hours of hunting survivors across open fields reveal the explicit intent carried by the attackers.
Furthermore, Posner addressed counter-arguments regarding non-Jewish casualties, such as foreign laborers and Arab citizens, noting that international jurisprudence, such as the rulings from the Rwanda tribunal, establishes that genocide does not require 100% of victims to belong exclusively to the protected group, provided the group itself was the object of the attack.
Posner then evaluated serious bodily and mental harm under Article II(b), analyzing extensive documentation of torture, mutilation, and conflict-related sexual violence.
Citing findings from UN Special Representative Pramila Patten and local crisis center reports, Posner outlined evidence of rape and gang rape committed systematically across multiple locations, noting that recovered instructions found on dead terrorists even included phrases in Hebrew demanding victims take off their pants.
Comparing these findings to the legal precedent where the Rwanda tribunal recognized systematic sexual violence as an act of genocide, Posner argued that these actions carried no military value other than harm directed at the group.
Can a single-day massacre count as genocide?
To test whether a single-day massacre can legally constitute genocide, Posner conducted a detailed comparison with the 1995 Srebrenica massacre. While acknowledging numerical differences, Posner applied the legal principle established in the Krstic case that genocidal intent and impact must be judged against the specific community within the perpetrators’ reach.
He pointed out that at the level of the individual communities attacked, such as Be’eri and Nir Oz, the proportion of residents killed or abducted matched or exceeded the community-level destruction seen at Srebrenica.
Posner contended that, while the Srebrenica massacre was an administrative operation conducted over days, Hamas’s inability to kill more people during a fast-moving, multi-hour raid is constrained only by opportunity under the Krstic doctrine, especially given explicit orders to maximize casualties.
Posner draws attention to international double standard
Posner pointed out how international bodies and human rights organizations applied the genocide framework exclusively to Israel while omitting any formal analysis of the October 7 attack.
He detailed how the International Association of Genocide Scholars issued an August 2025 resolution declaring Israel’s military actions in Gaza to be genocide while entirely ignoring its own earlier peer-reviewed policy brief by scholar Sara Brown, which had concluded that Hamas’s attacks constituted genocidal violence.
Posner similarly highlighted that the UN Commission of Inquiry scrutinized public statements by Israeli leaders like Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant as direct evidence of genocidal intent, yet failed to apply that exact same standard to Hamas’s explicit charter provisions, Sinwar’s pledge to wipe out Israel, or Fathi Hammad’s call to slaughter Jews globally.
Furthermore, he noted that while Amnesty International and B’Tselem formally accused Israel of genocide, their reports on October 7 categorized the atrocities merely as war crimes or crimes against humanity without testing them against the Genocide Convention.
Posner argued that applying a standard selectively to one party while ignoring it for another invalidates the standard entirely.
Posner concluded by challenging critics with a falsifiable standard, demanding that anyone seeking to refute the conclusion of genocide must provide a valid military rationale for executing infants and the elderly, explain away the explicit house-to-house execution instructions, reconcile the 1988 Covenant’s eliminationist text with the physical reality of the massacre, and offer an alternative interpretation for leaders’ explicit public pledges to repeat the violence again and again.

Knesset legal adviser urges vote as Israel enters fourth month without comptroller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:58:42 UTC
02:58:42 KST

Israel has not had a state comptroller for three months, and the Knesset is obligated to hold a repeat vote for the position as soon as possible, Knesset legal adviser Sagit Afik told the High Court of Justice on Monday.
The July judgment invalidating the election of attorney Michael Rabello must be implemented, preferably before the current Knesset’s term ends following the October 27 general election, she said.
The authority to convene the Knesset or set a date for the vote rests with Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, who is expected to submit a separate response through private counsel.
Afik has repeatedly told Ohana the plenum should be convened, but he has so far declined to set a date. Once his response is filed, the court will decide how to proceed with the petition and whether further intervention is required.
The petition, filed by Yaron Gadot, asks the court to compel Ohana to convene the plenum and complete the election process.
Afik said four developments since the July 2 judgment could affect the timing and conduct of the vote, but none cancels the Knesset’s obligation to comply with the ruling.
Changes in Knesset create obstacles for holding new vote
The composition of the Knesset has changed: Factions have split, MKs have switched parties, five MKs have resigned, and five others who did not participate in the original vote have replaced them.
Holding a secret vote during a general-election campaign could increase the weight MKs give to party and factional considerations, Afik said. The secrecy requirement is intended to allow MKs to vote according to their judgment and conscience, free from coalition or party pressure, she added.
The Knesset is in an election recess, when MKs are focused largely on campaigning and previously scheduled events. Therefore, sufficient notice would be needed to allow all MKs who want to participate to attend, Afik said.
Under the State Comptroller Law, the speaker must convene the Knesset to elect a comptroller even during a recess, Afik said.
Because the court had ordered the second round of voting to be held again, Ohana would not be required to repeat the formal consultation with his nine deputies or provide the three weeks’ written notice ordinarily required before an initial comptroller election, she said.
Reasonable advance notice would nevertheless be necessary, Afik said, adding that none of the Knesset factions or deputy speakers had asked Ohana to convene the plenum for a repeat vote.
Position left vacant after previous comptroller completed term with no successor
The vacancy began in early July, when Matanyahu Englman completed his seven-year term without a successor in line to take office. Rabello’s election had been invalidated two days earlier, leaving the State Comptroller’s Office without either a permanent comptroller or a temporary replacement.
The office’s professional staff can continue routine work, but several core powers are vested personally in the comptroller and cannot be delegated, its legal adviser said in July. These include signing and publishing reports, opening new audits, imposing sanctions under party-financing laws, and granting protective orders to public employees who report suspected corruption.
The last of those functions is exercised by the comptroller in his parallel role as ombudsman. Without a serving comptroller, the State Comptroller’s Office has said it cannot legally grant relief to workers who claim they were targeted after exposing wrongdoing.
The office initially asked the Knesset to appoint an acting comptroller during the vacancy. Afik rejected that proposal on grounds that the relevant provisions apply when a serving comptroller is temporarily unable to perform the job, not when a term has expired and no successor has entered office.
The legally proper solution was to complete the election rather than create an interim appointment through a provision that did not cover the situation, she said.
Rabello was chosen over retired Supreme Court justice Yosef Elron on June 3 after two rounds of voting. Elron led the first round 60-57, leaving both short of the 61 votes required.
The vote was then restarted after allegations emerged that coalition MKs had photographed or filmed their ballots behind the voting screen.
Rabello won the second round 61-57.
On July 2, a five-justice High Court panel unanimously invalidated the second ballot. The documentation of votes had caused a material breach of the legally required secret ballot, it ruled. The court ordered the Knesset to hold that round again and said it was presumed that it would complete the process as soon as possible.
Afik had previously defended the original result and said there was insufficient evidence that MKs had been instructed to document their votes. Since the court issued its final judgment, however, she has consistently maintained that it must be implemented.
If the repeat vote is held by the outgoing Knesset, it would complete the second-round contest between Rabello and Elron.
If the process is postponed until the next Knesset, a further legal question will arise over whether lawmakers can simply repeat the second round or must begin the election process again, Afik said.

Kalaniyot faculty network strengthens campus ties to Israeli scholars, fights academic boycotts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:58:40 UTC
02:58:40 KST

Dr. Yossi Sheffi has been a defining fixture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). Serving as the director of the Center for Transportation and Logistics, the engineering professor has managed multi-million-dollar research portfolios, authored foundational texts, and launched a steady stream of successful technology startups.
"I am the number one influencer in my field in the world," Sheffi noted, reflecting on a career in which his name alone sold books and his global influence was well established. By all conventional standards, his place within the elite institution was secure and celebrated.
"And then on October 7 everything changed," Sheffi recalled. Describing himself as "what you might call an October 8 Jew," he admitted that prior to the Hamas attacks, while he knew antisemitism existed, he never expected to encounter it himself. In the wake of the atrocities committed in Israel, MIT, like many elite North American universities, was swept up in an unprecedented wave of intense agitation and rising hostility.
Describing the collapse of institutional norms, Sheffi noted that "law and order disintegrated" at MIT, as a wave of antisemitism and anti-Zionism swept the campus and transformed corridors that once resonated with scholarly debate into environments of intimidation where classes were disrupted, research laboratories were targeted with graffiti, and Jewish and Israeli students and faculty members faced open vitriol.
Jewish, Israeli students, faculty targeted by pro-Palestine students
Recalling the nature of the campus demonstrations, Sheffi pointed to the hostile rhetoric of the student protesters, shouting slogans "from the river to the sea" without knowing which river or sea they meant. He noted that these agitators immediately began shouting "Kill the Jews" and demanding that "Palestine should be free," alongside what he described as "the big lie, the genocide," adding that they "started screaming about genocide and writing about genocide."
Sheffi explained that he started with helping Jewish students who were "completely traumatized." He noted that these students were "shunted from study groups," attacked, vilified, and "threatened with bodily harm." The atmosphere of fear became so acute that students started walking with pepper spray and constantly looking behind their backs.
Sheffi also highlighted specific incidents of intimidation targeting faculty, recalling how one Israeli faculty member had pictures of the hostages put up right inside her office, only for hostile supporters to enter the workspace, threaten her, and strip everything off the walls, while the department allegedly told neighbors and victims never to call campus police again.
The hostile climate led to departures from the institution. Sheffi pointed out that about 12 students left MIT without finishing their studies due to the unbearable environment, alongside professors who were also driven out by antisemitism.
Expressing profound shock regarding the fallout of the high-profile congressional hearings in late 2023, where university leaders were questioned by the House Committee on Education and the Workforce regarding surging campus antisemitism and their failures to protect Jewish students, Sheffi underscored the stark double standard.
He noted with disbelief how university presidents at Penn and Harvard lost their jobs after evasive, legalistic exchanges regarding whether calling for the genocide of Jews violated campus codes of conduct, yet MIT's leadership managed to evade similar accountability.
Expressing deep frustration, Sheffi emphasized: "Unlike Penn and Harvard, where the presidents had to step down after failing to give straight answers to Elise Stefanik’s questions, at MIT there was no investigation into antisemitism whatsoever; they completely managed to dodge any formal inquiry or institutional reckoning."
For Sheffi, the administrative response was the ultimate breaking point. "That was one of the most shameful things that got me over the edge," Sheffi stated, pointing directly to "the response of the administration."
Rather than protecting vulnerable scholars, administrators routinely downplayed the hostility, offering empty bureaucratic pronouncements while avoiding decisive disciplinary action against disruptors. Reflecting on the institutional response, Sheffi noted that the administration was "still trying to shove it under the carpet."
Sheffi documents MIT antisemitism in Unsafe at MIT: A Chronicle of a Campus War on the Jews
Determined to ensure that these incidents were permanently recorded rather than swept aside, Sheffi channeled his investigative background into writing Unsafe at MIT: A Chronicle of a Campus War on the Jews. Drawing on extensive interviews with dozens of students, postdocs, and professors, the book serves as a rigorous historical ledger of institutional failure.
To ensure the text was bulletproof against potential legal challenges and bad-faith denials, Sheffi subjected the manuscript to strict pre-publication legal vetting. Sheffi entirely self-funded the book, and the university made it clear it would not fund any promotion or distribution of the work.
Amid the isolation felt by Jewish students at MIT, Sheffi fostered a vital support system by creating and building a community through the MIT Israel Alliance. What began quietly as informal, bi-weekly lunch gatherings organized to offer safe spaces for shaken students soon transformed into a robust, proactive initiative that provided peer support, shared resources, and a united front against campus hostility.
Realizing that isolated student support was only part of the solution, the network expanded into a new initiative called Kalaniyot.
Named after the Hebrew word for anemone flowers - regarded as Israel's national flower, which mark the rejuvenation of Israel's southern deserts following winter rains - Kalaniyot evolved into a constructive counter-infrastructure designed to directly strengthen institutional ties with Israeli researchers. Bypassing institutional inertia, the initiative successfully secured independent funding from private donors who refused to watch academic centers capitulate to radical elements.
At its core, Kalaniyot focuses on bringing top-tier Israeli scientists, postdoctoral fellows, and visiting researchers to universities across the continent on one- or two-year fellowships in order to counter academic boycotts. By pairing them with sympathetic local faculty mentors, the network establishes a secure pipeline for professional collaboration, mentorship, and financial protection that deepens binational academic ties and keeps high-level scientific cooperation thriving.
Kalaniyot spreading to other major educational institutions
"Kalaniyot was the response to the BDS," Sheffi explained. "And it's going very well. It's now in several universities and growing, bringing Israeli scientists and creating science collaboration with Israeli engineers and scientists."
Sheffi emphasized that a major success of Kalaniyot is its growth into a national organization that began at MIT and has since expanded, with formal chapters established at other major institutions, including Harvard, Dartmouth, Penn, Columbia, USC, and Cornell.
Looking ahead, Sheffi shared that the ultimate big dream for Kalaniyot is to scale this infrastructure into a permanent, nationwide network embedded across every major research university in North America, ensuring that Israeli academics always have a secure, well-funded home abroad regardless of shifting political tides or administrative hostility.
For Sheffi and the leaders driving Kalaniyot, the overarching lesson is clear: when institutional leadership falters and university bureaucracy turns a blind eye, the only path forward is to take matters into your own hands, standing up for academic excellence, refusing to wait for permission, and building lasting, constructive safeguards that ensure Israeli scholarship continues to thrive globally.

Iranian commanders warn any new war would trigger wider regional conflict
TEHRAN- Iranian military commanders have issued a series of increasingly forceful warnings against any renewed US or Israeli military action, saying the Islamic Republic is fully prepared to respond and cautioning regional states against allowing their territory or military facilities to be used in a new conflict.
The warnings, delivered separately by Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei, Chief of Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces Major General Ali Abdollahi, Army Commander Major General Amir Hatami and Brigadier General Ali Fadavi, head of the advisory group to the commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), underscore Tehran’s stated policy of treating any renewed attack as a broader regional security crisis rather than a conflict confined to Iranian territory.
In a message issued Monday, Abdollahi said reports suggesting that the United States and Israel could be preparing for another war against Iran appeared to be linked to renewed allegations concerning Iran’s nuclear program.
He said the Iranian people would not submit to pressure or accept attempts to impose another war on the country, stressing that the Armed Forces remain prepared to confront threats at any level.
Abdollahi warned that another Israeli attack would carry consequences for the entire region, saying the Israeli regime had already experienced the consequences of previous confrontations with Iran and would face a powerful response if it made another “miscalculation.”
 
“We are confident that the vicious Zionist regime has neither now nor at any other time had, or will have, the ability to confront a powerful Iran,” he said.
Warning to Washington
The senior Iranian commander also delivered a direct warning to Washington, saying Iran would respond to any US military action without restrictions, regardless of when such action might occur.
“If the US, itself or at the instigation of the child-killing Zionist regime, takes action against the Islamic Republic of Iran, the Iranian Armed Forces will immediately and forcefully target US interests without limitation in a painful manner,” Abdollahi warned.
His reference to the US congressional elections appeared intended to underline that Tehran considers its response to any military action independent of the US domestic political calendar.
Abdollahi also addressed countries in the region that host US military forces, warning them against allowing their territories to become launch points for attacks on Iran.
He argued that the continued deployment of American forces in the region is itself a source of insecurity and economic pressure, and cautioned regional governments that a new conflict would not necessarily remain limited to the territory of the parties directly involved.
“Be aware that if a new war against Iran begins, its flames will engulf everyone,” he said.
Iran rejects nuclear allegations
Abdollahi further rejected Israeli allegations that Iran’s nuclear program had entered a military phase, describing such claims as part of an effort to portray the Islamic Republic as a threat.
He questioned the credibility of such accusations when made by Israel, which possesses a substantial nuclear arsenal while not being a party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT).
The commander also warned international organizations, particularly the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), against issuing ‘unfounded statements concerning Iran’s nuclear facilities.’
He concluded by saying Iran was “stronger than ever” and prepared to confront any threat, while expressing confidence in God help.
Mohsen Rezaei has also warned that any further miscalculation by Iran’s adversaries would lead to new fronts and larger surprises.
“Every miscalculation by the enemy against Iran has resulted in a heavy defeat for it,” Rezaei wrote on social media platform X on Monday. “The next mistake will open new fronts and bring bigger surprises.”
Rezaei said Iran would overcome the current complex circumstances with the wise leadership of Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, national unity and coordination among state institutions.
Army chief: war has not ended
Separately, Army Commander Major General Amir Hatami said the confrontation with Iran had not ended and that the Armed Forces would maintain their readiness to deliver a “crushing response” to any renewed threat.
Addressing commanders of Army units in Fars Province, Hatami said the failure of the enemy to achieve its objectives through military means had led it to pursue other forms of pressure, including economic sanctions, efforts to put the Iranian population under economic strain, and attempts to create insecurity and unrest.
He stressed that Iran’s Armed Forces would maintain a high level of vigilance and respond decisively should the enemy make another mistake.
Hatami also called for the opportunities created by the recent US-Israeli-imposed wars to be used to consolidate Iran’s strategic gains and prevent the recurrence of war, emphasizing the importance of continued resilience and perseverance.
“War is an arena of resilience,” the Army chief said, arguing that the side capable of demonstrating greater endurance would ultimately prevail.
He said Iran, as the defending side, possessed significant resilience both among its population and within its Armed Forces.
IRGC general warns regional states
Ali Fadavi, meanwhile, issued one of the most explicit warnings to regional countries hosting US forces, saying any location used to launch an attack against Iran would be considered a legitimate target.
Speaking in a televised interview, he said Iran had already communicated its red lines to regional governments.
Fadavi stressed that Iran had not targeted regional countries themselves, but had struck US military bases located on their territory, arguing that Tehran regards American military facilities abroad as extensions of US territory when they are used in operations against Iran.
“We have declared our red line to the countries of the region,” Fadavi said. “Any point from which an action against Iran originates will be targeted.”
He said the southern Persian Gulf states host some US military installations and warned that if attacks against Iran were launched from those facilities, they would be subject to retaliation.
His remarks reflect Tehran’s long-standing warning that regional countries could avoid becoming parties to a confrontation by preventing their territory and military infrastructure from being used for offensive operations against Iran.
Hormuz and the US military presence
Fadavi also linked the warnings to the strategic importance of the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, saying the waterway had remained firmly under Iran’s control in recent months.
He stated that, despite the longstanding US military presence in the Persian Gulf, American forces had moved significantly farther from Iran’s shores and that no US vessel was currently present in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf of Oman or even the northern Indian Ocean.
“The Americans have fled and moved more than 1,000 kilometers away from our borders,” Fadavi said, attributing the repositioning to the military power of Iran and the IRGC Navy rather than a voluntary US decision.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a substantial share of global seaborne oil and LNG trade normally passes, has remained central to the wider security equation surrounding Iran and the Persian Gulf. Any major military confrontation in or around the waterway would therefore carry consequences well beyond the immediate parties, potentially affecting energy markets, shipping insurance, maritime security and regional trade.
Taken together, the statements by Abdollahi, Hatami and Fadavi present a consistent message from Iran’s military establishment: Tehran says it does not seek a new war, but regards itself as prepared for one and would respond directly to any renewed attack. The commanders’ warnings also make clear that, in Tehran’s assessment, the geography of a future conflict would not necessarily be confined to Iran and Israel or Iran and the United States, but could extend to military facilities and strategic infrastructure across the wider region if they were used against the Islamic Republic.

The Insider confirms Russia ties of UK businessman involved in VexPay project, promoted by A7 “shadow banking” network to evade sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:58:08 UTC
02:58:08 KST

British payments specialist Michael Donald, a former board member of Visa UK, appears in documents related to VexPay, a Kyrgyz payment platform that the Kremlin-linked A7 shadow banking network has promoted as an alternative to SWIFT. According to meeting minutes from inside A7 reviewed by the Financial Times, in 2025 fugitive Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor named Donald as VexPay’s chief executive. Donald denies ever working for the company or agreeing to run it.
The Insider found that Donald and his business had ties to Russia well before the VexPay episode. In 2020, ImageNPay, a company founded founded by Donald, identified Russia and other former Soviet states as key markets and used Russian programmers while attempting to enter the Russian market via the Skolkovo Innovation Center outside Moscow.
A man named Dmitry Kuptsov also held a 27.2% stake in the British company ImageNPay. A businessman with the same name, described by Bloomberg as an Irish passport holder born in Russia, appeared in luxury real estate deals in Monaco and was also connected to ImageNPay’s circle through another Monaco company.
A7 is a Russian payment network created by Shor in cooperation with Russian state-owned Promsvyazbank, which serves Russia’s defense sector. The network’s purpose is to process international payments for Russian companies amid sanctions and restricted access to the Western financial system. As the Financial Times previously reported, from late 2024 through August 2025 the network moved more than $6.9 billion through international banks using hundreds of intermediary companies — and, according to the FT, ran an “industrial-scale forgery operation.”
On Oct. 1, the U.S. Treasury Department designated A7 as a “significant transnational criminal organization.” U.S. authorities say the network disguises payments linked to sanctioned entities as ordinary trade transactions and uses companies in third countries to gain access to the global financial system. According to the Treasury Department, A7 intermediaries processed more than $17 billion from January 2025 through June 2026.
Shor named Michael Donald as the head of VexPay – which he denies
The new documents obtained by the FT date from the period March to August 2025. They indicate that A7 representatives took part in developing VexPay in Kyrgyzstan. The project was pitched to local officials as an alternative international payment channel that would allow transactions to be processed outside the conventional SWIFT system.
According to meeting minutes, Shor introduced VexPay’s new management at an Aug. 12 meeting in Moscow and named Michael Donald as one of the platform’s executives. Donald confirmed to the FT that he attended the Moscow meeting but said he was never an employee or director of VexPay and never agreed to take the position. He said he was only advising Kyrgyz state company Processing KG on international payments, card acceptance, Apple Pay, and relations with Visa. Donald also says he has never met or spoken with Shor.
His statements contrast with the meeting minutes described by the FT, in which Shor is said to have introduced Donald to other participants as a VexPay executive. The document’s description alone, however, does not prove that Donald accepted the position or took part in any illegal activity.
Formally, VexPay is linked to Kyrgyz state company Processing KG, not A7, and the Kyrgyz side denies that the company is under outside control. The leaked documents outlined by the FT, however, show that Shor and A7 employees took part in discussions about the project’s structure, accounts, staffing, and technical setup.
The Insider finds Donald’s earlier ties to Russia and Skolkovo
Using open sources, The Insider found that as early as 2020 — five years before the meeting in Moscow, Michael Donald was actively seeking opportunities to expand his payments business in Russia. In June 2020, the official Skolkovo website published an interview with Donald in which he said ImageNPay viewed Russia and the CIS countries as key markets for the coming years and was already using a team of Russian programmers. Donald described Russia as a major fintech market and praised Russian payments developers.
ImageNPay took part in Skolkovo’s Soft-Landing program, a two-week course for foreign companies seeking to enter the Russian market. The next step could have been obtaining Skolkovo resident status, which can provide tax breaks and access to grants. In the interview, Donald called Skolkovo an excellent place for a foreign company seeking to enter the Russian market.
Donald’s ties to Russia went back even further. His public LinkedIn profile lists Moscow among his work locations and Russian among the languages he speaks. One recommendation posted on the social network says he helped arrange business contacts and distribution in Russia, including helping establish relationships with the Ritz-Carlton and Grand Havana Club in Moscow.
ImageNPay’s shareholder was born in Russia and appeared in Monaco luxury real estate deals
The Insider found that ImageNPay’s Russia ties went beyond its attempt to enter the market through Skolkovo. Corporate filings for Britain’s ImageNPay UK Limited from 2020 list Dmitry Kuptsov as a shareholder.
A document filed with Companies House on July 1, 2020, shows that after 250 ordinary shares were transferred from Switzerland’s ImageNPay AG, they were divided among four owners. Michael Donald received 127 shares, Dmitry Kuptsov 68, Mark Schlittler 42 and Xupery Limited 13. Kuptsov controlled 27.2% of ImageNPay UK, making him the second-largest shareholder after Donald, who held 50.8%.
A businessman with the same name previously appeared in a Bloomberg investigation into Monaco’s luxury real estate market. In April 2026, the outlet cited leaked emails and documents from the Mareterra development project while reporting on two little-known aviation executives: Dmitry Kuptsov and Konstantin Krivchenko. Bloomberg said both were born in Russia but hold Irish passports.
According to Bloomberg, in 2017 Kuptsov and Krivchenko planned to buy four villas in the Mareterra luxury development for 100 million euros each. Special-purpose companies were created for the purchases and were approved by Monaco authorities in late 2017. The buyers later missed payments on some of the properties and eventually scaled back their plans to a single villa of about 2,300 square meters — still replete with a hammam, sauna, movie theater, massage rooms, and a wine-tasting room. A representative for the businessmen declined to comment to Bloomberg at the time.
Bloomberg’s investigation focused on the origins of money in Monaco’s ultra-luxury property market. The outlet reviewed documents from the Mareterra project, including correspondence among the developer, notaries, banks, and prospective buyers. Bloomberg separately stressed that publication of the documents did not mean the people named in them had committed any wrongdoing.
Kuptsov’s connection to ImageNPay’s circle can also be traced through another company in Monaco corporate records. In September 2018, Dmitry Kuptsov was appointed manager of Monaco-registered FM-CRAFT, according to the official Journal de Monaco. He replaced Konstantin Krivchenko, the same person who appeared with Kuptsov in Bloomberg’s real estate investigation. The document lists Kuptsov’s Monaco address as 54 Boulevard du Jardin Exotique.
FM-CRAFT was engaged in the design, purchase, sale, import, export, and rental of pleasure yachts and related equipment. Kuptsov stepped down as manager in April 2022 and was replaced by Maria Christova Mundt.
By then, Mundt was already connected to Donald’s business. Companies House records show that she became a director of ImageNPay UK on Sept. 1, 2021, and she remains in the role. The British registry lists her address as 27 Boulevard de Belgique in Monaco, the same address that appears in the official notice of her appointment as FM-CRAFT manager. In August 2024, FM-CRAFT’s owners decided to dissolve the company early and appointed Mundt as liquidator.
Taken together, the documents show several points of overlap: Dmitry Kuptsov owned more than a quarter of Britain’s ImageNPay, a person with the same name managed FM-CRAFT in Monaco, and he was later replaced in that role by current ImageNPay director Maria Kristova Mundt.
The Insider, however, was unable to find a document bearing a unique identifier directly linking ImageNPay shareholder Dmitry Kuptsov to the person of the same name who is associated with FM-CRAFT and the Bloomberg investigation.

The Republic of Türkiye, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan convened an emergency meeting of the Strategic-Political and Defense Committee of the Makkah Alliance for Defense in Riyadh on 5 October 2026 to address the security developments and threats facing the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
As part of the institutional development of the Makkah Alliance for Defense, the Committee decided to appoint His Excellency Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood (Ret.) of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan as the first Secretary-General for a three-year term. The Parties welcomed His Excellency, wished him every success in the discharge of his duties, and expressed their confidence in his contribution to advancing the Alliance and achieving its objectives.
The Parties also condemned in the strongest terms the attempted targeting of Makkah and Madinah, as well as the continuing attacks targeting cities and civilian and economic facilities in the Kingdom, reaffirming their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the Kingdom’s security and territorial integrity.
The Republic of Türkiye and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan commended the vigilance and readiness of the Saudi Armed Forces, as well as the professionalism and high level of competence they have demonstrated in countering the threats and attacks facing the Kingdom and in safeguarding its security and territorial integrity.
The Committee reviewed the outcomes of the political and military consultations preceding the meeting and approved the recommendations submitted to it, affirming that the Makkah Alliance for Defense embodies a firm commitment to collective defense and a unified position in confronting threats.
The Committee decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the Parties, thereby enhancing readiness, military integration, and the collective capacity to confront and counter threats.
The Parties affirmed that the security of each Party is an integral part of the collective security of the three countries, and that translating the Makkah Agreement for Joint Defense into practical measures demonstrates the credibility of the commitment to collective defense, strengthens the effectiveness of deterrence, and reaffirms the unity and determination of our three countries to defend their security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, in accordance with the provisions of the Agreement.

German air travelers favor Istanbul over Frankfurt on flights to Asia, Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:56:50 UTC
02:56:50 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Travelers flying between Germany and Asia are increasingly choosing Istanbul and Gulf airports over Frankfurt and Munich, driven by higher European climate charges and rising German aviation costs, a report released Monday found.
“Air travelers generally have a wide range of options on which airline to take to a long-haul destination,” said the report by German aviation organizations, adding that Istanbul, Doha, and Dubai are increasingly preferred as their fares are lower and their connections are wider.
Transfers through non-EU hubs rose to 54% of all passenger traffic from Germany to the Far East and Southeast Asia in 2024, according to the joint study by the Federal Association of German Aviation Industry (BDL) and the German Aerospace Center (DLR). Those figures were up from 43.8% in 2019 and 33.7% in 2010.
Connecting traffic through airports in Türkiye and the Gulf saw the sharpest gains, more than doubling from 12.6% in 2010 to 28.2% in 2024. Over the same period, direct flights from Germany and transfers through domestic hubs combined tumbled from 56% to 36%.
The report singled out Turkish Airlines and Istanbul’s new mega-airport, alongside the Gulf’s leading hubs—Dubai and Doha —as key drivers of the shift. Beyond offering lower fares, these hubs often streamline travel itineraries—allowing passengers to reach destinations as far as Australia with a single layover, compared to two connections when flying via Western Europe. 
Germany's hub status at risk
Rising climate charges, higher government taxes, and mounting operating fees have steadily inflated ticket prices for flights originating in Western Europe. Facing broad carrier choices—such as flying Lufthansa via Frankfurt, Turkish Airlines via Istanbul, or Emirates via Dubai—price-sensitive travelers are routinely opting for more affordable non-EU options, according to the report.
The same shift was not limited to flights toward Asia and also showed up on routes between Germany and Africa, where, excluding Mediterranean states, transfers through Türkiye and the Gulf climbed from 11% in 2010 to 23.4% in 2019 and 32% in 2024.
The report also said Germany’s position as a leading air-freight hub was at risk, because more cargo bound for the country is being handled at airports abroad. “Frankfurt Airport, for instance, has lost its top spot in Europe to Istanbul Airport,” it said.
BDL Chief Executive Joachim Lang warned that Germany is slowly disconnecting from international air networks as passengers and cargo are shifting to hubs outside western Europe.
“For an exporting nation, this poses a serious challenge to its competitiveness as a business location,” he said. “Moreover, nothing is gained for the climate if emissions are merely shifted elsewhere. We need lower location costs and a level playing field on climate protection regulations so that the same conditions apply to all competitors.”

Conservative plans to slash aid budget would ‘irreparably damage’ UK’s global credibility, charities say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:56:47 UTC
02:56:47 KST

Conservative plans to slash the aid budget by 90% would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank and “irreparably damage” Britain’s global credibility, several organisations and charities have told the Guardian.
In a series of announcements at the Tory party conference in Birmingham, Kemi Badenoch said that as prime minister she would reduce the aid budget from £9bn a year to £1bn, to part-fund 50,000 new prison places in England and Wales. The culture budget would also be slashed by £1bn a year to fund the plans.
Overseas aid has been targeted by all political parties in recent years. Keir Starmer’s government reduced aid from 0.5% of GDP to 0.3% by 2027, and last year Nigel Farage announced that Reform UK would cap overseas aid at £1bn a year, or about 0.03% of GDP.
But those with knowledge of the UK’s commitments to global institutions such as the World Bank and the UN, suggested Badenoch’s plan to follow Farage’s policy was impractical, and one source described the move as “posturing”.
One source said that about 70% of the budget proposed by the the Conservatives would be swallowed up by funding the work done by British diplomats around the world. “I think any party in government would soon realise that £1bn is not enough to cover the very basics and would not be possible,” said one. “This feels both a morally questionable policy and disingenuous one.”
Multilateral overseas aid totalled £2.8bn in 2024, the most recent year for which complete figures are available. Existing commitments to the UN, the World Bank’s International Development Association, the Gavi vaccine alliance and the Global Fund to Fight Aids, Tuberculosis and Malaria total more than £1.6bn a year.
Cutting those immediately would be almost impossible, sources suggested, as most settlements are agreed in advance and cover several years. Even if the total could be brought down to £1bn, there would be no funding left to respond to new natural disasters such as devastating glacial floods in Nepal or the outbreak of new pandemics.
Gideon Rabinowitz, the director of policy at Bond, the umbrella group for development NGOs, said a £1bn limit would amount to the UK “shooting itself in the foot” and renouncing its position on the global stage.
“We currently have a front-row seat and can influence global policy thanks to our contributions and engagement with global bodies like the World Bank and the United Nations. We can’t do that without paying our dues,” he said.
“The number of extreme natural disasters is multiplying. If we cannot play our role in responding to those disasters on the international scale, then we are likely to find that displacement of people will grow, creating challenges for neighbouring regions and the UK.
“This decision would irreparably damage the UK’s reputation and credibility, leaving us more isolated at a moment where cooperation is more important than ever.”
Monica Harding, the Liberal Democrats’ international development spokesperson, accused the Conservatives of forcing the world’s poorest people to pay for prison places. “Britain should look to lead on the world stage, not retreat from it,” she said. “This is a desperate move from a Tory leader more concerned about chasing Reform voters than acting in Britain’s long-term interest. It would diminish Britain – it is un-British, unpatriotic, and unwise.”

Trump points to Ukraine strikes, US refinery closures as gas prices rise, not war on Iran

17:55:22 UTC

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure and refinery closures in Democratic-led US states are contributing to higher gasoline prices, as fuel costs remain elevated across the country.
“What’s driving up gasoline is no longer the Strait of Hormuz, because record numbers of barrels are coming out now on an almost daily basis,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
He said higher prices were being driven in part by Russian facilities “being blown up by Ukraine” and US refineries being closed in states such as California.
The comments come after Trump previously urged Kiev to avoid attacks on Russian petroleum facilities.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has meanwhile said Ukraine plans to intensify strikes on Russian oil refineries as part of its response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian military-industrial and infrastructure targets.
Gas prices remain well above last year
The national average for regular gasoline stood at about $4.37 per gallon Monday, according to AAA, compared with $4.15 a month ago and $3.13 a year earlier. Prices have eased from a recent peak but remain historically high for this time of year.
Global supply disruptions have continued to weigh on energy markets.
Russia has extended a temporary ban on exports of diesel and other fuel products by direct producers through October 31, while Ukrainian attacks have disrupted parts of Russia’s refining capacity.
The broader energy picture also includes continued volatility linked to the Middle East and the Strait of Hormuz, although oil shipments through the route have been recovering.
G7 moves to boost oil supplies
G7 leaders agreed Friday to begin a coordinated release of 100 million barrels from emergency oil reserves over four months, seeking to ease pressure on global energy markets and reduce volatility.
With fuel prices becoming an increasingly prominent economic issue ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections, the administration and lawmakers face pressure to contain costs for motorists and businesses.
Trump has continued to emphasise supply disruptions and energy-market conditions as key factors behind higher prices, while policymakers pursue measures aimed at improving fuel availability and easing pressure at the pump.

UK threatens to expel Israeli diplomats over planned East Jerusalem consulate closure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:53:46 UTC
02:53:46 KST

The UK has threatened to expel one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat forced to leave Israel as a result of Israel’s decision to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem later this week.
This could mean as many as 27 Israeli diplomats being expelled from the UK, a step that would arguably mark the lowest point in British-Israeli diplomatic relations since the formation of the state of Israel.
The mass expulsion threat – more reminiscent of British-Russian diplomatic relations – was first reported by the Israeli newspaper Ynet, citing a message sent to Israeli officials. The UK Foreign Office said it would not comment on speculation, rather than denying the report outright.
Israel has threatened to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem in protest at the UK decision to ban trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and to impose sanctions on British firms that aid, support or facilitate the construction of further illegal settlements.
The Foreign Office has been advised informally by the former UK attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel is acting unlawfully if it closes the consulate on the basis it is sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.
Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, has said that Britain’s decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused Britain’s ruling Labour party of being hostile towards the country.
The consulate, which Israel’s foreign ministry has said will close on Thursday, is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza. It is located in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East Jerusalem.
An Israeli diplomatic source said: “There is no reason for us to respond to speculation about decisions that other countries may or may not take in the future.
“We have already demonstrated that any step taken against Israel will be met with an appropriate response, and that will continue to be the case.”
The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Jerusalem last week in an effort to persuade the Israeli government to rescind or defer the closure of the consulate but the talks failed.
It has been reported that Powell opposed the decision of the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, to press ahead with the settlement trade ban decision, fearing that it might play to the advantage of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, in the national election on 27 October as he seeks to bolster his case that only his brand of leadership can bring Israel security. There is no evidence yet that the UK decision has featured in the campaign, but tit-for-tat expulsions of diplomats may raise its profile.
The incident highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this.
Diplomats from other western countries have been very worried about the closure setting a precedent, and suggest that Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it has implications beyond the immediate dispute.
Shutting down the consulate involves Israel claiming authority in Jerusalem that it does not have under international law, so it is effectively a challenge to the status quo.
“We are all concerned because if this (closure of the consulate) goes ahead it would be an incredibly damaging precedent for the status of missions in Jerusalem, which are monitoring the status quo,” said one western diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity.
“It would be inconceivable for the British government to accept (the closure) because they don’t recognise the authority of the Israeli government over Jerusalem under international law. Particularly as Israel is taking this step over British measures which are simply applying international law.”
Israel has also said it is to revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine, in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza means diplomats need Israeli accreditation to operate in Palestine. The decision also in effect bars them from Israel-controlled East Jerusalem.
France and Canada, which also joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.
Miliband received a very warm reception at the UK Labour party conference last week during a speech in which he highlighted his decision to get tough with Israel over illegal settlements.
UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza begun by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis as the UK became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the death of thousands of Palestinians in a bid to render Hamas inoperative, a task both the Conservative and Labour governments thought was unachievable through his methods.
The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel as a result and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds that he believes this is a matter for international courts alone to determine.

Meet Kyiv’s New Jet-Drone Killer—12+ Sky Sentinel Turrets Are Already on the Hunt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:53:04 UTC
02:53:04 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Meet Kyiv’s New Jet-Drone Killer—12+ Sky Sentinel Turrets Are Already on the Hunt
Russia’s attempt to outrun Ukraine’s air defenses with faster jet-powered attack drones is now facing a different kind of threat over Kyiv—an AI-guided gun system that does not need to chase its target to shoot it down.
More than 12 automated .50-caliber turrets deployed across Kyiv to counter Russia’s jet-powered attack drones are Ukrainian-made Sky Sentinel systems, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat confirmed in an exclusive comment to UNITED24 Media.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“These are Sky Sentinel systems. They are already on combat duty and are being used to counter Russian attack drones,” Ihnat told UNITED24 Media. “The systems have already demonstrated results in combat. There are confirmed cases of them successfully engaging and shooting down jet-powered UAVs,” he added.
Ihnat’s confirmation comes after he revealed earlier on October 5 that the automated turrets had already intercepted Russia’s Geran-5 jet-powered drone.
“There have already been shootdowns of even jet-powered UAVs, even the Geran-5, using those same turrets,” Ihnat said during Ukraine’s national telethon.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy first revealed the deployment a day earlier, saying that more than 12 automated “fifties” had already been installed in Kyiv, with another eight set to be deployed across the Kyiv region.
Sky Sentinel is a Ukrainian-developed automated anti-drone turret that uses machine vision and artificial intelligence to detect, track, and engage aerial targets.
The system combines a heavy machine gun with an automated fire-control module. Once a target is acquired, its optics track the drone while onboard software calculates its speed, trajectory, distance, and the lead required for an interception.
Unlike an interceptor drone, Sky Sentinel does not need to chase its target. It calculates where the UAV will be and fires toward that point, allowing it to engage fast-moving aircraft within its firing envelope.
Previously published specifications indicate that Sky Sentinel can engage aerial targets traveling at speeds of up to around 800 kilometers per hour, placing Russia’s jet-powered attack drones within its theoretical capability.
The Geran-5, now increasingly used by Russian forces, flies substantially faster than conventional propeller-driven Shahed-type drones. Its vulnerability to Sky Sentinel, however, depends on altitude and range.
At higher altitudes, a jet-powered drone may remain beyond the reach of heavy machine-gun fire. But as it descends toward a target or operates at lower altitude, it can enter the turret’s engagement zone.
At that point, the key factor is no longer whether a weapon can catch the drone, but whether it can track it and calculate a firing solution quickly enough. Sky Sentinel’s machine vision continuously follows the target while its software determines the interception point in real time.
The system had already seen combat before its deployment around Kyiv.
UNITED24 raised approximately $3.3 million for 22 Sky Sentinel systems. In August, five were delivered to Ukraine’s 636th Separate Anti-Aircraft Machine Gun Battalion operating in the Sumy region to strengthen defenses against Russian attack drones.
The system had already demonstrated combat effectiveness during earlier deployments, with a Sky Sentinel prototype reportedly destroying multiple Russian Shahed-type drones.
Sky Sentinel is designed as a relatively inexpensive final layer of air defense around critical infrastructure, bridges, military positions, and other high-value sites.

World War III and the diplomatic track
Ham-Mihan analyzed growing speculation about a possible Third World War and the diplomatic options available to the parties involved. Political discussions have recently been dominated by concerns over whether another conflict is becoming unavoidable.
Several developments have intensified these fears, including the deployment of a third US aircraft carrier group to the CENTCOM region, meetings involving American, Israeli, and Arab military commanders, Netanyahu's visit to Abu Dhabi, and Trump’s increasingly aggressive rhetoric. Despite these signs of escalation, war cannot yet be considered inevitable. Diplomatic channels remain open, and proposals have reportedly been exchanged between the two sides. However, Trump may be less willing to return to earlier diplomatic arrangements, particularly after criticism within the United States and developments in the Strait of Hormuz. Following claims that the United States helped restore navigation through the strait, Trump may now seek greater concessions from Iran, especially regarding its nuclear program, while offering limited benefits in return. The paper concludes that although military tensions are rising, opportunities for diplomacy still exist.
Siasat-e-Rooz: US will have no choice but to leave
Siasat-e-Rooz focused on the USS Roosevelt aircraft carrier which is heading toward the Arabian Sea. It argued that although American officials continue to speak about military options and highlight the carrier’s presence in West Asia, recent developments show that economic and political tools have become more important than military threats. The newspaper pointed to Trump’s economic promises and discussions surrounding international energy negotiations as evidence that military pressure has lost much of its effectiveness. Whether the Roosevelt was sent for military purposes or merely as a display of power makes little difference. The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz depends on meeting Iran’s conditions. Any military miscalculation would trigger a stronger and faster response than previous confrontations. Iran is the key actor shaping regional developments, and the United States will eventually be forced to reduce its presence and withdraw from the region. From this perspective, military deployments are largely symbolic and cannot fundamentally alter regional realities.
Hamshahri: The new reality of Hormuz
In a commentary, Hamshahri discussed the transit of an Iraqi oil tanker carrying two million barrels of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz. While some observers viewed the event as evidence that the waterway had reopened, the newspaper argued that this interpretation is inaccurate. According to the article, there is a significant difference between a strait being physically open and functioning normally for commercial traffic. Although ships can still pass through Hormuz and the route has not been blocked, normal shipping conditions have not returned. The Iraqi tanker’s journey is presented not as proof of a fully reopened strait but as an example of a new operational reality. Passage remains possible, yet each voyage entails extensive risk management. Political authorization, security concerns, insurance coverage, transportation costs, cargo destination, and legal responsibility all play central roles in determining whether ships can travel through the waterway. As a result, Hormuz continues to function, but under much more complicated conditions than before.
Sobh-e-No: Iran has entered America’s electoral battle
Sobh-e-No examined comments made by Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader in the US House of Representatives, and the broader political challenges facing Trump. Jeffries accused Republicans of pursuing a costly and reckless confrontation with Iran that has placed increasing pressure on American citizens. According to the newspaper, Trump’s reaction highlights the deep political divisions within Washington and demonstrates how Iran has become an important issue in domestic US politics rather than merely a foreign policy concern. The article argues that Democrats are attempting to present themselves as advocates of peace and stability, while Trump seeks to draw public attention to economic security and political competition at home. Both parties are effectively competing to define which costs matter most to voters: the costs associated with war and inflation or the costs of losing political power. In this sense, Iran has become a key topic in America’s electoral debate.
Donya-e-Eqtesad: A deepening energy crisis
Donya-e Eqtesad examined the energy consequences of the continuing US-Iran conflict. It noted that many observers initially expected the confrontation to be brief and that Trump had predicted a quick resolution. Months later, however, the conflict remains unresolved. The article argues that two critical maritime chokepoints, the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, are no longer operating without restrictions. Strategic reserves have declined, fuel costs have risen, and refining capacity has faced growing pressure. According to the newspaper, the crisis demonstrates that the effects of conflict extend beyond oil prices. Shipping disruptions, reduced exports, difficulties in imports, vulnerabilities in energy infrastructure, and refining constraints have combined to place significant pressure on global markets. The paper warns that a prolonged conflict could further weaken reserves and alternative supply networks, especially if energy facilities become targets, increasing strain on the global economy.

Finnish workers report better work ability as burnout persists
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:50:48 EEST
02:50:48 KST

Finnish workers are reporting stronger work ability than a year ago, but more than a quarter remain at increased risk of burnout, according to new research from the Finnish Institute of Occupational Health.
The institute’s How is Finland doing? study found that 43% of employed people rated their work ability as excellent in summer 2026, up from 39% a year earlier. Researchers examined five areas of work ability, covering physical, cognitive, social, emotional and skills-related demands.
Physical work ability received the strongest results, with 67% of respondents saying they were fully able to meet physical demands such as standing or lifting. Emotional work ability ranked lowest, with 41% saying they could fully handle demands involving other people’s emotions.
“Work ability is more multidimensional than many people think,” research professor Jari Hakanen said. He said an employee might perform well in one area while needing support in another.
Younger workers reported stronger physical and cognitive work ability than older groups. More than half of workers under 30 rated their overall work ability as excellent.
Their results were weaker on other measures of workplace wellbeing.
28% of workers aged 18 to 29 experienced boredom at work daily or several times a week. The rate was 23% among those aged 30 to 45, 15% among 46 to 55-year-olds and 12% among workers aged 56 to 66.
Fewer than half of workers aged 18 to 29 experienced work engagement daily or several times a week, compared with 65% among workers in their 50s and early 60s.
The institute found that younger workers also reported more loneliness and weaker social work ability, which measures their ability to deal with teamwork and informal workplace interaction.
Senior researcher Janne Kaltiainen said the findings should not be viewed only as characteristics of younger employees. Differences in experience, occupations and the social demands of jobs employing younger people also play a role.
Burnout symptoms showed no difference between age groups. Overall, 26% of employed Finns faced an increased risk of burnout or symptoms consistent with burnout. The level remained above that recorded before the Covid-19 pandemic.
Researchers identified bureaucracy and conflicting workplace roles as factors linked to burnout symptoms.
Researcher Jie Li said rigid procedures, poor tools, slow information flows and conflicting expectations add unnecessary demands and reduce the time employees spend on their main work.
Job insecurity, excessive workloads, repetitive tasks and physical demands were also associated with burnout, though the study found weaker links across the working population.
The amount of remote work had no association with workers’ overall assessment of their ability to work.

What if Russia uses nuclear weapons? Can we say Ukraine brought peace to world? Norwegian professor who nominated Zelenskyy and Ukrainians for 2026 Nobel Peace Prize takes on tough questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:48:50 UTC
02:48:50 KST

It is rare to hear a European say "I'm sorry" to the Ukrainians. Dag Øistein Endsjø, who nominated the Ukrainian people and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for the Nobel Peace Prize 2026, shared it several times during our interview.
Mr. Endsjø is a professor of religious studies at the University of Oslo in Norway. He comes across as courteous and reserved. But when he talks about Europe not helping Ukraine as much as it could, his eyes give away deep personal emotion.
"Just thank you for keeping us safe. Thank you for the extreme sacrifice you've been making for all of us. And I'm sorry that my government and the other governments haven't done enough," he said, speaking to me not as a journalist but as one of the Ukrainians.
These words cut through because tens of millions of us live under daily psychological and physical terror, feeling forgotten and betrayed.
At the same time, Professor Endsjø names things as they are, even when it is uncomfortable. When the full-scale invasion began, he says, he doubted Ukraine would hold. And he admits that Norway has profited from the war: by its own Finance Department's calculation, about €106 billion in additional revenue from higher oil and gas prices.
He was honest with us. Our questions were sharp too, even those about US President Donald Trump's chances to win this year's award, and he answered them the way he answers everything: straight.
Do you think people who fight the war can be nominated for a Nobel Peace Prize?
People who defend themselves, yes! Who defends a free and democratic state against unprovoked aggression, yes, I think so.
Many say Ukraine should stop fighting and negotiate. Wouldn't a peace prize reward the war?
It's not a reward for the war, because the war could stop tomorrow if Russia just realized they didn't want to break international rules and pulled out. This is not about continuing the war. On the other hand, the war would stop the moment Ukraine threw out Russia. That, regrettably, seems to take more time.
This is not, in any way, about rewarding or promoting war as such. This is about standing up against war, because not standing up against war has only provoked more war and aggression from Russia.
Russia is attacking free and democratic countries unprovoked. They started in 2008 with Georgia, and then moved on to Ukraine, and as so many others point out, they have their plans.
"Moldova, if Ukraine hadn't been able to resist this invasion, would also have been under Russian rule now for sure. Poland and the Baltics would have been under extreme pressure, maybe also invaded," Mr. Endsjø says.
If there was a moment when you thought that Ukraine might lose the war?
Yes, in the beginning, when I saw those lines of tanks heading for Kyiv, I was afraid that everything was lost. Also noting the lackluster reaction from the free world and how they only came with condemnations and no ammunition, just a flight out.
If Ukraine is defending peace, why is the war getting closer to Europe's borders?
That is because of Russia. If Ukraine hadn't defended itself and just given up, the war would have been even closer to Europe. We would be even more under threat with probably even more degrees of sabotage and terrorist attacks around in Europe.
Does Ukrainian resistance escalate the risk of direct war between NATO and Russia?
No. The other way around. If Ukraine had given up, it would have been a more direct threat to NATO countries.
But some politicians say that in this case, Russia will just negotiate and sell energy as it did in the past
Yes, while sabotaging and even murdering people around in Europe, and acting like a state of terrorism. So, no, it would remain aggressive. You can listen to various prominent Russians on Russian TV. You know, you're not allowed to say anything on Russian TV unless the government approves it...
People are again and again threatening Finland, Poland, Britain, and the Baltic. Just as they made up these fake republics in Luhansk and Donetsk in 2014, they have tried to do the same in Estonia and Latvia already.
So if it hadn't been for Ukraine and Ukraine's resistance, the risk of direct war between NATO and Russia would have been even greater. Because Ukraine keeps Russia at bay.
If Ukraine agrees to a ceasefire, will you consider this a failure or a victory?
I, as a non-Ukrainian but fellow European, like any other European, have no right whatsoever to tell the Ukrainians what to do.
If the Ukrainians themselves find that this most horrible war is too much, and you want a ceasefire and you want to stop, and it's not for me to criticize. It's not for any European to criticize. We cannot tell the Ukrainians what to do after that horrible sacrifice you've made already.
I only hope that Europe and the rest of the free world will assist Ukraine even more, so that you will be even more successful in throwing out the Russian occupation army of the entire of Ukraine, including Crimea.
What if Russia uses nuclear weapons? Can we say that Ukraine brought the world to peace?
They will not use nuclear weapons. If they wanted to do it, they would have done that already. China and India are completely clear that they will not accept any use of nuclear weapons, so that would mean that Russia would be completely isolated and completely devastated economically in weeks. So that's not going to happen.
Putin says the war ends if Ukraine gives up Donbas. Why give a Nobel Peace Prize to a country that refuses?
This is just a proposal from Putin and American so-called negotiators. They're supposed to be negotiating, but this is not a negotiation. This is just about trying to make Ukraine give up without even a fight, which Russia is unable to do, and, incredibly, in some way, try to force Ukraine to give up its rightful ownership of its occupied territories.
This is just appeasement, just as what Chamberlain did in 1938 and what Europe has done again and again in 2008 and 2014. This would be a completely terrible mistake.
"Ukraine deserves the Nobel Prize, no matter how long they keep on fighting against this horrible aggression by this dreadful kleptocracy," Mr. Endsjø says.
Europe says Ukraine keeps the peace for everyone. Can it then demand that Ukrainian refugees go back and fight?
I, as a European, think that other Europeans cannot demand anything of the Ukrainians, whoever they are. This must be up to the Ukrainian people and the Ukrainian government.
Do people in Norway still genuinely believe that Ukraine can win this war, dragging on for so long?
I think so. Very many do believe that. But this depends on whether the West keeps on, and the free world continues to support Ukraine. Here in Norway, we are in a particular situation because, as our own Finance Department calculated last year, we have earned an extra 106 billion euros from the war (additional government revenues generated by high energy prices — ed.) due to higher oil and gas prices.
We don't support you as much as we should. We should have given you those 106 billion euros.
Why should someone in Europe care whether Ukraine wins or loses?
That is the point: that this is a war against the free world from a horrible dictatorship. More or less, you can call it a kleptocracy — that's the most, I guess, the most precise definition of Russia today. It's not a democracy whatsoever. It's most of all a kleptocracy where the top leaders just steal whatever they can get their hands on.
If Ukraine had fallen, it's not just that that would be horrible for Ukraine as such, but that would mean also that Russia would have had its hands on all the immense resources Ukraine has. Also, all the million men and women who probably would have been forced into the Russian army, and made it an even more dangerous enemy to the West.
So this is about the survival of all of us. Ukraine is the free world. We belong together. Ukraine should have been in NATO and the EU a long time ago.
If Russia says it only wants Donbas, why not just give it to them and let the war end?
This is like World War II all over again. They say: "If we only get Donbas, we're going to at least have proper negotiations."
Donbas, that is the Ukrainian Sudetenland. That's just what the West forced Czechoslovakia to do in 1938 and 1939. The Sudetenland wasn't just a nice little border region. It was the defense line of Czechoslovakia. So the moment the Germans got that, they were defenseless against the full-scale invasion that followed in the months afterward.
"Donbas, it's not just a small border region. It's the most important line of defense," Mr. Endsjø says.
Forcing Ukraine to give up anything whatsoever is rewarding the Russian aggression.
But I have to give Putin right in one thing when he says: "We are, you know, continuing World War II." That's true, because you have to remember what Russia did in World War II. They started it together with Nazi Germany in 1939. They occupied the Baltic countries, they occupied Moldova, they occupied half of Poland, they split Poland with Nazi Germany, and they tried to occupy Finland.
When Norway was invaded by Nazi Germany, Russia congratulated Germany. They were on Germany's side. The only thing that made Russia shift sides in World War II was the German invasion. What did they do after World War II? They didn't liberate any country - they occupied. They just changed one occupation for another.
"Eastern Europe wasn't liberated before 1990 and 1991. That's the actual end of World War II, when the Russian occupation of Eastern Europe ended," he stresses.
They even talk about the northern parts of Northern Norway. In 1945, they did have designs. They wanted Svalbard and the northern islands. They had plans to take the regions closest to Norway, which were also part of the Soviet Union. They want everything they have ever had, and they want it back.
Trump has made no secret of his desire for the Nobel Peace Prize. Could the Committee deny Ukraine the award simply to avoid provoking him?
Trump has been nominated for the Peace Prize several times, but I don't think he really has a chance. What I did note is that last year's recipient, Mrs. Machado from Venezuela, was probably chosen partly due to it. I don't criticize the prize, as she is a democratically elected leader, a good candidate, and a good recipient.
"But I believe part of the reason she got it was that the Nobel Committee wanted a recipient who would not provoke President Trump," he says.
I consider that they are going to worry about that again, about whether the recipient is going to provoke Trump or not. You never know what his reaction will be anyway. I don't think they really see him as a serious candidate — someone who just started an immense war in Iran, drawing the whole world economy down.
