A Saudi-led coalition says it has reclaimed territory overrun by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:30:34 UTC
01:30:34 KST

A Saudi-led coalition says it has reclaimed territory overrun by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Yemen’s military spokesman said that more than 1,100 attacks had been launched against Houthi positions.
- The Houthis had captured territory overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital waterway for traffic passing through the Suez Canal.
- The Houthis denied Yemeni government claims that they had been driven out of towns near the strait.
BEIRUT — Yemen’s embattled government and a Saudi-led coalition have launched a major campaign aimed at dislodging Iran-backed Houthis who had recently seized vital parts of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
The offensive, which had already reclaimed territory overlooking a key waterway, marks a sharp escalation in what thus far been an ancillary conflict in the wider U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
In a televised address on Sunday evening, Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Yemeni government’s Presidential Leadership Council, announced a military operation to “extend the authority of the state and its institutions over the entire national territory.”
The operation would continue, he said, “until the country is liberated from the control of terrorist militias.”
The campaign comes almost a month after a blitzkrieg offensive by the Houthis saw Saudi-backed government forces collapse in disarray and give up wide swaths of territory along the Red Sea coast, including the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an important maritime chokepoint.
The Houthis also made important gains inland, all but besieging the strategic city of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, in a move that augured more Houthi advances.
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which links the Mediterranean Sea with the Indian Ocean, is a new tinderbox in the Iran war.
On Sunday, the group said it seized Turbah, a garrison town that lies on the sole supply route linking Taiz to Aden, a key port on the Arabian Sea.
On Monday, Yemen’s military spokesman Majed al-Nuzaily said that “Operation Yemen Dawn” had launched more than 1,100 attacks against Houthi positions. He added that pro-government factions succeeded in clawing back Mokha, the town of Bab el-Mandeb and a nearby airport from the Houthis — claims the group denied.
Video posted on social media by activists accompanying pro-government factions depicted what was said to be the aftermath of attacks on Houthi positions along the Red Sea coast.
“They ran away into the sea. We captured some of them, and the rest were killed,” said one fighter from the Giants Brigade, a pro-government group.
Meanwhile, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a military spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, said in a post on X that 100 warplanes participated in a Monday raid that destroyed 324 “high-value targets.”
Later, he said the warplanes were providing “air protection” over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait as well as “round-the-clock air support for Yemeni armed forces on the ground.”
When it was first formed in 2015, the Saudi-led coalition consisted of nine nations, including the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Bahrain along with Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, Sudan and Senegal.
The fighting represents the sharpest escalation since a 2022 ceasefire between the Houthis, Yemen’s government and Saudi Arabia broke down in July.
Officially known as Ansar Allah (“Supporters of God”), the Houthis occupy much of Yemen’s north — its most populated section — and have long clamored for greater control over the rest. Iran has incorporated the rebels as members of its anti-U.S. coalition, the so-called Axis of Resistance, and has provided weapons, training and other aid to the Houthis, which belong to a branch of Shiite Islam.
The Yemeni government is a fragile body that, despite being internationally recognized, has no real foothold in the country it ostensibly rules.
In the days after the ceasefire broke down, the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi shipping, and launched attacks crippling Saudi Arabia’s oil export infrastructure. That included the East-West Pipeline, the main conduit Saudi Arabia has used to circumvent Iranian and American closures of the Strait of Hormuz.
Then in early September, the Houthis scythed through the Red Sea port of Mokha, along with Dhubab, Bab el-Mandeb and Perim Island. The offensive essentially granted the group control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a move that rocked energy markets already made skittish by the U.S. and Israel’s war on Iran.
Vessels using the Suez Canal must pass through the strait to reach the Mediterranean Sea to the north or Arabian Sea to the south.
This week’s offensive is not the first time the Yemeni and Saudi governments have tried to roll back the Houthis.
After the Houthis took over the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and a coalition of Arab nations launched a bombing campaign in support of anti-Houthi forces. That campaign managed to expel the rebels from Aden, but the Houthis — tough mountain fighters who received Iranian training to field and eventually manufacture drones and missiles — proved a difficult adversary.
The war turned into a grinding conflict, killing hundreds of thousands of people and spurring successive health crises and famine. In 2022, after years of stalemate, the government and rebels signed on to a ceasefire.
With front lines frozen, infighting among pro-government factions — which had never been the happiest of allies — broke out into open war, causing a still-unresolved rift between Saudi Arabia and the Emirates.
Experts say those dynamics are likely to bedevil the government’s ambitious plans for a march on Sanaa.
“The government doesn’t have the capabilities, the materiel, nor the cohesion of the forces,” said Hisham Al-Omeisy, a senior Yemen advisor at the European Institute of Peace. He added that previous assaults — when the Saudi-led coalition was larger, there was less fragmentation in anti-Houthi forces and the Houthis were less capable — couldn’t achieve the war objectives the government has now placed.
“It would require a lot more investment, not only from Saudi Arabia, but also from the U.S,” he said.
In any case, Al-Omeisy said Saudi Arabia was not looking for a “zero-sum game” involving the Houthis’ defeat, but was likely more interested in rolling back some of the group’s recent gains.
“They want a better hand for when they sit down for negotiations — and inevitably there will be negotiations,” Al-Omeisy said.
Faced with escalating Houthi attacks and a reluctant U.S. administration unwilling to intervene, Saudi Arabia is actively seeking regional defense partnerships.
In recent weeks, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman — the de facto leader of Saudi Arabia — reached out to President Trump for the U.S. military to attack the Houthis. But Trump demurred, appearing unwilling to provoke a new front in the war of Iran.
In remarks to the press on Monday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. intended “to live by” the defense and security agreement it has with Saudi Arabia, but would not go into details about any U.S. involvement in the current campaign.
He added that the U.S. was expecting the counteroffensive would happen.
“Obviously the Saudis have come under Houthi attack and see the threat that that poses, and they have a right to defend themselves,” he said.
There have since been reports of some 200 U.S. military advisors stationed at planning centers in Saudi Arabia, along with U.S. tankers providing aerial refueling capabilities for Saudi warplanes. But it all falls short of the military involvement Bin Salman reportedly wants.
With the U.S. on the sidelines, Saudi Arabia has turned to other nations, including Turkey and Pakistan, with which it recently signed a tripartite, NATO-style mutual defense agreement.
On Monday, Turkish officials and Pakistan’s foreign and defense ministers and army chief met with their counterparts in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, to discuss how to “institutionalize” the pact, according to official statements.
But observers expect the participation would be limited to protecting Saudi Arabia’s borders from ground assault by the Houthis or providing air-defense equipment against ballistic missiles and drones.

730 days without a barber – “Man Utd” fan has not had a haircut for exactly two years
Kyiv • UNN
Frank Ilett has not had a haircut since October 5, 2024, waiting for Man Utd to win five matches in a row. His hair has already had to be braided into dreadlocks.
Today, October 5, fan of English club "Manchester United" Frank Ilett started a challenge: not to cut his hair until "United" achieve five consecutive victories. Since then, the fan’s hair has grown so much that he has even had to braid it into dreadlocks, reports UNN.
Details
Exactly two years ago today, I decided to start this challenge. To be honest, I didn’t think anything would come of it, but I simply thought it would be a fun way to provide a little humor for other "Manchester United" fans, because we were going through a difficult period at the time. The decision to start the challenge was partly connected with the feeling that we were also being somewhat underestimated. A few months before that, we had won the FA Cup (and five consecutive matches a few months before that), but by that point in the 2024/25 season we had already played 10 matches... 3 wins, 4 draws, and 3 defeats. Unfortunately, since then we have continued to struggle, and this has lasted MUCH longer than I ever expected
He noted that "United" have already played seven matches this season, recording two wins, two draws, and three defeats, adding that he very much hopes the club will manage to turn the season around, return to winning ways, and compete for trophies again.
Contrary to what some people think, I genuinely want those five wins and a new hairstyle to come as soon as possible. I won’t pretend that this hasn’t been an interesting journey... I am incredibly grateful for the opportunities and experiences I have gained thanks to it. I have met incredible people, fulfilled real dreams, and enjoyed this journey. But this was not my plan. I never thought it would interest so many people, never thought it would last this long, and never thought I would become a "social media personality" or a "content creator"
Additional information
On this day, October 5, 2024, "United" fan Frank Ilett launched a challenge whose premise was not to cut his hair until the English club achieved five consecutive victories. October 5, 2024 was the last time Ilett had his hair cut.
It should be noted that the Englishman started the challenge when "United" were managed by Erik ten Hag. The day before, "Man United" drew 3–3 with "Porto" in the Europa League, and the day after the challenge began, the team drew 0–0 with "Aston Villa".
Overall, the challenge has already outlasted three "United" managers — ten Hag, Rúben Amorim, and Michael Carrick, who currently manages the "Red Devils".
“Manchester United” will again be led by a former club legend - insider12.01.26, 22:48 • 4413 views
Ilett came closest to visiting the barber in February this year. At that time, "United" first defeated their arch-rivals "Manchester City" 2–0, then beat "Arsenal" 3–2, followed by a victory over "Fulham" by the same score, and then a 2–0 win over "Tottenham". However, in the fifth and decisive match, "United" somehow managed to draw with "West Ham" — 1–1.
In September, Ilett met Rúben Amorim, sharing a photo on Instagram. According to him, Amorim apologized to the fan.
He saw me, pointed at my hair, and said: "Sorry about this." I still love him
It should be noted that Ilett’s hair has already grown so much that he eventually had to visit a barber to have dreadlocks made.
The fan’s story also attracted the attention of "Manchester City" forward Erling Haaland, who himself recently changed his hairstyle.

If that were the case, he would have cut his hair after the fifth victory, in the match against "United," rather than after the seventh, against "Sunderland."

Merz goes to Kiev to 'escape' low ratings in Germany — Berliner Zeitung
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:29:11 UTC
01:29:11 KST

BERLIN, October 5. /TASS/. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Ukraine last weekend to escape low ratings in Germany and defeats in regional elections, Harald Neuber, head of the news and international departments at Berliner Zeitung, said.
Merz visited Ukraine for the first time this year last weekend. As Neuber points out, the visit came amid a decline in approval of the chancellor’s performance to a record low - only 10% of the country’s residents rate his performance positively, while 88% view it negatively. In contrast, he is popular in Ukraine - in August, 64% of respondents in one poll said they viewed the chancellor positively.
"A German chancellor who is six times more popular in Kiev than in Berlin is a sociological curiosity and a political diagnosis. Anyone who is popular in Kiev but punished in Magdeburg [the poor showing by Merz’s party in the elections in Saxony-Anhalt - TASS] should ask whether the trip to a war zone was a duty or an escape. The answer is unpleasant: both," Neuber wrote.
He noted that in Kiev, Merz promised new military assistance and called for continued support for the country. And although polls show that slightly more than half of Germany’s residents share the chancellor’s view on policy toward Russia, this does not automatically mean they are ready to send more weapons to Kiev. "Quite the opposite. Poll data show the opposite trend," the journalist wrote. He recalled that a recent Infratest poll showed that 42% of Germans - the highest level since February 2022 - believe the current volume of military assistance to Ukraine is excessive.
Polls also show that Germans do not consider it necessary to resume gas supplies from Russia, in line with Merz’s position, Neuber wrote. "The question is how long a chancellor with a 10% approval rating can credibly speak on behalf of the majority [of the country’s residents]. Will Merz’s rule come to an end together with Ukraine, or will the federal government’s Ukraine policy [come to an end] together with Merz?" the author asks. In his view, Germans are not opposed to helping Ukraine as such, but are against "help without an end goal."

Senior British officials have made it clear to Israel that if the British Consulate in East Jerusalem is closed and British diplomats are expelled, the UK will respond by expelling 27 Israeli diplomats, along with their families, two sources familiar with the matter told The Jerusalem Post on Monday.
The consulate is expected to close on October 8, following an order issued by Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar.
The move reportedly follows Britain's economic sanctions on the West Bank.
There is no reason for us to address speculation regarding decisions other countries might make in the future, diplomatic sources told the Post.
"We have already demonstrated that any move against Israel will be met with an appropriate response, and this will continue to be the case in the future," the sources added.
In addition, Britain's top national security official quietly visited Israel last week in a bid to prevent the closure of the consulate, three sources told Reuters.

UK claims Israel's actions were undermining the possibility of a two-state solution
In announcing the sanctions, Britain said that Israel's actions were undermining the possibility of a two-state solution, the idea of a Palestinian state co-existing peacefully alongside Israel. Israel has rejected the idea of Palestinian statehood.
Britain cited Israeli government-backed plans to expand settlements and rising extremist settler attacks targeting Palestinians in the West Bank. The British sanctions are to take effect next year.
The British consulate, located in the Sheikh Jarrah neighborhood, handles the country's relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza. It also provides consular services to Palestinians.
Sa'ar has said that Britain's decision to impose sanctions was "morally distorted," accusing Britain's ruling Labour Party of being hostile towards the country, and of interfering in Israel's upcoming general election on October 27.

Jewish contingent marches separately on 90th anniversary of the Battle of Cable Street
Unknown

2026-10-05

A Jewish group organized a separate march on the 90th anniversary of the historic Battle of Cable Street on Sunday to commemorate resistance against fascism in the United Kingdom, after being dismissed as provocateurs and told they were unwelcome by organizers marking the event.
Reporting live from East London, GB News presenter and comedian Josh Howie highlighted how in 1936, thousands of Jewish residents stood shoulder-to-shoulder with Irish dockers, trade unionists, and socialists to block Oswald Mosley’s fascists from marching through the heart of the East End.
Ninety years later, however, mainstream groups organizing the official anniversary, such as Unite the Union, produced promotional material that omitted any mention of Jews or antisemitism entirely.
Jewish Zionist participants rejected from main march
The rally organizer Eve Kay explained in an interview with GB News’s Free Speech Nation program that, when Jewish community members reached out to coordinate their presence, they were met with hostility and dismissed as provocateurs. Branded as Zionists or fascists, Jewish participants were told they were unwelcome and that their safety could not be guaranteed on the main route.
Recognizing that the official demonstration had become a hostile environment, Kay and others formed the “Cable Street Jews” committee, establishing a separate contingent to march just 10 minutes ahead of the main procession under police protection.
Roughly 300 people joined the Cable Street Jews march, filling the streets with defiant chants, “Am Yisrael Chai,” as well as “90 years and we’re still here,” and “they shall not pass.”
'1936-2026, Right or Left, No to Jew Hate'
Demonstrators also chanted “here to stay, here to fight, no to the antisemite!” Participants held blue flags, placards featuring images and names of individuals from the 1936 era under the banner of “Cable St Jew,” and signs that read “1936-2026, Right or Left, No to Jew Hate.”
Addressing the gathered crowd through a megaphone, Howie told attendees: “The Jews who stood in these streets in 1936 would think about our lives today... They’d be shocked. Shocked Jews murdered in Manchester, ambulances blown up, Jews in the streets stabbed, synagogues firebombed... And now, marching parallel to us, is another group of people who didn’t want us there, who were trying to erase those who came before... The best way to honor them, those people who stood here 90 years ago, is to fight so that we can ensure that, in 90 years, we will still be here.”
Elsewhere during the main rally, circulating footage captured protesters surrounding and aggressively confronting an individual perceived as a Zionist, shouting, “Zionists are not welcome here” and chanting, “Go! Go! Go! Go!” directly at him. Police officers stepped in to separate the crowd, managing the escalating hostility as the man was escorted away from the scene.

====================================================================================================

US antisemitism envoy tells 'Post' people should understand Zionism, ‘not be ignorant about it’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:28:25 UTC
01:28:25 KST

US Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism, Ambassador Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun, told The Jerusalem Post on Monday that Zionism must be understood through Jewish history rather than equated with racism.
In a wide-ranging State Department briefing, he said more than 250,000 visas had been revoked under the administration, described US efforts to change antisemitic educational material abroad, criticized the use of the term “genocide” against Israel, and said a two-state solution could not advance while one side called for the eradication of the other.
Kaploun said Monday that people using the term Zionism should understand its historical meaning and “not be ignorant about it.”
Kaploun made the comments during an on-the-record briefing at the State Department’s Washington Foreign Press Center after the Post asked whether his office was addressing what appeared to be a growing international misconception about the meaning of Zionism.
“I think people have to have an understanding of history to know what Zionism is,” Kaploun said. “For the last 3,000 years, we say we lift up our eyes, and we pray to Zion. That is something that people have said for 3,000 years. That is not anything new.”
Kaploun said modern Zionism also meant that “the Jewish community has a state now,” pointing to the diversity of Israeli society.
“In Israel, you will see it’s one of the few countries you will see black Jews, white Jews, Middle Eastern Jews from all walks of life,” he said, referring also to Jewish communities expelled from other countries who found a home in Israel.
He cited Israeli universities and hospitals, where Jews, Arabs and Druze study and work alongside one another.
“I don’t think that it’s racism,” Kaploun said. “I think people should understand the term and understand and know about it and not be ignorant about it.”
US to raise UK Zionism controversy
Earlier in the briefing, Kaploun was asked about a motion adopted at the Green Party of England and Wales conference equating Zionism with racism.
He said the United States would make representations on the issue.
“I think a lot of countries are being hypocritical in the sense of they will only focus on Israel. They will not focus on other countries,” Kaploun said.
He argued that countries criticizing Israel should apply the same standards they use for other states.
Asked separately about debate in Italy over formally adopting the IHRA definition of antisemitism, Kaploun rejected concerns that doing so would prevent legitimate criticism of Israel.
“The IHRA definition doesn’t say that you can’t criticize Israel,” he said. “The IHRA definition says that if you’re criticizing Israel, you have to hold that same standard across the board.”
“It does not restrict you from criticizing Israel,” he added. “What it does is hold you accountable so that you can’t only criticize Israel.”
More than 250,000 visas revoked
In his opening remarks, Kaploun outlined several measures undertaken by the Trump administration as part of its campaign against antisemitism.
He said the administration implemented “a rigorous visa vetting process” and revoked more than 250,000 visas.
Kaploun also cited renewed hate-crime prosecutions, cooperation with counterterrorism agencies, and work with foreign governments to address antisemitism in educational systems.
“We have been involved with the Saudi government to have their curriculum changed to remove unprecedented levels of antisemitic questions, and that is a priority of this office,” he said.
Later, Kaploun gave an example of a question he said had appeared in a textbook in one country: “If someone killed 127 Israelis in one day, how many Israelis would be killed if they did that for nine days?”
He said such questions were now being removed from textbooks as a result of efforts involving US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, US President Donald Trump, State Department officials and US ambassadors.
“This office believes that most people who hate are ignorant,” Kaploun said, arguing that education grounded in respect and human dignity could reduce antisemitism as well as hatred directed at other religious groups.
‘Genocide’ term being used by ‘uneducated people’
Asked about South Africa’s accusations against Israel, Kaploun sharply criticized what he described as misuse of the term genocide.
“The term genocide is being thrown around here by a lot of uneducated people, or left-wing or right-wing radicals, or people who are literally antisemitic, trying to tar and feather the Jewish community and Israel with the level of genocide,” he said.
Kaploun questioned why a six-year-old Jewish child attending school in the United States should be called a “baby killer” or told that he or she was responsible for genocide.
“I think people have to take a very strong look at how that term is being used,” he said.
Two states: ‘Don’t put the cart in front of the horse’
Kaploun was also asked about the Trump administration’s policy toward a two-state solution.
“I think for a second, the one thing that separates this administration from other administrations is that we have a very good dose of realism, a very good dose of reality,” he said.
“If you want to talk about a two-state solution, you can’t be talking with one of those states calling for the eradication of another state first and foremost.”
Kaploun said the administration’s immediate focus was on economic opportunity in Gaza, education, Hamas disarmament, and implementation of benchmarks contained in existing agreements.
“Nothing is off the table with this administration,” he said. “But we expect people to live up to their agreements.”
“Let’s not put the cart in front of the horse right now,” he added.
Kaploun also described what he said was an Iranian-backed plot targeting a synagogue in Belgium.
He recalled visiting a firebombed synagogue during his first diplomatic visit to Belgium and meeting about 100 members of the Jewish community who, he said, were frightened.
Following discussions with Belgian officials, Kaploun said the military protected Jewish communities in Brussels, Antwerp and Liège.
“Three days later, they caught three teenagers who were being hired by the Iranian government to firebomb a synagogue,” Kaploun said.
He added that the IRGC was subsequently designated as a terrorist organization, presenting the episode as an example of how diplomatic intervention could lead to concrete protection for Jewish communities.
Kaploun also expressed concern about conditions facing Jewish communities in Canada and Mexico.
“The Jewish community in Canada is under siege,” he said, adding that members of Mexico’s Jewish community also felt under siege.
Kaploun argued that governments should be judged by how well they protect their own citizens and whether people can freely worship, attend school and participate in public life without fear.
He said current levels of antisemitism were at levels he had not seen since the period before World War II and called for political leaders to confront hatred directly.
Kaploun also addressed antisemitism on social media, saying he believed X/Twitter had seen a significant reduction in antisemitic posts after introducing greater visibility into account locations.
“We believe very strongly in freedom of speech,” he said. “You have the right to say what you want to say, but by the same token, we also have the right to say that it’s not true, and it can be disproven that it’s not true.”
Kaploun concluded by arguing that combating antisemitism required changing attitudes before they turned into violence.
“If I can teach a seven-year-old child to not hate, so when he’s 18 or 19, he’s not influenced to go take a gun and go shoot up something, because he’s now informed, he’s not an ignorant person - that’s our success,” he said.

Jerusalem man charged over year-long contact with alleged foreign agent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:27:43 UTC
01:27:43 KST

The State Attorney’s Office indicted Tarek Oweida, 53, of Jerusalem, on Monday for allegedly maintaining contact for about a year with a foreign agent who sought photographs and information from across the capital.
The indictment, filed in Jerusalem District Court, alleges that the operative offered Oweida money to photograph Jewish residential neighborhoods and locations used by police and security forces. Prosecutors have asked the court to keep him in custody until the proceedings conclude.
The case is narrower than several recent foreign-agent prosecutions: The indictment explicitly states that Oweida did not complete any of the proposed assignments and did not transmit the requested material. He also received no payment.
Oweida was arrested on September 9. Roughly a year earlier, he allegedly sought to join a Telegram group called “The Resistance,” through which he began corresponding with the suspected agent approximately once every two weeks.
Prosecutors allege that the person was acting on behalf of either a foreign state or a terrorist organization.
During the correspondence, the operative allegedly asked Oweida to photograph locations in Jerusalem in exchange for money. At the agent’s request, Oweida downloaded a separate application intended to allow them to communicate securely and through encrypted messages, the indictment states.
On August 23, the operative asked whether Oweida had a driver’s license or another means of transportation. Oweida replied that he used an electric bicycle, prompting the operative to ask whether he could mount a camera on it and record his journeys without attracting attention. Oweida replied he was in the area of al-Aqsa Mosque, according to the filing.
Later in the exchange, he asked the operative to stop contacting him. When the operative replied that he would request activities that would “please God,” Oweida allegedly continued the conversation and asked what information was wanted.
Four days later, Oweida agreed to a request to mount a camera on his bicycle and photograph a mosque, but did not carry out the assignment, prosecutors commented.
On September 7, two days before his arrest, the operative again asked him to install a camera on the bicycle and film while riding near al-Aqsa Mosque or in other areas that could assist them. Oweida did not reply and did not perform the task, according to the indictment.
He is charged with one count of contact with a foreign agent. Unlike several recent cases involving alleged foreign handlers, he has not been charged with providing information to the enemy or completing an intelligence-gathering assignment.
The indictment includes general background on an increase in Iranian efforts to recruit Israelis through social media and messaging applications since the October 7 massacre. It does not, however, identify the operative in Oweida’s case as Iranian.
Charged with contact with an alleged Iranian intelligence operative
In March, Jerusalem prosecutors charged Ali Jaber, 23, of Eilat, with contact with an alleged Iranian intelligence operative and three counts of providing information that could assist the enemy. Jaber allegedly received hundreds of dollars after photographing locations in Eilat, areas inside Ovda Air Base, where he was working, and the road leading to the base.
In December, Vadim Kupriyanov, 40, of Rishon Lezion, was charged after allegedly using a dashboard camera to record the street and entrance outside former prime minister Naftali Bennett’s Ra’anana home for an Iranian handler. Prosecutors claimed he completed other paid photography assignments.
Those cases illustrate a recurring method described by Israeli authorities: approaching potential recruits through Telegram or job advertisements, initially offering payment for apparently simple photographs and later requesting access to more sensitive locations.

The Brazilian real also strengthened over the course of the day, trading at 4.98 reais to the dollar, compared with 5.22 at Friday’s close.
Although inflation has been brought under control and unemployment has fallen to a historic low during Lula da Silva’s third term, Brazilians complain of a loss of purchasing power.
Flávio Bolsonaro, of the far-right Liberal Party, won more than 56 million votes (47.03%), while the left-wing candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured the backing of almost 53.9 million voters (45.16%).

Russian women's volleyball team allowed to compete at 2027 World Cup
The Russian women's national volleyball team has been allowed to compete at the 2027 Women's Volleyball World Cup.
Source: International Volleyball Federation (FIVB)
Details: The Russian team qualified for the tournament based on the world rankings, without going through the qualifying stage. The Netherlands, Germany, Czechia, Belgium, France, Slovenia, Sweden, Mexico, Greece, South Korea, Bulgaria, Switzerland and Ukraine also qualified on the same basis.
The Ukrainian and Russian national teams will appear at the same major international tournament for the first time since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Russian team currently ranks 11th in the FIVB world rankings for women's national teams.
The upcoming World Cup will be held in the United States and Canada. The competition will begin on 20 August and end on 5 September. The 2027 World Cup will also be one of the qualifying tournaments for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.
The Russian women's national team have won the world championship twice in their history, in 2006 and 2010.
Background:
- In July, the International Olympic Committee decided to temporarily lift the suspension of Russia's National Olympic Committee, which had been imposed on 12 October 2023, and suspended its recommendations restricting the participation of Russian athletes.
- Following the decision, a number of international sports organisations lifted restrictions on athletes from Russia competing internationally. The FIVB was also among them.
- The European Volleyball Confederation previously allowed both the Russian men's and women's national teams to compete in competitions under its auspices. Ukrainian Volleyball Federation President Mykhailo Melnyk said the decision had been made following a vote.
- In addition, it emerged in August that, for security reasons, the Russian men's national volleyball team will not compete at the 2027 World Championship in Poland.

'Golden Mandarin' case sent to court
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:23:02 EEST
01:23:02 KST

Anti-corruption agencies have sent to court the "Golden Mandarin" case involving the misappropriation and legalization of UAH 54.18 million in state budget funds through manipulation of a European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruling, allegedly organized by Heorhii Lohvynsky, a People's Front MP in Ukraine's 8th convocation parliament, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine's (NABU) press service reported.
"NABU and SAPO have sent to court the case involving the misappropriation and legalization of UAH 54.18 million in state budget funds," NABU said on Telegram Monday.
According to law enforcement, between 2013 and 2016 a former MP devised and carried out a scheme to misappropriate state budget funds by misleading the ECHR about a disputed legal relationship between Zolotoy Mandarin Oil LLC, a company under the scheme's participants' control showing signs of being fictitious, and PJSC Kyivenergo.
In September 2013, a representative of Zolotoy Mandarin Oil, acting on the defendant's instructions, filed an application with the ECHR seeking to recover UAH 54.18 million from Ukraine's state budget as outstanding debt owed by PJSC Kyivenergo under a court ruling that, according to the application, had gone unenforced since 2009.
Investigators established that, at the time of the ECHR filing, the company had taken no steps to actually collect the debt, since all its property and accounts had been seized to secure obligations exceeding UAH 70 million owed to state-owned JSC Rodovid Bank, and the company's director had been criminally charged with financial fraud.
In addition, the defendants concealed from the court the fact that, shortly before filing with the ECHR, the claim against PJSC Kyivenergo had been assigned to another company in exchange for UAH 54.18 million.
According to the investigation, the former MP subsequently arranged, in agreement with the Justice Ministry's then-leadership, for the government's ECHR representative to prepare a declaration of friendly settlement, which in effect acknowledged the state's guilt for failing to enforce a court ruling in a dispute between two private companies - a claim that had already been sold on.
On the basis of this declaration, UAH 54.18 million was transferred from Ukraine's state budget to a company controlled by the defendant and his associates. These funds were then laundered through conversion centers, according to the investigation.
The statement does not name the main suspect, but according to media reports, the scheme's key organizer is former MP Heorhii Lohvynsky.
According to NABU, the former MP was notified of suspicion as the crime's organizer in July 2023. The notice of suspicion became possible after the termination of his immunity, which he held as a relative of a European Court of Human Rights judge. Since the suspect left Ukraine shortly before his immunity was terminated, he was notified of suspicion under Articles 135 and 278 of Ukraine's Criminal Procedure Code.

An Israeli mathematics lecturer at Bar-Ilan University has been indicted for planning a series of mass-casualty terrorist attacks targeting Palestinian citizens of Israel and Palestinians in the occupied East Jerusalem and the occupied West Bank, according to a report by Haaretz.
The professor, who is in his 60s and whose identity remains under a gag order, developed a plan he called “Am Ya’aseh Transfer” (“the nation will carry out a transfer”), with the stated objective of forcing Palestinian populations to flee or be expelled to Jordan, Lebanon and Gaza.
Prosecutors said that he spent more than three years developing the plan, conducting reconnaissance, preparing detailed documents and attempting to recruit participants.
The State Prosecutor’s Office said the suspect sought assistance from “subversive elements” in the Israeli Air Force, artillery and armored corps, The Times of Israel reported.
Divided cells for coordinated attacks
The indictment describes a highly organised scheme involving 72 Jewish operatives divided into 12 cells, with plans for coordinated attacks in mixed Jewish-Palestinian cities and Palestinian communities in Israel.
The plan included attacks on civilians and instructions to show no mercy, including towards women and children.
It estimated that 600 to 700 people would be killed and stipulated that at least half of the attackers, including the professor, should hold gun licenses.
It also envisioned support from elements within the Israeli military and sought to exploit social media coverage of the attacks to create panic and encourage Palestinian citizens of Israel to flee the country.
The professor attempted to recruit former security officials, journalists, academics and right-wing political figures, including former Knesset member Moshe Feiglin, whose Zehut faction has teamed up with extremist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party ahead of the October 27 parliamentary election.
Around June, he asked his daughter to recruit acquaintances among the so-called “hilltop youth,” a term referring to extremist illegal Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, but she refused.
The Central District Attorney’s Office filed the indictment at Lod District Court and asked that he remain in custody until the end of the proceedings.
Bar-Ilan University has suspended the lecturer and said it was “appalled” by the allegations, stressing that it has zero tolerance for such conduct.
Palestinian Israelis make up about 21 percent of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Ukrainian pilots will begin training on French Rafale aircraft in France in the very near future,” Zelensky said. “This is a strong step for Ukrainian combat aviation.”
New aid package as Russia steps up strikes
Paris is also preparing a new package of military supplies for Ukraine, which Kyiv expects to receive soon, Zelensky said. While he did not disclose what the package would include, he confirmed that its contents were on the agenda during the call.
In a post on X, Macron reaffirmed France’s full support for Ukraine.
“With President Zelensky, we took stock of the concrete support we can provide to help Ukraine intercept drones and thwart Russia’s aggression,” he said, noting that France would continue providing support to the country despite intimidation or escalation by Russia.

Russia Strikes Kharkiv With Guided Bombs Killing 6, Wounding 59, Including Children
The groundwork for the cooperation was laid in July, when Paris agreed to support licensed production in Ukraine of AASM Hammer glide bombs, Aster 30 interceptors for SAMP/T air defense systems, and SCALP cruise missiles.
The two countries are also working to advance FREYJA, a Ukraine-led initiative to develop an affordable anti-ballistic missile defense system. Launched in Paris in July, the project brings together Ukraine, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden and the UK.
Zelensky said he and Macron had discussed ways to speed up the work and agreed to go over the details when they meet in person, though no date has been set publicly.
From 100-jet plan to first 16 aircraft
Zelensky’s latest announcement follows France’s earlier confirmation that it had started preparing Ukrainian pilots for the aircraft.
According to UNN citing French Minister Delegate for European Affairs Benjamin Haddad, the training follows the standard French Air Force path; first, the pilots start on Grob G-120TP light trainers, move on to Dornier Alpha Jet advanced trainers and only then transition to frontline fighters.
Once the course is complete, Ukraine could receive its first four Rafales.
The training is the first practical step in a deal that has been taking shape for nearly a year. In November 2025, Zelensky and Macron signed a letter of intent for Ukraine to acquire up to 100 Rafales.
In July, Kyiv and Paris agreed on a roadmap for the first 16 jets, along with an unspecified amount of weaponry, which is expected to be financed through the EU’s €90 billion ($103 billion) Ukraine Support Loan and other sources.
As part of the same July agreement, France pledged two more SAMP/T air defense systems by the end of 2026 and four to eight upgraded SAMP/T NG systems in the following years.
Deliveries of Aster 30 interceptors, which are in short supply in Ukraine, were also expected to increase from October.

Breadcrumb
Iran executes two men linked to anti-govt protests
Iran's judiciary said two men were executed on Monday for involvement in the deaths of four police officers during anti-government protests that peaked in January.
Authorities accused them of murdering the officers in the central city of Isfahan during protests that began in the capital, Tehran, in December over economic grievances before spreading nationwide.
The movement rapidly evolved into large anti-government rallies that peaked on 8 and 9 January, causing unprecedented destruction and thousands of deaths.
"Alireza Sepahi and Alireza Raissi were hanged this morning after the Supreme Court upheld the verdict," the judiciary's Mizan Online website said, without specifying the dates of their arrest or trial.

Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths in the unrest, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel.
Foreign-based NGOs, citing much higher death tolls, maintain, however, that Iranian security forces fired on protesters.
The number of executions in Iran has risen since the start of the Middle East war, which was triggered in late February by US-Israeli strikes.
In 2025, Iran executed at least 1,639 people, the largest number in any year since 1989, according to the NGOs Iran Human Rights and Together Against the Death Penalty.
Amnesty International says Iran carries out more executions than any country except China.
On Saturday, Iran announced the execution of another man convicted of a raft of charges, including firing a military-grade weapon at police officers during the protests.

The Armed Forces of Ukraine will receive the Varkhan robotic system — technical specifications and battlefield strengths
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:17:02 EEST
01:17:02 KST

The Armed Forces of Ukraine will receive the Varkhan robotic system — technical specifications and battlefield strengths
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukrainian Varkhan unmanned ground complex transports hundreds of kilograms of cargo over dozens of kilometers. The system has all-wheel drive, replaceable batteries and several control systems.
The Ministry of Defence has codified and authorized the Varkhan unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) for supply to the Armed Forces of Ukraine. It is designed to perform a wide range of military logistics missions: delivering weapons, ammunition, equipment, hardware, and more, UNN reports, citing the Ministry of Defence.
Tactical and technical characteristics (TTC) of the Varkhan UGV
The Varkhan UGV was manufactured at a Ukrainian defense enterprise in response to requests from military personnel who need the appropriate equipment to perform logistics tasks. The engineers incorporated all the defenders’ requirements into its design.
The Varkhan unmanned ground platform is highly versatile, reliable, and durable. It is built on an all-wheel-drive chassis with a 4×4 wheel arrangement, dependent suspension, and ground clearance of more than 200 mm. The design ensures good off-road capability and allows the system to move confidently across difficult terrain, in severe off-road conditions, marshland, and sand.
The platform is equipped with quick-release batteries, enabling it to carry out missions continuously.
Strengths of the Varkhan system on the battlefield
The Varkhan unmanned ground vehicle demonstrated high tactical and technical characteristics during testing. Its capabilities are sufficient to transport hundreds of kilograms of cargo over several dozen kilometers. In addition, the Varkhan UGV has several communication/control systems.
The Varkhan system meets the requirements of modern high-intensity warfare:
-  continuous operation; 
-  reliable, durable components and assemblies; 
-  a clear control algorithm; 
-  availability of spare parts and consumables; 
-  high tactical and technical characteristics; 
-  extensive logistics capabilities; 
-  ease of maintenance. 
The Varkhan UGV is part of an ecosystem of integrated solutions. It includes T-Bone ground control stations, antennas, masts, repeaters, and rotary mechanisms.
Combining these products makes it possible to develop integrated solutions for controlling unmanned systems and ensuring stable communications.
It should be recalled
Earlier, the Ministry of Defence codified the Zmiі Mini Strike reconnaissance and strike UGV. It was designed jointly with engineers from one of the most effective combat brigades of the Defense Forces and manufactured taking into account more than four years of wartime experience and analysis of the combat use of ground drones on the battlefield.

ICC unseals arrest warrants for Taliban education ministers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:16:48 UTC
01:16:48 KST

ICC unseals arrest warrants for Taliban education ministers
The International Criminal Court on Monday unsealed warrants for Afghan Education Minister Habibullah Agha, and Higher Education Minister Neda Mohammad Nadeem, accusing two senior Taliban officials of crimes against humanity for denying Afghanistan's women and girls over 12 their rights to an education.
The International Criminal Court on Monday unsealed arrest warrants for two Afghan education ministers accused of committing crimes against humanity through the Taliban government's restrictions on women and girls.
The warrants, for Habibullah Agha, minister of education, and Neda Mohammad Nadeem, minister of higher education, were issued on September 9, 2025 and remained under seal until Monday.
The two officials are accused of gender-based persecution linked to policies that have barred girls over the age of 12 from school and excluded women from higher education following the Taliban's return to power in August 2021.
The ICC warrants were likely to increase international pressure on the Taliban government.
AFP has approached Taliban authorities for comment.
The two warrants against the ministers were issued after the ICC authorised warrants in July 2025 for Afghanistan's Supreme Taliban Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and Supreme Court President Abdul Hakim Haqqani – parts of which have been made public.
Both Agha and Nadeem have played key roles in implementing the supreme leader's vision for Afghanistan.
"There are reasonable grounds to believe" the suspects committed "the crime against humanity of persecution on gender grounds", the court said.
It said the persecution was directed against women and girls, and the deprivation of their fundamental rights was committed "in connection with" other alleged crimes under the Taliban government's policies, including "imprisonment, torture, rape and enforced disappearance".
The court said the alleged crimes were committed in Afghanistan from the Taliban's takeover until at least January 20, 2025.
'Worsening' oppression
The ICC's disclosure of the warrants came the same day the UN Human Rights Council urged the Taliban authorities to repeal their "worsening" and "systematic oppression of all women and girls in Afghanistan".
The council's 47 member countries unanimously criticised that discrimination "and the harms that it has entrenched, which are unbearable, unjustifiable and should shock the conscience of humanity".
The ICC's Pre-Trial Chamber II said it decided to unseal all four warrants – with redactions – after concluding that doing so would not unduly affect ongoing investigations and could "prevent the commission of further crimes by the suspects".
Publication could also "promote cooperation by the international community... in relation to the situation in Afghanistan", it said.
Afghans across the country have told AFP journalists of severe mental health problems tied to the education ban, with teenage girls and women mostly staying at home.
Afghan universities are now men-only zones, where smartphones are banned and students can be chastised if their beards are not long enough.
Some women and girls have tried to continue their education by studying online, but their efforts are hampered by internet and electricity problems across Afghanistan.
Women are increasingly absent from public life and need to abide by a strict dress code when they leave home, covering everything but their eyes.
They are banned from most jobs and a host of public places – including parks – and must have a close male relative escort them on long journeys.
The higher education ban has led to staff shortages in hospitals, multiple healthcare workers told AFP, as women are no longer allowed to qualify as doctors.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Israel is rewriting the Palestinian curriculum in East Jerusalem to erase Palestinian identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:15:52 UTC
01:15:52 KST

Sally Assi, 34, recalled watching her 11-year-old daughter, Aline, a third-grader at Nour al-Huda School in the town of Beit Hanina in occupied East Jerusalem, arrange her drawing supplies before asking her, “Do you know why we draw Jerusalem?”
“Because it’s beautiful… right?” Aline answered.
Assi smiled, but her question to her daughter wasn’t really about drawing. “Jerusalem isn’t just walls and the Dome of the Rock,” Assi told Mondoweiss. “Jerusalem, to our generation and the generations before us, is a living history. It has cities, people, prisoners, stories, dreams.”
What Assi is describing from her kitchen in the town of Betunia, adjacent to Ramallah, is not an isolated worry among Palestinian parents whose children attend schools in East Jerusalem, under the control of the Israeli Ministry of Education. It is the front line of a rapid, Israeli-driven transformation of Palestinian education in the occupied city, where the Israeli curriculum has become mandatory for every first- and seventh-grade class as of this school year, affecting well over a third of Palestinian students in East Jerusalem.
Now, these tens of thousands of Palestinian children, for the first time since Israel illegally annexed and occupied the city in 1967, are using the Israeli curriculum as part of an effort to “Israelize” the schools. In addition, the remaining two-thirds of the Palestinian student body have been subjected to invasive Israeli alterations to the existing Palestinian curriculum, which has included the wholesale deletion of phrases, images, and symbols that denote Palestinian national identity, most significantly references to the Nakba of 1948 and altered phrasings around themes such as Jerusalem, prisoners, and Palestinian heritage.
It’s this quiet encroachment on Palestinian textbooks, as much as the wholesale replacement, that worries Assi most. “We don’t want our children to learn hatred, and we don’t want them to carry pain without meaning,” she said in an indirect reference to Israeli claims that Palestinian textbooks teach children to “hate.”
“But we want them to know the truth,” she added.
For Assi, the issue isn’t one deleted page, one cut poem, or one changed word, but the collective memory of the Palestinian people that is being altered. “Whoever deletes a page from an entire history is asking children to deny a part of themselves,” she said.
A conflict that moved inside the classroom
In East Jerusalem, the fight over education is no longer about the number of schools or classroom seats alone. It has moved into the classroom itself, into the book students open each morning, the terms their eyes land on, the images they study, the history they’re taught, and the narrative that will shape how they understand themselves in their city for years to come.
With the start of the 2026-2027 school year, the Israeli curriculum was imposed on all new first- and seventh-grade classes in municipal schools located in areas under the jurisdiction of the Israeli-run Jerusalem Municipality.
Israel’s own data shows the scale — the share of Palestinian students studying the Israeli curriculum rose to roughly 36% in 2025-2026, and more recent figures put this year’s number at close to 45,000 students, about 38% of all East Jerusalem students.
The Palestinian Authority (PA) Minister of Education and Higher Education, Amjad Barham, detailed to Mondoweiss a set of edits documented in correspondence and circulating records.
“In the first-grade civic and life education textbook, the Palestinian national anthem is marked for deletion,” Barham said. “The documents also describe the removal of a second-grade page containing an image of a prison and an attempt to break free from it, along with the deletion of prisoners’ names”.
In third grade, the poem “Ala Dalauna”, a traditional Palestinian folk song that often appears in nationalist anthems about the homeland, is among the material reportedly cut from the Arabic curriculum. The lesson, “Bride of the Sea,” the commonly used nickname for the coastal Palestinian city of Jaffa, now occupied by Israel, was also altered, its questions rewritten.
The edits surface even where they seem furthest from politics. In mathematics, Barham said, a reference to the “separation and annexation wall” was struck, along with a map of Palestine showing Jerusalem as its capital.
The changes intensify with grade level. From fourth through ninth grade, the documents describe substituted terminology — “mujahid” (freedom fighter) replaced with “defender,” “aseer” (prisoner) replaced with “the wronged” — alongside deleted or revised material on Jerusalem, prisoners, the Palestinian revolution, resistance, settlement, strikes, and select historical events.
“In their place”, Barham said, “content on peace, coexistence, and cooperation has been introduced.” References to the Palestinian village of Umm Khalid were recast in light of its proximity to present-day Netanya, an Israeli city. Language on the Judaization of Jerusalem was rewritten toward a vocabulary centered on peace rather than confrontation,” he noted.
Ma’arouf al-Rifai, spokesperson for the PA-run Jerusalem Governorate — the parts of the West Bank Israel annexed in 1967 and incorporated within the boundaries of Israel’s Jerusalem municipality — warned that Israel’s decision to impose the Israeli curriculum on East Jerusalem’s municipal schools represents “a dangerous and unprecedented escalation,” the most serious since 1967.
In a statement, al-Rifai described the move as a direct assault on the national and cultural identity of generations of Jerusalemites. “The decision is part of a systematic policy targeting Palestinian education in Jerusalem, one aimed at replacing the curriculum with the Israeli narrative in full,” the statement read.
Al-Rifai cited figures showing the scale of that replacement: nearly 45,000 students, around 38% of the roughly 120,000 Palestinian students in East Jerusalem, are now enrolled in the Israeli curriculum. The trajectory, he said, reveals a rapid and dangerous escalation — from 10,347 students in the 2020-2021 school year, to 19,402 in 2024-2025, to 27,041 in 2025-2026.
Six years ago, he noted, the number stood at under 13,000. Fifteen years ago, it was a few hundred.
A trajectory decades in the making
Israeli affairs analyst Esmat Mansour says this shift didn’t begin this year, nor was it imposed by sudden decree. It’s a trajectory that has accumulated for decades, starting with early attempts to impose the Israeli curriculum after the 1967 occupation of East Jerusalem, which was blocked by parent and teacher resistance, keeping the Jordanian curriculum in place for years.
“When the Palestinian Authority was established, the Palestinian curriculum became the city’s reference text,” Mansour told Mondoweiss. “But it never entered classrooms without passing through Israeli review. Books were revised before approval, so the cover stayed Palestinian while the content was reshaped from within. Today, that has escalated into something bolder: direct expansion of the Israeli curriculum itself, not as a marginal alternative but as a primary track competing for the city’s children”.
That pattern of internal revision is exactly what Hebrew University researcher Samira Alian documented in a recent academic study examining 28 social studies textbooks for grades three through ten. She found substantive changes to material on Jerusalem, Palestinian identity, colonialism, Zionism, and the Nakba: altered wording about Jerusalem itself, deleted or amended references to the occupation, changed lesson titles, and removed images tied to the wall and settlements. One textbook, the study found, excluded entire lessons on Palestinian political history, replaced with material carrying none of the same weight.
Imad Hawas, an Arabic teacher at a municipal school in Anata under Israeli jurisdiction, says the change can’t be reduced to a passing word.
“A textbook doesn’t just transmit information,” Hawas said. “It determines how a child learns to name a place, understand events, and connect the past to the present he lives in every day. When the word ‘Palestine’ changes, or a reference to the occupation is deleted, or the image of the wall a child sees with his own eyes on his way to school is altered, the material no longer stays what it was in its original version. It becomes another text, carrying a Palestinian title but different content.”

A former poet laureate and a Pulitzer winner lead TS Eliot prize shortlist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:15:34 UTC
01:15:34 KST

The former poet laureate Andrew Motion and Pulitzer prize winner Jorie Graham are among the 10 poets shortlisted for this year’s £25,000 TS Eliot prize, the UK and Ireland’s most prestigious award for a single volume of poetry.
Motion has been selected for Gravity Archives, while Graham, who was previously shortlisted in 2012, is on the list for Killing Spree.
Motion was the UK’s poet laureate between 1999 and 2009, and has written more than 15 poetry collections, alongside nonfiction books including biographies of Philip Larkin and John Keats. In a Guardian review, Sandeep Parmar wrote that Gravity Archives showcases Motion’s “rooted and resolute eye surveying the mortality of others as well as his own”.
Graham, who has published 16 collections, won the 1996 Pulitzer prize for poetry for The Dream of the Unified Field, a book of selected poems. In 2012, she was shortlisted for the TS Eliot prize for the collection PLACE, which won the Forward prize for best collection.
Along with Motion and Graham, this year’s shortlist features the British poet and writer Keith Jarrett, whose second collection, Hide Me Under the Blood and I Shall Be Satisfied, is also shortlisted for this year’s Forward prize. He is a poetry slam champion, and his work has previously been projected on to the facade of St Paul’s Cathedral.
Other shortlisted poets include Imani Mason Jordan, whose PIVOT is their debut collection; the Canadian poet Sylvia Legris, shortlisted for Sleep Gate; and Shara McCallum, whose collection Behold is her seventh.
“Though very different in voice, style and preoccupation, these 10 collections share a determination to meet the challenges faced in difficult times with closer attention to language,” said chair of judges and poet Leontia Flynn. “Each of these books reminds us why, when nothing else makes much sense, it’s to poetry we turn to reorient ourselves.”
The remaining poets on the list are 2022 Forward prize winner Kim Moore, for The House of Broken Things; Holly Pester, for Cafés; Jana Prikryl, for The Channel; and the Irish poet Billy Ramsell, for Render. Mason Jordan’s PIVOT is the only debut on the shortlist.
Flynn appeared on the judging panel alongside the poets Ishion Hutchinson and Daisy Lafarge. The 10 collections were selected from 174 submissions by 65 British and Irish publishers.
The prize was established in 1993 by the Poetry Book Society to mark its 40th anniversary and honour its founding poet, TS Eliot.
The winner will receive £25,000, with each shortlisted poet receiving £1,500. Last year’s prize was won by the Canadian poet Karen Solie for Wellwater. Other recent winners include Joelle Taylor, Jason Allen-Paisant, Anthony Joseph and Bhanu Kapil.
The shortlisted poets will read from their work at the Southbank Centre’s Royal Festival Hall in London on 17 January, with the winner announced at a ceremony at the Wallace Collection the following day.

When growth is not enough: housing and inflation, Sanchez's main challenges before elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:15:22 UTC
01:15:22 KST

Spain's economy is still outpacing the eurozone and employment is at its highest since 2008, but Sánchez's term end is marred by inflation, weak productivity and a housing crisis now dominating the election debate.
The President of the Spanish Government, Pedro Sánchez, will face the snap elections on 29 November hoping that the strong economic figures that have marked much of his time in office will help him overcome a widespread feeling across the country: macro-level growth is not enough.
Spain's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 2.8% in 2025 and is expected to continue expanding at a relatively brisk pace, with growth forecast at 2.4% for 2026, as the European Commission's country report on Spain points out (source in Spanish). Since the pandemic, moreover, Spain has grown faster than the main economies of the euro area.
However, as the protests over the housing crisis that have gripped the country for weeks make clear, that growth has not translated into an improvement in Spaniards' quality of life. The Commission attributes part of this to a sharp increase in the population, driven by migration flows, but also to weak labour productivity.
Hourly productivity has improved since 2019, but productivity per employee and per full-time worker has remained virtually flat. That is one of the main reasons why aggregate growth is not being reflected to the same extent in per capita income in a Spain that Sánchez has governed since June 2018.
Immigration, in fact, has become one of the engines of the Spanish labour market. While employment grew by 2.6% in 2025, the number of jobs filled by people born abroad accounted for 7.9% of all the posts created that year.
The latest consolidated figures nevertheless show that the labour market still has a strongly seasonal pattern. In August, unemployment rose by 44,419 people, to 2,355,918, although this was the lowest figure recorded in that month since 2007. In September, the jobless total increased again, by 23,587 people, which was also a low for that month since 2007.
The main pillar of Spanish growth has been the services sector, and specifically exports of services and tourism. Spain received 58.1 million international tourists between January and July 2026, an unprecedented figure and 4.6% more than a year earlier. Tourist spending rose by 7.8%, reaching a record 82.054 billion euros, according to the Frontur and Egatur data published (source in Spanish) by the National Statistics Institute (INE).
The European Commission stresses that the increase in exported services has helped widen the current account surplus and improve the country's international investment position. But it also warns that a significant share of activity remains concentrated in sectors with relatively low productivity, such as agriculture. More than 82% of the jobs created were in low-productivity activities, limiting the scope for wage growth.
Inflation adds another layer of tension. In September, annual inflation in the country stood at 5%, well above the 3.8% recorded on average in the euro area, and only behind Lithuania (6.1%), Bulgaria (5.6%), Cyprus and Luxembourg (5.2%) and Greece (5.1%).
In September, inflation in Spain stood at 4.9%. The INE mainly attributed the Spanish spike to rising fuel prices and the behaviour of package holidays.
Housing, the big problem
If there is one issue that sums up the imbalance between economic growth and quality of life, it is housing. Here, Spain faces a serious mismatch between supply and demand, both for buying and renting, especially in large cities and tourist areas.
"The severe rate of housing deprivation increased, which indicates poor living conditions", says the Commission's country report. Social housing accounts for barely between 1.5% and 1.7% of the total stock, compared with an average of between 6% and 7% in the European Union.
On top of that, prices have been rising steadily since 2014 and have accelerated in recent years, while high costs are also making labour mobility more difficult.
This is precisely where the economy and politics collided on Monday. After the Government failed to ratify two decrees last week to tackle the housing crisis because it lacked the support of its partners in Congress, Prime Minister Sánchez dissolved parliament and called elections for November.
Thus, the economic balance sheet of Sánchez's term in office so far has two sides: one in which Spain is growing, creating jobs and benefiting from the arrival of foreign workers and the strength of the tourism sector; and another, which GDP growth alone cannot solve, weighed down by low productivity, the loss of purchasing power and the difficulty of accessing housing.

Russia burned 628,000 new school textbooks in Kharkiv at the peak of back-to-school season
Unknown

16:14:23 UTC
01:14:23 KST

Russian missiles and drones destroyed 13 million Ukrainian books this summer, The Guardian reported. That is about a third of all books printed in Ukraine this year, the government estimates.
Russia is striking civilian warehouses, including those where publishers store their books. The uncertainty is pushing publishers toward safe international bestsellers, Publishers Weekly reported. "We'll all end up fed up with safe, non-risky books—if there are still publishers around to publish them," said Iryna Baturevych, co-founder of the publishing news outlet Chytomo.
Millions of Ukrainian books on fire
Ranok is one of Ukraine's largest publishing houses and a leader in children's literature and school textbooks. On one day in August, Russia destroyed more than 85% of its stock, The Guardian reported.
Viktor Kruhlov, the publisher's co-founder and chief executive, was on the warehouse floor at its headquarters in Kharkiv. The facility, built on the site of a former bread factory, covered about 10,000 m².
Together with five senior colleagues, he was discussing plans for the upcoming school year, the peak of the distribution season. Moments after the meeting began, a strike hit about 30 meters from where the staff had gathered. Kruhlov heard an explosion and almost at once saw a huge fire. As colleagues tried to put out the flames, a second strike came, and he realized there could be a third and a fourth, so the staff evacuated. Fifty people were on shift that day, and no one was injured, Kruhlov told The Guardian.
Eight million books, including 628,000 new school textbooks, were in the warehouse at the time. None could be saved. Firefighters battled the blaze for a week.
Several editorial staff members who saw the remains of the warehouse for the first time looked shaken as they recognized fragments of books they had helped create.
"When you see what was produced with your brain, with your hands, with your imagination, spoiled by Russia, it's an awful feeling," Kruhlov said.
He predicted shortages at Ranok's stores this fall, when the books in stock run out and there is nothing to replace them.
Literature is part of Ukrainian identity
Kruhlov is convinced that Russia deliberately targeted the book warehouse, but Bohdana Laiuk, Ukraine's deputy culture minister, sees the strikes as part of Russia's broader campaign against warehouses, The Guardian wrote.
"They cannot occupy Kyiv. So they target warehouses around Kyiv to take the possibility of everyday life from us—and books are part of everyday life," she said.
Books also matter to Russia's occupiers, Laiuk said.
"When the Russians occupy, the first thing they do—and we know this from the areas that were occupied and then liberated in 2022 in the Kherson and Kharkiv regions—is to go to the libraries, take the Ukrainian language books out, and destroy them," Laiuk said.
Before 2022, about 70% of the Ukrainian book market consisted of Russian-language titles, most of them imported from Russia.
Russian dominance in Ukrainian publishing developed over centuries, from tsarist bans on publishing in Ukrainian in the 19th century to Soviet Russification. Ukrainian writers were purged, and Ukrainian literature stayed in the shadow of Russian literature, the article notes.
Laiuk calls the dominance of Russian books a form of colonialism. Russia deliberately built its own information space in Ukraine through books, media, and television, she argues, so that everything would be ready for it once its tanks arrived.
Even after independence, a commercially successful Ukrainian-language novel was long seen as unlikely. But at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukrainian bookstores stopped selling Russian imports, and interest in Ukrainian literature grew, from 1920s classics and poetry to contemporary authors and translations.
"So people are asking: what does it actually mean to be Ukrainian? Literary culture gives us the place to understand who we are," Laiuk told The Guardian in 2023.
The future of Ukrainian literature is uncertain
Ranok is now rushing to reprint textbooks and bestsellers: schools need the former, while sales of popular titles will help the publisher make up for lost revenue.
For debut authors and writers of less commercial or experimental books, the situation is particularly difficult. Even before the strike on Ranok's warehouse, some publications had been delayed by attacks on printing infrastructure.
Ksenia Shpak's debut novel, an urban fantasy about a girl displaced from eastern Ukraine to the Carpathians, was due out in February 2025 but was published only that November, the article says. Half of the print run was in Ranok's Kharkiv warehouse when it was attacked.
It was her first published book, and Shpak fears the publisher will now focus on bestsellers and reprint her novel only if money allows. The Ukrainian book market is also feeling demand level off and the cost of living rise, she said.
Despite the loss of 8 million books, Kruhlov remained optimistic. Looking over the ruined warehouse in Kharkiv, he said he planned to rebuild everything—and to do it better.

How light became a remote control for the brain, and won a Nobel Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:14:11 UTC
01:14:11 KST

Optogenetics, the technique that lets scientists control brain cells with light, has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine for their work in light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, a method that lays the foundation "of a new era in neuroscience", the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet announced on Monday.
But what exactly is optogenetics, and how did the laureates develop the technique?
Optogenetics is a method for controlling selected cells using light as a remote control. It allows scientists to switch cells on or off in a living brain and investigate how particular cells and neural circuits influence behaviour.
This new method was given the name optogenetics in 2006, but the story behind the technique began more than a decade earlier, when Peter Hegemann was studying the unicellular alga Chlamydomonas, an organism famous for swimming towards light.
Hegemann wanted to understand what makes algae move towards light. He studied its eyespot, a tiny orange dot on the cell’s surface that detects light. Through a series of experiments, Hegemann and his colleagues identified light-sensitive proteins called channelrhodopsins, which allow algae to detect light and respond to it.
Together with Georg Nagel at the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics in Frankfurt, he inserted the algal genes into frog egg cells and human kidney cells and proved that channelrhodopsin was indeed a light-controlled ion channel.
When exposed to blue light, the channel opened in just 0.2 milliseconds, allowing positively charged ions to flood into the cell and generate a tiny electrical impulse.
Years later, Karl Deisseroth, the third laureate, introduced the channelrhodopsin gene into rat nerve cells. By shining blue light on the cells, they could trigger nerve signals, showing that the protein could act as a light-controlled switch. He then used the technique to control nerve cells in the brains of living mice.
For example, scientists could trigger movements in a mouse's whiskers or wake sleeping mice simply by switching on a light.
What does the future hold?
The discovery “provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, in a press release.
Optogenetics is currently used primarily as a research tool. By allowing researchers to turn targeted cell types on or off using pulses of light, it enables scientists to establish direct cause-and-effect relationships between neural activity, brain function, and behaviour.
It allows researchers to map the neurons involved in emotional states such as fear, anxiety or reward. They can also map specific neural circuits governing pain, thirst, attention or aggression.
Optogenetics is also widely used in research into neurological or psychiatric conditions such as depression, schizophrenia, anxiety, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease and epilepsy.
The science has also entered clinical trials to treat retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic disease that causes blindness due to the loss of light-detecting cells in the retina.
By delivering light-sensitive opsin genes into surviving retinal cells, researchers have enabled a blind patient wearing light-emitting goggles to regain partial vision and perceive high-contrast objects.
