As Air Force Goes Big on Autonomy, Are Cargo Drones Next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:13:38 UTC
01:13:38 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force’s plans to field 1,000 semi-autonomous fighter and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance drones within just a few years made headlines at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference last month.
But beyond the service’s signature Collaborative Combat Aircraft and Massed Modular Aircraft programs, a half-dozen or so firms are pitching another kind of autonomous aircraft: cargo drones to solve some of the thorniest logistics problems.
Textron Aviation and Merlin Labs unveiled a cockpit-less Cessna equipped with Merlin’s autonomy software and a nose hatch opening to a cavernous cargo bay.
“By pairing a proven aircraft platform with autonomy technology, we’re exploring new approaches to contested logistics operations while also examining how autonomy may enable more efficient cargo aircraft designs that increase usable volume, improve cargo accessibility and support mission sustainment requirements,” Bob Gibbs, Textron’s vice president for defense and special mission sales, said of the company’s Cessna SkyuCourier UX concept.
Reliable Robotics is offering its own modified Cessna 208B Caravan. Its aircraft flew in multiple Agile Flag exercises in 2024, installing actuators, sensors, and other gear in the cockpit and using a human pilot to command high-level direction from a ground station. Reliable announced a $17.4 million deal with the Air Force in 2025 to provide an aircraft for a yearlong test.
In a May blog post, Reliable’s certification flight test lead Chris Baughman wrote that the firm is targeting the start of fiscal 2027 to begin the test, which will focus on the Indo-Pacific region. The company is also seeking FAA certification for its autonomy software to operate in U.S. airspace, targeting 2028 for that certification.
Joby Aviation, which previously acquired autonomy startup Xwing, is also flying a modified Cessna Caravan, racking up 40 hours and 7,000 miles during last summer’s Resolute Force Pacific. Joby did not exhibit at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber, but sought to capitalize on the timing by announcing soon after that it completed 3,199 miles of autonomous flight across the U.S. this summer, including stops at Shaw Air Force Base, S.C., and near Washington D.C. At a press event Sept. 24, Joby’s Head of Defense Policy John Barranco told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the aircraft carried a safety pilot for those flights in case human intervention was needed, but the autonomy software never required a pilot intervention.
Coming at the same time that other vendors are developing autonomous fighters and reconnaissance aircraft with clean-sheet designs, the modified Cessnas might seem like minimalist efforts. But aviation firms see a gap they can fill in the Air Force’s logistics enterprise, a small airlifter that can do jobs that USAF’s workhorse C-130 cannot do as efficiently. The Hercules can haul 40,000 pounds of cargo, and the Air Force has only about 270. A Cessna could be ideal for shorter hops and smaller loads at a fraction of the cost.
“It’s a really robust, reliable existing cargo airframe that’s in the world, and there are many of them, and so we can retrofit a lot of those for the customers,” Barranco said.
USAF officials have spent years talking about Agile Combat Employment—the concept of dispersing small teams of Airmen and aircraft from large bases to operate from remote or austere locations and move quickly to counter adversary long-range missile attacks. But the ACE logistics is complex, especially in the vast and watery Indo-Pacific region.
Having small, unmanned aircraft to island-hop and resupply those forces so they can generate airpower—without taxing manned airlifters—could be a solution.
“Historically it’s about a logistics train where you’re trying to move a really big airframe and move a lot of stuff, and that takes time, and it takes Airmen, and it takes support, and that’s a really important mission,” said Barranco. “Sometimes you need to move a lot less really, really quickly, without standing up a mission, without 24 hours’ notice, without pulling folks together.”
Other concepts are also emerging to chase this possible market. DZYNE Technologies put its autonomous cargo drone, called Grasshopper, on display.
DZYNE and the Air Force Research Laboratory unveiled Grasshopper last May, as a self-guided glider capable of carrying up to 500 pounds after being dropped out the back of a C-130; from there, it could glide tens of miles to resupply troops in “high-risk environments.”
DZYNE has since offered a “Long-Range” powered variant with a turbine engine that can fly “10 times” further than Grasshopper and launched from “standoff” distances.
U.S. Special Operations Command has tested the concept, using the Long-Range Grasshopper in Exercise Trojan Footprint 26 in Romania and North Macedonia, where the drones were launched from a Romanian Air Force C-27J.
But the firms pursuing this niche want more than a narrow special ops use case, focusing on any mission where moving cargo quickly without risking crews could be attractive.
Grid Aero won $6 million in seed funding from the Air Force’s innovation arm, AFWERX, last August. CEO Arthur Dubois compared his company’s drone to a “flying pickup” truck at the time, saying it would be able to carry somewhere between 1,000 and 8,000 pounds from “Guam to Japan,” for example, a trek of some 1,500 miles.
Grid Aero’s Lifter Lite hasn’t made its first flight yet, but the firm was among seven selected in September to compete for the Air Force’s Massed Modular Aircraft program. It’s unclear if Lifter Lite or some other design is what the company envisions as its entry.
Dubois said last year that the idea for Lifter Lite sprang from asking military and commercial air cargo stakeholders about their pain points. For the military, that’s executing logistics in areas where U.S. assets could be attacked.
Lt. Gen. Kenyon K. Bell, deputy chief of staff for logistics, engineering, and force protection, noted as much during the conference: “The era of uncontested logistics is over,” Bell declared. “We will have to continue to fight our way in from a logistics standpoint and be able to sustain and regenerate ourselves while we’re in contact. … That is a concept that we certainly need to think through.”
Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach endorsed the concept of autonomous cargo drones during a media roundtable at the conference, albeit without completely committing to it.
“We believe that there’s some value in that as well,” he said in response to a question. “It certainly could be valuable in the Pacific, with the ranges that we’re talking about. And so we’re looking at several different options and evaluating them, but I would say, no program of record just yet, but certainly taking a look at some demonstrators and the like to see what’s available to us.”
Congress and Pentagon officials are also tuning in. When Undersecretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael culled the department’s list of “critical technology areas” from 14 to just six last November, “contested logistics technology” survived the cut.
The House Armed Services Committee directed the the Air Force to present a briefing on the topic in their version of the 2027 defense policy bill. Lawmakers also expect a proposed timeline for developing an acquisition strategy that could include rapid prototyping. They also want a strategy for the use of “low-cost and attritable Group 4 and 5 unmanned aircraft systems in contested logistics operations.”
Staff Writers Matthew Cox and Stephen Losey contributed reporting.

Britain's national security adviser made an undisclosed visit to Israel last week but failed to reach a deal to prevent the closure of the U.K. Consulate in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem, three sources familiar with the talks said.
Jonathan Powell, whose visit has not been disclosed by Britain's government, held talks with Israeli officials but failed to reach an agreement to keep the consulate open, said the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Israel on Sept. 8 ordered Britain to close the East Jerusalem consulate within 30 days and remove its diplomats from the city, after Britain said it would ban goods made in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
France and Canada joined in the sanctions. Israel has not taken action against them.
The incident highlighted growing frustration among Israel's longtime allies over its unlawful settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law.
The 30-day deadline for Britain to close the consulate runs out on Thursday. Two of the sources said talks were still ongoing, and while an agreement to keep it open was possible, it is unlikely one would be struck by the Thursday deadline.
Asked about Powell's visit and talks with London over the consulate, a spokesperson for Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar told Reuters that it would close on Thursday, as announced.
A U.K. government spokesperson had no immediate comment.
In announcing the sanctions, Britain said that Israel's actions were undermining the possibility of a two-state solution - the idea of a Palestinian state co-existing peacefully alongside Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government openly rejects the idea of Palestinian statehood.
Britain cited Israeli government-backed plans to expand illegal settlements and rising settler violence targeting Palestinians in the West Bank. The British sanctions are to take effect next year.
The British consulate, in the Sheikh Jarrah neighborhood of East Jerusalem, handles the country's relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza. It also provides consular services to Palestinians.
The British sanctions announcement and Israel's response marked a new low in the relationship between the once steadfast allies. Britain has repeatedly criticized Israel over its violations in the war in Gaza and over Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians.

Monday, 5 October 2026, 18:16
PHOTO Pexels
Font size
Some 58% of Bulgarians have no money set aside for unexpected expenses, while only one in 10 could manage for more than six months without an income, according to a nationally representative survey conducted by polling agency Trend.
The survey, the third in a series commissioned jointly by Finance Academy and UBB Asset Management, found that 67% of respondents do not save money and 91% do not invest. Nearly half of Bulgarians (49%) describe their standard of living as average, with the proportion higher among people under 60.
Respondents were far more likely to associate an improvement in their standard of living with earning additional income than with saving or investing money they already have.

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin
PHOTO BGNES
Font size
Bulgaria and 16 other EU member states have called for cohesion and agricultural funding to be maintained in the bloc’s 2028–2034 budget, the Bulgarian government press office said.
In a joint letter to European Council President António Costa and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, whose country holds the rotating EU Council presidency, the leaders warned that cuts could weaken the EU budget and public support for the bloc. The 17 countries, known as the Friends of Cohesion group, are seeking to protect funding for cohesion policy and the Common Agricultural Policy as negotiations continue over the EU’s next long-term budget.
They said new priorities, including security and defence, competitiveness, energy security and resilience, should receive adequate additional resources rather than be funded at the expense of cohesion policy and agriculture.
The appeal comes ahead of an EU summit on October 15–16, when leaders are due to discuss the 2028–2034 budget.

Norway plans temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:11:31 UTC
01:11:31 KST

Norway is planning a temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places, amid rising global concern at the spread of the AI-enabled recording devices.
The Oslo government is planning a bill to prevent the use of the camera-enabled spectacles in parks, beaches, museums, shopping centres, schools, daycare centres, healthcare facilities, gyms and public events, although private use would still be allowed.
There is already a growing patchwork of restrictions on the use of the glasses including in UK and US courtrooms and in pubs, cinemas and restaurants where owners have raised privacy fears.
Torgeir Micaelsen, Norway’s minister of digital affairs, said he was “worried that new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without knowing it”.
“We do not want a society where people worry about being recorded without their knowledge, photographed or filmed in places and situations where they are accustomed to not being monitored,” he said.
Norway’s Labour party, which heads a minority government, needs the support of other parties to pass the proposed ban. It said it planned to submit a bill “as soon as possible”, while tasking an expert group with drawing up permanent regulations on the issue.
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta sells “smart” versions of Ray-Ban and Oakley glasses that allow users to film, take photos, make phone calls, play music and execute AI prompts. It has sold at least 9m pairs of the Ray-Ban versions since the start of 2023.
In the UK restaurateurs such as Jeremy King, who created the Wolseley and Delaunay restaurants, and pub chain Wetherspoons have already said they do not want customers using the devices. Cinemas said in August they had begun introducing policies to ban or restrict the use of smart glasses citing both privacy and film piracy concerns.
Last week the governor of California, Gavin Newsom, vetoed legislation that would have penalised citizens for using smart glasses to record people without their permission in changing rooms, doctors’ offices and other spaces people generally consider private. The state already has laws governing unlawful recording.
In France, the child welfare group E-enfance said it had this year received about 20 reports of women being filmed without their knowledge using glasses fitted with a camera, the majority of which involved Meta smart glasses. It said the incidents often followed the same pattern: a young girl or woman approached in a public place, filmed without her knowledge, with the clip then posted on social media in the form of a prank or a street interview.
Meta has stressed that each pair of glasses is fitted with a tamper-proof LED light that blinks white when the user is recording or taking pictures. It advises users: “Not everyone loves being photographed. Stop recording if anyone expresses that they would rather you not.”
A Meta spokesperson said: “We’re excited that our glasses continue to be very popular for listening to music, making calls, or getting live translations, so we’re continuing to expand styles and features around the world. Every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video. It can’t be turned off and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it -- something smartphones and other camera’s don’t have.”

PHOTO Facebook / Мяра
Font size
If Bulgaria’s presidential election were held in early October, 46.9% of voters would back Iliana Iotova and Kiril Valchev, compared with 25.3% for Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev, according to a survey by polling agency Myara.
Kostadin Kostadinov and Petar Volgin would receive 8.8%, followed by Ivelin Mihaylov and Yuliana Mateeva with 4.2%, Ivan Hristanov and Stoyanka Cherkezova with 2.7%, and Radostin Vasilev and Krasimir Manov with 2.2%.

Expected voter turnout stands at 35.4%, based on respondents’ stated intentions, the agency said.
The independent survey was conducted between September 26 and October 4 through face-to-face interviews and an online questionnaire among 1,000 Bulgarian adults. It has a maximum margin of sampling error of ±3.1 percentage points for a 50% share. One percentage point of the total sample, rather than of those intending to vote, represents approximately 53,000 people.

Separatists win Quebec election in test for Canada PM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:08:47 UTC
01:08:47 KST

Quebec separatists vow independence vote after provincial election win
The separatist Parti Québécois won provincial elections on Monday, but fell just short of enough seats to govern alone in Canada's French-speaking province, Quebec. The victory comes just two weeks ahead of a vote in Alberta, Canada's economic powerhouse, on whether it wants to begin the process of leaving the country.
Separatists won provincial elections in Quebec on Monday, with a promise to hold a vote on leaving Canada after US President Donald Trump leaves office, testing Prime Minister Mark Carney's message of national unity.
But the Parti Québécois fell short of a majority government in Canada's French-speaking province, offering some solace for the federalist camp.
The PQ win still upends Canada's political landscape as the country confronts a trade war and annexation threats levelled by the United States.
It also comes just two weeks before Canada's oil-producing province of Alberta, an economic powerhouse, holds a vote on whether it wants to begin the process of leaving Canada.
Read moreCarney says Alberta 'essential' to Canada as separatist push advances
The results make PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, a 49-year-old lawyer known by his initials PSPP, Quebec's next premier.
At a jubilant victory party in Montreal, he invoked "the courageous struggle" francophones have endured in a part of the world increasingly dominated by English speakers.
That struggle "will find meaning when (francophones) obtain their own country", he said.
"We deserve it," he added, calling a referendum a chance "to decide what our national future will be".
Independence after Trump?
Carney congratulated PSPP, saying that "building a stronger Quebec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada".
The prime minister is popular in Quebec, and the separatist win was not seen as a repudiation of his stance toward Trump, whose confrontational policies have infuriated Canadians.
Instead, the PQ's rise after more than a decade in opposition has been tied to frustration over affordability and an enduring desire to protect the French language in a majority anglophone country.
Surveys suggest that only about 30 percent of Quebecers want independence, but PSPP has maintained he will call a referendum on leaving Canada, just not while Trump is in office.
He has said a decision on Quebec's independence "requires conditions that allow for an informed and calm debate".
That shouldn't be "hijacked by the theatrics of an unpredictable president", he added, ruling out a referendum until at least 2029.
Read moreTrump threatens EU with tariffs over 'laughable' Canada association plan
Quebec has held two previous votes on leaving Canada. Federalists won comfortably in 1980, but the 1995 result was excruciatingly close, with just 50.58 percent voting to stay in Canada.
First-time voter Alexia Gomez, 19, invoked tensions with the United States when she told AFP she opposed an independence referendum.
"If Quebec becomes independent it would make us politically, economically and militarily vulnerable," she said.
Lydie Periard, a 22-year-old student, said she was "very worried" by the PQ's victory, condemning what she termed the party's "populist" stance on immigration. The PQ has backed immigration cuts, particularly for non-French speakers.
The PQ replaces a party, known as the Coalition for Quebec's Future (CAQ), that advocated strongly for the province's distinctive culture within Canada, without supporting separatism.
Lacking a majority, the PQ will struggle to advance its separatist agenda.
The two largest opposition parties after Monday's vote, the Liberals and Conservatives, both declared they would never back a referendum on independence.
'Abolish the monarchy?'
PSPP may not have majority backing for an independent Quebec, but his plans to target the British monarchy appear far more popular.
Canada is part of the British Commonwealth. King Charles III, Canada's head of state, is represented in Ottawa by the governor general. Lieutenant governors represent the monarchy in the provinces, including Quebec.
In a 2025 Leger poll, 87 percent of Quebecers said they felt no attachment to the British monarchy, and only 31 percent expressed a favorable view of King Charles.
PSPP has said his government could cut off funds for the lieutenant governor, calling it a "masquerade that wastes money".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Glasgow city council reaches pay deal with union to avert fire-and-rehire plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:08:14 UTC
01:08:14 KST

Glasgow city council has reached an agreement with the trade union Unison over pay and grading, averting one of the UK’s biggest ever fire-and-rehire exercises.
Talks between the council and the GMB, Unite and Unison unions previously broke down when Unison refused to ballot its members on a new pay and grading system, designed to resolve historical equal pay issues.
The collapse of talks prompted the council to contact 23,000 workers, its entire non-teaching staff, at the end of last month to inform them they were at risk of being dismissed and reappointed, many on less favourable terms. The move led to significant backlash from opposition parties, unions and council employees.
The original proposal that led Unison to walk out of negotiations would have resulted in wage cuts for 11% of staff, but on Monday the council agreed to protect their pay for three years.
Unison said many issues remained unresolved and that negotiations would continue, but that it would ballot its members this month. The council has agreed to continue negotiating on issues including the equality impacts of the new pay structure.
Ricky Bell, the leader of Glasgow city council, said he was “delighted that we have been able to reach agreement with Unison” and “remove the unpalatable prospect of fire-and-rehire”.
“This is a strong and fair deal,” he added. “Both GMB and Unite have already agreed to take it to their members and, with all three unions now engaging with their memberships, we are moving closer to the outcome we have always wanted to achieve: ending pay discrimination in Glasgow city council once and for all.”
Bell emphasised there was no further money to come as part of the package, but said he looked forward to seeing the outcome of the union ballots. He thanked the Scottish government for additional support to help “unlock [the] agreement”.
Chris Sermanni, Unison’s Glasgow city branch secretary, said: “Unison stood firm because Glasgow’s workers deserved better than what was originally put on the table.
“That position has secured significant movement. There’s now a path for Unison members to give their verdict without the immediate threat of dismissal and re-engagement hanging over them.
“The period ahead will be used to keep fighting to give the whole workforce the information they need to make their decision.”
The ballot will last four weeks, with a timeline to be laid out in the coming days.

Sanction Israel to save Palestinian state, officials tell EU

Sanction Israel immediately to save Palestinian state, officials tell EU
More than 500 former European politicians and diplomats have urged the EU to take immediate action against the Israeli government as it prepares to move forward with the E1 settlement designed to block the establishment of a Palestinian state in the occupied West Bank.
Writing in the French newspaper Libération, the officials called on European governments to agree to an EU-wide trade ban on Israeli settlements and impose sanctions on all banks and companies involved in the settlement project.
Among the names attached to the list are former French prime ministers Dominique de Villepin and Alain Juppe, former Belgian prime minister Yves Leterme, and former EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell.
The E1 area is situated between occupied East Jerusalem and the Maale Adumim settlement bloc. If built, the project would effectively cut the West Bank in two, making a future contiguous Palestinian state impossible.
Israel's attorney-general recently postponed a construction tender for 1,234 housing units until after the 27 October general election, though a second tender for 2,167 units is expected to open two days before the vote.
"The time has undoubtedly come for the EU and its member states to act," the former officials wrote ahead of next week's meeting of European foreign ministers.
"The 27 will meet after another year of violence and ethnic cleansing by the Israeli government against the Palestinian people in Gaza and the West Bank," the op-ed read.
Successive attempts to impose EU-wide sanctions on Israel have been scuppered by close Israeli allies Germany and Italy, which have blocked the qualified majority needed to partially suspend the association agreement.
In the absence of an EU-wide consensus, several European countries are implementing trade bans with Israeli settlements, including France, the Netherlands, Ireland, Spain, Norway and Belgium.
Meanwhile, the UK last month became the first G7 country to announce plans to impose sanctions on Israeli banks, construction companies, and real estate firms involved in the settlements.
"While the fact that some EU member states have taken national action against illegal settlements is to be welcomed, others, notably Germany and Italy, continue to systematically block the adoption of measures at the European level, thus becoming de facto complicit in the weakening of EU values and the two-state solution," the op-ed said.

NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party on Monday came down heavily on Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi and accused him of misleading the public over the Supreme Court's observation on Form 6 and the Election Commission's decision on the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra compared Rahul's claims to the Congress leader's earlier statements on the Rafale issue.
"Rahul Gandhi misled the public on two counts. First, he claimed that Form 6 was illegal - specifically mentioning the Bharatiya Janata Party in this context. However, the Court did not declare Form 6 illegal today. It noted that the petition mentioned a modification to Form 6, so the Court said it would look into the matter," Patra said."We had not consented to any such modification. If any modification has indeed taken place, that will become clear only after a notice is issued. Yet, when we read the detailed order and look at the Election Commission's press release dated September 26, 2026, it becomes evident that the Commission had clearly stated there were no changes to Form 6 and that the Supreme Court had validated the declaration form attached to it," he said.
This comes hours after Rahul Gandhi alleged that the CEC had changed Form 6 "illegally and unilaterally", citing the Supreme Court's observation which came earlier in the day."It is now established beyond doubt that Gyanesh Kumar changed Form 6 illegally and unilaterally. This is just one more proof of him abusing his position to help the BJP," Rahul said."He and everyone else involved in this criminal assault on our democracy will be held accountable," he added.The Congress leader also shared a screenshot of the September 26 Election Commission statement which read: "The declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court. For non-SIR period, the Forms applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used."In its response, the EC said the order for the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Bihar, issued on June 24, 2025, had received the unanimous approval of the Commission and was subsequently upheld by the Supreme Court in its judgment dated May 27, 2026.EC officials also clarified that Form 6 itself had not been changed, but that a declaration had been attached to the form under the Bihar SIR order, as quoted by PTI.This came after the Supreme Court said it had not approved any modification to Form 6 used by the EC during the SIR exercise in various states."Any modification to Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let's be clear. When records are produced, we would like to see who has modified it," a bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said.
What is Form 6
Form 6 is the application used by eligible voters for inclusion in the electoral roll.The declaration was attached to Form 6 during the Bihar SIR, which began with the EC's June 24, 2025, order. The declaration sought additional details, including information about the applicant's parents.
According to EC officials, the form itself remained unchanged, while the declaration was a separate document attached to it for the SIR exercise. Outside SIR, the forms prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, apply.The declaration was later withdrawn from the EC's online portals.The online version of Form 6 and the declaration also used a single OTP for both, rather than requiring separate OTP verification, which had led to suggestions that the declaration was part of Form 6.

Ukraine’s Farsight Vision Builds Ground Robot Navigation to Work Without GPS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

01:06:49 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Farsight Vision Builds Ground Robot Navigation to Work Without GPS
Ukrainian defense technology company Farsight Vision presented a navigation module on October 5 that allows ground robotic systems to orient themselves without GPS by combining laser sensing with 3D terrain data.
Oboronka reported the development on October 5, citing information provided by Farsight Vision. The system generates a real-time point cloud around the vehicle, identifying obstacles, holes, slopes, and other terrain features while refining its planned route.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The solution is based on the concept of a digital twin of the terrain," Farsight Vision stated. The company explained that operators receive a continuously updated model of the surrounding area rather than relying solely on satellite imagery.
Before a mission, the FSV Platform creates a 3D model of the terrain. During movement, the onboard module adds sensor-generated point cloud data to the model, allowing the operator to compare the vehicle's actual surroundings with the planned route.
If GPS becomes unavailable and the ground system loses its position, the combination of the prebuilt 3D model and live sensor data helps restore orientation. The three-dimensional view can also show terrain geometry that may be difficult to assess through a conventional video feed.
Farsight Vision CEO Viktoriia Yaremchuk noted that the company wants to eliminate the need to launch a separate reconnaissance drone simply to guide a ground robotic system. Such support creates additional risk and consumes resources, she added.
"By the end of the year, Farsight Vision aims to enable the drone to autonomously return to the point where communication was lost or to a designated base," Yaremchuk stated. The initial target is several kilometers, with later scaling to 30–40 kilometers at the platform's maximum speed.
Earlier, on September 24, Ukraine codified the domestically produced Varkhan ground robotic complex, a 4×4 platform that can carry up to 300 kilograms over 37 kilometers to positions where sending personnel would be too risky.
Unmanned ground vehicles completed more than 25,000 logistics and evacuation missions in August alone, up from 7,511 in January. Kyiv aims to build at least 50,000 combat and logistics ground robots this year.

Ukraine Adds New Varkhan 4×4 Ground Robot to Its Military Arsenal. Here’s What It Can Do

Ukraine Adds New Varkhan 4×4 Ground Robot to Its Military Arsenal. Here’s What It Can Do
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense has codified and approved the domestically produced Varkhan unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) for use by the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the ministry announced on October 5.
The Varkhan is designed primarily for military logistics missions, including transporting weapons, ammunition, equipment, and other supplies. According to the ministry, the system was developed by a Ukrainian defense company in response to operational requirements provided by the military.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The UGV is built on a four-wheel-drive 4×4 chassis with dependent suspension and ground clearance of more than 200 millimeters. Its design allows the vehicle to operate across difficult terrain, including off-road conditions, marshy ground, and sand.
The platform is also equipped with quick-release batteries, allowing operators to replace power sources and continue missions without extended interruptions.
During testing, the Varkhan demonstrated the ability to transport hundreds of kilograms of cargo over distances of several dozen kilometers, according to the Defense Ministry. The platform is also equipped with several communication and control systems.
The ministry said the UGV was designed for sustained operation in high-intensity combat conditions, with an emphasis on durability, straightforward controls, accessible spare parts and consumables, and ease of maintenance.
According to the statement, the Varkhan also forms part of a broader ecosystem of unmanned-system equipment that includes T-Bone ground control stations, antennas, masts, repeaters, and rotating mechanisms. Together, these components are designed to provide integrated control of unmanned systems and maintain stable communications.
Ukrainian forces in the Sumy region managed to retrieve an unmanned ground vehicle damaged by a mine after receiving help from a local woman who happened to be cycling past the area, Ukraine’s 71st Separate Airmobile Brigade reported.
The brigade said the UGV struck a mine during a combat mission, putting the damaged vehicle at risk of being lost.

Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Russian attacks have repeatedly caused damage to Amic Energy’s infrastructure in Ukraine. The latest strike targeted an oil depot that had already been seriously damaged at the start of the full-scale invasion.
In the first weeks of the war, Russian troops entered the site. At that time, the oil depot was full of fuel, which Amic Energy reported to the relevant Ukrainian authorities to ensure the supplies were not used by the occupying forces. As a result of the fighting on the depot’s premises, four storage tanks were burnt out and process equipment was damaged. Now this same facility has been hit again — this time by a direct Russian attack.
“The most important thing for us is that none of our employees were harmed. This is by no means Amic Energy’s first loss. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, three of the company’s oil depots, a data centre and several petrol stations have been damaged. And that’s not even counting the petrol stations the company has lost as a result of the occupation of part of Ukraine’s territory. That’s why we understand, not just in theory but from our own experience, just how real these threats are, and what the cost of this war is,” says Gintaras Macijauskas, CEO of Amic Energy in Ukraine.
Despite the damage to its infrastructure, the Amic Energy network continues to operate as normal. The company is stepping up security measures and working on additional solutions to protect its staff, including the installation of mobile shelters near petrol stations.
Amic Energy is also documenting the losses incurred by the company as a result of Russian aggression and is asserting its right to compensation. In 2023, the company filed a claim to this effect with the European Court of Human Rights. According to preliminary estimates, the amount of damages claimed in this case exceeds 300 million hryvnias — approximately 8.5 million euros.

Flávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:05:20 UTC
01:05:20 KST

Flávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, leaving progressive voters reeling.
The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.
“Miracles are possible in politics. But I don’t see that happening,” the political scientist Miguel Lago said of Lula’s chances of snapping back. “I don’t see Flávio losing this election now.”
Speaking outside the White House on Monday, Donald Trump told reporters: “Well, it’s a big victory: close but a very, very big victory. Amazing, actually.”
Trump, who is a longtime ally of the Bolsonaro family, predicted the runoff would be “a very close election”.
The far-right surge was a triumph – albeit an incomplete one – for the Bolsonaro clan and its 71-year-old patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro.
The disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, saw four relatives elected to congress. His 44-year-old wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, won a seat in the senate, as did his second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, who is 43. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, 28-year-old Jair Renan Bolsonaro, and the ex-president’s 62-year-old brother, Renato Bolsonaro, both won seats in the lower house of congress.
Across Latin America’s biggest democracy, key congressional and gubernatorial races were also won by staunch Bolsonaristas including Tarcísio de Freitas, who was re-elected as the governor of São Paulo state, and Sérgio Moro, who was elected governor of the southern state of Paraná. Both men were ministers during Bolsonaro’s 2018-22 government.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) will now boast the largest caucus in the senate with 28 of its 81 seats. Combined with the seats of other hard-right parties, that number rises to 43, giving the movement an upper house majority.
Meanwhile, pro-Lula senate candidates, including the former environment minister Marina Silva, the leftwing veteran Benedita da Silva, and the centrist former planning minister Simone Tebet, suffered bitter defeats.
Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, two young Bolsonarista social media warriors, became the best-voted congresspeople in Brazilian history, securing more than 3m votes.
“We are experiencing a revolution … The far right is growing in a very consistent way, election after election,” said Lago, calling the election the worst for progressive and moderate centrist parties since the late 80s.
Lago believed Lula had managed to interrupt the advance of Bolsonaro’s populist movement in 2022, thanks to positive voter memories of his first two terms, from 2002 to 2010. Back then, a global commodities boom allowed Brazil’s first working-class president to fund major social welfare programmes that helped millions escape poverty. “But it was just an interregnum,” Lago said.
Control of the senate should allow pro-Bolsonaro politicians to approve an amnesty for their movement’s charismatic leader, allowing the former president to emerge from the Brasília mansion where he is living under house arrest and reassert his leadership of the far right.
“I think he will be freed and I think he will be very important during Flávio Bolsonaro’s [presidency],” said Lago. “Flávio will be running the country and [Jair] Bolsonaro will be doing what he has always done: leading the revolution.”
The senate majority may also help Bolsonaro’s third son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, return from self-imposed exile in the US. The 42-year-old, who has close ties to Donald Trump’s Maga movement, was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison earlier this year for coercion – the result of his lobbying the Trump administration to interfere in his father’s coup trial. Eduardo Bolsonaro reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.
The result is good news for Trump, who has been accused of trying to sway the election in Bolsonaro’s favour, and his attempt to expand the conservative “orange wave” sweeping Latin America to its biggest democracy and economy. Recent years have seen a succession of pro-Trump presidents win power in the region, from Costa Rica, Honduras and El Salvador to Chile and Colombia.
One of Trump’s most enthusiastic regional cheerleaders, the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, celebrated Bolsonaro’s “historic” victory against “the communist Lula”. “The American continent belongs to citizens who want to live in freedom,” Milei wrote on X.
The prime minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, wished Bolsonaro “good luck in the final” and celebrated his “great victory”. He wrote on X: “I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil.”
Speaking after Sunday’s result was confirmed, Lula put a brave face on what analysts called a catastrophic night for the left. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil,” he said, vowing to expose his rival’s “dark past”, which involves well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld and corruption allegations, which Bolsonaro has denied.
But the mood at Lula’s post-election event was reportedly funereal and Bolsonaro goes into the second round as the firm favourite. He is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates – Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema – who, between them, won more than 5.5m votes.
Santos quickly announced he would endorse neither candidate, considering both Lula and Bolsonaro to be “crooks”. Zema has vowed to vote against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) in the runoff, while Caiado has yet to declare his intentions.
Lula’s best hope may be convincing some of the record 33 million Brazilians who did not vote to turn out next time. “He will need to mobilise these apathetic voters who, in a sense, have already abandoned politics, which will be an extremely difficult task,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right.
Rocha has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters and identified “a great deal of voter apathy, especially among those who are not aligned with Bolsonarismo, and who could potentially vote for Lula”.
Although Flávio Bolsonaro has held political office for more than 20 years, “for undecided voters, his main positive characteristic is this idea of ‘renewal’, despite his possible involvement in corruption and with paramilitary groups,” Rocha added.
Lago believed only a dramatic shift from Lula’s campaign – such as changing the candidate, or a severe scandal involving Bolsonaro – could change the election’s outcome. But he was doubtful that would occur.

Brazil's Lula weighs VP Alckmin as next finance minister to woo centrist voters
BRASILIA, Oct 5 - Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is considering tapping Vice President Geraldo Alckmin to be his next finance minister if re-elected, two people familiar with the proposal said, in a bid to bolster his fiscal credibility and win over centrist voters after Senator Flavio Bolsonaro beat expectations in the first-round vote.
Under the proposal, Alckmin would remain vice president while also becoming finance minister next year, cementing his authority over economic policy, the sources said, speaking on condition of anonymity because the deliberations are private. The proposal is still under discussion.
The Brazilian presidency did not respond to a request for comment.
Alckmin, a veteran centrist, unsuccessfully challenged Lula for the presidency in 2006 and has served two terms as governor of Sao Paulo. He also ran Lula's Development, Industry and Trade Ministry until earlier this year, making him a key interlocutor with Washington since the US imposed sweeping tariffs on Brazilian goods.
Alckmin is widely considered a moderating force in Lula's government, with strong ties to the business community, although critics say his influence has been overshadowed in Lula's current term by policies widely seen as tilting to the left.
Lula also considered making Alckmin his finance minister in 2022 but ultimately chose Workers' Party member Fernando Haddad as finance minister after winning in both the first and second rounds.
Seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, Lula finished second on Sunday behind Senator Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro and an ally of Trump, in a first-round result that defied most polling forecasts, which had pointed to a narrow lead for the president.
The outcome, along with the electoral success of Bolsonaro's right-wing allies in Congress, sparked a strong market rally on Monday as investors bet a Bolsonaro administration would be more likely to deliver faster fiscal consolidation with broader legislative support.
Since Lula took office, Brazil's gross public debt has risen by more than 10 percentage points of GDP to 82.9%, a key vulnerability for the leftist leader despite inflation running below historical averages, stronger-than-expected economic growth, record-low unemployment and gains in real wages.
In remarks after the first-round results on Sunday, Lula signaled the importance of Alckmin to his runoff strategy, declaring that "no one in this country has the moral authority to lecture me or Alckmin on fiscal policy or fiscal responsibility, given what he did in Sao Paulo state and what we did in Brazil."
Elevating Alckmin could help attract voters concerned about fiscal credibility who are unwilling to back Bolsonaro but have grown disillusioned with what they see as an increasingly populist turn by Lula's government, the sources said. REUTERS

Teenager loses hand picking up grenade in France school protests

Unknown Publisher

Teen loses hand picking up police grenade as France school protests continue
A 15-year-old student lost a hand on Monday picking up a police grenade as part of nationwide protests in France over classroom conditions that have disrupted lessons at hundreds of schools since last week.
Some students returned to classrooms but others maintained actions outside their schools, ahead of a day of larger demonstrations expected on Tuesday.
Authorities said the teenager was injured in the northern town of Lens. A police union source told French news agency AFP he appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police and that it exploded in his hand.
Since late September, students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of schools, complaining of teacher absences, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings ill-adapted to rising temperatures, among other grievances.
Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old protester, told CBS News his school had a rat infestation. Student leader Daphnee Die said the violence has been sparked by the students' frustration.
"It's understandable, but it's getting really dangerous, and that's why we're warning students to be safe during these events," Die told CBS News.
The unrest erupted months before elections next year that will determine the successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron.
The government has sought to address the grievances, while accusing hard-left activists of having hijacked the protest movement.
The French Human Rights League on Monday accused security forces of using disproportionate methods against protesters, many of whom are legally minors.
"We can see that in the instructions given to the police, there is no directive to show restraint, even though they are dealing with children," league President Nathalie Tehio said.
"We're missing our lessons to give you one"
More than 400 out of France's 3,700 high schools, known as lycees, were partially or totally closed on Monday morning, the education ministry said.
A third of the 468 lycees for teenagers aged 15 to 17 were expected to be closed in the Paris region, authorities said.
In central Paris, dozens of teenage students demonstrated outside a school while passing cars honked their horns. Some classmates made their way inside to attend lessons.
"We're missing our lessons to give you one," read one cardboard sign outside the Turgot high school, located in Paris' 3rd arrondissement.
In Bordeaux, in the southwest, some students returned to the classroom while others continued to demonstrate in the presence of riot police.
Some protesters outside the Gustave Eiffel high school set off fireworks in the direction of the police, who responded sporadically with tear gas, but overall the situation remained calm, AFP reporters said.
In the northern city of Lille, masked protesters destroyed bus shelters and set fire to dustbins, as police fired tear gas toward demonstrators.
The movement started on Sept. 17 at a high school in the Paris suburb of Creteil, in support of teachers striking over a lack of staff and resources.
It gained momentum and spread across France, at times spiraling into vandalism, including the destruction of bus shelters, the burning of school entrances and clashes between protesters and security forces.
Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education minister.
More than 5,000 people, 85% of them minors, have been arrested.
Protesters have also accused the police of using excessive force, and internal investigations have been opened into at least three instances of alleged police brutality.
French leaders scramble to respond
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu set out a timetable on Sunday urging local authorities to prioritize filling gaps left by long-term teacher absences and unfilled posts.
He called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss overhauling the country's often-dilapidated school buildings.
The government is also pushing legislation to make those responsible for damaging public property pay for repairs themselves, instead of drawing on public funds.
Government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon defended the bill.
"When you have 14-, 15-, 16-year-olds who, at 9 a.m., are burning bus shelters or — perhaps even more seriously — the high school where they study, that raises the question of parental responsibility," she told the Europe1/CNews broadcaster.
Lecornu has said the draft law could allow compensation payments to be recovered from family allowances and housing benefits while preserving a minimum income threshold.
The head of the main CGT labor union, Sophie Binet, slammed what she called a "populist announcement," which she said would "end up targeting the most vulnerable families."

Ukraine is working on a satellite system of its own, something similar to SpaceX's Starlink, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 4 October, Interfax-Ukraine reported. He argued Kyiv should be free to turn Starlink on Russian military targets, warning that China and other states will share comparable satellite technology with Moscow within months. Ukraine's battlefield communications still ride on a network owned by Elon Musk, who has clashed with Kyiv and once limited its wartime use.
Low-orbit satellite internet has turned into a frontline utility that a single company or government can switch on or off, and both armies are now racing to own that link instead of renting it. Control of the network decides whose drones can see the battlefield and fly through the jamming to strike it—leverage Kyiv has gone without while its connection rode on hardware it does not run.
Working on a Starlink of its own
Zelenskyy said there was groundwork in place and that Ukraine was working on a system similar to Starlink. He called it fair for Ukraine to aim Starlink at military sites inside Russia. The timing is the reason, he said: some states will share the technology with Russia late this year or early next, and the Chinese are among them. Moscow is already fielding its own Starlink-style constellation, Rassvet, though for now it reaches Ukraine only in brief passes.
Ukrainian brigades detail Starlink crackdown: Russian terminals “became just bricks,” assaults disrupted
Ukraine's troops and drones lean heavily on Starlink, a network Kyiv neither owns nor controls. Musk has used that control against Kyiv before: in 2022 SpaceX refused a Ukrainian request to extend Starlink over occupied Crimea for a drone strike on Russia's warships, and it has since restricted the network's use for drone operations.
Sanctions, and satellites of its own
Zelenskyy has asked US President Donald Trump several times to sanction the Russian and Chinese companies building Russia's Rassvet network, most recently at the UN General Assembly in New York, he said in a recent Financial Times interview.
The EU sanctioned Russia’s Starlink rival but not the company that builds it. Experts call that the gap that matters
Denys Shtilerman, co-founder and chief designer at Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, told the Financial Times in May that the firm had launched two satellites this year and planned dozens more in 2027, aiming to reduce reliance on the US government and Western tech companies. To strike deep inside Russia and gather intelligence, he has said, Ukraine needs its own constellation covering all of Russia.

The U.S. State Department has approved potential arms sales worth a combined $2.27 billion to Egypt, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates, including missiles, defense support and precision-guidance equipment.
The largest of the three is a possible sale to the UAE of Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System-II guidance sections and related equipment at an estimated cost of $1.041 billion, the department said in a statement.
The UAE "has requested to buy up to ten thousand (10,000) Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System-II guidance sections consisting of a combination of air-to-air and air-to-ground configurations," it added.
For Egypt, the department approved a possible sale of Javelin missile systems at an estimated cost of $832 million.
Cairo has requested to buy up to 2,020 Javelin FGM-148F missiles, including 20 fly-to-buy missiles, and up to 200 Javelin Lightweight Command Launch Units, according to the notification.
For Kuwait, it approved a possible sale of Patriot missile repair and return services and related equipment at an estimated cost of $400 million.
The sale comes more than seven months into the Iran war, which began on Feb. 28 when the U.S. and Israel launched coordinated strikes on Iran.
Iran retaliated with attacks on U.S. bases in Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Kuwait, Jordan and Saudi Arabia.
The U.S. and Iran signed a framework agreement in June outlining immediate steps to restore freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and address Iran's nuclear program, but it expired in August without a final deal.

Ukraine offers combat-tested drone tech to JEF
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:00:59 BST
01:00:59 KST

Ukraine has proposed deeper defence technology cooperation with the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force, including the use of Ukrainian drone, counter-drone and battlefield sensing technology across the Baltic and North Atlantic regions, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara set out the proposals during an address to a meeting of JEF countries, arguing that Ukraine’s experience of countering drones and other threats during the war with Russia could be applied directly to security challenges faced by the ten-member grouping.
The areas identified include counter-UAS operations, protection of critical undersea infrastructure, responses to hybrid threats and efforts to counter Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, all of which have become increasingly prominent areas of activity for the JEF.
According to a news update from Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence, Khmara said: “Ukraine is ready to build a mutually beneficial partnership with you. We need it. So does the security of our region. And of the entire continent. Our shared future lies in this partnership.”
Ukraine said its existing battlefield technologies include mass-produced low-cost interceptor drones, detection systems and systems able to combine information from multiple sources into a common real-time air picture.
Khmara said: “We see how Russia uses drones for reconnaissance, sabotage and strikes on infrastructure. And we have already built solutions that work in real combat.”
The Ukrainian government argues that those technologies and the operational experience developed around them could be applied to the Baltic Sea and other areas covered by the JEF, particularly where participating countries are seeking ways to detect and respond to drones while protecting maritime infrastructure. Kyiv is proposing to expand the relationship through several existing cooperation models, including Drone Deal arrangements, Train with Ukraine and Build with Ukraine.
The Drone Deal initiative is intended to allow Ukraine to export drone technologies developed and refined during the war, while Build with Ukraine covers joint production arrangements for drones and counter-drone equipment. Ukraine said a number of those manufacturing projects are already under way with JEF member countries.
Train with Ukraine is intended to transfer operational experience gained by Ukrainian forces to partner militaries, giving allied personnel access to lessons developed during large-scale combat operations. The Joint Expeditionary Force was established under UK leadership in 2015 and comprises Britain, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. Its geographical focus covers Northern Europe, including the High North, North Atlantic and Baltic regions. In recent years its work has increasingly included the protection of critical maritime infrastructure and responses to hybrid activity alongside more conventional military exercises.
Ukraine became an Enhanced Partner of the JEF in 2025 after Ukrainian representatives attended a meeting of JEF defence ministers for the first time. The arrangement provides a framework for closer cooperation without Ukraine becoming one of the ten full JEF participant nations. The latest proposals would expand that relationship into the development, production and use of military technology, with Kyiv seeking to connect systems already being used by Ukrainian forces with the requirements of Northern European militaries.

The dispute relates to the Tata's Mithapur facility in Gujarat.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday directed that no coercive action be taken against Tata Chemicals while it considers the company's challenge to a Gujarat high court ruling concerning alleged environmental damage to a marine sanctuary in the Gulf of Kutch.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued notice on Tata Chemicals' plea against the high court's May 25 judgment. The bench asked the Gujarat government to respond by November 2."Meanwhile, no coercive action shall be taken against the petitioners," the Supreme Court said according to news agency PTI.Senior advocate Abhishek Singhvi, representing Tata Chemicals, told the court that the case concerns allegations of environmental degradation and encroachment.The dispute relates to the company's Mithapur facility, where open channels have historically been used to discharge wastewater into the sea. Tata Chemicals had challenged a 2006 order passed by the district collector, who rejected the company's claim over the land on which these channels were located.
The Gujarat high court dismissed that challenge on May 25. It also rejected Tata Chemicals' argument that it had pre-existing rights over the legacy open wastewater channels.
The high court found that government land forming part of the marine sanctuary had been encroached upon. It further directed the Gujarat Pollution Control Board to appoint experts to assess the environmental damage caused to the area.The experts have also been asked to recommend suitable measures to restore or remedy the damage and determine the compensation that may be payable. The exercise was directed to be completed within three months.The Supreme Court's order means that no coercive steps will be taken against Tata Chemicals for the time being as the court examines the company's challenge to the Gujarat high court judgment.

Sexual satisfaction is more closely tied to orgasm for women than for men, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:00:43 UTC
01:00:43 KST

A study of Italian adults in heterosexual relationships found that men report reaching orgasm more often than women. For both genders, more frequent orgasms went along with greater sexual arousal, a greater variety of sexual activities, and wanting sex more often. Other links differed by gender: women’s orgasm frequency was more closely tied than men’s to their sexual satisfaction and to oral sex, while men’s was linked to a different set of practices, including the use of sex toys and erotic media. The paper was published in Sexuality & Culture.
Orgasm is an intense psychophysiological experience of sexual pleasure that usually represents the height of a sexual act. It is accompanied by characteristic bodily responses such as rhythmic muscular contractions, changes in blood flow, and hormonal activity. Although its basic physiological mechanisms are broadly similar in men and women, in heterosexual relationships women report experiencing orgasm less often than men. This is known as the orgasm gap.
Researchers have proposed several explanations for the orgasm gap, including anatomy, patterns of sexual stimulation, stress, body image, and sexual self-confidence. Relationship factors such as emotional closeness, communication, responsiveness, and satisfaction also seem to play an important role, particularly for women.
Specific sexual practices matter as well, because intercourse alone may not provide the stimulation most likely to produce orgasm for many women. Sexual experiences are also shaped by cultural “scripts” that influence how men and women are expected to behave, respond, and experience pleasure during sex. These expectations can affect both sexual behavior and the meaning people attach to orgasm within intimate relationships.
Most research on the orgasm gap has drawn on samples from the United States and other English-speaking countries. The authors chose Italy in part because traditional cultural and religious influences there coexist with growing sexual openness and changing gender roles.
Study author Cristina Civilotti of the University of Turin and her colleagues examined how often people experience orgasm and which factors are associated with it in a large group of Italian heterosexual adults. More specifically, they examined how orgasm frequency related to the quality of people’s romantic relationships, aspects of sexual satisfaction, non-coital practices (sexual activities other than intercourse), and sexual habits.
Study participants were 579 heterosexual adults in Italy who reported being in a stable relationship. They were between 18 and 60 years of age, and most were middle-aged, highly educated, steadily employed, and had been with their partners for more than 10 years. They were recruited through centers of the Italian Federation of Scientific Sexology in northern, central, and southern Italy and through an online survey link.
Participants completed a sociodemographic questionnaire and assessments of relationship quality (a short version of the Dyadic Adjustment Scale) and of sexual attitudes and behaviors (the Sexual Activity Questionnaire). They also answered questions about their sexual history and functioning (e.g., “How often do you orgasm during sexual activity with your partner?”, “How often do you and your partner have sexual intercourse?”, “How often would you like to have sexual intercourse with your partner?”). Orgasm frequency was rated on a five-point scale ranging from “almost always” to “never.”
As expected, men reported reaching orgasm more often than women. Men’s average rating fell between “almost always” and “usually,” closer to “almost always,” while women’s average was close to “usually.” Additional analyses showed that this difference was not explained by participants’ age, education, employment status, parenthood, or relationship status.
For both genders, those reporting more frequent orgasms also tended to report greater ease of sexual arousal, a greater variety of sexual activity, and wanting sex more often. More frequent orgasms were also linked to better relationship quality in both men and women, including agreement with the partner on important matters, time spent together in conversation and shared activities (which the authors describe as emotional closeness), and overall happiness with the relationship. These links were somewhat larger among women, but the difference between genders was not statistically significant.
The clearest gender difference involved sexual satisfaction. Among women, more frequent orgasms were moderately linked to greater satisfaction with the sexual relationship, enjoyment of the partner’s behavior, ease of arousal, and affectionate touch, while among men these links were weak or absent. Women who reported more oral sex and more sharing of sexual fantasies also tended to report more frequent orgasms, a pattern not seen in men.
For men, orgasm frequency was linked to anal sex, sex toys, and erotic films, books, and websites, practices that were unrelated to orgasm frequency among women. The authors interpret these links as a sign that men’s orgasms are tied to sexual novelty and stimulation. However, the direction of these correlations as reported in the paper does not match that interpretation, so this finding should be treated with caution.
“These findings point to persistent gender differences in orgasmic experience and suggest that men’s orgasm is more strongly influenced by sexual novelty and stimulation, while women’s orgasm is more strongly associated with emotional and relational factors. A better understanding of these differences is essential for promoting more satisfying and equitable sexual experiences in couples,” the study authors concluded.
That summary goes somewhat beyond the data on relationships, since the paper’s own tests found no statistically significant gender difference in how relationship quality was linked to orgasm. The clearer differences involved sexual satisfaction and specific sexual practices.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of sexual experiences and of the “orgasm gap.” However, its design does not allow causal inferences, so it cannot show whether better relationships or particular practices lead to more frequent orgasms, or the reverse. All data were collected using self-report measures, leaving room for reporting bias, and orgasm frequency was measured with a single question.
Recruitment through sexology centers may have attracted people who are unusually comfortable discussing sex, and the sample was mostly middle-aged, highly educated, and in long-term relationships. The results may also not apply to LGBTQ+ adults, who were excluded from the analysis.
The paper, “Revisiting the Gender Orgasm Gap: Relational, Sexual, and Behavioral Correlates of Orgasm Attainment Among Cisgender Heterosexual Adults,” was authored by Cristina Civilotti, Giulia Di Fini, Vieri Boncinelli, Ivan De Marco, Camilla Branda, Gabriella Gandino, and Fabio Veglia.

Tusk and Zelensky last met at the Carpathian 8 Summit on Sept. 18, where the countries of the Carpathian region discussed economic, cultural, and security cooperation.
The president also held a phone call with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten later that day to discuss ways to strengthen Ukraine's air defenses and the status of peace talks.
"A significant share of (Russian) drones are shot down specifically by the F-16s that the Netherlands transferred to Ukraine, and there are opportunities to support their operation with the necessary means," Zelensky said.

GELENDZHIK, October 5. /TASS/. Markets in Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America are promising destinations for Russian biotechnology exports, Russian Industry and Trade Minister Anton Alikhanov told reporters on the sidelines of the Bioprom forum.
"For biotechnology, markets where food production, livestock farming, aquaculture, and pharmaceuticals are growing but domestic technology chains are not yet sufficiently developed are particularly promising. These include Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and Latin America," he said.
Following reduced access to European markets, Russian companies have been expanding more actively into China, India, Turkey, the UAE and other Persian Gulf countries, CIS countries, Africa, and Latin America.
Products being promoted in export markets include feed enzymes, probiotics and starter cultures, amino acids, feed proteins and concentrates, enzyme preparations for the food industry, starch products, biological crop protection products, and others.
"These products are in demand because they help reduce the cost of producing meat, milk, fish, bread, and food ingredients. Russian suppliers also benefit from the relatively low cost of grain feedstock, energy, and a number of production resources," the minister noted.
Speaking about potential joint projects with other countries, Alikhanov stressed that Russia always welcomes any cooperation between domestic producers and friendly countries. "First and foremost, this facilitates technology transfer and scientific development, which has a significant impact on the development of Russia’s biotechnology industry," he concluded.

Behind Hamas’s offer to mediate between Yemen and Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:58:29 UTC
00:58:29 KST

Behind Hamas’s offer to mediate between Yemen and Saudi Arabia
TEHRAN – Many assumed that Hamas’s offer to mediate between Yemen and Saudi Arabia was primarily an attempt to avoid choosing sides.
On the one hand, Hamas cannot afford to move in a direction that runs counter to many Arab and regional countries. This is particularly true of the countries that host senior members of the Palestinian resistance movement. It also applies to those working to mediate between Hamas and the Israeli regime, or leading reconciliation efforts between Hamas and other Palestinian parties.
Qatar, Turkey, Egypt, and some other countries have all made no secret of their sympathy and solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
On the other hand, Hamas cannot disregard what its own officials call a “blood partnership” with Ansarallah. That partnership was manifested in Ansarallah’s decision to militarily support Gaza. It was also evident in its missile and drone attacks on Tel Aviv and deep inside territories occupied by the Zionist regime.
The Yemeni Armed Forces (YAF) also succeeded in disrupting the regime’s port of Eilat. The port remains severely impaired, reducing its operating capacity by 85 percent, according to Israeli sources.
The resulting war subjected Yemen to thousands of Israeli and U.S. airstrikes. Washington eventually reached a separate agreement with Ansarallah. It also did so without requiring Ansarallah to refrain from targeting the occupation regime’s interests and assets in the Red Sea or on land.
The conflict exacted a heavy toll on Ansarallah and on Yemen as a whole. Many senior political and military leaders were killed alongside civilians. A wide range of civilian and economic facilities were also damaged or destroyed.
But the real surprise came during a private meeting with one of Hamas’s senior leaders. He revealed that the initiative had not originated with Hamas. It had come from the government in Sanaa itself.
Ansarallah were the ones who asked Hamas to intervene. They specifically wanted the movement to act through the three-party mediation channel working on Gaza: Qatar, Turkey, and Egypt. They hoped the mediators could open a political and negotiating track between Sanaa and Riyadh.
The objective was to move beyond a simple de-escalation. A truce alone, Ansarallah argues, could never produce lasting peace and stability. The remaining economic, financial, and political issues would also have to be addressed.
That, according to the Palestinian Hamas leader, was the position conveyed by Ansarallah.
Hamas subsequently passed Ansarallah’s proposal on to the three mediating parties. It appears that Hamas has virtually no direct channel to Riyadh. The movement itself is also not regarded by Saudi Arabia as the most suitable mediator.
Ansarallah is well aware of this. Their calculation instead rested on the close relationships Hamas has developed with the three members of the Gaza mediation triangle. The response from the parties concerned, however, has not been sufficiently positive to suggest that this track is likely to be activated anytime soon.
Analysts believe Saudi Arabia is not yet ready for an initiative of this kind. Riyadh does not want to publicize its role in the war. It also sought to avoid that role during the de-escalation and ceasefire negotiations of 2022 by emphasizing it was a Yemeni-Yemeni conflict.
Significance of the initiative
Ansarallah’s initiative, which was entrusted to Hamas, comes against the backdrop of the close and mutually reinforcing relationship between the two allies. It also recalls a proposal made by Sayyed Abdul-Malik al-Houthi in 2020.
At the time, Sayyed al-Houthi offered to exchange a Saudi pilot held by his group for the release of several Hamas members detained in the Kingdom.
Hamas welcomed Ansarallah’s proposal, but Saudi Arabia ignored it. The detainees were eventually released between 2022 and 2024. This happened either as a result of third-party mediation efforts or because their prison sentences had expired.
Today, Ansarallah’s initiative appears intended, among other things, to strengthen Hamas’s political standing and give the movement greater credit.
Some Arab and international actors view Hamas as part of the region’s problems. Through this initiative, Ansarallah appears to be trying to present Hamas instead as part of the solution.
However, the initiative remains at a very early stage. Quite frankly, it may already have died there. Nevertheless, the initiative carries several messages for Yemeni and regional actors. The first message is that Ansarallah is not just attached to Tehran and the IRGC.
The Sanaa government does not conceal its alliance with Iran or the ties that bind it to Tehran. Yet, according to most assessments, Ansarallah acts according to its own calculations and interests. At the same time, they take care, wherever possible, not to stray too far from the Islamic Republic.
The second message is that the movement is seeking to build relationships with the most influential and major Arab and regional powers. There is little doubt that Ansarallah is closely watching the increasingly prominent roles being played by the three mediators.
This applies both to the wider illegal war against Iran and to the conflicts unfolding close to Yemen. These include the conflicts on the other side of the Red Sea, around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, and in the Horn of Africa. None of these conflicts is remote from Yemen. Nor are they remote from the regional actors involved.
The third message Ansarallah wants to convey is that however long a “truce” may last, it is not a solution. Four years after the guns fell silent, the parties have still failed to put the remaining outstanding issues on a genuine path toward resolution. These include sanctions, the blockade, salaries, fuel, ports, and airports.
Under such circumstances, it was only natural that the conflict would eventually erupt again. This has happened in conflicts and disputes around the world. The underlying causes remain unresolved, and the roots of the conflict continue to run deep.
The fourth message is that war is not a solution in Yemen. It was not the answer during the seven-year war, and it will not be the answer going forward. Economic isolation and blockade, combined with the absence of any political horizon, are a recipe for renewed conflict. They are not a way to preserve the already difficult status quo indefinitely.
The initiative and the regional framework
The Yemeni initiative that Hamas has brought into the public arena fits into the broader effort to establish a regional framework for cooperation and collective security.
Qatar presented this concept from the highest UN platform. Oman’s foreign minister subsequently elaborated on it in two articles published in France’s Le Monde and Britain’s The Economist.
There appears to be a new trend among some Arab and regional actors. They seem increasingly willing to embrace containment rather than exclusion, participation rather than domination, and cooperation rather than confrontation.
If this concept of collective security is given a chance to take shape, one of its priorities should be to address the region’s various unresolved problems. They should be placed on a path toward comprehensive negotiated settlements. Such an approach would need to safeguard the legitimate and balanced interests of neighboring states.
Yemen may well be the first to require a political solution. The alternative is to embark on another dangerous conflict. The region may recognize it has begun, but it has no way of knowing how or when it will end. The case for diplomacy, dialogue, and negotiation becomes even stronger given the limited appetite among regional and international actors for escalation, military victory, mobilization, and the beating of war drums.
The U.S. has shown no willingness to launch another round of aggression against Ansarallah. Neither have the three mediators for Hamas. Pakistan and Turkey, which formed the “Mecca” alliance with Riyadh, have not joined Saudi airstrikes in Yemen either. As Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar indicated, they favor a political solution.
Some observers, however, believe that the mediating parties’ reluctance to become directly involved in Yemen may stem from a different calculation. They assume that without resolving the larger regional conflict, it is impossible to resolve the smaller conflicts. That argument is generally valid, but it is not always true.
If influential actors within local conflicts are prepared to engage, limited solutions and interim settlements may still be possible. Such steps could become part of a longer process of confidence-building within the region.
There is therefore nothing wrong with giving Hamas some of the credit it deserves. The mediators need some of it as well. They are facing the fascism of the Israeli regime, its dismissal of any initiatives or roadmaps, and its determination to continue waging wars.

Brazilian assets rally as Flavio Bolsonaro tops first-round vote
