2026-10-05
15:58:00 UTC
00:58:00 KST

Brazilian assets were trading higher on Monday after right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro, came in first in the first round of Sunday's presidential election.
The Bovespa benchmark stock index gained more than 8% and the country's currency strengthened against the U.S. dollar following the vote.
The eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro won 47% of the votes and will face leftist incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who secured about 45% of the vote, in a runoff on Oct. 25. Polls had forecast Lula would lead the first round of voting by around three percentage points.
Investors cheered on Monday morning as Bolsonaro's strong showing was matched by gains for his allies in Congress. Analysts say a friendlier legislature would make it easier for him, if elected, to push through a pro-market agenda of tighter public spending, privatizations and tax cuts.
"Brazil wants change," Bolsonaro said on Sunday evening, heralding the "end of the era of (Lula's) Workers' Party."
Shares in retailer Magazine Luiza, stock exchange operator B3, lender BTG Pactual, homebuilder Cyrela and conglomerate Cosan jumped more than 20% each, putting them among the top gainers.
J.P. Morgan upgraded Brazil's equities to "overweight" on Monday, saying a more favorable political backdrop after recent election developments had improved the outlook for the region's largest market and could drive a period of outperformance.
Brazil's real currency strengthened more than 4% against the U.S. dollar in early trading, moving below 5.00 per greenback, from around 5.22 previously, in line with analyst forecasts and with the currency's performance four years ago when then-President Jair Bolsonaro did better than expected in the first-round vote against Lula.
The elder Bolsonaro went on to lose to Lula in the second round of that election and was subsequently convicted of trying to carry out a coup to overturn the result. The former president was sentenced to about 27 years in prison and is currently under house arrest.
Brazil's international debt also rallied on Monday, while broader fixed-income markets were jittery. The 2056 bond was up 1.4 cents on the dollar to bid at 93.5 cents, Tradeweb data showed.
Bolsonaro has pitched himself as a "more centered" version of his father to investors concerned about Brazil's burgeoning fiscal pressures.
"It remains to be seen whether the senator would ultimately prove more fiscally responsible than Lula would be in a fourth non-consecutive presidential term. However, markets are likely to give him the benefit of the doubt," said Thierry Larose, portfolio manager at Vontobel.
If he is elected, Bolsonaro would enjoy some room to maneuver with Congress after his Liberal Party emerged as the biggest winner in congressional races on Sunday.
Bolsonaro's party increased its representation in the Senate from 15 to 28 seats, the strongest result for a party since Brazil's return to democracy in 1985. It also is projected to secure 121 seats in the lower house, up from its current 98 seats.
"The likelihood of advancing reforms is much greater," said Pedro Paulo Silveira, an analyst at Terra Investimentos. He noted that during the previous Bolsonaro government, reforms often depended on costly political bargaining or stalled altogether.
Analysts also expect the real to continue strengthening into 2027. Societe Generale forecast that it would move to 5.10 by the end of 2026, with scope to move below 5.00 in the first half of 2027. Morgan Stanley forecast the real could strengthen past 4.90 and toward 4.50 in the first quarter of next year.
"The market wants change, it wants reform; it doesn't want a high public deficit; with the current government, all of this will continue," said Pedro Galdi, investment analyst at the AGF Investments platform.
Bolsonaro's strong showing is likely to boost market confidence in the near term, said Bryan Harris, a managing partner at Sabio.
"The market will be looking for clear signals from Bolsonaro that he is serious about tackling the country's problems," Harris said.
Heading into Sunday's vote, most private polls, which largely underestimated the younger Bolsonaro's strength, had shown the 45-year-old senator and Lula, who will turn 81 later this month, about even in a runoff vote.
Addressing a crowd at a hotel in Sao Paulo, Lula said he had been convinced he would win the election in the first round.
"Starting tomorrow, we begin a new campaign," the leftist leader said, promising to show voters what he had accomplished as president.

FlyDubai co-pilot planned to crash jet into Israeli airport, official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:54:40 UTC
00:54:40 KST

FlyDubai co-pilot planned to crash plane into airport, shouldn't have been cleared to fly to Israel, sources say
The Omani co-pilot who allegedly attempted to hijack a FlyDubai flight to Israel told interrogators in the United Arab Emirates last week that he planned the attack even before he was employed by the Emirati airline more than a year ago, according to an Israeli official.
He had intended to crash the FlyDubai jet into Israel's Ben Gurion Airport, the official said, adding that the co-pilot, who multiple sources familiar with the investigation have identified to CBS News as Omani national Hamam al Hamami, had flown to Israel in the past.
A series of major security failures preceded the alleged hijacking attempt, and insiders told CBS News on Monday that the incident should have been prevented long before the plane even took off.
"A huge failure"
Israel's own security protocols should've prohibited al Hamami from ever flying to Tel Aviv, according to Eytan Ben David, a former deputy head of aviation security at El Al, Israel's flagship airline.
The Sept. 30 flight was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain with the plane's crash ax and attempted to crash the aircraft, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, passengers on board the plane and the flight captain.
Israel receives lists of passengers and crew for all flights into the country in advance, and, at least in the past, each individual was checked by a security division inside the transportation ministry to make sure they posed no threat, Ben David told CBS News.
An Omani pilot should never have been permitted to fly into Israel under its current guidelines, as Oman does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel, said Ben David, who is also a former deputy head of Israel's National Security Council.
"It's enough that you see that he is of Omani nationality to say, 'Stop, he cannot fly to Israel because he is Omani, replace him with another pilot,'" said Ben David.
"It's a huge failure, and it's a big miracle," he added of the seemingly narrowly averted catastrophe.
Ben David said he once personally prohibited a pilot with Iranian citizenship from flying a Turkish Airlines plane into Israel under the same rules, which extend to Iran.
Sources familiar with the investigation told CBS News it is possible al Hamami has dual citizenship, which could explain how he was allowed to fly to Israel.
Smit Machchhar, the FlyDubai captain, was able to fight off his co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door, he told India's leader last week from a hospital bed in Saudi Arabia where he was recovering from stab wounds.
A group of Israeli passengers and FlyDubai staff then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Israel's government passed a law in 2023 that requires foreign airlines to submit a list of passengers and crew ahead of all flights to Israel, aimed at preventing terrorist incidents.
Following the alleged attempted hijacking last week, Israel's transportation ministry, as well as its domestic and foreign security agencies, have all said they were not responsible for vetting foreign flight crews.
Ben David said the responsibility to properly vet foreign pilots primarily falls on the security branch inside Israel's transportation ministry.
Israel has made efforts for many years to secure its own airlines and vet their personnel. But foreign airlines and their crews have emerged as a potential gap in aviation security, and Israel's near tragedy last week is likely to trigger a reevaluation, Ben David said.
"I'm sure all the countries in the world heard about this and said to themselves, 'Let's check what the situation is for us,'" he told CBS News.
Other security lapses?
Failing to block him based on his nationality is just one example of the apparent failures that took place before al Hamami boarded the flight to Tel Aviv last week.
He had also been removed from his role as a pilot by his previous employer, Oman Air, with which he underwent new pilot training, sources told CBS News over the weekend.
Surveillance by Omani authorities revealed that he was visiting radical websites, the sources said.
Oman Air transferred him to an office job. One of the sources said al Hamami resigned from his job at Oman Air after being placed on desk duty, leaving the airline around 2024.
Al Hamami then moved to Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates, where he was hired by FlyDubai. The Emirati carrier hired the Omani without vetting him with Oman's government, the sources told CBS News, and as he was not fired by the first airline, he may not have raised any red flags anyway.
FlyDubai told CBS News on Monday that it could not respond to questions on the incident due to the ongoing investigation.
Al Hamami is an Omani citizen but was not born in Oman and lived most of his life outside the Persian Gulf nation, the sources told CBS News. They said his mother is Syrian and his father is Omani.
Oman's government has not publicly confirmed the co-pilot's nationality.
Vice President JD Vance indicated Monday that while there may not have been specific U.S. intelligence on al Hamami, it was clear he should not have been flying a commercial jet.
"We knew that guy was a problem — not United States intelligence, but if you look historically, that person should not have been flying an airline, and so we're certainly looking at our procedures within the United States to make sure that people who are obviously flight risks are not getting behind the wheel of an airplane," Vance told a reporter at Joint Base Andrews.
He declined to comment on any possible links between the co-pilot and Iran, deferring to U.S. intelligence agencies.
President Trump has been the only senior U.S. or Israeli official to suggest a possible Iranian link, telling reporters the day after the incident that "based on what I'm hearing," the co-pilot could have been working for or with the Islamic Republic.

Spain's gambler PM Sanchez seeks to defy the odds again on a snap election

Spain's gambler PM Sanchez seeks to defy the odds again on a snap election
MADRID, Oct 5 - Spain's Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, on Monday lived up to his reputation as a political gambler by calling a snap election that surveys indicate will cost him his job and usher in a right-wing government.
But then, the 54-year-old has managed to remain in office for eight years without ever winning a majority in parliament.
His appetite for risk has led him to openly accuse Israel of genocide in Gaza, a charge it rejects, and to defy US President Donald Trump's demands that Madrid spend much more on defence and let the US use its airbases in Spain for its war on Iran.
His latest gamble - to bring the election forward to November 29 from next year - appears to be based on a calculation that anger over a mounting housing crisis will be directed more at his opponents than at his own party.
SANCHEZ AIMS TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF HOUSING CRISIS
On Friday, his right-wing opponents blocked his attempt to answer protesters' anger over the eviction of 87-year-old tenant Maricarmen Abascal with a decree capping rents and blocking further evictions.
With thousands of activists camped in the capital outside the office of the Madrid regional government, led by the conservative People's Party, Sanchez could be trying to make the election a referendum on housing.
It could also shift the narrative from damaging headlines about his government's handling of a migrant crisis in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta this summer, and investigations into alleged corruption in his party and influence peddling by his wife and brother. Anger still lingers, too, at an amnesty for Catalan separatists that allowed him to clinch a third term in 2023.
"Faced with an inability to legislate on the issue of greatest public concern, the aim is to capitalise on social mobilisation," said political analyst Eduardo Bayon.
"The logic is to transform a tangible problem into a choice between political blocs: 'This is what I am trying to do, but the right-wing parties are blocking me'."
Surveys indicate the housing measures rejected by the PP, Vox and the Catalan nationalists Junts have support across Spanish society. A 40dB survey for El Pais and Cadena Ser on Friday found that 68% of Spaniards, including a majority of PP and Vox voters, were in favour of capping rents to make housing more accessible.
"In contrast to their (opposition parties') penthouses, their budget cuts and their subservience to the elites, our pledge to the people is for affordable housing, public services and social rights," Sanchez wrote on X on Monday. "Spain must continue to move forward, and to do so, we need the public to strengthen our position in parliament."
SANCHEZ ALWAYS DEFYING THE ODDS
Sanchez has defied the odds throughout his political career. He first grabbed power by leading a move to remove his conservative predecessor, Mariano Rajoy of the PP, in Spain's first successful no-confidence vote over corruption.
In two subsequent elections, he has mobilised his base by pitching himself as a progressive bulwark against the far right returning to power for the first time since the end of Francisco Franco's 36-year right-wing dictatorship in 1975.
In 2023, he called a snap election after the Socialists performed badly in local ballots. It paid off: With no political party prepared to endorse Vox, Sanchez cobbled together an eclectic alliance to back him for a third term, even though the PP had won the most seats.
Still, the chances of that happening look even slimmer than in 2023, with support for the Socialists and their minority coalition partners Sumar well below what it was then.
Sanchez could also be playing a long game, betting that, even if he does not win, he can wait in the wings as an effective opposition leader, said Lorenzo Bernaldo de Quiros, an economist and president of the consultancy Freemarket Corporate Intelligence.
Sanchez's Socialists are betting that, although a PP-Vox coalition government is now a possibility, it would be beset by policy conflicts, which has been the case in the four regional governments where the PP and Vox currently rule in coalition.
"It is a government that (the Socialists) believe will not last," Bernaldo de Quiros said. REUTERS

Green party drops longstanding opposition to nuclear power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:53:49 UTC
00:53:49 KST

Green party members have voted to end the party’s opposition to nuclear power, dropping a commitment to phase out the technology in a major shift in its energy policy.
The motion, adopted at conference, removes a “blanket opposition to nuclear fission” and instead commits the Green party of England and Wales to assessing nuclear projects alongside other low-carbon technologies.
Its electricity generation policy still prioritises offshore wind, onshore wind and rooftop solar as the primary sources of electricity, but allows elected representatives to support new nuclear reactors on a case-by-case basis.
The Green MP Carla Denyer said the decision recognised there was a role for nuclear while the country moved towards an electricity system based primarily on renewables. “This evolution of our policy does not commit the party to backing new nuclear, but accepts this power source is here to stay for now, while we transition to electricity generation based primarily on renewable sources,” she said.
Denyer said keeping existing nuclear stations running could be a low-carbon option because a significant proportion of their carbon footprint came from construction. “So if I were energy secretary, my evidence-based approach would be to keep existing nuclear plants in operation, but to consider proposals for new nuclear power very carefully, bearing in mind the cost, speed and environmental impacts.”
Her comments strike a different tone from her assessment in 2023, when she described nuclear energy as “incredibly slow and incredibly expensive”. She said at the time: “Renewables is simply the way forward. Nuclear is not going to help us out in this climate emergency.”
Other senior Greens have previously criticised the technology. The party’s leader, Zack Polanski, has described it as outdated and compared investment in new nuclear reactors to “creating a fax machine”.
Last year, Adrian Ramsay, then a Green co-leader, criticised government support for Sizewell C. “The money being spent on this nuclear gamble would be far better spent on insulating and retrofitting millions of homes, bringing down energy bills and keeping people warmer and more comfortable,” he said.
The Green’s previous opposition to nuclear fission was rooted in its staunch opposition of nuclear weapons, one of the party’s founding principles.
Eugene McCarthy, a co-founder of Greens for Nuclear and a supporter of the motion, said the urgency of the climate crisis demanded a willingness to consider all available options. “We are at the throw-the-kitchen-sink-at-it phase of the climate crisis where you cannot be ruling anything out for things like Chernobyl happening in the 1980s,” he said.
The motion allows elected representatives to assess individual proposals on their merits, McCarthy said. “We will not say we support or don’t support any particular technology. This motion basically lets our elected members of parliament take it on a case-by-case basis and go: ‘This makes sense, we will extend the lifetime of Sizewell B,’ and on a different case say: ‘Actually the numbers don’t add up here.’”
Asked about Polanski’s previous criticism of nuclear, McCarthy said the leader remained entitled to his views. “He’s still fully entitled to say that, and a lot of the nuclear technology that we are using is quite outdated, to be frank. What this means is that he can now take a nuanced position.”
Prof Andrew Stirling, who has advised government on nuclear power and energy policy, said the motion was “completely irrational”. “Why would a party that pioneered concerns about nuclear power that have been so broadly vindicated by history, choose now to shift its position?” he said.
“All authoritative sources agree that climate action is much faster, affordable and impactful with combined renewables and storage,” he added. “Why spend scarce resources on less effective actions?”
McCarthy said: “Renewables are cheaper and have much more capacity, and you can roll them out much quicker. [But] there are issues with baseload, which nuclear can help with.”

US State Department approves arms sales worth $2.27B to Egypt, Kuwait, UAE

Rabia Iclal Turan
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
The US State Department has approved three possible foreign military sales to Egypt, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates with a combined estimated cost of about $2.27 billion.
The largest of the three is a possible sale to the UAE of Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System-II guidance sections and related equipment at an estimated cost of $1.041 billion, the department said in a statement.
The UAE "has requested to buy up to ten thousand (10,000) Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System-II guidance sections consisting of a combination of air-to-air and air-to-ground configurations," it added.
For Egypt, the department approved a possible sale of Javelin missile systems at an estimated cost of $832 million.
Cairo has requested to buy up to 2,020 Javelin FGM-148F missiles, including 20 fly-to-buy missiles, and up to 200 Javelin Lightweight Command Launch Units, according to the notification.
For Kuwait, it approved a possible sale of Patriot missile repair and return services and related equipment at an estimated cost of $400 million.
The sale comes more than seven months into the Iran war, which began on Feb. 28 when the US and Israel launched coordinated strikes on Iran.
Iran retaliated with attacks on US bases in Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Kuwait, Jordan and Saudi Arabia.
The US and Iran signed a framework agreement in June outlining immediate steps to restore freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and address Iran's nuclear program, but it expired in August without a final deal.

Italy’s Meloni moves to trademark voice amid AI deepfake fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:53:00 UTC
00:53:00 KST

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has moved to trademark her voice across the EU in an effort to guard against its unauthorized use in AI-generated deepfakes.
The application filed with the EU agency includes a four-second audio recording of Meloni repeating the phrase, in Italian, "Io sono Giorgia Meloni” ("I am Giorgia Meloni”), according to the EU office's records on Monday.
The filing, first reported by Italian daily La Repubblica, was confirmed by an Italian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
Meloni’s move comes as governments, regulators and public figures grapple with the rapid spread of artificial intelligence tools capable of convincingly replicating voices and images.
The recorded phrase echoes Meloni’s famous declaration at a 2019 political rally: "I am Giorgia, I am a woman, I am a mother, I am Italian, I am Christian.” The slogan became widely known in Italy and inspired a viral dance remix. "Io sono Giorgia” was also the title of her 2021 autobiography.
Manipulated images of Meloni have repeatedly circulated online in recent years and have at times been passed off as authentic. Among them was a fake image showing her sitting on a bed in her underwear.
Meloni has warned that deepfakes can "deceive, manipulate and harm anyone,” urging users to verify online content before sharing it.
"I can defend myself, but many others cannot,” she said in May, after fake images of her surfaced online.
Pop star Taylor Swift was among the most prominent targets of deepfakes in 2024, after sexually explicit AI-generated images falsely depicting her spread widely online, fueling calls for stronger legal protections against unauthorized digital replicas.
Matthew McConaughey was one of the first major celebrities to use trademark registrations to secure rights to voice clips and motion elements.
Fellow actor Scarlett Johansson also raised concerns about AI-generated voices after objecting to an OpenAI chatbot voice that she said sounded "eerily similar” to her own. She had declined to participate in the project. OpenAI denied intentionally imitating Johansson’s voice and later withdrew the feature.
And in Japan last week, a court awarded legal protection to the human voice for the first time. The case involved a popular Japanese anime voice actor who demanded that TikTok close an account over its unauthorized use of an AI clone of his trademark baritone.
Italian media reported that even if Meloni's application is approved, the trademark will not automatically prevent AI-generated imitations of her voice. It could, however, provide an additional legal tool against unauthorized use.
The filing follows a separate legal battle launched by Meloni in 2024 against a man accused of creating and posting deepfake pornographic images using her likeness. The case remains pending before an Italian court.

Satellite images of the Ilsky Oil Refinery in the Krasnodar Krai following the attack indicate that all of the facility’s primary refining facilities were damaged.
Analysts at the Dnipro Osint group released the images.
On September 26, FP-1 drones attacked the Ilsky Oil Refinery in the Krasnodar Region. The facility has a capacity of over 6.6 million metric tons of crude oil per year.
Satellite images show at least six strikes on equipment at the AVT-5 and AVT-6 units, which handle most of the refinery’s primary oil processing.
Another, less powerful unit—AVT-3—suffered extensive damage and was almost completely destroyed by fire.

Analysts from the Absolutely Reliable group released the images.
At the Samara-1 pumping station site, vertical steel tanks (VSTs) with a capacity of 20,000 cubic meters were damaged.
One tank is on fire and is believed to have been destroyed; two others sustained significant damage; and two more sustained surface damage or show signs of fire damage to their walls.
The Samara-2 pumping station area contains storage tanks with a total capacity of 50,000 cubic meters. One of them sustained significant damage, while two others sustained surface damage.
At the oil blending site, tanks with a total capacity of 20,000 cubic meters were damaged. One sustained significant damage, two had their roofs destroyed, and two more sustained surface damage. A pipeline was also damaged.
In total, four to five RVS-20,000 tanks and one RVS-50,000 tank sustained significant damage.
Thus, the strikes on the Ilsky Oil Refinery and the Samara Oil Pipeline caused damage to key oil infrastructure facilities, including primary processing units, the tank farm, and pipeline equipment.

Ukraine says Russian drones behind Turkish ship sinking
October 5, 2026
Romanian authorities said on Monday that two people were killed and another one was wounded after a fire broke out in a commercial vessel on Romanian waters in the Black Sea.
The Turkish-owned civilian vessel subsequently sank. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the incident was caused by a Russian drone attack.
Romania's Interior Ministry said the Coast Guard was alerted at around 11 a.m. local time (14:00 UTC) and the afflicted vessel was in Romania's exclusive economic zone, some 30 nautical miles (55 kilometers) south of Sfantul Gheorghe in Tulcea County.
"Eleven crew members have been rescued. Two deceased individuals have also been located," the ministry said, adding that a helicopter had airlifted the injured.
Zelenskyy accuses Russia of 'horrific strike'
Authorities did not identify the cause of the fire, but Romanian media reported that the ship was carrying grain and was hit by a drone.
"A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Türkiye. Azerbaijani and Indian citizens were on board," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X.
"As of now, unfortunately, we know that the ship's captain was killed ... The fate of one other person is still being established," he added.
The Ukrainian government says it has repeatedly proposed taking steps to de-escalate the situation in the Black Sea, which is putting maritime trade at risk.
"But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian vessels instead of normal maritime navigation," Zelenskyy wrote on social media.
Rising threat to Black Sea maritime traffic
The Black Sea is a major commercial shipping route, which connects Ukraine's grain exports with the rest of the world. The waterway has faced heightened security concerns since Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine in 2022.
There has been an increase in war-related objects found in the Black Sea, mostly in Romanian, Bulgarian and Turkish waters, with analysts saying the trend is expected to continue.
The incident is the latest to take place on Romanian waters. In August, a Romanian F-16 fighter jet destroyed a marine drone near an offshore gas project in the Black Sea.
Two months before, a Ukrainian maritime drone exploded in Romania's Black Sea port of Constanta, with Ukraine saying the drone had been knocked off course by Russian electronic interference.

Bosnia and Herzegovina elections: Return to a nationalist political order?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:47:40 UTC
00:47:40 KST

‘Trend reached us’: Nationalists gain ground in Bosnia and Herzegovina
Results raise the prospect of a new conservative alliance and further political polarisation, analysts say.
Bosnia and Herzegovina’s general election did not bring about many surprises in voter trends, but some developments could change the country’s political atmosphere, analysts have told Al Jazeera.
Most voters on Sunday moved further along ethnic lines, turning away from the idea of a civic society that gained momentum in the previous election when the centre-right Bosniak Party of Democratic Action (SDA) did not participate in the state government.
This trend has long been a fixture in the Bosnian entity of Republika Srpska, where Milorad Dodik’s Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) once again swept aside its competition in Sunday’s elections.
Voters in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina elected a candidate of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina (HDZ BiH), Darijana Filipovic, to the state presidency; for eight years that seat had been held by Zeljko Komsic of the Democratic Front, a civic-oriented party.
Sacir Filandra, a professor of political science at the University of Sarajevo, said the results were in line with a broader pattern – the strengthening of conservative forces in an uncertain European environment marked by “rising walls” and fear.
“We are witnessing the strengthening of conservative views and the revival or consolidation of political right-wing forces as part of wider European trends,” Filandra told Al Jazeera. “In these times of crisis and transition, that trend has also reached us, which is why nationalist and conservative parties have gained greater prominence. The basis of this voter choice is insecurity, anxiety, uncertainty and, to some extent, fear, as well as global developments in Europe.”
The clearer picture of what comes next will emerge only after parties negotiate coalitions and form governments.
“In our society, political parties reflect longstanding divisions within society,” Filandra said. “The situation is highly conservative, status quo prevails and politics has been reduced to a redistribution of power. It was not realistic to expect encouraging breakthroughs in terms of political reconciliation”, he added.
Changes in the presidency
During the years Komsic held the seat, the nationalist Croat leadership headed by Dragan Covic complained that Croats were being outvoted by Bosniaks, who helped Komsic to win the seat twice in a row.
Under Bosnia’s electoral system, Croat and Bosniak members of the state presidency are elected in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with every citizen, regardless of nationality, entitled to vote for any of the candidates. Over the past eight years, many Bosniaks have cast their ballots for Komsic, who was running for the Croat seat.
It could be argued that Filipovic’s victory is the most significant shift.
The results mean that the only member of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s tripartite presidency representing a declared multi-ethnic political orientation will be Bosniak Denis Becirovic, of the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and its partners, who won a second term in the state presidency.
However, with Filipovic and Zeljka Cvijanovic, the candidate of Dodik’s hardline Serb nationalist SNSD, on the presidency, the national interests of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s constituent peoples are likely to play a much greater role than they have over the past eight years.
The elections for the state and entity parliaments, as well as cantonal assemblies, also saw the SDA perform – it was the leading party in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in terms of the number of votes won, alongside traditionally strong performances by HDZ and SNSD. HDZ secured a convincing victory among Croat voters, while Dodik’s party won the largest number of votes in both the entity and state parliamentary elections.
‘A relaxation of Croat-Bosniak relations’
Over the past eight years, HDZ BiH leader Dragan Covic has warned of the “endangerment of Croats”, fuelled by Komsic’s victories over HDZ candidates in elections for the state presidency.
These votes could usher in an end to the pattern that Covic described, with the election of the Croat member of the Presidency.
Filipovic defeated Komsic’s preferred candidate, Slaven Kovacevic.
Covic publicly “thanked Bosniaks” for the outcome.
The question now is how this change will affect the political environment in Bosnia.
“Part of the public in Bosnia and Herzegovina is not unhappy with the outcome and sees the change as an opportunity to ease Croat-Bosniak relations,” historian and columnist Dragan Markovina told Al Jazeera. “I do not believe anything fundamental will change, but at least the atmosphere between political parties … could become less tense.”
Another striking feature of the election was the low turnout. About 40 percent took to the polls, some 10 percent fewer than four years ago.
Some interpret that as growing apathy.
Srecko Latal, an independent analyst, believes new technologies have also played a role, eliminating allegedly fraudulent ballots.
‘Worries’ for Bosnia’s future
Markovina believes the election results point clearly towards a possible coalition and the emergence of a new conservative axis between SDA, SNSD and HDZ, a scenario that evokes Bosnia’s political past.
The dominance of the three conservative parties in post-war Bosnia has been associated with obstruction, political deadlock and ethnonationalist narratives that have hindered progressive processes.
Amid declining support for civic or multi-ethnic parties, the political balance is changing.
“It would be fair to say that a coalition of SDA, SNSD and HDZ is likely to emerge. Much of post-war Bosnia’s history has been spent with these parties in coalitions, and nothing has improved, nor has any fundamental problem been resolved,” said Markovina, expressing little optimism about the future.
“Bosnia is moving backwards,” Markovina believes. “We are not the only ones who have nationalists. There are more and more of them around us (in Europe), and that is what worries me most when it comes to Bosnia’s future.”

Experts say Carney’s concern about Trump’s possible invasion of Canada is valid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:47:34 UTC
00:47:34 KST

Experts say Carney’s concern about Trump’s possible invasion of Canada is valid
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney touched on a wide range of topics during an hour-long interview with the New York Times last month — F-35 jets, Starlink satellites, trade in potash and automobiles and more — but the biggest takeaway was that he had prepared over the past year for the “extreme tail risk” that U.S. President Donald Trump might order military action against Canada.
“I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” said Carney, using a term from the financial world that was his metier as a former central banker for Britain and Canada. “That’s just risk management … it would be irresponsible not to.”
The expression refers to a scenario that is considered unlikely but not impossible — the “tail” of a probability curve where the center represents the most likely outcomes.
Carney told the Times that, based on Trump’s threats to make Canada a 51st state, he had carefully examined the possibility of U.S.-led military action, but declined to discuss in detail what that involved.
Timothy Sayle, a professor at the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto, said Carney’s comments indicate a valid concern.
“It makes sense to me that it’s at the real extreme end of possibilities, but I don’t think it’s a zero percent chance,” he told National Post.
The U.S. incursion into Venezuela this year and its threats against Greenland made its allies, including Canada and Europe, take notice, Sayle said.
“It can seem outlandish, but … the United States has made these decisions to enter Venezuela and then to attack Iran that were pretty low-probability events, and yet they did happen. So that’s why I can understand the prime minister’s point that it’s maybe very very very low risk but, as he said, can’t be totally ignored.”
As to what form a potential invasion might take, Sayle said the “wild unpredictability of the current American administration” made it difficult to predict, but he imagined several small-scale scenarios. They included “some sort of hot pursuit of a suspected criminal, or somebody that ICE was seeking, across the Canadian border.”
He added: “You could imagine an increase of U.S. forces, like the strengthening of U.S. forces in Canada in some way.” (According to the U.S. Department of Defense, as of March there were 159 active duty military personnel serving in Canada, plus 33 civilian DoD staff.)
Sayle also suggested “the presence of naval ships, the presence of or overflights by aircraft and … what could be described as something in the shared interest, but in which Canada was not consulted in the usual means. Americans could either publicly or invisibly flex their might and indicate that Canada’s sovereignty wasn’t quite as secure as we’d like to think.”
The notion has been ridiculed at high levels. This month, when a Canadian reporter asked Admiral Samuel J. Paparo, commander of the U.S. Pacific Command, about the possibility of military action against Canada, he was met with incredulity. Paparo called it “preposterous” and added: “Would you ask me please, also, what my attack plans are for the Martians?”
Sayle said that could change. “Canada and the United States militaries obviously have worked so closely together for so long,” he said. “I’m sure there’s a lot of goodwill and close relationships in the senior ranks, but we are, of course, seeing changes to how general officers are selected in the United States, and who keeps their jobs.”
Paparo concluded his remarks by saying he will ultimately follow the orders of the commander-in-chief. “And so we have, I think, lots of protections against this; relationships, friendships, common sense,” said Sayle. “But these things don’t always govern in a crisis.”
Carney is hardly the first to speculate on the possibility of war between
Canada and the U.S. Back in 1921, Lieut.-Col. James “Buster” Sutherland Brown drafted Defence Scheme No. 1, a plan for a Canadian pre-emptive attack against the United States in the event of a conflict between them and the British Empire.
A Washington Post article from 2005 said the plan called for Canadian soldiers to make for Albany, Minneapolis, Seattle and Great Falls, Mont., at the first signs of a possible U.S. invasion. The article quotes Floyd Rudmin, Canadian author of the 1993 book “Bordering on Aggression: Evidence of U.S. Military Preparations Against Canada,” as saying Brown even entered the country in civilian clothing to do reconnaissance.
“He had a total annual budget of $1,200,” said Rudmin, “so he himself would drive to the areas where they were going to invade and take pictures and pick up free maps at gas stations.” The plan was terminated in 1928, and many of the documents relating to it were destroyed.
Vincent Rigby, Canada’s former national security and intelligence adviser, told National Post this year that a U.S. invasion “falls into the category of very low probability, but very high impact, to put it mildly.”
Rigby, who spent 14 years with the Department of National Defence, said the Canadian military is supposed to plan for all scenarios. “They’re very good at it and, given the current situation in the world, given the current state of Canada-U.S. relations, given the current state of U.S. foreign policy, I’m not completely surprised that they’re looking at possible scenarios.”
Carney’s comments to the New York Times also included talk of the trade war, a fact Sayle calls salient.
“It’s a signal to the whole world,” he said. “I don’t think it’s a significant signal to the American government, but maybe a signal more broadly to American politicians and industry leaders as to how seriously Canada is taking this current difficult period with the United States, and I think in some ways it might strengthen the Canadian negotiating hand when it comes to trade issues, because the prime minister is signaling that this was a sort of existential moment for Canada.”
He added: “Even though it’s an American news outlet, this is a major headline in an international paper that Canadians will see too. So … there may be these instrumental reasons for doing it, like the trade negotiations, and signaling to Canadians just how serious he’s taking this moment. But it’s obviously a pretty important signal of the state of the relationship with the United States, and how different that is than anything in our living memory.”

Preppers used to be ridiculed – but we’re all stockpiling now | Zoe Williams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:47:12 UTC
00:47:12 KST

There is no national food stockpile and there hasn’t been since it was wound up in the 1990s. It feels like a metaphor for the delusions of that era: nothing bad can possibly happen again; no two countries with a McDonald’s have gone to war with each other (according to the journalist Thomas L Friedman, also in the 90s). Now, we all have a McDonald’s and wars regularly disrupt food supplies. The problem with metaphors is you can’t eat them – not even satisfying ones.
For people who remember the second world war, or feel as if they do, there is always enough muscle memory to do topical household stockpiling. My mum kept a trunk of food that was mainly filled with condensed milk in case of a nuclear war, all the way through the 80s. When the Berlin Wall came down, we should have had a ceremonial toffee-sauce-making event where we ate it all, but we didn’t; in 1990, she was stockpiling again, to mark the Gulf war.
The spectre of Y2K saw a large amount of bottled water enter the house, but by then I’d left home. When 9/11 happened, the water had gone off, but it was still fine for washing, apparently, so all she needed was a load of new water – and all that remained for the wider family was to call her mad and occasionally steal her anchovies.
The 2008 financial crash may have brought almost 20 years of roiling turmoil to the world, but the period spent wondering whether the cash would stop coming out of the wall was only a couple of days, during which if you had got your arse into gear enough to buy beans, you would have been considered hysterical. It would be dispiriting to go through all the events since that have made stockpiling seem like a good idea and impossible to pinpoint the date on which having a three-day food stash went from “crazy prepper idea from someone who probably also keeps a crossbow” to “something any sensible person who reads the news and listens to the authorities would do”.
The UK government’s resilience campaign, urging households to prepare for threats unknown, doesn’t feel like an overreaction. But nor does it feel realistic.
A record number of households – one in eight, or one in six with children – experience food insecurity already, which is to say can’t be sure they have enough even without external events. The range of possible disasters is so wide that it’s hard to consider them practically without freaking out: are we planning for crop failures in the UK or for the collapse of the global food supply, which would mean us relying on our own crops? Are we anticipating a hostile foreign act such as a cyber-attack, or something more meat-world?
Power outages, extreme weather, floods – they all seem possible, but none of them seem as if they’d be over in three days. You can see that having a torch would be better than no torch, but a stash of tinned pineapple wouldn’t meet the moment. The advice is to have three litres of drinking water a day for each person, but can you seriously imagine having that and not sharing it? There is no household solution that doesn’t hinge on the emergency being very short-lived and a collective response being ready to go within only a few hours. The more you think about emergencies, though, the less likely they seem to be short-lived. The chance of inoculating yourself household by household seems vanishingly small.
The essence of old-school prepping – the reason people who did it were mocked and viewed with suspicion – was that it was implicitly off-grid, or rather planning for a world without a grid and without meaningful order. The modern preppers’ problem is that stockpiling for your own household – even having a workable first aid kit and some non-perishables – feels ridiculous unless you believe there’s a bigger plan under way. The government has the unenviable task of asking us to trust the future less while trusting its authority more. It’s enough to make you want to do something helpful – more helpful, even, than buying a gigantic bag of rice.
Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Women suffer more pain than men across the whole body, major global study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:47:00 UTC
00:47:00 KST

Women report suffering more pain than men, a major new global study has found.
That was true for all types of pain the researchers measured, and comes amid continuing concern about the gender pain gap, which means women are less likely to be prescribed the pain relief they need.
Researchers from all over the world carried out “one of the largest harmonisation efforts in pain epidemiology to date”. Data was collected from more than 6 million people from 118 countries from 1990 to 2025, and included people from aged five years to more than 100.
The research, published in Nature Medicine, looked at how pain, as the leading global cause of disability, was distributed both around the world and across the human lifespan.
It found women’s self-reported pain across 11 bodily sites – head, face, neck or shoulder, foot or ankle, hand or wrist, elbow, chest, back, stomach or abdomen, hip and knee – was higher than for men.
That was particularly true for headache, facial and abdominal pain.
For men and women, the steepest increase in pain happened before people turned 55, then peaked at or beyond 75, with back, hip and knee pain increasing across the lifespan.
That indicated “that a substantial share of lifetime pain burden develops during working-age adulthood”, the authors wrote.
About 40% of participants reported back pain, while facial pain was the rarest at 2%.
Those in the lowest Human Development Index regions had substantially “higher late-life prevalence of bodily pain”, and almost twice the rates of low back pain in their older age.
High-intensity pain peaked at about 50, while generalised pain peaked around 70.
“Overall, our results suggest that, although the likelihood of experiencing any pain rises steadily with age, the most disabling forms of pain followed an inverted-U trajectory, peaking in mid-to-late adulthood before declining,” the study authors wrote.
“This distinction, between pain accumulation and pain that intensifies and then resolves, has direct implications for where prevention and care should be concentrated across the lifespan.”
The authors wrote that current estimates focus on diagnoses, which may mean people with limited healthcare access are left out, which is why they analysed rates of self-reported pain. That could provide a foundation for more equitable monitoring and prevention efforts, they wrote.
“Trajectories varied markedly by phenotype: headache, abdominal and facial pain peaked earlier in life before declining, whereas musculoskeletal pain generally rose progressively with age,” they wrote.
“Within musculoskeletal sites, upper body pain (including neck, shoulder and elbow) peaked around midlife and declined thereafter, whereas lower body pain (including back, hip and knee) continued to increase across the lifespan, consistent with the greater role of cumulative mechanical and degenerative load at weight-bearing sites.”
The study found 18.3% of the global pain burden was due to smoking, obesity and low household incomes. This ranged from 12.6% in sub-Saharan Africa to 27.1% in eastern Europe.
In Oceania, 6.6% of pain was attributable to smoking compared with 2.5% in sub-Saharan Africa and 8.5% in eastern Europe, while 11.2% of pain was attributable to obesity, compared with 2.7% in central and southern Asia and 14.6% in North America. And 8% was attributable to lower incomes, compared with 6.6% in sub-Saharan Africa and 8.6% in eastern Europe.
The authors noted that there were important limitations on the research which could affect interpretations but did not alter the overall patterns. Those limitations included different ways of measuring pain, uneven coverage across different regions and oldest and youngest age groups, and that they described patterns for particular age groups, rather than following the same people over time.
Professor Andrew Horne, the director of the Centre for Reproductive Health at the University of Edinburgh in the UK, described the research as a landmark study, showing that women experience more pain than men at every body site studied.
“Pain also rises most steeply before age 55, during women’s working, caring and reproductive years. It is strong evidence that the gender pain gap is real, consistent and global. Yet women’s pain is still too often dismissed, underresearched and undertreated,” he said.
“Closing the gap means taking women’s pain seriously in the clinic, routinely analysing data by sex, properly funding research into the biological and social causes, and developing better, more personalised treatments for women.”
Prof Rebeccah Slater, professor of Paediatric Neuroscience at the University of Oxford agreed. “The troubling paradox is that women experience more pain, yet their pain is also more likely to be dismissed, diagnosed late or undertreated,” she said. “This enormous study shows that the higher burden of pain in women is remarkably consistent across the body and in a remarkably diverse global population.”

Trump's Ukraine-Russia peace gambit begins to unravel. Again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:43:14 UTC
00:43:14 KST

Trump's Ukraine-Russia peace gambit begins to unravel. Again
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during a visit to the Fort Bragg U.S. Army base on Feb. 13, 2026, in Fort Bragg, (Nathan Howard/Getty Images)
U.S. President Donald Trump's latest push for peace between Ukraine and Russia is facing growing uncertainty, with few in Kyiv believing it can deliver a breakthrough — or even bring the three sides together for talks, the Kyiv Independent can reveal.
The latest effort began in early September, when Trump's envoys traveled to Kyiv and Moscow seeking progress before the U.S. midterm elections.
The trips produced one tangible outcome: an agreement in principle to hold a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. The sides were expected to discuss proposals for an energy ceasefire, a possible reopening of the Black Sea grain corridor, and humanitarian issues such as prisoner-of-war exchanges.
Kyiv never expected the talks to produce a full ceasefire by spring 2027, according to a senior Ukrainian official. Still, Kyiv agreed to participate.
A month later, even the trilateral meeting itself remains uncertain. Moscow has shown little urgency to commit to the talks, people familiar with the negotiations said.
"The U.S. wants to organize meetings. I think we will support it. But it is very important that not only Ukraine but also the Russian side support these meetings," President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters during a side gaggle on Oct. 4.
The US keeps pushing
The latest sign that Washington is still trying to move the process forward came on Oct. 4, as Zelensky was meeting German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv.
Zelensky's phone buzzed with a message from Trump's peace envoy Steve Witkoff. He told the Ukrainian president that Washington wanted to hold the trilateral meeting in late October. Zelensky texted back that Ukraine would support it.
But the proposed timing represents a significant delay. The meeting was initially expected to take place in early October in the UAE, where the sides were expected to discuss the energy initiative and a possible reopening of the Black Sea grain corridor.
People close to the negotiations attributed the delay to Russia's position.
Ukrainian and U.S. officials have already shared their vision for the next steps with Moscow, people familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent.
The effort has also continued through Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's envoy, who visited the U.S. twice in September for meetings with Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
It remains unclear why the trilateral meeting was pushed back by almost a month.
One major issue expected to be discussed is an energy ceasefire. Ukraine and Russia have repeatedly targeted each other's energy infrastructure throughout the war.
Ukraine has struck Russian energy facilities and exports to disrupt a key source of funding for Moscow's war effort. Russia, meanwhile, has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian power plants and substations, seeking to leave civilians without electricity and heating.
The urgency of the issue has grown as winter approaches.
Russia struck Kyiv's energy infrastructure overnight and throughout the day on Sept. 30 in a renewed campaign to push Ukraine into the dark, and reviving fears of another winter of attacks on the electricity grid.
One senior Ukrainian official said Russia could have little incentive to rush into talks while it can still inflict damage on Ukraine's energy system. The official suggested Moscow may be seeking to destroy as much Ukrainian energy infrastructure as possible before negotiations, potentially giving Russia greater leverage at the talks.
Since late August, Russia has also intensified attacks on Kyiv. The Ukrainian president said Moscow had effectively removed restrictions on its targets, including schools, energy infrastructure, and civilian sites.
"Russia is deliberately escalating things as much as possible to provoke a response from Ukraine, so that it can continue the escalation and keep raising the stakes as much as possible before any talks with the Americans," Zelensky said.
No change to the current track
The uncertainty surrounding the trilateral meeting raises a broader question: after months of failed attempts to broker a ceasefire, can another round of U.S.-led diplomacy produce a different result?
Trump has sought to broker an end to Russia's war against Ukraine since returning to office in January 2025. So far, his efforts have failed to deliver.
Washington is not the only outside power that has tried to find a way forward.
India has proposed a ceasefire plan combining a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure with measures to protect shipping in the Black Sea. India's proposal incorporates elements of initiatives put forward by other countries, including Turkey, Egypt, and the United States, according to a Ukrainian official familiar with the matter.
Russia has rejected the proposal, the official said.
The rejection is significant for Kyiv because it suggests that the problem is not simply finding another intermediary or drafting another proposal. Moscow has also resisted initiatives from countries it maintains close relations with.
For now, Washington continues to pursue the same track, even as Kyiv grows increasingly doubtful about what it can achieve.
"Putin doesn't seem afraid. He feels he can do whatever he wants. There's no pressure from the U.S. … but he's afraid of Trump, no matter what," Zelensky said.

Flydubai passenger feared possible landing in Iran, Yemen after attempted hijack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:37:31 UTC
00:37:31 KST

Passengers on flydubai flight 1073 thought they were being flown to Iran even after the co-pilot had been subdued, The Jerusalem Post has learned.
The Omani co-pilot, Hamam al-Hammami, had attacked the pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, with the cockpit axe and was attempting to crash the plane with 182 people on board. The attack was miraculously thwarted by the pilot and a group of Israelis who overpowered Hammami and stabilized the plane shortly before it would have crashed into the Arabian Desert.
It was “10 minutes of horror,” Uri Pintov told the Post.
But even with the pilot tied up, the passengers were not fully relaxed until they landed and were taken into the terminal at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia – a six-hour drive from Jerusalem if the borders were open.
Pintov, who was on the flight with his wife, Michelle, and three children, following a family vacation in Thailand, said the passengers “did not trust” the crew, including the rescue pilots who had locked themselves in the cockpit.
“What was the copilot’s plan? Was he planning to crash us into Ben-Gurion [Airport]? Did he want to hijack the plane and bring us to Yemen or Iran? I felt like I was held hostage for an hour and a half,” he said.
“It was an hour and a half where we didn’t know where we were going, where they were taking us,” he added. “We didn’t trust anyone, so we separated the crew and put them in different places on the plane.”
The rescue crew did not speak to the passengers until 10 minutes before landing, Pintov said.
“It was so fast, and once they got into the cockpit, they locked the door, and no one could go in,” he said. “It could have been that they had their hands full, but they said nothing to us.
“As we were landing, I forced the crew member sitting next to me to tell me where we were, and then I understood it was Saudi Arabia. But we still didn’t know what their intentions were… if we were going to be hostages or not once we landed. We were ready for whatever was coming.”
The Pintov family sat in row 9, not far from business class and the cockpit. While they couldn’t see what was happening in the cockpit during the attack, Michelle told the Post, “We saw all the blood, and then we heard Yaniv saying that ‘we are in a critical situation, and we couldn’t rely on anyone on the flight.’”
Her family chose flydubai because the price was lower than El Al’s, she said, adding that she had no concerns regarding the airline. Even when she realized that the entire crew was male, she didn’t pay much attention to it.
“Everything was normal, until it wasn’t,” Michelle said. “I remember Tali coming out and screaming something. In my head, I was imagining that someone had a heart attack. But then I understood that something more dramatic was happening, and then we started falling.”
Still visibly shaken by the traumatic experience, Michelle recounted how she remembered the passengers screaming and the looks on her children’s faces as the plane plunged toward the ground at almost the speed of sound.
“I remember more screaming, and I was seeing my own death – our deaths,” she said. “It wasn’t even a question. I remember looking at my son Daniel, who is only 10 years old, and he was in shock with his eyes closed. My daughter Emma was sitting near the window and looked at me, terrified.
“Mia was sitting next to the window, and I saw her sending a voice note to her boyfriend, saying goodbye. I took my phone, too, and left a message for my mother that I loved her.
“I felt that I couldn’t say bye to my kids. I couldn’t say it out loud to the kids,” Michelle said, still visibly shaken.
For the Pintovs, the pilot wasn’t only a hero; he was a miracle.
“I went to help the pilot,” Uri said. “He was saying that he couldn’t breathe. He lost tons of blood from the attack. So, he is a miracle. He saved us.”
The plane, too, was miraculous. With its rapid descent, it could have easily come apart, but it did not.
“Boeing did something right,” Uri said with a small smile.
Saudis at airport welcomed and cared for Israeli passengers
Once they landed in Saudi Arabia, they were segmented into groups of 10 before being brought into the lounge. The Pintovs said the Saudis were very welcoming and caring for the Israeli passengers, offering them food and medical care.
Then came the questions of how they were going to get back to Israel.
“People were terrified of boarding the rescue plane,” Uri Pintov said, adding that they understood Israeli pilots were not going to be able to land in Saudi Arabia.
“It was surreal that we had to go on another flydubai plane,” he said. “How did they think we were going to board the flight?
“I am still shocked that no one in Israel was able to check the crew of the rescue flight and let us know it was safe to board that plane. Doing checks on pilots flying into Israel isn’t something new, but the Transportation Ministry did not do their job. This is a lawsuit.”
Although the attempted attack occurred close to the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre, Michelle said she did not see the connection.
For Uri, the hatred for Israel that has spread around the world is one of the reasons behind the copilot’s attempt to kill everyone on board.
“There is so much hate toward Israel around the world,” he said. “Since October 7, instead of making people understand the situation, it’s only gotten worse, and people like this terrorist are a result of the hate.”
Despite the attack, the Pintovs plan to fly again, perhaps during the Hanukkah vacation in December. But they said one thing is certain: They don’t plan on flying flydubai again.

Norway parliament to consider proposal for national terror list naming Hamas, IRGC - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:37:28 UTC
00:37:28 KST

Tomorrow, Norway’s parliament is set to consider a proposal calling for the country to establish its own terror blacklist, which will include Hamas, Hezbollah, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
At present, Norway does not maintain its own terrorist organization list, and instead relies upon the UN sanctions framework. Hamas, Hezbollah, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and the IRGC are not on the relevant UN list.
Norway’s Christian Democratic Party (KrF) is looking to change this.
KrF Whip Joel Ystebo told The Jerusalem Post that his party is proposing that Norway create its own independent designation system.
The motion – which the Post has seen – says that the Storting, Norway’s parliament, should instruct the government to bring forward legislation establishing a Norwegian list of terrorist organizations. Specifically, organizations “involved in preparing, promoting, or glorifying terrorism, and makes it a criminal offense to engage in activities within such a terrorist organization, cf. the conditions set out in Section 136a of the Penal Code.”
The KrF proposal explicitly said that the list should include Hamas, Hezbollah, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and the IRGC.
For clarity, parliament is not voting tomorrow to place Hamas and the IRGC on an operative Norwegian terror list, but instead on whether it should instruct the government to develop and submit a system for creating such a list in the first place.
If the motion passes, the government would then be obligated to work out the legal and administrative details of the list.
Creating terror blacklist could protect Norway's security, Jewish community
“We have been working on this for some time,” Ystebo told the Post. “The reason why we are putting forward this proposal is that many of our allies have their own lists, and we think that would be very good for Norway, too, because it is important to take a stand when it comes to terrorism and antisemitism.”
Ystebo added: “But also, this is not only a foreign policy issue – this is also a domestic issue. It’s about our homeland security. What worries me the most right now is seeing how some of these organizations, especially Hamas, have significant influence in other countries, including Norway, particularly concerning young people and radicalized young people in some of these communities.”
While parliament does not have a say over who would control such a designation list – i.e. the police of the Department of Justice – Ystebo told the Post it would be “smart” to do this through the Department of Justice because it involves both foreign policy and foreign organizations, as well as homeland security.
“It’s important to put forward this proposal, because in my opinion and in our opinion, the Norwegian government has been very naive when it comes to the influence these organizations have in our own country, despite different reports being very clear that this is an increasing problem,” Ystebo said. “So, to us, this is just so important when it comes to our homeland security and our minorities, especially the Jewish community.”
Establishing terror blacklist 'essential for protecting Norwegian society'
On Elpeleg, a Norway-based Israeli activist and the head of the advocacy group StoppNRK, told the Post that his group has been fighting for this motion for a long time, especially following the police report it filed against an NTNU professor who glorified the October 7 massacre.
“Establishing a Norwegian list of terrorist organizations is essential not only for protecting the Jewish community, but Norwegian society as a whole,” Elpeleg told the Post.
He said this is not about targeting Muslims or legitimate political views, but instead about “drawing a clear line against organizations that use terrorism and violence to achieve their goals.”
“Norway should join other democratic European nations in formally designating Hamas as a terrorist organization, along with Hezbollah, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, the IRGC, and other organizations that meet the criteria,” he said. “A democracy must be able to defend itself and its citizens.”

Despite comments by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, reports in March said Tehran had attempted to strike Diego Garcia with two intermediate-range ballistic missiles, which would have required a range far beyond 2,000 km.
“The missiles that we used during the war, particularly those used by our ground forces to target enemy bases, which were used in Kuwait, and our naval forces also used naval missiles, or sea-launched missiles, sea cruise missiles, against enemy vessels,” he said.
“These were actually very good and effective missiles, and we have now reached the conclusion that we need to increase their speed and range, because the enemy is located at a greater distance from our forces. They are located at a distance of up to 1,000 kilometers, and God willing, we will upgrade them as well.”
Iran already possesses several missiles capable of traveling more than 1,000 km, including the Khorramshahr, a liquid-fueled medium-range ballistic missile with a reported range of up to 2,000–3,000 km; the Sejjil, a solid-propellant medium-range ballistic missile capable of striking targets roughly 2,000 km away; and the Shahab-3, a foundational medium-range ballistic missile with a reported range of up to around 1,300 km, capable of reaching Israel and parts of the wider region. Later variants of the Shahab-3, including the Ghadr-1, have reported ranges of up to roughly 1,950 km.
Iran claims attacks forced out US troops
The spokesperson’s claims came after IRGC Rear Admiral Ali Fadavi alleged that Iranian attacks forced the US military out of the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters.
In comments made to Iranian state media IRIB, Fadavi alleged on Sunday that “The Americans fled and moved more than 1,000 kilometers away from our borders. This was not their choice; it was due to the authority of the Islamic Republic and the authority of the IRGC Ground Force.”
“The Americans must use their vessels because you cannot exercise full sovereignty with air power. You can bomb the region every day, but unless your forces have a physical presence, you cannot impose your will,” he continued, going on to deny that the Islamic Republic targets assets and infrastructure of Islamic nations.
“...Any base belonging to the Americans, any vessel belonging to the Americans, will be targeted by the grace of God.”

At least 75 pro-Palestinian protests planned worldwide on Oct. 7 anniversary, many deemed high risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:37:14 UTC
00:37:14 KST

At least 75 pro-Palestinian demonstrations and anti-Israel events across the world are set to take place on Wednesday, October 7, the day that marks three years since the Hamas attack on Israel in 2023.
The figures were released by the Ministry for Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism ahead of the third anniversary of October 7.
A large proportion - 29% of all events - are to take place on October 7 itself. The rest are spread out between October 1 and October 14, with most events expected over the weekend following October 7, 2026.
The Ministry identified 262 events in 37 countries worldwide. Of these, approximately one-third of all identified events have been classified as posing a medium or high level of risk.
The countries with the highest number of events are the United States (45), Spain (40), Australia (21), the United Kingdom (19), and Italy (16). Germany and Canada each have 14 events, France has 10, and the Netherlands has eight.
As mentioned, 87 events have been classified as posing a medium or high level of risk. The “high-risk” hotspots span numerous countries: Canada stands out with four events classified as high risk. Two high-risk events were identified in Greece, Italy, the United States, and Australia. Additional hotspots were identified, among other locations, in Barcelona, Bogotá, Paris, Istanbul, Bangkok, Santiago, London, Berlin and Amsterdam.
The Ministry's report also finds that 45 events are expected to take place in proximity to an Israeli embassy, consulate or another property associated with the State of Israel. Of these events, 30 are located within 2.5 kilometers of an Israeli property.
Among the notable locations identified are a planned demonstration in Dam Square in Amsterdam, an event in Helsinki approximately 300 meters from the Israeli Embassy, a high-risk event on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, approximately 350 meters from the Israeli Embassy, and an event in Frankfurt approximately 370 meters from a hotel used by Israeli visitors.
PFLP-linked organizing groups, grassroots spread
The Jerusalem Post went a bit deeper than the Ministry's analysis.
The ministry identifies 262 events in 37 countries, but the distribution is actually extremely uneven. As noted, the US accounts for 45, Spain 40, Australia 21, UK 19, and Italy 16. Those five countries alone account for about 54% of the entire database.
This makes an interesting geographical distinction. Spain's events appear to take the form of a mass grassroots/BDS network, with dozens of small local events across cities and towns.
In North America, the events are much more networked around student, Palestinian youth, and activist organizations such as Palestinian Youth Movement (PYM), Students for Justice in Palestine (SJP), and American Muslims for Palestine.
Australia has a strong concentration of organized Palestine networks, including Palestine Action Group Sydney and Canberra, Free Palestine Melbourne, and Students for Palestine.
The UK has fewer events in terms of numbers but some of the largest established national organizations, particularly Palestine Solidarity Campaign and Friends of Al-Aqsa.
The actual spread differs per country, and is therefore a mixture of large established national organizations, transnational networks and local grassroots groups.
Furthermore, the Post delved deeper into the high-risk geography.
Canada has 4 high-risk events, and Greece, Italy, the US, and Australia have 2 each.
Canada therefore stands out; it has only 14 events overall, but four are classified as high risk.
Then there is the risk level associated with proximity to Israeli embassies or important assets.
Although only 11% of events are within 2.5 km of an Israeli asset, nearly half of those nearby events are classified as medium or high risk.
This suggests that higher-risk events are disproportionately likely to occur where there is a symbolic Israeli target nearby.
The 'Post' explores terror ties of anti-Israel demonstrations
Finally, the Post explored organizing groups, and whether any have ties to terror groups. While the ministry report does not itself identify Hamas, PFLP, PLO or Samidoun as organizers of any of the 262 events, the table does contain a number of organizations that have documented links, joint activity or ideological overlap with those networks.
This is particularly the case with PYM, which is behind planned events in Los Angeles, New York, Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto - all five of which are categorized as high risk. PYM is also associated with 8 other events.
As such, PYM appears to be functioning as one of the major transnational organizational hubs connecting North American demonstrations.
This is relevant, given Israeli research has documented PYM's connection to the PFLP: the group has previously appeared alongside PFLP-affiliated figures and Samidoun at pro-Palestinian events.
Similar concerns have been raised by Palestine Solidarity Campaign in the UK, which is behind several of the UK protests including the high-risk October 10 event at Victoria Embankment Gardens.
The UK government's review of political violence and disruption says PSC has a history of alleged support for Hamas, notes that two former leaders met Ismail Haniyeh in 2012, and says PSC has advocated Palestinians' right to armed resistance. The report also notes that PSC opposed the UK's decision to proscribe Hamas in its entirety.
