IAF soldiers reveal air force's initial response to flydubai attempted hijacking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:36:54 UTC
00:36:54 KST

An Israel Air Force officer who first identified a distress signal from a flydubai aircraft last week said the situation initially appeared routine, but quickly escalated after a second signal indicated the plane may have been hijacked.
Lt. N., an air force aerial image identification officer, was on duty at 8:30 a.m. when he detected the first distress signal from the aircraft.
He told Walla that the initial alert did not immediately suggest a major emergency.
"It was an emergency signal transmitted by the aircraft. In retrospect, this was already after the drastic descent it had carried out," he said. "First, I was trying to understand why the aircraft was activating it, whether it was some kind of malfunction, perhaps a malfunction in our systems, or whether it was really a genuine signal, and I was trying to understand details about that flight. I wasn't alarmed at first, before I really understood what the incident was."
N. then checked the aircraft type and flight path and passed the information to other air force officials.
He said the situation still appeared consistent with a possible technical problem at that stage.
"When I understand that the aircraft is supposed to arrive in Israel, I alert the management position, and from there they really try to understand more details," said N. "From my perspective, it is a standard flight. There can be malfunctions during the procedures. It can be a procedure and a decision made inside the aircraft in order to make clear that there is something unusual here, but until that point, it was not something I had encountered before."
Second aircraft distress signal indicated possible hijacking
As air force personnel waited for the results of additional checks, a second distress signal arrived from the aircraft. This time, the code indicated a possible hijacking.
N. said the second signal immediately changed the assessment.
"Another emergency signal, but it became the signal for a hijacked aircraft," he emphasized. "I tell myself, this is already something unusual. There is no way this is a malfunction, because it is not a coincidence, and there is a high probability that this really is a hijacked aircraft. And from there, we basically set the incident in motion in the air force."
He said it was the first time he had encountered such a signal during a real incident.
"I'm not alarmed. A little stressed. It is the first time I have experienced a signal like this. I encountered something like this in the past, but it was due to a malfunction. Not a real incident. Since finishing the control course, it crosses your mind, but the chances are low," he continued. "This is not what an air traffic controller thinks about at night when he goes to sleep. Our world thinks more about UAVs and cruise missiles."
Once N. relayed the hijacked-aircraft code and issued the alert, the air force and senior command went on heightened alert.
He said there was no room to dismiss the possibility that the aircraft had been hijacked, particularly with Israelis potentially on board.
"I'm not prepared to take the risk that someone really may have hijacked the aircraft, and there may be Israeli passengers on board, and there is no way we let something like this pass without a response," N. said.
Maj. D., a reservist who serves as head of national airspace defense in the Air Control Array, said the aircraft was first detected between Saudi Arabia and Jordan and appeared to be headed for Tel Aviv.
According to D., the second signal prompted the air force to escalate its response within seconds and scramble fighter jets.
"We first detected the aircraft between Saudi Arabia and Jordan and saw that it was due to land in Tel Aviv," D. noted. "It looked strange. When we received the second signal about a hijacking, we decided within a few seconds to escalate the report and scramble fighter jets. We moved to prepare a response for every scenario, while at the same time we worked to obtain more intelligence and information about the incident.
"Throughout the incident, there was a great deal of uncertainty, D. continued. "It was not always clear to us whether the aircraft was in contact with another party, and during the incident a great deal of information flowed to us, some of it incorrect."
The uncertainty increased further when the aircraft began turning away from Israel.
D. said the team spent roughly half an hour running through possible scenarios as information continued to come in.
"As we are identifying what is happening, the aircraft begins turning around and moving away from the country, which added even more uncertainty for us," he added. "Amid that uncertainty, we sat as a team and spent about half an hour running what were essentially war games. What happens in this situation... One of the scenarios is that it really reaches our territory with the distress signal, under the assumption that it has been hijacked.
"During the incident, you try to disconnect from emotion as much as possible," he continued. "Only after I came out of the incident did I think about the fact that my brother is abroad, and I wondered whether he could have been on the flight. We prepare for the most severe scenario that could happen, and we have very clear procedures for it."
IAF tensions remained high amid Israeli media reports of pilot dispute
As the aircraft turned toward Saudi Arabia and Israeli media reports began circulating about a dispute between the pilots, tension remained high in the air force operations room.
N. said officials did not consider the incident over until they had confirmation that the aircraft had landed safely and that the Israeli passengers were no longer at risk.
"Until we receive information that the aircraft has actually landed safely and that the incident is really over, nothing is fine," N. noted. "We don't listen to rumors. We understand that the aircraft is landing in Saudi Arabia. I'm concerned. Why? A civilian aircraft landing with Israelis in a Muslim country, and not at a civilian airport. Until they announced that the rescue flight had departed, or that the Israeli civilian passengers had boarded the rescue flight, I couldn't be calm."
Capt. A., a reservist and air force air traffic manager, said his unit began clearing Israeli airspace once the incident was formally classified as unusual.
The aircraft was still far from Israel at the time, but the air force needed to prepare the airspace for fighter jets that had been scrambled.
"I go into action after the incident is defined as unusual," said A. "At this stage, the aircraft is still very far from the country, so we act to clear the airspace in a way that meets the needs of the fighter jets being scrambled. The skies are crowded with crop-dusting aircraft, sports aviation, commercial flights to Eilat or eastward, air force training, drones and helicopters, and the clearance we carried out was immediate.
"We call it moving to sterile airspace because it is possible that it will reach us later, and we need to plan ahead and check what other takeoffs and what other flights are planned in the airspace," A continued. "It is very possible that if this incident gets closer to the country, we will have to stop takeoffs completely. I have been an air traffic controller for more than a decade, and I have never had to close the skies because of a significant incident."
Asked about the possibility that the prime minister could soon be receiving updates from the IDF chief of staff and air force commander as officials prepared for the most extreme scenario, shooting down the aircraft, A. said his unit remained focused on its defined responsibility.
"At the end of the day, we come to do the job according to the procedures we know. We are in the air traffic section, and our role is clear and defined: clearing the airspace. All those other things, as they say, are not with us..." the captain concluded.

Talking points from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:36:45 UTC
00:36:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Talking points from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia
Tropical storms, software bugs and a bad tyre choice may have delayed them, but in the end the three generational talents of modern Formula One stood on the podium.
After a race weekend that placed a premium on experience, preparation and pure talent, AFP Sport looks at three things we learned from Sunday's delayed, rain-hit Bahrain Grand Prix held in Malaysia:
Verstappen and Red Bull poised for run-in
Having committed himself to a fresh long-term deal with Red Bull, Verstappen has galvanised the team and, with the keen and able support of Isack Hadjar, led them back to the front of the field.
It was Verstappen's first win this year. It was also Red Bull's first with their own power unit, which they developed around a Ford engine. The victory confirmed they have recovered from the implosion that followed Christian Horner's exit and the loss of design genius Adrian Newey and others.
Verstappen also moved level with Michael Schumacher on 72 wins for the same team.
The German set his total with Ferrari between 1996 and 2006. They are behind only Lewis Hamilton, who won 84 for Mercedes between 2013 and 2024.
Verstappen's loyalty and leadership have helped forge a new spirit of unity under Laurent Mekies' soft power as team chief, setting an example in commitment and work ethic that makes Red Bull a threat to Mercedes.
Sepang shines despite storms and bugs
The unprecedented crowds, relishing a spectacular return event after a nine-year gap, were evidence of the success of Formula One's lateral thinking in taking the Bahrain Grand Prix to Malaysia after it was cancelled in April.
A thunderous downpour caused a 100-minute delay to the start, exacerbated by a software failure, in programmes controlled by the International Motoring Federation (FIA). That led to bizarre scenes on an aborted formation lap. What followed was a memorable race.
"It was insane," said Verstappen, who was one of many to lose power. "At some points, we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn't understand it... I saw eight cars crawling, and Lewis stopped... It's not what you want for the sport."
Hamilton came to a complete halt and did a full restart before the FIA abandoned the lap and reloaded new software. The ruling body apologised for the chaos.
The energy management cutouts, in systems created as part of car controls for the new 'hybrid era', may have delivered frustration, but they also enticed teams to take risks.
Ferrari chose dry slick tyres, sending both Hamilton and Charles Leclerc down the order after starting in the wet.
Red Bull and Mercedes stayed on intermediates.
"When I saw they were on "inters", my heart sank," said Hamilton.
He produced a vintage recovery from 19th to third ahead of Leclerc and thrilled an enthusiastic crowd as Verstappen reprised his 2017 win.
"The software was tested," said the FIA's Nikolas Tombazis. "It just wasn't tested in those specific conditions."
Antonelli benefits from Russell's bad luck
George Russell's continued ill fortune enabled Antonelli to pull 84 points clear with seven races remaining, this time due to a power failure while running third in the closing laps.
It was a reminder of F1's adage that "to finish first, first you must finish" and painful for both Russell and Mercedes boss Toto Wolff.
Mercedes introduced an extensive upgrade package but ended the weekend well beaten by Verstappen and wondered whether the changes had worked.
Antonelli suggested the problem may be that their cars are sensitive to open, low-grip asphalt.
"I'm sure the team - with a lot of data, especially after this weekend - will come with a better view of the package for Singapore. Hopefully, we can extract full potential."
For the precocious 20-year-old, it could prove a key race in his charge for Italy's first drivers' title since 1953.
Russell admitted it was "exceptionally unlikely" that he could become champion.
But the Englishman won last year in Singapore, where Mercedes have taken five of the last 10 races, including three with Hamilton, and where Verstappen has never won.

The formal application followed several attempts, beginning in July, to obtain permission for a camp near the Supreme Court, the Knesset, and the prime minister’s official residence. The petition said the family was turned away even when it proposed using existing protest sites or infrastructure.

If responsibility for the investigation has not been transferred to the Shin Bet by then, the family plans to file a new petition with the assistance of the Association for Civil Rights in Israel, a protest organizer told The Jerusalem Post. A new filing would be required because the existing petition had been withdrawn.

“Thank you to everyone who supports and strengthens us,” Tesfaye said. “Please come to the protest tent.”

Who gets to choose Brazil's future?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:36:35 UTC
00:36:35 KST

- Marcus Vinicius De Freitas is visiting professor at the China Foreign Affairs University and a senior fellow at the Policy Center for the New South, based in Morocco.
Brazil's voters have issued warnings that neither Brasília nor foreign capitals can afford to ignore. Senator Flavio Bolsonaro's first round lead over President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva reflects frustration with the cost of living, insecurity, debt, and institutions, particularly the Supreme Court. Foreign endorsements featured in the campaign, but the discontent was Brazilian. Defending sovereignty cannot excuse failing to govern.
Lula's most formidable opponent is his own record. His political camp has held the presidency for roughly 16 years since 2003, with a brief interruption. It cannot indefinitely present itself as the answer to problems that persisted under its watch. Earlier achievements remain relevant, but political memory does not pay today's supermarket bill. The difficulty is convincing voters that familiar leadership can produce a different future. Political exhaustion cannot be overcome by invoking past accomplishments alone.
 
Diplomacy or sponsorship?
Yet domestic disappointment does not entitle foreign governments to realign Brazil's loyalties. Benjamin Netanyahu's video endorsement, Javier Milei's appearance at Bolsonaro's campaign launch, and Donald Trump's reception of the candidate revealed explicit preferences. A presidential audience alone proves little; Trump also met Lula. Together, however, these gestures raise a question about where diplomacy ends and political sponsorship begins.
Economic pressure makes that boundary harder to defend. Washington offered trade and diplomatic justifications for tariffs and visa restrictions. Yet official terminology does not erase political consequences. Trump publicly linked earlier tariffs to the treatment of former President Jair Bolsonaro, while members of the Bolsonaro family claimed credit for mobilizing American pressure. A country subjected to economic punishment cannot expect those imposing it to be disinterested observers.
On Oct. 2, two days before the first round vote, the United States suspended in-person consular services, and Australia closed its embassy, citing security concerns. Brazilian police reported finding no concrete evidence of an attack plan. The episode fueled online speculation about a coup, although claims of an official coup warning were false. Whatever the intentions, such measures risk reinforcing a narrative of instability at a politically sensitive moment.
The larger issue is Washington's understanding of the hemisphere. Trump's revival of the Monroe Doctrine recalls a persistent historical confusion: the belief that excluding outside powers gives the United States authority over its neighbors. Latin American independence was not achieved to exchange European tutelage for an American entitlement to obedience. Geography creates shared interests and responsibilities; it does not establish a hierarchy of sovereignty.
Viewed through this lens, pressure on Brazil also advances Washington's ambition to reduce Chinese influence. Brazil's markets, infrastructure, and critical minerals, including rare earths, make its partnerships strategically significant. Lula has defended the country's right to maintain those partnerships without seeking permission. Whatever his administration's shortcomings, that principle serves the enduring national interest. Brazilian diplomacy must turn international competition into development opportunities while resisting demands for exclusive loyalty. Brazil needs access to competing sources of investment, technology, and markets, and the freedom to negotiate.
A change of government may legitimately alter diplomatic priorities. It should not mortgage the country's future to foreign leaders' preferences. Mineral wealth must underpin Brazil's development. Alignment that narrows commercial and diplomatic possibilities carries costs long after the applause at campaign rallies has faded.
 
Israel, the Arab world, and partisan diplomacy
Israel's involvement has a distinct political logic. Netanyahu's endorsement resonates with evangelical and conservative voters for whom Israel holds religious and civilizational significance. In February 2024, Israel's foreign minister declared Lula persona non grata after Lula compared Israel's actions in Gaza to the Holocaust. Bolsonaro's promised embassy relocation to Jerusalem would mark a diplomatic reversal.
Brazil's relationships across the Arab world matter both commercially and diplomatically. A country aspiring to speak across regional divisions weakens its credibility when partisan affinity becomes the organizing principle of its foreign policy. Friendship with Israel need not require abandoning independent judgement about its government's misconduct.
The BRICS group of countries, a quintessential platform for Brazil's global ambitions, poses another test. Bolsonaro's willingness to consider withdrawal warrants scrutiny, but Brazil's economic structure constrains ideological freedom. Fellow member China is deeply embedded in trade and production, and influential domestic constituencies favor preserving those ties. A political downgrading of involvement appears more plausible than withdrawal: less commitment to the grouping and less ambition to organize the Global South.
None of this relieves Lula of responsibility for the frustrations driving the vote. Nor does Bolsonaro's domestic support render foreign pressure politically innocent. A serious account must acknowledge both.
The coming Oct. 25 runoff will demand answers that neither foreign endorsements nor sovereignty speeches can provide. Lula must explain what another mandate would change. Bolsonaro, whose undistinguished political career has also been marred by controversy, must explain what closer alignment would cost. Brazil's partners must recognize that cooperation confers no right to dictate Brazil's political direction. The choice belongs to Brazilians, including their right to disappoint Washington, Tel Aviv, or any other capital. Whoever wins will receive a temporary mandate to govern a sovereign country, not a license to place its future in someone else's hands.

MOSCOW, October 5. /TASS/. There are currently no grounds for restoring the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline, chief energy director at the Institute of Energy and Finance Alexey Gromov believes.
"To be frank, I do not believe in any initiatives involving some kind of extension of Russian gas supplies to Europe or the restoration of any Nord Stream 2 pipeline routes," he said at a press conference. Gromov noted that despite the rationale behind the idea, Europe was unlikely to change its chosen political course.
"So, I don’t think we should harbor any illusions. Russian gas has left Europe, and I see no grounds for its return. Yes, Europe will pay for this, and it is already paying an increasingly high price," the expert added.
Vyacheslav Kulagin, director of the Center for Oil and Gas Research at the Institute for Economics and Regulation of Infrastructure Industries at HSE University, believes, for his part, that if tensions in Europe’s gas market increase, politicians in the region will raise the issue of returning to Russian gas.
On September 26, 2022, a terrorist attack was carried out on the Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines, leaving only one of the system’s four pipelines intact - a string of Nord Stream 2. The 1,224-km Nord Stream gas pipeline runs along the bottom of the Baltic Sea from Vyborg in Russia to Greifswald in Germany and has a capacity of 55 bln cubic meters per year. Construction of Nord Stream 2, which has the same capacity, was completed on September 10, 2021, but the pipeline was never commissioned. The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office initiated a criminal case over an act of international terrorism.

First ton-scale drone lifeline: Ukraine flies 4 more tons of aid into a starving Russian-occupied town of Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:34:31 UTC
00:34:31 KST

Nearly 400 parcels containing food, medicine, and children's kits were delivered to occupied Oleshky on the night of 4 October, weighing almost 4 tons in total, Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said. All the parcels reached their destinations, he added.
The operation was the second ton-scale drone delivery into the blockaded occupied town in a week. Ukrainian drone deliveries to Oleshky have run regularly since March, and on 27 September Ukrainian forces flew about 4,000 kg of food to 100 locations across the town.
What happens to the parcels after they land
Delivery does not mean the aid stays with the people it was meant for. Kherson Oblast head Oleksandr Prokudin said Russian forces shoot down drones carrying food and take supplies from residents. He also said Russian forces detain and use violence against people who receive the aid.
Russia holds 2,000 people hostage in Oleshky without food or water—Ukraine flew 4,000 kg of food to locals across the Dnipro
Prokudin also said Russian forces take food intended for children and sell it, according to Radio Svoboda. Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, said Russian troops question residents about where the food came from and treat receiving Ukrainian aid as cooperation with Ukraine.
Monitors describe a blockade, and the Kremlin blames Ukraine
About 2,000 people remain in Oleshky, including nearly 50 children, Prokudin said. In June, Danielle Bell, head of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, said that food could not get into Oleshky and that sick and injured people were not receiving the medical assistance they needed. Residents had reported that no shipments had reached the town for nearly a month.
The Institute for the Study of War has described Russia's restrictions on the town as an effective blockade. The Kremlin acknowledged a "genuine humanitarian catastrophe" in Oleshky but blamed Ukraine for it: spokesman Dmitry Peskov claimed to The New York Times that Ukraine was preventing residents from leaving and disrupting supplies of food and water with drones.
The drone crews behind the deliveries
Several Ukrainian units carried out the 4 October delivery. Vyhivskyi named the National Guard's 11th Mykhailo Hrushevskyi Brigade and 34th Kherson Regiment, the 30th Marine Corps, the 34th Separate Marine Brigade Borysfen, and the 79th Border Guard Detachment. The Perun drone crew also rescued six animals from the occupied territory, he said.
What has changed since 2023
Drone aid to Oleshky is not new. In 2023, Ukrainian drone operators dropped water and other supplies to civilians in Oleshky and nearby settlements. What distinguishes the current effort is its repeated, ton-scale deliveries into the occupied town.

Birzeit University memorial destruction aims to crush Palestinian memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:14:28 UTC
00:14:28 KST

Birzeit University memorial destruction aims to crush Palestinian memory
Israeli soldiers removed the monument to students and alumni killed by Israel and replaced it with a fig sapling.
After Israeli soldiers stormed Birzeit University near Ramallah to demolish a stone memorial dedicated to dead students, Rania Washaha, 47, felt the pain of bereavement again.
Her brother, Fadi, 34, was shot in the head by an Israeli soldier near the northern entrance to el-Bireh in the central West Bank in May 2021.
His name was among the 38 students from the university killed by Israel and listed on the stone pillar known as the Martyrs’ Monument.
Israeli soldiers raided the university campus at dawn on Monday, accompanied by 10 military vehicles. A bulldozer demolished the pillar, and soldiers took away the marble stone. In its place, the Israelis left a planter containing a fig sapling, bearing the inscription: “Water it twice.”
Targeting the University
This raid marks the fifth Israeli incursion into the campus since the beginning of 2026 and the 28th since 2002.
Birzeit University’s administration condemned the recent raid, describing the destruction of the Martyrs’ Monument as a violation of international law and an attack on education and national memory.
“Bulldozers won’t erase the memory of the martyrs, military vehicles won’t extinguish the light of knowledge, and these assaults won’t break the university’s resolve to pursue its academic and national mission,” a statement by the university pledged.
It came 10 days after another incursion by Israeli forces during the daytime, a day before the start of the new fall semester.
Nardeen al-Memi, the university’s public relations and media officer, told Al Jazeera in the brief minutes of their incursion, Israeli soldiers approached the monument for the first time and photographed it.
The Martyrs’ Monument was erected between 1994 and 1996, bearing the names of students and alumni at Birzeit killed by Israeli forces. The list starts with Sharaf al-Tayyibi, who was shot dead by Israeli forces on the campus in 1984. The names of other students and alumni were added during the years that followed.
“The last name inscribed on the monument was that of student Omar al-Naasan, whom soldiers killed in al-Mughayyir east of Ramallah on September 2 while he was confronting settler incursions,” said Nardeen. “Days after his death, his father came and personally wrote his son’s name on the monument.”
University students organised a protest at the site of the destroyed memorial on Tuesday afternoon, most viewing it as an Israeli attempt to intimidate them.
Sami Adel, a Birzeit student who wanted to use a pseudonym due to his fear of being detained, told Al Jazeera the memorial holds a place in the heart of everyone who has attended the university since the 1990s.
In recent years, Israel has tried to suppress any student activity dedicated to commemorating the martyrs, he said.
“Soldiers detained me for several hours three weeks ago and threatened that if I participated in any political student activity on campus, I would face a long and harsh detention,” he added.
Erasing memory
The removal of the memorial is part of a broader Israeli policy targeting memorials dedicated to Palestinians killed by Israel in the occupied West Bank.
The Israeli far-right has made the issue part of its campaign to erase markers of Palestinian identity.
Zvi Sukkot, a member of the Knesset from the Religious Zionism Party, destroyed one such memorial in the village of Madama, south of Nablus, with a sledgehammer in August. The Israeli military later said that it routinely removes “symbols of incitement”.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich submitted a list of approximately 40 Palestinian memorials, proposing their destruction, to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
There has been a wider targeting of civic and cultural symbols across the West Bank, particularly in Jenin, by Israeli authorities.
“Jenin Horse”, a monument constructed from the wreckage left behind by an Israeli incursion into the city, was removed. A memorial dedicated to Al Jazeera journalist Shireen Abu Akleh in Jenin was also targeted in 2023.
A cemetery containing the bodies of Iraqi soldiers killed during the 1948 war, also located in Jenin, has been raided by Israelis from illegal settlements.
Other landmarks embedded in the city’s collective memory, including the “Watermelon Roundabout”, have also been targeted.
Crushing resistance
Israel’s targeting of Palestine’s collective memory has coincided with a wider campaign of suppression in the occupied West Bank.
Palestinian universities have been a particular target in this pressure campaign, with campuses raided, students detained, and strict restrictions on activities and events within university grounds.
Israeli authorities are likely focusing on Palestinian universities because they hold a special significance for Palestinian resistance. They historically served as spaces for anti-occupation activism and have been an integral part of the Palestinian political landscape for decades.
Political analyst Mohammed al-Qeeq, who served as president of the Birzeit University Student Council between 2006 and 2007, told Al Jazeera that Israel has targeted writers, influencers, and activists, along with students, to deter any resistance to the occupation.
Universities have historically served as a “fundamental pillar” of Palestinian resilience and identity.
“Israel had also sought to weaken Palestinian political and social cohesion inside universities by deepening divisions between factions and creating chaos”, he said.
Remembering Fadi
For Rania, the memorial served to cement the names of the martyred students in the minds of the next generation of Berzeit students, including her brother’s.
“I cannot deny that I felt a pang of anguish when the memorial was demolished,” she told Al Jazeera. “I realised the goal wasn’t simply to uproot a physical object; I felt the suppressed violence Israel inflicts upon us.”
The memorial, constructed in 1996, stood on the campus when Fadi studied at Birzeit University. He had been arrested multiple times, spending a total of eight years in detention, and Israel denied Fadi the chance to wear a graduation gown.
“He didn’t even complete two years of study due to repeated arrests and injuries from soldiers’ gunfire,” Rania said. “Yet, he loved Birzeit University dearly and would stand by the memorial, contemplating the names of the student martyrs, never knowing that his own name would one day be added to theirs.”
This year, Rania’s son enrolled at Birzeit University as a first-year student. Shortly before classes started last September, an Israeli officer phoned him, threatening him if he participated in any student activities on campus. “Remember what we did to your uncle,” they warned him.

Three Iranians face UK trial for allegedly spying for Tehran

Breadcrumb
Iranians charged with spying 'on behalf of' Tehran go on trial in UK
Three Iranian men went on trial in the United Kingdom Tuesday charged with spying for Iran, allegedly laying the groundwork for a violent attack against at least one London-based journalist.
The Iranian nationals visited addresses linked to people including two journalists working for the Farsi-language Iran International television news network, which Tehran has labelled a terror organisation.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Noori, 57, who have all pleaded not guilty, appeared at a court in London accompanied by translators.
Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones told the jury the three were accused of conduct likely to assist a foreign intelligence service, "in other words ... they spied on people of interest to the Iranian regime".
The trio undertook surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and February 2025, with Sepahvand allegedly earmarked to carry out any attack, he said.
The trial would focus on steps taken "on behalf of the Iranian regime to target journalists and others considered to be hostile to or even just critical" of it.
Iran International, which is based in London, had been critical of the Iranian government and supportive of opposition groups, he said.
Another of the men's targets was lawyer Jonathan Turner, a founder member of the group UK Lawyers for Israel.
The three accused do not deny visiting the addresses and taking photos and videos, but Sepahvand claimed he had been coerced and acted out of fear, the prosecution said.
Prosecutors labelled his claims "bogus" and alleged he was seeking payment and looking to have a criminal conviction for theft in Iran "fixed" in return for his actions.
Manesh and Noori said they were not aware that what they were doing was to assist the Iranian intelligence services, the prosecution added.
Emlyn Jones told the jury their intention was to "locate and target at least two journalists associated with ... Iran International and others".
'Retribution'
"Their ultimate objective was that one or more of their targets would be subjected to serious violence, no doubt as retribution for their criticism of the Iranian regime and to try to silence and deter others who might dare to voice their criticism," he added.
Those who attracted the attention of the trio included political satirist and Iran International journalist Kambiz Hosseini, who is long said to have been the subject of threats and intimidation from the Iranian intelligence services.
Mobile phone network data showed all three men visited the address where Hosseini was living.
Another target was Mojtaba Pourmohsen, also a journalist for Iran International and known as a poet and writer.
The three defendants, whom authorities said were Iranian-born but living in London at the time of their arrests, are all charged under the National Security Act.
Sepahvand is also charged with engaging in surveillance, reconnaissance and open-source research with the intention to commit serious violence.
Manesh and Noori are further charged with engaging in surveillance and reconnaissance, with the intention that serious violence would be committed by others.
The trial is expected to last up to six weeks.

Ukraine says no to EU membership without access to selling grain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

Ukraine says no to EU membership without access to selling grain
A permanent restriction on Kyiv’s market access would “run counter to the very logic” of full EU membership, Ukraine’s agriculture minister told POLITICO.
From left: European Council President António Costa, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. They speak to the media in Brussels, on June 18, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
Ukraine “cannot agree” to an EU membership model that would permanently limit sales of certain food products to the bloc, the country's Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi told POLITICO.
The European Commission endorsed this model Tuesday, as part of a so-called pre-enlargement policy review to prepare the EU for future enlargements.
“For us, there is a fundamental difference between a transitional period and a permanent restriction. Ukraine is prepared for the former. The latter would run counter to the very logic of full European Union membership,” Vysotskyi said in a written statement.
Advertisement
The potential accession of Ukraine to the EU raises fundamental questions about farm support and imports. Ukraine exports millions of tons of grain to the world market and sells to the EU under a strict quota regime. Some countries, such as Poland, have blocked grain imports from Ukraine to protect their own farming sectors.
The Commission’s proposal states it wants to “significantly limit financial support and market access for sensitive agricultural products.”
Instead of giving Kyiv full market access, the Commission would rather help Ukraine get back into its “historic” export markets, which include Africa and the Middle East, the draft states.
But Vysotskyi insists Ukraine should not "solely" be seen as a threat to European farmers. He argues the country could help the EU become less dependent on imports from third countries for commodities such as fertilizers, soybeans and lysine for animal feed, and give EU producers better access to Black Sea export routes. Ukraine could also be a place to invest in food processing facilities, Vysotskyi said.
"Our goal is to reach membership with a sector that sells Europe not only grain and other raw materials but also animal feed, ingredients, processed products, and biofuels," he added.
Vysotskyi confirmed Ukraine is open to transition periods — which could include phasing in farm support, temporary quotas and safeguards for sensitive products. But he maintained that they must have an end date.

Hunting for cannon fodder: How Russia&#039;s private recruitment market for the war in Ukraine really works
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:34:38 UTC
00:34:38 KST

The prosecutor's office in the Russian city of Nizhny Tagil proposed scrapping payments to recruiters who sign up contract soldiers for the war in Ukraine, citing a rise in fraud cases. Amid a shortage of willing volunteers, Russia has developed a vast state-backed intermediary recruitment market, with multilayered networks of middlemen, “ready-made creatives,” and region-specific rates. The Insider examined several of the schemes and traced how money from regional budgets reaches private headhunters. Spending on recruitment alone, excluding payments to contract soldiers, may run into billions of rubles a month, and private recruiters can receive up to 1.25 million rubles (almost $15,000) for bringing in a single soldier.
In the fifth year of Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine, the Russian army continues to lose tens of thousands of soldiers every month. As of Aug. 28, 2026, Mediazona and the BBC had confirmed by name the deaths of 242,747 Russian servicemen — and these are only the deaths that have become publicly known. Actual monthly losses of killed and wounded exceed 30,000, and direct recruitment of contract soldiers is no longer enough to replace them.
The state now separately funds organizations that seek out and recruit people for the war in Ukraine. The Insider examined court records, NGO reports, procurement requests, and internal materials from recruitment agencies, reconstructing the chain through which some of this money flows – from regional budgets to intermediaries and ultimately to the individuals who bring recruits directly to military enlistment offices.
A million rubles per head: the cannon-fodder market
As recently as 2024, Ivanovo’s Center for Creative Solutions was engaged in activities that had little to do with military recruitment. For example, the organization ran a quiz called “Favorite Ivanovo Region” at polling stations during the presidential election, with prizes including tickets to sporting events and a car. Another of its projects, “Urban Treasures: A Family Quest,” received a regional grant of almost 1 million rubles (almost $12,000).
On July 4, 2025, Ivanovo businessman Dmitry Gruzdev took over as head of the organization. That same month, the regional budget allocated funds for an entirely different purpose: “financing costs associated with providing services to attract and select candidates for military service under contract.” The Center for Creative Solutions was among the recipients of this funding.
The Insider found that a November 2025 order by the regional government awarded the center a 260 million ruble ($3.1 million) subsidy specifically for recruiting and selecting prospective contract soldiers. The sums it received were on an entirely different scale from its previous earnings from civilian quizzes.
In 2025, the organization received 1.06 billion rubles ($12.5 million), and a similar amount under the same budget line was awarded by the Moscow Region government to the non-profit Dobryye Dela (Good Deeds), which then passed the money on to its contractor, Russia's Agency for Communication Strategies.
As is often the case, the Center for Creative Solutions and Dobryye Dela appear to be the main distributors of budget funds to a long chain of other organizations. They outsource most of the work to private contractors, who in turn often subcontract it.
One such subcontractor emerged through an ordinary commercial dispute. In February 2026, Nizhny Novgorod businessman Alexander Kondratyev sued the center in the Nizhny Novgorod Region Arbitration Court, seeking 24.78 million rubles ($297,000) in unpaid debt. Court documents identify the contract as being for the “provision of services to attract and select candidates for military service under contract.” In March, the parties reached a settlement, with the Center for Creative Solutions acknowledging the full amount of the debt.
The court documents make it possible to determine how much the recruiter earned per contract soldier, as the debt was the result of two certificates of completed work. Kondratyev was owed 12.98 million rubles ($153,000) for November and another 11.8 million ($139,000) for the first half of December.
Both sums divide evenly by 590,000 rubles: the first amounts to 22 such payments and the second to 20. In other words, Kondratyev appears to have been paid 590,000 rubles (just under $7,000) for each contract recruit, with the two certificates covering 42 people.
In virtually all similar schemes in different regions examined by The Insider, recruiters are paid only after a candidate signs a contract, and the commission varies considerably. For example, at the previously mentioned Agency for Communication Strategies, one of the largest recruitment organizations, a recruiter gets 1.25 million rubles ($14,700) for a person who signs a contract through Moscow. Through Orenburg, the rate is 850,000 rubles ($10,000) “per head”; through Voronezh, 680,000 ($8,000); and through Balashikha, 530,000 ($6,250). In other areas, the rates ranged from 150,000 to 450,000 rubles ($1,750 to $5,300).
Debtors, addicts, bankrupts: recruiters target the vulnerable
Instructions for recruiters from the Agency for Communication Strategies (ACS) reveal who makes up the main pool of prospective contract soldiers. Its “target audiences” include former prisoners and Wagner PMC members, bankrupts, clients of microfinance organizations, residents of economically depressed regions, 18- and 19-year-olds with limited educational prospects, people with gambling or substance addictions, and “socially vulnerable groups.” They also include people who face legal trouble, particularly if they have not yet been convicted.
ACS advises recruiters to seek potential targets through advertising platforms and by buying ads in social media communities.
A recruit’s suitability directly affects the payment: if a prospective soldier fails a stricter medical examination in one region, he can simply be sent to another. An internal ACS information sheet divides medical commissions into “strict,” “moderate,” “lenient,” and “very lenient.”
Moscow, for example, is listed as having a strict commission. Voronezh, on the other hand, is described as “very lenient,” accepting recruits people with hepatitis A, B, or C, HIV, and “serious medical conditions subject to approval that would disqualify them in other regions.”
“Very lenient” Voronezh accepts people with hepatitis A, B, or C, HIV, and “serious medical conditions subject to approval”
Ufa’s commission is also described as “very lenient”: candidates with hepatitis, psoriasis, HIV, and “serious medical conditions subject to approval” may be accepted there. Orenburg and Cheboksary, meanwhile, are designated as merely “lenient.”
Under certain conditions, candidates with a Group III disability, diabetes, hypertension, missing organs, blindness in one eye, psychiatric or addiction records, signs of self-harm, or a history of tuberculosis may still be eligible to sign a contract.
Bonuses for recruiters
Although organizations like the Center for Creative Solutions and the Agency for Communication Strategies do not recruit soldiers themselves, they do provide smaller private businesses with the infrastructure for recruitment: up to 400,000 rubles ($4,700) per recruit, along with “ready-made creatives,” CRM, scripts, and training for new recruiters. The service works with candidates for contract military service from across Russia and attempts to maximize the number of contracts signed through Moscow, where bonus payments are higher.
For people looking to sign a contract, the organization can select a destination, arrange travel, meet them on arrival, and help with accommodation, food, medical examinations, and paperwork.
The page for prospective recruiters states the job’s purpose plainly: “The partner’s task is to get the candidate to sign a contract.” Payment is tied to that outcome – “for one signed contract.” The site promises that earnings are “unlimited.”
The Contract Call service is run by sole proprietor Fyodor Shchepetov, whose main business is “other personnel recruitment.” Public sources identify Shchepetov as a political consultant, conflict-resolution specialist, and internet technologist. He also serves on the public council of Rosprirodnadzor, Russia’s environmental regulator.
The demand for personnel in military recruitment is clearly substantial. Recent job postings offer “military recruiters” up to 300,000 rubles ($3,550) for each contract recruit they bring in, with no experience required and training provided. The job involves handling incoming inquiries, conducting initial interviews, “working with objections,” and managing candidates in Bitrix24 through to the final result.
“Military recruiters” are offered up to 300,000 rubles per contract recruit, with no experience required
The Agency for Communication Strategies has also launched a referral program called “Bring a Colleague.” Partners are promised an additional 100,000 rubles ($1,200) if a recruiter they refer brings in someone who signs a contract through Moscow, and 50,000 rubles ($600) if the contract is signed through another region.
In short, the agency pays not only for new contract soldiers but also for new recruiters who supply them. According to ACS itself, more than 250 “partners” work with the organization, and it has helped arrange more than 6,000 contracts.
How much does it cost the state to recruit one soldier?
There is no fixed price per recruit in this market, as payments vary widely from region to region. Much also depends on the numerous intermediaries involved. In the schemes examined by The Insider, recruiters who directly bring candidates to the point of signing a contract can receive the ruble equivalent on more than $10,000, but a substantial share of the money is absorbed by the intermediary organizations participating in the process.
Adding only the recruiter’s fee and the contract soldier’s enlistment bonus, the total can be much higher. For example, for a contract signed through St. Petersburg, ACS promises the soldier 4.5 million rubles ($53,000) and the recruiter 150,000 ($1,750). According to Re:Russia’s calculations, by mid-May 2026 the average “effective” bonus in the regions where a large share of contracts are signed had reached about 2.74 million rubles ($32,300).
In some schemes, the two visible payments – to the contract soldier and the recruiter – already total 4.65 million rubles per person
The scale of the spending becomes even more evident when these sums are compared with the rate at which the army is being replenished. CSIS estimates that in 2026 Russia has been recruiting an average of 27,000 new service members a month. Applying Re:Russia’s estimate of an average effective bonus of 2.74 million rubles, one-time payments to new contract soldiers alone would amount to about 74 billion rubles a month ($872.4 million).
As for recruiters, even using 300,000 rubles ($3,550) per contract soldier as a rough benchmark would put direct payments to the middlemen at more than 8 billion rubles ($94.3 million) a month.
After four years of war, Russia has built a system in which the army’s need for manpower has created a rapidly growing market fueled by public money. A region allocates the funds, an intermediary gets the contract, a recruiter searches for “leads,” and a person placed at the disposal of the Russian military machine.
As long as the Russian army continues to suffer losses, this market will persist. The state may even increase its funding, and professional recruitment agencies will devise ever more “creative” approaches to get their share of the outlays.

Jack Dorsey’s Bitchat taken off Indian app stores over law-and-order concerns: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:18:29 UTC
00:18:29 KST

NEW DELHI: Jack Dorsey’s Bluetooth-based messaging app Bitchat has been removed from Indian app stores following government intervention, putting the spotlight on concerns over decentralised communication. Government sources quoted by news agency PTI said on Tuesday that the app posed a law-and-order concern and therefore had to be taken down.The sources told PTI that Bitchat allows users to send messages through multiple Bluetooth “hops” without relying on conventional internet connectivity, raising concerns that it could be used to bypass restrictions imposed by authorities.“The government is duty-bound to maintain law and order,” sources said, adding that the app's ability to facilitate communication through Bluetooth was a concern.On proposals to restrict minors' access to social media, government sources said there was no such proposal under consideration. They pointed to Australia's experience, saying restrictions had not prevented children from accessing social media without accounts.The government is instead consulting industry representatives and experts, including those with expertise in psychology, sources said.“We have to find a better solution...when the right solution comes, we will bring it in front of you,” the sources said, stressing that a solution needed to be found.
Apple removed Bitchat from the India App Store following a demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Dorsey said in an X post on Saturday.“Government of India officially removes Bitchat from the App Store,” Dorsey wrote, sharing a screenshot of Apple's App Review notice.
The notice said the removal was “per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)” because the app “includes content that is illegal in India”. It cited Section 69(A) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, under which the takedown demand was issued.Google has also removed the app from the Play Store in India, while Apple said it remained available in other territories selected by the developer. Its TestFlight version would also no longer be available for testing in India.Bitchat had previously faced government action in July. The Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C) had then directed GitHub to restrict access to its repositories, citing concerns that the decentralised network could enable communication during internet restrictions and make lawful detection more difficult.

Seoul backs Ukraine, but sanctioned tankers carried fuel from South Korea to Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:37:29 UTC
00:37:29 KST

Seven tankers made 14 trips from South Korea to Russia's Far East in July and August, carrying more than 176,000 metric tons of fuel, most of it diesel, the Guardian found in a 6 October analysis of port records and ship-tracking data. The UK and EU have sanctioned three of the ships, and one loaded its fuel from another tanker at sea off South Korea instead of at a terminal.
Ukrainian strikes have cut Russia's fuel output as Moscow scrambles for supplies, while fuel loaded at South Korean ports has flowed to Russia. Loadings began to surge in July, the same month South Korean President Lee Jae-myung pledged $100 million for Ukraine's reconstruction, the Guardian reported. That creates a tension in Seoul's policy toward the war: South Korea has provided Ukraine with humanitarian and non-lethal aid but ruled out sending weapons directly, while the fuel trade appears legal under South Korean law even though three of the tankers are under UK and EU sanctions.
Russia imported 368,000 metric tons of oil products by sea in August, 112,000 of them from South Korea, according to Kpler data analyzed by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) and cited by the Guardian. CREA's own August report gives 172,000 metric tons in total, including 18,000 from South Korea. Neither explains the gap.
Where the tankers said they were going
The Layla, a tanker under UK and EU sanctions, made two voyages from Ulsan to Vladivostok, carrying a total of 57,000 metric tons of diesel. It left South Korea on 19 July and 10 August. On the first trip, it told South Korean authorities it was bound for Vladivostok; on the second, it declared Niigata, Japan, but sailed to Vladivostok again.
The Astoria, a Russian-flagged tanker under UK, EU, and Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 metric tons of fuel at Ulsan on 1 August. It declared Japan as its destination but sailed to Vladivostok.
The Chongchon did not berth at a South Korean port. Instead, it took about 26,000 metric tons of fuel from the unsanctioned Celeste I at an anchorage off Yeosu in early August. It declared Singapore as its destination but headed to Vladivostok. The owners and managers of the four tankers did not respond to the Guardian's requests for comment.
Why Russia needs the fuel
Ukrainian drone strikes have severely disrupted Russia's refining capacity, the Guardian reported. In July, Ukraine's General Staff said the strikes had knocked out 42% of Russia's refining capacity, costing the industry billions of dollars.
Russian refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% from a year earlier, the International Energy Agency said, according to the Guardian.
Russia has also restricted fuel exports to protect domestic supplies, extending its diesel export ban until the end of October; on 2 October, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow could consider partially lifting the ban if there was overproduction, according to the Moscow Times.
Responses to the shipments
Seoul's non-lethal aid has included helmets, body armor, and demining vehicles, and in 2023 it pledged $2.3 billion in support, mostly in loans.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at CREA, told the Guardian:
"It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia. This undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea's support for Ukraine."
South Korea's Foreign Ministry did not address the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, it said the government supports international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery. The ministry said it was strictly enforcing its export controls and had expanded them to cover 1,402 non-strategic items with high potential for diversion to military use. The UK Foreign Office did not answer the Guardian's questions about UK-sanctioned tankers using South Korean ports, saying only that it remains committed to monitoring its sanctions.
Ties between Kyiv and Seoul are also strained over Ukraine's disclosure of its transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul said should have remained private.

Air Force: Drone interceptors will not be available in necessary quantities until at least end of November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:30:00 UTC
00:30:00 KST

Air Force: Drone interceptors will not be available in necessary quantities until at least end of November
According to Ukrinform, Colonel Yurii Cherevashenko, deputy commander of the Ukrainian Air Force for air defense, announced this during a meeting of the Temporary Investigative Commission.
“The number of jet-powered drones has increased significantly since July. It now accounts for about 40% of all unmanned aerial vehicles deployed across Ukraine, and in certain areas, it makes up as much as 60% of attacks. And it continues to grow. We predict that jet-powered drones will account for about 80% of attacks,” he said.
According to Cherevashchenko, to counter attack drones, the Air Force is actively collaborating with manufacturers of jet-powered UAV interceptors. Currently, about 20 companies are in communication with the military, each at different stages of readiness for their products. The Air Force has established test zones where these drones are being deployed in combat conditions.
“Fourteen companies already have specific products and have begun test flights; of these, six companies have achieved certain results in destroying jet-powered drones, and three of them have results that can be considered promising solutions. We are currently actively collaborating to improve their performance,” said the deputy commander.
He noted that mass production of such drones is not currently on the table, as they are quite expensive and the companies do not always have their own funding. Production is currently in the tens of units.
“One of them has already been adopted into service and has shown the best results. Two have undergone codification, one of which is the ‘Predator,’” Cherevashchenko reported.
Some of these systems, he said, were originally designed for other tasks but were quickly adapted specifically for intercepting aerial targets. In response to a follow-up question about how they work, the deputy commander confirmed that an operator on the ground views the drone’s feed and controls it in real time.
“Their speed is about 460–500 kilometers per hour. Some manufacturers claim speeds of up to 700,” he noted.
Regarding scaling up production, Cherevashchenko noted that it would be best to check with the manufacturers for specific volumes.
“For our part, we are already training personnel: first, basic pilot training, then specialization specifically in interception,” explained the deputy commander.
According to him, the Air Force is considering two types of interceptor drones: classic rotorcraft and high-speed jet drones; deliveries of interceptors in the required quantities are not expected until at least the end of November.
As reported by Ukrinform, Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, stated that air defense forces have already begun shooting down enemy UAVs using robotic turrets.
